X. EXPLANATION OF THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON DICTATED IN THE WITTENBERG SCHOOL.

IN THE YEAR 1555.

BY PHILIPP MELANCHTHON.

AND THIS IS THE LATEST.

Melanchthon first published a Latin version of the Proverbs of Solomon inscribed thus: "Sentences of Solomon according to the Hebrew truth, rendered with the greatest care. By the author Philipp Melanchthon, 1524." (without place.) — It was dedicated to John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, and read the dedicatory epistle above in the Epistles, Vol. I, p. 774. — This book was reprinted in Nuremberg, a. 1525, in Leipzig 1531, and more often. Afterwards the same version appeared with Melanchthon's annotations, but without Melanchthon's knowledge and against his will (as he himself professed in the dedicatory epistle of the new edition in the year 1529, which may be seen in its place), inscribed thus: "Παροιμίαι (Proverbs), or Proverbs of Solomon with annotations by Phil.

Mel. Nuremberg by Jo. Petreius. 1525. 8vo. 18 sheets." — Item at Hagenau by Jo. Sercerius 1525. 1 Alphabet 11 sheets. — In German: "Exposition of Philipp Melanchthon on the Proverbs of Solomon, translated into German with his favor and will by Justus Menius from Erfurt. M.D.XXVI." (At the end: Printed at Erfurt by Melchior Sachsen, at the Leopard near St. George's, in the year M.D.XXVI.

(4to. 17 sheets.) There appeared "New Scholia by Phil. Mel. on the Proverbs of Solomon, written in the manner of almost a full commentary. Hagenau, Jo. Sercer. 1529. in the month of May. 8vo. 20 sheets." — Melanchthon dedicated this book to Magnus, Duke of Mecklenburg (see above, Epistles for the year 1529). — These scholia were reprinted at Hagenau in 1531. Again in 1532. At Hall in Swabia 1538. Afterwards Melanchthon treated the book of Solomon again, and it appeared: "Explanation of the Proverbs of Solomon recently dictated in the Wittenberg School by Phil.

Melanchthon. Frankfurt, from the workshop of Peter Brubach, in the month of May 1550. 8vo. 16 sheets." — which book Melanchthon revised and published in a more corrected form in the year 1555: "Explanation of the Prov. of Sol. in the School of Wit. dictated in the year 1551 by Phil. Mel. Wittenberg 1555. 8vo. 12 sheets." — The book was dedicated to John Albert, Duke of Mecklenburg, and see the dedicatory epistle above in the Epistles, Vol. VII, p. 705. Peucer included this latest edition in the works of Melanchthon, Vol. II, p. 872, which we have also provided here.

PREFACE OF PHILIPP MELANCHTHON ON THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON.

It is a common observation that there are two ways of teaching, of which one is the complete Dialectical method, proceeding in order, and building up as it were a complete edifice, so that the entire doctrine may be gathered into one body. As when a physician speaks first about the construction of the body, about the members and the humors, afterwards about the causes and kinds of diseases, and then about the remedies. The other way is when brief sentences are delivered, as aphorisms, and this is often done promiscuously without great care for order: as Phocylides, Theognis, and others wrote moral precepts. Such a heaping together of sentences is this book of Solomon, which has the title in the Latin edition: Proverbs.

And although there is a distinction both among the Greeks between γνῶμαι (maxims) and παροιμίαι (proverbs), and among the Latins between sentences and proverbs: yet among the Hebrews, both are signified indiscriminately by one name.

A sentence or γνώμη (gnome) is a brief saying, containing a precept about morals, or an admonition about rewards and punishments, or a description of events in life, the consideration of which is also useful for admonition.

The precepts are: Spurn pleasures, pleasure bought with pain is harmful, Μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν (Remember to be distrustful). Γνῶθι σεαυτόν (Know thyself).

Concerning rewards and punishments: εὐσεβέων παίδεσσι τὰ λώϊα, δυσσεβέων δ'οὐ (To the children of the pious, the best things; to the impious, not so).

Concerning events.

Minds usually luxuriate in favorable circumstances.

Fortune, whom she favors too much, makes a fool.

But a Proverb is a highly celebrated saying, and usually signifies something by some figure, whether by metaphor, or comparison, or image, or hyperbole, or irony, whether it contains a sentence or any other kind of description, such as: A leaking jar.

To the Greek Calends, Go to the crows.

More changeable than the Euripus.

These and many others contain no sentences.

But others signify time, others place, others other circumstances figuratively.

Although, therefore, a proverb is one thing and a sentence another: yet many proverbs are at the same time sentences, such as: You have obtained Sparta, adorn it.

It is a sentence, admonishing that everyone should understand his own vocation, as we call it, and keep himself within its bounds, and rightly do those things which are of his office.

But it is also a proverb, because it is adorned with a figure, and is highly celebrated.

We do not see the wallet that is on our back, is a sentence, reproving blind self-love (φιλαυτία), which nevertheless judges others more harshly.

But at the same time it is a proverb, because it is figurative, and highly celebrated.

Thus are sentences and proverbs: He grants pardon to the crows, he vexes the doves with censure. Τὰν ἀρετὰν καὶ τὰν σοφίαν νικᾶντι χελῶναι, that is, tortoises conquer virtue and wisdom, that is, money.

Since, however, there are many such sayings in this little book, which are at once sentences and proverbs, the title of Proverbs does not fit badly, but whether the title will be sentences or proverbs, it must be known that here a heap of the sweetest sentences has been collected, which are precepts about all virtues.

We often admonish, however, that the sum of the doctrine concerning virtues, so that it can be comprehended in some way, must be included in the Decalogue.

The same must be done here, and the kinds of sentences should be distributed according to the Decalogue.

Some speak of the first table, others of the second.

These kinds can be named thus: Some are Theological, which discourse about God and the precepts of the first table.

Others are Political, which contain the duties of governors.

Others are Ethical, which give precepts about the common morals of all.

Others are Oeconomical, which speak about marriage and domestic government.

Since, however, sentences are pleasing in all languages, because they give precepts briefly about honest things, and are sought after as constant monitors in this great variety of human actions, it must be known that in these most ancient sayings of Solomon there is a singular sweetness, both because of the figures and because of the things themselves.

For they admonish much about secret affections, much about the causes and seeds of the greatest changes in life, and about the chief moments of government, which are not rustic, or Bucolic, as many think.

How charming a picture of marriage it is, when it paints with the image of the doe and the fawn the mutual love of husband and wife, simple, sincere, sweet, having nothing of deceit, nothing of suspicion, nothing of moroseness?

What sweetness is in the oeconomical precept: Let your fountains be derived abroad, and you remain the master of them.

What is more lovable than fountains and rivulets, irrigating both your gardens and your neighbors'?

How copious a doctrine is contained in this saying.

It approves the distinction of properties, it commands justice and frugality, so that everyone may hold his own, and abstain from another's, may diligently cultivate his own lands, and also exercise beneficence, but in such a way that he is not shaken out of his land, but rather helps others from the fruits.

Such are many sentences in this whole heap, which signify the greatest things with most charming images and sweetest figures.

It is necessary, however, to be admonished at this beginning, that there is a great difference between ethnic γνωμολογίας (gnomologies), such as those of Phocylides or Theognis, and these handed down by Solomon in the Church of God, just as it is said elsewhere in general about the difference between philosophy and the doctrine sounding in the Church.

As philosophy retains a particle of the law, so also Phocylides says something about the wrath of God, and about the punishments of crimes.

But about the Mediator, about the remission of sins, about reconciliation, about true invocation, faith and hope, about the presence of God in our calamities, he does not speak, otherwise however recites many precepts, pertaining to the second table of the Decalogue.

But Solomon often preaches about the true knowledge and invocation of God, and about the other virtues pertaining to the first table, as: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

Item: Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own wisdom; in all your ways think of Him, and He will direct your steps.

Concerning the cross: Whom the Lord loves, He chastises; do not fail because of Him.

And concerning salvation after this life: The righteous man hopes in his death.

Julian the Emperor opposed Phocylides to Solomon, when he argues that no greater wisdom is handed down in the prophetic and apostolic books than what is found among the Heathens.

And Cyril, refuting Julian, only prefers Solomon to him because he preceded Phocylides in age.

For Phocylides, who was a Milesian, and Theognis, who was a Megarian, lived in the age of Cyrus and Thales.

But this childish response does not satisfy the magnitude of this dispute.

For it should have been said concerning the true sources of doctrines, that the doctrine of the Law is one thing, and that of the Gospel another.

And it should have been conceded that Phocylides recites a good part of the law, but that there is another doctrine proper to the Church, namely, concerning the revelation of God, made by illustrious testimonies, concerning the published promises, concerning the Gospel, announcing the remission of sins, and offering eternal life on account of the Son, concerning consolation in the cross.

Concerning these highest matters, the heathen writers are mute.

This distinction must always be in sight, so that we may know what is the proper doctrine of the Church.

In the preface, this also must be added: Since this book was written in the true Church of God, in which the promise concerning the Messiah was known, let us understand that he also intends this, that faith should shine forth, looking upon the Messiah in the use of all the sentences, whether he speaks of faith or of works, as when he says in chapter 8: Trust in the Lord with all your heart, understand, on account of the Mediator, just as David had taught before: Kiss the Son, blessed are all who trust in Him.

For Solomon expressly commands that the doctrine handed down by God in this people be embraced.

And where mention is made of faith, it is necessary to look upon the promises.

Thus, when he says concerning marriage: Rejoice with the wife of your youth, understand, with faith shining forth, that you should conclude that it is acceptable to God on account of the Mediator, and that on account of Him, works divinely ordained are pleasing to Him.

Thus, everywhere, the doctrine concerning the Messiah, which is handed down more perspicuously in the Psalms and Prophets, must be embraced at the same time.

It is signified here also, however, because mention is made of the wisdom of God preaching in the human race, which is the Son sent to the Church.

And Solomon commands that the doctrine handed down by God in this people be known.

Item, when mention is made of eternal life, it is necessary to look upon the promises.

Latin:

X. EXPLICATIO PROVERBIORUM SALOMONIS IN SCHOLA WITEMBERGENSI DICTATA.

ANNO M.D.LV.

A PHILIPPO MELANTHONE.

ESTQUE HAEC POSTREMA.

Primum Melanthon edidit versionem latinam proverbiorum Salomonis sic inscriptam: „Sententiae Salomonis iuxta hebraicam veritatem summa cura redditae. Autore Philippo Mel. 1524.“ (sine loco.) — Dicata est Ioanni Friderico Duci Saxon., et epistolam nuncupatoriam lege supra in Epistolis T. I. p. 774. — Recusus est hic liber Norimbergae, a. 1525, Lipsiae 1531. et saepius.

Postea eadem versio prodiit cum annotationibus Melanthonis, sed inscio et invito Melanthone (ut ipse professus est in epistola dedicatoria novae editionis anno 1529, quae videatur suo loco), sic inscripta: »Παροιμίαι, sive Proverbia Salomonis cum annotationibus Phil. Mel. Norimbergae per Io. Petreium. 1525. 8. 18 pl.“ — Item Haganoae apud Io. Sercerium 1525. 1 Alph. 11 pl. — Germanice: „Auslegung Philipps Melanchthon yber die Sprüch Salomo mit seiner gunst und willen verdeutschet durch Justum Mendum aus Erffurdt.

M.D.XXVI.“ (In fine: Gedruckt zu Erffurdt durch Melchior Sachsen, zum Leoparden bei S. Georgen, im Jahr M.D.XXVI. (4. 17 pl.) Prodierunt „Nova Scholia Phil. Mel. in Proverbia Salomonis ad iusti pene commentarii modum conscripta. Haganoae Io. Sercer. 1529. mense Maio. 8. 20 pl.“ — Hunc librum Melanthon dicavit Magno, Duci Megapolitano (vid. supra Epp. ad ann. 1529). — Recusa sunt haec scholia Haganoae 1531. Iterum 1532.

Halae Suevor. 1538. Postea Melanthon denuo librum Salomonis tractavit, et prodiit: „Explicatio Proverbiorum Salomonis in Schola Witebergensi recens dictata a Phil. Melanthone. Francof. ex officina Petri Brubachii, m. Maio 1550. 8. 16 pl.“ — quem librum Melanthon recognovit et emendatiorem edidit anno 1555: „Explicatio Prov. Sal. in Schola Wit. dictata a. 1551. a Phil. Mel. Witeb. 1555. 8. 12 pl.“ — Dicatus est liber Ioanni Alberto, Duci Megalburgensi, et epist. dedicatoriam vide supra in Epistolis Tom. VII. p. 705. Hanc postremam editionem Peuceri inseruit operibus Melanthonis T. II. p. 872, quam hic etiam dedimus.

PRAEFATIO PHILIPPI MELANTHONIS IN PROVERBIA SALOMONIS.

Usitata admonitio est, de duobus modis docendi, quorum alter est integra Dialectica methodus, ordine procedens, et quasi integrum aedificium extruens, ut universa doctrina in unum corpus redigatur. Ut, cum medicus primum de fabricatione corporis, de membris et de humoribus, postea de morborum causis et generibus, deinde de remediis dicit. Alter modus est, cum breves sententiae traduntur, tanquam aphorismi, idque saepe fit promiscue sine magna cura ordinis: ut praecepta moralia scipserunt Phocylides, Theognis, et alii. Talis coacervatio sententiarum est hic liber Salomonis, cui titulus est in Latina editione: Proverbia.

Etsi autem discrimen est tum apud Graecos inter γνώμας et παροιμίας, tum apud Latinos inter sententias et proverbia: tamen Ebraeis uno nomine promiscue utrunque significatur.

Sententia seu γνώμη est breve dictum, continens praeceptum de moribus, aut commonefactionem de praemiis et poenis, aut descriptionem eventuum in vita, quorum consideratio etiam prodest ad commonefactionem.

Praecepta sunt: Sperne voluptates, nocet emta dolore voluptas, Μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν. Γνῶθι σεαυτόν.

De praemiis et poenis: εὐσεβέων παίδεσσι τὰ λώϊα, δυσσεβέων δ'οὐ.

De eventibus.

Luxuriant animi rebus plerunque secundis.

Fortuna quem nimium fovet, stultum facit.

Sed Proverbium est valde celebratum dictum, et plerunque figura aliqua, seu metaphora, seu collatione, seu imagine, seu hyperbole, seu ironia aliquid significans, sive sententiam contineat, sive aliam qualemcunque descriptionem, ut: Dolium pertusum.

Ad Calendas Graecas, Eat ad corvos.

Euripo mutabilior.

Haec et multa alia nullas sententias continent.

Sed alia tempus, alia locum, alia alias circumstantias figurate significant.

Etsi igitur aliud est proverbium, aliud sententia: tamen multa proverbia simul sunt sententiae, ut Spartam nactus es, hanc orna.

Sententia est, monens ut suam quisque vocationem, sicut nominamus, intelligat, et intra metas eius se contineat, et recte faciat ea quae sunt sui officii.

Ideo autem et proverbium est, quia figura ornatum est, et valde celebratum.

Non videmus manticae quod in tergo est, sententia est, reprehendens caecam φιλαυτίαν, quae tamen de aliis acerbius iudicat.

Simul autem proverbium est, quia figuratum est, et valde celebratum.

Ita sunt sententiae et proverbia: Dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas. Τὰν ἀρετὰν καὶ τὰν σοφίαν νικᾶντι χελῶναι, id est, virtutem et sapientiam vincunt testudines, id est, pecunia.

Cum autem talia dicta multa sint in hoc libello, quae simul et sententiae sunt et proverbia, titulus Proverbiorum non male congruit, sed sive titulus erit sententiae, sive proverbia, sciendum est, hic collectum esse acervum dulcissimarum sententiarum, quae sunt praecepta de omnibus virtutibus.

Saepe autem monemus, summam doctrinae de virtutibus, ut aliquo modo comprehendi possit, includendam esse in Decalogum.

Idem hic faciendum est, et genera sententiarum iuxta Decalogum distribuantur.

Aliae de prima tabula, aliae de secunda loquuntur.

Haec genera sic nominari possunt: Aliae sunt Theologicae, quae de Deo et de praeceptis primae tabulae concionantur.

Aliae Politicae, quae gubernatorum officia continent.

Aliae Ethicae, quae de communibus omnium moribus praecipiunt.

Aliae Oeconomicae, quae de coniugio, et de domestica gubernatione loquuntur.

Cum autem sententiae in omnibus linguis gratae sint, quia breviter de rebus honestis praecipiunt, et expetuntur, tanquam assiduae monitrices in hac tanta varietate actionum humanarum, sciendum est, in his vetustissimis dictis Salomonis singularem esse dulcedinem, et propter figuras, et propter res ipsas.

Multa enim de arcanis affectibus, multa de causis et seminibus maximarum mutationum in vita, et de praecipuis momentis gubernationis monent, quae non sunt agrestia, seu Bucolica, ut multi putant.

Quam blanda pictura est coniugii, cum mariti et coniugis mutuum amorem, simplicem, sincerum, dulcem, nihil fuci, nihil suspicionis, nihil morositatis habentem, pingit imagine capreae et hinni?

Quanta suavitas est praecepti oeconomici: Fontes tui deriventur foras, et tu dominus eorum maneto.

Quid amabilius est fontibus et rivulis, rigantibus et tuos hortos, et vicinos?

Quam copiosa doctrina continetur in hoc dicto.

Approbat distinctionem dominiorum, praecipit iustitiam et frugalitatem, ut suum quisque teneat, et ab alieno abstineat, suos fundos diligenter colat, beneficentiam quoque exerceat, sed ita, ne ex fundo excuciatur, verum iuvet alios ex fructibus.

Tales sunt multae sententiae in hoc toto acervo, quae blandissimis imaginibus et dulcissimis figuris significant res maximas.

Necesse est autem et hoc initio moneri, magnum discrimen est inter γνωμολογίας ethnicas, ut sunt Phocylidis aut Theognidis, et has a Salomone in Ecclesia Dei traditas, sicut alias in genere dicitur de discrimine philosophiae et doctrinae sonantis in Ecclesia.

Ut philosophia particulam legis retinet, ita et Phocylides aliquid dicit de ira Dei, et de poenis scelerum.

Sed de Mediatore, de remissione peccatorum, de reconciliatione, de vera invocatione, fide et spe, de praesentia Dei in calamitatibus nostris, non dicit, caeterum utcunque recitat multa praecepta, pertinentia ad secundam tabulam Decalogi.

Salomon vero de vera agnitione et invocatione Dei, et de caeteris virtutibus ad primam tabulam pertinentibus saepe concionatur, ut: Initium sapientiae timor Domini.

Item: Confide Domino in toto corde tuo, et non innitare sapientiae tuae, in omnibus viis tuis cogita illum, et ipsi diriget gressus tuos.

De cruce: Quem diligit Dominus castigat, ne deficias ab eo.

Et de salute post hanc vitam: Sperat iustus in morte sua.

Iulianus imperator opposuit Salomoni Phocylidem, cum disputat, nihilo maiorem sapientiam tradi in libris propheticis et apostolicis, quam qualis apud Ethnicos reperitur.

Et Cyrillus refutans Iulianum, tantum eo antefert Salomonem, quod aetate antecesserit Phocylidem.

Nam Phocylides, qui fuit Milesius, et Theognis, qui fuit Megarensis, Cyri et Thaletis aetate vixerunt.

Sed haec puerilis responsio non satisfacit magnitudini huius disputationis.

Dicendum enim fuerat de veris fontibus doctrinarum, aliam esse doctrinam Legis, aliam Evangelii.

Et concedendum fuerat, Phocylidem recitare bonam partem legis, sed tamen aliam propriam Ecclesiae doctrinam esse, scilicet de patefactione Dei, facta illustribus testimoniis, de editis promissionibus, de Evangelio, annuntiante remissionem peccatorum, et offerente aeternam vitam propter Filium, de consolatione in cruce.

De his summis rebus muti ethnici scriptores.

Id discrimen semper in conspectu esse oportet, ut sciamus, quae sit doctrina Ecclesiae propria.

In praefatione et hoc addendum est: Cum hic liber in vera Ecclesia Dei scriptus sit, in qua nota erat promissio de Messia, intelligamus eum et hoc velle, ut praeluceat fides, intuens Messiam in usu omnium sententiarum, sive de fide loquatur sive de operibus, ut cum dicit capite 8.: Confide Domino toto corde tuo, intellige, propter Mediatorem, sicut antea David docuerat: Osculamini Filium, Beati omnes qui confidunt in eum.

Expresse enim iubet Salomon doctrinam in hoc populo a Deo traditam, amplecti.

Et ubi fit mentio fidei, necesse est intueri promissiones.

Sic cum de coniugio dicit: Laetare cum uxore adolescentiae tuae, intellige, praelucente fide, statuas de propter Mediatorem Deo acceptum esse, et propter eum placere ei opera divinitus ordinata.

Sic ubique simul complectenda est doctrina de Messia, quae in Psalmis et Prophetis magis perspicue tradita est.

Significatur tamen hic quoque, quia fit mentio sapientiae Dei concionantis in genere humano, quae est Filius missus ad Ecclesiam.

Et iubet Salomon cognosci doctrinam in hoc populo traditam a Deo.

Item cum fit mentio, et vitae aeternae, intueri promissiones necesse est.

## 1:1 Argument
Chapter I. Proposition.

The sentences of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, written so that you may learn wisdom, discipline, prudence, and receive understanding, justice, judgment, and rectitude, and that circumspection may be given to the incautious, and knowledge and consideration to the young.

Admonition.

A wise man will hear and will profit, and an intelligent man will possess counsels, and will understand the sentences and the interpretation and the words of the wise, and their enigmas.

First precept.

The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

Fools despise wisdom and discipline.

The proposition is clear, in which he says that he has collected these sentences for the sake of great utility, so that the more unlearned and the younger may be admonished, taught, and turned toward diligence in the governance of morals, toward God and toward men.

He describes these utilities in many words, whose proper significations should be considered.

Wisdom signifies the knowledge of God, when fear and true faith shine in the heart.

Discipline or erudition is generally preparation or instruction.

Prudence signifies the governance of morals.

Understanding signifies discernment, where, when many probable propositions are set forth, the choice is difficult, as when Jeremiah advises surrender against the opinion of others, or Zechariah advises that servitude should be tolerated, and that sedition should not be stirred up.

Justice signifies obedience universally, according to all the precepts.

Judgment signifies accusation, chastisement, and punishment.

Rectitude is opposed to hypocrisy, and as if one were to say, sincerity. Circumspection is opposed to stupidity, which rushes rashly without deliberation. Knowledge signifies discernment. Consideration is the same thing as deliberation, as to what is fitting for the diversity of places, times, and persons. The wise man will hear and will profit, etc. To the proposition he adds an admonition as to what kind of hearer one ought to be. The wise hearer will profit, just as the Lord says: To him who has, it shall be given. Item: He will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask, not to those who despise, not to those who resist with barbaric and cyclopean ferocity. He says here that these despisers of God, like the Epicureans and their like, do not profit, but others do, in whom are the beginnings of the fear of God, and who ask to be ruled by God, just as it is said: Ask and you shall receive.

The first commandment.

He begins the commandments from that which is first, namely, from the fear of the true God. For because he names Jehovah, who is celebrated among the people of God, he leads us first to the recognition of the doctrine concerning the true God, and wishes true invocation to be distinguished from the cults of other nations. By usage, however, the Fear of God is named the whole true worship of God, and not simulated, or universal obedience, according to all the commandments, as in this saying: Blessed are all who fear the Lord. This fear embraces at the beginning the knowledge of true doctrine, then the fear which is perceived by the senses, and the faith which distinguishes this fear, when true invocation is joined to it, from servile or impious fear, which is to flee and rage against God. It also embraces in the true recognition of God, in true fear and faith, the invocation which asks for and receives reconciliation, and asks for and expects help in the whole governance of life. And let this saying be understood not only of the beginning, that is, of the inception, but of the sum, as if he were to say: The fear of the Lord is the sum of wisdom, governing all counsels in favorable and adverse circumstances.

Hear, my son, the instruction of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother. He spoke before of the sum of doctrine and worship: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; now he shows the persons who teach, and commands that they be heard, because there must be a ministry of teaching, and it is necessary to hear the ministry. And the first degree in the order of persons is the degree of parents, and their first duty is to rightly hand down to their offspring the doctrine concerning God, just as it is written to the Ephesians: Bring up your children in the doctrine and discipline of the Lord. Let this saying be joined to the former: Hear the instruction of your father, namely, of him who teaches about the fear of the Lord, this very doctrine which the Church of Israel sounds forth, which he named; this I also call the law of your mother, namely, of the Church, handed down by God with certain and illustrious testimonies in Israel. Thus let us know that we are bound to a certain kind of doctrine, when he says: Do not cast away the law of your mother. For by the appellation of mother he signifies the Church of Israel. It is manifest, however, that this commandment has been often repeated, so that we may embrace this unique kind of doctrine concerning God, which has been handed down to the Church in the prophetic and apostolic writings. Just as the eternal Father says concerning the Son: Hear him, etc. And the Lord says: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, etc.

But just as the Lord there adds the promise of all things to this commandment concerning the knowledge and profession of doctrine, so here Solomon adds a promise, which, so that it may be more alluring, is taken as a metaphor from childish ornaments. A crown signifies a kingdom or preeminence, and the meaning is: God will place you among salutary governors, and will promote and aid your counsels, so that they may be salutary to you and to the people, so that you may be a vessel of mercy to yourself and to the people, just as Samuel, David, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah; do not be a vessel of wrath, like Saul, Absalom. The ornaments of the neck signify eloquence, that is, salutary doctrine and salutary counsels. With these great gifts God will adorn you, if you hear the law of your mother.

My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. This is an admonition against the allurements which draw very many away from God, namely, against the multitude of the impious, and against the favorable circumstances of the impious. In vain is the net spread rightly before the bird. That is, even if the impious think they are hidden, just as bird-catchers hide themselves: yet they are not hidden. Because God, the avenger, discerns all things.

Psalm 57: Truly there is a God who judges men on the earth. Psalm 61: You render to each one according to his works. Solomon therefore exhorts not to be [moved] by the examples of the multitude and by the [favorable] things... by the wickedness of the impious, so that we might act against God, and he adds a threat of punishment.

Among punishments, however, the saddest is: Then they will call, and I will not hear. He does not mean by this that those who have fallen cannot return to repentance, or that repentance is useless. Rather, he calls us to repentance and promises the mitigation of present punishments and the remission of eternal punishment, as it is said in Isaiah 1: If your sins are as scarlet, they shall be white as snow.

The meaning of the saying, however, is that those who do penance are heard before the punishment comes. But when the punishment comes, it is already present. If it is bodily, it is mitigated for the one doing penance: if it is eternal, there is no hearing, as in the destruction of Saul and Judas.

At the end is the antithesis: He who hears or obeys rests securely.

Latin:

Caput I. Propositio.

Sententiae Salomonis, filii David, regis IsraëL, scriptae, ut hinc discas sapientiam, disciplinam, prudentiam, et accipias intelligentiam, iusticiam, iudicium et rectitudinem, et ut detur incautis circumspectio, et adolescentibus scientia et consideratio.

Admonitio.

Audiet sapiens et proficiet, et intelligens possidebit consilia, et intelliget sententias et interpretationem et sermones sapientum, et aenigmata eorum.

Primum praeceptum.

Timor Domini initium sapientiae.

Sapientiam et disciplinam stulti despiciunt.

Propositio perspicua est, in qua ait, se collegisse has sententias, magnae utilitatis causa, ut rudiores et iuniores commonefiant, doceantur, et ad diligentiam flectantur in gubernatione morum, erga Deum et erga homines.

Has utilitates describit multis verbis, quorum propriae significationes considerentur.

Sapientia significat agnitionem Dei, cum lucent in corde timor et vera fides.

Disciplina seu eruditio generaliter est praeparatio seu institutio.

Prudentia significat gubernationem morum.

Intelligentia, diiudicationem, ubi multis probabilibus propositis, difficilis est electio, ut cum Hieremias suadet deditionem contra aliorum opinionem, Zacharias suadet tolerandam esse servitutem, non movendam esse seditionem.

Iusticia significat universaliter obedientiam, iuxta omnia praecepta.

Iudicium accusationem, castigationem et poenam.

Rectitudo opponitur hypocrisi, ac si diceretur sinceritas. Circumspectio opponitur stoliditati, quae temere ruit sine deliberatione. Scientia significat delectum. Consideratio idem est, quod deliberatio, quid conveniat pro diversitate locorum, temporum et personarum. Audiet sapiens et proficiet, etc. Propositioni addit admonitionem, qualem oporteat auditorem esse. Sapiens auditor proficiet, sicut Dominus inquit: Habenti dabitur. Item: Dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus, non contemnentibus, non repugnantibus barbarica et cyclopica ferocia. Hos contemtores Dei, ut Epicureos et similes, ait hic non proficere, sed alios, in quibus sunt initia timoris Dei, et qui petunt se regi a Deo, sicut dicitur: Petite et accipietis.

Primum praeceptum.

Orditur autem praecepta ab eo quod primum est, videlicet a timore veri Dei. Quia enim nominat Iehova in populo Dei celebratum, deducit nos primum ad agnitionem doctrinae de vero Deo, et vult discerni veram invocationem ab aliarum gentium cultibus. Usitate autem Timor Dei nominatur totus cultus Dei verus, et non simulatus, seu universalis obedientia, iuxta omnia praecepta, ut in hoc dicto: Beati omnes qui timent Dominum. Hic timor complectitur initio cognitionem verae doctrinae, deinde timorem, qui sensu percipitur, et fidem quae discernit hunc timorem, cum est vera invocatio coniuncta, a timore servili seu impio, qui est fugere et fremere adversus Deum. Complectitur item in vera agnitione Dei, in vero timore et fide, invocationem, quae petitet accipit reconciliationem, et petitet expectat auxilium in tota gubernatione vitae. Nec de initio tantum, id est, de incoatione intelligatur hoc dictum, sed de summa, quasi dicat: Timor Domini est summa sapientiae, gubernans omnia consilia in rebus secundis et adversis.

Audi fili eruditionem patris tui, et matris tuae legem ne dimittas. Prius dixit de summa doctrinae et cultuum: Initium sapientiae timor Domini, nunc monstrat personas docentes, et iubet has audiri, quia oportet esse ministerium docendi, et necesse est ministerium audire. Ac primus gradus est in ordine personarum, gradus parentum, et horum officium primum est, recte tradere natis doctrinam de Deo, sicut et ad Ephesios scriptum est: Educate natos in doctrina et disciplina Domini. Adiungatur autem hoc dictum priori: Audi eruditionem patris tui, scilicet, docentis de timore Domini, hanc ipsam doctrinam quam sonat Ecclesia Israël, quam nominavit, hanc etiam nomino legem tuae matris, scilicet Ecclesiae, traditam a Deo certis et illustribus testimoniis in Israël. Ita sciamus nos ad certum genus doctrinae alligari, cum ait: Legem matris tuae ne abiicias. Significat enim appellatione matris Ecclesiam Israël. Manifestum est autem, hoc mandatum saepe repetitum esse, ut unicum hoc doctrinae genus de Deo amplectamur, quod Ecclesiae traditum est in scriptis propheticis et apostolicis. Sicut inquit aeternus pater de Filio: Hunc audite etc. Et Dominus inquit: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, etc.

Ut autem ibi Dominus promissionem omnium summam addit huic praecepto de cognitione et professione doctrinae, ita hic Salomon addit promissionem, quae ut sit blandior, metaphora sumta est a puerilibus ornamentis. Corona significat regnum seu praestantiam, estque sententia: Deus collocabit te inter salutares gubernatores, et provehet et iuvabit consilia, ut sint salutaria, tibi et populo, ut sis vas misericordiae tibi et populo, sicut Samuel, David, Iosaphat, Ezechias, non sis vas irae, sicut Saul, Absalon. Ornamenta colli, significant eloquentiam, hoc est, salutarem doctrinam, et salutaria consilia. His ingentibus donis te Deus ornabit, si legem matris tuae audies.

Fili mi, si lactaverint te peccatores, ne obsequaris. Admonitio est contra illecebras, quae plurimos abstrahunt a Deo, scilicet, contra multitudinem impiorum, et contra res secundas impiorum. Frustra panditur recte coram volucri. Id est, etiamsi putant se latere impii, sicut aucupes se abscondunt: tamen non latent. Quia cernit Deus omnia vindex.

Psal. 57.: Utique est Deus, iudicans homines in terra. Psal. 61.: Tu reddis unicuique iuxta opera sua. Hortatur ergo Salomon, ne exemplis multitudinis et rebus [se-] cundis impiorum moveamur, ut faciamus contra Deum, et addit comminationem de poena.

Inter poenas autem tristissima est: Tunc invocabunt, et non exaudiam. Non hoc vult, non posse lapsos redire ad poenitentiam, aut poenitentiam inutilem esse. Imo vocat nos ad poenitentiam, et promittit mitigationem praesentium poenarum, et remissionem poenae aeternae, ut dicitur Esaiae 1.: Si peccata vestra fuerint sicut coccinum, eritis candidi sicut nix.

Est autem dicti sententia, ante poenam exaudiri agentes poenitentiam. Sed cum venit poena, et iam adest. Si est corporalis, mitigatur agenti poenitentiam: si est aeterna, nulla est exauditio, ut in interitu Saul et Iudae.

In fine est antithesis: Audiens vel obediens quiescit secure.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter II.

The entire second chapter is an exhortation to hear and learn this doctrine, which God has handed down to the Church, and binds us to it, and commands us to flee other wisdom that fights against this doctrine.

For figuratively, by the name of an adulterous woman, he understands wisdom, which leads minds away from God. For he says by name that to leave that wandering woman is to leave the master, that is, the teacher God, to whom she had been betrothed. For such a mind is like an adulteress, who, having left and spurned the true master to whom she had been betrothed, wanders most petulantly, plays with impious opinions, just as the Epicureans rejoice in their audacity, and idolaters rejoice in their cults, because they think that on account of them they have great successes and all good things.

He adds, however, in this chapter promises and threats, according to the saying: Seek first the kingdom of God, and all things will be added to you, etc. Likewise Psalm 1: Blessed is the man, etc. He also warns how we can progress, for he joins two causes, the help of God and our own study, just as it is said elsewhere: How much more will he give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

Likewise: Ask and it will be given to you, Seek and you will find, etc. And in the book of Wisdom, chapter 6: Wisdom is easily found by those who love her, and she anticipates those who seek her. These sayings promise help to those who are learning.

Latin:

Caput II.

Totum secundum caput est adhortatio ad audiendam et discendam hanc doctrinam, quam Deus Ecclesiae tradidit, et ad hanc nos alligat, ac praecipit fugere aliam sapientiam, pugnantem cum hac doctrina.

Figurate enim nomine mulieris adulterae intelligit sapientiam, quae a Deo mentes abducit. Nominatim enim inquit, illam mulierem vagabundam relinquere magistrum, id est doctorem Deum, cui desponsata fuerat. Talis enim mens est velut adultera, quae relicto et spreto vero magistro, cui fuerat desponsata, vagatur petulantissime, ludit impiis opinionibus, ut laetantur sua audacia Epicurei, laetantur et idolatrae suis cultibus, quia putant se propter eos habere magnos successus, et omnia bona.

Addit autem in hoc capite promissiones et comminationes, iuxta dictum: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et omnia adiicientur vobis etc. Item Psalmus 1.: Beatus vir etc. Monet etiam quomodo proficere possumus, coniungit enim duas causas, auxilium Dei, et nostrum studium, sicut alibi dicitur: Quanto magis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus.

Item: Petite et dabitur vobis, Quaerite et invenietis etc. Et in libro Sapientiae capite 6.: Sapientia facile invenitur ab his qui diligunt eam, et antevertit eos, qui expetunt eam. Haec dicta promittunt auxilium discentibus.

## 3:1 Argument
Chapter III.

At the beginning of the third chapter, exhortations are repeated, and a promise is inserted: Mercy and truth shall not forsake you, namely, the mercy of God.

It is a customary phrase regarding God and men: He has done mercy and truth, that is, he has shown beneficence and faithfulness. As, Jonathan did mercy and truth to David, that is, he was beneficent and faithful toward him, that is, he loved him constantly and without simulation, and did good to him. So it is said here: God will do good to you, and faithfully, that is, he will always protect you, according to the saying: To him who fears the Lord, no good thing shall be lacking.

Latin:

Caput III.

Initio tertii capitis repetitae sunt adhortationes, et promissio inserta est: Misericordia et veritas non deserent te, scilicet misericordia Dei.

Usitata phrasis est de Deo et hominibus: Fecit misericordiam et veritatem, id est, beneficentiam et fidelitatem praestitit. Ut, Ionathas fecit misericordiam et veritatem Davidi, id est, fuit erga eum beneficus et fidelis, id est, constanter et sine simulatione eum dilexit, et ei benefecit. Ita hic dicitur: Deus benefaciet tibi, et fideliter, id est, semper te proteget, iuxta dictum: Timenti Dominum non deerit ullum bonum.

## 3:1
Precepts.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart. Three precepts follow.

The first is about the acknowledgment of God, about faith, and about fear. The second is about the preservation of the ministry of doctrine. The third is about the cross. The doctrine in each precept is very extensive.

The first commands faith, and an antithesis is added. Do not lean on your own prudence, which is to be understood in three categories: regarding the acknowledgment of God, regarding morals, and regarding counsel in the choice of useful things. Thus, acknowledge God as he has revealed himself in this doctrine; I do not want you to wander like the heathens and invent various deities, cults, and opinions about God; I want you to do in morals what has been commanded, not to follow your own imaginations, as the Lacedaemonians allowed one to make a pact with a man about his wife.

The Pope forbids marriage. I want you in the choice of useful things to follow my precepts, to do what is necessary, not with meddlesomeness [πολυπραγμοσύνῃ], not by hope or fear to attempt anything outside your calling.

Be mindful of the saying in Ezekiel: Walk in my precepts. Honor God with your wealth, etc. He commands that each person, according to their means, should help the preservation of the ministry of doctrine in temples and schools, and a most sweet promise is added, just as it is written in Matthew 10: Whoever gives a cup of water to one of the least of... mine because of the, shall have his reward. Do not spurn the chastening of God, and do not abhor his correction. Here the whole doctrine of the cross is to be understood, and the distinction between Philosophy and the

Evangelical. Philosophy and human reason judge differently concerning the causes of death and human calamities than the voice of the Gospel. It is necessary, however, that the causes be known for which the Church is subjected to the cross. Furthermore, both the philosophical and evangelical places of consolation are to be compared. Christian and philosophical patience must be distinguished.

Latin:

Praecepta.

*Confide Domino in toto corde tuo.* Sequuntur tria praecepta.

Primum de agnitione Dei, de fide, et de timore. Secundum de conservatione ministerii doctrinae. Tertium de cruce. Amplissima est doctrina in singulis praeceptis.

Primum praecipit de fide, et addita est antithesis. Ne innitaris prudentiae tuae, quod intelligatur de tribus generibus, de agnitione Dei, de moribus, et de consiliis in delectu utilium. Sic agnoscas Deum, sicut se in hac doctrina patefecit, nolo te vagari ut Ethnicos, et comminisci varia numina, cultus, opiniones de Deo, volo te in moribus facere quae praecepta sunt, non sequi tuas imaginationes, ut Lacedaemonii concedebant pacisci cum viro de uxore.

Papa prohibet coniugium. Volo te in delectu rerum utilium sequi mea praecepta, facere necessaria, non πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, non spe vel metu tentare aliquid extra vocationem.

Sis memor dicti in Ezechiele: In praeceptis meis ambulate. Honora Deum de facultatibus tuis etc. Praecipit ut singuli pro suis facultatibus iuvent conservationem ministerii doctrinae in templis et scholis, et addita est dulcissima promissio, sicut et Matth. 10. scriptum est: Qui deder...i...t potum aquae uni ex minimis meorum propter doctrinam, habebit mercedem. Castigationem Dei ne averseris, et non abomineris correptionem. Hic tota doctrina de cruce comprehendenda est, et considerandum discrimen Philosophiae et

Evangelii. Philosophia et humana ratio aliter de causis mortis et humanarum calamitatum iudicat, quam vox Evangelii. Necesse est autem sciri causas, propter quas Ecclesia subiecta est cruci. Deinde et loci consolationum philosophici et evangeli......ci conferendi sunt. Discernenda et patientia Christiana et philosophica.

## 3:13
Blessed is the man who finds wisdom etc.

He returns to common exhortations, and commands that we learn the doctrine handed down by God, and that we obey it, and not prefer our own wisdom or cunning, and he adds promises and threats. All these things are opposed to human wisdom, which plays most audaciously by inventing opinions about God, religions, and cults, etc., and does not wish to be bound by the word of God. Likewise, that which in the counsels of life seeks its own safeguards through cunning, and does not remain within the boundaries handed down by the word of God. And these exhortations agree with the whole Psalm: Blessed are the undefiled etc. But these praises of wisdom are rightly understood concerning revealed wisdom, that is, concerning the word of God made manifest in the Church, concerning the Decalogue and the Gospel. Nor is it alien, however, that antiquity adapted these praises of wisdom to the person who is the Son of God, who is the manifestor of the word sounding in the Church, and is efficacious through that word, and in it shows what kind of God He is, and what His will is.

Precepts.

Latin:

Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam etc.

Redit ad communes adhortationes, ac praecipit, ut discamus doctrinam a Deo traditam, et ei obediamus, nec anteferamus nostram sapientiam aut calliditatem, et addit promissiones et comminationes. Haec omnia opponuntur sapientiae humanae, quae audacissime ludit fingendis opinionibus de Deo, religionibus et cultibus etc. et non vult esse alligata verbo Dei. Item quae in consiliis vitae, calliditate sua quaerit praesidia, nec manet intra metas verbo Dei traditas. Et congruunt hae adhortationes cum toto Psalmo: Beati immaculati etc. Recte autem intelliguntur hae laudationes sapientiae de sapientia revelata, id est, de verbo Dei patefacto in Ecclesia, de Decalogo et Evangelio. Nec tamen alienum est quod vetustas accommodavit has laudes sapientiae ad personam, quae est Filius Dei, qui est patefactor verbi sonantis in Ecclesia, et est efficax per id verbum, et in eo ostendit, qualis sit Deus, et quae sit eius voluntas.

Praecepta.

## 3:27
Do not forbid him to do good who is able to do good, and do you do good when your hand is able.

Do not hinder the vocation of others, and obey your own vocation studiously and faithfully.

Latin:

Non prohibeas benefacere illum, qui potest benefacere, et benefacito tu, cum manus tua potest.

Non impedias aliorum vocationem, et tuae vocationi studiose et fideliter obtemperes.

## 3:28
Do not say to your neighbor, go and return, tomorrow I will give, when you are already able to give.

Do not plot evil against your neighbor, but let him dwell securely with you.

This precept and the following ones pertain to the commandment: You shall not kill. But evil is constructed against others in two ways: either by manifest violence, or by frauds, calumnies, thefts, etc. John prohibits both kinds when he says: Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely.

Do not litigate with a man without cause, when he has done you no evil.

He prohibits every kind of calumny and unjust contention.

Do not emulate the iniquitous man, and do not choose his ways.

It is a common precept that we should not, offended by the scandal of the cross and the successes of the impious, fall away from God, and imitate the impious in the hope of power, riches, tranquility, and other comforts, as happens in great part, so that the Church is subjected to the cross and the impious dominate. The whole Psalm preaches about this scandal: Do not emulate etc.

Latin:

Non dicas proximo tuo, vade et redito, cras dabo, cum iam possis dare.

Non machineris proximo tuo malum, sed habitet apud te secure.

Hoc praeceptum et sequentia pertinent ad praeceptum: Non occidas. Dupliciter autem struitur malum aliis, aut manifesta violentia, aut fraudibus, calumniis, furtis etc. Utrumque genus prohibet Iohannes, cum inquit: Neminem concutiatis neque calumniemini.

Non litiges cum homine sine causa, cum tibi malum non fecerit.

Prohibet omne genus calumniarum, et contentionum iniustarum.

Non aemuleris virum iniquum, et non eligas vias eius.

Commune praeceptum est, ne offensi scandalo crucis et successibus impiorum deficiamus a Deo, et imitemur impios spe potentiae, opum, tranquillitatis et aliorum commodorum, sicut magna ex parte fit, ut Ecclesia sit subiecta cruci, et impii dominentur. De hoc scandalo concionatur totus Psalmus: Noli aemulari etc.

## 3:35
The exaltation of fools will be ignominy.

It agrees with the saying: They are lifted up on high, so that they may fall with a heavier crash.

Latin:

Stultorum exaltatio erit ignominia.

Congruit cum dicto: Tolluntur in altum, ut lapsu graviore ruant.

## 4:1 Argument
Chapter IV.

He returns again to common exhortations, and commands that we learn the doctrine and obey it.

The fourth chapter is a general exhortation to learn the doctrine, and to the zeal of obeying, and to the diligence of governing discipline, and to circumspection, lest we be deceived by the examples of the impious, and mention of rewards and punishments is inserted.

There is obscurity in one saying: The beginning of wisdom is to acquire wisdom, but the sentence is plain concerning the manner and the beginning of conversion to God: to hear the doctrine, and to truly seek it, and to ask for guidance from God, according to the doctrine, is the beginning of conversion, as it is said elsewhere: He will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. And the Prophet says: Convert me and I shall be converted. And Wisdom 6: It is found by those who seek it, and it meets those who seek it first. And above, chapter 2: If you seek it, you will find it. James 1: If any man lacks wisdom, let him ask of God etc. Likewise: God draws, but He draws the willing.

Latin:

Caput IV.

Redit iterum ad communes adhortationes, et praecipit ut doctrinam discamus, et ei obediamus.

Quartum caput generalis adhortatio est ad discendam doctrinam, et ad studium obediendi, et ad diligentiam regendi disciplinam, et ad circumspectionem, ne decipiamur exemplis impiorum, et inseritur mentio praemiorum et poenarum.

Obscuritas est in uno dicto: Principium sapientiae est acquirere sapientiam, sed plana est sententia de modo et incoatione conversionis ad Deum, audire doctrinam, et eam vere expetere, et petere gubernationem a Deo, iuxta doctrinam, est incoatio conversionis, sicut alibi dicitur: Dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Et Propheta inquit: Converte me et convertar. Et Sapientiae 6.: Invenitur ab his, qui quaerunt eam, et prior occurrit expetentibus eam. Et supra cap. 2.: Si quaesieris eam, invenies. Iacobi 1.: Si quis indiget sapientia petat a Deo etc. Item: Trahit Deus, sed volentem trahit.

## 5:1 Argument
Chapter V.

The fifth chapter pertains to two commandments of the Decalogue. You shall not commit adultery, and, You shall not steal. For at the beginning of the fifth chapter he prohibits adulteries and all wandering lusts, and adds discourses concerning punishments, because without any doubt to this divine rules correspond to events: God will punish fornicators and adulterers.

And here in chapter 6. The adulterer will lose his own soul, as private and public histories show, David, Troy, Thebes, etc.

And although God mitigates punishments for some who perform penance, nevertheless some punishments always accompany them, and often the sins of the seed are punished in the seed, that is, in the offspring.

Inserted, however, is a most sweet discourse, which approves of marriage and mutual love, and the sweetness of marriage, and prohibits adulteries.

The approval of marriage and mutual love is, when it says: May you be delighted with the wife of your youth, that is, whom you marry as a youth.

Then it paints mutual love with a distinguished image, Let love be such as that of the stag and the doe, or as that of the roe and the fawn, that is, let it be an ardent love, without simulation and without coercion, let it be sweet, without moroseness and disgust, let it be sincere, without suspicions, and without pride, and let spouses acquiesce in mutual love, lest they be torn apart or desire others.

There exists a description of this ardor in Oppian concerning stags: Yet the stag himself with swift feet follows her When she flees, and stops to embrace his beloved. But with swift feet he reached her as she ran, And he catches her as she flees and holds his spouse in his arms.

Antithesis, however, is declared by examples.

Tiberius unwillingly marries Julia; here simulation and coercion make marriage unpleasant.

Q. Cicero's Pomponia is more morose.

Many natures of men and women are suspicious, proud, distrustful, not observing equality in conversation: all such vices are removed, by considering the sincere and sweet affection of the roe and the fawn, or the stag and the doe.

And the text repeats the most sweet approval of love and the conjugal covenant, when it says: May her breasts inebriate you, that is, let there be true and ardent love, and let it not be wandering.

Let the emphases be considered, breasts signify affection (στοργή).

Inebriate signifies great love.

And then it is said: In her love you shall be ignorant, namely of others.

And the sum is, truly love your spouse, and be content with her alone, just as this law concerning marriage was immediately sanctioned in Paradise: They shall be two in one flesh, that is, one male and one female inseparably joined.

Because even then, although the nature of men had remained intact, God would have wanted men to understand chastity, and to provide the exercise of obedience, by the preservation of this order, namely, by avoiding wandering lusts.

But since the understanding of all virtues was therefore placed in the minds of men, so that this very distinction between honorable and shameful things might be a testimony that God exists, and might show what He is like, and that He is a judge, so also God wants chastity to be understood, and most severely punishes wandering lusts, so that we may know Him to be a chaste mind, and by this consideration distinguish Him from unclean natures.

Let us also think of this, that in the Church of God alone has the incorrupt doctrine of avoiding wandering lusts remained.

And let us often remind ourselves of the punishments.

For wandering lusts are punished both by most sad examples in this life, and by eternal torments, if conversion to God does not take place, according to that saying of Paul 1.

Corinthians 6: Fornicators and adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God. And in histories and many daily troubles let us consider the judgment of God.

Concerning the other Precept.

Drink water from your own fountains etc.

At the same time, this embraces precepts concerning particular justice, abstaining from the things of others, and concerning parsimony, and concerning liberality.

And first, let this distinguished testimony be observed against the Monks and Anabaptists, who praise Platonic community.

For here it is expressly said: You, remain the Lord of your own things, and not others with you.

Just as in the precept, You shall not steal, the distinction of ownership is sanctioned: so let us know that it is confirmed here, when it says: You, remain the Lord of your own things, and not others with you.

And concerning parsimony, it commands above: Do not give your wealth to others, and your years to the cruel one.

He calls them cruel, Leeches, who abuse the wealth of others.

This rapacity is more conspicuous in courts, and is painted in the fable of Actaeon, whom his own dogs tear apart.

Concerning adultery, however, and alms, it is said most sweetly: Let your fountains be derived abroad, and you remain the Lord of them, that is, you may give of the fruits, so that you can retain the estate.

He shows, therefore, the manner of liberality, he wants ownerships to be preserved, not for profusions and dissipations of inheritances to occur, and yet he wants the needy to be helped according to one's means, just as the Lord says: Give according to your means.

I was almost in all evil, in the midst of the congregation.

In this chapter, let this distinguished sentence also be observed concerning the examples of the multitude: I was almost in every evil, in the midst of the congregation, that is, the contagions of the people harm everyone, because man is led by nature to imitation, and learns by imitation. Since, therefore, he hears the false opinions of many and great men, and perceives their rites and customs, he follows them, and it is easier to imitate vices; afterwards, habit confirms the beginnings of diseases. Therefore, many sayings exist which command that we should not follow examples or the multitude, leaving behind the rule. Exod. 23 it is expressly said: You shall not follow the multitude to do evil, and you shall not answer in judgment by declining to the multitude that declines. We see, however, especially in religions, how much the opinion of the multitude prevails. Against such contagions, let us confirm ourselves with these sayings: Thy word is a lamp to my feet. Likewise: Hear me, etc. God wants us to be ruled by His word, not by opinions and examples departing from the word of God, etc.

Latin:

Caput V.

Caput quintum ad duo praecepta Decalogi pertinet. Non moechaberis, et, Non furtum facies. Initio enim quinti capitis prohibet adulteria et omnes vagas libidines, et addit conciones de poenis, quia sine ulla dubitatione huic divinae regulae respondent eventus: Scortatores et adulteros puniet Deus.

Et hic cap. 6. Adulter perdet animam suam, ut historiae privatae et publicae ostendunt, David, Troia, Thebae etc.

Et quanquam Deus mitigat poenas aliquibus agentibus poenitentiam, tamen semper aliquae poenae comitantur, et saepe peccata seminis puniuntur in semine, id est, in sobole.

Inserta est autem dulcissima concio, quae approbat coniugium et mutuum amorem, et suavitatem coniugii, et prohibet adulteria.

Approbatio coniugii et mutui amoris est, cum inquit: Delecteris uxore adolescentiae tuae, id est, quam adolescens ducis.

Deinde pingit amorem mutuum insigni imagine, Talis sit amor, ut est cervi et cervae, seu ut est capreae et hinnuli, id est, sit ardens amor, sine simulatione et sine coactione, sit suavis, sine morositate et fastidio, sit sincerus, sine suspicionibus, et sine superbia, et acquiescant coniuges in mutuo amore, ne divellantur aut appetant alios.

Extat ardoris descriptio apud Oppianum de cervis: Ipse tamen cervus pedibus velocibus ipsam Cum fugit assequitur, sistitque amplexus amatam. Ἀλλὰ ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι θεὼν ἐκίχανε θέουσαν φεύγουσαν μάρπτει δὲ καὶ ἀγκὰς ἔχει παράκοιτιν.

Antithesis vero declaratur exemplis.

Tyberius invitus ducit Iuliam, hic simulatio et coactio reddit coniugium insuave.

Q. Ciceronis Pomponia est morosior.

Multae naturae virorum et mulierum sunt suspicaces, superbae, diffidentes, non servantes aequalitatem in conversatione: talia vitia omnia removentur, considerato sincero et dulci affectu capreae et hinnuli, seu cervi et cervae.

Et repetit textus dulcissimam approbationem amoris et foederis coniugalis, cum ait: Ubera eius inebrient te, id est, sit verus et ardens amor, et non sit vagus.

Considerentur emphases, ubera significant στοργὴν.

Inebrient significat magnum amorem.

Et deinde dicitur: In dilectione eius ignores, videlicet alias.

Estque summa, vere diligito tuam coniugem, et ea unica contentus esto, sicut haec lex de coniugio statim in Paradiso sancita est: Erunt duo in carnem unam, id est, unus mas et una foemina inseparabiliter iuncti.

Quia tunc quoque etiamsi natura hominum mansisset integra, voluisset Deus homines intelligere castitatem, et praestare exercitium obedientiae, huius ordinis conservatione, videlicet, vitandis vagis libidinibus.

Ut autem omnium virtutum intellectus ideo mentibus hominum inditus est, ut hoc ipsum discrimen honestorum et turpium sit testimonium, quod sit Deus, et ostendat qualis sit, et quod sit iudex, ita et castitatem vult Deus intelligi, et severissime punit vagas libidines, ut sciamus ipsum esse mentem castam, et hac consideratione discernamus eum a naturis immundis.

Cogitemus et hoc, in sola Ecclesia Dei mansisse incorruptam doctrinam de vitandis vagis libidinibus.

Et saepe nos commonefaciamus de poenis.

Puniuntur enim vagae libidines et tristissimis exemplis in hac vita, et aeternis cruciatibus, si non fiat conversio ad Deum, iuxta dictum illud Pauli 1.

Corinth. 6.: Scortatores et adulteri non possidebunt regnum Dei. Et in historiis et multis aerumnis quotidianis consideremus iudicium Dei.

De altero Praecepto.

Bibe aquam de tuis fontibus etc.

Simul complexus est hic praecepta de iustitia particulari, abstinente a rebus alienis, et de parsimonia, et de liberalitate.

Ac primum observetur hic insigne testimonium contra Monachos et Anabaptistas, laudantes Platonicam communionem.

Hic enim expresse dicitur: Tu Dominus rerum tuarum maneto, et non alii tecum.

Sicut in praecepto, Non furtum facies, sancitur distinctio dominiorum: ita sciamus eam hic confirmari, cum ait: Tu Dominus rerum tuarum maneto, et non alii tecum.

Ac de parsimonia supra praecipit: Non des facultates tuas alienis, et annos tuos crudeli.

Crudeles nominat, Hirudines, quae abutuntur alienis facultatibus.

Haec rapacitas in aulis conspectior est, et pingitur in fabula Actaeonis, quem sui canes dilacerant.

De adulterio vero et eleemosynis dulcissime dicitur: Deriventur fontes tui foras, et tu Dominus eorum maneto, id est, largiaris de fructibus, ita ut retinere possis fundum.

Ostendit igitur modum liberalitatis, vult dominia conservari, non fieri profusiones et dissipationes haereditatum, et tamen vult iuvari egentes pro facultatibus, sicut Dominus inquit: Date pro facultatibus.

Pene fui in omni malo, in medio congregationis.

In hoc capite et haec insignis sententia observetur de exemplis multitudinis: Pene fui in omni malo, in medio congregationis, id est, contagia populi nocent omnibus, quia homo na- tura ad imitationem ducitur, et imitatione discit. Cum igitur multorum et magnorum falsas opinio- nes audit, et cernit ritus et mores, sequitur eos, et facilius est vitia imitari, postea consuetudo confirmat morborum initia. Ideo multa dicta ex- tant, quae praecipiunt, ne relicta regula exempla vel multitudinem sequamur. Exod. 23. expresse dictum est: Non sequaris multitudinem ad facien- dum malum, et non respondebis in iudicio decli- nans ad multitudinem declinantem. Videmus autem, praecipue in religionibus, quantum va- leat multitudinis opinio. Adversus talia conta- gia, confirmemus nos his dictis: Lucerna pedi- bus meis verbum tuum. Item: Audite me etc. Vult nos Deus suo verbo regi, non opinionibus et exemplis discedentibus a verbo Dei etc.

## 6:1 Argument
Chapter VI.

In the sixth chapter, the first sentence dissuades from giving pledges, narrating that they are dangerous, because very many sponsors fail; therefore, a saying was celebrated which was written in the Delphic temple: If you pledge, damage is at hand, that is, if you have pledged, you will be afflicted with damage. And Homer says in Odyssey 8: Δειλαί τοι δειλῶν γε, καὶ ἐγγυαι ἐγγυάασθαι, that is, bad are the pledges of bad men for bad men. In general, however, this saying warns that the faith of agreements is to be ratified, and that sincere and faithful men are rare. On the contrary, there are many unstable, masked, unfaithful, and perfidious men, as many complaints are read: Nowhere is faith safe. Flee those whom you believe to be faithful, and you will be safe. And that of Epicharmus: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν, ταῦτα γὰρ ἄρθρα φρενῶν ἐστὶν. Likewise in the Psalm: Do not trust in princes, and in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. And in Jeremiah: Cursed is he who trusts in man.

Here if anyone should ask: What then, is nothing to be believed? I answer: First, concerning the doctrine of God, one must believe the word of God, since indeed God has added illustrious testimonies, the resurrection of the dead and others. But men asserting something about God, by their own audacity, outside the doctrine handed down by God, are not to be believed, according to the saying: You shall add nothing nor take away. Next, in the arts, doctrine is certain because of demonstrations and other causes of certainty, because κριτήρια and demonstrations are also an order divinely instituted, which God wants to be perceived by human minds. But many things are mutable in affairs, and most mutable are the wills of men, and they are often fallacious; therefore, a distinction must be applied in this place, and it must be considered where and to what extent one should assent to human promises, and where one should not.

There is, however, a virtue which is named Candor, which judges wills, the extremes of which are calumny and foolish credulity. For candor is a virtue near to truth, approving the wills of others on account of probable reason, and not generating vain suspicions through malevolence or κακοηθίᾳ, bending even certain ambiguous things to the better part, and indeed hoping well, but nevertheless, as concerning mutable things, thinking that human wills can be changed, and that a man can err concerning the will of another, since the hidden places of the human breast are not thoroughly looked into. As David thinks well of Jonathan, because he has a probable reason why he should hope his will is firm, because he knows him to fear God, and to be adorned with divine testimony. He did not think well of Ahithophel, because he noticed him not to fear God. Thus, therefore, let the saying of 1 Corinthians 13 be understood: Love believes all things, that is, it is candid, it is not suspicious, it does not think ill of another without a probable and grave reason.

Concerning labors or concerning diligence.

In this sixth chapter, the second precept is concerning labor, which it also illustrates by example, commanding us to look at the ants and to imitate their diligence. First, therefore, let us learn here that God has ordained the degrees of offices or vocations, and that it is the command of God that each one should perform the labors of his own vocation, and not thrust himself into another's vocation, but in his own should provide diligence and faith. Thus these sayings of 1 Thessalonians 4 command: We exhort you to excel, and to be so ambitious, namely that you be quiet, and do your own things, and labor with your own hands. Eccles. 9: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might. And that by the counsel of God the degrees of offices are ordained and distinguished is manifest from the sayings of Rom. 12 and 13 and 1 Corinthians 12. There are distinctions of ministries. And 1 Corinthians 7: Each one as he has been called by the Lord, so let him walk. Where both are taught, that the degrees are distinct by the counsel of God, and that each one ought to know the limits of his office, and to perform the labors of his own degree. However, as often as mention is made of labor, let the invocation and help of God be included at the same time, according to the sayings: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his own. Likewise: Unless the Lord builds the house, etc. Likewise: Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act. Likewise: Ask and you shall receive. Likewise: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Likewise Daniel 2: God gives wisdom to the wise. Colossians 3: Everything that you do, in word or in deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus. And above, Proverbs 3: In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will direct your steps. Let there always be a conjunction of invocation and labor. This virtue is named Diligence, of which let this be the definition:

Diligence is a virtue by which we constantly and firmly desire to perform labors suitable to our vocation for the sake of God and the common salvation, with the help of God, who promised help to those who ask, as: David is a diligent soldier, Paul is a diligent teacher. The extremes of this virtue are Sloth and πολυπραγμοσύνη (meddlesomeness). The slothful person ceases too much, the meddlesome person or busybody attempts many unnecessary things or πάρεργα (side-tasks), and inserts himself into the vocations of others, just as Achas, Pericles, and Demosthenes draw wars upon themselves through unnecessary contentions, which could have been avoided. Thus, the Church is often disturbed by unnecessary disputes and contentions, or when teachers insert themselves into civil affairs, as if having one foot in the court and the other in the temple. I have said these things briefly about Diligence.

Let students collect together both the sayings in the prophetic and evangelical writings pertaining to this, and other wisely spoken things, such as: You have obtained Sparta, adorn it. Here both diligence is enjoined, and meddlesomeness is prohibited. A verse of Nazianzen warns to do necessary things: τὸ μὲν πάρεργον οὐδαμῶς ἔργον λέγω (I by no means call a side-task a task). This saying of Nazianzen is an admonition about association: καὶ γὰρ χερὸς χεὶρ, καὶ πόδος ποῦς ἐνδεής (For hand is in need of hand, and foot of foot). The hand is in need of the hand, and the foot of the foot.

A man of Belial, that is, useless, is not only a slacker, but a disturber.

I said that diligence is between the vicious extremes, sloth and meddlesomeness, and neighboring vices are ambition and quarrelsomeness; these also are censured in this place, because both are very pernicious to the common society, as Juvenal says concerning vicious ambition: 'Yet the desire for glory and titles of a few once overwhelmed the fatherland.' Likewise Claudian: 'For luxury turns other kingdoms upside down with vices and hatreds and pride.' Concerning the desire for contentions, and concerning dissensions, these sayings are well known: 'By concord small things grow, by discord the greatest fall apart.' However, let the definitions be held. True glory, and that which is justly sought, is the approval of a rightly judging conscience, and of others who judge rightly. That this is to be sought is manifest from these sentences: 'A good name is better than gold and silver.' Likewise: 'Live without scandal.' Likewise: 'Woe to the man through whom scandal comes.' Likewise: This is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience. Likewise: 'Let each one test his own work, so he will have glory in himself, and not from others.' And since it is a command of God to seek the approval of one's own rightly judging conscience, and of some who judge rightly in the Church, it is a virtue to seek this glory in order. The opposite vices are Levity and Impudence. Levity is to care for neither one's own conscience nor the right judgments of others, according to the verse: 'He is light, nor does the honor of glory stimulate him.' Impudence and arrogance and vanity is to attribute to oneself things that are not present. Then in the sixth and seventh chapters he preaches again about chastity, about which it was also spoken above, so that there may be known sermons about the punishments of adulteries, and of other wandering lusts, handed down here and there in the scriptures.

Latin:

Caput VI.

In sexto capite prima sententia dissuadet sponsiones, narrans esse periculosas, quia pluri- mi fallunt sponsores, ideo celebratum est dictum, quod in templo Delphico scriptum fuit: Spondeto damnum praesto est, id est, si spoponderis damno afficieris. Et Homerus inquit Odysseae ϑ.: Δει- λαί τοι δειλῶν γε, καὶ ἐγγυαι ἐγγυάασθαι, id est, malae sunt sponsiones spondendo pro malis. In genere autem hoc dictum monet, ratam esse fidem pactorum, et raros esse sinceros et fideles. Contra vero multos instabiles, fucatos, infidos, perfidos, ut multae querelae leguntur: Nusquam tuta fides. Quos credis fidos effuge, tutus eris. Et illud Epicharmi: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν, ταῦτα γὰρ ἄρθρα φρενῶν ἐστὶν. Item in Psal- mo: Nolite confidere in principibus, et in filiis hominum, in quibus non est salus. Et apud Ie- remiam: Maledictus qui confidit in homine.

Hic si quis interroget: Quid igitur, nihil- ne credendum est? Respondeo: Primum de do- ctrina de Deo, credendum est verbo Dei, cum quidem Deus addiderit illustria testimonia, re- suscitationem mortuorum et alia. Sed homini- bus asseverantibus aliquid de Deo, propria audacia, extra doctrinam a Deo traditam, non est creden- dum, iuxta dictum: Nihil addatis neque detraha- tis. Deinde in artibus certa est doctrina propter demonstrationes et alias causas certitudinis, quia κριτήρια et demonstrationes etiam sunt ordo di- vinitus institutus, quem vult Deus conspici ab humanis mentibus. Sed multa sunt mutabilia in rebus, et maxime mutabiles sunt hominum vo- luntates, et saepe sunt fallaces, ideo adhibendum est hoc loco discrimen, et considerandum est, ubi et quatenus assentiendum sit humanis pro- missis, ubi non sit assentiendum.

Est autem virtus quae nominatur Candor, quae diiudicat voluntates, cuius extrema sunt ca- lumnia et stulta credulitas. Nam candor est vir- tus vicina veritati, propter probabilem rationem approbans alienas voluntates, et non gignens va- nas suspiciones malevolentia seu κακοηθίᾳ, quae- dam etiam ambigua in meliorem partem flectens, ac bene quidem sperans, sed tamen ut de rebus mutabilibus, cogitans posse mutari voluntates humanas, et posse hominem errare de voluntate alterius, cum non penitus introspiciantur latebrae humani pectoris, Ut, David bene sentit de Iona- tha, quia habet probabilem rationem, quare illius voluntatem speret firmam esse, quia scit eum ti- mere Deum, et ornatum esse testimonio divino. Non bene sensit de Achitophel, quia animadver- tit eum non timere Deum. Sic igitur intelligatur dictum 1. Corinth. 13.: Dilectio credit omnia, id est, est candida, non est suspicax, non male sentit de alio sine probabili et gravi ratione.

De laboribus seu de sedulitate.

In hoc sexto capite secundum praeceptum est de labore, quod exemplo etiam illustrat, iubet nos intueri formicas, et earum sedulitatem imi- tari. Primum igitur hic discamus, et ordinasse Deum gradus officiorum seu vocationum, et man- datum Dei esse, ut suae quisque vocationis labo- res faciat, nec ingerat se alienae vocationi, sed in sua praestet diligentiam et fidem. Sic praeci- piunt haec dicta 1. Thessa. 4.: Hortamur vos ex- cellere, et sic ambitiosos esse, nempe ut sitis quieti, et propria faciatis, et laboretis propriis manibus. Eccles. 9.: Quicquid invenit manus tua ad faciendum, hoc totis viribus facito. Et quod Dei consilio gradus officiorum ordinati et distincti sint, manifestum est ex dictis Rom. 12. et 13. et 1. Corinth. 12. Distinctiones sunt mi- nisteriorum. Et 1. Corinth. 7.: Unusquisque si- cut vocatus est a Domino sic ambulet. Ubi utrunque docetur, et distinctos esse gradus con- silio Dei, et unumquemque debere nosse metas sui officii, et sui gradus labores facere. Quoties autem laboris mentio fit, simul com- prehendantur invocatio et auxilium Dei, iuxta dicta: Scio Domine non est hominis via eius. Item: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum etc. Item: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Item: Petite et accipietis. Item: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Item Daniel 2.: Deus dat sapientiam sapientibus. Coloss. 3.: Omnia quae facitis, in sermone aut in opere, omnia in nomine Domini nostri Iesu facite. Et supra Proverb. 3.: In omnibus viis tuis consi- deres eum, et ipse diriget gressus tuos. Sit sem- per coniunctio invocationis et laboris. Haec vir- tus nominatur Sedulitas, cuius sit haec definitio:

Sedulitas est virtus, qua constanter et firmi- ter volumus propter Deum et communem salutem labores facere vocationi convenientes, iuvante Deo, qui petentibus auxilium promisit, ut: Da- vid est sedulus miles, Paulus est sedulus doctor. Huius virtutis extrema sunt Ignavia et πολυπραγ- μοσύνη. Ignavus nimium cessat, πολυπράγμων seu ardelio multa non necessaria seu πάρεργα mo- litur, et se ingerit alienis vocationibus, ut Achas, Pericles, Demosthenes non necessariis contentio- nibus attrahunt bella, quae vitari poterant. Ita saepe turbatur Ecclesia non necessariis disputa- tionibus et contentionibus, aut cum ingerunt se doctores civilibus negociis, tanquam alterum pe- dem in curia, alterum in templo habentes. Haec breviter de Sedulitate dixi.

Colligant autem studiosi simul et dicta in scriptis propheticis et evangelicis, huc pertinen- tia, et alia sapienter dicta, ut: Spartam nactus es, hanc orna. Hic et sedulitas praecipitur, et prohibetur πολυπραγμοσύνη. Versus Nazian- zeni monet necessaria facere: τὸ μὲν πάρεργον οὐδαμῶς ἔργον λέγω. Hoc dictum Nazianzeni admonitio est de consociatione: καὶ γὰρ χερὸς χεὶρ, καὶ πόδος ποῦς ἐνδεής. Manus est indi- gens manu, et pes pede.

Homo Belial, id est, inutilis, non est tan- tum cessator, sed turbator.

Dixi sedulitatem esse inter extrema vitiosa, ignaviam et πολυπραγμοσύνην, et vicina vitia sunt ambitio et rixositas, haec etiam hoc loco ta- xantur, quia utrumque valde perniciosum est communi societati, ut de ambitione vitiosa di- cit Iuvenalis: Patriam tamen obruit olim, Gloria paucorum laudis, titulique cupido. Item Clau- dianus: Nam caetera regna luxuries vitiis odiis- que superbia vertit. De cupiditate contentionum, et de dissidiis haec dicta nota sunt: Concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia maximae dilabun- tur. Teneantur autem definitiones. Vera gloria, et quae iuste appetitur, est ap- probatio conscientiae recte iudicantis, et aliorum recte iudicantium. Hanc esse appetendam mani- festum est ex his sententiis: Melius est nomen bonum, quam aurum et argentum. Item: Vivite sine scandalo. Item: Vae homini, per quem ve- nit scandalum. Item: Haec est gloriatio nostra, testimonium conscientiae nostrae. Item: Probet unusquisque opus suum, sic habebit gloriam apud sese, et non ex aliis. Et cum mandatum Dei sit, appetere approbationem conscientiae suae recte iudicantis, et aliquorum recte iudicantium in Ec- clesia, virtus est hanc gloriam ordine expetere. Opposita vitia sunt Levitas et Impudentia. Levitas est, nec suae conscientiae, nec aliorum recta iudicia curare, iuxta versum: Levis est, nec illum stimulat gloriae decus. Impudentia et arrogantia et vanitas est tri- buere sibi quae non adsunt. Deinde in sexto et septimo capite rursus con- cionatur de castitate, de qua et supra dictum est, ut sint notae conciones de poenis adulteriorum, et aliarum vagarum libidinum, passim in scri- pturis traditae.

## 8:1 Argument
Chapter VIII.

In the eighth chapter, after he repeated the precepts of the Decalogue at the beginning, he now returns to a general exhortation, that we may learn this wisdom, and obey it. For he names the wisdom proposed and revealed to us by God, and binds us to this; he does not speak of the wisdom of Pericles or Alcibiades, or of similar men, which is the cunning of increasing power and wealth by any occasion, whether in a just or unjust way. Nor indeed is there any doubt that Solomon speaks of the word revealed in the Church, of the law of God, and of the Gospel, because he says: 'Wisdom cries out in the gates of the city.' But yet, since the eternal and unmoved wisdom, which is in God himself, has been revealed by the voice of the law and the Gospel, and has been revealed through the Son himself, through whom the Father speaks the decrees concerning order of the creation and restoration of man: Antiquity understood in this place the wisdom which is the Son speaking, namely, to the Church. I approve of this opinion rightly understood. But the Arians falsely excerpted certain sayings, in order to confirm that the Son is a creature. For where Solomon says: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, the Arians read: The Lord created me in the beginning of his ways. But it must be known that in the Hebrew reading the word for possessing, not creating, is placed, and by the word for possessing and the continuous series of the narrative the Arians are clearly refuted. For as it is written in John: In the beginning was the Word, so here it is most sweetly said: The Lord possessed me in the beginning. Likewise: Before the ages I was ordained. And this wisdom says that she was the artificer or fashioner, just as it is said in John 1: All things were made through him. Likewise Hebrews 1: Upholding all things by the word of his power.
