Because it is the same Son, through whom the decree concerning the order of the creation and restoration of man is said. Therefore here by the same name he names the wisdom creating and issuing the Law and the Gospel. And it follows: Playing before him at all times, playing in the world of the earth, and my delights were with the sons of men. This wisdom first supremely gladdens the Father, then shows to angels and men the Father in the wondrous order of the workmanship of the world, and afterwards in the promulgation of the word, in the assumption of human nature, and the resurrection, in the restoration of men, and the preservation of the whole Church, in the flood of Noah, in the Red Sea, and all other miracles, it shows and glorifies the Father, and rejoices in the vivification and restitution of the Church. All these wondrous works he here calls the games and delights of the wisdom of God. Let pious readers attentively consider this most sweet opinion, and this same wisdom, that is, the Son, teaches outside the Church by the promulgated word, and sustains, teaches, and illuminates it within, and because he preserves the human race for the sake of the Church, insofar as just things are done in polities, they are done by him sustaining and teaching the governors by the published word, and governing them in a secret way. Therefore he says: By me kings reign, and judges decree just things. This wisdom of God, the directress promulgated through the word, he then distinguishes from human cunning. Divine wisdom is happy, effective, and salutary, and finally brings happy outcomes, even if they are delayed for some time. But the cunning of Pericles, Alcibiades, Demosthenes, and the like is destructive to the fatherland and to themselves. Therefore the wisdom of God says: With me is counsel and success, that is, those counsels are just which agree with the word of God, and these counsels will finally have happy outcomes, with the help of that Son of God, who indeed wishes to be present to those persevering in the word handed down, and to those invoking him, according to the saying: Commit thy way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will do it. Proverbs 3: In all thy ways know him, and he will direct thy steps. Likewise: It is God who works in you, both to will and to perform. Conversely, however, punishments follow injustice universally, although in the present they were for a little while pleasing pleasures, or power grew.

Latin:

Caput VIII.

In octavo capite postquam initio Decalogi praecepta repetivit, nunc redit ad generalem ad- hortationem, ut hanc sapientiam discamus, et ei obediamus. Nominat enim sapientiam a Deo nobis propositam et revelatam, et ad hanc nos alligat, non loquitur de sapientia Periclis aut Alcibiadis, aut similium, quae est calliditas augendi potentiam et opes quacunque occasione, sive iusto, sive iniusto modo. Nec vero du- bium est, Salomonem loqui de verbo revelato in Ecclesia, de lege Dei, et de Evangelio, quia dicit: Sapientia in portis civitatis clami- tat. Sed tamen cum sapientia aeterna et im- mota, quae est in ipso Deo, revelata sit voce legis et Evangelii, et sit revelata per ipsum Fi- lium, per quem Pater dicit decreta de ordine creationis et reparationis hominis: Vetustas in- tellexit hoc loco sapientiam quae est Filius loquens scilicet ad Ecclesiam. Hanc sententiam recte in- tellectam probo. Sed Arriani falso excerpserunt quaedam di- cta, ut confirmarent Filium esse creaturam. Ubi enim Salomon inquit: Dominus possedit me ini- tio viae suae, legerunt Arriani: Dominus creavit me initio viarum suarum. Sed sciendum est in Ebraica lectione verbum possidendi, non creandi positum esse, ac verbo possidendi et continua se- rie narrationis perspicue refutantur Arriani. Ut enim in Iohanne scriptum est: In principio erat verbum, ita hic dulcissime dicitur: Dominus possedit me initio. Item: Ante secula ordinata sum. Et inquit haec sapientia, se fuisse artifi- cem seu formatricem, sicut Iohannis 1. dicitur: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Item Ebrae. 1.: Gestans omnia verbo potentiae suae. Quia idem Filius est, per quem dicitur decretum de ordine creationis et reparationis hominis. Ideo hic eo- dem nomine sapientiam creantem et edentem le- gem et Evangelium nominat. Ac sequitur: Lu- dens coram eo in omni tempore, ludens in orbe terrae, et delectationes meae cum Filiis homi- num. Haec sapientia primum summe laetificat Patrem, deinde ostendit angelis et hominibus Pa- trem in mirando ordine opificii mundi, ac postea in promulgatione verbi, in assumtione naturae humanae, et resurrectione, in hominum repa- ratione, et totius Ecclesiae conservatione, in di- luvio Noë, in mari rubro, et omnibus aliis mi- raculis ostendit et glorificat Patrem, et laetatur vivificatione et restitutione Ecclesiae. Haec omnia miranda opera nominat hic ludos et delectationes sapientiae Dei. Hanc dulcissimam sententiam attente considerent pii lectores, et haec eadem sapientia, id est, Filius docet foris Ecclesiam pro- mulgato verbo, et intus eam sustentat, docet et illustrat, et quia propter Ecclesiam servat genus humanum, quatenus iusta fiunt in politiis, fiunt ipso sustentante et docente gubernatores edito ver- bo, et gubernante eos arcano modo. Ideo in- quit: Per me reges regnant, et iudices iusta de- cernunt. Hanc sapientiam Dei rectricem per ver- bum promulgatam, discernit deinde ab humana calliditate. Sapientia divina est felix, efficax et salutaris, et tandem adfert laetos exitus, etiamsi aliquandiu differuntur. Calliditas vero Periclis, Alcibiadis, Demosthenis et similium est exitiosa patriae et ipsis. Ideo inquit sapientia Dei: Penes me est consilium et successus, id est, illa consi- lia sunt iusta, quae congruunt cum verbo Dei, et haec consilia tandem habebunt laetos exitus, ad- iuvante ea Filio Dei, qui quidem vult adesse per- severantibus in verbo tradidit, et invocantibus eum, iuxta dictum: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Proverb. 3.: In omnibus viis tuis cognosce eum, et ipse diriget gressus' tuos. Item: Deus est qui facit, ut velitis et ut perficiatis. Contra vero poenae sequuntur universaliter iniusticiam, quanquam in praesen- tia aliquantisper voluptates gratae fuerunt, aut potentia crevit.

## 10:1 Argument
Chapter X.

Latin:

Caput X.

## 10:3
The Lord will not suffer the soul of the just to famish.

It is a common doctrine concerning providence, which has been often repeated in the whole work. But God distinguishes right and not right by eternal rewards and punishments, because this is the order of justice, that right things be preserved, and not right things be destroyed, according to the saying: God is a consuming fire, and God wishes the distinction of the right and the not right to be made more conspicuous by the mention of punishments and rewards. But right things are those conforming to God or his law. Not right things are those fighting with God or with the law.

But temporal and eternal punishments must be distinguished. Temporal punishments are imposed first to recall men to repentance, then in those not doing repentance, they are the beginnings of destruction and eternal punishments, as the punishments of Saul, Judas, Nero, and all others rushing into eternal punishments.

Let bodily and eternal goods also be distinguished. The Church will certainly have eternal goods. For rational creatures were founded for this reason, that they might be some organs by which God communicates himself, his light, wisdom, justice, life, and eternal joy. But in this mortal life the Church is still subject to the cross by the certain counsel of God, therefore many members are harshly exercised, some more, some less, and yet because God wishes the Church in this life to be gathered by the voice of the ministry, and not otherwise, he always preserves some assembly, which cannot live without food, drink, and lodging. Thus therefore he mitigates the cross, so that he also gives to this assembly the things necessary for the preservation of bodily life, and preserves among these also these rules concerning external life, universally: atrocious crimes are accompanied by atrocious punishments, as, for example, David’s adultery and the crimes of Manasseh were followed by horrible punishments; but for the pious, many punishments are mitigated, and for many the course of life is more tranquil. Here, therefore, promises both eternal and corporal are often inculcated, as is said in this place: The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish. Psalm 33: The lions have suffered hunger, but to them that fear the Lord no good thing shall be lacking.

May this common doctrine concerning the distinction, which the eternal and immovable wisdom of God has sanctioned between right and not right, and concerning rewards and punishments, always be in sight, and at the same time let the universal doctrine concerning the Church be considered, concerning the distinction between the eternal promise and corporal things. Also the doctrine concerning the cross.

There are, however, four principal causes for which promises concerning corporal goods have been given to the Church:

First. That they may be testimonies of providence, against Epicurean opinions, so that we do not think these external goods are scattered by chance, and especially in the Church they are given by the singular counsel of God, and in a singular manner. Indeed, even to the whole human race, the nature of things is preserved for the sake of the Church.

Second. That they may testify that God will preserve the Church, even in this life, and that we may think that in this mortal life the Church must be begun.

Third. That faith and invocation may be exercised in daily necessity, in seeking peace, food, good health, and success in government.

Fourth cause. That they may be reminders of the eternal promise, because in every petition, faith must shine forth, which receives the remission of sins for the sake of the Mediator, and we must always think that the Church in this life also is preserved for his sake and through him, as he says: I will carry you in my bosom, just as a shepherd carries lambs recently born. Let us know, therefore, that the promises concerning corporal goods are not void, and confirmed by this divine voice, let us seek and expect the necessities of life in invocation.

Latin:

Non sinet esurire Dominus animam iusti.

Communis doctrina est de providentia, quae saepe repetita est in toto opere. Discernit autem Deus recta et non recta aeternis praemiis et poe- nis, quia hic est ordo iusticiae, ut recta conser- ventur, et non recta destruantur, iuxta dictum: Deus est ignis consumens, et vult Deus mentione poenarum et praemiorum fieri conspectius discri- men rectorum et non rectorum. Sunt autem re- cta conformia Deo seu legi eius. Non recta sunt pugnantia cum Deo seu cum lege.

Discernendae autem sunt poenae temporales et aeternae. Poenae temporales imponuntur pri- mum ut revocent homines ad poenitentiam, de- inde in non agentibus poenitentiam, sunt initia destructionis et poenarum aeternarum, ut suppli- cia Saul, Iudae, Neronis, et aliorum omnium ruentium in aeternas poenas.

Discernantur et bona corporalia et aeterna. Ecclesia certo habebit aeterna bona. Ideo enim conditae sunt rationales creaturae, ut sint aliqua organa, quibus Deus communicet sese, suam lu- cem, sapientiam, iusticiam, vitam et laeticiam aeternam. Sed in hac vita mortali Ecclesia adhuc certo consilio Dei subiecta est cruci, ideo multa membra duriter exercentur, alia magis, alia mi- nus, et tamen quia vult Deus Ecclesiam in hac vita voce ministerii, et non aliter colligi, semper aliquem coetum servat, qui sine cibo, potu, et hospitiis vivere non potest. Sic igitur mitigat crucem, ut huic coetui quoque det necessaria ad vitae corporalis conservationem, et servat inter hos quoque has regulas de externa vita, universaliter: Atrocia delicta comitantur atroces poenae, ut, Davidis adulterium, Manassis scelera, secutae sunt horribiles poenae: piis vero mitigantur multae poenae, et multorum est tranquillior cursus. Hic igitur saepe inculcantur promissiones et aeternae et corporales, ut hoc loco dicitur: Non sinet esurire Dominus animam iusti. Psal. 33.: Leones esurierunt, timentibus autem Dominum non deerit ullum bonum.

Haec communis doctrina de distinctione, quam sanxit aeterna et immota sapientia Dei inter recta et non recta, et de praemiis et poenis semper sit in conspectu, et simul consideretur universa doctrina de Ecclesia, de distinctione promissionis aeternae et corporalium. Item doctrina de cruce.

Sunt autem praecipuae causae quatuor, propter quas Ecclesiae traditae sunt promissiones de bonis corporalibus:

Prima. Ut sint testimonia de providentia, contra Epicureas opiniones, ne existimemus haec bona externa casu spargi, ac praesertim in Ecclesia dantur singulari consilio Dei, et singulari modo. Imo et toti generi humano servatur natura rerum propter Ecclesiam.

Secunda. Ut testentur Deum servaturum esse Ecclesiam, etiam in hac vita, et cogitemus in hac mortali vita oportere incoari Ecclesiam.

Tertia. Ut fides et invocatio exerceantur in quotidiana necessitate, in petenda pace, victu, bona valetudine, successu in gubernatione.

Quarta causa. Ut sint commonefactiones de promissione aeterna, quia in omni petitione, oportet praelucere fidem, quae accipit remissionem peccatorum propter Mediatorem, et semper cogitemus Ecclesiam in hac vita quoque propter eum et per eum servari, sicut dicit: Ego gestabo vos in sinu, sicut pastor agnos recens editos gestat. Sciamus igitur promissiones de bonis corporalibus non esse irritas et confirmati hac voce divina, petamus et expectemus necessaria vitae in invocatione.

## 10:4
Slothful hands make for poverty.

Solomon joins promises and precepts concerning labor, because God commands both, that we should perform the works of our vocation, and at the same time seek and expect good outcomes from him, according to the saying: Commit thy way unto the Lord, and hope in him, and he shall bring it to pass.

Latin:

Egestatem efficit manus ignava.

Coniungit Salomon promissiones et praecepta de labore, quia utrumque praecipit Deus, et ut faciamus opera vocationis, et simul petamus et expectemus ab ipso bonos eventus, iuxta dictum: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

## 10:12
Hatred stirreth up strifes, but love covereth all sins.

This is a precept concerning ἐπιεικεία [equity/clemency] and candor, pertaining to the fifth and eighth commandments. Here it is first necessary to know the common definitions and distinctions of justice.

Particular justice is the virtue that gives to each his own.

Thus, the justice of a judge is the virtue that gives defense to the just, and punishments to the unjust. But because there are degrees of crimes, as the crime of the devil is more atrocious than that of Adam, the guilt of Judas is more atrocious than that of Peter: there are also distinct degrees of vindictive justice, severity and equity, and both are justice, and the extremes are the same, cruelty and indulgence. Sulla was cruel, who even after victory killed a promiscuous multitude, as the poet says: The medicine exceeded the measure. Julius spared Cicero, Marcellus, and others, and in the city exercised no cruelty.

But let them be discerned in this saying of Solomon: Love covereth all sins: the judge and the private person. A judge, by divine mandate, is compelled to use severity against those who have sinned atrociously, as against blasphemers, perjurers, murderers, those polluted by adulteries and incestuous lusts. Deut. 19: Thou shalt put away the evil from the midst of thee, thou shalt not pity him, but it shall be soul for soul, because God wishes punishments to be seen, so that he himself may be acknowledged as discerning right and not right, and judging and punishing crimes, and then so that the common society may be defended. But the same judge will also understand where punishments are to be mitigated, just as the laws themselves concerning murder committed by ambush are more atrocious than concerning accidental killing. This moderating virtue ἐπιεικεία [equity/clemency], which is justice, mitigating either certain laws or certain punishments for a probable reason, and many examples of this mitigation have been most wisely handed down. As David, when hungry, made use of the loaves of the priests.

Thrasybulus decreed an ἀμνηστίαν [amnesty], and did not cast the possessors out of the property of the exiles, so that new wars would not arise.

Emperor Conrad made peace with Welf at the town of Weinsberg, when, contrary to the understanding of the pact, the women had carried out their husbands and sons from the fortress, because the emperor had permitted that the women could depart with those things which they were able to carry.

Let these things be said concerning the judge, whom it behooves to understand where severity and where leniency should be used, as must be said elsewhere.

But concerning private persons and private offenses, it must first be known that necessary defense is permitted, but outside the case of necessary defense, private injuries must be remitted and buried in oblivion, according to the saying: Forgive and it shall be forgiven you. But since such injuries happen very frequently in the custom of men, and it is madness to hope for a life in which many do not run into you, let us not think that this precept speaks of rare offenses, but let us know that this forgiveness is necessary in many affairs of life regarding private offenses.

And forgivenesses must be made, first for the sake of God, then for the sake of common tranquility. And God not only commands this virtue, but also wishes it to be a reminder of His own forgiveness. Therefore He says: Forgive and it shall be forgiven you. He also wishes us, in the contemplation and exercise of this virtue, to be reminded of His mercy, and of the Gospel, in which the immense ἐπιείκεια (clemency) of the law is proposed, because an incipient, meager, and sordid obedience is accepted, and because many infirmities are forgiven, and punishments are daily softened, according to the saying: It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed. That the oblivion of private offenses is necessary for common peace is most manifest.

However, younger people must be warned not to admit the false interpretation of those who twist this saying into an error, which feigns that our works merit the remission of sins. Love covers sins, therefore your love covers sins before God. The consequence must be denied, because the saying is political, and speaks of forgiveness between men, and of covering the sins of others, and of repressing the desire for vengeance, as it is commanded in Leviticus 17: Do not exercise vengeance, nor be mindful of injury against your fellow citizens. For it is said specifically of citizens, to signify that for the sake of common concord, many injuries must be overlooked. But let us be ashamed of our pride and impatience, when the Son of God not only forgives us many and great sins, but also derived the punishment upon Himself, prostrate before the Father, and sustaining the curse against our sins, as if He Himself had been polluted by my and your crimes. Therefore He says: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. Warned by this example and precept, let us bear it patiently when we are thrust down as if from a superior place, when indeed we truly deserve punishments for many great sins, and let us restrain our impulses, lest greater hatreds, dissensions, and wars be kindled. Let us cherish this virtue, ἐπιείκεια (clemency), for this very reason, so that this name itself may often remind us of the Gospel, in which the sweetest ἐπιείκεια of the divine law is proposed, as has been said. But just as virtues are neighbors, severe justice and ἐπιείκεια, so are the virtues neighbors, Truth, which judges severely concerning the words or deeds of others, and Candor. The extremes are Flattery and Calumny. But candor moderates harsher judgments, so that often something said rather negligently by good writers must be softened by an interpretation congruent with the perpetual intent of the author.

Latin:

Odium suscitat rixas, universa autem delicta operit dilectio.

Praeceptum est de ἐπιεικείᾳ et de candore, pertinens ad quintum et octavum praeceptum. Hic primum scire necesse est communes definitiones et distinctiones iusticiae.

Iusticia particularis est virtus suum cuique tribuens.

Sic iusticia iudicis est virtus tribuens iustis defensionem, et poenas iniustis. Quia vero gradus sunt delictorum, ut atrocius scelus est diaboli quam Adae, atrocior est culpa Iudae quam Petri: distincti sunt et gradus iusticiae vindicis, severitas et aequitas, et utraque est iusticia, ac extrema sunt eadem, crudelitas et indulgentia. Sylla crudelis fuit, qui etiam post victoriam occidit promiscuam multitudinem, sicut inquit poëta: Excessit medicina modum. Iulius pepercit Ciceroni, Marcello et aliis, et in urbe nullam saevitiam exercuit.

Discernantur autem in hoc dicto Salomonis: Universa delicta operit dilectio: iudex et privata persona. Iudex mandato divino cogitur severitate uti adversus eos qui atrociter deliquerunt, ut adversus blasphemos, periuros, homicidas, pollutos adulteriis et incestis libidinibus. Deutero. 19.: Auferes malum de medio tui, non misereberis eius, sed sit anima pro anima, quia Deus vult conspici poenas, ut agnoscatur ipse discernens recta et non recta, et iudicans ac puniens scelera, deinde ut communis societas defendatur. Idem autem iudex intelliget quoque, ubi leniendae sint poenae, sicut leges ipsae de caede ex insidiis facta sunt atrociores, quam de caede fortuita. Haec virtus moderatrix ἐπιεικεία, quae est iusticia, seu leges aliquas, seu poenas propter rationem probabilem mitigans, et sapientissime tradita sunt multa exempla huius mitigationis. Ut David esuriens usus est panibus sacerdotum.

Thrasybulus sanxit ἀμνηστίαν, nec eiecit possessores ex facultatibus exulum, ne nova bella orirentur.

Conradus imperator fecit pacem cum Guelpho ad oppidum Weinsberg, cum contra intellectum pacti mulieres extulissent viros et filios ex arce, quia imperator permiserat, ut mulieres discederent cum iis rebus quas possent asportare.

Haec de iudice dicta sint, quem oportet intelligere, ubi severitate, ubi lenitate utendum sit, ut alibi dicendum est.

Sed de privatis personis et de privatis offensionibus primum sciendum est, necessariam defensionem concessam esse, sed extra casum necessariae defensionis remittendae sunt privatae iniuriae, et obruendae oblivione, iuxta dictum: Remittite et remittetur vobis. Cum autem tales iniuriae in consuetudine hominum plurimae accidant, et insania sit, sperare vitam, in qua non multi in te incurrant, non existimemus hoc praeceptum de raris offensionibus loqui, sed sciamus hanc condonationem in multis vitae negotiis necessariam esse in privatis offensionibus.

Et faciendae sunt condonationes, primum propter Deum, deinde propter communem tranquillitatem. Ac Deus non solum praecipit hanc virtutem, sed etiam vult eam esse commonefactionem de sua condonatione. Ideo inquit: Remittite et remittetur vobis. Vult etiam nos in huius virtutis cogitatione et exercitio commonefieri de sua misericordia, et de Evangelio, in quo proponitur ingens ἐπιείκεια legis, quod recipitur incoata obedientia exigua et sordida, et quod multae infirmitates condonantur, et quotidie leniuntur poenae, iuxta dictum: Misericordia Domini quod non consumti sumus. Quod autem communi paci necessaria sit privatarum offensionum oblivio, manifestissimum est.

Monendi sunt autem iuniores, ne admittant falsam interpretationem detorquentium hoc dictum ad errorem, qui fingit nostra opera mereri remissionem peccatorum. Delicta tegit dilectio, ergo tua dilectio tegit delicta coram Deo. Neganda est consequentia, quia dictum est politicum, et loquitur de condonatione inter homines, et de alienis delictis tegendis, et de reprimenda cupiditate vindictae, ut Levit. 17. praecipitur: Non exerceas vindictam, nec sis memor iniuriae adversus cives tuos. Nominatim enim de civibus dicitur, ut significet, propter communem concordiam multas iniurias dissimulandas esse. Pudeat autem nos nostrae superbiae et impatientiae, cum Filius Dei non solum remittat nobis multa et magna peccata, sed etiam poenam in sese derivaverit prostratus coram Patre, ac iuram adversus nostra delicta sustinens, quasi ipse se meis et tuis sceleribus polluisset. Ideo inquit: Discite a me, qui mitis sum et humilis corde. Hoc exemplo et praecepto moniti patienter feramus cum quasi de superiori loco detrudimur, cum quidem nos revera multis magnis peccatis meriti simus poenas, et coërceamus nostros impetus, ne maiora odia, dissidia, bella accendantur. Diligamus hanc virtutem ἐπιείκειαν hanc ipsam ob causam, ut saepe nos hoc ipsum nomen admoneat de Evangelio, in quo dulcissima ἐπιείκεια legis divinae proponitur, ut dictum est. Sicut autem virtutes vicinae sunt, severa iustitia et ἐπιείκεια, ita sunt vicinae virtutes, Veritas severe iudicans de alienis dictis aut factis, et Candor. Extrema sunt Assentatio et Calumnia. Moderatur autem candor iudicia duriora, ut saepe aliquid negligentius dictum in bonis scriptoribus leniendum est interpretatione congruente ad perpetuam autoris sententiam.

## 10:14
The mouth of the fool approaches confusion.

There are many sayings in Solomon concerning speech or the bridling of the tongue. But the vices proper to the tongue are: Lying, garrulity, precipitation, curiosity, evil-speaking, railing, petulance of the tongue, calumnies, vanity or boasting, θρασωνισμὸς (braggadocio), irony, δυσωπία (shamefacedness/bashfulness), ἀκκισμὸς (affectation), impudence, φιλονεικία (contentiousness), scurrility, obscenity, being scoptic (mocking), futility, flattery. These vices must be considered for this reason, that we may learn to avoid them with greater care, and bridle our impulses, and not pour out all our thoughts, etc.

Latin:

Os stulti confusioni appropinquat.

Multa sunt dicta in Salomone de sermone seu de lingua frenanda. Sunt autem vitia linguae propria, Mendacium, garrulitas, praecipitantia, curiositas, maledicentia, conviciatio, petulantia linguae, calumniae, vanitas, seu iactantia, θρασωνισμὸς, ironia, δυσωπία, ἀκκισμὸς, impudentia, φιλονεικία, scurillitas, obscoenitas, scopticum esse, futilitas, assentatio. Haec vitia ideo consideranda sunt, ut maiore cura vitare ea discamus, et frenemus impetus nostros, nec omnes cogitationes effundamus etc.

## 10:22
The blessing of the Lord makes rich and adds no sorrow.

Profane men think that wealth and victories are prepared only by human industry and labors, as they think Alexander wins; because he excels the Persian multitude in counsel, labors, and the strength of his army, just as it is commonly said: Persistent labor conquers all things. And Plato says that he is blessed whose fortune does not depend on others, but all things necessary for happiness are placed within himself. And thus says Nebuchadnezzar: I have made Babylon so great by my own strength. Such imaginations confirm the confidence in our own cunning and our own powers, by which elated men neglect God, and move things that should not be moved, as when Antony sees that he is better equipped than Augustus, and hopes that he can be crushed, he moves an unjust war. There are very many such sad errors of men. But the divine voice teaches that the causes of good outcomes are not the labors of men alone, but God helping just labors, and the obedience of men in their calling.

Therefore, the negative proposition is expressly handed down: Unless the Lord builds the house, he labors in vain who builds it. Likewise, Ecclesiastes 9: There is not to the swift the race, nor to the strong the battle, nor to the wise bread. And Psalm 33: A horse is a vain thing for safety. And Psalm 59: You will not go out, O God, in our virtues. Give us help from tribulation, for vain is the salvation of man. And Jeremiah 10: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his own. John 3: A man cannot take anything to himself, unless it be given to him from God. And John 5: Without me you can do nothing. These testimonies do not prohibit the labor of one's calling, but teach that the cause of good outcomes is not the wisdom of men alone and the labors of men alone.

Therefore, they condemn our self-confidence. Afterward, the divine voice joins these causes of good outcomes: God helping the labors of one's calling, and our obedience in that calling. Therefore, it commands just labors, congruent with one's calling, as in Ecclesiastes 9: Whatever your hand can do, do it with all your might. And 1 Thessalonians 4: Study to do this, that you may be quiet, and do your own business, and work with your own hands. And Genesis 3: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread. And Psalm 127: Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you. And Proverbs 10: The hand of the diligent shall be rich. But it must be known that these labors are happy and follow with good outcomes only when God helps those who labor according to their calling.

Promises of divine help and commands concerning invocation are therefore handed down, so that God may be acknowledged. Likewise, so that His presence may be acknowledged in private and public governance, as in Psalm 36: Be subject to the Lord, and pray to Him. Likewise: Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in Him, and He shall do it. And Psalm 33: There is no want to those who fear God. And Psalm 54: Cast your care upon the Lord, and He shall sustain you. Psalm 90: I will protect him, because he has known my name; I am with him in tribulation. Daniel 2: He gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding. Proverbs 16: The heart of man thinks out his way, but the Lord confirms his steps. Proverbs 21: The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord gives the victory. Proverbs 20: That the eye may see, and the ear may hear, the Lord makes both. Isaiah 46: I have made you, I will carry you even into old age. Isaiah 40: I have carried you as a shepherd carries suckling lambs. Deuteronomy 30: He is your life, and the length of your days. Deuteronomy 8: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Exodus 19: I have carried you on the wings of eagles. Deuteronomy 8: Do not say, 'My strength and the power of my hand have given me these things,' but remember the Lord your God, that He Himself has provided you with strength. It is profitable to have these and similar testimonies in view, so that we may cast out profane imagination from our minds, and not trust in our own diligence or our own strength, but truly believe that our labors are happy only when they are helped by God, and let us seek the help of God, according to the saying of the Psalm: Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in Him, and He shall do it.

And Proverbs 16: Commit your works to the Lord, and your thoughts shall be directed. Let us look to this rule of life in all counsels and business, making the labors of our calling, and seeking and expecting help from God. And let the doctrine concerning the invocation of God and His promises be joined to this. Furthermore, let this also be considered: that even the heathens, compelled by experience, confess that the more powerful and wiser are often defeated, namely when they act unjustly, and move forward with a confidence in their own strength that is not necessary; and for many, confidence in their own strength has been their ruin, as is said of Ajax: that when he had said he could win even without God, because of this impious self-confidence he was punished with madness, by which he brought death upon himself.

And the story of Milo of Croton is often recited, who, when he was stuck in a split tree, was torn apart by wolves. And Pegasus threw off Bellerophon when he wanted to ride into heaven. And the head of the Gorgon was finally the ruin of Perseus. Chapter XI. A fraudulent balance is an abomination to the Lord, and a just weight is pleasing to Him.

This is a commandment concerning particular justice and truth in contracts, and it pertains to the saying of the Decalogue: You shall not steal. And the warning, often repeated, should be understood to be repeated here as well: Atrocious crimes are punished with atrocious penalties, even in this life.

According to the sayings: He who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword. Likewise: Woe to you who plunder, for you shall be plundered.

And in the consideration of this order, God wills that He be acknowledged, and that this order be understood to have been divinely sanctioned. And let us know that marriages, political society, contracts, judgments, and punishments are works of the wisdom and justice of God, and are effectively preserved by God, as much as any of the order remains, even if in the meantime great tumults are stirred up by devils and by the organs of the devil.

Just as a shepherd of a flock preserves some part of the herd, even if wolves snatch away some sheep. Thus he says below concerning the political order in the sixteenth chapter. The weight and the scales are the judgments of the Lord, and all the works of the scales are His. This admonition is necessary against the Manichaean and Anabaptist furies, as has been said copiously elsewhere.

When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom. It is common for men to become more negligent in prosperous circumstances, because, protected by manifest defenses, they fear less and grieve less; therefore, the invocation of God becomes more languid, as is said in Moses: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. Item: Minds generally grow wanton in prosperous circumstances. But when the fear of God is extinguished, men, feeling secure, in order to increase their power, attempt many things outside their calling, and inflict injuries upon others.

Thence follow punishments by divine order, according to the sayings: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Item: He has put down the mighty from their seat, and has exalted the humble. And experience has compelled even the heathens to confess that punishments inevitably follow pride that rushes outside the bounds of one's calling. This order they named Adrasteia, and a sign of impending ruin is notable insolence, according to the saying of Claudian: They are lifted up on high, so that they may fall with a heavier crash, etc. This is also the sentiment of Solomon in this place.

But on the contrary, he says that wisdom is with the humble, as Peter says: He gives grace to the humble. And it is said in Isaiah: Where shall the Lord dwell? In a contrite and humbled spirit, and in one who keeps my words. Let the definitions of Humility and Pride be noted.

Humility, or ταπεινοφροσύνη (humility of mind), is to acknowledge and confess one's own infirmity in the fear of God, and not to break out beyond one's calling, but to serve God within the bounds of one's calling, in the hope of divine aid, and not to despise or oppress others, but to assign to each their degree, in which they have been placed by order, and to feel that they also can be salutary organs of God, and not to be angry with God in punishments. An illustrious example of this virtue is Jonathan. But the highest of all is the Son of God Himself, obedient in His own calling, and He says here: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart. Pride, however, is to be secure and without the fear of God, and to trust in one's own strength, and in self-confidence to break out beyond the bounds of one's calling, to wish to increase power for oneself, to despise and oppress others, to stubbornly prefer one's own wisdom to good counsel, and to be angry with God and men when the outcome is unhappy, as Pharaoh, Goliath, Saul, Ahithophel, and the like.

If retribution is made to the just on earth, how much more to the impious and the sinner? This is a notable admonition, from which Peter's saying is also taken, that it is time for judgment to begin at the house of God.

But if it begins with us, what is the end of those who do not believe the Gospel? And if the just is scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear? There is, however, a doctrine concerning repentance and the punishments that will come upon the impious, and a consolation concerning the scandal of the cross. The argument is instituted from the lesser. Since the just are afflicted in this life, who nevertheless seek amendment, how much more will the impious, who stubbornly and furiously persist in their crimes, be punished; it is necessary, therefore, that another judgment remain after this life, so that just as David was punished for adultery and murder, undoubtedly others who are worse will be punished, such as Dionysius, Tiberius, even if they had peaceful ends in this life; therefore, another judgment remains.

Here, however, two rules are to be compared, and a reconciliation considered. The former is: Atrocious crimes are punished with atrocious punishments in this life; this accords with the order of justice in God, and because it happens so generally, the congruence of these examples is a testimony concerning the providence and presence of God in the human race.

The other rule is: The Church is subject to the cross, and tyrants exercise cruelty against it. This seems not to accord with the order of justice, so reason disputes whether there is providence.

But the Church responds: First, it accords with the order of justice in God to punish even the Church, because sin still clings to it. And the Church knows many reasons why it is subject to the cross.

Next, concerning tyrants, the second rule remains true for tyrants, because they too are often snatched away to punishments in this life, according to the saying: "Few kings descend to the son-in-law of Ceres without slaughter and bloodshed, and tyrants by a dry death.

Although therefore they flourish for a while, yet afterwards they are cast out from their empires. Secondly, the Church knows it to be consistent with the justice of God that He punishes crimes not only with present and brief punishments, but with eternal ones. Therefore, it answers to this argument.

It is fitting for the just to be well, for the unjust to be ill. The Church is just, Tyrants are unjust, therefore it is well for the Church, and ill for Tyrants. The Church answers to the major premise: It is fitting for the just to be well, and for the unjust to be ill, according to the declaration of the Gospel, which teaches why the Church is subjected to the cross in this life, and yet that some group is always preserved by God, and that the Church will afterwards possess eternal goods, but the impious will be in eternal punishments.

Indeed, these very examples are testimonies of the coming judgment.

Because Abel is killed by Cain, and God, being just, previously showed that He loves Abel. Therefore, another judgment remains, in which the dissimilarity between Cain and Abel will be shown. Then, let it be answered to the minor premise: The Church is just, namely by imputation and inchoation, not yet by consummation.

Therefore, it is exercised for a time, so that it may acknowledge the judgment of God against sin, as it is said in Isaiah: Chastisement is discipline for them, so that they may cry out to You. The conclusion therefore follows: tyrants are often punished in this life, but universally they will afterwards be in eternal punishments; the Church, even if it is afflicted, yet even in this life feels mitigation, and afterwards will have eternal goods.

Latin:

Benedictio Domini facit divites et non addit dolorem.

Prophani homines cogitant, opes et victorias parari tantum humana industria et laboribus, ut existimant Alexandrum vincere; quia consilio, laboribus, et robore exercitus antecellit multitudini Persicae, sicut usitate dicitur: Labor omnia vincit improbus. Et Plato inquit, hunc esse beatum, cui non ex aliis pendet fortuna, sed sui in seipso posita sunt omnia, quae ad beatitudinem necessaria sunt. Et sic dicit Nabuchodonosor: Ego Babylonem feci tantam meo robore. Tales imaginationes confirmant fiduciam nostrae calliditatis et nostrarum virium, qua elati homines negligunt Deum, et movent non movenda, ut, Quia videt Antonius se instructiorem esse Augusto, et sperat eum posse opprimi, movet bellum iniustum. Talia valde multa sunt tristia errata hominum. Sed vox divina docet, causas esse bonorum eventuum, non labores hominum solos, sed Deum iuvantem iustos labores, et hominum obedientiam in vocatione.

Ideo expresse tradita est negativa propositio: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum, frustra laborat qui aedificat eam. Item Eccle. 9.: Non est velocium cursus, nec fortium bellum, nec sapientium panis. Et Psal. 33.: Fallax equus ad salutem. Et Psal. 59.: Non egrederis Deus in virtutibus nostris. Da nobis auxilium de tribulatione, vana salus hominis. Et Hiere. 10.: Scio Domine non est hominis via eius. Iohan. 3.: Non potest sibi homo sumere quicquam, nisi datum sit ei a Deo. Et Iohan. 5.: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Haec testimonia non prohibent laborem vocationis, sed docent bonorum eventuum causam esse, non solam hominum sapientiam et solos hominum labores.

Damnant igitur fiduciam nostri. Postea vox divina coniungit has causas bonorum eventuum, Deum iuvantem labores vocationis, et obedientiam nostram in vocatione. Praecipit igitur labores iustos, congruentes vocationi, ut Ecclesiast. 9.: Quicquid potest facere manus tua, operare omnibus viribus. Et 1. Thessal. 4.: Studiose hoc agatis, ut sitis quieti, et propria faciatis, et laboretis manibus vestris. Et Gene. 3.: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Et Psal. 127.: Labores manuum tuarum quia manducabis, beatus es, et bene tibi erit. Et Proverb. 10.: Manus sedulorum dives erit. Sed sciendum est hos labores ita felices esse, et sequi bonos eventus, cum Deus adiuvat laborantes iuxta vocationem.

Traditae sunt igitur promissiones de auxilio divino, et mandata de invocatione, ut Deus agnoscatur. Item ut agnoscatur praesentia eius in gubernatione privata et publica, ut 36. Psal.: Subditus esto Deo, et ora eum. Item: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Et Psal. 33.: Non est inopia timentibus Deum. Et Psal. 54.: Iacta in Deum curam tuam, et ipse te sustentabit. Psal. 90.: Protegam eum, quoniam cognovit nomen meum, cum ipso sum in tribulatione. Dan. 2.: Dat sapientiam sapientibus, et scientiam intelligentibus. Proverb. 16.: Cor hominis cogitat viam suam, sed Deus confirmat gressus eius. Proverb. 21.: Equus paratur ad diem belli, Deus autem dat victoriam. Proverb. 20.: Ut oculus videat, et auris audiat, Deus facit utrunque. Esaias 46.: Ego feci vos, ego gestabo vos etiam in senecta. Esa. 40.: Gestavi vos sicut pastor lactentes agnos. Deut. 30.: Ipse est vita tua, et longitudo dierum tuorum. Deut. 8.: Non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit ex ore Dei. Exod. 19.: Gestavi vos super alas aquilarum. Deut. 8.: Ne dicas, fortitudo mea et manus meae haec mihi dederunt, sed recorderis Domini Dei tui, quod ipse vires tibi praebuerit. Haec et similia testimonia prodest in conspectu habere, ut imaginationem prophanam eiiciamus ex animis, nec confidamus nostra diligentia, aut nostris viribus, sed vere credamus, ita tantum labores nostros felices esse, cum a Deo adiuvantur, et petamus auxilium Dei, iuxta dictum Psalmi: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Et Proverb. 16.: Commenda Deo opera tua, et dirigentur cogitationes tuae. Hanc regulam vitae in omnibus consiliis et negotiis intueamur, faciendo esse labores vocationis, et petendum et expectandum auxilium a Deo. Et adiungatur huc doctrina de invocatione Dei, de promissionibus. Praeterea et hoc consideretur, Ethnicos quoque experientia coactos fateri, saepe potentiores et sapientiores vinci, videlicet cum aut iniusta faciunt, et non necessaria movent fiducia virium suarum, et multis fiducia virium suarum exitio fuit, sicut de Aiace dicitur: Cum dixisset se etiam sine Deo vincere posse, propter hanc impiam fiduciam sui punitum esse furore, quo sibi mortem concivit.

Et saepe recitatur historia de Milone Crotoniata, qui cum in divulsa arbore haereret, laceratus est a lupis. Et Bellerophontem Pegasus excussit, cum vellet invehi coelum. Et Perseo tandem fuit exitio caput Gorgonis. Caput XI. Libram fraudulentam abominatur Dominus, et pondus aequale placet ei.

Praeceptum est de particulari iustitia, et veritate in contractibus, et pertinet ad Decalogi dictum: Non furtum facies. Et comminatio saepe repetita, hic quoque repeti intelligatur: Atrocia delicta puniuntur atrocibus poenis, etiam in hac vita.

Iuxta dicta: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. Item: Vae qui spolias, quia spoliaberis.

Et in huius ordinis consideratione vult Deus se agnosci, et intelligi hunc ordinem divinitus sancitum esse. Ac sciamus, coniugia, politicam societatem, contractus, iudicia, poenas, opera esse sapientiae et iusticiae Dei, et efficaciter a Deo conservari, quantum ordinis reliquum manet, etiamsi a diabolis et ab organis diaboli interea magni tumultus moventur.

Sicut custos gregis servat aliquod agmen, etiamsi lupi aliquas pecudes rapiunt. Sic dicit infra de politico ordine capite decimo sexto. Pondus et statera iudicia Domini sunt, et opera eius omnes lapides lancis. Haec admonitio necessaria est contra furores Manichaeos et Anabaptisticos, ut saepe alias copiose dictum est.

Cum venit superbia, venit et ignominia, et in humilibus est sapientia. Usitatum est homines in secundis rebus fieri negligentiores, quia muniti praesidiis manifestis, minus metuunt et minus dolent, ideo et invocatio Dei fit languidior, sicut in Mose dicitur: Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et surrexit ludere. Item: Luxuriant animi rebus plerumque secundis. Extincto autem timore Dei, homines securi, ut augeant potentiam, multa extra vocationem tentant, et alios iniuriis afficiunt.

Inde sequuntur poenae ordine divino, iuxta dicta: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Item: Deposuit potentes de sede, et exaltavit humiles. Ac Ethnicos experientia coëgit fateri, divino ordine inevitabiliter sequi poenas superbiam ruentem extra metas vocationis. Hunc ordinem nominaverunt ἀδράστειαν, et signum sequuturae ruinae est insignis insolentia, iuxta dictum Claudiani: Tolluntur in altum, ut lapsu graviore ruant etc. Haec est et hoc loco sententia Salomonis.

Contra vero ait in humilibus sapientiam esse, sicut Petrus inquit: Humilibus dat gratiam. Et apud Esaiam dicitur: Ubi habitabit Dominus? in Spiritu contrito et humiliato, et tenente sermones meos. Notae sint autem definitiones Humilitatis et Superbiae.

Humilitas seu ταπεινοφροσύνη est in timore Dei agnoscere et fateri propriam infirmitatem, et non erumpere extra vocationem, sed intra metas vocationis Deo servire, spe auxilii divini, et non despicere, nec premere alios, sed tribuere singulis gradum, in quem ordine collocati sunt, et sentire illos etiam posse organa Dei salutaria esse, et non irasci Deo in poenis. Exemplum illustre huius virtutis est Ionathas. Omnium vero summum est ipse Filius Dei in sua vocatione obediens, et hic inquit: Discite a me, quia mitis sum, et humilis corde. Superbia autem est, securum et sine timore Dei esse, et confidere propriis viribus, et fiducia sui extra metas vocationis erumpere, sibi potentiam velle augere, despicere et premere alios, pertinaciter anteferre propriam sapientiam bonis consiliis, et irasci Deo et hominibus cum exitus est infelix, ut Pharao, Goliad, Saul, Achitophel, et similes.

Cum iusto in terra fiat retributio, quanto magis impio et peccatori? Insignis admonitio est, ex qua et Petri dictum sumitur, quia tempus est ut incipiat iudicium a domo Dei.

Si autem primum a nobis, quis finis est eorum qui non credunt Evangelio? et si iustus vix salvatur, impius et peccator ubi apparebunt? Est autem doctrina de poenitentia et de poenis venturis impiorum, et consolatio de scandalo crucis. Argumentum autem instituitur a minore. Cum iusti in hac vita affligantur, qui tamen quaerunt emendationem, quanto magis impii, contumaciter et furenter in sceleribus perseverantes punientur, necesse est igitur post hanc vitam restare aliud iudicium, ut cum David punitus sit propter adulterium et caedem, punientur haud dubie alii deteriores, ut Dionysius, Tyberius, etiamsi in hac vita habuerunt placidos exitus, restat igitur aliud iudicium.

Hic autem duae regulae conferantur, et conciliatio consideretur. Prior est: Atrocia delicta puniuntur atrocibus poenis in hac vita, id congruit ordini iusticiae in Deo, et quia sic plerumque fit, horum exemplorum congruentia testimonium est de providentia et praesentia Dei in genere humano.

Altera regula est: Ecclesia subiecta est cruci, et tyranni exercent crudelitatem adversus eam. Id videtur non congruere ordini iusticiae, disputat igitur ratio, an sit providentia.

Sed Ecclesia respondet: Primum congruit ordini iusticiae in Deo, etiam punire Ecclesiam, quia adhuc haeret in ea peccatum. Et scit Ecclesia multas causas quare subiecta sit cruci.

Deinde de tyrannis tyrannis manet vera altera regula, quia ipsi quoque plerumque in hac vita rapiuntur ad poenas, iuxta dictum: Ad generum Cereris sine caede et sanguine pauci descendunt reges, et sicca morte tyranni.

Quanquam igitur florent aliquandiu, tamen postea excutiuntur ex imperiis. Secundo scit Ecclesia iusticiae Dei convenire, ut scelera non tantum praesentibus et brevibus suppliciis puniat, sed aeternis. Ideo respondet ad hoc argumentum.

Iustis congruit bene esse, iniustis male. Ecclesiae est iusta, Tyranni sunt iniusti, Ergo Ecclesiae bene sit, Tyrannis male. Respondet Ecclesia ad maiorem: Congruit iustis bene esse, iniustis male, iuxta declarationem Evangelii, quod docet quare Ecclesia subiecta sit cruci in hac vita, et tamen semper a Deo servari coetum aliquem, et postea habituram esse Ecclesiam aeterna bona, impios autem fore in aeternis poenis.

Imo haec ipsa exempla sunt testimonia venturi iudicii.

Quia Abel a Cain interficitur, et Deus iustus antea ostendit se diligere Abel. Ergo restat aliud iudicium, in quo ostendetur dissimilitudo Cain et Abel. Deinde ad minorem respondeatur: Ecclesia est iusta, videlicet imputatione et inchoatione, nondum consummatione.

Igitur ad tempus exercetur, ut agnoscat iudicium Dei adversus peccatum, ut in Esaia dicitur: Castigatio est eis disciplina, ut ad te clament. Sequitur ergo conclusio, tyranni saepe in hac vita puniuntur, sed universaliter postea erunt in poenis aeternis, Ecclesia etsi affligitur, tamen et in hac vita sentit mitigationem, et postea habebit aeterna bona.

## 12:1 Argument
Chapter XII.

Many things are said in the twelfth chapter, often repeated concerning the providence of God, that the unjust are about to pay penalties.

Also concerning labor, the vices of the tongue, lying, sophistry, calumnies, boasting, and ostentation. But especially let the reader remember this saying: Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord. Let us know that love and care for maintaining truth are commanded, both in the doctrine concerning God and in the arts, and in all honest pacts and contracts, and because truth is among the chief and most conspicuous virtues, therefore the contrary vice is condemned with a harsh word, and is named an abomination, that is, such an evil that God detests with a singular agitation, just as idols are named βδελύγματα (abominations).

Latin:

Caput XII.

Multa sunt dicta in duodecimo capite, saepe repetita de providentia Dei, quod iniusti sint daturi poenas.

Item de labore, de linguae vitiis, de mendacio, de sophistica, de calumniis, de iactantia et ostentatione. Praecipue vero meminerit lector hoc dictum: Abominatio Domino labia mendacia. Sciamus praecipi amorem et curam tuendae veritatis, et in doctrina de Deo et in artibus, et in omnibus honestis pactis et contractibus, et quia veritas est inter praecipuas et maxime conspicuas virtutes, ideo atroci verbo damnatur contrarium vitium, et nominatur abominatio, id est, tale malum quod Deus singulari commotione detestatur, sicut et idola nominantur βδελύγματα.

## 13:1 Argument
Chapter XIII.

Among the proud is contention, and among the deliberating is wisdom.

There is a Greek saying: ὄρος ὄρει οὐ μίγνυται, that is, mountain does not mix with mountain, by which it is signified that it is not fitting for two equally haughty people to agree. Although there are many causes of discords, yet more often the cause is pride, when, namely, natures that admire themselves and wish to excel take occasions for strife from wherever they can, and are not moved by the magnitude or smallness of things, but fight over reputation and the applause of the people; it is known what evils follow public discords.

Whence these sayings are: Yet the glory of a few, and the desire for praise and titles, once overwhelmed the fatherland. Also from Claudian: For luxury turns other kingdoms to vices and pride to hatreds. Since therefore these two affections are most bitter, the desire for glory and irascibility, or the desire for vengeance, as in Marius and Sulla, in Pompey and Julius, and others, the Son of God specifically commands with most grave words that these two affections be curbed: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.

One virtue is opposed to pride, another, meekness, to the desire for vengeance. Meekness, however, is a virtue which first comprehends justice, so that it does not fight where it is not necessary: then, in necessary combat, it moderates anger, and by a probable reason softens something of just anger, or of punishment.

But that deliberation is opposed to contention signifies that minds impeded by ambition, anger, or other affections, either do not discern the truth, or when they do discern it, yet do not wish to be seen to be overcome, as it is said: A frequent friend has given gold and wealth and vessels, He who wishes to yield to talent will be rare. Wherefore, in deliberation, truth must be sought from its own fountains, and the inquiry must not be hindered by the waves of affections.

Those things also must be thought upon: By too much arguing, truth is lost. Item: For whoever is not wise in excess, he is wise. Believe me, to be wise is not to be wise in excess. But once the truth is found, let the mind acquiesce, give thanks to God, and apply the truth to use in life, as it was said above: A lying lip is an abomination before God.

Much food is in the furrows of the poor, and others accumulate without measure.

This is an economic precept concerning moderation and the diligence of maintaining moderate means, according to the saying: Praise great fields, cultivate a small one.

The sentiment is that it is better to possess moderate means, and to administer them rightly, and to enjoy them with piety and tranquility, than to accumulate great wealth, which cannot happen without offenses.

The saying of Paul pertains to this: Those who wish to become rich fall into foolish and pernicious desires.

Let the saying be transferred to other things: It is better to be in a small government, and to adorn it, than in the highest position, where we are less able to sustain the magnitude of things.

And let the well-known verse be noted, which Aristotle cites in the 4th book of Politics from Phocylides: Many things are best in the middle; I wish to be in the middle in the city.

Latin:

Caput XIII.

Inter superbos est contentio, et apud deliberantes est sapientia.

Graecum dictum est: ὄρος ὄρει οὐ μίγνυται, id est, mons monti non miscetur, quo significatum est, non convenire inter duos pariter elatos. Quanquam autem plures sunt discordiarum causae, tamen saepius causa est superbia, cum videlicet naturae, quae sese admirantur, et volunt antecellere, sumunt undecunque occasiones certaminum, nec moventur magnitudine, aut parvitate rerum, sed dimicant de existimatione, et de populi applausu, postea quae mala sequantur publicas discordias, notum est.

Unde sunt haec dicta: Patriam tamen obruit olim gloria paucorum, laudis titulique cupido. Item Claudiani: Nam caetera regna luxuries vitiis odiisque superbia vertit. Cum igitur hi duo affectus sint acerrimi, cupiditas gloriae, et iracundia, seu cupiditas vindictae, ut in Mario et Sylla, in Pompeio et Iulio, et aliis, nominatim Filius Dei gravissimis verbis praecipit ut isti duo affectus frenentur: Discite a me, quia mitis sum et humilis corde.

Altera virtus opponitur superbiae, altera mansuetudo cupiditati vindictae. Est autem Mansuetudo virtus, quae primum comprehendit iustitiam, ne pugnet ubi non est necesse: deinde in pugna necessaria moderatur iram, et probabili ratione lenit aliquid de iusta ira, seu de poena.

Quod autem opponitur deliberatio contentioni, significatur animos impeditos ambitione, ira vel aliis affectibus, aut non cernere verum, aut cum cernunt, tamen non velle videri vinci, sicut dicitur: Aurum et opes et vasa frequens donavit amicus, Qui velit ingenio cedere, rarus erit. Quare in deliberatione veritas ex suis fontibus quaerenda est, nec impedienda est inquisitio fluctibus affectuum.

Cogitanda sunt et illa: Nimium altercando veritas amittitur. Item: Nam quisquis nimium non sapit, ille sapit. Crede mihi sapere est non nimium sapere. Inventa autem veritate mens acquiescat, agat Deo gratias, et veritatem ad usum in vita conferat, sicut supra dictum est: Abominatio coram Deo labium mendax.

Multum escae in sulcis pauperum, et alii sine modo cumulant.

Praeceptum oeconomicum est de mediocritate et diligentia tuendi mediocres facultates, iuxta dictum: Laudato ingentia rura, Exiguum colito.

Estque sententia, melius esse possidere mediocres facultates, et eas recte administrare, et frui eis cum pietate et tranquillitate, quam magnas opes cumulare, quod sine offensionibus fieri non potest.

Huc pertinet dictum Pauli: Qui volunt fieri divites, incident in cupiditates stultas et perniciosas.

Transferatur dictum ad alia: Melius est in parva gubernatione esse, et eam ornare, quam in summa fastigio, ubi magnitudinem rerum minus sustinere possumus.

Et versiculus notus sit, quem Aristoteles 4. Politicorum citat ex Phocylide: πολλὰ μέσοισιν ἄριστα, μέσος θέλω ἐν πόλει εἶναι.

## 14:1 Argument
Chapter XIV.

There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death.

This is an admonition concerning the darkness and infirmity of human judgment, and concerning the many great errors of counsel, as it is manifest that men often err in judging and in deliberations.

They are deceived either by their own imaginations, or by the examples of others, or by custom, etc., and once deceived, they rush more headlong, fascinated by the devil, just as it is written of Judas: Satan entered into his heart.

Thus a great multitude has assented and assents to impious cults, and heretics tenaciously retain monstrous dogmas.

And Pompey and Josiah err in the deliberation about war.

Complaints exist concerning this infirmity of many, according to the sayings: The number of fools is infinite.

Item: No man is wise in all things.

Item: Often ideas deceive the appearance.

Item Simonides: Seeming does violence to the truth.

Against these evils, this is the only remedy: to piously acknowledge the word of God, and to do what is necessary according to the word of God with invocation, according to these sayings: Your word is a lamp to my feet.

Item: Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act.

Item Deut.

4: This is your wisdom, to walk in my commandments.

Latin:

Caput XIV.

Est via recta coram homine, cuius exitus tamen est via mortis.

Admonitio est de caligine et infirmitate humani iudicii, et de multis magnis erroribus consiliorum, sicut manifestum est, saepe errare homines in iudicando et in deliberationibus.

Decipiuntur autem vel suis imaginationibus, vel exemplis aliorum, vel consuetudine etc. et decepti magis ruunt fascinati a diabolo, sicut de Iuda scriptum est: Intravit Satanas in cor eius.

Ita magna multitudo assensit et assentitur impiis cultibus, et haeretici portentosa dogmata mordicus retinent.

Et Pompeius, Iosias errant in deliberatione de bello.

De hac multorum infirmitate querelae extant, iuxta dicta: Stultorum infinitus est numerus.

Item: οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων ἐστὶν ἅπαντα σοφός.

Item: πολλάκι τὴν μορφὴν ἐξαπατῶσ’ ἰδέαι.

Item Simonides: τὸ δοκεῖν βιάζεται τὴν ἀλήθειαν.

Adversus haec mala hoc unicum remedium est, pie agnoscere verbum Dei, et iuxta verbum Dei facere necessaria cum invocatione, iuxta haec dicta: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum.

Item: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Item Deut.

4.: Haec sapientia vestra ambulare in praeceptis meis.

## 15:1 Argument
Chapter XV.

A soft answer mitigates wrath, a harsh word provokes wrath.

The whole law of God is a description of what God is like, and it has been revealed to men so that we may know what God is like, and that He wishes us to be conformed to Him.

Just as therefore He commands: You shall not kill, so He Himself is a God not of destruction, but of salvation, just as He also swears: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live.

Many precepts concerning peace have therefore been handed down, which pertain to the commandment: You shall not kill.

Those who disturb peace without a just cause violate it.

Let the sayings therefore be noted: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.

Rom.

12: As much as is in you, have peace with all men.

Precepts are also handed down concerning the manner of retaining peace.

First, let no one inflict injury upon another.

Then, it is not enough not to initiate unjust struggles, but there should also be a limit in repelling injury, in defending oneself, let the repulsion not be more atrocious than the injury, as it is said: Defense should not be offense.

If one contends with words, and the crimes are atrocious, you should respond moderately with words; if the crimes are not atrocious, it is often a virtue to overlook them, and to forgive them for the sake of common tranquility, and to refute them rather by the testimonies of one's life than by recriminating, as Cicero says: It goes badly with me if my speech rather than my life clears me.

And Demosthenes says that he will not respond to private insults, but opposes his life as a witness: if you know me to be such as he describes, rise up immediately as if I were condemned.

And David says: They were slandering me, but I was praying.

This moderation pertains to these virtues: gentleness, patience, and the piety owed to the Church or to public tranquility.

But the extremes are philoneikia, that is, the desire for contention, and gentleness.

Many, however, sin by philoneikia; that evil is much more pernicious.

Now philoneikia is, either in stirring up struggles, to kindle unjust or unnecessary contentions, whether by pride, or by ambition, or by moroseness of nature, or by emulation, or by irascibility, or by superstition, or in responding, neither to yield nor to soften anything, but to wish to win by bitterness, and from all sides to take material for inflaming hatreds, as Lucan says: And he finds causes for arms.

Item: He goes wandering, and the fires of the soul adds to the burning [tribes/factions]. Such are many of a tribunitian nature, restless and quarrelsome, like many Roman tribunes, and many heretics in the Church. And an old saying is cited in Stobaeus, by which he signifies that the desire... for contention is the cause of huge calamities, 'Great evils do not arise otherwise than from contentiousness.'

Since, therefore, this vice must be avoided, Solomon provides an admonition regarding the manner.

A soft answer breaks wrath, that is, not only should you not first inflict injury upon another, but even when you answer, you should strive to soothe somewhat. And there are many similar precepts which teach that one should not contend with the angry, such as: Do not stir up fire with a sword.

And these verses are praised: 'Of two speaking, when one is angered, he who does not contend in words is the wiser.' But here some object against this, 'Reprove in season, out of season, etc.' and zeal is used as a pretext for private hatreds, pride, or other affections.

But let good minds know that in this kind, the rules handed down by God must be followed.

Let teachers rightly teach in their place, and indeed the necessary things; let them not sow empty logomachies, let them not litigate about side-issues or matters alien to their office; let auditors, when asked about doctrine, answer, as Peter says: 'Ready to give an account to all who ask, with meekness.' The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, and the prayer of the upright pleases him.

This doctrine has been often repeated in the Prophets, concerning the three kinds of works: concerning ceremonies, concerning moral works, and concerning faith.

This discourse is of the whole Psalm 49: 'I will not eat the flesh of bulls, etc.', taxing the abuse of ceremonies.

And in Jeremiah 7 it is said: 'I did not command you concerning burnt offerings.' And in the last chapter of Isaiah it is said: 'He who slaughters a beast is as one who strangles a dog.'

And Ecclesiastes 4: 'Better is obedience than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know what they are doing.' And Hosea 6: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.'

John 4: 'True worshipers will worship the Father in Spirit and in truth,' that is, by true knowledge according to the word of God, and by the motions of the heart, fear, faith, hope. Let these and similar sayings be most familiarly known to all, and let the younger ones know that there are three degrees of works or worships.

The first, Ceremonies, that is, external signs.

For God instituted some ceremonies for two causes: both that they might be signs of the promises, and that they might be the sinews of the public congregation, for God wills that the Church should not be in hiding, but be seen and distinguished from other nations, by voice and ceremonies.

But it must be prudently considered how ceremonies are to be used, because men are prone to false worships, and especially to the abuse of ceremonies.

For when the knowledge of the promises is lost, and the light of faith is extinguished, they turn their eyes to ceremonies, and think that these merit the remission of sins before God, and are righteousness.

This persuasion wanders most widely among the human race at all times.

Thus the Gentiles felt about their sacrifices, thus a great part of the people of Israel felt.

Thus the Pharisees taught, thus the Monks taught concerning the Mass, concerning vows, and other ceremonies.

But the Prophets most sharply tax this common error, as was said concerning Psalm 49 and other testimonies.

Indeed, even the Gentiles reproved this superstition, which keeps ceremonies without good moral works, as Plato says: 'It is necessary to worship God, not by simulating gestures with art, but by truly honoring virtue, not by posturing with techniques, but by honoring virtue with truth.'

But this ethnic reproof is not enough.

For although it is true that there must be in men a righteousness of a good conscience, yet in the Church we know that one must speak not only of legal doctrine, but also of the mediator, of the promise of grace, and of faith.

For it is necessary that the knowledge of the mediator and the promise, and trust in the mediator, should shine before all moral and ceremonial works, so that hearts may believe that they are received and heard on account of the mediator, although we are unworthy, and by this faith approach God, as the Lord says: 'No one comes to the Father except through the Son.'

Item: 'Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.'

God demands this faith in invocation and in the whole of life, and in the petition for help he demands hope and expectation, according to the saying: 'For the coming one will come, and will not delay, etc.'

Item: 'Offer the sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord.'

Afterwards, good moral works are pleasing for this end, not that they may merit the remission of sins, but that we may obey God, and others may learn the doctrine, and celebrate God, and the devil may not triumph in us against God. Ceremonies instituted by God are pleasing, done for this end, not that they merit remission, but because they are signs, reminding us of the promise so that faith may be kindled. Also, because they are signs of confession. Also, because they are the sinews of the congregation. It is necessary that these true ends be understood in the Church, and that impious opinions be removed.

Latin:

Caput XV.

Mollis responsio mitigat iram, Sermo asper provocat iram.

Tota lex Dei est descriptio qualis sit Deus, et hominibus patefacta est, ut sciamus qualis sit Deus, et quod velit nos sibi conformes esse.

Sicut igitur praecipit: Non occides, ita ipse est Deus non perditionis, sed salvationis, sicut et iurat: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat.

Multa sunt igitur tradita praecepta de pace, quae pertinent ad mandatum: Non occidas.

Id violant, qui sine iusta causa pacem turbant.

Nota sint igitur dicta: Beati pacifici, quia Filii Dei vocabuntur.

Rom.

12.: Quantum in vobis est, pacem habete cum omnibus.

Traduntur etiam praecepta de modo retinendae pacis.

Primum, nemo alium iniuria afficiat.

Deinde non satis est non incoare iniusta certamina, sed etiam modus sit in repellenda iniuria, ἐν τῷ ἀμύνεσθαι, non sit repulsio atrocior quam iniuria, sicut dicitur: Defensio non sit offensio.

Si verbis contenditur, et sunt atrocia crimina, moderate respondeas verbis, si non sunt atrocia crimina, saepe est virtus, dissimulare ea, et condonare communi tranquillitati, et refutare ea potius vitae testimoniis, quam recriminando, sicut Cicero inquit: Male mecum agitur, si me oratio potius quam vita mea purgat.

Et Demosthenes inquit, se non responsurum esse de privatis conviciis, sed opponit vitam testem: si talem me esse scitis, qualem ipse describit, statim surgite tanquam me condemnato.

Et David inquit: Detrahebant mihi, Ego autem orabam.

Haec moderatio pertinet ad has virtutes, mansuetudinem, patientiam, pietatem debitam Ecclesiae vel publicae tranquillitati.

Sed extrema sunt φιλονεικία, id est, cupiditas contentionis, et lenitas.

Plures autem peccant φιλονεικία, id malum est multo perniciosius.

Est autem φιλονεικία, seu in movendis certaminibus vel iniustas vel non necessarias contentiones accendere, aut superbia, aut ambitione, aut morositate naturae, aut aemulatione, aut iracundia, aut superstitione, seu in respondendo neque cedere, neque aliud lenire, sed acerbitate velle vincere, et undique sumere materiam inflammandi odia, sicut inquit Lucanus: Et causas invenit armis.

Item: It vagus, atque ignes animis flagrantibus addit. Tales multae sunt tribunitiae naturae, inquietae et rixatrices, ut Romani multi tribuni, et in Ecclesia multi haeretici. Ac citatur dictum vetus in Stobaeo, quo significat cupiditatem contentionis, causam esse ingentium calamitatum, τὰ μεγάλα κακὰ οὐκ ἄλλως, ἢ ἐκ φιλονεικίας συνίσταται.

Cum igitur fugiendum sit hoc vitium, Salomon tradit admonitionem de modo.

Mollis responsio frangit iram, id est, non solum prior alium non afficias iniuria, sed etiam cum respondes, lenire aliquid studeas. Ac multa sunt similia praecepta, quae docent, cum iratis non contendendum esse, ut: Ignem gladio ne fodias.

Et laudantur hi versus: δυοῖν λεγόντοιν θατέρου θυμουμένου, ὁ μὴ ἀντιτείνων τοῖς λόγοις σοφώτερος. Sed hic contra obiiciunt aliqui, Increpa opportune, importune etc. et praetexitur zelus privatis odiis, superbiae, aut aliis affectibus.

Sed sciant bonae mentes, in hoc genere regulas a Deo traditas sequendas esse.

Doctores suo loco recte doceant, et quidem necessaria, non serant inanes λογομαχίας, non litigent de παρέργοις aut rebus alienis a suo officio, auditores interrogati de doctrina respondeant, sicut Petrus inquit: Parati ad rationem reddendam omnibus qui interrogant, cum mansuetudine. Victima impiorum abominatio Domino, et precatio rectorum placet ei.

Saepe repetita est haec doctrina in Prophetis, de tribus generibus operum, de ceremoniis, de operibus moralibus, et de fide.

Haec concio est totius Psalmi 49.: Non manducabo carnes taurorum etc. taxans abusum ceremoniarum.

Et Hieremiae 7. dicitur: Non praecepi vobis de holocaustis. Et Esaiae ultimo dicitur: Mactans pecudem est velut strangulans canem.

Et Ecclesiast 4.: Melior est obedientia, quam stultorum victimae, qui nesciunt quid faciant. Et Oseae 6.: Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium, et agnitionem Dei magis quam holocausta. Iohan.

4.: Veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu et veritate, id est, vera agnitione iuxta verbum Dei, et motibus cordis, timore, fide, spe. Haec et similia dicta familiarissime nota sint omnibus, et sciant iuniores, tres esse gradus operum seu cultuum.

Primus, Ceremoniae, id est, externa signa.

Instituit enim enim Deus aliquas ceremonias propter duas causas, et ut sint signa promissionum, et ut sint nervi publicae congregationis, qui Deus vult Ecclesiam non esse in latebris, sed conspici et discerni a caeteris gentibus, voce et ceremoniis.

Prudenter autem considerandum est, quomodo utendum sit ceremoniis, quia homines proni sunt ad falsos cultus, et praesertim ad abusum ceremoniarum.

Amissa enim noticia promissionum, et extincta luce fidei, flectunt oculos ad ceremonias, et has cogitant mereri remissionem peccatorum coram Deo, et esse iusticiam.

Haec persuasio in genere humano omnibus temporibus latissime vagatur.

Sic de suis sacrificiis Ethnici sentiebant, sic in populo Israël magna pars sentiebat.

Sic docebant Pharisaei, sic Monachi de Missa, de votis, et aliis ceremoniis docuerunt.

Hunc autem communem errorem acerrime taxant Prophetae, ut dictum est de Psalmo 49. et aliis testimoniis.

Imo et Ethnici reprehenderunt hanc superstitionem, quae ceremonias servat, sine bonis operibus moralibus, ut Plato dicit: Oportet colere Deum, non gestus arte simulantes, sed vere honorantes virtutem, οὐ σχήμασι τεχνάζοντες, ἀλλὰ ἀληθείᾳ τιμῶντας ἀρετήν.

Sed haec ethnica reprehensio non sufficit.

Etsi enim verum est oportere in hominibus esse iusticiam bonam conscientiae, tamen in Ecclesia scimus, non tantum de legali doctrina dicendum esse, sed etiam de mediatore, de promissione gratiae et de fide.

Oportet enim omnibus operibus moralibus et ceremonialibus praelucere noticiam mediatoris et promissionis, et fiduciam mediatoris, ut corda credant se recipi et exaudiri propter mediatorem, quanquam indigni sumus, et hac fide ad Deum accedant, sicut inquit Dominus: Nemo venit ad patrem nisi per Filium.

Item: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis.

Hanc fidem in invocatione et in tota vita postulat Deus, et in petitione auxilii postulat spem et expectationem, iuxta dictum: Quia veniens veniet, et non tardabit etc.

Item: Sacrificate sacrificium iusticiae et sperate in Domino.

Postea placent bona opera moralia hoc fine, non ut mereantur remissionem peccatorum, sed ut Deo obediamus, et alii discant doctrinam, et celebrent Deum, et non triumphet diabolus in nobis adversus Deum. Placent et ceremoniae institutae a Deo, factae hoc fine, ut non mereantur remissionem, sed quia sunt signa, commonefacientia nos de promissione ut accendatur fides. Item, quia sunt signa confessionis. Item, quia sunt nervi congregationis. Hos veros fines in Ecclesia intelligi oportet, et removeri impias opiniones.

## 16:1 Argument
Chapter XVI.

It is for man to prepare the heart, but from God is the answer of the tongue. A similar saying follows shortly in the same chapter: The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his step. These sayings do not take away the freedom of human will, or choice, but signify that there are some choices of human will, both in the unregenerate, as in Pompey, and in the regenerate, as in Joshua, David, etc. But in these choices, men sometimes err, as when Josiah moved a war not necessary against the Egyptian king; his will had a choice, but an erring one, and the outcome did not respond. And it must be diligently considered that choice in us is one thing, and success is another.

But in order for a choice to be happy, it is necessary that the help of God be added in two ways, namely in judging, and afterwards in governing the events. For unless judgment is governed by the Word of God, and by divine light, many errors occur, as Josiah, Zedekiah, Demosthenes, Pompey, and Cicero err in choosing war, and grim outcomes follow, because they are not helped by God. Sometimes even when the mind does not err in judgment, and yet God does not help the agents, because of other causes, as in the battles against Benjamin, even sad outcomes follow, because the Israelites trusted in their own strength.

Let us know, therefore, that the cause of happy actions is not only human choice and diligence; therefore Jeremiah says: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, that is, man without divine help often errs in his counsels, and cannot have happy successes. Therefore it is written: Unless the Lord builds the house, etc. Also: No one can take anything for himself, unless it is given to him by God. Also: Without me you can do nothing, that is, without my help you cannot do salutary things.

God wants us to acknowledge this weakness of ours, and likewise wants us to be governed by His Word in our calling, and to fear Him, and by faith to seek divine help, according to the saying: Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in Him, and He will act. Also: Ask and you shall receive. Also: When we do not know what should be done, behold our eyes are directed to You, O Lord. Let this rule of life be noted, which he repeats here also: Commit your works to the Lord, then your thoughts will be confirmed, that is, do the commands of God according to your calling, seek help from God, then the counsels will be happy, for you and for the people. This doctrine must be thought upon often, so that we may stir up in ourselves the care of governing life by the Word of God, and of seeking divine help, etc.

To this use let these sayings be accommodated, not to Stoic opinions about necessity. For it does not follow: The outcome did not respond to Zedekiah, Therefore Zedekiah did not freely will the war. Rather, because he willed it, and willed it without a command, and without the invocation of God, therefore the outcome did not respond.

God does everything for His own sake, even the wicked for the day of evil. The preceding sentences were precepts about seeking the help of God. This saying preaches about providence, concerning which there are many sad doubts in the minds of men.

There are, however, two kinds of things, namely, Good things, in which order is seen, and bad things, which are the destruction of order, such as crimes and calamities. Regarding good things, the mind is moved in some way to think that they did not arise by chance, or are preserved by chance, and yet assent is troubled. And many Philosophers have argued that the matter of heaven and earth is such by some necessity of its own, and has always been such, and generates other bodies, and that these were neither freely fashioned by an eternal mind, nor are they freely preserved. From these Cyclopean furies, this discourse draws us back to the first article of faith concerning creation.
