Rather, he says, things are not such by chance, but truly there is a wise and good God, who most freely created and preserves good things, namely, those ordered by Him: the heaven, the earth, the cycles of the seasons, the fertility of the earth, the generation of living creatures in individual species, the society of the human race, the political order, the Church, and in the good minds of individuals His own gifts, wisdom and virtues, and many deliverances for those who call upon Him.

All these things both have been done, and are done by God most freely, and indeed to this end, that they may be testimonies that God exists, and that He is a wise and good creator and ordainer. Therefore he says: God created all things for His own sake.

But the Epicureans object many disordered things: Since God wills order, whence come evils, crimes, and calamities?

Solomon answers concerning punishments: Nay, even punishments are testimonies of providence, as it is universal, that atrocious crimes are punished with atrocious punishments, even in this life, according to the saying: He who takes up the sword, shall perish by the sword.

And universally, Death and all calamities are punishments of original sin and other sins, according to the saying of Paul: Through sin death entered, etc. Meanwhile, this is true, that God neither wills, nor effects, nor approves of sin, but after men have abused their own liberty, the justice of God is seen in this order, that by punishment compensation is made.

And the Syntax in the word "Facit" (He makes) is to be observed.

For he does not say: He makes the impious man, but a predicate is added: He makes the evil man for the day of evil, that is, he who is impious, sinning against the will of God, He snatches away to punishment. This also is a testimony of providence, as when I say, a sculptor makes a figure of Alexander out of marble.

This sculptor does not beget the marble, but is the fabricator of the figure; so God is by no means the cause of impiety, but by the order of justice He punishes and destroys the impious. Therefore, this whole sentiment is an admonition concerning Providence, and it warns us to acknowledge that God freely makes and preserves good things, and most freely punishes, according to the sayings of Psalm 32: The Lord looked down from heaven, He saw all the sons of men, etc. Psalm 61: You render to each one according to his works.

An abomination to the Lord is every proud man in heart, and he shall not be unpunished, even if hand be joined to hand.

Also this saying from Luke 16 is cited: That which is sublime among men, is an abomination before God. And Sirach says: The beginning of all sin is pride.

Here let the definitions handed down above be considered, and let the contrary examples of Jonathan and Antony the Triumvir be considered.

And always keep in sight the saying: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. By mercy and truth iniquity is expiated, and by the fear of the Lord one departs from evil.

Repetita is the admonition concerning the distinction of worships, as above in the saying: The victim of the impious is an abomination.

And Hosea 9: I desire the knowledge of God, and not burnt offerings, and mercy, not sacrifice. In the same way he says here, that men are not just because of sacrifices, but if they have the fear of God, mercy, and truth.

And this is the customary summary of doctrine: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience.

The fear of the Lord signifies true conversion to God, in which there is fear and faith, just as it is often expressly said elsewhere concerning faith. The phrase is customary among the Hebrews, concerning sincere and not feigned love toward men, as Jonathan does mercy and truth with David, that is, he does good to him, and faithfully, without simulation, and he does this constantly.

Thus it is said below in chapter 20: Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is supported by clemency, that is, beneficence and fidelity are the nerves of empire. But if truth is understood here toward God, it signifies the true recognition of God, which is faith.

Divination is in the lips of the king, in judgment his mouth shall not err.

The weight and balance are the judgments of the Lord, all the weights of the bag are His work. These sayings affirm that the whole political order, Magistrates, laws, the distinction of dominions, contracts, judgments, punishments, are works ordained by the wisdom of God in the human race.

And although devils and men with many horrible furies disturb this order, yet lest the human race be utterly extinguished, something of political order remains. Let us know that this is effectively preserved by God, just as Daniel also says: God transfers and establishes kingdoms.

Then, when we know that the order of God is His work, let us love it, and strive to defend it by our duties, and modestly obey it for God's sake, and give thanks to God the preserver, and let us know that the furies of devils and men, who disturb the political order, are displeasing to God, just as this whole doctrine is recited in a long discourse in Romans 13. But why does he say: Divination is in the lips of the king, in judgment his mouth shall not err?

These members must be joined together. The saying speaks of the King and of judgment. diciis, not about the Tyrant and about Calumnies. The King's voice is understood: If your brother sins against you, argue with him between you and him alone. Pastors and others, especially those who have the office of teaching, when they know someone is erring, or otherwise acting unjustly, should first admonish him privately. If he does not amend himself, then let a public accusation be made. Let there be Truth and Candor in the monitor, and let him not seek calumniously for what to reprehend. Let the one admonished be docile, not stubborn. In neither should there be φιλονεικία [love of strife], that is, a desire for contention. Thus, in this place, precepts are given both to the monitor and to the one admonished.

The evil man only seeks quarrels, that is, he does not seek the truth and the salvation of the Church, but endless disturbances, just as Cleon and Alcibiades in Athens kept sowing the seeds of wars. The Cynics and Academics contradicted everyone, and recently Valla, Cornelius Agrippa, Karlstadt, Osiander, Stancarus, and many others have such quarrelsome natures. These do not seek the truth, but pervert rightly spoken things with artifice, or petulantly stir up unnecessary conflicts, nor do they yield when admonished, but defend their errors more rabidly. Of these, Solomon says in this place: It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly, just as when a deluded Papist defends manifest errors.

Therefore, these sentences condemn calumnies and the desire for contentions, and persistence in errors.

They command, however, that order be kept in admonition, and they order that truth, candor, and ἐπιείκεια [gentleness/equity] be employed, and they order those admonished to be docile, according to the saying: Cease to do evil. Likewise: Repent and believe the Gospel. Therefore it is said: He who hides another's fault acquires friendship, that is, when he has admonished the erring one with order, he heals him, does not make a public tumult, saves the man, and nourishes public concord. Conversely, when this order is neglected, from quarrels arise the discord of princes, wars, and devastations, as is said in the verse of Empedocles: Φοιτᾷ δὲ βροτολοιγὸς ἔρις κενεὸν λελακυῖα, Discord, sounding vainly, brings forth cruel slaughters.

They also denounce punishment here for quarrelsome monitors and those admonished. A cruel messenger will meet him, that is, those who either ignite or nourish discords with calumnies will eventually pay the penalty, because truth, even if suppressed for a while, nevertheless eventually wins. Ἰσχυρὸν τὸ ἀληθὲς [Truth is strong], as Demosthenes says. And Paul orders that heretics be avoided after one or two admonitions, and says: They sin being αὐτοκατάκριτοι [self-condemned].

Latin:

Caput XVI.

Hominis est praeparare cor, sed a Deo est responsio linguae. Simile dictum sequitur mox in eodem capite: Cor hominis cogitat viam suam, et Dominus confirmat gressum eius. Haec dicta non tollunt libertatem voluntatis humanae, seu electionis, sed significant, esse aliquas electiones humanae voluntatis, cum in non renatis, ut in Pompeio, tum in renatis, ut in Iosua, Davide etc. Sed in his electionibus aliquando errare homines, ut cum Iosias movit bellum non necessarium adversus regem Aegyptium, voluntas eius habebat electionem, sed errantem, et successus non respondit. Ac diligenter considerandum est, aliud esse electionem in nobis, aliud successum.

Ut autem sit felix electio, necesse est accedere auxilium Dei dupliciter, videlicet in iudicando, et postea in regendo eventus. Nisi enim iudicium regatur verbo Dei, et luce divina, multi errores accidunt, ut Iosias, Zedechias, Demosthenes, Pompeius, Cicero errant in eligendo bello, et sequuntur tetri eventus, quia non iuvantur a Deo. Interdum etiam cum non errat mens iudicio, et tamen Deus non adiuvat agentes, propter alias causas, ut, in praeliis adversus Beniamin etiam eventus tristes sequuntur, quia Israëlitae confidebant suis viribus.

Sciamus ergo, causam felicium actionum esse, non solam humanam electionem et diligentiam, ideo inquit Ieremias: Scio Domine, non est hominis via eius, id est, homo sine auxilio divino saepe in consiliis errat, et non potest habere felices successus. Ideo scriptum est: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum etc. Item: Nemo potest sibi sumere quidquam, nisi sit ei datum a Deo. Item: Sine me nihil potestis facere, id est, sine meo auxilio non potestis facere salutaria.

Hanc nostram imbecillitatem vult nos Deus agnoscere, et similiter vult regi nos suo verbo in vocatione, et timere ipsum, ac fide petere auxilium divinum, iuxta dictum: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Item: Petite et accipietis. Item: Cum nescimus quid agendum sit, ecce oculi nostri ad te Domine diriguntur. Nota sit igitur haec regula vitae, quam hic quoque repetit: Commenda Deo opera tua, tunc confirmabuntur cogitationes tuae, id est, fac mandata Dei iuxta vocationem, pete auxilium a Deo, tunc erunt felicia consilia, tibi et populo. Haec doctrina saepe cogitanda est, ut curam in nobis exuscitemus regendi vitam verbo Dei, et petendi auxilium divinum etc.

Ad hunc usum accommodentur haec dicta, non ad Stoicas opiniones de necessitate. Non enim sequitur: Zedechiae non respondit eventus, Ergo Zedechias non libere voluit bellum. Imo quia voluit, et voluit sine mandato, et sine invocatione Dei, ideo eventus non respondit.

Omnia facit Deus propter sese, etiam impium ad diem malum. Superiores sententiae fuerunt praecepta de petendo auxilio Dei. Hoc dictum concionatur de providentia, de qua multae, tristes dubitationes sunt in mentibus hominum.

Sunt autem duo genera rerum, videlicet, Res bonae, in quibus ordo conspicitur, et res malae, quae sunt ordinis destructio, ut, scelera et calamitates. De rebus bonis utcunque movetur mens, ut cogitet eas non casu ortas esse, aut casu servari, et tamen adsensio turbatur. Ac multi Philosophi disputarunt, materiam coeli et terrae sua quadam necessitate talem esse, et semper talem fuisse, et alia corpora gignere, nec libere haec a mente aeterna fabricata esse, nec libere conservari. Ab his Cyclopicis furoribus retrahit nos haec concio ad primum articulum fidei de creatione. Imo, inquit, res non sunt casu tales, sed vere est Deus sapiens et bonus, qui liberrime condidit et servat res bonas, videlicet, ordinatas ab ipso, coelum, terram, vices temporum, foecunditatem terrae, generationem animantium in singulis speciebus, societatem generis humani, ordinem politicum, Ecclesiam, et in bonis mentibus singulorum sua dona, sapientiam et virtutes, et multas liberationes invocantium.

Haec omnia et facta sunt, et fiunt a Deo liberrime, et quidem ad hunc finem, ut sint testimonia, quod sit Deus, et quod sit sapiens et bonus conditor et ordinator. Ideo inquit: Propter sese condidit Deus. Sed obiiciunt Epicurei multa inordinata: Cum Deus velit ordinem, unde sunt mala, scelera et calamitates?

Respondit Salomon de poenis: Imo et poenae testimonia sunt de providentia, ut universale est, Atrocia delicta puniri atrocibus poenis, etiam in hac vita, iuxta dictum: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit.

Et universaliter, Mors et omnes calamitates sunt poenae peccati originalis et aliorum peccatorum, iuxta dictum Pauli: Per peccatum mors intravit etc.

Interea hoc verum est, Deum nec velle, nec efficere, nec approbare peccatum, sed postquam propria libertate homines abusi sunt, conspicitur iustitia Dei in hoc ordine, quod per poenam fit compensatio.

Ac Syntaxis in verbo Facit observanda est. Non enim dicit: Facit impium, sed additur praedicatum: Facit ad diem malum, id est, eum qui impius est, peccans non volente Deo, rapit ad poenam.

Id quoque providentiae testimonium est, ut cum dico, statuarius facit ex marmore figuram Alexandri. Hic statuarius non gignit marmor, sed figurae fabricator est, ita Deus nequaquam est causa impietatis, sed ordine iusticiae punit ac destruit impium.

Tota igitur haec sententia commonefactio est de Providentia, et monet ut agnoscamus, Deum libere facere et conservare res bonas, et liberrime punire, iuxta dicta Psal. 32.: De coelo respexit Dominus, vidit omnes filios hominum etc. Psal.

61.: Tu reddis unicuique iuxta opera sua. Abominatio Domino est omnis superbus corde, nec erit impunitus, etiamsi erit manus ad manum.

Citatur et Lucae 16. hoc dictum: Quod sublime est inter homines, abominatio est coram Deo. Et Siracides inquit: Omnis peccati initium est superbia.

Hic definitiones cogitentur supra traditae, et considerentur exempla contraria Ionathae et Antonii Triumviri.

Et semper in conspectu dictum: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Misericordia et veritate expiatur iniquitas, et timore Domini receditur a malo.

Repetita est admonitio de discrimine cultuum, ut supra in dicto: Victima impiorum abominatio.

Et Oseae 9.: Scientiam Domini volo, non holocausta et misericordiam, non sacrificium. Eodem modo hic ait, non esse homines iustos propter sacrificia, sed si habeant timorem Dei, misericordiam et veritatem.

Et est usitata summa doctrinae: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Timor Domini significat veram conversionem ad Deum, in qua est timor et fides, sicut alibi saepe expresse dicitur de fide. Phrasis usitata Ebraeis est, de sincera et non fucosa dilectione erga homines, ut Ionathas facit misericordiam et veritatem cum Davide, id est, benefacit ei, et fideliter, sine simulatione, et constanter hoc facit.

Sic infra dicitur capite 20.: Misericordia et veritas custodiunt regem, et fulcitur clementia solium eius, id est, beneficentia et fidelitas sunt nervi et imperii. Sed si hic intelligitur veritas erga Deum, significat veram agnitionem Dei, quae est fides.

Divinatio in labiis regis, in iudicio non delinquet os eius.

Pondus et statera iudicia Domini sunt, opus eius omnia pondera lancis. Haec dicta affirmant, totum politicum ordinem, Magistratus, leges, distinctionem dominiorum, contractus, iudicia, poenas, esse opera ordinata Dei sapientia in genere humano.

Et quanquam diaboli et homines multis horribilibus furoribus turbant hunc ordinem, tamen ne funditus extinguatur genus humanum, aliquid politici ordinis reliquum manet. Id sciamus efficaciter a Deo conservari, sicut et Daniel inquit: Deus transfert et stabilit regna.

Deinde cum cognoscimus ordinem Dei opus esse, amemus eum, et tueri nostris officiis studeamus, et modeste propter Deum ei obediamus, et Deo conservatori gratias agamus, et sciamus furores diabolorum et hominum, qui turbant politicum ordinem, displicere Deo, sicut tota haec doctrina longa concione ad Romanos 13. recitatur. Sed quare dicit: Divinatio in labiis regis, in iudicio non errat os eius?

Coniungenda sunt haec membra. Dictum loquitur de Rege et de iudicio. diciis, non de Tyranno et de Calumniis. Regis vox comprehenditur: Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, argue eum inter te et ipsum. Pastores et alii, praesertim qui habent officium docendi, cum sciunt errare aliquem, aut alioqui iniuste facere, primum admoneant eum privatim. Si ille non emendat se, postea fiat accusatio publica. Sit autem in monitore Veritas et Candor, non quaerat calumniose quod reprehendat. Monitus sit docilis, non contumax. In neutro sit φιλονεικία, id est, cupiditas contentionis. Ita hoc loco praecepta dantur et monitori et monito.

Malus tantum quaerit rixas, id est, non quaerit veritatem et salutem Ecclesiae, sed sine fine turbas, ut Cleon et Alcibiades Athenis subinde bellorum semina spargunt. Omnibus contradicebant Cynici et Academici, et recens Valla, Cornelius Agrippa, Carolostadius, Osiander, Stancarus, et multi habent tales rixatrices naturas. Hi non quaerunt veritatem, sed recte dicta arte depravant, aut petulanter movent non necessaria certamina, nec moniti cedunt, sed rabiosius defendunt errores. De his dicit hoc loco Salomon: Satius est occurrere ursae orbatae catulis, quam stulto in stulticia sua, ut cum fascinatus Papista defendit manifestos errores.

Damnant igitur hae sententiae calumnias et cupiditatem contentionum, et pertinentiam in erroribus.

Praecipiunt autem, servari ordinem in admonitione, et iubent adhiberi veritatem, candorem et ἐπιείκειαν, et monitos iubent esse dociles, iuxta dictum: Desinite male facere. Item: Agite poenitentiam et credite Evangelio. Ideo dicitur: Qui celat alienum delictum, acquirit amiciciam, id est, cum ordine monuit errantem, sanat eum, non tumultuatur publice, servat hominem, et alit publicam concordiam. Contra vero neglecto hoc ordine ex rixis oriuntur discordiae principum, bella et vastationes, sicut in versu Empedoclis dicitur: Φοιτᾷ δὲ βροτολοιγὸς ἔρις κενεὸν λελακυῖα, Vana sonans adfert saevas discordia caedes.

Poenam etiam hic rixosis monitoribus et monitis denunciant. Nuncius malus occurret ei, id est, qui calumniis aut accendunt aut alunt discordias, tandem dabunt poenas, quia veritas etiam si aliquandiu reprimitur, tamen tandem vincit. Ἰσχυρὸν τὸ ἀληθὲς, ut inquit Demosthenes. Et Paulus iubet haereticos post unam et alteram admonitionem vitari, et ait: Peccant αὐτοκατάκριτοι.

## 17:1 Argument
Chapter XVII.

He who hides another's fault acquires friendship: but he who makes it public, separates princes. A rebuke terrifies a prudent man more than a hundred stripes a fool. An evil man only seeks discords, and a cruel messenger will meet him. It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly. These sentences are related, and they all pertain to the order in judging, which in the saying of Christ toi, that is, because those convicted in their conscience do not wish to be seen as convicted, they already condemn themselves by their own testimony.

But someone might ask, how can a man be convicted? I answer: In forensic matters, a man is convicted by a legitimate trial and the sentence of a judge. In philosophy, by common norms, which are called κριτήρια (criteria), which are three: universal experience, principles, and the understanding of consequences. In the doctrine of the Church concerning the law and the articles of faith, a man is convicted by testimonies correctly cited from the Prophets and Apostles, and by the creeds. For the doctrine of the Church concerning the foundation is not ambiguous.

It must be known, however, that it is a divine command that, once the truth is acknowledged, we should acquiesce in it for the sake of God, and give thanks to God that He has shown His light, and that we should apply it to use, as it is commanded in Zechariah 8: Love truth and peace. And he who does not assent to the truth concerning God violates the first and second commandments of the decalogue: You shall have no other gods. Item: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. And to oppose the acknowledged truth concerning God is blasphemy, of which it is said: The blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. In other matters, the commandment is violated: You shall not bear false witness.

Latin:

Caput XVII.

Qui celat alienum delictum, acquirit amiciciam: qui vero palam facit, distrahit principes. Increpatio prudentem magis perterrefacit, quam centum plagae stultum. Tantum discordias quaerit malus, et nuncius crudelis occurret ei. Melius est occurrere ursae orbatae catulis, quam stulto in sua stulticia. Vicinae sunt sententiae, et pertinent omnes ad ordinem in iudicando, qui in dicto Christi τοι, id est, quia convicti in conscientia non volunt videri convicti, iam suo testimonio sese damnant.

Quaerat autem aliquis, quomodo potest homo convinci? Respondeo: In forensibus negociis convincitur homo legitimo iudicio et sententia iudicis. In philosophia per normas communes, quae nominantur κριτήρια, quae tria sunt: Experientia universalis, principia, et intellectus consequentiae. In doctrina Ecclesiae de lege et de articulis fidei convincitur homo per testimonia recte citata ex Prophetis et Apostolis, et per symbola. Non est enim ambigua doctrina Ecclesiae de fundamento.

Sciendum est autem, mandatum divinum esse, ut agnita veritate, in ea acquiescamus propter Deum, et Deo gratias agamus, quod lucem suam monstravit, et eam ad usum conferamus, ut praeceptum est Zachariae 8.: Diligite veritatem et pacem. Et non assentiens veritati de Deo, violat primum et secundum praeceptum decalogi: Non habebis Deos alienos. Item: Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui falso. Et agnitae veritati de Deo adversari, blasphemia est, de qua dicitur: Blasphemia Spiritus non remittetur. In aliis negociis violatur praeceptum: Non dicas falsum testimonium.

## 18:1 Argument
Chapter XVIII.

The just man is at first his own accuser; afterwards he inquires into another.

In all men, in this weakness, these are the sources of many sins: φιλαυτία (self-love) and pride. We please ourselves, and we exalt ourselves above others. Therefore we flatter ourselves, and we love κολακίας (flatteries), and we do not see our own vices; we even wish others to be seen as inferior, and we judge them harshly, while we spare ourselves and are the censors and Momuses of others. In our own vices we are blind, in those of others we are Lynceuses. We are wise abroad, but not wise at home.

Hence those sayings: To each his own is beautiful. And Cicero says to Atticus: To each his own bride, to me my own. To each his own love, to me my own. Not wisely said, etc.

Hence also the fable about the two wallets, of which Catullus says: Truly we are all deceived, nor is there anyone Whom you could not see as a Suffenus in some matter, To each his own error is attributed. But we do not see the wallet that is on our back.

And Horace: Since you see your own evils with bleary, anointed eyes, Why do you see so sharply into the vices of your friends? And Persius: As no one tries to descend into himself, no one: But the wallet on the preceding back is looked at. Item: Live with yourself, and you will know how short your own furniture is.

And in the Gospel, the hypocrite is severely censured, who, having a beam in his eye, wishes to remove a speck from another's.

Against this φιλαυτία (self-love) and perversity of judgments, let the admonition be held which is delivered in this sentence: The just man is at first his own accuser, that is, he inquires into himself, acknowledges his own infirmity and his own lapses, because it is just to begin punishment from ourselves, according to the saying: It is shameful for a teacher to be refuted by the fault he himself commits. Furthermore, even the just have some blemishes, according to the saying: There is no just man on earth who, although he does well, does not also sin. But because they are just, they confess the truth, nor do they defend their own errors or lapses; they grieve, and they punish themselves first, and amend.

Afterwards, they consider when and in what order they ought to judge others, and they do not judge from light suspicions, but from true arguments. Therefore the text uses the word 'He shall explore,' saying: Let each one test his own work, and thus he will have glory in himself, not from another, that is, if he does his duty correctly, he has a tranquil conscience, and does not depend on the applause of the mob.

Many sayings pertain to this: It is true that everyone should measure themselves by their own rule and foot. Item: He who measures his own weights can bear them, etc.

The Greek interpreter in Solomon used a significant word.

The just man in his πρωτολογία (first speech/accusation) accuses himself. Now πρωτολογία is a forensic term, namely the speech of the accuser before the defendant is heard. But it is difficult afterwards to uproot from minds an opinion once conceived, as Demosthenes says.

Now consider how many such censors there are everywhere, such as the picture of the hypocrite describes, who, having a beam in his eye, wishes to remove a speck from another.

But many vices concur in this perversity of judgments: φιλαυτία (self-love), pride, poly- pragmosynē (busyness/meddling), cruelty, when hypocrites spare themselves and exercise cruelty toward others, etc. Let us each acknowledge our own vices, and be moved with mercy toward those who can be healed, and according to our calling, let us strive to heal them, and let us be mindful of the saying of Nazianzen: If you know you are being wronged, show gentleness, For mercy is weighed by God with mercy.

He who finds a wife finds a good thing, and will draw pleasure from the Lord. Let the phrase be considered. To find signifies to lead happily. Finding a wife, that is, leading happily, or in Greek, eutykhōs eutykhōn (happily finding). It signifies, therefore, that it is a singular gift of God, a happy, placid, and pious marriage, in which there is mutual love and the spouses are in harmony with the Church, and at the same time with God, according to the verse: And in God let there be one mind, let there be one love. Therefore in the following chapter: A prudent wife is from the Lord. At the same time, these sayings are illustrious testimonies which affirm that marriage is pleasing to God. And with singular emphasis it is said here: He will draw pleasure from the Lord, as if to say, Great are the dangers of life, and common miseries are many; in these, however, God will be the guardian of such spouses who, in harmony, call upon Him and rejoice in God, because they know that they are His care. Such were the spouses Zacharias and Elizabeth, and other pious ones, whom God then miraculously protected when the armies of the most wicked nations were wandering everywhere in Judea. When Lamyrus killed thirty thousand Jews and forced the captives to feed on the corpses of the slaughtered Jews, then God protected Zacharias, Elizabeth, Mary, and her parents, just as He saved the three men in the Babylonian furnace. In these examples, let us consider what it is to draw pleasure from the Lord. He used the significant verb 'to draw' (hauriendi), alluding to fountains and springs, to signify a manifold, efficacious, and sweet consolation, and as it were, a recreation.

Let there be noted here the whole doctrine concerning Chastity and Marriage. God created Male and Female because He wills the human race to be the Church; and by a certain law He joined male and female, and set boundaries, and prohibited wandering lusts, so that there might be an understanding of chastity in the human race. For God wills it to be understood that He is a chaste mind, and by this thought to be distinguished in invocation from unclean natures. For it is necessary for us to think about whom we are invoking. And because we do not embrace God with our arms, but address Him with our mind, we must think about what He is like and where He has revealed Himself. We say, therefore: Almighty God, eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of heaven and earth, of angels and of men, together with Thy Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and Thy Holy Spirit, wise, good, truthful, just, merciful, judge, chaste and most free, have mercy on us for the sake of Jesus Christ Thy Son, whom Thou didst will to be for us a victim, and mediator and intercessor, and justify us for His sake, and through Him, and sanctify us with Thy Holy Spirit, truthful and chaste, etc.

Let there be noted, therefore, also the doctrine concerning chastity, and let us hold to the most severe divine threats which are recited in Leviticus 18 and 1 Corinthians 6: Fornicators, adulterers, murderers, etc., will not possess the kingdom of God. And to the Hebrews: God will judge fornicators and adulterers. And in sight are examples of punishments, as it is expressly said in Leviticus: That the Canaanites were destroyed because of the confusions of lust. And there is no doubt that a great part of the calamities in the whole human race are the punishments for lusts. Let us, therefore, be more ardent in seeking chastity from God, because the more God is angered at the defilement of men, and the devil more inflames men, the more God wills to guard us, as we seek chastity. Let us also keep the rule: To avoid sins is to avoid the occasions of sins. Item:

Walk accurately, not as the foolish. Item: If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the spirit, you will live, etc.

Latin:

Caput XVIII.

Iustus initio accusator est sui; postea inquirit in alium.

In omnibus hominibus in hac imbecillitate hi fontes sunt multorum peccatorum, φιλαυτία et superbia. Nobis placemus, et nos efferimus supra alios. Ideo nobis blandimur, et amamus κολακίας, et nostra vitia non cernimus, volumus etiam alios videri inferiores, ac de eis acerbe iudicamus, nobis parcimus et aliorum sumus censores et Momi. In nostris vitiis caecutimus, in alienis sumus Lyncei. Foris sapimus, domi non sapimus.

Hinc illa dicta sunt: Suum cuique pulcrum. Et ad Atticum inquit Cicero: Suam cuique sponsam, mihi meam. Suum cuique amorem, mihi meum. Non scite hoc etc.

Hinc et Apologus est de duabus Manticis, de quibus Catullus inquit: Nimirum omnes fallimur, neque est quisquam, Quem non in aliqua re videre Suffenum Possis, suus cuique attribntus est error. Sed non videmus manticae quod in tergo est.

Et Horatius: Cum tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Cur in amicorum vitiis tam cernis acutum? Et Persius: Ut nemo in sese tentat descendere, nemo: Sed praecedenti spectatur mantica tergo. Item: Tecum habita, et noris quam sit tibi curta supellex.

Et in Evangelio severe taxatur hypocrita, qui habens trabem in oculo, vult alteri festucam eximere.

Contra hanc φιλαυτίαν et perversitatem iudiciorum teneatur admonitio, quae in hac sententia traditur: Iustus initio accusator est sui, id est, inquirit in sese, agnoscit suam infirmitatem, et suos lapsus, quia iustum est, incoare poenam a nobis ipsis, iuxta dictum: Turpe est doctori cum culpa redarguit ipsum. Praeterea et iusti habent aliquos naevos, iuxta dictum: Non est iustus in terra, qui quanquam benefacit, non etiam peccet. Sed quia sunt iusti, vera fatentur, nec defendunt suos errores aut lapsus, dolent, ac sese primum puniunt, et emendant.

Postea considerant, quando et quo ordine de aliis iudicare debeant, nec iudicant ex levibus suspicionibus, sed ex veris argumentis. Ideo textus utitur verbo Explorabit, inquiens: Probet unusquisque suum opus, et sic habebit gloriam apud sese, non ex alio, id est, si recte facit officium, habet tranquillam conscientiam, et non pendet ex applausu vulgi.

Huc pertinent multa dicta: Metiri se quenque suo modulo ac pede verum est. Item: Qui sua metitur pondera ferre potest etc.

Interpres Graecus in Salomone usus est insigni verbo.

Iustus in πρωτολογία seipsum accusat. Est autem πρωτολογία forense vocabulum, videlicet oratio accusatoris antequam reus auditur. Difficile est autem postea evellere ex animis opinionem primum conceptam, ut Demosthenes inquit.

Iam cogita, quam multi sint tales censores passim, qualis describit pictura hypocritae, qui habens trabem in oculo, alteri vult eximere festucam.

Concurrunt autem multa vitia in hac perversitate iudiciorum, φιλαυτία, superbia, πολυ- πραγμοσύνη, crudelitas, cum sibi parcunt hypocritae, et in alios saevitiam exercent etc. Agnoscamus autem singuli nostra vitia, et adficiamur misericordia erga sanabiles, et iuxta vocationem sanare eos studeamus, et simus memores dicti Nazianzeni: εἰδὲ οἶδας ὄφλων καὶ πρόχρησον τὸ πρᾶον, οἴκτῳ γὰρ οἶκτος, τῷ θεῷ σταθμίζεται.

Inveniens uxorem invenit bonum, et hauriet voluptatem a Domino. Phrasis consideretur. Invenire significat feliciter ducere. Inveniens uxorem, id est, feliciter ducens, seu Graece εὐτυχῶς εὐτυχῶν. Significat igitur singulare Dei donum esse, felix, placidum et pium coniugium, in quo mutuus est amor et coniuges concordes sunt Ecclesia, simul Deum, iuxta versum: Inque Deo sit mens una, sit unus amor. Ideo in sequenti capite: Uxor prudens a Domino. Simul autem haec dicta sunt illustria testimonia, quae adfirmant, Deo placere coniugium. Et singulari emphasi hic dictum est: Hauriet voluptatem a Domino, quasi dicat, Magna sunt vitae pericula, et communes miseriae multae, in his tamen Deus erit custos talium coniugum, qui concordes ipsum invocant, et laetantur in Deo, quia sciunt, se ei curae esse. Tales fuerunt coniuges Zacharias et Elisabeth, et alii pii, quos Deus mirabiliter tunc protexit, cum assidue pessimarum gentium exercitus passim in Iudaea vagerentur. Cum Lamyrus triginta millia Iudaeorum occidit, et captivos coëgit vesci cadaveribus interfectorum Iudaeorum, tunc Zachariam, Elisabeth, Mariam, et eius parentes protexit Deus, sicut servavit tres viros in fornace Babylonica. In his exemplis cogitemus, quid sit haurire voluptatem a Domino. Usus est autem verbo insigni Hauriendi, alludens ad fontes et scaturigines, ut significet, multiplicem, efficacem et dulcem consolationem, et quasi recreationem.

Nota sit autem hic tota doctrina de Castitate, et de Coniugio. Condidit Deus Marem et Foeminam, quia genus humanum vult esse Ecclesiam: et certa lege coniunxit marem et foeminam, et metas circumdedit, ac prohibuit vagas libidines, ut sit in genere humano intellectus castitatis. Vult enim Deus intelligi, se mentem castam esse, et hac cogitatione discerni in invocatione a naturis immundis. Necesse est enim nos cogitare, quid invocemus. Et quia non amplectimur Deum brachiis, sed mente eum alloquimur, cogitandum est, qualis sit, et ubi se patefecerit. Dicimus igitur: Omnipotens Deus, aeterne pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, conditor coeli et terrae, angelorum et hominum, una cum Filio tuo Domino nostro Iesu Christo, et Spiritu tuo sancto, sapiens, bone, verax, iuste, misericors, iudex, caste et liberrime, miserere nostri propter Iesum Christum Filium tuum, quem voluisti pro nobis esse victimam, καὶ μεσίτην καὶ ἱκέτην, et iustifica nos propter eum, et per eum, et sanctifica nos Spiritu tuo sancto veraci et casto etc.

Nota sit igitur et doctrina de castitate, et teneamus severissimas comminationes divinas, quae recitantur Levitici 18. et 1. Cor. 6.: Scortatores, adulteri, homicidae etc. non possidebunt regnum Dei. Et ad Ebraeos: Scortatores et adulteros iudicabit Deus. Et in conspectu sunt exempla poenarum, ut in Levitico expresse dicitur: Cananaeos deletos esse propter confusiones libidinis. Nec dubium est, magnam partem calamitatum in toto genere humano poenas esse libidinum. Simus igitur ardentiores in petenda castitate a Deo, quia quo magis irascitur Deus inquinationi hominum, et diabolus magis incendit homines, eo magis vult nos Deus custodire, petentes castitatem. Servemus etiam regulam: Vitare peccata est vitare occasiones peccatorum.

Item: Ambulate accurate, non ut fatui. Item: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis, vivetis, etc.

## 19:1 Argument
Chapter XIX.

Delights do not befit a fool.

Nor does it befit a servant to rule over leaders. All men in this weakness of nature become more negligent in prosperous circumstances, as it is commonly said: Minds usually grow wanton in prosperous circumstances. Item: Whom fortune favors too much, she makes a fool. Item: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play, etc. Finally, in many writings this admonition is repeated, because when minds are not troubled, they invoke God less, and they are less intent on doing necessary things.

But since nature cannot be entirely idle, and is prone to pleasures and vices, those not occupied with necessary cares rush toward depraved things, as Cato says: Men learn to do evil by doing nothing. Item: If you remove idleness, Cupid's bows perish, and his extinguished torches lie without light. Item: Idleness is treacherous to the secure.

David, when idle, admits and feeds the fires of love. Therefore it is said here: Luxury does not befit a fool, that is, those not tamed, not previously disciplined, become more audacious and worse in prosperous circumstances, just as Rehoboam becomes more insolent, having been made king in such great tranquility. In Alexander, many vices grow after the course of so many victories.

Universally, therefore, there is a precept concerning discipline in Sirach ch. 33: Fodder, a rod, and a burden for an ass. Thus bread, discipline, and work for a servant, that is, let men not be idle, but occupied with certain honest labor.

But yet let there be a measure; let them have fodder, but let them also have inspectors who are exactors of works and ἐργοδιῶκται [taskmasters], that is, those urging works, and let them punish the contumacious, so that others may be kept in their duty by the fear of punishments. This precept is a warning, both concerning one's own body and concerning economic governance, and the rule: Let kingdoms not be merely slaughterhouses for the people, but let them leave fodder for the citizens, and take care that they are occupied with honest labors, and punish the contumacious. Now, discipline is mostly neglected, and the resources of the citizens are exhausted by immoderate exactions, so that ordinary men do not have the necessities of life, and the expenses for educating and instructing their offspring.

But the divine voice has predicted that in this delirious old age of the world, empires will be more deformed, and it commands us to seek from God a mitigation of public and private punishments, and a moderate preservation of honest society and the Church. When the scoffer is struck, the inexperienced will be more cautious.

After the mind of men was plunged into sin, destruction followed, namely Death, because human nature ceased to be the dwelling of God, as it had been before, according to the saying: In Him was life, that is, man lived through the Word dwelling in man; with the Word cast off, God the ruler and vivifier was cast off, and death followed. But yet, because for the sake of the Son God willed to gather an eternal Church in the human race, the first parents were not immediately destroyed, but were vivified again, with the Word dwelling in them again, the promise having been issued. Since, therefore, the human race exists, and there are many sins, punishments are accumulated, and innumerable calamities precede death.

Physicists say the cause of death and many calamities is matter, which by its own nature, as in fruits, withers or rots. They say also that some miseries are brought on by human errors and wills. These things are rightly said concerning immediate causes.

But why is the matter of men now such? Whence is there ignorance in men, and the depravity of the will? Here the doctrine of the Church shows the principal causes, namely sin. After man, having cast off the Word of God, cast off God the ruler, sins followed, and from original sin, innumerable actual sins arise afterward.

There is, however, an order of justice in God, that nature should be destroyed, just as it is written: God is a consuming fire. Therefore punishments follow.

There are, however, four causes of punishments to be considered primarily. The first is the order of justice in God, because it is just that guilty nature be destroyed.

Then final causes are added. God wills that the distinction between honest and base things be recognized; He wills that He Himself be recognized as to what He is, and He wills it to be understood that He is the judge and avenger of crimes.

Therefore, the second cause of punishments is that punishments may be warnings of what God is and what He is like, so that because He destroys Sodom, we know God to be chaste; and a lover of chastity, and that He is horribly angered by incestuous lusts. The third cause is utility, so that the human race may be preserved, because there would be no end to robberies if there were no punishments.

The fourth cause is that others may be warned by the example, and be restrained by fear, and some may be converted to God. Concerning this cause, it is said in this place: When the scoffer is struck, the inexperienced will be more cautious, just as the Gibeonites, with their neighbors destroyed, became more cautious and sought peace.

The punishment of Sisamnes made Otanes more cautious, who was placed in the chair on which his father's skin was spread, as Herodotus narrates in Terpsichore. He says by name: Strike the mockers, that is, those who sin atrociously, who, when punishments are delayed, deride admonitions with Epicurean contempt, and become more furious, so that the punishment may be more conspicuous, as it is said: They are lifted on high, That they may fall with a heavier crash. The other part of the saying: Correction increases knowledge in the prudent, signifies that not all are amended by examples of punishments, but some, not the furious, who hear admonitions and, being warned, obey.

Latin:

Caput XIX.

Non decent stultum deliciae.

Nec servum dominari ducibus. Omnes homines in hac imbecillitate naturae in rebus secundis fiunt negligentiores, sicut usitate dicitur: Luxuriant animi rebus plerumque secundis. Item: Fortuna quem nimium fovet, stultum facit. Item: Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et surrexit ludere etc. Denique in multis scriptis haec commonefactio repetita est, quia cum non anguntur animi, minus invocant Deum, et minus sunt intenti in rebus necessariis agendis.

Cum autem natura non prorsus ociosa esse possit, et prona sit ad voluptates et ad vitia, non occupati necessariis curis ruunt ad prava, ut Cato ait: Homines nihil agendo mala agere discunt. Item: Ocia si tollas periere Cupidinis arcus, Contemtaeque faces, et sine luce iacent. Item: Ocia securis insidiosa nocent.

David ociosus admittit et alit incendia amoris. Ideo hic dicitur: Deliciae non decent fatuum, id est, non domiti, non cicurati antea, fiunt audaciores et peiores in rebus secundis, ut Roboam fit insolentior, factus rex in tanta tranquillitate. In Alexandro multa vitia post tot victoriarum cursum crescunt.

Universaliter igitur de disciplina praeceptum est in Siracide cap. 33.: Pabulum, virga, et onus asino. Sic panis, disciplina et opus servo, id est, homines non sint ociosi, sed certo labore honesto occupati.

Sed tamen modus sit, habeant pabulum, habeant autem et inspectores, qui sint exactores operarum et ἐργοδιῶκται, id est, urgentes operas, et puniant contumaces, ut alii metu poenarum in officio contineantur. Hoc praeceptum commonefactio est, et de suo cuiusque corpore, et de oeconomica gubernatione, et regula: Regna non sint tantum carnificinae populi, sed relinquant papulum civibus, et curent ut sint occupati honestis laboribus, et puniant contumaces. Nunc plerumque negligitur disciplina, et immoderatis expilationibus exhauriuntur facultates civium, ut mediocres homines non habeant res vitae necessarias, et sumtus ad educandam et instituendam sobolem.

Sed vox divina praedixit, in hac delira mundi senecta, imperia fore deformiora, et iubet nos a Deo petere mitigationem poenarum publicarum et privatarum, et mediocrem conservationem honestae societatis et Ecclesiae. Subsannatore percusso imperitus erit cautior.

Postquam mens hominum mersa est in peccatum, sequuta est destructio, videlicet Mors, quia humana natura desiit esse domicilium Dei, sicut antea fuerat, iuxta dictum: In ipso vita erat, id est, per Verbum habitans in homine vivebat homo, excusso verbo excussus est Deus rector et vivificator, et sequuta est mors. Sed tamen quia propter Filium voluit Deus colligere Ecclesiam aeternam in genere humano, non mox deleti sunt primi parentes, sed rursus vivificati sunt, verbo iterum habitante in eis, edita promissione. Cum igitur sit genus humanum, et multa sint peccata, cumulantur et poenae, et innumerabiles calamitates mortem antecedunt.

Physici causam mortis et multarum calamitatum dicunt esse materiam, quae sua natura, ut in pomis arefit aut putrescit. Dicunt item, aliquas miserias accersi erroribus et voluntatibus humanis. Haec de immediatis causis recte dicuntur.

Sed cur hominum materia nunc est talis? Unde est in hominibus ignorantia, et voluntatis pravitas? Hic doctrina Ecclesiae monstrat principales causas, scilicet peccatum. Postquam homo excusso verbo Dei excussit Deum rectorem, sequuta sunt peccata, et ex originali postea innumerabilia actualia oriuntur.

Est autem ordo iusticiae in Deo, ut natura destruatur, sicut scriptum est: Deus est ignis consumens. Ideo poenas sequuntur.

Sunt autem quatuor causae poenarum praecipue considerandae. Prima est ordo iusticiae in Deo, quia iustum est, ream naturam destrui.

Deinde accedunt finales causae. Vult Deus agnosci discrimen honestorum et turpium, vult se agnosci qualis sit, et vult intelligi, quod sit iudex et vindex scelerum.

Est igitur secunda causa poenarum, ut poenae sint commonefactiones, quod sit Deus et qualis sit, ut quia destruit Sodoma, scimus Deum castum esse; et amantem castitatis, et horribiliter irasci incestis libidinibus. Tertia causa est utilitas, ut conservetur genus humanum, quia non esset finis latrociniorum, si nullae essent poenae.

Quarta causa est, ut exemplo alii commonefiant, et metu coërceantur, et aliqui ad Deum convertantur. De hac causa hoc loco dicitur: Subsannatore percusso imperitus erit cautior, ut Gabeonitae deletis vicinis facti sunt cautiores, et petierunt pacem.

Poena Sisamnis facti cautiorem Otanem collocatum in sellam, in qua pellis paterna expansa erat, ut Herodotus narrat in Terpsichore. Nominatim vero dicit: Percuti subsannatores, id est, atrociter delinquentes, qui cum poenae differantur, Epicureo contemtu derident admonitiones, et fiunt furiosiores, ut poena sit conspectior, ut dicitur: Tolluntur in altum, Ut lapsu graviore ruant. Altera pars dicti: Correctio apud prudentem auget scientiam, significat non omnes emendari exemplis castigationum, sed aliquos, non furiosos, qui audiunt admonitiones, et moniti obtemperant.

## 20:1 Argument
Chapter XX.

The hearing ear and the seeing eye, God makes both. In a happy government these two things must concur: Good counsels of the governors, and the obedience of the people. And Solomon says both are a gift of God. As, Jeremiah was a good monitor, but he did not have King Zedekiah obeying him, therefore Jerusalem was destroyed. Hezekiah obeyed Isaiah, therefore the city was saved. This is the principal meaning of this most sweet saying: The hearing ear and the seeing eye, God makes both. He warns, however, that not only should polities and economies be ruled by human wisdom, but that the help of God should be sought both in giving counsel, and in bending the wills of men to obedience, and in ruling events, as Jeremiah says: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself. Item: Unless the Lord build the house. Item: Commit thy way unto the Lord, and hope in him, and he shall bring it to pass.

Furthermore, the saying of Solomon is to be applied in general to all excellent craftsmen, whose minds find and discover many things in the arts divinely, which others do not discern, as it is said in Daniel: God gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding. It is evil, it is evil, they say, when they possess it. But after they have lost it, they praise it, etc.

As much as possible, let us consider our diseases, so that we may in some way correct them. For we all bring many vices with us at birth. Among these is the loathing of present goods, which arises either from the mobility and inconstancy of the mind, or from weariness, or from impatience, when, offended by some inconveniences, we desire a change. Many proverbs censure this loathing: A lazy ox desires horse-trappings, a horse desires to plow. And there is a fable among Aesop's, about an Ass constantly changing its condition for the worse. And there are verses of Sophocles in Ajax: Foolish men do not recognize a good thing while it is in their hands, before they lose it; afterwards, when it is lost, they desire it. Finally, individuals discover in themselves such loathings of their present state, just as he in Terence says: We are displeased with ourselves.

And it is most common to bear present rule with difficulty, and to desire others, as it is said in Thucydides: ἀεὶ τὸ παρὸν βαρύ [The present is always burdensome]. Against this instability of minds, many divine precepts have been handed down concerning patience. As: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Item: Do not murmur against God. And philosophical [precepts] concerning the moderation of the mind: Στέργειν τὰ παρόντα [Be content with present things]. Item: What you are, wish to be, and prefer nothing else. And there is a verse of Pythagoras: ὧν ἂν μοῖραν ἔχεις ταύτην ἔχε, μηδ᾽ ἀγανάκτει [Whatever portion you have, keep it, and do not be indignant]. And Stigelius: Be an ass, whatever ass harsh fate has made you, He who knows how to bear his lot calmly, he is wise. Item: Sufficient for the day is its own affliction.

And Pindar warns most gracefully that, since evils are mixed with goods, the good things are to be selected and cherished, and evils are to be softened by art: ἓν παρὰ ἐσθλὸν πήματα σύνδυο δαίονται βροτοῖς ἀθάνατοι· τὰ μὲν ὧν οὐ δύνανται νήπιοι κόσμῳ φέρειν ἀλλ᾽ ἀγαθοὶ τὰ καλὰ τρέψαντες ἔξω. [For one good thing, the immortals deal out two evils to mortals; which fools cannot bear with order, but the good, turning the good things outward.] Let us learn this art, which is necessary in life. It belongs to justice to embrace present goods with gratitude. Then it belongs to prudence and tolerance to bear certain inconveniences moderately, lest we bring more evil upon ourselves by foolish changes, as Periander warns: μὴ κακῷ κακὸν ἰῶ [Do not cure evil with evil]. To this doctrine let this saying of Solomon also be referred, by which he properly censures the loathing of present goods, and signifies that what is lost is again desired and sought.

Let this saying be referred to the common topic concerning the loathing of present things, and concerning patience, which is, to be willing to obey God in these burdens in bearing the things which He commands to be borne, and at the same time to seek and expect help from God, just as Paul joins these: Always rejoice, always give thanks, always pray.

An inheritance which is hastened to in the beginning, will eventually lack a blessing. There is a precept concerning the expectation of a calling. Absalom could have become king if he had expected the death of his father, but because he seizes dominion before the time and without a calling, he is cast out again and oppressed with horrible punishments.

The sons of Ephraim invaded the land of Canaan before Moses, with a carnal trust in the divine promise, because the land of Canaan had been promised to the lineage of Abraham: but because they move to war without a calling, by human persuasion, they are killed, and the whole plan was useless, 1 Paralip.

7. For the promise had given a right to the thing, not yet the thing itself.

On the contrary, David, although he knows the kingdom has been promised to him, nevertheless, while Saul is alive, he by no means calls himself king, nor does he cast him out of the kingdom, nor does he kill him, although he had just causes, because Saul had killed the priests, and often armed, sought him, so that he might kill him.

Let us therefore discern necessary things from unnecessary ones, and let us move nothing without a compelling calling.

It is a ruin to a man to offer holy insult, and afterwards to make vows.

In the Latin writing and version there are errors, which have provided an occasion for foreign and fictitious interpretations, and for accommodation to monastic vows.

Otherwise, Solomon's sentiment is clear.

He censures the most common superstition of the greatest part of men, who, polluted by impiety, hatred of the Gospel, and other crimes against their conscience, afterwards anxiously observe certain ceremonies, and because of these, they dream that they please God, and they exalt themselves above others, just as Spanish adulterers and assassins watch the Mass with great solicitude, or on certain holidays lacerate their backs with public flagellation.

But above, it was spoken concerning the distinctions of worships, in the sentiment: The sacrifices of the impious are an abomination, but the prayer of the upright pleases God, etc.

And in Ecclesiastes 4 it is said: Obedience is better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know how much evil they do.

Latin:

Caput XX.

Aurem audientem et oculum videntem, Deus facit utrunque. In gubernatione felici haec duo concurrere oportet: Bona consilia gubernantium, et obedientiam populi. Et utrunque dicit Salomon donum Dei esse. Ut, Ieremias erat bonus monitor, sed non habebat regem Zedechiam obtemperantem, ideo Hierosolyma deleta est. Esaiae obtemperabat Ezechias, ideo civitas servata est. Haec est principalis sententia huius dulcissimi dicti: Aurem audientem et oculum videntem, Deus facit utrunque. Monet autem, non solum sapientia humana regi politias et oeconomias, sed petendum esse auxilium Dei et in dando consilio, et in flectendis voluntatibus hominum ad obedientiam, et in regendis eventibus, sicut Ieremias inquit: Scio Domine quod non est hominis via eius. Item: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum. Item: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Caeterum et dictum Salomonis in genere accommodandum est ad omnes excellentes artifices, quorum mentes inveniunt et deprehendunt multa in artibus divinitus, quae alii non cernunt, sicut in Daniele dicitur: Deus dat sapientiam sapientibus, et scientiam intelligentibus. Malum est, malum est dicunt, cum tenent. Sed postquam amiserunt laudant etc.

Quantum fieri potest morhos nostros consideremus, ut aliquo modo eos corrigamus. Omnes enim nascentes multa vitia nobiscum adferimus. Inter haec est fastidium bonorum praesentium, quod oritur vel ex mobilitate et inconstantia animi, vel ex defatigatione, vel ex impatientia, cum offensi aliquibus incommodis, mutationem appetimus. Hoc fastidium taxant multae sententiae: Optat Ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus. Et Apologus apud Aesopum extat, de Asino subinde mutante conditionem in deteriora. Et Sophoclis versus sunt in Aiace: Stulti homines non agnoscunt bonum, dum in manibus est, priusquam amittunt, postea amissa desiderant. Denique singuli in seipsis deprehendunt talia fastidia praesentis status, sicut et ille apud Terentium inquit: Nostri nosmet poenitet.

Et usitatissimum est, praesentia imperia aegre ferre, et appetere alia, sicut apud Thucydidem dicitur: ἀεὶ τὸ παρὸν βαρύ. Adversus hanc instabilitatem animorum multa praecepta tradita sunt divina de patientia. Ut: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei. Item: Non murmurate adversus Deum. Et philosophica de animi moderatione: Στέργειν τὰ παρόντα. Item: Quod sis, esse velis, nihilque malis. Et versus est Pythagorae: ὧν ἂν μοῖραν ἔχεις ταύτην ἔχε, μηδ᾽ ἀγανάκτει. Et Stigelius: Sis asinus, quemcunque asinum sors aspera fecit, Qui placide sortem ferre scit, ille sapit. Item: Sufficit diei afflictio sua.

Et Pindarus venustissime monet, cum bonis mala admixta sint, bona excerpenda et fovenda esse, et arte lenienda mala: ἓν παρὰ ἐσθλὸν πήματα σύνδυο δαίονται βροτοῖς ἀθάνατοι· τὰ μὲν ὧν οὐ δύνανται νήπιοι κόσμῳ φέρειν ἀλλ᾽ ἀγαθοὶ τὰ καλὰ τρέψαντες ἔξω. Hanc artem in vita necessariam discamus. Iusticiae est cum gratitudine amplecti praesentia bona. Deinde prudentiae et tolerantiae est, quaedam incommoda moderate ferre, ne stultis mutationibus plus mali accersamus, ut monet Periander: μὴ κακῷ κακὸν ἰῶ.

Ad hanc doctrinam referatur et haec sententia ...Salomonis, qua proprie taxat fastidia praesentium bonorum, et significat amissa rursus desiderari et requiri. Referatur autem hoc dictum ad locum communem de fastidio praesentium, et de patientia, quae est, velle obedire Deo in his oneribus ferendis, quae iubet ferre, et simul petere et expectare auxilium a Deo, sicut Paulus haec coniungit: Semper gaudete, semper gratias agite, semper orate.

Haereditas ad quam properatur initio, tandem benedictione carebit. Praeceptum ...est de expectanda vocatione. Absalon potuisset fieri rex, si expectasset mortem patris, sed quia ante tempus et sine vocatione rapit dominationem, rursus excutitur et opprimitur horribilibus poenis.

Filii Ephraim ante Moysen invaserunt terram Cananaeam, carnali fiducia divinae promissionis, quia stirpi Abrahae terra Canaan promissa erat: sed quia sine vocatione, persuasione humana movent bellum, interficiuntur, et totum consilium inutile fuit, 1.

Paralip. 7. Promissio enim dederat ius ad rem, nondum in re.

Contra vero David etsi scit sibi regnum promissum esse, tamen vivo Saule nequaquam se nominat regem, nec illum ex regno excutit, nec eum interficit, cum iustas causas haberet, quia Saul interfecerat sacerdotes, et saepe armatus quaerebat illum, ut eum interficeret.

Discernamus igitur necessaria a non necessariis, et nihil sine vocatione cogente moveamus.

Ruina est homini, sancta contumelia afficere, et postea vota facere.

In Latina scriptione et versione mendae sunt, quae praebuerunt occasionem alienis et commentitiis interpretationibus, et accomodationi ad vota monastica.

Caeterum Salomonis sententia perspicua est.

Taxat usitatissimam superstitionem maximae partis hominum, qui polluti impietate, odio Evangelii et aliis sceleribus contra conscientiam, postea ceremonias aliquas anxie observant, et propter has somniant se Deo placere, et se efferunt supra alios, ut Hispani adulteri et sicarii magna solicitudine spectant Missam, aut in feriis certis publica flagellatione lacerant tergora.

Supra autem de discriminibus cultuum dictum est, in sententia: Victimae impiorum abominatio, oratio autem rectorum placet Deo etc.

Et Ecclesiastae 4. dicitur: Melior est obedientia, quam stultorum victimae, qui nesciunt quantum mali faciant.

## 21:1 Argument
Chapter XXI.

There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against God.

A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is from God.

A necessary rule of life is that the duties of one's calling must be performed, and the help of God must be sought: thus, with God helping, labors become useful and salutary.

But unjust businesses, or those undertaken out of curiosity, or whatever businesses are undertaken without trust in God and invocation, are unhappy, even if great cunning is employed.

Always, therefore, let the precepts concerning the Calling be in sight.

As Paul says to the Thessalonians: Do this ambitiously, so that you may do your own things.

Likewise, to the Corinthians: In whatever calling each one is called, let him walk in it.

And then the precepts concerning the invocation of God, and the promise of help, as in the Psalm: Commend your way to God, and hope in Him, and He will act.

Likewise, to the Corinthians: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord.

And John 15: He who remains in me, and I in him, he bears much fruit.

Let us oppose these consolations to the difficulties which make spirits languish, doubting whether the labor will be profitable.

And both faith and invocation must be aroused, and with the hope of divine help, labors must be diligently performed, and it must be known that God wills that faith, invocation, and hope be exercised in these hardships of the stages of life, as the Psalm says: Be subject to God, and pray to Him, etc.

Let us also know that the trust in our own strength is censured, [Greek: polypragmosynēn] (meddlesomeness) and [Greek: kakozēlian] (bad zeal), etc.

According to these sentiments: There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord.

Item: A man cannot take anything for himself, unless it has been given to him by God.

Item: Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it.

Latin:

Caput XXI.

Non est sapientia, non prudentia, non consilium contra Deum.

Equus paratur ad diem belli, a Deo autem est victoria.

Regula necessaria est vitae, facienda esse officia vocationis, et petendum esse auxilium Dei: ita Deo iuvante labores fiunt utiles et salutares.

Sed iniusta negocia, aut curiositate suscepta, aut quaecunque negocia suscepta sine fiducia Dei et invocatione, sunt infelicia, etiam si magna calliditas adhibetur.

Semper igitur in conspectu sint praecepta de Vocatione.

Ut ad Thess. inquit Paulus: Ambitiose hoc agite, ut propria faciatis.

Item, ad Corinthios: Qua vocatione quisque vocatus est, in ea ambulet.

Et deinde praecepta de invocatione Dei, et promissione auxilii, ut in Psalmo: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Item, ad Corinthios: Non erit inanis labor vester in Domino.

Et Iohan. 15.: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, hic fert fructum copiosum.

Has consolationes opponamus difficultatibus, quae languefaciunt animos, dubitantes utrum labor profuturus sit.

Et fides et invocatio excitanda est, et spe auxilii divini labores sedulo facienda sunt, et sciendum est, Deum velle exerceri fidem, invocationem et spem in his aerumnis graduum vitae, ut Psalmus inquit: Subditus esto Deo, et ora eum etc.

Sciamus etiam taxari fiduciam nostrarum virium, πολυπραγμοσύνην et κακοζηλίαν etc.

Iuxta has sententias: Non est sapientia, non prudentia, non consilium contra Dominum.

Item: Non potest sibi homo sumere quicquam, nisi sit ei datum a Deo.

Item: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum, in vanum laborant, qui aedificant eam.

## 22:1 Argument
Chapter XXII.

A good name is better than many riches.

It is rightly said: A good conscience is a work for me before God, a good reputation for my neighbor.

And it must be known that a good reputation is a good thing, that is, an approval ordained by God, and it is to be sought, because God wills that by public testimonies I have shown the distinction between right and not right, and he wishes those doing rightly to be approved and preserved, and those not doing rightly to be censured and destroyed. He wishes these testimonies to be observed, so that we may learn the law, and consider that there is a God, and what sort he is, and that he is the avenger of crimes.

Good reputation is therefore a testimony divinely ordained, of many judging rightly, approving right things, and doing rightly, by which testimony those doing rightly may be fortified, and an honorable place in common society may be granted to them, so that other men may be taught and invited to right things.

Since therefore good reputation is an approval divinely ordained, and is in many ways useful to life, it is manifest that it is a good thing and to be desired. Therefore also Sirach ch. 41 says: Have a care for a good name. For it is more durable than great treasures. But let the causes be considered.

I. First because God wishes us to look upon the judgments of honest men, as Sirach ch. 6 says: Stand in the assembly of the elders, and if there is anyone wise, cleave to him. It is arrogance and impudence to be unwilling to look upon the judgments of the sound.

II. Then he also wishes honest examples to be provided to others. Therefore 1 Cor. 10 it is said: Do all things for the glory of God, and do not offend the Church. And to Philip. 4: Take care of these things which are true, grave, just, friendly, laudable, virtue and praise.

First, Truth is demanded, which is the preservation of true doctrine, and in other honest businesses to keep words and pacts. Moreover, the preservation of true doctrine is a virtue of the first table.

Gravity is constancy in speech and honest gestures befitting a person, and is a part of modesty.

Particular justice is to affect no one with injury.

Chastity is to avoid prohibited lusts.

He names as friendly things Beneficence and Ἐπιείκειαν, without which concord cannot be retained.

He names as laudable things virtue, which is the diligence of avoiding scandals, which is named φιλοτιμία, the honest desire of honor or good reputation.

Afterwards Paul expressly names Virtue and Praise, so that he may signify that good reputation is to be obtained by right deeds, not by empty ostentation.

Thus also in Romans 14 he says: He who in these things serves Christ, pleases God, and is approved by men, where he also wishes us to consider and respect the judgments of honest men. Those who do not consider these things are arrogant and impudent. Therefore it is rightly said in the Tragedy of Seneca: He is fickle, nor does the glory of honor stimulate him.

Let the younger ones remember also congruent sentiments in other writings, as in the verse of Publius: An honest reputation is a second inheritance. And Plautus: If I shall have preserved an honest reputation, I shall be rich enough. And Hesiod instructs to avoid a bad reputation, and adds that common reputation is not entirely empty: φήμη δ᾽ οὔτις πάμπαν ἀπόλλυται, ἥντινα πολλοὶ λαοὶ φημίζουσι, θεὸς νύ τις ἐστὶ καὶ αὐτή.

The rich and the poor are together, and God makes them both.

The prosperous affairs of the unjust and the calamities of the just disturb assent concerning the providence of God, and some seek other causes for events, and many run to physical causes and fates. It must be known, therefore, that God has set forth testimonies of providence in ordinary and extraordinary works, and in his express word.

Ordinary works show the presence of God, such as this very beautiful order of the bodies of the world, the turns of winter and summer, the annual fertilization of the earth, the preservation of human society, the punishments of murderers, the law and judgment of conscience in individuals, the generation and first nourishment of offspring, etc.

Then Extraordinary works strike the eyes more, such as all miracles, the leading out of the people from Egypt, the resurrection of the dead, and others.

And since these deeds testify that divine sayings are true, let there be in sight many sentiments which affirm that prosperous and adverse things do not happen by chance, but that these things also are ruled by the counsel of God. Let this faith shine in hearts, and let it seek and expect good outcomes from God.

Thus Jeremiah says in Lamentations: Who is this, who says, From the mouth of the Lord shall not proceed good and evil?

And Zephaniah 1: I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will visit the men settled in their dregs, who say in their hearts: The Lord will not do good and will not do evil.

Likewise in Psalm 32: From heaven the Lord looks down, he sees all the sons of men.

Item Matthew 10: One of these sparrows shall not fall upon the ground without the will of my Father. Item: All the hairs of your head are numbered. By these and similar testimonies let us confirm ourselves against Epicurean furies. Let us also consider the commands of God concerning the seeking of corporal things from Him, and the promises, which are also testimonies of providence. Then let us know this, that one must judge concerning the will of God from His own word, as it is said: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet. It is necessary, therefore, to obey the word of God, even if the righteous are often harshly afflicted, because there are certain causes why God wills the Church to be subject to the cross. And let the sentence be noted: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but out of them all God delivered them. Although, therefore, Lazarus is a pauper, yet he should not for that reason cast away his assent concerning providence, but judge from the word of God, which affirms that there is providence, and that liberation will follow. These things are expressly handed down in the word. But why he himself is a pauper, and does not have the empire of Tiberius, is not to be scrutinized. But the rule of Sirach chapter 3 must be held: Think reverently upon those things which have been commanded to you. For it is not necessary for you to look upon hidden things with your eyes. Thus let it be discerned between things revealed and things not revealed, and let each one obey God in his own vocation. This is what this saying teaches in sum: The rich and the poor are together, and God makes them both, that is: Know that there is providence, and that it is not by chance that some are rich and others poor, but by the counsel of God, and let each one serve rightly in his own place, according to the saying: In whatever vocation each was called, in that let him walk. Let not the pauper fret against God, but let him obey this saying: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, and let him hold this consolation. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Item Proverbs 17: He who despises the poor, reproaches his Maker. And Proverbs 15: Better is a little with the fear of God, than great treasures with tumult. Item: Sufficient for the day is its own affliction. Item: Pray without anger and without hesitation.

Do not remove the ancient landmarks, which your fathers have set.

To the commandment, Thou shalt not steal, belongs also this prohibition, that landmarks should not be dug up, and boundaries disturbed, as it is expressly said, Deut. 19: Do not remove the boundaries etc. And chapter 27:

Cursed is he who removes the boundaries of his neighbor. And in the ff. tit. de termino moto, there are laws of Julius, Nerva, and Hadrian concerning the punishments of those who dig up landmarks.

Nor is the commandment obscure, but it is cited allegorically, concerning not changing laws which antiquity has handed down with grave authority, if there is no evident necessity. For among the precepts of political life this also is often repeated, that old laws are not to be changed rashly, as the verse also warns: The Roman state stands by ancient customs and men.

And let the narrative be known to all which exists in Demosthenes in the oration against Timocrates concerning the Locrians, among whom there was a law: That if anyone were to propose a new law, he should persuade it publicly with his neck inserted into a noose, so that if the law did not please, the citizens would immediately strangle the proposer.

The words of Demosthenes are these. I wish, judges, to tell you the example of the Locrians. For you will not be the worse for having heard the example, especially of that state which is governed by honest laws. They so much feel that old laws are to be retained, and ancestral institutions are to be fortified and preserved, and that new laws are not to be borne for the desires of any, or for evading actions of injuries, that if anyone wishes to propose a new law, he is compelled to persuade it with his neck inserted into a noose. But if the people judge the law to be honest and useful, the proposer departs alive and unharmed. But if it does not please, the proposer is immediately killed by the tightened noose. Therefore they do not dare to propose new laws. But they use the old ones with great care and severity. And for very many years only one new law was proposed. For when there was a law there, that to one digging out an eye, an eye should be dug out in return, and not be punished by a pecuniary fine: But a certain man having two eyes threatened an enemy who had one eye, that he would dig out the only eye he had, this one-eyed man fearing his calamity dared to propose a new law, That if anyone having two eyes should dig out the eye of one having only one, he should be punished by having both eyes dug out, so that the calamity of both might be equal. This they say is the only new law established within more than 200 years. These are the words of Demosthenes.

If such severity existed now, we would not have so many new Dogmatists and Lycurguses concerning wax candles and bells, and similar things, the change of which is absolutely not necessary, and brings no utility.

…And political men command that some small inconveniences be condoned to custom, lest the Republi ca be moved, just as in a sick body, greater evils happen.…

Because we see it was not falsely said by Xenophon: πᾶσαι μεταβολαὶ πολιτειῶν θανατηφόροι (all changes of republics bring slaughter), that is, all changes of republics bring slaughter. Therefore, this saying is also often repeated: An evil well established is not to be moved.

But here it is necessary to add this correction.

When doctrine is impious, and laws establish impious opinions and idols, it is necessary that the rules be preferred: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema.

Item: It is necessary to obey God rather than men. Item: Blasphemy will not be forgiven either in this or in the future age. And when amendment is necessary, the boundaries of the fathers are not transferred, but restored.

Because the doctrine handed down by God to the first fathers is restored, as was said by Tertullian: Everything first is most true. But true antiquity must be diligently inquired into, and it is a great confirmation of faith, having known the series of times of the Church, to choose the testimonies of those who have retained the foundation.

Latin:

Caput XXII.

Melius est nomen bonum, quam divitiae multae.

Recte dicitur: Bona conscientia mihi propter Deum opus est, bona fama propter proximum.

Et sciendum est, Bonam famam esse rem bonam, id est, approbationem ordinatam a Deo, et appetendam esse, quia Deus vult publicis testimoniis ostendi discrimen inter recta et non recta, et vult recte facientes approbari et servari, et non recte facientes vituperari et deleri. Haec testi- monia vult conspici, ut discamus legem, et co- gitemus esse Deum, et qualis sit, et quod sit vindex scelerum.

Est igitur bona fama testimonium divinitus ordinatum, multorum recte iudicantium, appro- bantium recta, et recte facientium, quo testimo- nio muniti sint recte facientes, et eis honestus locus in communi societate tribuatur, ut alii ho- mines doceantur et invitentur ad recta.

Cum igitur bona fama sit approbatio divini- tus ordinata, et multipliciter sit utilis vitae, ma- nifestum est, eam rem bonam et appetendam esse. Ideo et Siracides cap. 41. inquit: Cura sit tibi de bono nomine. Durabilius est enim quam magni thesauri. Causae autem considerentur.

I. Primum quia Deus vult nos honestorum hominum iudicia intueri, ut Siracides cap. 6. in- quit: In coetu seniorum consistito, et si quis est sapiens ei adhaereto. Arrogantia et impu- dentia est, nolle intueri sanorum iudicia.

II. Deinde vult etiam honesta exempla aliis praeberi. Ideo 1. Cor. 10. dicitur: Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite, et non offendite Ecclesiam. Et ad Philip. 4.: Haec curate quae sunt vera, gra- via, iusta, amicabilia, laudabilia, virtutem et laudem.

Primum flagitatur Veritas, quae est verae doctrinae conservatio, et in aliis honestis nego- ciis servare dicta et pacta. Est autem virtus pri- mae tabulae, verae doctrinae conservatio.

Gravitas est constantia in sermone et ge- stibus honestis personae conveniens, et est pars modestiae.

Iusticia particularis est, neminem iniuria afficere.

Castitas est vitare prohibitas libidines.

Amicabilia nominat Beneficentiam et Ἐπιείκειαν, sine qua non potest retineri con- cordia.

Laudabilia nominat virtutem, quae est diligentia vitandi scandala, quae nominatur φιλο- τιμία, honesta appetitio honoris seu bonae famae.

Postea expresse nominat Paulus Virtutem et Laudem, ut significet, recte factis, non nani ostentatione bonam famam parandam esse.

Sic et Romanos 14. inquit: Qui in his seruit Christo, placet Deo, et probatus est hominibus, ubi etiam vult, nos iudicia honestorum hominum intueri et vereri. Haec qui non intuentur sunt arrogantes et impudentes. Ideo recte dictum est in Tragoedia Senecae: Levis est, nec illum sti- mulat gloriae decus.

Meminerint iuniores et congruentes senten- tias in aliis scriptis, ut in versu Publii: Honestus rumor alterum patrimonium est. Et Plautus: Honestam famam si servasso, sat ero dives. Et Hesiodus praecipit vitare malam famam, et addit, communem famam non prorsus inanem esse: φήμη δ᾽ οὔτις πάμπαν ἀπόλλυται, ἥντινα πολλοὶ λαοὶ φημίζουσι, θεὸς νύ τις ἐστὶ καὶ αὐτή.

Dives et pauper simul sunt, et Deus facit utrunque.

Res secundae iniustorum et calamitates iu- storum turbant assensionem de providentia Dei, et alii alias causas eventuum quaerunt, et multi ad physicas causas et fata decurrunt. Sciendum est igitur, Deum proposuisse testimonia provi- dentiae in operibus ordinariis et extraordinariis, et in expresso verbo suo.

Ordinaria opera ostendunt praesentiam Dei, ut hic ipse pulcerrimus ordo corporum mun- di, vices hyemis et aestatis, foecundatio annua terrae, conservatio societatis humanae, poenae homicidarum, lex et iudicium conscientiae in sin- gulis, generatio et prima nutricatio sobolis etc.

Deinde Extraordinaria opera magis in- currunt in oculos, ut omnia miracula, eductio populi ex Aegypto, resuscitatio mortuorum, et alia.

Et cum haec facta testentur, vera esse dicta divina, sint in conspectu multae sententiae, quae affirmant, non casu res secundas et adversas acci- dere, sed regi haec quoque consilio Dei. Haec fides luceat in cordibus, et petat et expectet bonos eventus a Deo.

Sic Ieremias inquit in Threnis: Quis est iste, qui dicit, Ex ore Domini non egredientur bona et mala?

Et Zophoniae 1.: Scrutabor Hierusalem lu- cernis, et visitabo viros defixos in fecibus suis, qui dicunt in cordibus suis: Non faciet Dominus bene et non faciet male.

Item Psalmo 32.: De coelo respicit Dominus, videt omnes filios hominum.

Item Matthaei 10.: Unus de istis passeribus non cadet super terram, sine voluntate patris mei. Item: Omnes capilli capitis vestri numerati sunt. His et similibus testimoniis confirmemus nos contra Epicureos furores. Intueamur et man- data Dei de petendis corporalibus ab ipso, et pro- missiones, quae etiam sunt testimonia provi- dentiae. Deinde hoc sciamus, de voluntate Dei iudi- candum esse ex ipsius verbo, sicut dicitur: Lu- cerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Necesse est igitur obtemperare verbo Dei, etiamsi iusti saepe duriter affliguntur, quia certae causae sunt, quare Deus Ecclesiam vult subiectam esse cruci. Et nota sit sententia: Multae tribulationes iustorum, sed ex omnibus illis liberavit eos Deus. Quanquam igitur Lazarus est pauper, tamen non propterea abiiciat assensionem de providen- tia, sed iudicet ex verbo Dei, quod affirmat esse providentiam, et sequuturam esse liberationem. Haec in verbo expresse tradita sunt. Quare autem ipse sit pauper, et non habeat imperium Tyberii, non est scrutandum. Sed tenenda est regula Si- racidae capite 3.: Quae mandata sunt tibi haec cogita sancte. Non enim necesse est, te occulta aspicere oculis. Ita discernatur inter revelata et non revelata, et in sua vocatione quisque Deo obediat. Haec in summa docet et hoc dictum: Dives et pauper simul sunt, et Deus facit utrunque, id est: Scito esse providentiam, nec casu alios divites, alios pauperes esse, sed Dei consilio, et suo quisque loco recte serviat, iuxta dictum: Qua vocatione quisque vocatus est, in ea am- bulet.
