Pauper non fremat adversus Deum, sed obediat huic dicto: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, et hanc consolationem teneat. Beati pauperes spiritu, quia talium est regnum coelo- rum. Item Proverbiorum 17.: Qui despicit pau- perem, exprobrat factori eius. Et Proverb. 15.: Melius est parum cum timore Dei, quam thesauri magni cum tumultu. Item: Sufficit diei afflictio sua. Item: Orate sine ira et sine haesitatione.

Non transferas limites antiquos, quos sta- tuerunt patres tui.

Ad praeceptum, Non furaberis, pertinet et haec prohibitio, ne limites effodiantur, ac con- turbentur fines, sicut expresse dictum est, Deut. 19.: Non transferas terminos etc. Et cap. 27.:

Maledictus qui transfert terminos proximi sui. Et in ff. tit. de termino moto, leges sunt Iulii, Nervae et Adriani de poenis eorum, qui limites effodiunt.

Nec praeceptum obscurum est, sed citatur allegorice, de non mutandis legibus, quas vetu- stas gravi autoritate tradidit, si non sit evidens necessitas. Nam inter praecepta vitae politicae hoc quoque saepe repetitum est, non temere mu- tandas esse veteres leges, ut et versus monet: Mo- ribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque.

Ac nota sit omnibus narratio quae extat apud Demosthenem in oratione contra Timocratem de Locrensibus, apud quos lex fuit: Ut si quis no- vam legem laturus esset, suaderet eam publice collo inserto in laqueum, ut si non placuisset lex, cives mox strangularent suasorem.

Verba Demosthenis haec sunt. Volo iudi- ces Locrense exemplum vobis narrare. Non enim deteriores eritis audito exemplo, praesertim eius civitatis, quae honestis legibus gubernatur. Illi adeo sentiunt veteres leges retinendas esse, et pa- tria instituta munienda et conservanda esse, nec ferendas esse novas leges ad cupiditates ullorum, aut ad eludendas actiones iniuriarum, ut si quis velit novam legem ferre, cogatur eam suadere collo inserto in laqueum. Quod si populus iudi- cat, legem honestam et utilem esse, discedit sua- sor vivus et incolumis. Sin autem non placet, suasor statim interficitur constricto laqueo. Ideo non audent ferre novas leges. Veteribus autem magna cura et severitate utuntur. Ac valde mul- tis annis tantum una lex nova lata est. Cum enim ibi lex esset, ut effodienti oculum vicissim oculus effoderetur, nec multa pecuniaria puniretur: Qui- dam autem habens duos oculos inimico unoculo minatus est, se ei oculum quem habebat unicum effossurum esse, hic unoculus metuens calamita- tem suam ausus est novam legem suadere, Ut si quis habens geminos effoderet oculum habenti unicum, puniretur effosso utroque oculo, ut aequalis esse utriusque calamitas. Hanc solam dicunt novam legem conditam esse intra annos plures 200. Haec sunt verba Demosthenis.

Talis severitas si nunc esset, non haberemus tot novos Dogmatistas et Lycurgos de cereis et no- lis, et similibus rebus, quarum mutatio prorsus non necessaria est, et nullam adfert utilitatem.

Ac iubent viri politici aliqua parva incom- moda condonare consuetudini, ne mota Republi- velut aegro corpore, maiora mala accidunt.

Quia videmus non falso dictum esse a Xenophonte: πᾶσαι μεταβολαὶ πολιτειῶν θανατηφόροι, id est, omnes mutationes Rerumpublicarum adferunt caedes. Ideo et hoc dictum saepe repetitur: Malum bene conditum non est movendum.

Sed hic necesse est addi hanc correctionem.

Cum doctrina est impia, et leges stabiliunt impias opiniones et idola, necesse est anteferri regulas: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit.

Item: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus. Item: Blasphemia non remittetur neque in hoc neque futuro seculo. Et cum sit necessaria emendatio, non transferuntur limites patrum, sed restituuntur.

Quia doctrina primis patribus a Deo tradita restituitur, sicut dictum est a Tertulliano: Primum quodque verissimum est. Sed diligenter inquirenda est vera antiquitas, et magna est confirmatio fidei, cognita serie temporum Ecclesiae eligere testimonia eorum, qui fundamentum retinuerunt.

## 23:1 Argument
Chapter XXIII.

When you sit to eat with a powerful man, be cautious, and put a knife to your throat, and save your life etc. This is a courtly admonition.

Since the familiarities of the powerful are dangerous, be cautious and circumspect in speaking, as if moving a sword to your throat, lest you say something rashly that brings destruction upon you.

As Alexander killed Clitus in a banquet for contradicting him too freely. There exist many similar admonitions about courtly dangers.

Horace says: The cultivation of a powerful friend is sweet to the inexperienced, The experienced man fears it. etc.

And long is Ovid's elegy: Live for yourself, and as much as you can, avoid high places, A savage lightning bolt comes from a high citadel.

For although the powerful can alone be of benefit, They do not benefit, rather they are accustomed to do the greatest harm etc. And Aesop said to Solon going to Croesus, When speaking with a king, ἢ ὡς ἥκιστα, ἢ ὡς ἥδιστα (either as little as possible, or as sweetly as possible), either as sparingly as possible, or as sweetly as possible.

It is necessary that there be governors and ministers, and God has adorned this rank in such a way that He has granted it the fellowship of His own name.

I said, You are gods, that is, having a divine office. And those called to offices should be faithful, prudent, and modest. But it is to be lamented that in this highest station few perform their duty correctly, and very many are either slothful or cruel.

And it is a wonder that the devil rages so horribly in that seat of God, as the examples of all ages show. And because many abuse power, they draw upon themselves tragic punishments.

There are, therefore, many complaints about the inconstancy of fortune in courts.

These are the verses of Seneca in Agamemnon: Not so does the sea rage on the Libyan Syrtes, Rolling alternating waves, Not does the wave of the Euxine swell from the lowest Depths, stirred up, near the snowy Pole, where the bright Bootes turns his wagon Free from the azure waters: As Fortune rotates The precipitous falls of kings.

Although, however, there are many dangers in courts, yet common evils in human natures are Ambition and Pride.

Ambition desires high things: as Seneca says, that the minds of men tend upward, because they are fiery. Pride in those who have power is to abuse their position, and to take for themselves unjust license, which punishments follow afterward. Solomon, therefore, in order to repress ambition and pride, delivers an admonition, by which he commands modesty and circumspection.

But let the rules be noted.

To seek offices for which we are moderately qualified is just.

But our petition should not impede the judgments of those electing, nor should it fight in unjust ways. And such a petition is to indicate oneself, and to show a pious will, and to offer oneself to the fellowship of more difficult labors and huge dangers.

Concerning such a petition it was said: He who desires the Episcopate, desires a good work.

Item: God loves a cheerful giver. Item, Paul to Titus commands to learn honest arts, so that we may be of use in government.

But vicious ambition is to seek in such a way that you desire to impede the judgments of those electing, and to fight in unjust ways, or afterward to break out beyond the boundaries of one's vocation.

Against this ambition it is said: He who exalts himself will be humbled.

Item: Every proud person in heart is an abomination before God. There is also a vicious ambition, which is named ἀξιοσμός (self-estimation), of those who, although they are most ambitious, nevertheless want to appear to flee that which they most desire. Aristotle calls such people βαυκοπανουργους [baucopanourgous], that is, those who feign disdain. Furthermore, those who are elevated usually abuse their power for private desires, just as David indulged himself in his kingdom, and many others even more so.

Here let us be mindful of the saying of the son of Sirach, chapter 3: The greater you are, the more you should humble yourself, thus finding grace before God. Let the saying of Plutarch also be known: A prince should imitate the sun, which, when it reaches its highest point in the northern part, is slower, so that it may be more secure: imitating the sun of the ruler, who, when he takes the greatest height, having risen in the north, moves the least, by a slower course establishing his path in safety.

Do not be anxious in your mind, so that you may become rich, let go of your own prudence.

Previously he preached about Pride.

Here he preaches about Avarice.

However, this sentence by no means prohibits diligence and labor according to one's calling, nor diligence in one's calling. For it is very often expressly commanded to be diligent and to labor, as the example of the ant is proposed above.

And in Ecclesiastes chapter nine. Item: Let those who are in charge be diligent. Item: Diligence, not sloth, etc.

And 1 Cor. 4: This is required, that we be faithful.

The parable of the Talents, Matthew 25, also pertains to this. Let us know, however, that labors will be happy when the help of God is added, according to the saying of the Psalm: Unless the Lord builds the house, etc.

Therefore, he wants the invocation of God and our diligence in the labors of our callings to be joined, according to the saying: Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act. He prohibits πολυπραγμοσύνην [polypragmosynen - meddling] and unjust grasping, which a man seeks because he distrusts God, and is tormented by this distrust.

He censures this distrust, not diligence in commanded labor. Therefore, this Solomon says here that human plans, namely those undertaken outside of one's calling and which are unjust, are vain, and that riches flee like eagles flying away. Therefore, he calls us back to the goals of our calling, and to seeking the help of God, and to the diligence and prudence divinely commanded.

Do not eat bread with an envious man, nor desire his food, because in his soul it is like a phantom, etc.

Above he said that the familiarities of the powerful or courtly are dangerous, then he warned not to seek power and wealth outside of one's calling. Now he warns that envious people are to be avoided.

For there are envious people who grieve that other good or mediocre people excel in some gift or virtue, or in other good things. Cain grieves that his brother excels in this great glory, because God adorned him with this public testimony. This grief is the cause of horrible evils in life, as the examples of Cain, Esau, Saul, Marius, Pompey, and countless similar ones show. But the source of envy is Pride.

For because all men want to excel, and are φιλαρχικοί [philarchikoi - ambitious for power], just as the devil addresses Eve: You will be like Gods. And Seneca says: Human souls are fiery, and therefore tend upward: Men grieve when they see others excel, and especially when it happens that they themselves are cast down.

Therefore it is written in Sirach: Pride is the beginning of all sin. And so common are the evils of pride and envy, that it has been said in a Greek verse, that envy always accompanies all honorable things: ἀεὶ τὰ σεμνὰ πάντα ἕπεται φθόνος [aiei ta semna panta hepeta phthonos].

And Cicero says: It is the blight and stain of this age to envy virtue. But this grief is unjust here, because it gives what is due neither to God nor to men.

As, Cain does not give thanks to God who gives testimony of His presence, and of the gathering of the Church. Nor does he want his brother to have the gifts given by God, and afterwards, raging, he tries to take him away.

Thus also Saul does not give thanks to God for the many benefits which He gives to the Church through David and his testimonies, and grants many victories to his kingdom. Nor does he want David to have those gifts handed down by God; he is inflamed with indignation, and plots against his life. A neighboring vice is ἐπιχαιρεκακία [epichairekakia], that is, joy in the calamity of the just or those who are tolerable, just as the devil is most manifestly ἐπιχαιρεκακος [epichairekakos]. These vices are condemned in this place, and warnings are given about avoiding the company of the envious and the suspicious.

Item, about showing true benevolence of heart in all duties. As the beginnings of other virtues are from judgment, will, and heart: so also beneficence ought to [arise] from the same sources. Therefore it is written: God loves a cheerful giver. And most sweet is the Greek saying: 'The spirit of graces is best.' The mind in benefits should be best. And among Seneca is read the saying of Fabius, who says: 'A benefit proudly given by a harsh man is like stony bread.'

Let there be, therefore, in giving benefits a benevolent will, eager to help, favoring the salvation of others. And when it is such, if the recognition of God, faith, love of common salvation, and a will referring these duties to the glory of God shine in the breast, this virtue becomes the worship of God.

But on the contrary, in an envious, malevolent, and suspicious man, there is a great confusion of the worst affections. Therefore he says here: 'In such a heart there is a specter.'

And indeed, in reality, such a heart is a sewer of the devil.

Therefore it is written in John: 'He who does not love his brother is a murderer.' And it is most manifest that many calamities arise from such people, when malevolence indulges in suspicions, and reasons falsely, and in order to fortify itself, attempts to destroy others, about whom it suspects evil. And it is a singular happiness to avoid such people, as he says here: 'Do not eat bread with an envious man.' And let there be moderate diligence in considering the wills of men, just as Christ says: 'Be simple as doves,' that is, without malevolence, 'and prudent as serpents,' which protect their head, and among many in a crowd recognize their enemy, and attack him, leaving the others aside.

Latin:

Caput XXIII.

Cum sedes ut comedas cum potente, sis cautus, et pone cultrum in gutture tuo, et serves vitam tuam etc. Aulica admonitio est.

Cum periculosae sint familiaritates potentum, sis cautus et circumspectus in loquendo, tanquam gladium gutturi admovens, quid temere dicas, quod tibi exitium adfert.

Ut Alexander Clitum liberius contradicentem in convivio interfecit. Extant similes admonitiones multae de aulicis periculis.

Horatius inquit: Dulcis inexpertis cultura potentis amici, Expertus metuit. etc.

Et langa est Ovidii elegia: Vive tibi, quantumque potes praelustria vita, Saevum praelustri fulmen ab arce venit.

Nam quamvis soli possunt prodesse potentes, Non prosunt, potius plurimum obesse solent etc. Et Aesopus dixit Soloni eunti ad Croesum, Cum rege loquendum, ἢ ὡς ἥκιστα, ἢ ὡς ἥδιστα, aut quam parcissima, aut quam dulcissima.

Necesse est esse gubernatores et ministros, et Deus hunc gradum sic ornavit, ut tribuerit ei societatem sui nominis.

Ego dixi Dii estis, id est, habentes officium divinum. Et vocati ad officia sint fideles, prudentes et modesti. Sed dolendum est, quod in hoc summo fastigio pauci recte faciunt officium, et plurimi sunt vel ignavi, vel crudeles.

Ac mirum est, in illa sede Dei tam horribiliter grassari diabolum, ut ostendunt exempla omnium aetatum. Et quia multi potentia abutuntur, attrahunt tragicas poenas.

Sunt igitur multae querelae de inconstantia fortunae in aulis.

Versus Senecae hi sunt in Agamemnone: Non sic Libycis Syrtibus aequor Furit alternos voluere fluctus, Non Euxini turget ab imis Commota vadis unda, nivali Vicina polo, ubi caeruleis Immunis aquis lucida versat Plaustra Bootes: Ut praecipites regum casus Fortuna rotat.

Quanquam autem multum est periculorum in aulis, tamen communia mala sunt in hominum naturis Ambitio et Fastus.

Ambitio appetit celsa: sicut Seneca inquit, hominum animos sursum tendere, quia sint ignei. Fastus in his qui habent potentiam, est abuti loco, et sibi iniustam licentiam sumere, quam postea sequuntur poenae. Salomon igitur ut reprimat ambitionem et fastum, tradit admonitionem, qua praecipit modestiam et circumspectionem.

Sint autem notae regulae.

Petere officia ad quae mediocriter idonei sumus, iustum est.

Sed petitio nostra non impediat iudicia eligentium, non pugnet iniustis modis. Ac talis petitio est indicare sese, et ostendere piam voluntatem, et offerre sese ad societatem difficiliorum laborum et ingentium periculorum.

De tali petitione dictum est: Qui Episcopatum desiderat, honestum opus desiderat.

Item: Hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Item, Paulus ad Titum iubet discere honestas artes, ut possimus esse usui in gubernatione.

Sed vitiosa ambitio est, ita petere, ut cupias impedire iudicia eligentium, et pugnare iniustis modis, aut postea extra vocationem metas erumpere.

Contra hanc ambitionem dicitur: Qui se exaltat humiliabitur.

Item: Abominatio est coram Deo omnis superbus corde. Est et vitiosa ambitio, quae nominatur ἀξιοσμός, illorum, qui cum sint ambitiosissimi, tamen volunt videri defugere id, quod maxime appetunt. Tales nominat Aristoteles βαυκοπανουργους, id est, ficte fastidientes. Praeterea qui sunt evecti deinde plerumque abutuntur potestate ad privatas cupiditates, sicut David in regno sibi... indulsuit, et multo magis alii.

Hic simus memores dicti Siracidae, capite 3.: Quo maior es, tanto magis te humilia, sic inveniens gratiam coram Deo. Notum sit etiam Plutarchi dictum: Princeps imitetur solem, qui cum in summum fastigium venit in parte boreali tardior est, ut sit securior: μιμουμένου τὸν ἥλιον τοῦ ἄρχοντος, ὃς ὅταν ὕψωμα λάβῃ μέγιστον, ἐξαρθεὶς ἐν τοῖς βορείοις, ἐλάχιστα κινεῖται, τῷ σχολαιοτέρῳ τὸν δρόμον εἰς ἀσφαλὲς καθιστάμενος.

Non angaris animo, ut fias dives, prudentiam tuam omillito.

Antea de Superbia concionatus est.

Hic concionatur de Avaricia.

Nequaquam autem prohibet haec sententia sedulitatem et laborem iuxta vocationem, neque diligentiam in vocatione. Saepissime enim expresse praecipitur de diligentia et labore, ut supra formicae exemplum proponitur.

Et in Ecclesiastae capite nono. Item: Qui praesunt sint diligentes. Item: Diligentia non ignavi etc.

Et 1. Cor. 4.: Hoc requiritur, ut fideles simus.

Huc et parabola pertinet de Talentis, Matth. 25. Sciamus autem, labores ita felices fore, cum accedit auxilium Dei, iuxta dictum Psalmi: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum etc.

Vult igitur coniungi invocationem Dei et nostram diligentiam in laboribus vocationum, iuxta dictum: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Prohibet autem πολυπραγμοσύνην et iniusta aucupia, quae homo quaerit, quia Deo diffidit, et hac diffidentia cruciatur.

Hanc diffidentiam taxat, non diligentiam in mandato labore. Dicit igitur hic Salomon, humana consilia videlicet extra vocationem suscepta et iniusta, irrita esse, et fugere divitias ceu Aquilas avolantes. Revocat igitur nos ad metas vocationis, et ad petendum auxilium Dei, et ad diligentiam ac prudentiam divinitus praeceptam.

Ne cum invido comedas panem, neque concupiscas cibos eius, quia in anima eius tanquam spectrum est, etc.

Supra dixit, periculosas esse familiaritates potentum seu aulicas, deinde monuit, ne extra vocationem appetamus potentiam et opes. Nunc monet, fugiendos esse invidos.

Sunt autem invidi, qui dolent, alios bonos seu mediocres aliquo dono seu virtute, seu aliis bonis rebus antecellere. Cain dolet, fratrem antecellere hac magna gloria, quod Deus eum hoc publico testimonio ornavit. Hic dolor causa est horribilium malorum in vita, ut ostendunt exempla Cain, Esau, Saul, Marii, Pompeii, et similia innumerabilia.

Est autem fons invidentiae Superbia. Quia enim omnes homines volunt eminere, et sunt φιλαρχικοί, sicut diabolus Evam alloquitur: Eritis sicut Dii. Et Seneca inquit: Humanos animos igneos esse, ac ideo sursum tendere: Dolent homines, cum vident alios antecellere, ac praecipue cum hoc accedit, ut ipsi deiiciantur.

Ideo scriptum est in Siracide: Superbia initium est omnis peccati. Et adeo communia mala sunt superbia et invidentia, ut dictum sit in Graeco versu, omnia honesta semper comitari invidiam: ἀεὶ τὰ σεμνὰ πάντα ἕπεται φθόνος.

Et Cicero inquit: Labes atque macula huius seculi est, invidere virtuti. Ideo autem hic dolor iniustus est, quia nec Deo nec hominibus tribuit debitum.

Ut, Cain non agit gratias Deo edenti testimonium de sua praesentia, et de collectione Ecclesiae. Nec vult fratrem habere dona a Deo data, et postea furens tollere eum conatur. Sic et Saul non agit Deo gratias pro multis beneficii, quod per Davidem et testimonia dat Ecclesiae, et tribuit multas victorias suo regno. Nec vult Davidem habere illa dona a Deo tradita, incenditur indignatione, et insidiatur eius vitae.

Vicinum est vitium ἐπιχαιρεκακία, id est, laeticia in calamitate iustorum seu tolerabilium, ut diabolus manifestissime est ἐπιχαιρεκακος. Haec vitia hoc loco damnantur, et traduntur admonitiones de fugienda societate invidorum et suspicacium.

Item de vera benevolentia cordis in omnibus officiis praestanda. Ut caeterarum virtutum initia sunt a indicio, voluntate et corde: ita et beneficentia debet ex iisdem fontibus oriri. Ideo scriptum est: Hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Et dulcissimum est Graecum dictum: χαρίτων δέ τε θυμὸς ἄριστος. Animus in beneficiis est optimus. Et apud Senecam legitur dictum Fabii, qui inquit: Beneficium superbe datum ab homine duro, simile est pani lapidoso.

Sit igitur in dandis beneficiis voluntas beneficia, cupida iuvandi, favens alienae saluti. Et cum talis est, si luceant in pectore agnitio Dei, fides, amor communis salutis, et voluntas referens ad gloriam Dei haec officia, fit haec virtus cultus Dei.

Contra vero in homine invido, malevolo et suspicaci, magna confusio est pessimorum affectuum. Ideo hic dicit: In tali corde spectrum esse.

Et quidem reipsa tale cor cloaca est diaboli.

Ideo scriptum est in Iohanne: Qui non diligit fratrem, homicida est. Et manifestissimum est, multum calamitatum a talibus oriri, cum malevolentia indulget suspicionibus, et falsa ratiocinatur, et ut se muniat, alios delere conatur, de quibus male suspicatur. Et singularis felicitas est tales cavere, ut hic dicit: Ne comedas cum invido panem tuum. Et sit mediocris diligentia in considerandis hominum voluntatibus, sicut Christus inquit: Estote simplices sicut columbae, id est, sine malevolentia, et prudentes sicut serpentes, qui caput tuentur, et inter multos in turba agnoscunt hostem suum, et illum petunt, caeteris omissis.

## 24:1 Argument
Chapter XXIV.

Deliver those who are drawn to death, and those who are rushing to slaughter, when you can.

These precepts are known: 'Do not kill,' etc. 'Do not share in the sins of others.'

God commands both the magistrate and private individuals not to kill the innocent. He also commands not to aid unjust cruelty.

But when and in what order the magistrate ought to remove the guilty, an explanation is added to the Decalogue, as in Deut. 19 and elsewhere.

But let the magistrate be the guardian of the life of the innocent, as it is written in Rom. 13: 'He is God's minister, an avenger for punishment to him who does evil.' And let private men, without sedition, as much as they can according to their vocation, oppose unjust cruelty.

Examples of this matter are cited worthy of consideration. Jonathan opposes his father, and not only by testimony, but also by other duties helps David, without sedition.

Obadiah secretly fed the Prophets, driven out by Jezebel. A eunuch draws Jeremiah out of prison.

The Egyptian midwives save the Israelite infants. Rahab saves the Israelite scouts.

In the time of Diocletian, a nobleman in the city of Nicomedia in Bithynia publicly tore down the emperor's edict about killing Christians, to show that he disapproved of unjust cruelty. A contrary example is Doeg, who, doing the will of Saul's fury, cruelly killed the innocent priests.

Thus, many at this time confirm unjust cruelty, which is exercised against our Churches, either openly or by their silence. Let these people consider this saying of Solomon and similar ones, and, being warned by the most sad threat of Christ, let them amend themselves.

For it is written in Matthew 23: 'All the righteous blood shed upon the earth will come upon them, from the blood of righteous Abel even to Zachariah.' Also worthy of memory is the most honest voice of Trajan, who, giving a sword to the Master of the Horse, said: 'I hand this sword to you, that you may use it for me when I do what is just: but use it against me if I do what is unjust.'

'Do not lie in wait impiously for the dwelling of the just: for seven times the just man falls and rises again,' etc. He repeats the precept: 'Do not kill,' with an added warning about epikhairekakia (rejoicing in evil) and sarcasm.

For when impious and cruel men see the calamities of the pious, they rejoice in this very deformity of theirs, and become more rabid, just as Shimei curses David. For when he says: 'He falls seven times a day,' he speaks especially of the evil of punishment, that is, of calamities.

And yet sometimes evils of fault occur, which attract calamities. Yet from these the just man emerges, like David, Manasseh, and countless others.

'Fear the Lord, my son, and the king, and do not mix with the seditious: For their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of the seditious.' This sentence is also to be observed among the most important of this book, which commands obedience, and indeed ordains it. First, He commands to obey God, and then the king, because the primary duty, even of a political governor, is that he himself be the voice of the Decalogue, and punish those who violate the Decalogue. And for this primary reason God has subjected the multitude to magistrates, because He wishes His law to be heard and understood, so that He Himself may be acknowledged. A second reason, then, is that the society of the human race may not be dissipated by infinite tumults. God has ordained, however, that we obey for His sake, and that we know He punishes the contumacious. He has also surrounded power with limits, so that it may not command things contrary to divine mandates. Therefore it is said here first: Fear God. Wherefore the rule of the Apostles is also comprehended here: It is necessary to obey God rather than men.

However, the entire doctrine concerning the causes of political order and magistrates, which is recited more copiously in Romans 13 and elsewhere, must be considered in this place.

But specifically, it commands here to avoid the seditious, where it is necessary to judge in dissensions who are the seditious.

And judgment is easier in political affairs, because the ordinary power stands far above the multitude and is seen with the eyes.

And it is manifest what the duties of ordinary power are, namely: To sound the voice of the Decalogue, and to punish the contumacious. Item, to enact proper laws not conflicting with the Decalogue, and to punish the contumacious. Item, to exercise judgments, and to pass sentences according to the laws. And in doubtful matters, sentences are valid not only because of probable reason, but also because of the authority divinely attributed to magistrates, whom God wishes us to obey in civil affairs even when they were previously doubtful. And because God sometimes gives more peaceful and mild empires, and sometimes less, He wishes us also to bear certain harder burdens, provided they are tolerable, and are not atrocious and notorious injuries, and obedience is not a sin. Concerning these, the rule of Paul must be held: It is necessary to obey, not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience. But the contumacious sin, that is, those not willing to obey legitimate empires, and the seditious sin more, that is, those who are contumelious against magistrates in words, or who attempt to remove them by force, factions, and arms.

To these, He threatens punishment in this place, just as the Lord says: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword, that is, he who draws a sword not given by the laws, as perished Absalom, Seba, Adonias, Joab, Cassius, Brutus, and innumerable others.

But against atrocious and notorious injuries, defense is conceded, as the written law in the Digest (ff.) concedes that a Consul caught in adultery may be killed by the father of the woman. And Marius absolved the youth who killed a military Tribune in defense of chastity. Victorinus, governor of Germany, was killed in Cologne by a scribe whose wife he had violated, although otherwise his virtue is so praised that it is compared to Nerva and Trajan.

But the Gospel concedes the use of political laws, when they are congruent with reason. Indeed, if such defense were not conceded, the Gospel would be transformed into a political doctrine, and would stabilize infinite tyranny. But this dispute is spoken of more copiously elsewhere.

But concerning the reprehension of errors in the Church, it must be known that those who oppose Princes and Bishops defending errors do not sin at all. For it is necessary to obey God in the confession of truth, just as the Apostles say: It is necessary to obey God rather than men. Item: If anyone denies me before men, I also will deny him before my heavenly Father. Item: If anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him. Item: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. By these mandates of God, let us confirm ourselves against the clamors of Kings and Bishops, who vociferate that we are seditious because by teaching and confession we tax errors and idols, just as God commands.

Let us know, however, that the ministers of the Gospel do not bear the sword, and when those who hold ordinary power exercise cruelty, injuries must be tolerated, according to these sayings, 2 Cor. 10: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal. Item: As the Father sent me, so I send you. And: My kingdom is not of this world.

Latin:

Caput XXIV.

Libera eos qui trahuntur ad mortem, et qui properant ad necem, cum potes.

Nota sunt haec praecepta: Non occidas etc. Non communices alienis peccatis.

Deus et magistratui et privatis praecipit, non occidere innocentem. Praecipit etiam non adiuvare iniustam crudelitatem.

Quando autem et quo ordine magistratus tollere debeat sontes, addita est Decalogo explicatio, ut Deut. 19. et alibi.

Sit autem magistratus custos vitae innocentum, sicut scriptum est Rom. 13.: Dei minister est, vindex ad poenam ei, qui male facit. Et privati homines sine seditione, quantum possunt pro vocatione, adversentur iniustae saevitiae.

Eius rei exempla recitantur digna consideratione. Ionathas adversatur patri suo, et non solum testimonio, sed etiam aliis officiis iuvat Davidem, sine seditione.

Abdias clam pavit Prophetas, pulsos a Iesabel. Ieremiam Eunuchus extrahit ex carcere.

Aegyptiae obstetrices servant infantes Israëliticos. Rahab servat exploratores Israëliticos.

Tempore Diocletiani vir nobilis in urbe Bithyniae Nicomedia, edictum imperatoris de interficiendis Christianis publice concerpsit, ut ostenderet, se iniustam crudelitatem improbare. Contrarium exemplum est Doëg, qui furori Saul morem gerens, crudeliter interfecit innocentes sacerdotes.

Ita multi hoc tempore iniustam saevitiam, quae exercetur adversus nostras Ecclesias, confirmant aut palam, aut suo silentio. Hi cogitent hoc dictum Salomonis et similia, et commonefacti tristissima comminatione Christi emendent se.

Scriptum est enim Matthaei 23.: Veniet super eos omnis sanguis iustus effusus super terram inde usque a nece Abel iusti, usque ad Zachariam. Digna memoria est etiam honestissima vox Traiani, qui dans gladium Magistro equitum: Hunc, inquit, gladium tibi trado, ut eo pro me utaris, cum iusta facio: Contra me vero utaris, si iniusta facio.

Ne insidieris impie habitaculo iusti: septies enim cadit iustus et resurgit etc. Repetit praeceptum: Non occidas, addita commonefactione de ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ et σαρκασμῷ.

Cum enim vident impii et saevi homines calamitates piorum, hac ipsa deformitate eorum laetantur, et fiunt rabiosiores, sicut Semei maledicit Davidi. Cum enim inquit: Septies in die cadit, praecipue de malo poenae, id est, de calamitatibus, loquitur.

Et tamen accedunt interdum mala culpae, quae attrahunt calamitates. Ex his tamen emergit iustus, ut David, Manasse, et alii innumerabiles.

Time Dominum fili, et regem, et cum seditiosis ne commiscearis: Quia subito veniet exitium eorum, et ruinam seditiosorum quis novit. Est et haec sententia inter praecipuas huius libri observanda, quae praecipit obedientiam, et quidem ordinat eam. Primum iubet Deo obedire, et deinde regi, quia primum officium est, etiam politici gubernatoris, ut ipse sit vox Decalogi, et puniat violantes Decalogum. Ac propter hanc causam praecipuam Deus subiecit multitudinem magistratibus, quia vult exaudiri et intelligi suam legem, ut ipse agnoscatur. Altera causa deinde est, Ne societas generis humani infinitis tumultibus dissipetur. Sanxit autem Deus, ut propter ipsum obediamus, et sciamus eum punire contumaces. Circumdedit etiam metas potestati, ne praecipiat contraria mandatis divinis. Ideo prius hic dicitur: Time Deum. Quare et Apostolorum regula hic comprehenditur: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus.

Cogitanda est autem hoc loco integra doctrina de causis politici ordinis, et de magistratibus, quae Roman.

13. et alibi copiosius recitata est. Nominatim autem hic praecipit, vitare seditiosos, ubi necesse est in dissensionibus iudicari, qui sint seditiosi.

Et facilior diiudicatio est in politicis negotiis, quia ordinaria potestas longe eminet supra multitudinem, et conspicitur oculis.

Ac manifestum est, quae sint officia ordinariae potestatis, scilicet: Sonare vocem Decalogi, et punire contumaces. Item, proprias leges ferre non pugnantes cum Decalogo, et punire contumaces. Item, exercere iudicia, et ferre sententias iuxta leges. Ac in dubiis rebus valent sententiae non solum propter probabilem rationem, sed etiam propter autoritatem divinitus attributam magistratibus, cui vult Deus in civilibus negotiis etiam antea dubiis nos obedire. Et quia Deus alias dat magis placida et mitia imperia, alias minus, vult nos etiam quaedam duriora onera ferre, modo sint tolerabilia, et non sint atroces et notoriae iniuriae, et obedientia non sit peccatum.

De his regula Pauli tenenda est: Necesse est obedire, non solum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam. Peccant autem contumaces, id est, non volentes obedire legitimis imperiis, et plus peccant seditiosi, id est, qui contra magistratus contumeliosi sunt verbis, aut qui vi, factionibus et armis eos excutere conantur. His poenam hoc loco minatur, sicut et Dominus inquit: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit, id est, qui gladium stringit, non datum a legibus, ut perierunt Absalon, Seba, Adonias, Ioab, Cassius, Brutus, et alii innumerabiles.

Sed contra iniurias atroces et notorias concessa est defensio, ut lex scripta in ff. concedit interfici Consulem deprehensum in adulterio a patre mulieris. Et Marius absolvit adolescentem, qui Tribunum militarem in defensione pudiciciae interfecit. Victorinus praeses Germaniae in Colonia Agrippina interfectus est a scriba, cuius uxorem compresserat, cum alioqui adeo laudetur eius virtus, ut Nervae et Traiano conferatur.

Concedit autem Evangelium uti legibus politicis, cum ratione congruentibus. Imo si talis defensio non esset concessa, transformaretur Evangelium in doctrinam politicam, et stabiliret infinitam tyrannidem. Sed de hac disputatione alias copiosius dicitur.

Sed de reprehensione errorum in Ecclesia sciendum est, nequaquam peccare eos, qui adversantur Principibus et Episcopis defendentibus errores. Necesse est enim obedire Deo in confessione veritatis, sicut Apostoli dicunt: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus. Item: Si quis negabit me coram hominibus, negabo et ego eum coram patre meo coelesti. Item: Si quis dixerit blasphemiam contra Spiritum sanctum, non remittetur ei. Item: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. His mandatis Dei confirmemus nos contra clamores Regum et Episcoporum, qui vociferantur nos seditiosos esse, quia docendo et confessione taxamus errores et idola, sicut Deus praecipit.

Sciamus autem, ministros Evangelii non gerere gladium, et cum illi qui tenent ordinariam potestatem, exercent saevitiam, iniurias tolerandas esse, iuxta haec dicta, 2. Cor. 10.: Arma militiae nostrae non sunt carnalia. Item: Sicut pater misit me, sic ego mitto vos. Et: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo.

## 25:1 Argument
Chapter XXV. The glory of the Lord is to conceal a word, But the glory of kings is to search it out.

The doctrine proper to the Church of God differs from human wisdom, and often in government even outstanding men err, preferring political wisdom to the word of God, just as Nebuchadnezzar instituted a cult, dreaming that a similarity of ceremonies would be profitable for the concord of the kingdom.

Thus heretics bend the Gospel to their own imaginations. Here, therefore, he warns that the Word of God is the arcane wisdom, and is to be learned with true study; that is, God wants us to be disciples of His voice, He does not want us to prefer our own thoughts, and to fashion new dogmas or rites. Thus, it is the glory of kings, and of all who are preeminent, to inquire into arcane wisdom, namely by listening, not by disturbing it with cavils. Just as Paul also commands: Let the wisdom of God dwell in you, that is, let the sources be wisely inquired into, and let the testimonies be compared, and let us remember that we ought to be disciples of the divine voice, as Solomon says: The wise man who listens will be wiser.

Human wisdom in David commanded that Saul be killed, but the Holy Spirit in David did not want such an example to be shown among the people of God.

Latin:

Caput XXV. Gloria Domini est verbum celare, At gloria regum est inquirere illud.

Differt doctrina propria Ecclesiae Dei ab humana sapientia, et saepe in gubernatione errant praesertim praestantes homines, anteferentes sapientiam politicam verbo Dei, sicut Nabuchodonosor instituit cultum, somnians ad regni concordiam profuturam esse similitudinem ceremoniarum.

Sic haeretici flectunt Evangelium ad suas imaginationes. Hic igitur monet, Verbum Dei esse sapientiam arcanam, et discendam vero studio, id est, vult Deus nos discipulos esse suae vocis, non vult nos anteferre nostras cogitationes, et fingere nova dogmata seu ritus. Sic gloria regum est, omnium praestantium, inquirere arcanam sapientiam, scilicet audiendo, non turbando cavillationibus. Sicut et Paulus praecipit: Sapientia Dei habitet in vobis, id est, sapienter inquirantur fontes, et conferantur testimonia, et meminerimus, nos debere discipulos esse vocis divinae, sicut Salomon inquit: Audiens sapiens sapientior erit.

Humana sapientia in Davide iubebat interfici Saulem, sed Spiritus sanctus in Davide, noluit tale exemplum ostendere in populo Dei.

## 25:20
Vinegar upon Nitre, singing to a heart that is wrong.

The natures of salt and nitre are similar; they gnaw and burn bodies, and there is a singular power in nitre to repel, and it is irritated by vinegar and lime, as Pliny says: For ulcers that spread, apply nitre with lime and vinegar. This similitude therefore signifies that when the stubborn are admonished, they only become more rabid, just as nitre, when ignited, is dissipated and repelled much more vehemently by the infusion of vinegar, on account of antiperistasis.

Thus Saul, when admonished, becomes much more savage. Such are many of the impious, in whom furies grow when they are admonished.

However, this sentiment does not forbid the true doctrine from being taught.

But it speaks of the fact or event, and shows that listeners are different; some are docile, others are stubborn and do not want to be taught, as it is said in Romans 11 concerning the blasphemous: Their eyes have been blinded, so that they may not see.

Although, as I have said, this sentiment does not forbid the true doctrine from being taught, it nevertheless signifies that listeners must be discerned. The docile are to be instructed piously and diligently, as Paul says: Him who is weak in faith, receive. Concerning other blasphemers, it has been said: Do not give what is holy to dogs. And Proverbs 13: Do not speak to the ears of a fool, for he despises the wisdom of your speech. And yet, before you can discern the listeners, the doctrine must be proposed to all. Afterwards, let us follow the rule of Paul: A heretical man, after one or two admonitions, avoid.

Latin:

Acetum super Nitrum, canens carnem cordi pravo.

Salis et Nitri naturae similes sunt, rodunt et urunt corpora, et singularis vis est Nitrii in pellendo, et irritatur aceto et calce, sicut inquit Plinius: Ulceribus quae serpunt Nitrum cum calce et aceto illini. Significat igitur haec similitudo, pertinaces cum admonentur, tantum fieri rabiosiores, ut Nitrum incensum infuso aceto multo vehementius dissipatur et pellitur propter ἀντιπερίστασιν.

Sic Saul admonitus fit multo saevior. Tales multi sunt impii, in quibus crescunt furores cum admonentur.

Non prohibet autem haec sententia doceri veram doctrinam.

Sed loquitur de facto seu eventu, et ostendit, dissimiles esse auditores, alios esse dociles, alios pertinaces nolle doceri, ut Rom. 11. dicitur de blasphemis: Excoecati sunt oculi eorum, ne videant.

Etsi autem ut dixi haec sententia non prohibet doceri veram doctrinam, tamen significat discernendos esse auditores. Dociles pie et sedulo erudiendi sunt, ut Paulus inquit: Infirmum in fide assumito. De aliis blasphemis dictum est: Non detis sanctum canibus. Et Proverb. 13.: Auribus stulti ne loquaris, quia contemnit sapientiam eloquii tui. Et tamen priusquam auditores discernere possis, omnibus doctrina proponenda est. Postea sequamur regulam Pauli: Haereticum hominem post unam atque alteram admonitionem, vitato.

## 25:26
A troubled fountain and a muddy spring is the just man falling before the impious.

It is manifest that the minds of all the wise are greatly troubled by the deformity of the Church when they see empires, wealth, and wisdom in the hands of the impious: meanwhile, the Church is small, wretched, and without a certain empire, scattered among the most dissimilar nations. Likewise, that innocent men are killed by the most base tyrants: the infants of the Israelites by Pharaoh, the Baptist by Herod, Paul by Nero. These wondrous spectacles move the wise to think that these miserable men are not a care to God.

But the divine voice teaches that the true Church is there where God has manifested Himself by an issued promise and illustrious testimonies, by the resurrection of the dead and other things, and that this is a care to God, and is heard, protected, and is an heir of eternal glory before God: and indeed that it is small, and subject to the cross for certain causes.

Let us confirm ourselves by these divine testimonies against these spectacles, which are usually called the Scandal of the cross, and let us be mindful of these sayings. Matthew 11: You have hidden these things from the wise, and have revealed them to little ones. Likewise 1 Corinthians 1: Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, etc. To this pertains the whole doctrine of Paul in chapter 9 to the Romans and many Psalms. As: Do not emulate those who do evil. Likewise Psalm 72: My feet were almost moved.

Thus it happens privately. When David is driven into exile, the impious delight in his calamity, and mock him with manifest sarcasms. These judgments are described by this image: A muddy fountain is the just man before the impious. But let the pious hold to true consolations, and let them know what the Church is, and let them consider the causes why it is subject to the cross, and from where firm consolations are to be sought.

1. First, because He wants sin to be acknowledged, which still clings to this nature of men.

2. Because the Church often has manifest lapses, and God wants us to be recalled to repentance.

3. Because He wants to be invoked, and to show His presence in miseries, which cannot be healed by human counsel.

4. Because He wants the testimonies of the Saints to be necessary concerning doctrine, and concerning the coming judgment.

Latin:

Fons conturbatus et scaturigo lutulenta iustus cadens coram impio.

Manifestum est, valde turbari omnium sapientum mentes deformitate Ecclesiae cum vident imperia, opes, sapientiam penes impios esse: interea vero Ecclesiam exiguam, aerumnosam, sine certo imperio sparsam in dissimilimas gentes. Item, a turpissimis tyrannis innocentes homines interfici, Israëlitarum infantes a Pharaone, Baptistam ab Herode, Paulum a Nerone. Haec mirabilia spectacula movent sapientes, ut cogitent, hos miseros homines non esse Deo curae.

Sed docet vox divina, ibi esse veram Ecclesiam, ubi se Deus edita promissione et illustribus testimoniis, resuscitatione mortuorum et aliis patefecit, et hanc esse Deo curae, et exaudiri, protegi, et haeredem esse aeternae gloriae apud Deum: et quidem exiguam esse, et subiectam esse cruci propter certas causas.

His divinis testimoniis nos confirmemus adversus haec spectacula, quae usitate nominantur Scandalum crucis, et simus memores horum dictorum. Matth. 11.: Abscondisti haec a sapientibus, et revelasti ea parvulis. Item 1. Cor. 1.: Non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes etc. Huc pertinet tota doctrina Pauli cap. 9. ad Rom. et multi Psalmi. Ut: Noli aemulari in malignantibus. Item Psalmo 72.: Moti erant pene pedes mei.

Ita fit privatim. Cum David pellitur in exilium, delectantur eius calamitate impii, et manifestis sarcasmis ei illudunt. Haec iudicia describuntur hac imagine: Fons lutulentus iustus coram impio. Sed teneant pii veras consolationes, et sciant, qualis sit Ecclesia, et cogitent causas, quare cruci subiecta, et unde sint petendae firmae consolationes.

1. Primum, quia vult agnosci peccatum, quod adhuc haeret in hac natura hominum.

2. Quia saepe et manifestos lapsus habet Ecclesia, et vult nos Deus revocari ad poenitentiam.

3. Quia vult invocari, et ostendere suam praesentiam in aerumnis, quae non possunt humano consilio sanari.

4. Quia vult neces Sanctorum testimonia esse de doctrina, et de venturo iudicio.

## 26:1 Argument
Chapter XXVI.

As snow in summer, as rain in harvest: so glory does not befit a fool. He speaks of the outcome, as in this saying: Fortune makes a fool of him whom she favors too much. For he relates that men not yet chastened or tamed become insolent in prosperous circumstances, and loosen the reins to various desires, just as Alexander, though he had been most modest and mild at the beginning, later wishes to be God, and becomes cruel.

For when men are not troubled, they become secure, they do not seek help from God, and, drunk with successes, they magnify their own counsels and themselves. Therefore, the falls of heroes are great and sad, such as those of Hercules, Nebuchadnezzar, Julius, Pompey, and countless others.

Although he speaks here only of the outcome, which pertains to the rule concerning things that commonly happen, yet he silently includes an admonition or precept concerning modesty, which Sirach recites in chapter 3: The greater you are, the more you humble yourself, and you will find grace before the Lord.

Item: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. And above I cited the saying of Plutarch: Let princes imitate the sun, which, when it comes to the highest point, raised toward the northern part, moves most slowly, so that the slowness makes the course safer.

As a bird flies, and a swallow flits away: so a curse of a fool does not stick.

This rule of life must be held: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience.

Having these, we shall also have the approval of some honest men. And this is to be sought, as Sirach says, in chapter 41: Take care of a good name.

But yet there are always many envious people who try to deform those whom they envy, as Cicero says: It is a certain blight and stain of this age to envy virtue.

And many are by nature virulent, whom slander itself delights. It is a source of gain for many, as Plautus says: That treasure is situated in the tongue of fools, so that they may have it for gain, to speak evil of their betters.

And the verses of Menander are known: ὁ βίος μάλιστα τοῖς πονηροῖς ἥδεται. Life is delighted most by the wicked.

πράττει δ᾽ ὁ κόλαξ ἄριστα πάντων, δεύτερος ὁ συκοφάντης, ὁ κακοήθης τρίτατος. The flatterer does best of all, the slanderer second, the malicious man third. And the histories of all times show that many honest men have been oppressed by calumnies, such as Joseph, Palamedes, Aristides, Theramenes, Socrates, and countless others.

And it is said in Ecclesiastes: Calumny troubles the wise man, and breaks the strength of his heart.

As experience shows, good men are often hindered by calumnies. Here, therefore, a consolation against calumnies is provided, namely, that false slanders, even if they wound for a while, are nevertheless later uncovered and refuted, as it is said: Truth can labor for a time, it cannot be destroyed.

The Psalm adds a sweeter consolation: They will curse, and you will bless.

And David says concerning the insults of Shimei: God will give me something good for these curses.

Let us hold these consolations, but yet in such a way that we retain the integrity of our conscience, as is often commanded: This is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience. And to the Galatians: Let each one test his own work, and thus he will have glory in himself, and not from others, that is: Do rightly, lest your conscience condemn you, and when the conscience is not wounded, you have glory, a cause, namely, not hanging from the foolish applause of others, but such as is the true approval of conscience, and in the believer it is a necessary work, and pleasing to God.

Let us know that these precepts and these consolations are given to us divinely, because calumny is no light torture, even if Truth, once revealed, eventually refutes it. As, when Socrates had been put to death, later the tragedy about Palamedes was presented, in which this verse was recited: You killed, you killed the best of the Greeks, the nightingale that harmed no one.

After this tragedy, the citizens expelled the accusers of Socrates from Athens. Now follow other sayings, which pertain to this purpose, and warn that one must judge wisely when calumny is to be refuted, and when it is not to be refuted.

Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him etc. Two conflicting opinions are recited, which differ for this reason, because sometimes slanders are to be refuted, sometimes it is not necessary to refute, but one must judge prudently whether it should be done.

But the judgment is easy for pastors teaching in a public office.

They always have different listeners, pious, firm, and weak, yet teachable, and stubborn and incurable adversaries, as has been most elegantly said in the Greek les.

ciles [are] however, and [to] stubborn and incurable adversaries.

It is necessary, however, for pastors to serve the better part, where the voice of doctrine, uncorrupted, refutes the adversaries. And let these discern insults. Some tear apart doctrine, others deform the person of the teacher.

There is, however, a mandate concerning illustrating and defending doctrine. 2 Tim. 1: Guard the honest deposit through the Holy Spirit, dwelling in us. To Titus 1: Whose mouths it is necessary to stop. And in the same place: Convince them severely. And to Titus 2: Convince with all authority, that is, commanding with express assertion, so that they may assent to the word.

Let them fight, however, about necessary matters, and let them strive to take up the weak in faith, as Paul says, and let them strive to join [them], not disturb [them] with inextricable dissipations, nor alienate [them] with bitterness. Private insults, however, let them either refute modestly, or pass over entirely, as it is said in the Psalm: They were slandering me, but I was praying.

In other private meetings, however, let Doctors and others consider the differences of the auditors. If there are those who can be healed present, let them be taught rightly.

If, however, anyone falls into an incurable crowd, as John, when he had come into the bath to the crowd of Cerinthus, here, having shown his confession, so that he might not seem to collude with them, as soon as possible, if he can, let him depart from them, according to the saying: Avoid a heretical man after one or another admonition, just as John immediately went out from the bath. Item, Do not give what is holy to dogs.

Especially, however, it is fitting either not to refute private insults, just as David was silent when Shimei was cursing him, or to refute them with few words. And there are many examples of great governors who ignored insults, as Pericles, Fabius, Scipio, and others did. The Lacedaemonians, provoked by Mardonius, who, when he had become more insolent because of the silence of the Lacedaemonians, Herodotus says, [learned] that he was elated by ψυχρῇ νίκῃ, that is, a cold victory. And in the book of Herodotus, a narrative is recounted about a Spartan legate, who had answered Gelon the Sicilian proudly; to this man Gelon says: Reproaches cast at a man are wont to kindle anger: You, however, even if you have affected insult in speech, you will not, however, persuade [me] to do unseemly things by compensating for insults.

Furthermore, for the most part, men are driven to insults by anger. It is folly, however, to wrangle with an angry man, as it has been said most elegantly in Greek verses: When two are speaking, when one is angry, he who does not contend in return by speaking is the wiser. Δυοῖν λεγόντοιν, θατέρου θυμουμένου, ὁ μὴ ἀντιτείνων τοῖς λόγοις σοφώτερος.

Finally, concerning private insults, let us be mindful of the saying of Peter, 1 Pet. 3: Not rendering insult for insult. Let us also remember this, that in refutation not only are the errors of another to be reproved, but also necessary doctrine is to be proposed with clear assertion, because it is not enough, in the academic manner, to contradict others, but it must also be shown what is to be thought, as Demosthenes warns, when he says: To find fault is for everyone, to give counsel is not for everyone.

He who conducts business through a foolish messenger is like one lame in his feet.

It agrees with the Homeric [saying], which Pindar praises: It is noble and well-made, when a messenger knows what is fitting.

It is a very useful thing, if the messenger himself is wise.

An artisan shapes his work: And he who hires a fool, hires one who corrupts the work.

A jurist says: Great is the difference between artisans. And there are many sayings about the difference between artisans, about impostors and busybodies, who sell themselves as artisans when they are not. As, there are very many impostors who want to seem to be physicians. Very many are unlearned preachers who flatter the common people or the powerful.

Therefore, an admonition is handed down here, which pertains to prudence, that suitable persons be chosen in every matter. At the same time, it is also commanded to those who profess arts, that they not be impostors or busybodies, but as Paul says, that they be Faithful, that is, that they rightly know the arts which they profess, and in practice show faith and diligence. Virtue embraces all these things, which is named Diligence, which is both to understand and to do faithfully the work of one's own office or vocation.

To this pertain the sayings: Let each one practice the art which he knows. Item: No one can teach what he knows little of. Item: One thing is the scepter, another is the plectrum. Item: For being a builder you were not doing carpentry, that is, being a craftsman, you were not doing craft-work. Item Phocylides: For never let unskilled men judge. Item: Let him who has learned it lead the oar. Item this from Sylla: It is necessary to be a rower before steering the rudder. And it usually happens that the unlearned are more audacious, according to the saying: ἀμαθία θράσος ἀπεργάζεται, Ignorance brings audacity. As a dog returns to its vomit, so the fool repeats etc.

Regarding the causes of punishments in this life, it has often been said elsewhere, namely, that there are four principal causes. 1. The first, because God is just, and because of His justice He destroys contrary things. 2. The second, because He wishes it to be understood that He is just, and that a distinction between just and unjust things should be learned. 3. The third, so that pernicious members may be removed. 4. The fourth, so that punishments may be warnings to us and to others, and deter us from sinning, as was said above, chap. 19: When the scoffer is struck, the simple will be wiser.

And 1 Corinthians 11, Paul says that the punishments of the people of Israel are examples. And the Lord says to Abraham that He is therefore recounting to him the example of the punishment of the Sodomites, so that He may warn posterity about the judgment of God.

And some who are curable, having been warned by punishments, subsequently become more cautious, of whom it is said: The struck one is wise. Item: παθήματα μαθήματα (Sufferings are lessons). Item: It is shameful to strike against the same stone twice. Item regarding the examples of others it is said: βλέπων πεπαίδευμαι εἰς τὰ ἄλλων κακά, By looking at the evils of others I have been instructed.

But many are blind and iron-hearted, and are corrected neither by the examples of others nor by their own punishments; many are even puffed up and become more rabid in their punishments. Some, repressed for a little while, like Saul, soon relapse into the same crimes. This saying speaks of such relapsers, just as God also very often warns elsewhere, lest by relapsing we attract greater punishments, as it is said in Amos 1: For three sins I have spared, for the fourth I will not spare. And Christ and Peter say: The last state becomes worse for such people than the first. And Solomon says: Relapsers are like dogs.

But it is much sadder that the Lord says the devil returns with seven other spirits more wicked than himself. Here let horrible public and private examples be considered. Fury grows in Pharaoh, Saul, Absalom, Ahab. And the citizens of Sodom, who had seen that they had been divinely liberated when Abraham defeated the army of the enemies, then soon forgetting their former punishments and liberations, furiously rush into the most terrible crimes. After the most sorrowful calamities and liberations, with the Maccabean brothers killed, the Jews most petulantly tore apart the doctrine with the dissensions of sects, the Pharisaic and Sadducean. They also tore apart the kingdom with civil wars. In that history we see the image of Germany even now: with the doctrine amended, many return to their former errors, and afterwards become utterly ἄθεοι (godless).

Many overwhelm the light of true doctrine with new errors, and stir up seditions. Many teachers, having omitted the investigation of doctrine, hand over the scriptures to the common people. The common people are delighted by license, and loosen the reins on their desires. Thus we attract greater punishments.

Yet He will preserve some remnants of the true Church. If we wish to be members of this, let us seriously convert to God, and let us ask to be converted, ruled, and confirmed by the Son of God, lest we relapse. And let there be in us ourselves the diligence to avoid the enticements and occasions of sins, just as Paul commands: See that you have not received the grace in vain. Item: Walk accurately, not as fools etc. Item, the saying is known: To avoid sins is to avoid the occasions of sins. Item Siracides: He who loves danger will perish in it.

Latin:

Caput XXVI.

Sicut nix in aestate, sicut pluvia in messe: sic non decet stultum gloria. De eventu loquitur, ut hoc dictum: Fortuna quem nimium fovet stultum facit. Narrat enim homines nondum castigatos seu cicuratos fieri insolentes rebus secundis, et laxare frenos variis cupiditatibus, ut Alexander cum initio modestissimus et mitissimus fuisset, postea vult esse Deus, et fit crudelis.

Cum enim homines non anguntur, fiunt securi, non petunt auxilium a Deo, et ebrii successibus, sua consilia et sese magnificiunt. Ideo magni et tristes sunt heroum casus, ut Herculis, Nabuchodonosor, Iulii, Pompeii, et innumerabilium aliorum.

Etsi autem hic de eventu tantum dicit, qui ad regulam pertinet de communiter accidentibus, tamen tacite complectitur admonitionem seu praeceptum de modestia, quod recitat Siracides capite 3.: Quo maior es, eo magis te humilia, et coram Domino invenies gratiam.

Item: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Et supra recitavi dictum Plutarchi: Solem imitentur principes, qui cum in summum fastigium venit, elatus in partem borealém, tardissime movetur, ut tarditas cursum reddat tutiorem.

Sicut avis fugit, et hirundo avolat: ita maledictum fatui non adhaerescit.

Tenenda est regula vita: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Haec habentes habebimus etiam aliquorum honestorum approbationem. Et haec expetenda est, ut Siracides inquit, capite 41.: Curam habe de bono nomine.

Sed tamen semper multi sunt invidi, qui deformare eos quibus invident conantur, ut Cicero inquit: Est quaedam huius seculi labes et macula, invidere virtuti.

Ac multi natura sunt virulenti, quos ipsa maledicentia delectat. Multis in quaestu est, ut Plautus inquit: Istic thesaurus stultis in lingua situs, ut quaestui habeant, male loqui melioribus.

Et noti sunt versus Menandri: ὁ βίος μάλιστα τοῖς πονηροῖς ἥδεται. Vita maxime delectatur improbis.

πράττει δ᾽ ὁ κόλαξ ἄριστα πάντων, δεύτερος ὁ συκοφάντης, ὁ κακοήθης τρίτατος. Et omnium temporum historiae ostendunt, multos honestos calumniis oppressos esse, ut Ioseph, Palamedem, Aristidem, Theramenem, Socratem, et alios innumerabiles.

Ac in Ecclesiastes dicitur: Calumnia turbat sapientem, et frangit robur cordis eius.

Sicut experientia ostendit, saepe bonos viros impediri calumniis. Hic igitur consolatio contra calumnias tradita est, videlicet, falsa maledicta, etiamsi aliquantisper sauciant, tamen postea retegi et improbari, sicut dicitur: Veritas aliquandiu laborare potest, deleri non potest.

Psalmus addit dulciorem consolationem: Maledicent illi, et tu benedices.

Et David de conviciis Semei inquit: Deus dabit mihi aliquid boni pro his maledictis.

Has consolationes teneamus, sed ita tamen, ut conscientiae nostrae integritatem retineamus, sicut saepe praecipitur: Haec est gloriatio nostra, testimonium conscientiae nostrae. Et ad Galatas: Opus suum unusquisque probet, et sic habebit gloriam apud sese, et non ex aliis, id est: Recte facito, ne te conscientia tua damnet, et cum non est saucia conscientia, habes gloriam, causae videlicet, non pendentem ex stulto applausu aliorum, sed talem, quae est vera conscientiae approbatio, et in credente est opus necessarium, et Deo placens.

Haec praecepta et has consolationes sciamus nobis divinitus dari, quia calumnia non est levis carnificina, etiamsi tandem Veritas patefacta eam refutat. Ut, cum Socrates interfectus esset, postea repraesentata est tragoedia de Palamede, in qua recitatus est hic versus: ἐκάνετε ἐκάνετε τὸν ἄριστον ἑλλήνων, μηδένα βλάψασαν ἀηδόνα.

Post hanc tragoediam cives expulerunt ex Athenis accusatores Socratis. Nunc sequuntur alia dicta, quae ad hoc propositum pertinent, et monent sapienter iudicandum esse, quando refutanda sit calumnia, quando non sit refutanda.

Ne respondeas stulto de stulticia eius, ne similis eius fias etc. Duae pugnantes sententiae recitantur, quae ideo dissentiunt, quia aliquando refutanda sunt maledicta, aliquando non necesse est refutare, sed prudenter iudicandum est, utrum faciendum sit.

Facilis autem diiudicatio est pastoribus in publico munere docentibus.

Hi semper habent auditores dissimiles, pios, firmos et infirmos, dociles tamen, et adversarios pertinaces et insanabiles, sicut elegantissime dictum est in Graecis les.

ciles tamen, et adversarios pertinaces et insanabiles.

Necesse est autem pastores servire meliori parti, ubi vox doctrinae incorrupta refutat adversarios. Et hi discernant maledicta. Alia lacerant doctrinam, alia deformant personam docentis.

Mandatum est autem de doctrina illustranda et propugnanda. 2. Tim. 1.: Honestum depositum custodi per Spiritum sanctum, habitantem in nobis. Ad Titum 1.: Quibus oportet os obstruere. Et ibidem: Convincito eos severe. Et ad Titum 2.: Convincito cum omni imperio, id est, praecipiens expressa asseveratione, ut verbo assentiantur.

Pugnent autem de rebus necessariis, et studeant assumere infirmos in fide, ut Paulus inquit, et adiungere studeant, non turbent dissipationibus inextricabilibus, neque alienent acerbitate. Privata autem convicia aut modeste refutent, aut omnino praetereant, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Illi detrahebant mihi, ego autem orabam.

In aliis autem privatis congressibus, Doctores et alii considerent discrimina auditorum. Si adsunt sanabiles, recte doceantur.

Si quis autem incidit in turbam insanabilem, ut Ioannes cum in balneo venisset ad Cherinthi turbam, hic ostensa confessione, ne videatur cum illis colludere, quamprimum, si potest, discedat ab eis, iuxta dictum: Haereticum hominem post unam atque alteram admonitionem vitato, Sicut Iohannes statim ex balneo egressus est. Item, Ne detis sanctum canibus.

Praesertim autem decet, privata convicia aut non refutare, sicut David tacuit, cum ei malediceret Semei: aut paucis refutare. Et exempla multa sunt magnorum gubernatorum, qui convicia dissimularunt, ut Pericles, Fabius, Scipio et alii fecerunt. Lacedaemonii docuerunt provocati a Mardonio, qui cum factus esset insolentior propter silentium Lacedaemoniorum, inquit Herodotus, eum elatum esse ψυχρῇ νίκῃ, id est, frigida victoria. Et in libro Herodoti narratio recitatur de Spartano legato, qui Geloni Siculo superbe responderat, ad hunc Gelon inquit: Probra obiecta homini solent iram accendere: Tu vero etsi contumeliam e sermone affecisti, non tamen persuadebis, ut indecora faciam, compensando convicia.

Praeterea plerumque ira impelluntur homines ad convicia. Stulticia est autem cum irato rixari, sicut elegantissime dictum est in Graecis versibus: Duobus dicentibus, cum alter est iratus, qui non contratendit dicendo, sapientior est. Δυοῖν λεγόντοιν, θατέρου θυμουμένου, ὁ μὴ ἀντιτείνων τοῖς λόγοις σοφώτερος.

Denique de privatis conviciis simus memores dicti Petri, 1. Pet. 3.: Non reddentes convicium pro convicio. Hoc etiam meminerimus, in refutatione non tantum alterius errata reprehendenda esse, sed etiam doctrinam necessariam perspicua adseveratione proponendam esse, quia non satis est, academico more contradicere aliis, sed etiam ostendendum est, quid sentiendum sit, sicut Demosthenes monet, cum inquit: ἐπιτιμᾷν παντός ἐστι, συμβουλεύειν δ᾽ οὐ παντός.

Qui per nuncium stultum agit negocium, est velut claudus pedibus.

Congruit cum Homerico, quod laudat Pindarus: ἐσθλὸν καὶ τὸ τέτυκται, ὅτ᾽ ἄγγελος αἴσιμα εἴδη.

Commoda res valde est, sapiat si nuncius ipse.

Artifex format opus: Et conducens stultum, conducit corrumpentem opus.

Iurisconsultus inquit: Magna est artificum differentia. Et multa sunt dicta de discrimine artificum, de impostoribus et ardelionibus, qui se venditant pro artificibus, cum non sint. Ut, plurimi sunt impostores, qui volunt videri medici. Plurimi indocti concionatores sunt, qui adulantur vulgo aut potentibus.

Traditur ergo hic admonitio, quae ad prudentiam pertinet, ut eligantur in qualibet re idonei. Simul etiam praecipitur his qui profitentur artes, ne sint impostores aut ardeliones, sed ut Paulus inquit, sint Fideles, id est, recte sciant artes quas profitentur, et in usu praestent fidem et diligentiam. Haec omnia complectitur virtus, quae nominatur Sedulitas, quae est proprii officii seu vocationis opera et intelligere et fideliter facere.

Huc pertinent dicta: Quam quisque norit artem, in hac se exerceat. Item: Quodque parum novit, nemo docere potest. Item: Aliud est sceptrum, aliud est plectrum. Item: τέκτων γὰρ ὢν ἔπραττες οὐ ξυλουργικὰ, id est, faber existens, non faciebas fabrilia. Item Phocylides: μὴ πότε γὰρ κρίνειν ἀδαήμονας ἄνδρας ἐάσῃς. Item: Remum ducat qui didicit. Item hoc Syllae: Remigem prius esse oportet, quam clavum gubernare. Et plerumque fit, ut indocti sint audaciores, iuxta dictum: ἀμαθία θράσος ἀπεργάζεται, Inscitia audaciam affert. Sicut canis redit ad vomitum, ita stultus iterat etc.

De causis poenarum in hac vita saepe alias dictum est, videlicet, causas praecipuas quatuor esse. 1. Prima, quia Deus iustus est, et propter suam iusticiam destruit contraria. 2. Secunda, quia vult intelligi, se iustum esse, et disci discrimen inter iusta et iniusta. 3. Tertia, ut perniciosa membra tollantur. 4. Quarta, ut poenae nobis et aliis sint commonefactiones, et deterreant nos a peccando, sicut supra dictum est, cap. 19.: Derisore percusso imperitus erit cautior.

Et 1. Corinth. 11. inquit Paulus, poenas populi Israël esse exempla. Et Dominus dicit ad Abraham, se ideo ei commemorare exemplum poenae Sodomorum, ut posteros moneat de iudicio Dei.

Et aliqui sanabiles moniti poenis, deinde fiunt cautiores, de quibus dicitur: Ictus sapit. Item: παθήματα μαθήματα. Item: Turpe est bis impingere ad eundem lapidem. Item de alienis exemplis dicitur: βλέπων πεπαίδευμαι εἰς τὰ ἄλλων κακά, Intuens aliorum mala eruditus sum.

Sed multi coeci et ferrei, nec alienis, nec seu poenis emendantur, multi etiam efferuntur et fiunt rabiosiores in poenis. Aliqui repressi paulisper, sicut Saul, mox relabuntur in eadem scelera. De talibus relabentibus loquitur hoc dictum, sicut et saepissime alias monet Deus, ne relabendo attrahamus maiores poenas, ut Amos 1. dicitur: Ter peccantibus peperci, quarto non parcam. Et Christus et Petrus inquiunt: Postrema talibus fieri peiora prioribus. Et Salomon ait: Relabentes similes esse canibus.

Sed multo tristius est, quod Dominus inquit redire diabolum, cum aliis septem nequioribus spiritibus. Hic horribilia exempla publica et privata considerentur. Crescit furor in Pharaone, Saul, Absolone, Achab. Et cives Sodomorum, qui viderant, se divinitus liberatos esse, cum Abraham profligavit exercitum hostium, deinde mox obliti priorum poenarum et liberationum, furenter ruunt in teterrima scelera. Iudaei post tristissimas calamitates et liberationes interfectis Maccabaeis fratribus, petulantissime lacerarunt doctrinam dissidiis sectarum, Pharisaicae et Saducaeae. Lacerarunt et regnum civilibus bellis. In ea historia et nunc Germaniae imaginem videmus: Emendata doctrina multi redeunt ad priores errores, et postea prorsus fiunt ἄθεοι.

Multi novis erroribus lucem verae doctrinae obruunt, et seditiones movent. Multi doctores omissa inquisitione doctrinae, tradunt grafa vulgo. Vulgus delectatur licentia, et laxat frenos cupiditatibus. Ita poenas maiores attrahimus.

Servabit tamen aliquas verae Ecclesiae reliquias. Huius si volumus esse membra, serio convertamur ad Deum, et petamus nos converti, regi et confirmari, a Filio Dei, ne relabamur. Et sit in nobis ipsis diligentia vitandi illecebras et occasiones peccatorum sicut Paulus praecipit: Videte ne gratiam frustra acceperitis. Item: Ambulate accurate, non ut fatui etc. Item, notum est dictum: Vitare peccata est vitare occasiones peccatorum. Item Siracides: Qui amat periculum, peribit in illo.

## 27:1 Argument
Chapter XXVII.

Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the present day will bring forth. It agrees with the Roman saying: You do not know what the late evening may carry. Item: Divine power plays with human affairs, And the present hour hardly has certainty. Item: All things of men hang by a thin thread, And those things which were strong fall by sudden chance. Item: Irus, and suddenly he who was just now Croesus. Finally, all books are full of such admonitions about the inconstancy of fortune, which are therefore proposed to us, so that they may warn us about modesty, and prohibit these two greatest vices, confidence in ourselves, and the rashness of moving non-necessary things, with foolish hope, and include us within boundaries, so that we may only perform the necessary duties of our vocation, as Paul says: Do your own work.

And indeed in the acknowledgment of our infirmity let us add the invocation of God, according to the saying: Be subject to God, and pray to Him. Item: Without me you can do nothing. And Jeremiah says: I know, Lord, that it is not of man, his way, that is, his calling. For it does not say that men do nothing, but that without the help of God, neither counsels nor actions are happy. We must therefore always keep this rule in mind: that necessary and present things must be done rightly, as the reason of duty demands, and that help must be sought from God, lest, trusting in our own strength or in foolish hope, we move toward unnecessary things, just as Pericles moved toward an unnecessary war for a very slight cause, which could have been neglected, as many judged even then.

Alcibiades crossed into Sicily without necessity. Hannibal brought war upon the Romans without necessity. Pompey could have retained peace on honorable conditions. All these wars were destructive to the states of those men. Charles the Bold, without cause, brought war upon the Lorrainers and the Swiss, in which, fighting unhappily in battle, he was killed. Finally, generally unhappy is πολυπραγμοσύνη [meddlesomeness], that is, to do unnecessary things out of foolish hope, as it is said: "Fools think foolish things out of desire."

It is useful to consider these admonitions in life, to which also pertains the saying of Christ: "Tomorrow's day will be anxious for itself."

The day's own affliction is sufficient, that is, do the necessary things in the present, which by themselves have enough difficulties, and do not heap up difficulties with empty reasoning and anxiety about future things. *

Heavy is a stone, and heavy is sand: but the anger of a fool is heavier than both.* Discriminations of sentences must often be thought upon.

Some expressly command something, or forbid it; others are divine promises or threats; others narrate Events. These together warn covertly how minds should be fortified against those events. Thus this sentence is a narrative about an event, namely, about the common malady of many who are more irascible and less placable. Such angry people are for the most part those who are more foolish and more unskilled, who do not consider the infirmity of men, and do not think that many of the errors of others must be placidly tolerated and healed. Therefore it is said: "To the unskilled, nothing is ever more unjust." But as goodness shines in God, and He Himself tolerates many maladies even in His own, and commands: "Forgive and it shall be forgiven you." Thus wise men turn their minds more toward goodness, and think about their own common infirmity and that of others, and are mindful of the divine precept: "Forgive and it shall be forgiven you."

Nor can a more illustrious image of the foolish and implacable be painted than the image proposed in the Gospel of the cruel servant, who owed sixty talents of gold. Although, however, this sentence in this book of Solomon is only a narrative about an Event, yet it warns of many things: It bids us consider human infirmity, and to remember the precept of ἐπιεικείᾳ [gentleness/equity], and to moderate anger: It also warns us to avoid the foolish, who know neither how to recognize nor how to forgive. Many sayings pertain to this: The greater each one is, the more placable he is to anger, And a generous mind easily takes up gentle motions. And Seneca says: "Nothing is great that is not placid."

And most sweet are the verses of Homer, 7th Odyssey: " Guest, do not think my heart to be such, That it should rashly or too much burn with flaming anger. In all things, moderation is the most beautiful virtue." [Greek text: "Guest, not such a heart is in my breast, to be angry in vain. Better are all things that are fitting."] And Pliny says:

"He who hates vices, hates men." But yet that saying must be understood prudently. For Pliny does not speak of enormous vices, nor of approval, but of tolerating affections that are somewhat aberrant without wickedness.

Furthermore, let there be precepts divinely delivered about moderating anger, as in Matthew 5 and 8. Also Romans 12 and elsewhere. *

As a bird deserting its nest: so is a man, deserting his place.* No kind of life, no function is without many troubles and dangers; therefore, in any kind of life, weariness quickly creeps in, according to that: "The lazy ox desires horse-trappings, the horse desires to plow."

It warns, therefore, that we should not, broken by weariness, rashly desert the kind of life to which we have been rightly called. Paul says: "Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called, before God." Many precepts delivered against inconstancy pertain to this, such as is the desultory life, which constantly changes its institutions: "As a stone often rolled is not covered with moss," [Greek text: "A rolling stone does not gather moss."] Item:

"A plant that is often transferred does not take root." Item: "Be an ass, whatever ass harsh fate has made you, he who knows how to bear his lot placidly, he is wise." Item: "For an elegant Doctor, a bad Poet: [Greek text: "Instead of a gentle doctor, a bad poet."]" Iron is sharpened by iron: so a man sharpens the face of his friend.

Let us acknowledge our infirmity, and let us know that individual men are ignorant of many things, and often err and slip, as Solomon says: The number of fools is infinite. Item: There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end leads to death. And this complaint exists in the writings of many.

Euripides says: No one man sees all things, 'One man does not see all things.' Theognis: 'No one of men is wise in all things.' And God for this reason created us especially for the communication of speech, so that others might teach others, and guide them with counsel.

Therefore Paul says: Teach and admonish one another. And Sirach chapter 6: If you see a wise man, go to him early, and let your feet wear out the steps of his door. Finally, there are very many sayings that command us to listen to the counsels and judgments of experts, and to confer our thoughts with others.

And daily experience shows how dangerous it is to 'rely on one's own counsel.' And this is said about craftsmen: Everyone is the worst teacher to himself. And Euripides said most sweetly: 'Conversation gave birth to the arts,' when, namely, many confer their thoughts, and others are admonished by the judgments or examples of others.

And the thing itself shows that doctrines are corrupted by those who do not listen to others, but hidden away like those who flee the light, they invent new opinions from themselves, abhorring the approved form of doctrines. There are many such now, who boast that they are 'self-taught,' and admire their own dreams, and do not listen to the judgments of other sound men. But let us obey the precepts, which command us to listen to the experts, and let us confer our thoughts with others, as Paul says: Teach and admonish one another.

This sentence also speaks about this collation of judgments and counsels: Iron is sharpened by iron, so an artisan sharpens an artisan. This diligence is first a part of modesty, of one who considers his own infirmity. Then, prudence is the zeal of learning what you do not know. And above, Solomon, praising faithful counsel, says: As fragrant odors are sweet to the heart, so is a sweet friend, giving counsel to the soul.
