No invocation was or is pleasing to God, unless the mind recognizes the supreme Priest offering our vows and our groans to the eternal Father.

And so, even then, the Prophets taught those performing repentance to receive the remission of sins, to be reckoned righteous, to be gifted with the Holy Spirit, and to be heirs of eternal life certainly by faith in the Redeemer, not on account of their own dignity or the law.

But this knowledge of the Redeemer shone forth in some more, in others less; many also, as happens in all ages, only dreamed that men were righteous by that discipline of the law, and that sins were taken away by the slaughter of victims.

But yet the Prophets and many of their hearers were guardians of the true of doctrine and the trust of the Redeemer, they rightly called upon God.

Regarding the others who thought they could appease the wrath of God with their sacrifices, Solomon says: They know not how much evil they do. In this brief complaint of Solomon, there is a sad rebuke of the blindness of many in all ages, who have been fascinated by a similar error. Many now also do not know how much evil they do, who establish idols in the Mass, and in the invocation of the dead. But it was necessary for them to hear the divine voice, which censures errors and shows the true invocation.

I have said these things briefly concerning the argument of this book of Solomon, which, because it is profitable for it to be familiarly known to all who learn letters, for indeed it contains many most useful admonitions, I have recently read over again in school as best I could.

Although I see that the commentary is too meager, I did not wish to publish it, and yet I resisted the less because some thought that many would read Solomon himself, once they were made aware of the magnitude of the things which the book contains.

In the edition, however, I have added your name, because I know in my heart that you too, in that militia of yours, often seek these consolations, which affirm that pious labors in government are pleasing to God, and will not be entirely in vain, even if good counsels are hindered in various ways.

There is no doubt that devils lie in wait for the human race, who incite some to try to destroy the Church by force, and others to disturb it with the deceits of sophisms.

To these evils are added many other difficulties. But we know that the Son of God, sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, is the guardian of His Church. Let us pray to Him that He may rule us, and make us vessels of mercy and salutary instruments, that He may aid pious labors, and cherish the sorrowful Churches, and repress the devil raging with tyranny and sophistry. We know that these our prayers are not in vain. Fare well and happily, Cal. Oct.

Argument on Ecclesiastes.

Therefore, in commentaries, the arguments and counsels of the writer are recited at the beginning, so that the younger ones, being forewarned, may grasp the sum of the work in their minds as best they can, and consider to what use the written material is to be accommodated, whether the end is knowledge, or indeed some Action profitable for life.

But to speak now of the writings in the Church.

One part is doctrine, such as the recitation of the articles of faith, because God wills to be known from His revelations, He wills us to hear His voice, and to know the illustrious testimonies which He has added to His voice. He also wills us to assent to His sayings, and He declares this assent to be a virtue.

But the ultimate end is not knowledge; rather, He wills that fear and consolation should follow after knowledge, because God revealed Himself for this reason, that He might gather to Himself an eternal Church in the human race, and deliver it from sin and death. Therefore, hearers are to be raised up by consolation, which is made by Faith, which is the beginning of eternal life, and it is necessary for minds in this course to have consolation, so that invocation may be possible.

Afterwards, they shall enjoy light, wisdom, goodness, and divine joy in all eternity, when God shall be all in all, that is, when He shall be efficacious in us, without the ministry of the word, but by His own light, which we shall see openly. Although, therefore, some part in the writings of the Church is dogmatic (δογματικὴ) or doctrine, yet afterwards those further ends are to be looked to.

Thus let the preacher know that the members of his discourse are to be distributed, and as Paul admonished: Be assiduous in reading, in doctrine, and in consolation.

Let the pious Preacher read the Prophetic and Apostolic books. Thence let him take the matters of the Church to be set forth, and let him not feign new opinions or fabricated divinities, like Numa Pompilius, or the like. But the pious Preacher, having taken his matters from the fountains, should expound them perspicuously and without corruptions, and should show somewhere definitions and distinctions. These are the duties of one teaching; Thirdly, let him transfer doctrine to stirring up Fear and Faith, which is consolation and restoration of life.

But after the reader has considered these discourses of Solomon, that these are the counsels of the writers, let him know that principally this whole book, whose title is Ecclesiastes, to be a doctrine, namely, an Assertion concerning providence. He affirms that God is wise, truthful, just, a judge, acting most freely, to be worshipped according to the doctrine handed down by Him, and not otherwise, punishing those who despise Him, and merciful and saving those who call upon Him and begin to obey Him. Therefore, the principal work of this book is dogmatic, namely, an Assertion concerning providence against the Epicureans, Pyrrhonians, Stoics, and other thoughts which undermine the assent to providence. And these assertions are expressed in these words in the last chapter: "God will bring all things into judgment, He is about to judge all hidden things, both good and evil." Also chapter 11: "Know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment." And chapter 3: "God will judge the just and the impious." In these words and similar ones, know that the principal proposition of the whole discourse is recited and repeated.

This assertion is followed by the doctrine of obedience. Since God has given the law and added threats, and in great mercy has also issued the voice of the Gospel concerning reconciliation and the most ample promises, and certainly punishes those who despise Him, but receives and saves those who flee to the Son the Mediator, it is necessary to obey Him according to His doctrine; let there be in hearts a Fear dreading His judgment, let there be faith resting in the Mediator, and determining that you are received, heard, invoked, protected, and saved, and let the members be restrained so that they do not rush against the commandments of God.

Thus the doctrine is transferred to use, when obedience follows the assent to providence, and in that obedience hearts are sustained by divine consolation, and are freed from eternal death, and the celestial life is begun, which it is necessary for us to behold as the final goal. But many confusions in life seem to oppose the assertion concerning providence. When a just judge has the power, he defends the just, and suppresses those about to do unjust things, and punishes those who have transgressed.

But in the human race, the just generally lie oppressed by great miseries. How many thousands of innocent infants, Virgins, and matrons perish daily in wars, fires, and other calamities. Meanwhile, the wicked are not only not suppressed, but they even flourish and possess empires and wealth. Since such is the confusion, how can life be seen to be governed by God? This complaint exists in the writings of many, as is known. And there is no man who is not tormented by this dispute. Furthermore, good and evil men seem to perish by fortuitous accidents, just as violets are trampled on the ground, or winds shake flowers and fruits from trees.

Often also the efforts of the wise and the just are in vain, and the wicked win. There was a true Church among the people of the Jews, when Nebuchadnezzar made a desolation in all Judea, with Jerusalem and other cities destroyed. This spectacle then also moved many to think that that nation was not a care to God. And although there are many testimonies of the presence of God in nature, and in the preservation of the human race, such as the order of celestial motions, certain notions in the mind, the preservation of species, and the regular punishments of atrocious crimes, yet the Epicureans can be refuted with difficulty, since they collect these spectacles of confusion against providence.

But Solomon here opposes firm and true responses, which are not born of human reason, but are the voice of God concerning the future judgment after this life. And first he says that in this life also the crimes of many are punished, as he says in chapter 8: "Impiety will not save the impious, nor will there be an escape for him in war." Then he confesses that the judgment is deferred for a while, and he complains that by this, however brief, delay, the audacity of the wicked is confirmed. But yet he opposes eternity. This life is a short shadow. Neither are punishments in this life long-lasting, nor is joy. But eternal goods and evils are not fleeting shadows.

He commands all to behold this eternity, and to beware, lest they fall into the eternal wrath of God, and the horrendous torments that will never cease, and to seek and expect eternal goods. In this response, faith in those converted to God rests, flees the eternal wrath of God, seeks and expects eternal salvation, and therefore obeys God, and sustains itself by the recognition of the presence of God and of divine aid in present miseries. The Church also knows why it is burdened in this life with such a mass of miseries. Therefore, although Epicurus might laugh at Solomon's response, yet the pious mind assents and believes in God asserting concerning the future judgment.

Therefore this sermon of Solomon is prophetic, and is the divine voice in the Church of God concerning the future judgment, such as is the sermon of the Son of God in the chapter of Matthew 25 and in other places. This book of Solomon, therefore, is not to be read like the Epistles of Crates or Seneca concerning the contempt of riches, and the writings of the Monks concerning the desertion of political society, but it is a doctrine of faith concerning the judgment of God, and concerning the distinction between the wicked and the Church, and amidst the horrendous confusions of the human race it shows the wrath of God to the contumacious, and consolation to the pious.

And therefore the narrations of confusions and scandals are prolix, so that it may teach afterwards that one must by no means judge from these spectacles in this life concerning the will of God, but must assent with firm faith to the divine voice, and that the word of God ought to be the norm of all counsels and actions, just as it is written: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet.

It is necessary, therefore, in the reading of this book to have known the sum of ecclesiastical doctrine, concerning the creation of the world and of man, concerning the fall of men, concerning the causes of calamities, concerning the promise, and concerning the Mediator, through whom and for whom the Church is gathered again, concerning faith receiving the remission of sins, concerning the law of God, concerning eternal life, concerning the final judgment, concerning the eternal punishments of the wicked, concerning the salvation of the pious.

It is necessary to embrace this whole doctrine when one speaks of providence. For since confusions in this short life cast darkness upon minds, so that they perceive providence less, it is necessary to look upon that other life, in which there will be a clear distinction between the evil and the good in all eternity.

However, the series of parts in this book of Solomon must be considered.

First, he recites the objections which seem to oppose providence, and in this recitation he is prolix, because these profane thoughts excite great and constant tumults in human minds. And therefore this part of the book is also more prolix.

But he inserts brief responses here and there.

Fear God, another judgment remains.

These very brief sayings are responses, which we ought to embrace with firm assent and faith.

For it is most certain that they are divine decrees, which are often repeated in the Church by the voice of the Prophets, of Christ, and of the Apostles, and faith opposes certain and brief divine sayings to the turbulent thoughts of reason. The form of objections and responses in this book imitates these very struggles of human reason.

But following the asseveration concerning providence, there follow the Law and the commination.

Likewise the Gospel and consolation: after you establish that there is a God, and that He is a judge and avenger, hear the precepts and obey, and because the infirmity of men is great, and the many furies of the devils, which increase the confusions of the human race, there are many impediments to obedience. Here consolation is necessary.

Therefore the voice of the Gospel must be heard, which teaches what obedience is, and how it pleases, it commands the governor not to cast away the duties of his vocation, even if in this confusion of life the outcomes of the counsels of rulers are for a time dissimilar, and it warns us not to be broken by despair, even if the unjust flourish for a time, and the true Church is oppressed, because even if the judgment of God is deferred for a time, yet after a while, both in this life and in all eternity, the wicked will be punished.

He has often interwoven this consolation into this Writing, which is comprehended in the whole of Psalm 36. Fret not thyself, and in many sermons of the Prophets and of the Son of God, as in the chapter of Matthew 10: Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Eternity is to be preferred by far to the very short space of this mortal life, and yet in this life atrocious crimes are accompanied by atrocious punishments, according to that: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword, and experience has brought forth these sayings: He who fashions evil for another, fashions evil for his own liver.

As it is said concerning Archelaus, the Macedonian king, who although he was for a time a glorious king, yet because he had invaded the kingdom through crime, he was killed by his own, and individual ages see many such examples.

Now the reader who is not entirely ignorant of common life easily understands what the use of this book is, and what utility is to be taken from it.

The assent concerning providence must be confirmed by the sayings of this preacher, which are proposed in the Church not by human authority, but divinely.

Then let each one in his own place obey God, and perform the duties of his vocation, which, although many things impede, let him hold to the consolations which are proposed here, let him know that his course in his vocation pleases God, let him know that God is the ruler of his assembly, and that He wills that divine help be sought, and that He most truly brings aid to those faithfully serving in their vocation, and that He will finally place the Church into that eternal custom. with divinity, in which God will be all in all.

By this faith, let him obey God, do what is right, and find rest in God; let him not cast away the duties of his calling in indignation or despair, nor fall into the Epicurean contempt of God.

With this admonition regarding the use of the book considered, the reading will be both clearer and sweeter, and the sum of the work is contained almost entirely in these sweetest rules of life.

Psalm 36: Be subject to God, and pray to him.

Commit your way to God, and hope in him, and he will act.

Wait for the Lord, and keep his way.

Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you.

Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest will be added to you.

Do not be anxious about tomorrow; the affliction of the day is sufficient.

Do what is necessary, and ask for and expect help from God, and do not stir up what is not necessary.

But looking to the commands of God, you should follow this norm, and know from the Gospel that obedience is pleasing because of the Mediator, and that through him and for his sake your labors will be salutary, as he says: Without me you can do nothing.

And Paul says: Your labor in the Lord will not be in vain.

The Son of God himself will bring it about that your course benefits the Church, as it is written: He ascended, he gave gifts to men, Prophets, Apostles, teachers, etc.

And in the Psalm it is said: Who gives salvation to kings.

Good minds understand that these consolations are true and salutary.

And because a great part of these consolations pertains to the virtue which is called Patience, I will briefly add this admonition at the beginning.

Let the distinction between philosophical and Christian patience be known.

Philosophical patience is to obey reason in enduring those labors and hardships which reason commands one to bear, and to do nothing against justice, and to moderate grief with this consciousness of rectitude.

Sometimes, however, this philosophical patience is without any hope of help, when, namely, reason does not show help or mitigation before death, as Aristides and Camillus bore injuries and exiles with an even mind, nor did they expect help from God.

But Christian patience is to obey God in bearing those labors and hardships which God commands one to bear, and to do nothing against justice, and to ask for and expect help and mitigation from God because of the Mediator, and to moderate grief with this confidence in the presence of God.

Thus in David, in Jeremiah, and in similar figures, these virtues, faith and hope, are always joined with obedience, and these virtues, faith and hope, beget joy in the heart, according to those sayings: Being justified by faith, we have peace.

Item: May the peace of God guard your hearts.

To this pertains the Pauline rule written to the Thessalonians: Always rejoice, pray incessantly, give thanks in all things.

But in order that this faith may be kindled in our hearts, it is necessary to know the Gospel concerning the remission of sins, and concerning reconciliation because of the Mediator, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Faith looks to him, and knows that through him we are led to the eternal Father; it knows that this Mediator is a shade by which we are covered, lest we be extinguished by the horrendous wrath of God, and lest the devil be able to exercise his rage against us, as they desire; it knows that the Church is helped and preserved through this Mediator, the Son of God.

Let this confidence in the Mediator shine before all other actions, as is often and copiously said.

I omit long recitations of how this book has been obscured by the interpretations of others.

Some have sought a physical explanation; others, fanatical ones, as if the book condemns marriages, governments, and necessary labors in the Church, the State, and the Household, and they have ordered that one's calling be deserted.

It is necessary to be warned at the beginning that these ravings of the Monks are to be rejected.

Solomon does not condemn the creatures of God, nor one's calling; rather, he commands that they be used reverently and in order, but he condemns the perversion of order in the human heart, which is so moved by the spectacles of events that it doubts providence.

Since, however, false interpretations of this book have cast a great shadow over the doctrine of the Gospel, it is useful for the younger generation to be reminded of the simple meaning.

A false interpretation of the saying is spread throughout the Church: No one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred.

That saying is explained against the meaning of this book.

You should always doubt whether you are pleasing to God, when yet Solomon wishes to remedy this doubt.

Jeremiah or other believers do not doubt that they are pleasing to God, even if they see their country burning and themselves being led into exile: for Solomon himself wishes this, that one should judge concerning the will of God from his word, not from favorable or adverse events in this life.

It is enough to have said this concerning the Argument.

Latin:

XI. ENARRATIO BREVIS CONCIONUM LIBRI SALOMONIS, CUIUS TITULUS EST ECCLESIASTES. AUTORE PHILIPPO MELANTHONE.

( Hoc modo inscriptus, hic liber primum prodiit Witebergae, Excudebat Ios. Clug. Anno 1550. 8. 11 pl. — Recusus est liber Witeb. 1551. et iterum anno 1556, quam postremam editionem Peucerus repetiit in operibus Melanth. T. II. p. 915, unde hic librum dedimus. Epistola nuncupatoria, Ioachimo Mollero inscripta, supra dedimus in Epistolis d. 1. Oct. 1550. — Germanice prodiit cura Stephani Riccii, discipuli Melanthonis: „Ecclesiastes, ausgelegt von Phil. Mel., und verdeutscht von Stephan Reich. Wittenb. 1561. 8. 21 pl.“)

Clarissimo viro, eruditione et virtute praestanti, D. Ioachimo Moller Hamburgensi, Doctori Iuris, Philippus Melanthon S. D. Multi omnibus temporibus intuentes tristissimas humani generis confusiones, ruinas regnorum, promiscuos interitus hominum sceleratorum aut aliorum, quorum mores fuerunt modesti et inculpati, dubitarunt, an providentia divina regantur res humanae, an vero sine consilio vel physicis motibus vel temere et coeca vertigine et casu omnia volvantur. Adversus hanc dubitationem, etsi Deus multa testimonia in ipsa natura opposuit, ipsam mundi figuram, vices motuum coelestium et temporum, mirandam fabricationem naturae humanae, et in mentibus hominum numeros, cognitionem ordinis, immotum discrimen honestorum et turpium, conscientiae dolores, terrae foecundationem, conservationem singularum specierum, poenas atrocium scelerum, tamen et prodiens ex arcana sede allocutus est universum genus humanum, ac de salute hominum et de venturo iudicio concionatus est, in quo universale et aeternum discrimen inter bonos et malos efficiet, ac ut sciremus has conciones veras esse, resuscitatione mortuorum, et aliis mirandis operibus ostendit eas Dei decretum esse. Etsi autem in genere humano pauci eis adsentiuntur, tamen semper fuit, est et erit aliqua Dei Ecclesia, alias magis, alias minus frequens, quae firma adsensione divinam vocem amplectitur. Haec celebrat et invocat verum Deum, et causas confusionum praecipuas didicit, nec dissimilitudine fortunae movetur, ut de providentia dubitet. Et quanquam sunt in hac vita dissimilia spectacula, tamen in illud venturum iudicium semper intuens, scit esse unicam vitae normam divinitus traditam, qua regi iudicia in mente, et omnes actiones humanae oporteat. Haec dubitationi opponit et testimonia naturae impressa, et vocem a Deo traditam, et exempla resuscitationis mortuorum et similia. Confirmantur pii et singulari testimonio in cordibus, quod nequaquam eis dubium est. Nam et in sensu irae Dei agnoscunt eum vere irasci peccatis, et rursus cum in consolatione eriguntur fide, illucescit pectori flamma, agnoscunt se ex inferis retrahi, et sentiunt initia vitae aeternae. De hoc testimonio loquitur Paulus inquiens: Spiritus sanctus dat testimonium spiritui nostro.

Quanque autem de argumento huius libri alii aliter locuti sunt, tamen in hac sententia acquiesco, et iudico summam operis hoc modo recte distribui: Totam concionem esse doctrinam, videlicet, Adseverationem de providentia, ac refutationem in qua consolationes sunt, et comminationes.

Etsi magna est in hac vita confusio, imperia tenent homines iniusti, qui Deum contemnunt, florent opibus impii: Ecclesia recte invocans Deum horribiliter premitur, vox recte docentium et bona suadentium saepe est inutilis, magna multitudo est hominum insanabilium, tamen non propterea existimes nullam esse providentiam: sed venturum est iudicium in quo fiet aeternum discrimen bonorum et malorum.

Sunt et consolationes intextae, in quibus ducuntur Argumenta a necessario, a possibili et ab utili.

Cum necesse sit Deo obedire, facias officia vocationis, quicunque erunt eventus.

Nec erunt prorsus irriti conatus.

Aderit Deus invocanti, et labores, pericula, impedimenta reget, sicut Psalmus inquit: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Nec semper erit infelix labor, respondebunt aliquando boni eventus.

Sparge, inquit, panem velut in aquam, quia tamen rursus inveniens.

Mira imago est, iubet spargere salutarem doctrinam et consilia, ac si panem in aqua spargeremus, qui perire ibi videtur.

Sed melius promittit hic concionator.

Aliqua ex parte hi tui labores, Ecclesiae, patriae, posteritati profuturi sunt, etiamsi non poteris constituere statum qualem constituit Iosue, Samuel, David, Salomon, Iosias, at servies utiliter tuo loco, sicut in misera et oppressa patria serviebant Zacharias, Simeon et alii his inferiores, quorum tamen fuit similis voluntas.

Postremo cum non respondent eventus, tamen in Deo acquiescito, scias ipsi et in officiis vocationis, et deinde in eventibus obediendum esse, sicut scriptum est: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei.

Non est similis temporum fortuna, et Deus ipse praedixit maiores imperiorum et Ecclesiae dilacerationes in extrema senecta mundi futuras esse quam fuerunt Patrum et Prophetarum temporibus.

Et tamen quaelibet aetas multa tristia exempla habet.

Sed nunc urgemur non solum aetatis infirmitate, sed etiam mole poenarum, quae cumulatae sunt propter idola et alia scelera.

Maior etiam in diabolo rabies est, sentiente iam instare tempus extremi iudicii, in quo sibi maiores cruciatus in omnem aeternitatem certo propositos esse novit.

Addit Salomon et comminationes, tradit regulam: Atrocia scelera et in hac vita puniri.

Non est iniustis, inquit evasio in praelio.

Item: Etsi differuntur poenae, tamen certo secuturae sunt.

Bene erit timentibus Deum.

Ac nequaquam bene erit impio, nec diuturna eius vita erit, sed sicut umbra evanescit.

Haec sunt praecipua membra in hac concione Salomonis.

Iam apud sese lector reputet, quam sit utilis doctrina, quae confirmat in mente sententiam de providentia, et de venturo iudicio, quae admonitionem de officiis vocationis, et consolationes de difficultatibus et eventibus proponit.

Nam exordium in omni gravi deliberatione est cogitatio de providentia et iudicio Dei, et de auxilio divino.

Sciat autem lector et hoc, has conciones in Ecclesia Dei recitari, ubi notam esse oportet doctrinam de veri Dei invocatione, et de Redemptore Filio Dei.

Praelucere agnitionem Filii Dei, et Redemptoris oportet his laboribus, de quibus haec concio loquitur: Ut ipse Salomon hic universam doctrinam Ecclesiae cognosci et audiri praecipit, et cultus inutiles taxat inquiens: Ingrediens domum Dei, accede ut audias.

Melior est obedientia, quam stultorum victimae, qui nesciunt quantum faciant mali.

Vides gravissime praecipi, ut doctrinam in domo Dei, id est, in vera Ecclesia sonantem audiamus, quae totam fundamenti doctrinam complectitur.

Nam et tunc necesse erat discerni verum Deum ab omnium gentium commenticiis numinibus, et oportebat promissiones de Redemptore notas esse, intelligi doctrinam de iustitia fidei.

Nulla fuit neque est Invocatio grata Deo, nisi mens agnoscat summum Sacerdotem perferentem nostra vota, et nostros gemitus ad aeternum Patrem.

Itaque tunc quoque Prophetae docebant agentes poenitentiam accipere remissionem peccatorum, reputari iustos, donari Spiritu sancto, et haeredes esse vitae aeternae certo fiducia Redemptoris, non propter propriam dignitatem, aut legem.

Fulsit autem haec noticia Redemptoris in aliis magis, in aliis minus, multi etiam ut fit omnibus aetatibus tantum somniarunt homines illa disciplina legis iustos esse, et peccata tolli mactatione victimarum.

Sed tamen Prophetae et multi eorum auditores custodes fuerunt verae doctrinae et fiducia Redemptoris Deum recte invocarent.

De caeteris qui putabant se iram Dei placare suis sacrificiis, inquit Salomon: Nesciunt quantum faciant mali. In hac brevi querela Salomonis, tristis vituperatio est coecitatis multorum omnibus aetatibus, qui simili errore fascinati sunt. Multi nunc quoque nesciunt, quantum faciant mali, qui idola stabiliunt in Missa, et in invocatione mortuorum. Sed audire eos vocem divinam oportebat, quae taxat errores et monstrat veram invocationem.

Haec de argumento huius libri Salomonis breviter dixi, quem quia prodest familiariter notum esse omnibus, qui discunt literas, nam profecto multas utilissimas admonitiones continet, recens in schola utcunque relegi.

Etsi autem video enarrationem nimis ieiunam esse, edi non volebam et tamen eo minus repugnavi, quia aliqui existimabant plures ipsum Salomonem lecturos esse, utcunque commonefactos de rerum magnitudine, quas liber continet.

In editione vero tuum nomen addidi, quia te quoque in illa tua militia has consolationes saepe requirere animo scio, quae adfirmant pios labores in gubernatione placere Deo, et non prorsus irritos fore, etiam si bona consilia variis modis impediuntur.

Insidiari humano generi diabolos non dubium est, qui incitant alios, ut vi Ecclesiam delere conentur, alios ut sophismatum praestigiis eas turbent. Ad haec mala accedunt multae difficultates aliae.

Sed scimus Filium Dei sedentem ad dextram aeterni patris, custodem esse suae Ecclesiae. Hunc oremus ut nos regat, et faciat nos vasa misericordiae et organa salutaria, adiuvet pios labores, et foveat moestas Ecclesias, et reprimat diabolum grassantem tyrannide et sophistica. Haec nostra vota scimus non esse irrita. Bene et feliciter vale, Cal. Oct.

Argumentum in Ecclesiasten.

Ideo in enarrationibus argumenta et consilia scriptoris initio recitantur, ut iuniores praemoniti utcunque summam operis mente complectantur, et cogitent ad quem usum materia scripta accommodanda sit, an finis sit cognitio, an vero Actio aliqua vitae profutura.

Ut autem iam de scriptis in Ecclesia dicamus.

Una pars doctrina est, ut recitatio articulorum fidei, quia Deus vult se agnosci ex patefactionibus suis, vult nos audire suam vocem, et nosse illustria testimonia, quae addidit suae voci. Vult etiam nos assentiri suis dictis, et hanc assensionem esse virtutem pronunciat.

Sed non est ultimus finis cognitio, verum postea vult ad cognitionem accedere timorem et consolationem, quia ideo se patefecit Deus, ut colligat sibi aeternam Ecclesiam in genere humano, et eam a peccato et morte liberet. Erigendi sunt igitur auditores consolatione, quae fit Fide, quae est incoatio vitae aeternae, et oportet mentes in hoc cursu habere consolationem, ut fieri possit invocatio. Postea fruentur luce, sapientia, bonitate et laeticia divina in omni aeternitate, cum erit Deus omnia in omnibus, id est, cum erit efficax in nobis, sine ministerio verbi, sed sua ipsius luce, quam palam cernemus.

Quanquam igitur pars aliqua in scriptis Ecclesiae est δογματικὴ seu doctrina, tamen postea illi fines ulteriores intuendi sunt. Sicut et eruditus concionator alias recitat ordine articulos symboli aut legem: alias proponit comminationes, accusat reos, ut timorem iudicii divini in animis exuscitet: alias recitat vocem Evangelii et consolationes, quas Filius Dei Dominus noster Iesus Christus Ecclesiae tradidit, et accendit fidem et invocationem, et lenit moesticiam, ne corda opprimantur desperatione, et ruant in exitium.

Ita sciat concionator membra suae orationis distribuenda esse, et ut Paulus monuit: Sis assiduus in lectione, doctrina et consolatione.

Legat pius Concionator libros Propheticos et Apostolicos. Inde sumat res Ecclesiae proponendas, non fingat novas opiniones aut commenticia numina, ut Numa Pompilius, aut similes. Sumtas autem res ex fontibus pius Concionator perspicue et sine corruptelis exponat, monstret alicubi definitiones, ac distinctiones. Haec sunt docentis munera, Tertio transferat doctrinam ad excitandum Timorem et Fidem, quae est consolatio et restitutio vitae.

Postquam autem lector harum concionam Salomonis consideravit, haec esse consilia scribentium, sciat principaliter totum hunc librum, cui titulus est Ecclesiastes, esse doctrinam, videlicet, Asseverationem de providentia. Affirmat esse Deum sapientem, veracem, iustum, iudicem, liberrime agentem, colendum iuxta doctrinam ab ipso traditam, non aliter, punientem contemnentes ipsum, et misericordem ac servantem eos, qui ipsum invocant et ei obedire incipiunt. Est igitur praecipuum opus huius libri δογματικὸν, videlicet, Asseveratio de providentia contra Epicureas, Pyrrhonias, Stoicas et alias cogitationes, quae labefactant assensionem de providentia. Suntque expressae asseverationes in his verbis capite ultimo. Cuncta quae sunt, adducet Deus in iudicium, Omnia abscondita iudicaturus est, et bona et mala.

Item cap. 11.: Scito quod pro omnibus his adducet te Deus in iudicium. Et cap. 3.: Iustum et impium iudicabit Deus. In his verbis et similibus scito principalem propositionem totius concionis recitari et repeti. Hanc asseverationem sequitur doctrina de obedientia. Cum Deus dederit legem et addiderit comminationes, ingenti misericordia etiam vocem Evangelii de reconciliatione, et amplissimas promissiones ediderit, et certo puniat contemnentes ipsum, recipiat vero et servet confugientes ad Filium Mediatorem, necesse est ei obedire iuxta suam doctrinam, sit in cordibus Timor metuens eius iudicium, sit fides acquiescens in Mediatore, et statuens te recipi, exaudiri, invari, protegi et servari, et frenentur membra ne ruant contra mandata Dei.

Ita doctrina transfertur ad usum, cum obedientia sequitur assensionem de providentia, et in illa obedientia corda sustentantur divina consolatione, et liberantur a morte aeterna, et incoatur coelestis vita, quam ultimam metam intueri nos necesse est. Sed asseverationi de providentia videntur adversari multae confusiones in vita. Iustus iudex cum potest, defendit iustos, et reprimit facturos iniusta, et eos qui deliquerunt, punit.

At in genere humano plerumque iusti iacent oppressi magnis aerumnis. Quam multa millia innocentum infantum, Virginum, matronarum quotidie in bellis, incendiis, et aliis calamitatibus pereunt. Interea scelerati non solum non reprimuntur, sed etiam florent et habent imperia et opes. Talis cum sit confusio, quomodo videri potest regi vita a Deo. Extat haec querela in plurimorum scriptis, ut notum est. Et nemo est hominum, qui non hac disputatione excrucietur. Praeterea videntur homines boni et mali fortuitis casibus perire, sicut conculcantur violae in terra, aut venti flores et poma decutiunt ab arboribus.

Saepe etiam sapientum et iustorum conatus irriti sunt, et vincunt mali. Erat vera Ecclesia in populo Iudaeorum, cum Nabogdonosor fecit vastitatem in tota Iudaea deletis Ierosolymis et aliis urbibus. Hoc spectaculum tunc quoque multos movit, ut existimarent eam gentem non esse curae Deo. Etsi autem multa sunt testimonia praesentiae Dei in natura, et in conservatione generis humani, ut ordo motuum coelestium, noticiae certae in mente, conservatio specierum, poenae regulares atrocium scelerum, tamen Epicurei difficulter refutari possunt, cum contra providentiam haec spectacula confusionum colligunt.

Sed Salomon hic opponit responsiones firmas et veras, quae non nascuntur in humana ratione, sed sunt vox Dei de venturo iudicio post hanc vitam. Ac primum ait, in hac vita quoque multorum scelera puniri, ut cap. 8. dicit: Non salvabit impietas impium, nec erit ei evasio in bello. Deinde fatetur aliquantisper differri iudicium, et queritur hac quamvis brevi mora, tamen confirmari audaciam sceleratorum. Sed tamen opponit aeternitatem. Haec vita brevis umbra est. Nec poenae in hac vita diuturnae sunt, nec laeticia. Sed aeterna bona et mala non sunt fugaces umbrae.

Hanc aeternitatem iubet omnes intueri, et cavere, ne incidant in aeternam Dei iram, et horrendos cruciatus nunquam desituros, et petere, et expectare aeterna bona. In hac responsione fides in conversis ad Deum acquiescit, fugit aeternam Dei iram, petit et expectat aeternam salutem, ideoque Deo obtemperat, et sustentat se agnitione praesentiae Dei, et auxilii divini in praesentibus aerumnis. Scit autem etiam Ecclesia, quare in hac vita onerata sit tanta mole miseriarum. Etsi igitur Epicurus rideret Salomonis responsionem, tamen pia mens assentitur et credit Deo asseveranti de futuro iudicio.

Ergo haec concio Salomonis prophetica est, et vox divina in Ecclesia Dei de futuro iudicio, qualis est concio Filii Dei in capite Matth. 25. et in aliis locis. Non igitur hic liber Salomonis legendus est, ut Cratetis aut Senecae Epistolae de contemtu divitiarum, et Monachorum scripta de desertione societatis politicae, sed doctrina fidei est de iudicio Dei, et de distinctione impiorum et Ecclesiae, et inter horrendas confusiones generis humani ostendit iram Dei contumacibus, et consolationem piis.

Ideoque prolixae sunt narrationes confusionum et scandalorum, ut postea doceat, nequaquam ex his spectaculis in hac vita iudicandum esse de voluntate Dei, sed firma fide assentiendum esse voci divinae et verbum Dei oportere normam esse omnium consiliorum et actionum, sicut scriptum est: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum.

Necesse est igitur in huius libri lectione novisse summam doctrinae ecclesiasticae, de creatione mundi et hominis, de lapsu hominum, de causis calamitatum, de promissione, et de Mediatore, propter quem et per quem rursus Ecclesia colligitur, de fide accipiente remissionem peccatorum, de lege Dei, de vita aeterna, de iudicio postremo, de poenis aeternis impiorum, de salute piorum.

Hanc totam doctrinam complecti necesse est, cum de providentia dicitur. Cum enim confusiones in hac brevi vita caliginem offundant mentibus, ut minus cernant providentiam, necesse est intueri illam alteram vitam, in qua discrimen erit illustre malorum et bonorum in omni aeternitate.

Consideranda est autem series partium in hoc libro Salomonis.

Prius recitat obiectiones, quae videntur adversari providentiae, et in hac recitatione prolixus est, quia magnos et assiduos tumultus excitant in humanis mentibus hae profanae cogitationes. Et igitur et haec pars libri prolixior.

Passim vero breves responsiones inserit.

Timeto Deum, restat aliud iudicium.

Haec brevissima dicta sunt responsiones, quas firma assensione et fide amplecti nos oportet.

Certissimum est enim esse eas decreta divina, quae in Ecclesia voce Prophetarum, Christi et Apostolorum saepe repetuntur, et fides certa et brevia dicta divina opponit turbulentis cogitationibus rationis. Haec ipsa certamina rationis humanae imitatur forma obiectionum et responsionum in hoc libro.

Sequuntur autem asseverationem de providentia, Lex et comminatio.

Item Evangelium et consolatio: postquam statuis esse Deum, et esse iudicem et vindicem, audi praecepta et obtempera, et quia magna est infirmitas hominum, et multi furores diabolorum, qui augent confusiones generis humani, multa sunt impedimenta obedientiae. Hic necessaria est consolatio.

Audienda est igitur vox Evangelii, quae docet, quae obedientia, et quomodo placeat, iubet gubernatorem non abiicere vocationis officia, etiamsi in hac vitae confusione aliquantisper dissimiles sunt eventus rectorum consiliorum, et monet, ne frangamur desperatione, etiamsi aliquantisper florent iniusti, et premitur vera Ecclesia, quia etiamsi aliquantisper differtur iudicium Dei, tamen aliquanto post et in hac vita, et in tota aeternitate punientur scelerati.

Hanc consolationem saepe intexuit huic Scripto, quae comprehensa est et in toto Psalmo 36. Noli aemulari, et in multis concionibus Prophetarum et Filii Dei, ut in capite Matth. 10.: Non timete eos, qui occidunt corpus, animam autem non possunt occidere, sed timete eum, qui potest animam et corpus perdere in gehennam.

Longe anteferenda est aeternitas brevissimo spatio huius vitae mortalis, et tamen in hac vita comitantur atroces poenas atrocia delicta, iuxta illud: Qui gladium acceperit gladio peribit, et experientia peperit haec dicta: τεύχων ὡς ἑτέρῳ τὶ, ἑῷ κακὸν ἥπατι τεύχει.

Ut de Archelao rege Macedonico dictum est, qui etiamsi fuit aliquantisper gloriosus rex, tamen quia per scelus regnum invaserat, a suis interfectus est, et singulae aetates multa vident talia exempla.

Iam facile intelligit lector non omnino rudis vitae communis, quis sit usus huius libri, quae inde utilitas capienda sit.

Confirmanda est assensio de providentia dictis huius concionatoris, quae in Ecclesia proponuntur non humana autoritate, sed divinitus.

Deinde suo quisque loco obediat Deo, et faciat officia vocationis, quam cum multa impediant, teneat consolationes quae hic proponuntur, sciat cursum in vocatione Deo placere, sciat Deum rectorem esse sui coetus, et velle peti auxilium divinum, et verissime opem ferre fideliter servientibus in vocatione, et tandem collocaturum esse Ecclesiam in illam aeternam consuetudinem. cum divinitate, in qua Deus erit omnia in omnibus.

Hac fide obtemperet Deo, recta faciat, et acquiescat in Deo, non indignatione, non desperatione abiiciat officia vocationis, non ruat in contemtum Dei Epicureum.

Hac admonitione de usu libri considerata, lectio et magis perspicua et dulcior erit, ac propemodum summa operis continetur in his dulcissimis regulis vitae.

Psalmo 36.: Subditus esto Deo, et ora eum.

Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Expecta Dominum, et custodi viam eius.

Iacta curam tuam in Dominum, et ipse te sustentabit.

Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis.

Ne sitis soliciti de crastino, sufficit diei afflictio.

Fac necessaria, et pete ac expecta auxilium a Deo, nec moveas non necessaria.

Sed intuens in mandata Dei, hanc normam sequaris, et scias ex Evangelio placere obedientiam propter Mediatorem, et per eum ac propter eum labores tuos fore salutares, sicut inquit: Sine me nihil potestis facere.

Et Paulus inquit: Non erit inanis labor vester in Domino.

Efficiet ipse Filius Dei, ut cursus tuus prosit Ecclesiae, sicut scriptum est: Ascendit, dedit dona hominibus, Prophetas, Apostolos, doctores etc.

Et in Psalmo dicitur: Qui dat salutem regibus.

Has consolationes veras et salutares esse, bonae mentes intelligunt.

Et quia magna pars harum consolationum pertinet ad virtutem, quae nominatur Patientia, breviter initio et hanc admonitionem addam.

Notum sit discrimen patientiae philosophicae et Christianae.

Patientia philosophica est obedire rationi in perferendis iis laboribus et aerumnis quas iubet ratio ferre, et nihil facere contra iusticiam, et hac recti conscientia moderari dolorem.

Interdum autem haec philosophica patientia est sine ulla spe auxilii, cum videlicet ratio non ostendit auxilium aut mitigationem ante mortem, ut Aristides, Camillus, aequo animo ferunt iniurias et exilia, nec expectant auxilium a Deo.

Sed patientia Christiana est obedire Deo in his laboribus et aerumnis ferendis, quas iubet Deus ferre, et nihil facere contra iusticiam, et petere ac expectare auxilium ac mitigationem a Deo propter Mediatorem, et hac fiducia praesentiae Dei moderari dolorem.

Ita in Davide, in Ieremia et similibus semper cum obedientia coniunctae sunt hae virtutes, fides et spes, et hae virtutes, fides et spes gignunt laeticiam in corde, iuxta illa dicta: Iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Item: Pax Dei custodiat corda vestra.

Huc pertinet regula Paulina scripta ad Thessalonicenses: Semper gaudete, incessanter orate, in omnibus gratias agite.

Ut autem haec fides accendatur in cordibus nostris, necesse est nosse Evangelium de remissione peccatorum, et de reconciliatione propter Mediatorem Filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Hunc intuetur fides, et scit per eum nos duci ad aeternum patrem, scit hunc Mediatorem umbraculum esse, quo tegimur, ne horrenda ira Dei extinguamur, et ne diaboli rabiem suam exercere in nos possint, ut cupiunt, scit iuvari et servari Ecclesiam per hunc Mediatorem Filium Dei.

Haec fiducia Mediatoris praeluceat omnibus aliis actionibus, ut saepe copiose dicitur.

Omitto longas recitationes, quomodo hic liber alienis interpretationibus obscuratus sit.

Alii physicam enarrationem quaesiverunt: alii fanaticas, quasi liber damnet coniugia, gubernationes, labores necessarios in Ecclesia, Politia et Oeconomia, et iusserunt deseri vocationem.

Haec deliramenta Monachorum reiicienda esse initio moneri necesse est.

Non damnat Salomon creaturas Dei, nec vocationem, imo iubet his reverenter et ordine uti, sed damnat in humano corde perversionem ordinis, quod ita movetur spectaculis eventuum, ut dubitet de providentia.

Cum autem falsae interpretationes huius libri magnam caliginem offuderint doctrinae Evangelii, utile est iuniores de simplici sententia commonefieri.

Sparsa est in Ecclesiam falsa interpretatio dicti: Nemo scit an amore vel odio dignus sit.

Id dictum contra huius libri sententiam enarratur.

Semper dubites an Deo placeas, cum tamen Salomon huic dubitationi mederi velit.

Non dubitant Ieremias vel alii credentes se placere Deo, etiamsi vident conflagrare patriam, et se in exilium abduci: hoc ipsum enim vult Salomon, de voluntate Dei ex eius verbo, non ex secundis aut adversis eventibus in hac vita iudicandum esse.

Haec de Argumento dixisse satis est.

## 1:1 Argument
Chapter I.

The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king of Jerusalem. In the title, he names himself Solomon and King, and Ecclesiastes, that is, a preacher, by which appellation he signifies that it pertains to the office of princes to ensure that the Churches are rightly taught, just as it is said in the Psalm: And now, O ye kings, understand. Item: Lift up your gates, O ye princes. Item: In the gathering of kings and peoples into one that they may serve the Lord. It was necessary for both princes and peoples to often think upon this sweet verse: because it is commanded to both, that they should gather, that is, that they should protect the common congregation and the ministry of the divine voice, and learn true doctrine, and with true consensus call upon God and strive to preserve the doctrine: Moreover, kings ought to be the leaders and authors of this pious consensus: therefore here too Solomon calls himself a preacher, signifying that he wishes to be the author of pious consensus in the Church and the guardian of true doctrine. *Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.

What hath a man more of all his labour?* First, you should know that this is not said to mean that things are evil, but the sentiment in Genesis must be most firmly held: God saw all that He had made, and they were very good, that is, ordered by His own wisdom and goodness, congruent to His own wisdom, pleasing to Him, and created for uses pleasing to Him and preserving nature.

It is necessary to remember this interpretation well at the beginning. And Genesis speaks of things created and remaining in their order, but Solomon speaks of human affairs. And he expressly says, under the Sun, to signify that he does not include God, the word of God, and whatever ministries are governed by the word of God under the appellation of vanity. For these things, too, when they retain their own order, are good things. But here it is spoken of the depravity of order, that is, he speaks of things and affairs brought to the human heart, which mixes in the disturbances of order. Therefore he says: All things are vain that are under the Sun, that is, affairs, human things are brief, fleeting, unstable, miserable, not bringing perpetual rest to the heart, not pleasures, not riches, not human wisdom and virtue, not glory, not the magnitude of empire. To all these things and affairs are mixed many great miseries on account of human weakness. But only the mercy of God, recognized in the promises, brings firm and perpetual tranquility and joy into hearts. I said, however, at the beginning that this book is a consolation. Therefore, the second part of the proposition is a complaint, which recounts miseries, and affirms that souls cannot find rest in human things or affairs. Therefore, things or events should not be preferred to the word of God. And so an Antithesis is added, which is the other part of the proposition and the sum of the work: Let the word of God govern minds, whatever the events in affairs may be. Thus they will find rest in God, just as Paul also commands: Let the peace of God govern your hearts, etc. The Sun ariseth and goeth down, and returneth to his place, all rivers enter the sea etc. Afterwards, he adds a similitude taken from the motions of the Sun and the waters, the application of which should be prudently considered.

For it is proposed only as an image of the instability and revolution of similar miseries in human affairs, and signifies that those miseries can be hindered neither by counsel nor by human wisdom. Just as when there had been great tumults and frequent seditions in the Roman Republic under the Consuls and Tribunes, afterwards a monarchy was sought, and yet similar miseries returned: so in Israel, when great calamities had occurred in the Aristocracy before the kingdom, the people wanted a kingdom to be established, and hoped that with the form of the Republic changed there would be a happier state, but some time later greater lacerations followed. Since, therefore, human things are unstable and do not bring rest, make it necessary and find rest in God. The simplest application of this similitude, therefore, is this: Just as the Sun and water have constant revolutions and are turned about, so human affairs, together with the miseries that are admixed, are turned about, and calamities cannot be hindered in general by human counsel or wisdom. In private and in public affairs we repeatedly attempt other counsels to effect a better state, and yet similar miseries return. To this sentiment he says: Nothing new under the Sun, and afterwards he adds the cause: The perverse are difficult to correct, and the number of fools is infinite, that is, no human wisdom can prohibit or avoid all lapses and sad accidents.

Because this nature is weak and foolish, therefore such things as happened before, such will happen in all ages and afterwards in general.

human. From this declaration it can be understood that this narrative in the text pertains to a complaint, that is, that it is a description of human miseries recurring in a similar way, just as Thucydides says: Similar things happen as long as the same nature of men remains, sometimes somewhat more mildly, sometimes somewhat more atrociously, as circumstances dictate. This consideration is necessary, however, so that, forewarned, we may prepare ourselves to bear adverse events, and know that help is to be sought from God and that we must acquiesce in Him, who mitigates calamities both for the Church and for those who invoke Him privately, and does not kindle all His wrath. Incidentally, however, let students observe here the statements which affirm that the Earth stands still and the Sun is moved. I omit other physical disputations.

Latin:

Caput I.

Verba Ecclesiaste filii David regis Ierusalem. In titulo nominat se Salomon et Regem, et Ecclesiasten, id est, concionatorem, qua appellatione significat ad officium principum pertinere ut curent recte doceri Ecclesias, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Et nunc reges intelligite. Item: Aperite portas principes vestras. Item: In conveniendo reges et populos in unum ut serviant Domino. Hunc dulcem versiculum saepe cogitare oportebat et principes et populos: quia utrisque praecipitur, ut conveniant, id est, tueantur communem congregationem et ministerium vocis divinae, et discant veram doctrinam, et vero consensu Deum invocent et doctrinam conservare studeant: Huius autem pii consensus reges debent esse duces et autores: ideo hic quoque Salomon se concionatorem nominat, significans se velle autorem esse pii consensus in Ecclesia et custodem verae doctrinae. *Vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas.

Quid habet homo amplius de universo labore suo?* Primum scias non hoc dici, res esse malas, sed sententia in Genesi firmissime retinenda est: Vidit Deus omnia quae fecerat, et erant valde bona, id est, ordinata ipsius sapientia et bonitate, congruentia ad ipsius sapientiam, placentia ipsi, et condita ad usus placentes ipsi et conservantes naturam.

Hanc interpretationem bene meminisse initio oportet. Et Genes. loquitur de rebus conditis et manentibus in suo ordine, sed Salomon loquitur de negotiis humanis. Ac diserte inquit, sub Sole, ut significet se non comprehendere vanitatis appellatione Deum, verbum Dei et ministeria quaecunque, quae reguntur verbo Dei. Nam haec quoque cum suum ordinem retinent, sunt res bonae. Sed hic de ordinis depravatione dicitur, id est, loquitur de rebus et negotiis collatis ad cor humanum, quod miscet conturbationes ordinis. Ideo dicit: Omnia sunt vana, quae sub Sole sunt, id est, negocia, humana sunt brevia, fugacia, instabilia, aerumnosa, non adferentia perpetuam quietem cordi, non voluptates, non divitiae, non sapientia et virtus humana, non gloria, non magnitudo imperii. His rebus et negotiis omnibus miscentur multae magnae miseriae propter hominum imbecillitatem. Sed sola Dei misericordia agnita in promissionib. adfert firmam et perpetuam tranquillitatem et laetitiam in cordibus. Dixi autem initio hunc librum consolationem esse. Ideo pars altera propositionis querela est, quae recitat miserias, et affirmat, non posse acquiescere animos in rebus seu negotiis humanis. Non igitur anteferantur res aut eventus verbo Deo. Itaque Antithesis additur, quae est altera pars propositionis et summa operis: Gubernet mentes verbum Dei, qualescunque sunt eventus in negotiis. Ita acquiescent in Deo, sicut et Paulus praecipit: Gubernet corda vestra pax Dei etc. Oritur Sol et occidit, et ad locum suum redit, omnia flumina intrant mare etc. Postea addit similitudinem sumtam a motibus Solis et aquarum, cuius accommodatio prudenter consideretur.

Tantum enim proponitur tanquam imago instabilitatis et revolutionis similium miseriarum in negotiis humanis, et significat eas miserias nec consilio nec sapientia humana impediri posse. Ut cum fuissent magni tumultus et crebrae seditiones in Republica Romana sub Coss. et Tribunis, postea expetita est monarchia, et redierunt tamen similes miseriae: ita in Israël, cum in Aristocratia ante regnum magnae calamitates accidissent, populus voluit regnum constitui, ac sperabat mutata forma Reipublicae feliciorem statum fore, sed aliquanto post secutae sunt maiores dilacerationes. Cum igitur instabilia sint humana, et non adferant quietem, fac necessaria et acquiescas in Deo. Simplicissima igitur accommodatio similitudinis haec est: Sicut Sol et aqua habent assiduas circumgyrationes et revolvuntur, ita humana negocia una cum miseriis quae admixtae sunt, revolvuntur, nec consilio aut sapientia humana impediri aerumnae in universum possunt. In privatis et in publicis negotiis subinde alia consilia tentamus ad efficiendum statum meliorem, et tamen redeunt similes miseriae. In hanc sententiam dicit: Nihil novi sub Sole, et postea addit causam: Perversi difficulter corriguntur, et stultorum infinitus est numerus, id est, nulla sapientia humana prohibere aut vitare potest omnes lapsus et tristes casus.

Quia haec natura est imbecilla et stulta, ideo qualia acciderunt antea, talia omnibus aetatibus et postea accident in genere.

humano. Ex hac declaratione intelligi potest, hanc narrationem in textu ad querelam pertinere, id est, descriptionem esse miseriarum humanarum simili modo recurrentium, sicut et Thucydides inquit: Similia accidere donec maneat eadem hominum natura, alias aliquanto mitius, alias aliquanto atrocius ut ferunt cicumstantiae. Necessaria est autem haec consideratio, ut praemoniti praeparemus nos ad ferendos adversus casus, et sciamus a Deo petendum auxilium et in eo acquiescendum, qui calamitates et Ecclesiae et privatim invocantibus mitigat, et non accendit totam iram suam. Obiter autem observent hic studiosi dicta, quae affirmant, Terram stare, et Solem moveri. Caeteras physicas disputationes omitto.

## 1:12
I, Ecclesiastes, was king in Jerusalem, etc.

First, you should know here that Solomon is not speaking of physical consideration, in which, if a sober observation of order and art in the workmanship of the world is made, he shows illustrious testimonies about God and providence. But Solomon speaks of Wisdom, that is, of the consideration of counsels, actions, and events in human government, whether political or economic. Therefore he expressly says that he had considered those things which are under the Sun, that is, the counsels and events of human actions, just as Pericles, Demosthenes, and Cicero are wise governors. Solomon speaks here of such wisdom; he names this very wisdom, or deliberations in government, an evil affliction, and adds that it was given to men by God.

These things seem absurd, but first let the calling be distinguished from the wisdom or government of Pericles or Cicero itself.

The calling is good and ordained by God, but that governing wisdom in Pericles is an evil affliction in two ways. First, how often he errs in counsels, and then because even with good counsels, events often do not respond.

Therefore, it is an affliction, that is, a punishment or torment, just as Demosthenes says that he would rather go straight to death than to the highest honors, if he were allowed to undo his life: and Aeschines says that he rejoices to have been freed from government as if from a rabid dog.

Finally, all prudent heads of families and governors feel that government is full not only of cares, but also of impediments, errors, and sad events, all of which greatly torment the mind. Hence those poems were invented about Prometheus fixed to the Caucasus, about Sisyphus rolling the stone, and the like.

But why does he say that this affliction was given by God? I answer: It is generally true that God wills punishment, yet it does not follow from this that God is the cause of sin.

He wills that Nero be punished, yet He Himself does not impel him to those foul crimes, but lets him fall. Thus, the plain answer here is: God lets governors err, He lets impediments and sad events happen, so that He may punish human rashness. Likewise, so that He may warn some, lest they yield to desires, ambition, or curiosity, but that their minds may be ruled in their calling by the Word of God, and be contained within those bounds, that they may seek and expect favorable events from God, and in sad events obey God. Josiah brings war upon the Egyptian, which is not necessary. Pericles moves war out of restlessness of mind and πολυπραγμοσύνῃ (meddlesomeness). Marius out of ambition. These err in their counsels. Often, indeed, even with good counsels, events do not respond, just as the Israelites often fight unsuccessfully even in a most just cause, as when they are defeated by the Benjaminites, because God willed that both sides be punished. He also wishes to teach us not to move toward unnecessary things, trusting in our own wisdom or power. Likewise, that in necessary things we may be humble, and confess that we deserve punishment. Likewise, that by faith we may seek and expect good events from God. Likewise, that we may obey God even when He punishes us and does not give the events we desire. In this sense he says that this affliction was divinely imposed upon the human race, because it is a common misery, which accompanies, as it were a punishment, the depravity of nature and many sins.

Latin:

Ego Ecclesiastes fui rex in Ierusalem etc.

Primum hic scias Salomonem non loqui de physica consideratione, in qua si fiat sobrie animadversio ordinis et artis in opificio mundi, illustria testimonia de Deo et de providentia ostendit. Sed loquitur Salomon de Sapientia, id est, de consideratione consiliorum, actionum et eventuum in gubernatione humana, politica vel oeconomica. Ideo expresse dicit, se considerasse ea quae sunt sub Sole, id est, consilia et eventus actionum humanarum, ut Pericles, Demosthenes, Cicero, sunt sapientes gubernatores. De tali sapientia hic loquitur Salomon, hanc ipsam sapientiam seu deliberationes in gubernatione, nominat malam afflictionem, et addit hominibus a Deo datam esse.

Haec videntur absurda, sed primum discernantur vocatio, et ipsa Periclis vel Ciceronis sapientia seu gubernatio.

Vocatio bona est, et a Deo ordinata, sed illa sapientia rectrix in Pericle, est afflictio mala dupliciter. Primum quam saepe errat in consiliis, deinde quia etiam bonis consiliis saepe non respondent eventus.

Est igitur afflictio, id est, poena seu cruciatus, sicut Demosthenes inquit, Se malle recta ad mortem ire, quàm ad summos honores, si retexere vitam liceret: et Aeschines ait, Gaudere se a gubernatione velut a rabiosa cane liberatum esse.

Denique omnes prudentes patresfamilias et gubernatores sentiunt plenam esse gubernationem non tantum curarum, sed etiam impedimentorum, errorum, tristium eventuum, quae omnia valde cruciant animos. Hinc illa poëmata ficta sunt de Prometheo affixo ad Caucasum, de Sisypho saxum volvente, et similia.

Sed cur dicit, a Deo hanc afflictionem datam esse? Respondeo: Generaliter verum est, Deum velle poenam, nequaquam tamen inde sequitur Deum causam esse peccati.

Vult puniri Neronem, nec tamen ipse impellit eum ad illa tetra scelera, sed sinit eum ruere. Ita hic plana responsio est, Deus sinit errare gubernatores, sinit accidere impedimenta et tristes eventus, ut puniat humanam temeritatem. Item, ut commonefaciat aliquos, ne obsequantur cupiditatibus, ambitioni aut curiositati. sed ut mentes in vocatione regantur verbo Dei, et intra eas metas contineantur, petant et expectent secundos eventus a Deo, et in tristibus eventibus Deo obtemperent. Iosias infert bellum Aegyptio non necessarium. Pericles movet bellum inquietudine animi et πολυπραγμοσύνῃ. Marius ambitione. Hi errant in consiliis. Saepe vero etiam bonis consiliis non respondent eventus, ut Israëlitae saepe infeliciter pugnant etiam in causa iustissima, ut cum vincuntur a Beniamitis, quia Deus volebat utrosque puniri. Vult etiam docere, ne confisi nostra sapientia aut potentiam moveamus res non necessarias. Item, ut in necessariis simus humiles, fateamur nos poenam meritos esse. Item, fide petamus et expectemus bonos eventus a Deo. Item, ut Deo obtemperemus etiam cum nos punit, nec dat eventus quales optamus. In hanc sententiam inquit hanc afflictionem divinitus impositam esse generi humano, quia communis miseria est, quae tanquam poena comitatur pravitatem naturae et multa peccata.

## 1:16-18
I spoke in my heart, etc. My mind contemplated many things wisely, etc. For in much wisdom there is much indignation, and he who adds knowledge, adds also sorrow.

As was said above, Solomon is not speaking of physical consideration of order in the workmanship of the world, or of the knowledge of the Word of God, but he speaks of the consideration of counsels, actions, and human events, in which we perceive life to be full of confusions, errors, vices, and calamities. Those wiser and experienced in government perceive present evils more closely, and reason out from present ones many dreadful events to come. Therefore they are tormented with great grief on account of the present and future miseries, and indeed, once mutual debts have arisen, greater confusions follow, as when war was set in motion by Pericles, the destruction of almost all the great cities in Greece followed.

And it is too true what Pindar says: It is easy for anyone to move a city, but to set it in tranquility belongs to God alone.

So far the complaint has been recited in the first chapter, and the consolation, which follows later, has not yet been added.

But this is the summary.

We see that there are great confusions in life, great errors, and many sad events.

Therefore, we cannot find rest in the things themselves; the very confusion of things does not produce tranquility, nor yet, because of these miseries, should one fall away from God, but one must obey Him patiently, and expect defense and liberation from Him, and in Him one must find rest by faith according to His word.

This is the summary not only of this chapter but also of the entire book, consistent with these sayings: Be subject to God and pray to Him.

Item: Cast your care upon God, and He will sustain you.

This consolation will be added later in the third chapter, and subsequently.

Latin:

Locutus sum in corde meo etc. Mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter etc. Eo quod in multa sapientia, multa sit indignatio, et qui addit scientiam, addit et dolorem.

Ut supra dictum est, non loquitur Salomon de physica consideratione ordinis in opificio mundi, aut cognitione verbi Dei, sed loquitur de consideratione consiliorum, actionum et eventuum humanorum, in quibus cernimus vitam plenam esse confusionum, errorum, vitiorum et calamitatum. Sapientiores et versati in gubernatione propius cernunt praesentia mala, et multos tetros casus futuros ex praesentibus ratiocinantur. Ideo magno dolore excruciantur propter praesentes et futuras miserias, et quidem semel ortis mutuationibus sequi maiores confusiones, ut moto bello a Pericle, secuta sunt excidia pene omnium magnarum urbium in Graecia.

Et nimis verum est, quod dicit Pindarus: Facile est civitatem movere cuivis, sed in tranquillum sistere solius Dei est.

Hactenus querela recitata est in primo capite, ac nondum addita est consolatio, quae postea sequitur.

Est autem haec summa.

Videmus magnas in vita confusiones esse, magna errata et multos tristes eventus.

Ideo non possumus acquiescere in ipsis rebus, non parit tranquillitatem ipsa rerum confusio, neque tamen propter has miserias a Deo deficiendum est, sed ei obediendum patienter, et ab ipso expectanda defensio et liberatio, et in ipso fide acquiescendum est iuxta verbum ipsius.

Haec est summa non solum huius capitis, sed etiam universi libri, congruens cum his dictis: Subditus esto Deo et ora eum.

Item: Iacta curam tuam in Deum, et ipse te sustentabit.

Haec consolatio postea in capite tertio, et deinceps addetur.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter II.

I said therefore in my heart: I will go and abound in delights, and I will enjoy good things.

And I saw that this also was vanity.

Themistocles, Lucullus, and many others finally gave themselves over to pleasures, weary of the Republic because of many useless contentions and the ingratitude of men.

Thus men slide from extremes to extremes; weary of labors, they then indulge profusely in pleasures.

This method of seeking tranquility he also calls vanity here, nor is it a condemnation of things; rather, God Himself, in His immense goodness, has seasoned this life with many most sweet pleasures.

And one must use food, drink, and other things divinely created according to divine ordination, with invocation and thanksgiving: but it is vanity to wish to find rest in these, when one must find rest in God.

Moreover, many sorrows are mixed into these pleasures, as there are many complaints in poems.

Ovid says: To such an extent is there no sincere pleasure, and something anxious intervenes in joyful things.

And Plautus: It is a small matter of pleasures in life, except for what is troublesome.

Item, sorrow follows as a companion to pleasure.

Thus he says here: I understood laughter to be foolishness, that is, that the pleasures of the body are neither lasting nor whole.

Nor should another meaning be sought far away.

But he signifies that men cannot find rest in the pleasures of the body, nor should they be broken so that they fall away from God when pleasures are hindered or snatched away, just as he warned above, that one should not fall away from God because of sad events and the confusions of government, but should patiently obey God, and expect good things from Him.

I magnified my works, I built houses for myself and planted vineyards etc.

There follows a complaint about another neighboring pleasure, that is, about magnificence and splendor in life, and about the curiosity of the investigation of many things.

For this desire also is no light torture, since, with necessary things omitted, unnecessary things are sought with great care and great labor.

I possessed servants and handmaids, and much family etc.

He adds other businesses, such as the diligence of increasing family property, which is sometimes fruitless, and often great patrimonies are pernicious to descendants.

Concerning all these things, concerning the investigation of doctrine, concerning faculties as above, he advises that they are good things, and that one must serve one's vocation, necessary things must be learned, family property must be sought, but in such a way that we do not think we will find tranquility in these businesses.

For many things are added, useless occupations, many errors.

Nor should we be consumed by the pain of cares when events do not respond to our efforts or hope, but we should patiently grieve the will of God, and do what is necessary.

This conclusion the text itself puts forward, saying: Tranquility is from the hand of God.

Item: God gives wisdom and joy to a man who pleases Him, but to the sinner, affliction.

Therefore, he does not disapprove of the investigation of doctrine, but he wants everyone to obey his own vocation, and us to find rest in God, whether labors proceed or do not proceed, let us not desert our vocations, let us not be angry with God, even if we do not become rich in the same way.

Necessary studies should not be deserted, even if we cannot find everything, nor does the knowledge of things take away death, or most other miseries, as he says here: The learned man dies as the unlearned.

He narrates those things which we see happening before our eyes, and he wants the vocation not to be deserted because of such events.

Aristotle was learned, and died an exile. Indeed, they say he was extinguished by grief, because he could not find the cause of the flux and reflux of the Euripus. Therefore, let all things be referred to the rule often handed down: let us use things as they are ordained, let us serve in political government, let us seek our livelihood, let us learn necessary things, and let us acknowledge God, who ordained all these things, and let us give thanks to Him for all these gifts; and if anything happens otherwise, let us patiently tolerate His will, and let us acquiesce in Him, as has often been said: Be subject to God and pray to Him.

Latin:

Caput II.

Dixi ergo in corde meo: Vadam et adfluam deliciis, et fruar bonis.

Et vidi quod hoc quoque esset vanitas.

Themistocles, Lucullus et multi alii tandem se voluptatibus dediderunt pertaesi Reipublicae propter multas inutiles contentiones, et ingratitudinem hominum.

Ita ab extremis ad extrema delabuntur homines, pertaesi laborum deinde voluptatibus effuse indulgent.

Hunc modum quaerendae tranquillitatis hic etiam nominat vanitatem, nec est rerum reprehensio, imo Deus ipse immensa bonitate multis dulcissimis voluptatibus hanc vitam condivit.

Ac utendum est cibo, potu et aliis rebus divinitus conditis iuxta divinam ordinationem, cum invocatione et gratiarum actione: sed vanitas est velle in his acquiescere, cum in Deo sit acquiescendum.

Praeterea in his voluptatibus multi dolores admixti sunt, ut in poëmatis multae sunt querelae.

Ovidius inquit: Usque adeo nulla est sincera voluptas, solicitumque aliquid laetis intervenit.

Et Plautus: Statin parva res est voluptatum in vita praeterquam quod molestum est.

Item, voluptati moeror comes consequitur.

Ita hic dicit: Risum intellexi esse stulticiam, id est, voluptates corporis nec diuturnas nec integras esse.

Nec procul alia sententia quaeratur.

Sed significat non posse homines acquiescere in voluptatibus corporis, nec frangi debere, ut deficiant a Deo, cum voluptates impediuntur aut eripiuntur, sicut supra monuit, non deficiendum esse a Deo propter tristes eventus et confusiones gubernationis, sed Deo patienter obediendum esse, et ab ipso expectanda bona.

Magnificavi opera mea, aedificavi mihi domos et plantavi vineas etc.

Sequitur querela de alia vicina voluptate, id est, de magnificentia et splendore in vita, et de curiositate inquisitionis multarum rerum.

Nam et haec cupiditas non est levis carnificina, cum omissis necessariis, magna cura et magno labore non necessaria inquiruntur.

Possedi servos et ancillas, multamque familiam etc.

Addit et alia negocia, ut diligentiam augendae rei familiaris, quae interdum est irrita, saepe magna patrimonia posteris perniciosa sunt.

De his omnibus de inquisitione doctrinae, de facultatibus ut supra, monet res bonas esse, et vocationi serviendum esse, necessaria discenda, rem familiarem quaerendam, sed ita, ne existimemus nos tranquillitatem in his negociis inventuros esse.

Multae enim accedunt, inutiles occupationes, multa errata.

Nec conficiamur curis dolore, cum non respondent eventus nostris conatibus aut spei, sed patienter doleremus voluntatem Dei, et necessaria faciamus.

Hanc conclusionem textus ipse ponit inquiens: Tranquillitas de manu Dei est.

Item: Deus dat homini placenti sapientiam et laetitiam, peccatori vero afflictionem.

Non igitur non inquisitionem doctrinae improbat, sed vult suae quemque vocationi parere, et nos in Deo acquiescere, sive procedant labores, sive non procedant, non deseramus vocationes, non irascamur Deo, etiamsi non pariter ditescimus.

Non deserantur studia necessaria, etiamsi non omnia invenire possumus, nec rerum cognitio tollit mortem, aut alias plerasque miserias, ut hic inquit: Moritur doctus ut indoctus.

Narrat ea quae fieri nostris oculis cernimus, et vult, ne propter tales eventus deseratur vocatio.

Aristoteles fuit doctus, et mortuus est exul. Imo dicunt eum dolore extinctum esse, quod causam invenire non potuit fluxuum et refluxuum Euripi. Omnia igitur ad regulam saepe traditam referantur, utamur rebus, ut sunt ordinatae, serviamus in gubernatione politica, quaeramus rem familiarem, discamus necessaria, et Deum agnoscamus, qui haec omnia ordinavit, et ei gratias agamus pro omnibus istis donis, et si quid secus accidit, patienter voluntatem eius toleremus, et in eo acquiescamus, ut saepe iam dictum est: Subditus esto Deo et ora eum.

## 3:1 Argument
Chapter III.

In the third chapter, now expressly after the complaints, he adds a conclusion and an asseveration. God made all things good in their time, that is, the use of things, as it is ordained by God, is good and is happy in its time, that is, when we use things according to the ordinance of God and with God helping, according to that: A man cannot take anything for himself, unless it be given to him from above.

Therefore, afterwards he adds a long catalog: All things have a time, that is, it is not of human counsel without a calling and without the help of God to choose happy times. Brutus, Cicero, Hircius, and Pansa think that the old state of the Roman Republic can be restored, and they are deceived, and always in this way many have been deceived, and will be deceived. But affairs proceed when we obey our calling, and indeed with God helping, and yet sometimes more, sometimes less difficultly. To this pertains the saying of the Psalm: Commend your way to God, and He will act. And He has put the world in their heart. But man cannot find the work that the Lord does, neither the beginning nor the end. That is, God created things in such a way that hearts should sweetly enjoy them, and celebrate the author, and have tranquility in God; He gave foods, pleasures, riches, arts, empires, virtue, but to men the use becomes unpleasant, because they have wandering desires, they mix vain anxieties because of distrust, they seek new things and move unnecessary matters, as Jeremiah said most briefly and most significantly: The heart of man is perverse and miserable.

Antonius obtained a most flourishing part of the empire, but his restless nature, when it desires the whole empire, brings destruction upon itself. Bellerophon is carried by Pegasus at the beginning to perform useful deeds, but afterwards, having become too proud, when he wanted to be carried higher to the conversation of Jove, he is narrated to have been thrown off by Pegasus. Against these evils, men ought to remain in their calling, and by faith acquiesce in God, and to do this, says Solomon: It is the gift of God. Therefore it follows in the text: There is nothing better for a man than to rejoice and do good in his life. For every man who eats and drinks, and sees good from his labor, this is the gift of God. These words are not said mimetically [in a mocking way] in the person of a glutton, but are an asseveration of one rightly teaching, pertaining to the established conclusion, which approves the use of things as it is ordained by God; he says this use is happy and sweet with God helping; he commands, therefore, to use things according to the ordinance of God, and shows from where it must be sought so that the use may be happy, and where one must acquiesce.

Faith looks to God, let it perform the duties of the calling, let it seek and expect help and success from God, and let it bear inconveniences, and insofar as labor is happy, let it know that it is helped and governed by God, and let it give thanks to Him. This is the meaning of the words, "He who sees good from his labor, it is the gift of God." He approves and demands labor, and says that with God helping it is happy and pleasing. This sentiment agrees with the whole Psalm: Unless the Lord builds the house, etc. As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of the strong. Such was the government of Jehoshaphat, which, although it itself had some offenses, yet for the most part was salutary and happy with God helping, and he himself acquiesced in God.

On the contrary, the government of Ahaz was restless and unhappy, since he himself was without faith, and attempted many things by human wisdom outside of his calling. All the works that God does are firm. He dwells on the previous sentiment: Human counsels without God are unhappy, like the government of Ahaz and Agesilaus. On the contrary, the works of God are firm, that is, salutary, happy, and proceeding, even if the devil tries to hinder them in various ways, as the battles of David are happy, and the government of Jehoshaphat is salutary.

But especially to be observed is the epiphonema: God does this, that He may be feared. This particle about the fear of God, repeated several times in this book, shows that Solomon is not [making] empty complaints to cite in the philosophical manner, or as it is said in poems: "While we speak, envious time will have fled; seize the day, trusting as little as possible in the morrow": but to hand down a rule of life most necessary, to set boundaries for our calling, to condemn trust in ourselves, curiosity, and other wandering desires, and to show the will of God, to teach fear, and God will judge the just and the impious.

Again, there follow examples of human miseries and confusions: many things are done unjustly even in a government that is not tyrannical, because good men cannot inspect all business, and many things are carried out by negligent men, many by the wicked obeying depraved affections; meanwhile, however, God preserves the political order in some way, and judges in his own time.

I said in my heart concerning the sons of men.

He adds at the end a general complaint concerning the confusion of human life in its external appearance: he says that the destruction of beasts and of men seems similar.

In this place, interpreters have labored much: they have said that these things are recited in the person of an Epicurean man, but Solomon speaks of the external appearance.
