If only eyes and human reason were consulted without the word of God, this life of men seems to be ruled by chance in such great confusion, and men to be like a swarm of ants, and to be crushed just as swarms of ants are crushed; and against this appearance, he will later advise that the word of God must be opposed.

What has been done, it remains.

Solomon speaks of events, and illustrates the sentiment: Human counsels, when they are not governed divinely, are vain, as Antony tries in vain to seize the monarchy, but Augustus wins.

Nor can Augustus be hindered by human counsels, because God governs this event.

He speaks of such events when he says: What has been done, it remains, that is, those things which God does and helps, come to pass, and this doctrine agrees entirely with the common rule: Unless the Lord builds the house, etc.

Item: A man cannot take anything for himself, unless it is given to him from heaven.

Item: Without me you can do nothing.

Those things which are to be, have already been.

That is, those things which are to happen, happen, because they were decreed by God long before.

Cyrus will be king, nor can he be killed by Astyages, because this was decreed long before.

This explanation is the simple, native meaning of the text, but it has often been said that many admonitions are contained in this doctrine.

Since human efforts without God are vain, you should only do the commandments divinely, and ask that he himself may rule and help you, for he wishes to help those serving in their calling, and those calling upon him.

As the Psalm says: Commit your way to God, and he will act.

Latin:

Caput III.

In tertio capite, iam expresse post querelas addit conclusionem et asseverationem. Cuncta fecit Deus bona suo tempore, id est, rerum usus, ut a Deo ordinatus est, est bonus et est felix suo tempore, id est, cum utimur rebus iuxta ordinationem Dei et Deo iuvante, iuxta illud: Non potest sibi homo sumere quicquam, nisi sit ei datum desuper.

Ideo postea longum catalogum addit: Omnia tempus habent, id est, non est humani consilii sine vocatione et sine auxilio Dei eligere tempora felicia. Brutus, Cicero, Hircius, Pansa cogitant restitui posse veterem statum Reipublicae Romanae, et falluntur, et semper hoc modo multi decepti sunt, et decipientur. Sed procedunt negocia cum obtemperamus vocationi, et quidem iuvante Deo, et tamen alias magis, alias minus difficulter. Huc pertinet dictum Psalmi: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet. Et dedit mundum in cor eorum. Sed homo non potest invenire opus quod facit Dominus, nec initium nec finem. Id est, Deus res ita condidit, ut corda suaviter eis frui deberent, et celebrare autorem et habere tranquillitatem in Deo, dedit cibos, voluptates, divitias, artes, imperia, virtutem, sed hominibus fit usus insuavis, quia habent, vagas cupiditates, miscent vanas solicitudines propter diffidentiam, appetunt nova et movent res non necessarias, sicut brevissime dixit et significantissime Ieremias: Cor hominis perversum et aerumnosum.

Antonius adeptus est florentissimam partem imperii, sed natura inquieta cum appetit totum imperium accersit sibi exitium. Bellerophontes Pegaso vehitur initio ad res utiles gerendas, postea factus elatior, cum vellet altius ad Iovis colloquium vehi, narratur a Pegaso excussus esse. Contra haec mala debebant homines manere in vocatione, et fide acquiescere in Deo, et hoc facere, inquit Salomon: Est donum Dei. Sequitur ergo in textu: Non est melius homini, quam laetari et benefacere vitae suae. Omnis enim homo qui comedit et bibit, et videt bonum de labore suo, hoc donum Dei est. Haec verba non dicuntur μιμητικῶς in persona helluonis, sed sunt asseveratio recte docentis pertinens ad institutam conclusionem, quae approbat rerum usum, ut a Deo ordinatus est, hunc usum ait felicem et suavem esse Deo iuvante, iubet igitur uti rebus iuxta ordinationem Dei, et ostendit unde petendum sit, ut sit usus felix, et ubi acquiescendum sit.

Fides intuetur Deum, faciat officia vocationis, petat et expectet a Deo auxilium et successus, et perferat incommoda, et quatenus labor est felix, sciat eum a Deo iuvari et gubernari, et ei gratias agat. Haec est sententia verborum, Qui videt bonum de labore suo, Dei donum est. Approbat et postulat laborem, et dicit, iuvante Deo felicem et gratum esse. Haec sententia congruit cum toto Psalmo: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum etc. Sicut sagittae in manu potentis, ita filii fortium. Talis fuit gubernatio Iosaphat, quae quanquam et ipsa offensiones aliquas habuit, tamen magna ex parte salutaris et felix fuit iuvante Deo, et acquievit ipse in Deo.

Econtra gubernatio Achas inquieta, infelix fuit, cum ipse esset sine fide, et multa humana sapientia extra vocationem conaretur. Omnia opera, quae facit Deus, firma sunt. Commoratur in superiore sententia: Humana consilia sine Deo sunt infelicia, ut gubernatio Achaz, Agesilai. Econtra Dei opera firma sunt, id est, salutaria, felicia, procedentia, etiamsi diabolus variis modis impedire conatur, ut Davidis ...praelia felicia sunt, gubernatio Iosaphat salutaris est.

Praecipue vero observandum est epiphonema: Haec facit Deus, ut timeatur. Haec particula de timore Dei aliquoties repetita in hoc libro ostendit, Salomonem non inanes querelas recitare more philosophico, aut sicut in poëmatis dicitur: Dum loquimur fugerit invida aetas, carpe diem quam minimum credula postero: sed tradere regulam vitae maxime necessariam, circumdare nobis metas vocationis, damnare fiduciam nostri, curiositatem et alias errantes cupiditates, et monstrare voluntatem Dei, docere timorem et Iustum et impium iudicabit Deus.

Rursus sequuntur exempla miseriarum humanarum et confusionum: multa fiunt iniuste etiam in gubernatione non tyrannica, quia nec inspicere omnia negocia boni possunt, et multa geruntur per homines negligentes, multa per impidem obtemperantes pravis affectibus, interea tamen Deus servat utcunque politicum ordinem, et suo tempore iudicat.

Dixi in corde meo de filiis hominum.

Addit in fine generalem querelam, de confusione vitae humanae in externa specie: dicit videri similem interitum pecudum et hominum.

In hoc loco interpretes multum sudarunt: dixerunt in persona hominis Epicurei haec recitari, sed Salomon de externa specie loquitur.

Si tantum oculi et ratio humana consulerentur sine verbo Dei, videtur haec vita hominum in tanta confusione casu regi, et homines esse velut agmen formicarum, et conteri perinde ut conterentur agmina formicarum, et contra hanc speciem postea monebit opponendum esse verbum Dei.

Quod factum est, ipsum permanet.

Loquitur Salomon de eventibus, et illustrat sententiam, Humana consilia cum non gubernantur divinitus, sunt irrita, ut Antonius frustra conatur occupare monarchiam, sed vincit Augustus.

Nec potest impediri humanis consiliis Augustus, quia Deus hunc eventum gubernat.

De talibus eventibus loquitur, cum ait: Quod factum est ipsum permanet, id est, ea quae Deus agit et iuvat, eveniunt, et prorsus congruit haec doctrina cum communi regula: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum etc.

Item: Non potest sibi homo sumere quicquam, nisi sit ei datum de coelo.

Item: Sine me nihil potestis facere.

Ea quae futura sunt, iam fuerunt.

Id est, ea quae eventura sunt, eveniunt, quia a Deo multo ante decreta sunt.

Cyrus erit rex, nec potest ab Astyage interfici, quia multo ante hoc decretum est.

Haec enarratio simplex est nativa sententia textus, saepe autem dictum est, multas admonitiones in hac doctrina contineri.

Cum humani conatus sine Deo irriti sint, tantum facias mandata divinitus, et petas, ut ipse te regat et adiuvet, vult enim adiuvare servientes in vocatione, et invocantes ipsum.

Sicut Psalmus inquit: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet.

## 4:1 Argument
Chapter IV.

I turned myself to other things, and I saw the calumnies which are done under the Sun, and the tears of the innocent.

At the beginning of chapter 4, he returns to injuries, which are a notable example of confusion in human life.

And if consolation had not been proposed in the Gospel, the voice would be true: It is best not to be born.

Again I contemplated that all the labors of men are exposed to envy.

Another example concerning envy.

This also is a great impediment to necessary and useful actions in life, as the envious drag Scipio back from Africa.

The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.

He adds other examples concerning the slothful.

Item, concerning the miser, and in the censure of the miser he enters into the topic of the praise of society: and he warns that the association of men, of duties, of arts, of craftsmen, and of orders is necessary for life. All orders are in need of mutual aid, and individual men [must] refer they owe their labors to the common association, to protect the congregation, to take care that no dissipations occur, according to those sayings: The Good is conservative, congregative, and communicative of itself. Conversely, Evil is dissipative and destructive of itself, but man, being greedy (πλεονεκτικὸς), wishes to consult his own utility, even with the ruin of the community. This evil he censures. Better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king. Another example concerning the ambitious and the restless in government. The restless in governments also disturb many things without necessity, and afterwards are punished, as Saul, Eurystheus, and countless others.

Latin:

Caput IV.

Verti me ad alia, et vidi calumnias, quae sub Sole geruntur, et lacrimas innocentum.

Initio capitis 4. redit ad iniurias, quae sunt insigne exemplum confusionis in vita humana.

Ac si consolatio in Evangelio non proposita esset, vera esset vox, Optimum non nasci.

Rursus contemplatus sum omnes labores hominum patere invidiae.

Aliud exemplum de invidiae.

Haec quoque magnum impedimentum est necessariarum et utilium actionum in vita, ut Scipionem invidi retrahunt ex Africa.

Stultus complicat manus suas et comedit carnes suas.

Addit alia exempla de ignavo.

Item de avaro, et in vituperatione avari ingreditur in locum de laude societatis: et monet necessariam vitae esse consociationem hominum, officiorum, artium, opificum et ordinum, Omnes ordines mutuis auxiliis indigent, et singuli homines referre suos labores debent ad communem consociationem, tueri congregationem, cavere ne fiant dissipationes, iuxta illa dicta: Bonum est conservativum, congregativum et communicativum sui. Econtra, Malum est dissipativum et destructivum sui, sed homo πλεονεκτικὸς suae utilitati vult consulere, etiam cum pernicie communi. Id malum vituperat. Melior est pauper sapiens rege sene et stulto. Aliud exemplum de ambitiosis et inquietis in imperio. Inquieti in imperiis etiam multa sine necessitate turbant, ac postea plectuntur, ut Saul, Eurystheus et alii innumerabiles.

## 5:1 Argument
Chapter V.

Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear.

Here he returns to the precepts, and at the beginning distinguishes the true worship of God from hypocrites, and recalls us from the external appearance of human confusions to the acknowledgment of God, to the consideration of the divine commandments and promises. And by the testimony of this chapter, those inept people are manifestly refuted who have dreamed that this book of Solomon is a profane or Epicurean discourse. And at the beginning he teaches that the chief worship is to hear the word of God, that is, the commandments and promises, and in true faith to obey the word of God, just as it is commanded in the same words in Jeremiah 7. I did not command them concerning burnt offerings, but this I commanded them: Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.

Therefore, the whole doctrine of the first commandment is to be thought of here. Nor does he make mention of the house of God without cause. For he warns that the doctrine concerning the Church and the true ministry should be sought, and that we should hear the teaching Church, as it is said elsewhere: If they had not plowed with my heifer, they would not have found it.

And Deut. 17: You shall come to the priest, and they shall teach you according to the law of God, where he expressly joins the Law and the Doctors.

This is better than the sacrifices of fools. Many dream that only ceremonies are the worship of God, just as the Gentiles worship God with gestures, as Plato names it. Their foolishness is manifest, because the law says: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.

Others, when they do not acknowledge that ceremonies are not enough, demand an external discipline of moral works, like the Pharisees, but neither is discipline without repentance and faith the worship of God, as it is said in Matthew 5: Unless your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the Pharisees, etc.

But it is necessary that repentance and faith, which receives the remission of sins on account of the Mediator, should approach in the heart. Concerning these distinctions, Solomon here preaches: he wishes first that hearts be ruled by the word of God, by fear and by faith.

But it has always been customary to accumulate sacrifices and to invent various forms of worship, and thus the Gentiles, the Pharisees, and the Monks departed from the voice of God. This audacity of man he condemns and affirms to be a foul sin, even if men think this superstition to be an excellent virtue. Therefore he adds: They know not how much evil they do.

Be not rash to speak or to utter a word. Before, he commanded us to hear, to learn, to deliberate from the word of God, according to the saying: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet.

Here he adds the consequence of that sentiment: Since the word of God is to be heard, there follows a prohibition, that you should not teach, affirm, or do anything against the word of God, as the Gentiles, Pharisees, Popes, and Monks have invented forms of worship and deities against the word of God. Samosatenus and Arius most audaciously invented dogmas against the word of God, as in the case of Absalom.

Antonius and many others moved governments without a calling and against the word of God. Josiah, although a holy man, nevertheless fell, moving a war that was not necessary.

Therefore, the saying of Solomon preaches to all men that they should hear the word of God, that they should affirm nothing in the Church which is not handed down by God: that they should not move governments without a calling and without necessity. Thus says Peter: If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God, namely in teaching, and if any man minister, let him minister as of the ability which God supplies, that is, let him remain within the bounds of his calling, which God aids, who does not wish to aid those who, by their own curiosity, attempt things alien to their calling, according to that: Commit thy way unto the Lord, and he shall bring it to pass.

These sayings of Peter entirely agree with this place of Solomon. But Solomon adds a threat: God is in heaven, that is, the inspector, judge, and avenger.

Psalm 32: He beholds all the sons of men, he understands all their works. Item:

He renders to everyone according to their works.

Latin:

Caput V.

Custodi pedem tuum ingrediens domum Dei, et appropinqua ut audias.

Hic redit ad praecepta, et initio discernit veros cultus Dei ab hypocritis, et revocat nos ab externa specie confusionum humanarum ad agnitionem Dei, ad considerationem mandatorum et promissionum divinarum. Ac manifeste refutantur huius capitis testimonio inepti, qui hunc librum Salomonis somniarunt prophanum vel Epicureum sermonem esse. Ac principio docet praecipuum cultum esse audire verbum Dei, id est, mandata et promissiones, et in vera fide obedire verbo Dei, sicut Ieremiae 7. iisdem verbis praecipitur. Non praecepi ei de holocaustis, sed hoc praecepi eis: Audite vocem meam, et ero vobis Deus, et eritis mihi populus.

Tota igitur doctrina primi praecepti hic cogitanda est. Nec sine causa facit mentionem domus Dei. Monet enim ut quaeratur doctrina de Ecclesia et vero ministerio, et audiamus docentem Ecclesiam, sicut alibi dicitur: Nisi vitula mea arassent non invenissent.

Et Deut. 17.: Venies ad sacerdotem, et hi doceant te iuxta legem Dei, ubi expresse coniungit Legem et Doctores.

Hoc melius est quam stultorum victimae. Multi solas ceremonias somniant esse cultum Dei, sicut Ethnici colentes Deum gestibus, sicut nominat Plato, Horum stulticia manifesta est, quia lex dicit: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde.

Alii cum non agnoscant non sufficere ceremonias, postulant externam disciplinam operum moralium, ut Pharisaei, sed nec disciplina sine poenitentia et fide est cultus Dei, ut Matth. 5. dicitur: Nisi iusticia vestra abundabit supra Pharisaeorum iusticiam etc.

Oportet autem accedere in corde poenitentiam et fidem accipientem remissionem peccatorum propter Mediatorem. De his discriminibus hic concionatur Salomon: vult primum corda regi verbo Dei, timore et fide.

Semper autem usitatum fuit cumulare sacrificia, et varios cultus comminisci, atque ita a voce Dei discesserunt Ethnici, Pharisaei, Monachi. Hanc audaciam hominis damnat et adfirmat tetrum peccatum esse, etiamsi homines hanc superstitionem putant esse excellentem virtutem. Ideo addit: Nesciunt quantum faciant mali.

Ne sis velox ad loquendum aut proferendum sermonem. Antea iussit nos audire, discere, deliberare ex verbo Dei, iuxta dictum: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum.

Hic addit consequens eius sententiae, Cum audiendum sit verbum Dei, sequitur prohibitio, ne quid doceas, adfirmes, facias contra verbum Dei, ut Ethnici, Pharisaei, Papae, Monachi, fnxerunt cultus et numina verbum Dei. Samosatenus, Arius, audacissime finxerunt dogmata contra verbum Dei, sic in facto Absalon.

Antonius et multi alii moverunt imperia sine vocatione et contra verbum Dei. Iosias quanquam vir sanctus, tamen lapsus est, movens bellum non necessarium.

Itaque dictum Salomonis concionatur omnibus hominibus, ut audiant verbum Dei, nihil adfirment in Ecclesia, quod non est a Deo traditum: non moveant imperia sine vocatione et sine necessitate. Sic dicit Petrus: Qui loquitur, loquatur oracula Dei, scilicet in docendo, et qui administrat, administret tanquam ex virtute, quam suppeditat Deus, id est, maneat intra metas vocationis, quam Deus adiuvat, qui non vult iuvare sua curiositate tentantes aliena a vocatione, iuxta illud: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet.

Haec dicta Pétri prorsus cum hoc loco Salomonis congruunt. Addit autem comminationem Salomon: Deus in coelo est, id est, inspector, iudex et vindex.

Psalm. 32.: Videt omnes filios hominum, intelligit omnia opera eorum.

Item: Reddit unicuique iuxta opera eorum.

## 5:3
Many cares follow dreams, and in many words is found foolishness. Cares of labor, care about the outcome, and care outside of one's calling differ.

The care of labor is most severely commanded in Rom. 12: He who presides, let him be diligent. 1. Cor. 4: This is required in the ministry, that one be faithful. But affected negligence is similar to treachery.

Therefore, the care of David is to be praised, when he foresees the times and places opportune for battle, as Alexander said to Parmenion: Do you think I could have slept before I had determined how we were to draw up the battle line?

But David is accustomed to seek a happy outcome of the battle from God, and he commends this care to God.

On the contrary, one sins in both ways, when through foolish persuasion someone promises himself certain victory because of his strength or fortune, as Pompey did, or when he is tormented by diffidence, as Aratus was.

Solomon here reproves such care, which is anxious about the outcome.

There is also this care to be reproved: to move things that are not necessary, things alien to one's calling.

This is the polypragmosyne (meddlesomeness) often prohibited, as in Paul: Do your own work. And in Peter: Do not be allotrioepiskopoi (busybodies in other men's matters). These two kinds of cares are useless, and they torment minds in vain.

Therefore it is added here: Such cares produce many dreams.

And although they thus relate that they produce many anxieties of the mind, yet I think this is signified, that the cares themselves, which are prohibited, are empty dreams: the polypragmosyne of Cassius and Brutus, concerning the establishing of a beautiful state of the Republic, was only a most vain dream.

To this pertains the saying: The vain think vain things through desire. But let this rule concerning cares be held: Commend your way to God, and he will act.

The first part commands concerning the care of labor in one's calling and concerning faith; the second part adds the promise: He will act.

Latin:

Multas curas sequuntur somnia, et in multis sermonibus invenitur stulticia. Differunt cura laboris, cura de exitu, et cura extra vocationem.

Cura laboris severissime praecipitur Rom. 12.: Qui praeest, sit diligens. 1. Corinth. 4.: Hoc requiritur in ministerio, ut fidelis sit. Est autem adfectata negligentia similis perfidiae.

Laudanda est igitur cura Davidis, cum tempora et loca oportuna dimicationi praevidet, ut Alexander dicebat Parmenioni: An putas me dormire potuisse, priusquam constituissem, quomodo instructuri simus aciem?

Petere autem a Deo felicem exitum praelii David solet, et hanc curam Deo commendat.

Econtra vero utroque modo peccatur, cum stulta persuasione propter vires aut fortunam aliquis sibi certam victoriam promittit, ut Pompeius, aut cum diffidentia excruciatur, ut Aratus.

Talem curam hic reprehendit Salomon, quae angitur de exitu.

Est et haec cura reprehendenda, movere non necessaria, aliena a vocatione.

Haec est πολυπραγμοσύνη saepe prohibita, ut apud Paulum: Propria agite. Et apud Petrum: Non sitis ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοποι. Haec duo genera curarum inutilia sunt, et frustra excruciant mentes.

Ideo hic additur: Tales curas parere multa somnia.

Etsi autem sic enarrant, quod multas anxietatis animi pariant, tamen opinor hoc significari, curas ipsas, quae prohibitae sunt, inania somnia esse: πολυπραγμοσύνη Cassii et Bruti, de constituendo pulcro statu Reipub. erat tantum vanissimum somnium.

Huc pertinet dictum: μάταιοι μάταια λογίζονται διὰ ἐπιθυμίας. Regula autem de curis ista teneatur: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet.

Prior pars praecipit de cura laboris in vocatione et de fide, Altera pars addit promissionem: Ipse faciet.

## 5:3
The voice of the fool in a multitude of words.

He often repeats this admonition, so that men may not pronounce rashly concerning dogmas and in deliberations, but rightly and after long consideration of the sources and true causes: and it is manifest that those who are precipitate and judge many things often err.

Therefore, Prov. ch. 10 says: In a multitude of words there will not be wanting sin. And there exist many similar admonitions, which prohibit garrulity, the precipitation of judgments, and similar vices.

If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it.

To the rashness of the tongue he adds an example concerning vows: but let us know at the same time that many other things are to be included, oaths, pacts, promises, judgments concerning doctrine, deliberations.

For in all these it is necessary to avoid precipitation and rashness, and soon a most grave admonition concerning providence is added.

Because that rashness is proper to a secure heart, which does not care for the judgment of God, and is incited either by admiration of its own wisdom, or by emulation, or by other desires, and disturbs dogmas, or moves things that should not be moved.

Let this admonition concerning providence be fixed in minds, and let assent be confirmed in us by the examples of all the punishments which we read, and which we see daily, and let the divine voice be opposed, which preaches about providence, and whose examples we see in punishments, to foolish security, and to human doubt, and to all Epicurean and Cyclopean opinions.

Before the Angel. It is customary for the fathers and Prophets to call the Son of God the Angel, because they know this Lord, promised to the Church, to be the messenger of the wonderful decree concerning the liberation of the human race.

Thus also Jacob calls him the Angel, and adds a description which distinguishes him from created Angels. Because he says: May the Angel bless you, who has delivered me from all evils.

He affirms, therefore, that this Angel is omnipotent, delivering from sin and from death, and makes mention of him: because he knows properly that this is the Lord and guardian of the Church.

If you see the oppressions of the poor and violent judgments.

Soon he adds an admonition, that one should not therefore doubt concerning providence, because many injuries are permitted, as Diogenes used to say, that Harpalus was a living testimony against the gods, because he lived in great pleasures after many crimes.

This objection must be answered from experience itself: Although injuries are permitted for a time, yet punishments follow, and God keeps the rule, which is the nerve of discipline; atrocious deeds are punished even in this life with atrocious punishments, according to those sayings: He who takes the sword will perish by the sword.

Item: Woe to you who plunder, because you will be plundered.

Therefore Solomon soon adds a commination, and declares that there remain other Judges, by whom those who have done unjust things are punished, as Augustus punished Antony.

And a notable description of a king is to be observed here, when he says: The king is over all on earth for the cultivation... of fields, where he distinguishes the king from the tyrant; the tyrant dissipates and devastates, the good prince fosters society, and protects the cultivation of the earth, of the Church, of the arts, and of all good things.

The covetous man shall not be filled with money, and he who loves riches shall not reap fruit from them.

Afterwards follow long discourses railing against Avarice, and he repeats the sentiment placed above, which commands us to use things according to the ordinance of God—food, drink, marriage—and to serve our vocation with a good conscience and faith: but as for events, which are not in our power, to commend them to God, as he has often warned, and the saying must be repeated from time to time: Commit thy way unto the Lord, and he shall bring it to pass.

Latin:

Vox stulti in multiloquio.

Saepe hanc admonitionem repetit, ne temere pronuncient homines de dogmatibus et in deliberationibus, sed recte et diu consideratis fontibus et veris causis: ac manifestum est, saepe errare praecipites et multa iudicantes.

Ideo cap. 10. Proverb. inquit: In multiloquio non deerit peccatum. Et extant similes admonitiones plurimae, quae prohibent garrulitatem, praecipitantiam iudiciorum, et similia vitia.

Si quid vovisti Deo, non moreris reddere.

Temeritati linguae addit exemplum de votis: sciamus autem simul alia multa complectenda esse, iuramenta, pacta, sponsiones, iudicia de doctrina, deliberationes.

Nam in his omnibus opus est evitare praecipitantiam et temeritatem, et mox additur gravissima admonitio de providentia.

Quia temeritas illa est propria securi pectoris, quod non curat iudicium Dei, et vel admiratione propriae sapientiae, vel aemulatione, vel aliis cupiditatibus incitatur, et turbet dogmata, aut moveat non movenda.

Sit infixa animis haec admonitio de providentia, et confirmetur assensio in nobis exemplis poenarum omnium quae legimus, et quae quotidie cernimus, et opponatur vox divina, quae concionatur de providentia, et cuius exempla in poenis cernimus, stultae securitati, et dubitationi humanae, et omnibus opinionibus Epicureis et Cyclopicis.

Coram Angelo. Usitatum est patribus et Prophetis Filium Dei, nominare Angelum, quia sciunt hunc Dominum, Ecclesiae promissum, nuncium esse miradi decreti de liberatione generis humani.

Sic et Iacob nominat eum Angelum, et addit descriptionem, quae discernit eum a creatis Angelis. Quia inquit: Benedicat vobis Angelus, qui liberavit me ex omnibus malis.

Adfirmat ergo hunc Angelum omnipotentem esse, liberantem a peccato et a morte, et facit eius mentionem: quia proprie scit hunc esse Dominum et custodem Ecclesiae.

Si videris calumnias egenorum et violenta iudicia.

Mox addit admonitionem, ne propterea dubitetur de providentia, quia multae iniuriae permittuntur, ut Diogenes dicebat, Harpalum dicere vivum testimonium contra Deos, quod in magnis voluptatibus post multa scelera vivebat.

Huic obiectioni respondendum est ex ipsa experientia, Quanquam aliquandiu permittuntur iniuriae, tamen sequuntur poenae, et Deus regulam servat, quae est nervus disciplinae, Atrocia delecta etiam in hac vita puniuntur atrocibus poenis, iuxta illa dicta: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit.

Item: Vae qui spolias, quia spoliaberis.

Ideo Salomon mox addit comminationem, et dicit reliquos esse alios Iudices, a quibus puniantur illi qui iniusta fecerunt, ut Augustus punit Antonium.

Et insignis descriptio regis hic observanda est, cum ait: Super omnes est rex in terra ad culturam agrorum, ubi discernit regem a tyranno, tyrannus dissipat et vastat, bonus princeps fovet societatem, et tuetur culturam terrae, Ecclesiae, artium et omnium rerum bonarum.

Avarus non implebitur pecunia, et qui amat divitias, fructum non capiet ex eis.

Postea sequuntur longae conciones vituperantes Avariciam, et repetit sententiam supra positam, quae iubet uti rebus iuxta ordinationem Dei, cibo, potu, coniugio, et servire vocationi bona conscientia et fide: eventus vero, qui non sunt in potestate nostra, commendare Deo, sicut saepe monuit, et subinde repetendum est dictum: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet.

## 6:1 Argument
Chapter VI.

Even if someone is famous, yet this is known, that he is a man, and cannot contend with him that is mightier.

At the end of the sixth chapter he places a sentiment that may rule us, so that we may perform the duties of our vocation, and not cast away our vocation because of the dissimilarity of events; for he says thus: Whosoever is called a man, he cannot contend with him that is mightier, that is, he cannot govern events, and it follows: For they are vain words, that is, these cares and imaginations are vain, and profit a man nothing.

Our text says:

What need is there for a man to seek greater things, but the Hebrew reading only says: They profit a man nothing.

They warn, however, as I have said, that we should consider which cares pertain to us and which do not, just as we made three degrees above: the care of labor according to one's vocation, this pertains to us; others are cares about the outcome.

Likewise, about other things outside one's vocation.

These do not pertain to us.

Latin:

Caput VI.

Etiamsi quis celebris est, tamen hoc scitur, quod homo sit, et non potest certare cum eo quod est potentius.

In fine sexti capitis ponit sententiam, quae regat nos, ut officia vocationis faciamus, nec abiiciamus, vocationem propter dissimilitudinem eventuum, sic enim ait: Quisquis homo nominatur, non potest certare cum eo, quod est potentius, id est, non potest eventus gubernare, et sequitur: Sunt enim inania verba, id est, hae curae et imaginationes inanes sunt, et nihil prosunt homini.

Noster textus inquit.

Quid necesse est homini maiora se quaerere, sed lectio Ebraea tantum inquit: Nihil prosunt homini.

Monent autem ut dixi, ut consideremus, quae curae ad nos pertineant, quae non pertineant ad nos, sicut supra tres gradus fecimus, curam laboris iuxta vocationem, haec ad nos pertinet, aliae sunt curae de eventu.

Item de rebus aliis extra vocationem.

Hae non pertinent ad nos.

## 7:1 Argument
Chapter VII.

A man knows not what is good for him in this life in the days of vanity.

He speaks, however, of things under the Sun, that is, of events in this mortal life, both prosperous and adverse.

Joseph thinks his being sold is harmful to him, and it was profitable.

Therefore it follows, Neither can a man know things to come under the Sun, that is, what will happen after prosperous or adverse things.

David is brought back into the kingdom from the greatest calamity; Saul falls from the greatest glory into destruction, etc.

He commands, therefore, to obey God in prosperous and adverse things, and to commend the outcomes to him, not to attempt things by an unjust or unnecessary confidence in prosperity, nor to be broken by adversity and fall away from God, but to remember the rule of Job: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.

A good name is better than precious ointment.

Here he gathers many sentiments, of which some exhort to action, others to patience, others console the needy, others the afflicted, as I shall show in each case, to which they are to be referred.

The first, concerning a good name or glory, is an exhortation to action.

It has been said elsewhere, however, what, speaking correctly, glory or a good name is before human judgment.

For it is the approval of our own conscience judging rightly, and of others judging rightly, as Scipio, freeing the bride of another, has glory, that is, his own conscience remains unharmed, and he has also the approval of others who judge rightly.

Thraso has no glory, because he himself does not judge rightly, arrogating false things to himself: nor do others who lie by assenting; but God commands both, that we do what is right, and that we approve of things rightly done, according to that: Thou shalt not bear false witness.

He wants the knowledge of virtues to exist, and that we recognize what he himself is, and that it may be the guide of life.

And so that the distinction between virtues and vices may be seen, God wants crimes to be punished by human judgments as well: he also wants things rightly done to be approved for two reasons, so that the distinction between virtues and vices may be more conspicuous, and that others may be instructed by examples.

He wants, therefore, the infamous to be cast out of society, but that an honest place in society be given to those whose morals are without infamy.

Since, therefore, such approval is sanctioned divinely, and is a good thing, it is manifest that this glory is to be sought, and indeed it is a command of God that we avoid scandals, as Paul says: Do all to the glory of God, and be not a scandal to the Church.

And Augustine well said: I have need of a good conscience for God's sake, and a good name for my neighbor's sake.

Elsewhere he said: A good name is better than great riches.

There the degrees

it, teaches that reputation is to be preferred to wealth and riches. A sponsor would rather lose his wealth than his reputation. Here is a sweeter admonition: A good reputation is better than balsam, that is, just as balsam heals and refreshes bodies, so a good reputation is a great relief to the heart, and conversely, a bad reputation is a horrible torture. Thus it is said in Proverbs: A good reputation makes the bones fat. And Pindar says: Not even warm water refreshes exhausted bones as much as glory. And Thucydides: Honor is food for the aged. Let these things be understood rightly, and let the glory of conscience and human approval be distinguished from the glory of justice before God, of which it is said elsewhere: He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.

Elsewhere, however, he speaks of the approval of conscience. This is our boasting, the soundness of our conscience. Item: Let each one test his own work, and thus he will have glory in himself, not in others, that is, let him examine his own deeds, which if they were done rightly, you will have the approval of your conscience, which is the glory of which we spoke: Do not do this, which many do, so that you may grow by the detraction of others or the applause of the multitude.

Latin:

Caput VII.

Ignorat homo quid sibi prosit in hac vita in diebus vanitatis.

Loquitur autem, de rebus sub Sole, hoc est, de eventibus in hac mortali vita prosperis et adversis.

Ioseph putat sibi nocere venditionem et profuit.

Ideo sequitur, Nec potest scire homo futura sub Sole, id est, quid sit futurum post res prosperas aut adversas.

David ex summa calamitate reducitur in regnum, Saul ex summa gloria ruit in exitium etc.

Iubet igitur Deo obtemperare in prosperis et adversis rebus, et ipsi commendare exitus, non fiducia prosperitatis iniusta aut non necessaria tentare, nec frangi adversitate ac deficere a Deo, sed meminisse regulam Iob: Etiamsi occiderit me, sperabo in eum.

Melius est nomen bonum, quam unguenta pretiosa.

Hic coacervat multas sententias, quarum aliae hortantur ad agendum, aliae ad patientiam, aliae consolantur egentes, aliae adflictos, ut in singulis, quo referendae sunt, ostendam.

Prima de bono nomine seu gloria est adhortatio ad agendum.

Dictum est autem alibi, quid, recte loquendo, sit gloria seu bonum nomen coram iudicio humano.

Est enim adprobatio conscientiae nostrae recte iudicantis, et aliorum recte iudicantium, ut Scipio liberans sponsam alterius, habet gloriam, id est, ipsius conscientiae manet illaesa, habet et adprobationem aliorum recte iudicantium.

Thraso non habet gloriam, quia nec ipse recte iudicat, arrogans sibi falsa: nec alii qui mentiuntur adsentando, Deus autem utrunque praecipit, et ut recta faciamus, et ut recte facta adprobemus, iuxta illud: Non dicas falsum testimonium.

Vult noticiam virtutum extare, et ut agnoscamus qualis ipse sit, et ut sit rectrix vitae.

Et ut conspici discrimen virtutum et vitiorum possit, vult Deus humanis iudiciis quoque puniri scelera: vult et recte facta adprobari propter duas causas, ut discrimen virtutum et vitiorum sit conspectius, et ut alii exemplis erudiantur.

Vult igitur famosos eiici ex societate, tribui vero honestum locum in societate illis, quorum mores sunt sine infamia.

Cum igitur talis adprobatio sit sancita divinitus, et sit res bona, manifestum est hanc gloriam adpetendam esse, et quidem mandatum Dei est, ut scandala vitemus, ut Paulus inquit: Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite, et non sitis scandalo Ecclesiae.

Et bene dixit Augustinus: Bona conscientia mihi opus est propter Deum, Bona fama propter proximum.

Alibi dixit: Melius est nomen bonum, quam divitiae multae.

Ibi gradus

dit, docet famam anteferendam esse facultatibus et divitiis. Sponsor potius amittat facultates quam famam. Hic dulcior est admonitio: Bona fama est melior balsamo, id est, ut balsamum sanat et recreat corpora, ita bona fama magna levatio est cordi, Et econtra mala fama horribilis carnificina est. Sic in Proverbiis dicitur: Bona fama pinguefacit ossa. Et Pindarus inquit: Non aqua tepida sic reficit ossa defatigata sicut gloria. Et Thucydides: Seni honos est alimentum. Haec dextre intelligantur, et discernantur gloria conscientiae et adprobationis humanae, et gloria iusticiae coram Deo, de qua alibi dicitur. Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur.

Alibi vero loquitur de adprobatione conscientiae. Haec est gloriatio nostra, incolumitas conscientiae nostrae. Item: Probet opus suum unusquisque, et sic habebit gloriam apud sese, non apud alios, id est, examinet sua facta, quae si recte facta sunt, habebis adprobationem tuae conscientiae, quae est gloria de qua diximus: Non hoc ages quod faciunt plurimi, ut crescas obtrectatione aliorum vel adplausu multitudinis.

## 7:1
Better is the day of death than the day of birth.

This saying is a consolation. But the comparison is not simply of life and death, but of calamities and liberation, which, however, must be recognized by faith, and in the Church this saying is neither obscure nor ambiguous concerning believers. For it agrees with that saying in Revelation 14: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. And such sayings are testimonies about the future life, just as Proverbs 14 says: The righteous man retains hope in his death. And Job: Even if he kills me, I will hope in him. Nor should I seek other interpretations, nor add those pagan ones, that it is best not to be born, or to be abolished as quickly as possible. These things are foreign to the doctrine of the Church.

Latin:

Melior est dies mortis, quam dies nativitatis.

Hoc dictum consolatio est. Fit autem collatio non simpliciter vitae et mortis, sed calamitatum et liberationis, quae tamen fide agnoscenda est, Et in Ecclesia hoc dictum nec obscurum, nec ambiguum est de credentibus. Congruit enim cum illo dicto Apocal. 14.: Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur. Et talia dicta sunt testimonia de futura vita, sicut Proverb. 14. inquit: Spem retinet iustus in morte sua. Et Iob: Etiam si occidet me, sperabo in eo. Nec quaeram alias interpretationes, nec addam illa ethnica, Optimum non nasci, aut quam celerrime aboleri. Haec aliena sunt a doctrina Ecclesiae.

## 7:2
It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting.

These sayings agree with the most well-known maxims, for minds usually luxuriate in prosperous circumstances. Item: The people sat down to eat, and rose up to play. Item: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your justifications. Item: Vexation gives understanding. In prosperous times, men become more negligent, they think less about the wrath of God, and seek less the help of God, then they become more insolent, they trust in their own industry, their own power, and are easily driven by the devil. Therefore, from that height they later fall into great calamities, according to that: They are lifted up on high, so that they may fall with a heavier crash. Conversely, troubles are reminders of our infirmity, and of seeking the help of God, and they are a bridle for many desires. Therefore, the Church is subjected to the cross, as is often said elsewhere about the causes of the calamities of the Church, and about true consolation.

At the end of these sentences, Solomon signifies that this joy of fools is by no means lasting, that they quickly fall from security and insolence into tragic calamities, as Saul, David, Croesus, Xerxes, Alexander, Pompeius, Caesar, Antony, and other innumerable ones were oppressed by most sad events, so that the examples of the wrath of God may be seen, so that they may remind others of repentance, of the fear of God, and of invocation. For God keeps the rule: That which is sublime before men is an abomination before God. Item, he destroys the proud in the intent of their heart. Therefore, concerning the brevity of the joy of fools, Solomon says it is such as the sound of burning thorns which quickly flare up.

Latin:

Melius est ire ad domum luctus, quam ad domum convivii.

Haec dicta congruunt cum notissimis sententiis, Luxuriant animi rebus plerumque secundis. Item: Sedit populus manducare, et surrexit ludere. Item: Bonum mihi quod humiliasti me, ut discam iustificationes tuas. Item: Vexatio dat intellectum. In rebus secundis fiunt homines negligentiores, minus cogitant de ira Dei, et minus expetunt auxilium Dei, deinde fiunt et insolentiores, confidunt sua industria, sua potentia, et facile impelluntur a diabolo. Ideo ex illo fastigio postea ruunt in magnas calamitates, iuxta illud: Tolluntur in altum, ut lapsu graviore ruant. Econtra aerumnae sunt commonefactiones de nostra infirmitate, et de petendo auxilio Dei, et sunt frenum multarum cupiditatum. Ideo Ecclesia subiecta est cruci, ut saepe dicitur alibi de causis calamitatum Ecclesiae, et de vera consolatione.

In fine harum sententiarum significat Salomon; nequaquam diuturnam esse hanc laetitiam stultorum, cito eos ex securitate, et insolentia ruere in tragicas calamitates, ut Saul, David, Croesus, Xerxes, Alexander, Pompeius, Caesar, Antonius, et alii innumerabiles oppressi sunt tristissimis casibus, ut exempla irae Dei conspiciantur, ut caeteros commonefaciant de poenitentia, de timore Dei, et de invocatione. Servat enim regulam Deus, Abominatio est coram Deo, quidquid est sublime coram hominibus. Item, disperdit superbos mente cordis sui. Itaque de brevitate laetitiae stultorum inquit Salomon, talem esse, qualis est sonitus spinarum ardentium quae cito conflagrant.

## 7:7
Calumny disturbs the wise man, and destroys the generous heart.

There is a detestation of calumny, as it is manifest in every government that calumny is a most harmful plague, as Palamedes, Miltiades, Aristides, Cimon, and Themistocles, who deserved the best, were oppressed by calumnies. Neither are the examples of this evil rare or obscure, and the sources are known. Men are by nature proud, some more, some less: therefore they envy the glory of others, and to diminish it, they seek sophisms to deprave the counsels and deeds of others. This sophistic depravation is called Calumny. But it is much more harmful in the Church, where sophisms and cavils are sought to elude the simple truth, and for the depravation of those things which have been rightly handed down. But it is established that it is divinely commanded in the second commandment, that the truth of doctrine should not be corrupted. Item concerning other matters, Do not speak false testimony. Let these precepts confirm us, so that we may detest and flee from sophistry and calumnies.

Latin:

Calumnia conturbat sapientem, et perdit cor beneficum.

Detestatio est calumniae, ut manifestum est in omni gubernatione nocentissimam pestem esse calumniam, ut Palamedes, Miltiades, Aristides, Cimon, Themistocles, optime meriti calumniis oppressi sunt. Nec rara, nec obscura sunt huius mali exempla, et fontes noti sunt. Homines natura superbi, aut magis, aut alii minus: ideo alienae gloriae invident, et ut eam extenuent, sophismata quaerunt ad depravanda aliorum consilia et facta. Haec sophistica depravatio nominatur Calumnia. Est autem multo nocentior in Ecclesia, ubi quaeruntur sophismata et cavillationes ad eludendam veritatem simplicem, et ad depravationem eorum, quae recte tradita sunt. Constat autem divinitus praecipi in secundo praecepto, ne corrumpatur veritas doctrinae. Item de caeteris negotiis, Non dicas falsum testimonium. Haec praecepta confirment nos, ut sophisticen et calumnias detestemur et fugiamus.

## 7:8
Better is the end of a counsel than the beginning.

He warns generally that the end must be looked to in deliberations, as if to say, It is better to look to the end of a counsel than the beginning, according to that: Whatever you do, do it prudently, and look to the end. the end.

Or let this be a simple explanation: Let the saying of Solomon be understood concerning good and honest counsels.

In these, the end is better in two ways: first, by the constancy of the will in performing an honest thing, and then also by the outcome. Many are "Thrasydeiloi" (cowardly boasters) who are brave at the beginning in teaching, in stirring up wars, in rioting: afterwards, broken by a slight moment, they cast away their confession, desert the battle line, etc. Therefore, it demands in this saying, perseverance in good counsels, just as it is said in the Gospel: He who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved. Furthermore, the honest cause is also better in its outcome: for although many adverse things must be endured, yet the honest cause wins in the end.

Better is the patient than the arrogant.

Pride is the fountain of impatience, of the desire for revenge, and of contention, as it is said in Proverbs: Among the proud there is contention. Hence great dissensions arise in empires and in the Church, just as because Alcibiades and Coriolanus bear injuries impatiently, they bring wars upon their fatherland.

Camillus, Fabius, and Scipio endure injuries. The verse is known: For he did not place rumors before safety. Concerning this gentleness and tolerance it is said: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.

Likewise, Prov. 16: Better is the patient than the conqueror of cities.

Therefore, the following sentence also says: Be not quick to be angry, because anger rests in the bosom of a fool. And very many admonitions have been handed down in all writings concerning the moderation of anger.

Latin:

Melior est finis consilii, quam initium.

Generaliter monet, finem in deliberationibus prospiciendum esse, quasi dicat, Melius est finem consilii prospicere quam initium, iuxta illud: Quidquid agas, prudenter agas, et respice finem.

Aut sit haec simplex enarratio, Intelligatur dictum Salomonis de bonis et honestis consiliis.

In his melior est finis duobus modis: primum constantia voluntatis in re honesta perficienda, deinde et eventu. Multi Θρασύδειλοι sunt fortes initio in docendo, in bellis movendis, in tumultuando: postea levi momento fracti confessionem abiiciunt, deserunt aciem etc. Postulat igitur in hoc dicto, In bonis consiliis perseverantiam, sicut in Evangelio dicitur: Qui perseveraverit in finem, hic salvus erit. Praeterea et eventu causa honesta melior est: quanquam enim multa adversa patientia sunt, tamen vincit tandem causa honesta.

Melior est patiens arrogante.

Superbia fons est impatientiae, cupiditatis vindictae et contentionis, ut in Proverbiis dicitur: Inter superbos est contentio. Hinc magnae dissensiones in imperiis et in Ecclesia oriuntur, ut quia Alcibiades et Coriolanus impatienter ferunt iniurias, inferunt bella patriae.

Camillus, Fabius, Scipio tolerant iniurias. Notus est versus, Non ponebat enim rumores ante salutem. De hac mansuetudine et tolerantia dictum est: Beati mites, quia possidebunt terram.

Item, Proverb. 16.: Melior est patiens expugnatore urbium.

Ideo et sequens sententia inquit: Non sis velox ad irascendum, quia ira in sinu stulti quiescit. Et plurimae sunt traditae admonitiones in omnibus scriptis de moderatione irae.

## 7:10
Do not say, why were the former times better?

This admonition also preaches about patience.

For as Thucydides says about empires, so it happens almost in the whole of life, "aei to paron bary" (the present is always burdensome). The present state is always more troublesome, for present inconveniences are felt more closely. Therefore, we praise the times of others, and we seek another state. However, the rule must be held: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that is, do not rage against God, obey patiently in bearing those burdens which God imposes on each one in his own place and time, just as Job says: The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord.

Every time has its own inconveniences. The government of David is happier than that of Hezekiah, and yet it had its own calamities.

And the evils of Hezekiah’s own age must be endured. And it is wisdom to bear adverse things rightly, and not to increase them by foolish treatment, according to the admonition: "me to kakon to kako" (do not cure evil with evil).

To this pertains the rule often repeated: Be subject to God, and pray to Him. And the verse of Pythagoras is known: "on an moiran eches, tauten phere, med' aganaktei" (whatever portion you have, bear it, and do not be indignant).

*Wisdom is good with an inheritance, and better than seeing the Sun, that is, than life itself.

Wisdom protects, money also protects. But the doctrine of wisdom is something better, because it gives life.*

It meets an objection. Since he said before that wisdom is an affliction, because men are often deceived, and outcomes often do not correspond to good counsels, it seems to deter men from the care of learning and governing.

On the contrary, he says, I command that you learn, that you govern the Church, the common society, households, that you seek resources. For these labors, and the things themselves, peace, resources, are good things, but let the outcomes be commended to God, as has often been said already: Do the duties of your vocation, and commend the outcome to God. Therefore, he soon adds: Consider the works of God, because no one can make straight that which He has made crooked, that is, human diligence cannot either avoid or heal all evils, nor for that reason should government be cast aside, but God must be obeyed in one's vocation, and this sweetest consolation must be held, which Paul proposes: Your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

In adverse things, however, the mind should not rage against God. The following consolation pertains to the same: In the good day enjoy good things, that is, when outcomes are favorable, give thanks to God, and use that good, neither trusting in favorable things, nor, puffed up by this foolish confidence, pressing others or moving things that should not be moved, as Xerxes, Pompey, and many others do, but be modest, prepare yourself to bear adverse things, because soon there will be changes.

Moreover, he adds the reason why God wills these changes to be, lest, he says, men find something else, that is, lest by their curiosity in favorable things they seek what is not granted, just as Bellerophon, puffed up by favorable things, wishes to be carried into heaven by Pegasus. But let us be modest, and remain within the bounds of our vocation, and let us be restrained by the fear of the punishment which follows insolence, injustice, neglect of vocation, etc.

He also proposes consolations in adverse things, Lest men find something else, that is, lest they con they flee to forbidden aids, just as Saul consulted a magic woman, and the emperors of Constantinople attracted the Turks: but let us seek and expect help from God, and let us use the remedies ordained by Him.

Nor is it obscure that men sin very greatly when they attempt to remedy adversities with forbidden remedies. *

The just man perishes in his justice, and the impious man lives long in his malice.* There are two rules which, although they seem to disagree, are nevertheless true, and do not disagree when each is assigned its own place.

The other is entirely political:

Atrocious crimes are punished with atrocious penalties in this life, according to that saying: He who has taken the sword shall perish by the sword.

These things happen thus regularly in the whole human race, whether the fallen remains in impiety, or is converted to God, and thus for the converted, penalties are mitigated.

Although, however, no one is without faults, yet those who are not polluted by atrocious crimes do not fall into such tragic cases, as the end of Augustus is peaceful.

The other rule is, the Church is subject to the cross, as Abel, Jeremiah, the Baptist, the Apostles and martyrs are killed.

These are singular cases not pertaining to that political judgment.

The Church knows there are other causes for the death of Abel, and others for the death of Absalom: but men without the doctrine of the Church are troubled by these examples, so that they doubt providence.

On the contrary, however, let us know that it is an illustrious testimony of providence, those very regular and ordinary ends of murderers.

Furthermore, concerning the Saints, we have more manifest testimonies of the presence of God; Paul previously recalled the dead to life, he was therefore a care to God, and will be even if he is killed by Nero. Be not too just nor too wise, lest you cause devastation.

There is no doubt that Solomon speaks of political justice, and the governor of this external life, and this is a clear accommodation of this saying, and it is a very useful precept.

Justice dwells in the middle between negligence and cruelty. Excessive severity becomes cruelty, as it was in Aurelian; excessive indulgence, which does not punish atrocious crimes, confirms the wicked, such as it was in Arcadius.

But a salutary governor, like Augustus, sees the middle, which has a probable reason.

This middle, this admonition of Solomon commands to be sought, and let goodness prevail.

Nor should the middle be sought too subtly, just as in God mercy surpasses judgment.

Diligently, however, the warning must be observed which he adds: Lest you cause devastation; excessive severity causes devastation, many curable people are killed without necessity, many good people flee from government.

Soon he adds a similar admonition concerning wisdom, Be not too wise.

As excessive severity becomes cruelty, so excessive wisdom, that is, excessive subtlety, becomes cavilling, quarrelsome, πολυπραγμονικὴ (meddlesome), sophistic, ἀντιλογικὴ (contentious), as Menander says: Laws are good, but if anyone interprets them too subtly, he becomes a sycophant, like one who, having agreed to a 30-day truce, ravaged the fields by night.

The Emperor is the lord of Milan, the French king can find a subtlety by which he says Milan pertains to him.

Life is full of such examples, and it is manifest that wars and devastations arise from thence.

Therefore, many admonitions exist about fleeing that cavilling wisdom.

And Agesilaus said: τὸ λίαν δίκαιον πρόφασις ἐστὶ (excessive justice is a pretext). *

Be not too impious, nor be foolish, lest you die, not in your own time.* This admonition coheres with the previous one which speaks of the other extreme, namely of negligence:

Let not the magistrate tolerate atrocious and enormous crimes, let not the faithful doctor be silent about necessary matters and about idolomania, do not swallow camels while straining out a gnat.

And he proposes an atrocious penalty for negligence: Lest you die not in your time, that is, lest if you have negligently governed your own morals, and have too much loosened the reins of desires, God punishes you either through the magistrate or by other means, just as David himself fell into penalties by indulging himself too much.

But when he wishes the middle to be sought, he adds afterwards, Who is he who discerns the middle with God showing, and ruling his counsels and hand, namely, he who fears God: thus he warns that without the fear of God, without invocation, without divine help, there is no happy government, according to those sayings: Unless the Lord guards.

Item: Commend your way to God, and he himself will act. *The good which you have apprehended in this and in that, let not your hand let go.

He who fears God will escape from all these.*

When severity is good, exercise it; again, when leniency is profitable, use leniency. that moderation suitable to affairs or circumstances should be sought, so that some may be harder, others milder, just as a physician gives different medicines to different people.

Fabius sees when one must fight, and when one must not fight.

Saul, with foolish zeal, kills the Gibeonites; Joshua spared them.

However, one must observe the emphasis in the word 'Apprehend'.

For it signifies that the true cause must be sought for acting either severely or leniently, just as Paul says: 'Let each one be certain in his own mind.'

The good that you apprehend—that is, when the conscience, after deliberating the matter, has found the true reason to which one must firmly assent—that reason should be preferred to anger and other affections.

But someone might say, how can that moderation or virtue suitable to the circumstance be found?

He answers: 'He who fears God will escape from all these things,' that is, he will choose the better opinion, because he who fears God looks to the divine law, and at the same time is ruled by the Holy Spirit, and asks for his counsels to be governed, moderates his impulses, wishes to consult for the Church and the public safety, and does not indulge private grief and private desires.

Wisdom comforts the wise man more than ten princes in a city.

This is a general admonition, which signifies that good counsels and moderation excel physical strength; a governor is better fortified by diligence in avoiding dangers, by moderation in curbing affections, and by the invocation of God, than if he surrounded himself with great garrisons and great armies, as Alexander of Pherae was killed by his wife and her brothers, even though he slept at night among guards in a tower, which had to be ascended by ladders.

Alexander's father was killed in a public procession while princes and bodyguards were watching.

Julius was killed in his Senate, and there are innumerable examples: but milder princes have had a more tranquil government and peaceful ends, such as Jehoshaphat, Augustus, and Theodosius.

There is no just man on earth who, although he does good, does not also sin.

This is a political maxim, not about sin inherent in nature, but about external errors and lapses: even the just and deserving sometimes sin, not in the same action, but in different ones.

David is a good and salutary prince, and for the most part he acts rightly, and yet he neglects many things; indeed, he fell ruinously by seizing his friend's wife and killing her husband, a holy and brave man.

Josiah was a good and salutary prince, yet he was involved in an unnecessary war.

Thus, not even the just are without some lapses.

Here the verse of Theognis may be applied: 'But a good man is sometimes bad, at other times good.'

Likewise Euripides: 'He who does many things also commits many errors.'

Hence, descriptions of good and bad governors are also taken.

A good governor is one who has the desire to do right, and for the most part does right, even if he sometimes falters.

Such were the good princes David, Josiah, and Augustus.

But a bad governor is one who does not have the desire to do right, and for the most part acts wickedly, even if he sometimes does right, as Cambyses did.

The distinction is therefore taken from the perpetual will or prohairesis (choice).

Just as Paul also established this goal: 'This is required, that we be faithful.'

Let us, however, recognize in such admonitions our own immense infirmity, let us fear the snares of the devil, and let us assiduously pray that God may both rule us and heal our errors, just as Peter commands: 'Be vigilant, because your adversary goes about.'

Do not apply your heart to all words.

This is an admonition concerning detractions, so that we may neither be detractors ourselves, nor be broken by detraction or calumnies.

Detraction is contrary to truth and candor, either perverting what was rightly done or excusable, or spreading a false opinion about those who act rightly because of some errors.

And so many delight in detraction, as Pindar says, that 'slanderous words are a relish.'

This vice is prohibited in the eighth commandment: 'Do not bear false witness.'

And in Leviticus: 'Do not be a whisperer among the people.'

Above, however, it was said concerning the judgment of conscience and fame.

And although the preservation of both must be cared for, the prior care should be that the conscience does not become wounded; afterwards, let a good reputation be sought, as Augustine says: 'I need a good conscience for the sake of God, a good reputation for the sake of my neighbor.'

And because there are many detractors, let us not on that account grieve too much if some do not judge candidly, but let us console ourselves with the testimony of conscience, as Paul says: 'This is our boast, the testimony of our conscience.'

Likewise: 'Let each one test his own work, and thus he will have glory in himself, and will not depend on another.

Solomon in this place commands them to be less angry at detractions, because we ourselves often sin in the same way.

For Solomon recites the common vices of men.

I have tested all things in wisdom, I said, I will be wise, and it itself receded further from me.

Afterwards in the text follows a repetition.

He denies that all errors can be foreseen and avoided by men, and it is manifest that great and sad lapses belong to the highest and wisest of men.

In this complaint, being reminded of our infirmity, let us ask to be ruled by God, as it is often said: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his own.

Item: Commit your way to God, and he will act.

I found a woman more bitter than death, who is a snare of hunters etc.

Afterwards he speaks about women.

For whenever our infirmities and calamities are recited, in that catalog the diseases of women themselves occupy some part, and the furies in men, who on account of women bring great calamities upon themselves and others, as Samson, David, Paris, and others innumerable.

God made man upright, but he himself seeks many deliberations.

He does not speak principally about Creation, but about the mode of actions, which God proposed as right to men, that is, God instituted an order, by which you may eat, drink, be a husband, serve in a certain vocation, and remain within the boundaries of your vocation.

But man seeks various deliberations.

David had his wives outstanding in form and virtue, and yet he desires another's.

Antony has a great empire, but he desires a Monarchy.

He censures these wandering desires, and hallucinating wisdom, as Pericles, Demosthenes, Brutus, Cicero, and many others fall under the guise of wisdom.

Nor is the saying poorly accommodated to doctrines.

God gave man a certain kind of doctrine, and within those boundaries he wishes our minds to be restrained, but the wandering geniuses of men seek other opinions, and are delighted by the variety of imaginations as if by games.

This huge evil is most severely censured in many places, as in Jeremiah: This I commanded, hear me.

Latin:

Ne dicas, cur priora tempora meliora fuerunt?

Haec admonitio etiam de patientia concionatur.

Ut enim Thucydides inquit de imperiis, ita fit propemodum in tota vita, ἀεὶ τὸ παρὸν βαρύ. Semper praesens status molestior est, propius enim sentiuntur praesentia incommoda. Ideo et aliorum tempora laudamus, et alium statum expetimus. Tenenda est autem regula: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, id est, non freme adversus Deum, obedite patienter in ferendis iis oneribus, quae Deus suo cuique loco et tempore imponit, sicut inquit Iob: Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit, sit nomen Domini benedictum.

Habent sua incommoda, quaelibet tempora. Est felicior gubernatio Davidis, quam Ezechiae, et tamen habuit suas calamitates.

Et Ezechiae suae aetatis mala ferenda sunt. Et sapientia est adversa recte ferre, nec augere stulta curatione, iuxta admonitionem: μὴ τὸ κακὸν λῷ κακῷ.

Huc pertinet regula saepe repetita: Subditus esto Deo, et ora eum. Et notus sit versus Pythagorae: ὦν ἂν μοῖραν ἔχῃς, ταύτην φέρε, μηδ᾽ ἀγανάκτει.

*Bona est sapientia cum haereditate, et melior, quem videre Solem, id est, quam vita ipsa.

Prolegit sapientia, protegit et pecunia. Sed doctrina sapientiae quiddam melius est, quia dat vitam.*

Occurrit obiectioni. Cum antea dixerit, Sapientiam esse adflictionem, quia saepe falluntur homines, et saepe non respondent eventus bonis consiliis, videtur deterrere homines a cura discendi et gubernandi.

Imo inquit, Praecipio ut discatis, gubernetis Ecclesiam, communem societatem, oeconomias, quaeratis facultates. Nam et hi labores, et res ipsae, pax, facultates, sunt res bonae, sed eventus Deo commendentur, sicut saepe iam dictum est: Facias vocationis officia, et eventus Deo commenda. Ideo mox addit: Considera opera Dei, quia nemo potest directum facere, id quod curvum fecit, id est, humana diligentia, non potest omnia mala vel cavere, vel sanare, nec propterea abiicienda est gubernatio, sed Deo obediendum in vocatione, et haec dulcissima consolatio tenenda, quam Paulus proponit: Non inanis est labor vester in Domino.

In adversis vero mens non fremat contra Deum. Eodem pertinet sequens consolatio: In die bona fruere bonis, id est, cum eventus sunt secundi, age Deo gratias, et eo bono utaris, nec confido rebus secundis, nec hac stulta fiducia elatus premito alios aut moveas non movenda, ut faciant Xerxes, Pompeius et alii multi, sed sis modestus, praepares te ad ferenda adversa, quia mox erunt vices.

Addit autem causam, Quare Deus velit has vices esse, ne, inquit, homines inveniant aliud, id est, ne sua curiositate in rebus secundis quaerant inconcessa, sicut Bellerophontes elatus rebus secundis, Pegaso vult intra coelum ferri. Sed simus modesti, et maneamus intra metas vocationis, et reprimamur metu poenae, quae sequitur insolentiam, iniusticiam, neglectionem vocationis etc.

Proponit etiam consolationes in rebus adversis, Ne homines aliud inveniant, id est, ne con fugiant ad inconcessa auxilia, sicut Saul consulit mulierem magicam, et imperatores Constantinopolitani attraxerunt Turcas: sed petamus et expectemus a Deo auxilium, et utamur remediis ab ipso ordinatis.

Nec obscurum est, valde multa peccare homines, cum mederi adversis conantur, inconcessis remediis.

Iustus perit in sua iusticia, et impius vivit diu in malicia.

Duae regulae sunt, quae, etsi videntur discrepare, tamen verae sunt, et non discrepant, cum suus cuique locus tribuitur.

Altera est prorsus politica: Atrocia delicta puniuntur atrocibus poenis in hac vita, iuxta illud: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit.

Haec ita regulariter fiunt in toto genere humano, sive lapsus maneat in impietate, sive convertatur ad Deum, et sic conversis mitigantur poenae.

Quanquam autem nemo est sine delictis, tamen qui non polluti sunt atrocibus sceleribus, non incidunt in tales tragicos casus, ut Augusti exitus placidus est.

Altera regula est, Ecclesia subiecta est cruci, ut Abel, Ieremias, Baptista, Apostoli et martyres, interficiuntur.

Haec sunt singularia non pertinentia ad illud politicum iudicium.

Scit Ecclesia alias esse causas necis Abel, et alias necis Absalonis: sed homines sine doctrina Ecclesiae turbantur in his exemplis, ut dubitent de providentia.

Econtra vero sciamus illustre testimonium providentiae esse, illos ipsos regulares et ordinarios exitus homicidarum.

Deinde de Sanctis testimonia praesentiae Dei manifestiora habemus, Paulus antea revocavit mortuos in vitam, fuit igitur curae Deo, et erit etiamsi a Nerone interficitur. Non sis nimis iustus nec nimis sapiens, ne facias vastitatem.

Non dubium est Salomonem loqui de iusticia politica, et gubernatrice huius externae vitae, et hanc perspicua est accommodatio huius dicti, et valde utile praeceptum est.

Iusticia versatur in medio inter negligentiam et crudelitatem, Nimia severitas fit crudelitas, ut fuit in Aureliano, Nimia indulgentia, quae non punit atrocia delicta, confirmat facinorosos, qualis fuit in Arcadio.

Sed gubernator salutaris, ut Augustus videt medium, quod habet probabilem rationem.

Id medium haec admonitio Salomonis iubet quaeri, et vincat bonitas.

Nec subtilissime quaeratur medium, sicut in Deo misericordia superat iudicium.

Diligenter autem et comminatio observanda est, quam addit: Ne facias vastationem, Nimia severitas facit vastationem, Multi sanabiles sine necessitate interficiuntur, Multi boni fugiunt gubernationem.

Mox addit similem admonitionem de sapientia, Non sis nimis sapiens.

Ut nimia severitas fit crudelitas, ita nimia sapientia, hoc est nimia subtilitas, fit cavillatrix, rixosa, πολυπραγμονικὴ, sophistica, ἀντιλογικὴ, ut dicit Menander: Leges bonae sunt, sed si quis eas nimis subtiliter interpretatur, fit sycophanta, ut qui pactus 30 dierum inducias, noctu populatus est agros.

Imperator est dominus Mediolani, rex Gallicus subtilitatem invenire potest, qua dicat ad se pertinere Mediolanum.

Plena est vita talium exemplorum, et inde oriri bella et vastitates manifestum est.

Ideo multae extant admonitiones de fugienda illa cavillatrice sapientia.

Et Agesilaus dixit: τὸ λίαν δίκαιον πρόφασις ἐστὶ.

Ne sis nimis impius, nec sis stultus, ne moriaris, non tuo ipsius tempore.

Haec admonitio cohaeret cum proxima quae loquitur de altero extremo, scilicet de negligentia, Non toleret magistratus atrocia et enormia delicta, non taceat fidelis doctor de rebus necessariis et de idolomania, non devores camelos, colato culice.

Ac atrocem poenam negligentiae proponit: Ne moriaris non tuo tempore, id est, ne si negligenter rexeris tuos mores, et nimium laxaveris frenos cupiditatum, Deus te puniat vel per magistratum vel aliis modis, sicut ipse David ruit in poenas nimium sibi indulgens.

Cum autem velit quaeri medium postea addit, Quis sit ille, qui medium cernit Deo monstrante, et consilia eius ac manum regente, scilicet, timen Deum: ita monet sine timore Dei, sine invocatione, sine auxilio divino, non esse felicem gubernationem, iuxta illa dicta: Nisi Dominus custodierit.

Item: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet. Bonum quod apprehenderis in hoc et in illo, non dimittat manus tua.

Timens Deum evadet ex omnibus illis.

Cum severitas est bona, exerceas eam, rursum cum lenitas prodest, utaris lenitate. mediocritatem negotiis seu circumstantiis convenientem quaeri, ut alias duriores, alias leniores sint, ut medicus aliis dat alia pharmaca.

Fabius videt quando pugnandum sit, quando non sit pugnandum.

Saul stulto zelo interficit Gabaonitas, Iosue pepercit eis.

Observanda est autem emphasis in verbo Apprehendere.

Significat enim quaerendam esse veram causam vel severe vel leniter agendi, sicut Paulus inquit: Unusquisque certus sit in sua sententia.

Bonum quod apprehenderis, id est, cum re deliberata invenerit conscientia veram rationem, cui firmiter assentiendum est, illa ratio anteferatur iracundiae, et aliis affectibus.

Sed dicat aliquis, quomodo potest inveniri illa mediocritas seu virtus conveniens circumstantiae.

Respondet: Timens Deum evadet ex his omnibus, id est, eliget meliorem sententiam, quia timens Deum intuetur legem divinam, et simul regitur Spiritu sancto, et petit sua consilia gubernari, moderatur impetus, vult consulere Ecclesiae et publicae saluti, non gerit morem privato dolori et privatis cupiditatibus.

Sapientia magis confortat sapientem, quam decem principes in civitate.

Generalis admonitio est, quae significat bona consilia et moderationem antecellere viribus, gubernator melius munitus est diligentia in cavendis periculis, moderatione in frenandis affectibus, invocatione Dei, quam si magna praesidia et magnos exercitus sibi circumdet, ut Alexander Pheraeus interfectus est a coniuge et eius fratribus, etiam si noctu inter praesidia in turri cubabat, quo ascendendum erat per scalas.

Pater Alexandri in publica pompa spectantibus principibus et satellitibus interfectus est.

Iulius in Senatu suo interfectus est, et sunt innumerabilia exempla: sed principes mitiores et tranquillio rem gubernationem et placidos exitus habuerunt, ut Iosaphat, Augustus, Theodosius.

Non est homo iustus in terra, qui quanquam bona facit, non etiam peccet.

Politica sententia est, non de peccato haerente in natura, sed de erratis et lapsibus externis: etiam iusti et benemerentes tamen aliquando peccant, non in eadem actione, sed in diversis.

Bonus et salutaris princeps est David, et plerumque recte facit, et tamen multa negligit, imo ruit perniciose rapta amici coniuge et marito interfecto, viro sancto et forti.

Iosias bonus et salutaris princeps, tamen erat moto bello non necessario.

Ita nec iusti sunt sine aliquibus lapsibus.

Huc Theognidis versus accommodetur: αὐτὰρ ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς πότε μὲν κακὸς ἄλλοτε ἐσθλός.

Item Euripides: ὁ πολλὰ πράττων πολλὰ καὶ ἁμαρτάνει.

Hinc et descriptiones sumuntur bonorum et malorum gubernatorum.

Bonus gubernator est, qui studium habet recte faciendi, et plerumque recte facit, etiam si aliquando cessat.

Ita fuerunt boni principes, David, Iosias, Augustus.

Sed malus gubernator est, qui non habet studium recte faciendi, et plerumque scelerate facit, etiam si aliquando recte facit, ut Cambyses.

Sumitur igitur discrimen a perpetua voluntate seu προαιρέσει.

Sicut et Paulus hanc metam constituit, Hoc requiritur, fideles ut simus.

Agnoscamus autem in talibus admonitionibus ingentem infirmitatem nostram, metuamus insidias diaboli, et assidue petamus, ut et regat nos Deus, et sanet errata nostra, sicut Petrus praecipit: Vigilate, quia adversarius vester circumit.

Non omnibus sermonibus accommoda cor tuum.

Admonitio est de obtrectationibus, ne vel ipsi simus obtrectatores, vel frangamur obtrectatione seu calumniis.

Est autem obtrectatio contraria veritati et candori, recte facta aut excusabilia depravans, aut propter aliqua errata de recte facientibus serens pravam opinionem.

Adeoque multi delectantur obtrectatione, ut Pindarus dicit, Sermones maledicos ohsonium esse.

Hoc vitium prohibetur in praecepto octavo: Non dicas falsum testimonium.

Et in Levitico: Non sis susurro in populis.

Supra autem dictum est de iudicio conscientiae et de fama.

Etsi autem utriusque conservatio curanda est, tamen prior sit cura, ne conscientia fiat saucia, postea expetatur et bona fama, ut inquit Augustinus: Bona conscientia mihi opus est propter Deum, Bona fama propter proximum.

Et quia multi sunt obtrectatores, non propterea nimium doleamus, si qui non iudicant candide, sed consolemur nos testimonio conscientiae, sicut Paulus inquit: Haec est gloriatio nostra, testimonium conscientiae nostrae.

Item: Probet unusquisque opus suum, et sic apud sese gloriam habebit, et non pendebit ex alio.

Salomon hoc loco iubet eos minus irasci obtrectationibus, quia nos ipsi saepe eodem modo peccamus.

Recitat enim Salomon communia hominum vitia.

Cuncta tentavi in sapientia, Dixi, sapiens efficiar, et ipsa longius recessit a me.

Postea in textu sequitur repetitio.

Negat ab hominibus omnes errores prospici et caveri posse, et manifestum est, magnos et tristes lapsus esse summorum et sapientissimorum hominum.

In hac querela commonefacti de nostra infirmitate, petamus nos regi a Deo, ut saepe dictum est: Scio Domine, quod non est hominis via eius.

Item: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet.

Inveni amariorem morte mulierem, quae laqueus est venatorum etc.

Postea de mulieribus loquitur.

Quandocunque enim recitantur infirmitates et calamitates nostrae, in eo catalogo partem aliquam occupant ipsarum mulierum morbi, et furores in viris, qui propter mulieres magnas calamitates sibi et aliis accersunt, ut Samson, David, Paris, et alii innumerabiles.

Deus fecit hominem rectum, sed ipse quaerit multas deliberationes.

Non principaliter de Creatione loquitur, sed de modo actionum, quem Deus hominibus rectum proposuit, id est, Deus instituit ordinem, quo comedas, bibas, sis maritus, servias in vocatione certa, et maneas intra metas tuae vocationis.

Sed homo quaerit varias deliberationes.

David habebat suas coniuges forma et virtute praestantes, et tamen appetit alienam.

Antonius habet magnum imperium, sed appetit Monarchiam.

Has errantes cupiditates, et hallucinantem sapientiam taxat, ut Pericles, Demosthenes, Brutus, Cicero, et alii multi sapientiae specie labuntur.

Nee male accommodatur dictum ad doctrinas.

Deus dedit homini certum doctrinae genus, et intra eas metas vult coërceri mentes nostras, sed hominum ingenia vagabunda quaerunt alias opiniones, et delectantur varietate imaginationum tanquam ludis.

Hoc ingens malum severissime taxatur multis locis, ut apud Ieremiam: Hoc praecepi, audite me.

## 8:1 Argument
Chapter VIII.

The wisdom of a man is the light of his countenance, and the stubborn will be worthy of hatred.

Although it is a general saying, Wisdom brings cheerfulness, because a good conscience is tranquil.

But evil is a horrible torture, and other external punishments accompany it, so that finally tyrants are oppressed: yet it seems here to be spoken properly still about the matter of the previous chapter, Wisdom, that is, discernment and choice, where severity is profitable, where leniency is profitable, where one must fight, where one must yield, it brings joy: but the stubborn, that is, the hard, who does not listen to those rightly admonishing, but indulges his own anger, destroys himself and others.

Just as the stubbornness of Pericles and Demosthenes was destructive to all of Greece.

I observe the mouth of the king and the words of the oath of God.

This sentence is very worthy of consideration and memory, and indeed it clearly shows that this book does not teach monastic idleness, as many have foolishly interpreted: but here it leads man to all necessary actions, and to many difficult and dangerous struggles, and so that there may not be license, it surrounds the life of man with boundaries, and ordains obedience.
