He commands to observe the Mouth, that is, the mandates of the king, and adds a restriction: And the words of the oath of God, that is, the law of God.

For he names the law an oath elsewhere, because God by swearing confirmed promises and threats.

Therefore there is no doubt that crimes are punished, but punishments are mitigated for those doing penance.

For that also is included in the oath.

Thus let obedience be ordered: First let us obey the divine voice, which the mouth of the king also ought to sound.

Then also the king commanding things not fighting with the divine voice.

These agree with the rule: It is necessary to obey God rather than men.

Now consider what kind of boundary is set around man, Let there not be license, which indulges all desires, nor let there be idleness, nor let there be meddlesomeness [πολυπραγμοσύνη], but do the mandates divinely, and the duties of the vocation, into which you have been placed by the king, do not rush by curiosity, ambition, or any desire to other business.

It is added therefore in the text.

Do not hasten to depart from his face, that is, do not depart from your vocation, do not disturb the order, do not seize dominion, nor stand in evil work, that is, do not do those things which you know are prohibited by law. Afterwards follow the sayings about punishments, where in the end he says: There shall be no escape. Above, however, he says: Because whatever he wills, the king shall do, namely with God defending legitimate empires. For he speaks of legitimate power, or legitimate order, which God protects, just as it is said in Rom. 13: Those who resist power shall have punishment.

This doctrine has been repeated often elsewhere. He who keeps the commandment shall not fall into punishments. The wise heart understands time and judgment, because for every business there is a time and judgment that will come. But great is the calamity of man who does not know the past and the future. Nor does man have power over his life, nor does he have power over his death, and there is no escape in war, and wickedness shall not deliver the wicked.

This continuous discourse preaches about punishments, and hands down this general rule: Atrocious crimes are punished with atrocious punishments even in this life, such as homicides, perjuries, adulteries, incestuous lusts, robberies, and the like, as it is written: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword.

Item: God will judge whoremongers and adulterers. On the contrary, he promises a more tranquil life to the modest: He who keeps the commandment shall not fall into punishments.

Then Solomon meets a tacit objection. For because punishments are deferred, boldness is confirmed in many. To this foolish imagination and security he opposes the following sayings.

Nay, he says, the wise man understands time and judgment, that is, he knows that punishments will come in their own time even if they are deferred for a little while, and he knows that for every business there will be a judgment, that is, he is not a cyclopian, he does not despise providence, but knows that the most true is the divine threatening which is recited in Ps. 61: You will render to each one according to his works, and Ps. 57: Truly there is a God judging in the earth. And the law of nature and experience have shown the same doctrine even to the Gentiles, according to those sayings: God has an avenging eye. Item: God knows how to judge. Item: Yet late punishment comes with silent feet. Item: It compensates for the slowness of punishment with the gravity of the punishment. Then the words that follow contain the detestation of that cyclopian security.

Great calamity it is, he says, that men neither care for the past, nor the future, that is; at all times we see horrendous spectacles of punishments, and yet many laugh at such atrocious examples: he speaks of such past punishments, clearly, and examples. Afterwards he adds an express threatening.

There will come, he says, punishments, which you will in no way be able to hinder or ward off. Man does not have in his power his life or death, that is, he cannot retain life or ward off death, when God oppresses him with punishments. There is no escape, he says, in war, And in no way shall wickedness be unpunished.

These sayings do not need another explanation, but let us assent to the divine voice threatening punishment to all who do not do penance, just as the Lord says in Luke 13: Unless you do penance, you shall all likewise perish.

Let us by no means know these thunderbolts to be an empty sound, but let us truly tremble with the thought and fear of present and eternal punishments, and let us be converted to God, let us curb unjust impulses, and let us pray to the king by God etc.

Sometimes man dominates man to his own harm. Previously the assertion about providence has been clearly set forth, it has been expressly said that crimes are punished. Now he adds objections, which he refutes with mixed complaints. On the contrary he says: We see the wicked often flourish in wealth and power, the just oppressed and killed.

This injustice would not be tolerated, if there were providence. He recites this most well-known objection here too, and refutes it in this way. Although the wicked often flourish, and the just are often oppressed, yet it is most certain that in the end these unjust ones will also pay punishments, and it will be better for the just.

This solution David also recites in Psalm 56: I saw the wicked exalted like the cedars of Lebanon, I passed by, and behold he was not. But the salvation of the just is from the Lord. Saul dominates for a little while, who drives away David, kills the priests, Herod the Baptist, Nero Paul, but a little while after these tyrants are oppressed in this life by manifest punishments.

But someone may say, what does this profit the good who are killed? This question torments men, which Solomon also deplores here: because human reason ignores the causes, why nature is universally subject to such great miseries, but the doctrine of the Church shows the cause, namely sin in all. In the meantime, however, there is its own place for political justice, and it does not profit the wicked to act wickedly, since it is nonetheless certain that they are punished, and therein the example of God’s providence is seen.

Thus, one part of the objection can be judged by reason, as is also said in poems: 'Yet punishment comes slowly with silent feet.' The other part of the objection, what becomes of the good, is not judged by human wisdom, but in the word of God, deliverance is proposed to them, in which one must rest by faith.

Abel, the Baptist, know that God is just, and they await the future deliverance and salvation of the Church, of which the resurrection of the Son of God, and of other saints, and other miracles in the Church testify. Therefore, Solomon also says elsewhere: 'To the just there is hope in death.' And Job says: 'Even if He kills me, I will hope in Him.' Thus the Church responds to that objection.

But because punishments are delayed, security and boldness grow in men.

Solomon weaves this complaint in here too, because the decree against evil deeds is not made quickly, the hearts of men burn to act wickedly.

To this complaint, he again adds a solution and an affirmation. Even if the wicked are tolerated for a long time, yet I know that it will be well for those who fear God, who fear before His face, and it will not be well for the impious, nor will his days be prolonged, but like a shadow they will pass away who do not fear His face.

Solomon therefore teaches that we should not, offended by that inequality in this life, fall away from God, but rest in the word of God, which promises deliverance and salvation to the just, while punishments are denounced against the impious, both by word and by manifest examples.

Therefore, many sayings exist regarding punishments even among the poets, as in Claudian: 'Often a doubtful opinion has drawn my mind, whether the gods care for the earth, or if no Ruler exists, and mortal things flow by uncertain chance; for when I watched the ordered covenants of the world, and the prescribed limits of the sea and the courses of the year, and the changes of light and night, then I thought all things were confirmed by the counsel of God, who by law commanded the stars to move, who commanded the fruits to be born at different times, who commanded the changing Moon to be filled with alien fire, and the Sun with its own, who stretched out the shores for the waves, and balanced the earth on a central axis.

But when I wished to look upon the affairs of men in such great darkness, and saw the joyful wicked flourishing for a long time, and the pious being vexed, again Religion fell, shaken, and I did not willingly follow the path of another cause, which thought the seeds of things run by empty motion.' 'He affirms, and that Fortune, through the void, does not rule new figures by art, which thinks the divine powers are either null or ignorant of us by ambiguous sense. At last, the punishment of Rufinus removed this tumult and absolved the gods; now I do not complain that the unjust have grown to the heights of things; they are lifted up on high, that they may fall with a heavier crash.'

There are just men to whom evils happen.

He dwells on the established discourse concerning providence, and repeats the doctrine in which there is this affirmation: That providence is not to be denied on that account, even if the punishments of the wicked are delayed, or the just are oppressed in this life.

And the true refutation of the objection is that another judgment remains, in which not a momentary compensation will be made, but an eternal one. He comprehends this refutation when he commands to fear God, and sets forth the affirmation: 'It will be well for those who fear God.'

But that human wisdom seeks the causes why the just are often harshly oppressed and the wicked flourish, is vanity, that is, a fruitless labor, because this counsel of God is not found by the keenness of the human mind, but the causes have been revealed to the Church in general, for which it is subjected to the cross, as is said in its own place. Solomon therefore commands, having omitted this inquiry of human reason, to remain in the fear of God and to use the present gifts of God according to the precepts: food, drink, political and economic vocation. This is the summary of the long narration in this very chapter.

For this question torments all men, and many, because they see the prosperity of the wicked and the adversity of the just, think there is no providence; but it is the excellent strength of faith not to be broken by these spectacles, but to retain the true knowledge of God, and to await the judgment.

The same discourse is copiously recited in Psalm 36: 'Fret not thyself.'

And let the studious consider where poets or other writers enter into this matter, as often happens: sometimes they recite doubts, sometimes affirmations, as, 'Learn justice, being warned, and do not despise the gods.' And Aristotle in his Rhetoric recites the saying of Stesichorus: 'Do not treat anyone with injury.' Because the cicadas will sing this in the fields, that is, the poor oppressed in their fields sound these complaints and move God to punish the tyrants.

Latin:

Caput VIII.

Sapientia hominis est lumen vultus, et pertinax erit dignus odio.

Etsi generale dictum est, Sapientia adfert hilaritatem, quia bona conscientia tranquilla est.

Mala vero est horribilis carnificina, et comitantur eam aliae poenae externae, ut tandem opprimuntur tyranni: tamen videtur hic proprie dici adhuc de materia proximi capitis, Sapientia, id est, diiudicatio et delectus, ubi prosit severitas, ubi prosit lenitas, ubi sit praeliandum, ubi sit cedendum, adfert laeticiam: sed pervicax, id est, durus, qui non audit recte monentes, sed suae iracundiae morem gerit, perdit sese et alios.

Sicut Periclis et Demosthenis pertinacia fuit exitiosa toti Graeciae.

Ego os regis observo et verba iuramenti Dei.

Haec sententia valde digna est consideratione, et memoria, et quidem perspicue ostendit hunc librum non docere ocium monasticum, ut multi insulse interpretati sunt: sed hic deducit hominem ad omnes necessarias actiones, et ad multa difficilia et periculosa certamina, et ne sit licentia, circumdat vitae hominis metas, et ordinat obedientiam.

Iubet observare Os, id est, mandata regis, et addit restrictionem: Et verba iuramenti Dei, id est, legem Dei.

Nominat enim et alibi legem iuramentum, quia Deus iureiurando sanxit promissiones et comminationes.

Igitur non dubium est puniri scelera, sed mitigantur poenae agentibus poenitentiam.

Nam id quoque in iuramento comprehenditur.

Sic sit ordinata obedientia: Primum voci divinae obediamus, quam et os regis sonare debet.

Deinde et regi mandanti non pugnantia cum voce divina.

Haec congruunt ad regulam: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus.

Iam considera qualis meta circumdata sit homini, Non sit licentia, quae indulgeat omnibus cupiditatibus, nec sit ocium, nec sit πολυπραγμοσύνη, sed facias mandata divinitus, et officia vocationis, in quam a rege collocatus es, non ruas curiositate, ambitione, vel quacunque cupiditate ad alia negocia.

Additum est igitur in textu.

Non festines recedere a facie eius, id est, non discedas a vocatione, non turbes ordinem, non rapias dominationem, nec stes in opere malo, id est, non facias ea quae scis prohiberi lege. Postea sequuntur dicta de poenis, ubi in fine dicit: Non erit evasio. Supra vero inquit: Quia omne quod voluerit, faciet rex, scilicet Deo defendente legitima imperia. Loquitur enim de legitima potestate, seu legitimo ordine, quem Deus tuetur, sicut Rom. 13. dicitur: Qui potestati resistunt, poenam habebunt.

Haec doctrina alias saepe repetita est. Qui custodit praeceptum, non ruet in poenas. Tempus et iudicium intelligit cor sapiens, quia cuiuslibet negotii tempus et iudicium veniet. Sed magna est calamitas hominis nescientis praeterita et futura. Nec habet homo potestatem suae vitae, nec habet potestatem suae mortis, et non est evasio in bello, et non liberabit impietas impium.

Haec continua oratio de poenis concionatur, et hanc generalem regulam tradit: Atrocia delicta puniuntur atrocibus poenis etiam in hac vita, ut homicidia, periuria, adulteria, incestae libidines, rapinae, et similia, ut scriptum est: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit.

Item: Scortatores et adulteros iudicabit Deus. Econtra promittit tranquilliorem vitam modestis: Qui custodit praeceptum, non ruet in poenas.

Deinde occurrit tacitae obiectioni Salomon. Quia enim differuntur poenae, confirmatur in multis audacia. Huic stultae imaginationi et securitati opponit sequentia dicta.

Imo, inquit, Sapiens intelligit tempus et iudicium, id est, scit poenas suo tempore venturas esse etiamsi aliquantisper differantur, et scit cuiuslibet negotii venturum esse iudicium, id est, non est cyclopicus, non contemnit providentiam, sed scit verissimam esse comminationem divinam quae recitatur Psal. 61.: Reddes unicuique iuxta opera sua, et Psal. 57.: Utique est Deus iudicans in terra, Et lex naturae et experientia eandem doctrinam etiam Ethnicis ostenderunt, iuxta illa dicta: ἔχει θεὸς ἔκδικον ὄμμα. Item: θεὸς οἶδε δικά-ζειν. Item: Sera tamen tacitis poena venit pedibus. Item: Tarditatem poenae gravitate supplicii compensat. Deinde verba quae sequuntur, continent detestationem illius cyclopicae securitatis.

Magna calamitas est, inquit, homines nec praeterita curare, nec futura, id est; omnibus temporibus videmus horrenda spectacula poenarum, et tamen tam atrocia exempla rident multi: de talibus praeteritis poenis videlicet et exemplis loquitur. Postea addit expressam comminationem.

Venient, inquit, poenae, quas nullo modo poteris impedire aut arcere. Homo non habet in potestate sua vitam aut mortem, id est, non potest retinere vitam aut arcere mortem, cum Deus eum poenis opprimit. Non est evasio, inquit, in bello, Et nequaquam erit impunita impietas.

Haec dicta non indigent alia enarratione, sed adsentiamur voci divinae minitanti poenam omnibus qui non agunt poenitentiam, sicut inquit Dominus Lucae 13.: Nisi poenitentiam agetis, omnes similiter peribitis. Haec fulmina nequaquam sciamus esse inanem sonitum, sed vere expavescamus cogitatione et metu praesentium et aeternarum poenarum, et ad Deum convertamur, frenemus iniustos impetus, et oremus regi a Deo etc.

Interdum dominatur homo homini in malum suum.

Antea perspicue posita est adseveratio de providentia, expresse dictum est puniri delicta. Nunc addit obiectiones, quas refutat admixtis querelis. Contra inquit: Videmus sceleratos saepe florere opibus et potentia, iustos opprimi et interfici.

Haec iniusticia non toleraretur, si esset providentia. Hanc notissimam obiectionem et hic recitat, et hoc modo refutat. Quanquam saepe florent scelerati, saepe opprimuntur iusti, tamen certissimum est, tandem et hos iniustos daturos esse poenas, et melius fore iustis.

Hanc solutionem recitat et David Psalmo 56.: Vidi impium exaltatum ut cedros Libani, praeterii, et ecce non erat. Salus autem iustorum a Domino. Dominatur aliquantisper Saul, qui pellit Davidem, interficit sacerdotes, Herodes Baptistam, Nero Paulum, sed aliquanto post hi tyranni in hac vita manifestis poenis opprimuntur.

Sed dicat aliquis, quid hoc prodest bonis interfectis? Haec quaestio excruciat homines, id quoque Salomon hic deplorat: quia humana ratio causas ignorat, quare universaliter tantis aerumnis natura subiecta sit, sed doctrina Ecclesiae monstrat causam, scilicet peccatum in omnibus. Interea tamen suus locus est politicae iusticiae, et non prodest sceleratis scelerate facere, quia tamen certum est eos puniri, et ibi exemplum providentiae Dei conspicitur.

Ita una pars objectionis ratione iudicari potest, ut etiam in poëmatis dicitur. Sera tamen tacitis poena venit pedibus. Altera pars objectionis, quid de bonis fiat, non iudicatur humana sapientia, sed in verbo Dei proposita est ipsis liberatio, in qua fide acquiescendum est.

Abel, Baptista, norunt Deum esse iustum, et expectant futuram Ecclesiae liberationem et salutem, de qua testificatur resurrectio Filii Dei, et aliorum sanctorum, et alia miracula in Ecclesia. Ideo et alibi inquit Salomon: Iusto spes est in morte. Et Iob inquit: Etiamsi occidet me, sperabo in eum. Sic Ecclesia respondet ad illam objectionem.

Sed quia differuntur poenae, crescit in hominibus securitas et audacia.

Hanc querelam et hic intexit Salomon, quia non cito fit decretum contra mala facta, aestuant hominum corda ad scelerate faciendum.

Huic querelae rursus addit solutionem et adseverationem. Etiamsi diu tolerantur scelerati, tamen scio, quod erit bonum timentibus Deum, qui timent a facie eius, et non erit bonum impio nec prolongabuntur dies eius, sed sicut umbra transibunt qui non timent faciem eius.

Docet igitur Salomon, ne offensi illa inaequalitate in hac vita deficiamus a Deo, sed acquiescamus in verbo Dei, quod promittit liberationem, et salutem iustis, poenae vero denunciantur impiis, et verbo et exemplis manifestis.

Ideo de poenis multa extant dicta etiam apud poëtas, ut apud Claudianum: Saepe mihi dubiam traxit sententiam mentem, Curarent superi terras, an nullus inesset Rector, et incerto fluerent mortalia casu, Nam cum dispositi spectabam foedera mundi, Praescriptosque maris fines annique meatus, Et lucis noctisque vices, tunc omnia rebar Consilio firmata Dei, qui lege moveri Sidera, qui fruges diverso tempore nasci, Qui variam Phoeben alieno iusserit igne Compleri, Solemque suo, porrexerit undis Littora, tellurem medio libraverit axe.

Sed cum res hominum tanta caligine volui Aspicerem, laetosque diu florere nocentes, Vexarique pios, rursus labefacta cadebat Relligio, causaeque viam non sponte sequebar Alterius, vacuo quae semina currere motu. Adfirmat, magnumque novas per inane figuras Fortuna non arte regi, quae numina sensu Ambiguo vel nulla putat vel nescia nostri. Abstulit hunc tandem Ruffini poena tumultum Absolvitque Deos, iam non ad culmina rerum Iniustos crevisse queror, tolluntur in altum, Ut lapsu graviore ruant.

Sunt iusti quibus mala accidunt.

Immoratur institutae concioni de providentia, et repetit doctrinam, in qua est asseveratio: Non propterea negandam esse providentiam, etiamsi poenae sceleratorum differuntur, aut iusti in hac vita premuntur.

Ac vera refutatio est objectionis, restare aliud iudicium, in quo non momentanea compensatio fiet, sed aeterna. Hanc refutationem comprehendit, cum iubet timere Deum, et ponit asseverationem: Bene erit timentibus Deum.

Sed quod quaerit humana sapientia causas, quare iusti saepe duriter premantur et mali floreant, vanitas est, id est, irritus labor, quia hoc consilium Dei non invenitur acie humanae mentis, sed Ecclesiae patefactae sunt causae in genere propter quas cruci subiectae est, ut suo loco dicitur. Iubet igitur Salomon, omissa hac inquisitione humanae rationis, manere in timore Dei et praesentibus donis Dei iuxta praecepta uti, cibo, potu, vocatione politica, oeconomica. Haec est summa longae narrationis in hoc ipso capite.

Excruciat enim haec quaestio omnes homines, et multi quia vident res secundas malorum et res adversas iustorum, cogitant non esse providentiam sed excellens robur fidei est his spectaculis non frangi, ac retinere veram agnitionem Dei, et expectare iudicium.

Eadem concio copiose recitatur in Psalmo 36.: Noli aemulari.

Et studiosi considerent, ubi poetae aut alii scriptores in hanc materiam ingrediantur, ut saepe fit: interdum recitant dubitationes, interdum asseverationes, ut, Discite iusticiam moniti, et non spernere divos. Et Aristoteles in Rhetoricis recitat Stesichori dictum: Neminem afficias iniuria. Quia cicadae canent hoc in campis, id est, pauperes oppressi in suis agris sonant has querelas et movent Deum, ut puniat tyrannos.

## 9:1 Argument
Chapter IX. There are just and wise men and their works are in the hand of God, and man knows not love or hatred in all things that are before him. All things happen similarly to all, to the just, the wicked, the good, and the unclean, just as to the one offering in the unclean, and to the one not offering. As it happens to the good, so it happens to the sinner. As it happens to the perjurer, so it happens to the one fearing an oath. This is the worst of all things that happen under the Sun, that the events are similar. Therefore the hearts of men are filled with malice, and foolishness remains in their hearts in all their life, until they die.

Although this part of the text has been obscured by foreign interpretations, yet it is manifest that the complaint is repeated concerning this external appearance, which moves many to deny providence because of the prosperous affairs of the wicked and the adverse affairs of the just. Salomon, however, preaches about this external appearance for this reason, that he may lead us away from it, lest we judge from these events: but that we may embrace with the firmest faith the divine voice, which affirms what things are to be done, and that the judgment is to be awaited. This is the simplest opinion of Salomon, who expressly condemns here the frenzies of those denying providence, because he says that foolishness is destructive to those very people who, because of these spectacles or external appearance, fall away from God.

Having established this simplest opinion, now the interpretation of the monks, spread into the Church concerning this saying: No one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, must be refuted.

The monks do not see that this saying is an admonition, lest one judge concerning providence from prosperous or adverse things, but they transfer the saying to the doubt of a conscience seeking concerning the remission of sins, concerning which it must be asserted from the voice of the Gospel, not from events. It is manifest, however, that the monks wrongly twist this saying to doubt.

Because it must certainly be confessed that those sinning against their conscience know that they are in hatred. David, taking the wife of another, knows that he is committing a crime, at which God is horribly angry. Although the monks concede that in sins against conscience the wrath of God is known, yet afterwards they say that concerning the converted one must always doubt whether he is in grace. But it must be known most certainly that this imagination of the monks is false and impious, and is a deletion of the Gospel.

Because this is the external and immovable voice of the Gospel, that those doing penance should by faith establish that their sins are truly remitted to them, and that they are received into grace because of the Mediator, and that they should struggle out of doubt, according to that Ephesians 3: By whom we have boldness to approach in confidence through faith in Christ. Likewise to the Hebrews: Having such a high priest, let us approach the throne of grace with confidence. And it must be known that there ought to be certainty on both sides.

David, taking the wife of another, should certainly know that God is horribly angry, just as it is most true. And this wrath is shown in the preaching of Nathan and in the most sad punishments. Afterwards David, having heard the absolution in his conversion, should resist doubt and establish that he is again most truly received into grace, and by this assent and faith he should sustain himself even in exile and in the highest sorrows.

But the monks object, nay, even the saints have sins of ignorance, therefore they should not affirm that they please God.

I answer: Let the saints confess both, that they have sins of ignorance and many other diseases, just as David says: No one living shall be justified in thy sight, and yet that they please God because of the Mediator by faith, and that their uncleanness is covered by the Mediator, just as it is written: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus. Likewise: Blessed are they whose iniquities are remitted, and whose sins are covered. This consolation is the proper voice of the Gospel.

But the monks, not understanding the distinction between Law and Gospel, have brought darkness into the Church. Afterwards they twisted this saying of Salomon to their own ravings, when Salomon is only doing this, that we should not judge from external appearance, and indeed he leads us to the word of God.

David, not even after hearing absolution, should judge himself to be cast away, even if he is in great punishments, and the event shows the wrath of God, but he ought to judge not from the event, but truly from the word of God. Much less should he judge concerning others from external appearance: Saul and Ionathas perish in the same way, nor can human wisdom discern these events, but the doctrine of the Church discerns them.

The end of Saul agrees with the rule: He who takes the sword, shall perish by the sword. The end of Ionathas has other causes: because God had previously testified that Ionathan pleased Him, but Ionathas and David know the causes why the Church is subjected to the cross.

What then is to be chosen? In the living there is hope, And a living dog is better than a dead lion.

A complaint was recited earlier, that similar things happen to the just and the unjust: This confusion disturbs minds, and weakens the will to act rightly. Therefore, he opposes a precept to this offense. Indeed, he says: It is necessary, however, to obey God, and he began from the question.

What then is to be chosen? Is labor to be chosen, when rewards do not follow? Solomon answers: One must entirely obey one's calling, and events must be commended to God, as has been often said above: Commend your way to God, and he himself will act.

But you will not be able to be a happy warrior such as Asa was. You cannot be a leader like Scipio; be therefore like Fabius, provided you serve faithfully in your own place, just as Paul says: This is required, that each one be faithful. But our sufficiency is from God.

Therefore Solomon says: In the living there is hope, that is, let the living person do something according to his calling. And a living dog is better than a dead lion, that is, even if you cannot be a lion, be a mediocre puppy. Why do we now seek lions, heroic leaders and governors, such as those ancients were, Gideon, Samson, David? Let us use our own, who even if they are not like them, as lions, are however like puppies; let them do something in their own place, and pray to God, that he may make them vessels of mercy.

Solomon dwells long on this sentiment. He says that the dead have already departed from the governance of this life, that the present must be used, and he commands to obey one's calling, and to acquiesce in God with faith, and a good conscience, whatever the events may be.

Go, eat your bread in gladness, Because your works are pleasing to God. That is, what you do according to your calling, just as he says later: This is your portion in life and in your labor which God has given you. And later: Everything that your hand finds, do it with strength.

This saying must be diligently observed, which indeed shows quite clearly that Solomon is not teaching the desertion of common society or of business, or the idleness of monks, but is proposing a most serious doctrine and consolation. He commands us to zealously obey our calling and to commend events to God, and indeed he demands faithfulness and diligence, when he says here: Work with strength. And he adds a most sweet consolation: Let the pious know that such a course according to one's calling pleases God, and is governed divinely, although many impediments occur, many offenses.

But soon another objection is added. What does it profit to labor, when there is not the race of the swift nor the victory of the strong? I answer: I want you to labor, and yet I want men not to trust in their own wisdom and strength, not to move unnecessary things by the confidence of their own wisdom or strength: but to seek and expect help from God, and whatever the events are, not to fail from God, nor to rage against him, but to acknowledge our own infirmity.

A similar saying is that one: I know, Lord, that the way of man is not his own. Item: A man cannot take anything for himself, unless it be given to him from heaven. These sayings speak of events, as was said in its place, they do not mean this, that there is absolutely no freedom in the very election of the will.

Time and chance prevail in all things. It agrees with the saying: Unless the Lord builds the house, he who builds it labors in vain. For he means this, that efforts are happy only then, when God helps them, gives a happy moment, and directs the events.

For let not time and chance be understood in the Epicurean manner. But Solomon reproves the confidence of our own powers and of our own wisdom, which imagines that human diligence suffices without God. And soon Solomon adds a nearby admonition about our infirmity: Man does not know his end, but is caught like a fish, that is, men often, incited by false persuasions and foolish hope, dream of good events, when yet in the middle of their course they are oppressed by great calamities, as happened to Marius, Pompey, Julius, and countless others who burst forth outside their calling.

To this pertain the common sayings: All things of men hang by a thin thread, And things that have flourished fall by a sudden chance. Item: μάταιοι διὰ ἐπιθυμίας μάταια λογίζονται (vain men through desire calculate vain things).

Therefore, the saying already very often recited must be repeated: Commend your way to God, and hope in him, and he himself will act. That is, you will do what is necessary according to your calling, and you should ask to be helped by God, mindful of your own infirmity.

A poor and wise man shall deliver the city, and one sinner shall destroy many good things.

It is very profitable to consider in life, as has also been said above: There are two kinds of men, some are vessels of wrath, others are vessels of mercy.

Vessels of wrath are unhappy men, who are a destruction to themselves and others, even if they are sometimes great and wise, as Solon says: Republics are overturned by great and excellent minds.

Such were the vessels of wrath Achas, Zedekiah, and in Rome Catiline, Antony and many others, and in the Church Samosatenus, Arius, Manichaeus, and many other pernicious teachers.

Concerning all such he says: One sinner shall destroy many good things, often the whole city suffers for the evil of one man.

But vessels of mercy are men whose course is salutary to themselves and others, such as Samuel, David, Jeremiah.

And properly such a poor man in the city, as he himself writes, was Jeremiah, who, although very many did not obey him, yet in that great confusion he especially preserved the Church.

This distinction being considered, let us pray to God with constant groans, each one, that He may make us vessels of mercy, and not allow us to become plagues, the avenging spirits of the human race, as the Prophets cry out in the Psalm: Look upon thy servants, and direct the work of our hands.

And Isaiah: Thou O Lord art our father, we are thy clay, thou formest us, we are the work of thy hands, be not very angry.

At the same time, this saying warns that good counsels are heard by the few, and that worse counsels please the multitude.

Therefore he says: The wisdom of the poor man is despised.

The words of the wise are heard by the silent, that is, not by those raging with some desire, but by those seeking the truth, and those things which are salutary.

Elsewhere Solomon says: It is better to meet a bear that has lost her cubs, than a fool in his folly, that is, it is most difficult to oppose one occupied by some desire, or fascinated by a foolish persuasion.

Latin:

Caput IX. Sunt iusti et sapientes et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt, et amorem et odium nescit homo in omnibus quae sunt coram ipso. Omnia eveniunt similiter omnibus, iusto, malo, bono et mundo, sicut in mundo offerenti, et non offerenti. Sicut evenit bono, sic evenit peccatori. Sicut evenit periuro, sic evenit timenti iusiurandum. Hoc est pessimum omnium, quae sub Sole fiunt, quod similes sunt eventus. Ideo corda hominum implentur malicia, et stulticia manet in cordibus eorum in omni vita, donec moriuntur.

Etsi peregrinis interpretationibus haec pars textus obscurata est, tamen manifestum est repeti querelam de hac externa specie, quae multos movet, ut negent providentiam propter res secundas malorum et res adversas iustorum. Salomon autem ideo concionatur de hac externa specie, ut nos ab ea abducat, ne ex his eventibus iudicemus: sed firmissima fide amplectamur vocem divinam, quae affirmat, quae facienda sint, et expectandum esse iudicium. Haec est simplicissima sententia Salomonis, qui expresse damnat hic furores negantium providentiam, quia dicit stulticiam esse exitialem illis ipsis, qui propter haec spectacula seu externam speciem deficiunt a Deo.

Constituta hac simplicissima sententia, iam refutanda est interpretatio monachorum, sparsa in Ecclesiam de hoc dicto: Nemo scit an amore vel odio dignus sit.

Monachi non vident hoc dictum admonitionem esse, ne de providentia ex rebus secundis aut adversis iudicetur, sed transferunt dictum ad dubitationem conscientiae quaerentis de remissione peccatorum, de qua asseverandum est ex voce Evangelii, non ex eventibus. Manifestum est autem monachos male detorquere hoc dictum ad dubitationem.

Quia certe fatendum est, delinquentes contra conscientiam, scire se in odio esse. David rapiens coniugem alterius, scit se facere scelus, cui Deus horribiliter irascitur. Quanquam autem concedunt monachi, in delictis contra conscientiam sciri iram Dei, tamen postea dicunt de conversis semper dubitandum esse, an sit in gratia. Sciendum est autem certissime, et hanc imaginationem monachorum falsam et impiam esse, et esse deletionem Evangelii.

Quia haec est vox externa et immota Evangelii, ut agentes poenitentiam fide statuant vere sibi remitti peccata, et se recipi in gratiam propter Mediatorem, et eluctentur ex dubitatione, iuxta illud Ephes. 3.: Per quem audemus accedere in fiducia per fidem Christi. Item ad Ebrae.: Habentes talem pontificem, accedamus ad thronum gratiae cum fiducia.

Ac sciendum est oportere certitudinem in utraque parte esse. David rapiens coniugem alterius, certo sciat Deum horribiliter irasci, sicut verissimum est. Et ostenditur haec ira in concione Nathan et tristissimis poenis.

Postea David, audita absolutione in conversione, repugnet dubitationi et statuat se rursus verissime recipi in gratiam, et hac assensione et fide se etiam in exilio et summus doloribus sustentet.

Sed obiiciunt monachi, imo habent et sancti peccata ignorantiae, ideo non affirment se placere Deo. Respondeo: Utrunque fateantur sancti, se habere peccata ignorantiae et alios morbos multos, sicut inquit David: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens, et tamen se placere Deo propter Mediatorem fide, et tectam esse immunditiem a Mediatore, sicut scriptum est: Nulla nunc damnatio est his qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Item: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata.

Haec consolatio est propria vox Evangelii. Sed monachi non intelligentes discrimen legis et Evangelii, tenebras in Ecclesiam invexerunt.

Postea hoc dictum Salomonis detorserunt ad sua deliramenta, cum Salomon hoc tantum agat, Ne ex specie externa iudicemus, et quidem deducat nos ad verbum Dei. David ne se quidem audita absolutione iudicet abiectum esse, etiamsi est in magnis poenis, et eventus iram Dei ostendit, sed non ex eventu, verum ex verbo Dei iudicare debet.

Multo minus ex specie externa de aliis iudicet: pereunt eodem modo Saul et Ionathas, nec discernere hos eventus humana sapientia potest, sed doctrina Ecclesiae discernit. Exitus Saul congruit cum regula: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. Exitus Ionathae habet alias causas: quia Deus antea testatus est, Ionathan sibi placere, sed sciunt Ionathas et David causas, quare Ecclesia cruci subiecta sit.

Quid igitur eligendum est? In vivente spes est, Et melior est canis vivus leone mortuo.

Antea recitata est querela, quod iustis et iniustis similia eveniant: Haec confusio turbat mentes, et languefacit voluntatem recte agendi. Opponit ergo huic offensioni praeceptum. Imo inquit: Necesse est tamen Deo obedire, et a quaestione exorsus est.

Quid igitur eligendum est? Estne eligendus labor, cum non respondeant praemia? Respondet Salomon: Est omnino vocationi obtemperandum, et eventus Deo commendandi sunt, ut supra saepe dictum est: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet.

At non poteris esse felix praeliator qualis fuit Asa. Non potes esse dux similis Scipioni, Sis igitur similis Fabio, modo servias tuo loco fideliter, sicut Paulus inquit: Hoc requiritur, fidelis ut sit quisque. Sufficientia vero nostra ex Deo est.

Inquit igitur Salomon: In vivente spes est, id est, vivens agat aliquid iuxta vocationem. Et melior est vivus canis leone mortuo, id est, etiamsi non potes esse leo, sis mediocris catulus. Quid iam quaerimus leones, heroicos duces et gubernatores, quales illi veteres fuerunt Gedeon, Samson, David? Utamur nostris, qui etiamsi non sunt illis similes, ut leones, sunt autem velut catuli, Aliquid suo loco agant, et orent Deum, ut faciat eos vasa misericordiae.

In hac sententia diu commoratur Salomon. Dicit mortuos iam discessisse ab huius vitae gubernatione, praesentibus utendum esse, et iubet vocationi parere, et acquiescere in Deo fide, et bona conscientia, qualescunque sint eventus.

Vade, comede in laeticia panem tuum, Quia Deo placent opera tua. Id est, quae facis iuxta vocationem, sicut postea dicit: Haec est pars in vita et labore tuo quem tibi dedit Deus. Et postea: Omne quod invenit manus tua, fortiter facito.

Hoc dictum diligenter observandum est, quod quidem satis perspicue ostendit, non doceri a Salomone desertionem societatis communis aut negotiorum, aut ocium monachorum, sed proponi gravissimam doctrinam et consolationem. Iubet nos studiose obtemperare vocationi et eventus Deo commendare, et quidem fidelitatem et diligentiam postulat, cum hic ait: Fortiter operare. Et addit consolationem dulcissimam: Pii sciant talem cursum iuxta vocationem Deo placere, et gubernari divinitus, quanquam multa incidunt impedimenta, multae offensiones.

Mox autem alia obiectio additur. Quid prodest laborare, cum non sit velocium cursus nec fortium victoria? Respondeo: Volo ut labores, et tamen volo homines non confidere propria sapientia et fortitudine, non movere res non necessarias fiducia propriae sapientiae aut fortitudinis: sed petere et expectare auxilium a Deo, et qualescunque sunt eventus, non deficere a Deo, nec fremere adversus eum, sed agnoscere nostram infirmitatem.

Simile dictum est illi: Scio Domine, non est hominis via eius. Item: Non potest sibi homo sumere quicquam, nisi datum sit ei de coelo. Haec dicta de eventibus loquuntur, ut suo loco dictum est, non hoc volunt, prorsus nullam esse libertatem in ipsa electione voluntatis.

Tempus et casus valent in omnibus. Congruit cum dicto: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum, frustra laborat qui aedificat eam. Nam hoc vult, tunc demum felices esse conatus, quando Deus eos adiuvat, dat felix momentum et regit eventus.

Non enim intelligantur tempus et casus Epicureo more. Sed reprehendit Salomon fiduciam nostrarum virium et nostrae sapientiae, quae imaginatur sufficere humanam diligentiam sine Deo. Ac mox addit vicinam admonitionem Salomon de nostra infirmitate: Nescit homo finem suum, sed velut piscis capitur, id est, homines saepe falsis persuasionibus et stulta spe incitati somniant bonos eventus, cum tamen in medio cursu magnis calamitatibus opprimantur, ut accidit Mario, Pompeio, Iulio et aliis innumerabilibus erumpentibus extra vocationem.

Huc pertinent communia dicta: Omnia sunt hominum tenui pendentia filo, Et subito casu quae valuere ruunt. Item: μάταιοι διὰ ἐπιθυμίας μάταια λογίζονται.

Repetendum est ergo dictum saepissime iam recitatum: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Id est, facies necessaria iuxta vocationem, et petas te iuvari a Deo memor tuae infirmitatis.

Vir pauper et sapiens liberabit urbem, et unus peccator multa bona perdet.

Valde prodest considerare in vita, ut supra quoque dictum est: Duo esse hominum genera, alii sunt vasa irae, alii vasa misericordiae.

Vasa irae sunt homines infelices, qui sibi et aliis exitio sunt, etsi interdum magni et sapientes sunt, sicut Solon inquit: Everti Respublicas a magnis et excellentibus ingeniis.

Ita erant vasa irae Achas, Sedechias, et Romae Catilina, Antonius et multi alii, et in Ecclesia Samosatenus, Arius, Manichaeus, et multi alii perniciosi doctores.

De talibus omnibus inquit: Unus peccator, multa bona perdet, πολλάκι καὶ ξύμπατα πόλις κακοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἐπαυρεῖ.

Sed vasa misericordiae sunt homines, quorum cursus salutaris est ipsis et aliis, ut Samuel, David, Ieremias.

Ac proprie talis Vir pauper in civitate, ut ipse scribit, fuit Ieremias, qui, quanquam ei plurimi non obtemperabant, tamen in illa tanta confusione praecipue servavit Ecclesiam.

Hoc discrimine considerato, oremus Deum assiduis gemitibus singuli, ut faciat nos vasa misericordiae, nec sinat nos fieri pestes τε ἀλάστορας generis humani, sicut clamant Prophetae in Psalmo: Respice servos tuos, et dirige opus manuum nostrarum.

Et Esaias: Tu Domine pater noster es, Nos lutum tuum, tu formas nos, Opera manuum tuarum sumus, ne irascaris valde.

Simul autem monet hoc dictum, Bona consilia a paucioribus audiri, et multitudini placere deteriora consilia.

Ideo inquit: Sapientia pauperis contemta est.

Verba sapientum audiuntur a silentibus, id est, non furentibus aliqua cupiditate, sed quaerentibus veritatem, et ea quae sunt salutaria.

Alibi vero inquit Salomon: Melius est occurrere ursae, quae amisit catulos suos, quam fatuo in stulticia sua, id est, occupato aliqua cupiditate, aut fascinato stulta persuasione adversari difficillimum est.

## 10:1 Argument
Chapter X.

Dead flies corrupt sweet ointments.

That is: Good counsels, good doctrine, arts rightly constituted are daily corrupted by busybodies who are heard more easily in courts and among the people than modest and poor men, who teach rightly, or give salutary counsel.

Folly is a little better than wisdom and glory.

It agrees with the saying: For he did not place rumors before salvation.

Fabius is thought to be a little foolish, but afterwards the event shows that his counsels were salutary, and it agrees with what follows: The hearts of the wise are in the right hand, that is, they are held more firmly, so that they do not yield to anger, grief, or ambition.

The hearts of fools are in the left, that is, they are held less firmly, they rush where anger, the desire for glory, grief, or other blind affections drive them.

And a rule is handed down concerning the property, universally joined with the false persuasion of wisdom, namely that all are arrogant, admire themselves, and despise others and judge them to be fools, just as Epicureans and hypocrites judge the Apostles to be insane.

Pompey judges the dissuaders of war to be in error.

If the impulse of a more powerful person prevails over you, do not leave your place.

For healing will make great sinners cease.

That is: Even if for a while the envious or sycophants, or glorious Thrasos prevail, yet let not the one doing right be moved to desert his station because of the perversity of judgments or grief.

A good and faithful pastor should not be moved by calumnies or the clamors of the mob, so as to desert the Church, or change himself and bend to unjust judgments.

Because in the meantime he will be able to heal many things.

Then follows a complaint, deploring this common evil, that often fools and wicked men reign, so that a flatterer playing to the affections of the Lord is more pleasing in court than a wise and faithful counselor, according to the verses: Life delights most in the wicked, And the flatterer acts best, the sycophant second.

He who digs a pit shall fall into it.

To the previous complaint respond these following sayings about punishments, which warn that the outcomes of evil counsels are sad, according to the rule often repeated: Atrocious crimes are punished by atrocious punishments in this life.

Item: With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you.

Thus he says here: He who digs a pit shall fall into it and this agrees a proverb with the usual sayings: "The evil counsel is most evil to the one who counsels." Item: "He who fashions something for another, fashions evil for his own liver."

Latin:

Caput X.

Muscae venenatae corrumpunt suavia unguenta.

Id est: Bona consilia, bona doctrina, artes recte constitutae quotidie corrumpuntur per ardeliones qui facilius audiuntur in aulis et in populo, quam homines modesti et pauperes, recte docentes, aut salutaria consulentes.

Paulisper melior est stulticia quam sapientia et gloria.

Congruit cum dicto: Non ponebat enim rumores ante salutem.

Fabius paulisper stultus esse existimatur, sed postea eventus ostendit, eius consilia fuisse salutaria, et congruit quod sequitur: Sapientum corda in dextra manu esse, id est, firmius teneri, ne obtemperent iracundiae, dolori, ambitioni.

Stultorum corda sunt in sinistra, id est, infirmius tenentur, ruunt quo ira, cupiditas gloriae, dolor aut alii coeci affectus impellunt.

Et regula traditur de proprietate, universaliter coniuncta cum falsa persuasione sapientiae, videlicet quod omnes sint arrogantes, sese admirentur, et alios despiciant ac iudicent fatuos esse, sicut Epicurei et hypocritae iudicant insanire Apostolos.

Pompeius iudicat errare dissuasores belli.

Si praevaluerit impetus potentioris super te, locum tuum ne relinquas.

Nam sanatio faciet cessare magnos peccatores.

Id est: Etiamsi aliquantisper vincunt invidi aut sycophantae, aut gloriosi Thrasones, tamen non moveatur recte faciens, ut deserat suam stationem propter perversitatem iudiciorum aut dolorem.

Bonus et fidelis pastor non moveatur calumniis aut vulgi clamoribus, ut deserat Ecclesiam, aut sese immutet et inflectat ad iniqua iudicia.

Quia interea tamen multa sanare poterit.

Sequitur deinde querela, deplorans hoc commune malum, quod saepe regnant stulti et mali, ut gratior est in aula assentator alludens ad affectus Domini, quam sapiens et fidelis consiliarius, iuxta versus: δ βίος μάλιστα τοῖς πονηροῖς ἥδεται, πράττει δὲ ἄριστα κόλαξ, ὁ συκοφάντης δεύτερος.

Qui fodit foveam, incidit in eam.

Superiori querelae respondent haec dicta sequentia de poenis, quae monent tristes esse exitus malorum consiliorum, iuxta regulam saepe repetitam: Atrocia delicta puniuntur atrocibus poenis in hac vita.

Item: Qua mensura mensi fueritis, eadem remetietur vobis.

Ita hic dicit: Qui fodit foveam incidit in eam et congruit hoc proverbium cum usitatis dictis: ἡ δὲ κακὴ βούλη τῷ βουλεύσαντι κακίστη. Item: τεύχων ὡς ἑτέρῳ τὶ, ἑῷ κακὸν ἥπατι τεύχει.

## 10:8
He who tears down a hedge, a serpent shall bite him.

This is a peculiar punishment for those who change Republics, whether by meddlesomeness (πολυπραγμοσύνῃ), or for other unapproved causes. Usually, the leaders themselves are oppressed by the petulance of those very people to whom they have given free rein, just as his own fellow soldiers killed Julius, and that very thing often happens which was pronounced about Julius: "I saved them, so that there would be those who would destroy me." A hedge signifies a moderately constituted polity. Serpents are those who abuse the liberty obtained by another's labor with license.

Latin:

Qui diruit sepem, mordebit eum coluber.

Haec peculiaris poena est eorum qui Respublicas mutant, sive πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, sive aliis causis non probandis. Plerumque petulantia illorum ipsorum, quibus laxaverunt frenos, opprimuntur et ipsi duces, sicut Iulium interficiunt sui commilitones, et saepe accidit illud ipsum, quod de Iulio pronunciatum est: Men' servasse, ut essent qui me perderent. Significat autem sepes politiam mediocriter constitutam. Colubri sunt, qui licentia abutuntur alieno labore parta libertate.

## 10:9
He who moves stones, shall be afflicted by them.

It is a common figure of speech: "To move stones" for that which is to change the laws and the form of the Republic. It agrees with the previous sentence: He who changes the form of the Republic will be exercised by great dangers, whether he changes it divinely or by human meddlesomeness (πολυπραγμοσύνῃ) or ambition, but then the outcomes are worse, as with Brutus, Cassius, and Antonius. And let the saying of Pindar always be in sight: "It is easy to move a city, but to set it back into tranquility is for God alone."

The following figure is more general: He who cuts wood, shall be wounded by them. He who shapes the various minds of the people or of students, like preachers and teachers, is usually wounded by his own listeners.

As iron that has been blunted is not sharpened again except with great labor, so wisdom is the companion of great diligence.

This is a precept about diligence in acting and in enduring many difficulties, as it is said: "Sufferings are learnings" (παθήματα μαθήματα). It censures the slothful in any vocation whatsoever, and demands vigilance, care, labor, and serious intention, as is commanded in many other sayings. Christ rebukes the slothful servant who had gained nothing with his talent: and there are many admonitions about diligence in all the scriptures, according to that:

"Life has given nothing to mortals without great labor."

Item Epicharmus: "The gods sell us all good things in exchange for labors." Hesiod: "Diligence increases work."

However, let the intention be diligent in the duties of one's vocation, and in necessary things; let there not be meddlesomeness (πολυπραγμοσύνῃ), attempting various things outside one's vocation, just as useless hunting dogs do not follow one piece of game, but are constantly turning aside to other things. And the saying of Seneca is known: "We are ignorant of necessary things, because we learn unnecessary ones."

A calumniator is like a serpent, which bites secretly.

It agrees with the superior saying: Calumny disturbs the wise man, and kills the strength of his heart. Calumny is altogether a savage plague, and it is a torch of great dissensions, from which later arise confusions of religions, wars, and devastations. Therefore, it is also commanded in Moses: "Do not be a whisperer among the people." Thus, this whole class of calumniators and detractors is censured here.

Latin:

Qui transfert lapides, affligetur ab eis.

Figura sermonis usitata est: Transferre lapides, pro eo, quod est mutare leges et formam Reipublicae. Congruit cum sententia proxima: Mutans formam Reipublicae, exercebitur magnis periculis, sive mutet divinitus, sive humana πολυπραγμοσύνῃ seu ambitione, sed tunc exitus deteriores sunt, ut Bruti, Cassii, Antonii. Et semper sit in conspectu Pindari dictum: Facile est movere civitatem, sed rursus in tranquillum sistere, solius Dei.

Figura sequens generalior est: Qui secat ligna, vulnerabitur ab eis. Qui format seudo-lat varia ingenia populi vel discipulorum, ut concionatores et doctores, plerumque vulneratur a suis auditoribus.

Sicut ferrum hebetatum non nisi magno labore rursus acuitur, ito magnae diligentiae comes est sapientia.

Praeceptum est de diligentia in agendo et in perferendis multis difficultatibus, sicut dicitur: παθήματα μαθήματα. Taxat autem ignavos in quacunque vocatione, et postulat vigilantiam, curam, laborem et seriam intentionem, sicut in multis aliis dictis praecipitur. Christus vituperat servum ignavum, qui suo talento nihil lucratus erat: et multae sunt admonitiones de diligentia in omnibus scriptis, iuxta illud:

Nil nisi magno vita labore dedit mortalibus.

Item Epicharmus: τῶν πόνων πωλοῦσιν πάντα ἡμῖν ἀγαθὰ θεοὶ. Hesiodus: μελετὴ δέ τε ἔργον ὀφέλλει.

Sit autem diligens intentio in officia vocationis, et in res necessarias, non sit πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, varia tentans extra vocationem, sicut inutiles canes venatici non sequuntur unam feram, sed subinde avertuntur ad alia. Et notum est dictum Senecae: Necessaria ignoramus, quia non necessaria discimus.

Calumniator similis est serpenti, qui clam mordet.

Congruit cum dicto superiori, Calumnia conturbat sapientem, et necat robur cordis eius. Est omnino saeva pestis calumnia, et fax est magnarum dissensionum, unde postea confusiones religionum, bella et vastitates oriuntur. Ideo et in Moyse praeceptum est: Non sis susurro in populo. Ita hic totum hoc genus calumniatorum et obtrectatorum taxatur.

## 10:12
The words of the mouth of the wise are grace.

He distinguishes wise counselors and teachers from the foolish who have a persuasion of wisdom, when nevertheless they are foolish, because they do not direct their counsels to the true norm, but to their own or others' blind affections, just as Mardonius advises Xerxes to war, or just as Pompey had instigators. He says these men are ignorant of what happened before, that is, such men do not care for the examples of those who came before, who by foolish counsels or pernicious doctrine ruined themselves and others, nor do they foresee the coming punishments.

Latin:

Verba oris sapientis gratia.

Discernit sapientes consiliarios et doctores a stulti qui habent persuasionem sapientiae, cum tamen desipiant, quia non dirigunt consilia ad veram normam, sed ad suos vel aliorum coecos adfectus, sicut Mardonius Xerxi bellum suadet, vel sicut Pompeius habuit instigatores. Hos ait ignorare, quid antea acciderit, id est, tales non curant exempla priorum, qui stultis consiliis aut perniciosa doctrina se et alios everterunt, nec prospiciunt venturas poenas.

## 10:15
The labor of the foolish afflicts them, because they do not know the way to the city.

That is: Those perversely wise men labor in vain at many things, attempt to reform many things, and bring many sad events upon themselves and others, nor do they know the feelings of men, nor do they consider the importance of affairs, nor do they see what is necessary to do. He encompasses these things when he says: "They do not know the way to the city," or to the court, just as the shepherd is described to whom a mirror had recently been given at court, in which, when he had contemplated himself, he became more insolent from the admiration of his own form, and later fell into punishments, of which Francis Petrarch says: Let that wretch groan eternally, who first gave Evil gifts to the shepherds of the court. Woe to the land whose King is a child, and whose Princes eat in the morning. The sentence is clear, and it speaks not only of those who are children in age, but also of the elderly, who have always lived in leisure and pleasures, and have not become more cautious through doctrine, nor through the experience of life and common hardships.

And where governors seek mainly the pleasures of the body, there jurisdiction, the governance of discipline, and military exercises are neglected. Such are the suitors of Penelope, born to consume the fruits. Contrary is the verse which Polybius cites from Hesiod: [blind ones rejoicing in war, or in a feast].

Latin:

Labor stultorum affligit eos, quia nesciunt viam ad urbem.

Id est: Illi perverse sapientes multa frustra moliuntur, multa conantur reformare, et sibi et aliis accersunt multos tristes casus, nec norunt hominum sensus, nec considerant momenta negociorum, nec vident quid necesse sit agere. Haec comprehendit, cum ait: Nesciunt viam ad urbem, seu ad aulam, sicut describitur pastor cui recens in aula fuerat speculum donatum, in quo, cum se contemplatus esset, admiratione formae suae factus est insolentior, et postea in poenas incidit, de quo dicit Franciscus Petrarcha: Aeternum gemat ille miser, pastoribus aulae Qui primus mala dona dedit. Vae terrae cuius Rex puer est, et cuius Principes mane comedunt. Perspicua sententia est, nec tantum loquitur de his qui aetate pueri sunt, sed etiam de senibus, qui semper in ocio et voluptatibus vixerunt, nec doctrina, nec usu vitae et communibus aerumnis facti sunt cautiores.

Et ubi gubernatores praecipue quaerunt voluptates corporis, ibi negliguntur iurisdictio, gubernatio disciplinae, exercitia militaria. Tales sunt sponsi Penelopes fruges consumere nati. Contrarius est versus quem ex Hesiodo citat Polybius: ἀλαοὶ πολέμῳ κεχαρηότες, ἠέ γε δαιτὶ.

## 11:1 Argument
Chapter XI.

Cast your bread upon the waters etc.

This whole chapter is the light of this book. For it shows that in these discourses, a confirmation of the doctrine of providence has been established, and a refutation of the arguments by which men are moved by nature to doubt providence.

Let the first sentence, therefore, which is placed here at the end, be: God will bring you into judgment for all these things. He expressly affirms that God both judges and will judge the deeds of men, and he will repeat this assertion at the end with this discourse: Fear God, and keep his commandments.

With this sentence established, that God will judge and that one must obey Him according to His commandments, now come the consolations.

When the mind doubts, what shall I do? I see many labors are vain, many are ungrateful, I see hatreds and hardships being summoned, shall I desert the society of life, and hide myself in some solitudes, and follow that old saying: [live unnoticed]? By no means.

But as he said above: You shall bravely do the labor which God has attributed to you.

So here he says: Keep His commandments, but commend the outcomes to God, and do not be broken by sorrow if adversities occur, but in these things obey God, and by faith retain the tranquility of mind, invocation, and hope. Know that you please God in that obedience, that your labors will not be entirely vain, even if sometimes fierce storms arise.

As, for Moses, many huge tumults disturb the governance.

For David, a son stirs up sedition.

Let us know that these things happen so, and let us not cast away hope, the peace of hearts, invocation, and the duties commanded to us, and let us think on the saying often repeated: Commend your way to God, and hope in Him, and He will act.

And that of Paul: Your labor will not be vain in the Lord.

And Psalm 1: His leaf will not wither.

All understand that this whole doctrine and consolation is very necessary in life, which indeed is handed down divinely, because reason is offended by this confusion, and doubts about providence and the help of God.

This is the narration of this whole chapter, nay, of the whole book.

And here he says concerning the works of governance: Cast your bread upon the waters, that is, let the teacher scatter doctrine among the people, as if he were scattering food into the water to be caught by fish, or if he were sending grain to other places.

Let the governor scatter his labors in the same way.

For even if something perishes, yet these labors will benefit others, and the utility will be seen among posterity.

The governance of Jeremiah was full of hardships, but it nevertheless profited all posterity.

While there is opportunity, perform the duties of your calling, just as Paul also commands that the time be redeemed, because the days are evil, that is, he commands to use the opportunity, because in such great miseries good counsels are often hindered.

If the clouds are full, they will pour out rain.

Afterwards, consolations and admonitions are mixed in the text. If the clouds are full, they will pour out rain, i.e., the outcomes are not in your power, but you should wisely bear those things which happen for the time.

Sometimes one thing will happen, sometimes it rains, sometimes there is serenity.

The clouds were full in the time of Moses, that is, the time had come to lead the people out of Egypt.

Again, in another way, the clouds were full in the time of Jeremiah, that is, they were heaped up with sin, which brought rain and exile to this people.

And after the outcome happens, what is done cannot be undone.

Where the tree falls, there it lies, this agrees with the old verse: [For never can that which is ordained be un-happened].

It signifies that outcomes are not in our power and are to be borne wisely: he dwells on this sentence also hereafter.

He who wants to have certain and circumscribed outcomes beforehand will do nothing.

Therefore he says: He who observes the wind, does not sow etc.

He then adds an admonition, that not all outcomes can be foreseen, just as it is said in Herodotus to be an ancient saying: [that the end of everything should not appear at the same time as the beginning].

And most wisely he proposes here the image of the fetus, just as we do not know how we are formed in the mother's womb, so the governance of many events cannot be foreseen.

And here a consolation must be added, just as in this very image we see that the fetus is a ...care to God, that the pregnant mother is preserved, that life is given to the one being born in the womb, that nourishment is created in the breasts, that the joints are wonderfully opened when the birth is brought forth: so let us know that the rest of life is also a care to God, according to those sayings: In Him we are, we live, and we move. Item: He is your life and the length of your days.

And in many great dangers He preserves the human race without secondary causes, as it is said: All the hairs of your head are numbered. In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening etc. He repeats the previous admonitions and consolations, and weaves in a discourse on death and on judgment.

Do not be broken in spirit, even if some adversities hinder you, you nevertheless perform the duties of your calling, In the morning and in the evening sow your seed, that is, redeem the time, as Paul says: Because the days are evil, that is, when there are great impediments, you should be intent on opportunities for doing good, for helping the Church, for propagating doctrine, etc.

Then a consolation is added: The light is sweet, rejoice in your youth, that is, as long as God grants it, use His gifts reverently; when He takes them away, patiently obey Him, and rest in Him, as Paul says: Let the peace of God dwell in your hearts.

Item: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, and when I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light.

Latin:

Caput XI.

Mitte panem tuum super aquas etc.

Totum hoc caput lumen est huius libri. Ostendit enim, in his concionibus institutam esse confirmationem sententiae de providentia, et refutationem argumentorum, quibus homines natura moventur, ut de providentia dubitent.

Sit igitur prima sententia, quae hic in fine ponitur: De his omnibus abducet te Deus in iudicium. Expresse affirmat, Deum et iudicare et iudicaturum esse hominum facta, et hanc asseverationem in fine repetet, cum hac concione: Deum time, et mandata eius serva.

Constituta hac sententia, quod et iudicaturus sit Deus, et quod ei iuxta mandata obediendum sit, iam accedunt consolationes.

Cum dubitat animus, quid faciam? video multos labores esse irritos, multos ingratos, video accersi odia et aerumnas, deseram ne vitae societatem, et abdam me in aliquas solitudines, ac sequar illud vetus dictum: λάθε βιώσας? Nequaquam.

Sed ut supra dixit: Fortiter facias laborem, quem Deus tibi attribuit.

Ita hic inquit: Mandata eius serva, Eventus vero commendes Deo, nec frangaris dolore, si incidant adversa, sed in his Deo obedias, et fide retineas animi tranquillitatem, invocationem et spem. Scias te placere Deo in illa obedientia, labores tuos non fore prorsus irritos, etiamsi interdum saevae tempestates orientur.

Ut, Moisi gubernationem turbant multi ingentes tumultus.

Davidi movet seditionem filius.

Haec ita fieri sciamus, et non abiiciamus spem, pacem cordium, invocationem, et officia nobis mandata, et dictum saepe repetitum cogitemus: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Et illud Pauli: Labor vester non erit inanis in Domino.

Et Psal.

1.: Folium eius non defluet. Hanc totam doctrinam et consolationem in vita valde necessariam esse omnes intelligunt, quae quidem ideo divinitus traditur, quia ratio hac confusione offenditur, et dubitat de providentia et de auxilio Dei.

Haec est enarratio huius totius capitis, imo totius libri.

Et hic de operibus gubernationis dicit: Mitte panem tuum super aquas, id est, doctor spargat doctrinam in populo, ut si spargeret escas in aquam piscibus excipiendas, vel si mitteret frumentum in alia loca.

Gubernator labores spargat eodem modo.

Etsi enim aliquid peribit, tamen aliquib. proderunt hi labores, et utilitas apud posteros conspicietur.

Fuit aerumnosa gubernatio Ieremiae, at profuit tamen universae posteritati.

Donec occasio est, facito officia vocationis, sicut et Paulus iubet tempus redimi, quia dies mali sint, id est, iubet uti occasione, quia in tantis miseriis saepe bona consilia impediuntur.

Si nubes fuerint plenae, effundent imbrem.

Postea miscentur in textu consolationes et admonitiones. Si nubes fuerint plenae, effundent imbrem, i. e. non sunt in tua potestate eventus, sed sapienter feras ea quae pro tempore fiunt.

Evenient alias alia, alias pluit, alias est serenitas.

Nubes plenae erant tempore Moisi, id est, venerat tempus educendi populum ex Aegypto.

Rursus alio modo nubes plenae erant tempore Ieremiae, id est, peccato cumulata erant quae adferebant imbrem et exilium huic populo.

Et postquam accidit eventus, factum infectum fieri non potest.

Quo cadit arbor, ibi iacet, id congruit cum veteri versu: οὐ πότε γὰρ δύναται τὸ τετυγμένον εἶναι ἄνυκτον.

Significat eventus non esse in nostra potestate et sapienter ferendos esse: in hac sententia etiam deinceps commoratur.

Qui prius vult habere certos et circumscriptos eventus, nihil aget.

Ideo dicit: Qui observat ventum, non seminat etc.

Addit deinde admonitionem, nec praesciri posse omnes eventus, sicut et apud Herodotum dicitur antiquum dictum esse: μὴ ἅμα ἀρχῇ πᾶν τέλος καταφαίνεσθαι.

Et sapientissime proponitur hic imago foetus, sicut nescimus, quomodo in alvo matris formemur, sic gubernatio multorum eventuum prospici non potest.

Et hic addenda est consolatio, sicut in hac ipsa imagine videmus Deo curae esse foetum, servari matrem gravidam, ...dari vitam nascenti in utero, creari alimentum in uberibus, mirabiliter aperiri iuncturas cum partus editur: ita sciamus et reliquam vitam Deo curae esse, iuxta illa dicta: In ipso sumus, vivimus et movemur. Item: Ipse est vita tua et longitudo dierum tuorum.

Et in multis magnis periculis servat genus humanum sine causis secundis, sicut dicitur: Omnes capilli capitis vestri numerati sunt. Mane seminato semen tuum et vespere etc. Repetit priores admonitiones et consolationes, et intexit concionem de morte et de iudicio.

Non frangaris animo, etiam si quae adversationes impediunt, tu tamen facito officia vocationis, Mane et vespere seminato semen tuum, id est, redimito tempus, ut Paulus inquit: Quia dies mali sunt, id est, cum sint magna impedimenta, vos sitis intenti in occasiones bene merendi, iuvandae Ecclesiae, propagandae doctrinae etc.

Deinde consolatio additur: Dulce est lumen, laetare in adolescentia tua, id est, donec Deus concedit, reverenter utaris ipsius donis, cum aufert, patienter ei obedias, et in ipso acquiescito, sicut Paulus inquit: Pax Dei habitet in cordibus vestris.

Item: Iram Domini portabo, et cum sedebo in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est.

## 12:1 Argument
Chapter XII.

Remember your creator. In prosperous and adverse things remember your creator, obey Him, and rest in Him, and by faith according to His promises, which He delivered in immense goodness on account of the Mediator of the Church, know that He most truly hears those who call upon Him, and those who wish to obey Him, and that He horribly punishes the contumacious.

Therefore He repeats the reminder about judgment, and adds mention of old age and death, so that by this argument He may confirm the assertion about providence, and exhort us to the fear of God, to faith, and to obedience.

Do not securely despise God, because diseases and death show our weakness.

Even if you are drunk with the indulgence of fortune, and have great hopes, yet the hour of death will suddenly shake off these dreams.

And if you have despised God in judgment, you will rush into eternal wrath, and into eternal punishments.

He proposes this reminder about death and judgment, so that He may draw us back from carnal security, and from doubts to the consideration of providence, to the fear of God, to faith, and to obedience.

Moreover, the description of old age is figurative, which appears to have been taken from nature itself and from physical signs.

But not all metaphors are clearly understood. Before the Sun and the Moon and the stars are darkened. That is, for the old, the view of the whole of nature is duller and sadder. And the clouds return after the rain. That is, new miseries, new calamities come one after another; when one evil has passed, another comes.

As it is said in the Homeric lament: ὡς μοὶ δέχεται κακὸν ἐκ κακοῦ αἰεί (as evil ever awaits me from evil).

Item: φόβου τὸ γῆρας, οὐ γὰρ ἔρχεται μόνον (fear old age, for it does not come alone).

Fear old age, for it does not come alone. The keepers of the house tremble. That is, the hands: because the nerves, tendons, and ligaments become weaker or flaccid. The strong men totter. That is, the legs and shins. The grinders shall be idle and fewer. That is, the teeth will be weaker and will fall out. Those looking through the holes shall be darkened. That is, the eyes will be duller. The doors shall be shut. That is, the lips will dry up and become flaccid. They shall rise at the voice of a bird. That is, sleep will be shorter, and old men are easily awakened by the crowing of a cock. The daughters of song shall be brought low. That is, either the ears become deaf, or the organs of the voice are wrinkled.

Because in the old, both the spirits of the heart are diminished, and the lungs and trachea become weaker either from cold humidity or from dryness. They shall be afraid of high places on the way. That is, the head will be tremulous with vertigo.

The almond tree shall flourish. That is, grayness will happen, as in almond trees.

The locusts are burdened. That is, the shoulder blades and hips are bent, that is, old men walk stooped. And the figure of the protruding shoulder blades, and the hips and the spine of the back, is similar to a locust.

And desire shall fail. That is, there is loathing and nausea for food, drink, and other pleasures: because vigor is weakened, poor digestion occurs, little good blood and spirits, meager nourishment, etc.

Afterwards he speaks of the internal parts.

Latin:

Caput XII.

Memento creatoris tui. In rebus secundis et adversis memento creatoris tui, obtemperes ei, et in eo acquiescito, et fide iuxta ipsius promissiones, quas immensa bonitate propter Mediatorem Ecclesiae tradidit, scias verissime exaudire eum invocantes, et volentes ei obedire, et horribiliter punire contumaces.

Ideo repetit commonefactionem de iudicio, et addit mentionem senectae et mortis, ut hoc argumento confirmet adseverationem de providentia, et hortetur nos ad timorem Dei, ad fidem et ad obedientiam.

Ne securus contemnas Deum, quia morbi et mors ostendunt nostram imbecillitatem.

Etiam si ebrius indulgentia fortunae, et magnas spes habes, tamen haec somnia subito excutiet hora mortis.

Et si contemsisti Deum in iudicio, rues in aeternam iram, et in aeternas poenas.

Hanc commonefactionem de morte et de iudicio proponit, ut nos retrahat a carnali securitate, et a dubitationibus ad considerationem providentiae, ad timorem Dei, ad fidem et ad obedientiam.

Est autem descriptio senectae figurata, quam apparet ex natura ipsa et physicis signis sumtam esse.

Sed non omnes metaphora plane intelliguntur. Antequam Sol et Luna et stellae obscurabuntur. Id est, senibus aspectus totius naturae hebetior et tristior est. Et redit nubes post pluviam. Id est, subinde novae miseriae, novae calamitates veniunt, cum praeteriit aliquod malum, venit aliud.

Sicut in querela Homerica dicitur: ὡς μοὶ δέχεται κακὸν ἐκ κακοῦ αἰεί.

Item: φόβου τὸ γῆρας, οὐ γὰρ ἔρχεται μόνον.

Time senectam, non enim venit sola. Tremunt custodes domus. Id est, manus: quia nervi, tendines et ligamenta fiunt languidiora seu flaccida. Nutant viri fortes. Id est, Crura et tibiae. Ociosae erunt molentes et pauciores. Id est, Dentes erunt imbecilliores et excident. Caligabunt videntes per foramina. Id est, Oculi erunt hebetiores. Claudentur ostia. Id est, Labra arefient et erunt flaccida. Surgent ad vocem volucris. Id est, Somnus erit brevior, et facile cantu galli excitantur senes. Inclinatae sunt filiae carminis. Id est, vel aures fiunt surdae, vel vocis organa corrugantur.

Quia in senibus et minus et spirituum cordis, et pulmo et trachea vel frigida humiditate, vel siccitate fiunt debiliores. Excelsa formidabunt in via. Id est, Caput erit tremulum vertigine.

Florebit amygdalus. Id est, accidet canicies, ut in amygdalis.

Onerantur locustae. Id est, incurvantur scapulae et coxae, id est, senes incedunt curvi. Et figura extantium scapularum, et coxae et spinae dorsi incurvae similes est locustae.

Et perit voluptas. Id est, fastidia sunt et nauseae cibi, potus et aliarum voluptatum: quia virtus est languefacta, fit mala coctio, parum boni sanguinis et spirituum, exigua nutritio etc.

Postea de interioribus loquitur.

## 12:6
Before the silver cord be loosed.

I understand the nerves and tendons, the ligaments: for nerves are similar to white threads. And since they are the instruments of sense and motion, they have the primary power in the human body.

And the golden bowl run down.

That is, the heart, which is the fountain and source of all virtues and of vital heat.

Latin:

Antequam rumpatur funiculus argenteus.

Intelligo nervos et τένοντας, ligamenta: sunt enim nervi similes albis filis. Et cum sint instrumenta sensus et motus, praecipuam vim habent in corpore humano.

Et decurrat fons aureus.

Id est, cor, quod est fons et scaturigo omnium virtutum, et vivifici caloris.

## 12:6
The pitcher shall be broken at the fountain.

That is, the vein above the liver.

For since he named two fountains or two sources, it seemed fitting that the golden bowl be understood as the heart. Because the likeness of gold corresponds more to the heart and to the spirits. Afterwards, let the pitcher be the vein, which draws blood from the liver and pours it into the whole body, and is most truly the nurse and canal of the whole body. And it is consistent that Solomon did not omit here the mechanism of the veins, which brings primary utility in nourishment, and is distributed throughout the whole body with wonderful art and providence, so that nourishment may be carried to all parts.

I clearly understand the cistern as the stomach.

Because the word signifies a deep cavity, and the circles above the stomach signify the neighboring parts, namely the intestines, which are placed like circles or orbs, and the mesentery almost makes the appearance of a wheel, to which the intestines are attached.

He inserted this mention of old age and death so that he might remind readers of the future judgment, just as he soon repeats this sentiment: God shall bring all things into judgment, and he wishes that by the thought of judgment faith in providence be confirmed, and the fear of God, invocation, and the care of doing right be excited.

Because the fear of eternal wrath and rejection and of horrible torture that will last for all eternity is no sluggish monitor to a mind that is not profane, and he refers this whole sermon to this sum.

Latin:

Conteretur hydria super fontem.

Id est, vena super epar.

Cum enim duos fontes seu duas scaturigines nominaverit, visum est concinne fontem aureum intelligi cor. Quia auri similitudo magis congruit ad cor, et ad spiritus. Postea hydria sit causa vena, quae sanguinem haurit ex epate, et in totum corpus effundit, et verissime est nutrix et canalis totius corporis. Et consentaneum est, Salomonem hic non omisisse opificium venarum, quod in nutricatione praecipuam affert utilitatem, et miranda arte et providentia in totum corpus distributum est, ut omnibus partibus advehatur nutrimentum.

Cisternam plane intelligo ventriculum.

Quia vocabulum significat profundam cavitatem, et gyri super ventriculum significant vicinas partes, scilicet intestina, quae collocatae sunt tanquam gyri seu orbes, et μεσεντέριον pene speciem rotae efficit, cui implicita sunt intestina.

Hanc mentionem senectae et mortis inseruit, ut lectores de futuro iudicio commonefaciat, sicut mox repetit hanc sententiam: Cuncta adducet Deus in iudicium, vultque cogitatione iudicii confirmari fidem de providentia, et excitari timorem Dei, invocationem et curam recte faciendi.

Quia metus aeternae irae et abiectionis et horrendi cruciatus in tota aeternitate duraturi, non est segnis monitor menti non prophanae, et hanc summam refert totam concionem.

## 12:13
Fear God, and keep his commandments, this is the primary thing for all men.
