He embraces, however, the whole worship and the whole obedience, and leads us to this true God, who revealed himself in this people of Israel, and delivered to them promises and the law, with illustrious and unfailing testimonies; he wants this God to be acknowledged, heard, invoked, and worshipped according to this very voice which he delivered, and he proposes the highest norm, which ought to be the ruler of all deliberations and actions: Look to God and his doctrine, and do not depart from this norm, and know that he who departs will without any doubt fall into darkness, the snares of the devil, and most sad punishments; refer all counsels and all actions to this end, that you may render obedience to God and celebrate him.

You should also hold this rule in judging all doctrines; consider which disputes, which doctrines, which discourses dissent from the word of God, or do not profit for nourishing the fear of God in minds, and for confirming faith; and there are always, have been, and will be many Epicurean and many idle opinions, and many cults of idols. All these things must be judged and avoided with the highest vigilance.

He refers the sermons in this book to this sum, which indeed is also the sum of the universal doctrine in the Church, according to those sayings: Blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it. Likewise, the whole Psalm: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Likewise: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our abode with him. Solomon refers his own sermons to this same sum.

I shall therefore do as Solomon did, and I will recite the argument and sum of this book again at the end.

Solomon wishes in this book principally to propose an assertion concerning providence. Then, however, to refute the objections which are opposed against providence. For since there are many and great confusions in life, and the multitude of the impious is great, and few are those who rightly acknowledge and fear God, and the impious flourish in glory and riches, while the pious are miserable, and many are killed by the worst, and the faithful governance profits little, all things seem to be carried by chance.

To this objection Solomon responds: Although such confusion is great in large part, nevertheless you should be ruled by the word of God, and retain the opinion concerning providence with firm faith, and do not because of these scandals fall away from God, nor cast away the fear of God, and the confidence resting in God, nor desert your calling, and to those confusions oppose these two ordered things. The judgment will come, in which God will take away this confusion, and all the impious will be cast into eternal punishments, and it will be well for the just. Now also in this life God moderates confusions, punishes atrocious crimes, and does not allow governance to be altogether vain; He gathers for Himself an eternal Church, and preserves some polities and economies. Indeed, this very thing is a testimony of the presence of God, that, although there is such great weakness of the nature of men, such great and savage furies of many, we see nevertheless that the Church of God is miraculously preserved, and some of its shelters.

The objection therefore concerning confusions is a fallacy from a statement in a certain respect to a statement simply: Many things are done inordinately in this life, Therefore all things and always are inordinate. The consequence must be denied. For this confusion will be altogether taken away at length, and in this life many things are done orderly.

The whole machine of the world is most beautifully ordered: the figure and position of the heaven, of the air, of the water and the earth, the motion of the stars, the changes of the seasons, the fertilization of the earth, and the nourishment of the human body, the preservation of species, generation, regular notions in the mind, the preservation of society, the punishments of atrocious crimes. These ordered and regular things must be opposed to the confusions.

But much more the divine revelation itself, which is the published word, the Law, the threats, the Gospel and the promises, must be opposed to all spectacles that run into the eyes, and faith must be firmly retained, and in faith one must serve one's calling. Do rightly, because there will be an eternal distinction in the coming judgment, even if punishments are digested for a little while.

Perform the duties of your calling, even if many labors will be vain and ungrateful, yet at some time you will profit; God will be present to the one laboring and calling upon Him. With this faith scatter doctrine and labors, as bread upon the waters. With this faith and hope soothe your pain.

Thus He prohibits despair and confidence in ourselves, and teaches that one must rest in faith in God. Nor will you be able in life to heal pains otherwise, even if you attempt contrary things, or desert the society of life. Miseries are not avoided by human counsel, but only when hearts rest in faith in God.

To this summary, the recitations concerning various businesses and events placed above are to be accommodated, and from time to time responses are added, in which he opposes the word of God, and ordered events, the punishments of atrocious crimes, which are testimonies of the coming judgment, and the very mention of judgment so often repeated. It is profitable, however, in any matter to consider what is the counsel, what is the will of the writer, and to what end the speech is instituted. Let us know, therefore, that this book is principally a doctrine concerning providence.

Then a consolation against the various confusions of life, so that we do not because of them doubt concerning providence, nor cast away the care of doing rightly, and the common labors of life, nor desert our calling. And the places of consolation are drawn from the necessary, from the possible, and from the useful, from rewards and punishments.

From the Necessary, because it is necessary to obey God. And this assertion must be most firmly retained: that the human race was created by God. And although many sad confusions have approached, nevertheless we are preserved by Him, and labors are ordered by Him; let us most firmly maintain that He is the inspector, judge, and helper.

Therefore He often repeats these sayings: Fear God, because God will bring all things into judgment, good and evil, even the hidden things. Arguments are from the Possible: Although there are great confusions, and in many things governance is useless, as he says: That which is crooked cannot be made straight, and often even the just fall: nevertheless God will not allow the labors of the calling to be altogether vain; He will be present to the one calling upon Him, as it is said here: Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it.

In the morning and in the evening sow, etc. Finally, this consolation is often repeated, both here and elsewhere.

As in Paul: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord. And in Psalm 1: His leaf will not fall.

And to the place from the possible pertain the remedies of pains. Rages ignite, and pain burns in the hard bones of Pericles, and similar ones, because counsels most beautifully thought out concerning the defense of the fatherland do not proceed.

But Jeremiah rests in God, even when things are adverse; Jeremiah has these remedies. that he knows that God must be obeyed, and that God will miraculously preserve the Church, as it is said in Isaiah: I will carry you, even in old age.

Item: And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

The third place is from the Useful, from rewards and punishments, that the punishments of atrocious crimes are discerned even in this life, and yet after this life the Church will be adorned with eternal goods, and the impious will be cast into eternal torments.

This, therefore, is the third place in this book, namely the warning, which denounces punishments to all who sin, not only outside the Church, but also in the Church, as he says: I know that it will be well with those who fear God, and it will not be well with the impious.

It is certain that these are the principal places of this book.

Afterwards, many sayings about common events and about many virtues are mixed in.

But the entire doctrine is referred to this chapter: Fear God, and keep his commandments, where he embraces the whole of worship, fear, faith, and good works.

And thus the admonitions of this book will be profitable, when the doctrine of faith is added, concerning the true God, concerning conversion or repentance, concerning the recognition of the Son of God, concerning the righteousness of faith, and concerning new obedience.

For he preaches to the hearers in the true Church, to whom God has revealed himself and delivered promises.

And thus the works of one's calling are pleasing to God, and these labors of life become the worship of God, when faith shines forth, by which we are accounted righteous before God on account of the Son, the redeemer, and by this very faith, governance and help are sought from God, just as the Lord says: Without me you can do nothing.

Item: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

And when faith governs labors, it simultaneously refers them to the glory of God.

For the worship of God is a work commanded by God, done in reliance on the Son of God, the principal end of which is that this obedience may offer honor to God, and show that we invoke this true God, who revealed himself in the Church.

This faith also brings peace to the heart, because it subjects us to God, and establishes that God is present as a helper and deliverer, of which Paul says: The peace of God, which surpasses all the counsels of the human mind, guard your hearts.

But since various sentences are scattered throughout these discourses, prudence should be used in judging the distinction between them.

And in general, in all writings that contain sentences, it is necessary to distinguish the genres.

In the sacred books, some sayings are Legal, others Evangelical, others Dogmatic, others Consolatory, others simply Narratives about events, whether good or bad.

It is Legal, as the commandment about one's calling, often repeated in this book: Diligently perform the labors which God has given you.

And to the commandments are added warnings, as here: It will not be well with the impious.

They are Evangelical, such as: He who believes in the Son has eternal life.

And to this are referred other sayings about faith, about invocation, and about consolations, which are scattered here and there in divine discourses, such as: Ask and you shall receive.

How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

And in this book: He who sees good from his labor, it is a gift of God.

For although he speaks more obscurely about faith, yet he signifies that help must be sought and expected, just as the Psalm says: Commit your way to God, and hope in him, and he will act.

It also agrees with this saying: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord.

Others are Dogmatic, such as those concerning the essence of God, concerning providence, concerning the will of God, concerning judgment.

Such as: You shall know no other God besides me, nor is there any other God.

Item in this book: God will judge the manifest and the hidden.

Consolatory [sayings] are referred to the Evangelical, such as: God is near to those who are troubled in heart.

Item: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you.

Narratives about events are, as there are many in this book: The learned man dies like the unlearned.

Crooked things cannot be made straight.

There is no righteous man on earth who, when he does right, does not also sin.

And sayings that contain decisions and promises must be prudently distinguished from narratives, such as: Fortune makes a fool of him whom it favors too much.

Or: Minds often grow wanton in prosperous circumstances.

And in this book: I saw iniquity in the place of justice.

Such narratives do not approve of evils, but show that we, being warned, should consider them and be intent on avoiding them, just as a physician reviews and describes diseases.

I have said this concerning the genres of sentences in the prophetic and apostolic books.

Now let philosophical sentences also be considered.

In these, there are no Evangelical or Dogmatic [sentences].

But they are either Legal, or Narratives about events, such as: Do not trust the crowd, the crowd is fickle [lit. 'of many turns'].

Let the distinction between sentences, such as those of Hesiod, Phocylides, Theognis, and those which are contained in the sacred books, be in view. And often, profane narratives are to be understood in one way, and narratives in the sacred books in another. For example, one thing is said in this verse: Fortune rules life, not wisdom. Another thing in the saying of Solomon: The race is not to the swift, nor bread to the wise, etc. Because Solomon commands that we do things regularly, in accordance with divine mandates, and forbids human curiosity, which moves trust in oneself to things outside one's calling. He also forbids trust in ourselves in the works of our calling, and wants the help of God to be sought, and for us to obey God, whether events respond or do not respond. Solomon therefore confirms the opinion concerning providence. But in that profane saying: Fortune rules life, not wisdom, something else is said.

There exists a saying in the life of Pomponius Atticus: Each man's own character makes his fortune. This saying seems to differ from another rule: Many are the tribulations of the righteous. But this is the reconciliation. The one is a political rule, consistent with these sayings: Atrocious crimes are punished by atrocious punishments in this life. Item: He who takes up the sword, shall perish by the sword. On the other hand, the course of life is more peaceful for men who live modestly. But in the Church there is an exception, where although God spares many who are weak, yet He exercises some harshly. And the causes are rightly noted in the institutions, why the Church is more oppressed than other men. For it behooves us to become similar to the image of the Son of God.

The prophetic sentence says: Cursed is he who trusts in man. That agrees with the saying: That Epicharmian [saying] is the nerve and sinew of wisdom: Μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν (Remember to be skeptical). So also Plato warns, that our hope should not depend on fortune, or on the associations of men: but he says nothing about trust in God.

Cicero renders the words of Plato, placed in his epitaph, in this way: For to the man for whom all things that lead to living happily are suited from within himself, and not dependent on others or on good luck, or the contrary, for him the method of living best has been prepared. He rightly warns that hopes should not depend on fortune, or on the associations of men. But that he leads us to our own virtues is not enough. For it was necessary that we be led to God, because many things happen to a man where human virtue succumbs without the help of God. Here, even when all human counsels desert us, God wants Himself to be acknowledged and invoked, and He promises help. And the thing itself shows that for those who invoke Him, calamities are mitigated, just as it was said: The Lord is near to those who are of a broken heart. Item: Turn to me, and I will turn to you. Item: If your sins are as scarlet, they shall be white as snow, etc.

This Ennian [saying] also seems to conflict: Fortune is given to brave men. And this of Solomon: The race is not to the swift. But the true reconciliation is this. The one censures the slothful. The other condemns trust in our own virtue, and the neglect of God, and yet it is true that David, when he conquers Goliath, is not idle, not slothful, not incautious.

In this way, it must be prudently considered in sayings, to which genera they should be referred. And because sentences are for the most part common rules of life, it is profitable to have many notes familiarly, and because they are monitors in life, and because they beget arguments or confirmations and refutations in all causes, and add gravity to speech, when they are woven in appropriately and modestly.

Discriminations of persons and hyperboles must also be considered. Nero says: The sword protects the prince. Seneca replies: Better is Faith. Item, that Greek [saying]: Πάντα ἀνθρώπων μανιώδη εἶναι (All things of men are full of madness). This hyperbole should by no means be transferred to those things which are ordained divinely, to the voice of the Gospel, to the confession of the saints, to the legitimate duties of government, [and] to the institutions of education. Such also is this hyperbole: No faith and piety [exists] in men who follow the camps. Item: The Fates rule men, all things stand by a certain law. It is necessary that these sayings be corrected by an erudite and true interpretation.

ARGUMENT ON ECCLESIASTES, REPEATED IN THE YEAR 1554.

It is necessary to consider the counsels of those writing, or their intention, in reading; that is, one must think about what the writer wanted to do, whether he is handing down a doctrine concerning some Proposition, or whether he is commanding that something be done, or whether a Consolation is being instituted, and in sum, the end of the writing must be looked to, as to what the writer wishes to take away or make the reader do.

Therefore, in rhetorical books, the genera are also distinguished, the didascalic and the deliberative. torical books, the kinds are distinguished: the didascalic and the deliberative. This distribution is a reminder to consider the counsel or intention of the writer, or the end of the oration.

First, therefore, concerning the book of Solomon, whose title is: Ecclesiastes, I say this: that its principal part is doctrine, namely, the assertion concerning providence, that is, concerning this article of faith, that God is truly the judge of things done rightly and otherwise, and that He wills us to do what is right, and for those doing what is right according to His word and calling to commend the outcomes to Him, even if many great labors seem to be in vain, as the labors of Jeremiah, which, although they do not prevent the destruction of the fatherland, are nevertheless salutary. Again, He also commands us to firmly establish that God will punish those who do not act rightly, even if punishments are sometimes delayed. This assertion concerning providence is the principal part of the book.

But because the assent concerning providence is disturbed by the horrible confusions of human life, namely, that many labors, and most of them undertaken with a great appearance of wisdom, but without a mandate, and some even undertaken according to mandates and calling, seem to be in vain. Likewise, the Church is subject to the cross, and the just are afflicted, while the unjust reign, holding empires and wealth, like the Turks and others. Solomon recounts these arguments that disturb the assent concerning providence, and opposes an assertion which has the testimony of the word of God, which Solomon wills to be preferred to all spectacles that fall before the eyes.

This foundation of doctrine having been laid, he adds then a rule of life: Obey the word of God, according to your calling, and do not depart from it because of the specious counsels of reason, or because of favorable or adverse things. But commend the outcomes to God. As the Israelites depart from the word and calling because of specious counsel when they seek a king, and wish to constitute a new form in this divinely constituted polity by their own wisdom. Jeroboam departs from the word of God, constituting a new cult, because he did not want to appear not to be equal to the king of Judah, etc. Much more do Marius, Catilina, and Antonius depart from their calling, who, having stirred up seditions, attempt to constitute kingdoms. Those broken by affairs against the pontiffs depart from the word of God, such as Menelaus, Alcimus, and others in the times of the Maccabees, and now many are moved by the power and glory of the Turkish kingdom and the pontifical, so that they fall away from the true God. Therefore, the rule often repeated here must be held: Obey the word of God, and commend the outcomes to Him, because God is certainly going to judge.

This rule is also often repeated elsewhere, as in Psalm 37: Commend your way to God, and hope in Him, and He Himself will act. With this rule established, consolations follow thereafter. Even if there are great confusions of the human race.

The multitude of the impious is greatest, and the unjust hold empires, the just are oppressed, and most counsels of men without God are useless. Indeed, even the labors of the pious in such great contumacy of the impious multitude and the fleetingness of life seem to be in vain, and for a while well-constituted Churches and cities are quickly disturbed, yet do not depart from the rule: Obey God, and rejoice in Him, and do not cast away the labors and the order instituted by God because of the mandate. These consolations are often repeated, but they are built upon the assertion concerning providence and the coming judgment, as chapter 3 says: God will judge the just and the impious.

And the last chapter: God will bring all things that are done into judgment. And chapter 11: For all these things God will bring you into judgment. To this foundation is added the precept of the last chapter: Fear God, and observe His mandates, let every man do this.

And concerning mandated labors, he says in chapter 9: Whatever your hand can do, do it with all your strength. Likewise chapter 11: Cast your bread upon the passing waters, yet you will find it. Just as Paul says: Your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Consolations are also added so that we may acquiesce and rejoice in God, when indeed many adverse things hinder necessary and useful labors.

Chapter 9: Go and eat your bread in gladness, because your works are pleasing to God. Let these rules of life and consolations always be in sight, and let not the assent concerning providence be disturbed by various spectacles, which do not accord with the order, as when the just are oppressed, the impious flourish, etc., nor let mandated labors be cast away because many impediments occur.

Therefore, this writing is principally dogmatic or didascalic, namely, an assertion concerning providence confirming the pious against Epicurean and Academic opinions. Then are added precepts or rules of life and consolations; this itself is the sum of this writing.

The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king of Jerusalem. In the title, he names himself both Solomon and King and Ecclesiastes, that is, the Preacher, by which appellation he signifies that it pertains to the office of princes to ensure that the Churches are rightly taught, just as it is said in the Psalm: And now, O ye kings, understand. Item: Open your gates, O ye princes. Item: in gathering the peoples and kings together, that they may serve the Lord. It was necessary for both princes and peoples to often ponder this sweet verse, because it is commanded to both that they should gather, that is, that they should protect the common congregation and the ministry of the divine voice, and learn true doctrine, and with true consent call upon God, and strive to preserve the doctrine. Of this pious consent, kings ought to be the leaders and authors. Therefore, here too Solomon names himself the Preacher, signifying that he wishes to be the author of pious consent in the Church, and the guardian of true doctrine.

Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, what hath a man more of all his labour which he laboureth under the Sun.

At the beginning, he poses an objection against the assertion concerning providence, as if he were saying: what providence can there be, when the labors of men are equally either vain or unhappy for both the good and the bad. For Solomon is not speaking of the things themselves created by God and remaining in their order, when he says: All is vanity. But he speaks of human labors, namely counsels, affections, and strivings; therefore he says more expressly: What does a man gain by his labor? Item: Wherefore does he labor under the Sun? By no means, therefore, does he include in the appellation of vanity God, the word of God, and the ministries insofar as they are governed by the word of God, nor the creatures themselves created by God. For the sentiment stated in Genesis must be retained: God saw all that He had made, and they were very good.

But in this place, Solomon speaks of labors under the Sun, that is, in this miserable life of men, in which men either err in their counsels and affections, and strive for many things in vain, and accumulate miseries, just as it is said in the fable about the Ass, about whom there are verses: Be an ass, whatever harsh fate has made you an ass: He who knows how to bear his lot calmly, he is wise: Or human counsels and human affections are uselessly mixed with good things and divine ministries.

As good things are seeking a living, governing economies, polities, Churches, yet how many useless cares and evil affections do men mix in. Saul tries to pass the kingdom to his descendants. David hopes that he will pass the kingdom to Absalom. These thoughts fall out far otherwise. Much more are the hopes and counsels of the impious deceived, however specious they may be, as Pompey, Cato, Marcellus, who hope for victory in a cause (as they think) just, just as they say: The cause bids the gods above to hope for better success. Brutus and Cassius think that, with Caesar killed, they will restore the old form of the Republic. Antony thinks that, with Augustus oppressed, he will be the monarch.

Finally, concerning the vain strivings of men, the sayings are most often cited: Vain men think vain things through their desires.

Item: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, that is, by human counsels and strengths alone, no calling is happy. Item: Unless the Lord build the house, he labors in vain who builds it. Item: No man is wise in all things. Item: Alas, how much blind night do hearts possess. And further on in this book: The number of fools is infinite. From this, therefore, they argue: since there are such great confusions, the impious dominate, the pious are oppressed, just counsels are hindered, what providence can there be?

I will answer this objection later.

Nay, he says: Judgment follows, even if now there seems to be a confusion of order; therefore, obey the commands of God, and know that not all labors in divine ministries will be in vain. Just as Paul also says: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord.

The Sun ariseth and goeth down, and returneth to his place.

He began earlier with a complaint about human affairs, or an objection against the assertion concerning providence, that human labors are equally vain, for both the good and the bad; life itself is uncertain and fleeting; Alexander, Julius, are oppressed in the course of the greatest things; empires, even if best constituted, are not durable. After Cyrus, the tyranny of Cambyses soon followed, the defection of Babylon, and after Darius, all of Asia was afflicted by the war of Xerxes.

Finally, the complaints are often repeated: Great things fall in a moment. Item: And it is denied to the highest To stand long, and heavy falls under too great a weight.

Because of this instability of human affairs, and various confusions, he said at the beginning that business under the Sun is vanity, that is, both fleeting and full of confusion. Now he adds a comparison taken from the motions of the Sun and the waters, the application of which should be prudently considered: for it is proposed only as an image of the instability and revolution of similar miseries in human affairs, and it signifies that these miseries can be hindered neither by counsel nor by human wisdom, as when there had been great tumults and frequent seditions in the Roman Republic under the Consuls and Tribunes, afterwards a monarchy was sought, and yet similar miseries returned. So in Israel, when great calamities had occurred under the Aristocracy before the kingdom, the people wanted a certain king to be established, and hoped that with the form of the Republic changed, the state would be happier. But some time later, sadder lacerations followed.

Therefore, the simplest application of this comparison is: Just as the Sun and water have constant circumgyrations and revolve, so human affairs, together with the miseries that are mixed in, revolve, and troubles cannot be hindered in general by human counsel or wisdom.

In private and public business, other counsels are tried from time to time to bring about a better state, and yet similar miseries return. To this sentiment he says there is nothing new under the Sun, that is, similar desires, similar counsels, similar events, causes of wars, wars, and calamitous outcomes return, just as Thucydides says: As long as the nature of men is such, similar things will happen, sometimes less, sometimes more atrociously.

He says, therefore: All things are difficult, that is, many things happen whose causes cannot be foreseen. Why is Pompey defeated, in a cause that seems better? Item: Government is most difficult, when the great multitude does not want to be amended, therefore he says: The perverse cannot be corrected by laws, vigilance, and the severity of governors.

This whole speech and complaint is about human miseries, and an objection against providence, but afterwards he will provide a refutation and consolation.

This is the common refutation, that a judgment will follow, and the consolation, that individuals ought to obey divine commands according to their vocation, and that those labors will not be entirely in vain, even if many adverse things happen, that this rule must be held: Commit your way to God, and hope in him, and he himself will act.

Incidentally, let students observe here the testimonies which affirm that the earth stands still and the Sun is moved: for it is profitable to have even divine testimonies against the absurd opinions of those who, playing around, undermine the common doctrine of physicists. I omit other physical disputes here.

I, the Preacher, was King, and I thought to seek wisely concerning all things that are done under the Sun.

It is fitting to speak at the beginning about consideration. For because we see dissimilar events, we are moved to inquire about providence, and Solomon is not speaking about physical consideration, which shows illustrious testimonies of divine providence, and as it were the footprints of God in the whole nature of things, because it is impossible for the most beautiful order to exist and remain by chance, in the position, adornment, and motion of the bodies of the world, and in natural notices, and the conservation of species, and distribution for diverse uses. Paul preaches about these testimonies, Rom.

2 and Acts 1 and 17. But Solomon speaks about the consideration of counsels, actions, and events in political and economic government: therefore he expressly says that he had considered those things which are done under the Sun, the actions and events of human counsels, as Pericles, Demosthenes, Cicero are wise governors, and yet the specious counsels of these have grim outcomes, because he said before: All things are difficult, nor can man explain them in speech, that is, all deliberations are difficult, because for the most part dangers occur on both sides.

Nor does human wisdom foresee everything. And afterwards it is said, wisdom often fails, when he says, the number of fools is not [to be counted], or errors are innumerable.

But Solomon calls this very wisdom or deliberations a bad affliction, and says it was given to men by God. These things seem absurd, but first let the vocation or divine order be distinguished from human infirmity or darkness and doubts.

The order is that marriage, judgments, magistracies, which things are good in their own kind, insofar as they are ordained by God, and the order is not disturbed by the vices and furies of men, but the wisdom of God is the ruler. In Pericles there is a bad affliction, that is, torment, which is the evil of punishment, as we commonly speak.

But torment is twofold, because doubt and error torment men, as doubt first torments Pompey, then error, when he saw the calamitous outcome. Often even wise governors err, often they sin through ambition, as Perdiccas after Alexander, often through a false appearance of justice, as Brutus, often through πολυπραγμοσύνῃ [meddlesomeness] and restlessness of spirit, as Pericles, often through anger, as Marius: furthermore, often events do not respond to good counsels, as when the Israelites fought against the tribe of Benjamin: finally, all heads of families, all governors, experience that government is full not only of cares, but also of impediments, errors, and sad events, all of which greatly torment the soul.

Solomon embraces all these miseries at once when he says that this guiding wisdom is a grievous affliction.

Hence the poetic myths about Prometheus, who is said to be fixed to the Caucasus. And about Sisyphus rolling the stone, and the like. Demosthenes says that if life were to be unraveled, he would rather go to a certain death than to the highest honors in the Republic. And Aeschines says that he rejoices to have been freed from the government of the Republic, as if he had been freed from a rabid dog.

But why does he say that this affliction was given to man by God, so that government is full of miseries and errors?

I answer: It is generally true that God wills punishment, either for the sake of conversion, or for ultimate destruction, but it does not follow from this that God is the cause of sins, or that He wills or aids sins, which are the means to punishment or ultimate destruction.

God preserves His order among the errors of governors, as He preserves the polity of Israel, even if Saul, Absalom, and the like disturb the order for a while. But government becomes more miserable for David, because either others disturb him, or even he himself, by his own fall, is the cause of impediments. But because God wills that men be punished, either for the sake of conversion or because of ultimate destruction, He does not prohibit the means which arise from human weakness and the furies of devils, which do not arise from God: and a governor who experiences impediments suffers more than a private man, just as David suffers more than a private man.

When they enter, as is said in Solon's verse: Into the chambers, public disasters, yours.

But yet, supreme governors usually sustain more danger and misery, as it is said: βίος ἰδιώτων ἄριστος, the life of private men is best.

Item: λάθε βιώσας, remain in private life. Item: More often the huge pine is shaken by the winds, And tall towers fall with a heavier crash, And lightning strikes the highest mountains. Item, ὄγκου δὲ μεγάλου πτῶμα γίγνεται μέγα. The fall of great pride becomes great. Item: Irus is suddenly what Croesus was just now. And in Euripides, Oedipus says: I who surpassed kings in wisdom, now go out from my country like a shadow.

Solomon says, therefore, that in great wisdom there is great indignation, that is, in the consideration of human confusions, which happens without the knowledge of the will of God, and without trust in divine aid, great pain follows, as Pompey and Cato are carried along, not knowing the causes of their ruin, when they think they have undertaken a just defense, and Cato does not yield to fortune, but wants to continue the war with human counsels, and to afflict himself and the Republic more.

Thus, very often men try to overcome fatal calamities with human counsels, and they do not want to yield to God, and without His calling, and for necessary causes, they proceed to be tumultuous, they only accumulate calamities, both for themselves and for others, as Zedekiah, Turnus.

Therefore it is said: μὴ πιαίζειν τὴν τυχὴν, do not provoke fortune. Item: μὴ κακὸν ἰῶ κακῷ, do not heal evil with evil. He says here, therefore: What does knowledge add, that is, consideration and corrections without the acknowledgment of the will of God, and without trust in divine aid? It adds pain, namely, he will suffer more by raging against God, and drawing upon himself greater evils, with counsels that will not profit, just as the Jewish kings in vain fortify themselves with various practices, when at one time they made treaties with the Babylonians, at another with the Egyptians, at another with the Syrians.

Solomon speaks of such counsels in government, which for the most part arise from πολυπραγμοσύνῃ [meddlesomeness] and the desires of men; he does not speak of physical consideration, in which there are many illustrious testimonies of the providence, goodness, and presence of God. As in the first chapter a general complaint was recited, that many things are done against the rule, which disturb the assent concerning providence: so in the second chapter he specifically enumerates many kinds of life, and finally in the third chapter he adds a spectacle, in which there is the greatest confusion, because the death of men and of beasts is similar.

Thus he said before: The wise and the foolish die alike, etc.

In these sayings, let us know that Solomon speaks of spectacles which strike the eyes, as if he were commemorating arguments μιμητικῶς (mimetically) or recitatively, which disturb the assent concerning providence; he is not yet speaking of the judgment to come, of which he speaks afterwards.

The wisdom of Palamedes, Theramenes, Socrates, Pompey, Julius, and Cicero was excellent, and yet they had tragic ends, just as many for whom folly was their destruction.

Demades had been more cautious than Demosthenes, and yet he was killed, when indeed his sons had first been killed in his sight, as it is said: An old fox is hardly caught, but it is caught nonetheless.

The End.

Latin:

Deum time, et mandata eius observa, hoc est praecipuum omnibus hominibus.

Complectitur autem totum cultum et totam obedientiam, et deducit nos ad hunc verum Deum, qui se patefecit in hoc populo Israël, et tradidit ei promissiones et legem, illustribus et non fallentibus testimoniis, hunc Deum vult agnosci, audiri, invocari, coli iuxta hanc ipsam vocem, quam tradidit, et proponit summam normam, quae debet esse rectrix omnium deliberationum et actionum: Intuere Deum et ipsius doctrinam, et ab hac norma non discedito, et scias, discedentem sine ulla dubitatione ruiturum esse in tenebras, laqueos diaboli et tristissimas poenas, referas omnia consilia et omnes actiones ad hunc finem, ut Deo praestes obedientiam, et eum celebres.

Hanc regulam etiam in iudicandis omnibus doctrinis teneas, considera quae disputationes, quae doctrinae, qui sermones dissentiant a verbo Dei, aut non prosint ad alendum timorem Dei in mentibus, et confirmandam fidem, et semper sunt, fuerunt et erunt multae Epicureae et multae ociosae opiniones, et multi idolorum cultus. Haec omnia summa vigilantia iudicanda et vitanda sunt.

Ad hanc summam refert conciones in hoc libro, quae quidem et summa est universae doctrinae in Ecclesia, iuxta illa dicta: Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt. Item, totus Psalmus: Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini. Item: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Ad hanc eandem summam refert Salomon et suas conciones.

Faciam igitur exemplo Salomonis, et argumentum ac summam huius libri in fine rursus recitabo.

Vult in hoc libro Salomon principaliter proponere asseverationem de providentia. Deinde vero refutare obiectiones, quae contra providentiam opponuntur. Cum enim multae et magnae sint in vita confusiones, et magna sit impiorum multitudo, et pauci sint Deum recte agnoscentes et timentes, et impii floreant gloria et opibus, pii sint aerumnosi, et multi interficiantur a pessimis, et gubernatio fidelis parum proficiat, videntur omnia casu ferri.

Ad hanc objectionem respondet Salomon: Etsi magna ex parte talis est confusio, tamen tu regaris verbo Dei, et retineas sententiam de providentia firma fide, nec propter haec scandala deficias a Deo, nec abiicias timorem Dei, et fiduciam acquiescentem in Deo, nec deseras vocationem tuam, et illis confusionibus haec duo ordinata opponito. Veniet iudicium, in quo Deus tollet hanc confusionem, et omnes impii abiicientur in aeternas poenas, et iustis bene erit. Iam quoque in hac vita Deus moderatur confusiones, punit atrocia scelera, nec sinit gubernationem prorsus irritam esse, colligit sibi aeternam Ecclesiam, servat aliquas politias et oeconomias. Imo hoc ipsum testimonium est praesentiae Dei, quod, cum tanta sit infirmitas naturae hominum, tanti, tam saevi multorum furores, videmus tamen mirabiliter servari Ecclesiam Dei, et aliqua eius hospitia.

Obiectio igitur de confusionibus est fallacia a dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter: Multa fiunt inordinate in hac vita, Ergo omnia et semper sunt inordinata. Neganda est consequentia. Nam prorsus tolletur haec confusio tandem, et in hac vita multa fiunt ordinate.

Tota machina mundi pulcherrime ordinata est, figura et situs coeli, aëris, aquae et terrae, motus siderum, vices temporum, foecundatio terrae, et nutricatio corporis humani, conservatio specierum, generatio, noticiae regulares in mente, conservatio societatis, poenae atrocium scelerum. Haec ordinata et regularia opponenda sunt confusionibus, Sed multo magis ipsa revelatio divina, quae editum est verbum, Lex, comminationes, Evangelium et promissiones, opponenda est omnibus spectaculis, quae incurrunt in oculos, et firmiter retinenda est fides, et in fide serviendum vocationi.

Recte facito, quia discrimen erit aeternum in venturo iudicio, etiam si aliquantisper digeruntur poenae. Fac officia vocationis, etiam si multi labores erunt inanes et ingrati, at aliquando proficies, aderit Deus laboranti et invocanti ipsum.

Hac fide spargito doctrinam et labores, ut panem in aquas. Hac fide et spe lenias dolorem. Ita prohibet desperationem et fiduciam nostri, et docet, fide in Deo acquiescendum esse.

Nec poteris in vita aliter mederi doloribus, etiamsi contraria tentes, aut deseras vitae societatem. Non vitantur miseriae humano consilio, sed tantum cum acquiescunt corda fide in Deo. Ad hanc summam recitationes de variis negociis et eventibus supra positae accommodandae sunt, et subinde adiunguntur responsiones, in quibus opponit verbum Dei, et ordinatos eventus, poenas atrocium scelerum, quae sunt testimonia venturi iudicii, et ipsam mentionem iudicii toties repetitam.

Prodest autem in qualibet materia considerare, quod sit consilium, quae voluntas scriptoris, et ad quem finem instituta sit oratio. Sciamus igitur, hunc librum principaliter doctrinam esse de providentia. Deinde consolationem contra varias confusiones vitae, ne propter eas de providentia dubitemus, nec abiiciamus curam recte faciendi, et communes labores vitae, nec deseramus vocationem.

Et consolationis loci ducuntur a necessario, a possibili, et ab utili, praemiis et poenis. A Necessario, quia necesse est Deo obedire.

Et firmissime retinenda est haec asseveratio: Genus humanum a Deo conditum esse. Et quanquam accesserunt multae tristes confusiones, tamen nos ab eo servari, et labores ab eo ordinatos esse, ipsum inspectorem, iudicem et adiutorem esse firmissime statuamus. Ideo saepe repetit haec dicta: Deum timeto, quia omnia adducet Deus in iudicium, bona et mala, etiam arcana.

Argumenta sunt a Possibili: Etsi magnae confusiones, et in multis gubernatio est inutilis, ut inquit: Curva non possunt fieri recta, et saepe etiam iusti labuntur: tamen Deus non sinet labores vocationis prorsus irritos esse, aderit invocanti, ut hic dicitur: Sparge panem velut in aquas, quia inveniens eum. Mane et vesperi seminato etc.

Denique saepe repetita est haec consolatio, et hic et alibi. Ut apud Paulum: Non erit labor vester inanis in Domino.

Et in Psalmo 1.: Folium eius non defluet. Et ad locum a possibili pertinent remedia dolorum.

Ignescunt irae, ac duris dolor ossibus ardet Pericli, et similibus, quod consilia pulcherrime cogitata de defensione patriae non procedunt.

Sed Ieremias acquiescit in Deo, etiam cum res adversae habet haec remedia Ieremias. quod scit, Deo obediendum esse, et Deum mirabiliter servaturum esse Ecclesiam, ut apud Esaiam dicitur: Ego gestabo vos, etiam in senecta.

Item: Et portae inferorum non praevalebunt adversus eam.

Tertius locus est ab Utili, praemiis et a poenis, discerni poenas atrocium scelerum etiam in hac vita, et tamen post hanc vitam Ecclesia ornabitur aeternis bonis, et impii abiicientur in aeternos cruciatus.

Hic igitur tertius locus est in hoc libro, scilicet comminatio, quae denunciat poenas omnibus peccantibus, non solum extra Ecclesiam, sed etiam in Ecclesia, ut inquit: Scio, quod bene erit timentibus Deum, et non bene erit impio.

Hos esse principales locos huius libri certum est.

Postea multa dicta de communibus eventibus, et de multis virtutibus miscentur.

Sed universa doctrina refertur ad hoc caput: Deum time, et mandata eius observa, ubi totum cultum, timorem, fidem et bona opera complectitur.

Et ita profuturae sunt huius libri admonitiones, cum adiungitur doctrina fidei, de vero Deo, de conversione seu poenitentia, de agnitione Filii Dei, de iustitia fidei, et de nova obedientia.

Concionatur enim auditoribus in vera Ecclesia, quibus Deus se patefecit, et promissiones tradidit.

Atque ita placent Deo opera vocationis, et hi labores vitae fiunt cultus Dei, cum fides praelucet, qua coram Deo propter Filium redemptorem iusti reputamur, et hac ipsa fide petitur gubernatio et auxilium a Deo, sicut Dominus inquit: Sine me nihil potestis facere.

Item: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus.

Et cum fides regit labores, simul refert eos ad gloriam Dei.

Est enim cultus Dei opus a Deo mandatum, factum fiducia Filii Dei, cuius finis principalis est, ut haec obedientia Deo praestet honorem, et ostendat, nos hunc verum Deum invocare, qui se in Ecclesia patefecit.

Haec fides etiam affert pacem cordi, quia subiicit nos Deo, statuit Deum adesse adiutorem et liberatorem, de qua Paulus dicit: Pax Dei superans omnia consilia mentis humanae, custodiat corda vestra.

Cum autem variae sententiae in has conciones sparsae sint, prudentia adhibeatur in iudicando discrimine earum.

Ac in universum in omnibus scriptis quae continent sententias, genera distingui necesse est.

In sacris libris alia dicta sunt Legalia, alia Evangelica, alia Dogmatica, alia Consolatoria, alia simpliciter Narrationes de eventibus, seu bonis seu malis.

Legale est, ut in hoc libro saepe repetitum praeceptum de vocatione: Sedulo facito labores, quos tibi Deus dedit.

Et ad praecepta adiunguntur comminationes, ut hic: Non bene erit impio.

Evangelica sunt, ut: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam.

Et huc referantur alia dicta de fide, de invocatione et de consolationibus, quae passim sparsae sunt in divinis concionibus, ut: Petite et accipietis.

Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus.

Et in hoc libro: Qui videt bonum de labore suo, donum Dei est.

Etsi enim obscurius de fide loquitur, tamen significat, petendum et expectandum esse auxilium, sicut Psalmus inquit: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Congruit et cum hoc dicto: Non erit labor vester inanis in Domino.

Alia sunt Dogmatica, ut de essentia Dei, de providentia, de voluntate Dei, de iudicio.

Ut: Alium Deum praeter me nescias, nec est alius Deus.

Item in hoc libro: Manifesta et occulta iudicabit Deus.

Consolatoria referantur ad Evangelica, ut: Prope est Deus his, qui tribulato sunt corde.

Item: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et ego eripiam te.

Narrationes de eventibus sunt, ut in hoc libro multae sunt: Moritur doctus ut indoctus.

Curva non fiunt recta.

Non est iustus in terra, qui cum recte facit, non etiam peccet.

Et prudenter discernenda sunt dicta, quae continent decisiones et promissiones, a narrationibus, ut: Fortuna quem nimium fovet, stultum facit.

Vel: Luxuriant animi rebus plerumque secundis.

Et in hoc libro: Vidi in loco iustitiae iniquitatem.

Tales narrationes non approbant mala, sed ostendunt, ut moniti consideremus ea, et simus intenti ad cavendum, sicut medicus recenset et describit morbos.

Haec dixi de generibus sententiarum in libris propheticis et apostolicis.

Iam considerentur et philosophicae sententiae.

In his non sunt Evangelicae et Dogmaticae.

Sed sunt aut Legales, aut Narrationes de eventibus, ut: λαῷ μὴ πίστευε, πολύτροπος ἐστὶν ὅμιλος.

Discrimen igitur sententiarum, quales sunt Hesiodi, Phocylidis, Theognidis, et earum quae in sacris libris continentur, sit in conspectu. Et saepe narrationes profanae aliter accipiendae sunt, aliter narrationes in sacris libris. Ut, aliud dicitur in hoc versu: Vitam regit fortuna, non sapientia. Aliud in dicto Salomonis: Non est fortium cursus, neque sapientum panis etc. Quia Salomon praecipit, ut regularia faciamus, convenientia mandatis divinis, et prohibet humanam curiositatem, quae sui fiduciam movet res extra vocationem. Prohibet etiam fiduciam nostri in operibus vocationis, et vult peti auxilium Dei, et nos obtemparare Deo, sive respondeant eventus, sive non respondeant. Confirmat igitur Salomon sententiam de providentia. Sed in illo profano dicto: Vitam regit fortuna non sapientia, aliud dicitur.

Extat dictum in vita Pomponii Attici: Sui cuique mores fortunam faciunt. Hoc dictum videtur discrepare ab alia regula: Multae tribulationes iustorum. Sed conciliatio haec est. Alterum est politica regula, congruens cum his dictis: Atrocia scelera puniuntur atrocibus poenis in hac vita. Item: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. Contra vero placidior cursus vitae est hominum, qui modeste vivunt. Sed in Ecclesia exceptio est, ubi quanquam Deus multis infirmis parcit, tamen aliquos duriter exercet. Et recte institutis notae sunt causae, quare Ecclesia magis prematur, quam caeteri homines. Oportet enim nos similes fieri imaginis Filii Dei.

Sententia prophetica dicit: Maledictus qui confidit in homine. Id congruit cum dicto: Nervus atque artus esse sapientiae illud Epicharmion: Μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν. Sic et Plato monet, ne spes nobis a fortuna, aut ab hominum coniunctionibus pendeant: sed nihil dicit de fiducia Dei.

Verba Platonis, in epitaphio posita, reddit Cicero hoc modo: Nam cui viro ex se ipso apta sunt omnia, quae ad beate vivendum ferunt, nec suspensa aliorum aut bono casu, aut contrario, huic optime vivendi ratio comparata est. Recte monet, ne pendeant spes a fortuna, aut ab hominum coniunctionibus. Sed quod deducit nos ad nostras virtutes, non satis est. Oportebat enim nos ad Deum deduci, quia multa accidunt homini, ubi virtus humana sine auxilio Dei succumbit. Hic, etiam cum destituunt nos humana consilia omnia, se vult agnosci et invocari Deus, et pollicetur auxilium. Et res ipsa ostendit, invocantibus mitigari calamitates, sicut dictum est: Prope est Dominus his, qui tribulato sunt corde. Item: Convertimini ad me, et ego convertar ad vos. Item: Si peccata vestra erunt sicut coccinum, eritis candidi sicut nix etc.

Pugnare videntur et hoc Ennianum: Fortibus est fortuna viris data. Et hoc Salomonis: Non est fortium cursus. Sed vera conciliatio est. Alterum taxat ignavos. Alterum damnat fiduciam nostrae virtutis, et neglectionem Dei, et tamen verum est, Davidem, cum vincit Goliath, non esse ociosum, non ignavum, non incautum.

Hoc modo prudenter considerandum est in dictis, ad quae genera referenda sint. Et quia sententiae plerumque sunt communes regulae vitae, prodest multas habere familiariter notas, et quia sunt monitrices in vita, et quia gignunt argumenta seu confirmationes et refutationes in omnibus causis, et addunt orationi gravitatem, cum in loco et verecunde intexuntur.

Consideranda sunt etiam personarum discrimina et hyperbolae. Nero dicit: Ferrum tuetur principem. Respondet Seneca: Melius Fides. Item, Graecum illud: Πάντα ἀνθρώπων μανιώδη εἶναι. Haec hyperbole nequaquam transferatur ad ea quae sunt ordinata divinitus, ad vocem Evangelii, ad confessionem sanctorum, ad officia legitima gubernationis, educationis institutiones. Talis et haec hyperbole est: Nulla fides pietasque viris qui castra sequuntur. Item: Fata regunt homines, certa stant omnia lege. Haec dicta necesse est corrigi erudita et vera interpretatione.

ARGUMENTUM IN ECCLESIASTEN, REPETITUM ANNO M.D.

LIIII. Consilia scribentium seu intentionem necesse est in legendo considerare, id est, Cogitandum est quid scriptor voluerit agere, an doctrinam de Propositione aliqua tradat, an vero praecipiat agi aliquid, seu an Consolatio instituatur, et in summa prospiciendus est finis scripti quid velit scriptor auferre aut facere lectorem.

Ideo et in Rhe toricis libellis genera discernuntur, didascalicon et deliberativum. Haec distributio est commonefactio de considerando consilio seu intentione scribentis, seu de fine orationis.

Primum igitur de libro Salomonis, cui titulus est: Ecclesiastes, hoc dico, principalem partem esse doctrinam, videlicet, asseverationem de providentia, hoc est, de hoc articulo fidei, quod Deus vere sit iudex recte et secus factorum, ac velit nos recta facere, et facientes recta iuxta verbum et vocationem ipsi commendare eventus, etiamsi multi magni labores videntur esse irriti, ut labores Ieremiae, quanquam non impediunt excidium patriae, tamen sunt salutares. Rursus etiam iubet certo statuere Deum puniturum esse non recte facientes, etiamsi interdum differuntur poenae. Haec asseveratio de providentia est principalis pars libri.

Quia vero turbatur assensio de providentia horribilibus confusionibus vitae humanae, videlicet quod multi labores, ac plerique magna specie sapientiae suscepti, sed sine mandato, aliqui etiam suscepti iuxta mandata et vocationem videntur irriti. Item Ecclesia subiecta est cruci, et iusti affliguntur, iniusti vero regnant, tenent imperia et opes, ut Turci et alii. Recitat Salomon haec argumenta turbantia assensionem de providentia, et opponit asseverationem, quae habet testimonium verbi Dei, quod vult Salomon omnibus spectaculis, quae in oculos incurrunt, anteferri.

Hoc doctrinae fundamento iacto, addit deinde regulam vitae: Obedias verbo Dei, iuxta vocationem, nec ab eo discedas propter speciosa rationis consilia, aut propter res secundas aut adversas. Deo autem commendes eventus. Ut propter speciosum consilium discedunt a verbo et vocatione Israëlitae cum petunt regem, et volunt in hac politia divinitus constituta novam formam sua sapientia constituere. Discedit a verbo Dei, constituens novum cultum, Ieroboam, quia nolebat videri se non esse parem regi Iuda etc. Multo magis discedunt a vocatione Marius, Catilina, Antonius, qui motis seditionibus regna constituere conantur. Discedunt a verbo Dei fracti rebus adversus pontifices, Menelaus, Alcimus et alii Maccabaeorum temporibus, et nunc multi moventur potentia et gloria regni Turcici et pontificii, ut deficiant a vero Deo. Tenenda est igitur regula hic saepe repetita: Obedias verbo Dei, et ipsi commendes eventus, quia certo Deus iudicaturus est.

Haec regula et alibi saepe repetita est, ut Psalm. 37.: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Hac regula constituta sequuntur deinde consolationes.

Etiamsi magnae sunt confusiones generis humani. Maxima est multitudo impiorum, et iniusti tenent imperia, iusti opprimuntur, et plurima consilia hominum sine Deo sunt inutilia. Imo et labores piorum in tanta contumacia impiae multitudinis et fugacitate vitae videntur esse irriti, et aliquantisper bene constitutae Ecclesiae et civitates cito turbantur, tamen non discedas a regula: Obtemperes Deo, et in ipso laeteris, nec abiicias mandato labores et ordinem a Deo institutum.

Hae consolationes saepe repetuntur, sed sunt extructae supra asseverationem de providentia et de venturo iudicio, ut cap. 3. dicit: Iustum et impium iudicabit Deus. Et cap. ult.: Cuncta quae fiunt adducet Deus in iudicium. Et cap. 11.: Pro omnibus his adducet te Deus in iudicium. Ad hoc fundamentum adiungitur praeceptum cap. ult.: Deum time, et mandata eius observa, hoc faciat omnis homo.

Et de laboribus mandatis inquit cap. 9.: Quicquid potest facere manus tua omnibus viribus facito. Item cap. 11.: Mitte panem tuum super aquas transeuntes, tamen invenies eum. Sicut Paulus inquit: Labor vester non est inanis in Domino.

Adduntur et consolationes ut in Deo acquiescamus et laetemur, cum quidem multa adversa impediant necessarios et utiles labores. Cap. 9.: Vade et comede in laetitia panem tuum, quia Deo placent opera tua. Hae vitae regulae et consolationes semper sint in conspectu, nec turbetur assensio de providentia variis spectaculis, quae non congruunt cum ordine, ut cum iusti opprimuntur, florent impii etc., nec abiiciantur mandati labores propterea quod multa impedimenta occurrunt.

Est igitur principaliter hoc scriptum δογματικὸν sive διδασκαλικὸν, videlicet asseveratio de providentia confirmans pios contra Epicureas et Academicas opiniones. Deinde adduntur praecepta seu regulae vitae et consolationes, haec ipsa summa est huius scripti.

Verba Ecclesiastae filii David regis Hierusalem. In titulo nominat se Salomon et Regem et Ecclesiasten, id est, Concionatorem, qua appellatione significat ad officium principum pertinere, ut curent recte doceri Ecclesias, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Et nunc reges intelligite. Item: Aperite portas principes vestras. Item: in conveniendo populos et reges in unum, ut serviant Domino. Hunc dulcem versiculum saepe cogitare oportebat et principes et populos, quia utrisque praecipitur ut conveniant, id est, tueantur communem congregationem et ministerium vocis divinae, et discant veram doctrinam, et vero consensu Deum invocent, et doctrinam conservare studeant. Huius autem pii consensus reges debent esse duces et autores. Ideo hic quoque Salomon se Concionatorem nominat, significans se velle autorem esse pii consensus in Ecclesia, et custodem verae doctrinae.

Vanitas vanitatum et omnia vanitas, quid habet homo amplius de labore suo quo laborat sub Sole.

Initio ponit objectionem contra asseverationem de providentia, quasi dicat, quae potest esse providentia, cum labores hominum pariter vel irriti vel infelices sint bonorum et malorum. Non enim loquitur Salomon de rebus ipsis a Deo conditis et manentibus in suo ordine, cum ait: Omnia sunt vanitas. Sed de humanis laboribus, videlicet consiliis, affectibus et conatibus, ideo expressius inquit: Quid homo lucratur suo labore. Item: Quo laborat sub Sole. Nequaquam igitur comprehendit vanitatis appellatione Deum, verbum Dei et ministeria quatenus reguntur verbo Dei, nec creaturas ipsas a Deo conditas. Nam retinenda est sententia dicti in Genesi: Vidit Deus omnia fecerat, et erant valde bona.

Sed loquitur hoc loco Salomon de laboribus sub Sole, id est, in hac aerumnosa hominum vita, in qua homines aut errant consiliis et affectibus, et multa frustra conantur, et miserias cumulant, sicut in fabula dicitur de Asino, de quo sunt versus: Sis asinus quemcunque asinum sors aspera fecit: Qui placide sortem ferre scit, ille sapit: Aut bonis rebus et ministeriis divinis inutiliter miscentur humana consilia et humani affectus.

Ut bonae res sunt quaerere victum, regere oeconomias, politias, Ecclesias, tamen quantum inutilium curarum et malorum affectuum miscent homines. Saul conatur traducere regnum ad suos posteros. David sperat se regnum traditurum esse Absaloni. Hae cogitationes longe secus cadunt. Multo magis falluntur spes et consilia impiorum quanquam speciosa, ut Pompeius, Cato, Marcellus, sperant victoriam in causa (ut putant) iusta, sicut dicunt: Causa iubet superos melior sperare secundos. Brutus et Cassius cogitant, interfecto Caesare veterem formam Reipub. se instauraturos esse. Antonius cogitat, se oppresso Augusto monarcham fore.

Denique de irritis conatibus hominum saepissime citantur dicta: Μάταιοι μάταια λογίζονται δι᾽ ἐπιθυμίας.

Item: Scio Domine non est hominis via eius, id est, solis humanis consiliis et viribus nulla vocatio felix est. Item: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum, frustra laborat qui aedificaverit eam. Item: οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων ἐστὶν ἅπαντα σοφὸς. Item: Heu pectora quantum coecae noctis habent. Et infra in hoc libro: Stultorum infinitus est numerus. Inde igitur argumentantur, cum tantae sint confusiones, impii dominentur, pii opprimantur, iusta consilia impediantur, quae potest esse providentia.

Huic obiectioni postea respondebo.

Imo inquit: Sequitur iudicium, etiam si nunc confusio ordinis esse videtur, ideo mandatis Dei obtemperato, et scias non omnes labores in ministeriis divinis irritos fore. Sicut et Paulus inquit: Non erit labor vester inanis in Domino.

Oritur Sol et occidit, et ad locum suum redit.

Prius incoavit seu querelam de negotiis humanis, sive obiectionem contra asseverationem de providentia, quod labores humani pariter sint irriti, bonorum et malorum, vita ipsa est incerta, et fugax, Alexander, Iulius, in cursu maximarum rerum opprimuntur, non sunt durabilia imperia optime constituta. Post Cyrum mox secuta tyrannis Cambysis, defectio Babylonis, post Darium bello Xerxis afflicta tota Asia.

Denique saepe repetuntur querelae: Magna momento ruunt. Item: Summisque negatum est Stare diu, nimioque graves sub pondere lapsus.

Propter hanc instabilitatem rerum humanarum, et varias confusiones, dixit initio, negocia sub Sole vanitatem esse, id est, et fugacia, et plena confusionum. Nunc addit similitudinem sumtam a motibus Solis et aquarum, cuius accomodatio prudenter consideretur: tantum enim proponitur, tanquam imago instabilitatis et revolutionis similium miseriarum in negociis humanis, et significat eas miserias nec consilio nec sapientia humana impediri posse, ut cum fuissent magni tumultus, et crebrae seditiones in Repub. Romana sub Consulibus et Tribunis, postea expetita est monarchia, et redierunt tamen similes miseriae. Ita in Israël, cum in Aristocratia, ante regnum magnae calamitates accidissent, populus voluit regem certum constitui, ac sperabat mutata forma Reipub. feliciorem statum fore. Sed aliquanto post secutae sunt tristiores dilacerationes.

Simplicissima igitur accommodatio similitudinis haec est: Sicut Sol et aqua habent assiduas circumgirationes, et revolvuntur, ita humana negocia una cum miseriis, quae admixtae sunt, revolvuntur, nec consilio aut sapientia humana impediri aerumnae in universum possunt.

In privatis et publicis negociis subinde alia consilia tentantur, ad afferendum statum meliorem, et tamen redeunt similes miseriae. In hanc sententiam dicit nihil novi sub Sole, id est, redeunt similes cupiditates, similia consilia, similes eventus, bellorum causae, bella, et calamitosi exitus, sicut Thucydides inquit: Donec talis erit hominum natura, accident similia, alias minus, alias atrocius.

Inquit igitur: Cunctae res sunt difficiles, id est, multa fiunt, quorum causae provideri non possunt. Cur vincitur Pompeius, in causa ut videtur meliore. Item: Difficilima est gubernatio, cum maxima multitudo nolit emendari, ideo dicit: Perversi non possunt corrigi legibus, vigilantia, et severitate gubernatorum.

Haec tota oratio et querela est de miseriis humanis, et obiectio contra providentiam, postea vero tradet refutationem et consolationem.

Refutatio communis haec est, secuturum esse iudicium, consolatio vero, singulos pro vocatione debere mandatis divinis obtemperare, eosque labores non omnino fore irritos, etiamsi multa adversa accidunt, Tenendam esse regulam: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet.

Obiter observent hic studiosi testimonia, quae affirmant terram stare et Solem moveri: prodest enim habere etiam divina testimonia, contra absurdas opiniones eorum, qui ludentes, labefactant communem physicorum doctrinam. Caeteras physicas disputationes hic omitto.

Ego Ecclesiastes fui Rex, et cogitavi quaerere sapienter, de omnibus quae fiunt sub Sole.

Congruit initio dicere, de consideratione. Quia enim videmus dissimiles eventus, movemur, ut quaeramus de providentia, nec loquitur Salomon de consideratione physica, quae ostendit illustria testimonia providentiae divinae, et tanquam vestigia Dei in tota rerum natura, quia impossibile est, casu existere, et manere pulcerrimum ordinem, in positu, ornatu, et motu corporum mundi, et noticiis naturalibus, et conservatione specierum, et distributione ad diversos usus.

De his testimoniis concionatur Paulus, Rom. 2. et Act. 1. et 17. Sed loquitur Salomon de consideratione consiliorum, actionum, et eventuum in gubernatione politica et oeconomica: ideo expresse dicit se considerasse, ea quae fiunt sub Sole, actiones et eventus humanorum consiliorum, ut Pericles, Demosthenes, Cicero, sunt sapientes gubernatores, et tamen horum speciosa consilia habent tetros eventus, quia antea dixit: Cunctae res sunt difficiles, nec potest homo eas explicare sermone, id est, omnes deliberationes sunt difficiles, quia plerumque utrinque pericula occurrunt.

Nec humana sapientia prospicit omnia. Et postea dicitur, sapientia saepe fallit, cum inquit, stultorum non est numerus, seu errata sunt innumerabilia.

Nominat autem Salomon hanc ipsam sapientiam seu deliberationes malam afflictionem, et ait hominibus, a Deo datam esse. Haec videntur absurda, sed primum discernatur vocatio, seu ordo divinus, et hominum infirmitas seu caligo, et dubitationes.

Ordo est, ut coningium, iudicia, magistratus, quae res suo genere bonae sunt, quatenus ordinatae sunt a Deo, et ordo non turbatur hominum vitiis et furoribus, Sed sapientia Dei rectrix est. In Pericle est mala afflictio, id est, cruciatus, qui est malum poenae, sicut usitate loquimur.

Est autem cruciatus dupliciter, quia dubitatio et error cruciant homines, ut Pompeium cruciat primum dubitatio, deinde error, cum vidit calamitosum exitum. Saepe errant etiam sapientes gubernatores, saepe peccant ambitione, ut Perdicas post Alexandrum, saepe falsa specie iuris, ut Brutus, saepe πολυπραγμοσύνῃ et inquietudine animorum, ut Pericles, saepe ira, ut Marius: deinde etiam bonis consiliis saepe non respondent eventus, ut cum Israëlitae dimicarent cum tribu Beniamin: denique omnes patresfamilias, omnes gubernatores, experiuntur plenam esse gubernationem non solum curarum, sed etiam impedimentorum, erratorum, tristium eventuum, quae omnia valde cruciant animos.

Has aerumnas omnes, simul complectitur Salomon, cum ait, hanc sapientiam rectricem esse malam afflictionem.

Hinc sunt poëtica figmenta de Prometheo, qui dicitur affixus in Caucaso. Et de Sisypho volvente saxum, et similia. Demosthenes inquit, se si retexenda esset vita, malle ad certam mortem ire, quam ad summos honores in Repub. Et Aeschines inquit, laetari se liberatum esse a gubernatione Reipub, ac si liberatus esset a rabiosa cane.

Sed cur dicit, a Deo hanc afflictionem datam esse homini, ut gubernatio sit plena aerumnarum et errorum?

Respondeo: Generaliter verum est, Deum velle poenam, seu conversionis causa, sed ad ultimam destructionem, sed tamen inde non sequitur Deum causam esse peccatorum, aut velle, vel adiuvare peccata, quae sunt media ad poenam, vel ultimam destructionem.

Deus servat ordinem suum inter errata gubernatorum, ut servat politiam Israël, etiamsi aliquantisper turbant ordinem, Saul, Absalon et similes. Fit autem Davidi gubernatio aerumnosior, quia vel alii turbant eum, vel etiam ipse suo lapsu, causa est impedimentorum. Quia autem vult Deus homines puniri, seu conversionis causa, seu propter ultimam destructionem, non prohibet media, quae ab humana imbecillitate et a furoribus diabolorum oriuntur, non oriuntur a Deo: et gubernator qui experitur impedimenta magis dolet, quam homo privatus, ut magis dolet David, quam homo privatus.

Quangunt, ut in Solonis versu dicitur: Intrant in thalamos, publica damna, tuos.

Sed tamen plerumque plus periculi, et miseriarum sustinent summi gubernatores, ut dicitur: βίος ἰδιώτων ἄριστος, vita privatorum optima.

Item: λάθε βιώσας, maneas in vita privata. Item: Saepius venti agitatur ingens Pinus, et celsae graviore casu Decidunt turres, feriuntque summos Fulmina montes. Item, ὄγκου δὲ μεγάλου πτῶμα γίγνεται μέγα. Fastus magni lapsus fit magnus. Item: Irus et est subito, qui modo Croesus erat. Et apud Euripidem Oedipus inquit: Ego qui reges antecellui sapientia, nunc exeo ex patria velut umbra.

Inquit igitur Salomon, in magna sapientia est magna indignatio, id est, in consideratione confusionum humanarum, quae fit sine cognitione voluntatis Dei, et sine fiducia auxilii divini, sequitur magnus dolor, ut Pompeius, Cato, feruntur nescientes causas ruinae suae, cum existiment se iustam defensionem suscepisse, et Cato non cedit fortunae, sed humanis consiliis vult continuare bellum, et magis sese, et Rempub. affligere.

Sic saepissime homines cum consiliis humanis fatales calamitates, vincere conantur, nec volunt cedere Deo, et sine vocatione sua, et necessariis causis tumultuari pergunt, cumulant tantum calamitates, et sibi et aliis, ut Zedechias, Turnus.

Ideo dictum est: μὴ πιαίζειν τὴν τυχὴν, non premito fortunam. Item: μὴ κακὸν ἰῶ κακῷ, ne malum sanato malo. Dicit igitur hic: Quid addit scientiam, id est, considerationem, et correctiones sine agnitione voluntatis Dei, et sine fiducia auxilii divini, addit dolorem, scilicet magis dolebit fremens adversus Deum, et attrahens maiora mala, non profuturis consiliis, ut reges Iudaici variis practicis frustra se muniunt, cum alias cum Babyloniis foedera fecerunt, alias cum Aegyptiis, alias cum Syriacis.

De talibus consiliis in gubernatione loquitur Salomon, quae magna ex parte a πολυπραγμοσύνῃ et cupiditatibus hominum oriuntur, non loquitur de consideratione physica, in qua plurima sunt illustria testimonia providentiae, bonitatis et praesentiae Dei. Ut in primo capite generalis querela recitata est, quod multa fiant contra regulam, quae turbant assensionem de providentia: ita in secundo capite specialiter enumerat multa vitae genera, et tandem in tertio capite addit spectaculum, in quo est maxima confusio, quod similis sit interitus hominum et pecorum.

Ita prius dixit: Sapientes et insipientes similiter mori etc.

In his dictis sciamus Salomonem loqui de spectaculis, quae incurrunt in oculos tanquam μιμητικῶς seu recitative commemorantem argumenta, quae turbant assensionem de providentia, non iam loquitur de iudicio secuturo, de quo postea dicit.

Fuit excellens sapientia Palamedis, Theramenis, Socratis, Pompeii, Iulii, Ciceronis, et tamen habent tragicos exitus, sicut multi quibus stulticia fuit exitio.

Fuerat cautior Demades quam Demosthenes, et tamen interfectus est, cum quidem in conspectu eius primum filii essent interfecti, sicut dicitur: Vetula vulpes vix capitur, sed capitur tamen.

Finis.

# Matthew

## 1:1 Introduction: Sermons on Matthew
SERMONS EXPLAINING THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

A book has appeared, with the title: "Sermons explaining the entire Gospel of Matthew, delivered at Wittenberg by M. Sebastian Froeschelius of Amberg, Archdeacon in the same Church, written by Philipp Melanchthon." Wittenberg 1558. 8vo. 2 alphabets, 10 sheets. Reprinted in the works of Melanchthon, Wittenberg. Vol. III. p. 247 ff. — Reprinted also at Wittenberg, 1560.

Regarding the genesis of this writing, Froeschelius in his dedicatory epistle to the Senate of Amberg, dated 29 September 1558, committed these things to writing: Since, by reason of my office, I was to have an evening sermon every Saturday in this Church, and by the judgment of my reverend Pastor I had undertaken to explain the Gospel of Matthew to our hearers. I, however, conscious of my own weakness and the infancy known to all, feared to invent or carve out something from my own head: I asked the reverend man D. Philipp Melanchthon, a faithful teacher and indeed our most kind Father, about eighteen years ago, while Luther was still living (who was also an auditor and arbiter of these sermons for more than five years), that he might be of assistance to me in the more obscure passages, and if he could, through his most grave occupations, distinguish the text of the Evangelist, and reduce it into certain places, and show what doctrine or consolation should be proposed to the hearers in each place. He undertook this labor willingly, although most occupied, as he is prepared for all to perform such works, from which some utility might be expected to return either to the Church and posterity, or to those very people who seek his work: so that he truly lives not for himself nor for his own, but entirely for others, that is, for the Church, for literary matters, and for all requiring his help. Therefore, he wrote for me, while I was present, every Friday, first the dispositions and certain brief summaries of the individual chapters. Then, when we arrived at the 5th chapter, he wove together almost proper sermons, for some time in the vernacular language, so that I might more properly propose the things themselves to my hearers; the rest, from chapter 9, he explained in Latin speech, meanwhile, however, admonishing and instructing me, by what words in our language they could be most properly expressed and rendered, and what Latin words used in the Church could be [used], which German words we sometimes leave in this printed example the Latin words inserted, so that the less learned may become more accustomed to rendering Latin properly into German.

However, the writing of this work, begun by Philipp, was often interrupted, either by the public dangers and dissipations of this School, as when Professors were expelled from here on account of plague or war: or by his own private journeys, undertaken by order of the Elector for imperial assemblies, colloquies, or similar deliberations.

Therefore, it was very difficult for me to obtain annotations on the whole Gospel of Matthew, especially since, even while he was here, many occupations occurred which hindered his writing.

I took care, however, that the explanation of Matthew was so often undertaken by me publicly in the Church, until at length I elicited an almost complete commentary on his entire history, and it was finished three years ago.

I was keeping this Treasure among my most cherished possessions, and I was already at work on it, intending to transcribe the entire work with my own hand, with the intention that a copy might be sent to you in your homeland.

For when some were urging that this commentary be published, I noticed that the author was completely averse to publication, so much so that he would sometimes respond rather heatedly to those pressing him, saying he would not permit it to be published, because these little sermons had been written by him incidentally and at long intervals of time, and sometimes in hurried work, adapted to the grasp of unlearned listeners, to whom sometimes the most serious matters had to be explained ἀμαθέστερον καὶ σαφέστερον (more simply and more clearly).

Thus it happened that, without doubt, many things would be found in them that were mutilated, concise, not in proper order and method, nor explained with equal diligence, in some places even annoyingly repeated, and finally, that most were unpolished and unworthy to be exhibited to the eyes of the learned.

It could also have happened that, in such a variety of business and in the haste of this writing, some little words might have slipped out here and there, which would provide a cause for criticism to the suspicious and severe censors of others' writings.

Finally, that it is the misfortune of this age that it has produced and admires certain talents which seek for themselves the highest praise of learning and piety among the unlearned, even if they interpret the words of others wrongly, and declare that various seeds of errors and heresies lie hidden and concealed therein.

He did not want to provide, by the publication of these unlearned little sermons, a cause for new struggles over doctrine, or for renewing and confirming previous ones, especially since he was not now granted as much leisure as would be sufficient for reading through and revising these pages, which hurried and often interrupted work had poured forth rather than written to this end, that it might provide me with a cause for thinking more diligently about the sayings of the Evangelist Matthew, not that those pages should be scattered into the hands of many.

That there exist just and learned commentaries of others on this Evangelist, which he would prefer to be inspected and consulted by a preacher, rather than these little annotations of his.

Since, therefore, I saw that Lord Philipp was seriously confirmed in this opinion, that he did not want to grant the publication of this commentary, I began, as I said before, to transcribe it with my own hand, so that a copy of it might be sent to you in your homeland.

For I had many reasons why I decided that this most useful labor of my Teacher, which I had used in teaching this Church not without profit to the listeners, as I hope, should be shared with you.

For besides those most sacred bonds of our common fatherland, by which we are mutually obligated to one another to perform any duties, I was moved by your munificence, by which you have liberally advanced my studies in the Leipzig Academy and here in Wittenberg, and by your other benefits, with which you have long since favored me, though absent from here.

Furthermore, I judged that I owed this to my fatherland, that since I could not be present to serve and benefit it in the illustration and propagation of the pure doctrine of the Gospel, I should, while absent, impart to it those things which I had drawn and collected here from men who are learned and outstanding in the excellence of their gifts.

Moved by these and other reasons, while I was laboring to prepare a copy of my sermons for you, some colleagues and friends of mine here rushed upon me in a single impulse, who with great zeal contend with me that I should see to it that this commentary on Matthew, as it is, written by Philipp, be printed, to whom, although I explained what stood in my way, namely the prohibition of the author himself, whom I did not think should be offended by this edition, since I had found him so prompt, easy, and kind in writing my own sermons: yet they began to urge seriously, and at the same time to show letters sent here from elsewhere (which I myself had also received frequently from various places). ram) which they were demanding with the greatest effort, that a copy of this commentary might be made, by whatever means, for all ministers of the Churches.

As far as the author's reasons were concerned, they said that these were not to be valued so highly that this work, which would be profitable to very many if it were published, should therefore be confined within the walls and desk of one man.
