For even if there are some things in these sermons that are less accurate, less copious, less orderly, and more simply explained because of haste, than they ought to be to be subjected to the more severe censure of the learned, yet they thought, nay, they affirmed, that fair readers, if they are forewarned for whom these sermons were written, and by how busy a man, how hastily, and at what long intervals of time—which could easily have erased from the memory of the writer the previous opinion and order of the annotators—would undoubtedly show such candor in reading and judging that they would embrace with a grateful heart the things themselves, faithfully explained, and would attribute and forgive the rest, which, compared with other more accurate writings of the same author, as far as the method of teaching and the manner of speaking are concerned, will seem to agree less, due to these impediments which I have said were occasionally placed in the way of the writing of this narrative.

But as for the remaining Momuses, who seek the praise of learning and piety by some new institution, and trust that they will be the greatest in the Church if they render all the words of others, who previously taught in the Church with some authority, however simply and rightly spoken, odious and suspect to the common people by the tricks of cavils and sinister interpretations, they contended that they were not to be cared for at all, so that for that reason the edition of this writing should be hastened rather than omitted, so that if those men attempt to seize it in their own way and deform it with false criticisms, they may more openly display and reveal their own desire to harm and their impotence of mind to all good men, which will do no harm to the author or the writing, since it is certain that these annotations were not written to be published, nor did the author wish them to be published.

Why then do you dare to publish them? someone will say.

I am complying with the constant admonitions, petitions, and entreaties of those who, when they had extorted from me by their prayers this commentary to be read in secret, returned it to me afterwards in such a way that they said they had been much helped and delighted by reading it, and that its publication would be profitable to very many, and especially to those engaged in the ecclesiastical ministry.

Some also added this, that by publishing these sermons, the mouths of those who cry out to the common people that the same doctrine no longer sounds in this Church as was handed down here while Luther was alive, must be stopped, since a pious reader can learn from this writing that the same purity of doctrine is preserved here, and that the corruptions of heavenly doctrine, such as were proposed in the book INTERIM and in the writings of certain others, were freely criticized in public sermons during that most dangerous time.

There were also some who openly threatened me that if I did not wish to publish these sermons, they would by every artifice lie in wait for that writing, and would not rest until they took it from me, so that it might be printed elsewhere, even while I was still alive and unaware, or at least be scattered after my death.

Overcome by these reasons, I finally consented and permitted this commentary to be published, although I had entirely determined to keep it in hiding and to obey the prohibition of my teacher Philip, whom, indeed, if I offend by this publication, I reverently pray that he may mercifully grant me pardon, because I have preferred the prayers, exhortations, and commands of so many good and serious men (among whom also the reverend and holy man the Lord D. Johannes Bugenhagen, while he lived, was especially a persistent demander of it) to the prohibition of him alone, which arose only from consideration of this corrupt age and from fear of unjust censures, seeking or aiming at nothing else than that, if—as many men outstanding in piety and prudence judge and certainly promise me will be the case—the ministers of the word and other learned men can derive some benefit from the reading of these sermons, it may not seem that through me those things were withheld from them and obstructed through envy or πλεονεξίαν.

Christ himself commands us to share doctrine liberally with others, when he says: Let your light shine before men, that your Father who is in heaven may be glorified. Likewise, sending his Apostles to teach the Gospel, among other things he also gives them this command: What I say to you in darkness, you speak in the light, and what you hear in the ear, you preach upon the housetops. Looking toward this end with this edition, may my teacher Philip, the Lord, forgive me, nor let him think that all disobedience is always a crime and detestable, but that some at times not only excusable, but even worthy of praise.

In several places, the Evangelists proclaim the disobedience and lack of restraint of the tongue of those who, having been freed from serious illnesses by the divine power and kindness of Christ, and having been ordered to keep that benefit hidden in silence, do not at all obey their benefactor Christ, overcome by the magnitude of their joy, but as Mark says in chapter 7: The more they are ordered to be silent, the more clamorously they proclaim that wondrous healing to everyone they meet.

May this act of mine, therefore, be received kindly, for I did not wish to keep to myself alone this writing—which was written against the author's will, but by the reading of which I profess myself to have been greatly helped, and I have learned that all others to whom I gave the power to inspect it have judged the same—but I thought it should be shared with many, and I did so having been asked so many times by friends, importuned by my elders, and ordered and even almost compelled by those whose authority I ought not to have avoided.

BRIEF COMMENTARIES ON MATTHEW, WRITTEN BY PHILIP MELANCHTHON.

Always at the beginning, before the exposition of the books that recount the history of the Gospel, let there be a discussion about the distinction between the Law and the Gospel.

Then, when the promise has been discussed, let it be added that these Narratives were written so that the Apostles might be witnesses, and that posterity might be certain that the Messiah was sent and manifested.

Thirdly, let it be said that these four things are contained principally in the evangelical reading: 1. Narratives, who Christ is, and whence he is. 2. Miracles testifying that he is not an Impostor, but truly sent by God, and that his doctrine is true. 3. Sermons of the Gospel, that is, promises, such as: Everyone who believes in the Son shall not perish. Come to me all who labor, etc. Likewise concerning eternal life. 4. Sermons concerning good works, which are as it were sermons of the Law and interpretations of the Law. And they pertain to the doctrine of repentance.

And the distinction between Precepts and Promises must be diligently observed, lest this light be lost, that the remission of sins is gratuitous. And so much for the Introduction.

Latin:

CONCIONES EXPLICANTES EVANGELIUM MATTHAEI.

Prodiit liber, cui titulus: "Conciones explicantes integrum Evangelium Matthaei, Witebergae habitae a M. Sebastiano Froeschelio Ambergense, Archidiacono in eadem Ecclesia, scriptae a Philippo Melanchtone." Witebergae 1558. 8. 2 alph. 10 pl. Recusae in operibus Melanchtonis Witeberg. Tom. III. p. 247 sqq. — Recusae etiam Witeberg. 1560.

De genesi huius scripti Froeschelius in epistola dedicatoria ad Senatum Ambergensem d. d. 29. Septb. 1558. haec literis mandavit: Cum officii mei ratione mihi singulis diebus Saturni vespertina Concio esset habenda in hac Ecclesia, et iudicio reverendi Pastoris mei sumsissem explicandum auditoribus nostris Evangelium Matthaei. Ego autem conscius mihi meae imbecillitatis, et notae omnibus infantiae, vererer aliquid ex meo capite affingere aut exculpere: rogavi reverendum virum D. Philippum Melanchtonem praeceptorem fidelem, atque adeo Patrem benignissimum nostrum, ante annos octodecim ferme, adhuc vivente Luthero (qui etiam harum concionum amplius quinquennium auditor et arbiter fuit) ut mihi in locis obscurioribus esset adiumento, et si per gravissimas occupationes suas posset, textum Evangelistae distingueret, et in locos certos redigeret, et quae in quolibet loco vel doctrina vel consolatio proponenda auditoribus esset commonstraret. Hunc laborem ille in se recepit libenter, quamvis occupatissimus, ut est paratus omnibus ad eiusmodi operas praestandas, ex quibus utilitas aliqua reditura vel ad Ecclesiam et posteritatem, vel ad illos ipsos, qui operam eius expetunt, sperari potest: ita ut vere vivat nec sibi nec suis, sed prorsus aliis, hoc est, Ecclesiae, rei literariae, et omnibus opem ipsius requirentibus. Scripsit igitur singulis diebus Parasceves mihi praesenti primum dispositiones et summas quasdam breves singulorum capitum. Deinde ubi ad 5. caput pervenimus, iustas ferme conciones contexuit, aliquandiu vernacula lingua, ut magis proprie res ipsas auditoribus meis proponere possem, reliqua a cap. 9. explicavit Latina oratione, subinde tamen me admonens ac instruens, quibus verbis nostra lingua quam propriissime efferri et reddi Latina vocabula in Ecclesia usurpata possent, quas Germanicas voces Latinis insertas etiam in hoc excuso exemplo interdum relinquimus, ut rudiores magis proprie Latina Germanicis reddere assuescant.

Hanc autem Philippi institutam scriptionem saepe interruperunt, vel publica huius Scholae pericula et dissipationes, ut cum propter pestem aut bellum hinc expellebantur Professores: vel privatae ipsius profectiones, iussu Electoris susceptae ad conventus imperiales, colloquia, aut similes deliberationes.

Itaque mihi perdifficile fuit, annotationes in totum Evangelium Matthaei impetrare, praesertim cum etiam dum hic erat, multae inciderent occupationes, quae ipsius scriptiones impedirent.

Dedi tamen operam, ut toties suscepta sit a me explicatio Matthaei publice in Ecclesia, donec tandem in totam eius historiam integrum quasi commentarium elicerem, isque completus fuit anno ab hinc tertio.

Hunc ego Thesaurum inter res mihi carissimas reponebam, et iam in eo eram labore, ut integrum opus mea manu describerem, eo consilio, ut ad vos exemplum mitteretur.

Suadentibus enim aliquibus edi publice hunc commentarium, animadvertebam autorem prorsus a publicatione abhorrere, adeo quidem, ut instantibus aliquibus interdum commotius responderet, non permissurum se, ut ederetur, eo quod obiter et per longa saepe intervalla temporum, et interdum festinata opera a se scriptae istae conciunculae essent, accommodatae ad captum rudium auditorum, qui bus interdum res gravissimae exponendae essent ἀμαθέστερον καὶ σαφέστερον.

Ita factum esse, ut haud dubie multa in iis reperirentur mutila, concisa, non iusto ordine ac methodo, nec pari diligentia omnia explicata, alicubi etiam eadem moleste repetita, denique pleraque inculta, et indigna esse, quae eruditorum oculis exhiberentur.

Fieri etiam potuisse, ut in tanta negotiorum varietate, et scriptionis huius festinatione, alicubi voculae aliquae sibi exciderint, quae suspicacibus et severis alienorum scriptorum censoribus reprehensionum causam praebiturae essent.

Postremo esse huius seculi eam infelicitatem, ut ingenia quaedam talia produxerit et admiretur, quae in hoc sibi summam eruditionis et pietatis laudem quaerant apud indoctos, si etiam recte aliorum dicta secus interpretentur, et varia ibi errorum et haereseon semina latere et occultari pronuncient.

Eis se nolle harum rudium conciuncularum editione causam praeberi, nova certamina de doctrina excitandi, aut priora renovandi et confirmandi, praesertim cum nequaquam sibi tantum otii nunc concederetur, quantum ad perlegendum et retexendum has pagellas satis esset, quas tumultuaria et interrupta saepe opera effuderit potius quam scripserit in hunc finem, ut mihi concionatorum causam diligentius cogitandi de dictis Matthaei Evangelistae praeberet, non ut in plurium manus illae pagellae spargerentur.

Extare aliorum iustos et eruditos in hunc Evangelistam commentarios, quos malit a concionatoris inspici et consuli, quam has suas annotationculas.

Cum igitur in hac sententia serio confirmatum viderem Dominum Philippum, quod nollet concedere editionem huius commentarii, coepi, ut ante dixi, mea manu eum transcribere, ut eius exemplum ad vos in patriam mitteretur.

Multas enim causas habebam, cur hunc Praeceptoris mei utilissimum laborem, quo ego in docenda Ecclesia hac non sine fructu auditorum, ut spero, usus eram, statuerem vobiscum communicandum esse.

Nam praeter illa sanctissima communis patriae vincula, quibus inter nos mutuo obligati sumus ad quaevis officia praestanda, movebant me vestra munificentia, qua mea studia in Academia Lipsica et hic Witebergae liberaliter provexistis, et alia beneficia vestra, quibus me longo iam tempore ab hoc absentem affecistis.

Deinde iudicabam me hoc patriae meae debere, ut cui in illustratione et propagatione purae doctrinae Evangelii coram prodesse ac servire non possem, absens ei impertirer illa, quae hic a viris eruditis et donorum excellentia praestantibus hausissem et collegissem.

His et aliis rationibus motus, dum exemplum vobis mearum concionum adornare laboro, uno quasi impetu in me irruunt aliquot hic collegae et amici mei, qui magno studio a me contendunt, ut hunc commentarium in Matthaeum, ut est, a Philippo scriptum, typis excudi curarem, quibus etsi ego, quid mihi obstaret, exponebam, nempe auctoris ipsius prohibitionem, quem offendendum hac editione non putarem, cum ipsum ad conscribendas meas conciones tam habuissem promptum, facilem et benignum: tamen illi urgere serio coeperunt, et ostendere simul literas aliunde huc missas (quae etiam ipse ex diversis locis frequentes acceperem). ram) quae summopere flagitabant, ut huius commentarii copia fieret, quacunque ratione, omnibus Ecclesiarum ministris.

Quod ad scriptoris rationes attineret, dicebant eas tanti non faciendas esse, ut hoc opus profuturum plurimis, si vulgetur, propterea intra unius parietes et scrinium concluderetur. Ut enim maxime sint aliqua in iis concionibus propter festinationem minus accurate, minus copiose, minus ordine, et simplicius explicata, quam ut debeant eruditorum censurae severiori subiici, tamen existimabant, imo affirmabant, aequos lectores, si praemoniti sint, cui hae conciones scriptae sint, a quam occupato, quam festinanter, quam longis interdum intervallis temporum, quae prius annotatorum sententiam et ordinem facile ex memoria scribentis delere potuerint, haud dubie eum candorem adhibituros esse in legendo et iudicando, ut res ipsas fideliter explicatas grato animo amplectantur, et cetera, quae cum aliis accuratioribus eiusdem auctoris scriptis, quod ad docendi methodum et eloquendi rationem attinet, minus congruere videbuntur, his impedimentis, quae scriptioni huius enarrationis subinde obiecta fuisse dixi, tribuant et condonent.

Reliquos vero Momos, qui novo quodam instituto laudem eruditionis et pietatis aucupantur, et summos se in Ecclesia fore confidunt, si omnia aliorum, qui antea cum auctoritate aliqua in Ecclesia docuerunt, quantumvis simpliciter et recte dicta, cavillationum strophis et sinistris interpretationibus odiosa ac suspecta vulgo reddant, adeo non curandos esse contendebant, ut eam ob causam etiam maturanda potius quam omittenda sit editio huius scripti, ut si illud more suo arripere mordicus et deformare falsis reprehensionibus isti conentur, suam cupiditatem nocendi et animi impotentiam omnibus bonis apertius prodant et patefaciant, nihil nocituram scriptori aut scripto, cum constet, non in hoc scriptas esse has annotationes, ut publicentur, nec autorem eas publicari voluisse.

Cur tu igitur eas edere audes? dicet aliquis.

Obsequor assiduis illorum monitionibus, petitionibus, obtestationibus, qui cum legendum hunc secreto commentarium a me precibus suis extorsissent, ita mihi eum reddiderunt postea, ut dicerent se eius perlectione multum adiutos et delectatos fuisse, et publicationem eiusdem plurimis ac praesertim versantibus in ministerio ecclesiastico, profuturam esse.

Aliqui etiam hoc addebant, editis his concionibus os obturandum esse iis, qui ad vulgus clamant, non amplius eandem doctrinam sonare in hac Ecclesia, quae vivente Luthero hic sit tradita, cum pius lector ex hoc scripto cognoscere possit, et eandem puritatem doctrinae hic conservari, et libere taxatas esse in publicis concionibus illo periculosissimo tempore corruptelas doctrinae coelestis, quales erant propositae in libro INTERIM, et aliis quorundam scriptis.

Erant etiam quidam, qui mihi aperte minitarentur, si non vellem edere has conciones, se omni arte illi scripto insidiaturos esse, nec quieturos, donec id a me auferrent, ut vel adhuc vivente me et ignorante, alibi excudatur, vel post mortem saltem meam spargatur.

His ego rationibus victus tandem consensi, et permisi, ut ederetur hic commentarius, etsi omnino constitueram eum in latebris asservare, et praeceptoris Philippi prohibitioni auscultare, quem quidem si hac publicatione offendi, reverenter oro, ut mihi clementer det veniam, quod tot bonorum et gravium virorum preces, hortationes, mandata, (inter quos etiam reverendus et sanctus vir Dominus D. Iohannes Bugenhagius Pastor meus, dum viveret, erat maxime assiduus flagitator) ipsius unius prohibitioni, tantum ex consideratione huius corrupti seculi et metu iniquarum reprehensionum profectae, anteposui, aliud nihil quaerens aut captans, quam si, quod multi pietate et prudentia praestantes viri existimant et certo mihi spondent futurum esse, aliquam utilitatem ex lectione harum concionum percipere poterunt ministri verbi et alii docti viri, ne per me illa eis interclusa et impedita per invidiam vel πλεονεξίαν fuisse videatur.

Iubet Christus ipse nos liberaliter doctrinam cum aliis communicare, cum inquit: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut glorificetur pater vester qui in coelis est. Item mittens Apostolos suos ad docendum Evangelium, inter alia etiam hoc ipsis mandatum dat: Quod dico vobis in tenebris, vos dicite in lumine, et quod in aure auditis, vos praedicate super tectis. Hunc finem spectanti mihi hac editione, ignoscat Dominus Praeceptor Philippus, nec existimet omnem inobedientiam semper scelus et detestandam esse, sed aliquam interdum non modo excusabilem, verum etiam laude dignam esse.

Praedicatur aliquot in locis ab Evangelistis inobedientia et linguae incontinentia eorum, qui a gravibus morbis divina virtute et benignitate Christi liberati, iussique id beneficium silentio occultare, minime obsequuntur benefactori suo Christo, victi magnitudine gaudii, sed ut Marcus inquit cap. 7. : Quanto magis iubentur tacere, tanto ipsi clamosius sanationem illam mirandam omnibus obviis praedicant.

Clementer igitur accipiatur et hoc meum factum, quod contra autoris voluntatem hoc scriptum, cuius lectione ego me plurimum adiutum profiteor, et alios omnes, quibus eius inspiciendi potestatem feci, idem iudicasse cognovi, solus asservare nolui, sed cum pluribus communicandum duxi, idque feci toties rogatus ab amicis, flagitatus a maioribus meis, iussus atque adeo propemodum coactus ab iis, quorum autoritatem ego defugere non debui.

BREVES COMMENTARII IN MATTHAEUM, CONSCRIPTI A PHILIPPO MELANTHONE.

Semper initio ante enarrationem Librorum, qui recitant historiam Evangelii, dicatur de discri- mine Legis et Evangelii.

Deinde cum de promissione dictum est, addatur ideo scriptas esse has Narrationes, ut Apostoli sint testes, et posteritas certa sit, quod missus sit Messias et exhibitus.

Tertio dicatur, In lectione evangelica haec quatuor contineri praecipue. 1. Narrationes, quis sit Christus, et unde sit. 2. Miracula testificantia eum non esse Impostorem, sed vere missum a Deo, et doctrinam eius esse veram. 3. Conciones Evangelii, id est, promissiones, ut: Omnis qui credit in Filium, non peribit. Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis etc. Item de vita aeterna. 4. Conciones de bonis operibus, quae sint velut Legis conciones et interpretationes Legis. Et pertinent ad doctrinam de poenitentia.

Estque diligenter observandum discrimen inter Praecepta et Promissiones, ne amittatur haec lux, quod remissio sit gratuita. Et tantum de Exordio.

## 1:1 Notes on Matthew: Argument
PHIL. MEL. ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

PRELIMINARY REMARKS.

Melanchthon expounded the Gospel of Matthew in the school at Wittenberg at the end of 1519 and the beginning of 1520. Regarding this exposition, Luther (T. I. Epp. p. 124. — in the Letters of Luther edited by de Wette, Vol. I. p. 380.) wrote on December 18, 1519: "I am sorry that I cannot send all the brothers to the theological lecture of Philip on Matthew at the sixth hour in the morning. That little Greek surpasses me even in Theology itself." However, Melanchthon himself, in a letter to Johann Hess (April 27, 1520, see above Vol. I. p. 158.), judged his exposition differently. For he wrote: "I have not yet finished Matthew. Nor is there any reason for you to desire our annotations or scholia. We have treated the Evangelist more briefly than is proper, speaking more in proverbs [παροιμιαζόμενοι] and preluding to a proper exposition." — That he truly had in mind to publish this exposition, he himself professed in a letter to Schwebelius on December 11, 1529 (Vol. I. p. 128.), when he wrote: "We are now doing the same on Matthew, and perhaps we shall publish Commentaries on Matthew." Which, however, he did not do later. But without Melanchthon's knowledge, in the year 1523, a bookseller published these scholia, which had been taken down by the pen by certain students, inscribed as follows:

Annotations on the Gospel of Matthew by Phil. Melanth. (without place). Month of May 1523. 8vo. 5 1/2 sheets. The bookseller did not profess his name. — The same book, augmented with scholia on the history of the passion, which truly did not have Melanchthon as their author, as the bookseller himself professed, appeared in the same year:

Annotations of Phil. Mel. on the Gospel of Matthew, now recently edited for the benefit of students. At Hagenau by Io. Secerius, 1523, month of November. (8vo. 7 1/2 sheets.)

Mel. on the Gospel of Matthew and on the history of the passion of the Lord. At Strasbourg, month of December, year 1523. 8vo.

Furthermore: Annotations of Phil. Mel. on the Gospel of Matthew, edited for the use of those progressing in Christ. Printed in the year M.D.XXIII, month of December. 8vo. — (It exists in the library of the Gotha Gymnasium.)

Basle. Vol. I. p. 131.

Finally: Annotations of Philippi Mel. on the Gospel of Matthew and on the passion of the Lord. Also, on the same Evangelist and on Luke, brief but learned scholia by a certain scholar, with a preface by Melanth. At Hagenau by Io. Secerius, 1526. 8vo. — The book was reprinted ibid. 1531. 8vo. 19 1/4 sheets. — (We have not seen this book.)

Strobelius, in his booklet: "On Melanchthon's Merits for the Holy Scripture," p. 72, mentioned that these Scholia of Melanchthon were also reprinted in Italy, with Melanchthon's name changed slightly to Hippophilus Melangaeus, and that Daniel Gerdesius wrote in his book: "Specimen Italiae Reformatae": "To this day, there exists in the Index of Prohibited Books a commentary on the Gospel of Matthew by Hippophilus Melangaeus, among the prohibited books, from which we gather that even under this mask that book of Melanchthon was brought into Italy.

He touches the secret Jews, who had more confidence in their works and in Abraham than in his faith, and it is a judgment. The Lord's winnowing fan, that is, the judgment, will purge his threshing floor, that is, the earth, and will gather the elect into grace, that is, the wheat, and will burn the chaff, that is, the non-believers in Christ, with unquenchable fire. But our baptism is also a trial and adversity.

Latin:

PHIL. MEL. ANNOTATIONES IN EVANGELIUM MATTHAEI.

PRAEMONENDA.

Evangelium Matthaei Melanthon enarravit in schola Witebergensi anno 1519 exeunte et 1520 ineunte, de qua enarratione Lutherus (T. I. Epp. p. 124. — in Epp. Lutheri a de Wettio editis Tom. I. p. 380.) d. 18. Decb. 1519 scripsit: „Doleo me non posse vel omnes fratres ad lectionem theol. Philippi in Matthaeum hora sexta matutina mittere. Superat iste Graeculus me queque in ipsa Theologia.“ Ipse autem Melanthon in epist. ad Ioann. Hessum (d. 27. April 1520, vid. supra Vol. I. p. 158.) aliter iudicavit de sua enarratione. Scripsit enim: „Matthaeum nondum absolvi. Nec est, quod annotationes seu scholia nostra desideres. Brevius aequo tractavimus Evangelistam magis παροιμιαζόμενοι ac praeludentes justae enarrationi.“ — Illum vero in animo habuisse hanc enarrationem in lucem edere, ipse professus est in ep. ad Schwebelium d. 11. Decb. 1529 (Vol. I. p. 128.), dum scribit: „Idem nunc in Matthaeum agimus, et forte Commentarios in Matthaeum publicabimus.“ Quod autem postea non fecit. At inscio Melanthone a. 1523 bibliopola haec scholia, a quibusdam studiosis calamo excepta, in lucem edidit, sic inscripta:

In Evangelium Matthaei annotationes Phil. Melanth. (sine loco). Mense Maio 1523. 8. 5 1/2 pl. Librarius nomen suum non professus est. — Idem liber, auctus scholiis in historiam passionis, quae vere Melanthonem non habuerunt auctorem, ut librarius ipse professus est, prodiit eodem anno:

Annotationes Phil. Mel. in Evangelium Matthaei, iam recens in gratiam studiosorum editae. Hagenoae per Io. Secerium 1523. mense Novb. (8. 7 1/2 pl.)

Iterum: Annotationes Phil. Mel. in Evangelium Matthaei inque historiam passionis domini. Argentorati, mense Decb. anno 1523. 8.

Porro: Annotationes Phil. Mel. in Evangelium Matthaci in usum proficientium in Christo in lucem editae. Excudebatur anno M.D.XXIII. mense Decb. 8. — (Extat in bibliotheca Gymnasii Gothani.)

Recusae in operibus Melanth. Basileens. Tom. I. p. 131.

Denique: In Evang. Matth. inque passionem domini Philippi Mel. annotationes. Item in eundem Evangelistam et in Lucam eruditi cuiusdam brevia quidem sed docta scholia cum praef. Melanth. Haganoae per Io. Secerium 1526. 8. — Recusus est liber ibid. 1531. 8. 19 1/4 pl. — (Hunc librum non vidimus.)

Strobelius in libello: Von Melanchthons Verdiensten um die heilige Schrift p. 72., commemoravit, haec Melanthonis Scholia in Italia quoque recusa esse, mutato paululum Melanthonis nomine in Hippophilum Melangaeum, et Danielem Gerdesium in suo libro: „Specimen Italiae Reformatae“ scripsisse: „Extat in hunc usque diem in Indice librorum prohibitorum Hippophili Melangaei commentarius in Evangelium Matthaei, inter libros prohibitos, unde colligimus, etiam sub hac larva illum Melanchthonis librum in Italiam esse delatum.“

Tangit clanculum Iudaeos, qui plus fiduciae habebant in Abraham quam in eius fidem, et opera. Ventilabrum domini, id est iudicium, Repurgabit aream suam, et terram, et congregabit triticum, id est convocabit electos in gratiam, Paleam autem, id est, non credentes in Christum, Baptismos sine fide nihil est. Baptismus nostrarum tentationum et adversitatum est ancora.

## 1:1 Sermons on Matthew: Argument
Chapter I. of Matthew. The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, etc. I.

The first chapter narrates the series of the Fathers from Abraham onwards, and then the Nativity of Christ from a virgin.

And thus Matthew testifies that the Messiah has been manifested, and he recites the testimonies and miracles of others. This is the summary of the first chapter.

II.

But the very recitation of the fathers suggests many things.

First, that there has always been a Church, and what kind it was and where it was, and that without the promise concerning the Messiah, there was no Church, nor can there be.

The Church is therefore such a visible assembly embracing the Gospel, in which through the ministry

of the Gospel or of the promise, God is efficacious and regenerates all who truly believe. But to this multitude are mixed many who consent by external profession, but yet do not truly believe in their heart. And such a Church is bound to its promise, and in this faith it calls upon God, even if meanwhile it is variously exercised by the cross; in external appearance it is miserable, dispersed into various empires.

Such was the Church of Abraham; Shem was the Bishop, afterwards he himself also became a Bishop, and they have many good and truly believing listeners, such as his son Isaac, Sarah the mother, Hagar, Abimelech. But there are also some hypocrites, such as perhaps Ishmael, and certainly some, such as later Esau.

Now consider what kind of Church this of Abraham was; it learned the word of God, and by faith in the promise acknowledged mercy, and thus called upon God. By this faith it was pleasing, as the text says: Abraham believed God etc.

Then he lived also in good works, he exercised faith in the cross, in exiles, in dangers, he was a father of a family, a preacher, a warrior, and he was patient, where God demands patience. Thus the perpetual Church must be thought of backwards, to confirm us, so that we may know whence this word is, which we learn. Also that we may consider whether the present doctrine agrees with the doctrine of Abraham. Also that, looking upon them, we may know what kind of thing the Church is, and compare ourselves to that image, so that we may console ourselves against the scandal of the cross, and not think that we are therefore not the Church of God, because we are pressed by many miseries etc. Let these things be said in general, afterwards let the promise made to Abraham be briefly repeated.

III.

It can be briefly said that the seed of the Gentiles is also in this series in the ancestors of Christ, so that it may be signified that the Church is to be gathered from the Gentiles.

IIII.

The histories of individual persons would provide individual books, but nevertheless let the pious readers themselves consider the notable examples which profit us, such as the example of David doing penance. The example of Manasseh doing penance. This consideration shows the Church of all times, and confirms faith in us.

V.

I will not speak about reconciling the genealogies, but I will leave these to the schools, but the reconciliation is easy. Luke leads Christ from Nathan the son of David; from whose natural descendants Christ was born. Matthew from Solomon, because he was the father by law, because he was King.

VI.

A notable example is the destruction of Jerusalem and the return from Babylon. This is a notable doctrine, God had promised that He would preserve that polity. Because of this promise the Jews thought in carnal security that their kingdom could not be destroyed, and yet it was destroyed, because God wants us to live in true penance, and He keeps His promises, not in such a way as we dream, just as, in the first place, this example splendidly teaches.

After the return the state was more deformed than before, even greater sins followed. The sects of the Pharisees, of the Sadducees: and yet God preserved the remnants, the true Church remained.

Herod killed the entire council of the seventy elders, the Sanhedrin.

Some time before Herod, Ptolemy Lathyrus killed twenty thousand Jews, and forced the captives to eat the flesh of the dead.

Latin:

Caput I. Matthaei. Liber generationis Iesu Christi etc. I.

Primum Caput narrat seriem Patrum inde usque ab Abraham, et deinde Nativitatem Christi ex virgine.

Et sic testatur Matthaeus Messiam exhibi- tum esse, et recitat aliorum testimonia et mira- cula. Haec est summa primi capitis.

II.

Sed ipsa recitatio patrum multa monet.

Primum quod semper fuerit Ecclesia, et qua- lis et ubi fuerit, et quod sine promissione de Mes- sia, nulla fuerit Ecclesia, nec esse possit.

Est igitur Ecclesia talis coetus visibilis am- plectens Evangelium, in quo per ministerium

Evangelii seu promissionis Deus est efficax, et re- generat omnes vere credentes. Sed huic multitu- dini sunt admixti multi externa professione con- sentientes, sed tamen non vere in corde creden- tes. Et talis Ecclesia est alligata suae promissioni, et in hac fide invocat Deum, etiamsi interea varie exercetur cruce, Specie externa est misera, di- spersa in varia imperia.

Talis fuit Ecclesia Abrahae, Sem fuit Epi- scopus, postea et ipse fit Episcopus, et habent mul- tos auditores bonos et vere credentes, ut filium Isaac, Saram matrem, Agar, Abimelech. Sed aliqui etiam sunt hypocritae, ut fortassis Ismaël, et certe aliqui, ut postea Esau.

Iam cogita, qualis haec Ecclesia Abrahae fuerit, didicit verbum Dei, et fide promissionis agnovit misericordiam, et sic invocavit Deum. Hac fide placuit, ut dicit textus: Credidit Abra- ham Deo etc.

Deinde vixit et in bonis operibus, exercuit fidem in cruce, in exiliis, in periculis, fuit Pater- familias, praedicator, bellator, et fuit patiens, ubi Deus postulat patientiam. Ita retro cogitanda est perpetua Ecclesia, ad nos confirmandos, ut sciamus, unde sit hoc ver- bum, quod discimus. Item ut consideremus, an praesens doctrina consentiat cum Abrahae doctri- na. Item ut intuentes in illos, sciamus, qualis sit Ecclesia, et ad eam imaginem nos ipsos confe- ramus, ut consolemur nos contra scandalum cru- cis, nec putemus nos propterea non esse Eccle- siam Dei, quod multis aerumnis premimur etc. Haec in genere dicantur, postea breviter re- petatur promissio facta Abrahae.

III.

Breviter dici potest, quod etiam semen gen- tium sit in hac serie in den voreltern Christi, ut significetur Ecclesiam ex gentibus colligendam esse.

IIII.

Historiae singularum personarum praeberent singulos libros, sed tamen ipsi pii legentes consi- derent insignia exempla, quae nobis prosunt, ut exemplum David agentis poenitentiam. Exem- plum Manasse agentis poenitentiam. Haec consideratio monstrat Ecclesiam omnium temporum, et fidem in nobis confirmat.

V.

Non dicam de genealogiis conciliandis, sed relinquam haec scholis, sed facilis est conciliatio. Lucas ducit Christum a Nathan filio David; ex cuius posteris naturalibus, Christus natus est. Matthaeus a Salomone, quia hic fuit Pater lege, quia fuit Rex.

VI.

Insigne exemplum est destructio Ierosolymae et reductio ex Babylone, Haec est insignis doctri- na, Deus promiserat se illam politiam servatu- rum esse. Propter hanc promissionem Iudaei carnali securitate putabant non posse destrui suum re- gnum, et destruebatur tamen, quia Deus vult nos in vera poenitentia vivere, et servat promissiones, non tali modo, qualem nos somniamus, sicut in- primis, hoc exemplum splendide docet.

Post reditum erat deformior status quam an- tea, etiam peccata maiora sequebantur. Sectae Pharisaeorum, Sadducaeorum: et tamen Deus servavit reliquias, mansit vera Ecclesia.

Herodes interfecit totum concilium seniorum septuaginta, Sanhedrin.

Aliquanto ante Herodem Ptolemaeus Lamy- rus interfecit viginti millia Iudaeorum, et coëgit captivos vesci carne mortuorum.

## 1:2 Sermons on Matthew
Abraham begat Isaac.

The enumeration is useful for this, that with the order of the Fathers and histories known, we may know for certain when and by what testimonies the promises were handed down, and whence Christ was born, and we may know that this doctrine concerning the Messiah was handed down by God with certain testimonies, and is not an empty fable. Therefore, in the histories of the individual Fathers, wonderful testimonies must be considered.

In Abraham, that Isaac is born from an old and sterile mother.

In Isaac, that he was miraculously liberated in his immolation.

In Jacob, that he was miraculously defended against Esau and Laban.

In Nahshon, that he was present at the leading out through the Red Sea.

In David, that he defeated Goliath and others with divine aid.

In Abijah, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah, that they had miraculous victories.

In Shealtiel, that he was miraculously brought back from Babylon.

These and similar works of God are testimonies of the doctrine.

Latin:

Abraham genuit Isaac.

Enumeratio ad hoc prodest, ut cognito or- dine Patrum, et historiarum, certo sciamus, quando, et quibus testimoniis promissiones tradi- tae sint, et unde Christus natus sit, et sciamus hanc doctrinam de Messia certis testimoniis a Deo traditam esse, et non esse inanem fabulam. Ideo in singulorum Patrum historiis miranda testimo- nia consideranda sunt.

In Abraham, quod nascitur Isaac ex matre anu et sterili.

In Isaac, quod in immolatione mirabiliter liberatus est.

In Iacob, quod mirabiliter defensus est con- tra Esau et Laban.

In Nahasson, quod interfuit eductioni per mare rubrum.

In David, quod vicit auxilio divino Goliath et alios.

In Abia, Iosaphat, Ezechia, Iosia, quod habuerunt mirandas victorias.

In Salathiel, quod mirabiliter reductus est ex Babylone.

Haec et similia opera Dei sunt testimonia doctrinae.

## 1:18 Sermons on Matthew
She was found to be with child, etc.

The following narrative recounts the history of the Conception and Nativity of the Messiah from a virgin.

Here first let the beginning of the narrative of John be added, and let it be spoken of the two natures in the Messiah.

Secondly, let the listener be admonished to observe in order the testimonies concerning the conception and nativity from a virgin; God wishes us to be certain about this Messiah: therefore many witnesses are recited here, the Angel confirms Joseph, afterwards Elizabeth also becomes a witness concerning the conception.

Then follow the witnesses concerning the Nativity: Angels, Shepherds, Magi, Simeon, Anna.

On the office of Christ.

He shall save his people from their sins. Here the error of the Pharisees is censured, who dreamed that the Messiah would deliver the Jews from bodily servitude and give them the empire of the world.

On the saying of Isaiah.

Behold, a virgin is with child, and shall bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel. Here it is spoken of the appellation, which embraces the doctrine concerning the person of Christ, that there are two natures in him, and concerning his office, that God is with us, and being appeased, saves us, etc.

Latin:

Inventa est in utero habens etc.

Sequens narratio recitat historiam de Con- ceptione et Nativitate Messiae ex virgine.

Hic primum addatur initium narrationis Io- hannis, et dicatur de duabus naturis in Messia.

Secundo admoneatur auditor, ut observet ordine testimonia de conceptione et nativitate ex virgine, vult nos Deus certos esse de hoc Messia: ideo multi hic testes recitantur, Angelus confir- mat Ioseph, postea et Elizabeth fit testis de con- ceptione.

Deinde sequuntur testes de Nativitate, An- geli, Pastores, Magi, Simeon, Anna.

De officio Christi.

Salvabit populum a peccatis. Hic taxatur error Pharisaeorum, qui somniabant Messiam liberaturum esse Iudaeos, a corporali servitute, et daturum eis imperium mundi.

De dicto Esaiae.

Ecce virgo est gravida, et pariet filium, et vocabis nomen eius Emmanuel. Hic dicatur de appellatione, quae complectitur doctrinam de persona Christi, quod duae sint in ea naturae, et de officio, Quod Deus sit nobiscum, placatus salvet nos etc.

## 1:18 Sermons on Matthew
On Joseph.

Why is he called just, not wishing to defame his spouse? This example teaches that we ought to spare another's reputation when we do not have certain causes for our own reproach.

Latin:

De Ioseph.

Quare dicitur iustus nolens infamare coniugem? Hoc exemplum docet, nos debere parcere alienae famae, cum non habemus certas causas nostrae reprehensionis.

## 2:1-12 On the Epiphany of the Lord
On the Epiphany of the Lord. The Gospel

Matth. 2. Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the East to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the East, and are come to worship him. When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And when he had gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people together, he demanded of them where Christ should be born. And they said unto him: In Bethlehem of Judea. For thus it is written by the Prophet: And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel. Then Herod, when he had privily called the wise men, enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said: Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also. When they had heard the king, they departed; and, lo, the star, which they saw in the East, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy. And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh. And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.

Five points. I. The testimony concerning the born Messiah. II. Concerning the calling of the Gentiles. III. The testimony of the Prophet concerning the place, and the place is named, so that it might confirm us also concerning the time, namely that while the polity of this people stood, it was necessary for Christ to come. IV. Persecution follows immediately upon the birth of Christ. V. The Magi offer gifts, so that the infant and his parents might have sustenance.

Concerning the first. We often say that a distinction must be observed between empires and the Church. The victories of Alexander are seen by the eyes of all, and have the testimonies of all nations: but the things which are done in the Church do not so strike the eyes, and yet there must be certain testimonies. Although, therefore, not everyone knew that the Messiah had been born there, yet many testimonies are set forth, so that faith may be certain. The mother knows that she gave birth as a virgin, Joseph hears the same from angels: the angels announce to the shepherds that the Messiah is born: now the star warns the Magi, who were afterwards witnesses that the Messiah was born, nor does it matter whether it was a new star, or an angel, as Chrysostom understands it. Thus, the remaining testimonies are to be considered in turn, so that we may confirm our faith, and know for certain that the Messiah has been exhibited, and that this is the savior, and that he will do the things which he promised, will hear us, etc.

Concerning the second. Concerning the calling of the Gentiles.

The Magi were properly called the priests of the Persians, whom it is necessary to have had some doctrine concerning the coming savior: for otherwise why would they seek a king in Judea, whom they knew to be oppressed by miserable servitude? I believe, however, that there were remnants of the Church of Daniel, who was a governor of Persia: and that they were pious, such as were very many among the Gentiles, who called upon God by the faith of the promises handed down.

to the people of Israel, even though they were not burdened by ceremonies. Moreover, they knew from Daniel that the Messiah would also come around those times.

And this example is a notable testimony that the Gospel pertains to the Gentiles. And when it is spoken of the calling of the Gentiles, this doctrine is simultaneously included, that the remission of sins is given freely, not on account of the law. Let this consolation also come to mind.

On the third. On the passage of Micah.

It is a useful testimony for refuting the Jews at this time, that Christ had to be born in Bethlehem: therefore it is necessary that he has already come, because he had to be born while that polity stood, which God utterly destroyed, so that it might testify that Christ has come. O wondrous counsels of God, the Jewish destruction confirms the pious, and convicts the obstinacy of the Jews.

Moreover, this also is to be observed in the saying of Micah, that he discourses about both natures in Christ; he says: that a leader would come from Bethlehem, that is said concerning the birth from a virgin. Then he adds: His going forth is before the beginning of the world. Here he testifies that he was born of the Father before the beginning of the world. Now here it must be said what kind of leader he is who delivers: namely, from true evils, from sin, from the wrath of God, and from eternal death: and he effects this liberation by his word in believers, not on account of our dignity. These things are to be thought upon in this place.

On the fourth. On the persecution.

When Christ was born, Herod and the Pharisees immediately feared a change of kingdom: therefore they attempt to remove him. And here simulation must be diligently considered. Thus the Church is always attacked by simulation and open force.

On the fifth. The Magi offer gifts.

The Magi recognize this infant to be the Messiah, because they were undoubtedly such as I described above, disciples of the Prophets, who held the doctrine concerning the future Messiah, just as this doctrine was widely scattered throughout the whole world. And they had already heard the prophecy of Micah in Jerusalem, by which they were also confirmed. Nor is there any doubt that they conferred much about such scriptures there with Joseph, Zechariah, and the rest of the fellowship.

Furthermore, this whole example is an illustrious picture of the Church, what it is like, in what dangers it is involved, how it is defended and nourished, not by human counsels, but by God governing. The Church is a gathering of a few, dispersed—Mary, Joseph, Zechariah, Elizabeth, Simeon, Anna, the Shepherds, the Magi, and the like—while in the meantime the Pontiffs and other impious men, warring against the word of God, assumed the title for themselves, whereas the Church is only there where the word of God is. The enemies are Herod and the Pontiffs, and this Church is defended against Herod and nourished by the gifts of the Magi. Here God preserves the Church in a wondrous way, even in this life, as the Psalm says, I have not seen the righteous forsaken in famine, etc.

Allegory.

The Magi offer Gold, Frankincense, and Myrrh; in these is a beautiful significance, although first the bodily benefit must be considered, which God wished to provide for the sustenance of the mother and the child through the gift offered by the Magi. Because God wills that churches be sustained by the liberality of some pious princes or wealthy people. And that Christ esteems these benefits highly, he himself testifies when he says: Whatever you did to one of these least of mine, you did to me. Likewise: Whoever shall give to anyone a cup of cold water in my name, etc. Thus also Paul most sweetly gives thanks to Philemon, because he had received and helped the poor and needy ministers: The hearts of the saints, he says, have been refreshed by you.

Gold regularly signifies the pure doctrine of faith. As in the Psalm: Thy law is like the purest gold. Frankincense signifies invocation and confession. Myrrh [signifies] the cross and the afflictions which follow confession.

We too ought to offer these gifts to Christ. The first act of worship is the study of doctrine, and faith. The second is invocation. For thus He is truly worshipped, not when we give to Him, but when we ask from Him. But He must be invoked with faith, that is, with confidence in the mediator Christ, not on account of our merits. Afterwards follow afflictions, not only bodily ones, but also the snares of the devil. And God wills the Church to be subject to afflictions, so that faith may be exercised in them.

Latin:

In Epiphaniis Domini. Evangelium

Matth. 2. Cum autem natus esset Iesus in Bethlehem Iudae in diebus Herodis regis, Ecce Magi ab Oriente venerunt Ierosolymam, dicentes: Ubi est qui natus est rex Iudaeorum? vidimus enim stellam eius in Oriente, et venimus adorare eum. Audiens autem Herodes rex, turbatus est, et omnis Ierosolyma cum illo. Et congregans omnes principes sacerdotum et scribas populi, sciscitabatur ab eis, ubi Christus nasceretur. At illi dixerunt ei: In Bethlehem Iudaeae. Sic enim scriptum est per Prophetam: Et tu Bethlehem terra Iuda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Iuda, ex te enim exibit mihi dux, qui regat populum meum Israël. Tunc Herodes clam vocatis Magis, diligenter didicit ab eis tempus stellae quae apparuerat, et mittens illos in Bethlehem, dixit: Ite et exquirite diligenter de puero, et cum inveneritis, renunciate mihi, ut et ego veniens adorem eum. Qui cum audissent regem, abierunt. Et ecce stella, quam viderant in Oriente, antecedebat eos, usque dum veniens staret supra ubi erat puer. Videntes autem stellam, gavisi sunt gaudio magno valde. Et intrantes domum, invenerunt puerum cum Maria matre eius, et procidentes adoraverunt eum. Et apertis thesauris suis, obtulerunt ei munera, Aurum, Thus et Myrrham, Et oraculo admoniti in somnis, ne redirent ad Herodem, per aliam viam reversi sunt in regionem suam.

Loci quinque. I. Testimonium de nato Messia. II. De vocatione gentium. III. Testimonium Prophetae de loco, et locus nominatus est, ut de tempore etiam nos confirmet, quod videlicet stante politia huius populi, venire Christum oportuerit. IV. Nato Christo mox sequitur persecutio. V. Magi offerunt munera, ut infans et parentes habeant victum.

De primo. Saepe dicimus dissimilitudinem observandam esse imperiorum et Ecclesiae. Alexandri victoriae conspiciuntur omnium oculis, et omnium gentium testimonia habent: sed res, quae geruntur in Ecclesia, non sic incurrunt in oculos, et tamen oportet esse certa testimonia. Quanquam igitur non omnes norant ibi natum esse Messiam, tamen multa sunt testimonia proposita, ut fides sit certa. Mater scit se virginem peperisse, Ioseph audit idem ex angelis: Nunciant angeli pastoribus, natum esse Messiam: nunc stellam monet magos, qui postea erant testes nati Messiae, nec refert utrum stella nova, aut angelus fuerit, ut Chrysostomus intelligit. Ita deinceps reliqua testimonia consideranda sunt, ut fidem nostram confirmemus, et certo sciamus exhibitum esse Messiam, et hunc esse salvatorem, et facturum ea, quae promisit, exauditurum nos etc.

De secundo. De vocatione gentium.

Magi proprie dicebantur Persarum sacerdotes, quos necesse est aliquam habuisse de venturo salvatore doctrinam: alioqui enim cur in Iudaea quaererent regem, quam sciebant oppressam esse misera servitute? Arbitror autem fuisse reliquias Ecclesiae Danielis, qui fuit praefectus Persiae: ac fuisse pios, quales plurimi erant inter gentes, qui invocabant Deum fide promissionum traditarum.

populo Israël, etiamsi ceremoniis non oneraban- tur. Sciebant autem ex Daniele etiam circiter ea tempora venturum esse Messiam.

Estque hoc exemplum insigne testimonium, quod Evangelium ad gentes pertineat. Et cum de vocatione gentium dicitur, simul comprehen- ditur haec doctrina, quod gratis, non propter le- gem donetur remissio peccatorum. Haec conso- latio simul • niat in mentem.

De tertio. De loco Micheae.

Utile testimonium est ad refutandos hoc tem- pore Iudaeos, oportuit nasci Christum in Beth- lehem: ergo necesse est eum venisse iam, quia oportuit eum stante politia illa nasci, quam Deus funditus delevit, ut testetur venisse Christum. O mira Dei consilia, excidium Iudaicum confir- mat pios, et convincit Iudaeorum pertinaciam.

Est autem et hoc observandum in dicto Mi- cheae, quod de utraque natura in Christo concio- natur, dicit: ducem venturum esse ex Bethlehem, id de nativitate ex virgine dicitur. Deinde addit: Egressus eius ante initium mundi. Hic testatur eum esse natum ex patre ante initium mundi. Iam hic dicendum est, qualis sit dux, qui liberat. vi- delicet, a veris malis, a peccato, ab ira Dei, et a morte aeterna: et hanc liberationem verbo suo efficit in credentibus, non propter nostram di- gnitatem. Haec cogitanda sunt hoc loco.

De quarto. De persecutione.

Nato Christo statim metuunt mutationem re- gni Herodes et Pharisaei: ideo conantur eum tol- lere. Et diligenter hic consideranda est simu- latio. Sic semper Ecclesia oppugnantur simu- latione et aperta vi.

De quinto. Magi offerunt munera.

Magi agnoscunt hunc infantem esse Messiam, quia haud dubie fuerunt tales, quales supra de- scripsi, discipuli Prophetarum, qui tenuerunt doctrinam de futuro Messia, sicut haec doctrina late toto orbe terrarum sparsa fuit. Et iam Hie- rosolymis audierant vaticinium Micheae, quo etiam confirmati sunt. Nec dubium est, quin de talibus scripturis multa cum Ioseph, Zacharia et reliquo sodalitio ibi contulerint.

Porro hoc totum exemplum est illustris pi- ctura Ecclesiae, qualis sit, in quibus periculis versetur, quomodo defendatur, et alatur, non humanis consiliis, sed Deo gubernante. Ecclesia est coetus paucorum dispersus, Mariae, Ioseph, Zachariae, Elisabeth, Simeonis, Annae, Pasto- rum, Magorum, et similium, cum interim sibi titulum sumerent Pontifices, et alii impii cum verbo Dei belligerantes, cum Ecclesia tantum ibi sit, ubi est verbum Dei. Hostes sunt Herodes et Pontifices, et defenditur haec Ecclesia adversus Herodem, et alitur muneribus Magorum. Hic Deus mirabili modo servat Ecclesiam, etiam in hac vita, sicut inquit Psalmus, Non vidi iustum derelictum in fame, etc.

Allegoria.

Magi offerunt Aurum, Thus, Myrrham, in his est pulcra significatio, quanquam prius con- siderandum est beneficium corporale, quod Deus munere oblato a Magis voluerit curare victum matri et puero. Quia Deus vult sustentari Eccle- sias liberalitate aliquorum piorum principum aut locupletum. Et quod haec beneficia magni aesti- met Christus, testatur ipse, cum dicit: Quod- cunque fecistis uni ex minimis meis, mihi fecistis. Item: Qui dederit alicui potum aquae frigidae in nomine meo etc. Sic et Paulus dulcissime gratias agit Philemoni, quod exceperit et iuverit paupe- res et egentes ministros: Refecta sunt, inquit, abs te viscera sanctorum.

Aurum regulariter significat puram doctri- nam fidei. Sicut in Psalm.: Lex tua sicut aurum purissimum. Thus significat invocationem et confessionem. Myrrha crucem et afflictiones, quae sequuntur confessionem.

Haec munera nos quoque debemus offerre Christo. Primus cultus est studium doctrinae, et fides. Secundus est invocatio. Nam sic vere colitur, non cum ipsi damus, sed cum ab eo pe- timus. Sed invocari debet fide, id est, fiducia mediatoris Christi, non propter nostra merita. Postea sequuntur afflictiones, non tantum corpo- rales, sed etiam diaboli insidiae. Et Deus vult Ecclesiam subiectam esse afflictionibus, ut in his exerceatur fides.

## 2:1 Sermons on Matthew: Argument
Chapter II. The history of the Magi.

First, it must be said that God has provided testimonies concerning the born Son, so that the Church might be certain. For although those things which are done in the Church do not strike the eyes as much as the battles of Alexander or Julius, yet God grants testimony even to these things which are done in the Church. And let us gather these testimonies to confirm ourselves. The Angels, Shepherds, Simeon, Anna, Zacharias, Elizabeth, and the Magi testify that the Son of God, the Messiah, was born.

Second doctrine.

Even the Gentiles belong to the Church, and this is the first confession of the Gentiles after Christ was born. But when it is spoken of the gathering of the Church from the Gentiles, it is said at the same time that the remission of sins is given freely, not because of the law, but because of the Messiah, according to that: In your seed shall all nations be blessed.

3. Who were those Magi? Persian men, undoubtedly the remnants of the school of Daniel. For Daniel was a governor in Persia. Thus God has always gathered some Church from the Gentiles: and therefore the Israelites were dispersed, so that they might teach elsewhere, and it is consistent that in Germany formerly many were rightly recognizing and calling upon God in the acknowledgment of the promise concerning the Messiah.

4. The miracle of the star is a testimony of the presence of God among these Magi, because this was a new star closer to the earth than others, because it was the pointer of the very house in which Mary was. And it is necessary that they were learned men, who knew the differences of the stars in some way.

5. Doctrine, Herod and the Princes are terrified: Thus, with the preaching of the Gospel having arisen, Princes always fear for their tranquility.

6. The saying of Micah: And you, Bethlehem, teaches of the divine and human generation, and affirms that the Messiah was before the beginning of the world. And yet that he was to be born in Bethlehem. Therefore he will assume human nature. He speaks also of his office: A leader who shall feed my people Israel, a leader who shall deliver us from the highest evils, from sin, death, and the kingdom of the devil.

7. The deceits of Herod. The Gospel is opposed by force and fraud.

8. The Magi come to the child, and there they show their confession, they affirm that this is the Messiah, and there were undoubtedly sweet conversations concerning the prophetic promises. They gave gold and other things, so the rich must always contribute something to support the ministry.

9. There is also this sweet allegory of the gifts: Gold is faith: Doctrine is Frankincense, Invocation, Sacrifice: Myrrh is the Cross.

10. The flight of Christ and Mary, and the solicitude of God for the Church: he commands them to flee, and gives them hospitality elsewhere.

11. The persecution, the slaughter of the children carried out by Herod. Here let it first be said concerning the Infants. This history is a testimony that infants in the Church are pleasing to God, have the Holy Spirit, and are heirs of eternal life, because these infants were without any doubt holy, and are praised as holy, through the saying which the Apostle cites concerning the truly holy, because the children of Rachel are the children of the Church and heirs of eternal life.

And where there is the inheritance of eternal life, there is the Holy Spirit. Therefore, as in these infants, so in ours, the Holy Spirit is efficacious, etc. And the Anabaptists are to be condemned for teaching the contrary.

Here it must be learned that there are various causes of afflictions in the Church; it is true that we are often punished for certain sins.

As David is punished for adultery. But besides this cause there are also others, namely, the enormity of the hatred in the devil, who often rages even against those who do not have their own sins, as Daniel, Jeremiah, and the like, did not have sins for which they themselves, like the others, were led away into exile, but there were other causes why they were involved in a common calamity.

So now, when calamities come, let us know that there are many whose sins have deserved them. But let us know at the same time that the devil, because of the magnitude of his hatred, rages against many innocent people. Wherefore let us not despair, but let us know that God will hear the cries of the Church and will repress the cruelty of the devil, just as in this history, in the saying of Jeremiah, the Church weeps and cries out and fears universal destruction, as it says: She refused to admit consolation, because they are not, because they all seem about to perish.

And God wants us in such dangers not only to pray for our own sins, but also against the devil, and to know that God wants to hear us asking for help against the devil.

For our sins we suffer justly. But as far as the devil is concerned, we suffer unjustly, therefore God hears us.

Here let us also consider how great this persecution was. Not only did the children suffer, but much more the parents, because no human pain is greater than the pain from the calamity of one's children.

Why? Because God wanted this affection to be a sign of His love toward the Son and toward us. Consolation is to be considered; the Church then had no defense, and yet it was preserved.

Herod killed the children, and before that he had killed seventy Elders, who were the highest government.

The Pharisees themselves had killed Zechariah, and many such things were done. Therefore let us not be so delicate, tender, that we are unwilling to suffer anything, but let us recognize the customary cross of the Church, and let us hope that God will nevertheless preserve a remnant.

Nazirite.

Nazirites were those under a vow among the people, to whom God had handed down the form of the vow, and they did not drink wine, did not shave their hair, etc.

This was an institution like many other external exercises in the law, so that there might be a more notable confession, because singular ceremonies make a man more conspicuous, but it signified a true preacher dedicated to God, not corrupting the doctrine with his drunkenness, etc., not drunk with the desire for glory, with human opinions.

Christ, however, was not such a Nazirite by ceremonies, because He drank wine, but He was the signified Nazirite, that is, the purest, and a preacher dedicated to God, not drunk with human opinions, but preaching the word purely.

Likewise without the desire for glory, etc. Chapter III.

First, let the state of the Church of that time be considered here.

There were three sects, and one was entirely impious, the Sadducees.

And the Pharisees were also for the most part impious; a few perhaps, just like some Monks among us, were sounder. This example shows that often the greater part of the Church errs greatly.

Meanwhile, however, God preserves some, as there were then Zechariah, Simeon, Elizabeth, Anna, Mary, Joseph, and many others. Thus God preserves a seed for Himself, even if the impious dominate.

Let us propose this image to ourselves, so that we may be comforted now also, when the adversaries cry out that the Church does not err, and that they are the Church, etc. In such darkness God again kindles the light, calls John, and commands him to institute baptism and to preach the Gospel in the desert.

Thus God, by His wonderful mercy, from time to time restores the Church. But here it is asked whether it is permitted to act against the ordinary power, just as John departed from the temple.

I answer: It is always necessary that the command of God be preferred to the ordinary power, just as the Apostles said: We must obey God rather than men.

What did John teach? 1. The doctrine of repentance.

2. Of the remission of sins.

3. Of the good works of all estates.

4. Of the calling of the Gentiles.

On the calling of the Gentiles.

5. On the end of the Jewish polity, and the future preaching of the Gospel. 6. On the future judgment and eternal life.

Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance.

Who they are must be learned from the other sermons of John. The first fruit is to grow in faith; John often inculcates this: Behold the Lamb of God. John 5: Everyone who believes in him has eternal life. The second fruit, the works of the second table, and it is the most common: Alms. He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none. Behold, he teaches who ought to give, and to what kind of people, according to the rule of Paul: Not that there may be tribulation for you, and relief for others. Let those give who have and can bestow something of their own; let it be given to the truly needy, who cannot work and are honest; Solomon: Do not give your substance to the cruel.

Two sermons for magistrates and soldiers.

These ask, What shall we do? because they are Gentiles, and they doubt whether it is necessary to perform ceremonies. John answers that it is not necessary to observe ceremonies, but to perform the works of one's vocation in faith, which he commands them when he baptizes. Now he adds doctrine concerning the works of one's vocation. The works of magistrates and soldiers, of quaestors, of jurisconsults, of judges, are especially these: Not to slander, not to extort, not to exact more, but to be content with one's wages. And in these three members is contained the sum of bodily government in bodily matters, namely, justice is commanded in these three things: There are three kinds of injustice in government: 1. To acquire the goods of others with cunning and false pretense. 2. To harm someone or extort something with public force. 3. To burden subjects too heavily with unnecessary taxes. And this sermon of John, all rulers, officials, judges, etc. should note well, for God does not leave such injustice unpunished; whatever you judge, will redound upon you.

The difference between John and Christ. I baptize you with water.

Here the learned ask what the difference was between the baptism of John and that of the Apostles.

I answer: John baptized into Christ who was to suffer and rise again; the Apostles later baptize into Christ who has suffered and has risen again. And this is the only difference. As to the effect, the baptism is the same, the ministry is exactly the same, and it is a Sacrament instituted by God, which both administer, and faith is required in adults, and the remission of sins, grace, and the Holy Spirit are given, whether John administers it or the Apostles, because they think impiously who imagine it to be a human ceremony, which John therefore began for the sake of passing the time.

But also the baptism of John is truly a huge work of God, instituted to signify the death of the Son of God and the promise of the remission of sins.

Question.

Why therefore does John say: I baptize you with water? I answer: He distinguishes all ministers from the Messiah.

On the baptism of Christ.

He was baptized on the sixth day of January or thereabouts, ἐπιφάνεια, that is, the apparition of God, because there God manifested Himself.

There are four notable things in this history. 1. First, the baptism of Christ, why Christ wished to be baptized. 2. The confession of John. 3. The testimony of God, who revealed Himself there more illustriously than anywhere else. 4. The opening of heaven, the hearing of God.

On the first. Why He wished to be baptized.

1. Cause, because He wished to give testimony to the baptism of John, that He might approve it, lest He be thought to agree with the Pharisees and Priests, who condemned it. Because when God sends a word, individuals ought to show testimonies of their confession.

2. Because He wished to show that this is the beginning of the New Testament, and He wished to show Himself to be a member of this new Church.

3. Cause, why is He baptized, since He does not need the remission of sins? Therefore, because He testifies that He also is baptized into death, and to die for our sins, just as our baptism is a testimony that we are baptized into the death of Christ, so that sin may be blotted out in us.

The Confession of John.

John does not wish to baptize him, and openly confesses him to be the Messiah.

But Christ answers and teaches that at this time he submits himself to the ministry which the eternal Father instituted, and wishes now to be inferior to this ministry, for reasons, as has been said.

1. That he might give testimony to this ministry.

2. That he might approve of baptism, which is the beginning of the New Testament.

3. That he might become a member of this Church.

4. That he might show that he is baptized into death.

Therefore he says to John: Thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.

Let this be understood distributively. Although others speak of this here, that Christ alone has fulfilled all righteousness, we do not wish to speak of that same understanding now, but rather, as Christ speaks here of both persons, let such things remain. All righteousness is called the work, calling, and obedience of every person. You ought to do your office, I mine; you ought to baptize whoever desires it; I am now in this calling, that I wish to let myself be baptized, and show my obedience with your baptism and my death, which this baptism signifies.

III. The Testimony of God who appears.

This revelation teaches many things. It is a testimony concerning the Trinity.

And we always look to this manifestation in our invocation, because we ought to separate our invocation from that of the heathens.

IIII. The opening of heaven, Heaven stands open through the Baptism. God wishes to hear, wishes to make [us] safe. He testifies to all these things together with this voice: This is my beloved Son. Item: Just as he sent the Holy Spirit there, so he testifies that he sends him to us.

On the feast of John the Baptist.

This feast is celebrated especially for these reasons, that men may be taught that God miraculously preserves the Church, and from time to time raises up suitable and salutary teachers, and adds testimonies that they were sent by him.

Item, that men may be taught what the true Church of God is, and what kind it is.

And it matters greatly in such confusion of the kingdoms of the world, and in the changes of kingdoms, to know which and where the Church of God is, and how it is preserved, and how it is governed.

And when we learn these things, let us at the same time give thanks to God for his immense mercy.

But first consider what the state of the Church was in the time of Zacharias, and compare those times to our own age, because there is a great similarity.

In Judea reigned the impious king Herod, who killed many elders. And the Pontiffs were impious, and the chief Doctors were Pharisees and Sadducees, who were corrupting the promises concerning the Messiah. And the greatest multitude among the people agreed with them.

Now I ask, were these the Church of God, when they were the supreme governors, and the chief part of the people, who wished to have the name of Church?

I answer: By no means were they the Church of God, because Christ says expressly to them: You are of your father the devil. By no means are any men or groups the Church of God who are ignorant of the Gospel, or who are enemies of the Gospel.

Behold what kind of darkness there was? Such a multitude, which boasted itself to be the Church, was not the Church.

Where then was the Church? Was it completely extinguished? It was by no means extinguished, because God always preserves some remnants, but often they are small, as is said in Isaiah chapter one: Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have been as Sodom and Gomorrah.

But there were Zacharias, Simeon, Anna, Maria, Elizabeth, Joseph, and many others, because these were not without listeners, but yet, before the multitude of the impious, the Church was small.

Consider this whole image diligently, and learn first who the Church are, namely those holding to the true doctrine.

Then know this, that it is not true that the greater part is the Church. Just as now the Pope and Bishops and Kings, and the very great multitude agreeing with them, boast themselves to be the Church, only on account of the titles of their offices, and on account of the greater multitude.

But let us confirm ourselves with the example, that just as the smaller group in the time of Zechariah was the Church, so now and often at other times the smaller group is the Church of God. And remember this example well.

Secondly, let this example also confirm us in other temptations. Although the cruelty of Herod and the Pharisees was great, yet God preserved the public ministry of Zechariah and others, and defended many. Because He always wills there to be some public ministry. Thus now, although the Pope and his adherents wish to destroy our Churches, yet God will preserve us and many others, and will not allow the public ministry to be entirely destroyed, just as then, even if many Pontiffs and Priests were impious and Epicureans, yet it was necessary for some to be pious, who had some listeners; such were Simeon, Zechariah, Elizabeth, Mary.

The thought of these examples is a great consolation.

After, therefore, you have considered the example, now learn from it that the word of God must be heard and learned, and truly determine for yourselves that you are members of the Church and the people of God, when you embrace the Gospel by faith, and do not care that your adversaries condemn you.

Secondly, also give thanks to God that He preserves the Church and you, and pray that He may preserve it for a longer time.

II.

On the mission of the Prophets and others teaching the truth.

Now consider how God from time to time restores the Church.

And in this consideration give thanks to God for His immense goodness, that He does not leave the human race perpetually in darkness.

When Adam and Eve had fallen, there was then no Church of the human race, and they would have had to perish entirely if God had not of His own accord come forth with immense mercy and given a promise. But the promise having been issued, He began the Church again.

Thus afterwards, often when the world had almost forgotten the promise and the doctrine of the Gospel, then He called new teachers, as after Noah and Shem He called Abraham, then Joseph, afterwards Moses, afterwards Samuel, Elijah, and others.

Thus when there was now great darkness, God called John. And God always adds miracles, so that we may know for certain that they were sent by God. Therefore John is born by a great miracle from a sterile and elderly mother. And although the Gentiles have miracles which the devil performs, yet the devil cannot imitate this miracle. Let us know, therefore, that John is a teacher sent by God, and let us believe his testimony: and let us seek what he taught.

III. On the doctrine of John.

Whenever we speak of the Saints, let us first ask what they taught. Papists speak of the Saints in such a way that they command them to be invoked, and they heap insult upon God and the Saints. This idolatry is to be condemned and fled from. Let us hear the histories of the Saints in such a way that we may learn from them that God preserves the Church, and how He preserves it, and let us give thanks to God that He reveals Himself so often by sending Prophets and Teachers. Let us also learn what each one taught, and whether their doctrine agrees. Know, therefore, that John preached the Gospel most properly and most plainly. Indeed, the doctrine of John and our own is entirely the same, except that John pointed to the present and visible Lord. We point to Him reigning in heaven. The remaining articles of the whole doctrine are the same.

Articles of faith.

He acknowledged the Trinity, he saw three persons in the baptism of Christ. He acknowledges two natures in the Messiah, because he says: He is before me. Likewise: From his fullness we have all received. He hands down the doctrine that by faith we receive the remission of sins, and that we are righteous by faith; he also says: Everyone who believes in the Son has eternal life. He preaches repentance and conversion, and teaches that the remission of sins is given on account of Christ: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. He teaches concerning good works, he calls the Gentiles. These things are to be considered principally in the history of John. How he was clothed, and what he ate, this pertains nothing to us. The doctrine pertains to us. And remember diligently these words of John: Behold the Lamb of God.…

Likewise: Everyone who believes in the Son has eternal life.

By these words let us confirm ourselves, and let us know that John is not a futile teacher, but sent by God, and that it is the command of God that we believe him. Therefore, let us oppose the authority of John to our Pharisees, who say that men merit remission by their own works.

Likewise, those who obscure the doctrine of faith. Let us hold rather to this consolation: Everyone who believes in the Son has eternal life. This saying agrees with the words of Christ and Paul: This is the will of God, that everyone who believes in the Son may have eternal life.

Think diligently on these principal things concerning John, and give thanks to God that He preserves the Church, and pray that He may preserve it hereafter as well.

Chapter IV. Concerning the temptations of Christ. Preface.

Although those temptations are great and obscure, and cannot be sufficiently understood or explained by us, yet they are not written in vain, but the Holy Spirit wished to teach us something when He willed those mysteries to be written.

But first, they warn of this: that there is a great war between the Son of God and the devil, just as it was immediately foretold in Genesis: I will put enmity between you and the seed of the woman. Therefore, the devil has always attacked the Church in various ways—with slaughters, errors, and many great confusions—so that he might draw many away from the truth of God.

II.

It is not enough to know of the struggle, but it must also be known how we can conquer. It is therefore foretold that the Son of God is the victor. And thus Genesis says: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. The exact same thing is understood in this saying: The Son of God came to destroy the works of the devil.

III.

Therefore, the battle of Christ and the devil is narrated here so that we may see an example that Christ was the victor, and that we may learn that we too must conquer. We shall conquer, however, not alone, without Christ as our leader, but by faith and the invocation of the Son of God.

IIII.

And the war is marvelous. The devils are most powerful and most cunning spirits, and the Church is a gathering of the most infirm and foolish men, children, women, and other miserable people. The devil rages against these, as if robust men were to break into a gathering of infants, and some were to seize others and dash them against the walls.

In such a battle, however, we miserable ones conquer, but we do not conquer by our own strength, but by the invocation of the Son of God, because He drives those robust ones away from the infants daily.

These things concerning the application—that we ought to run to Christ the victor in every temptation—should be learned first in this history; afterwards, the history may be viewed.

There are three principal persecutions by which the devil has attacked the Church. Types of these persecutions are proposed in the person of Christ. 1. Corporal persecution, famine and the sword. 2. Persecution through heresies. 3. Persecution through manifest idolatry.

Thus, Christ is first tempted concerning sustenance.

If you are the Son of God, if you are the Messiah, feed yourself. There is irony in the saying: Command that these stones become bread, as if he were saying, "Forsooth, you will have your sustenance from stones."

Just as now pastors and other ministers go hungry, and many are deterred from the ministry because of poverty.

Christ opposes the word of God and sustains Himself by faith.

Thus He teaches us also to do battle, to seek the word of God, to stir up faith, and to gaze upon the victor Himself. Then we shall not only have spiritual consolation, but temporal evils will also be mitigated.

Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

It is a great consolation that the word of God is to be sought first and received by faith. This is more the cause of life than natural instruments.

Example. Let us first seek the Gospel, and receive it by faith, then we shall have defense through God more than through armies.

We should always carry this consolation in our minds. Many are greatly anxious about their own sustenance and that of their children, but from this they ought to seek consolation.

And universally in every government this rule must be held. First embrace the word of God, and obey God, afterwards commend the outcomes to God.
