Item: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and drink, He who believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly. And He calls all: Come to me all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. These things were said for this reason, that in invocation we might consider the works of the persons, and having considered the works, we might learn to distinguish them rightly, and to invoke them, and to give thanks to God, because He has revealed Himself to the human race.

But let us also seek the appellations of the persons, and let us use them distinctly and prudently. The Father is called the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ; the Son is called the Word and the image of the Father, as it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: The brightness of glory, that is, of light, and the image of the Father's substance.

I have explained these words in some way above. He is called the Word, because He is born by thinking; He is called the Image, because the word is the image of the thing thought. Many also name Him the Word for this reason, because He is the person speaking with the fathers, just as it appears that the Son speaks with Daniel.

Then

In the Gospel of John, chapter 14, the title of Paraclete, that is, Advocate, is attributed to the Holy Spirit. However, someone might wonder why this title is attributed to the Holy Spirit. But it appears primarily that this appellation signifies the presence and offices of the Holy Spirit; in ministry and confession, the Church accuses the world, and in turn is accused by the world, yet it could sustain neither, unless it had the advocate, the Spirit of God, teaching minds so that they might judge rightly, and confirming them so that they might dare to profess truly, refute errors, and endure hatreds and punishments.

For that the Holy Spirit teaches is testified by the saying in John 16: "When that Spirit of truth shall come." Also John 14: "He will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all things that I have said to you." And 1 John 2: "The anointing teaches you about all things, and it is truth, and is no lie.

I. Let us learn, therefore, that among the benefits of the Holy Spirit in renewal, the first is to teach. And indeed He teaches in a twofold way: publicly through the ministry, and inwardly He kindles a light in the hearts, so that they may receive the voice of the Gospel rightly and correctly, and not invent alien opinions, just as many, because of the judgments of reason, corrupt the sayings of the Gospel. As now many corrupt the doctrine of grace and justification, fascinated by human opinions, because they imagine that righteousness is merely some kind of discipline, and they detect in their souls a doubt, which they think is not evil. Likewise, the pontiffs have transferred many sayings to their own authority which speak of spiritual government, such as the sayings about the keys. Finally, men often stray from the true light. Therefore, let us ask for this benefit, that the Holy Spirit may kindle in us the light of doctrine, and where the Holy Spirit is promised, let us know that only this benefit is promised.

II. Furthermore, when He teaches, He confirms the assent, which the devil tries to undermine in various ways. For many, although they had felt rightly at the beginning, later, driven by scandals or contrary speculations, began to doubt, and finally became entirely atheists [ἄθεοι]. For Christ speaks of these in the parable of the sower, when He says: "The devil snatches the word from their heart." Against such a great temptation, let us be at our station and on watch, and as Paul says: "Let us cast off the fiery darts, and have at hand firm testimonies, through which the Holy Spirit confirms the heart."

III. But after the Holy Spirit has taught and confirmed the assent, He incites the will and the heart to obey the law of God, that is, He excites the fear of God, trust, love, and invocation. These works are described in these sayings of Paul, Rom. 8: "You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in whom we cry Abba Father." This spirit gives testimony to our spirit, that we are the sons of God, that is, the Holy Spirit excites in us such motions, by which motions the mind invokes God, and truly determines that God is propitious to us, that He will save us, and there arises in the mind a certain light, joy, and fortitude, which overcomes human evils and subjects us to the will of God.

Therefore Christ says: "I will not leave you orphans," as if to say, in the world you will be as orphans, without defenders, without empires, without a certain seat, but I will give you the Spirit, the Advocate, teaching and confirming you, directing your counsels and government, and ruling events wonderfully, which cannot be foreseen by human prudence. The Apostles were orphans, nor could they see how they, as wanderers, could gather any Church and associate, or how such scattered groups could coalesce into one doctrine. So now we are orphans; the Turks and others threaten that they will extinguish the light of the Gospel. But nevertheless, the Spirit, the Paraclete, is present, who kindles light and strength in the pious, so that they do not cast away the Gospel, and it will be God's care to rule the events; while the doctrine of the Gospel is retained, He will provide some polities and some hospices. Moreover, it agrees with the previous sayings and the sweetest sentiment in Zechariah concerning the effects which are excited by the Holy Spirit: "I will pour upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of prayers," that is, I will give the Spirit, through whom they will acknowledge mercy, and will determine that they are in grace, will flee to God, and will invoke Him. For without the Holy Spirit, hearts remain in doubt, flee from God, and are oppressed by desperation and terrors.

Conversely, when the evil conscience is laid aside, the recognition of mercy through the Gospel shines in the hearts, the Holy Spirit is conceived, who effects peace and joy of heart, and helps so that we may determine that we are received and heard, and impels us to invoke God, and to ask for and expect good things, and in these motions, renewal is kindled and grows, concerning which the Gospel preaches. The same [passage] absolutely intends the statement in 2 Corinthians 3: We, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord; that is, we, with our face unveiled, acknowledge ourselves to be guilty, and we behold the glory, that is, the splendor of God shown in Christ, namely, the immense amplitude of mercy. We are transformed, however, into the same image, that is, the likeness of Christ is begun in us, kindled by a new light, which is the firm knowledge of God, and by new motions kindled—fear, trust in God, invocation, hatred of sin—from glory to glory, that is, by this light and clarity increasing by degrees. And these things happen, he says, through the Spirit of the Lord, given and poured out upon us.

Let us therefore propose these most serious sentiments to ourselves, so that we may know that this is a promised gift, and let us ask for it seriously, just as Christ commands, saying: How much more will your Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Then let us also beware, lest we resist the Holy Spirit, indulging in depraved desires, against conscience, and lest we expel him, and as Paul speaks, lest we grieve him.

And one lapse in various ways grieves the Holy Spirit, just as David's lapse grieved the Holy Spirit, first in the heart of David, from whence he was cast out, afterwards in all those to whom the magnitude of the scandal brought pain, but especially in the women who were raped by force, who were in extreme mourning, and perhaps some were extinguished by pain and despair. Thus, those who defend false dogmas grieve the Holy Spirit most, because they disturb many pious people, whom they lead into doubt, and they excite dissensions, which produce innumerable scandals.

Let us therefore be vigilant, and let us learn to attribute true worship to God, and true invocation, and to ask for and retain the gifts of God. In these exercises, the doctrine concerning the three persons will become clearer to us.

Sermon on the ministry of the Apostles.

The Gospel of Matthew 16. Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, and asked his disciples, saying: Whom do men say that the Son of man is? But they said: Some John the Baptist, but others Elias, and others indeed Jeremias, or one of the Prophets. Jesus says to them: But whom do you say that I am? Simon Peter answering, said: Thou art Christ the Son of the living God. And Jesus answering, said to him: Blessed art thou, Simon Bar Jona, because flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to thee: Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatsoever thou shalt bind upon earth, it shall be bound also in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth, it shall be loosed also in heaven.

There are four topics.

I. Concerning the recognition of God, and his Son. II. The distinction between ethnic and true recognition, and what must always be considered, that God has revealed himself, and why he has revealed himself. III. The distinction between Christ and the Prophets. IIII. The institution of the ministry of the Gospel and its efficacy and preservation.

Concerning the first. It is most useful always to consider that men were not born by chance, but created by God, and created for this end, that they might be his images, celebrating him. And the human mind ought to have been like a mirror, in which the illustrious knowledge of God might shine. And therefore God revealed himself to man in a twofold way. By an innate natural knowledge, and by a promulgated certain word, which he confirmed with certain testimonies. Creation is a great benefit, but it is much greater that God also revealed himself by his word, and wishes to be known and invoked, so that he may give eternal life. And this revelation is a testimony that men are not born by chance, and do not live by chance. For God did not reveal himself in vain, but so that he might be invoked, and might save. These beginnings must always be thought upon.

Concerning the second. When the heathens discourse about God, they wander in their minds, and stray from the true God, because they do not seek that God who revealed himself in his word.

And although by natural judgment they recognize the law in some way, yet they do not know the remission of sins promised on account of the Son. Therefore they flee from God, and are angry with him, because he created this weak nature only for destruction. Those ignorant of the Gospel, and fleeing from God, cannot call upon Him. Because invocation requires a faith that asks, and expects good things from God. Let ethnic recognition of God, therefore, be distinguished from true recognition. For true recognition calls upon this God who created us, and revealed Himself in immense goodness, and sent the Son concerning whom He cried out: "Hear Him," and on account of whom He granted the remission of sins and restored eternal life. Therefore, in invocation, the mind should always contemplate this God the Creator, who revealed Himself by promulgating His Word and sending the Son, who was made a victim for us; and He did not reveal Himself in vain, nor did He send the Son in vain. Wherefore, in prayer, you should always think: I call upon You, almighty, eternal, and living God, eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Creator and Preserver of all things, with Your Son Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, wise, good, merciful, judge, and strong, who revealed Yourself by giving the Gospel and bestowing the Son for us; have mercy on me on account of Your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, whom You willed to be a victim, mediator, and intercessor for us; and sanctify, rule, help, and teach me by Your Holy Spirit. This form of prayer must be diligently pondered, so that we may distinguish true invocation from ethnic, Jewish, or Turkish [invocation]; and when the mind considers the testimonies by which God revealed Himself, many Epicurean and academic doubts are excluded.

Concerning the third point.

When we thus consider God revealing Himself, the illustrious revelations made to the fathers, the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles should be thought of in order. But here, a distinction must be observed between the Prophets and Christ. The Prophets are teachers through whom the voice of God sounds, but they are not victims who merit the remission of sins, nor are they givers of the Holy Spirit and eternal life; rather, they are merely ministers of the divine voice, or preachers. Just as John significantly said: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness." But Christ’s office is something greater. He interceded for us before the Father, and by the wonderful counsel of the Godhead was sent so that He might become a victim and be the giver of the Holy Spirit and eternal life, established as mediator, on account of whom God receives us as we bring the confidence of this mediator. We do not yet sufficiently understand this wonderful counsel, but we only know it to be a testimony of immense wrath against sin, and, in turn, of immense love toward the human race. For it is necessary that there be a true and immense wrath, which no thing could appease except the Son. And, in turn, it is necessary that there be a great force of divine love, in that He did not will for this creature to perish, but to be restored by the giving of the Son.

But many think otherwise concerning Christ. They imagine He was a legislator who only handed down precepts concerning morals, like other philosophers, or they imagine He is similar to the Prophets—just as the Jews still expect the Messiah as a legislator or a political governor, not as a victim or a giver of eternal life. Therefore, it is said here in the question that some judge differently concerning Christ. But the true Church distinguishes Christ and the Prophets. Therefore, this profession is set forth here: "Whom do you say that I am?" Peter answered: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."

He asserts two things: that this one born of Mary is the Messiah, that is, the promised Savior; and that this Savior is the Son of God, not as others are called sons by adoption, but Son by nature, just as Peter had learned from the Psalm: "You are my Son, today I have begotten You." Furthermore, this distinction between Christ and the Prophets should be held not only in teaching, but daily in invocation. Let us know that the Prophets were only teachers, not placators of God and givers of eternal life. But faith should contemplate and call upon this Messiah in such a way that it establishes Him to have been a victim for our sins, and that He is now mediator or propitiator, and giver of the Holy Spirit and eternal life, and that He is the Son of God by nature—that is, reigning, liberating, defending, and vivifying with the same power as the Father. Peter embraces all these things in his confession, which will be more clearly understood by us when, in invocation, we think upon the benefits of Christ and propose this mediator to the Father, and truly take refuge in God.

Concerning the fourth point.

With the profession published, the ministry is instituted, but Christ prefaces it concerning the end or utility of this profession, and whence this light comes. The end or utility is that, by this knowledge, confession, and invocation of Christ, we may obtain eternal salvation. Therefore, it is said here: "Blessed are you, Simon," just as it is said elsewhere: "This is eternal life, that they may know You, the only God, and Jesus whom You have sent to be Christ." Thus also Isaiah said: "By the knowledge of Himself, My servant shall justify many."

Not the law, not any other human thing, abolishes sin and death, but the recognition and invocation of this Son brings righteousness and eternal life. Afterwards it is said, whence this light is: Flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my heavenly Father. The Gospel is not wisdom invented by men. Nor does the human mind assent to the Gospel, unless God helps. But God helps not those who proudly resist the word of God, but those who believe the word of God, and ask to be helped, as Christ says: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?

After Christ has prefaced what the utility of this doctrine is, and whence it is, he afterwards adds a statement about the ministry, or propagation, and about the Church: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. Insofar as you sound this voice, and profess that this one born of Mary is the Messiah, and the Son of God, to that extent you are Peter, that is, a rock, which will not be overturned; you will be a minister of this voice and a propagator. I give this command to you, that you preach this confession. And upon this rock, that is, upon this ministry of preaching this voice, I will build my Church. This passage teaches what the Church is, and where it is to be sought. Then, that it is to endure perpetually. What then is the Church? It is a congregation of those sounding this voice about Christ, preached through the Apostles, just as the Apostles confessed him, in which congregation it is necessary that some be gifted with new light by the heavenly Father, and will have eternal life.

But why is it not rather said, upon me I will build the Church? Is the Church bound to the person of Peter or the Apostles? I answer. It was said with great wisdom, upon this rock. For the Church is bound to the ministry of the Apostles, that is, Christ wants us to believe this very voice, when the Apostles will preach it later, just as we believe his own voice, and just as we believe the voice sounding from heaven. Therefore it is written to the Ephesians that the Church is built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, namely, as it pertains to the propagation and ministry, and the testimony of the doctrine. But it is built upon Christ, as it pertains to the merit, the source of the doctrine, and the efficacy, that is, because of Christ the Church is chosen, and called from the beginning of the world, and because of him it is preserved and saved, and through Christ the Gospel was revealed from the bosom of the Father; and the Son is efficacious, he gives the Holy Spirit through the Gospel.

Therefore 1 Corinthians 3 says: No other foundation can be laid than that which is laid, Jesus Christ. Item: The Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself revealed it to us. Item: I am the way, the life, and the truth. Item: I will not leave you orphans, but I will come to you. Item, Acts 2: Exalted therefore to the right hand of God, receiving the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he poured it out.

But it is a great consolation that we know that testimony was given to the Apostles so many times by Christ, that the Church is to be gathered by their voice and ministry, that by this very word, which the Apostles preach, God will preserve the Church, just as John 7 says: I pray not for them only, but for all who will believe through their word. And 20: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. After it has been said where the Church is, namely wherever this confession of the Apostles sounds, and what it is, the following sentences speak about its perpetual conservation. The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

The Church is subject to the cross at all times: but yet at times it is less vexed, at other times it is shaken more harshly: as in the time of David and Solomon it was more tranquil than in the time of Jeremiah and the Maccabees. But it was said concerning the last times, that the Church would be most distressed, and would suffer most sad tyrannies and dispersions: just as we now see the Turkish barbarity, kings and pontiffs, and among the doctors themselves, there are atrocious dissensions. No princes are firm, no seat of the Church seems likely to endure, in short it is truly, as Daniel calls it, a Dispersion. In such a time, minds must be diligently fortified, lest they fail from God, because of this sad appearance: nor should they think the Church of God is utterly extinct, but they should know that the Church is such a dissipated assembly, of those acknowledging Christ, and yet that it will endure. Thus Christ predicted in Luke 21: There will be distress of nations in anguish.

And Paul says: There will be savage times. And although these evils are in sight, yet many are lightly affected by such horrendous spectacles. Wherefore let us contemplate them, so that we may seek true consolations, and stir ourselves to invocation. May our groans seek the defense and preservation of the Church, of studies, of polities, because the Churches have need of hospitality.

And

lest we be broken by despair, let us hold fast to the testimonies which preach about the perpetuity of the Church, as here: And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

Item: I am with you even unto the end of the world. Item, Psalm 10: Thou art a priest forever.

Isaiah 59: This is my covenant with them, saith the Lord, My spirit that is upon thee, and my words which I have put in thy mouth, shall not depart out of thy mouth, nor out of the mouth of thy seed, saith the Lord, from henceforth and for ever. Item, Jeremiah 31: The holy temple of the Lord shall not be plucked up, and shall not be destroyed any more for ever.

By these words let us confirm ourselves, so that we may establish that the whole human race has not been cast away, but that the Church still remains, that we are heard, and that it will remain perpetually.

But at the same time, that conservation must be sought from God, and we must labor so that we may retain the word of God. For the Church does not remain among those who cast away the word of God, but God gathers a people for himself elsewhere, just as when the Jews were cast away, the doctrine was propagated among the Gentiles, as it is said in Hosea: Because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will reject thee.

Let us also consider that in such great dangers we do not sustain these struggles alone, but that the Son of God is present with us, just as Daniel says concerning this very last time. At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people, that is, Christ.

The last saying speaks of efficacy: I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

As a sword signifies empires, so keys signify domestic government. For Christ wishes the kingdom of the Church to be more like a household than like empires. Therefore he uses the term keys. They signify, however, not a part of the administration, but the whole office, that is, the power or mandate of teaching the Gospel, of administering the sacraments, of calling ministers, of announcing the remission of sins, and of excluding the contumacious from the kingdom of God, without corporal force.

In these great actions God is present, and saves those who are obedient to the Gospel, and condemns the contumacious, just as it is said in Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.

Even if it seems ridiculous to the impious when they hear that by the voice of the Gospel men are certainly made heirs of eternal life, nevertheless let us gratefully acknowledge and embrace this great benefit.

Let us know that God did not reveal himself in vain, nor did he send his Son in vain, nor did he give the Gospel in vain with the addition of illustrious testimonies, and let us believe the voice of God, by which he has so often promised eternal life to those who embrace the Gospel, and has testified that he will be present with them, just as Christ says: We will come unto him, and make our abode with him.

I have expounded the passages of the Gospel containing doctrine most useful to pious minds, concerning the recognition of Christ and the Church, which, although they pertain to the light of faith in the mind, have nevertheless been distorted by a certain perverse imitation toward the pontifical kingdom.

The Church is founded upon the ministry, that is, the word of the Apostles, not upon the successors of Peter who abandon the word of the Apostles. Nor do the keys signify worldly empires, or the power of making laws, but simply the office of teaching the Gospel and the administration of the sacraments, as I said before, without corporal force.

Latin:

De Trinitate. Evangelium Matth. 3.

Tunc accedit Iesus a Galilaea ad Iordanem ad Iohannem, ut baptizaretur ab illo. At Iohannes prohibebat illum, dicens: Mihi opus est, ut abs te baptizer, et tu venis ad me? Respondit autem Iesus, et dixit ad illum: Omitte nunc, sic enim decet nos, ut compleamus omnem iusticiam. Tunc omittit illum. Et baptizatus Iesus, ascendit protinus de aqua: et ecce aperti sunt illi coeli, et vidit Spiritum Dei descendentem tanquam columbam, et venientem super ipsum. Et ecce vox de coelis, dicens: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, quo delector.

Haec lectio proponatur, ut doceantur homines, quae sit voluntas Dei, et quomodo sit invocandus. Nam haec est propria Ecclesiae doctrina. Et hae semper fuerunt quaestiones omnium maximae.

sicut Philippus inquit: Domine, ostende nobis patrem.

Duae sunt autem viae quaerendi definitionem, seu quid sit Deus.

Altera rationis, sine verbo Dei, ut Plato intuens certas leges motuum coelestium, et ordinem tradit, Deus est mens aeterna, causa boni in natura, ac potest addere: quae vult nos sibi obedire, iuxta discrimen honestorum et turpium, impressum mentibus humanis. Nec exiguum miraculum est, quod haec notitia utcunque lucet in mentibus humanis, quae tamen multo illustrior esset, si natura hominum non esset corrupta. Sed quia iam in hac naturae corruptione obscurata est, Deus immensa bonitate iterum se patefecit sua voce, et misso Filio.

Est ergo altera via quaerendi, quid sit Deus. Plato intuetur naturae ordinem, nos intuamur testimonia.

Propone tibi baptismum Christi, in quo audis vocem aeterni patris: Hic est Filius meus dilectus. Filium stantem in Iordane vident oculi, et descendit Spiritus sanctus specie columbae. Considerentur et aliae similes revelationes et conciones, in quibus Christus discernit personas.

Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Item: Dabit vobis alium paracletum, spiritum veritatis.

Ad haec testimonia referamus mentem, oculos et aures, et statuamus Deum sic velle agnosci, ut se patefecit, velle non sola ratione investigari, sed per sua testimonia, sicut inquit Christus: Nemo novit patrem, nisi Filius, et cui voluerit Filius revelare. Discernamus nos ab ethnicis, Iudaeis, Mahometistis, haereticis, omnes illi quaerunt Deum sine ipsius verbo ac testimonio.

At Deus iussit nos audire Filium, Hunc audite, et addit testimonia resurrectionis mortuorum, et alia, ut sciamus vere ipsum velle sic agnosci et invocari, sic ut se in hoc verbo patefecit. Constituamus ergo definitionem.

Primum cogitemus Deum esse quandam essentiam intelligentem, aeternam, immensae potentiae. Haec docet 1. cap. Genesis de omnipotentia: In principio creavit Deus coelum et terram.

Quod sit essentia intelligens, testatur Genesis, cum inquit: Dixit Deus. Nam dicere est naturae cogitantis et sapientis.

Adde amplius: Deus est essentia intelligens, aeterna, omnipotens, sapiens, iusta, verax, bona seu benefica. Nam quod sit iusta, verax et bona, etiam Genesis indicat, inquiens: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram.

Mens autem hominis intelligit discrimen iustorum et iniustorum, et iustitiam, veritatem et bonitatem approbat. Ergo et divina mens talis est.

Haec, quae hactenus dixi, agnoscit etiam Plato: addendae sunt igitur plures descriptiones, et haec sumendae sunt ex testimoniis divinis.

Haec essentia aeterna, intelligens, est pater gignens Filium, qui refert patrem, qui cum de substantia patris natus sit, est eiusdem essentiae. Postea vero assumsit humanam naturam, et propiciator constitutus est, propter quem recipimur, exaudimur et salvamur. Et ab utroque procedit Spiritus sanctus ab aeterno, per quem incoat in nobis vitam aeternam, condens novam lucem, timorem Dei, fidem, et alios bonos motus.

Haec est integra descriptio, ignota Platoni, sumta ex testimoniis, in quibus Deus se patefecit. Et quoties precamur, haec omnia primum cogitanda sunt, quid invoces, quem Deum, ubi se patefecerit, quae sit eius voluntas, an velit exaudire. Utilissimum est mente intueri baptismum Christi, item, nostrum baptismum.

Ut summum opus est invocatio, ita pauci sunt qui recte invocant. Ethnicae, Iudaicae, Turcicae invocationes propter multas causas damnatae sunt, quia nec directae sunt ad verum Deum, nec fiunt in agnitione verbi Dei, nec fiducia Christi. Item, prorsus fiunt in dubitatione. Praeterea multi titulo Christiani currunt ad statuas, aut recitant preces, ne quidem cogitantes de Deo, quem Deum invocent, et an exaudiat. Quidam eremita dixit, difficillimum omnium operum esse precationem, et verum est, quia non est tantum recitatio versuum, sed requirit cogitationem de vero Deo, et fidem.

Primum cogites de obiecto, scilicet, de vero Deo, ad ipsum dirigatur invocatio. Deinde cogitentur praeceptum, et promissio Dei de invocatione. Tertio adsit et fiducia Christi, propter quem credamus nos recipi et exaudiri. Quarto petatur res certa, et agantur gratiae.

Sit igitur talis aliqua forma precationis, comprehendens tres personas, ut discernatur nostra invocatio ab ethnica, Iudaica et Turcica.

Omnipotens, aeterne, et vive Deus, aeterne pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui te patefecisti immensa bonitate, et clamasti de Filio tuo, Hunc audite: conditor omnium rerum, et conservator, cum Filio tuo coaeterne, Domine nostro Iesu Christo, et Spiritu sancto tuo, sapiens, bone, misericors, iudex et fortis, miserere mei propter Iesum Christum Filium tuum, quem voluisti pro nobis esse victimam, mediatorem et deprecatorem, sanctifica, rege, doce, iuva me Spiritu sancto tuo, serva et rege Ecclesiam tuam, et politias, quae praebent hospitia Ecclesiis.

Hac forma complecteris tres personas, primo simul in creatione, quia creatio est commune opus, et invocas unam illam essentiam conditricem rerum, sicut se patefecit. Deinde admones Deum suarum promissionum de Filio incarnato, et petis fiducia Filii, eique tribuis proprium munus, quod constitutus sit mediator, et fuerit victima. Tertio tribuis Spiritui sancto suum munus, quod per eum regamur, sicut scriptum est: Effundam de Meo spiritu super omnem carnem. Sic in invocatione exerceatur doctrina de personis, et cogitentur discrimina penes officia, sicut revelatae sunt personae.

Teneamus autem et communem doctrinam, quod sit una essentia divina trium personarum. Estque persona substantia intelligens, individua, incommunicabilis.

Prima est pater, qui est substantia aeterna, intelligens, bona et omnipotens, quae intuens et cogitans se, gignit ab aeterno imaginem sui de sua essentia.

Haec proprietas, scilicet, gignere, discernit patrem a Filio. Secunda persona est Filius, qui est imago patris, ab aeterno genita de essentia patris, et dicitur λόγος, quod sit ita natus, ut ex mente nascitur cogitatio seu sermo.

Nam et cogitatio qualiscunque imago est cogitatae rei. Nec sunt in creaturis exempla, quae propius depingant hanc mirandam generationem, quam haec duo: mens cogitationem gignens, et lux spargens radium. Ideo Epistola ad Ebraeos vocat fulgorem paternae lucis. Sed tamen non omnino conveniunt hae similitudines.

Nostra cogitatio non est persona, nec est substantialis imago. At Filius est substantialis imago aeterni patris, et sicut in Symbolo dicitur: Deus de Deo, lumen de lumine. Et quod sit alia persona a patre, inde manifestum est, quia haec imago patris assumsit postea humanam naturam, quam non assumsit pater. Cum igitur se Deus ita patefecerit, quod pater et haec imago sint distinctae personae, credamus Deo haec revelanti, et patrem, cum hac sua imagine coaeterna, et simul condente res, invocemus.

Haec Iohannes clare expressit in exordio suo, ubi dicit: λόγον, qui est Filius, fuisse ab initio, et per eum omnia condita esse. Cum pater quasi deliberat cum Filio, fulget in Filio idea operis fabricandi, sicut in creatione hominis haec deliberatio describitur: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram. Haec arcana lux nondum conspicitur, sed aspicienda erit in vita aeterna. Nunc nos de Filio cogitantes, intuearum eum exhibitum nobis, assumta humana natura, praedicantem, passum, resuscitatum, stantem in Iordane, ascendentem in coelum, et de ipsius proprio munere cogitemus, quod mirando Dei consilio factus sit pro nobis deprecator, et victima placans iram Dei.

Et sit Emmanuel, inter vos versatus, regnans inter nos, ideo exhibitus nobis, ut nos miseros regat et servet. Ideoque ante assumtam humanam naturam, se cernendum praebuit patribus, ut Danieli, et aliis, etc. Alligetur ergo cogitatio nostra de Filio ad Christum, qui se patefecit, et nobiscum versatus est, crucifixus, resuscitatus est, et ascendit in coelum, et ostendit se Stephano, et aliis.

Ac sciamus ideo nobiscum versatum esse, ut testaretur se semper curare et exaudire invocantes. Et quia Philippo interroganti de patre, respondit: Qui videt me, videt patrem: cum de patre cogitamus, primum hunc Filium patefactum mente intuemur, et hunc patrem invocemus, qui de eo edidit hanc vocem, Hunc audite. Et semper simul cogitemus de ipsa patefactione, non frustra Deum se ostendisse, et familiariter cum hominibus collocutum esse, sed certo testatum esse hac ipsa re, quod vere nos curet.

Nec ulla est illustrior confirmatio adversus epicureos et academicos furores, quam haec ipsa cogitatio de patefactione et miraculis, quae omnia fuerunt principaliter testimonia patefactionis. Quoties autem sic de Filio cogitamus, simul veniat in mentem, quod mediator sit, et intercessor pro nobis, quod propter ipsum exaudiamur. Tertia persona est Spiritus sanctus, qui est agitator, procedens a Patre et Filio, eiusdem substantiae, per quem in mentibus sanctorum novi motus placentes Deo excitantur, et per quem Ecclesia vivit vita aeterna.

Ac proprie tribuitur Spiritui sancto vocabulum Procedere, quod ut aliquo modo declaretur, sicut supra de imagine quaesivimus qualecunque exemplum, in intellectu hominis: ita iam intuearum voluntatem hominis, seu cor. Generatio propria est intellectionis, quia pingit imagines intellectio. Spiratio vero voluntatis est aut cordis. Ut autem voluntas in homine, aut cor, non pingit imagines, sicut pars cognoscens, sed habet impetus aut motus, aut flatus, quibus attrahit aut pellit obiectum, amat quasi attrahens, odit quasi pellens: sic a voluntate aeterna Patris et Filii, impetus seu status efficacissimus est, qui est de ipsa Patris et Filii essentia. Hic flatus non dicitur genitus, sed procedens. Et hic ipse flatus statim initio describitur a Mose: Et spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas, id est, fovebat aquas, impertiebat eis vigorem, ubi significatum est, Deum per Spiritum sanctum impertire vitam et agitationem creaturae suae.

Sed aliud est loqui de generali agitatione seu vita, aliud de renovatione hominis, in qua fiunt motus obedientes Deo, agnitio Dei, et iusticia, de hac proprie dicamus. Supra dictum est, creationem esse opus commune trium personarum. Sic et renovatio seu sanctificatio est opus commune trium personarum. Sed modus discernitur, Pater, et Filius, et Spiritus sanctus recipiunt hominem, propter Filium mediatorem, et Pater et Filius mittunt Spiritum sanctum, per quem fiunt novi motus incoantes vitam aeternam in hominibus.

Haec magna res expresse descripta est in donatione Spiritus sancti, cum Christus insufflaret Spiritum sanctum in Apostolos, dicens: Accipite Spiritum sanctum. Hic flatus revera erat persona Spiritus sancti, per quam et in Apostolis novi motus excitabantur. Ita cum ad Mariam diceretur: Spiritus sanctus veniet super te, et potentia altissimi obumbrabit tibi, persona Spiritus sancti vere erat praesens, et per eum in corde virginis fiebat umbraculum, id est, non incutiebatur sensus horrendae irae Dei, sed accendebatur agnitio misericordiae, et laetitia in illa agnitione misericordiae.

Haec declaratio diligenter consideretur, et in invocatione discatur, in qua petamus accendi in nobis novam lucem, et regi nos Spiritu sancto. Nam opera Spiritus sancti aliter intelligi non possunt, nisi in nobis accendantur. Sunt autem haec opera Spiritus sancti, in mentibus piorum, per verbum Dei accendere lucem, id est, agnitionem irae Dei adversus peccatum, et rursus agnitionem misericordiae promissae propter Filium, excitare fiduciam, quae in veris pavoribus erigit mentes, et consolatur conspectu misericordiae promissae propter mediatorem.

Cum hac fiducia excitat invocationem, et flectit mentes, ut se Deo subiiciant. De his operibus concionatur Christus, cum inquit: Spiritus glorificabit me, id est, accendet agnitionem mei in mentibus, quae assentiuntur Evangelio. Item: S. S. arguet mundum de peccato, de iusticia, et de iudicio.

Dixi, quomodo tres personae discernendae et agnoscendae sint. Discernantur hoc modo: Pater gignit ab aeterno Filium, intuens sese et cogitans. Filius genitus est a patre, et est imago patris. Spiritus sanctus procedit a patre et Filio, et est flatus seu agitator, per quem fit sanctificatio.

Discernantur autem et agnoscantur per externa testimonia, hoc modo: Pater clamat de Filio, Hunc audite. Filius assumsit humanam naturam, et factus est mediator. Spiritus sanctus est missus et ostensus in flatu, in specie columbae, in linguis igneis, et per eum nova lux et agnitio Dei, et nova iusticia accenditur.

Haec nobis clariora essent, si invocatione cogitarentur, et si revera crederemus Deum nobis velle quoque hanc lucem impertire, et hac fiducia peteremus, ideo clamat Christus: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus se. Vult agnosci Deus, vult in nobis habitare, modo admittamus eum, sicut inquit: Ego sto ad ostium et pulso. Item: Veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Item: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, et bibat, Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre eius fluent aquae vivae. Et vocat omnes: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos.

Haec ideo dicta sunt, ut in invocatione consideremus opera personarum, et consideratis operibus, discamus eas recte discernere, et invocare, et Deo gratias agere, quod se generi humano patefecerit. Quaeramus autem et appellationes personarum, eisque distincte et prudenter utamur.

Pater, dicitur pater domini Iesu Christi, Filius, dicitur verbum et imago patris, ut in Epistola ad Hebraeos scriptum est: Fulgor gloriae, id est, lucis, et imago substantiae patris. Haec vocabula utcunque supra declaravi. Dicitur Verbum, quia nascitur cogitando, dicitur Imago, quia verbum est imago cogitatae rei.

Multi etiam ideo nominant verbum, quia sit persona loquens cum patribus, sicut apparet Filium loqui cum Daniele. Deinde

In Evangelio Iohan. cap. 14. tribuitur Spiritui sancto appellatio paracleti, id est, advocati. Miretur autem aliquis, cur hic titulus Spiritui sancto attributus sit. Sed apparet principaliter hanc appellationem significare praesentiam et officia Spiritus sancti, in ministerio et confessione, Ecclesia accusat mundum, et vicissim a mundo accusatur, neutrum autem sustinere posset, nisi haberet advocatum spiritum Dei, docentem mentes, ut recte iudicent, et confirmantem ut ausint vere profiteri, refutare errores, et perferre odia et supplicia.

Quod enim doceat Spiritus sanctus, testatur dictum Iohan. 16.: Cum venerit ille spiritus veritatem. Item Iohan. 14.: Docebit vos omnia, et rediget vobis in memoriam omnia quae dixi vobis. Et 1. Iohan. 2.: Unctio docet vos de omnibus, et est veritas, et non est mendacium.

I. Discamus igitur inter beneficia Spiritus sancti in renovatione primum esse docere. Et quidem dupliciter docet, publice per ministerium, et intus accendit lumen in cordibus, ut dextre et recte accipiant vocem Evangelii, nec fingant alienas opiniones, sicut multi propter iudicia rationis corrumpunt dicta Evangelii. Ut nunc multi corrumpunt doctrinam de gratia et iustificatione, fascinati humanis opinionibus, quia imaginantur iusticiam tantum esse qualemcunque disciplinam, et deprehendunt in animis dubitationem, quam putant non esse malam. Item multa dicta ad imperium transtulerunt pontifices, quae loquuntur de spirituali gubernatione, ut dicta de clavibus. Denique saepe deerrant homines a vera luce. Ideo petamus hoc beneficium, ut Spiritus sanctus accendat in nobis lucem doctrinae, et ubi promittitur Spiritus sanctus, sciamus hoc tantum beneficium promitti.

II. Praeterea cum docet, confirmat assensionem, quam diabolus varie labefactare conatur. Multi enim cum initio recte sensissent, postea vel scandalis, vel speculationibus contrariis impulsi, dubitare coeperunt, et tandem prorsus ἄθεοι facti sunt. De his enim loquitur Christus in parabola sementis, cum inquit: Diabolus rapit verbum ex corde eorum. Adversus hanc tantam tentationem simus in statione et in excubiis, et ut Paulus inquit: Depellamus tela ignita, et habeamus in promptu firma testimonia, per quae Spiritus sanctus confirmat cor.

III. Postquam autem docuit Spiritus sanctus, et confirmavit assensionem, incitat voluntatem et cor ad obediendum legi Dei, id est, excusitat timorem Dei, fiduciam, dilectionem et invocationem. Haec opera describuntur in his dictis Pauli, Rom. 8.: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum in quo clamamus Abba pater. Hic spiritus testimonium dat spiritui nostro, quod simus filii Dei, id est, Spiritus sanctus excusitat in nobis tales motus, quibus motibus mens invocat Deum, et vere statuit Deum nobis propicium esse, nos servaturum esse, et exoritur in mente quaedam lux, laetitia et fortitudo, quae superat humana mala, et subiicit nos voluntati Dei.

Ideo Christus inquit: Non relinquam vos orphanos, quasi dicat, in mundo eritis ut orphani, sine defensoribus, sine imperiis, sine certa sede, sed dabo vobis spiritum advocatum, docentem et confirmantem vos, dirigentem consilia et gubernationem, et regentem eventus mirabiliter, qui prospici humana prudentia non possunt. Erant orphani Apostoli, nec videre poterant, quomodo vagabundi colligere aliquam Ecclesiam, et consociare possent, aut quomodo tam dissipati coetus coalescere in unam doctrinam possent. Ita nunc sumus orphani, Turci et alii minantur se lucem Evangelii extincturos esse. Sed tamen adest spiritus paracletus, qui lucem et robur in piis accendit, ne Evangelium abiiciant, et Deo curae erit, ut regat eventus, dum doctrina Evangelii retinetur, dabit aliquas politias et aliqua hospitia. Congruit autem cum superioribus dictis et dulcissima sententia apud Zachariam de effectibus, qui per Spiritum sanctum excitantur: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum, id est, dabo spiritum, per quem agnoscent misericordiam, et statuent se esse in gratia, confugient ad Deum, et invocabunt. Nam sine Spiritu sancto corda manent in dubitatione, fugiunt Deum, et opprimuntur desperatione et pavoribus.

Econtra cum deposita mala conscientia, lucet in cordibus agnitio misericordiae per Evangelium, concipitur Spiritus sanctus, qui pacem et laetitiam cordis efficit, et adiuvat, ut statuamus nos recipi et exaudiri, et impellit ut invocemus Deum, ac petamus et expectemus bona, et in his motibus accenditur et crescit renovatio, de qua concionatur Evangelium. Idem prorsus vult dictum 2. Corinth. 3.: Nos retecta facie gloriam Dei intuentes, ad eandem imaginem transformamur, a gloria in gloriam, tanquam a Domini spiritu, id est, nos retecta nostra facie, nos agnoscimus esse reos, et intuemur gloriam, id est, splendorem Dei in Christo monstratam, videlicet immensam amplitudine misericordiae. Transformamur autem ad eandem imaginem, id est, incoatur in nobis similitudo Christi, accensa nova luce, quae est firma Dei noticia, et accensis novis motib. timore, fiducia Dei, invocatione, odio peccati, a gloria in gloriam, id est, crescente subinde hac luce et claritate. Et haec fiunt inquit, per Domini spiritum, datum et effusum in nos.

Has gravissimas sententias ideo nobis proponamus, ut sciamus promissum esse hoc tantum donum, et serio petamus, sicut Christus iubet, inquiens: Quanto magis pater vester dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Deinde etiam caveamus, ne resistamus Spiritui sancto, indulgentes pravis cupiditatibus, contra conscientiam, neve eum expellamus, et sicut Paulus loquitur, ne eum contristemus.

Ac varie unus lapsus contristat Spiritum sanctum, ut Davidis lapsus contristabat Spiritum sanctum, primum in corde Davidis, unde eiiciebatur, postea in omnibus quibus magnitudo scandali dolorem attulit, maxime vero in mulieribus, quae per vim stupratae sunt, quae in summo luctu fuerunt, et fortassis aliquae dolore ac desperatione extinctae sunt. Sic maxime contristant Spiritum sanctum, qui falsa dogmata defendunt, quia conturbant multos pios, quos in dubitationem adducunt, excitant dissidia, quae pariunt innumerabilia scandala.

Simus igitur vigilantes, et discamus Deo veros cultus tribuere, et veram invocationem, et petere ac retinere dona Dei. In his exercitiis fiet nobis doctrina de tribus personis illustrior.

Concio de ministerio Apostolorum.

Evangelium Matthaei 16. Venit Iesus in partes Caesareae Philippi, et interrogabat discipulos suos, dicens: Quem dicunt homines esse Filium hominis? At illi dixerunt: Alii Ioannem Baptistam, alii autem Eliam, alii vero Ieremiam, aut unum ex Prophetis. Dicit illis Iesus: Vos autem quem me esse dicitis? Respondens Simon Petrus, dixit: Tu es Christus Filius Dei vivi. Respondens autem Iesus dixit ei: Beatus es Simon Bar Iona, quia caro et sanguis non revelavit tibi, sed pater meus qui in coelis est. Et ego dico tibi: Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, et portae inferi non praevalebunt adversus eam. Et dabo tibi claves regni coelorum. Et quodcunque ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum in coelis, et quodcunque solveris super terram, erit solutum in coelis.

Quatuor sunt loci.

I. De agnitione Dei, et Filii eius. II. Discrimen inter agnitionem ethnicam et veram, et quod semper considerandum sit, quod Deus se patefecit, et cur se patefecerit. III. Discrimen Christi et Prophetarum. IIII. Institutio ministerii Evangelii et efficacia et conservatio.

De primo. Utilissimum est semper considerare, homines non ortos esse casu, sed a Deo conditos, et ad hunc finem conditos, ut sint imagines eius, celebrantes ipsum. Ac humana mens tanquam speculum esse debebat, in quo luceret illustris Dei noticia. Ideoque se patefecit Deus homini dupliciter. Insita naturali noticia, et promulgato certo verbo, quod certis testimoniis confirmavit. Magnum beneficium est creatio, sed multo maius, quod Deus etiam se verbo suo patefecit, et vult agnosci et invocari, ut det vitam aeternam. Et haec patefactio testimonium est, homines non casu nasci, non casu vivere. Non enim frustra patefecit se Deus, sed ut invocetur, et salvet. Haec initia semper cogitanda sunt.

De secundo. Ethnici cum disserunt de Deo, vagantur animis, et deerrant a vero Deo, quia non quaerunt illum Deum, qui se in verbo suo patefecit.

Et quanquam naturali iudicio legem utcunque agnoscunt, tamen non norunt remissionem peccatorum promissam propter Filium. Ideo fugiunt Deum, et irascuntur ei, quod hanc imbecillem naturam tantum ad exitium condiderit. ignari Evangelii, et fugientes Deum, non possunt eum invocare. Quia invocatio requirit fidem petentem, et expectantem bona a Deo. Discernatur igitur ethnica agnitio Dei a vera. Nam vera agnitio hunc Deum invocat, qui nos condidit, et se immensa bonitate patefecit, misit Filium de quo clamavit: Hunc audite, et propter quem donavit remissionem peccatorum, et restituit vitam aeternam. Semper igitur in invocatione mens intueatur hunc Deum conditorem, qui se patefecit promulgato verbo suo et misso Filio, qui pro nobis factus est victima, et non frustra se patefecit, nec frustra misit Filium. Quare semper in precatione cogites: Te invoco, omnipotens, aeterne et vive Deus, aeterne pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, conditor et conservator omnium rerum, cum Filio tuo Iesu Christo, et Spiritu sancto, sapiens, bone, misericors, iudex et fortis, qui patefecisti te dato Evangelio, et donato Filio pro nobis, miserere mei propter Filium tuum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, quem voluisti pro nobis esse victimam, mediatorem et deprecatorem, et sanctifica, rege, iuva, doce me Spiritu sancto tuo. Haec forma precationis diligenter cogitanda est, ut discernamus veram invocationem ab ethnica, Iudaica, Turcica, et cum mens considerat testimonia, quibus se Deus patefecit, multae dubitationes epicureae et academicae excluduntur.

De tertio.

Cum ita consideramus Deum se patefacientem, ordine illustres revelationes factae patribus, Prophetis, Christo, Apostolis cogitentur. Sed hic discrimen attendatur inter Prophetas et Christum. Prophetae sunt doctores, per quos sonat vox Dei, sed non sunt victimae, quae merentur remissionem peccatorum, nec sunt datores Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae, sed tantum sunt ministri vocis divinae, seu concionatores. Sicut Iohannes significanter dixit: Ego sum vox clamans in deserto. Sed aliud maius officium est Christi. Hic intercessit pro nobis apud patrem, et mirabili consilio divinitatis missus est, ut fieret victima, et esset dator Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae, constitutus mediator, propter quem Deus recipit nos afferentes fiduciam huius mediatoris. Hoc mirandum consilium nondum satis intelligimus, sed tantum scimus testimonium esse ingentis irae adversus peccatum, et rursus immensi amoris erga genus humanum. Necesse est enim esse veram et ingentem iram, quam nulla res placare potuit, nisi Filius. Et rursus necesse est, magnam vim amoris divini esse, quod non voluit hanc creaturam perire, sed dato Filio restitui.

Sed multi de Christo aliter sentiunt. Fingunt fuisse legislatorem, qui tantum praecepta de moribus tradiderit, sicut caeteri philosophi, aut fingunt similem esse Prophetis, ut Iudaei adhuc expectant Messiam tanquam legislatorem, aut gubernatorem politicum, non victimam aut datorem vitae aeternae. Ideo hic in quaestione dicitur, alios aliter de Christo iudicare. Sed vera Ecclesia discernit Christum et Prophetas. Ideo haec professio hic exponitur. Vos quem me esse dicitis? Respondit Petrus: Tu es Christus Filius Dei viventis.

Duas res asseverat, hunc natum ex Maria esse Messiam, id est, promissum salvatorem, et hunc salvatorem esse Filium Dei, non ut caeteri dicuntur filii adoptione, sed natura filium, sicut ex Psalmo didicerat Petrus: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Porro non solum in docendo, sed quotidie in invocatione teneatur hoc discrimen Christi et Prophetarum. Sciamus Prophetas tantum fuisse doctores, non placatores Dei, et datores vitae aeternae. Sed fides intueatur et invocet hunc Messiam, ita, ut statuat eum fuisse victimam pro nostris peccatis, et nunc esse mediatorem seu propiciatorem, et datorem Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae, et esse natura Filium Dei, id est, eadem potentia cum patre regnantem, liberantem, defendentem, vivificantem. Haec omnia complectitur Petrus in sua confessione, quae a nobis clarius intelligentur, cum in invocatione cogitabimus beneficia Christi et hunc mediatorem patri proponemus, et ad Deum vere confugiemus.

De quarto.

Edita professione instituitur ministerium, sed Christus praefatur de fine seu utilitate huius professionis, et unde sit haec lux. Finis seu utilitas est, ut hac cognitione, confessione et invocatione Christi, consequamur aeternam salutem. Ideo hic dicitur: Beatus es Simon, sicut et alias dicitur: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te solum esse Deum, et quem misisti Iesum esse Christum. Sic et Esaias dixit: Agni-tione sui iustificabit servus meus multos.

Non lex, non alia res humana ulla abolet peccatum et mortem, sed agnitio et invocatio huius Filii affert iusticiam et vitam aeternam. Postea dicitur, unde sit haec lux: Caro et sanguis non revelavit tibi, sed pater meus coelestis. Evangelium non est sapientia ab hominibus inventa. Nec mens humana assentitur Evangelio, nisi Deo adiuvante. Adiuvat autem Deus non eos, qui superbe repugnant verbo Dei, sed qui credunt verbo Dei, et petunt se iuvari, sicut Christus inquit: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum S. petentibus?

Postquam praefatus est Christus, quae sit utilitas huius doctrinae, et unde sit, postea addit sententiam de ministerio, seu propagatione, et de Ecclesia: Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Tu quatenus sonas hanc vocem, et profiteris hunc natum ex Maria esse Messiam, et Filium Dei, eatenus es Petrus, id est, rupes, quae non evertetur, eris minister huius vocis et propagator. Hoc tibi mandatum do, ut hanc confessionem praedices. Et super hanc petram, id est, super hoc ministerium praedicandae huius vocis, aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Hic locus docet quid sit Ecclesia, et ubi sit, quaerenda. Deinde quod sit perpetuo mansura. Quid est igitur Ecclesia? Est congregatio sonantium hanc vocem de Christo, praedicato per Apostolos, sicut eum confessi sunt Apostoli, in qua congregatione necesse est aliquos esse nova luce donatos a patre coelesti, et habituros gloriam aeternam.

Sed cur non potius dicitur, super me aedificabo Ecclesiam? An alligatur Ecclesia ad Petri aut Apostolorum personam? Respondeo. Magno consilio dictum est, super hanc petram. Alligatur enim Ecclesia ad ministerium Apostolorum, id est, vult nos Christus huic ipsi voci, cum praedicabunt eam postea Apostoli, credere, sicut suae voci, et sicut voci de coelo sonanti. Ideo ad Ephesios scriptum est, Ecclesiam extructam esse super fundamentum Prophetarum et Apostolorum, videlicet, quod attinet ad propagationem et ministerium, et testimonium doctrinae. Sed est extructa super Christum, quod attinet ad meritum, doctrinae fontem, et efficaciam, id est, propter Christum Ecclesia est electa, et vocata a principio mundi, et propter eum servatur et salvatur, et per Christum ex sinu patris revelatum est Evangelium; et Filius est efficax, dat Spiritum sanctum per Evangelium.

Ideo 1. Corinth. 3. dicitur: Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, Iesus Christus. Item: Filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse revelavit nobis. Item: Ego sum via, vita et veritas. Item: Non relinquam vos orphanos, sed veniam ad vos. Item, Act. 2.: Ad dextram igitur Dei exaltatus, promissionem Spiritus sancti accipiens a patre effudit.

Magna autem consolatio est, quod scimus testimonium datum esse Apostolis toties a Christo, quod eorum voce et ministerio colligenda sit Ecclesia, quod hoc ipso verbo, quod Apostoli praedicant, Deus servaturus sit Ecclesiam, sicut Iohan. 7. dicitur: Oro non pro ipsis tantum, sed pro omnibus credituris per verbum eorum. Et 20.: Sicut misit me pater, sic mitto vos. Postquam dictum est ubi sit Ecclesia, videlicet ubicunque haec confessio Apostolorum sonat, et quid sit, sequentes sententiae loquuntur de perpetua conservatione. Portae inferi non praevalebunt adversus eam.

Ecclesia est subiecta cruci omnibus temporibus: sed tamen alias minus vexatur, alias quassatur durius: ut tempore Davidis et Salomonis fuit tranquillior, quam tempore Ieremiae et Maccabaeorum. Dictum est autem de postremis temporibus, Ecclesiam futuram angustissimam, et passuram tristissimas tyrannides et dispersiones: sicut iam grassari in eam videmus Turcicam barbariem, reges et pontifices, et inter se doctorum esse atrocia dissidia. Nulli principes firmi sunt, nulla sedes Ecclesiae duratura videtur, denique vere est, ut vocat Daniel, Dispersio. Hoc tali tempore diligenter muniendi sunt animi, ne deficiant a Deo, propter hanc tristem speciem: nec cogitent extinctam esse Ecclesiam Dei penitus, sed sciant Ecclesiam esse talem dissipatum coetum, agnoscentium Christum, et tamen mansuram esse. Sic praedixit Christus Lucae 21.: Erit pressura gentium in angustia.

Et Paulus inquit: Erunt tempora saeva. Etsi autem haec mala sunt in conspectu, tamen multi leviter afficiuntur tam horrendis spectaculis. Quare ea intueamur, ut quaeramus veras consolationes, et excitemus nos ad invocationem. Gemitus nostri petant defensionem et conservationem Ecclesiae, studiorum, politiarum, quia Ecclesiis opus est hospitio.

Et

ne desperatione frangamur, testimonia teneamus, quae de perpetuitate Ecclesiae concionantur, ut hic: Et portae inferi non praevalebunt adversus eam.

Item: Ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi. Item, Psal. 10.: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum.

Esaiae 59.: Hoc foedus meum cum eis, dicit Dominus, Spiritus meus qui est in te, et verba mea, quae posui in ore tuo, non recedent de ore tuo, nec ab ore seminis tui, dicit Dominus, deinceps et in sempiternum. Item, Iere. 31.: Sanctum templum Domini non evelletur, et non destruetur ultra in perpetuum.

His dictis confirmemus nos, ut statuamus non abiectum esse totum genus humanum, sed adhuc manere Ecclesiam, nos exaudiri, et perpetuo mansuram esse.

Sed simul petendam esse a Deo conservationem, et laborandum, ut verbum Dei retineamus. Nam apud eos non manet Ecclesia, qui verbum Dei abiiciunt, sed Deus alibi sibi populum colligit, ut abiectis Iudaeis propagata est doctrina inter gentes, ut in Osea dicitur: Quia repulisti scientiam, repellam te.

Cogitemus item in tantis periculis nos non solos sustinere haec certamina, sed Filium Dei nobis adesse, sicut Daniel inquit de hoc ipso postremo tempore. Illo tempore stabit pro filiis populi sui dux magnus Michaël, id est, Christus.

Postremum dictum de efficacia loquitur: Dabo tibi claves regni coelorum.

Ut gladius significat imperia, ita claves significant domesticam gubernationem. Vult enim Christus Ecclesiae regnum magis oeconomiae, quam imperiis simile esse. Ideo utitur appellatione clavium. Significant autem non partem administrationis, sed totum munus, id est, potestatem seu mandatum docendi Evangelium, administrandi sacramenta, vocandi ministros, annunciandae remissionis peccatorum et excludendi contumaces ex regno Dei, sine vi corporali.

His tantis actionibus adest Deus, et salvat obedientes Evangelio, et damnat contumaces, sicut Rom. 1. dicitur: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti.

Etsi impiis ridiculum videtur, cum audiunt voce Evangelii homines certo fieri haeredes vitae aeternae, tamen nos hoc tantum beneficium grati agnoscamus et amplectamur.

Sciamus Deum non frustra se patefecisse, nec frustra Filium misisse, nec frustra dedisse Evangelium additis illustribus testimoniis, et credamus voci Dei, quo toties promisit vitam aeternam amplectentibus Evangelium, et testatus est se illis affuturum esse, sicut Christus inquit: Veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Exposui locos Evangelii, continentes doctrinam maxime utilem piis mentibus, de agnitione Christi et de Ecclesia, qui cum ad fidei lumen in mentibus pertineant, tamen quadam prava imitatione detortae sunt ad regnum pontificium.

Ecclesia fundata est super ministerium, id est, verbum Apostolorum, non super successores Petri, relinquentes verbum Apostolorum. Nec claves significant imperia mundana, aut potestatem ferendi leges, sed simpliciter munus docendi Evangelii, et administrationem sacramentorum, ut prius dixi, sine vi corporali.

## 4:1 Invocavit Sunday
Invocavit Sunday. Gospel

Matt. 4.

Then Jesus was led into the desert by the spirit, to be tempted by the devil.

And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry.

And the tempter coming to him, said: If you are the son of God, say that these stones become bread.

Who answering said: It is written, Not in bread alone does man live, but in every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

Then the devil took him into the holy city, and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: If you are the son of God, cast yourself down, for it is written, That he will give his angels charge over you, and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone.

Jesus said to him: It is written again, You shall not tempt the Lord your God.

Again the devil took him up into a very high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him: All these I will give you, if falling down you will adore me.

Then Jesus says to him: Begone Satan, for it is written, The Lord your God you shall adore, and him only shall you serve.

Then the devil left him.

And behold, angels came, and ministered to him.

I. Topic: That we are not tempted by chance. II. Concerning the tyranny and snares of the devil. III. How man is liberated from this servitude, namely through the Son of God. IIII. The victory of the Son of God benefits us, and just as He conquered in His own person, so He wishes to conquer the snares of the devil in believers, even though He also wishes us to struggle, so that we may experience His help. V. The three temptations in the person of Christ are examples of the temptations of the Church, and of persecutions. First, the Church is pressed by poverty, and is tormented by tyrants. Second, it is lacerated by impious teachers, who spread their dogmas with their own audacity without the Word of God. Third, it is contaminated by manifest idolatry. Concerning the first four topics.

Although so many horrible crimes, idolatries, lusts, slaughters, wars, the destruction of kingdoms, and great calamities which follow crimes, sufficiently show that some savage and powerful enemy is raging against the human race: yet such is the stupor of men that they consider these things light, and think they happen by chance. But the doctrine of the Gospel reveals the true causes, shows that the devil is raging against the human race, and that men, because of sin, are subject to his tyranny. Again, it also shows us a liberator, who fights with the devil. As John says: The Son of God appeared that He might destroy the works of the devil. Therefore, in summary, these admonitions concerning temptations, concerning the causes, and concerning the liberator, must be held.

It is certain that such great evils of men do not happen by chance, but that the devil, out of hatred for God, is raging hostiley against all, and wounding individuals with a notable bite, just as in the beginning he wounded Eve and Adam. Wherefore let each one look at his own life, and he will detect some notable wound. The devil insidiously drags one either to crime or to calamity, so that from there he may drag them into despair and blasphemy. Let us consider these snares, and let us learn to flee to our leader Christ the Son of God, who fights against the devil, just as it was said in the beginning in Genesis: This seed shall crush the head of the serpent, which voice entirely agrees with that saying of John: The Son of God appeared, that He might destroy the works of the devil, that is, sins, calamities, death. These things in summary must be observed here, so that we may prepare our minds, because these are not light struggles that must be undergone. In these, let faith shine and be exercised, and let the help of the Son of God be implored, who for this reason conquered the devil in these temptations, so that He might show that He will be the victor, even in these battles in which the devil attacks us.

V. Concerning the temptations of Christ, let us think that it was a certain wondrous, insidious, and vehement struggle, and much sharper and greater than can be thought by us. He was tempted often at other times: but these temptations are described by name, because they undoubtedly signify something to the whole Church.

VI. Concerning the first temptation, the histories are well known; in the time of the Apostles and Martyrs, the bodies and resources of the pious were always in danger. The same is accustomed to happen whenever struggles concerning doctrine are moved, as now: and this temptation is breaking out again under the Turkish tyranny. Here the devil insults the minds of many: If you are the sons of God, if you serve God, namely, you will have to live from stones. For it is the irony of one who objects to poverty, hunger, and other miseries, and reproaches them. Here, consolations must be sought and opposed.

First, let us know that the Church will remain, and cannot be overturned by the gates of hell. Then, let us know that those who call upon Christ will have help, according to this saying: The Son of God appeared, that He might destroy the works of the devil. Item: Man does not live by bread alone; in the Church he is nourished, preserved, and defended not only by common and visible helps and means, but also by divine ones, which reason does not perceive. If, however, the Church remains in the acknowledgment of the Word of God, it shall not fail from the Word of God. The Psalm says: Know that the Lord makes His holy one wondrous. Thus, even if we do not now see what the future Church will be, even if the Turks were to possess all of Europe, yet if we retain the Word of God, it will be God's care that we have defense. Furthermore, this doctrine must also be applied to individuals; let each one in his own poverty, in his own dangers, think that he cannot protect his life, vocation, and state by human counsels alone: but that divine help must be sought and expected, so that we may live in faith and in the invocation of God.

But few live thus, all seek wealth, so that they may have certain aids in sight and at hand, and the doctrine of Christ is laughed at: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you.

VII. Concerning the second.

The order of histories shows that after bodily vexations, heresies followed, as is aptly signified here. Standing on the pinnacle of the temple is someone excellent in doctrine; he casting himself down, that is, spreading dogma without the word of God, tempts God. Such were, are, and will be many, but then there were Ebion, Cerinthus, Marcion, Manes, Samosatenus, Arius, Pelagius, and the like.

To tempt God properly is to contend with God by the confidence of one's own wisdom, justice, and strength, and to be unwilling to be ruled by the very word of God, and by His ordination and calling. But, having spurned these, to seek something else, by the confidence of our own wisdom, which pleases us more. As by human wisdom the Pontiffs commanded celibacy, Samosatenus corrupted the doctrine concerning the Son of God, and sought something else more harmonious. The pseudo-apostles sought by human judgment something more plausible when they did not want the law to be abrogated. Therefore Peter says: Why do you tempt God? That is, by the confidence of your wisdom and human reasons you contend with God, you depart from His word. And afterwards the Pontiffs truly horribly tempted God with many depraved dogmas, concerning the abuse of the sacraments, concerning the ignorance of faith and true invocation, and concerning monastic cults.

VIII. Concerning the third.

The final temptation is to establish and defend manifest idolatry for the sake of the kingdom. Just as both the kingdom of the Pope and of Mahomet have as their chief nerves, indeed idolatry. Christ therefore warns us that we should learn to judge these final kingdoms oppressing the Church, and that we should avoid idolatries, and not flee from struggles, and the outcome of the struggles is signified.

Latin:

Dominica Invocavit. Evangelium

Matth. 4.

Tunc Iesus ductus est in desertum a spiritu, ut tentaretur a diabolo.

Et cum ieiunasset quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, postea esuriit.

Et accedens ad eum tentator, dixit: Si filius Dei es, dic ut lapides isti panes fiant.

Qui respondens dixit: Scriptum est, Non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit de ore Dei.

Tunc assumsit eum diabolus in sanctam civitatem, et statuit eum supra pinnaculum templi, et dixit ei: Si filius Dei es, demitte te deorsum, scriptum est enim, Quia angelis suis mandabit de te, et in manibus tollent te, ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum.

Ait illi Iesus: Rursum scriptum est, Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum.

Iterum assumsit eum diabolus in montem excelsum valde, et ostendit ei omnia regna mundi et gloriam eorum, et dixit ei: Haec omnia tibi dabo, si cadens adoraveris me.

Tunc dicit ei Iesus: Vade Satana, scriptum est enim, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies.

Tunc reliquit eum diabolus.

Et ecce, angeli accesserunt, et ministrabant ei.

I. Locus: Quod non casu tentemur. II. De tyrannide et insidiis diaboli. III. Quomodo liberetur homo ex hac servitute, scilicet per Filium Dei. IIII. Victoria Filii Dei prodest nobis, et sicut in sua persona vicit, ita vult in credentibus vincere insidias diaboli, etsi vult nos quoque certare, ut experiamur auxilium. V. Tres tentationes in persona Christi sunt exempla tentationum Ecclesiae, et persecutionum. Primum Ecclesia premitur inopia, et excruciatur a tyrannis. Secundo laceratur a doctoribus impiis, qui dogmata spargunt sua audacia sine verbo Dei. Tertio contaminatur manifesta idololatria. De primis quatuor locis.

Etsi tot horribilia scelera, idololatriae, libidines, caedes, bella, excidia regnorum, et magnae calamitates, quae sequuntur scelera, satis ostendunt grassari aliquem saevum et potentem hostem adversus genus humanum: tamen tantus est stupor hominum, ut haec ducat levia, et putet casu accidere. Sed doctrina Evangelii patefacit veras causas, ostendit diabolum grassari adversus genus humanum, et homines propter peccatum subiectos esse eius tyrannidi. Rursus etiam ostendit nobis liberatorem, qui cum diabolo praeliatur. Sicut Iohannes inquit: Filius Dei apparuit ut destruat opera diaboli. Itaque in summa de tentationibus tenendae sunt hae admonitiones, de causis, et de liberatore.

Certum est, non casu accidere tanta hominum mala, sed diabolum odio Dei hostiliter grassari contra omnes, et insigni morsu sauciare singulos, sicut initio Evam et Adam sauciavit. Quare suam quisque vitam intuetur, et deprehendet aliquod insigne vulnus. Insidiose pertrahit diabolus vel ad scelus, vel ad calamitatem, ut inde pertrahat in desperationem et blasphemiam. Has insidias consideremus, et discamus confugere ad ducem nostrum Christum Filium Dei, qui praeliatur adversus diabolum, sicut initio in Genesi dictum est: Hoc semen conteret caput serpentis, quae vox prorsus convenit cum illo dicto Iohannis: Filius Dei apparuit, ut destruat opera diaboli, id est, peccata, calamitates, mortem. Haec in summa hic observanda sunt, ut praeparemus animos, quia non levia certamina subeunda sunt. In his luceat et exerceatur fides, et imploretur auxilium Filii Dei, qui ideo vicit diabolum in his tentationibus, ut ostendat se victorem fore, etiam in his praeliis, in quibus nos adoritur diabolus.

V. De Christi tentationibus cogitemus fuisse mirum quoddam, insidiosum et vehemens certamen, et multo acrius et maius, quam a nobis cogitari possit. Tentatus est alias saepe: sed hae tentationes nominatim describuntur, quia haud dubie significant aliquid toti Ecclesiae.

VI. De prima tentatione historiae notae sunt, tempore Apostolorum et Martyrum corpora et facultates piorum semper erant in periculo. Idem solet accidere quandocunque moventur certamina de doctrina, ut nunc: et haec tentatio sub Turcica tyrannide recrudescit. Hic insultat diabolus multorum animis, Si filii Dei estis, si Deo servitis, scilicet victitandum vobis erit ex lapidibus. Est enim ironia obiicientis inopiam, famem, et alias miserias exprobrantis. Hic quaerendae et opponendae sunt consolationes.

Primum sciamus mansuram esse Ecclesiam, et non posse everti a portis inferorum. Deinde sciamus invocantes Christum habituros esse auxilium, iuxta hoc dictum: Filius Dei apparuit, ut destruat opera diaboli. Item: Non in solo pane vivit homo, in Ecclesia alitur, conservatur, defenditur non tantum communibus et visibilibus auxiliis et modis, sed etiam divinis, quae non perspicit ratio. Si tamen Ecclesia maneat in agnitione verbi Dei, non deficiat a verbo Dei. Psalmus inquit: Scitote quod mirificat Dominus sanctum suum. Ita, etsi iam non videmus, qualis sit futura Ecclesia, etiamsi Turci tota Europa potirentur, tamen si retinebimus verbum Dei, curae erit Deo, ut habeamus defensionem. Caeterum haec doctrina etiam singulis accomodanda est, unusquisque in sua inopia, in suis periculis cogitet, se solis humanis consiliis non posse tueri vitam, vocationem, statum: sed petendum et expectandum esse auxilium divinum, ut in fide et invocatione Dei vivamus.

Sed pauci sic vivunt, omnes quaerunt opes, ut habeant certa auxilia in conspectu et in promtu, et ridetur do- ctrina Christi: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis.

VII. De secunda.

Ordo historiarum ostendit post corporales vexationes accessisse haereses, sicut hic apte signi- ficatur. Stans in fastigio templi, est aliquis ex- cellens doctrina, Is se deiiciens, id est, spargens dogma, sine verbo Dei, tentat Deum. Tales fuerunt, sunt et erunt plurimi, sed tunc erant, Ebion, Cerinthus, Marcion, Manes, Samosate- nus, Arius, Pelagius, et similes.

Tentare Deum proprie, est certare cum Deo fiducia propriae sapientiae, iusticiae et virium, ac nolle regi ipsius Dei verbo, ac ordinatione et vocatione. Sed his spretis aliud quaerere, fidu- cia nostrae sapientiae, quod nobis magis placet. Ut humana sapientia Pontifices mandarunt coeli- batum, Samosatenus corrupit doctrinam de Filio Dei, et quaerebat aliud concinnius. Pseudo- apostoli quaerebant humano iudicio aliquid plau- sibilius cum legem abrogari nollent. Ideo dicit Petrus: Quid tentatis Deum? id est, fiducia vestrae sapientiae et humanarum rationum certa- tis cum Deo, disceditis ab eius verbo. Et postea Pontifices profecto horribiliter tentaverunt Deum multis pravis dogmatibus, de abusu sacramento- rum, de ignoratione fidei et verae invocationis, de monasticis cultibus.

VIII. De tertia.

Postrema tentatio, est regni causa manife- stam idolatriam constituere et defendere. Sicut utrunque regnum Papae et Mahometi habet prae- cipuos nervos, terram idolatriam. Praemonet igitur nos Christus, ut haec regna postrema op- pressura Ecclesiam, iudicare discamus, et vite- mus idolatrias, et non defugiamus certamina, et significatur exitus certaminum.

## 4:1 Notes on Matthew: Argument
Chapter IV.

Let us be baptized by Christ etc. etc.

ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

Annotations on the Gospel of Matthew, delivered at Wittenberg by M. Sebastian [missing name], in the same Church, written by Philipp Melanchthon.

[Reference to] Vol. III p. 247 sqq. — Also reprinted at Wittenberg.

[Reference to] A letter of this same Melanchthon to the Senate of Amberg, dated September 29. I undertook this labor willingly, although I am very busy, so that I might be ready to perform such works for all, from which some benefit might return either to the Church or to posterity, or to those themselves who seek my work, neither for my own sake nor for others, that is, the Church, for whom hope can be had: but entirely for others, that is, for those requiring his help. Therefore, I have prepared for individuals on the days of Preparation [Friday] the summaries of certain chapters.

Then, when I arrived at chapter 5, I composed almost just sermons in the vernacular language, so that I might be able to propose the matter more properly to my listeners, yet explaining the rest in Latin speech, sometimes admonishing and instructing, by which words our Latin terms could be most properly expressed and rendered, which could be used in the Church, which German [words]... inserted into the Latin in this printed edition might provide a cause for new struggles to be stirred up regarding doctrine, or for earlier ones to be renewed and confirmed, especially since by no means was so much leisure now granted to him as would be sufficient for reading through and revising these pages, which a hurried and often interrupted work had poured forth rather than written to this end, that it might provide me, as I was about to preach, a cause for thinking more diligently about the sayings of the Evangelist Matthew, not that those pages should be scattered into the hands of many.

There exist just and learned commentaries by others on this Evangelist, which he would prefer to be inspected and consulted by those about to preach, rather than these little annotations of his.

Since, therefore, I saw Master Philippus seriously confirmed in this opinion, that he would not grant the publication of this commentary, I began, as I said before, to transcribe it with my own hand, so that I might send a copy of it to you in our homeland.

For I had many reasons why I decided that this most useful labor of my teacher, which I had used in teaching in this Church not without fruit for the listeners, as I hope, should be shared with you.

For besides those most sacred bonds of our common homeland, by which we are mutually obligated to one another to perform any duties whatsoever, I was moved by your munificence, with which you liberally advanced my studies at the Academy of Leipzig and here at Wittenberg, and by your other benefits, with which you have favored me for a long time now while I have been absent.

Furthermore, I judged that I owed this to my homeland, that to it, whom I could not benefit and serve in person in the illustration and propagation of the pure doctrine of the Gospel, I might impart while absent those things which I had drawn and collected here from learned men and those excelling in the excellence of their gifts.

Moved by these and other reasons, while I was laboring to prepare a copy of my sermons for you, some colleagues and friends of mine here rushed upon me in a single, as it were, assault, and with great zeal contended with me that I should take care to have this commentary on Matthew, as it was written by Philippus, printed; to whom, although I explained what stood in my way—namely, the prohibition of the author himself, whom I did not think should be offended by this edition, since I had found him so prompt, easy, and kind in writing these sermons for my own benefit and that of the Church—nevertheless, they began to urge me seriously, and at the same time to show me letters sent here from elsewhere (such as I myself have frequently received

Reimann, in his Catalogus bibliothecae theologicae, p. 323, passed this judgment on this little book: "It is a booklet taken from the mouth of the Author, interpolated, not polished, nor brought to a conclusion, to be recommended only for... the antiquity and rarity of the edition." (See Strobel, ibid., p. 67.) We, who have had the booklet in our hands and have read it, certainly approve of Reimann's judgment.

It is a booklet compiled from the manuscripts of certain students, who were not very learned. The style is often alien to Melanchthon's elegance and clarity, nor do the disciples seem to have correctly understood the Master's words everywhere.

Although, therefore, Hervagius inserted these "annotations on Matthew" into the works of Melanchthon published at Basel, we nevertheless cannot consider this booklet sufficiently trustworthy or as representing the genuine words of Melanchthon. Nor could Peucer, Melanchthon's son-in-law, bring himself to insert this booklet into the works of Melanchthon published at Wittenberg.

But so that the Readers themselves might be able to judge the booklet in some way, we have wished to provide a part of it here as an example, namely the complete scholia on the second and third chapters of Matthew.

(EXCERPTS FROM THE ANNOTATIONS OF PHIL.

MEL. ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.) Chapter II.
