When Jesus was born in Bethlehem, city of Judea etc. First, God shows the Savior to the Magi, that is, to the wise men or priests of the Persians, by which he signified that Christ was also born for the Gentiles. And just as the Evangelist previously taught why Christ came, so now he adumbrates our calling.

First, a star rises, that is, a certain celestial light, which, when it has fallen into darkness, places us before our own eyes, and affects us with a certain thirst for divine mercy, with the anxious sighs of souls that truly thirst for God, seeking where Christ the Savior is, who was born King of the Jews, having called us away from created things, so that we might take some comfort from them. And thus he shows us to ourselves, so that, although the grasp of nature does not see that there is a path to God, through certain obscure things, and always against the affections of nature, the Spirit leads our counsels, and we do not feel anything except our own vices, and so God does not seem to be reconciled, so that God is thought to be more irritated.

This struggle of the Spirit and our nature first breaks and humbles us. What seemed pleasant, sweet, and good to the flesh, this withers, becomes invisible, becomes a lying evil, until the mind of man becomes so pure that nothing is left in it except an anxious desire for God, and as the prophet says: "All my desire is before thee," likewise: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks etc." That affection begins here and is completed in death; there is no path to God except these anxious sighs. We are taught, therefore, on whom it behooves us to depend: that Christ was born in Bethlehem, that is, that one cannot arrive at God except through Christ born in Bethlehem.

To him, since he was born in Bethlehem, that is, born in the infirmity of our flesh, one must flee. And thou Bethlehem, land of Judah, art not the least etc. Micah 5: "And thou Bethlehem Ephratah, art little among the thousands of Judah," which reading is clearly different from the Evangelist's reading. But he reported the meaning more than the words.

For if you read in the prophet, through an interrogative of admiration, "Art thou Bethlehem?" as if he were saying, "Certainly not." Why not?

"Because out of thee shall come forth unto me, that is to be ruler in Israel." The Evangelist rendered this emphasis, with the addition of a negation, because this had already been fulfilled, which the prophet had previously predicted. Otherwise, Bethlehem is small in appearance, great in spirit, just as the Church is despised in appearance, but renowned in spirit.

In which sense the prophet called it small, but the Evangelist, with the mystery now revealed, called it great. That I may come and worship him also. An example of impiety has been produced. Thus we are accustomed to cloak the appearance of piety with all our own desires, and there is almost no one for whom God is not worshipped in the place of an idol.

XII. ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. to use as a pretext, and there is almost no one for whom a god is not worshipped in place of an idol.

However, those who act like Herod are primarily those who seek their own interests under the guise of piety, who use the name of Christ as a pretext for their tyranny in the Church.

Admonished by an oracle.

This is an argument for hope and faith, where God's solitude for His own is commemorated, as Paul also says in Ro.

8: "He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all,

how will He not also with Him freely give us all things?"

Behold, an angel of the Lord appears in a dream to Joseph, etc.

And this passage is an argument for impiety, that Christ deserted Judea, which presented an appearance of piety, and sanctified sinful Egypt.

This means that we should understand that Christ came to save sinners.

Furthermore, it is not in vain that he brings forth the Prophet Hosea's saying.

For even there in Hosea, it is not so much about Christ as about the entire faithful people.

EXCERPTS TAKEN IN PASSING on Chapter Three.

Christ flees Judea, i.e., external worship and appearance, so that He might sanctify Egypt, i.e., that He might save those who showed themselves to be sinners and humble.

That Christ is called out of Egypt means at the same time that the whole world is called out of the vices of Egypt, so that we may understand that Christ came to earth for the sake of our justification.

Bethlehem, that is, house of bread.

Magi, Persian priests.

The star is the grace of our God, which is poured out upon us through God.

Bethlehem, a village not far from Jerusalem.

Herod was a most wicked man, who at one time killed his own sons by tyrannical murder.

From this Augustus took the saying, that he would rather be Herod's pig than his son.

When they had seen the star.

It is believed that there was an angel there.

Herod had ordered all two-year-olds or younger to be killed.

A voice in Rama, that is, on high.

Rachel is used for Bethlehem.

Allegorically, the gifts are interpreted thus: By gold, a sincere and pure spirit.

By frankincense, a spirit burning towards God.

By myrrh, a vehement and most ardent spirit for the glory of God.

584 Chapter III.

In Christ's birth and infancy, it has been briefly discussed why He was born, how we are called by the guidance of a star, that is, how we are reborn in Christ, and that the first rudiments of Christ's life are to suffer adversities and exiles.

Now, however, a more mature age is to be pursued; we are engrafted into Christ through repentance and baptism.

Therefore, it seems necessary to discuss repentance and baptism in a little more detail.

Repentance is the renewal of life in Christ, which renewal is the conversion of sins.

The conversion of a

sinner occurs in this way: God transfuses the spirit of grace into the soul of the sinner, who, with sinful affections first repressed by the word of God, is terrified, afflicted, tormented, becomes anxious about his sin, so much so that he thirsts for the justifying spirit. There is no refuge or rest for the sinner there except Christ, into whom if he casts his sin, it is abolished through faith.

There are therefore two works of grace: first, to humble; next, to tranquilize, to uplift, to govern.

Grace performs the first work through the word of the law, the second through the word of Christ.

Horror and the recognition of sin come from the law; the absolution of sins comes through the Gospel.

The first work of grace is signified when it is said, "Turn back"; the next, "and I will turn to you."

The first work is done through the word of John, the next through the word of Christ.

John terrifies, so that Christ may be desired more vehemently.

Therefore, the repentance of John and Christ is the same, but the works of grace are different.

God terrifies through the word of John, that is, the law, and at the same time impels to the desire for grace.

Christ heals; otherwise, the law without grace either does not affect us, or it terrifies us so much that we despair, and God becomes hateful to us.

Grace, however, first makes the soul humble, deserted, dry, and thirsty, then it calms it.

Therefore, you see how harsh and full of threats John's sermon is.

For this reason, the sacred writers say that John's baptism did not have the remission of sins.

For it is Christ alone who forgives sins, who tranquilizes the conscience; John's baptism did not confer grace, but Christ's baptism does confer it.

Wherever the prophets commend grace, they first indicate the wrath and judgment of God, so here John says: "The axe is laid to the root."

He himself will baptize you.

That Christ baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire signifies that Christ is God and the author of justi-34

ENARRATIONES EVANGELIUM MATTHAEI.

Enarrationes Evangelii Matthaei, Witebergae habitae a M. Sebastiano Fröschelio, in eadem Ecclesia, scriptae a Philippo Melanthone.

Tom. III. p. 247 sqq. - Recusae etiam Witeberg.

De genere huius scripti Enarrationis ad Senatum Ambergensem d. d. 29. Septb. MDXLIIII. haec annotavi: Cum adivi meo marte in singulis diebus S. Hunc laborem ille in se recepit libenter, quamvis occupatissimus, ut est paratus omnibus ad eiusmodi operas praestandas, ex quibus utilitas aliqua reditura vel ad Ecclesiam et posteritatem, vel ad illos ipsos, qui operam eius expetunt, sed prorsus aliis, hoc est, Ecclesiae, rei literariae, et omnibus opem ipsius requirentibus. Scripsit igitur singulis diebus Parasceves mihi praeseti primum dispositiones et summas quasdam breves singulorum capitum.

Deinde ubi ad 5. cap. pervenimus, iustas ferme conciones contexuit, aliquandiu vernacula lingua, ut magis proprie res ipsas auditoribus meis proponere possem, reliqua a cap. 9. explicavit Latina oratione, subinde tamen me admonens ac instruens, quibus verbis nostra lingua quam propriissime efferri et reddi Latina vocabula in Ecclesia usurpata possent, quas Germanicas. manicas voces Latinis insertas etiam in hoc excurso editione causam praeberi, nova certamina de doctrina excitandi, aut priora renovandi et confirmandi, praesertim cum nequaquam sibi tantum ocii nunc concederetur, quantum ad perlegendum et retexendum has pagellas satis esset, quas tumultuaria et interrupta saepe opera effuderit potius quam scripserit in hunc finem, ut mihi concionaturo causam diligentius cogitandi de dictis Matthaei Evangelistae praeberet, non ut in plurium manus illae pagellae spargerentur.

Extare aliorum iustos et eruditos in hunc Evangelistam commentarios, quos malit a concionaturis inspici et consuli, quam has suas annotatiunculas.

Cum igitur in hac sententia serio confirmatum viderem Dominum Philippum, quod nollet concedere editionem huius commentarii, coepi, ut ante dixi, mea manu eum transcribere, ut eius exemplum ad vos in patriam mitterem.

Multas enim causas habebam, cur hunc Praeceptoris mei utilissimum laborem, quo ego in docenda Ecclesia hac non sine fructu auditorum, ut spero, usus eram, statuerem vobiscum communicandum esse.

Nam praeter illa sanctissima communis patriae vincula, quibus inter nos mutuo obligati sumus ad quaevis officia praestanda, movebant me vestra munificentia, quam mea studia in Academia Lipsica et hic Witebergae liberaliter provexistis, et alia beneficia vestra, quibus me longo iam tempore absentem affecistis.

Deinde iudicabam me hoc patriae meae debere, ut cui in illustratione et propagatione purae doctrinae Evangelii coram prodesse ac servire non possem, absens ei impertirer illa, quae hic a viris eruditis et donorum excellentia praestantibus hausissem et collegissem.

His et aliis rationibus motus, dum exemplum vobis mearum concionum adornare laboro, uno quasi impetu in me irruunt aliquot hic collegae et amici mei, qui magno studio a me contendunt, ut hunc commentarium in Matthaeum, ut est, a Philippo scriptus, typis excudi curarem, quibus etsi ego, quid mihi obstaret, exponebam, nempe auctoris ipsius prohibitionem, quem offendendum hac editione non putarem, cum ipsum ad conscribendas in... meam et Ecclesiae gratiam et utilitatem has conciones tam habuissem promptum, facilem et benignum: tamen illi urgere serio coeperunt, et ostendere simul literas aliunde huc missas (quales etiam ipse ex diversis locis frequentes acceperunt

Reimannus in Catalogo bibl. Theol. p. 323. de hoc libello Mel. hoc tulit iudicium: „est opusculum ex ore Auctoris exceptum, interpolatum, non expolitum, nec ad coronidem deductum, sola editionis et antiquitate et raritate commendandum.” (Vid. Strobel. l. l. p. 67.) Nos, qui libellum in manibus habuimus et legimus, iudicium Reimanni utique comprobamus.

Est opusculum, ex manuscriptis quorundam studiosorum, parum doctorum, compilatum. Stylus a Melanthonis elegantia et perspicuitate saepe alienus, neque discipuli ubique Magistri dicta recte intellexisse videntur.

Quanquam igitur Hervagius has „annotationes in Matthaeum operibus Melanchonis Basileae editis inseruit, nos tamen hunc libellum non potuimus habere satis fide dignum et genuina dicta Melanchonis referentem. Neque Peucerus, gener Melanchonis, potuit a se impetrare, ut hunc libellum operibus Melanchonis Witebergae editis insereret.

Ut vero Lectores ipsi aliquo modo iudicare de libello possent, partem eius, ut exemplo sit, hic dare voluimus, nempe scholia integra in caput secundum et tertium Matthaei.

(EXCERPTA EX ANNOTATIONIBUS PHIL.

MEL. IN EVANGELIUM MATTHAEI.) Caput II.

*Cum natus esset Iesus in Bethlehem, civitate Iudae etc.* Primum Magis, hoc est Persis sapientibus, sive sacerdotibus ostendit Deus salvatorem, quo significaret, etiam Christum in gentes natum esse. Atque ut antea Evangelista, quid Christus venerit docuit, ita modo adumbrat vocationem nostram.

Primum stella oritur, hoc est, lux quaedam coelestis, quae cum in tenebras inciderit, nos nobis ante oculos ponit, et siti quadam divinae misericordiae afficit, anxiis suspiriis animorum, quae vere Deum sitiunt, quaerunt, ubinam sit Christus salvator, qui natus est rex Iudaeorem, avocatos de creaturis lux, ut quid ex eis solatii capiamus. Et ita nos nobis ostendit, ut captus tamen naturae non videat, quod ad deum iter sit, per obscura quaedam, et semper contra naturae affectus, consiliaque ducit spiritus, nec sentimus nos nisi vitia nostra, adeoque non videtur reconciliari deus, ut magis irritari putetur deus.

Haec pugna spiritus et naturae nostrae, primum frangit et humiliat, Quod carni iucundum, suave, boverum visum est, hoc marcescit, invisum, malum mendax fit, donec adeo pura fiat mens hominis, ut nihil praeter anxium desiderium dei in ea relinquatur, et cum propheta dicat: Omne desiderium meum aute te, item: Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum etc. Affectus ille hic incipit, et absolvitur morte, nullum ad deum est iter, praeter haec anxia suspiria. Docemur itaque ex quo pendere nos oporteat, Christum natum esse in Bethlehem, hoc est, perveniri ad deum non nisi per Christum natum in Bethlehem.

Ad hunc, quandoquidem natus est in Bethlehem, hoc est, natus in infirmitate carnis nostrae, confugiendum est. Et tu Bethlehem terra Iuda, nequaquam minima es etc. Micheae 5. Et tu Bethlehem Euphrata parvulus es in millibus Iuda, quae lectio plane diversa est ab Evangelistae lectione. Sed hic sententiam magis quam verba retulit.

Nam si legas apud prophetam, per interrogationem admirationis notam, Tune Bethlehem? quasi dicat, certe non.

Quare non? Quoniam ex te mihi egredietur, qui sit dominator in Israel. Hanc emphasim reddidit Evangelista, addita negatione, quia hoc iam impletum erat, quod antea propheta praedixit. Caeterum parvula est Bethlehem specie, spiritu magna, perinde ut Ecclesia in speciem contempta, spiritu inclyta.

Quo sensu et propheta parvam dixit, Evangelista vero revelato iam mysterio, magnam. Ut et ego veniam et adorem illum. Exemplum impietatis proditum est. Sic solemus pietatis speciem omnibus nostris cupidita

XII. ANNOTATIONES IN EVANGELIUM MATTHAEI. tibus praetexere, et fere nemo est, cui non idoli vice deus colatur.

Oraculo admoniti.

Est argumentum spei et fidei, ubi solitudo dei pro suis commemoratur, ut Paulus etiam Ro.

8.: Qui proprio filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum.

Qui fieri potest, ut non cum eodem omnia nobis donet?

Ecce angelus domini apparet in somniis Ioseph etc.

Et hic locus impietatis argumentum est, quod Christus Iudaeam, quae speciem pietatis prae se ferebat, deseruit, et vitiosam Aegyptum sanctificavit.

Id quod eo pertinet, ut intelligamus Christum venisse, ut peccatores salvos faceret.

Ex quo Augustus proverbii locum sumebat, se malle eius esse porcum quam filium.

584 Caput III.

In Christi natali et infantia paucis tractatum est, cur genitus sit, quo modo nos vocemus stella duce, hoc est renascamur Christo, et prima rudimenta esse vitae Christi pati adversitates et exilia.

Nunc autem aetas maturior prosequenda est, inserimur Christo per poenitentiam et baptismum.

Proinde de poenitentia et baptismo paulo pluribus agendum videtur.

Poenitentia est innovatio vitae in Christum, quae innovatio est peccatorum conversio.

Fit autem conversio

peccatoris in hunc modum. Spiritum gratiae transfundit deus in animam peccatoris, qui per verbum dei repressis primum peccato affectibus terretur, affligitur, cruciatur, anxius fit pro peccato suo, adeo ut sitiat spiritum iustificantem, ibi non est peccatori perfugium neque quies nisi Christus, in quem si peccatum reiecerit, per fidem aboletur.

Duplex est ergo gratiae opus, primum humiliare, proximum tranquillare, erigere, gubernare.

Primum opus facit gratia per verbum legis, secundum per verbum Christi.

Horror et agnitio peccati ex lege est, Absolutio peccatorum per Evangelium.

Primum gratiae opus significatur cum dicitur, convertimini: proximum, et ego convertar ad vos.

Primum opus fit per verbum Ioannis, proximum per verbum Christi.

Ioannes terret, ut vehementius desideretur Christus.

Eadem ergo poenitentia est Ioannis et Christi, opera autem gratiae diversa.

Deus terret per verbum Ioannis, hoc est legis, et simul impellit ad desiderium gratiae.

Christus medetur, alioqui lex sine gratia aut non afficit nos, aut ita terret ut desperemus, ac invisus nobis fiat deus.

Gratia vero primum humilem, desertum, aridum, sitibundum reddit animum, deinde serenat.

Propterea Ioannis contio vides quam aspera sit, et plena minarum.

Ob id sacri scriptores baptismum Ioannis non habuisse remissionem peccatorum dicunt.

Solius enim Christi est condonare peccata, tranquillare conscientiam, Ioannis baptismus non conferebat gratiam, confert autem Christi baptismus.

Prophetae ubicunque gratiam commendant, prius iram et iudicium dei indicant, ita hic Ioannes inquit: securis ad radicem posita est,

Ipse vos baptizabit.

Christum baptizare spiritu sancto et igni, significat Christum deum esse et authorem iusti-34

## 5:1 All Saints’ Day, Matt. 5
The Gospel on All Saints’ Day, Matt. 5.

Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up on the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. and opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God. Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For so persecuted they the Prophets which were before you.

There are three points.

I. The general doctrine is against the opinions concerning the scandal of the cross. II. And there are added promises of good works, interpreting the law. III. And at the same time, the doctrine is delivered concerning faith to be exercised in these works.

On the first.

Promises are twofold. Some are legal, which have the condition of works, and are added to good works, or merits, as: He that shall give to one of the least a cup of water, shall not lose his reward. And here: Blessed are the meek, Blessed are the poor in spirit, etc.

But since no one satisfies the law, here it must be asked, how good works please God, and how these promises become valid.

Therefore we answer, as has often been said elsewhere: The law without Christ does not profit, but just as the law is valid, so also are the legal promises valid, when the promise of grace given for Christ's sake has first been apprehended. And so, when we are righteous by faith, then the begun obedience pleases God, and merits rewards, and the promises are then valid, because that obedience is said to be a certain fulfillment of the law. There is therefore another promise proper to the Gospel, gratuitous, namely of reconciliation and righteousness to be imputed for Christ's sake. This promise must always shine before all works and promises, because through the Son we have access to the Father. We have therefore prefaced this, so that it may be known how these legal promises are valid and ratified, according to that: By faith we establish the law.

Hence an objection can also be explained. Since he says here that men are blessed by meekness, why do you say elsewhere that men are justified by faith alone? I answer: These do not conflict. It is necessary first for men to be made righteous or accepted by God, by faith, freely for Christ's sake, afterwards they are also blessed, that is, having gifts and rewards from God, for other virtues. These things, explained in this way without sophistry, can be easily understood. Let us learn therefore that legal promises or those of good works are delivered here, which are to be accepted in such a way that the evangelical promise of the grace of Christ always shines forth.

On the second. Promises proposed in this place dissent from the judgment of reason, and are an exposition of the Mosaic law: the law says, it shall be well with the good. But here Christ says that the righteous will be in poverty, mourning, and persecution. But Christ answers that the chief rewards are deferred, even if in this life also it is necessary for the Church to be preserved by the wonderful benefits of God.

Let it be well with the righteous.

Abel is righteous. Therefore let it be well with Abel.

I answer first to the minor premise: Abel is righteous by imputation, and has begun obedience, but because sin still clings to him, death remains, and this vicious nature is subject to the cross. Therefore rewards are deferred to perfected righteousness. Then you should answer to the major premise: Let it be well with the righteous, according to the counsel of God, and after this life. For God, in order to preserve the Church, even in this life imparts huge gifts, but amidst wonderful struggles, just as he preserved the Church in the flood, in Egypt, in the Babylonian captivity, and in the times of the martyrs. Let us therefore hold to this interpretation of the law, which Christ delivers here, when he promises rewards, and testifies that they are given partly in this life, partly after this life.

On the third.

But this is especially to be learned in these discourses, how faith is to be exercised in these promises. We rejoice in faith, and we especially flee the exercises of faith. Christ predicts the Church to be in hardships, because in these He wishes faith to be exercised.

How? In eight ways.

First, by acknowledging the grace promised on account of Christ. Second, by calling upon God. Third, by being impelled to good works, so that the benefit of God may be retained. Fourth, by seeking and expecting help, against the devil, against enemies, against one's own weakness. Fifth, by expecting compensation or rewards. Sixth, by seeking help in endurance. Seventh, by showing gratitude, and examples, so that the doctrine may be propagated, and the glory of God adorned. Eighth, so that faith, stirred and awakened by these exercises, may grow, and other gifts may grow.

An example: Paul in afflictions first considered whether he pleased God, because afflictions and adverse events seem to be signs of God's wrath.

He therefore stirs up faith, and feels that he pleases God on account of Christ, and flees to God. Second, he calls upon Him. Third, acknowledging the mercy of God toward him, he strives to retain the benefit, and takes care not to lose righteousness. Fourth, by faith he seeks and expects liberation in afflictions and help against the devil. Fifth, he expects rewards, and looking with faith to the promised end, he endures present hardships. Sixth, by faith he seeks help and strength of spirit, so that he may be able to show patience, even if death must be faced. Seventh, he determines that these duties are necessary to show gratitude, for the propagation of the Gospel, he acknowledges God, by a wonderful counsel, thus wishing to abolish sin in our flesh, and to glorify the Church in a wonderful way. Eighth, he makes an effort so that faith may grow, and other gifts. Thus a believing rich man calls upon God, strives to retain righteousness, obeys God in the duty of liberality, expects in turn help from God in his hardships, and expects compensation or the preservation of his resources, shows gratitude by his example, desires gifts to be increased, faith to be increased.

But because few believe, few expect the preservation of resources: therefore their minds are more narrow and illiberal. These generalities must always be held regarding legal promises, so that we may remember that even in these promises of rewards, faith must be exercised.

Blessed are the poor in spirit.

He does not wish resources to be abandoned without a calling, He does not approve of Monasticism, according to that: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men, but Christ preaches about the true poverty of the pious and those fleeing the gains of the impious, whether the poverty be accidental, or whether it happened on account of the profession of the Gospel. He consoles all these needy ones, and testifies that poverty is not a sign of God's wrath and a curse, but rather He promises rewards.

And this is a sentiment opposed to the law, and to the empires of the world. The law teaches that the loss of resources is a punishment for sins and a curse: here Christ teaches the pious that the judgment concerning the cross is different according to the Gospel. For afflictions for the pious are not signs of wrath, but become exercises of faith, just as the Gospel cries out everywhere, that the Church is subject to the cross.

In the most severe afflictions, the greatest lights of the Church have been Christ, John the Baptist, Jeremiah, Abel, etc.

Likewise, the empires of the world are said to flourish when they have wealth, and the Pontiffs think the same about the Church. But Christ here testifies that the Church flourishes rather in poverty, so that we may not despair on account of need.

He adds, however: Poor in spirit, that is, in spiritual obedience, patiently bearing poverty, or prepared to bear it, if they have been stripped of their resources, just as Abraham at one time had resources, at another wandered needy without fixed dwellings.

Blessed are those who mourn.

And here He speaks of the true sorrows of the pious, whether they happen on account of their profession, or arise from the punishments or bites of the devil, as when David, driven into exile, acknowledged his guilt and felt that he was being punished. In such hardships, the conscience cries out that we have been cast off or deserted by God. But the voice of the Gospel teaches otherwise: A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit.

Likewise: Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and here consolation is promised, both in this life and after this life, as the whole of Psalm 4 teaches: Know that the Lord makes His holy one wonderful, and hears me when I cry to Him. Likewise Psalm 35: The poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.

Blessed are the meek.

He consoles the oppressed, who have no avenger and defender, and teaches that private vengeance must be commended to God, just as Joseph, the Israelites in Egypt, David under Saul, the pious under Antiochus,

The Church under Diocletian was without defense. However, this passage is understood more clearly when the antithesis is considered. Tyrants think that empires are maintained and increased by the bitterness of vengeance. On the contrary, the Gospel teaches that we should be constant in a just cause, yet not seek private vengeance, but commend the outcomes to God. And when vengeance must be exercised by virtue of one's office, we should mitigate it, just as the examples of David illustrate this whole doctrine. He never wanted to kill Saul; then, while reigning, he nevertheless often tempered necessary vengeance with mercy, and spared Shimei.

Hither pertain many things in the Psalms, such as Psalm 37: The raging shall be exterminated, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the earth. Pharaoh was destroyed, Israel conquered. The Apostles were killed, yet the Church remained when the tyrants were destroyed. Therefore, this little verse promises to the oppressed, and to those lacking an avenger and not desiring private vengeance, preservation even on earth. Although these things are written properly for the sake of the Church, yet so that the matter may be more clear, let us also consider political examples. In political justice, clemency is useful for princes, and gentleness for private citizens. On the contrary, cruelty has been the ruin of many, not only of monstrous tyrants who were also polluted by other crimes, such as Phalaris, Dionysius, and Nero, but also of those otherwise mediocre, such as Pertinax and Aurelian. And we often see that great private offenses are healed by patience. Christ demands this gentleness most of all, because dangerous offenses occur in the Church; therefore He says so often: Forgive, and it will be forgiven you. And Christ, washing the feet of the Apostles, wishes us to heal offenses by every kind of service; therefore He says: I have given you an example. And Peter says: Love covers a multitude of sins. Let all these sentences be transferred here. And because in dangers to our reputation or property, if an avenger is lacking, we fear that we and our belongings will perish, therefore preservation is promised here, when He says: They shall possess the earth, just as Israel was preserved in Egypt, even though the command had been given that the infants should be killed.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.

To thirst for righteousness is to be affected with true sorrow and zeal, so that the glory of God may be propagated, that the government may be just, and that scandals and bad examples may be removed. This clause is, as it were, a certain declaration of the previous one. Before, He said that clemency is salutary; now He adds that this clemency ought not to be dissolution or sloth. Let zeal be added; let everyone be vigilant, intent, and sharp in their own office. And the sentiment is opposed to the Epicureans, who care nothing for any vices whatsoever, whether of religions or others, just as the Epicureans now mock us when we complain about idolatry or lusts. Christ detests this sloth, and commands zeal, and adds a promise. For the impious say that the pious strive in vain for amendment. Christ, on the contrary, promises that labors will not be empty; they shall be satisfied, He says. Likewise, let these who thirst be understood not as Cynics, who only criticize the vices of others while winking at their own, but as those who also amend themselves, according to that saying: The just man is the first accuser of himself, afterwards he encounters another.

Blessed are the merciful. A reward is promised to those who do good, who defend or help the afflicted, such as those who cover those who are afflicted on account of the profession of the Gospel, according to the Psalm: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor, etc.

Blessed are the pure in heart, that is, chaste, just as it is said to the Hebrews: Pursue sanctification, that is, chastity, without which no one will see God.

And a common punishment for lusts is blindness, as is said in Romans 1 and Ephesians 4.

Blessed are the peacemakers, that is, those who rightly judge dogmas, who rightly heal the unjust discords of the Church or of kingdoms, yielding to others in good conscience for the sake of peace. The greatest part of the Decalogue is contained here. For these virtues pertain to the first commandment: Truth and fortitude in confession, concerning which He says: Blessed are those who suffer persecution. Likewise: Faith expecting these promises and retaining the truth on account of these promises. Likewise: Patience in any hardships whatsoever. For these virtues are the worship concerning which the first commandment preaches. To the second table pertain gentleness in mitigating vengeance, beneficence, chastity, and charity or equity in making peace. To the first commandment pertains thirsting for righteousness, that is, zeal, etc.

Concerning the saying: I have not come to abolish the law.

The moral law is an eternal and immutable sentence in the divine mind, which is the rule of justice, prescribing what all intelligent creatures ought to be, and what they ought to do and omit. what ought to be, and what they ought to do and omit, and denouncing the wrath of God and punishments, both present and eternal, to those who do not perform perfect obedience.

But although God is a most free agent, yet as this proposition is eternal and immovable—God is wise, just, good—so these propositions are eternal and immovable: God wills just things, obedience is owed to God.

Nor let us imagine that the moral law of God is something mutable, which can be abrogated and deleted, just as a tablet fixed to a wall can be removed, or as the Spartan law could be changed regarding bronze coinage. There remains in God knowledge, which is the rule of acting justly. There remains a will that truly, not feignedly, wills just things, and truly, not feignedly, rejects unjust things, as the Psalm says: "You are not a God who wills impiety." And similar to these divine notices are those impressed upon the human mind, which always remain and judge deeds. Wherefore, let not the abrogation of the law be imagined as such, as if God now does not grow angry at one rushing against the moral law, just as He does not grow angry at one eating swine's flesh.

But let someone say: If the moral law is an eternal and immovable sentence, it follows that there is no remission of sins. I answer: Since every law obliges to obedience or to punishment, and we, having fallen, could not be restored unless the punishment were paid. But the punishment was derived onto the Son of God, nor does God receive the fallen except on account of the Son, nor does He approve of sin even if He receives believers, but He declared His wrath against sin to be immense in the passion of the Son. When, therefore, we think about the remission of sins, let us in faith look upon the Son crucified for us, so that He might pay the penalty, and let us acknowledge that God truly and horribly grows angry at sin, but that He receives us on account of the Son.

Therefore Christ says that He fulfills the law. And Paul says: "Christ is the end of the law," that is, the law testifies of Christ, just as all the victims signifying Christ admonish that the Lord was to come, who alone would fulfill the law; He fulfills it, however, in three ways. First, by sustaining the punishment for us, since He Himself was without sin and had perfect obedience, and yet was made a victim for us.

Secondly, He fulfills it effectively, because He Himself restores human nature and gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life, so that true obedience may again exist in man, which is begun here and perfected in the resurrection, and will be eternal, as it is said: "I will put my law in their hearts," where it is expressly said, "my," so that we may know that new and eternal life is truly wisdom, justice, and obedience, congruent to the very law sounding on Mount Sinai.

Therefore, when it is said that Christ fulfills the law, this degree also must be understood, namely, that by the given Holy Spirit He brings it about that true, integral, and eternal obedience is restored in us. And because He says "my law," it can be sufficiently understood that the moral law is an eternal sentence in the divine mind, because He wills to restore it in the hearts of men. It is not, therefore, abolished, just as the calendar of the past year is thrown away, as some foolishly speak.

Thirdly, Christ fulfills the law by teaching, that is, He testifies that He does not abolish it lest it be done, but proposes it so that it may argue against sins and teach what works God demands. For God wills that we be ruled by His word, nor does He want us to devise works and worships by our own imaginations, as the Gentiles devised, who fashioned idols without end, permitted themselves lusts, and meanwhile accumulated sacrifices and performed some civil works by which they thought themselves to be just and to please God, just as now the sacrificers praise their own works, Masses, observations of rites, and the obedience which they perform by their own laws, while they neglect the divine laws concerning true doctrine, true worship, and chastity. But Christ calls us back to the law of God; this He wills to be the doctrine of repentance and the rule of good works.

Latin:

Evangelium in die omnium Sanctorum, Matth. 5.

Videns Iesus turbas ascendit in montem, et cum sedisset, accesserunt ad eum discipuli cius, et aperiens os suum, docebat eos, dicens: Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum.

Beati mites, quoniam ipsi haereditabunt terram. Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur. Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt iusticiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Beati pacifici, quoniam ipsi filii Dei vocabuntur. Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iusticiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum. Beati estis, cum exprobraverint vobis homines, et persecuti vos fuerint, et dixerint omne malum verbum adversus vos mentientes, propter me. Gaudete et exultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in coelis. Sic enim persecuti sunt Prophetas qui fuerunt ante vos.

Tres sunt loci.

I. Doctrina generalis est, contra opiniones de scandalo crucis. II. Et sunt adiectae promissiones bonorum operum, interpretantes legem. III. Et simul traditur doctrina de fide exercenda in his operibus.

De primo.

Duplices sunt promissiones. Aliae legales, quae habent conditionem operum, et sunt additae bonis operibus, seu meritis, ut: Qui dederit uni ex minimis potum aquae, non perdet mercedem suam. Et hic: Beati mites, Beati pauperes spiritu etc.

Sed cum legi nemo satisfaciat, hic quaerendum est, quomodo bona opera placeant Deo, et quomodo hae promissiones fiant ratae.

Ideo respondemus, sicut alias saepe dictum est: Lex sine Christo non prodest, sicut autem valet lex, sic et valent legales promissiones, cum prius apprehensa est promissio gratiae donatae propter Christum. Itaque cum fide iusti sumus, deinde placet Deo incoata obedientia, et meretur praemia, ac promissiones tunc ratae sunt, quia illa obedientia dicitur esse quaedam legis impletio. Est igitur alia promissio propria Evangelii, gratuita, videlicet reconciliationis et iusticiae imputandae propter Christum. Haec promissio semper praeluocere debet omnibus operibus et promissionibus, quia per Filium habemus accessum ad patrem. Haec ideo praefati sumus, ut sciatur, quomodo hae promissiones legales valeant et ratae sint, iuxta illud: Per fidem stabilimus legem.

Hinc explicari etiam obiectio potest. Cum hic dicat, homines beatos esse mansuetudine, cur alibi dicitis, sola fide iustificari homines? Respondeo: Haec non pugnant. Oportet primum homines fieri iustos seu acceptos Deo, fide, gratis propter Christum, postea sunt etiam beati, id est, habentes dona et praemia a Deo, propter caeteras virtutes. Haec sine sophistica hoc modo explicata facile intelligi possunt. Discamus igitur tradi hic promissiones legales seu bonorum operum, quae sic accipiendae sunt, ut semper praeluceat promissio evangelica gratiae Christi.

De secundo. Promissiones hoc loco propositae dissentiunt a iudicio rationis, et sunt expositio legis Mosaicae: lex dicit, bonis bene fore. At hic dicit Christus, iustos futuros in paupertate, luctu, persecutione. Sed respondet Christus, differri praemia praecipua, etsi in hac vita etiam conservari Ecclesiam oportet mirabilibus beneficiis Dei.

Iustis bene sit.

Abel est iustus. Ergo Abelo bene sit.

Respondeo primum ad minorem: Abel est iustus imputatione, et habet incoatam obedientiam, sed quia in eo adhuc haeret peccatum, manet mors, et haec natura vitiosa est subiecta cruci. Ideo differuntur praemia ad consummatam iusticiam. Deinde respondeas ad maiorem: Iustis bene sit, iuxta consilium Dei, et post hanc vitam. Nam Deus, ut servet Ecclesiam, etiam in hac vita impertit ingentia dona, sed inter mirabilia certamina, sicut servavit Ecclesiam in diluvio, in Aegypto, in captivitate Babylonica, et martyrum temporibus. Teneamus igitur hanc interpretationem legis, quam hic Christus tradit, cum praemia pollicetur, et testatur partim in hac vita dasi, partim post hanc vitam.

De tertio.

Sed hoc praecipue discendum est in his concionibus, quomodo fides in his promissionibus exercenda sit. Laetamus fidem, et maxime fugimus exercitia fidei. Christus praedicit Ecclesiam fore in aerumnis, quia in his vult exerceri fidem.

Quomodo? Octo modis.

Primo, agnoscendo gratiam promissam propter Christum. Secundo, invocando Deum. Tertio, impellendo ad bona opera, ut retineatur beneficium Dei. Quarto, ad petendum et expectandum auxilium, adversus diabolum, adversus hostes, adversus imbecillitatem propriam. Quinto, ad expectandam compensationem seu praemia. Sexto, ad petendum auxilium in tolerantia. Septimo, ad ostendendam gratitudinem, et exempla, ut propagetur doctrina, et ornetur gloria Dei. Octavo, ut his exercitiis agitata et excuscitata fides, crescat, et crescant caetera dona.

Exemplum, Paulus in afflictionibus primum cogitabat, an placeret Deo, quia afflictiones et adversi casus videntur esse signa irae Dei.

Excitat igitur fidem, et sentit se propter Christum placere, et confugit ad Deum. Secundo invocat. Tertio, agnoscens misericordiam Dei erga se, studet retinere beneficium, et cavet, ne amittat iusticiam. Quarto fide petit et expectat liberationem in afflictionibus et auxilium adversus diabolum. Quinto, expectat praemia, et intuens fide in finem promissum, perfert praesentes aerumnas. Sexto, fide petit auxilium et robur spiritus, ut possit praestare patientiam, etiamsi mors oppetenda sit. Septimo, statuit haec officia necessaria esse ad ostendendam gratitudinem, ad propagationem Evangelii, agnoscit Deum, mirabili consilio, sic velle abolere peccatum in carne nostra, et Ecclesiam mirabili modo glorificare. Octavo, dat operam ut crescat fides, et caetera dona. Sic dives credens invocat Deum, studet retinere iusticiam, Deo obtemperat in officio liberalitatis, expectat vicissim auxilium a Deo in suis aerumnis, et expectat compensationem seu conservationem facultatum, ostendit gratitudinem suo exemplo, cupit augeri dona, augeri fidem.

Sed quia pauci credunt, pauci expectant conservationem facultatum: ideo animi sunt angustiores et illiberales. Haec generalia semper de promissionibus legalibus tenenda sunt, ut meminerimus et in his promissionibus praemiorum exercendam esse fidem.

Beati pauperes spiritu.

Non vult deseri facultates sine vocatione, non approbat Monachatum, iuxta illud: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum, sed concionatur Christus de vera inopia piorum et fugientium impios quaestus, sive inopia sit fortuita, sive acciderit propter professionem Evangelii. Hos inopes omnes consolatur, et testatur inopiam non esse signum irae Dei et maledictionem, imo pollicetur praemia.

Estque opposita sententia legi, et imperiis mundi. Lex docet detrimenta facultatum esse poenas peccatorum et maledictionem: hic Christus docet pios, aliud esse iudicium de cruce secundum Evangelium. Nam afflictiones piis non sunt signa irae, sed fiunt exercitia fidei, sicut ubique clamat Evangelium, Ecclesiam subiectam esse cruci.

In durissimis afflictionibus summa lumina Ecclesiae fuerunt, Christus, Iohannes Baptista, Ieremias, Abel etc.

Item imperia mundi dicuntur florere, cum habent opes, sic de Ecclesia et Pontifices sentiunt. At Christus hic testatur Ecclesiam potius florere in paupertate, ne desperemus propter inopiam.

Addit autem: Pauperes spiritu, id est, spirituali obedientia, patienter ferentes paupertatem, seu parati ad eam ferendam, si fuerint excussi ex facultatibus, sicut Abraham alias habebat facultates, alias vagabatur inops sine certis sedibus.

Beati lugentes.

Et hic loquitur de veris doloribus piorum, sive propter professionem accidant, sive a poenis aut morsibus diaboli oriantur, ut cum David pulsus in exilium agnovit culpam, et sensit se puniri. In talibus aerumnis clamat conscientia, nos a Deo proiectos vel desertos esse. Sed vox Evangelii diversum docet: Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus.

Item: Multae tribulationes iustorum, et hic promittitur consolatio, cum in hac vita, tum post hanc vitam, sicut docet totus Psalmus 4.: Scitote quoniam mirificat Dominus sanctum suum, et exaudit me cum clamo ad eum. Item 35.: Pauper clamavit, et Dominus exaudivit eum.

Beati mites.

Consolatur oppressos, qui non habent vindicem et defensorem, et docet privatam vindictam Deo commendandam esse, sicut Ioseph, Israëlitae in Aegypto, David sub Saule, pii sub Antiocho,

Ecclesia sub Diocletiano, erant sine defensione. Clarius autem intelligitur hic locus, considerata antithesi. Tyranni existimant imperia retineri, et augeri acerbitate vindictae. Econtra, Evangelium docet, ut in causa iusta simus constantes, nec tamen quaeramus privatam vindictam, sed exitus Deo commendemus. Et cum ex officio exercenda est vindicta, mitigemus eam, sicut exempla David, totam hanc doctrinam pingunt. Nunquam voluit Saulem interficere, deinde regnans, necessariam vindictam, tamen saepe temperavit misericordia, pepercit Semei.

Huc pertinent multa in Psalmis, ut Psalm. 36.: Saevientes exterminabuntur, sustinentes autem Dominum haereditabunt terram. Pharao deletus est, vicit Israël. Apostoli interfecti sunt, mansit tamen Ecclesia deletis tyrannis. Promittitur igitur hic versiculus oppressis, et vindice carentibus, ac non cupidis privatae vindictae, conservationem etiam in terra. Quanquam autem haec proprie scribuntur propter Ecclesiam, tamen ut res sit magis perspicua, etiam politica exempla consideremus. In politica iustitia, clementia principibus, et mansuetudo privatis utilis est. Econtra, saevitia multis exitio fuit, non solum monstrosis tyrannis, qui etiam aliis sceleribus polluti erant, ut Phalaridi, Dionysio, Neroni, sed etiam alioqui mediocribus, ut Pertinaci, Aureliano. Et saepe videmus, privatas offensiones magnas patientia sanari. Hanc lenitatem maxime flagitat Christus, quia in Ecclesia incidunt periculosae offensiones, ideo toties dicit: Remittite, et remittetur vobis. Et Christus lavans pedes Apostolis, vult nos sanare offensiones omni genere officii, ideo dicit: Exemplum dedi vobis. Et Petrus inquit: Dilectio tegit peccata. Hae sententiae omnes huc transferantur, Et quia in periculis famae, aut rerum, si desit vindex, timemus nos et nostra peritura esse, ideo hic promittitur conservatio, cum ait: Possidebunt terram, sicut Israël in Aegypto conservabatur, etiamsi mandatum erat ut infantes interficerentur.

Beati qui sitiunt et esuriunt iusticiam.

Sitire iusticiam est, vero dolore et zelo affici, ut propagetur gloria Dei, ut iusta sit gubernatio, et scandala, et mala exempla tollantur. Est autem haec particula quasi declaratio quaedam superioris. Antea dixit salutarem esse clementiam, nunc addit hanc clementiam non debere esse dissolutionem seu ignaviam. Accedat zelus, sit vigilans, intentus, acer, unusquisque in suo officio. Estque opposita sententia Epicureis, qui nihil curant qualiacunque vitia, seu religionum, seu alia, ut nunc rident nos Epicurei, cum de idololatria aut de libidinibus querimur. Hanc ignaviam detestatur Christus, et praecipit zelum, ac addit promissionem. Nam impii dicunt pios frustra moliri emendationem. Christus econtra promittit labores non fore inanes, saturabuntur, inquit. Item, hi sitientes intelligantur non Cynici, aliena vitia tantum reprehendentes, ad sua conniventes, sed sese quoque emendantes, iuxta illud: Iustus primum accusator est sui, postea occurrit alteri.

Beati misericordes. Promittitur merces beneficiis, qui defendunt aut adiuvant afflictos, ut qui tegunt eos, qui propter professionem Evangelii affliguntur, iuxta Psalmum: Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem etc.

Beati mundo corde, id est, casto, sicut ad Ebraeos dicitur: Sectamini sanctificationem, id est, castitatem, sine qua nemo Deum videbit.

Et usitata poena est libidinum coecitas, ut Rom. 1. et Ephes. 4. dicitur.

Beati pacifici, id est, recte diiudicantes dogmata, recte sanantes iniustas discordias Ecclesiae, vel regnorum, cedentes aliis bona conscientia, propter pacem. Continetur autem hic maxima pars Decalogi. Nam ad primum praeceptum pertinent hae virtutes, Veritas et fortitudo in confessione, de qua dicit: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur. Item: Fides expectans has promissiones et retinens veritatem, propter has promissiones. Item: Patientia in qualibuscunque aerumnis. Nam hae virtutes sunt cultus, de quibus concionatur primum praeceptum. Ad secundam tabulam pertinent mansuetudo in mitiganda vindicta, beneficentia, castitas, caritas vel aequitas in facienda pace. Ad primum praeceptum pertinet sitire iusticiam, id est, zelus etc.

De dicto: Non veni solvere legem.

Lex moralis est aeterna et immutabilis sententia in mente divina, quae est regula iusticiae, praecipiens quales omnes creaturas intelligentes esse oporteat, et quae facere et omittere debeant. et iram Dei ac poenas praesentes et aeternas denuncians iis, qui non praestant perfectam obedientiam.

Etsi autem Deus est agens liberrimum, tamen ut haec propositio aeterna et immota est, Deus est sapiens, iustus, bonus, ita hae propositiones sunt aeternae et immotae, Deus vult iusta, Deo debetur obedientia.

Nec imaginemur legem Dei moralem quiddam mutabile esse, quod abrogari ac deleri possit, sicut tabula adfixa parieti amoveri potest, aut sicut lex Spartana de nummo aeneo mutari potuit. Manet in Deo noticia, quae est regula iuste faciendi. Manet voluntas vere, non simulate volens iusta, et vere, non simulate reiiciens iniusta, sicut Psalm. inquit: Non Deus volens impietatem tu es. Et harum noticiarum divinarum similes impressae sunt humanae menti, quae semper manent et iudicant facta. Quare abrogatio legis non fingatur talis, quasi nunc Deus non irascatur ruenti contra legem moralem, sicut non irascitur edenti carnem suillam.

Sed dicat aliquis: Si lex moralis est aeterna et immota sententia, sequetur, non esse remissionem peccatorum. Respondeo: Cum omnis lex obliget ad obedientiam, vel ad poenam, nec nos lapsi nisi persoluta poena restitui potueramus. Est autem poena derivata in Filium Dei, nec recipit Deus lapsos nisi propter Filium, nec approbat peccatum etiamsi credentes recipit, sed iram suam adversus peccatum ingentem declaravit in passione Filii. Cum igitur de remissione peccatorum cogitamus, fide intuemur Filium pro nobis crucifixum, ut persolveret poenam, et agnoscamus Deum vere et horribiliter irasci peccato, nos autem propter Filium recipere.

Ideo dicit Christus, se implere legem. Et Paulus inquit: Finis legis est Christus, id est, lex testificatur de Christo, ut victimae omnes significantes Christum, admonent venturum fuisse dominum, qui solus impleret legem, implet autem tripliciter. Primum sustinendo poenam pro nobis, cum ipse fuerit sine peccato, et habuerit integram obedientiam, et tamen pro nobis factus sit victima.

Secundo effective implet, quia ipse instaurat humanam naturam, et dat Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam, ut rursus in homine existat vera obedientia, quae hic incoatur, et perficitur in resurrectione, et erit aeterna, sicut dicitur: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum, ubi diserte dictum est, meam, ut sciamus novam et aeternam vitam, vere esse sapientiam, iusticiam, obedientiam, congruentem ad ipsam legem sonantem in monte Sina.

C. igitur dicitur, Christum implere legem, etiam hic gradus comprehendendus est, quod videlicet efficiat dato Spiritu sancto, ut in nobis vera, integra, et aeterna obedientia restituatur. Et quia dicit legem meam, satis intelligi potest, legem moralem esse aeternam sententiam in mente divina, quia vult eam restituere in hominum cordibus. Non est igitur abolita, sicut abiicitur Calendarium praeteriti anni, ut aliqui insulse loquuntur.

Tertio implet legem Christus docendo, id est, testatur se eam non abolere ne fiat, sed proponere eam, ut peccata arguat, et doceat quae opera Deus postulet. Vult enim Deus nos verbo suo regi, nec vult nos nostris imaginationibus excogitare opera et cultus, sicut Ethnici excogitarunt, finxerunt idola sine fine, permiserunt sibi libidines, et interim cumularunt sacrificia, et aliqua opera civilia exercuerunt, quibus arbitrabantur se iustos esse, et placere Deo, sicut iam sacrificuli sua opera laudant, Missas, observationes rituum, obedientiam, quam propriis legibus praestant, et negligunt leges divinas de vera doctrina, vero cultu, et castitate. Revocat autem nos Christus ad legem Dei, hanc vult esse doctrinam poenitentiae, et regulam bonorum operum.

## 5:1 All Saints' Day
The Gospel on All Saints' Day.

Matth. 5. Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up into the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him.

his, and opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God. Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil word against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad, for your reward is great in heaven. For so persecuted they the Prophets which were before you.

There are three points.

I. The general doctrine is against the opinions concerning the scandal of the cross. II. And there are added promises of good works, interpreting the law. III. And at the same time, the doctrine of faith to be exercised in these works is delivered.

On the first.

There are two kinds of promises. Some are legal, which have the condition of works, and are added to good works, or merits, as: He who shall have given to one of the least a cup of water, shall not lose his reward. And here: Blessed are the meek, Blessed are the poor in spirit, etc.

But since no one satisfies the law, here it must be asked how good works please God, and how these promises become valid. Therefore we answer, as has often been said elsewhere: The law without Christ is of no avail, but just as the law is valid, so too are the legal promises valid, when the promise of grace given on account of Christ has first been apprehended. Therefore, when we are righteous by faith, then the begun obedience pleases God, and merits rewards, and the promises are then valid, because that obedience is said to be a certain fulfillment of the law.

There is, therefore, another promise proper to the Gospel, a gratuitous one, namely, of reconciliation and righteousness to be imputed on account of Christ. This promise must always shine forth above all works and promises, because through the Son we have access to the Father. We have prefaced this so that it may be known how these legal promises are valid and ratified, according to that saying: Through faith we establish the law.

Hence an objection can also be explained. Since he says here that men are blessed by meekness, why do you say elsewhere that men are justified by faith alone? I answer: These do not conflict. It is necessary first for men to become righteous or accepted by God, by faith, freely on account of Christ; afterwards they are also blessed, that is, having gifts and rewards from God, on account of other virtues. These things, explained in this way without sophistry, can be easily understood. Let us learn, therefore, that legal promises or promises of good works are delivered here, which are to be accepted in such a way that the evangelical promise of the grace of Christ always shines forth.

On the second. Promises proposed in this place dissent from the judgment of reason, and are an exposition of the Mosaic law: the law says, it shall be well with the good. But here Christ says that the righteous will be in poverty, mourning, and persecution. But Christ answers that the chief rewards are deferred, even though the Church must also be preserved in this life by the wonderful benefits of God.

It is well with the righteous. Abel is righteous, Therefore it is well with Abel. I answer first to the minor premise: Abel is righteous by imputation, and has begun obedience, but because sin still clings to him, death remains, and this vicious nature is subject to the cross. Therefore, rewards are deferred until perfected righteousness.

Then you should answer to the major premise: It is well with the righteous, according to the counsel of God, and after this life. For God, in order to preserve the Church, even in this life bestows immense gifts, but amidst wonderful struggles, just as He preserved the Church in the flood, in Egypt, in the Babylonian captivity, and in the times of the martyrs. Let us therefore hold to this interpretation of the law, which Christ delivers here, when He promises rewards, and testifies that they are given partly in this life, and partly after this life.

On the third.

But this must be learned especially in these contentions, how faith is to be exercised in these promises. Let us rejoice in faith, and let us especially flee to the exercises of faith. Christ predicts the Church to be in miseries, because in these He wishes faith to be exercised. How? In eight ways.

First, by acknowledging the grace promised on account of Christ. Second, by calling upon God. Third, by being impelled to good works, so that the benefit of God may be retained. Fourth, by seeking and expecting help against the devil, against enemies, against one's own weakness. Fifth, by expecting compensation or rewards. Sixth, by seeking help in endurance. Seventh, by showing gratitude, and examples, so that the doctrine may be propagated, and the glory of God adorned. Eighth, so that faith, agitated and excited by these exercises, may grow, and other gifts may grow.

Example: Paul in afflictions first considered whether he was pleasing to God, because afflictions and adverse events seem to be signs of God's wrath. He therefore excites faith, and feels that he is pleasing on account of Christ, and flees to God. Second, he invokes. Third, acknowledging the mercy of God toward him, he strives to retain the benefit, and takes care not to lose righteousness. Fourth, by faith he seeks and expects liberation in afflictions and help against the devil. Fifth, he expects rewards, and looking by faith to the promised end, he endures present miseries. Sixth, by faith he seeks help and strength of spirit, so that he may be able to provide patience, even if death must be faced. Seventh, he determines that these duties are necessary to show gratitude, for the propagation of the Gospel, he acknowledges God, by a wonderful counsel, thus wishing to abolish sin in our flesh, and to glorify the Church in a wonderful way. Eighth, he makes an effort so that faith may grow, and other gifts. Thus the believing rich man invokes God, strives to retain righteousness, obeys God in the duty of liberality, expects in turn help from God in his miseries, and expects compensation or the preservation of his resources, shows gratitude by his example, desires gifts to be increased, faith to be increased. But because few believe, few expect the preservation of resources: therefore their minds are more narrow and illiberal. These generalities must always be held regarding legal promises, so that we may remember that even in these promises of rewards, faith must be exercised.

Blessed are the poor in spirit.

He does not wish resources to be abandoned without a calling, He does not approve of Monasticism, according to that: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men, but Christ preaches about the true poverty of the pious and those fleeing the gains of the impious, whether the poverty is accidental, or has happened on account of the profession of the Gospel. He consoles all these needy ones, and testifies that poverty is not a sign of God's wrath and a curse, but rather He promises rewards. And this is a sentiment opposed to the law, and to the empires of the world. The law teaches that the loss of resources is a punishment for sins and a curse: here Christ teaches the pious that the judgment concerning the cross is different according to the Gospel. For afflictions for the pious are not signs of wrath, but become exercises of faith, just as the Gospel cries out everywhere, that the Church is subject to the cross. In the most severe afflictions, the greatest lights of the Church have been Christ, John the Baptist, Jeremiah, Abel, etc. Likewise, the empires of the world are said to flourish when they have wealth, and the Pontiffs think the same about the Church. But Christ here testifies that the Church flourishes rather in poverty, so that we may not despair on account of poverty. He adds, however: Poor in spirit, that is, in spiritual obedience, patiently bearing poverty, or prepared to bear it, if they have been shaken out of their resources, just as Abraham at one time had resources, at another wandered needy without fixed abodes.

Blessed are those who mourn.

And here He speaks of the true sorrows of the pious, whether they happen on account of their profession, or arise from punishments or the bites of the devil, as when David, driven into exile, acknowledged his guilt and felt that he was being punished. In such miseries, the conscience cries out that we have been cast away or deserted by God. But the voice of the Gospel teaches otherwise: A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit. Likewise: Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and here consolation is promised, both in this life and after this life, as the whole of Psalm 4 teaches: Know that the Lord makes His holy one wonderful, and hears me when I cry to Him. Likewise 33: The poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.

Blessed are the meek.

He consoles the oppressed, who have no avenger and defender, and teaches that private vengeance must be commended to God, just as Joseph, the Israelites in Egypt, David under Saul, the pious under Antiochus,

The Church under Diocletian was without defense. This passage is understood more clearly, however, when the antithesis is considered. Tyrants think that empires are maintained and increased by the bitterness of vengeance. Conversely, the Gospel teaches that we should be constant in a just cause, and yet not seek private vengeance, but commend the outcomes to God. And when vengeance must be exercised by virtue of office, we should mitigate it, just as the examples of David illustrate this whole doctrine. He never wanted to kill Saul, and then, while reigning, he nevertheless often tempered necessary vengeance with mercy; he spared Shimei.

To this pertain many things in the Psalms, such as Psalm 37: The raging shall be exterminated, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the earth. Pharaoh was destroyed, Israel conquered. The Apostles were killed, yet the Church remained when the tyrants were destroyed. This little verse is therefore promised to the oppressed, and to those lacking an avenger, and who are not desirous of private vengeance, [promising] preservation even on earth.

Although these things are written properly for the sake of the Church, yet so that the matter may be more clear, let us also consider political examples. In political justice, clemency is useful for princes, and gentleness for private citizens. Conversely, cruelty has been the ruin of many, not only monstrous tyrants who were also polluted by other crimes, such as Phalaris, Dionysius, and Nero, but also those otherwise mediocre, such as Pertinax and Aurelian. And we often see that great private offenses are healed by patience. Christ demands this leniency most of all, because dangerous offenses occur in the Church; therefore He says so often: Forgive, and it will be forgiven you. And Christ, washing the feet of the Apostles, wishes us to heal offenses with every kind of service; therefore He says: I have given you an example. And Peter says: Love covers a multitude of sins. Let all these maxims be transferred here. And because in dangers to our reputation or property, if an avenger is lacking, we fear that we and ours will perish, therefore preservation is promised here, when He says: They shall possess the earth, just as Israel was preserved in Egypt, even though the command had been given that the infants should be killed.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.

To thirst for righteousness is to be affected with true sorrow and zeal, so that the glory of God may be propagated, so that the government may be just, and that scandals and bad examples may be removed. This clause is, as it were, a certain declaration of the former. Before, He said that clemency is salutary; now He adds that this clemency ought not to be dissolution or sloth. Let zeal be added; let everyone be vigilant, intent, and sharp in their own office. And the sentiment is opposed to the Epicureans, who care nothing for any vices whatsoever, whether of religions or others, just as Epicureans now mock us when we complain about idolatry or lusts. Christ detests this sloth and commands zeal, and adds a promise. For the impious say that the pious strive in vain for amendment. Christ, on the contrary, promises that labors will not be empty; they shall be satisfied, He says. Likewise, let these who thirst be understood not as Cynics, who only criticize the vices of others while winking at their own, but as those who also amend themselves, according to that saying: The just man is the first accuser of himself, afterwards he encounters another.

Blessed are the merciful. A reward is promised to those who perform acts of kindness, who defend or help the afflicted, such as those who cover those who are afflicted on account of the profession of the Gospel, according to the Psalm: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor, etc.

Blessed are the pure in heart, that is, chaste, just as it is said to the Hebrews: Pursue sanctification, that is, chastity, without which no one will see God.

And a common punishment for lusts is blindness, as is said in Rom. 1 and Eph. 4.

Blessed are the peacemakers, that is, those who rightly judge dogmas, who rightly heal unjust discords of the Church or of kingdoms, yielding to others in good conscience for the sake of peace. Contained here, however, is the greatest part of the Decalogue. For these virtues pertain to the first commandment: Truth and fortitude in confession, concerning which He says: Blessed are those who suffer persecution. Likewise: Faith expecting these promises and retaining the truth on account of these promises. Likewise: Patience in whatever hardships. For these virtues are the worship concerning which the first commandment preaches. To the second table pertain gentleness in mitigating vengeance, beneficence, chastity, and charity or equity in making peace. To the first commandment pertains thirsting for righteousness, that is, zeal, etc.

Concerning the saying: I have not come to abolish the law.

The moral law is an eternal and immutable sentiment in the divine mind, which is the rule of justice, commanding what kind of [people] all intelligent creatures [ought to be]. must follow, while the Baptists withdraw into corners, invent speculations for themselves, and refuse to live in this civil society; by these means they think they receive the Holy Spirit, just as the monks and idolatrous Papists boast that they obtain the Holy Spirit through their ludicrous ceremonies, Masses, and works of tradition. By these means they think they receive the Holy Spirit, just as the Monks do, and the idolatrous Papists boast that they obtain the Holy Spirit through their ludicrous ceremonies, Masses, and works of tradition.

But let us learn that the Holy Spirit is given through the Word of God, whenever we comfort ourselves with the thought of Him, hearing, or reading, or thinking upon the Word of God, and we call upon God, and believe that we are forgiven for Christ's sake, and that we are helped. These things happen in true repentance, and in the daily invocation of all who practice repentance, and do not persevere in sins against their conscience.

I have spoken of the first part, namely, of the promise.

Now I will speak of the second, what the Holy Spirit does.

Here Christ makes an antithesis. I will not leave you orphans. The speech is brief, but it is a true image of the Church before the world, and as we ourselves generally judge, when we feel the burden of our miseries.

See if we are not orphans? The world persecutes us, we are a small, scattered, poorly cohesive group.

We have no human prince, king, or pontiff. It is ridiculous to the Pope and to kings when we call ourselves the Church.

Furthermore, let individuals consider their own miseries.

Are we not orphans, without a defender, without certain aids? And especially then we would understand that we are orphans, if we could in any way perceive the power of the devil. Therefore, against such great enemies, Christ promises the Holy Spirit, He says: I will not leave you orphans, but I am your pontiff, I will ask the Father.

Believe, the Son does not pray in vain, He obtains help for us from the Father.

What? The Spirit the Paraclete, who shines in us, gives counsel, lifts up the spirit, begins eternal life in us, just as it is said here: That He may remain with you forever. But so that we may be able to think about these benefits, and stir ourselves up, let us propose to ourselves the sweetest saying from Zechariah, where it is written: I will pour out upon the house of David the Spirit of grace and of supplications.

This voice embraces everything, and teaches what good works are, what are the highest and true worships of the Church. All nations, even the barbarians, have external worships of God, honest works.

But these are not yet those by which God is properly worshipped and apprehended; the Church alone has true worships, which it performs when it receives the spirit of grace and of supplications. What do these words signify?

The Spirit of grace signifies that we are helped by the Holy Spirit, so that we may establish that we are in the grace of God, that we certainly please God, that our sins are forgiven for Christ's sake.

This faith in every affliction recognizes that God is present as a helper, that He is propitious, that He will not leave orphans. By this faith the Holy Spirit is the παράκλητος (Paraclete), the comforter and vivifier.

There follows the other particle, the Spirit of supplications.

Since we are orphans in the world, we have need of God as a defender and helper. Therefore, hearts are stirred up by the Holy Spirit, so that they may call upon God, just as Paul also says: The Spirit helps us, so that we may cry Abba Father. Therefore the Church is burdened with huge dangers and miseries, so that we may exercise this invocation, that we may cry to God in faith, that we may expect help.

And do not think that these are only magnificent words. Pious believers experience that God is truly present as a helper and assistant, and great things and great miracles are thus done in the world.

Thus your family is saved against the devil. Thus kingdoms are saved, as Hezekiah and Isaiah drove back the Assyrians with prayers.

Other miracles, like those of Moses, are perceived more by the eyes, because God wants certain illustrious testimonies to exist. But yet the Church always has its own miracles, which happen in invocation, just as Moses, just as Elijah were governed by the Holy Spirit in their calling, and performed great and illustrious things.

Thus let us ask to be governed by the Holy Spirit, and let us know that the voice of Christ is true: He will give you the Spirit the Paraclete. Let us know that the Holy Spirit is given to us, that our prayers are heard, that we are helped in all public and private dangers; great things and great miracles are thus done in the world, even if the world does not perceive it: because the war between Christ and the devil is waged in a wonderful way, through weak vessels in the Church, which Christ nevertheless accomplishes by divine power through the Holy Spirit.

Remember therefore this voice: I will pour out the spirit of grace and of supplications. Stir yourself up by faith, so that you may believe that you are in grace for Christ's sake, ask for the Holy Spirit as a helper, call upon God in all business, so that you may experience this helper. Now also let us pray for the Church, that we may retain the Spirit of truth, because the devil most cunningly he lays snares for the truth.

A new sophistry attempts to overwhelm the Gospel, and the world delights in these lies and deceptions, because it knows neither the Holy Spirit nor Christ. But the pious, who know Christ and seek the spirit of truth, oppose such impostures with all their heart. God, however, will preserve the Church and will repel the Turks, for the sake of the Church, not for the sake of the impious and idolaters. These things must be briefly noted this day, so that the pious may receive these warnings of Christ, and together let us call upon God for the sake of the Son, and let us ask for the Holy Spirit, just as He promised: My heavenly Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.

Peter's Sermon, Acts 2.

But Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and spoke to them: You men of Judea, and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and perceive my words with your ears. For these are not drunk as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day. But this is what was said by the Prophet Joel: And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh. And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. And indeed upon my servants and my handmaids in those days I will pour out of my spirit, and they shall prophesy, and I will give wonders in heaven above, and signs on the earth below, blood and fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the Moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes. And it shall be: Everyone whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.

You men of Israel, hear these words, Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you, by miracles and wonders and signs, which God did through Him in your midst, as you know, this man, delivered by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken and by wicked hands have crucified and killed. Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, according to what was impossible for Him to be held by it. For David says concerning Him: I foresaw the Lord always before my face, because He is at my right hand, that I should not be moved. Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted, moreover also my flesh shall rest in hope. Because You will not leave my soul in hell, nor will You give Your holy one to see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life, You will fill me with joy with Your countenance. You men and brethren, let it be permitted to speak boldly to you concerning the patriarch David, because he is both dead and buried, and his sepulcher is with us unto this present day. Therefore, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath, that of the fruit of his loins one should sit upon his throne, foreseeing he spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that neither was He left in hell, nor did His flesh see corruption. This Jesus God has raised up, of whom we all are witnesses. Therefore being exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, He has poured out this gift, which you see and hear.

Peter's sermon contains three main parts in total.

The first is the saying of Joel, containing the promise of the Holy Spirit and of eternal salvation, proper to the New Testament. Therefore, the benefits of the New Testament are described first.

The second part is the sermon concerning the death and resurrection of the Messiah, who is the cause of the benefits of the New Testament. And this passage is a testimony that this Jesus is the Messiah, because He rose from the dead.

The third part is concerning the application, how we obtain these benefits of the New Testament, acquired through the Messiah, namely: Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Christ, for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. It is a long and very rich sermon, which cannot be fully recounted in a few words.

However, it is profitable to meditate often on such passages to nourish the knowledge of the benefits of Christ, and to confirm faith, and to excite thanksgiving, and love toward God. Therefore, let us first speak briefly concerning the first part of Peter's sermon, namely, concerning the grace of the New Testament and the donation of the Holy Spirit.

The Prophet says two things: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Likewise, concerning the donation of the Holy Spirit: I will pour out of my spirit. Both sentences are opposed to the law. The law teaches and demands many things, but it does not save; rather, it accuses, as Paul teaches: The law works wrath. But the preaching of the New Testament is different, which promises salvation, and indeed promises it to all, but to those who call upon Him. What is it to promise salvation? To promise liberation from sin, from the wrath of God, from eternal death, and the donation of eternal life.

The New Testament brings these things, not because of the law, but only to the one who calls upon Him. For this reason it says: Calling upon Him, so that it may distinguish the forms of worship, as if to say: That worship of the law will not be sought then, but another worship, namely, invocation alone, which is the voice of faith, of one believing and receiving the promise, and crying out: Abba Father. Therefore this saying will grow sweet to the soul when we consider that the promise is universal and pertains to us ourselves. And by invocation we understand faith, excluding one's own merits, and relying only on the Lord, who has already revealed Himself. For it is necessary that invocation be distinguished from the worship of the law. For even this very voice: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, is an abrogation of the law.

Here let the listener be admonished to diligently impress upon himself this clause: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, let him know that it is the sum of the Gospel, and let him understand invocation not in the manner of the law, that is, let him not think thus: the one who calls upon Him is saved, provided he is worthy, if he has enough works, etc., but the one who calls upon Him, that is, not fleeing from God, but believing in Him because of the Messiah sent by the heavenly Father.
