Cum autem audivisset populus, se per Messiam a damnatione, quae est poena, quam lex imponit, liberandos esse, audierunt etiam, quod finis futurus esset ceremoniarum Leviticarum, intelligebant doctrinam de libertate carnaliter, quasi iam concederetur licentia omnibus cupiditatibus, sicut multi ante annos viginti audita praedicatione libertatis Christianae, volebant esse liberi ab omnibus legibus, a reditibus et a disciplina. Huic stultae opinioni primum Christus hic opponit gravissimam sententiam de lege: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere.

Obiectio. Sed dicat aliquis: Si Christus non est legislator, cur praedicat legem?

Respondeo. Verum est, Christum non esse legislatorem, quia lex prius est lata et nota, sed venit principaliter propter promissionem.

Sed tamen quia in Ecclesia oportet sciri, quid sit peccatum, necesse est vocem Decalogi in Ecclesia sonare, quae est aeterna sententia Dei, et non parcit ullis hominibus, nisi confugientibus ad Filium Dei, ut prius dixi. Non potest cognosci medicina, nisi prius et morbus cognoscatur.

Ita non potest magnitudo misericordiae et remissio peccatorum intelligi, nisi intelligatur peccatum aliquo modo. Quomodo potes obligare vulnus, si non scias, ubi aut quale vulnus sit?

Ideo in Ecclesia semper etiam Decalogus recitatur, ut Paulus inquit: Per legem cognitio peccati. Et quia Pharisaei legem male interpretati fuerant, et suas traditiones pluris faciebant, quam legem Dei, sicut apud nos Papistae et Monachi. Ideo Christus ut fidelis doctor Decalogum saepe repetivit, et falsas interpretationes taxavit et de- levit, sicut nostro tempore Dominus Doctor Mar- tinus in praedicatione Decalogi tales pharisaicas interpretationes delevit. Interea tamen scias, aliud esse promissionem propriam Evangelii, et Christum habere alia prin- cipalia officia, scilicet, sonare vocem Evangelii, et fieri victimam, et dare remissionem peccato- rum, iusticiam et vitam aeternam. Iam videte verba. Non veni solvere legem. Solvere significat delere, weg thun, vnd austilgen. Affirmat igitur clare, quod ipse non velit de- lere legem, videlicet Decalogum. Nam Decalogus est illa pars legis, quae est fundamentum aliarum legum, et est sententia perpetua, et ad totum ge- nus humanum pertinet, non tantum ad populum Iudaicum. Quare autem non deletur Decalogus? Quia non est tantum pictura in libris vel parietibus, sed est ipsa sapientia et voluntas Dei, quae est aeterna, sicut ipse Deus. Sicut igitur sapientia et voluntas Dei non possunt deleri, ita lex non potest deleri, sicut videmus manere poenas in nobis ipsis, quia eas lex, id est, iusta voluntas Dei imponit. Ait ergo: Non veni solvere legem, sed im- plere. Haec verba plena sunt maximae sapientiae, et debent esse notissima omnibus, et saepe cogi- tanda sunt, ut paulatim magis magisque ea intel- ligere discamus. Ut autem pro nostra infirmitate utcunque de- claremus haec verba, sciendum est, quod Chri- stus implet legem quatuor modis. Primum, suae propriae obedientiae per- fectione, quia solus Christus perfecte facit legem. Secundo, solvendo poenas pro nobis. Tertio, efficiendo legem in nobis, dans Spi- ritum sanctum, et regenerans nos, et restituens nobis vitam aeternam, ut ita fiat lex in nobis, quia oportet nostras voluntates congruere cum sa- pientia et voluntate Dei. Quarto, quia ipse eam etiam docet et illu- strat, et testatur obedientiam esse necessariam.

## 5:17 Sermons on Matthew
On the saying: I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.

We have recently begun to speak about this most serious sentence: I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it. And I exhort you that you strive to remember it perpetually, and that you think upon it often.

I said, however, that the Lord fulfills the law in four ways.

First, by the perfection of his own obedience.

Second, by sustaining the penalty which we owe to the justice of God.

Third, by renewing us, so that we may be able to perform the law.

Fourth, by teaching, and by removing Pharisaical errors.

Concerning the first way, it is not necessary to speak at length, but this must be noted, that no man in the whole human race was without sin, and satisfied the law, except this Lord Jesus Christ alone, who was born of the Virgin Mary. And it was necessary for this Lord to be without sin, so that the penalty derived onto him might be valid, not for himself, but for others.

Concerning the second way.

The Lord speaks especially in this place about the second mode, although the other modes follow upon it.

Moreover, the second mode is most to be admired. Christ fulfills the law, namely by deriving the punishment into himself, and thus paying it off for us, so that we may be received on account of him.

Here let us learn that sin is a horrendous and most evil thing, since God did not wish to remit sin unless such a great compensation intervened.

And let us consider here how, in the redemption of man, the mercy and justice of God are joined together by his wondrous wisdom.

It is the justice of God that, after the fall, Adam and Eve should be condemned to eternal punishments, just like the devils. And thus Adam reasons, when he is accused by God.

But the Son of God intervenes, and prays for the human race, and so that the justice of the Father might be satisfied, this wondrous decree is made: that the Son should assume human nature, and obey the law, and sustain horrendous punishments for the human race.

Thus God through mercy receives men, namely on account of the interceding Son, but nevertheless justice is joined to it, in such a way that the Son should nevertheless sustain the punishment for the others. We do not sufficiently understand this wonderful counsel in this life, but this wisdom will have to be learned in heaven in all eternity. Now, however, this consideration must be begun.

And so that it might be begun, so many slaughters were instituted in the Law. All these were types and signs of this future sacrifice to be admired. God wants us to think that His wrath against sin is serious and immense, and that it was the greatest cause why the Son suffered. We are all too hard-hearted, and we cannot understand this magnitude of God's wrath. But yet the thought must be begun, and God must be prayed to, that He may kindle in us the sparks of this light and wisdom, so that we do not think sin to be a small matter. Although, therefore, others speak here only of types, Christ fulfills the ceremonial laws, because He Himself becomes the victim, which is signified by the ceremonies and the slaughter of animals: yet you should know that the principal fulfillment is that He suffers the penalty, which we owed to justice, because of the eternal law, which is recited in the Decalogue.

On the third mode.

Christ not only pays the penalty, but once the penalty is paid, He afterwards also applies His goods to us, and restores to us justice and life. Thus He fulfills the law, He renews us by the given Holy Spirit, so that we may now begin to be in ourselves such as the law teaches us to be. With our nature renewed and afterwards perfected in newness in the Resurrection, we shall be entirely such as the law teaches us to be. Meanwhile, however, we are accounted righteous, with the justice of Christ Himself imputed to us. You hear this doctrine daily.

And it is a necessary consolation. In this life we are righteous because of the Son of God, with His justice imputed to us, which must be received by faith. And when hearts are quickened in true terrors, obedience now begins in us, which will be perfected after this life. Thus says Paul in Rom. 8: He condemned sin in the flesh concerning sin, so that the justice of the law might be fulfilled in us. Here he speaks of these two modes, of the payment of the penalty, when he says that Christ was made sin for us.

Concerning the following benefit, when he says, That the justice of the law might be fulfilled in us, this is done in two ways. First, by imputation, with the justice of Christ given to us. And this must be received by faith. Then, also by the renovation of our nature, which renovation is begun in this life, and will be perfected after this life.

On the fourth mode.

Christ fulfills the law by teaching. For although Christ did not come primarily to give laws, because the law was already known and promulgated, but so that He Himself might become the victim: yet at the same time, as has been said, He taxes the errors of the Pharisees, and shows the pure meaning of the law, so that He may show the magnitude of sin, and draw us to repentance. Therefore, in this chapter He recites the sayings of the law, and rebukes the pharisaical interpretations, etc. Let the text be read.

Whoever shall break one of the least commandments, and shall so teach men, etc. Unless your justice shall have abounded above the justice of the Pharisees. It was said to the ancients: Thou shalt not kill. But I say to you: Whoever is angry with his brother without cause, is liable to judgment, etc. Exposition.

Here the Lord begins to rebuke the evil interpretations of the Pharisees. And now again He admonishes us concerning this common doctrine, that there must always be in sight the distinction between the Law and the Gospel. And let all men accustom themselves, so that when they hear the name of law, they know that mention is being made of the Decalogue. And because Christ now wants to be a Teacher, He taxes the errors by which the Decalogue has been depraved by the Pharisees, and He begins from the grosser precepts. Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not commit adultery, because in these we feel more our vicious desires and disorder (ἀταξίαν, vnb vnordnung), than in the first precept.

But in sum, this is the common error of the Pharisees.

God's law prohibits not only external works conflicting with the law, such as external homicide or external adultery. But it also wants the heart to be rightly ordered and similar to the law of God, so that not only, lest Saul kill David, but He also wants Saul to have a right heart, which for God's sake with true affection loves David. But the Pharisees taught that the law of God only speaks of external deeds. And does not speak of the interior affections, and afterwards they pretended that the law was satisfied in this way, when a man restrained his hands and other external members outwardly, and they said that a man was righteous before God, having this external appearance, and they knew nothing about Christ and the righteousness of faith.

But they taught such an external appearance, which is usually called external discipline, outward discipline. And they said nothing about true repentance, about true humility, about Christ, about the righteousness of faith, and about grace, or about those true consolations of which the Prophets preach in the promises.

Indeed, they most impiously corrupted those sayings about faith: The righteous shall live by his faith, just as the Jews most wickedly corrupt them now. The righteous shall live by his faith, they interpret it thus: anyone living honestly in his own religion, whether Jew, or Gentile, or Mahometan, shall live. Such horrible blasphemies do impious men invent when they lose the light of the Gospel.

Before these years, the Monks also taught these pharisaical furies in the same way as the Pharisees and Jews, that external works satisfy the law of God, that a man is righteous by such discipline, that interior uncleanness, doubts about God, and other wandering desires, other disorderly desires, are not sins. And they said nothing about the righteousness of faith; indeed, even now they defend these very errors.

But let us here learn from Christ's sermon the true understanding of the law, namely, that it condemns both exterior deeds contrary to the law and interior inclinations fighting against the law. And let us know that in this corrupt nature all are guilty of the wrath of God, and that no one born in this corruption could or can satisfy the law of God, as Paul clearly says in Rom. 8: The flesh cannot be subject to the law of God.

And it is necessary to know this doctrine, so that we may acknowledge the just wrath and judgment of God, and perform repentance, and flee to our Lord Jesus Christ. And the righteousness of faith cannot be understood as long as these shadows remain, that we are righteous by our own righteousness and fulfillment of the law: indeed, this error directly fights against the doctrine of the righteousness of faith. Wherefore it is necessary in the Church that this error be often and clearly censured.

I have said these things so that the sum of this whole sermon may be understood more plainly. Now I will speak briefly about the text.

First, Christ says: If anyone shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach so, etc., he shall be the least in the kingdom of heaven.

What does he call the least commandments? Truly they are the greatest: doubt in the heart about God, security, being without the fear of God, being full of pride, hatred, envy, inordinate loves, etc. Are these the least?

I answer: The Pharisees spoke thus. And the Lord uses their word to censure their blindness, as if he were saying: You worst and most proud hypocrites call these great evils, which greatly offend God, the "least," and you do not wish to acknowledge the judgment and wrath of God. Therefore you also shall be the least in the kingdom of God, that is, cast out and damned by those who are in the kingdom of God.

The second part.

Latin:

De dicto: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere.

Coepimus nuper dicere de hac gravissima sententia: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere. Et vos adhortor, ut eam perpetuo meminisse stu- deatis, et saepe cogitetis.

Dixi autem, Dominum quatuor modis im- plere legem.

Primum, perfectione propriae obedientiae.

Secundo, sustinendo poenam, quam nos de- bemus iusticiae Dei.

Tertio, renovando nos, ut possimus legem facere.

Quarto, docendo, et tollendo errores pha- risaicos.

De primo modo non est prolixe dicendum, sed hoc moneri opus est, quod nullus homo in toto genere humano fuit sine peccato, et satisfecit legi, nisi solus hic Dominus Iesus Christus, qui natus est ex Maria virgine. Et hunc Dominum oportuit esse sine peccato, ut poena in ipsum de- rivata valeret, non pro ipso, sed pro aliis.

De secundo modo.

Praecipue loquitur Dominus hoc loco de secundo modo, tametsi caeteri modi ad illum se- quuntur,

Est autem secundus modus maxime admiran- dus. Christus implet legem, scilicet derivando in se poenam, et ita pro nobis persolvendo, ut nos propter eum recipiamur.

Hic discamus peccatum esse rem horrendam et pessimam, siquidem Deus non voluit remittere peccatum, nisi tanta compensatione interveniente.

Et consideremus hic, quomodo miranda sa- pientia Dei in redemtione hominis copulentur mi- sericordia et iusticia.

Iusticia Dei est, ut post lapsum Adam et Eva sint damnati ad poenas aeternas, sicut diaboli. Et ita ratiocinatur Adam, cum a Deo accusatur.

Sed Filius Dei intervenit, et orat pro genere humano, et ut iusticiae patris satisfiat, fit hoc mirandum decretum, ut Filius adsumat humanam naturam, et obediat legi, et sustineat horrendas poenas pro genere humano.

Ita Deus per misericordiam recipit homines, scilicet propter deprecantem Filium, sed tamen co- pulata est iusticia, sic, ut Filius sustineret tamen poenam pro caeteris. Hoc mirandum consilium in hac vita non satis intelligimus, sed erit haec sapientia discenda in coelo in tota aeternitate. Nunc tamen incoanda est haec consideratio.

Et ut incoaretur, institutae fuerunt tot mactationes in lege. Hae omnes fuerunt typi et signa huius futuri sacrificii admirandi. Vult nos Deus cogitare esse seriam et ingentem iram suam adversus peccatum, et fuisse maximam causam, quare Filius passus sit. Nimis duri sumus omnes homines, et hanc magnitudinem irae Dei non possumus intelligere. Sed tamen cogitatio incoanda est, et Deus orandus est, ut in nobis accendat scintillas huius lucis et sapientiae, ut non parvam rem existimemus esse peccatum. Quanquam igitur alii tantum hic loquuntur de typis, Christus implet leges ceremoniales, quia ipse fit victima, quae est significata per ceremonias et mactationes pecudum: tamen sciatis principalem impletionem esse, quod patitur poenam, quam nos debuimus iusticiae, propter aeternam legem, quae est recitata in Decalogo.

De tertio modo.

Non solum poenam persolvit Christus, sed persoluta poena postea nobis etiam sua bona applicat, et restituit nobis iusticiam et vitam. Sic implet legem, renovat nos dato Spiritu sancto, ut iam incipiamus esse in nobis tales, quales lex esse docet. Renovata natura nostra et postea consummata novitate in Resurrectione, erimus prorsus tales, quales esse lex docet. Interea vero tamen reputamur iusti, imputata nobis ipsius Christi iusticia. Hanc doctrinam quotidie auditis.

Et est necessaria consolatio. In hac vita sumus iusti propter Filium Dei imputata nobis ipsius iusticia, quam oportet fide accipi. Et cum in veris pavoribus corda vivificantur, iam incoatur obedientia in nobis, quae perficietur post hanc vitam. Ita dicit Paulus Rom. 8.: De peccato damnavit peccatum in carne, ut iusticia legis impleatur in nobis. Hic loquitur de duobus his modis, de persolutione poenae, cum ait, Christum factum esse peccatum pro nobis.

De sequente beneficio, cum ait, Ut iusticia legis impleretur in nobis, id fit dupliciter. Primum imputatione, donata nobis iusticia Christi. Et hanc oportet fide accipi. Deinde et renovatione nostrae naturae, quae renovatio in hac vita incoatur, et post hanc vitam perficietur.

De quarto modo.

Christus implet legem docendo. Etsi enim Christus non ideo principaliter venit, ut leges ferat, quia lex antea et nota fuit, et promulgata, sed ut ipse fiat victima: tamen simul, ut dictum est, taxat errores Pharisaeorum, et ostendit puram sententiam legis, ut monstret magnitudinem peccati, et nos trahat ad poenitentiam. Ideo in hoc capite recitat dicta legis, et reprehendit pharisaicas interpretationes etc. Legatur textus.

Qui solverit unum de mandatis minimis, et sic docuerit homines etc. Nisi abundaverit iusticia vestra supra iusticiam Pharisaeorum. Veteribus dictum: Non occides. Ego autem dico vobis: Qui frustra irascitur fratri suo, reus est iudicii etc. Enarratio.

Hic incipit Dominus reprehendere malas interpretationes Pharisaeorum. Et iam iterum admonet nos de hac communi doctrina, quod oportet semper in conspectu esse discrimen Legis et Evangelii. Et assuefaciant se omnes homines, ut cum audiunt nomen legis, sciant fieri mentionem Decalogi. Et quia Christus vult iam esse Doctor, taxat errores, quibus Decalogus depravatus est a Pharisaeis, et orditur a praeceptis crassioribus. Non occides, Non moechaberis, quia in his magis sentimus nostras viciosas cupiditates et ἀταξίαν, vnb vnordnung, quam in primo praecepto.

Est autem in summa hic communis error Pharisaeorum.

Lex Dei prohibet non tantum opera externa pugnantia cum lege, ut externum homicidium aut externum adulterium. Sed vult etiam cor esse recte ordinatum et simile legi Dei, ut non solum, ne Saul occidat Davidem, sed vult etiam ut sit Saul cor rectum, quod propter Deum vero affectu diligat Davidem. Sed Pharisaei docebant, legem Dei tantum loqui de externis factis. Et non loqui de interioribus affectibus, et postea fingebant sic satisfieri legi, quando homo foris coërceret manus et alia externa membra, Et dicebant hominem iustum esse coram Deo, habentem hanc externam speciem, et nihil sciebant de Christo et de iusticia fidei.

Sed docebant talem externam speciem, quae usitate nominatur externa disciplina, Eusserliche zucht. Et nihil dicebant de vera poenitentia, de vera humilitate, de Christo, de iusticia fidei, et de gratia, vel de illis veris consolationibus, de quibus concionantur Prophetae in promissionibus.

Imo ista dicta de fide: Iustus fide sua vivet, impiissime corrumpebant, sicut nunc corrumpunt Iudaei sceleratissime. Iustus fide sua vivet, sic interpretantur, unusquilibet honeste vivens in sua religione, sive Iudaeus, sive Ethnicus, sive Mahometista, vivet. Tales horrendas blasphemias fingunt impii homines, quando amittunt lucem Evangelii.

Ante hos annos Monachi etiam hos pharisaicos furores eodem modo sicut Pharisaei et Iudaei docuerunt, quod externa opera legi Dei satisfaciant, quod homo sit iustus tali disciplina, quod interiori immundities, dubitationes de Deo et aliae errantes cupiditates, andere vnordentliche begirden, non sint peccata. Et nihil dixerunt de iusticia fidei, imo nunc quoque defendunt hos ipsos errores.

Sed nos hic discamus ex concione Christi verum intellectum legis, quod videlicet damnet exteriora facta contraria legi, et interiores inclinationes pugnantes cum lege. Et sciamus, quod in hac corrupta natura Omnes sint rei irae Dei, et quod nemo natus in hac corruptione potuerit aut possit satisfacere legi Dei, sicut Paulus clare dicit Rom. 8.: Caro non potest subiici legi Dei.

Et hanc doctrinam scire necesse est, ut agnoscamus iustam iram et iudicium Dei, et agamus poenitentiam, et confugiamus ad Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Et non potest intelligi iusticia fidei, donec manent hae tenebrae, quod simus iusti nostra iusticia et impletione legis: imo hic error directe pugnat cum doctrina de iusticia fidei. Quare in Ecclesia necesse est hunc errorem saepe et perspicue taxari.

Haec dixi, ut summa totius huius concionis planius intelligatur. Nunc breviter de textu dicam.

Primum dicit Christus: Si quis unum de his minimis mandatis solverit, et sic docuerit etc. erit minimus in regno coelorum.

Quid vocat minima mandata? Profecto maxima sunt, dubitatio in corde de Deo, securitas, esse sine timore Dei, esse plenum superbia, odio, invidentia, inordinatis amoribus etc. An haec sunt minima?

Respondeo: Pharisaei sic loquebantur. Et Dominus utitur verbo ipsorum, ut coecitatem eorum taxet, quasi dicat: Vos pessimi et superbissimi hypocritae vocatis Minima haec tanta mala, quae valde offendunt Deum, et non vultis agnoscere iudicium et iram Dei. Ideo vos quoque eritis minimi in regno Dei, id est, abiecti et damnati ab his, qui sunt in regno Dei.

Altera pars.

## 5:20 Sunday VI After Trinity
Sunday VI after Trinity.

The Gospel of Matthew 5.

Unless your righteousness shall have abounded more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.

You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill, but whoever shall have killed, shall be liable to judgment.

But I say to you: That everyone who is angry with his brother, shall be liable to judgment.

But whoever shall have said to his brother, racha, shall be liable to the council.

But whoever shall have said, you fool, shall be liable to the fire of hell.

If therefore you offer your gift at the altar, and there you have remembered that your brother has something against you, leave your gift before the altar, and go first, be reconciled to your brother, and then coming offer your gift.

Be agreeing with your adversary quickly, while you are in the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the minister, and you be cast into prison.

Amen I say to you, you shall not go out from there until you pay the last farthing.

There are eight principal points.

I. The necessity of the righteousness of works.

II. The distinction between the righteousness of the flesh and the spiritual.

III. Spiritual justice abounds over rational justice in five things. 1. Repentance. 2. Faith. 3. Newness of spirit. 4. Successes in one's calling. 5. Victories against the devil. IIII. That the law requires perfect obedience. V. How this begun and imperfect obedience is pleasing. VI. Concerning vengeance. VII. That ceremonies are of no benefit if you violate moral precepts against your conscience. VIII. Concerning hatred and reconciliation.

Concerning the first.

There is a manifest testimony that the justice of works must be present, because he says above: I have not come to abolish the law, and here he requires a justice greater than that of the Scribes; therefore, a justice of a good conscience is required here, and more. To this pertain also these sayings: Do not err, adulterers, fornicators, murderers, shall not possess the kingdom of God.

Concerning the second.

It is necessary that there exist in the Church a distinction between rational discipline, which is called the justice of the flesh, and spiritual justice. Discipline is to restrain the members by reason, so that they do not admit external acts against the law of God, even if the heart is without true fear of God, without repentance, without faith, and full of doubts. The Pharisees taught this discipline, and thought it to be the fulfillment of the law and justice before God. Nor does Christ rebuke the discipline, but the errors which the Pharisees added, and their interior uncleanness.

Concerning the third.

It must be diligently observed in what things spiritual justice abounds. First, repentance: for it is necessary that true terrors exist in the heart from the recognition of the wrath of God against sin, and the heart must recognize that not only external offenses are sins, but also doubts about God, security, diffidence, and seeking human protections out of diffidence and neglect of God. Likewise, manifold wandering motions, and the perpetual contumacy of human nature against the law of God. Second, spiritual justice abounds in faith, that is, trust in the mercy promised on account of Christ, by which faith reconciliation is received, and true invocation is made. For where this faith does not shine, there is no invocation.

Third, it abounds in newness of spirit, that is, in begun interior obedience, fear of God, faith, love, invocation, patience, chastity, love of truth, and mercy toward others, according to that: Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.

Fourth, it abounds in successes in one's calling; David, fortified by faith, performs salutary and useful things. Saul, because he is without faith, does not dare to fight, seeks magical counsels, and ruins many affairs because of diffidence, just as it is said of the impious: Destruction and unhappiness are in their ways. Conversely, it is said of the faithful: Whatever he does shall prosper, namely, in his calling.

Finally, the justice of faith abounds, because it overcomes the snares of the devil in many ways, whereas hypocrites horribly succumb and are overturned. Saul succumbed to the devil, conquered by hatred and the desire for vengeance, so that he killed the priests. Judas succumbed; many succumb who are demented by perverse opinions, such as the Anabaptists. Concerning such struggles, Peter says: The devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Therefore, let these degrees, in which spiritual justice abounds over rational discipline, be diligently considered.

Concerning the fourth.

Here a clear testimony stands that the law of God requires not only external discipline, but perfect interior and exterior obedience. As Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 3. But many, not understanding this preaching of repentance, imagine that only certain Stoic hyperboles are being taught here. Why, they ask, does Christ command what no one can perform? Is it, as the Stoics do, to show an idle image of virtue?

But it must be known that these sayings of Christ are not hyperboles, nor are they spoken in the Stoic manner, but are true and proper sentences of the judgment of God against sin clinging to the nature of man. And the principal reason why these discourses are proposed is that the wrath of God against our uncleanness may be acknowledged, and that external discipline is not the fulfillment of the law, does not take away sin, is not righteousness before God, but that there is need of the mediator Messiah.

Concerning the fifth.

But it is necessary that obedience be begun in the heart, and that there exist motions assenting to the law of God, fear, faith, love of God, patience, therefore it is said: Unless it shall abound, etc., so that David does not burn with the desire for vengeance, like Saul, and yet not even David satisfies the law of God; he acknowledges that he has other vicious affections, he acknowledges also the depravity of nature: for sometimes flames of hatred arise against Saul, which, however, he extinguishes again by the Spirit.rit.

The question is, therefore, how does this imperfect obedience please? I answer: Three things are required for this, that imperfect obedience may please.

First, it must be established that the person must receive reconciliation by faith, on account of the mediator. Secondly, it must be acknowledged that we have sins, and do not satisfy the law of God, as David says: Enter not into judgment with thy servant. Likewise: Against thee only have I sinned, that thou mightest be justified in thy words. Thirdly, it must be established that God nevertheless requires begun obedience, and for this beginning gives the Holy Spirit, and in those who are reconciled by faith receives even these acts of worship, on account of the mediator, and forgives that which is lacking, as Peter says: Offer sacrifices pleasing to God through Jesus Christ.

Concerning the sixth.

But when it is said that sin remains in the saints, and yet begun obedience is required, it is asked, what sins are remaining in the saints, and which ones truly cast off grace, and disturb the Holy Spirit?

I answer, original sin and depraved affections remain in the saints, but in such a way that the saints resist these evils.

But if they assent against conscience, and indulge, and do not resist, grace is lost, the Holy Spirit is disturbed and cast out, as in Saul the sins are mortal, not only the external injuries against David, but also the internal hatred itself, to which he indulges and assents.

Christ therefore added here a sermon about hatred, to which one indulges against conscience; he orders this to be laid aside, and orders one to return to grace.

For when he says: If thou rememberest that thy brother hath anything against thee, he makes mention of an affection clinging against conscience; he wants this to be laid aside, even if the natural disease cannot be laid aside.

Concerning the seventh.

There are many opinions about vengeance, which must be prudently distinguished.

For some speak of the office of the magistrate, which is not prohibited, nay, it is exercised by the command of God. Others speak of private vengeance, which is prohibited. But the desire for vengeance is a very sharp movement, especially in excellent natures, as it is said. But vengeance is a good, and sweeter than life itself, and often disturbs the Republic and the Churches. And I think that is why mention is made of the offering in this very matter, because from the desire for vengeance arise the greatest conflicts in the Church. Christ therefore warns us to offer, that is, to perform ecclesiastical duties without hatreds, without the desire for vengeance.

At the same time, this passage also teaches that ceremonies do not profit those who have minds contaminated by sins against conscience, namely by moral violation, just as it is said elsewhere: Circumcision profits, if you observe the law.

Concerning the eighth.

The text also warns from whom reconciliation should be begun.

Because the text says: If thou rememberest that thy brother hath anything against thee, etc. Because the injured party has a cause against the one who injured him, therefore let him who injured begin the reconciliation. But even if he is too hard to be willing to bend himself to health, yet the injured party ought not to nourish hatred, so that, even if Saul was not seeking pardon, yet David did not hate him, he did not indulge in the private desire for vengeance, but kept the rule: Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you.

This is often not observed by those irritated by slight injuries; they compensate for them with vengeance much more atrocious than the injury by which they themselves were affected, nay, they even mix public affairs with private contentions. This evil must be diligently considered and avoided, lest we rush against the will of God, and by our impatience and desire for vengeance harm the Church or the Republic.

But rather let us forget injuries, and heal, just as Christ reminds us by washing the feet of the Apostles, and adding the commandment: Love one another, and as I have done, so you should do. For... the washing of the feet most properly signifies that healing of offenses and errors, or injuries.

Latin:

Dominica VI. post Trinitatis.

Evangelium Matthaei 5.

Nisi abundaverit iustitia vestra plus quam Scribarum et Pharisaeorum non intrabitis in regnum coelorum.

Audistis quia dictum est antiquis: Non occides, qui autem occidererit, reus erit iudicio.

Ego autem dico vobis: Quia omnis qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit iudicio.

Qui autem dixerit fratri suo, racha, reus erit concilio.

Qui autem dixerit, fatue, reus erit gehennae ignis.

Si ergo offers munus tuum ad altare, et ibi recordatus fueris quia frater tuus habet aliquid adversum te, relinque munus tuum ante altare, et vade prius, reconciliare fratri tuo, et tunc veniens offeras munus tuum.

Esto consentiens adversario tuo cito, dum es in via cum eo, ne forte tradat te adversarius iudici, et iudex tradat te ministro, et in carcerem mittaris.

Amen dico tibi, non exibis inde, donec reddas novissimum quadrantem.

Octo sunt praecipui loci.

I. Necessitas iustitiae operum.

II. Discrimen iustitiae carnis et spiritualis.

III. Quinque rebus abundat iusticia spiri- tualis supra rationalem. 1. Pœniten- tia. 2. Fide. 3. Novitate spiritus. 4. Successibus in vocatione. 5. Vi- ctoriis adversus diabolum. IIII. Quod lex requirat perfectam obe- dientiam. V. Quomodo placeat haec obedientia in- coata et imperfecta. VI. De vindicta. VII. Quod ceremoniae non prosint, si contra conscientiam violes praecepta moralia. VIII. De odio et de reconciliatione.

De primo.

Testimonium manifestum est, quod opor- teat adesse iusticiam operum, quia supra dicit: Non veni solvere legem, et hic requirit iusticiam maiorem Scribarum, ergo requiritur hic iusticia bonae conscientiae, et amplius. Huc pertinent, et haec dicta: Nolite errare, adulteri, fornicato- res, homicidae, non possidebunt regnum Dei.

De secundo.

Extare in Ecclesia necesse est discrimen di- sciplinae rationalis, quae vocatur iusticia carnis, et iusticiae spiritualis. Disciplina est ratione coërcere membra, ne admittant externa facta con- tra legem Dei, etiamsi cor est sine vero timore Dei, sine poenitentia, sine fide, plenum dubi- tationum. Hanc disciplinam tradebant Phari- saei, et putabant esse legis impletionem et iu- sticiam coram Deo. Nec reprehendit Christus disciplinam, sed errores, quos addebant Phari- saei, et immunditiem interiorem.

De tertio.

Diligenter observandum est, quibus rebus abundet iusticia spiritualis. Primum poeniten- tia: necesse est enim in corde veros pavores exi- stere ex agnitione irae Dei adversus peccatum, et agnoscat cor non tantum externa delicta esse pec- cata, sed etiam dubitationes de Deo, securitatem, diffidentiam, quaerere humana praesidia ex diffi- dentia et neglectione Dei. Item multiplices er- rantes motus, et perpetuam naturae humanae contumaciam contra legem Dei. Secundo abundat iusticia spiritualis, fide, id est, fiducia misericordiae promissae propter Chri- stum, qua fide accipitur reconciliatio, et fit vera invocatio. Nam ubi haec fides non praelucet, nulla est invocatio.

Tertio abundat novitate spiritus, id est, in- coata obedientia interiore, timore Dei, fide, di- lectione, invocatione, patientia, castitate, amore veritatis, misericordia erga alios, iuxta illud: Qui spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei.

Quarto, successibus abundat in vocatione, David fide munitus res salutares et utiles gerit. Saul quia sine fide est, non audet dimicare, quae- rit consilia magica, et multa negocia propter diffi- dentiam corrumpit, sicut de impiis dicitur: Con- tritio et infelicitas in viis eorum. Econtra de fideli dicitur: Quicquid faciet prosperabitur, videlicet in vocatione.

Postremo abundat iusticia fidei, quia multi- pliciter vincit insidias diaboli, cum hypocritae horribiliter succumbant et evertantur. Succu- buit diabolo Saul, victus odio et cupiditate vin- dictae, ut interficeret sacerdotes. Succubuit Iu- das, succumbunt multi dementati pravis opinio- nibus, ut Anabaptistae. De talibus certaminibus inquit Petrus: Circumit diabolus tanquam leo rugiens, quaerens quem devoret. Diligenter igi- tur considerentur hi gradus, quibus abundat iu- sticia spiritualis supra disciplinam rationalem.

De quarto.

Hic clarum testimonium extat, quod lex Dei requirat, non tantum externam disciplinam, sed perfectam obedientiam interiorem et exteriorem. Sicut Paulus docet 2. Corinth. 3. Sed multi non intelligentes hanc praedicationem poenitentiae, fingunt hic tantum stoicas quasdam hyperbolas tradi. Cur inquiunt, praecipit Christus, quae nemo, praestare potest, an, ut stoici monstrat imaginem virtutis ociosam?

Sed sciendum est, haec Christi dicta non esse hyperbolas, nec stoico more dici, sed esse veras et proprias sententias iudicii Dei adversus peccatum haerens in natura hominis. Et prin- cipalis causa est, cur hae conciones proponantur, ut ira Dei adversus nostram immunditiem agno- scatur, et quod disciplina externa non sit imple- tio legis, non tollat peccatum, non sit iusticia coram Deo, sed quod sit opus mediatore Messia.

De quinto.

Oportet autem incoari obedientiam in corde, et existere motus assentientes legi Dei, timorem, fidem, dilectionem Dei, patientiam, ideo dictum est: Nisi abundaverit etc., ut David non ardet cupiditate vindictae, ut Saul, et tamen ne David quidem satisfacit legi Dei, agnoscit se habere alios viciosos affectus, agnoscit etiam naturae depravationem: nam interdum oriuntur flammae odii adversus Saulem, quas tamen spiritu iterum extinguit.

Quaestio est igitur, quomodo placeat haec imperfecta obedientia? Respondeo: Tria requiruntur ad hoc, ut placeat imperfecta obedientia.

Primum statuendum est, personam fide reconciliationem accipere debere, propter mediatorem. Secundo agnoscendum est nos habere peccata, et non satisfacere legi Dei, ut David inquit: Non intres in iudicium cum servo tuo. Item: Tibi tantum sum peccatum, ut iustificeris in sermonibus tuis. Tertio statuendum est, quod tamen Deus requirat incoatam obedientiam, et ad hanc incoandam det Spiritum sanctum, et in his qui sunt reconciliati fide recipiat etiam hos cultus, propter mediatorem, et condonet id quod deest, ut Petrus inquit: Offerte hostias placentes Deo propter Iesum Christum.

De sexto.

Cum autem dicitur, manere peccatum in sanctis, et tamen requiri incoatam obedientiam, quaeritur, quae peccata sint in sanctis reliqua, quae vero excutiant gratiam, et perturbent Spiritum sanctum?

Respondeo, manent in sanctis peccatum originis, et pravi affectus, sed ita ut repugnent sancti his malis.

Sed si assentiantur contra conscientiam, et indulgeant, ac non repugnent, amittitur gratia, conturbatur, et eiicitur Spiritus sanctus, ut in Saule peccata mortalia sunt, non solum externae iniuriae contra Davidem, sed etiam odium ipsum internum, cui indulget et assentitur.

Addidit igitur Christus hic concionem de odio, cui indulgetur contra conscientiam, id iubet deponi, et iubet redire in gratiam.

Cum enim inquit: Si recordatus fueris, quod frater tuus aliquid adversum te habeat, facit mentionem affectus contra conscientiam haerentis, hunc vult deponi, etiamsi morbus naturalis non potest deponi.

De septimo.

Multae sunt sententiae de vindicta, quae prudenter discernendae sunt.

Aliae enim loquuntur de officio magistratus, quod non est prohibitum, imo exercetur mandato Dei. Aliae loquuntur de privata vindicta, quae prohibita est. Est autem acerrimus motus, praesertim in excellentibus naturis cupiditas vindictae, ut dicitur. At vindicta bonum est, et vita dulcius ipsa, et saepe perturbat Respub. et Ecclesias. Ac arbitror ideo fieri mentionem oblationis in hac ipsa materia, quia ex cupiditate vindictae maxima existunt certamina in Ecclesia. Praemonet igitur Christus ut offeramus, id est, ut faciamus officia ecclesiastica sine odiis, sine cupiditate vindictae.

Simul etiam docet hic locus, ceremonias non prodesse istis, qui habent mentes contaminatas peccatis contra conscientiam, videlicet violatione morali, sicut alibi dicitur: Circumcisio prodest, si legem observes.

De octavo.

Monet etiam textus, a quo reconciliatio incoanda sit.

Quia textus inquit: Si recordatus fueris, quod frater tuus habeat aliquid adversum te etc. Quia laesus habet causam adversus laedentem, incoët ergo reconciliationem is qui laesit. Sed etiamsi is durior est, quam ut flecti sese ad sanitatem velit, tamen laesus non debet alere odium, ut, etiamsi Saul non petebat veniam, tamen David non oderat eum, non indulsit privatae cupiditati vindictae, sed servavit regulam: Remittite, et remittetur vobis.

Hanc saepe non observant irritati levibus iniuriis, compensant eas vindicta multo atrociore, quam fuerat iniuria, qua ipsi affecti sunt, imo etiam privatis contentionibus miscent publica negocia. Hoc malum diligenter considerandum et cavendum est, ne ruamus contra voluntatem Dei, et nostra impatientia et cupiditate vindictae noceamus Ecclesiae vel Reipub.

Sed potius obliviscamur iniurias, et sanemus, sicut Christus commonefacit nos lavans pedes Apostolis, et addens praeceptum: Diligite invicem, et sicut ego feci, ita vos faciatis. Nam... lotio pedum propriissime significat illam sanationem offensionum et erratorum, vel iniuriarum.

## 5:20 Sermons on Matthew
Unless your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.

Behold, here Christian righteousness is distinguished from hypocrisy. Here you see that Christ does not teach carnal security, and does not want us to remain such, in this raw, fearless state.

In how many ways, therefore, does righteousness excel in a Christian man?

In four ways. First, by Repentance, that is, by true sorrows on account of sins. There is not security in David as there is in Saul; David performs repentance and grieves, Saul despises the judgment of God, or in his punishment is angry at God.

Such are hypocrites universally, fearless, proud, and they think they are the true pillars of Christendom, etc.

Secondly, it excels by Faith. Hypocrites are completely ignorant of this; they trust in themselves, they do not flee to the Son of God, who is the mediator, they boast that they are righteous by their own righteousness, or they rush into despair, and of this consolation—that men ought to believe they are made righteous by imputed righteousness on account of Christ—they know nothing, nor do they wish to know.

Thus David raised himself by this faith. Saul could not raise himself, because he did not wish to embrace this doctrine.

Thirdly, by Invocation. These alone can invoke God, who perform repentance and believe in Christ. Rom. 10: How shall they invoke unless they believe?

Item: No one comes to the Father, except through the Son.

Item Solomon.

The prayer of the hypocrite is a sin.

They only mock God, who call upon Him, and yet do not believe that they are received or heard.

With invocation, it is necessary to embrace hope, and at the same time there are many virtues, which are only in Christians who are doing penance and believing.

Fourth, regarding Consolation, believers feel consolation, and faith and the joy of the heart grow in them, and other fruits of the Spirit.

Item, God also mitigates punishments for them, as for David, Manasseh, Jeconiah, etc.

But hypocrites rush more and more, as Saul is not only pressed by desperation and pain in his heart, but also by many other external calamities.

These four things must be diligently considered, so that we may know the difference between hypocrites and Christians, and stir ourselves to conversion, to penance, faith, and true invocation, and seek consolation in God, which indeed is very necessary in these great miseries.

Latin:

Nisi excellet iusticia vestra, supra iusticiam Pharisaeorum, non intrabitis in regnum coelorum.

Ecce hic discernitur iusticia Christiana ab hypocrisi. Hic videtis, quod non doceat Christus securitatem carnalem, et non velit nos manere tales, in diesem rohen furchtlosen wesen.

Quot modis igitur antecelluit iusticia in homine Christiano?

Quatuor modis. Primum Poenitentia, id est, veris doloribus propter peccata. Non est securitas in Davide sicut in Saul, David agit poenitentiam et dolet, Saul contemnit iudicium Dei, vel in poena irascitur Deo.

Tales sunt universaliter hypocritae, furchtlos, stolz, vnd meinen sie sind die rechten seulen der Christenheit etc.

Secundo excellit Fide. Hanc prorsus ignorant hypocritae, confidunt sibiipsis, non confugiunt ad Filium Dei, qui est mediator, gloriantur se sua justicia iustos esse, vel ruunt in desperationem, et de hac consolatione, quod deberent credere homines fieri iustos imputata iusticia propter Christum, nihil sciunt, nec volunt scire.

Ita David erexit se hac fide. Saul non potuit se erigere, quia hanc doctrinam non voluit amplecti.

Tertio, Invoctione. Hi soli possunt Deum invocare, qui agunt, poenitentiam et credunt in Christum. Rom. 10.: Quomodo invocabunt nisi credent?

Item: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per Flium.

Item Salomon.

Oratio hypocritae est peccatum.

Tantum derident Deum, qui invocant, et tamen non credunt se recipi vel exaudiri.

Cum invocatione oportet complecti spem, et simul sunt multae virtutes, quae sunt tantum in Christianis agentibus poenitentiam et credentibus.

Quarto, Consolatione, credentes sentiunt consolationem, et crescit in eis fides et laetitia cordis, et alii fructus Spiritus.

Item Deus etiam mitigat eis poenas, ut Davidi, Manassae, Iechoniae etc.

Sed hypocritae magis magisque ruunt, ut Saul non solum premitur desperatione et dolore in corde, sed etiam aliis multis externis calamitatibus.

Haec quatuor diligenter consideranda sunt, ut sciamus discrimen inter hypocritas et Christianos, et excitemus nos ad conversionem, ad poenitentiam, fidem, et veram invocationem, et quaeramus in Deo consolationem, quod profecto iam in his tantis miseriis valde necessarium est.

## 5:21 Sermons on Matthew
You have heard what was said to the ancients: You shall not kill.

We said above, that in the human race, hypocrites always understand the law of God only as external discipline, and pretend that this external discipline is righteousness before God, and merits the remission of sins, just as the Pharisees pretended, as the Monks did, and as some have pretended in all times.

God wishes this error to be amended in all times.

The prophets who cried out against this error were killed.

Christ also taxes this same error here.

Lord Doctor Martin also taxed it recently, because God wants sin to be acknowledged, which lurks within the heart, and He wants us to be terrified, He wants us to acknowledge the gratuitous remission of sins, and righteousness on account of the Son.

And Christ begins from the commandment, You shall not kill, which speaks of sins that can be more easily understood.

And the uncleanness of the heart fighting against this commandment is more known than subtle sins, diffidence toward God, which is held for wisdom, or trust in one's own righteousness, which hypocrites think to be a virtue and glory.

But envy and bitter and unjust hatred in the heart of Saul is felt and can be clearly judged, and Saul knows what kind of thing it is, but he does not want to be condemned, he says these evils are not sins.

Against this blindness, Christ says: But I say to you, Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause, is liable to punishment, [German: He is immediately guilty, that he must be punished].

Whoever says to his brother Raca, [German: Whoever shows a grim demeanor to his brother, whoever bears envy or hatred, he is guilty, that one should bring him to judgment].

Whoever says to his brother, Fool, is liable to the fire of Gehenna, [German: Whoever slanders his brother, insults him, falsely defames him].

He named three degrees, which are not external homicides done by hand, but are interior homicides, which are done in the heart.

And they are most common, as we see there is a great deal of hatred, envy, and slander even in those who want to appear just and holy, and they do not see these sins of theirs.

But what Christ says elsewhere: He is liable to punishment, he is liable to judgment, they are the same, because He expressly says he is guilty.

Since he is guilty, God justly condemns him.

But He speaks most harshly about the third: He is liable to the fire of Gehenna.

Thus He is accustomed to name the infernal regions and eternal punishments, and the name is taken from the valley of Ennon, where it was sacrificed to an idol, to which in sacrifice were offered boys, who were burned there.

Thence the name is taken for infernal punishment.

But why does He speak more harshly here, about the slanderers?

Because to slander is worse than to commit slaughter by hand, because he who kills by hand only kills the body, but the slanderer kills the body and snatches away reputation.

For pain on account of infamy brings even death, as Solomon truly says: Calumny disturbs the wise man, and breaks the strength of his heart.

Let slanderous men, of whom there are very many, consider this well, and let them know that they are doubly homicides.

They kill the body with pain,

and they kill the man regarding his reputation, which is a better thing than bodily life, as Solomon says in Proverbs

22: A good name is better than great riches.

Two Questions.

Two Questions follow here.

One: Is all anger a sin?

I answer: The text speaks of unjust anger, because it expressly says: Whoever is angry with his brother without cause.

And such unjust anger is much more frequent among men than just anger.

There is, however, a just anger, when we are angry at sinners on account of the glory of God or on account of justice, just as Christ is angry when he drives the money-changers from the temple, or as a Prince is angry at robbers or at the ravishers of virgins or of honest matrons. Concerning this anger it is said: The zeal of thy house hath eaten me up. And such anger ought to be in government, because it is a spur inciting to justice, and aiding justice. But this anger is rare.

Another, unjust anger is more common, just as Saul envies and is angry at David, just as the proud are universally angry at others, by whom they think themselves to be hindered, etc.

Consider this distinction, concerning just and unjust anger, and at the same time examine yourselves rightly. Everyone wants to be just, and seems to himself to be justly angry, but very often we have false imaginations, and we are hypocrites, and we paint over our depraved desires; we are angry out of pride, or avarice, because not everything we ask for is immediately given to us, which, however, is not justly owed to us. Such people are very many, and let everyone look into himself.

To this also pertain the ungrateful. There are many who, when they have been affected by all benefits for a long time, and once something is done against their will, begin to hate. Such people also pertain to this sermon of Christ: He who is angry at his brother without cause is liable to punishment. And Solomon says: Evil shall not depart from the house of the ungrateful.

Another question is general.

Since the hearts of all are full of uncleanness, and man cannot put off this uncleanness entirely, why does the law rebuke it? Are these things said in vain? Just as the Stoics said in vain that a man ought to be entirely without anger, without love, without joy, without fear. I answer: By no means are these things said in vain by Christ, and it is not a Stoic fantasy, but they are recited for two reasons.

First, for the sake of repentance, so that we may acknowledge our sins, and know that we do not satisfy the law, and do not merit remission. Second, for the sake of the beginning, because it is necessary that newness be begun in us, and it is necessary that we resist evil affections. And although a beginning is made, yet many remnants of sin remain in us. And we ought to know that we are just on account of the Son of God, not on account of our fulfillment of the law.

If thou offerest at the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath something against thee.

You often hear the distinction between these three: The promise, the precepts concerning moral works, [German: of necessary virtues], and ceremonies, [German: church-pomp]: or between faith, moral works, [German: necessary virtues and ceremonies]. And it is very necessary to know this distinction, because it is customary that men slip into ceremonies, and think these to be the whole of religion, [German: the whole holiness, Christianity and divine service], just as the Prophets often complain, and refute this error, as it is said in Psalm 49: Hear, O my people, I will not rebuke thee for thy sacrifices, etc. All Holiness.

Thus the whole religion of the Pope and the Monks is to observe the ceremonies of their Mass, the form of dress, the distinctions of foods, and celibacy, so that a priest may not take a wife, etc. But we ought to understand, tax, and flee these abominations, and know that religion is another thing.

When worldly wise men hear this, they acknowledge religion, [German: divine service], to be something other than these masks of ceremonies, and they learn the doctrine concerning moral works, [German: of worldly virtues, or of good manners], and they think this obedience to be the whole of religion, just as Cato says: If God is a spirit, as the poems tell us, He is to be worshipped by thee especially with a pure mind. And Plato: God is not honored by gestures, but by true virtue. That fantasy of the wise, that such virtues are the highest worship, is also false, because it is written: Without faith it is impossible to please God. Remember these distinctions well.

And consider this order. First, it is necessary that there be faith in man, acknowledging God, and apprehending the promise of grace, and the mediator the Son of God, and the justice given through him and on account of him.

Because no one comes to the father, except through the Son. And this faith shines in true repentance and true conversion of the heart to God. This faith knows also that the remission of sins is not given on account of any other thing, except on account of the Son of God, not on account of our ceremonies, or virtues.

But after the heart is already thus turned to God, and is already joined to God, and lives in God, virtues and ceremonies also follow in the right order, and in such an understanding, just as God wills that virtues and ceremonies be understood and performed. The Lord preaches about this very order here. Because the Pharisees also used to say that offerings were the highest worship, and that they merited grace and all good things, just as Papists say about the Mass. And they were full of hatreds, and contaminated by adulteries, and did injuries to many, and afterwards they pretended that they were wiping away all these sins with sacrifices, and thus they neglected the weightier matters of the law, as it is written in Matthew 23: Woe to you who tithe mint etc. and neglect the weightier matters of the law: judgment and mercy and faith. Behold, this saying of Christ warns of exactly the same thing that I said before, that the Pharisaical imagination is most false, that the whole of religion is that observation of ceremonies, but here faith and judgment and mercy are expressly named. Faith signifies, as you know, the true acknowledgment of God, and receiving the promise of grace promised on account of the Son.

Then judgment and mercy signify moral virtues: to act justly with men, and not to afflict them with injuries, and to do good to them where you can and ought to do good.

Thus in this place He speaks about the order: If you wish to offer, and you are conscious to yourself that you have unjustly harmed another, your sacrifice and your offering profit nothing; know that the offerings of those who come to God with an evil conscience, that is, with the purpose of sinning, do not please God.

But it is necessary that the rule be kept: Wage a good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. Sacrifices with an evil conscience are a mockery of God, just as they are often named abominations in the Prophets. And Proverbs 15 it is said: The victims of the impious are an abomination to the Lord, the vows of the just are pleasing. And in sum, Scripture is full of this order, that first there must be faith in us, afterwards a good conscience in moral works.

Thirdly, ceremonies ought to follow with true understanding.

But I wish to add only this saying of Hosea, which I often repeat, because it ought to be most known to all. Hosea 6 it is said: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God, more than burnt offerings.

He teaches the same thing that I have already said. He censures the most false opinion which pretends that sacrifices please God in those who neglect the acknowledgment of God, namely faith and mercy, that is, the works necessary for a good conscience. And He says: I desire the knowledge of God, that is, faith, more than burnt offerings. And: I desire mercy, that is, good works toward one's neighbor, which are necessary for a good conscience. Commit this saying of Hosea to memory, because it is a good and useful rule, from which many errors can be judged. The Pope inverts everything, he says: The Mass is better than faith and a good conscience. If an unlearned, impious, adulterous priest celebrates Mass, he does more good than another man who believes rightly and is a chaste husband. Such furies of the Papists God will without any doubt punish horribly in this life, and after this life. Therefore let us be firm in faith, and let us ask of God that He Himself may defend and preserve the Churches that love and proclaim the truth, and not allow them to be dissipated, and let us expect protection from God. Let these things be said about this order, about faith, the works of conscience, and offering.

II.

Now a question is raised. Who ought to seek reconciliation? Here you see that the Lord commands hatreds to be put aside, and to be reconciled again, with an external sign, so that the other may understand that the hatred has been put aside. But who ought to begin the reconciliation? I answer: The unjust party, who has harmed the other, ought to begin the reconciliation, and seek pardon, and submit himself to God and to justice, and offer this humility to God and to justice. But no one willingly humbles himself. Therefore all seek pretexts, that they have just causes, and no one in the world wants to have an unjust cause. This evil is so common that there is hardly another more common, and it is most used by hypocrites, who see the speck in their brother's eye, and …neglect the beam in their own eye. But here let each one examine his own conscience, with those pretexts removed which he knows to be fictitious and sophistical. And when his conscience accuses him, let him see to it that he seeks reconciliation. And it happens more often that those seek reconciliation who have sinned less, because it is said: The just man in the beginning is his own accuser; the just find in themselves also infirmities, and they confess them more willingly, and seek forgiveness from God and from men. If the other does not wish to be reconciled, afterwards your conscience is excused, if you have sought reconciliation; God will be the judge, and will hand over that implacable and furious man to the officer, who will lead him into prison.

This doctrine must not only be learned, but also practiced in life. Many offenses occur among us; you ought to heal these, and by mutual reconciliation aid the common peace, just as James also well says: Confess your sins to one another. You have sins, and I have them too. I forgive you, and you forgive me for the sake of God, and for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, because this is the will of God, that we live in mutual peace.

You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you, that everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her, has already committed adultery in his heart.

I said above why this exposition of the Decalogue was proposed by Christ, namely because he is the interpreter of the law, and a preacher of repentance, and he wishes to show that we are all guilty, and have sins, so that having acknowledged the wrath of God, we may flee to grace, and learn that another righteousness has been proposed to us, promised for the sake of the Son of God, and that we are not righteous by the fulfillment of the law.

And the Lord began with two commandments, which manifestly convict us, when they speak of inordinate flames and desires, which all can feel and judge, namely, of envy and hatreds, and of illicit loves, and the desire for adulteries.

Therefore here he adds an exposition to this commandment, You shall not commit adultery, this: Everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her, has already committed adultery. By this declaration he shows that by the commandment of God not only are external adulteries prohibited, but also all inordinate motions. And that God wishes the heart to be chaste, and obedient to his law, and loving chastity just as he himself is.

He accuses us all, therefore, that we are not such.

Objectio. Here again a man can object according to political wisdom, [in the wisdom of the world].

Why is it useful to propose impossible commandments? Why are inordinate motions prohibited, when no one can entirely strip them off? I answer: These sayings of Christ are not useless, because they are preachings of repentance, as I said; God wishes us to acknowledge that we are immersed in sin, and guilty of sin.

And he wishes us to grieve, and not to be iron-hearted and secure, as if we were righteous and clean by our own cleanliness, and he wishes us to seek grace, and to believe that for the sake of the mediator the remission of sins is given, and we are reckoned righteous.

And when we are converted to God, he wishes us to restrain our motions, and he wishes us not to pollute ourselves against our conscience with fornication or adulteries.

You often hear this doctrine of sin, grace, and new obedience elsewhere. And it ought to be known to you all.

Here I also add a brief admonition for the younger ones. Know that adulteries and fornications are great sins, and are punished by God without any doubt with great penalties, [that God punishes the whole land, the city, and the perpetrators].

Concerning these penalties, the text to the Hebrews first says expressly: God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

And in Leviticus 18, it is said concerning all prohibited modes of commixtion: Every soul that has done such abominations shall perish from the midst of the people. Keep my commandments, lest the land vomit you out, just as it vomited out the nations that did such things before.

Nor ought you to doubt that God punishes adulteries and similar crimes with wars and great devastations.

Examples are also written to show the rule.

1. God punished the world with a flood because of adulteries.

2. Sodom perished, and because of similar crimes now all Asia, Egypt, and Greece have been devastated.

3. Num. 25. God commands the princes of the people of Israel to be hanged, and moreover twenty-four thousand men are killed, because of fornications.

Likewise, the tribe of Benjamin was almost entirely destroyed, because certain nobles had raped a Levite's wife. Likewise, David was horribly punished because of adultery. And just as he himself polluted another man's wife, so in turn God permitted his own wives to be polluted.

And look at the families of kings and princes, where there are manifest examples that God punishes sins. of the seed in the seed, that is, in the children and in the posterity. Remember these things, and fear the wrath and judgment of God, and avoid adulteries and similar sins, and pray to God that He may rule you, because God loves chastity, and wishes that gift to be sought from Him, and He gives this gift willingly, and adorns it with great rewards, just as Joseph, avoiding adultery, receives great rewards.

Thus it is said in the book of Wisdom, chap. 8: I knew that I could not otherwise be chaste, unless God gave it. And this itself was of wisdom, to know whose gift it is. Therefore I prayed to the Lord. Let us do the same; let us ask for this gift from God, and let us ourselves add our own diligence, and let us strive to restrain ourselves, lest we fall, and let us avoid the occasions of adulteries, and let us learn: To avoid sins is to avoid the occasions of sins, [German: to flee sin is to flee the causes and circumstances that incite a man].

If one goes into a bath, he becomes wet. So, whoever wishes to follow such company, he falls all the more easily. Therefore we ought to be cautious, and not seek out the incitement to such things ourselves. Therefore St. Paul says: Walk cautiously, not as the foolish.

Another Precept.

If your eye has scandalized you, pluck it out. The Lord commands that occasions be avoided, [German: causes and circumstances] that incite a man. Keep your eyes, flee evil company, etc. All such incitements are forbidden here.

Furthermore, this commandment concerning the eye and the right hand contains another prohibition as well. The eye signifies a counselor. The right hand signifies a friend. Therefore Christ commands that we take care not to be seduced by evil counselors. Likewise, that we do not sin for the sake of friends or wives. You know, however, that men commit very many and great sins, urged on by counselors or friends. Men often sin to gain the favor of princes and friends, when otherwise they would not sin, unless they were moved by this foolish imagination: You must do a favor to your friends, you must be silent for the sake of the common peace, just as many in courts are silent about the truth, lest they offend their princes or friends. These sins are most common.

Therefore this text does not need a long explanation. But remember that Christ forbids this levity, that we value princes or friends more than God, just as He says elsewhere: He who loves father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me. But here He commands the eye to be plucked out, and the hand to be cut off.

Here you may learn to understand the discourse correctly. He does not wish that you should literally gouge out an eye, or cut off a hand, as some fools once castrated themselves, like Origen. And let the exposition be taken from the precept: Do not kill. For if all members that sin were to be cut off literally, then the heart would have to be gouged out, and thus a man would kill himself, which God expressly forbids. Therefore, let this saying not be understood as a corporal amputation, [German: of the bodily gouging out or cutting off], but as a prohibition, which is made with a firm purpose, by which the will forbids listening to those counsels or friends, [German: the gouging out and cutting off is, with true earnestness and firm resolve, to cut off this speech and friend, that is, to turn away from them, not to value their opinion, friendship, and favor more than God].

And thus to flee such friends is a great and difficult matter among the wise. Therefore this precept, of which Christ speaks here, is of great moment, as the wise know well, that they often sin so as not to offend friends. But young people do not yet know these things; they only know this, that they are often corrupted by evil associations and the examples of companions. There let them also see to it that they tear themselves away from evil associations. And let them remember this precept of Christ: If your right hand offends you, cut it off.

It is said: Whoever shall have dismissed his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce. But I say to you, etc. Because Christ repeated this sermon several times, in which He reproved divorces, such as were customary among the Jews and the Gentiles, it is sufficiently apparent that He greatly disapproved of that levity.

For it was customary to dismiss wives merely out of levity, when the woman had committed no sin, but …perhaps the husband saw another who pleased him more. Likewise, by artifice, one enticed another's spouse to himself, and they played with the appearance of law, as if any kind of divorce were permitted in the law of Moses. Hortensius asked Cato to yield his wife Martia to him, a beautiful and noble woman. Cato did so, and after her death took Martia back, which was also against the ethnic laws. Augustus practiced that Drusus should yield Livia to him. That such things were often and much done among the Jews also is very credible. Christ censures these levities, because the confusions of lusts are very displeasing to God. Therefore, I wish to speak about this matter in order. First, about chastity. Second, about marriage. Third, about divorce. Fourth, about the duty of the Magistrate in punishing adulteries and other lusts.

I. On Chastity.

What is chastity?

It is to obey God in this work, so that either in marriage or outside of marriage you abstain from every commixtion prohibited by the law of God. And let not virginity alone be thought to be chastity, but the conjugal life before God is truly chastity, when the faith of marriage is kept and adulteries are not mingled. God has established this order in such a way, and wishes the human race to understand chastity, so that we may know that He Himself is a chaste spirit, and in our prayers we may distinguish God from devils by this thought. Let us think that we are addressing God, who is chaste and truthful and beneficent, not addressing the devil, who is a liar, a murderer, eager to do harm, and who, out of hatred for God, incites men to wandering lusts and to polluting their bodies in various ways. Therefore, think diligently and often of this distinction between God and devils, and in prayer think of whom you wish to address. We do not grasp God with our arms, but it is necessary to address and contemplate Him with the mind, and think of what kind He is, and distinguish Him from all creatures, and from devils, from angels and men, and from all other things. Moreover, this distinction is clear, taken from chastity, by which He is distinguished from devils and men. And let us know simply that God wishes us to serve Him in this work, namely by abstaining from all prohibited lusts. This is His will expressed in the commandments and declared in the punishments. The commandments are: Thou shalt not commit adultery, Deut. 25: Cursed is he who sleeps with the wife of his neighbor. And 1 Corinthians 6 it is said: Do not err, fornicators and adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God. To the Galatians 5: Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God.

Remember these commandments, and do not despise them, because there is no doubt that it is the truth that those who persevere in adulteries or other prohibited lusts are not members of Christ.

Furthermore, consider the punishments. Concerning eternal ones, it has already been said. All who do not convert will fall into eternal punishments, as has already been said: Fornicators and adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God, namely, those who do not convert.

But the doctrine concerning punishments in this life must be added. You ought not to doubt that God also in this life punishes adulteries and other prohibited lusts with bodily punishments and wounds of the soul. Therefore it is written: God will judge fornicators and adulterers, namely, both in this life and after this life, if conversion does not take place.

Now see the examples of punishments in this life.

Among the causes of the flood, this sin is recounted, that the principal men in the Church began to practice wandering lusts, allerley vnzucht treiben.

2. Afterwards, Sodom and other cities are utterly destroyed. And indeed the Son of God Himself is on that journey with Abraham, and becomes the executor of this punishment with His own hand, to show that He is very angry at such filth.

3. Numbers 25. God commands many princes to be hanged on account of the defiled Moabite women.

4. Almost the entire tribe of Benjamin was destroyed, because certain scoundrels had violated the wife of a Levite.

5. David is driven from his kingdom by his son, and the son violates his father's wives, which calamity was the punishment for David's adultery.

6. Jeremiah, among the causes of the Babylonian exile, cites adulteries. Thus also other Prophets often speak of the punishments for adulteries.

7. The histories of all nations are full of examples; Troy was destroyed because of the abduction of Helen, and such histories are very many.

8. Consider also daily examples. You see many families, great and small, perishing because of lusts. And do not doubt that God punishes such crimes severely even in this life with corporal punishments.

9. Besides corporal punishments there are also spiritual punishments. Paul to the Ephesians 4 says that those contaminated by wandering lusts are punished with blindness, insensibility, and impenitence, mit blindheit vnd verstockung, that is, they become blind through the manifold furies of opinions and others.

And they are without any sorrow for sins, and without any repentance, but securely they seek obscene pleasures, and heap sins upon sins, etc., until at length they rush into eternal destruction.

Such is the life of Pontiffs, Canons, and many impious men. You see that the Canons are blind; they are Epicureans, and they neither wish to hear nor understand the Gospel. Afterwards, they proceed in this way in their sins, idolatries, and lusts, until they fall completely into eternal punishments.

Consider well all these things which I have now said, both the precepts and the punishments, and rouse yourselves to maintain chastity, and pray to God that He may help you, so that you may be able to be chaste.

Think also how miserable it is to live thus in fornication or adultery, so that you know that God is angry with you, and you cannot call upon Him, and you can seek neither help nor defense from God, and that you are a slave of the devil. Such a life is most miserable. These evils must be seriously avoided.

I have spoken about chastity.

II. On Marriage.

Now, after I have spoken about chastity, I add the doctrine on Marriage.

Since God wishes chastity to be understood, He established this order, that one man and one woman should be coupled inseparably. Marriage is, therefore, the lawful coupling of one male and one female, such that they are inseparably joined. And this order was instituted in Paradise, in these words: They shall be two in one flesh, that is, one male and one female inseparably joined. Behold, here the law has now been delivered: You shall not commit adultery, because it is comprehended in these words: They shall be two in one flesh. If only two, and inseparably joined, then it is not permitted to wander to many. In this order, God would have wished us to serve Him even then, if nature had remained intact.

Now know this: since such a union has been instituted and ordained by God, let us learn to obey God in this His ordination, and let us know that the married life pleases God, and that this kind of life is holy to believers, and let us give thanks to God, and let us not violate this divine ordination with blind frenzies, as the Gentiles did, and as many impious people still do, who are never in agreement among themselves, who easily commit adulteries, as if it were a game, etc.

Let there be true reverence for God in us, and let us honor this ordination of God in the true fear of God, as it is written to the Hebrews: Marriage is honorable.

God wishes it to be acknowledged that marriage is His ordination; He wishes individual families to be Churches, in which He is invoked concordantly, and thanks are given to Him. Therefore, He created two, male and female, so that there might be a sweet society, and that it might be a Church, just as He said: Let us make him a helper like unto himself, namely, that it might be a helper not only in procreation, and education, and the duties of bodily life, but also in the society of invocation, in teaching and ruling children. Therefore, male and female, so that there might be ordered love.

III. On Divorces.

First, let the complaint be recited: The dissensions and miseries of spouses are a great part of the calamities of the human race, and are a sign and punishment of original sin, because if the nature of men had not been immersed in sin, that society of one male and one female would have been full of mutual love and sweetness, and no divorces would have been made, nor would the husband have coveted another, nor the wife another man; there would have been no hatreds, no discords, but they would have joyfully raised and taught their offspring together, and together would have cultivated their little gardens and fields, would have given thanks to God, would have listened to the wisdom of the elders, and would have conversed much among themselves about doctrine and the works of God.

When, therefore, domestic calamities of any kind occur, let us think about original sin, and about other sins which we add, and let us know that these marital miseries are punishments for sins. Therefore, let us do penance, and let us pray to God that He may rule us, and let us ourselves be vigilant against the devil, lest quarrels grow, because the devil, having taken the opportunity, stirs up great fires from small sparks.

Let this, therefore, be the first rule. Let spouses know that it is the will of God that marriage be the lawful and indissoluble union of one male and one female, and that those persons who provide the cause for divorce, such as adulterers or deserters, undoubtedly sin.

That this is the mind of the Gospel is most certain. For although Moses permitted divorces, so that it was lawful for a husband to dismiss a wife, even one who had not sinned, nevertheless Christ disapproves of this custom, and expressly prohibits such Mosaic divorces, and draws marriage back to its first institution: They shall be two in one flesh. But in order that spouses may be able to remain together, let us learn that there is also need for mutual patience, and for prayer to God against the devil.

Second rule. It is certain that the adulterer and the adulteress sin, and likewise that the deserter and the desertress sin. However, after the bond of marriage has been torn asunder by such people, the question is, Is it lawful for the innocent person to contract a marriage again with another? Here the Pope says that another marriage is not to be granted to the innocent person. I do not wish, however, to recite a long disputation in this place; this text is clear enough, which says that a divorce can take place between such people, the innocent person and the adulterer or adulteress. Now, if another marriage were not granted to the innocent person, that would be a divorce in name, not in reality. What need would there have been to except the case of adultery, if he had wished the innocent person to be bound in the same way as he wishes them to be bound in other cases, namely, if a wife is too irritable, or is sick?

And that this custom once existed in the Church, that such divorces were granted to innocent persons, some ancient sayings and examples show.
