Jerome relates that there was a noble matron at Rome, Fabiola, who had an adulterous husband who lived most shamefully. She eventually married another man. And although Jerome argues about this deed, nevertheless the history shows that this custom was still in use. And other examples are read.

Third rule.

Just as Christ speaks expressly of the case of adultery, so Paul speaks of another case, namely, of the deserter or desertress. And he says, when one of the spouses becomes a fugitive and a deserter, then the innocent person is not subject to servitude, that is, is no longer bound to them, but another marriage is to be granted to them. A deserter or desertress, however, is a person who departs from a spouse without just cause, and is absent for a long time without just cause, out of malice, as often happens. Such people are also for the most part adulterers and adulteresses. In these two cases, this is also observed in our Consistories, that another marriage is granted to the innocent person.

But afterwards, one must ask about the punishment of the person who has sinned either by adultery or by desertion. I will speak of this punishment next.

Concerning judgments and punishments.

It was recently said in which cases a marriage may be granted to an innocent person. And I said clearly and expressly that no man can justly tear asunder a marriage. But the adulterer and the deserter tear it asunder against the will of God, and sin horribly. The innocent person does not tear it asunder, but is free, after the tearing asunder has already been done by the adultery or by the desertion of the other.

But here it must be known that it is necessary for such cases to be brought to a Judge ordained for this purpose. No one is their own judge against another. But if you wish the guilty person to be condemned, and yourself to be pronounced free, this must be done through an ordinary judge. Nor is it lawful for an innocent person to contract another marriage before an investigation is made by an ordinary judge. Pastors ought also to say this diligently and often to the people in their sermons, because it often happens that such persons contract [marriage] without a judgment, and afterwards insufficient causes for separation are found, and many evils follow.

Therefore it was rightly done that the authority in these Churches ordained singular judges and Consistories for these cases, so that men might know where the judges of these matters are to be sought, and it would be desirable that these judges be more supported by the superior authority, and by those who bear the sword. The Papists neglect such judgments almost entirely, just as they otherwise corrupt many good ordinances greatly. And because of the negligence of those people, our authorities are also more negligent. But let us pray to God that He may help us, and give us salutary governments.

Question concerning the sick.

Here also a question is raised concerning the sick, Whether a separation should be made on account of a perpetual disease?

Response. I do not wish to speak about all the questions of this matter in the sermon, but I leave these affairs to the Consistories for the most part. I will only say a few things, useful for the present people. And first I say this, when some person is by nature not suitable for marriage, such as, if a man has no male strength at all for a woman, such a union is not a marriage. And the judge knows that he ought to pronounce that it is not a marriage, and he ought to grant the power to the capable person to contract another marriage. And let it be enough to have said this much about this matter; the rest I commend to the Consistories.

But if there are other diseases, such as leprosy, the French disease [syphilis], or other similar diseases, in the husband or in the wife, here I say that such diseases by no means separate spouses and that they are by no means sufficient causes for divorce.

Someone will say: It is burdensome that I am forced to retain a sick spouse. Although it is burdensome, yet it is most just. I prove it thus.

The height of friendship is to do good to a friend in necessity and in misery.

Between husband and wife there is the height of friendship for as long as they are not torn apart by some crime. For as long as that is true of them: They shall be two in one flesh.

Therefore, on account of disease, marriage should by no means be dissolved, but in disease, faithfulness should be shown toward the sick person.

How great an injury this would be, if you had an honest spouse, and sons and daughters by her, and she began to be sick, if you then wished to cast her away.

You are coupled in such a way that you may tolerate joyful and sad things together, and one may bring help to the other. Just as parents ought not to cast away sons and daughters when they are sick, so a husband ought not to cast away a sick wife, nor a woman depart from a sick husband.

God therefore instituted the society of spouses, likewise of parents and sons and daughters, so that the infirm and the sick might have help, just as a mother cares for an infant and does not cast it away.

Let this be enough to have said about this case as well, and this admonition is necessary for many, because many become impatient, and some desert their sick spouses.

Let such impatient people know that it is the will of God that they ought to seek consolation from God, and obey God in such affliction, and they ought to remain with the sick, and by no means depart from them.

IV. Concerning the punishments of adulterers.

The last part remains concerning punishments, about which I will also speak briefly.

In the Church there is only one punishment, namely Excommunication, against all offenses which are manifest or shown in judgments. And although this punishment is very great, namely to be cast out of the Church of God and not to have the remission of sins, as it is said: Whose sins you shall retain, they are retained for them, yet impious men do not care about this punishment.

But it is the command of God that the Magistrate, who bears the sword, should severely punish adulterers with corporal punishments, as it is written in the law of God, Deut. 22: If a man shall sleep with the wife of another, both shall die, the adulterer and the adulteress, and you shall take away the evil from Israel.

And many other things are said in the same place concerning the punishments of adultery and fornication. And because the magistrate does not punish, God later punishes both, namely, the adulterers and the magistrates. Indeed, He punishes whole nations on account of this negligence, as appears in the example of Benjamin.

Noble youths had violated the Levite's spouse and had killed her; the husband cut up the corpse and sent the parts to all the tribes of Israel, and complained about this crime.

The tribes of Israel gathered and ordered that the guilty be sent to them, so that they might inflict just punishment upon them, but because they were the sons of noble men, no one wanted to hand them over for punishment. Therefore, a great war followed afterward, and almost the entire tribe of Benjamin was killed. Thus, we ought not to doubt that God punishes both adulterers and magistrates, and whole nations, on account of the negligence of the magistrates.

We preachers ought to warn of these things; we cannot do more. But I say to you: O Consuls and Magistrates: Fear the wrath of God, and consider public punishments. You yourselves know your negligence in punishing; therefore, amend yourselves and be more severe. Let these things said about this passage of Matthew, concerning adulteries and divorces, suffice.

You shall not perjure yourself.

The doctrine concerning an Oath must often be repeated in the Church, because it is necessary for men to be admonished, so that they may know in some way what an oath is, and what reverence for an oath there ought to be.

And what oaths are truly oaths. And what are the punishments for perjury.

But in the beginning it must be known what an oath is.

An oath is an asseveration of some statement with the invocation of God, so that He may be a witness of our heart, that we do not wish to deceive, and that He may be an avenger to punish us if we deceive; and it is an obligation by which we bind ourselves to God for punishment if we deceive, and it is not void, because God expressly ordained a punishment for such an insult, because perjurers wish to make Him a witness of a lie, and they despise the punishment.

An oath is such a confirmation of a speech, in which one at the same time calls upon God, and prays to Him, that He may be a witness of our heart, that we have no deceit in mind, and that He may be a punisher if we do not keep our word. And it is an obligation by which we bind ourselves to punishment if we do not keep our word. And this invocation and obligation is certain, for God has with explicit words ordained the punishment for this disgrace, that one has drawn Him in as a witness of a lie, and that one has despised His punishment.

From these words you learn now that in an oath, an invocation of God is actually contained, in which we bind ourselves to punishment if we make God a lying witness.

See therefore how many great things are contained in an oath. First, Truth, which must be kept by itself, even if an oath is not added. Secondly, Invocation of God, which ought to be serious, and not done to confirm a lie or another sin. Thirdly, Confession, that God is the avenger of perjury, and the punisher, when He is cited as a false witness. Fourthly, Promise, that we wish to sustain the punishment if we deceive, if we do not keep our word.

Thus, on the contrary, there are four great sins in perjury, in the breaking of an oath.

The first sin is Lying. That by itself would be a great sin, even if the violation of an oath did not occur. The second sin is false invocation, because the perjurer invokes God to confirm a lie. The third sin, Contempt of God's threatening, who threatens punishment to perjurers, but the perjurer sins, caring nothing for this divine threatening. The fourth sin, Lying in an obligation, a lying obligation; the perjurer binds himself to God, and lies to God, when he does not care for the judgment of God. Let these things be said thus crudely about the sins which are simultaneously in perjury, in the breaking of an oath, because no one can express how great the magnitude of sins is in a single perjury, and how great the contempt of God is, because God is alleged as a false witness, and because His threatening is despised.

Concerning punishment.

But you should know what is said in the second commandment: God will not hold him guiltless who uses the name of God in vain.

In this commandment is an express threatening. And you should know that such an ordinance of God is as certain as the ordinance is certain that when the Sun rises, day is made. Punishment follows after perjury among all men, by whatever name they are called, whether Christians, or Gentiles, or Turks, or by whatever name they are called.

Whoever commits perjury is certainly punished divinely, whether they be kings, or servants, or whoever they may be.

Experience shows this. 2 Maccabees 7.

Alcinus the high priest swears to the Jews that he does not wish to harm them, afterwards he kills them. But a little later he himself is also suddenly struck by God, and pays the penalty. And such examples are seen daily in life.

Second doctrine.

Concerning what matters a promise can be made with an oath. I answer: A promise with an oath ought to be made only concerning possible things, and not things prohibited by the law of God.

And when a man promises a thing which he knows to be impossible for himself, or which is prohibited by the law of God, then he sins, as when someone swears that he wishes to kill an innocent person. Such is when someone swears that he wishes to become a monk, because he swears many things prohibited in the law of God, namely, that he wishes to be an idolater. Such is when someone swears that he does not wish to contract a legitimate marriage.

Such promises concerning impossible or forbidden things are not oaths, and those who swear thus sin, and afterwards add greater sins, when they make such promises against the law of God, because it is manifestly said: Thou shalt not desire the impiety of God. This rule must be held, because great sins are confirmed when it is neglected, just as Herod neglected it, who, because he had sworn, afterwards pretended that he had to kill John, because he was bound by an oath. But this hypocrisy was a mockery of God, and contains many great sins. Such is the hypocrisy of monks and papist Priests, that they pretend they are keeping idolatries and impure celibacy, because they are bound by an oath. But God punishes and will punish these sins, and will punish this lie and this hypocrisy, that they say they remain in such impiety because of an oath.

Third rule.

One must swear only by the name of God. Not by creatures, not by heaven, not by the earth, not by holy men, living or dead, because it is said in Deut. 6: Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve him only, and shalt swear by his name. This rule is well to be considered, because it was and is a bad custom that in oaths it is added: I swear by God and by the Saints.

And the cause is to be considered, why such a form is to be reprehended. To swear is to say something with the invocation of God. It is certain, however, that the Saints are not to be invoked. Also, when I swear by God, I confess that a witness and avenger is present. These things belong only to the omnipotent nature. Therefore, no mention of the Saints should be made in an oath, who are not omnipotent, nor are they inspectors of hearts, nor are they executors of punishment, they are not the mighty punishers.

This rule is also handed down here: You shall not swear by heaven, by the earth, by your head. A bad custom had also grown among the Jews of changing the form of an oath. Concerning this bad custom he speaks here.

He does not forbid an oath altogether, which is done rightly and with reverence for God, as will be said more fully later. Now let it be enough to know these main points:

1. What an oath is. 2. What penalties follow perjury. 3. That promises concerning forbidden things are not oaths. 4. That only God is to be invoked in an oath.

Concerning oaths extorted by force.

Concerning an oath which we make compelled by force or fear.

Concerning oaths which men, having passed the years of childhood, make compelled by terror, at that age which has deliberation and free consent, it is to be thought thus: If anyone swears to an enemy, or even to a robber on the public road, in order to redeem his life, that he will give a hundred Joachimics, and by this pact escapes present danger, he, because he knowingly chooses a lawful thing, must necessarily keep his word, since such an action is in itself an oath. And the violation or evasion of this oath is truly perjury, an insult affecting God. And since it often happens in practice (for we also remember frequent examples of our own time), that, with the faith or religion of an oath interposed, either concerning a return or concerning a price agreed upon for a head, captives are sent away unharmed, the more inexperienced must be warned that such private oaths of safety given to an enemy or robber must necessarily be kept.

So that these things may be understood more correctly, I add a declaration worthy of memory and consideration. Even if such an oath was extorted by terror, nevertheless, things done even by fear are truly voluntary. And because in an oath simulation must be entirely absent, a promise in such cases is in itself an oath. For to a traveler, after he falls into danger, with threats proposed either by an enemy or by a robber, an option is given, and power is permitted, that he may choose whether he wishes to lose his life or to promise money. Power therefore being given to the traveler to choose between evils, it is manifest that in that comparison, the choice is made by an assenting will, so that by the loss of money the safety of the body may be redeemed. Wherefore, when the will is not hindered by judgment, then because of such a moment of time, it chooses the lesser evil, namely the loss of money, so that it may retain life, it is necessary to confess that the will, although he is disturbed by fear, yet in this promise he retains his liberty, and therefore the choice is voluntary. And when this terrible bond, namely an oath, has been added to it, such a pact is by no means void, but is judged to be sanctioned and confirmed by the very fact and by a voluntary oath. Therefore, let those who have bound their faith by an oath know that God wills that they fulfill what they have sworn, and not evade their promises by violating the oath. For there is no doubt that the wrath of God rages with bodily punishments against those who redeem their money or life by perjury. Remember diligently this true opinion which I have recited.

But so that you may repeat it in your memory more willingly and more often, I wish to tell you a story. A certain nobleman of the equestrian order in France, an enemy of the Swabian League, was captured by the Prince Palatine and, having given his word in place of an oath, confirmed that he would return to the designated place on the appointed day. By which law or condition, having been freed at that time, the power was immediately granted to him to return to his own people whenever he wished. Although he had ascertained here, he who had pledged his faith, that if he had returned according to the pact on the appointed day, not only would the excellent Prince Palatine have interceded with his authority so that violent hands would not be laid upon him, but he would also have exerted effort in his cause so that, with enmities laid aside and peace reconciled, the controversies on both sides would be settled on the most equitable conditions possible, yet, neglecting his faith and oath, he did not fulfill his promises. Indeed, a short time later, not far from the Joachim valley, he was struck by a leaden ball fired from a cannon and died, paying the penalty worthy of perjury by the just judgment of God.

Furthermore, the Roman Pope in canon law speaks perplexedly about oaths extorted by force, and plays craftily with the deceits of sophisms. For elsewhere he cunningly orders him who has sworn, broken by fear, to seek absolution from the Pontiff, and by this absolution he says that he is freed from the obligation of the oath. Elsewhere he says that such pacts sanctioned by an oath must be kept. This variety of responses disturbs consciences. But I will not linger on this dispute. Moreover, let human minds be instructed concerning the pretext of pontifical absolution, that it is an impiety and an error insulting to God that the Pope has assumed for himself the authority to absolve men so that they do not fulfill promises made by a legitimate oath. Let it suffice to have warned of this briefly in this place.

Is it permitted to swear? On the text.

Thus far these matters proposed in the two previous sermons have been moderately explained, namely: What an oath is, and which promises are in fact oaths by which consciences are bound.

And which oaths are void, and are not oaths in truth. Now we shall explain the text, the words of which are these: But I say to you: do not swear at all, neither by heaven, nor by earth etc. From this saying the Anabaptists have constructed that delusion of theirs, that it is not permitted for Christians to give any oath, and by this question they have everywhere seditiously disturbed the political bonds in cities.

For it is established that an oath is the chief bond of judgments and of the political order, just as it is customary in any government for the magistrate to demand that subjects or citizens swear that they will obey the laws. And in the forum for the sake of settling controversies, it is often resorted to that an oath is deferred to the litigant either by the magistrate or by the judges. He who condemns and disapproves of such oaths sanctioned by political order, does he not seditiously cut the nerves of civil society? Wherefore attend a little more diligently, so that you may learn to understand the text in Matthew correctly.

For it is clear that the pernicious error of the Anabaptists flows and arises from this ignorance and blindness, as if from the very head and source, because they are also completely ignorant of the distinction between Law and Gospel, and stubbornly exclude from their ears and minds a doctrine so very necessary and salutary. Christ, however, in this chapter does not establish a polity, nor does he speak of the business of vocations, but of the private purity of each person, and separately in the interpretation of the law, as if in the judgment of God, he convicts the hearts of individuals, and having shown the sin, he commands us to recognize the interior impurity, futility, and inordinate fires of the human heart: just as he preached a little earlier about unjust anger and the flames of adultery in the heart. And immediately afterwards he says: Do not resist evil, forbidding the... private desire for vengeance. These sayings do not speak of the political order, nor do they establish a certain bodily polity, but are sermons of repentance, convicting sin in the hearts of individuals. Meanwhile God allows the order to no one in empires and the entire political government to serve the common society, nor does it take away or abolish, but confirms and approves forensic ordinances, legitimate punishments, and norms of civil actions, consistent with the natural judgment of reason....atural judgment of reason. This doctrine is taught by Paul in Romans 13. And the text to the Hebrews 6 clearly says: The end of all controversy is an oath. By which words is expressly sanctioned and approved a legitimate oath, which is the bond of civil obedience and judgments. With this testimony concerning the political order of oaths, let us be content, and let us most firmly establish that this order in political life corresponds to the rectitude instituted by God. Thus, there exist examples of the pious from the very beginning, such as Abraham, Isaac, the Prophets, and the Apostles at times, and with great exaggeration of those swearing, which convince that to swear truly is a work good in its own kind, and ordained and granted by God.

Finally, the law of God in Deuteronomy 6 expressly says: You shall swear by the name of the Lord your God. Now, being rightly instructed, and understanding the foundations or sources of our explanation, namely the distinction between Law and Gospel, and political order, let them think and weigh how this passage in Matthew is to be understood rightly, or softened by a convenient interpretation.

But first, the particle in the text must be considered: Do not swear by heaven, not by earth, etc. For it is most certain that forms of swearing by creatures are illicit and prohibited, just as, alas, among all nations, and not only among Jews and Gentiles, but even among those who are Christians by profession and title, this shameful and detestable custom has spread, that in swearing, invocations are made not only of God, but also of creatures. Thus, now among Papists, such a form of swearing is commonly proposed in set words: So help me God, and all the Saints. Thus Jews swear by the temple, Gentiles by heaven and earth. These illicit modes the Lord censures, and prohibits the invocations of creatures. For an oath is an invocation of him who is cited, so that he may be a witness and avenger. But you know that only the true God, who revealed himself by sending his Son, is to be invoked, and that honor properly belonging to God is not to be attributed to any thing that is not God. For every invocation attributes to that thing which it invokes the honor or worship peculiarly owed to God, namely, the inspection of hearts and omnipotence. How great, therefore, is the impiety to transfer the honor of God to creatures! This is a plain and ready answer, namely, that the Lord does not prohibit licit oaths, by which an obligation is made immediately between God and man, but oaths made not by the name of God, which are invocations of creatures, as when in an oath the Saints are added, etc. Secondly, let the notable distinction be considered between an oath administered by a magistrate or judges, which in every empire is the highest bond, and oaths which are made privately out of human futility, without great cause and grave deliberation, without the mandate of authority.

Likewise, they break forth without a compelling calling. For an oath that magistrates and judges demand, or other necessity, must be given reverently and seriously, and then kept with holiness and great religion: if, however, it is conceived in a legitimate form, let it be done by the name of God alone, and in a licit matter, which can be performed without violation of the divine mandate. But the custom of swearing rashly about any matter without calling, mandate, and necessity.

Likewise, the rash use of unjust execrations, which are made with the invocation of God, so that it may harm or curse others without any grave cause, such as this horrible imprecation: May God destroy you, and similar ones, which nevertheless this age, with detestable vanity and profanity, furiously transfers to vulgar business. These are very sad sins, and flagitious abuses of the divine name, fighting against the second commandment of the Decalogue. It pertains, however, to the duty of parents to restrain children with the fear of paternal punishment, so that they do not transfer the name of God to foolish and unjust execrations, and likewise that they not be easy and futile in swearing. Political governors also ought to punish these sins with severe examples. But because parents and magistrates, slothful and negligent in punishing, fail in their duty, therefore later republics are punished by wars, devastations, and other public calamities.

Concerning which matter, you should think diligently and often. Concerning that human futility, not considering the magnitude of an oath, the text speaks in this chapter of Matthew, and argues against hearts, because in the highest security they lightly care for and little esteem the wrath of God, when in a false or illicit invocation they multiply insults upon him.

You have heard that it was said: An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth, etc.

Here the Lord returns to the fifth commandment: You shall not kill. And as I said above, it is commanded concerning the purity of the heart, and not only concerning the obedience of external things, but concerning the whole man, You shall not kill, namely not in heart, not in tongue, not in hand, but let the whole man conform to the law of God.

Thus here He adds an interpretation pertaining to this commandment: You shall not kill, because the Pharisees did not rightly understand the commandment concerning vengeance, because it is written: An eye for an eye. Therefore they pretended that it was a lawful thing for anyone to have hatred and the desire for vengeance against others.

The Lord censures this error. The Law says: An eye for an eye, but it speaks to the judge, who is in an office divinely ordained. Here, in a legitimate punishment, he must observe this rule, without private hatred, but with true obedience toward God, in which he may grieve even because of the common misery of the human race, and only be a minister of the just will of God.

The Pharisees were corrupting this just and most severe law of God, and were transferring it to their own hatreds and to carnal furies, and were teaching that it was lawful to hate others and to exercise vengeance in any way whatsoever.

Against this false interpretation, the Lord here provides a declaration of the law, and prohibits the hatreds and vengeance which a man seeks and pursues outside the office ordained by God. Therefore He says: But I say to you: Do not resist evil, but if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also, etc.

Concerning this text, Christians and heathens have disputed much in the past. Some said it was a ridiculous commandment: because, if no vengeance were lawful, there would be no punishments, no repressions of robbers and thieves and plunderers, and infinite license would be granted to evil men. Others said it was a counsel, not a commandment. But all those foolish disputes against this text arose from the fact that they did not understand how great a thing political government is, and that one must distinguish far between judicial punishments, which are divine, and our own hatreds and furies.

Therefore, hold this rule as the true declaration of this text: There is a twofold vengeance or punishment; one is ordained by God through judges. This is a lawful thing, and commanded by God, and necessary, and by no means to be omitted, as when a judge punishes a robber, or a thief, or an adulterer, or the like.

Concerning this punishment, let us know that it is a work of the justice of God, and let judges know in that work that they are ministers of God, and that they do nothing therein out of their own hatred.

God wills that such punishments be severely exercised in the world for four reasons.

1. First, because He is just, He wills that the unjust be removed, such as robbers and the like.

2. Because He wills that His justice be seen in such examples, and to remind and teach us through such spectacles that He is just, and that He is going to punish those who sin.

3. Because it is a necessity to remove such people, so that they do not do more harm, just as it is necessary to kill rabid dogs. And it is a wonder, when someone has once been polluted with human blood or slaughter, that afterwards he commits homicide again.

4. Because God wills that others also be terrified by such examples, so that they may be restrained by the fear of punishment, lest they commit homicides.

Consider these four reasons, and learn to fear the punishments of the laws, because God nevertheless executes such punishments, even when the magistrate cannot execute them, as it is written: He who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword. And learn to venerate authority and judicial punishments as works of the justice of God. And let this much be said concerning judicial punishments.

Another species is vengeance not ordained by God, but arising from our own hatred, [own vengeance and own vengefulness], outside the office of the judge. This vengeance is prohibited here. And this text is a commandment, and not only a counsel, as some foolish people have said, because God wills our hearts to be clean, without hatreds, and wills us to preserve the order which He instituted, as He says: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, namely through me immediately, as He punishes Pharaoh immediately by Himself, or through me, mediately, namely through magistrates, just as He punishes Antony through Augustus, or a robber through a judge.

Question.

Here a question is raised: What then, if another has harmed me or mine, shall I not defend myself, or shall I not ask the judge that he be punished? Or if someone wills occupy my inheritance, or shall I not ask the judge to examine the case?

I answer: Judgments are a divine and lawful matter. And you may ask the magistrate for defense or punishment. These things are just, and granted by God, as it is clearly said in Rom. 13: The magistrate is for the honor of the good work, and for the fear of the evil. Likewise, Paul also appeals to Caesar.

But God forbids this, that we should bring our own hatreds. Likewise, when the magistrate does not help us, let us not stir up seditions, as many now say: Because Caesar wants to oppress us unjustly, therefore we want to stir up seditions.

This text forbids these evils. You understand, therefore, that a very useful doctrine is contained here, and that Christ does not teach monastic hypocrisy, but teaches great things.

Another Question. But someone will say: How can a man who has been harmed be without hatred and indignation? I answer as above, when it was said: He who covets another's wife is an adulterer. No one in this depravity of nature is without concupiscence, no one without unjust hatreds, but yet this sermon of Christ must be heard as a sermon of repentance for two reasons.

The first is, that we may recognize sin in ourselves, and seek a mediator.

The second, that we may not obey evil inclinations, by acting against conscience.

Behold, this preaching of repentance is not proposed in vain, but for these reasons, as I have often said already. Give to him who asks you, and do not turn away from him who wants to borrow.

It was said above about tolerating injuries in the body. Here he speaks about property, and there are two precepts: one about alms, which are gifts, for which the same amount is not paid back in money.

The other precept is about lending, which is not a gift, but is giving with such a condition that the same amount is paid back in return.

Anabaptists and Monks also pervert these texts, when it is said in Luke: Give to everyone who asks. If my property must be open to all, and must be like a common pile of hay, from which everyone may snatch: what kind of life will this be? And the Anabaptists seize this text, and shout that all things ought to be common. And these shouts are very pleasing to evil men, who would gladly like to snatch the property of the rich, as we know many have been drawn to the Anabaptist sect for this very reason, because they hoped they would have many things from another's property.

Monks have acted out their fable more moderately and less tragically, and have not seditiously contended in the Gospel that the ownership of things should be taken away, as the fanatical Anabaptists furiously imagine: yet in reality the dream of the Monks is utterly false, since, fascinated by a foul hypocrisy, they teach that the voluntary abandonment of property, and the Platonic communion of things, is perfection, that is, an exceedingly holy work, and the chief worship of God, which might merit greater grace. Such an insipid and monstrous hypocrisy they have snatched from these texts, and both Monks and Anabaptists have drunk it in.

And the Roman Pontiff also talks nonsense in the book of Decretals, writing that the abdication of the ownership of all things for the sake of God is meritorious and holy, and is the way of perfection.

There is, therefore, a question: How should one think about property, or the distinction of ownership, and about alms? For this care and thought exercises everyone: If it is necessary to give to all, if nothing ought to be saved or reserved for necessary uses: we will be reduced to begging, and sustenance will be lacking for me and my children. Answer.

Against these questions, and the hypocrisy of the Anabaptists and Monks, let us first hold fast, and oppose the precept of the Decalogue: You shall not steal.

Behold, God has sanctioned this order by His own voice, so that everyone may hold his own, so that by divine and natural law legitimate inheritances, just wages, and things handed down through purchase and donation may be one's own. He also gave the right of holding paternal inheritance, He does not snatch away private property from anyone, but He has distinguished and fortified the possessions, houses, and things honestly earned or acquired of each person, with this law as a wall, He has placed boundaries for all men universally in the whole human race, He keeps kings, princes, subjects, and private individuals away from what is another's, He forbids thefts, He prohibits snatching from others' goods, he forbids the disturbance of ownership.

Because he directs both.

He approves of property, enjoining frugality, which guards one's own things: and yet he wishes that, by distributing necessary alms, the truly needy be kindly helped, according to one's means.

And these are the words of Solomon: Let your fountains be dispersed abroad, and you be the master of them.

This most sweet saying, as it proposes the excellent and true doctrine of the Church of God concerning this matter, is at the same time an elegant and useful economic precept, to be diligently considered by every head of a household.

He says expressly: You be the master of your own fountain, and not others with you.

Here he clearly confirms the legitimate distinction of ownerships, and at the same time warns that profusions and the dissipation of inheritances are to be avoided.

He wishes you to use your things frugally and in an orderly manner for necessity, lest, exhausted by usury or oppressed by foreign debt, you be reduced to beggary, but that you retain the ownership of the land with your patrimony intact: just as he commands in the same place: Drink water from your own cisterns, and drink the streams of your own fountain; do not steal, do not plunder, do not seize from others.

And a little before: Do not give your wealth to others, nor your substance to the cruel, that is, to lazy gluttons, who, like leeches, sucking your blood as it were, after they have abused your wealth and consumed your goods, afterwards mock you, petulantly harassing and persecuting you with biting words.

These sentences all agree with this rule often repeated in heavenly doctrine, namely, that by divine ordination and will, individuals have property and dominion in their own possessions, and that parsimony in preserving patrimonies and inheritances is pleasing to God, so that we do not exhaust our means with profuse expenses, so that the necessities are lacking for our own.

Hence let kings, powers, and princes also learn that they too are held and bound by divine law not to exhaust the goods of their subjects with immoderate exactions, but that there should be a tolerable mediocrity in requesting legitimate and ordinary stipends and tributes.

For they ought to spare the means of the citizens, lest ownerships be disturbed, and lest subjects be stripped of their lands, but that they may enjoy their own labors, and be able to hold their own possessions, villas, houses, and fortunes.

For that the people have property in their own things by divine law, the history of King Ahab occupying the vineyard of Naboth clearly testifies, because God, the avenger, specifically condemns this injury, and punishes Ahab with a memorable example, because he had snatched away a field from a just citizen, having expelled him from his possession.

Furthermore, Solomon speaks most beautifully concerning liberality and alms: Let your fountains be dispersed abroad, and rivers of waters in the streets, that is, you should kindly bestow the fruits of your field upon the truly needy: but yet in such a way that you remain the master of your fountain, that is, of your field and patrimony. He commands, therefore, that inheritances and lordships be preserved, he forbids vain profusions to be made, but with this end, that according to the measure of your means you may help the needy and the calamitous, as much as you can without notable detriment. Therefore, know that for this very reason diligence is commanded in guarding moderate means, in moderating expenses, in using fortunes sparingly, so that there may be the ability to bestow goods rightly and usefully, and that there may be enough from which you can consult and provide for the necessity and poverty of both your relatives and strangers.

The Lord delivers the same precept in this place: Give to him that asks you, and to him that would borrow of you, etc. Understand: not to thieves, rapacious people, cruel people, that is, to able-bodied beggars, to lazy and idle gluttons, to greedy vagabonds wandering about everywhere, who are accustomed to be called 'stelliones' [shrewd tricksters]. For Solomon says in express words: Do not give your means to the cruel, that is, to those impostors and harpies, or leeches, who abuse your means, and like hags secretly suck out your marrow and blood.

So the Lord himself says clearly in Luke: Give according to your means, out of that which you have and are able to give. Item 2 Corinthians 8, the mode of communication is described, that we should give in such a way that there is no affliction for us, and for others, lazy idleness.

You see that these sayings openly support our interpretation, and there is no doubt that the true, simple, native, and proper meaning of this place, or text in Matthew, is that very one which I have commemorated, namely, that property is divinely approved, and at the same time it is commanded that alms be dispensed from the goods of which we are truly the masters: yet that a measure and limits be set to liberality, so that we do not confirm the laziness of others by our profusions, but that we retain the lordship of the field or patrimony.

Because God in this bodily life most truly wills that economies and polities be preserved, and that human society be bound together by these as if by eternal bonds.

Your little children, poor mothers in the act of giving birth, in the nutrition and education of offspring, are in need of little huts and cottages, just as little birds making nests for themselves: they have need of food, drink, and other supports of life. All these things are a care to God, and are ordained divinely. And the Creator wills that we use the things ordained by Him reverently and willingly, and not that we wander about as wild beasts, and hide ourselves in different caves, but that many live together, not indeed so that one may defraud or hinder another, but rather, so that we may kindly help and assist the afflicted, and the poor, those hindered by ill health, or other true difficulties, for the present occasion, and according to the measure of our means.

The Psalm speaks of these pious and necessary duties: Blessed is he that considers the needy and the poor: the Lord will deliver him in the day of evil. He affirms that he is heaped with divine rewards and gifts, who is moved with mercy toward the poor or needy, that is, not toward the trickster, the able-bodied and idle beggar, the lazy glutton, but toward the truly calamitous, and one who asks for a true cause.

Know that alms of this kind please God, and merit the mitigation of present troubles. And remember the sweetest promise in this verse of the Psalm: The Lord will deliver him in the day of evil. God wills to do good to you in return, to soothe calamities, to drive away dangers, for this beneficence by which you have brought aid to others who are afflicted, laboring in poverty, or oppressed by disease.

Therefore you ought to be more kind toward the miserable, so that by these very duties you may show that you feel the divine promises, which it is most certain are not void. You ought also to meditate assiduously, and carry in your mind, the precepts so often repeated, by which God demands that the needy be liberally helped.

Question.

But why does the Lord say: To every one that asks? I answer: He does not will this, that you should give to able-bodied beggars, or pour out everything, but He says: to every one that asks, that is, do not distinguish between friends and enemies, give to all as much to enemies as to friends, with respect to true necessity and according to your means, do not omit [this] out of a desire for vengeance or unjust hatred.

Let these be the words concerning alms, that is, when moved by mercy, we liberally assist and freely give something to the needy, nor do we wish him to be obligated to an equal or mutual compensation not at any time to be repaid, either the principal or any interest.

But a loan is to help a petitioner for free, with money or grain, or another useful thing, which is however consumed by use, with this obligation, that the debtor after a ...certain time returns the same amount to the creditor.

You see therefore by this very saying that the legitimate distinction of ownerships is confirmed again by the Lord.

For if things were held in common, and ownership were abolished, neither would any loans take place, nor would the one receiving a loan be obligated to return the same in kind, or an equivalent.

Furthermore, many things could be usefully said here about lending, but we will touch upon some things briefly.

First, however, the differences in loans should be considered.

For just as two species of beggars are distinguished, of whom some are swindlers and impostors, and others are truly needy: so two kinds of those taking loans must be discerned.

For some are merely thieves, who strive to accumulate debts under various pretexts, and by perfidy defraud their creditors, and never care to return what they have taken.

You should remember that these can be refuted and judged by this one but universal rule, as if by a Lydian stone, which is certain: that all those who willingly take loans, do not willingly nor in good faith repay what they owe.

But this defrauding is in reality a species of theft.

Another kind is that of the truly poor, who are in need of another's benefit and help for economic uses, whose whole care is turned to this, that, even if some loss must be endured, they nevertheless keep their faith and satisfy their creditors.

To those former petitioners you should by no means give a loan, mindful of the sentence of Solomon, by which these leeches are censured: Do not give your resources to the cruel.

To the same point pertains the Apostle's saying: I do not want you to give freely, so that for others there is lazy idleness, and for you affliction.

But to these latter, who, although they are in need due to poverty, nevertheless abstain from what is another's, and keep their agreements, and faithfully pay back as much as they can, and almost more than they can, you should by all means give a loan.

Concerning this liberal and dutiful loan, it is commanded here, which is a work pleasing to God, for which in turn God will bless your fortunes, will increase your household, and will adorn you with a huge heap of rewards.

This very duty of lending is commended also by this saying: Give and it shall be given to you.

On usury.

We spoke recently about alms and about lending.

And in Luke mention is made of the precept which prohibits usury: Give a loan, hoping for nothing in return.

Wherefore something must also be said about usury in this matter.

But I will be brief.

And first I warn you all of this: There is a great difference between these three: First, the ordinary tributes of empires imposed on lands, which subjects are accustomed and ought to pay from those goods, after an assessment has been made, as when two or three medimni of grain are paid from one field.

Secondly, certain revenues bought for a portion in a certain estate, with a pact of redemption, or a condition of reselling.

Thirdly, usury or interest, which is this: when one giving money as a loan, and not buying an estate, or a certain revenue in an estate, but having explored when he is to receive the money, or the principal, nevertheless in addition bargains for and takes some profit above the principal, solely by reason of the loan, or because of the service of the loan.

But so that you may apply moderate prudence in judging, you ought to hold and consider these things.

Ordinary tributes of empires, and certain revenues bought from certain fields with a pact of reselling, are by no means usury.

And do not be so senseless and stupid as to indiscriminately confuse all these things as if into one chaos: public revenues established by legitimate authority, purchases with a pact of redemption, and usury, just as twenty-five years ago Struthius at Eisenach, in the sedition of the peasants, was not lightly disturbing men with strange tragedies he had stirred up, to such an extent that they did not want to pay debts to creditors, shouting that, without any distinction, all due payments, and whatever revenues there were, were usury.

These insanities and turbulent frauds and injuries fight against the seventh commandment: You shall not steal.

For God has sanctioned the distinction of ownerships and resources, prohibits an attack from being made on others' possessions, wants an equal compensation to be returned in good faith, and for as much as is owed to be counted out, in purchases, loans, and rentals, etc.

God has instituted and ordained this equality universally in contracts with inestimable wisdom and admirable counsels, so that, being reminded of His justice, we may recognize it and that He Himself is equal. Therefore, He accumulates His blessing in return upon those who show faithfulness in these duties and in corporal goods; but those who defraud others in the communication of things, and who grow by rapine and unjust gains, God also afflicts in this life with just punishments. And, to testify that He does not neglect the administration and acquisition of wealth, He eventually shakes them from their fortunes. Therefore the Prophet Isaiah says: Woe to you who plunder, for you shall be plundered in turn. And Christ the Lord says: With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you.

Now, what the ordinary tributes of empires are, should not be unknown, and it can easily be understood, namely, the legitimate and customary pensions, ordered upon the goods of subjects, so that magistrates may have the necessary expenses from them, and that they may be the nerves of the republic, by which both the subsidies of war and the ornaments of peace are contained. Such public revenues are not usury. Indeed, it is just for individuals to pay these legitimate stipends.

For Paul specifically demands this collection of tributes, Rom. 13: To whom you owe tribute, pay tribute.

It is likewise just to pay faithfully to those to whom they are owed the purchased fruits or revenues, with the agreement of reselling, because every true, legitimate, and non-simulated purchase is divinely ordained and approved. But whoever constructs fraud in purchases and sales, and pays the due prices maliciously, is a thief, exhausting the resources of others, and was to be severely punished by the magistrate. But even when the magistrate is lacking in his duty and tolerates other thefts, God will nevertheless drag this swindler to punishments.

This brief reminder suffices regarding these two cases. Furthermore, I have recently discussed lending. You should know that this too is a divine ordinance, which God wills to be faithfully observed on both sides, both by the creditor and by the debtor, so that the one giving a loan does not seek usurious addition because of the service of the loan, and the one taking the loan returns the same amount of money in good faith.

Thus, therefore, God has ordained the contract of lending, with the parties to the contract as if surrounded by boundaries. The creditor who gives a loan must not exercise gain by the stipulation of usury, nor demand anything beyond the principal, nor profit from another's property. For in Leviticus twenty-five, the divine Law says expressly: Fear God, so that your brother may live with you. Do not take usury from your brother, nor more than you gave. And in Psalm 14 it is said: Who dwells in your tabernacle, etc.?

He who has not given his money for usury. Likewise Ezech. 18, a most atrocious threat: He who has sinned shall die, and he who lends and impudently demands from the usurer more than the amount he gave in loan.

Furthermore, in Luke 6, Christ says: Lend, hoping for nothing in return. Let this saying not be understood so perversely nor so foolishly that we reason that it is not even permitted to hope for the principal or capital.

For this would not be a loan, but a gift, if it prohibited the principal from being sought. Therefore, this is the proper understanding and the simple and true interpretation of the words of Christ: Lend in such a way that you receive the same amount of money, and do not seek profit in the loan above the principal because of the loan itself. With these precepts agrees a memorable and very beautiful history, which exists in the fifth chapter of the book of Ezra: There was a great difficulty of grain and famine in the land of Palestine, therefore the wealthier and moneyed people gave loans to the needy citizens, but demanding a hundredth part as usury, that is, which equals the principal in the hundredth month, so that those poor people were compelled both to return the principal and to pay one out of a hundred every month, or to pay twelve gold pieces in one year for one hundred florins.

When Nehemiah had learned of this, he flared with anger, and having gravely rebuked those usurers, he proposed the divine command: You shall give a loan to your brother without usury. Wherefore the terrified creditors confessed their sins, and to those affected by the injury, they promised that they would make restitution of the hundredths. Let these things be said about those who give loans.

Again, let the one receiving a loan remember and observe the precept: You shall not steal. For if he refuses or does not strive to pay back what he owes, he is truly a thief. Therefore, he ought to faithfully pay the principal, which is equal to the loan, or pay back as much as he took.

For God has ordained that the duty is so pressing on both sides, namely, both of giving a loan liberally without entrapment and without usury, and of faithfully returning those things which you have received to be used. For the contract of lending differs from a gift, and it is to help one's neighbor by the transfer of money or grain, etc., but with this obligation, that on the appointed day the debtor returns the same in kind.

or equivalent. If he, keeping his faith, has paid the debt on the appointed day, and has not caused the creditor any delay, it would be unjust for the one lending on loan to demand and gain something more besides, when the other, who pays the interest, receives nothing. And that is finally, in the thing itself and properly, called usury, when someone, from an obliging debtor who faithfully pays on the appointed day, impudently seeks and demands profit beyond the principal, so that on account of the loan he receives more than he gave.

It pertains, however, to the office of the political governor to prohibit this rapacity by laws and punishments. For the civil magistrate is ordained by God primarily for these chief duties.

First, that he himself may sound, or take care to be promulgated, inculcated, and repeated, the voice of the Decalogue in the human race, so that men are not ruled by their own imaginations, but that the law of nature expressed in the Decalogue may be the norm of all counsels and actions, according to which evil and good works are discerned. Second, that the magistrate may be a vigilant guardian and executor of the laws of the Decalogue, and protect them with the severity of punishments, inflict capital punishment upon murderers and adulterers, and likewise restrain and punish thieves, robbers, highwaymen, and usurers.

But in sight, alas, is the affected sloth and negligence of magistrates. Adultery is rarely punished, usury not at all.

Nevertheless, we meanwhile, so that they may cease, must necessarily propose, announce, and preach the divine command. And God himself will be the guardian, avenger, and executor of his law, and will eventually shake thieves and moneylenders out of their possessions, just as he said: Woe to you who plunder and despoil, for you shall be despoiled in turn.

Which threat, by the common appellation of predators and plunderers, also embraces those impostors who sell vicious goods, who push out fallacious and deceptive wares, who corrupt and adulterate bread, beer, and wines. This is (O miserable and deplorable thing) a certain flagitious blight and stain of these regions, and a leech much more pernicious to private and public resources than other thefts.

Therefore come wars, immoderate plunderings, and other great calamities, because all strive competitively to obtain immoderate liberty and infinite license for all their desires, they exercise unjust schemes for seeking money, they draw away from others for the sake of their own advantage, they pluck from the resources of others to accumulate their own, they seek πλεονεκτήματα [gains], and through contracts they construct snares, so that they themselves may be enriched with the loss and injury of others.

But the fraudulent sale of bad beer, which for the sake of your profit you do not wish to brew correctly, with how many vices and sins is it stained? For by this pursuit you not only despoil and plunder buyers of their silver through snares, but also, by a drink too thin and raw, as if by certain mild poisons, you secretly harm the bodies of others and afflict their health.

Do not hope that such rapines, impostures, plunderings, and finally fraudulent killings will have long-term impunity.

For thus says the divine voice in Deut. 25: You shall not have in your bag diverse weights, nor shall there be in your house a greater and a smaller measure, but you shall have a just weight and measure, that you may live a long time in the land which the Lord your God will give you.

For the Lord your God abominates, and turns away from, all injustice. Remember this saying well, and always carry it in your minds.

Let the thought of the most severe and very sad threats move you. Let the force and weight of the punishments imminent at this time upon your necks obtain and extort from you that you may seriously perform penance, and with assiduous groans to God seek the mitigation of such great calamities.

How, I ask, can either present punishments be driven from our necks, or impending dangers be averted, if we do not, with manners seriously amended, put aside and avoid such enormities and affected flagitious acts, frauds, lies, perfidy, petulance, filth, and the turpitude of obscene pleasures?

A most dangerous fire has been ignited by the starting of a horrible war, the mass of which, where it is going to turn, how long the impetus will last, and what the outcome will eventually be, there is no man who can foresee: Fields, republics, and regions are being laid waste.

Hence famine, poverty, and a lack of necessary things will exist among the people. With increasing exactions and public plunderings, and other difficulties and burdens in the political regime, servitude will become harder, and that face of things presents itself to the observer, so that all things seem to threaten barbaric devastation and solitude to these regions.

Eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, may you mercifully soften and mitigate the punishments present and impending, and may He not allow infinite dissipations, barbaric confusions, and ethnic devastations to occur in these regions. I beseech you also for the sake of the glory of God, and for the sake of the immense sorrow of the whole Church, that for the sake of your own safety and that of your weak children, you may seriously amend yourselves, call upon God with joined and ardent prayers, live more modestly, faithfully perform civil duties, and exercise justice in contracts, and finally imprint this sentence upon your hearts as a seal: The Lord God abominates all injustice, that is, whoever from ambush or evil deceit detracts from and harms another, the malice of this person provokes the wrath of God, who will eventually remove such a defrauder from the midst.

Latin:

Audistis quod dictum est antiquis: Non occides.

Diximus supra, semper in genere humano hypocritas legem Dei intelligere tantum de externa disciplina, et fingere hanc externam disciplinam esse justiciam coram Deo, et mereri remissionem peccatorum, sicut Pharisaei fingebant, sic Monachi, et aliqui omnibus temporibus finxerunt.

Hunc errorem vult emendari Deus omnibus temporibus.

Prophetae clamantes contra hunc errorem interfecti sunt.

Christus etiam hic taxat eundem errorem.

Taxavit et recens Dominus Doctor Martinus, quia Deus vult agnosci peccatum, quod intus in corde haeret, et vult expavescere, vult nos agnoscere gratuitam remissionem peccatorum, et iusticiam propter Filium.

Et orditur Christus a praecepto, Non occides, quod loquitur de peccatis, quae magis intelligi possunt.

Et immundities cordis pugnans cum hoc praecepto est magis nota, quam subtilia peccata, diffidentia erga Deum, quae habetur pro sapientia, vel fiducia propriae iusticiae, quam putant hypocritae virtutem et gloriam esse.

Sed invidentia et acerbum et iniustum odium in corde Saulis sentitur et clare iudicari potest, et scit Saul, qualis res sit, sed non vult se damnari, dicit haec mala non esse peccata.

Contra hanc coecitatem dicit Christus: Ego autem dico vobis, Omnis qui irascitur fratri suo frustra, reus est poenae, Der ist alsbald schuldig, das er sol gestrafft werden.

Qui dixerit fratri Racha, Wer seinem Bruder ein grimmige geberde zeigt, wer neid oder haß tregt, der ist schuldig, das man ihn für Gericht führe.

Qui dixerit fratri suo Fatue, reus est gehennae ignis, Wer seinen Bruder lestert, schmehet, felschlich verleugt.

Nominavit tres gradus, qui non sunt externae homicidia manu facta, sed sunt interiora homicidia, quae corde fiunt.

Et sunt communissima, sicut videmus plurimum esse odiorum, invidentiae, maledicentiae etiam in illis, qui volunt videri iusti et sancti, et haec sua peccata non vident.

Quod autem alibi dicit Christus: Reus est poenae, reus est judicii, idem sunt, quia expresse dicit reum esse.

Cum sit reus, iuste eum Deus condemnat.

Sed durissime dicit de tertio: Reus est gehennae ignis.

Sic solet nominare inferos et poenas aeternas, et nomen sumtum est a valle Ennon, ubi fuit sacrificatum idolo, cui in sacrificio offerebantur pueri, qui ibi comburebantur.

Inde nomen sumitur pro poena infernali.

Sed cur hic durius loquitur, von den Lestertern?

Quia maledicere est peius, quam caedem manu facere, quia qui manu occidit, tantum necat corpus, sed maledicus occidit corpus, et eripit famam.

Nam dolor propter infamiam adfert etiam mortem, sicut Salomon vere dicit: Calumnia conturbat sapientem, et frangit robur cordis eius.

Haec bene considerent homines maledici, quales valde multi sunt, et sciant se esse dupliciter homicidas.

Occidunt corpus dolore, et

occidunt hominem quo ad famam, quae est melior res, quam vita corporalis, Sicut Salomon dicit Proverb.

22.: Melius est nomen bonum, quam divitiae multae.

Quaestiones duae.

Sequuntur hic duae Quaestiones.

Una: Estne omnis ira peccatum?

Respondeo: Textus dicit de iniusta ira, quia expresse dicit: Qui irascitur fratri frustra.

Et talis ira iniusta multo frequentior est apud homines, quam iusta ira.

Est autem iusta ira, quando propter gloriam Dei aut propter iusticiam irascimur peccantibus, sicut Christus irascitur, cum expellit ex templo numularios, vel sicut Princeps irascitur latronibus aut raptoribus virginum vel honestarum matronarum. De hac ira dictum est: Zelus domus tuae comedit me. Et talis ira debet esse in gubernatione, quia est calcar exuscitans ad iusticiam, et adiuvans iusticiam. Sed haec ira rara est.

Alia ira iniusta est communior, sicut Saul invidet et irascitur Davidi, sicut superbi universaliter irascuntur aliis, a quibus se impediri putant etc.

Hanc distinctionem considerate, de ira iusta et iniusta, et simul vos ipsos recte examinate. Unusquisque vult esse iustus, et videtur sibi iuste irasci, sed saepissime habemus falsas imaginationes, et sumus hypocritae, et fucamus nostras pravas cupiditates, irascimur ex superbia, vel avaricia, quia non statim omnia nobis dantur, quae postulamus, quae tamen non iuste debentur nobis. Tales valde multi sunt, et introspiciat unusquisque seipsum.

Huc etiam pertinent ingrati. Multi sunt, quando omnibus beneficiis longo tempore affecti sunt, et semel aliquid fit contra eorum voluntatem, incipiunt odisse. Tales etiam pertinent ad hanc concionem Christi: Qui fratri suo frustra irascitur, reus est poenae. Et Salomon dicit: Non recedet malum a domo ingrati.

Altera quaestio est generalis.

Cum omnium corda sint plena immunditiae, et homo non possit deponere hanc immunditiem totam, Quare lex eam arguit? An frustra haec dicuntur? sicut frustra dicebant Stoici, quod homo deberet esse prorsus sine ira, sine amore, sine laetitia, sine metu. Respondeo: Nequaquam haec frustra dicuntur a Christo, et non est stoica phantasia, sed propter duas causas recitantur.

Primum propter poenitentiam, ut agnoscamus nostra peccata, et sciamus, quod non satisfaciamus legi, et non mereamur remissionem. Secundo, propter incoationem, quia oportet incoari in nobis novitatem, et oportet nos repugnare malis affectibus. Et quanquam fit incoatio, tamen manent in nobis multae reliquiae peccati. Et debemus scire, quod simus iusti propter Filium Dei, non propter nostram impletionem legis. Si offers ad aram, et ibi recordatus fueris, quod frater tuus habet aliquid contra te.

Saepe auditis discrimen inter haec tria: Promissionem, praecepta de operibus moralibus, von nötigen Tugenden, Et ceremonias, Kirchengepreng: vel inter fidem, Opera moralia, nötige Tugenden vnd Ceremonien.

Et nosse hanc distinctionem valde necessarium est, quia usitatum est, quod homines delabuntur ad ceremonias, et has putant esse totam religionem, Die ganze heiligkeit, Christenthum vnd Gottesdienst, sicut saepe conqueruntur Prophetae, et refutant hunc errorem, sicut in Psalmo 49. dicitur: Audi populus meus, non in sacrificiis arguam te, etc. Alle Heiligkeit.

Sic tota religio Papae et Monachorum est servare ceremonias suae Missae, formam vestitus, discrimina ciborum, et coelibatum, ne sacerdos ducat uxorem etc. Sed has abominationes debemus intelligere, taxare et fugere, et scire, quod religio sit alia res.

Hoc cum audiunt sapientes mundani, agnoscunt utcunque religionem, Gottesdienst, non esse has larvas ceremoniarum, et discunt doctrinam de operibus moralibus, von weltlichen Tugenden, oder von guten Sitten, et hanc obedientiam existimant esse totam religionem, sicut dicit Cato: Si Deus est animus, ut nobis carmina dicunt, Hic tibi praecipue pura sit mente colendus. Et Plato: Deus non gestibus honoratur, sed vera virtute. Ista phantasia sapientum, quod tales virtutes sint summus cultus, etiam est falsa, quia scriptum est: Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. Haec discrimina bene mementote.

Et hunc ordinem considerate. Primum oportet in homine esse fidem, agnoscentem Deum, et apprehendentem promissionem gratiae, et mediatorem Filium Dei, et iusticiam per eum et propter eum donatam.

Quia nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per Filium. Et haec fides lucet in vera poenitentia et vera conversione cordis ad Deum. Haec fides scit etiam, quod remissio peccatorum non datur propter ullam aliam rem, nisi propter Filium Dei, non propter nostras ceremonias, aut virtutes.

Postquam autem iam cor sic ad Deum con- versum est, et est iam Deo copulatum, et vivit in Deo, sequuntur etiam virtutes et ceremoniae iusto ordine, et in tali intellectu, sicut vult Deus intelligi et fieri virtutes et ceremonias. De hoc ipso ordine concionatur hic Dominus. Quia Pha- risaei etiam dicebant, oblationes esse summum cultum, et mereri gratiam et omnia bona, sicut Papistae de Missa dicunt. Et erant pleni odiis, et contaminati adulteriis, et multis faciebant in- iurias, et posteá fingebant, se delere haec peccata omnia sacrificiis, et sic negligebant potiora legis, ut scriptum est Matthaei 23.: Vae vobis qui de- cimatis mentam etc. et graviora legis negligitis: Iudicium et misericordiam, et fidem. Ecce hoc dictum Christi prorsus idem monet, quod prius dixi, quod falsissima sit imaginatio pharisaica, quod tota religio sit illa observatio ceremoniarum, sed hic expresse nominantur, fides et iudicium et misericordia. Fides significat, ut scitis, veram Dei agnitionem, et accipere promissionem gratiae propter Filium promissae.

Deinde iudicium et misericordia significant virtutes morales, Iuste agere cum hominibus, et eos non afficere iniuriis, et his bene facere, ubi potes et debes benefacere.

Ita hoc loco dicit de ordine: Si vis offerre, et tibi conscius es, quod alterum iniuste laeseris, nihil prodest tuum sacrificium et oblatio tua, scias non placere Deo oblationes eorum, qui veniunt cum mala conscientia, id est, cum proposito pec- candi ad Deum.

Sed oportet regulam servari: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam. Sacrificia cum mala conscientia sunt derisio Dei, sicut saepe in Prophetis nominantur abominatio- nes. Et Proverb. 15. dicitur: Victimae impiorum abominatio Domino, vota iustorum placent. Et in summa, plena est scriptura de hoc ordine, quod primum oporteat in nobis fidem essé, postea bonam conscientiam in operibus moralibus.

Tertio debent sequi ceremoniae cum vero intellectu.

Sed volo addere tantum hoc dictum Oseae, quod saepe repeto, quia omnibus notissimum esse debet. Oseae 6. dicitur: Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium, et scientiam Dei, plus quam holocausta.

Idem docet, quod iam dixi. Taxat falsissi- mam opinionem, quae fingit Deo placere sacrificia in his, qui negligunt agnitionem Dei, scilicet fidem et misericordiam, id est, opera necessaria bonae conscientiae. Et dicit: Magis volo scientiam Dei, id est, fidem, quam holocausta. Et: Magis volo mise- ricordiam, id est, bona opera erga proximum, quae sunt necessaria ad bonam conscientiam. Hoc dictum Oseae mandate memoriae, quia est bona et utilis regula, ex qua multi errores iu- dicari possunt. Papa totum invertit, dicit: Melior est Missa, quam fides et bona conscientia. Si sacerdos in- doctus, impius, adulter celebret Missam, plus boni facit, quam alius homo recte credens, et castus maritus. Tales furores Papistarum sine ulla dubita- tione Deus horribiliter puniet in hac vita, et post hanc vitam. Ideo simus firmi in fide, et petamus a Deo, ut ipse Ecclesias, quae veritatem amant et sonant, defendat et servet, et non sinat eas dissipari, et expectemus protectionem a Deo. Haec dicta sint de hoc ordine, de fide, ope- ribus conscientiae, et oblatione.

II.

Iam movetur quaestio. Quis debet petere reconciliationem? Hic vides, quod Dominus praecipit deponi odia, et rursus reconciliari, cum significatione externa, ut alter intelligat odium depositum esse. Sed quis debet incipere reconciliationem? Respondeo: Pars iniusta, quae laesit alterum, debet incipere reconciliationem, et petere veniam, et se Deo et iusticiae subiicere, et hanc humili- tatem Deo et iusticiae praestare. Sed nemo libenter se humiliat. Ideo omnes quaerunt praetextus, quod habeant iustas causas, et nemo vult in mundo habere iniustam causam. Hoc malum ita commune est, ut vix aliud sit communius, et maxime usitatum est hypocri- tis, qui vident festucam in oculo fratris, et negligunt trabem in suo oculo. Sed hic unusquisque suam conscientiam ipse interroget, remotis illis praetextibus, quos scit ficticios et sophisticos esse. Et cum conscientia eum arguit, videat ut petat reconciliationem. Et magis accidit, ut illi petant reconcilia- tionem, qui minus peccaverunt, quia dictum est: Iustus in principio est accusator sui; Iusti in- Iustiveniunt in se etiam infirmitates, et libentius eas fatentur, et petunt veniam a Deo, et ab hominibus. Si alter non vult reconciliari, postea tua conscientia est excusata, si petiisti reconciliationem, Deus erit iudex, et tradet illum implacabilem et furiosum hominem lictori, qui ducet eum in carcerem.

Haec doctrina non solum discenda est, sed etiam in vita exercenda. Multae inter nos offensiones incidunt, has debetis sanare, et mutua reconciliatione iuvare communem pacem, sicut et Iacobus bene inquit: Confitemini invicem peccata vestra. Tu habes peccata, habeo et ego. Ego tibi condono, Tu et mihi condonato propter Deum, et propter Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, quia haec est voluntas Dei, ut in pace mutua vivamus.

Non moechaberis. Ego autem dico vobis, quod omnis, qui videt mulierem ad concupiscendum eam, iam moechatus est in corde suo.

Dixi supra, quare haec enarratio Decalogi a Christo proposita sit, scilicet quia est interpres legis, et praedicator poenitentiae, et vult ostendere nos omnes reos esse, et habere peccata, ut agnita ira Dei, confugiamus ad gratiam, et discamus aliam iusticiam nobis propositam esse, promissam propter Filium Dei, et nos non esse iustos impletione legis.

Et exorsus est Dominus a duobus mandatis, quae manifeste convincunt nos, cum loquantur de inordinatis flammis et cupiditatibus, quas sentire omnes et iudicare possunt, videlicet, de invidentia et odiis, et de illicitis amoribus, et cupiditate adulteriorum.

Ideo hic addit enarrationem huic praecepto, Non moechaberis, hanc: Omnis qui videt mulierem ad concupiscendum eam, iam moechatus est. Hac declaratione ostendit, quod praecepto Dei non solum externa adulteria prohibita sint, sed etiam omnes inordinati motus. Et quod Deus velit cor esse castum, et obediens ipsius legi, et amans castitatem sicut ipse est.

Accusat igitur nos omnes, quod non simus tales.

Objectio. Hic iterum potest obiicere homo secundum politicam sapientiam, nach der Welt weisheit.

Quare prodest proponere praecepta impossibilia? Cur prohibentur inordinati motus, cum nemo possit eos prorsus exuere? Respondeo: Haec dicta Christi non sunt inutilia, quia sunt praedicationes poenitentiae, ut dixi, vult nos Deus agnoscere, quod simus mersi in peccatum, et rei peccati.

Et vult nos dolere, et non esse ferreos et securos, quasi simus iusti et mundi nostra munditie, et vult nos quaerere gratiam, et credere quod propter mediatorem detur remissio peccatorum, et reputemur iusti.

Et quando sumus conversi ad Deum, vult nos frenare nostros motus, et vult nos non contra conscientiam polluere nos scortatione vel adulteriis.

Hanc doctrinam de peccato, gratia, et nova obedientia saepe alias auditis. Et debet vobis omnibus nota esse.

Hic etiam addo brevem admonitionem pro iunioribus. Scitote adulteria et scortationes magna peccata esse, et a Deo sine ullo dubitatione magnis poenis puniri, Daß Gott ganze Land, Stett, vnd die Theter straffet.

De his poenis primum dicit expresse textus ad Ebraeos: Scortatores et adulteros iudicabit Deus.

Et Levitici 18. dicitur de omnibus prohibitis modis commixtionum: Omnis anima quae fecerit tales abominationes, peribit de medio populi. Custodite mandata mea, ne terra vos evomat, sicut evomuit gentes, quae prius talia fecerunt.

Nec dubitare debetis, quin Deus bellis et magnis vastationibus puniat adulteria et similia delicta.

Scripta sunt etiam exempla ad regulam ostendendam.

1. Deus punivit mundum diluvio propter adulteria.

2. Sodoma perierunt, et propter similia delicta nunc tota Asia, Aegyptus, Graecia sunt vastata.

3. Num. 25. Iubet Deus suspendi principes populi Israel, et occiduntur praeterea viginti quatuor millia hominum, propter scortationes.

Item tribus Beniamin pene tota deleta est, quia Nobiles quidam stupraverant Levitae coniugem. Item David propter adulterium horribiliter punitus est. Et sicut ipse alterius viri uxorem polluit, ita vicissim Deus permisit pollui uxores ipsius.

Et videte familias regum et principum, ubi manifesta exempla sunt, quod Deus punit peccata. seminis in semine, id est, in filiis et in posteritate. Haec mementote, et timete iram et iudicium Dei, et vitate adulteria et similia peccata, et orate Deum, ut vos regat, quia Deus diligit castitatem, et vult donum illud a se peti, et libenter dat hoc donum, et magnis praemiis ornat, sicut Ioseph vitans adulterium, magna praemia accipit.

Ita dicitur in libro Sapientiae, cap. 8.: Scivi quod aliter non possem esse castus, nisi Deus daret. Et hoc ipsum erat sapientiae, scire, cuius sit donum. Ideo precatus sum Dominum. Ita et nos faciamus, petamus hoc donum a Deo, et nos ipsi addamus nostram diligentiam, et conemur nos frenare, ne clabamur, et vitemus occasiones adulteriorum, et discamus: Vitare peccata, est vitare occasiones peccatorum, Sünd fliehen, ist die vrsachen vnd vmbstend fliehen, die ein Menschen anreißen.

Wenn einer ins Bad gehet, so wird er naß. Also, wer solcher geselschasst nachgehen wil, der fellt desto leichter. Darumb sollen wir fürsichtig sein, und nicht selbs anreihung suchen zu solchen sachen. Darumb spricht S. Paulus: Wandelt fürsichtiglich, nicht als die Narren.

Aliud Praeceptum.

Si oculus tuus scandalizaverit te, erue eum. Praecipit Dominus vitari occasiones, vrsach vnd vmbstend, die ein Menschen anreißen. Halt deine Augen, fliehe böse geselschasst etc. Solche anreibungen alle sind hie verboten.

Praeterea hoc mandatum de oculo et de dextra continet aliam prohibitionem etiam. Oculus significat consiliarium. Dextra significat amicum. Praecipit igitur Christus, ut caveamus, ne a malis consiliariis seducamur. Item, ne propter amicos aut uxores, peccemus. Scitis autem valde multa et magna peccata homines facere, impulsos a consiliariis vel amicis. Saepe peccant homines in gratiam principum et amicorum, cum alioqui non peccarent, nisi moverentur hac stulta imaginatione: Oportet te gratum facere amicis, oportet te propter communem pacem tacere, sicut multi in aulis tacent veritatem, ne offendant principes vel amicos suos. Haec peccata sunt communissima.

Ideo hic textus non longa declaratione indiget. Sed mementote, quod Christus prohibet hanc levitatem, quod pluris facimus principes vel amicos, quam Deum, sicut alibi dicit: Qui diligit patrem aut matrem, plus quam me, non est me dignus. Hic autem iubet oculum erui, et praecidi manum.

Hic discatis recte intelligere sermonem. Non vult, ut corporaliter effodias oculum, vel praecidas manum, sicut olim stulti aliqui castraverunt se, ut Origenes. Et sumatur expositio ex praecepto: Non occidas. Nam si membra omnia peccantia corporaliter abscindenda essent, tunc cor effodiendum esset, ita homo se occideret, quod expresse prohibet Deus. Non igitur intelligatur hoc dictum de corporali abscissione, vom leiblichen ausstechen oder abschneiden, sed de prohibitione, quae fit firmo proposito, qua voluntas prohibet audire consilia vel amicos illos, Das ausstechen vnd abschneiden ist, mit rechtem ernst vnd festem fürsatz diese Redt vnd freund abschneiden, das ist, von inen weichen, jre meinung, freundschasst vnd genad nicht grösser achten, denn Gott.

Et ita fugere tales amicos, est res magna et difficilis apud sapientes. Ideo hoc praeceptum, de quo Christus hic loquitur, magni momenti est, sicut bene sciunt sapientes, se saepe peccare, ne offendant amicos. Sed iuvenes haec nondum sciunt, tantum hoc sciunt, quod saepe malis sodalitiis et exemplis sociorum corrumpuntur. Ibi videant etiam, ut se a malis sodalitiis avellant. Et hoc praeceptum Christi meminerint: Si te dextra manus offendit, abscinde eam.

Dictum est: Qui dimiserit uxorem suam, det ei libellum repudii. Ego autem dico vobis etc. Quia Christus aliquoties repetivit hanc concionem, in qua reprehendit divortia, qualia usitata erant Iudaeis et gentibus, satis apparet, quod illam levitatem valde improbavit.

Fuit enim usitatum, ut dimitterent uxores tantum ex levitate, cum mulier nihil peccasset, sed fortassis vir vidit aliam, quae magis placuit. Item arte alius alteram coniugem ad se pellexit, et ludebant specie iuris, quasi quaelibet divortia essent in lege Moisi concessa. Hortensius rogavit Catonem, ut sibi cederet coniugem Martiam, pulcram et generosam foeminam. Fecit Cato, et post mortem reduxit Martiam, quod erat etiam contra ethnicas leges. Augustus practicabat, ut Drusus sibi ce- deret Liviam. Talia saepe et multum facta esse apud Iudaeos quoque, valde credibile est.
