Therefore, often during invocation, think of and set before yourself the baptism of Christ, in which the three persons are most clearly revealed and made known: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.

And as often as you begin a prayer, look with your eyes, mind, and true faith into our Lord Jesus Christ, and consider both, and that no other divine being is to be invoked except this true God, who revealed Himself in Christ, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: and that this eternal God, always revealed in the church, surely wishes to hear you, to care for your groans, and to receive your prayers on account of the Son and mediator Christ.

This admonitory thought—whom you wish to address, or who that deity is whom you address—must be kept before your eyes in every invocation you undertake, and must be proposed attentively and seriously to your mind, so that the distinction between true invocation in the Church and heathen invocation may be in sight. Heathens do not know whom they invoke, nor can they determine that they are heard, nor do they think about why they are heard. But Christians know and look upon the wonderful revelations by which God showed Himself from the beginning in the Church, and they confirm their faith by the thought of them; they look upon the manifestations made in the leading out from Egypt. Likewise, the most evident testimonies exhibited through the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, in the resurrection of the dead. Let your heart recognize, call upon, and address this true God, made manifest by illustrious testimonies, and in the confidence of the Mediator, seek grace and other benefits, firmly believing that your groans are heard for Christ's sake.

Let this be the first admonition concerning invocation, from which it can be clearly understood that you are not to invoke statues, nor devils, nor Saints, nor any men, nor is the honor due to God to be attributed to any creatures. And let the saying of Christ be always in sight: You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.

The second admonition is that the command of God concerning the making of invocation should be considered, because no work pleases God that is not divinely commanded. Indeed, who would dare to approach God, and to call upon and address such great majesty? Unless He Himself had willed and commanded that He be worshipped in this way: especially since the hearts of all men, naturally oppressed by doubt, tremble and flee from God in true sorrows.

Therefore, God has proposed a most severe command, so that we might know to run and flee to Him eagerly and confidently, and that we ought to seek and expect help in dangers from Him, and that this invocation is the highest worship, and the greatest work of all, and most pleasing to God, just as Psalm 49 cries out: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. Likewise Matthew 7: Ask and it shall be given to you, knock and it shall be opened to you. And the whole of Scripture is full of such commands, the authority of which should be instilled into our minds, and should rouse and inflame us, so that we do not flee from God in fear, but that we dare to flee to Him willingly, eagerly, and as if familiarly.

But someone might say: I would willingly come into the sight of God, willingly approaching God I would ask for many things; certainly in such great miseries I understand that I have need of the help of God, but I am a most miserable sinner. Perhaps my prayers are not cared for; I feel that I am unworthy to be heard. What should I ask, when it is written: God does not hear sinners? In vain, therefore, do I cry to God, since I am multiply guilty of wrath.

Response. Here a third consideration must be held, pertaining to true invocation, namely, the promise, and the Son of God as Mediator. God not only most severely commanded that we ask, but also, in order to invite us to invocation, He added the clearest sentences of the sweetest and most ample promises, in which He confirms by oath that He certainly wills to hear us, to provide the good things we ask for, and to help us in all things, both in spiritual and in corporal dangers and necessities. And the promises are expressed in these words: Amen, amen I say to you: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give to you. Behold, here the Son of God swears that the Father certainly wills to hear us, and that our prayers are certainly accepted and pleasing. Likewise Matth. 7: Ask and you shall receive.

But again, you are deterred by your own unworthiness, arguing that you are a miserable sinner.

Response. Here it is necessary to know that, for this very reason, because we are oppressed by sin, God has appointed His beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, as our intercessor, pleader, mediator, and high Priest, for whose sake He certainly receives and hears us. Wherefore, in every invocation you ought to approach and flee to Christ the propitiator, so that first you bring repentance, or conversion to God, then you sustain and raise yourself with this consolation, that even for the sake of the mediator Christ you certainly receive the remission of sins, and being reconciled through Him, you are heard, and that the same is the high Priest entering into the Holy of Holies, who carries your groans, your vows, and your prayers into the secret counsel of the divinity.

The heathens, Jews, Turks, and Papists are ignorant of this great consolation; but only the true church, or the people of God, rightly acknowledging the Lord Jesus Christ, possesses this most efficacious and sweetest consolation. The magnitude of such a thing far exceeds the eloquence of all angels and men. For what greater and more admirable thing can be thought of than this goodness of God? Namely, that He wills to certainly receive, care for, look upon, and hear us miserable men on account of the intercession and sacrifice of the High Priest Christ.

Therefore, the Lord Himself says clearly: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, that is, in faith, which relies on me as the propitiator, or in the confidence of the Son of God, the mediator and placator. This is the most necessary consideration in every prayer, concerning which daily experience teaches pious and true Christians, who pray seriously and with great intention of mind, that hearts are bent, instructed, and raised up not without great struggle and labor, so that they may acquiesce in so many promises sanctified by the blood and resurrection of the Son of God, and that this struggle cannot happen without true groans.

Therefore, a fourth reminder must necessarily be added, concerning faith. For it is an empty murmur, and cannot be called invocation, if you think while reciting words by some custom: I do not know if I am a care to God, or if my prayers please Him and are truly received.

But it is necessary that you look upon the promise and the Son of God the mediator, embrace Him, and apprehend Him with true faith, acquiescing in God on account of Him; it is necessary that you, with the confidence of the promise of grace, resist diffidence and doubt, according to the saying of James: Let everyone ask in faith, doubting nothing. Likewise, it is said in 1 Timothy 2: Pray without anger and hesitation. Likewise, the text says to the Ephesians: Through Christ we dare to approach confidently through faith in Him.

Wherefore, know that it is necessary universally in every petition, first and above all, to bring and let shine forth this faith, by which you believe that the eternal God certainly receives you, forgives you, and wills to look upon, approve, and hear your prayers on account of the mediator Christ.

And in the petition for eternal goods, such as reconciliation, salvation, and the governance of the soul, you must most firmly establish that God wills to give and grant to you by name and in particular these very things which you ask without condition, namely, the remission of sins, gratuitous reconciliation, and eternal life. But concerning corporal goods, necessary in this life, faith asks and establishes with the condition: If it pleases God.

This prayer is indeed not void, but efficacious, and it obtains either this very thing which is asked by name, or at least a mitigation of calamities and miseries. For although God wills in this life that the church be subject to the cross, yet in His immense mercy He softens and mitigates the pains and troubles for those who invoke Him, so that they may be sustained and endured, lest we be oppressed by despair and sink into eternal death, just as He affirms in Isaiah that He dwells with the afflicted, etc.

Know therefore, even if corporal liberation is deferred, and the outcome does not respond to your thought, yet your prayer pleases, is received, and is heard, and is neither void nor an empty murmur.

These things are most certain and most true without any doubt, as it is also written in Sirach 35: The tears of the widow flow down to her cheek, but the prayer ascends and penetrates heaven. [The] fifth consideration is of the things to be asked, that the certain benefits which we seek be thought of and recited in prayer by name, namely: remission of sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit, divine governance in morals, counsels, and dangers, the confirmation or firmness of faith, chastity, and all necessary virtues; likewise the preservation of the evangelical ministry, the purity of doctrine and the church; likewise corporal benefits, good health, sustenance, salutary governments, public peace and concord, the happiness of children, the protection of your little home, your family, your fortunes, your little town, etc.

Being reminded by your own great miseries of these great necessities, and of so many and such varied kinds of dangers, you ought to exercise faith, invocation, and hope in the petition for the goods of the universal church, and for yourselves privately, and for your families, both spiritual and corporal. For on account of this very cause the church is subject to the cross, and sustains troubles inextricable by human counsel, so that, oppressed by the weight of things, we may be excited to invocation and be compelled to seek the help of God. For as long as men, drunk with pleasures and enjoying present comforts, live without great sorrows, they do not become ardent, but their petitions are too slothful, languid, and cold, because such is the stupor of the idle and the drunken.

of minds, so that they neither consider their own miseries, nor think that they have need of the help of God. And therefore God allows the Church to be reminded by constant persecutions and sad and various calamities, so that, convinced by experience itself, we may learn to cry out and take refuge in Him, and may recognize the presence of God and the wondrous liberations in the Church, by which we are invited to the fear of God, to faith, and to celebrating God, just as Psalm 33 teaches and exhorts: Approach God, and run together in great numbers, then your faces will not be ashamed; this poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him, etc.

This is the common doctrine concerning prayer, which you often hear. But it was to be thought upon daily in invocation, and transferred to practice. For it does not treat of idle subtleties and empty quibbles, but contains necessary doctrine to be exercised in daily life, and in all business, so that we may learn to offer to God the true worship for which we were created, and thus it proposes wholesome and effective reminders, so that in conversion they may bring life and eternal consolation to hearts.

Furthermore, I add again a brief explanation of the saying: God does not hear sinners.

This is a true statement concerning sinners who do not perform repentance, or who are unwilling to be converted to God, and who securely persevere in sins against their conscience, such as those who retain the intention of polluting themselves with adulteries, with the persecution of true doctrine, with rapine and thefts, etc.

But this saying must by no means be understood of other sinners who are performing repentance, or who are converted to God. For the voice of the divine oath speaks concerning those who are converted and seeking the remission of sins: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.

Let us now be content with these necessary reminders concerning invocation or petition. In the following sermon I shall discuss more about this passage, because Christ Himself proposes a form of praying, which we may learn to understand skillfully, clearly, and correctly, concerning which matter it will be necessary to speak later.

Thus therefore pray: Our Father who art in heaven, etc. Luke 11. When you pray, say:

It is profitable that this admonition be added first. There are certain hypocrites so much above other

saints in religiousness, that they say there is no need for words in prayer, that it is enough to invoke in spirit, and they do not know what spirit or flesh is; they only seek a pretext for their own sloth, who rarely or never recite the words of prayers. Against such hypocrites, the particle in the text must be held: say. Christ manifestly commands these words to be recited, which is not to be understood superstitiously, but the recitation of words is useful. But first, the recitation of the words which our Lord Jesus Christ Himself prescribed for us, or which the Holy Spirit delivered in the Psalms and elsewhere, leads to this: that through this form proposed by divine counsel we may be instructed and reminded of the true God, of true worship, of the will of God, and of divine promises, and that we may establish with firmer assent that God has revealed Himself, that He has shown how He wishes to be invoked, that the petition for benefits and divine help is pleasing to Him, and that He truly hears those who invoke Him, and wishes to bestow these very goods which He commanded to be asked for by name in this most learned form. This thought of revelation and promises is especially necessary in the recitation of the divinely delivered form, so that when the Son of God commands you to say: Forgive us our debts, think: Because Christ commands that we ask for reconciliation, it is certain that it is the immovable will of God that we should establish that we are forgiven by Him. For He would not command us to ask for remission unless He were truly going to give it. Likewise, when the Lord's Prayer teaches us to pray seriously: Give us this day our daily bread, you should think, because Christ commands us to ask for bodily benefits, He will undoubtedly grant them to the Church. Behold, such great consolation is proposed in this form and certain recitation of words, which the Lord prescribed and delivered, that it is clearly evident that those drunken Cyclopes are plainly raging, and are agitated by an evil spirit, who contend that there is no need for the recitation of these words. But let the text in Luke be opposed to that …insanity, which says by name: When you pray: say. Secondly, let the express recitation of words be, while praying, a certain confession against the devil. Let it also be a profession of faith before the Church, by which you separate yourself from all Gentiles, and disapprove of the furies of all sects. Thus, when the penitent thief hanging on the cross prays in express words: Lord remember me, when you come into your kingdom, preaching from on high, he edits an illustrious confession, and shows by his testimony that this Jesus, who is now a companion in punishment, is truly the Messiah, the one who forgives sins, and the author and restorer of eternal life.

Furthermore, if the commemoration of certain words is done publicly, it usefully reminds and instructs by testimony, and invites, excites, and confirms by example, both children and adolescents, as well as others older in age. You ought to consider all these things well and remember them diligently, so that you may accustom yourselves to the recitation of the Lord's Prayer, the Apostles' Creed, and the Psalms, willingly and frequently, to be practiced both privately and publicly. For pious minds will experience that God, through this recitation, will effectively provide them with consolation and light, and that the invocation will not be in vain, nor the cries useless, but that they will obtain the salutary things they seek.

Now I proceed to the very words of the Lord's Prayer.

Our Father who art in heaven.

When this part is recited, let the sweetest appellation of Father first hold your mind. Consider attentively whom you call Father, and why you name him so. And know that by this address, Our Father who art in heaven, you are speaking to the whole Godhead. For 'Father' in this place is a name of essence, not just of one person. It is therefore a word common to the whole Godhead, or it is placed essentially, not personally, embracing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Then it is necessary for you to simultaneously think of and contemplate in your mind the divine manifestations, so that the invocation may be directed to this true God, who revealed himself by sending his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified and resurrected. Wherefore, let some such form of invocation be thought of: Almighty, eternal, true and living God, eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of heaven and earth, together with your Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the Holy Spirit, I address you as a suppliant, I pray and invoke you, I take refuge in you, I implore your mercy and help with true groans, hear me, according to your promises, through your Son the Mediator Jesus Christ, you are our Father, that is, you wish to be appeased toward us, to receive and hear us on account of your Son, whom you have established as a propitiator for us. Great, true, and ardent is the love of parents toward their children, therefore with a true movement of the soul I take refuge in you, most loving Father, whom I firmly establish by the trust of the revealed Son, that you will help me in all dangers with wonderful and paternal benevolence, and will soothe calamities and miseries with divine consolation. By some such form or thought, remind yourself, and kindle and excite your faith, as often as you recite these words: Our Father.

Who art in heaven.

It follows: Who art in heaven, that is, who art almighty, a helper, and truly present everywhere. For to be in heaven, when we speak of God or his infinite nature, does not mean to occupy a certain part of heaven, and to sit on a throne above the sun, or above the sphere of the fixed stars: but it is to be present in all places and to all creatures by substance, and to be everywhere present and effective, just as the text of Jeremiah 23 affirms:

I fill heaven and earth. This assertion in the prayer is therefore a certain confession of the universal presence and infinite power of God, that he is truly present with you, regards you and hears you, sees and judges the movements and groans of your heart, and that his power is so great that he can certainly help you: and that you do not adore a wooden or stone statue, nor a golden or silver idol, but the one, true, eternal, almighty, living, wise, good, beneficent, truthful, chaste, just, and merciful God, who revealed himself through our Lord Jesus Christ by the resurrection of the dead, and by other miracles, and truly wishes and is able to bring us help. You must add this thought to these words: Who art in heaven.

In which recitation you should simultaneously consider what blindness and insanity it is to invoke the Saints who have departed from this life. For they neither behold your heart, nor hear you as present, nor are they everywhere. But an invocation calling upon dead Saints is as uncertain, empty, and vain as if you were to ridiculously call upon and address a man who is completely unknown, ignorant, absent, and far removed, in your own room.

For example, if you say: Ah, my Lord Pastor of the Church of Lübeck, help me, or pray for me. For he... nor does He see the movements, nor does He hear the vows of your heart, and He does not even know that He is being invoked. Such an invocation, which is made to the deaf and the ignorant, what, I ask, differs from the idolatrous and ethnic adoration of marble or wooden statues? Let your mind in your recitation simultaneously depict this manifest and gross idolomania in thought, and seriously detest it, so that you may certainly learn to invoke the true God, and not doubt that God is truly present to you, truly sees, judges, hears the groans of your heart, is willing and able to help you, to give life and salvation for the sake of His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Hallowed be Thy name. Now the petitions follow in order. You have heard above the admonition concerning the things to be sought, which are to be recounted in prayer. For those praying ought to seek from God by name some certain benefit, necessary either for the soul or the body, and to expect it. Furthermore, the first, highest, and most necessary good is the true knowledge of God, and true and uncorrupted doctrine, concerning which knowledge and celebration of God the first commandment also preaches. And just as the first commandment of the Decalogue requires and commands that you have no other gods, but that you rightly acknowledge the true God, believe in His word, have true trust toward God, true fear and love of God above all things: so the Lord teaches us at the beginning to pray, that we may be able to begin and perform interior worship, and obedience of the heart toward the first commandment. He begins, therefore, from the chief and of all things most necessary good: Hallowed be Thy name, as if he were saying: Ah Lord God, kindle in us a pure, true, and holy knowledge of Thy name, that is, give us pure and sincere doctrine without corruptions, so that we may neither embrace errors nor receive idolatrous worships, but bring it about that we may holily acknowledge Thee as the true and only God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who revealed Thyself through this Son Jesus Christ, sent from the beginning to the Church, crucified and resurrected, that we may truly believe in Thee, rightly invoke, worship, and celebrate Thee. Guard us mercifully, lest our minds be fascinated by fanatical and idolatrous furies, take away idolatry and all impious opinions, bring it about that Thou, the true God, may be rightly known, truly acknowledged, invoked with true faith, worshipped and celebrated.

For 'name' signifies knowledge or acknowledgment. Here, therefore, you will observe that the first commandment of the Decalogue and this first petition agree, and that they speak of the true revelation, acknowledgment, invocation, and celebration of God.

Thy kingdom come.

True knowledge should not be an idle speculation, but a burning light divinely kindled, bringing to hearts eternal justice, joy, and life, according to the saying of Christ: This is eternal life, that they may know Thee the true God, and Jesus whom Thou hast sent to be Christ. The effect, therefore, of true knowledge is justice and eternal life. Therefore, concerning the effect of the first petition it is said: Thy kingdom come, that is, do Thou, through the ministry and voice of Thy doctrine, regenerate, rule, and govern us by the Holy Spirit, begin in us Thy kingdom in this life, and perfect it after this life, be effective in us, kindle through the voice of the Gospel and the knowledge of Thee, true faith, justice, and eternal life in our hearts, destroy the kingdom of the devil. Do not grant to the devil that he may capture our minds with his deceits, and then, having implicated and ensnared them, horribly drive and overturn them. Let Jesus Christ Thy Son dwell and reign powerfully and effectively, and make His dwelling in us, just as He Himself promised, saying: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him.

Moreover, this very petition also pertains to the first and second commandment of the Decalogue. For it is necessary that these two be joined, and that both be simultaneously begun in us, namely, the true acknowledgment of God, divine efficacy, or divine movements excited and kindled through the light of celestial doctrine and the knowledge of God. For true knowledge precedes, vivification follows, and God is effective through His word, and by the thought of His voice He converts and vivifies those who assent. You seek, therefore, in these first and chief petitions the highest and most ample benefits, true light of doctrine, true faith, fear of God, love of God, hope, consolation, and eternal life, and finally victory against the Devil, and against your sins.

Latin:

Caput VI.

Supra dixit de enarratione et interpretatione praeceptorum: Non occidas, Non moechaberis, Non furtum facies. Horum praeceptorum interpretatio est de rebus crassioribus, quae facilius intelligi possunt. Nunc venit ad doctrinam de vana gloria, quae non ita facile intelligi potest, et est malum in profundo cordis infixum cupiditas vanae gloriae. Ut aliquo modo crasse doceamus populum de hac re, sciendum est, quod vocabulum superbia, et vitiosa ambitio, seu cupiditas vanae gloriae non significet ostentare res externas, ut pulcras vestes, aut aedificia splendida (etsi hae res externae arguunt et declarant interdum occultam et interiorem superbiam) sed significat in corde confidere propria sapientia, aut viribus, aut potentia, aut pecunia, ideoque despicere alios, et hac sui fiducia sine vocatione et extra vocationem magnas res suscipere, multa movere, imo etiam coram Deo se efferre, nec agnoscere se dignum esse poena, et frenere adversus Deum, tum vel impeditur cupiditas, vel iusto iudicio Dei sequitur infelix exitus.

Ista sunt arcana et occulta peccata, quae pauci homines intelligunt. Hanc superbiam perpetuo condemnat Deus, et in concionibus suis, et in poenis, inevitabiliter sequentibus insignem insolentiam. De hoc malo et Christus hic loquitur. Ac dictum Petri dignum est memoria: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Difficile est intelligere, quid sit superbia, et quid sit humilitas, quia sunt in corde: sed tamen externa signa et exempla utcunque ostendunt discrimen.

Sumamus igitur exempla. Saul initio est modestus et humilis, sicut textus manifeste dicit, servit suo patri, manet intra vocationem, quaerit asinas, etc. Sed postea evectus ad fastigium regni, cum aliquamdiu habuisset prosperos successus et insignes victorias, fit superbus, hoc est, erumpit extra metas vocationis, et appetit maiora, conatur ad se transferre regnum, et quasi per manus, haereditatis loco, tradere posteris suis. Cum quidem sciret, regnum in hoc populo esse peculiare donum Dei, nec haberet mandatum de constituenda haereditaria successione. Idem postquam videbat alium, nempe Davidem vocari, cui Deus suo consilio regnum traditurus esset, irascebatur Deo et hominibus, premebat et persequebatur Davidem, interficiebat Sacerdotes, elatus hac superbia, quod confidebat fastigio imperii seu autoritate regia, et sua potentia, quibus praesidiis putabat se satis munitum esse adversus omnes fortunae casus, ne hic cursus impediri posset.

Cum David interfecisset Goliath, et virgines composuissent hymnum triumphalem de ipso et Saule, magisque praedicarent ac celebrarent Davidem quam Saulem, ibi Saul incensus invidentia urebatur gloria sui ministri, ardebat aemulatione et ira, dolens istum sibi praeferri, et se quasi inferiorem duci: cum tamen debuisset Deo reverenter agere gratias, et ita potius cogitare: Ah Domine Deus, vere sunt nihil omnes homines, nec potest regni moles humanis viribus sustineri. Tibi autem gratias ago, quod tu tu Deus dedisti nobis victoriam per me et per alios, honi consulo alium praestantiorem electum esse. Tibi permitto atque concedo, ut tuo consilio, cuicunque volueris, dona superiora, ampliorem gloriam, et diuturniores successus tribuas. Confiteor me parum idoneum, imo indignum esse tot beneficiis, et ea gloria, qua me ornasti. Agnosco me miserrimum peccatorem esse etc.

Aliud exemplum. Absolon erat filius regis, magnificabatur et co-adjuvare patrem: sed non contentus hoc splendore, praecipuoque dignitatis gradu, appetit superiorem vocationem seu summum fastigium, nec expectat mortem patris, sed ante tempus invadit et occupat regnum excusso patre. In huiusmodi crassis et insignibus exemplis potest agnosci et conspici, quid sit superbia.

Et bene considerate haec signa: ubicunque sunt hi morbi, invidentia, livor, aemulatio, et maledicentia laedens aliorum famam, seu obtrectans alienae existimationi, atque despectio aliorum; item: ubi multa tentantur, et moventur extra vocationem; item: ubi est impatientia contra Deum, ibi superbiam esse nihil dubium est. Tales igitur superbos et arrogantes esse cogitemus, quales Esau, Saul, Absolon et similes fuerunt.

E regione ponemus illustre exemplum humilitatis.

Ionathas filius Saulis eminebat inter praestantissimos duces et capitaneos patris, ac praeterquam quod multas egregias res gesserat, et admirandis atque salutaribus victoriis a Deo fuerat ornatus, etiam regis erat filius, cui iure et more aliarum gentium et communi quadam hominum opinione, haereditas regni deberi putabatur. Sed est humilis, non ruit extra vocationem, continet se intra metas officii, et quia scit nihil esse maius in hominum vita, quam gubernationem, praesertim populi Dei, nec ulli regnum in hoc populo deberi, nisi quem Deus electum et unctum quasi diademate imposito collocarit ipse in sede regia, ideo nequaquam concupiscit aut conatur rapere dominationem, sed intra metas suae vocationis fideliter servit. Deinde postquam videt Davidem divinitus ad hanc gubernationem vocatum esse, acquiescit, gaudet alium praestantiorem electum esse, amanter cedit, honestissime cupit ac benefacit ei, cor ipsius nec accenditur aemulatione et invidentia, nec impatientia et indignatione cruciatur, non existimat iniuste secum agi, vel iniuriam sibi fieri, quia scit hoc ipsum regnum donum Dei esse, nec invadendum esse ab ullo homine. Imo laetus agit gratias Deo, quod pro salute populi nunc vocarit et excitarit, sapientem, bonum, felicem et sanctum regem, gratulatur reipublicae, optat ut Deus haec beneficia cumulet. Hic ipse mitis et fidelis animus in Ionatha est vera humilitas. Ac quoties auditis dici de superbia et humilitate, toties vobis in mentem veniant haec exempla Saulis, Absolonis et Ionathae. Itaque facillimum fuerit intelligenti fundamentum in hac doctrina, perspicere et diiudicare, cum in omnibus historiis tum in quotidianis exemplis, quae personae re ipsa sint superbae, quae humiles, et quid proprie superbia sit, quid humilitas: collatis item eventibus agnoscere et observare, quod verissimum sit Petri dictum: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus dat gratiam, et quod verissime statuendum sit, superbos ordine divino ex alto fastigio excussos, tandem tristissimis casibus opprimi, sed humilibus Deum opitulaturum, et ipsorum curriculo affuturum esse.

Caeterum ut haec omnia melius intelligatis, volo definire, quid sit humilitas, et regulam tradere, commonefacientem vos, in quibus rebus exercenda sit humilitas, seu circa quae versetur.

Vestrum erit diligenter ea considerare et meminisse.

Humilitas est verus timor Dei, qui sensu percipi potest in corde, et in agnitione propriae infirmitatis verus dolor de peccatis, et sordibus nostris; estque obedientia sese Deo subiiciens ac serviens intra metas vocationis, non stulta sui fiducia erumpens, nec suscipiens negotia supra vires, aut maiora appetens, sed spe auxilii divini diligenter faciens convenientia vocationi, et est iustitia tribuens suum cuique locum, non certans aemulatione et livore cum antecedentibus, nec despiciens, premens, impediens caeteros, sed agens Deo gratias, quod alios etiam facit organa salutaria; est denique patientia tribuens Deo laudem iustitiae, ac propter agnitionem delictorum moderate ferens poenas, nec irascens Deo, quasi crudeliter exerceat nos vel negligat, cum loco movemur, aut cursus noster impeditur. Iam videte, quot membra seu species complectatur, et ex quantis virtutibus composita sit humilitas.

Prima virtus est timor Dei. Secunda, agnitio peccati et imbecillitatis propriae. Tertia, continere se intra metas, nec omissa vel deserta vocatione propria, irruere in aliena, aut appetere superiora viribus. Quarta, neminem despicere, nec accendi invidentia. Quinta, non fremere adversus Deum in poenis, sed in calamitate patienter obedire. Harum omnium virtutum copulatio est humilitas.

Ita sunt humiles Ionathas, David, et casti Angeli. Sed omnium maxime filius Dei, adeo patienter exuens suam gloriam, et se abiiciens, ut coram aeterno patre iacuerit prostratus et supplex pro nobis, ac senserit derivata in sese vera et horribili ira Dei, summam confusionem, deformationem, miseriam et ignominiam, perinde ac si ipse nostris sceleribus et probris sese pollui-set.

Ah quid nos vilissimi et inquinatissimi vermiculi superbimus, ac irritati parvis iniuriis, aut aliquo convitio leviter aspera freminus, et coecis affectibus animos tanquam navem ventis permitti-mus? Pudeat nos arrogantiae et flagitiosae im-patientiae nostrae, cum filius Dei propter nos in tantam humilitatem sese abiecerit. Propterea ipse dicit: Discite a me, quia mitis sum et humilis corde. Haec vox Christi semper sit vobis in conspectu.

E contrario videte, quot ex vitiis conflata sit superbia, quantumque chaos foedissimarum sordium, turpitudinum, ac pestium, in cor superbum, tanquam in sentinam scelerum concluda-tur et confluat. Superbia est coecitas errore iudicii non agnoscens peccatum et propriam infirmitatem, ideoque securissime contemnens iram Dei, et est orta ex hac ipsa coecitate admiratio atque fiducia suarum virium, potentiae, industriae, neglectis metis vocationis erumpens, et maiora appetens, aliosque vel arrogantia despiciens ac premens, vel invidentia criminans et deformans. Est denique impatientia fremens adversus Deum in poenis.

Primum ergo vitium, comprehensum in superbia, est coecitas non agnoscens peccatum et propriam infirmitatem. Secundum, securitas carnalis, vel esse sine timore Dei. Tertium, considere sua sapientia, potentia, aut donis qualibuscunque, sine agnitione et fiducia auxilii divini. Quartum, arrogare sibi maiorem autorita-tem, quam convenit, et extra vocationem erumpere, ut Absolon, ut seditiosi, ut autores novorum dogmatum, quos ingenii propriaeque sapientiae fiducia et gloriae sitis impellit ad studia fa-ctionum et ambitiosa certamina, quales Arius, Mahomet, et omnes haeretici fuerunt. Quintum, invidentia et aliorum despectio. Sextum, impatientia, repugnans voluntati divinae. Talis confusio pessimorum affectuum est superbia.

Haec breviter dicta sint de vocabulorum de-finitionibus tanquam in parva tabella quoquo modo propositis, ut commonefacti discamus paulisper aspicere nos ipsos, et agnoscere sordes ac miserias humanas, utque mentes excitentur ad considerationem virtutum, quas continet humilitas, et oppositorum vitiorum, quae plura con-currunt in superbis.

De precatione.

Quando oras, non eris sicut hypocritae etc.

In hac doctrina de precatione, primum rursus prohibet superbiam: postea docet modum orandi, et quidem certam formam verborum proponit; cumque proxime de superbia dictum sit aliquid, non sane retulerit, nec operae pretium fuerit hunc tradita prolixe iam repetere.

Est omnino profundum et arcanum peccatum superbia, videlicet, immodice sibi placere, seipsum admirari et magnifacere, se oblectare donis, arrogare sibi laudem iustitiae et sanctita-tis, quas pestes indies magis magisque discamus agnoscere, ut maiore prudentia repugnemus omnibus his morbis. Ideoque cum in affli-ctionibus exercemur, et cruce praeparamur ad ferendam humilitatem, tunc sciamus deduci nos in hanc scholam erudiendos et domandos castiga-tione, ut agnita pristina superbia et arrogantia emendemur, ac proficere studeamus.

Ita Na-bogdonosor, velut ebrius sese aspiciens admirabatur suam virtutem et potentiam, tumebat superbia et sui fiducia, oblectabat se his vocibus: Ego sum ille gloriosus, pulcer et invictus rex, clarissimarum, maximarumque virtutum prae-stantia excellens, cuius sapientia, consiliis, et dimicationibus tantum imperium partum et con-stitutum est: Ego feci Babylonem tantam meo robore. Sed eundem dona sua immodice mirantem et amantem, elatumque fiducia propriae sa-pientiae, virtutis et potentiae, subito Deus ex summo gradu deturbat, et detrudit in acerbissi-mas calamitates, in quibus non solum regnum et autoritatem, sed mentem etiam amisit, cum furiosus vagaretur inter bestias etc.

Nec est quod quisquam securitatem et superbiam alens, promittat sibi placidos et optatos exitus.

Quin potius omnibus persuasum esse debet universaliter inter homines, quicunque excelso dignitatis gradu collocatus, amplissimisque for- tunae muneribus ornatus, eminet et antecellit, ideoque velut ebrius et infatuatus successibus superbe sua consilia et sese magnificat, eum hac ipsa sui fiducia sibi tragicas poenas accersere, a Deo que rursus ex alto fastigio deiectum horribiliter cadere, sicut admonui proxime, signum secuturae ruinae certissimum esse, insignem insolentiam.

Semper enim verae manent hae regulae: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam.

Item, abominatio Domino est omnis superbus corde, Proverb. 16. Discant autem homines, primum agnoscere, emendare et exuere crassam, insulsam, agrestem atque Thrasonicam superbiam.

Quae quidem superbia rustica et Thrasonica est, Cyclopico fastu palam despicere atque contemnere reliquos, eosque maledictis et probris vexare, et obtrectatione aliorum vel gloriam quaerere, vel sibi potentiam augere velle.

Item, stolida vanitate et arrogantia gloriose multa, sed falso de sese praedicare, et impudenter ea sibi tribuere, quae non adsunt.

Item: ingerere se alienis vocationibus, nec tribuere singulis gradum, in quem ordine collocati sunt, sed invadere in eorum functiones, et velle quouqomodo antecellere aliis.

Item: iniustam licentiam sibi sumere premendi et afficiendi alios iniuria, et offerre speciem terroris, asperumque fieri non colentibus et magnifacientibus nos, ut propter hanc ipsam insolentiam, nos potentiores, fortiores, et praestantiores esse putemur quam sumus, alii vero videantur inferiores.

Haec enormia, crassa, et petulanter accersita vitia, multipliciterque vitam hominum turbantia considerentur, et agnita vitentur, frenentur, ac deponantur, adsciscatur autem et praestetur humilitas coniuncta cum patientia Christiana.

Verum de his satis multa.

Nunc de precatione seu adoratione.

Prima regula sit: Ne abutamur oratione ad hypocrisin et exercendam superbiam, neve transferatur invocatio vel ad superstitionem vanamque fiduciam propriae iustitiae, vel ad inanem ostentationem atque pompam, dum simulatis ceremoniis et tragoediis externis sanctimoniam mentientes affectamus, ut homines praedicent nos in templo stantes, plurima legentes, incurvisque corporibus in genua considentes, tanta quidem specie fictae devotionis, ut (quod Germanis in proverbio est) Divorum pedes mordicus auferre velle videamur.

Secunda regula: Precatio non est inanis et otiosa et frigida βαττολογία, seu ethnico more propter consuetudinem inani labiorum motu, vocumque strepitu, et linguae volubilitate legere prolixas preces, et easdem superstitiose sine fine iterare: quemadmodum Monachi et sacrificuli ante haec tempora cogebantur recitare horas canonicas, cum immodice prolixas, tum ne ab ipsis quidem intellectas: aut sicut aniculae rosariorum naenias demurmurabant sine animorum intentione.

Tertia regula: Invocatio seu adoratio est necessarius et praecipuus cultus Dei, ac summa virtus, et propria solius Ecclesiae, seu vere Christianorum; estque vera fide aliquid petere a Deo propter mediatorem Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, et postea gratias agere Deo et mediatori pro acceptis beneficiis.

Itaque priore loco dicemus de petitione, quae est motus in corde, volens aliquid accipere a Deo, et petens, ut nobis dentur bona necessaria.

Ad petitionem vero necessaria est praecipue quinque rerum consideratio.

Primo cogitandum est, quem invokes, qui sit verus Deus, ubi se patefecerit, ut discernas tuam invocationem ab Ethnica et omnium sectarum damnatis invocationibus.

Quanquam enim Ethnici quoque precantes usurpant et retinent nomen Dei, tamen vagantur animis, ignorantes, quid sit Deus, aut quod Numen alloquantur: alius coelum nominat Deum, alius appellat solem.

Tu vero debes in precatione attente considerare, et tecum ipse quaerere, quid agas, quid invokes, ubi se Deus patefecerit, et dirigere mentem ac invocationem ad hunc verum Deum, qui se patefecit misso filio, Domino nostro Iesu Christo crucifixo et resuscitato.

Ideo saepe inter invocationem cogites et proponas tibi baptismum Christi, in quo clarissime patefactae et revelatae sunt tres personae: Deus Pater, Deus Filius et Deus Spiritus sanctus.

Ac quoties inchoas precationem, oculis, mente, veraque fide intuearis in Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, et consideres utrumque, nec aliud numen invocandum esse, nisi hunc verum Deum, qui se patefecit in Christo, videlicet Patrem, Filium et Spiritum sanctum: et hunc aeternum Deum semper in ecclesia patefactum, velle certo te exaudire, curare tuos gemitus, recipere tuas preces propter Filium et mediatorem Christum.

Haec cogitatio commonefaciens, quem velis alloqui, seu quod sit illud numen, quod alloquaris, in omni invocatione suscipienda ante oculos, et apud animum attente, serioque proponenda est, ut in conspectu sit discrimen verae invocationis in Ecclesia, et invocationis Ethnicae. Ignorant ethnici quid invocent, nec possunt statuere quod exaudiantur, nec cogitant, cur exaudiantur. Verum Christiani norunt et aspiciunt admirandas revelationes, quibus ab initio se Deus ostendit in Ecclesia, earumque cogitatione fidem confirmant, intuentur patefactiones in eductione ex Aegypto factas. Item evidentissima testimonia per filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum exhibita in resuscitatione mortuorum. Hunc verum Deum patefactum illustribus testimoniis agnoscat, compellet, et alloquatur cor tuum, et fiducia mediatoris petat gratiam et alia beneficia, certo statuens propter Christum exaudiri tuos gemitus.

Haec prima sit admonitio de invocatione, ex qua perspicue potest intelligi, non statuas, non diabolos, non Sanctos, non ullos homines invocandos esse, nec honorem Deo debitum ullis creaturis tribuendum esse. Sitque semper in conspectu dictum Christi: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies.

Secunda commonefactio est, ut mandatum Dei de facienda invocatione cogitetur, quia nullum opus Deo placet non divinitus praeceptum. Imo quis auderet ad Deum accedere, tantamque maiestatem compellare et alloqui? nisi vellet ipse atque iussisset hoc modo se coli: praesertim cum naturaliter omnium hominum corda dubitatione oppressa trepident, Deumque fugiant in veris doloribus.

Propterea proposuit Deus severissimum mandatum, ut sciremus alacriter et confidenter nos ad ipsum accurrere et confugere, auxiliumque in periculis ab ipso petere et exspectare debere, atque hanc invocationem summum esse cultum, et opus omnium maximum, Deoque gratissimum, sicut clamitat Psalmus 49.: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me. Item Matthaei 7.: Petite et dabitur vobis, pulsate et aperietur vobis. Ac universa scriptura plena est talium praeceptorum, quorum autoritas animis inculcetur, nosque exsuscitet et accendat, ne trepidantes fugiamus Deum, sed ut ausimus libenter, avide, et quasi familiariter ad ipsum confugere.

At dicat aliquis: Libenter venirem in conspectum Dei, libenter accedens ad Deum multa peterem, certe in tantis miseriis intelligo mihi opus esse auxilio Dei, sed sum miserrimus peccator. Fortassis meae preces non curantur, sentio me indignum esse, qui exaudiar. Quid petam, cum scriptum sit: Peccatores Deus non exaudit? Frustra igitur clamo ad Deum, cum sim multipliciter reus irae.

Responsio. Hic tenenda est tertia consideratio, pertinens ad veram invocationem, videlicet, promissio, et filius Dei mediator. Deus non solum severissime praecepit, ut petamus, sed etiam ut invitaret nos ad invocationem, clarissimas sententias dulcissimarum et amplissimarum promissionum addidit, in quibus iure iurando confirmat, se certo velle nos exaudire, praestare bona quae petimus, et opitulari nobis in omnibus, tum spiritualibus, tum corporalibus periculis et necessitatibus. Suntque promissiones expressae his verbis: Amen amen dico vobis: Quicquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Ecce hic iurat filius Dei, Patrem certo velle nos exaudire, certo accipi et placere nostras preces. Item Matth. 7.: Petite et accipietis.

At rursus, indignitate tua deterreris, disputans te miserum peccatorem esse.

Responsio. Hic necesse est scire, propter hanc ipsam causam, quia sumus oppressi peccato, Deum constituisse dilectum filium suum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, pro nobis deprecatorem, interpellatorem, mediatorem et summum Sacerdotem, propter quem certo recipiat et exaudiat nos. Quare debes in omni invocatione accedere et confugere ad propitiatorem Christum, ita, ut primum adferas poenitentiam, seu conversionem ad Deum, deinde sustentes et erigas te hac consolatione, quod et propter mediatorem Christum certo accipias remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliatus propter ipsum, exaudiaris, et quod idem sit summus Pontifex ingrediens in Sancta sanctorum, tuos gemitus, tua vota, tuas preces perferat in arcanum divinitatis consilium.

Ecce hanc tantam consolationem ignorant Ethnici, Iudaei, Turci et Papistae, sed tantum vera ecclesia, seu populus Dei, recte agnoscens dominum Iesum Christum, tenet hanc efficacissimam et dulcissimam consolationem. Magnitudo quidem tantae rei longe superat omnium Angelorum et hominum eloquentiam. Quid enim maius et admirabilius hac Dei bonitate cogitari potest? videlicet, quod nos miseros homines vult certo recipere, curare, respicere, exaudire propter intercessionem et sacrificium Pontificis Christi. Ideo diserte dicit ipse Dominus: Quicquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, id est, fide, quae nititur me propitiatore, seu fiducia filii Dei mediatoris et placatoris.

Haec est in omni precatione omnium maxime necessaria consideratio, de qua pios et vere Christianos, qui serio magnaque animi intentione orant, quotidiana docet experientia, non sine ingenti certamine ac labore flecti, erudiri, et erigi corda, ut acquiescant in tot promissionibus sanctis sanguine et resuscitatione filii Dei, nec eam luctam sine veris gemitibus fieri posse. Necessario itaque debet accedere quarta commonefactio, de fide.

Est enim inane murmur, nec dici potest invocatio, si quadam consuetudine recitans verba cogites: Nescio an sim Deo curae, an placeant et vere recipiantur meae preces. Sed necesse est te promissionem atque filium Dei mediatorem intueri, amplecti, et apprehendere vera fide, acquiescente in Deo propter ipsum, necesse est te fiducia promissionis gratiae repugnare diffidentiae et dubitationi, iuxta dictum Iacobi: Omnis petat in fide, nihil haesitans.

Item 1. Tim. 2. dicitur: Orate sine ira et haesitatione. Item, textus inquit ad Ephesios: Per Christum audemus accedere confidenter per fidem in ipsum.

Quare scias oportere universaliter in omni petitione primum et ante omnia afferre atque praelucere hanc fidem, qua credis, Deum aeternum certo te recipere, tibi ignoscere, velle tuas preces respicere, approbare et exaudire propter mediatorem Christum. Ac in petitione aeternorum bonorum, ut reconciliationis, salutis, et gubernationis animae, firmissime statuito, quod haec ipsa, quae sine conditione petis, videlicet remissionem peccatorum, gratuitam reconciliationem, et vitam aeternam, Deus tibi nominatim et in specie certo dare et praestare velit.

Sed de bonis corporalibus, in hac vita necessariis, fides petit et statuit cum conditione: Si Deo placet.

Quae quidem precatio non est irrita, sed efficax, et vel hoc ipsum, quod nominatim petitur, impetrat, vel certe mitigationem calamitatum et miseriarum. Etsi enim Deus in hac vita vult ecclesiam subiectam esse cruci, tamen immensa misericordia lenit ac mitigat invocantibus ipsum poenas et aerumnas, ut sustineri atque perferri possint, ne desperatione oppressi mergamur in aeternam mortem, sicut affirmat in Esaia, se habitare cum afflictis etc.

Scias igitur, etiamsi differtur liberatio corporalis, nec eventus tuae cogitationi respondet, tamen placere, recipi, exaudiri tuam precationem, nec esse irritam, nec inane murmur.

Haec sine ulla dubitatione certissima et verissima sunt, ut et Syracidae 35. scriptum est: Lacrymae viduae defluunt ad maxillam, sed oratio ascendit, et coelum penetrat. Quinta consideratio est rerum petendarum, ut cogitentur et recitentur in precatione nominatim certa beneficia quae petimus, videlicet, remissio peccatorum, donatio Spiritus sancti, gubernatio divina in moribus, consiliis et periculis, confirmatio seu firmitas fidei, castitatis et omnium necessariarum virtutum, item conservatio ministerii evangelici, puritatis doctrinae et ecclesiae; item corporalia beneficia, bona valetudo, victus, salutaria regimina, pax et concordia publica, felicitas liberorum, protectio tui tugurioli, tuae familiae, tuarum fortunarum, tui oppiduli, etc. Has tantas necessitates, tot et tam varii generis pericula, commonefacti ingentibus miseriis vestris, vobis proponere, et in petitione bonorum universae ecclesiae, et vobis privatim, et vestris familiis, necessariorum, cum spiritualium tum corporalium, fidem, invocationem, et spem exercere debetis.

Nam propter hanc ipsam causam Ecclesia subiecta est cruci, et aerumnas inextricabiles humano consilio sustinet, ut mole rerum oppressi ad invocationem excitemur, et auxilium Dei quaerere cogamur. Donec enim homines ebrii voluptatibus, et praesentibus commodis fruentes, vivunt sine magnis doloribus, non fiunt ardentes, sed nimis ignavae, languidae et frigidae petitiones, quia tantus est stupor otiosarum et temulentarum.

mentium, ut nec suas miserias considerent, nec putent sibi opus esse auxilio Dei. Ideoque Deus Ecclesiam sinit assiduis persecutionibus et tristi- bus ac variis calamitatibus commonefieri, ut ipsa experientia convicti discamus clamare et confugere ad ipsum, et agnoscamus Dei praesentiam miran- dasque liberationes in Ecclesia, quibus ad timo- rem Dei, ad fidem, et ad celebrandum Deum invitemur, quemadmodum docet et hortatur Psalm. 33.: Accedite ad Deum, et magna fre- quentia accurrite, tunc facies vestrae non confun- dentur, iste pauper clamavit, et Dominus ex- audivit eum, etc.

Haec est communis doctrina de precatione, quam saepe auditis. Sed erat quotidie in invo- catione cogitanda, et ad usum transferenda. Non enim tractat otiosas subtilitates, et inanes argu- tias, sed continet necessariam doctrinam exercen- dam in quotidiana vita, et in omnibus negotiis, ut discamus verum cultum, ad quem conditi su- mus, Deo praestare, adeoque salutares et effica- ces commonefactiones proponit, ut in conversione vitam et consolationem aeternam cordibus afferant.

Caeterum rursus adiicio brevem explicatio- nem dicti: Peccatores Deus non exaudit.

Vera est sententia de peccatoribus non agen- tibus poenitentiam, seu nolentibus converti ad Deum, ac secure perseverantibus in peccatis con- tra conscientiam, ut, qui retinent propositum polluendi se adulteriis, persecutione verae doctri- nae, rapinis et furtis, etc.

Sed de aliis peccatoribus agentibus poeni- tentiam, seu conversis ad Deum, nequaquam de- bet intelligi hoc dictum. Nam de conversis et quaerentibus remissionem peccatorum, loquitur vox iuramenti divini: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat.

His necessariis commonefactionibus de in- vocatione seu petitione, nunc contenti simus. In sequenti concione plura disseram de hoc loco, quia Christus ipse formam precandi proponit, quam dextre, perspicue ac recte discamus intelli- gere, qua de re postea dicendum erit.

Sic igitur orate: Pater noster qui es in coelis, etc. Lucae 11. Quando orabitis, dicite:

Hanc admonitionem primum addi prodest. Sunt quidam hypocritae adeo supra caeteros

Sanctos religiosi, ut dicant nihil opus esse verbis in precatione, satis esse spiritu invocare, et nesciunt, quid sit spiritus vel caro, tantum suae ignaviae praetextum quaerunt, qui raro vel nun- quam recitant verba precationum. Contra tales hypocritas tenenda est parti- cula in textu: dicite. Manifeste iubet Christus haec verba recitari, quod non intelligatur super- stitiose, sed recitatio verborum utilis est. Primum autem recitatio verborum, quae Dominus noster Iesus Christus ipse nobis prae- scripsit, aut quae Spiritus sanctus in Psalmis et alibi tradidit, eo conducit, ut per hanc formam divino consilio propositam erudiamur et commo- nefiamus de vero Deo, de vero cultu, de volun- tate Dei, et promissionibus divinis, utque fir- miori assensione statuamus, quod se Deus pate- fecerit, quod ostenderit, quomodo velit invocari, quod placeat ipsi petitio beneficiorum et auxilii divini, et quod vere exaudiat invocantes, velitque haec ipsa bona largiri, quae nominatim in hac eruditissima forma peti iussit. Haec cogitatio patefactionis et promissionum inprimis est necessaria in recitatione formae di- vinitus traditae, ut cum filius Dei iubet te dicere: Remitte nobis debita nostra, cogita: Quia prae- cipit Christus, ut petamus reconciliationem, cer- tum est immotam Dei voluntatem esse, ut sta- tuamus, ab ipso nobis ignosci. Nec enim iuberet petere remissionem, nisi vere daturus esset. Item, cum docet precatio Dominica serio orare: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, cogites, quia Christus iubet nos petere beneficia corporalia, haud dubie ea donabit Ecclesiae. Ecce tanta consolatio proponitur in hac for- ma et recitatione certa verborum, quae Dominus praescripsit et tradidit, ut liquido constet temu- lentos istos Cyclopes plane furere, et agitari malo spiritu, qui contendunt, nihil opus esse horum verborum recitatione. Sed illi insaniae opponatur textus in Luca, qui nominatim inquit: Cum oratis: dicite. Secundo, expressa recitatio verborum sit inter precandum confessio quaedam contra diabo- lum. Sit etiam professio fidei coram Ecclesia, qua te seiungis ab omnibus Ethnicis, et omnium sectarum furores improbas. Sic cum dexter latro pendens in cruce ex- pressis verbis orat: Domine memento mei, quando venies in regnum tuum, de sublimi concionans edit illustrem confessionem, et ostendit suo testimonio, hunc Iesum, qui nunc est supplicii socius, vere Messiam esse, remittentem peccata, et autorem atque instauratorem vitae aeternae.

Praeterea, commemoratio certa verborum si fiat publice, utiliter et testimonio commonefacit ac erudit, et exemplo invitat, excitat atque confirmat, cum pueros et adolescentes, tum alios grandiores natu. Haec omnia bene considerare diligenterque meminisse debetis, ut assuefaciatis vos ad recitationem precationis Dominicae, Symboli Apostolici, et Psalmorum libenter ac frequenter, tum privatim, tum publice exercendam. Nam piae mentes experientur, Deum per hanc recitationem efficaciter ipsis consolationem atque lucem suppeditaturum esse, nec irritam fore invocationem, nec clamores inutiles, sed salutaria quae petunt impetraturus esse.

Nunc ad ipsa verba orationis Dominicae accedo.

Pater noster qui es in coelis.

Hac parte recitata primum detineat animum tuum dulcissima patris appellatio. Consideres attente, quem Deum voces Patrem, et cur ita nomines. Ac scias hac te compellatione, Pater noster qui es in coelis, alloqui totam divinitatem. Pater enim hoc loco est essentiae nomen, non tantum unius personae. Est igitur vocabulum commune toti divinitati, seu ponitur essentialiter, non personaliter, complectens Patrem, Filium, et Spiritum sanctum. Deinde necesse est te simul cogitare et intueri mente patefactiones divinas, ut directa sit invocatio ad hunc verum Deum, qui se patefecit misso filio Domino nostro Iesu Christo crucifixo et resuscitato. Quare talis aliqua forma invocationis cogitetur: Omnipotens, aeterne, vere et vive Deus, aeterne Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, conditor coeli et terrae, una cum filio tuo Domino nostro Iesu Christo, et cum Spiritu sancto, te supplex alloquor, oro et invoco, ad te confugio, tuam misericordiam et opem veris gemitibus imploro, exaudi me, iuxta promissiones tuas, propter filium Mediatorem Iesum Christum, tu es Pater noster, hoc est, tu vis nobis esse placatus, nos recipere et exaudire propter filium tuum, quem constituisti pro nobis propitiatorem. Ingens, verus et ardens amor est parentum erga natos, propterea vero animi motu ad te patrem amantissimum confugio, quem fiducia patefacti filii certo statuo, miranda et paterna benevolentia mihi in omnibus periculis opitulaturum, et divina consolatione leniturum esse calamitates et aerumnas. Tali aliqua seu forma, seu cogitatione te commonefacias, ac fidem accendas et excites, quoties recitas haec verba: Pater noster.

Qui es in coelis.

Sequitur: Qui es in coelis, hoc est, qui es omnipotens, opitulator, et vere ades ubique. Nam esse in coelis, cum de Deo, seu infinita natura loquimur, non significat occupare certam quandam coeli partem, et in solio sedere supra solem, aut supra sphaeram stellarum fixarum: sed est substantia omnibus locis et creaturis adesse, ac ubique praesentem et efficacem esse, sicut textus affirmat Ieremiae 23.

Coelum et terram ego impleo. Est igitur haec asseveratio in precatione, quaedam confessio de universali praesentia et infinita potentia Dei, quod vere tibi adsit, te respiciat et exaudiat, videat et iudicet motus ac gemitus tui cordis, quodque tanta sit ipsius potentia, ut certo tibi possit opitulari: et quod non adores ligneam aut lapideam statuam, nec idolum aureum vel argenteum, sed unicum, verum, aeternum, omnipotentem, vivum, sapientem, bonum, beneficum, veracem, castum, iustum atque misericordem Deum, qui se per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum resuscitatione mortuorum, et aliis miraculis patefecit, ac vere vult et potest nobis opem ferre. Hanc cogitationem debes addere ad haec verba: Qui es in coelis.

In qua recitatione simul consideretis, quanta coecitas et insania sit, invocare Sanctos, qui ex hac vita decesserunt. Isti enim nec intuentur cor tuum, nec te praesentes audiunt, nec ubique adsunt. Sed invocatio compellans mortuos Sanctos tam est incerta, inanis, et irrita, quam si tu hominem prorsus ignotum, ignorantem, absentem, longeque disiunctum, ridicule compelles et alloquaris in cubiculo tuo.

Verbi causa, si dicas: Ah mi Domine Pastor Ecclesiae Lubecensis iuva me, vel ora pro me. Ille enim nec videt motus, nec audit vota tui cordis, ac nescit quidem se invocari. Talis invocatio, quae fit ad surdos et ignorantes, quid quaeso differt ab adoratione idololatrica et ethnica marmorearum seu lignearum statuarum? Hanc manifestam et crassam idolomaniam simul in recitatione tua mens cogitatione depingat, serioque detestetur, ut certo discas invocare verum Deum, nec dubites vere tibi Deum adesse, vere aspicere, iudicare, exaudire gemitus tui cordis, velle ac posse tibi opitulari, dare vitam et salutem propter filium suum, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Nunc sequuntur ordine petitiones. Audivistis autem supra commonefactionem de rebus petendis in precatione recensendis. Debent enim precantes certum aliquod beneficium, necessarium vel animae vel corpori a Deo nominatim petere, et exspectare. Porro, primum, summum, et maxime necessarium bonum est vera Dei agnitio, ac vera et incorrupta doctrina, de qua notitia et celebratione Dei concionatur etiam primum praeceptum. Ac sicut primum mandatum Decalogi requirit et praecipit, ne habeas Deos alienos, sed ut verum Deum recte agnoscas, credas eius verbo, habeas veram fiduciam erga Deum, verum timorem et dilectionem Dei super omnia: ita docet nos Dominus initio petere, ut possimus inchoare et praestare cultum interiorem, et obedientiam cordis erga primum praeceptum. Exorditur itaque a praecipuo et omnium maxime necessario bono: Sanctificetur nomen tuum, quasi dicat: Ah Domine Deus accende in nobis puram, veram, et sanctam agnitionem nominis tui, hoc est, da nobis puram et sinceram doctrinam sine corruptelis, ne vel errores amplectamur, vel idololatricos cultus recipiamus, sed effice, ut te verum et unicum Deum, Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui te patefecisti per hunc filium Iesum Christum, ab initio missum ad Ecclesiam, crucifixum et resuscitatum, sancte agnoscamus, tibi vere credamus, te recte invocemus, colamus, ac celebremus. Custodi nos clementer, ne fanaticis et idololatricis furoribus animi nostri fascinentur, tolle idololatriam et omnes impias opiniones, effice, ut tu verus Deus recte innotescas, vere agnoscaris, vera fide invoceris, colaris et celebereris.

Nomen enim significat notitiam seu agnitionem. Hic igitur observabis, quod primum Decalogi praeceptum, et haec prima petitio congruant, quodque loquantur de vera patefactione, agnitione, invocatione ac celebratione Dei.

Adveniat regnum tuum.

Vera agnitio non sit otiosa speculatio, sed lux ardens divinitus accensa, cordibus afferens aeternam iustitiam, laetitiam et vitam, iuxta dictum Christi: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te verum Deum, et Iesum quem misisti esse Christum. Effectus itaque verae agnitionis est iustitia et vita aeterna. Propterea de effectu primae petitionis dicitur: Adveniat regnum tuum, hoc est, tu per ministerium et vocem doctrinae tuae regenera, rege, guberna nos Spiritu sancto, inchoa in nobis regnum tuum in hac vita, et perfice post hanc vitam, sis in nobis efficax, accende per vocem Evangelii et agnitionem tui, veram fidem, iustitiam et vitam aeternam in cordibus nostris, destrue regnum diaboli. Non concedas diabolo, ut praestigiis suis nostros animos capiat, et deinde implicatos et irretitos horribiliter impellat et evertat. Habit et ac regnet Iesus Christus filius tuus potenter et efficaciter, ac mansionem faciat in nobis, sicut ipse promisit, inquiens: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et Pater meus diliget illum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Caeterum et haec ipsa petitio pertinet ad primum ac secundum praeceptum Decalogi. Oportet enim ista duo coniungi, et utrumque simul in nobis inchoari, veram scilicet agnitionem Dei, efficaciam divinam, seu motus divinos excitatos et accensos per lucem doctrinae coelestis et agnitionem Dei. Nam vera cognitio praecedit, vivificatio sequitur, ac Deus est efficax per suum verbum, suaeque vocis cogitatione convertit et vivificat assentientes. Petis ergo in his primis atque praecipuis petitionibus summa et amplissima beneficia, veram lucem doctrinae, veram fidem, timorem Dei, dilectionem Dei, spem, consolationem et vitam aeternam, victoriam denique adversus Diabolum, et adversus tua peccata.

## 6:10 Sermons on Matthew
Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. The Lord makes the beginning of the prayer from the true knowledge of God, and the efficacy, or divine governance, in us ourselves. Wherefore now follows the third petition, pertaining to the third and fourth commandments of the Decalogue, which speak of vocations and functions. And now you do not ask for private goods for yourself alone, but rather for those that are common and public, salutary for any vocations, orders, and states whatsoever. For you pray for the ministry of the Gospel, for magistrates and the polity, or for the good of the public state, for economic or domestic governance, both of your own family and of others: Ah Lord God, may You Yourself rule and aid Your functions, so that in every governance, administration, and vocation, Your will may be done, that is, that those things which You have commanded may be done, that they may be pleasing and acceptable to You, namely, that preachers and ministers of the Church may teach rightly, faithfully, and holily; that kings, princes, consuls, and all who are in authority may establish, rule, and defend republics with pious and salutary counsels; that fathers and mothers may honestly take care that their children are educated, instructed, and disciplined according to heavenly doctrine; and that each one in his own place may perform his duty rightly and happily, and that all may remain joined and coupled to You, O God, as living members to their true head, and that all may obey You, and not, being torn away, depart and wander from the true head.

Take away all scandals of governors and others which offend Your will. Do not grant that the devils may sow false doctrine, or scatter among us foul errors and contumelious things against God, by which they tear men away from God, just as they deceived Adam and Eve and drew them away from Your will. Let not the devils kindle tyrannies and unjust wars against Your will, lest there follow most sad devastations of Churches, the destruction of discipline, and of the pious studies of youth.

This third member speaks of these great matters: Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Therefore, as often as you recite these words, think that you are here asking not only for yourself, but for the whole body of the Church, for individual orders and states, for all governments, assemblies, and kinds of life. And you ought often and much to consider this in your mind, which I have previously warned must be diligently weighed and kept in sight. The Son of God Himself commanded that such great things be asked for, namely, the conservation of heavenly doctrine, the governance and divine efficacy in us, the salutary governance of Churches, and likewise of governments and polities, so that the little Churches may be cherished and protected. These are certainly matters and petitions of the greatest moment, and of all that can be thought of and named or comprehended in prayer, they are the highest and most ample; nevertheless, because our Lord Jesus Christ commanded that we ask for these great goods, neither will our vows be in vain, nor will our cries be empty and useless. Let us also remember that the greatest and most necessary things are therefore comprehended in this form of prayer, delivered by divine counsel, so that we, having embraced them in thought, might be moved by care for others and for the whole Church, lest living from day to day in Cyclopean security and wildness, we should be without solicitude, and not be grieved for others, but with the mind and thought of each one fixed on the public salvation, we might look upon and embrace the whole Church, and the entire political government, and moved by the calamities of the Church, the republic, parents, children, and friends, we might demand that aid be brought not only to us, but also to others. Therefore, let us consider common and private necessities, and especially the public dangers of regions, which grant us hospitality and honest studies, and let us ask to be ruled by divine light in our vocation, in all counsels, in defending the purity of the Church, in teaching, in governing the republic, and in honest discipline.

Latin:

Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in coelo sic et in terra. Dominus facit initium precationis a vera Dei agnitione, et efficacia, seu gubernatione divina in nobis ipsis. Quare nunc sequitur tertia petitio, pertinens ad tertium et quartum praeceptum Decalogi, quae de vocationibus et functionibus loquuntur. Nec iam privata tantum bona tibi ipsi petis, sed potius communia et publica quibuslibet vocationibus, ordinibus, et statibus salutaria. Oras etenim pro ministerio Evangelii, pro magistratibus et politia, seu pro bono statu publico, pro oeconomica seu domestica gubernatione, cum tuae familiae tum aliarum: Ah Domine Deus, tu regas ipse et adiuves tuas functiones, ut in omni gubernatione, administratione, vocatione, Tua voluntas fiat, id est, ut fiant ea, quae Tu mandasti, fiant tibi grata et placentia, videlicet, ut concionatores et Ecclesiae ministri recte, fideliter sancteque doceant, ut reges, principes, consules, ac omnes qui praesunt, piis et salutaribus consiliis constituant, regant ac defendant respublicas, ut patres matresque familias honeste curent suos liberos educari, erudiri et castigari iuxta doctrinam coelestem, utque singuli suo loco officium suum rite et feliciter faciant, ac maneant omnes adiuncti copulatique tibi Deo, tamquam membra viva suo vero capiti, et omnes tibi obediant, nec avulsi discedant et aberrent a vero capite.

Tolle omnia scandala gubernatorum et aliorum quae offendunt tuam voluntatem. Non concedas ut diaboli serant falsam doctrinam, spargant inter nos tetros errores et contumeliosos adversus Deum, quibus homines avellant a Deo, sicut Adam et Evam deceptos abstraxerunt a tua voluntate. Non accendant diaboli odio tui tyrannides et iniusta bella contra tuam voluntatem, ne sequantur tristissimae vastationes Ecclesiarum, interitus disciplinae et piorum sudiorum iuventutis.

De his tantis rebus loquitur hoc tertium membrum: Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in coelo, sic etiam in terra. Proinde quoties haec verba recitas, cogita, te hic non solum pro te petere, sed pro toto corpore Ecclesiae, pro singulis ordinibus et statibus, pro omnibus regiminibus, coetibus et vitae generibus. Ac saepe multumque debes hoc tuo cum animo considerare, quod antea monui diligenter expendendum et in conspectu tenendum esse. Filius Dei iussit ipse peti tantas res, videlicet, conservationem coelestis doctrinae, gubernationem et efficaciam divinam in nobis, gubernationem salutarem Ecclesiarum, item regiminum et politiarum, ut Ecclesiolae misellae foveantur et protegantur. Ilae certe sunt res atque petitiones maximi momenti, omniumque, quae cogitari ac nominari seu oratione comprehendi possunt, summae et amplissimae; veruntamen quia Dominus noster Iesus Christus praecepit, ut haec tanta bona petamus, nec irrita vota nostra, nec inanes et inutiles erunt clamores nostri. Meminerimus etiam, maximas maximeque necessarias res ideo comprehensas esse in hac forma precationis, divino consilio tradita, ut nos eas cogitatione complexi, afficeremur, aliorum et totius Ecclesiae cura, ne securitate et feritate Cyclopica viventes in diem, essemus sine solicitudine, nec angeremur pro aliis, sed mente et cogitatione cuiusque in publica salute defixis, intueremur et complecteremur totam Ecclesiam, et universum regimen politicum, motique calamitatibus Ecclesiae, reipublicae, parentum, liberorum, et amicorum, non nobis tantum, sed etiam aliis opem ferri flagitaremus. Itaque consideremus communes et privatas necessitates, inprimisque publica pericula regionum, quae nobis et honestis studiis hospitia concedunt, ac petamus nos luce divina regi in vocatione, in omnibus consiliis, in tuenda puritate Ecclesiae, in docendo, in regenda republica et honesta disciplina.

## 6:11 Sermons on Matthew
Give us this day our daily bread.

The preceding petitions, prescribed in the best order, have wisely begun from the first commandment, namely, from the knowledge of God, and the efficacy, or divine governance, in us. It is very profitable to well note and understand this most apt order, and it brings much light and clarity in teaching. This fourth petition: Give us this day our daily bread, speaks of corporal goods, of the life and safety of bodies, of good health, of food, hospitality, a home, peace, defense, and finally of all the comforts, protections, and supports of life, just as in the present life bodies are in need of many and diverse things: food, drink, good health, certain economies, possessions, little nests and huts, and the happy and pious administration of polities, which provide for us hospices, peace or public tranquility, contracts, etc., just as we see that this external and bodily life is in need of the help, services, works, and protections of many men. Nor is there any human wisdom and diligence so great that it can sufficiently understand and foresee, much less express, how many and how diverse things are needed for retaining and protecting the life of bodies. For I am not now declaiming about things not necessary for life, such as unnecessary equipment, pomp, and profusion, about which it is by no means fitting to understand this petition, which speaks only of all bodily goods necessary in this life.

These daily and necessary benefits, therefore, as far as it can be done, should all come to mind, and be in the sight of those reciting this petition: Our Father who art in heaven, give us this day our daily bread, that is, give us all the comforts of the body, sustain and prolong our life, give us good health, so that we may be able to endure the labors of our vocations, give us sustenance, food, drink, give us peace, moderate tranquility, hospices, governments, marriages, households, so that offspring may be cherished and educated, protect our homes, our little huts and small towns, give us favorable weather, fertility of the fields, crops, grain, give us good success in the duties of our vocation, happiness in political and economic administration, success in the communication of things through contracts in business, in my trade, grant my little ones long and happy spans of life, give strength of body and vigor of mind, do not allow in these regions either Turkish or civil wars, or seditions, for barbaric devastation to occur, defend our little houses, lest they perish by fires or other disasters. Remember that these and similar bodily necessities are to be considered and weighed by you with your own mind with true groans, as often as you pray: Give us this day our daily bread. In which reflection many most grave, most wholesome, and most important doctrines will have to be learned, meditated upon, and fixed in your innermost senses by you.

For first someone might say: What is the point of asking for these benefits, when God himself taxes, accuses, and prohibits anxiety about the morrow, or about feeding the belly, about sustenance, food, drink, defense, and other comforts of life? Also, what does the petition profit? Since God wishes us to be afflicted, to be prepared to bear poverty, and to offer ourselves to obedience in enduring adversities? Also, the Gospel commands us to seek eternal life, not present and bodily goods. Also, many doctors have written that these things are not a care to God, nor is bodily bread or the goods of the body to be understood in the customary prayer, but they contend that it speaks of heavenly and eternal goods. To such reasonings and objections, which undoubtedly come to the mind of all sensible people, it would be worth the effort to observe this response diligently, to understand it rightly, and to remember it well: about which, indeed, ecclesiastical writers have handed down very little.

Response. The eternal and omnipotent God most truly founded the human race in the beginning, with admirable counsel, ineffable wisdom, and immense goodness, for eternal life, joy, and communion with himself. The same God, after the fall, through and because of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, having redeemed men and received them into grace, again called them back from death, and restored them to life, righteousness, and eternal glory, and gave promises concerning the remission of sins, the restoration of salvation, the consummation of righteousness, and heavenly and eternal benefits. Let us establish that these things are most true, with the firmest assent. It is necessary, however, that in this life before bodily death, conversion to God should take place, and true faith, true knowledge of God, vivification, consolation, and obedience should begin and grow. For God wills that in this miserable mass, the eternal Church should exist and be gathered in this narrow course of mortal life. And unless in the present life these beginnings of divine light, wisdom, consolation, and newness are kindled in us, by which we are prepared for the eternal school, there will be no access for us afterwards to the heavenly Church, which will enjoy the sight, communion, wisdom, and goodness of God in all eternity. As these things are true, certain, and immovable, so it is absolutely necessary to learn them, to remember them, and to embrace them with the firmest faith.

Here, therefore, hold to the saying which ought to be most known to all: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, that is, who before they departed from here, acknowledged the Lord, and persevering in faith and true invocation, in this life commended themselves to the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ. they piously commended to Christ.

And so Paul says: We shall be clothed with eternal salvation, if only we are found clothed and not naked, that is, if at that judgment, which we are about to undergo after death, we bring the beginnings of eternal righteousness.

It must therefore be firmly and certainly established that it is necessary in this mortal life for the gathering of the eternal Church to take place through the Son of God, who gives life to those who believe by the voice of the Gospel, and that it is necessary for you yourself to be converted to God and to become a member or citizen of the Church of God before bodily death, if you wish after the resurrection to be given life with all the saved in eternal life, in which God will be seen visibly and immediately.

Every human being ought to fix this foundation in their minds, know it familiarly, constantly embrace it, and hold it with both hands.

From this foundation follows this: Since it is necessary for the Church to be begun in this life, which will celebrate God in all eternity, undoubtedly these beginnings of sanctification in the human race will be a care to God, and He will paternally consult and provide for this weak and fleeting life of men, in which He wishes to show His presence, wishes always for some Church to be surviving, and therefore wishes to grant some spaces of life, to preserve bodies, families, polities, to cherish, protect, and propagate our life, as long as it has seemed good to Him, for the sake of the salvation of His Church, to sustain and conserve by His immense goodness, while the functions of the body, generation, nutrition, and the like endure, this propagation and association of the human race, and until He Himself wishes offspring to be procreated and educated, the earth to be made fruitful, the ministry of His voice to be heard, political regimes to remain, and through the preaching of the Gospel many men to be called and prepared for the inheritance of eternal salvation.

For if many gatherings of men must in this way, namely, through the ministry of the Gospel in this mortal and miserable life, be converted to God and be given life and restored to eternal salvation, certainly the weak nature of men has need of food, drink, agriculture, contracts, buying, selling, division, and the ownership of things according to laws, public peace, the good state of empires, political rule, etc.

Therefore it is said in the Psalm: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, but we who live, we bless the Lord.

The dead cannot by the ministry of the human voice preach and celebrate divine benefits in this bodily life, but we who live testify and confess, giving praise to God for His mercy, so that His glory may be known in the whole human race.

From this foundation Paul hands down this rule, in the first to Timothy, chapter four: The Gospel, or piety, has the promise of the present life and of the future.

Therefore, let the promises of both kinds always be in your sight, and you ought to consider their differences and degrees, and the order in which they are to be sought.

For those inept writers lacked both learning and spiritual judgment who imagined that this prayer does not speak of bodily and present goods.
