Likewise, that it is unworthy to ask for the goods of the body from God.

Let these insipid statements, as if they were ravings born from pernicious darkness and full of impiety, be exploded.

On the contrary, you must firmly establish that God has handed down promises of both kinds, both eternal and temporal, and diligently learn how faith is to be exercised and stirred up in both.

Know that the promise of eternal salvation, by which God for Christ's sake offers and gives us the remission of sins, righteousness, the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life, is always to be embraced and held by faith.

And first and before all things, let faith receive and apprehend reconciliation and eternal benefits, and thus through and for the sake of the mediator Christ, approach and flee to God.

And do not doubt that you are a member of the Church of God and an heir of eternal life.

Know that this first and highest promise concerning eternal things is ratified, firm, and most certain for you at all times, and truly believe that you are a son of God received into grace, and an heir of eternal salvation, and sustain yourself with this faith and hope, whatever happens to your body in this life, whether you are rich or poor, whether in sound or afflicted health, whether in great power, or driven into exile, whether in punishments or outside of punishments.

These external and bodily things do not snatch away from you grace and eternal life, but let your heart most firmly believe at all times, even when you seem deserted and cast out by the whole nature of things, that the perpetual voice of the Gospel remains always and without any exception most true: God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life.

This promise and consolation is immovable and eternal, and is not changed on account of poverty, diseases, and other bodily or temporal punishments, if only we retain the faith of reconciliation and the hope of eternal life.

This, therefore, is the first, highest, and most efficacious consolation, and the chief doctrine concerning the eternal promise, which consolation ought always to be the principal one, whether we enjoy tranquility, or are exercised and oppressed by human miseries inextricable by human counsel in this life, just as David, cast out from his kingdom and stripped of all his glory, nevertheless retained the eternal consolation, sustaining himself with the promise of grace, even if he were not to be restored to the lost earthly kingdom. And Job says: Even if he slays me, I will hope in him. Indeed, it is necessary that in you yourself this faith, hope, patience, likewise consolation, light, righteousness, and eternal life be begun, kindled, and confirmed in this present miserable, weak, and mortal life. For this order has been established by the admirable counsel and most wise will of God. Nor let us ourselves be disturbed by the deceits of disputations, because this is the truth divinely revealed in the expressed word.

There follow now the other promises concerning bodily goods.

Because God wishes the Church to be gathered and begun in this life, he also gives bodily promises, and has taught us in this prayer to cry out, and specifically to ask of him all the goods of the body necessary for this life. Far, therefore, and utterly cast out from your minds those profane, delirious, and diabolical imaginations which pretend that bodily goods are not to be sought from God, nor that bodily things are a care to God.

But rather let it be weighed and considered that God, by a singular counsel, has also given bodily life, and does not wish it to be suddenly destroyed, but to preserve it, and wishes to begin his eternal Church in the custom of this mortal life, and effectively to show his presence, and wishes that the necessities of life be sought from him and expected in invocation, and in this way wishes the knowledge of himself to grow in invocation amidst dangers and miraculous deliverances. Let there be opposed, therefore, to these false imaginations the very words of the prayer, by which the Lord himself taught us to ask: Give us this day our daily bread.

Since, therefore, the Lord himself teaches you to pray and ask in this way, you ought certainly and firmly to conclude that God wishes to bestow these goods, that he demands that we seek them, and that we ask for them from him by faith and expect them, and to affirm that he is worshipped by this honor. And therefore he says expressly in the Psalm: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me; you shall establish and confess concerning the presence of God, that I am not far from you, but that I am present to hear, to guard, and to protect you, and that I am not an idle nor a slothful God, doing nothing, not efficacious, nor helping, but that I wish to assist you in this life, and afterwards to give eternal life through and for the sake of the Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.

To this let there be added also, for worthy consideration, the doctrine concerning the four most grave and principal causes for which the promises concerning bodily goods have been given to the Church.

The first is, God wishes us to know and believe that he is truly the creator, author, giver, and preserver of these benefits, and that bodily life itself and all external or temporal goods are truly divine works and gifts, and that they cannot be prepared, or increased, or retained by human diligence alone, without the will, help, and government of God. To this effect the text of Acts 17 says: In him we live, and move, and have our being, that is, through him our life is given, sustained, and cherished.

Likewise, Proverbs 10: The blessing of the Lord makes rich, that is, we do not become rich, we do not prepare nor guard wealth only by human industry and our own labors, but it is necessary that the help of God be added, assisting honest labors and our obedience in our calling. Thus also the Psalm says: Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it.

Second cause.

Since God begins his eternal Church in this mortal life, he also wishes to give to this assembly, in which his knowledge and true invocation shine, the necessities for the conservation of bodily life. And that we might have consolation, and not be broken by despair, but might propagate the doctrine with good hope, God has expressed this will of his in many promises most clearly and sweetly: and these words are known to you all: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you, that is, acknowledge God, seek the true doctrine and the glory of God, perform true worship, obey God according to the Gospel, and he will clemently provide you with the necessary supports of life.

Let us know also in this place that God always wishes to endure in this life until the end, and will certainly preserve the Church, because he has promised bodily goods, life, food, defense, and shelter, without which this assembly, to be gathered by the voice of the ministry, cannot live, according to the...

The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord, that is, the dead cannot with external confession and testimony sound forth a voice concerning God, among us who are living.

The third cause is, that God also wishes to be acknowledged in such a way that faith and invocation may be stirred up and exercised in daily necessity. For so many and so diverse temporal things, so many various external occasions and afflictions, so many manifold bodily affairs and dangers—such as life, good health, diseases, poverty, food, peace, wars, etc.—are to be thought of as being, as it were, certain schools and gymnasia, in which the true acknowledgment and true invocation of God is to be learned, exercised, and confirmed. God himself testifies to this in the Psalm: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me; that is, thou shalt behold my presence, thou shalt acknowledge that I am present with thee, that I truly hear your groans and cries, that I certainly will to help you; which honor I wish to be attributed to me, I do not wish to be removed as an idle, yawning, and sleepy God, who neither wishes to bring help, nor is effective.

The fourth cause: all promises of bodily benefits ought to be reminders of the highest, chief, and eternal promise of grace, or of reconciliation and eternal salvation on account of the mediator, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

For God wishes to give the good things of the body for this reason, because in this life, before bodily death, it is necessary that regeneration be begun, and that the beginnings of eternal salvation be made, so that he may gather and preserve some Church in the custom of the present life. Wherefore faith, universally in every petition for present goods, should at the same time look upon the redeemer and savior Christ, and first believe and receive the remission of sins; nay, it should know that one cannot approach God, nor can bodily help be sought or expected, unless after we have been raised up by the promise of grace and the confidence of reconciliation, we establish that God is appeased, that he receives us into grace, and that he forgives us on account of Christ. Thus the Lord himself says: No one can come to the Father, except through the Son. Likewise, 2 Corinthians 1: All the promises of God are Amen, that is, certain, ratified, firm, true, through and on account of Christ.

Remember these four causes well, and fix them in your minds, why God has handed down the promises of bodily goods, and how they are to be used; and learn in this way to exercise faith equally in both kinds of promises, both spiritual and bodily. For he who rightly thinks about and understands the kinds, degrees, and order of the promises, concerning the distinction of which we have just spoken, has both a most clear light in Christian doctrine and, in any temptation, whether spiritual or bodily, an effective consolation. Thus far I have recounted brief and necessary admonitions concerning the distinction of both kinds of promises, and concerning the petition for bodily goods, which he who will consider attentively and exercise assiduously will experience in the thing itself, that invocation, if it be done in this order, as has been said, is not vain but effective.

But here human weakness objects to the contrary: Since we know that in this life we must be afflicted, what is the point of asking? The brief and clear answer is: Let us know both, that we must be afflicted and yet that we must live, according to the verse of the Psalm: The Lord has chastened me, and has not delivered me to death. Thus Jeremiah cries out concerning the mitigation of the calamities of the Church: Correct me, O Lord, yet in judgment, not in fury, lest thou bring me to nothing. God has established and ordained both by a wonderful and ineffable counsel. He wishes to punish sin through and on account of his justice, he also wishes the Church to be subject to the cross, and yet when he has commanded and requires invocation, he wishes us to establish that prayer is never empty and vain, but that he himself, in his immense mercy, is about to mitigate both the punishment and the cross for those who call upon him, lest the Church be utterly destroyed on earth. Clearly, therefore, it can be understood that prayers are not for that reason useless, but are pleasing and effective to God, even if we are forced to carry a part of the holy cross after the example of Simon of Cyrene; nevertheless, Christ stands by, and helps and assists us. Let it suffice to have briefly warned of this in this place, for we shall add more reminders later concerning this kind of petition.

And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

You know, and you ought to meditate upon it diligently and always have it in your sight, that there are two kinds of divine promises: eternal and bodily. The promise concerning eternal goods is the promise of grace, of the remission of sins, of the gift of the Holy Spirit, and of eternal salvation. This is the chief promise of the Gospel, on account of which the Son of God was sent to us, and was appointed mediator, redeemer, liberator, and savior. For if only bodily goods were promised to us, and we were not to have eternal salvation, a consolation would be proposed to us that is neither firm, nor efficacious, but empty and vanishing. But God wishes to communicate to us in all eternity His wisdom and goodness, and He has decreed the consummation of His immense mercy and this admirable liberation in this way: that in eternal beatitude, wisdom, justice, and joy, we may live and enjoy His clear and visible sight, and without sin, without death, without any calamities, we may celebrate Him perpetually. This promise of grace and eternal goods must be distinguished far from the promises of bodily goods.

Secondly, the rule must always be held that in every petition, the first and highest promise of grace and the remission of sins on account of Christ must shine forth before other promises of bodily benefits.

Therefore, it is necessary for you, if you wish to approach God and ask for goods necessary for the body, first and perpetually to bring this faith concerning the remission of sins and gratuitous acceptance, by which you specifically ask for and receive reconciliation, and by which you certainly determine that your sins are remitted to you, that you are received, that your vows are regarded, and your prayers are heard on account of the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ. For one cannot approach, nor is there any access to God without the mediator and propitiator, the Son of God. Thirdly, it must be known that this is the eternal and immovable will of God, and a most severe and immutable command, that at all times you believe most firmly that the remission of sins, justification, the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal salvation are given to you freely through and on account of Christ.

Thus, the eternal promise concerning reconciliation and the mediator remains immovable, certain, and ratified for the believer, whether you obtain life and the benefits of the body, or whether bodily liberation does not happen.

Nevertheless, because God, in this miserable mortal life, kindles in us the beginnings of His light, justice, and eternal life, and wishes the Church to be begun through the ministry of the Gospel and conversion or repentance in this narrow course of mortal life, He grants and provides also bodily goods—life, safety of the body, good health, homes, governments, peace, food, a spouse, children, households, good success in labors, etc.

Therefore, He has expressed His will that He will truly give these bodily goods as well, and He adds to the Gospel specifically promises concerning bodily things, as when He says: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you. He also commands that faith and invocation be exercised daily, asking for and expecting the sustenance and defense of our bodies and other necessary things from His goodness and mercy on account of Christ.

You heard this doctrine concerning the distinction of promises in the previous sermon.

And because the preceding petition, "Give us this day our daily bread," etc., speaks of bodily benefits, therefore the Lord immediately adds and repeats the petition for the remission of sins, which indeed must be applied before all things in every prayer, whatever thing is asked, must be comprehended at the same time, and must always shine forth before other petitions.

For when our infirmity and unworthiness immediately clamor in our invocation, trembling minds always flee from God and think thus: "How willingly would I ask for help, if my sins did not deter me, which are so many and so great that I do not dare to flee to or approach God."

Likewise: "If I did not have such sad falls, God would undoubtedly mitigate the punishments for me." The hearts of all the pious experience and feel these doubts and trepidations, even if savage, barbaric, and Cyclopean men, or secure hypocrites, are ignorant of them.

Wherefore our Lord Jesus Christ Himself has proposed to us here the most ample and abundant consolation, adding immediately this sweetest petition: "Forgive us our debts," etc.

As if He were saying: "I am not unaware that you are distressed and terrified by the sight of your unworthiness and your most sad falls, that you think you are cast away, that your cries are in vain, that God rejects and does not care for your murmuring, that your sins are too many and great, that you must expect punishments, not help or liberation."

Against these reasonings, the Son of God consoles you thus: "It is right, and pleasing to God, that you acknowledge and confess your sins. But you must not fail in God, nor be oppressed by desperation; rather, know that God wishes to forgive you and remit your sins on account of Christ, and seriously commands that you ask for remission, and not only ask, but that you also believe certainly and firmly that all your sins, whether great or small, all stains and infirmities, are remitted to you freely on account of the mediator Christ, not on account of any merits of yours."

Here, therefore, let your mind attentively and seriously, while praying, [contemplate] the chief heads of the doctrine of the Gospel, which you hear illustrated daily by the benefit of God, concerning grace, concerning the remission of sins, concerning the mediator, concerning faith, let him diligently propose to himself, think upon, and contemplate.

Wherefore, fix this petition in your minds. For since our Lord Jesus Christ himself has commanded that remission be asked for, and indeed asked for daily, he undoubtedly wishes to remit to us all sins, however great they may be, and to forgive all daily and manifold infirmities and stains.

But at the same time you must be warned here that you must by no means persevere in sins against conscience, but you ought to know that it is necessary in any true invocation that repentance, or conversion to God, should come to be or grow in us, because the divine oath clearly says: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. For it is a copulative prayer; these two are joined: conversion and consolation, the remission of sins and life, just as these are faithfully explained elsewhere and are often repeated.

But as to what is added: As we also forgive our debtors, we are admonished and obligated by the command of Christ that we also should forgive.

And again, your conscience interpellates at this point: If I cannot receive remission unless I myself also forgive others, reconciliation becomes uncertain, nor shall I be able to struggle out of the doubt as to whether I shall obtain remission. Because however much I may struggle against hatreds and the desire for revenge, I feel that nevertheless there always remain some traces or scars of indignation and animosities against some people.

To this objection, let a clear and true response be held: The remission of sins is offered and given to you through faith, freely, on account of our Lord Jesus Christ, not on account of your forgiveness or any other work. This foundation you should remember well, observe diligently, and embrace firmly with both hands, or more truly, with your whole heart.

It is most true, however, that in this consolation, when hearts are sustained and raised up by faith, it is necessary that at the same time a good purpose should exist and be initiated, so that you do not persevere in crimes against conscience, but truly be converted to God, and do not henceforth retain the will to rush into adulteries or the desire to harm others. This conversion, or non-simulated change of a prior purpose, must exist in us, and this is most manifest.

Christ speaks of this serious amendment, that it is necessary that the righteousness of a good conscience, or a good purpose, should follow. For although there are and remain in us in this life many not light stains, depraved inclinations, the flames of vicious affections, and a huge and manifold infirmity remains, yet it is absolutely necessary that there be repentance in us, and that in conversion sins against conscience be laid aside, so that we do not indulge in internal hatred and private desire for revenge, so that we do not knowingly wish to harm or oppress others against the command of God, but that we strive to heal offenses as much as we can with reconciled or recovered wills. This is the true, native, and proper meaning of the words of Christ, which we should diligently and attentively consider and weigh in prayer.

For although it is most certain that our sins are remitted to us freely on account of Christ, not on account of any merits of ours, yet at the same time one must know that it is the most severe and immutable will of God that we be converted to him, and not persevere in sins against conscience. Wherefore, when the mind retains contempt for God, it is not heard; indeed, it cannot even approach and flee to God as long as perseverance in an evil purpose remains.

For with what mouth, with what conscience would such an invocation be made: Ah Lord God, have mercy on me, be propitious, forgive, spare me, while I meanwhile indulge in all the furies of opinions, lusts, and cruelty, and petulantly proceed to satisfy depraved desires with murders, rapines, thefts, impostures, and lies? These prayers God abominates and execrates, as Solomon also affirms in the twenty-eighth chapter of Proverbs: He who turns away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be execrable.

And Paul says in express words: Do not err, God is not mocked, neither adulterers, nor fornicators, nor murderers, etc., shall possess the kingdom of God. Likewise in John, chapter nine: God does not hear sinners, that is, those not doing repentance, nor casting away the purpose of violating the law of God against conscience.

See, Christ serves this necessary doctrine here, and added to the petition of remission, by which we are warned concerning repentance, that we should bring conversion to God, and not, while retaining the purpose of sinning, loosen the rein on beastly desires and diabolical furies, and meanwhile dream that we are invoking God and swell with the persuasion of holiness: just as, alas, in this last time the world takes to itself infinite license, and The savagery of many is so great that they endure no bonds of discipline, who nevertheless meanwhile pretend that they have faith, that they invoke God with true movements of the soul, that they are living and chosen members of the Church, while they live in security and Cyclopean brutality, and yield and submit to the devil, who drives them to adulteries, homicides, and other foul crimes.

Unless we correct this remarkable perversity, enormous petulance, and Cyclopean savagery with a serious amendment of morals, sad and horrible punishments will follow.

Indeed, public punishments are raging in plain sight; you see internal wars, the devastation of commonwealths, and a great multitude of calamities converging: and although God has hitherto mercifully mitigated the present hardships, I greatly fear, lest, being so often irritated by the savagery of our morals, He may vent His wrath more violently and implacably, and these regions be oppressed by much sadder punishments, because there is no limit to the petulance, contumacy, and affected wickedness of the younger generation.

O eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, for the sake of Thy glory help us, govern, protect, and preserve Thy Church, the purity and studies of heavenly doctrine, discipline, and moderate polities; do not allow the saddest and infinite devastations to occur, nor Ethnic and Turkish profanity full of filth and contempt for divine justice.

You ought to revolve this very admonition concerning conversion or repentance often and much in your prayer in your mind, and repeat it in thought and memory, and by it bend and rouse yourselves to repentance and amendment.

If anyone in conversion casts away an evil purpose, he at last can cheerfully invoke God with the confidence of a mediator, and feels in his heart peace, tranquility, joy, and consolation, according to the saying of Paul: Being justified by faith, we have peace.

But this confidence, peace, and joy resting in God can by no means exist in your heart at the same time with perseverance in sins against conscience, or with the purpose of indulging in any frenzies whatsoever, and polluting yourself with every crime of turpitude.

But after conversion has begun in the hearts, let faith most firmly lean and rest upon the mediator Christ, and let it certainly conclude that your invocation is pleasing and effective, and that the remission of sins is truly given to you.

You ought to keep this highest and most ample consolation fixed in your mind, and daily, looking upon and remembering it in all your prayer, exercise and confirm your faith, and truly give thanks to God for such great benefits.

And thus far concerning this petition: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

Latin:

Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie.

Praecedentes petitiones optimo ordine praescriptae sapienter exorsae sunt a primo praecepto, videlicet, ab agnitione Dei, et efficacia, seu gubernatione divina in nobis. Istum aptissimum ordinem bene animadvertere ac intelligere valde prodest, et in docendo plurimum lucis et perspicuitatis affert. Haec quarta petitio: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, loquitur de corporalibus bonis, de vita et incolumitate corporum, de bona valetudine, de victu, hospitio, domicilio, pace, defensione, omnibus denique vitae commodis, praesidiis, et adminiculis, sicut in praesenti vita corpora multis et diversis rebus indigent, ciho, potu, bona valetudine, certis oeconomiis, possessionibus, nidulis ac tuguriolis, felici ac pia administratione politiarum, quae praebent nobis hospitia, pace seu tranquillitate publica, contractibus etc., quemadmodum videmus hanc externam et corporalem vitam indigere plurimorum hominum ope, officiis, operis, et praesidiis. Nec est ulla humana sapientia et diligentia tanta, quae satis intelligere ac prospicere, nedum eloqui possit, quot et quam diversis rebus ad retinendam et tuendam vitam corporum opus sit. Non enim iam declamito de rebus vitae non necessariis, ut de non necessariis apparatibus, pompis et profusionibus, de quibus hanc petitionem minime convenit intelligi, quae tantum loquitur de omnibus bonis corporalibus necessariis in hac vita.

Haec igitur quotidiana et necessaria beneficia, quoad eius fieri potest, omnia veniant in mentem, ac in conspectu sint recitantibus hanc petitionem: Pater noster qui es in coelis, panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, hoc est, da nobis omnia corporis commoda, sustenta et proroga nobis vitam, da nobis bonam valetudinem, ut labores vocationum perferre possimus, da victum, cibum, potum, da pacem, mediocrem tranquillitatem, hospitia, politias, coniugia, oeconomias, ut soboles foveri et educari possit, protege domicilia, tuguriola et oppidula nostra, da commodas tempestates, foecunditatem agrorum, fruges, annonam, da bonos successus in officiis vocationis, felicitatem in administratione politica et oeconomica, successus in communicatione rerum per contractus in negotiatione, in opificio meo, concede parvis meis longa et felicia vitae spatia, da vires corporis et vigorem ingeniorum, non sinas in his regionibus vel Turcicis, vel civilibus bellis, vel seditionibus barbaricam vastitatem fieri, defende casulas nostras, ne incendiis aut aliis cladibus pereant. Has et similes corporales necessitates memineris tibi cum animo tuo considerandas et expendendas esse veris gemitibus, quoties oras: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Qua in cogitatione multae gravissimae, saluberrimae, maximique momenti doctrinae tibi discendae, meditandae, intimisque sensibus erunt infigendae.

Nam primo dicat aliquis: Quid attinet haec beneficia petere, cum Deus ipse taxet, accuset, et prohibeat solicitudinem de crastino, seu de pascendo ventre, de victu, cibo, potu, defensione, et aliis vitae commodis? Item quid prodest petitio? cum Deus nos velit affligi, paratos esse ad ferendam paupertatem, et offerre nos ad obedientiam in tolerandis adversis? Item, Evangelium iubet quaerere aeternam vitam, non praesentia et corporalia bona. Item, multi doctores scripserunt, Deo haec non esse curae, nec in usitata precatione intelligendum esse panem corporalem seu bona corporis, sed contendunt eam loqui de coelestibus et aeternis bonis. Ad istiusmodi ratiocinationes et obiectiones, quae cordatis omnibus haud dubie veniunt in mentem, hanc responsionem diligenter observare, recte intelligere, atque bene meminisse operae pretium fuerit: de qua quidem scriptores ecclesiastici valde pauca tradiderunt.

Responsio. Aeternus et omnipotens Deus verissime condidit initio genus humanum, admirando consilio, inenarrabili sapientia, et immensa bonitate, ad aeternam vitam, laetitiam, et consuetudinem cum ipso. Idem post lapsum homines per et propter filium Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, redemtos, et in gratiam receptos rursus revocavit ex morte, ac restituit ad vitam, iustitiam et gloriam aeternam, deditque promissiones de remissione peccatorum, restitutione salutis, consummatione iustitiae, ac coelestibus et aeternis beneficiis. Haec esse verissima, assensione firmissima statuamus. Necesse est autem, ut in hac vita ante mortem corporalem fiat conversio ad Deum, et inchoentur ac crescant vera fides, vera agnitio Dei, vivificatio, consolatio et obedientia. Vult enim Deus, ut in hac misera massa, sit et colligatur aeterna Ecclesia in hoc angusto curriculo vitae mortalis. Ac nisi in praesenti vita haec divinae lucis, sapientiae, consolationis et novitatis initia sint in nobis accensa, quibus ad aeternam scholam praeparamur, non erit postea nobis aditus ad coelestem Ecclesiam, quae Dei conspectu, consuetudine, sapientia et bonitate laeta fruetur in omni aeternate. Quae ut vera, certa et immota sunt, ita prorsus est necessarium ea discere, meminisse, ac firmissima fide amplecti.

Hic ergo teneatis dictum, quod omnibus notissimum esse oportuit, Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur, hoc est, qui antequam hinc decederent, agnoverunt Dominum, et in fide ac vera invocatione perseverantes, in hac vita se filio Dei Domino Iesu Christo pie commendarunt.

Sic et Paulus inquit: Superinduemur aeterna salute, si tamen vestiti et non nudi reperiemur, id est, si ad illud iudicium, quod post mortem subituri sumus, initia iustitiae aeternae afferemus.

Firmiter igitur et certo statuendum est, quod et oporteat in hac mortali vita Ecclesiae aeternae collectionem fieri per filium Dei vivificantem credentes voce Evangelii, et quod necesse sit te ipsum converti ad Deum, et membrum seu civem Ecclesiae Dei fieri ante mortem corporalem, si vis post resurrectionem cum omnibus salvatis vivificari vita aeterna, in qua Deus visibiliter et immediate conspicietur.

Hoc fundamentum singuli homines animis infigere, familiariter nosse, constanter amplecti, et utraque manu retinere debent.

Ex hoc fundamento iam sequitur illud: Cum necesse sit inchoari in hac vita Ecclesiam, Deum celebraturam in omni aeternitate, haud dubie Deo curae erunt haec initia sanctificationis in genere humano, et paterne consulet ac prospiciet huic infirmae fugacique vitae hominum, in qua vult ostendere suam praesentiam, vult semper aliquam Ecclesiam superstitem esse, ideoque vult tribuere aliqua vitae spatia, servare corpora, familias, politias, fovere, protegere et propagare vitam nostram, quamdiu ipsi visum fuerit, propter salutem Ecclesiae suae, immensa bonitate sustentare et conservare, durantibus officiis corporis, generatione, nutritione et similibus, hanc propagationem et consociationem generis humani, et donec ipse voluerit procreari et educari sobolem, foecundari terram, ministerium suae vocis audiri, regimina politica manere, et per Evangelii praedicationem multos homines vocari atque praeparari ad hereditatem salutis aeternae.

Nam si debent multi coetus hominum isto modo, videlicet, per ministerium Evangelii in hac mortali et aerumnosa vita ad Deum converti, et ad aeternam salutem vivificari ac restitui, certe opus est imbecilli hominum naturae cibo, potu, agricultura, contractibus, emtione, venditione, divisione, et proprietate rerum iuxta leges, pace publica, bono statu imperiorum, regimine politico, etc.

Propterea dicitur in Psalmo: Non mortui laudabunt te Domine, sed nos qui vivimus, benedicimus Domino.

Mortui non possunt ministerio vocis humanae praedicare et celebrare divina beneficia in hac vita corporali, sed nos qui vivimus testificamur et confitemur, tribuentes Deo laudem misericordiae, ut innotescat gloria eius in toto genere humano.

Ex hoc fundamento tradit Paulus hanc regulam, primae ad Timotheum quarto: Evangelium, seu pietas promissionem habet praesentis vitae et futurae.

Itaque semper in conspectu sint utriusque generis promissiones, quarum et discrimina gradusque intelligere, et ordinem, quo petendae sunt, considerare debetis.

Ineptis enim scriptoribus illis et eruditio et spirituale iudicium defuit, qui finxerunt hanc precationem non loqui de corporalibus et praesentibus bonis.

Item indignum esse bona corporis a Deo petere.

Haec insulse dicta tanquam deliramenta ex perniciosis tenebris orta, et plena impietatis, explodantur.

Tu contra firmiter statuito, Deum tradidisse utriusque generis promissiones, cum aeternas, tum temporales, et diligenter discito, quomodo fides in utrisque sit exercenda et excitanda.

Scias initio promissionem aeternae salutis, qua Deus propter Christum offert nobis et donat remissionem peccatorum, iustitiam, Spiritum sanctum, et hereditatem vitae aeternae, fide semper amplectendam et retinendam esse.

Ac primum et ante omnia fides accipiat et apprehendat reconciliationem et aeterna beneficia, atque ita per et propter mediatorem Christum accedat atque confugiat ad Deum.

Nec dubites te membrum Ecclesiae Dei et heredem esse vitae aeternae.

Hanc primam et summam promissionem de rebus aeternis scito tibi ratam, firmam, et certissimam esse omni tempore, et vere credito te esse filium Dei receptum in gratiam, ac heredem aeternae salutis, teque hac fide et spe sustentato, quicquid fiat de corporibus in hac vita, sive dives sive pauper, sive integra, sive afflicta valetudine, sive in magna potentia, sive in exilium pulsus, sive in poenis, sive extra poenas sis.

Hae res externae atque corporales non eripiunt tibi gratiam et vitam aeternam, sed omni tempore cor tuum firmissime credat, etiam cum a tota rerum natura desertus et proiectus videris, perpetuam Evangelii vocem semper et sine ulla exceptione manere verissimam: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam.

Haec promissio et consolatio immota et aeterna est, nec mutatur propter paupertatem, morbos, et alias corporales aut temporales poenas, si modo fidem reconciliationis et spem vitae aeternae retineamus.

Est igitur haec primum summa et efficacissima consolatio, ac praecipua doctrina de promissione aeterna, quam consolationem semper oportet esse praecipuam, sive fruamur tranquillitate, sive exerceamur et opprimamur aerumnis humano consilio inextricabilibus, in hac vita, ut David excussus ex regno, et exutus universa gloria sua, tamen retinebat aeternam consolationem, sustentans se promissione gratiae, etiam si non reducendus fuisset in amissum corporale regnum. Et Iob inquit: Etiam si occidet me, sperabo in eum. Imo necesse est in te ipso hanc fidem, spem, patientiam, item, consolationem, lucem, iustitiam et vitam aeternam inchoari, accendi et confirmari in praesenti aerumnosa, imbecilli et mortali vita. Hic enim ordo sancitus est admirando consilio, et sapientissima Dei voluntate. Nec conturbemus ipsi nos praestigiis disputationum, quia haec est veritas divinitus patefacta in verbo expresso.

Sequuntur iam caeterae promissiones de bonis corporalibus.

Quia vult Deus in hac vita colligi et inchoari Ecclesiam, tradit etiam promissiones corporales, et docuit nos in hac precatione clamare, nominatimque a se petere omnia bona corporis ad hanc vitam necessaria. Procul igitur et penitus ex animis reiicite profanas, deliras, et diabolicas imaginationes, quae fingunt, ne petenda esse a Deo bona corporum, nec corporalia Deo curae esse.

Sed potius expendatur et cogitetur, Deum singulari consilio etiam vitam corporalem dedisse, nec eam subito deleri, sed servare velle, velle in consuetudine huius vitae mortalis inchoare suam aeternam Ecclesiam, et efficaciter ostendere suam praesentiam, velle a se peti et exspectari necessaria vitae in invocatione, et hoc modo velle crescere agnitionem sui in invocatione inter pericula et mirandas liberationes. Opponantur itaque falsis imaginationibus istis ipsa verba precationis, quibus ipse Dominus petere nos docuit: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie.

Cum ergo te Dominus ipse doceat ita precari et petere, certo debes ac firmiter statuere, Deum velle haec bona largiri, postulare ut ea nos quaeramus, a seque fide petamus et exspectemus, et affirmare, se hoc honore coli. Ideoque expresse dicit in Psalmo: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me, statues et fateberis de praesentia Dei, quod non absim procul a te, sed quod praesens exaudiam, custodiam et protegam te, nec sim otiosus nec ignavus Deus, nihil agens, non efficax, nec adiuvans, sed quod velim vobis opitulari in hac vita, et postea dare vitam aeternam per et propter filium Dominum Iesum Christum.

Huc addatur etiam digna consideratione doctrina de quatuor causis gravissimis et praecipuis, propter quas Ecclesiae traditae sunt promissiones de bonis corporalibus.

Prima est, Deus vult nos scire et credere, se vere conditorem, autorem, datorem, et conservatorem esse horum beneficiorum, ipsamque corporalem vitam et omnia bona externa, seu temporalia, vere esse opera et dona divina, nec humana diligentia sola, vel parari, vel augeri, vel retineri ea posse, sine voluntate, ope, et gubernatione Dei. In hanc sententiam dicit textus Actorum 17.: In ipso sumus, vivimus, et movemur, id est, per ipsum datur, sustentatur, et fovetur vita nostra.

Item, Proverb. 10.: Benedictio Domini divites facit, hoc est, non ditescimus, non paramus nec tuemur opes tantum humana industria et nostris laboribus, sed necesse est accedere auxilium Dei, iuvantis honestos labores et obedientiam nostram in vocatione. Sic et Psalmus inquit: Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum, frustra laborant aedificantes.

Secunda causa.

Cum Deus inchoët aeternam suam Ecclesiam in hac mortali vita, vult etiam huic coetui, in quo lucet ipsius notitia, et vera invocatio, dare necessaria ad vitae corporalis conservationem. Utque consolationem haberemus, nec frangeremur desperatione, sed bona cum spe propagaremus doctrinam, Deus hanc suam voluntatem in multis promissionibus clarissime ac dulcissime expressit: et nota sunt vobis omnibus haec verba: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis, id est, agnoscite Deum, quaerite veram doctrinam et gloriam Dei, praestate veros cultus, obtemperate Deo iuxta Evangelium, et clementer suppeditabit vobis necessaria vitae praesidia.

Sciamus et illud hoc loco, Deum semper in hac vita usque ad finem durare velle, certoque servaturum esse Ecclesiam, quia bona corporis, vitam, victum, defensionem et hospitia promisit, sine quibus hic coetus voce ministerii colligendus vivere non potest, iuxta dictum:

Non mortui laudabunt te Domine, id est, mortui non possunt externa confessione et testificatione sonare vocem de Deo, inter nos viventes.

Tertia causa est, sic etiam vult agnosci Deus, ut fides et invocatio exsuscitentur et exerceantur in quotidiana necessitate. Quin tot et tam diversae res temporales, tam variae externae occasiones et afflictiones, tam multiplicia corporalia negotia et pericula, ut vita, bona valetudo, morbi, egestas, victus, pax, bella, etc. cogitentur esse ceu scholae et gymnasia quaedam, in quibus discenda, exercenda et confirmanda sit vera agnitio et vera invocatio Dei. Id testatur ipse Deus in Psalmo: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me, hoc est, conspicies meam praesentiam, agnosces me tibi adesse, me vere gemitus et clamores vestros exaudire, me certo velle opitulari, quem honorem volo mihi tribui, nolo me removeri tanquam ignavum, oscitantem, ac somniculosum Deum, qui nec velit opem ferre, nec sit efficax.

Quarta causa, omnes promissiones beneficiorum corporalium debent esse commonefactiones de summa, praecipua et aeterna promissione gratiae, seu reconciliationis et salutis aeternae propter mediatorem filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Nam Deus ideo vult dare bona corporis, quia in hac vita ante mortem corporalem inchoari regenerationem, et salutis aeternae initia fieri necesse est, ut colligat et servet aliquam Ecclesiam in consuetudine praesentis vitae. Quare fides universaliter in omni petitione bonorum praesentium, simul intueatur redemptorem et salvatorem Christum, ac prius credat et accipiat remissionem peccatorum, imo sciat, non posse accedi ad Deum, nec peti aut exspectari auxilium corporale, nisi postquam promissione gratiae, et fiducia reconciliationis erecti statuimus Deum placatum esse, recipere nos in gratiam, et nobis ignoscere propter Christum. Sic Dominus ipse dicit: Nemo potest venire ad Patrem, nisi per filium. Item, 2. Corinth. 1.: Omnes promissiones divinae sunt Amen, id est, certae, ratae, firmae, verae, per et propter Christum.

Has quatuor causas bene mementote, et animis infigite, quare Deus tradiderit promissiones bonorum corporalium, ac quomodo sit utendum, et hoc modo discite, fidem pariter in utriusque generis promissionibus, cum spiritualibus, tum corporalibus exercere. Nam qui genera, gradus et ordinem promissionum, de quarum distinctione modo diximus, recte cogitat et intelligit, is habet et clarissimum lumen in doctrina Christiana, et in quavis tentatione, sive spirituali sive corporali, efficacem consolationem. Hactenus admonitiones breves et necessarias recensui de distinctione utriusque generis promissionum, et de petitione bonorum corporalium, quas qui considerabit attente, et exercebit assidue, re ipsa experietur, invocationem, si fiat hoc ordine, ut dictum est, non irritam sed efficacem esse.

At hic contra obiicit humana imbecillitas: Cum sciamus in hac vita oportere nos affligi, quid attinet petere? Brevis et perspicua responsio est: Sciamus utrumque, et affligi, et tamen vivere nos oportere, iuxta versum Psalmi: Castigans castigavit me Dominus, et morti non tradidit me. Sic Ieremias clamat de mitigatione calamitatum Ecclesiae: Corripe me Domine, veruntamen in iudicio, non in furore, ne ad nihilum redigas me. Utrumque Deus mirabili et inenarrabili consilio sanxit et ordinavit. Vult punire peccatum per et propter suam iustitiam, vult et Ecclesiam subiectam esse cruci, et tamen cum mandaverit ac postulet invocationem, vult nos statuere, quod precatio nunquam sit inanis et irrita, sed quod ipse sit immensa misericordia mitigaturus invocantibus et poenam et crucem, ne prorsus in terris Ecclesia deleatur. Plane igitur et clare potest intelligi, non idcirco preces inutiles, sed Deo gratas et efficaces esse, etiam si nos exemplo Simonis Cyrenaei vere partem sanctae crucis gestare cogimur, veruntamen Christus adstat, et subvenit ac opitulatur nobis. Haec breviter hoc loco monuisse satis sit, plures enim postea de hoc genere petitionum commonefactiones addemus.

Et remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos remittimus debitoribus nostris.

Vos scitis, idque meditari diligenter, et in conspectu semper habere debetis, duplices esse promissiones divinas: aeternas et corporales. Promissio de bonis aeternis est promissio gratiae, remissionis peccatorum, donationis Spiritus sancti, et salutis aeternae. Haec est praecipua Evangelii promissio, propter quam filius Dei missus est ad nos, et constitutus mediator, redemptor, liberator et salvator. Nam si tantum corporalia bona promissa nobis essent, nec habituri essemus aeternam salutem, proponeretur nobis consolatio nec firma, nec efficax, sed inanis et evanescens. Atqui Deus vult communicare nobis in omni aeternitate sapientiam et bonitatem suam, atque consummationem immensae misericordiae et admirandae liberationis huius hoc modo decrevit, ut in aeterna beatitudine, sapientia, iustitia, laetitia vivi fruamur ipsius claro visibilique conspectu, et sine peccato, sine morte, sine ullis calamitatibus ipsum perpetuo celebremus. Haec promissio gratiae et aeternorum bonorum, procul discerni debet a promissionibus bonorum corporalium.

Secundo, semper tenenda est regula, in omni petitione oportere primam et summam promissionem gratiae et remissionis peccatorum propter Christum praelucere caeteris promissionibus beneficiorum corporalium.

Itaque necesse est te, si vis accedere ad Deum, et bona corpori necessaria petere, primum ac perpetuo afferre hanc fidem, de remissione peccatorum et acceptatione gratuita, qua nominatim petis et accipis reconciliationem, quaque certo statuis tibi remitti peccata, te recipi, tua vota respici, tuas preces exaudiri propter filium Dei, Dominum Iesum Christum. Non enim potest accedi, nec est ullus aditus ad Deum sine mediatore et propitiatore filio Dei. Tertio, sciendum est hanc aeternam et immotam esse voluntatem Dei, atque severissimum et immutabile mandatum, ut omni tempore firmissime credas, tibi gratis per et propter Christum donari remissionem peccatorum, iustificationem, Spiritum sanctum et haereditatem salutis aeternae.

Sic manet immota, certa, et rata credenti promissio aeterna de reconciliatione et mediatore, sive impetres vitam et beneficia corporis, sive non contingat liberatio corporalis.

Veruntamen quia Deus, in hac misera mortali vita, initia suae lucis, iustitiae et vitae aeternae in nobis accendit, et vult Ecclesiam per ministerium Evangelii, et conversionem seu poenitentiam inchoari in hoc angusto mortalis vitae curriculo, largitur et suppeditat etiam bona corporalia, vitam, incolumitatem corporis, bonam valetudinem, domicilia, politias, pacem, victum, coniugem, liberos, oeconomias, bonos successus in laboribus, etc.

Itaque voluntatem suam expressit, quod etiam haec corporalia bona vere daturus sit, et addit Evangelio nominatim promissiones de rebus corporalibus, ut, cum dicit: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis. Mandat etiam, ut fides et invocatio quotidie exerceantur petenda et exspectanda sustentatione ac defensione corporum, aliisque rebus necessariis, ab ipsius bonitate atque misericordia propter Christum.

Hanc doctrinam de distinctione promissionum audivistis in proxima concione.

Et quia praecedens petitio: Panem nostrum quotidianum, etc. loquitur de beneficiis corporalibus, ideo mox Dominus adiungit et repetit petitionem remissionis peccatorum, quam quidem universaliter in omni precatione, quaecunque res petitur, ante omnia adhiberi, simul comprehendi, et semper praelucere caeteris petitionibus oportet.

Quia cum statim in invocatione obstrepat infirmitas et indignitas nostra, semper trepidae mentes fugiunt Deum, ac ita cogitant: Quam libenter peterem auxilium, nisi me deterrerent mea peccata, quae tot et tanta sunt, ut non ausim confugere neque accedere ad Deum.

Item: Si non haberem tam tristes lapsus, Deus haud dubie mihi mitigaret poenas. Has dubitationes et trepidationes experiuntur atque sentiunt omnium piorum corda, etiam si homines efferi, barbarici, et Cyclopici, aut hypocritae securi ignorant eas.

Quamobrem Dominus noster Iesus Christus ipse nobis hic amplissimam et uberrimam consolationem proposuit: adiungens mox hanc dulcissimam petitionem: Remitte nobis debita nostra, etc.

Quasi diceret: Non sum nescius, quod angeris et terreris indignitatis tuae tristissimorumque lapsuum conspectu, quod cogitas te abiectum esse, tuos clamores irritos esse, Deum respuere nec curare tuum murmur, tua peccata esse nimis multa et magna, tibi poenas exspectandas esse, non auxilium nec liberationem.

Contra istas ratiocinationes filius Dei sic te consolatur: Rectum est, Deoque gratum, quod agnoscis et confiteris tua peccata. Sed non oportet te deficere a Deo, nec opprimi desperatione, imo scias Deum velle tibi ignoscere, et remittere peccata propter Christum, serioque praecipere, ut petas remissionem, nec solum petas, sed ut etiam certo firmiterque credas, omnia tua peccata, sive magna, sive parva, omnes labes, et infirmitates, gratis propter mediatorem Christum, non propter ulla tua merita tibi remitti.

Hic igitur attente atque serio mens tua inter precandum, praecipua capita doctrinae Evangelii, quae Dei beneficio quotidie auditis illustrari, de gratia, de remissione peccatorum, de mediatore, de fide, diligenter sibi proponat, cogitet et intuetur.

Quapropter infigite animis hanc petitionem. Cum enim Dominus noster Iesus Christus ipse iusserit peti remissionem, et quidem quotidie peti, haud dubie vult nobis omnia peccata, quantacunque sint, remittere, et omnes quotidianas et multiplices infirmitates atque sordes condonare.

Verum simul hic monendi estis, nequaquam perseverandum esse in delictis contra conscientiam, sed scire debetis, quod necesse sit in qualibet vera invocatione fieri aut crescere in nobis poenitentiam, seu, conversionem ad Deum, quia iuramentum divinum clare dicit: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Est enim copulativa oratio, coniunguntur haec duo: conversio et consolatio, remissio peccatorum et vita, sicut haec alias fideliter explicantur, et saepe repetuntur.

Quod autem additur: Sicut et nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, admonemur et obligamur mandato Christi, ut nos quoque remittamus.

Ac rursus interpellat hoc loco tua conscientia: Si non possum accipere remissionem, nisi et ipse condonem aliis, fiet incerta reconciliatio, nec eluctari potero ex dubitatione, utrum consequar remissionem. Quia quantumvis repugnem odiis et cupiditati vindictae, sentio tamen adhuc semper vestigia seu cicatrices aliquas indignationis et simultatum adversus aliquos manere.

Ad hanc obiectionem teneatur perspicua et vera responsio: Remissio peccatorum offertur et donatur tibi per fidem, gratis, propter Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, non propter tuam condonationem, aut ullum aliud opus. Quod fundamentum bene memineris, diligenter observes, et utraque manu, seu verius toto pectore firmiter amplectaris.

Verissimum est autem, in hac consolatione, cum fides sustentantur et eriguntur corda, necessario simul existere et inchoari bonum propositum, ne videlicet perseveres in sceleribus contra conscientiam, sed vere convertaris ad Deum, nec deinceps retineas voluntatem ruendi in adulteria, aut cupiditatem nocendi aliis. Hanc conversionem, seu non simulatam mutationem prioris propositi, oportet in nobis existere, idque manifestissimum est.

De hac seria emendatione loquitur Christus, quod videlicet necesse sit sequi iustitiam bonae conscientiae, seu bonum propositum. Etsi enim sunt et manent in nobis in hac vita multae non leves sordes, pravae inclinationes flammae vitiosorum affectuum, et ingens ac multiplex infirmitas reliqua est, tamen prorsus necessarium est, et in nobis esse poenitentiam, et in conversione deponi delicta contra conscientiam, ne indulgeamus odio interno et privatae cupiditati vindictae, ne scientes contra mandatum Dei velimus alios laedere, vel opprimere, sed ut studeamus reconciliatis seu recuperatis voluntatibus offensiones sanare quantum possumus. Haec est vera, nativa et propria sententia verborum Christi, quae nos in precatione diligenter et attente consideremus ac perpendamus.

Etsi enim certissimum est, gratis remitti nobis peccata nostra propter Christum, non propter ulla nostra merita, tamen simul oportet scire, severissimam et immotam Dei voluntatem esse, ut ad ipsum convertamur, nec perseveremus in peccatis contra conscientiam. Quare cum mens retinet contemptum Dei, non exauditur, imo ne potest quidem accedere et confugere ad Deum, donec manet perseverantia in malo proposito.

Quo enim ore, qua conscientia talis invocatio fieret: Ah Domine Deus, miserere mei, esto propitius, ignosce, parce mihi, ego tamen interim omnibus furoribus opinionum, libidinum, crudelitatis indulgebo, petulanter pergam caedibus, rapinis, furtis, imposturis et mendaciis explere pravas cupiditates? Has preces Deus abominatur et exsecratur, ut et Salomon affirmat, Proverbiorum vicesimo octavo: Qui declinat aures suas, ne audiant legem, oratio eius erit exsecrabilis.

Ac Paulus expressis verbis inquit: Nolite errare, Deus non irridetur, neque adulteri, neque scortatores, neque homicidae, etc. regnum Dei possidebunt. Item Iohannis nono: Peccatores Deus non exaudit, scilicet non agentes poenitentiam, nec abiicientes propositum violandi legem Dei contra conscientiam.

Ecce hanc necessariam doctrinam inservit hic Christus, et addidit ad petitionem remissionis, qua monemur de poenitentia, ut afferamus ad Deum conversionem, nec retinentes propositum peccandi, beluinis cupiditatibus et diabolicis furoribus frenum laxemus, et interea somniemus, nos invocare Deum, ac tumeamus persuasione sanctitatis: sicut proh dolor, hoc postremo tempore mundus infinitam sibi licentiam sumit, et plurimorum tanta est feritas, ut nulla disciplinae vincula patiantur, qui tamen interim fingunt se habere fidem, se veris animi motibus invocare Deum, se esse viva et electa membra Ecclesiae, cum vivant in securitate et immanitate Cyclopica, et cedant ac obsequantur diabolo, impellenti eos ad adulteria, homicidia, et alia tetra flagitia.

Istam insignem perversitatem, enormem petulantiam, Cyclopicamque feritatem, nisi seria morum emendatione correxerimus, tristes et horrendae poenae sequentur.

Imo grassantur in conspectu poenae publicae, videtis intestina bella, vastationem rerum publicarum, et magnam calamitatum multitudinem concurrere: et quanquam Deus aerumnas praesentes hactenus clementer mitigavit, tamen valde metuo, ne toties irritatus feritate morum nostrorum violentius et implacabilius exserat iram, haeque regiones multo tristioribus poenis opprimantur, quia modus nullus est petulantiae, contumaciae et affectatae nequitiae iuniorum.

O aeterne Deus, Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi propter tuam gloriam adiuva nos, guberna, tuere et serva Ecclesiam tuam, puritatem ac studia coelestis doctrinae, disciplinam et mediocres politias, non sinas fieri tristissimas et infinitas vastitates, non Ethnicam et Turcicam profanitatem plenam spurcitie, ac contemtu iustitiae divinae.

Hanc ipsam commonefactionem de conversione seu poenitentia saepe multumque in precatione vestra animo volvere, et cogitatione memoriaque repetere, eaque vos ad poenitentiam et emendationem flectere atque exsuscitare debetis.

Si quis in conversione abiicit malum propositum, is demum potest alacriter invocare Deum fiducia mediatoris, et in corde sentit pacem, tranquillitatem, laetitiam et consolationem, iuxta dictum Pauli: Iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Haec autem fiducia, pax et laetitia acquiescens in Deo, nequaquam simul existere potest in tuo corde, cum perseverantia in delictis contra conscientiam, seu cum proposito indulgendi quibuslibet furoribus, teque polluendi omni scelere turpitudinis.

Sed postquam inchoata est conversio in cordibus, fides firmissime nitatur et acquiescat in mediatore Christo, et certo statuat invocationem tuam placere et efficacem esse, tibique vere dari remissionem peccatorum.

Hanc summam et amplissimam consolationem debes infixam animo tenere, eamque quotidie in omni precatione tua intuens ac recordans exercere et confirmare fidem, proque tantis beneficiis Deo vere gratias agere.

Et hactenus de hac petitione: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos remittimus debitoribus nostris.

## 6:13 Sermons on Matthew
And lead us not into temptation.

That is, do not allow us to be led, or, do not allow us to slip, fall, be submerged, and oppressed when we are tempted; do not allow us to succumb to the devil in temptations.

For these phrases, or modes of speaking: Lead us not into temptation, signify permission, not causation, nor an effective will.

For the meaning of these words is by no means that God is the author and cause of temptations, and that He Himself incites us and would as it were invite us to sin, and that He takes delight and pleasure in our destruction and ruin.

Let this false interpretation be exploded.

But the authors and instigators, from whom temptations and the causes of sins arise, are most truly the devils and men.

Likewise our own futility, curiosity, and petulance, and depraved inclinations.

Again, however, many most grave and useful doctrines of great moment are comprehended in this petition.

For although the remarkable brevity of the words: Lead us not into temptation, as it were flies past our ears, yet these few words speak of the greatest and most serious matters, of the sharpest and most insidious enemies.

Now set before your eyes the first enemy, namely, the devil; how horribly has he raged? what a sad slaughter and ruin has he wrought? when in the beginning he drove Adam and Eve into a horrible fall, by which impulse he dragged the entire human race, torn away from God, into death and infinite miseries.

Likewise, how cruelly has he raged at all times? how great a quantity of the most flagitious lusts, horrible dissipations, tragic and saddest cases, and most bitter calamities has the devil brought in and excited, in devising and establishing idols, in kindling unnecessary wars, in effecting unjust slaughters, in stirring up seditions and discords, etc.

And do not imagine that the devil is a sleepy, sluggish, lazy, and idle spirit, but the text clearly and in express words says of Judas: Satan entered into him.

Likewise, the Lord to the Pharisees, who certainly were wise, and [their] morals and manners were led astray, [by] honest discipline, [he] says: You are of your father the devil.

Likewise, the testimony of Peter is manifest: The devil, as a roaring lion, walks about, seeking whom he may devour. Do not, therefore, dream that you are... in safety and beyond danger, and sitting as if out of reach of the arrow, and that you cannot be circumvented, wounded, or overturned by the devil.

Afterwards, let other enemies be considered, who are the inciters and causes of temptations, namely, evil men, as it is well known, that many thousands of adolescents are depraved by evil associations and examples, and finally lose their body and life, and some even suffer the loss of their soul.

Likewise, many princes and wise men, through their counselors, to whose fidelity they commit their heart and life, and to whom, as it is said, they show an open breast, are captured and seduced, so that they embrace and receive false and pernicious doctrine, so that they move unnecessary and pernicious wars, so that they are implicated in other evil causes and affairs. Thus also other private men are deceived and corrupted very often by evil counselors and teachers.

The third enemy, and the most intimate and near of all, is your own wisdom, your beautiful imagination, or splendid thought, and the depraved desire in your heart: when we are stimulated and impelled by our own curiosity or petulance of mind to invent, sow, or embrace new dogmas, or when we are inflamed by the wandering flames of vicious affections toward adultery, or the desire for vengeance, toward thefts, lies, impostures, and other crimes.

We can feel all these things ourselves.

And when we obey and indulge these depraved motions and inclinations, the devil's spectators of our furious efforts wander around us, and therefore they fly in immediately, and with a dire and poisonous breath they infect and impel the miserable, weak, and deserted heart, so that, weakened and languishing, it falls into manifest crimes. As, when David, looking at another man's wife, who was outstanding in form, was inflamed by love for her, and when, wishing to feed the fire that had arisen in his mind, and in his external gesture and speech also, he followed those vicious motions and flames, the devils, seeing him yield to the affection and admit the allurements, impelled him violently, and entangled him, prostrate, in inextricable falls.

Here, therefore, the third enemy, namely, one's own curiosity, and vicious appetite or desire, moves on slippery ground, and comes into great danger; we excite tumults, or, indulging in curiosity, we show off our talents and wisdom, we are authors of new dogmas, and we persuade ourselves that our happiness will be perpetual, just as Pompey used to say that he would fill all of Italy with armies against Julius Caesar by the stamping of his foot.

But on the contrary, when, as we undergo huge calamities, things happen that are inextricable to human counsel, then we waste away, broken in spirit by grief, we fall into impatience and despair, we flee from God, and sad torments and horrendous roarings follow in the heart.

We ought to recognize these so various enemies, and consider such manifold temptations, and therefore pray with true groans and tears: Lead us not into temptation, that is, do not allow us to be submerged, to succumb, and to be oppressed when we are tempted, when the devil's danger, plague, and destruction are plotted against our bodies, souls, wives, and children, when they attempt to tear apart the Churches and disturb the republics.

Likewise, when other men, by their counsels and incitements, wish to ensnare and implicate us in evil causes. Likewise, when, overcome by our own infirmity, we are snatched and impelled to dishonest or destructive affairs. And in sum: If anyone thinks that by his own wisdom and his own counsels, even without divine governance, custody, and help, he can rule his own morals, his own affairs, and dangers: he must be judged truly blind, senseless, furious, and out of his mind.

For no human wisdom and vigilance can be equal to such a mass of dangers and impediments, nor can it suffice to rule our life, to sustain our calling, to foresee, avoid, and flee the snares of the devil, to understand and beware of the seductions and impostures of... men, and finally to overcome our own infirmity, without the help and protection of God. Because the sentence of the Son of God is always true: Without me you can do nothing.

We are weak, and burdened with various calamities; therefore God sent to us his own Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, that he might be the defender and guardian of the Church, by whom we might know ourselves to be ruled, protected, and helped; provided that, truly and seriously invoking him, we ask for... divine aid and governance, and cast away those sins which hinder invocation and pollute the conscience, and do not, in Cyclopean security, furiously proceed to indulge and obey all depraved inclinations and vicious desires.

Thus the Lord himself says to the Apostles: Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation. Likewise, Paul says: Walk accurately, not as fools, but as wise, in whom God kindles the beginnings of his light. Propose all these things diligently to yourselves, and do not hope that the Cyclopean security and drunkenness of this dissolute life will depart without the saddest outcomes and human miseries and diabolical snares.

Nor is this significant and memorable sentence inserted into history in vain, when the Israelites were performing dances around the image made in imitation of the Egyptian calf, where the text says: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.

Certainly, the sadness of these times is immense in such great dangers and public miseries, and although the difficulties of the times and the confusions of governments do not greatly move the minds of the young, yet the elders, in such great distress of affairs and in the saddest spectacles of punishments and the fear of the greatest calamities, ought indeed to be tormented both by the horrendous wars, the devastations of Churches, and the collisions of empires, and also be affected by their own and domestic difficulties, poverty, diseases, the unhappiness of children, and the loss of property, so that, thinking with anxiety about storms and tribulations of this kind, and being more intent and circumspect in avoiding lapses, they might be more ardent in praying.

Therefore, thinking of these causes of public mourning and individual sadness with a serious and great movement of the soul, let us cry out to God in this petition, that he may not allow us to be dragged into the snares of the devil, nor to succumb to depraved inclinations, nor to rush into pride, arrogance, and trust in ourselves, nor to be submerged in sadness and despair, nor to be oppressed by other temptations, which are many and varied.

Wherefore, to those reciting the words of this petition, let there often come to mind the similar words of Christ, by which in his agony at the Mount of Olives he exhorts his disciples to pray, saying: Pray that you enter not into temptation, that is, that the devil may not shake your faith and pull you away from God through snares, impostures, deceits, and scandals, which he can stir up in many ways.

But deliver us from evil.

This is a general petition, and as it were a clause, which indeed most aptly coheres and agrees with the next preceding petition.

Furthermore, we shall not speak now of the Heathens, Turks, and similar impious people.

For these are not delivered from evil, but remain oppressed by sins, the wrath of God, the tyranny of the devil, and eternal punishments, whether they flourish in this life or sustain great miseries.

As Caesar Tiberius lived pleasantly, was a great and powerful emperor, had pleasures of every kind, polluted himself with the confusions of lusts, and unjustly killed many.

The same, after he had grown old, died peacefully without violence; yet he did not therefore obtain liberation from the highest and eternal evils, but perished, cast into horrendous, most bitter, and everlasting torments.

Wherefore, nothing needs to be said in this place about the examples of the Heathens.

For however much the Heathens may solicitously and seriously cry out: Ah Lord God, deliver us from dangers and miseries, yet their cries are horrible and mere blindness, and therefore it is not to be doubted that they are vain and fruitless.

For they do not address the true God; rather, they heap insults upon the Son of God.

Furthermore, when they have cried out anxiously for a long time, yet their minds, tumultuous and trembling, argue that God does not care for the groans, tears, and cries of those invoking him, that their prayers are of no value and are not received, and therefore they do not expect aid from God.

Wherefore, at length, with a horrible roaring, they grow angry and curse God.

In this place, therefore, we shall speak only of the living and true members of Christ, and of the afflictions of the pious and holy.

God has subjected his Church to the cross, and exercises it so harshly that there is hardly any time when it is not suffering significant and multiple calamities, but the same God so mitigates and softens such a mass of miseries with his inestimable goodness that some men nevertheless remain alive as survivors, to whom he grants both good health and sustenance, by which they may be able to endure the labors of their vocations, and to serve and be useful to others, according to the saying of the Psalm: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, that is, because they have already departed.

will give you, O Lord, that is, those who have already departed, as if from a garrison and station of life, will no longer perform the public ministry of teaching, nor will they sit at the helms of the republic, nor will they sustain the common burdens and necessary labors in civil society or mortal life.

God, however, wills that in this miserable mass, in this life, this highest benefit be begun, namely, the restitution of justice and eternal life, in which, with sin henceforth completely abolished and death destroyed, He Himself will be all in all; therefore, He grants to many men longer spans of life, gives good health, sustenance, the fruits of the earth, so that you may live longer, and serve the Churches piously, or at least in your own place, you may be able to keep your little children with you and educate them.

Therefore, do not by any means think that this petition is made in vain, or that the prayer is void, if all afflictions and miseries are not removed and do not cease, but God nevertheless hears and receives the groans and cries of the afflicted, and softens and mitigates many punishments.

If God, having mercy on us, had not mitigated the punishments then, when the Emperor Charles had occupied this little town, and held it armed for fourteen whole days with a garrison imposed upon it, all would have been killed, and would have perished utterly. Therefore, if the Devil, the tempter, could, even for the space of one hour, [keep you] all burdened with sad troubles along with your holy infants and families, and oppressed by such cruel accidents, so that they could neither perform the labors of their calling, nor serve usefully, for example, those who are tormented by grave and long-lasting diseases, or who undergo the cruelty of tyrannical persecutions, nevertheless it behooves us all to pray, whether we endure great and bitter, or milder pains, that God, in His immense mercy, may at last will to deliver us from evil.

[ You] know that it is the most severe command of God that we believe most firmly that we have been truly delivered from sin and from eternal punishments on account of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. Yet we must seek deliverance, and in this petition stir up and confirm faith, and firmly resolve that God, on account of the Son, the mediator, clemently and with ineffable goodness forgives sins, and that it is most true that in all eternity He wills to communicate to us His wisdom, justice, goodness, and joy, and that He will not cast us into eternal destruction to be tormented with the devils and all the impious.

These eternal things you must first contemplate and consider in your mind during the recitation of this petition; afterwards, think of and look also at all present and bodily miseries and troubles, and seeking deliverance, embrace both yourself and others as well, and firmly resolve that this prayer of yours is not void, but is received by God, and obtains mitigation for you along with the others. And even if we are exercised more harshly, and the punishments are not entirely taken away, because the Church is subject to the present miseries of bodies, yet God clemently softens and mitigates the punishments, so that [He would not] by any means be about to omit or delay [the Church, the state, and to devour]. Wherefore, let us pray with serious and true motions of our souls that God may clemently will to deliver us from evil, both the present, which we have already tasted and begun to feel, and the future or imminent, which, although we do not yet sustain, nor feel, nor even foresee, yet would have been about to oppress our necks, had not God in His immense goodness warded it off and driven it away.

Deliver us from evil, eternal and temporal, present and impending, particular and universal, which could happen, if God did not avert it.

Thus cry the Prophets, Jerem. 10: Correct me, O Lord, but in judgment, not in fury, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing. Item Hab. 3: O Lord, when you have been angry, remember your immense mercy. Thus we also pray with these words: Ah Lord God, clemently mitigate for us public and private calamities, and all the miseries and troubles of this life; do not allow Ethnic devastations, do not allow diabolical filth, do not allow Turkish furies to run rampant in the human race.

Amen. That is, may these things be so most truly, and may they be ratified. It is necessary that this appendix or clause be added in every true invocation. Because invocation without faith, and oppressed by doubt, is Ethnic impiety. As when someone says: Ah Lord God, help me, who yet meanwhile thinks to himself thus: I do not know if I am a care to God, I do not know if God wills to receive my prayers, I do not know why He should receive them. Certainly, he who does not struggle out of these doubts, he recites his prayer in the heathen manner. But pious minds, and those turned toward God, must think thus: It is the most severe and immutable will of God that we should call upon Him, and He certainly wills to hear us for the sake of His son Jesus Christ; indeed, for this very reason He delivered His promises, with the addition of an immutable mandate, that we should believe that He truly wills to hear us. Therefore, I most firmly establish that I am heard by God for Christ’s sake, and most certainly that my groans and cries are not empty, not useless, nor in vain. I also pray with ardent vows that God may confirm these beginnings of faith in me, just as that trembling man, having acknowledged the weakness of his faith, asks to be confirmed: I believe, Lord, but help my unbelief.

Latin:

Et ne nos inducas in tentationem.

Hoc est, ne sinas nos induci, seu, ne sinas nos labi, ruere, submergi et opprimi, cum tentamur, ne sinas nos succumbere diabolo in tentationibus.

Nam hae phrases, seu modi loquendi: Ne nos inducas in tentationem, significant permissionem, non effectionem, nec efficacem voluntatem.

Nequaquam enim sententia horum verborum est, quod Deus autor et causa sit tentationum, ac ipse nos incitet ac velut invitare velit ad peccandum, quodque delectetur et voluptatem capiat ex interitu et pernicie nostra.

Haec falsa interpretatio explodatur.

Sed autores et impulsores, a quibus oriuntur tentationes et causae peccatorum, verissime sunt diaboli et homines.

Item futilitas, curiositas et petulantia nostra, et pravae inclinationes.

Rursus autem in hac petitione multae gravissimae et utilissimae, magnique momenti doctrinae comprehenduntur.

Etsi enim velut praetervolat aures nostras verborum brevitas insignis: Ne nos inducas in tentationem, tamen haec pauca verba de maximis et seriis rebus, de acerrimis et insidiosissimis hostibus loquuntur.

Iam proponite vobis ante oculos primum hostem, scilicet, diabolum, quam is horribiliter grassatus est? quam tristem stragem atque ruinam edidit? cum initio Adam et Evam impulit in horrendum lapsum, qua impulsione universum genus humanum avulsum a Deo pertraxit in mortem et miserias infinitas.

Item, quam saeviit atrociter omnibus temporibus? quantum flagitiosissimarum libidinum, horribilium dissipationum, tragico-rum et tristissimorum casuum, acerbissimarum calamitatum diabolus invexit, et excitavit, in excogitandis et stabiliendis idolis, in accendendis non necessariis bellis, in efficiendis caedibus iniustis, in concitandis seditionibus et discordiis, etc.

Nec imaginemini, diabolum esse somniculosum, segnem, ignavum et otiosum spiritum, sed clare textus et expressis verbis inquit de Iuda: Intravit in eum Satanas.

Item, Dominus ad Pharisaeos, qui certe sapientes erant, et mores moderabantur, honesta disciplina, dicit: Vos ex Patre diabolo estis.

Item Petri testimonium manifestum est: Diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quaerens quem devoret. Non igitur somnietis, vos in tuto citraque periculum, et velut extra teli... iactum sedere, nec posse vos a diabolo circumveniri, sauciari vel everti.

Postea cogitentur et alii hostes, qui sunt incitatores atque causae tentationum, videlicet, mali homines, ut constat, multa millia adolescentum malis sodalitiis et exemplis depravari, tandemque corpus et vitam perdere, aliquos etiam animae iacturam facere.

Item, multi principes et sapientes viri, per suos consiliarios, quorum fidei cor et vitam suam committunt, et quibus, ut dicitur, apertum pectus ostendunt, capiuntur et seducuntur, ut amplectantur ac recipiant doctrinam falsam et perniciosam, ut non necessaria et perniciosa bella moveant, ut aliis malis causis et negotiis implicentur. Sic et alii privati homines decipiuntur et corrumpuntur saepenumero per malos consultores et doctores.

Tertius hostis et omnium intimus ac proximus est tua propria sapientia, tua bella imaginatio, seu splendida cogitatio, et prava cupiditas in tuo corde: quando propria curiositate seu petulantia ingeniorum exstimulamur et impellimur ad fingenda, serenda, vel amplectenda nova dogmata, aut cum errantibus flammis vitiosorum affectuum incendimur ad adulteria, aut cupiditatem vindictae, ad furta, mendacia, imposturas, et alia flagitia.

Haec possumus ipsi sentire omnia.

Cumque obtemperamus et indulgemus his pravis motibus et inclinationibus, vagantur circa nos diaboli spectatores furiosorum conatuum nostrorum, ideoque confestim advolant, et diro atque venenato afflatu cor miserum, imbecille ac desertum a Deo inficiunt ac impellunt, ut debilitatum et languefactum ruat in manifesta scelera. Ut, cum David intuens alienam coniugem forma praestantem incenderetur eius amore, cumque volens aleret incendium, in animo ortum, et in externo quoque gestu ac sermone obsequeretur vitiosis illis motibus et flammis, diaboli videntes eum cedere affectui, et admittere illecebras, praecipitatum violenter impellebant, prostratumque lapsibus inextricabilibus implicabant.

Hic itaque tertius hostis, nempe propria curiositas, et appetitio seu cupiditas vitiosa, versatur in lubrico, magnumque venit in periculum, tumultus excitamus, aut indulgentes curiositati ostentamus ingenia et sapientiam, sumus autores, novorum dogmatum, et nobis persuademus nostram felicitatem perpetuam fore, sicut Pompeius dicebat, se supplosione pedis Italiam totam exercitibus completurum adversus Iulium Caesarem.

At contra cum subeuntibus ingentes aerumnas accidunt inextricabilia humano consilio, tunc animis fracti moerore contabescimus, ruimus in impatientiam et desperationem, fugimus Deum, tristesque cruciatus et horrendi fremitus in corde sequuntur.

Hos tam varios hostes agnoscere, tamque multiplices tentationes considerare debemus, atque ideo veris gemitibus et lacrymis orare: ne nos inducas in tentationem, hoc est, ne sinas nos mergi, succumbere, et opprimi, cum tentamur, quando diaboli periculum, pestem, et exitium moliuntur corporibus, animabus, coniugibus et liberis nostris, quando dilacerare Ecclesias, et turbare respublicas conantur.

Item cum alii homines consiliis et incitationibus suis volunt nos irretire et implicare malis causis. Item, cum superati propria infirmitate rapimur et impellimur ad inhonesta vel exitiosa negotia. Ac in summa: Si quis cogitat sua sapientia suisque consiliis, etiam sine gubernatione, custodia et ope divina se regere posse suos mores, sua negotia et pericula: is vere coecus, vecors, furiosus, et mente captus indicari debet.

Nec enim ulla humana sapientia et vigilantia par esse tantae moli periculorum et impedimentorum, nec sufficere potest ad regendam vitam nostram, ad sustinendam vocationem, ad prospiciendas, vitandas et fugiendas insidias diaboli, ad intelligendas cavendasque seductiones et imposturas hominum, ad vincendam denique propriam infirmitatem, sine auxilio et protectione Dei. Quia semper vera est sententia filii Dei: Sine me nihil potestis facere.
