Samus imbecilles, et variis calamitatibus onerati; propterea Deus misit nobis filium suum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, ut esset defensor et custos Ecclesiae, a quo sciremus nos regi, protegi et iuvari, modo vere et serio invocantes ipsum petamus auxilium et gubernationem divinam, et abiiciamus ...ea delicta, quae impediunt invocationem atque polluunt conscientiam, nec in securitate Cyclopica furenter pergamus indulgere ac obedire omnibus pravis inclinationibus et vitiosis cupiditatibus.

Ita Dominus ipse dicit Apostolis: Vigilate et orate, ne intretis in tentationem. Item, Paulus inquit: Ambulatis accurate, non ut fatui, sed ut sapientes, in quibus Deus initia suae lucis accendit. Haec omnia diligenter vobis proponite, nec sperate istius dissolutae vitae Cyclopicam securitatem et temulentiam, sine tristissimis casibus et humanarum miseriarum, et diabolicarum insidiarum abituram esse.

Nec frustra haec insignis et memorabilis sententia inseritur historiae, cum Israëlitae choreas exercerent circum vituli Aegyptiorum imitatione facti simulacrum, ubi textus dicit: Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et surrexit ludere.

Certe horum temporum ingens est moestitia in tantis periculis, et publicis miseriis, et quanquam iuniorum animos non valde movent difficultates temporum, et confusiones gubernationum, tamen seniores in tanta rerum angustia tristissimisque poenarum spectaculis, et maximarum calamitatum metu, profecto debebant tum excruciari propter horrenda bella, propter vastationes Ecclesiarum, et imperiorum collisiones, tum affici suis, atque domesticis difficultatibus, inopia, morbis, infelicitate liberorum, detrimentisque facultatum, ut cum solicitudine de procellis et aerumnis huiusmodi cogitantes, et in vitandis lapsibus intenti magis ac circumspecti, et in precando ardentiores essent.

Has itaque causas publici luctus et moestitiae singulorum, serio magnoque animorum motu cogitantes, clamemus ad Deum in hac petitione, ne sinat nos pertrahi in laqueos diaboli, nec succumbere pravis inclinationibus, nec in superbiam, fastum, fiduciamque nostri ruere, nec in tristitiam et desperationem mergi, nec aliis tentationibus, quae multae variaeque sunt, opprimi.

Quare recitantibus verba huius petitionis saepe veniat in mentem similium verborum Christi, quibus in agone ad montem olivarum discipulos adhortatur ad precandum, inquiens: Orate ne intretis in tentationem, id est, ne diabolus excutiat vobis fidem, et avellat vos a Deo per insidias, imposturas, praestigias atque scandala, quae multipliciter excitare potest.

Sed libera nos a malo.

Haec est petitio generalis, et tanquam clausula, quae quidem aptissime cohaeret et congruit cum proxima praecedente petitione.

Caeterum non loquemur iam de Ethnicis, Turcis, et similibus impiis.

Hi enim non liberantur a malo, sed manent oppressi peccatis, ira Dei, tyrannide diaboli, et aeternis poenis, sive floreant in hac vita, sive sustineant magnas miserias.

Ut Caesar Tiberius suaviter vixit, fuit magnus et potens imperator, habuit omnis generis voluptates, polluit se confusionibus libidinum, iniuste multos interfecit.

Idem posteaquam consenuerat, placide sine violentia mortuus est; nec tamen ideo consecutus est liberationem ex summis et aeternis malis, sed periit abiectus in horrendos, acerbissimos et sempiternos cruciatus.

Quamobrem nihil hoc loco de Ethnicis exemplis dicendum erit.

Quantumvis enim Ethnici solicite serioque clament: Ah Domine Deus eripe nos ex periculis et miseriis, tamen ipsorum clamores sunt horribilis et mera coecitas, ideoque inanes et irritos esse minime dubitandum est.

Non enim alloquuntur verum Deum, imo filium Dei contumeliis afficiunt.

Praeterea cum diu anxie clamaverunt, tamen animi tumultuantes ac trepidantes disputant, Deum non curare gemitus, lacrymas, clamores invocantium, non valere nec recipi suas preces, ideoque non exspectant a Deo auxilium.

Quare tandem horribili fremitu irascuntur et maledicunt Deo.

Hoc igitur loco tantum de vivis ac veris Christi membris, deque piorum ac sanctorum afflictionibus verba faciemus.

Deus Ecclesiam suam subiecit cruci, adeo que duriter exercet, ut vix ullo tempore non expariatur illa insignes ac multiplices calamitates, sed idem tantam molem miseriarum inaestimabili bonitate sic mitigat et lenit, ut aliqui tamen homines maneant in vita superstites, quibus et bonam valetudinem et victum largitur, quo labores vocationum perferre, ac servire et prodesse possint aliis, iuxta dictum Psalmi: Non mortui lau-

dabunt te Domine, id est, qui iam decesserunt 667 668 dabunt te Domine, id est, qui iam decesserunt tanquam de praesidio et statione vitae, non fungentur amplius ministerio publico docendi, nec ad gubernacula reipublicae sedebunt, nec onera communia, laboresque necessarios in civili societate seu mortali vita sustinebunt.

Vult autem Deus in hac misera massa in hac vita inchoari hoc summum beneficium, videlicet, restitutionem iustitiae et vitae aeternae, in qua deinceps prorsus abolito peccato et deleta morte ipse erit omnia in omnibus, propterea multis hominibus tribuit vitae spatia longiora, dat bonam valetudinem, victum, fruges terrae, ut plures vivere, ac Ecclesiis pie servire, aut certe suo loco tu parvulos liberos tuos retinere tecum, ac educare possis.

Propterea nequaquam cogites ideo frustra fieri hanc petitionem, aut irritam esse precationem, si non tollantur ac desinant omnes afflictiones et miseriae, sed Deus exaudit tamen ac recipit afflictorum gemitus et clamores, atque plurimas poenas lenit ac mitigat.

Nisi Deus misertus nostri mitigasset poenas tunc, cum imperator Carolus occupaverat hoc oppidulum, idque totos quatuordecim dies imposito praesidio tenebat armatus, fuissent omnes interfecti, et periissent funditus. Ideo si Diabolus insidiator posset vel unius horae spatio vos universos cum sanctis infantibus et familiis vestris tristibus aerumnis onerati, tamque saevis casibus oppressi sunt, ut nec suae vocationis labores facere, nec utiliter servire possint, verbi causa, qui gravibus et diuturnis morbis excruciantur, aut qui tyrannicarum persecutionum crudelitatem subeunt, nihilominus tamen omnes nos precari oportet, sive magnos et acerbos, sive leniores dolores perferamus, ut Deus immensa misericordia nos tandem velit a malo liberare.

Scitis esse severissimum Dei mandatum, ut firmissime credamus, nos propter filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum vere liberatos esse a peccato et ab aeternis poenis. Attamen debemus petere liberationem, et in hac petitione fidem exsuscitare ac confirmare, certoque statuere, Deum nobis propter filium mediatorem clementer et inenarrabili bonitate peccata remittere, atque verissimum esse, quod in omni aeternitate velit nobis suam sapientiam, iustitiam, bonitatem, ac laetitiam communicare, nec abiecturum nos esse in sempiternum exitium cruciandos cum diabolis et omnibus impiis.

Has res aeternas primum debes in petitionis huius recitatione animo contemplari et considerare; postea cogites et intuearis etiam omnes praesentes atque corporales miserias et aerumnas, ac petens liberationem cum te ipsum tum alios quoque complectaris, certoque statuas hanc tuam precationem, non esse irritam, sed a Deo recipi, et impetrare cum tibi cum caeteris mitigationem. Ac etiamsi durius exercemur, nec prorsus auferuntur poenae, quia Ecclesia subiecta est praesentibus miseriis corporum, tamen Deus clementer lenit ac mitigat poenas, ut Ecclesiae, politiae, ac devorare, nequaquam praetermissurus nec dilaturus esset. Quamobrem serio verisque motibus animorum petamus, ut Deus nos clementer liberare velit a malo, cum praesenti, quod iam degustavimus ac sentire coepimus, tum futuro seu imminenti, quod etsi nondum sustinemus, nec sentimus, aut ne quidem prospicimus, tamen fuerat oppressurum cervices nostras, nisi Deus id immensa bonitate arceret ac depelleret.

Libera nos a malo aeterno, et temporali, praesenti et impendenti, particulari et universali, quod posset accidere, nisi Deus averteret.

Sic clamant Prophetae, Ierem. 10.: Corripe me Domine, veruntamen in iudicio, non in furore, ne forte ad nihilum redigas me. Item Abac. 3.: Domine cum iratus fueris, immensae misericordiae recorderis. Ita nos quoque petimus his verbis: Ah Domine Deus clementer mitigato nobis publicas et privatas calamitates, ac omnes huius vitae miserias et aerumnas, non sinas fieri Ethnicas vastitates, non spurcitiem diabolicam, non Turcicos furores grassari sinas in genere humano.

Amen. Id est, haec ita verissime fiant, et rata sint. Hanc appendicem seu clausulam necesse est addi in omni vera invocatione. Quia invocatio sine fide, et oppressa dubitatione, est Ethnica impietas. Ut cum dicit aliquis: Ah Domine Deus opitulare mihi, qui tamen interea secum sic cogitat: Nescio an sim Deo curae, nescio an Deus vult recipere meas preces, nescio cur recipiat. Certe qui non eluctatur ex his dubitationibus, is recitat Ethnico more suam precationem. At pias mentes et conversas ad Deum necesse est ita cogitare: Severissima et immutabilis Dei voluntas est, ut invocemus ipsum, et certo vult nos propter filium Iesum Christum, exaudire, quin hanc ipsam ob causam tradidit promissiones suas, addito mandato immutabili, ut credamus, quod vere velit nos exaudire. Propterea firmissime statuo, me propter Christum a Deo exaudiri, et certissime non inanes, non inutiles, nec irritos esse gemitus et clamores meos. Oro etiam ardentibus votis, ut haec initia fidei Deus in me confirmet, quemadmodum trepidus ille agnita imbecillitate fidei petit se confirmari: Credo Domine, sed opem fer diffidentiae meae.

## 6:16 Sermons on Matthew
When you fast, do not be, like the hypocrites, sad.

The Jewish people did not have certain and preordained days of fasting in the divine law, except for the single day of the tenth of the seventh month, which was called the feast of atonement. They themselves, however, called a fast the abstinence from all food, or the starvation of an entire day, that is, when they ate absolutely nothing for an interval of time as long as from the evening of the preceding day until the evening of the following one. But the Pharisees accumulated human traditions and observed frequent fasts, by which exercises they preached that they were meriting huge benefits, the remission of sins, and increments of piety and holiness.

Furthermore, you know from the Gospel that no fasts, whether divinely commanded or chosen and prescribed by men, merit the remission of sins. Indeed, it is a foul and horrible blasphemy to attribute this highest honor, and that which is owed to Christ alone, to our works, rites, and exercises, as if they were merits for the remission of sins, or as if they were righteousness before God; but this honor is proper to the son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, whose obedience alone merited for us the remission of sins, righteousness, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life. And it is necessary that this very amplitude of divine grace or mercy be apprehended and received by us by faith alone, resting in the mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ.

May no forgetfulness of this most firm foundation ever seize us, but may we perpetually carry its memory in our minds, concerning which matter you hear yourselves reminded very often. Nor allow yourselves to be led away and moved by diabolical deceptions from this salutary and most true doctrine of the Gospel, but with most firm assent establish that you certainly receive and have the remission of sins, and that righteousness is imputed to you for the merit of Christ, just as the Prophet affirms: By his stripes we are healed. Nor suffer darkness to be cast upon you in this doctrine.

Now this also is most certain and irrefragably true, that whenever this sweetest consolation is conceived and begun in hearts by faith, God certainly kindles and effects in us life and joy resting in the mercy of God, so that all true Christians, or those turned to God, feel and experience it, according to the saying: Being justified by faith we have peace toward God. Nevertheless, in this very vivification or regeneration, it is necessary for the trust of your heart to rest in the son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and not to rely on its own cleanliness or novelty. This very doctrine is most truly the voice of the holy Gospel, and an eternal and immovable truth, nor is there anything of obscurity or ambiguity, or of snares, or of sophistry in this sentiment which I have recounted. Therefore, embrace and retain it constantly, nor allow yourselves to be disturbed and circumvented by clouds and corruptions cast upon you, whether by the Pope, or by the Monks, or by the Augsburg Sphinx, whose name is the Interim, or by certain jugglers, who now, coming forth as if from the cave of Trophonius, boast that they are about to reveal new mysteries to us.

But it occurs to us, and it can be asked in this place, why fasts are not entirely disapproved and rejected here, and why Christ says: When you wish to fast, show a cheerfulness of countenance and eyes.

I answer. First, it must be known that no form of fasts or manner of exercises is prescribed in the Gospel, but it is free and granted to anyone both to lunch and to dine, and to eat either meat, or fish, or vegetables, or turnips, or whatever foods, divinely given and offered to each. But in general, temperance is commanded to all men, observing at all times a measure in food and drink suitable to the nature of their bodies.

Thus the Lord himself commands in Luke 21: Take heed, lest your hearts be burdened of surfeit and drunkenness.

But why does He say that hearts are weighed down? For it would seem that it should rather have been said that the belly, filled and stuffed with immoderate food and drink, is weighed down by an inert mass?

I answer. The Lord speaks specifically of the heart for this reason, because in the intoxicated, the invocation of God is extinguished.

Wherefore divine governance or action is hindered in us, as those who are intemperate violate the temple of God, namely the heart and the brain. In this way, hearts are weighed down by gluttony and debauchery.

To the same effect Peter also says in 1 Peter 4: Be temperate and sober for prayer. And it is written in Hosea 4: Whoredom, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart, that is, they loosen human spirits and drive them unbridled into fury, and they hinder intention in invocation, and the efficacy or effects of God Himself in the hearts.

Therefore, let this necessary precept be known to you from the beginning, namely that temperance in food and drink is a necessary work at any time.

And the Gospel speaks of these commanded exercises of fasting.

This, whether it be abstinence or a form of fasting, is not hypocrisy, and it ought to be done or performed cheerfully in faith, invocation, and thanksgiving to God. And faith and joy in God is that very most generous and precious balm, of which mention is made here, with which, indeed, those who fast ought to anoint themselves. And indeed, neither invocation nor thanksgiving can be performed cheerfully, ardently, and from the heart, as long as you are distended with food and drink, or still exhaling yesterday’s surfeit, and the spirits are disturbed and seething in the brain.

Let everyone look at and consider himself, then he will notice and discover whether the invocation of one who is fasting and sober is more ardent, or that of one who is intoxicated and distended with wine and surfeit.

Therefore, Scripture joins both together in Matthew 17: In fasting and prayer, to signify that invocation is too languid and cold, nay, is utterly hindered and extinguished in a life that is drunken, Cyclopean, and beastly.

Secondly, the Gospel speaks of another kind of fasting, far more difficult and more serious, when, namely, the heart is so full and consumed by true sorrows and anguish that, because the mind is occupied by sadness and cares, the stomach is weakened and does not even admit food, nor can it enjoy the drink brought to it.

Such was the fast of David when rebuked by the Prophet Nathan. Thus did some holy men in Nineveh fast after hearing the preaching of Jonah. Thus in Matthew 9 the Lord Himself says that it will come to pass that His disciples will fast then, when the bridegroom is taken away from them.

In this way Paul also fasted after his conversion. Likewise, poor families are thus compelled by poverty to fast and almost waste away from hunger, because they lack the necessities for sustenance, or things suitable to nature.

Thus also Hagar with her son almost perished from thirst, having no water in the wilderness. This kind of fasting, proper to the Church, is by no means a simulation or hypocrisy, if the heart, submitting itself to God, obeys patiently in afflictions.

And then indeed this consolation is most necessary, that joy and cheerfulness should approach, and the head be anointed with the most fragrant balm. For this joy and fragrance of balm is the very consolation by which the heart, enlivened by faith and hope, is raised up, and in enduring adversities, obediently invokes God, and firmly determines that God wills to be propitious, and, having mitigated our hardships, to be present with us and to help us, lest we be utterly submerged and overwhelmed as if by waves, just as these sayings affirm.

Psalm 49: Call upon me in the day of thy tribulation, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me. Psalm 33: The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart. Nahum 1: The Lord is good and comforting in tribulation, and knowing or accepting those who hope in Him. Therefore, as I have said, let us exercise patience, faith, and hope in this kind of fasting in these ways.

For this very consolation is that most salutary balm with which we then anoint and cover our heads. For although youth does not yet know or understand much about this fast, namely, about tolerance in the cross and great and true sorrows, nevertheless those who are older, whose age has already matured, know that the true members of the Church are not without the cares of their calling and sharp pains of the mind, by which they are often so harshly exercised that they cannot even admit food or drink.

Furthermore, there are many poor people who truly lack the things necessary for sustenance, and do not have food and drink suitable to nature.

Concerning this difficult, serious, and sad fast, which neither is neither hypocritical nor forced, let Christians remember the consolation, how it is to be tolerated and endured, and let them know the effective remedies that truly heal the sorrows of the heart.

The third fast is pedagogical, and an exercise chosen spontaneously or of one's own accord, so that, if anyone wishes to abstain from food and drink for a day, or to eat only once and a little bit, with this purpose, that the mind may be more fit for intention in prayer, studies, and business. This exercise, chosen by our own judgment, is in reality only a voluntary work of temperance moderating food and drink, and therefore it is free for anyone, as he judges it to be suitable to his age and strength, either to restrain the body by fasting for an entire day, or to use as little food and drink as possible in a day to restore strength.

And so it was customary in the Church at all times: for the saints to gather while fasting to pray.

Thus Acts 10: Cornelius fasts for four days, when, having sent an angel divinely, he receives the command to send for Peter. Regarding this custom of fasting, no general or universal law can be enacted, prescribing one mode or a certain form of such exercises, the variety of which cannot be comprehended by rules, since some things are suitable for some and others for others.

Nevertheless, individuals privately, as the state of their health and time allowed, ought often to devote a certain day to prayers and fasting, which they would spend entirely abstaining from food in pious meditation on divine revelations and promises, so that, namely, with the intention of the mind and the alacrity of the heart excited toward the thought of God, prayer might be kindled, and spiritual actions might not be hindered. But such is the barbarism among the people, that most are persuaded that, if they are fasting for one day, they cannot live through the night immediately following.

I will not speak at greater length on this matter, but I will only exhort you to the fast of the first kind, that is, to the temperance most severely commanded by God to all men, that we do not spend our lives in carousing, gluttony, and drinking bouts.

Concerning this diligence in curbing desires, the Lord preaches in Luke 21: Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with drunkenness and gluttony.

The matter itself speaks, and daily examples, alas, testify all too much, that in these regions almost all effort is spent on the preparations of banquets, and on drunkenness, and on those monstrous drinking vessels. Wherefore it is manifest that now we are being punished by God in various ways, such as by fires, wars, and convulsions and confusions of governments, or polities, for this more than beastly gluttony of the belly, and the custom of gluttonizing and drinking to excess.

Furthermore, how often do you see drunken men rushing headlong into their own ruin, and often clashing among themselves with bloody iron, nay, even engaging in mutual slaughter? Also, how many and how great are the complaints heard everywhere from those declaiming publicly and privately, that the prices of goods for sale are rising, and casting curses upon the farmers because they do not sell grain and meat for less? But how can a more relaxed supply of grain be hoped for, in such profusion, gluttony, and preparations of pompous banquets?

Indeed, I believe that God would by no means make the earth so benignly fruitful, but would punish us with a shortage of grain and the sterility of the fields, were He not to spare the women in childbirth, the infants, the childhood, and the poor and needy little families. That God may grant sustenance to these, He blesses the earth, fosters the seeds of growing things, and provides for human necessities with a greater abundance of crops and fruits. But here, indeed, very many things should have been added concerning gross abuses.

Others, because of avarice, sell vicious things and corrupt the gifts of God, so that neither bread nor drink that is healthy and suitable to the nature of bodies can be had. Others, like the Homeric Grillus, who, having been changed into a pig by Circe, did not want to receive the human form, are so delighted by filth, dirt, and mire, that they are accustomed, in the manner of a muddy pig, to corrupt and contaminate any things whatsoever, bread, meat, beer, and other things of that kind. You do not recognize these gross abuses, nor do you judge them to be sins; therefore, punishments are accumulated. The eternal God, having mercifully pitied us, grants to these regions salutary governments, which do not permit the honest bonds of discipline to be wantonly loosened.

Latin:

Quando ieiunatis, non sitis, sicut hypocritae, tristes.

Populus Iudaicus non habuit certos et in lege divina praefinitos dies ieiunii, praeter unicum diem decimum septimi mensis, qui dicebatur festum expiationis. Ipsi vero nominarunt ieiunium abstinentiam ab omni cibo, seu inediam integrae diei, id est, cum prorsus nihil edebant tanto temporis intervallo, quantum est a vespere diei praecedentis usque ad vesperam sequentis. Sed Pharisaei cumularunt humanas traditiones, et crebra ieiunia servaverunt, quibus exercitiis praedicabant se promereri ingentia beneficia, remissionem peccatorum, et pietatis ac sanctimoniae incrementa.

Porro vos scitis ex Evangelio, nulla ieiunia sive divinitus mandata, sive ab hominibus electa et praescripta, mereri remissionem peccatorum. Imo tetra et horribilis blasphemia est, tribuere hunc summum honorem, et soli Christo debitum, nostris operibus, ritibus ac exercitiis, quod sint merita remissionis peccatorum, aut quod sint iustitia coram Deo, verum hic honos proprius est filii Dei Domini nostri Iesu Christi, cuius unius obedientia meruit nobis remissionem peccatorum, iustitiam, donationem Spiritus sancti, et haereditatem vitae aeternae. Et hanc ipsam amplitudinem gratiae seu misericordiae divinae necesse est a nobis apprehendi et accipi sola fide, acquiescente in mediatore Domino nostro Iesu Christo.

Huius firmissimi fundamenti nulla nos unquam capiat oblivio, sed eius memoriam perpetuo circumferamus animis, qua de re vos commonefieri saepenumero auditis. Nec sinatis abduci vos et dimoveri diabolicis praestigiis ab hac salutari et verissima Evangelii doctrina, sed assensione firmissima statuatis certo vos accipere et habere remissionem peccatorum, et imputari vobis iustitiam propter meritum Christi, sicut affirmat Propheta: Livore eius sanati sumus. Nec patiamini vobis in hac doctrina tenebras offundi.

Iam hoc quoque certissimum et irrefragabiliter verum est, quod quandocunque fide concipitur et inchoatur in cordibus haec dulcissima consolatio, certo Deus accendat et efficiat in nobis vitam et laetitiam acquiescentem in misericordia Dei, ut omnes vere Christiani seu conversi ad Deum sentiant et experiantur, iuxta dictum: Iustificati fide pacem habemus erga Deum. Veruntamen in hac ipsa vivificatione seu regeneratione oportet fiduciam tui cordis acquiescere in filio Dei, Domino nostro Iesu Christo, et non sua munditie vel novitate niti. Haec ipsa doctrina verissime vox est sacrosancti Evangelii, ac aeterna et immota veritas, nec est quicquam vel obscuritatis vel ambiguitatis, vel insidiarum, vel sophistices in hac sententia, quam recensui. Itaque constanter eam amplectimini et retinete, nec sinite vos perturbari ac circumveniri offusis nebulis ac corruptelis, vel a Papa, vel a Monachis, vel ab Augustana Sphynge, cui nomen est Interim, vel a quibusdam praestigiatoribus, qui nunc velut ex antro Trophonio prodeuntes iactitant se nova nobis mysteria patefacturos esse.

Occurrit autem nobis et quaeri hoc loco potest, quare ieiunia non prorsus improbentur hic et reiiciantur, et cur dicat Christus: Cum ieiunare voles, hilaritatem vultus et oculorum prae te feras.

Respondeo. Primum sciendum est, non praescribi ullam ieiuniorum formam, aut modum exercitiorum in Evangelio, sed liberum esse cuilibet et concessum cum prandere, tum coenare, ac vesci vel carnibus, vel piscibus, vel oleribus, vel rapis, vel quibuscunque cibis frui, divinitus cuique datis et oblatis. Verum in genere temperantia omnibus hominibus est praecepta, servans omni tempore modum in cibo et potu, convenientem naturae corporum.

Sic ipse Dominus praecipit Lucae 21.: Attendite, ne graventur corda vestra crapulae et ebrietate.

Cur vero dicit corda gravari? videtur enim potius dicendum fuisse, ventrem pastu potuque immodico repletum ac refertum inerti mole gravari?

Respondeo. Dominus ideo nominatim de corde loquitur, quia in temulentis exstinguitur invocatio Dei.

Quare gubernatio seu actio divina impeditur in nobis, intemperantia templum Dei, nempe cor et cerebrum, violantibus. Hoc modo corda gravantur ingluvie et helluationibus.

In eandem quoque sententiam Petrus inquit 1. Petri 4.: Estote temperantes et sobrii ad precandum. Et Hoseae 4. scriptum est: Scortatio, vinum et ebrietas auferunt cor, hoc est, laxant humanos animos, et effrenatos in furorem agunt, ac impediunt intentionem in invocatione, ipsiusque Dei efficaciam seu effectiones in cordibus.

Itaque principio notum sit vobis hoc necessarium praeceptum, quod videlicet temperantia in cibo ac potu sit opus necessarium quocunque tempore.

Ac de his mandatis exercitiis ieiuniorum loquitur Evangelium.

Haec sive abstinentia sive forma ieiunii, non est hypocrisis, ac hilariter fieri seu praestari debet in fide, invocatione, et gratiarum actione ad Deum. Estque fides et laetitia in Deo illud ipsum generosissimum ac pretiosum balsamum, cuius hic fit mentio, quo nimirum se perfundere debent ieiunantes. Ac ne potest quidem hilariter, ardenter et ex animo fieri tum invocatio tum gratiarum actio, quam diu tibi cibo potuque distento, vel halanti etiamnum pridianam crapulam, spiritus turbantur et exaestuant in cerebro.

Intueatur et consideret sese unusquisque, tunc animadvertet ac deprehendet, utrum ieiunii et sobrii sit ardentior invocatio, an temulenti et vino crapulaque distenti.

Propterea coniungit utrumque scriptura Matth. 17.: In ieiunio et oratione, ut significet invocationem nimis esse languidam frigidamque, imo prorsus impediri et exstingui in vita ebriosa, Cyclopica et beluina.

Secundo, Evangelium loquitur de alio quodam genere ieiunii longe difficiliore magisque serio, cum videlicet cor adeo plenum veris doloribus angoribusque confectum est, ut ab animo moestitia et curis occupato ventriculus languefactus ne quidem admittat cibum, nec frui potu allato possit.

Tale fuit ieiunium Davidis obiurgati a Propheta Nathan. Sic in Ninive ieiunarunt aliqui sancti homines audita concione Ionae. Ita Matthaei 9. inquit ipse Dominus, fore, ut discipuli sui ieiunent tunc, cum sponsus ab eis auferetur.

Hoc modo ieiunavit et Paulus post conversionem. Item, sic pauperes familiae propter inopiam coguntur ieiunare ac propemodum contabescunt fame, quia desunt eis necessaria ad victum, seu res naturae convenientes.

Sic et Agar cum filio paene siti periit, in solitudine non habens aquam. Hoc ieiunii genus Ecclesiae proprium nequaquam est simulatio vel hypocrisis, si cor Deo sese subiciens patienter obediat in afflictionibus.

Ac tunc quidem haec consolatio maxime necessaria est, ut accedat laetitia et hilaritas, atque fragrantissimo balsamo caput perfundatur. Haec enim laetitia et balsami fragrantia est ipsa consolatio, qua cor fide ac spe vivificatum erigitur, et in adversis tolerandis obediens invocat Deum, certoque statuit Deum velle propitium esse, ac mitigatis aerumnis adesse nobis atque opitulari, ne prorsus mergamur et tanquam fluctibus obruamur, sicut affirmant haec dicta.

Psalmo 49.: Invoca me in die tribulationis tuae, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me. Psalmo 33.: Prope est Dominus his qui tribulati sunt corde. Nahum 1.: Bonus est Dominus et confortans in tribulatione, et agnoscens seu acceptans sperantes in se. Iis igitur, ut dixi, modis patientiam, fidem et spem in hoc genere ieiunii exerceamus.

Etenim haec ipsa consolatio est illud saluberrimum balsamum, quo tunc ungimus ac perfundimus capita nostra. Etsi enim iuvenilis aetas de hoc ieiunio, videlicet, de tolerantia in cruce et magnis verisque doloribus, nondum scit aut intelligit multa, tamen grandiores, quorum iam maturuit aetas, norunt, non deesse veris Ecclesiae membris et vocationis curas, et acres animi dolores, quibus saepe adeo duriter exercentur, ut ne possint quidem admittere cibum aut potum.

Praeterea multi sunt pauperes, qui vere indigent rebus ad victum necessariis, nec habent cibum et potum naturae convenientem.

De hoc difficili, serio, tristique ieiunio, quod nec hypocriticum nec accersitum est, Christiani meminerint consolationem, quomodo tolerandum perferendumque sit, ac norint efficacia remedia vere sanantia dolores cordis.

Tertium ieiunium est paedagogicum, ac sponte seu ultro electum exercitium, ut, si quis in die aut prorsus abstinere a cibo, potuque, aut semel duntaxat et pauxillum velit edere, hoc fine, ut magis idoneus sit animus ad intentionem in invocatione, studiis, ac negotiis. Hoc exercitium arbitrio nostro electum re ipsa tantum est opus voluntarium temperantiae moderantis cibum et potum, ideoque cuilibet liberum est, prout aetati viribusque suis convenire iudicat, vel inedia integri diei corpus coërcere, vel in die quam minimum cibi et potionis ad reficiendas vires adhibere.

Itaque usitatum fuit in Ecclesia omnibus temporibus: Sanctos convenire ieiunos ad precandum.

Sic Act. 10.: Cornelius quatriduum ieiunat, cum misso divinitus angelo mandatum accipit de accersendo Petro.

De hoc more ieiunandi non potest ferri lex aliqua generalis vel universalis, praescribens unum modum seu certam formam talium exercitiorum, quorum varietas nequit comprehendi regulis, cum alia aliis congruant. Singuli tamen privatim, prout valetudinis ac temporis ratio pateretur, debebant saepe tribuere precibus et ieiunio certum aliquem diem, quem totum a cibo se abstinentes consumerent in pia meditatione patefactionum et promissionum divinarum, ut videlicet animi intentione et cordis alacritate excitata ad cogitationem de Deo, accenderetur invocatio, nec spirituales actiones impedirentur.

Sed ea barbaries est in populo, ut plerisque persuasum sit, se, si unum diem ieiuni sint, noctem continuo sequentem non posse vivere.

Nec prolixius hac de re dicam, sed tantum vos ad ieiunium primi generis adhortabor, id est, ad temperantiam severissime mandatam a Deo omnibus hominibus, ne in comessationibus, helluationibus, certaminibusque poculorum vitam degamus.

De hac diligentia frenandi cupiditates Dominus concionatur Lucae 21.: Videte ne corda vestra graventur ebrietate et crapula. Loquitur autem res ipsa, et quotidiana exempla, proh dolor, nimis multa testantur, in his regionibus omne fere studium conviviorum apparatibus, et ebrietati, atque immanibus illis poculis impendi.

Quare manifestum est, nunc a Deo variis modis puniri, ut incendiis, bellis, et convulsionibus atque confusionibus regiminum, seu politiarum, plus quam belluinam istam ventris ingluviem, et helluandi perpotandique consuetudinem. Praeterea, quoties videtis temulentos homines ultro ruere in suas clades, et saepe cruento ferro inter se ipsos concurrere, imo et caedibus mutuis grassari? Item, quot et quantae passim audiuntur querelae declamitantium publice privatimque, crescere pretia rerum venalium, et in agricolas maledicta coniicientium, quod non minoris vendant fruges et carnes?

At quomodo potest laxior annona sperari, in tantis profusionibus, helluationibus, pomparum conviviorumque apparatibus? Equidem credo quod Deus nequaquam adeo benigne foecundaret terram, sed inopia frumenti et agrorum sterilitate nos castigaret, nisi puerperis, infantibus, pueritiae, ac misellis et egentibus familiolis parceret. His ut victum largiatur Deus, benedicit terrae, fovet semina rerum nascentium, largiorem esse, ubertate frugum et fructuum prospicit humanis necessitatibus.

Verum hic erant addenda sane plurima de crassis abusibus. Alii propter avaritiam res vitiosas vendunt, atque Dei dona corrumpunt, adeo ut nec panis nec potus salubris naturaeque corporum conveniens haberi possit. Alii Homerico Grillo similes, qui a Circe in porcum mutatus recipere hominis figuram noluit, adeo delectantur immunditie, sordibus et illuvie, ut in morem suis lutulenti quaslibet res, panem, carnes, cerevisiae et id genus alia corrumpere et contaminare soleant. Istos crassos abusum non agnoscitis nec iudicatis esse peccata, propterea cumulantur poenae, Deus aeternus clementer nostri misertus tribut his regionibus salutaria regimina, quae non permittant laxari petulanter honesta disciplinae vincula.

## 6:19 Sermons on Matthew
Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth.

Now follows a sermon on avarice and the trust that rests in money, wealth, and the abundance of family property.

Here, first, let the words of Paul in Ephesians 4 be familiarly noted by you: Let everyone labor with his own hands, working what is good, so that he himself may have, and may share with the needy. Likewise Gen. 3. God says: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat thy bread. Likewise Psalm 128: For thou shalt eat the labours of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee. And everywhere there exist very many divine sentences, which command just labours appropriate to one's vocation. And it is a prescription of nature itself and of reason, nay, the will of God, that a head of a family should have the necessities for sustenance, and by labours convenient to his vocation should prepare resources, increase and protect his household property.

This virtue, namely diligence, seeking sustenance rightly and in order, preparing wealth, and preserving acquired resources, pleases God, and can be named economy, diligent and just, and divinely ordered. The extremes, or vices contrary to this diligence, are: the one, prodigality, exhausting resources through profusion; the other, avarice, seeking riches through filth, thefts, and rapacity. Moreover, avarice is the desire to scrape together and accumulate wealth in any way whatsoever, namely by unjust gains and various rapines and thefts, both hidden and manifest, as when vicious and faked goods are pushed out, when bread and beer are corrupted and depraved, when adulterated things are paid for as good, when by fraudulent sales and impostures snares are laid for others, when under various pretexts a loan is taken, and whatever is owed to others is not faithfully paid. Likewise when usury is sought, when unjust traps for seeking money are practiced, when finally equality and justice are violated in defrauding others.

All these things are prohibited in the seventh commandment: Thou shalt not steal. Nor does any of these need a lengthy declaration, but let individuals examine themselves, and notice where they act faithfully and candidly, where fallaciously and insidiously, and let them amend their ways.

Because such injustice is not a light sin, but one which God punishes in this life with atrocious penalties, and will punish with eternal torments, unless there is a conversion to God. Thus says Isaiah 33: Woe to thee that spoilest, for thou shalt be spoiled. And so you see clearly those growing by peculation and various frauds, finally being shaken out of their fortunes. And from experience that saying has arisen: Ill-gotten gains ill decay.

Thus Paul says 1 Cor. 6: Adulterers, thieves etc. shall not be heirs of God and eternal life.

Furthermore, this too is a species of avarice, and a huge sin, when money, wealth, and supplies are preferred to pious doctrine and divine truth. How great is the number of these in many regions? Who, having acknowledged the truth, nevertheless flee the dangers of confusion, nay, even establish and assist the persecution or oppression of the purer doctrine, lest they bring into jeopardy or lose their dignity, goods, riches, and tranquility. This too is a species of avarice, when you have moderate resources, and do not wish, according to your means and place, to pluck off something for God, and contribute both to the conservation of the ministry of the Church, and to relieving the difficulties of the truly needy, just as Nabal did not wish to help David, whom nevertheless the present occasion commended to him.

To the species of avarice must be added this sad sin, when your heart rests and relies more on the trust of money, power, and wealth, than on faith in the presence and divine goodness, while secure and not acknowledging your own weakness, you allow both the fear of God and invocation to be extinguished in your heart, and by vain trust in your own riches you seek pleasures, indulge in the desire for vengeance, etc. Which are indeed secret, but sad and foul sins, about which there would hardly be a place to discourse more copiously now. All these sins are prohibited in this saying of Christ: Lay not up for yourselves treasures, in which the heart as it were clings and rests, and which are of more value to him than God himself.

Therefore he adds: Where your heart is, there is your treasure, which is entirely true of the avaricious, who make and esteem their gains, riches, and πλεονεκτήματα (covetousness) of much more value than God.

On prodigality.

I will not speak at length on prodigality, for the thing itself speaks, as is clear to anyone, that prodigals, who have poured out their resources on unnecessary things through luxury or through a vain desire to show off wealth, stripped of their patrimonies, are finally turned to thefts and rapines, or idle beggary, which itself is a certain species of theft.

Hence the German rhymes say: He who wants to consume more, than his own plow can earn, will perish in the end, and perhaps die on the gallows. The meaning of which is: If anyone wishes to consume more from his share of things, Than he can seek with vigilant diligence: He shall seek his living by begging, knocking at doors, Or the cross and the noose will bring him a sad death.

And there exists a divine command specifically prohibiting the squandering and dissipation of inheritances, Prov. 5: Do not give your substance to the cruel, nor let strangers be satisfied with your resources. For he calls those cruel and strangers who abuse the resources and generosity of others, and who, like harpies and leeches, drain their blood, and after they have devoured the resources of others, they mock and insult in their calamity those to whom they owed fidelity and gratitude.

Furthermore, it can be seen in courts and in administration or political government how many impediments and pernicious detriments are caused by vain profusion. When lords or powers spend ordinary tributes and legitimate pensions on unnecessary expenses, trappings, and pomp, and beyond the measure of their resources squander many things in a vain pursuit of glory where there is no need, afterwards they themselves are neither provided with money to conduct necessary affairs, nor do they spare the resources of the citizens, but by immoderate extortions they skin the people and accumulate intolerable burdens on their own territories and jurisdictions.

May you diligently consider and weigh all these things, and learn with thanksgiving to God to order and prudently both allocate and guard resources justly acquired, and may you not defraud others under any pretexts. Indeed, know also this: that resources, a living, and household property are offered by God and are benefits of God, and that one should not neglect God in the administration or acquisition of fortunes, but should wish to protect, increase, and promote them for those who use them rightly and serve faithfully in their calling; and that He also wills to attenuate and dissipate resources when notable abuses are committed against conscience, as experience proves and eyes testify that these things happen divinely in this way.

This common doctrine concerning property, or the distinction of ownerships, and the legitimate use of resources, you ought here to think upon and meditate on attentively. I did not wish to agitate arduous and subtle questions in this place, but to make mention of common affairs, cases, and vices, of which in the miseries and infirmity of this life examples are too frequent, and alas, are placed daily before our eyes, concerning thefts of all kinds, unjust pursuits and gains, and the manifold abuse of resources.

Christ also speaks of these very sins, and there is no doubt that we too, if we worshipped God with true piety, would be more diligent in these economic, however light they may seem, duties; namely, that in just order we would acquire or prepare, and administer or allocate these external and bodily goods, and that one would not, like wolves, dogs, and cats fighting over food, snatch away the morsel or food from another's jaws as if it were snatched from the throat. God certainly wills and demands that we declare our faith and fear of God even by this kind of obedience, and that we render to Him this honor and due worship; namely, that we kindly, faithfully, and justly communicate things and duties among ourselves, according to the saying of the Prophet: I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings, etc.

What else can we preachers do but sound the voice of the Decalogue and propose divine commands to you, the hearers? Furthermore, the duty of the political magistrate was in many such matters to protect justice by exercising judgments and the execution of punishments, or by punishing violators of justice and discipline.

But governments, alas, are more languid in these last times, and in this delirious old age of the world. May God mercifully grant just and salutary empires to the Church, and may He also turn your minds and ours—that is, the minds of all—to living piously, temperately, in order, circumspectly, and soberly, so that we may honor Him, and that in the government of morals, anxious minds may be kindled to invocation and other virtues congruent with the divine will, Amen.

The lamp of the body is the eye. This memorable saying is a general rule, reminding us that in any work we should principally consider the intention of the mind or the distinctions of the ends, and not look only at... the gesture or simulation of the external work.

For example: Abraham, likewise the widow of Zarephath, and other holy men gave alms. Now, very many rich men among the Gentiles or hypocrites distribute alms no less kindly.

Here hypocrites perform works similar to the works of the pious, nor do the external gestures differ; indeed, it can happen that Ethnic liberality far exceeds in magnificence the pious work of the widow of Zarephath, who in extreme poverty offers a little flour to the exiled Elijah. But the end makes the distinction, because the interior movements of the heart are clearly dissimilar. The impious, that is, Ethnics and hypocrites, do not do good to others for the sake of God, or so that they may obey God, but either out of a certain ostentation and the hunting of popular glory, or because they pretend that by their beneficence they merit the remission of sins, and are just before God, just as Mahomet and Papists teach concerning satisfactions and the compensation of offenses.

In this example it is clear that works similar in external appearance must be prudently and far distinguished. For some things are done with a true movement of the heart acknowledging God, and on account of the command of God, concerning which works the Lord delivers a general rule in this place: When the heart is hypocritical, then even the external work is a feigned gesture, and a painted hypocrisy full of sin and displeasing to God.

This rule encompasses very many examples, namely, all external ceremonies. Cain and Abel, Saul and David offer sacrifices, and the similarity of an external work imposes upon many, so that they judge that there is no difference, but the hearts are entirely dissimilar. Furthermore, the first and greatest commandment says: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart. Likewise, Rom. 10: With the heart one believes unto righteousness, etc. And in Isaiah 29, God criticizes and rejects hypocrisy with this voice: This people draws near with their mouth, and honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me, just as Cain, Saul, Ethnics, and Monks artfully simulate external gestures, but the heart in them is full of filth and uncleanness, it is not ruled by light or the true acknowledgment of God, it is without the fear of God, without faith, full of envy and hatreds, indeed it rushes into slaughters and blasphemies. Sacrifices and external gestures of this kind are foul sins, and worship horribly condemned and rejected, just as Solomon also affirms in Proverbs 28: The prayer of him who turns away his ears, so that they do not hear the law, shall be detestable. Likewise Ecclesiastes 4: Obedience is better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know how much evil they do. An example: Ethnics were without the true acknowledgment of God, full of turpitude, adulteries, and incestuous lusts, meanwhile, however, they heaped up sacrifices, by which they thought sins were wiped away.

The devil has always confirmed such blindness in the world; thus, impure Papistic sacrificers lived in manifest turpitude, who nevertheless, celebrating Masses, shamelessly dreamed and boasted that they appeased the wrath of God by the ceremony of their offering, and that the very reading of Masses merited huge benefits for the whole Church.

Solomon speaks of such insane and blind hypocrites, saying: These fools do not know how much evil they do. For they wander from the true God, ignorant of the divine will, and they do not even understand their own works, but their worship and sacrifices are superstitious affectations and horrible sins. Therefore, concerning this blindness, the Lord says here in general and universally: If your eye is evil, your whole body will be darkness; that is, it is necessary to maintain the distinction of external works. Wherever the heart is pious and sincere, there also external works are uncorrupted and unpolluted. But where the heart is impure and hypocritical, where the affectation of external works or deeds, however magnificent, plausible, and specious, is a feigned superstition and a grave sin. This is the simple and proper understanding of these words of Christ.

Question.

But you say: When, therefore, is the heart sincere? and how can it be known whether the movements of the heart are pure?

Response.

First, it is necessary that the heart know and understand the word of God, according to the verse of the Psalm: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths. It is necessary that this light first be kindled in us, and that it be received and apprehended by a true and firm faith of the heart, but truly, rightly, and piously understood, lest we be drawn away by monstrous speculations and wandering into heresies, fanatical delusions, Monastic dreams, and sophistic perplexities, just as the devil at all times incites and impels certain petulant and insane men, so that, failing from the word of God, they are entangled in the corruptions of doctrine, and embrace pernicious errors and the deceits of sophisms.

Whenever, therefore, a man is ruled by the word of God, and there is no lack of a sincere and true understanding of the divine voice or a right sentiment, which faith firmly embraced retains and rejoices in, then it shines upon the heart, what the law is, what the eternal promise and reconcilia- or grace, how God is to be acknowledged and invoked, why the Son of God was sent, and what his benefits are, what are the true forms of worship of God, and what order of all works ought to be established.… But when this light is kindled in human minds, it is necessary that there exist a true and serious conversion to God or repentance, that is, true fears arising from the recognition of divine wrath against our sins, and true faith and trust resting in God on account of the Son, the mediator.

Furthermore, wherever this faith shines, there subsequently all forms of worship, and other works, divinely instituted, commanded, and approved, or whatever observances, can be rightly ordered and judged.

Let us declare this with an example.

After Paul knew that he was accepted and pleasing to God, that he was righteous freely on account of the obedience of our Lord Jesus Christ, and there had burned in his heart true fear of God, true faith, and true invocation, he clearly understood that fasts, ceremonies, and whatever works chosen by us were by no means merits for the remission of sins, or righteousness before God, but were external exercises, which can be observed or omitted according to circumstances.

That the hermit Anthony might learn this order, he was admonished by a singular revelation, not to prefer his own fasts and the sweetest exercises of solitude to the very hard life of the Alexandrian cobbler.

Recite the history: They say that it once came into the mind of St. Anthony, that he desired to know whether the kind of life which he himself had undertaken in those harder exercises of solitude was more excellent, and more pleasing to God, than the duties of common life, which Christian fathers of families are accustomed to perform, in whom no manifest baseness dwells; there God, wishing to show the hermit through a dream or some revelation how much he was progressing in this kind of life, showed him the house of an Alexandrian cobbler near the gate, and ordered him to explore his exercises and gifts.

Coming therefore into the city of Alexandria, Anthony enters the house of the cobbler, addresses the father of the family, and first asks about his doctrine, whether he is a Christian, and whether he embraces with true faith the Creed and all the writings of the Prophets and Apostles?

Here he modestly answers about his doctrine, confesses that he is a Christian, affirms that he rejects and condemns heathen idol-manias, and invokes the true God in the recognition of Jesus Christ the mediator, and in sum says that he believes all the articles of the faith, and that he rejects impious opinions, which fight against any article of the Creed, and with true groans asks of God that these beginnings of true faith be confirmed in his breast, lest he fall into errors, heresies, and fanatic furies, just as in all ages the contagions of most sad errors have wandered far and wide.

But when these things were gladly heard, Anthony asks, what worship then does he perform, what exercises of piety does he use, by what works is he accustomed to venerate God?

Then the cobbler: This faith, he says, by which I truly believe in God, and give thanks for such great goodness and huge benefits, that God in his immense mercy freely accepts me on account of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, that he pronounces me righteous, that he wills to be propitious to me, is the highest and chief worship.

Therefore daily by the thought of such great benefits I am stirred to thanksgiving, and would that I could celebrate the divine goodness and benevolence with an ardent heart and true gratitude.

For besides this thanksgiving, and the proclamation of benefits, there would be nothing left by which I could show honor to God, and by which I could testify to the will of returning grace.

Furthermore, every day, rising in the morning from bed, I give thanks to God with a short prayer, and I ask for the remission of sins, life, consolation, government, food, defense, and the mitigation of miseries, for myself, my wife, my children, and the Church.

The same thanksgiving, and petition, I repeat sitting at the table, and when I am about to go to sleep.

When these things were highly approved by Anthony, he proceeds to ask about the order and manner of fasts and bodily exercises.

This man answers: After I have prayed in the morning with a few words for my family and the whole city, I gladly do my domestic works.

For I am pressed by the common burden of poverty, therefore the necessity lies upon me, with God's help, to seek food for my small children and my little family.

Therefore I apply myself to my craft, and I take care that my children are rightly taught, and that my family is invited and instructed in the recognition and invocation of God.

Furthermore, whatever legitimate authority commands in political affairs, I diligently execute, and I offer obedience in paying tribute, and in sustaining the common burdens of the citizens.

Have you no other, says Anthony, harder exercises? such as certain days of fasting, and certain peculiar observations? Do you think it is a small thing, says the other, for me to sustain labor and fastings? Since in the workshop I exercise my craft with constant works, and seek the sustenance of my domestic family, since I am conflicted with various miseries, having to endure both economic difficulties and burdens imposed by the republic, since many things happen from time to time that cruelly torture a father of a family. Furthermore, for him whom multiple domestic miseries fatigue, whom a mass of cares in civil government and political offices exercises, it is not right to look around idly and cease, nor will there ever be a lack of causes, occasions, and dangers by which he may be stirred up to invocation, to exercising faith and love.

I wonder, therefore, why in these public and private miseries you do not consider the exercises of a pious father of a family to be a sufficiently hard warfare, but rather a soft leisure, and I do not know what more difficult and perfect works you require. Great piety and holiness exist in the offices of common life: to acknowledge God rightly, to invoke Him truly in the recognition and trust of Christ, then to live chastely in marriage, to serve faithfully in economic and political labors, and in these miseries and dangers to exercise daily faith and invocation, and finally piety in retaining the possession of the doctrine concerning God. By this very grave response, Antonius was moved to understand that his monastic life in solitude did not excel, nor was it to be preferred to the labors, offices, and exercises of political and economic life, in which the fear of God and faith are confirmed by the testimony of His presence.

He learned, therefore, the degrees, order, and distinctions between faith and works, between the pious motions of the heart and external gestures. Here let us also compare David and Alexander, so that we may be admonished concerning the differences between both governors.

Alexander was a most fierce warrior, gifted with the empire of the whole world, so flourishing in wealth and power that the possession of his empire was five or six times greater in magnitude than the Israelite kingdom of David. Likewise, he fought many illustrious battles, obtained many glorious victories, and spared captives mercifully. Meanwhile, the heart of such a prince, divinely instructed in the excellence of virtues and happiness, was full of contempt for God, filth, and other turpitudes. And therefore, he abused the gifts with which he was adorned by God—authority, wealth, kingdoms, and victories—for pride, for pleasures, and for the magnificence of pageants. But in the heart of David shone the true recognition of God, whom he rightly invoked; he attributed victories and kingdoms to the glory of God and the propagation of saving doctrine. And since he knew that he owed obedience to God in this political degree in which he had been placed, he eagerly undertook and sustained such great labors; he fought most fiercely to defend the heavenly doctrine, and he did not feel that he was earning the remission of sins by these struggles and by this mass of cares and sorrows, nor did he protect the honor and power of the kingdom for this end, that he himself might enjoy huge glory, much less that he might be allowed to do anything with impunity, and that, acting unjustly, he could not be restrained or repressed by anyone.

By the consideration of these and similar examples, the sentence of the saying becomes illustrious and clear: If your eye is malicious, your whole body will be darkness, that is, when the heart within is not moved and ruled by true judgment nor by an honest purpose, then it is certain that the gestures of an external work are sins, and by no means can they receive the name of divine worships. All of which are worthy of observation, so that you may recognize the order or degrees of true divine worships, and in order you may exercise yourselves in these degrees. For without exercises, true sorrows of the soul, ardent invocation, and the sense of divine consolation, this doctrine can by no means be understood. But this text the Papists have foully torn apart with insipid interpretations, since they did not even understand or judge their own works, according to the gnome of Solomon, Ecclesiastes 4: They do not know how much evil they do.

And hypocrites are ignorant of what the worships of their own superstition are, and they do not know what they are doing, while they show off and peddle their ceremonies with distinguished titles. And so they have brought in foul and pernicious errors, they have horribly perverted and disturbed the order of works, they have preferred human traditions to divine commands, and have said that men earn remission by their own works. All these and similar errors are taxed and reprehended by this short saying of Christ: If your eye is evil, it will be necessary for the whole body to be darkness, by which rule is constituted the distinction between hypocrisy and legitimate or divinely ordained and approved works.

And thus far concerning that general rule.

The Sermon now follows.

No one can serve two masters etc.

Political governments or the empires of the world have their own order, distinct by certain degrees; individual citizens and subjects have many masters, namely the consuls of the city, the prefect, the prince; yet these degrees are established in such an order that every citizen should primarily serve and obey the supreme head or governor, and afterwards, in their place, the other inferior masters. Nor are those who serve authorities in this order said to serve two masters, as long as the superior master and the inferior magistrates are united in their wills and opinions.

But when they are distracted in their minds and wills, and dissent among themselves, then certainly no one can adhere to and serve both of the discordant parties equally, just as the same water cannot be simultaneously hot and cold, because contrary or conflicting things cannot be placed together, nor joined in the same subject, and even if they are together, one is soon driven out by the other.

A similar reason applies in this case, about which the Lord preaches: No one can serve two masters, namely, those who are not in agreement and harmony with each other, but are turbulent and discordant.

Likewise, when there is no legitimate authority with degrees distinct in a certain order, one subject to the other, as, no one can serve King Ferdinand and the Turkish tyrant equally, because they dissent among themselves with hostile hatreds.

For King Ferdinand affirms that Hungary is his, and therefore denies that he will allow it to be snatched from him. In this manifest dissension and grave enmity, it is clear that no soldier can earn wages from both, or serve both. Examples of this kind are illustrious, plain, and clear.

So too, Judas cannot equally and alike venerate, worship, and magnify money and God.

For the divine voice says: Do not aid the oppression of the innocent; but avarice clamors: Rather, for the sake of money, confirm and aid unjust cruelty. Many now imitate this example.

For some wish to simultaneously embrace the doctrine of the Gospel and have Bishoprics and Priesthoods conferred upon them by the Roman Pontiff, but the voice of the Gospel is: Flee from idols, that is, neither be devoted to idolatrous cults, nor approve of them.

But the Episcopate protests, commanding the worship and approval of idols, so that you may be raised to the pinnacle of such dignity and obtain a beautiful principality. Furthermore, how common it is in the courts of princes for noble men to wish to appear Evangelical, while in the meantime they simultaneously hunt for favor and play up to the affections of the powerful, who, hostile to pious doctrine, persecute the Gospel.

From these and similar examples, the meaning of this text can be clearly understood.

And in this place, a rule is to be learned and observed: that God must be served before all things, or that the worship and honor of God is to be preferred to all creatures, according to the first commandment of the Decalogue: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, from which it follows most truly that nothing of all things is to be worshipped and equally loved as God Himself, nor is divine honor or love owed to God to be attributed to any creature; so far is it from being the case that anything of all things should be preferred to God, or more worshipped, or more ardently loved, to the insult of God Himself, and which would be repugnant and opposed to divine goodness.

This is the saving summary of that rule, which the following words in the text pursue: You cannot serve God equally and Mammon, or riches, which indeed you will understand in the same way as the things above, as if the Lord were saying: You ought by no means to seek riches in any way, omitting God, nor for the sake of riches act against God; you ought not to accept opulent Bishoprics and rich prebends, as they call them, to confirm and stabilize impious doctrine or false dogmas.

Likewise: You ought not for the sake of money violate other divine commands, just as usurers, robbers, thieves, and other impostors do, of which kind of sins there are certainly very many in the world.

For what is so common as to violate justice for the sake of money? According to the common proverb in the Teutonic language, for the sake of money men become wicked and dishonest.

A few years ago in Vienna, a certain baker had a servant whose name was Paul.

This man, having thoroughly inspected and explored the house, and having learned in which small chests money was accustomed to be kept, one night, insinuating himself into the same house, committed the murders of five people most cruelly in order, and first indeed slaughtered the servant sleeping on a bench, then the maid, afterwards the father of the family and his wife lying together in the same bed.

When, having killed these, he approached another bed, in which the little daughter was still very small, she cried out wailing: Ah Paul, I beseech you spare me, and do not take my life, you shall have all my dolls, whenever you wish.

But the devil impelled this robber to proceed, and confirmed the fury in him; he killed, therefore, the poor little girl, and having plundered the house and taken the money, fleeing Vienna, he arrived at Regensburg, which is fifty German miles away from Vienna.

But God himself is the executor of his own rule: Whoever shall take the sword, shall perish by the sword. Therefore, that robber, although he had departed at an interval of so many miles, was nevertheless divinely drawn back to punishment, and brought to a capital trial, and was sent back to Vienna in chains, where, pierced through by a spear or javelin, he paid for the blood of the innocent with a deserved execution. Suspended, however, on the javelin, or affixed to a sharp stake, he cried out miserably, that all the other tortures of the body which he was enduring were by no means as bitter a pain to him as the sharp bite and sense of pain caused by the recollection of the voice of the girl, who had said to the assassin: Ah Paul, let me live, I will give you all my dolls. Thus died this thief and robber in the torments of a most atrocious execution and the horrendous tortures of conscience. Mammon entangles one in such great sins, and brings about such sad and tragic ends. Remember these notable and gross examples, and while thinking on them, see to it that Mammon does not hold you captured and seized.

Question.

But here a question arises, whether one should seek a livelihood, and maintain family property? I answer. You must by all means seek and retain wealth, but in this order: First, that you obey God, and learn before all things to invoke and worship him rightly, and that you do not violate divine commands against your conscience, or knowingly and willingly. Afterwards, you must by honest labors, in an orderly manner according to your calling, prepare, arrange, protect, and increase your family property, or wealth. Indeed, God himself wishes by his goodness and blessing to assist your labors, so that they may be happy; he wishes to promote and increase your wealth for you, just as afterwards near the end of the chapter the gnome is added: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added to you divinely. Thus were the rich Abraham, Isaac, Joseph, David, Job. But because you have often heard the true and clear explanation of this question, I will not discourse on it more prolixly in this place; it follows in the text:

Do not be anxious about tomorrow, what you shall eat, or what you shall drink etc.

Here wise men, without the light of faith, think that these are idle and empty words, and that impossible things are commanded. I oppose, therefore, a brief and clear answer: it is true that wise men, ignorant of the exercises of faith, judge that certain Stoic hyperboles are being taught here, and that these are frivolous, useless words, similar to fabulous tales. But you, who have rightly learned the beginnings of Christian doctrine, and in whom the spark of faith is kindled, know that human minds, destitute of divine consolation in poverty, persecutions, and calamities, in such great private and public dangers, are vehemently tormented and anguished in the innermost senses of the soul, now here now there seeking protections, connections, and aids, fortifying themselves with factions and various practices. The text speaks of this solicitude, which is a huge torture and anguish of a trembling soul, born from diffidence, because the heart is neither raised nor sustained by divine consolation.

Wherefore, learn that there is a twofold solicitude.

One is the solicitude of diffidence, or the trepidation and torture of the heart, because it is not ruled by divine light and consolation, because it neither asks for nor expects help, defense, livelihood, and governance from God. Therefore often, alas, it happens that some men, because of the loss of wealth or poverty, are so harshly exercised by perturbations of the mind, anxieties, and solicitudes, that they waste away with grief, or even commit suicide, just as we remember examples.

This solicitude, full of diffidence, trepidation, blindness, and devoid of all true consolation, is here most severely forbidden. For the will of God is immutable, that in all dangers and necessities we should flee to him, hope for and ask for help from him, and not be broken by despair. This is taught by the most beautiful little verse of the Psalm, which you all ought to remember and often meditate upon: Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you.

Indeed, for this very reason the Lord serves the daily prayer and included these words: Give us this day our daily bread. Therefore, since he himself has ordered that food and the goods of the body be asked of him, he wishes without any doubt to provide these bodily goods as well, livelihood, defense, wealth; he wishes us not to fail from him nor be oppressed by despair. From this declaration it is clear and manifest that this solicitude is prohibited, which is diffidence, doubt, and despair of divine aid. Another solicitude is the care in the believer, the sedulity and diligence, divinely ordained, of performing the labors of one's place and one's vocation.

For example: David is an emperor or leader of an army. In fulfilling this vocation, it is necessary for him to apply just diligence and solicitude in leading, distributing, and placing military forces in ambushes. Likewise, in fighting with the enemy, in looking out from which places provisions can be conveniently supported or conveyed to the army, and [how] the grain supply can be expedited, and finally in exploring where the enemies have settled and are staying; in sum, it behooves him, as a sedulous and keen soldier, not to be slothful, nor drunk or intoxicated in performing his vocation. But to this care and diligence proper to one's vocation, there is added in the heart consolation, tranquility, and joy, namely, that while retaining constancy of mind, he believes that God is present with him, that He looks upon him, cares for him, protects him, and will help him; and therefore he invokes [God] joyfully, nay, he undertakes and sustains all labors the more promptly and cheerfully, because he knows that he, called by God, is helped and defended divinely, and he hopes for good outcomes. This solicitude of labor and diligence, joined with faith, is ordained and commanded divinely, and this sedulity or care of performing one's vocation does not mix unjust counsels and evil practices into business and ordained labors, as that former solicitude of diffidence often uses wicked counsels in the presence of the fear of future inconvenience, and seeks forbidden protections. But it restrains itself within bounds, rightly undertakes and placidly tolerates the labors commanded by God, and does not depart from the rule on account of future uncertain hopes or fears. Concerning which diligence Paul commands in Rom.

12: He who serves, let him serve faithfully; he who presides, let him be diligent, etc. Likewise, Psalm 128: Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you. Having therefore recognized and rightly understood this distinction of solicitude—that which torments the mind with diffidence, and that of solicitude or diligence in performing one's vocation, to which faith acquiescing in God gives light—this text can be moderately understood, which indeed proposes very many salutary admonitions, doctrines, and most sweet consolations, of which, clearly, this is the sum.

It is necessary for individual Christians at all times to know the doctrine concerning the distinction of promises, for there are twofold promises. The first and highest promise is the promise of grace or reconciliation and of eternal life to be given freely on account of the mediator Christ. Another is the promise concerning necessary goods in this life, or concerning corporal aid in every kind of necessity and danger, such as concerning food, defense, good health, etc.

Here, therefore, know that both kinds of promise are received by faith, and that by the consolation which each promise proposes, minds ought to be raised up and to acquiesce in God; nevertheless, one must always begin from the promise of grace and eternal salvation. Before you ask for present or corporal benefits, it behooves you at the beginning to consider whether your heart determines that it has God as propitious, and that it pleases God. Here it is necessary for you to look upon the Savior, the Son of God, and with true confidence of heart to determine that God, certainly appeased on account of the Son, receives you freely with immense goodness, that He remits your sins, that, reconciled, He wishes His mercy to be acknowledged, and that He truly vivifies you and makes you an heir of eternal salvation. This first promise is the chief voice of the Gospel, drawn from the bosom of the eternal Father, and it remains perpetually valid and firm, and immovable to the believer, whether he has corporal goods or whether corporal liberation does not happen to him in this mortal life.

For faith ought to rely on this eternal promise, and to retain this highest good, even if all temporal goods are to be lost, and the corporal life itself is to be poured out, as David, driven from his kingdom and cast into exile, nevertheless embraced and retained the consolation or voice of absolution, by which the Prophet Nathan had said to him: The Lord has taken away your sin. Therefore he believed most firmly that he had the remission of sins, and reconciliation, and that his prayers were received, and that he was an heir of eternal life, even if, stripped of all his glory, he had lost the kingdom, and could not recover it by his own counsels and strength.

Therefore also Job says in chapter 13: Even if God should kill me, I will hope in Him.

Let us propose to ourselves this eternal and immovable consolation, which depends neither on the condition of our dignity nor on any corporal benefits, and having embraced it at the beginning by faith, let us imprint it upon our hearts as a seal.

There are other promises concerning temporal goods, necessary for the preservation of bodily life. Although, therefore, God does not bestow and distribute the goods of the body equally to all, and indeed allows some of the Saints, and even the chief lights of the Church, such as Abel, Jonathan, John the Baptist, Paul, and many others, to be cruelly killed, yet these promises of bodily goods are not empty or void, but have this most true and most certain interpretation: that God, even in this present life, always wishes to gather and preserve the Church, and therefore by His counsel wishes assiduously to give it the necessary bodily goods, but with the condition that some may be punished or chastened.

Thus David, driven from his kingdom, is cast into exile. Likewise, that the cross may not be removed, but that the Church may be exercised by hardships and afflictions. Meanwhile, however, He wishes to mitigate for us both the punishments or chastisements, and the exercises or the cross, for those who do penance and call upon Him. Thus He confirms it Himself in Psalm 50: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. Likewise in Isaiah 1: Be converted, if your sins be as scarlet and as the worm, you shall be white as snow. This is, the guilt and magnitude of the most sad or tragic punishments shall be taken away and removed from you. Although, therefore, profane men who despise God judge these promises concerning help in afflictions, dangers, and bodily necessities to be empty sounds, yet let us know for certain that God did not in vain hand down such large and sweet promises, such as are also repeated in this text: Seek first the kingdom of God, and God will abundantly add other goods to you.

Therefore, let us apprehend and embrace them by faith, and let us each, with this confidence, perform the labors appropriate to our calling, let us expect sustenance, help, and defense from God, let us ask for these very goods with true groans, and let us give Him thanks, and let gratitude shine in our morals. For it is most certain that each one who is stirred up by this faith to invocation, and to the expectation of divine help, and to thanksgiving, experiences in reality the benefits, defense, aid, and deliverance of God. These are without any doubt most true, just as Psalm 34 proposes the application of examples: This poor man cried out and the Lord heard him, and saved him from all his tribulations; hasten with great frequency and flee to God, and your faces shall not be confounded. It is the will of God that we men should diligently and in just order perform and urge the labors of our own calling, that we should orderly seek sustenance, defense, and the safeguards of life, yet that we should meanwhile know that human labors in no way suffice, but that the help of God and His efficacious blessing must be added. And so, let there always be a conjunction of invocation and labor. For on this account God has added to the Gospel most rich and most ample promises concerning temporal things, and promises that He will help us also in bodily necessities and dangers. These divine oracles we should by no means consider as empty and old-wives' tales, but we should truly hold that God is truthful, and wishes to bring us aid according to His promises. Nay, we are convinced by the testimony of experience itself and of events, that God (to whom be grace, praise, and glory for everlasting and infinite ages) has so often mercifully helped, covered, and defended us while we were in such great dangers, that, having been struck with terror, we each feared that all things would utterly perish; nay, for this very reason God handed down the promises of bodily help, because He wishes us to exercise faith and invocation even in daily necessity, and in the expectation of bodily help, according to the verse in Psalm 50: Call upon me in the day of your trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. For if anyone does not learn to call upon God in bodily necessity as in a training ground, nor in these things, as in the cradles and rudiments of faith, wishes to expect a fragment of bread from God, how much more will he flee from God when that eternal and immense and infinite treasure of spiritual goods is to be sought and expected?
