Wherefore let us learn the exercises of faith and invocation in both kinds of promises, and let the recognition of divine goodness and presence grow even in seeking, hoping for, and expecting the benefits necessary for the body. These admonitions I judge to be sufficient for the explanation of the saying: Be not solicitous what you shall eat or drink, of which, however, we shall say more in the following sermon, God willing.

Seek first the kingdom of God, and His justice, and all these things shall be added to you. Be not solicitous for tomorrow, for the morrow will be solicitous for itself, sufficient for the day is its own affliction. You have heard recently, and you ought to remember and frequently meditate, that there are two kinds of promises, one of eternal things, the other of bodily things, and that first one ought to embrace and retain with firm faith the eternal promise, concerning the remission of sins and the gratuitous mercy of God on account of Christ, and never to fail in the promised reconciliation or be oppressed by trepidations and doubts, whether the comforts necessary for bodily life remain or are taken away. For the first step is to seek eternal goods; indeed, for this the Son of God was sent, that, the anger of the eternal Father being appeased, He might restore to those freed from sin and eternal death, justice and everlasting salvation.

Since, however, God has ordained this admirable order with ineffable goodness, that in this mortal life a gathering of the Church and of those to be saved should take place, and therefore He seriously wishes that in the custom of this fleeting life the beginnings of eternal life and justice should be initiated, bestowals of promises, one of eternal things, the other of corporal things, and that because the former, the eternal promise concerning the remission of sins and the gratuitous mercy of God through Christ, ought to be embraced and retained by firm faith, and one ought never to fail from the promised reconciliation nor be oppressed by trepidations and doubts, whether the comforts necessary for corporal life remain or are taken away.

For the first step is to seek eternal goods; indeed, the Son of God was sent for this purpose, that, having appeased the wrath of the eternal Father, He might restore to those freed from sin and eternal death, righteousness and everlasting salvation. But since God has established this admirable order with ineffable goodness, that in this mortal life a gathering of the Church and of those to be saved should take place, and therefore He seriously wills that in the custom of this fleeting life the beginnings of eternal life and righteousness should be initiated, He also bestows the goods of the body, so that in the meantime the Church may have food, drink, lodging, clothing, etc., as long as it enjoys the use of this external and transitory life.

And you heard it declared just now concerning the distinction of the promises, but then that admonition was also added, that it is certain that this is the will of God, that faith and invocation should be exercised together in both kinds of promises. Wherefore you ought to seek both eternal and corporal goods, but with this order preserved, which the Lord prescribed in these words: First seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all other goods shall be added unto you.

Which words, just as they are clear and illustrious, so they propose both a rule concerning the principal duty which God requires, and a most rich and sweetest consolation. The rule is that one must begin from eternal goods, and the first step is to seek the kingdom of God and divine righteousness, that is, to learn rightly and embrace seriously the word of God, so that we may prefer this very thing to all comforts of the body and of our life, and in true conversion to God, be inserted, joined, and become a member of the elect Church.

For the promises do not pertain to the impious who persevere in the contempt of God, but these, oppressed by present and eternal punishments, shall waste away, according to the horrible threats so often repeated in Scripture, as Psalm 12.: The Lord shall destroy the proud, the despisers of divine wrath and doctrine. Indeed, Christ Himself in Matthew 25. promulgates in the final judgment the condemnatory sentence in the saddest words: Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. But concerning temporal punishments in this life, Solomon says in Ecclesiastes 8.: I have certainly known and I know that it shall be well with those who fear God, and that it shall by no means be well with the impious, nor shall his life be long-lasting, but like a shadow he shall vanish, and he himself shall be punished. And Scripture is full of such testimonies.

Furthermore, individuals are admonished by the weight of the punishments which they sustain on their necks and shoulders, even if for those converted to God or doing penance, the hardships are mitigated.

Therefore, let this be the principal and first necessary rule, the guide of all deliberations and actions of the entire human life, namely, first to learn the word of God, to be converted to God, or to do penance, and by faith to apprehend the Redeemer and Savior our Lord Jesus Christ.

With this faith shining forth, let us afterwards be stirred up to seek, hope for, and expect also corporal aid. For in these very words: And all these things shall be added unto you, all goods necessary for life are promised in the calling.

Concerning the cross.

But human minds object: I hear the most generous promises of the goods of the body being inculcated, to which if events responded, the Church would by no means be more harshly pressed and shaken than the rest of the human race; yet by what great storms of persecutions is it shaken? Abel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, John the Baptist, Christ, the Apostles, and many thousands of Saints are killed in all times, and are most cruelly attacked.

Response. Both propositions are true: God both wills to provide the goods of the body, and that faith be exercised by the expectation of corporal aid: and at the same time He wills the Church to be subject to the cross, but on this condition, that in the meantime He most truly preserves at all times some assembly and flower or body of the Church that acknowledges, invokes, and celebrates Him, and does not allow the Church to be utterly destroyed and devoured by the devil, while they plot destruction for the human race, as it is written concerning the perpetuity and repression of the devils, Matthew 16: The gates of hell shall not prevail against it; nevertheless, in this way the Savior Son of God preserves and covers the Church, so that at the same time it is necessary that it be exercised by afflictions and subjected to immense miseries; indeed, it is necessary that the excellent members and the chief leaders in the ministry become similar and conformed in the cross, miseries, and death to the Redeemer Himself, our Lord Jesus Christ. Just as when God promises David victory and the safety of the Israelite army, it would be absurd to interpret the promise in such a way that they would undertake no labors in the battle line, undergo no dangers, receive no wounds, and that it would not happen that any soldiers fighting would be killed, but it is absolutely necessary that some of the fiercest and bravest men fighting in the battle line pour out their life and blood, so that the rest of the army may remain safe and achieve a glorious victory: so God fortifies, nourishes, defends, and preserves the body of the Church, even when its chief lights are foully torn apart and killed by tyrants.

For there are many most grave and great causes for which the Church, by the wonderful counsel of God, is subjected to so many and such great miseries. And since we ourselves also have many sins, not small nor light, God wills that examples of His judgment be seen, and through these punishments we, being reminded, are called back to conversion. Meanwhile, however, His immense mercy, through the Mediator, softens and mitigates present punishments to such an extent that the whole Church is not destroyed utterly, just as Sodom and Gomorrah were utterly destroyed; therefore, as long as we are in this mortal life, He gives good health, food, and other goods necessary for the preservation of bodily life.

This consolation concerning labors divinely ordained and present miseries the Lord proposed in these words: Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will take care of its own things, or will be anxious for itself; sufficient for the day is its own affliction. With the brief word 'affliction' the Lord admonishes and reminds us that we are subject to the cross and calamities, and that each day brings its own afflictions, by which God wills us to be exercised. These words are brief, as I said, but they encompass the whole history of life, and they preach about the immense miseries imposed upon the human race; they warn us not to indulge in security and pride, but to look upon this whole course of life, and to understand that in this life, for each individual, miseries of every kind are proposed daily, and finally to consider that, if this very mass of difficulties and afflictions, which we bear day by day heaped upon our necks and shoulders, were not mitigated and lightened by the immense mercy of God, it would have come to pass that, oppressed by much more atrocious punishments, which we would deserve by our blindness and hardness, we would succumb and perish.

See how much the Israelite people of Moses stir up daily of new struggles, tumults, and seditions. So much so that they can scarcely enjoy at any moment of time this security, that a placid, peaceful, and tranquil government will be in the future. Thus, the whole of life, in such great impediments which the devil and the organs of the devil throw in our way, is full of miseries inextricable by human counsel, and we are certainly all involved in daily and continuous dangers, as regards our own bodies, as regards the safety of our spouses and children, as regards food, and finally as regards rule or government. Wherefore, may you well consider and remember this brief saying, so that you may cast off security and pride: 'Sufficient for the day is its own affliction.'

The histories of all ages teach this very thing, and daily examples are in sight.

Moreover, our Lord Jesus Christ adds a most wise and most useful precept, having handed down a singular rule for discerning the kinds of afflictions. Affliction is twofold. One is the necessary cross, not sought out by our own curiosity, but afflicting us by itself by the certain counsel of God, so that we may be chastened and exercised. The other is affliction sought out by our own curiosity, when, through meddlesomeness or preposterous and hallucinating wisdom, we voluntarily entangle ourselves in troubles, anxieties, and miseries, as when a man seeks and takes upon himself unnecessary business, when princes stir up or attract wars without necessity, which they could have avoided, etc. Concerning this distinction the Lord preaches here: Let each day be anxious for itself, let it take care of its own things, let it bring its own afflictions and difficulties.

Tolerate these impediments rightly in the present, and do not in any way heap miseries upon yourselves, but only do what is necessary and commanded, content with the daily labor which your calling brings, and do not, out of human blindness, add security and pride to common calamities, but know that diligence divinely ordained will have enough labors, impediments, and anxieties of its own, besides the fact that multiple punishments and afflictions are added.

Therefore, prepare yourselves for this cross with faith, and ask God for a mitigation of your troubles. But beware lest, through curiosity or meddling and restlessness of mind, you seek out unnecessary business and pursuits that are foreign to your calling, and summon upon yourselves more difficulties, annoyances, and miseries than the present time and occasion offer you. Just as the pious and holy king Josias, while dreaming of security and imagining himself to be such a pious and well-deserving prince that he would encounter no offenses, but rather perpetual successes and peaceful outcomes, whatever he might attempt, stirred up an unnecessary war against the king of Egypt, in which, having received a wound, he died some time later. Let each of you consider and recall the course of his own life, and he will undoubtedly discover that he has drawn upon himself a great many punishments, dangers, and most sorrowful misfortunes through certain unnecessary occupations, and that if he had remained quiet (as the little servant says in the comedy), no evil would have befallen him.

Therefore let this rule also be observed: In great matters, only what is necessary should be done, and nothing that is not necessary should ever be attempted or undertaken.

But here an answer is given to your question about what is necessary and what is not.

I answer, moreover, clearly, simply, and plainly. The works and tasks that God has commanded you and that the nature of your duty requires are necessary, that is, the duties proper to your calling, in which you have been placed by God. On the other hand, unnecessary actions and occupations are to break out beyond your calling through some curiosity or ambition, and to take up matters belonging to others contrary to God’s command, or to thrust yourself into others’ callings. For example.

What, I ask, does the role of a ruler in civil government have to do with the calling or ministry of Thomae Monetarii? Why does he intrude into an administration not his own and overstep the bounds of his office? Why does he have one foot in the court and the other in the church? Why does he want to direct civil affairs, establish a new form of government, and set up new principalities in Germania? etc.

The holy and wise Apostle Paulus repeats the same admonition in striking and meaningful words, and commands with great wisdom, 1. Thessal. 4.: “We exhort you to strive with exceptional diligence to excel in this matter, and to make it your ambition to act—” Prepare yourselves, therefore, for this cross with faith, that you may rest in your own [vocation] and not run beyond your boundaries by rushing into the vocations of others.

In sum, polypragmosyne [meddlesomeness], or the rashness of those who undertake unnecessary things either out of curiosity, or fear of future danger, or foolish and pernicious hope, is always most unhappy, whether this confusion of vocations and disturbance of duties exists in the highest or in the lowest orders.

This singular wisdom, therefore, which avoids curiosity, meddlesomeness, and ambition, is commended by this saying of Christ: "Tomorrow will be anxious for itself; sufficient for the day is its own trouble," as if He were saying: "Do what is necessary in the present, which will have enough difficulties of its own, and do not, by your own curiosity, heap upon yourself troubles, anxieties, and miseries by thrusting yourself into the vocations of others."

King Uzziah, a good and especially praised king (2 Chronicles 26), wished to perform the office of a Priest and to sacrifice in the temple by himself against the divine ordinance; but God, declaring His wrath by a sudden punishment, struck him with leprosy.

Thus, manifold inconveniences and destructive punishments perpetually follow meddlesomeness, or the counsels and attempts of those who either try actions outside their vocation or break into the functions of others, whether out of curiosity or their own ambition.

If anyone, therefore, wishes to live rightly, so that, retaining a good conscience, he may be able in his own labors, actions, and business to seek and expect divine help, let him keep and follow this rule of life, which the Lord delivers and prescribes in this place.

First, seek the kingdom of God; that is, learn the true knowledge of God, and, having turned to God, rest in Him through the Mediator.

Then, perform the works of your vocation, and in the labors divinely commanded to you, exercise the invocation of God, and endure difficulties with a tranquil mind, in which you should also resolve that you are being helped divinely, and joyfully await good outcomes, and do not, with the light of faith extinguished, be consumed by cares and sorrows, or be broken by desperation and impatience.

If you have learned and practiced this art of life, you will experience in reality that God will be present and will help you, and that the outcomes of your business and counsels will be peaceful, favorable, and salutary, according to the saying of the Psalm: "Be subject to God, and hope in Him."

The same Psalm repeats the same most sweet maxim: "Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in Him, and He will act."

He calls the legitimate or just vocation of each person their "way."

To depart from one's calling, either through curiosity, or fear, or ambition, is to wander entirely from the path, to rush into darkness, into the snares of the devil, and into most sorrowful punishments. Although, therefore, these rules preach about so many and such great matters, the magnitude of which no eloquence can exhaust, it is nevertheless most useful for individual men to learn something from them, so that each one, understanding the boundaries of his own calling, may consider how the degree of his own office is ordained by God, and may know what the norm of obedience is; both in enduring afflictions, and in undertaking labors, business, and struggles. Therefore, first, as we have narrated, let the true knowledge of God shine in the mind, and let there be a serious conversion to God; the first commandment also teaches about this beginning.

Secondly, you must know the boundaries of your office, which God has set around you, and not move toward unnecessary things out of curiosity, fear, or pride, that is, to undertake things alien to your calling. Thirdly, it is necessary to retain this consolation: Although every day brings multiple difficulties, hardships, and afflictions, and it is established that the Church is subject to the cross, and is pressed more harshly than other men: you, however, should firmly resolve that God truly wishes to be present and to help those who serve Him in their calling, and therefore you should seek help, and expect good outcomes, and also undertake and endure with alacrity, through this faith and hope, the labors which the necessity of your calling and a just occasion offer in the present. Concerning this consolation, it is said in the present sermon: Do not be anxious, that is, do not torment your mind with distrust, nor be oppressed by despair, but trust that God will be present as a helper and liberator to those who undertake the necessary works of their calling, however great the mass of temptations, impediments, dangers, and afflictions that may have been set before you.

Thus it is written in Psalm 34: The Lord is near to those who are of a troubled heart, and He will save those who are contrite in spirit. Likewise Isaiah 66: God affirms that He dwells among the afflicted, that He looks to the miserable and contrite in spirit and to those who tremble at His words. Likewise Paul says in 1

Corinthians 15: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord, as if to say: God will promote and prosper with His blessing the necessary labors which your calling demands, and will govern the events, and will provide successes, so that your efforts may not be in vain. Thus, in this text, rules or guiding norms for life, counsels, studies, and actions are delivered, and the sources of true and effective consolations are also shown.

Nor, indeed, will anyone be able in any way to understand this text who does not have the beginnings of true faith. For when one is ruled by one's own wisdom, one cannot help but trust in one's own power, wisdom, strength, and counsels; indeed, it is necessary for such a person to have their hope depend on the goods of fortune, the connections of men, friends, money, wealth, and similar external supports. But in those in whom a spark of faith has been kindled, they at last will be able to perceive, in some part, the sense and use of this salutary rule and consolation. Wherefore, we shall briefly conclude here the interpretation of the present text, since the magnitude of the matters surpasses all human eloquence.

May our Lord Jesus Christ Himself grant us His grace, and may He rule and instruct us by His Holy Spirit, so that our minds may rightly understand this very sermon of His, and our entire life may be perpetually directed toward and conform to the order which He Himself has divinely prescribed for us in this chapter. Chapter VII. By the benefit of God, the doctrine concerning both degrees, concerning the distinction between the ministry of the Gospel and political power, is illustrated so copiously and piously and so often, that I do not doubt it is most well-known to you.

You know that both the office and the degree are the principal and highest works of God in the human race. You know that to both governments, jurisdiction or judgments, and the execution or punishments, are attributed by divine authority, and that the duty of rebuking and punishing is divinely and expressly instituted, and is necessary, holy, and approved and pleasing to God in both regimes. The minister of the Gospel, or preacher, has the mandate to judge, rebuke, and condemn by the word of God, that is, by the voice of the Law and the Gospel, all sins, and while he sounds forth, or announces the word judging, at the same time the Holy Spirit is effective in converting and helping believers, just as the Lord most sweetly confirms, John

16: The Holy Spirit will rebuke the world. Thus the Prophets indicate, rebuke, and reprove: Samuel the king Saul, Nathan David, Isaiah king Ahaz, Jeremiah Zedekiah, etc.

In the same way, political power has a mandate to be a guardian of discipline and peace, and to restrain and punish the contumacious with corporal penalties, prison, ropes, the sword, or other more atrocious punishments, or, according to the manner, circumstances, and quality of the offense, to remove them from the midst and put them to death.

God himself aids and promotes this preservation of discipline and execution of penalties in political government; indeed, he himself rules the hands of power and arms them with the sword. For the magistrate, if destitute of the presence and aid of God, would by no means be equal to this duty of his, nor would he by his own authority alone restrain robberies and the audacity of criminals.

Therefore it is written in the most grave words in Daniel, chapter 2: It is God who establishes and transfers kingdoms. But this text, "Judge not," does not speak at all of the office of judging and rebuking, which either a minister of the Gospel or a political magistrate exercises by divine mandate. For in this place, the emphasis of Christ's words must be observed: "Judge not yourselves," that is, you men must not break out from private malevolence or curiosity outside your vocations, and arrogate to yourselves the office of God. God is the judge mediately through the ministers of the word and the political magistrate; do not by any means constitute yourselves judges without God and without a vocation. Thus you understand this text to speak clearly or distinctly not of ministries or offices ordained by God, but of judgments that are made outside or beyond divine vocations and governments.

I wished to preface these things at the beginning for the sake of admonition, lest this text be distorted and accommodated to the ravings of the deluded and furious Anabaptists, who atrociously condemn the office of political power and seditiously disturb and tear it down. Indeed, let us know also that the office of political power is expressly instituted and confirmed by God, that it is holy and pious, and that it pleases God, according to the saying of the holy king Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 19: You exercise the judgment not of men, but of the Lord. Thus you ought to venerate and honor the whole political order, and recognize in it the testimonies of the divine will and presence, just as these things are very often wont to be faithfully explained to you.

Question.

Since, therefore, it is certain that political judgments or the rebuke which is done through magistrates are not prohibited by the Lord, you now ask, what kind of judgments are censured and forbidden?

Response. All private judgments are prohibited which are made outside or against the order of public judgments divinely approved, such as all false accusations and calumnies. Likewise, sinister interpretations of ambiguous things. Likewise, curses, even true ones, which are uttered with the intent of harming and exciting greater disturbances, discords, dissipations, and seditions. Now let each one consider how widely this sin wanders, how common a vice is evil-speaking, so that almost all men seem to take delight in contumelious speeches against others, whether true, or false, or certain, or uncertain. Indeed, very many suspicious people constantly invent and concoct other and yet other accusations, and this zeal for suspecting, for interpreting ambiguities in the worse part, and for slandering, they deem to be a singular art, not of some common wisdom.

Such private, curious, calumnious, and poisonous, or virulent judgments are often prohibited in the word of God, as first in the eighth commandment: "You shall not bear false witness," etc. Likewise, Leviticus 19: "You shall not be a talebearer among your people." Likewise, in the 7th chapter of Ecclesiastes, Solomon says: "Calumny disturbs the wise man, and breaks the strength of his heart," that is, calumnious depravations of counsels or deeds crush those who are most deserving like homicidal daggers, and are often the torches of great dissensions. Indeed, calumny is more pernicious than pestilence itself, than bodily death. For is it not more tolerable for a man merely to have his life taken away, than to have at once his good reputation, health, and all the advantages both of body and of fortune taken from him? For how often do innocents, on account of calumnious and virulent detractions and denunciations, at once lose their good estimation or fame, their life and their possessions? Likewise, grief and sadness of heart arising from the sharp sense of the most noxious pestilence of calumny gradually weakens and extinguishes a man, which Solomon expressly affirms in chapter 7 of Ecclesiastes: "Calumny disturbs the wise man, and breaks the strength of his heart." Indeed, Ecclesiasticus 10 adds more: "The secret detractor and calumniator harms secretly, after the manner of a serpent lying in wait with its bite and its venomous disposition.

Since, therefore, God has so severely prohibited lies and calumnies, let us learn to recognize and avoid these sins, let us bridle the tongue, let us not take delight in detractions or evil-speaking, let us not let us seek pleasure or relaxation of our minds either by sowing insulting tales and accusations, or by willingly and greedily listening to conversations by which the reputation of others is harmed and diminished. For St. Paul says in express words in 1 Corinthians 6: Neither adulterers, nor murderers, nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God. And in Ecclesiasticus 21 it is said: A backbiter will pollute his own soul and will be hated in his neighborhood. And in this very place the Lord adds a threat, speaking of present and future punishments, that it will be repaid in full, so that in turn those poisonous slanderers may be judged and punished. To this, indeed, the examples of daily life and history clearly agree and respond, as the example of the cursed Shimei testifies in 2 Samuel 16. When, after the sedition stirred up by Absalom, King David, now old, was trembling in flight, one of the nobles who had previously flourished in the court of King Saul met the fugitive; this man raved with shouts against David the exile, and rejoiced in the misery or exile of the king, insulting him with this poisonous sarcasm: Come out, you man of blood, the Lord has returned upon you all the blood of the house of Saul, because you have seized the kingdom after he was cast out, etc. Now I leave it to each to consider and weigh how much those sarcasms and poisonous ironies increased David's immense grief, which he carried in his heart during his flight because of the wickedness of his son Absalom. Therefore, the brave men who had previously led armies under David, and were then companions in flight and partners in the king's dangers, were so inflamed that they desired and attempted to run through the cursing mocker, but they were forbidden by David, who did not wish to exercise vengeance or avenge his injuries at that time; indeed, not even after he was restored to the kingdom did he wish this cursing reviler to be killed. But after the death of David, King Solomon commanded this Shimei to keep himself at home and not to carry his foot outside the gates of the city, and when he neglected to do this, Solomon saw to it that he was subjected to the ultimate punishment. Thus, Shimei did not even escape political punishments in this bodily life. Nor is there any reason for anyone to promise themselves impunity for such sins in the present life, however much the execution of civil punishments, which the magistrate exercises, may be hindered by a sophistical conjurer, by which those cursing slanderers so gravely wrap, excuse, and, if I may say so, "peddle" their poisonous and feigned insults, cloaked in new colors and pretexts, that they seem hardly ever able to be convicted of slander in forensic examinations and trials. Nevertheless, God himself uncovers, refutes, and pursues these pernicious lies, sophistical evasions, and poisonous slanders with atrocious punishments even in this bodily life.

Another example.

In the history of Esther it is written about Haman, the enemy of the Jews, who, because Mordecai would not bend his knees to worship him in the Gentile manner, had obtained by slander an edict for the destruction of the entire Jewish race, falsely accusing him of having contumaciously violated the commands of King Ahasuerus. But after his wife Esther swayed King Darius Ahasuerus by exposing the slanders and crimes of Haman, the king saw to it that the slanderer Haman, thirsty for Jewish blood, was strangled, hung from the same gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai, and having issued contrary edicts throughout the province, he assigned the house and possessions of Haman to Mordecai. But the histories of all times and ages provide enough examples to one who wishes to pay a little more diligent attention. For just as, alas, there is hardly any sin more common and vulgar than sycophantic or slanderous backbiting, so God constantly represses and beats back sophistical and sycophantic impostures with punishments wandering through the human race, just as he repeatedly drags back those who are rampant with murders, thefts, or other crimes to their punishments.

Another example.

Philip, King of Macedonia, father of Alexander the Great, had ordered a certain soldier to sail to certain places for the sake of spying or scouting. Meanwhile, a storm having arisen, the ship, overcome by gales and the force of the waves, was broken, but God looking upon the shipwreck, a farmer ran up, whose farm or villa was not far from the sea. Having heard the soldier's cry, he helped the one in danger, and having received him from the waters into his boat, exhausted by the labor of swimming, overcome by hunger, lack of sleep, and anxious grief of mind, stiff with cold, and almost lifeless, he led him into his villa, refreshed him by the hearth, placed him on a small bed, and restored him with food and drink, and cherished him with every service until he recovered his spirit and strength; after three days, when he wished to leave, he even provided him with travel money.

The soldier, departing, goes straight to King Philip, narrates the shipwreck, boasts of his labors, exaggerates the dangers, and asks for some reward, but remains silent about the benefit of his host, to whom he had promised at length that he would return the favor.

Philip orders the soldier, both because of his bravery and because he seemed to have deserved well, and was especially dear to him, to ask by name for a house and possession or some villa that was currently vacant, and could be conferred by the king at his discretion. See what happened. That scoundrel asks by name for the house and estate of the rustic who saved him, because the shipwrecked man had barely crawled to this villa, and he pursued with singular affection the place marked by the memory of his calamity, or as a witness to his danger.

Meanwhile, there is no mention of the benefit or services of the rustic, but he conceals that he had been helped or refreshed by any of the inhabitants in such great dangers of life. He easily obtains it from the liberal king, to whom the rest was unknown regarding the faithful services of the farmer, by which he had saved and refreshed the shipwrecked man.

Therefore, Philip takes care to have a diploma drawn up, by which the ownership or property of that estate was confirmed to the soldier. And he was ordered to be inducted into the goods he had asked for.

When these things were being done, with the soldier occupying the estate, the rustic, expelled from his goods, did not bear the injury, but approached the king, commemorating his benefits, narrates that he had been his savior, and that he had fed, clothed, and refreshed the shipwrecked man received from the waters for three whole days with whatever services he could, and complains that it is unjust to be cast out from his paternal possession by an ungrateful pupil for his hospitable benefits.

Philip, having learned of the perfidy and ingratitude of this scoundrel, burned with such anger that he ordered the soldier to be thrown into chains, and afterwards, having been dishonorably discharged, to be branded with marks, and to have these words inscribed on his forehead: Ungrateful guest. He restored the estate to the former owner, with the soldier turning to the ground for the sake of exile.

Thus the perfidy of the ungrateful soldier fell back upon his own head, and the evil counsel was pernicious to its author. For God is a most just judge, punishing with present and eternal penalties sins of every kind, in all who do not practice repentance.

Wherefore there follows in the text this general rule: With what measure you measure, it shall be returned to you.

As God is wise and just, so He teaches us to exercise and cultivate justice among us, that is, to observe equality in not harming others, likewise in contracts, and in the order of persons, so that no injury is done to anyone. When we violate this equality or justice, and deviate from the prescribed norm, He himself nevertheless remains perpetually just, destroys whatever is unjust or deformed to His most just will, punishes and deletes the unjust, and certainly preserves this order, punishing with present and eternal torments all who do not convert to Him.

But you perhaps think these things to yourself: Relying on my power, I will somewhat press this weaker and inferior person, so that I may indulge my spirit, and according to my lust I will trample any weaker ones.

For what danger would threaten me from them, whose anger is vain and without strength? Who, furthermore, would demand the penalty of retaliation from me? These thoughts are mockeries and most pernicious impostures, by which minds are fascinated, and which are confirmed by the devil.

For although punishments are sometimes accustomed to be deferred for a while, yet it is most certain that those who accumulate crimes are at length oppressed and stuck in atrocious punishments, according to that: The punishment, though late, comes with silent feet.

And specifically concerning corporal punishments, the Lord says, Matt. 26: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword. Likewise Isaiah 33: Woe to you who plunder, because you shall be plundered in turn.

And in the book of Wisdom, it is clearly written about the penalty of retaliation, chap. 11: By what things one sins, by the same he is punished. All histories have enough examples, and so that they may not be sought from books, this age provides us with many.

Indeed, even to the Heathens this was most persuasive.

Hence they scattered and celebrated such maxims born from experience, such as this Mime: Expect from another what you have done to another.

And in the 8th chapter of Ecclesiastes, Solomon says: Men perform evils securely, furiously, and petulantly, because punishments are deferred, and judgment is not quickly brought against the wicked, but the wise man understands the time and judgment, and I know for certain that punishments will follow shortly, and that it will not be that they are long deferred.

You ought to consider all these things, and when you feel private troubles and miseries, or public calamities, wars, excessive pillaging, the dearness of grain or famine, and the rest of the mass of punishments, learn to fear the judgment of God, practice repentance, and amend your morals and life.

For unless conversion and amendment of morals follow, there will be added to the implacable corporal punishments the eternal and horrible wrath of God, casting those who persevere in wickedness into eternal destruction: which may God, for His immense goodness, mercifully avert from us for the sake of His Son. those doing penance, and converted to God, are delivered from eternal punishments, through and on account of the mediator our Lord Jesus Christ.

Indeed, by these, temporal punishments are also mitigated, even if they are not immediately taken away entirely.

At this very time, there moves before your eyes and in your sight a mass of public punishments, truly formidable: you see at the same time famine, pestilence, and war raging in many places.

For in Poland and Belgium there is such a scarcity of grain that many poor people are wasting away from hunger, and that difficulty or dearness of provisions causes the price of grain to increase even in the vicinity of Silesia and other places, because grain is being exported from there by neighbors.

And if the neighbors, exhausted, should perhaps be in need, and our fields are laid waste by continuous wars, while in the towns food will be lacking for families bearing heavier burdens in time of war, consider, I beseech you, what will happen, and foresee what great calamities and dangers hang over you.

Wherefore I seriously exhort and adjure you to consider well, much, and often this most severe rule or norm of divine judgment, because it does not need a long declaration: With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you.

May this threat stir up care, so that, acknowledging the magnitude and multitude of your sins, and converted to God by trust in the mediator, you may strive to move God with true piety, and seriously and with true groans seek the mitigation of punishments.

For since you see openly that horrible and destructive punishments are encroaching, with fatal conversions and ruins of all kingdoms and republics hanging over everywhere in the world, meditate and repeatedly call to memory the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ in Luke 21: Pray that you may be able to escape the wrath hanging over you and the evils to come.

Jerusalem did not stand longer than forty years after this voice of Christ, while in the meantime every kind of turpitude, wickedness, and petulance grew and accumulated in it day by day.

And although the profane multitude of the people and princes was neither affected nor amended by the complaints, admonitions, adjurations, and sermons of holy men—Zechariah, Simeon, John the Baptist, Christ, and subsequently the Apostles—yet these cries were not empty and entirely without fruit, but many were converted to God and saved in this life, and there is no doubt that those called hence to eternal salvation enjoy the clear sight of God.

Thus, even then, God, in the most sorrowful destructions and ruins of cities and empires, most clemently gathered and saved the Church.

In the same way, it happened in the history of the Ninevites when Jonah was preaching.

The king and very many men in Nineveh were converted, and therefore the city of the Ninevites was not destroyed at that time, but God, in His immense goodness, mitigated the punishments.

But in the eightieth year after, or thereabouts, when Sennacherib had already been removed, when sins were likewise growing and accumulating, Nineveh was finally utterly overturned and destroyed.

But whose spirit is not moved or turned to penance at the sight of the most bitter miseries of the present, who does not perceive this man to be senseless, furious, or bereft of his mind?

Therefore, I again exhort and adjure you individually, that, stirred up by care for the salvation of your souls, your children, and the universal Church of Christ, you may amend your morals and life, praying with ardent vows that God, appeased, may spare us, and in His immense mercy may soften the punishments on account of the merit and intercession of His son our Lord Jesus Christ, Amen.

Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?

You know that in this long sermon of our Lord Jesus Christ is contained a most learned explanation and declaration of the Decalogue, and in the present chapter the Lord began to recount the eighth commandment: Do not bear false witness.

But to whom among you is it obscure, since these are common and vulgar sins—to lie, to revile, to slander, to curse, to backbite, to accuse, to indulge in false suspicions, and from these to judge rashly, to pervert the good deeds or correctly spoken words of others, or to twist ambiguous things into a worse sense, and by calumniously and contumeliously exaggerating and traducing, to harm their reputation?

All these sins are forbidden in the eighth commandment: Do not bear false witness, in which sense the Lord commands in this chapter: Do not judge.

To which commandment must be added the example which follows here concerning a certain hypocrite.

For in an illustrious parable, the hypocrite is depicted, who, while blinking, refuses to see the notable log in his own eye, yet investigates with curious eyes and looks more diligently at the speck in another's eye.

And not even for this example is there need of a long declaration.

For how many is there whom the use of common life and daily experience does not convince? cat? so that he may confess these to be the common diseases of most men, namely self-love and evil-speaking, by which it happens that, while they act with a harsher censure toward others, most are accustomed to note, carp at, reprehend, and reform many things, but they flatter and forgive themselves, and think there is no need for reformation or amendment. Indeed, it usually happens that the most foul monsters of men, polluted by notable and enormous crimes, attempt not only to extenuate, mitigate, conceal, and remove their own turpitude from the eyes of men, but also to obtain some measure of reputation, commendation, and painted glory, by invidiously and calumniously exaggerating and ulcerating the blemishes or little warts of men who are inferior or of lower status or less graceful, who nevertheless are by no means contaminated by such enormous crimes as those censors are: even if they have their own certain infirmities, filth, and stains, and have somewhere fallen and hallucinated through weakness, or error, or negligence, or have even turned aside somewhat from what is honest, just as there is no man, even among the most holy, who does not often sin by some infirmity, ignorance, omission, or negligence: indeed, who does not have many lapses, many not light offenses, errors, and scandals.

As in 2 Kings 16, when David is driven into exile, the abusive Shimei exults, rejoicing with a gladiatorial spirit over the fallen man, whose calamity he delights in, to rush upon him, and to vomit forth all the virulence, bitterness, and ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν [malicious joy] of his soul; he plays the buffoon, celebrates triumphs, insults and mocks him with manifest sarcasms: "Get out, you man of blood," he says, calling him a turbulent man, thirsty for gore and seditious. And it is customary for this to happen to the pious, which Solomon says in Proverbs 25: "A troubled fountain and a muddy spring is a just man falling or lapsing before the wicked." In this saying, an image of the world's judgments concerning the Church is proposed. For so it is accustomed to happen: the wicked hold power and wealth, they flourish in influence, grace, and glory; therefore, having observed some infirmity or deformity or tragic calamity of the pious, they rejoice that an opportunity is offered to traduce them, and to exaggerate their vices, and to speak evil of and insult the afflicted: indeed, as if their senses were suffused with the highest delight, and as if tickled with pleasure, they are carried away with joy, and mocking with poisonous ironies, they prostrate, trample, and crush the calamitous.

All these things are seen with the eyes and confirmed by daily experience. But on the contrary, let the will of God be known to the pious; let them know how to conduct themselves, with what moderation and equity of mind they ought to bear these triumphs and sarcasms, and let them also hold to true and firm consolations, so that they may not be broken in spirit because of the calumnies, insults, reproaches, and unjust imprecations of the wicked. Furthermore, let the rule or admonition handed down here concerning the order of judgment be considered first. You ought to begin reformation and censure from yourself; first remove the beam from your own eye, then more curiously inspect the speck in the eye of another. There exist, however, many sayings even among the wisest of the Heathens, whom civil judgment of reason instructs, in letters and monuments, by which this curiosity, unjust inequality, and perversity of judgments is reprehended and deplored, namely, that there are many such Momuses and censors everywhere, who attempt to reform others, of whom they judge harshly, while they not only spare themselves, but even flatter themselves and please themselves wonderfully. Hence that sentence of Cato, even most familiarly known to boys: "It is shameful for a teacher when his own guilt convicts him." Nevertheless, I will interpret and propose only one single maxim of Solomon, which, since it exhorts each one to repentance, ought to be diligently learned by each of you, and thoroughly committed to memory, and attentively and much considered.

Thus Solomon commands in Proverbs 18: "The just man in the beginning is his own accuser, afterwards he inquires or explores his neighbor." Perpetually carry this rule in your minds, and looking back to it from time to time, rule your minds and tongues as if with this bridle. In the beginning, we ought to inquire into ourselves: let each one acknowledge his own infirmity, his own errors and lapses, his own sins, and let them first punish and amend themselves. For let each one look into his own bosom for me, and descend into himself, as it is in the Proverb, then he will be reminded by the sight of his own vices and filth, so that he may not rashly judge and act with a harsher censure toward others. Your own heart is full of darkness, carnal security, waves of doubt, flames of inordinate love, malevolence, hatred, and manifold negligence in your function or vocation. And indeed there are fewer than one might think who, led to the inspection of themselves, are not found to have notable and enormous vices.

suri. With this order of judging observed, namely, if you first examine and explore yourself, there will never be a lack of that from which you can begin reformation and punishment.

In this domestic censure, therefore, learn to recognize the wrath of God in true terrors and sorrows, and with true humility of heart seek and ask for the remission of errors and sins through and for the sake of Christ, and subsequently amend your morals and life, retaining faith and a good conscience.

This admonition is delivered in the former member of that illustrious sentence of Solomon: The just man is at the beginning the accuser of himself. To this is usually accommodated the Aesopic fable about two wallets, of which Catullus says: But we do not see the wallet that is on our back. For they imagined that individual men have two wallets or bags, one before the chest, the other hanging from the shoulders and the back. In the latter, which hangs on the back, we carry our own vices, in which we are blind: into the former wallet we cast the vices of others, in which we are Lyncean or most sharp-sighted, so that there is neither measure nor end to reformations and censures.

By this image, and many similar illustrious pictures, the ancients attempted to express, and in a way place before the eyes, the most shameful vices: self-love, backbiting, and the perversity of calumnious judgments. But let the saying of Solomon always be in your sight, and the example proposed in this parable, so that your minds may be affected, thinking on these sentences and pictures: and so that you may recognize and amend the vices which are censured in this text, and not loosen the reins and indulge in curiosity and petulance that rashly judges others, easily and willingly slandering, and suspiciously and calumniously depraving the right deeds and ambiguous actions of others, but remember that your tongues and minds must be curbed, and with singular diligence these plagues, of which you have now heard, must be avoided.

The other part of Solomon's saying is: After inspection or accusation of himself, the just man inquires into another. After you have punished and amended yourself, then first consider when and in what order you ought to judge others, then also, according to your vocation, strive to remove the splinter from another, and to heal the wounds of others, but with the order observed which is prescribed in the Gospel, namely, that you admonish the fallen or erring one lovingly and placidly, not bitterly or virulently, that you call them back to the way, and instruct them, not in taverns or inns, not in centauric banquets, that you proclaim and traduce the vices of another, so that you may indulge your own morbid desire, and be tickled by this little pleasure, or by the detraction of others strive to wash away or wipe off your own filth and stains, and to cover your moles and blemishes, and finally to gather and increase your reputation.

God by no means lets these vices of an unbridled and petulant tongue go unpunished and unavenged, as the punishment of the reviler Shimei, and the punishment of the calumniator Haman in the history of Esther most evidently testify. And the sentence of the old Mime is confirmed by daily experience: Expect from another what you have done to another. Believe me, there will not be lacking those who in turn can depict your life, and express and illuminate you with vivid colors, so that your impropriety and turpitude, as if brought into the light and exposed to the eyes of all, may be censured and spat upon by public execrations.

Let this brief admonition suffice in this place regarding those vulgar and common vices, backbiting, detraction, and calumnies: against which oppose the thought of the horrible judgment and wrath of God, so that you may learn to rule your minds as if with reins cast upon them, and with true groans deplore that horrible darkness and blindness in the breasts of all men, because we either do not see our own filth, our own vices, or we deem them light, but it is necessary for Christians to begin amendment, so that in some way, recognizing the magnitude of sin and divine wrath, they may tremble, and not persevere in such pernicious self-love, blind security, and gross pride: such as is here severely taxed in that hypocrite, who, having a beam in his eye, wants to remove a splinter from another. For these vices, self-love, security, and pride are in the eyes of God foul and abominable filth: because a secure and arrogant heart, since it neither fears nor magnifies the wrath of God, in reality detracts from God the honor due to Him, while it dreams that He does not punish sins, but is idle and slow.

This very security and blindness is horribly accused in the sermons of all the Prophets, as God cries out in Isaiah, chapter 48: Your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead brass. Likewise Jeremiah 8: They are not confounded, and they have not known how to blush. Indeed, these most sorrowful complaints are repeated everywhere in the Prophets.

But you, above all, remember and diligently weigh the saying of Isaiah chapter 66: To whom shall I look? says the Lord, except to the poor, and the contrite in spirit, and him who trembles at my words. Do not imagine or dream that the proud, the arrogant, and the secure who live without the fear of God, without a sense of divine wrath and judgment, [they] are children of God, or heirs of eternal life, nay, the very true Church and people of God; therefore [the Church] is burdened with so many, so various, and such great calamities, so that we may learn to recognize the wrath of God against our own huge and manifold sins: and, terrified, may flee to the mediator, and, resisting sin, may amend our life and morals. There is no one who does not see the punishments placed in plain sight—wars, famine, diseases—and it is to be feared that much harsher and more atrocious punishments will follow. In Lithuania, such a great famine is already raging that many parents are ending their own lives and those of their children by hanging, due to the intolerable cruelty of the famine; indeed, this difficulty, or the dearness of provisions, seems to creep in little by little and to flow toward our own regions, as if by some contagion.

May God, the eternal Father of our Lord and deliverer Jesus Christ, mercifully mitigate and soothe such great miseries and hardships through the merit and intercession of his Son, and may He spare, in His immense goodness, the tender flock of boys and girls, so that the heavenly doctrine may be preserved and propagated in our little families. O good, merciful, beneficent God, have mercy on us for the sake of your Son, and give sustenance and daily bread to the tender flock of our children. The consideration of these and similar miseries ought to exhort and impel the minds of individuals to the fear of God and to repentance, or a salutary amendment of vices. If this were done, we would very easily perceive, nay, we would be evidently convinced, that we ourselves are the ones most in need of reformation, or of an amending censure: and that glory is not to be sought through the disparagement of others, or by judging bitterly and chattering contumeliously about others, but enough of this for now.

Do not give what is holy to the dogs, etc.

Now follows another doctrine, which specifically instructs and consoles preachers and ministers of the Gospel: it also reminds the hearers to examine and consider themselves, to search and think about who they are. For it makes three kinds of hearers: some of whom are dogs, others swine, but some indeed are children of God.

By dogs, he understands rabid persecutors, who tear apart the preachers they have seized, as if with their teeth.

Swine are foul, muddy, filthy men, namely those persevering in enormous errors and sins against their conscience. Although these do not at all wish to appear as persecutors—nay, they simulate some zeal for true religion—they nevertheless do not seriously desire to perform repentance, they do not strive to amend their morals, but they persevere in security and the filth of crimes, in which, as unclean swine wallow assiduously in mud, they pollute themselves with lusts, practice thefts, robberies, and unjust schemes for seeking money; they retain a contempt for God, they do not truly fear the wrath and judgment of God, they do not call upon Him with true faith, [and] they approach public sermons and prayers in temples with a certain hypocrisy, or simulation of piety, etc.

However, since the number of such dogs and swine is not small, a minister of the word or some preacher, moved by the indignity of the matter and offended by the scandal, and also weary of the cares, troubles, labors, dangers, and struggles that accompany the ministry and profession of the Gospel, could think thus: "What shall I, a wretch, do? I see that I am accomplishing nothing, that my labors are vain and without fruit; I see that the doctrine is being scattered among the people in vain, since few are converted and amend their vices, etc." Here, there is need for consolation for the pious: whom our Lord Jesus Christ confirms and consoles in this text, commanding them to proceed cheerfully to perform their ministry, to preach to the remaining congregation, however small, of those who are not failing: and not to desert their calling because of the multitude of dogs and swine, nor to be deterred or grow faint in spirit, even if such beasts do not wish to hear them, or persevere in manifest errors and crimes, but to omit and leave them behind.

But concerning the third kind, namely, the truly believing and children of God, the Lord says afterwards: "Few enter through the narrow gate." For the sake of these few, or for the sake of these remnants, it is necessary that the salutary doctrine be scattered; in them the ministry will be effective and fruitful, for them your labors in the confession and propagation of the Gospel will be profitable, according to the saying of Christ, John 15: "In this is my Father glorified, that you bear much fruit." Likewise Paul, 1 Corinthians 15: "Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord." Likewise Isaiah 55: "The word shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed." Thus in the parable in Matthew 18 and Luke 8 concerning the sower, a part of the scattered seed is trampled, a part is snatched away and consumed by the beaks of birds, a part is choked among thorns: nevertheless, the remaining part of the seed falls into good soil, and bears a very rich [harvest]. the fruit.

In this way God gathers, selects, and preserves at all times some holy seed and a small congregation: and in order to serve it, the ministers of the Gospel must not desert their calling, but remain in their office and function, as if at a garrison and station, however much the remaining profane multitude of dogs and swine may rage.

Furthermore, let each of the listeners deliberate with himself and decide in what kind or congregation, and what sort they wish to be, whether to be numbered among the dogs and swine, or whether they prefer to join themselves to the children of God and heirs of eternal life.

Ah, what a great and deplorable misery it is that in the human race so many who are outstanding in dignity, gravity, counsel, and wisdom—Emperors, Kings, Princes, Pontiffs, Cardinals, Bishops, Prelates, Canons.

Likewise nobles and ignoble, patricians and plebeians, the learned and the illiterate—are for the most part truly dogs and swine, for the very reason that they despise and persecute the word of God, and meanwhile, in their pursuit of pleasures, ambition, pride, and the ostentation of magnificence, they rush against the divine will.

Dogs and swine are beasts ignorant of God and of the promised immortality, or of the life that follows after the destruction of the bodies; nor is there implanted in them a light that discerns between honorable and base things, or that distinguishes a wise and good nature from a brute and evil nature, but they live and are carried along by a certain blind impulse, just as they are incited or driven by untamed and beastly appetites, which accompany consent.

The impious in this life are clearly similar to these, since they study or care nothing to learn or know about God, about eternal life, about the coming judgment, about the punishments of sins, since they neither understand nor observe the difference between honorable and base things, virtues and vices, things done rightly or otherwise, since they neither call upon God, nor fear His wrath, nor flee to Him, but with a blind impulse proceed to loosen the reins and indulge in inordinate appetites and furious desires that wander outside the boundaries divinely established.

Thus, tyrants delight in pride and ostentation in pomp, or in magnificent displays, and they burn and are inflamed with the desire for vengeance, by which, being incited, they stir up the fiercest conflicts and attack others with their bites like rabid dogs.

Other men, barbaric, beastly, and Cyclopean, wallow as if in the mire of crimes, indulge in gluttony, drunkenness, and luxury, defile themselves with lusts, adulteries, and fornications, and practice thefts, robberies, and unjust pursuits of money-getting, etc.

Nevertheless, after this life, there will be a visible difference and a remarkable change.

Then at last both will learn in eternal torments and punishments that God exists, and that He is truly a judge who is horribly angry at sin.

Then they will be forced to acknowledge and confess that, before they were overwhelmed by death, they had lived beastly in the manner of dogs and swine: but there, namely among the torments of the underworld, there is no place for help or any hope of liberation, so much so that it seems much more tolerable to the damned themselves, and they would far prefer, if it were possible, to be reduced entirely to nothing, and they would wish for their souls to be dissipated into smoke, perishing together with their bodies, just as we see dogs, swine, and cattle extinguished and rotting away; but God restrains them with eternal and horrendous punishments, cast out together with the devils with whom they joined themselves and conspired against God.

All these things you ought to embrace in your mind and thought, and repeat them often in your memory, so that your minds, awakened to serious prayer, may with true groans ask God, for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, to be enlightened, taught, ruled, and confirmed by the Holy Spirit, so that you do not become dogs and swine, but that you may learn to acknowledge God, so that the true light of faith, firmly establishing [the truth] about immortality, about the coming judgment of God, about the life and eternal salvation of the blessed, may shine in your hearts: likewise that you may understand and in all your life retain and observe the difference between honorable and base things, or virtues and vices: and in sum, that you may be children and temples or dwellings of God, and not be cast into eternal punishments, overwhelmed by torments, terrors, consternations, and horrendous, perpetual, and infinite confusions of the soul.

Indeed, every single person ought to shudder with their whole heart and be truly terrified, having heard this voice of divine majesty, by which impious men are likened and compared to dogs and swine.

But let us be stirred and moved to repentance and a salutary amendment by the thought of this picture or parable, which is truly terrible, lest we ourselves remain swine and dogs, rushing into eternal destruction.

For whoever in this mortal life persists in contempt or hatred of God (as when gluttons most proudly continue to mock, or superstitious tyrants do not cease to furiously hate and persecute the Gospel), for him much more atrocious and far more horrible evils are imminent at death than for dogs and swine.

For cattle and brutes, are utterly extinguished by the death of their bodies, nor do punishments or torments remain, by which, as life flees, the corpse can be tortured.

But the souls of men are separable spirits, surviving after the bodies are extinguished, and they will again be joined to the resurrected bodies in which they lived before: therefore, to dead men, both bodies will be restored, and life will be returned to the bodies.

Those, therefore, who have persevered in contempt or hatred of God, recalled from death to judgment, will hear and undergo, together with the devils, that condemnatory sentence, Matt. 25: Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels.

If anyone is not moved by this sad and terrible sermon, it is certain that in him stubbornness, madness, and fury have been so confirmed by the devils that he is held clearly captive by those blasphemous spirits.

Furthermore, it must not be ignored that even in the present life, dogs and swine are oppressed by such tragic and atrocious punishments.

Do not rabid dogs—Pharaoh, Herod, Nero, Diocletian, Julian, and similar tyrants—finally perish in the highest torture, foully and miserably? Are not the muddy swine—that is, impious nations and cities, Sodom, Gomorrah, Rome, Asia, Greece—horribly devastated, plundered, and utterly destroyed by the saddest examples? What of the fact that before everyone's eyes there are daily punishments, wars, famines, tyrannies, and the tearing apart of empires, excessive pillaging, and the devastation of regions and provinces? With such punishments God burdens, chastises, and oppresses the dogs and swine of whom it is spoken here, so that by some it may be recognized and understood as the divine wrath against sin, and the others who are not curable may be taken from the midst.

I judge this brief admonition to be sufficient for the narration of this saying.

May God mercifully help and kindle our hearts, so that they may be truly affected by these most grave sermons of Christ, and may be bent toward conversion and the salutary amendment of life, Amen.

Ask and it shall be given to you, etc.

There must be a distinction between precepts and promises, and it must be perpetually known in the Church: which admonition is indeed often repeated, namely, that it is necessary for precepts and promises to be distinguished.

And thus far in these last two chapters you have heard it learnedly declared what some of the precepts of the Decalogue are.

Now Christ begins a sermon on prayer, or invocation, which virtue pertains also to the first and second commandment of the Decalogue.

For these works, namely, true petition or prayer, true thanksgiving, are the chief and highest worship that can be rendered to God, and by which honor can be attributed to him. Heathens, and Mahometans, or Turks, can also govern external morals with honest discipline, maintain chastity in legitimate marriage, give alms, live soberly and temperately, etc., but this excellent spiritual and interior worship, namely, true invocation and true thanksgiving, no one can render to God except Christians alone, and the true members of the Church, who feel the beginnings of the fear of God, of faith, and of eternal consolation in their hearts, and who know the difference between the pious and the hypocrites.

And let it be diligently observed in this place that precepts and promises are joined: the precept concerning praying affirms that you ought to render this worship to God, that you may invoke, that you may ask, that you may expect help from him in dangers: The promise proposes consolation, and certifies us that our invocation is not in vain, nor an empty and useless murmur.

But that we may be learned in order and fundamentally about this so great and necessary work, about the highest virtue, about the chief worship and that proper to the Church alone, and that we may learn to exercise invocation with true movements of the soul and seriously: we will repeat in order the chief chapters of the doctrine concerning the invocation of God, which indeed in this Church are often accustomed to be treated in a sermon, and as much as can be, faithfully and copiously explained.

Therefore, these three things concerning invocation must always be commemorated and familiarly held in order.

First place, what invocation or prayer is. Second, why it should be done, and for what causes invocation is necessary. Third, how it should be done, so that it may be heard, received, may please, may be efficacious, valid, and pleasing to God. Concerning the first. What invocation or prayer is.

Concerning the definition of invocation or adoration, it is necessary to know at the beginning that the word for prayer, or adoration, or invocation of God, comprises two works, namely, both to ask for something from God, and afterwards to give thanks for benefits. And that these degrees are distinct can be sufficiently understood from the fact that nothing is more customary and nearly daily, both toward God and toward men, than to ask for necessary goods, and to wish to expect or receive many benefits; yet few are grateful, few declare their gratitude with true works of life and with their voice, but having received benefits necessary for the time, they afterwards do not magnify nor celebrate the author of goods, but either despise him, or as if they had forgotten the benefits received, they scarcely acknowledge the benefactor.

This is what all men who have deserved well of others experience daily. Therefore, let us accustom ourselves to both works or duties, namely, to exercise ourselves both in petition in invocation, and in thanksgiving toward God. But first we shall speak of the former species, namely, of petition or prayer. There is scarcely any other of all human works more excellent, more grave, and more difficult than to approach God, and through a mediator to ask of Him and expect grace or reconciliation, bodily and eternal goods, help and liberation in all dangers and necessities. For that is what it means to ask or to pray, to seek necessary goods, and to expect certain benefits, not to murmur some words without thought or attention, as among the Papists, monks, and nuns, who with a wondrous volubility of tongue murmur the Psalter all day long, and do not understand what they are doing or reciting.

But as I said, petition is a movement of the soul desiring to receive something from God: as, when Moses standing between the waves of the Red Sea, saw Pharaoh leading a most well-equipped army approaching to oppress the unarmed and promiscuous multitude of Israelites, of men, women, and children trembling, and enclosed partly by the sea, partly by the mountains, there he is stirred by a great movement of soul, so that he cries out ardently and seriously, so that with true groans he may seek and desire to receive help and liberation from God. Thus it is commanded in this text, that we should seek, ask, knock, with the promise added that all who ask shall receive, whence it is clear that the word 'to ask' is to be understood in such a way that grace and help are asked of God and expected.

And so much for the name of asking or petition. Now concerning the second point. Concerning the second point. For what ends and why petition should be made.

I answer: First, let petition be referred to the glory of God, for God wills that this honor be attributed to Him, and demands it, so that we may learn to acknowledge who and what He is, what His will is, that He is not an empty name, not a slothful or idle Lord, to whom human affairs are not a care, to whom there is no business or familiarity and conversation with men.

For whoever thinks in this way: 'I do not know whether God hears and receives my prayers, perhaps He is good to Himself. But why should He look upon me? Why should He care for my murmuring? Why should He be beneficent toward me?' He in reality judges God to be an inert, slothful, and sleepy deity, and meanwhile seeks protections and implores the help of men or other creatures. Just as Saul in extreme desperation, and in the highest danger and crisis, consults a witch or Pythoness, who brings up spirits from Orcus, that is, he flees to the devil. Such a man, either an Epicurean or a desperate person, omitting invocation, does not attribute to God the due and proper honor, who says: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, the living and true, and Him only shall you serve.' Wherefore, first let us remember that prayer or petition is most severely commanded and ordained, principally for the sake of the acknowledgment of God, and therefore must necessarily be made, so that God may be truly acknowledged.

For those who omit invocation, or doubt whether God wishes to be invoked, and whether He cares for our prayers, are ignorant of what God is, and whether He sleeps or watches. Secondly, petition must necessarily be made for the sake of our own utility or necessity and indigence.

For how many are we each individually constantly surrounded, implicated, and as it were immersed in difficulties, snares, miseries, and dangers inextricable by human counsel! We are pressed by the weight of sin, burdened by punishments, chastised by diseases, wars, famine, the destruction of kingdoms and cities, and finally we live in the midst of death, we are detained and stuck. And if in such a great concurrence of calamities and various kinds of afflictions there were not proposed to man by God a consolation, nor hope of mitigation, help, and liberation: we could not but be broken in spirit, nay, we would be consumed by perpetual anxieties, and overwhelmed by desperation.

But so that hearts might be raised, and not succumb to sorrows in such a great mass of most miserable calamities, God has revealed His immense mercy toward the human race with ineffable goodness, and coming forth from His secret and eternal seat, He sounds this voice: I, the true, eternal, and omnipotent God, Myself will hear you, will regard you, will console, will sustain, will help, will rescue, and will deliver you in all dangers, difficulties, miseries, and hardships: as He affirms in Psalm 50: Call upon Me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you. Behold, thus in the second place, prayer and invocation are necessary for our sake, or for our own salvation and utility, so that we may know for certain where to take refuge, where to find rest, from where to seek and expect consolation and help, and that we may certainly be able and ought to obtain and receive them.

For it is for this very purpose and design that the true Church is exercised, burdened, and pressed by more and harder calamities than the rest of the human race, so that, being awakened by the sense of evils, it may have more causes to cry out to God and to implore the help of God, and that it may know that God is present in afflictions, that He wishes to dwell with us, to help us, and that He will neither desert us nor permit us to be submerged, to succumb, or to be overwhelmed.

And although there is such great hardness in the great multitude of profane and brutalized men that they are neither affected nor perturbed by domestic and private, nor by public and common miseries, but securely continue to gorge themselves and to loosen the reins to blind desires, little concerned (as is commonly said among the Germans) either about the utility of the harvest or about the scarcity and high price of grain: yet we are pressed, urged, and fatigued by such a mass of punishments imposed upon our necks and imminent at this time, that it is necessary for many to be vehemently anguished and moved in their minds at the sight and sense of so many most bitter calamities.

The cruelty of wars and famine moves before your eyes and faces: you remember the fires by which, within two years, so many towns and villages in this vicinity have burned.

To this are added the confusions of governments, the difficulties in administration: which evils are increased and accumulated day by day.

Furthermore, the rabies of the enemies of the Gospel grows, and the persecution of the Churches is renewed with more atrocious examples.

What of the fact that, by the petulance and perversity of men's minds, monstrous opinions are feigned, spread, and defended, and dissensions are kindled with poisonous calumnies?

And that minds and wills are distracted by more than Sinonian artifices, and more pernicious factions and sects arise, are fostered, and are confirmed daily?

By which furies the wrath of God is irritated and accumulated, public discipline is loosened, and Cyclopean barbarism, impious security, and Ethnic profanity are increased and confirmed, especially in the rude common people and the dull youth.

In addition to this, the Turkish robbers gradually advance further, and every day they approach us more closely.

Finally, almost all individual men in their own families and homes are exercised by a manifold kind of calamities, oppressed now by poverty, now by diseases, now by other hardships, such as the unhappiness of children, infamy, bereavement, the loss of family property, or in other ways.

Holding this immense mass of dangers and miseries in view, let us be moved in our minds to seek and seriously request divine consolation, help, and liberation.

From this admonition, therefore, you can understand both that prayer is necessary and for what causes it is necessary.

I proceed, therefore, to the third point: what kind of prayer or supplication there ought to be, so that it may please God, so that it may be heard, so that it may be efficacious: for that matter, the consideration of these five points is especially necessary.

First admonition: one must think about what you invoke, which God, and where you wish to address Him as revealed.

Second point, the consideration of the divine and most severe precept or command concerning invocation.

Third consideration is of the promise.

Fourth consideration is of faith.

Fifth consideration is of the things to be requested, so that the petition may not be an empty and idle recitation, or battologia (babbling), but that it may be considered what goods or benefits, both corporal and spiritual, God wishes to be requested of Him, and in what order they are to be requested.

I return, therefore, to the first point: Who is to be addressed in prayer, and to whom the mind ought to be directed, namely, to the true God, distinguished from feigned deities by the acknowledgment of the Son sent, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Heathens, Mahometans, and all other nations outside the true Church only pour forth empty sounds, which, soon scattered into the air, dissipate and vanish.

For they wander in their thoughts, ignorant of what they are doing or whom they are calling upon: as one invoked Jupiter, another Juno, this one the god Christopher, that one St. Anne. Thus in all times idols have been worshipped, and have been heaped up everywhere among the nations, and always in a great multitude of the human race there remain the seeds of diabolical superstitions. Against this sad and horrible sin God cries out in these very words, Deut. 6: You shall adore the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve.

Wherefore it is necessary for the one praying to consider what, and which God he is calling upon and addressing.

And our invocation must be distinguished from the invocation of the Gentiles, the Jews, the Turks, the hypocrites, and the heretics.
