Nor let us paint in our minds an idol of God, such as we ourselves wish, but let the heart behold by faith this true, living, and only God, who has revealed Himself through His Son our Lord Jesus Christ: just as the Lord Himself teaches, John 14: No one comes to the Father except through the Son. Wherefore, that you may remind yourself of the three persons and their benefits, often think of and recite this form while praying.

O almighty, eternal, living, and true God, eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of heaven and earth, and of the angelic and human Church, together with your beloved Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, etc. I pray to you and invoke you as a suppliant on account of the mediator and propitiator our Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me, forgive me my sins, rule and sanctify me with your Holy Spirit, mitigate my miseries for me, be present and help me in these miseries and dangers in which I am now involved, etc. Sometimes also think of your baptism, and attentively consider the form of words which the Son of God Himself delivered. In your baptism such an invocation was made, which by an illustrious distinction separating the true God from all fictitious deities, as a conspicuous mark separates you from the people of all other nations and sects: and teaches you to call upon, to address, and to truly recognize this true God, namely, the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Father's coeternal Son, who was made a victim for you and was constituted a mediator and constant intercessor, and the Holy Spirit coeternal with the Father and the Son, who rules and sanctifies you unto eternal life and salvation.

Let these things be said briefly concerning the first point. Now consider for yourselves how horrendous a crime it is, having rejected the true God, to flee to dead men, or to invent deities which do not exist, and to call upon idols.

Second reminder: One must consider the most severe precept or command of God concerning invocation. How great is this goodness! that God Himself not only invites us, but even by a certain severity compels and urges us, that we should ask of Him and expect help in dangers: indeed, He teaches that this is the highest worship and honor which can be bestowed upon Him, namely, if we truly flee to Him with the groaning of the heart, ask for good things from Him, and seek from Him mitigation, help, and liberation.

Ah, let us not be so hard and iron-hearted, but let us give God this honor, that we implore His aid and mercy.

Here you ought to know and keep in sight some sentences commanding invocation, which may often come to your mind while praying: as in this text, the saying: Ask, seek, knock. Likewise Psalm 50: Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you. Likewise Luke 18: The Lord says, it is necessary to pray always, and not to grow weary. Matt. 26: Watch and pray, that you do not enter into temptation. By the thought or recitation of these and similar sayings let us exhort ourselves, let us rouse ourselves, and as it were compel and stimulate ourselves to invocation. Nor let us indulge in our trepidation, thinking or contentiously arguing: What is the use of invoking? Or, why would God care for my groanings? Why would He receive my prayers, when I am unworthy and ill-deserving? To this incredulity and our unworthiness let us oppose the most severe commands, which order us to pray, which affirm that God wishes to be worshipped in this way. Wherefore let us know that this work and this worship is most necessary, and that it is a huge sin not to render this worship, nor to perform this obedience to God.

Third reminder: But that we may establish that our cries and groanings are not in vain, that our invocation is not an empty murmur, it is necessary that we in every prayer seek and behold the promises, in which God has revealed and made known His will, in which He asserts and holily promises that... He wishes to hear us, to receive our prayers, to help us, to grant what we ask, and to deliver and free us from miseries and troubles. Thus in the present text, or reading, the Lord expressly added the universal: Everyone who asks, receives. Item, John 16: Amen, amen I say to you: Whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give to you.

Here is placed a promise confirmed by the oath of the Son of God.

Let this great assertion correct doubt, let it lift up souls, so that they may believe the promise, and most firmly establish that God certainly wills to hear us, that our invocation is pleasing to Him, and is not in vain, that He truly wills to give eternal and temporal goods, and indeed He wills that the praise of truth be attributed to Him.

Now let the doctrine concerning the distinction and order of promises be most familiarly known and assiduously circulated in minds. At the beginning, let us propose to ourselves the first and highest promise, namely, the promise of grace or reconciliation and eternal life to be given freely on account of the mediator Christ: and let us know that it is certainly the command of God that in true conversion or repentance, we first ask, and by faith receive this, as the highest good, namely, the remission of sins and reconciliation or acceptance unto eternal life on account of Christ: let us establish that this is certainly given to us as we approach God with the confidence of Christ the mediator, according to that [passage in] Habakkuk 2, Romans 1, Galatians 3: The just shall live by his faith. Item Matthew 11: Come to me all you that labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Item Luke 11: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him. Item Ezekiel 33: I live, saith the Lord, I desire not the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live.

You see that this is truly the perpetual voice of the Gospel, that we should approach God with the confidence of the mediator, that we should certainly assent to the promise of grace: which indeed has been confirmed by both the oath and the blood of the Son of God: God wills that this be accepted and retained even when all bodily goods are lost, according to the saying of Job 13: Although he should kill me, I will trust in him. But yet I will reprove my ways in his sight, and he himself shall be my Savior, nor shall any hypocrite enter before him. Indeed, other goods or benefits cannot be asked for unless the promise of grace shines forth first, according to the saying of Christ, John 14: No man can come to the Father, but by the Son. Item John 16: Whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give to you. And to the Hebrews 4: Having a high priest Jesus, let us go with confidence to the throne of grace.

In vain would David ask for victory, unless he simultaneously asked for the remission of sins.

But after we have been reminded concerning reconciliation: then let the promises concerning necessary goods in this life be considered, and let us know that benefits of the body are to be asked for and expected from God, and that those prayers are not in vain, but always obtain some goods, nay, certainly obtain either the liberation or the mitigation of bodily troubles: and that God has a care for the Church, even if He exercises other members differently. For because by the voice of the Gospel, and not otherwise, God always gathers the Church in this life, He also grants some spans of life, and polities and economies, and therefore it is said, 1 Timothy 4: Piety has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. Item Matthew 6: Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you. Item Psalm 115: The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord, etc.

A fourth consideration is concerning faith asking with the confidence of the Son of God the mediator for eternal and present goods: for the promises were delivered for this reason, that faith might be kindled in invocation. And, as I have already said concerning the order or distinction of promises, so first it must be known here that it is necessary in every prayer that this faith shine forth, which establishes that you are received and heard on account of the Son of God: as it is said in Ephesians 3: Through whom we have access with confidence through faith in him, etc. Nor let faith shine only in this beginning of consolation, namely, that it establish that we are received, pleasing to God, receiving remission of sins, and that our groanings are heard: but let firm hope also approach, whereby we may expect either mitigation or liberation in this life, even if help is deferred, and the length of delay weakens the soul, as it is commanded in Habakkuk 2: If he make any delay, wait for him; for he will surely come, and will not tarry.

Next, the things that are asked for must be distinguished. For either faith asks for spiritual goods, concerning which the will of God is expressly and specifically stated, that He will give these very goods by name, and that He wills that they be asked for without condition, such as reconciliation and eternal life, the governance of the soul, the gift of the Holy Spirit, liberation from impiety and eternal death: these, I say, are the benefits proper to the Gospel and eternal, and faith must ask for and expect them specifically and by name without condition. Because it is the eternal and immutable command of God at all times that we be converted to Him and ask for remission, and establish that we are certainly received freely on account of the Son of God, not on account of our own dignity, or any of our virtues and actions, those who do not believe this ,

the enemies of God are present, and they accuse him of falsehood, and treat him with contumely, according to the saying in John 3: He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him.

But faith asks for bodily goods, which are not given to all in the same way, and in the asking of which we ought to offer ourselves and be prepared for obedience, if we are not delivered in this life, as we might wish: for these, I say, bodily goods, faith in general asks for mitigation, because it knows that the Church must be subject to the cross: therefore, concerning the thing itself, which is specifically asked for, it does not decree without condition.

And yet this faith, asking and expecting the benefits of the body with a condition, may decree that the petition for bodily goods is heard, and that prayer is never in vain, even if the Church is subject to the cross, and we individually owe obedience to God in bodily punishments and hardships according to those sayings in Psalm 145: The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth; he will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and will hear their cry. And Matthew 21: All things that you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.

Specifically, therefore, concerning bodily hardships, let us ask for either deliverance or mitigation. For prayer obtains, either that the punishment be removed, or that it be mitigated: as Job, David, Manasseh, asked with trembling, but yet asked, did He avert or mitigate the great evils? Thus the Prophets pray for mitigation, Jeremiah 10: O Lord, correct me in your judgment, lest you reduce me to nothing. And Isaiah 64: Behold, we are your clay, etc., do not be angry, O Lord, exceedingly. Item Psalm 78: He did not kindle all his wrath. Item Psalm 130: If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? that is, if you wished to execute all punishments, we would all be suddenly extinguished. And indeed in such prayer, let individuals not only ask for themselves, but first for the whole body of the Church: let us pray for it to be preserved, even if individual members ought to be prepared for obedience, if anything is to be endured, or if the outcomes do not respond as we might wish.

David, praying for the army, asks for victory, so that the Church may be safe: meanwhile he knows that some will come into danger, or be killed, and he offers his own obedience. Nor is his prayer in vain, for it is received by God, and obtains for many the mitigation of evil.

And God wishes us in prayer to be affected by the needs of others, and the care of the whole Church: therefore it is written in Psalm 122: Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem. The fifth and final admonition is concerning the things to be asked for, that is, that in the petition there be expressed some things necessary for us, for the Church, for the republic, for our families, and for others for whom we ask. Now the things to be asked for are things not prohibited by the commands of God, as the Apostle John says in 1 John 5: Whatever you ask according to his will, he will give you, that is, the things to be asked for are not those prohibited by God: let not Saul ask for David to be taken away, let not David ask for Uriah to be killed, but let them ask for necessary things, the petition for which agrees with the Decalogue and with divine promises. Now other promises speak of spiritual goods, others of bodily goods, just as was said a little before concerning the distinction of promises.

And God wishes faith and invocation to be exercised even by the petition for bodily things, according to the saying: Give us this day our daily bread: He wishes counsel to be asked of Him, success in one's vocation: and other comforts of life. And indeed concerning vocation it is said in John 15: Without me you can do nothing. And there are four principal causes for which God commands that we ask for the goods of the body, the first of which is: that we may recognize, and certainly decree, that chance does not rule in these external goods, nor are they scattered rashly or by accident, and thrown out to be torn apart, but are given, distributed, and preserved by the singular counsel of God and in a singular way, especially in the Church: for whose sake the nature of things is preserved for the whole human race, as Christ clearly says in Matthew 6: Your heavenly Father knows that you have need of the defense of your bodies. Item, you are better than many sparrows.

The second cause why God wishes them to be asked for is: that we may know that He Himself will preserve the Church, even in this life, and that we may think that in this mortal life the Church must be begun, according to the saying in Psalm 115: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord. Therefore, let not only our own cause be the reason for asking for the goods of the body, but also for the common necessity of the Church: let us individually ask for the mitigation of miseries, so that we may be able to serve the Church, and for this cause let us know that God wishes to bestow these benefits, as He often testifies, as when Christ says in Matthew 6: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you. seek the kingdom of God, and the other things shall be added unto you.

The third cause is that faith and invocation may be exercised in daily necessity, in seeking peace, food, good health, and success in governance. Thus, let soldiers seek success in battle, senators wisdom in giving counsel and governance, teachers and students in their studies, etc. So that God may be known in these goods, and faith, invocation, and thanksgiving for benefits may be exercised.

The fourth cause is that God wills, in these exercises of seeking corporal things, that another spiritual faith be confirmed and kindled, concerning the eternal promise, or concerning reconciliation: for bodies, families, and polities are preserved so that the eternal Church may be gathered.

Therefore, this rule must always be held: In the petition for corporal goods, faith must shine forth, which receives the promise of grace, or by which the remission of sins is received freely on account of the Mediator: through whom and on account of whom the Church is also preserved in this life, according to the saying of Paul, 2 Corinthians 1: In Christ all promises are ratified.

The order, therefore, of things to be sought is as follows: First, let us seek the remission of sins and reconciliation, and with these goods, the light of the Holy Spirit, which kindles and confirms in us the knowledge of God, faith, fear, tolerance, love, invocation, chastity, etc. Finally, [let us seek] Him who rules us in our vocation, and in all counsels, in teaching, and in governing the republic.

In the second place, let us seek also corporal goods, common and private, the peace of those regions which provide a refuge for Churches and pious studies, the fertility of fields, fruitful weather, good health, food, success in our political and economic administration, the defense of children, reputation, and possessions, honest discipline of cities, and tranquil civil government, as it is said in 1 Timothy 2, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all piety and honesty.

To this must be added an admonition concerning delay and the manner of liberation: because two circumstances in seeking exercise faith above all, namely: manner and time, as Moses thought nothing less than that he would wander for forty years with such a multitude in such great hardships in the desert. But he hoped perhaps it would be a journey of one month.

Thus, Joseph, Jonah, and many others in all times were liberated in a way far different from what they themselves had thought. For God wills that His presence be acknowledged in the Church, and that help be sought from Him and expected; He wills that faith, invocation, and hope be exercised, nor does He will that human counsels or human thoughts dominate in the governance of life: but He wills it to be known that the Church is governed divinely, as Psalm 4 says: The Lord makes His holy one wonderful, that is, God does not deliver by human counsels, but by wondrous ways, which human reason cannot foresee. Therefore, events are not given immediately, and in the ways that human reason thinks: but He exercises us, so that we may depend on Him by faith, and not be ruled by our own opinions, so that, although God had promised that He would preserve the stock of Judah until the Messiah was born, nevertheless the vain imaginations of the enemies of Jeremiah were present, who argued that the temple and the polity of that time could not be destroyed; for God could have preserved and restored it otherwise than they themselves thought.

But the rule must be held concerning circumstances: Habakkuk 2: If it makes delay, wait for it, because it will surely come, and will not tarry.

Likewise, Luke 18, in the example of the slothful judge and the widow, where it is added: It is necessary always to pray and not to grow weary.

It is not ours, therefore, to prescribe to God the manner and time, but these things must be commended entirely to His own counsel, so that our eyes meanwhile may look not at things and events, but at God, and may be kindled to invocation. An illustrious example of this rule exists in the history of Judith, chapter 8, where Judith rebuking the citizens, who had set five days for God, says: Who are you, who tempt the Lord; you have set a time for mercy for the Lord. To this belongs the saying of Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 20: When we do not know what is to be done, our eyes look to Thee, our God. And since this very sentiment contains the sweetest consolation, let it always be before the eyes in all ambiguities which cannot be untangled by human counsels: of which kind very many befall man.

Finally: Whenever we think of prayer, let thanksgiving be joined to it, which in general is a profession, whence the benefit has been received, and of binding oneself to mutual duties. For two supreme virtues are comprehended in it, which are called gratitude, namely, truth and justice: truth acknowledges whence the benefit has come, and celebrates the author: justice binds to mutual duties. Therefore, he is ungrateful, and a liar and unjust. But God wills to be understood by men gratitude be understood by men, so that we may exercise it especially toward Him, and be truthful and dutiful toward Him. And just as He demands petition in invocation, so that we may acknowledge that He is God, and that He is omnipotent, present, and a helper; and that in such acknowledgment He may communicate Himself to us: so He demands thanksgiving, so that this true acknowledgment may persevere, and that He may subsequently also communicate Himself to us; therefore Paul says in 1 Thess. last chapter: Pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks.

Thanksgiving toward God is, therefore, the truth, which confesses that benefits have been received from God, and that He is truly God, that He is omnipotent, present, and a helper; and it is a work of justice, by which you bind yourself to duties pleasing to God.

Since, therefore, lying and injustice are horrible sins: it is manifest that ingratitude toward God is a horrendous crime, so that, when Alexander the Macedonian thinks that his kingdom was obtained by chance or by his own virtue, and does not confess that it was given by God, he is a liar, and indeed against God: afterwards he becomes unjust, not rendering to God the due duty, when He commands Himself to be worshipped as God.

But great and shameful is the ingratitude of all men toward God; we receive from God life, talents, education, food, letters, the Gospel, the Church, governments, and daily many benefits; we are often defended against the devil, his snares being repelled by the Son of God, which we are entirely ignorant of; we are often helped divinely, when we do not even ask for help: meanwhile we play securely, or seek pleasures, and we argue that good things are offered to us by chance, we do not acknowledge God as the author of the benefit, we pretend that dangers were repelled by chance, we do not strive to retain the benevolence of God, we do not show our gratitude by the celebration of the benefactor and by our obedience, but we kindle His wrath by our petulance.

Let us deplore these evils, and let us amend ourselves, and when we have acknowledged the benefits of God, let us confess that we have received them from God, and let us not petulantly cast off God as our guardian and helper: but let us strive to please Him, and let us celebrate our gratitude with true duties of life, and with our voice; let us give thanks by name at any time for a recent benefit then received, let us also tell others, where we have been helped and delivered, so that others may be invited to the acknowledgment of God.

Gratitude is a gift pleasing to God in itself, but it is also demanded for the sake of example.

Therefore Paul most sweetly exhorts that many pray for him, so that more may afterwards give thanks for the benefit received. 1 Cor. 1, signifying that thanksgiving is the chief sacrifice and most pleasing to God, and that it is to be performed by many: because God demands more to be acknowledged and celebrated by many, and when many celebrate a received benefit, the example becomes more illustrious, and many others are invited to invocation, fear, and faith.

Since, therefore, thanksgiving is necessary, precepts are usually joined concerning petition and thanksgiving, because both are necessary for the acknowledgment of God, Psalm 50: Call upon me in the day of thy trouble, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.

Item 1 Tim. 2: I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, or petitions, intercessions for others, and thanksgivings be made for all men, etc.

Certainly, when the acknowledgment of God is extinguished in the ungrateful, God ceases to communicate Himself to them.

Just as usually secure men after received benefits play with such thoughts: Perhaps you were delivered by chance, etc. Thus they lose the acknowledgment of God, and of the presence of God, when they ought to nourish and confirm the acknowledgment of God, and faith, with the following commemoration and profession.

It is a huge labor for pious minds, even after a benefit is received, to retain this sentiment, that we are truly helped and saved by God. Therefore, when our dangers are repelled by the benefits of God, as often happens, let us keep in sight the sentences which confirm us, so that we may acknowledge that we have been helped by God, as in Psalm 34: This poor man cried unto the Lord, and the Lord heard him.

Psalm 116: Thou hast loosed my bonds, I will sacrifice to thee the sacrifice of praise. Psalm 127: Except the Lord build the house, etc.

Let us acknowledge, therefore, that by human counsels and defenses all dangers cannot be resolved, as Jeremiah clearly says in chapter 10:

I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, neither is it in man to direct his steps.

And Psalm 27: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me up.

How many things happen to Moses, Samuel, David, Hezekiah, and finally to all rulers that are inextricable by human counsel? Therefore, as they did, let us ask to be ruled and helped by God, and when the outcomes are peaceful, let us confess what is the case, that we have been helped and defended by God, and by this reminder let us celebrate the author and governor of the benefit.

Everyone that asketh receiveth.

You have heard just now the common doctrine concerning invocation or prayer, which in this Church it is often repeated: for the reason that we all need this reminder or repetition, so that daily while praying we may consider in our minds the chapters or passages about which I have admonished; but above all we look upon the sweetest promise so often repeated by God, so that we may establish with the firmest faith that God wills to hear us mercifully for the sake of the Son, and therefore we may flee to Him, and from Him expect help.

And in the previous sermon we collected some sentences inviting us to invocation with the most ample promises, as it is said in John 16: Amen, amen I say to you: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give to you. Propose this and similar sentences to your minds while meditating frequently, but above all, while praying, let them be in your sight, and think that God is truthful, and do not think that so many most clear promises are empty sounds.

For they are the most severe voices of the divine Majesty, which in these very words makes plain and reveals to us His good will and immense mercy toward us: so often with an oath added, so that we may establish with certainty without any doubt that our prayers are received, and that our groans and cries are not in vain, provided that we attribute this honor to God, namely, that we believe God wills to hear us for the sake of the Son, that we believe He is truthful and a keeper of His promises, that He wills to receive our groans and cries, and that He will help us. Thus in the present text the promise is often repeated and inculcated: Ask and you shall receive, seek and you shall find, knock and it shall be opened to you.

Everyone who asks receives. And it must be diligently observed that the universal particle 'everyone' is added here.

Because the hearts of individuals object, cry out, and anxiously dispute against this universal: Ah, so many thousands of people everywhere in the world at all times recite prayers, and yet they are not heard: likewise the text in John ch. 9 says: God does not hear sinners. However much, therefore, I and other sinners cry out for a long time and much, yet we are repelled by this single answer as if by a weapon: God does not hear sinners.

It is asked, therefore, how the other sentence in John 9 agrees with this saying: Everyone who believes, receives? Answer. First, concerning sinners, it must be known that the kinds of sinners must be distinguished.

For there are other sinners who, secure and willing, persevere in sins against conscience, or with manifest stubbornness retain the purpose of sinning, and do not wish to do penance, such as Pharaoh, Saul, and many other Epicureans, the profane, hypocrites, and contemners of God in all ages, who retain the purpose of violating divine commands against conscience, and are not converted to God.

Of these it is properly and most truly said: God does not hear sinners.

Likewise Proverbs 28: He who turns away his ears, so that he does not hear the Law, his prayer is an execrable abomination. Here you hear the true and genuine interpretation of the former saying: He who turns away his ears, and does not wish to hear the word of God, that is, he who proudly and contumaciously perseveres in the contempt of God without penance, as those who do not wish to cast away the worship of idols, to avoid lusts and adulteries, to omit unjust persecutions, such sinners are not heard, and their prayer is truly an execrable abomination.

Therefore we must by no means be placed in this number, or wish to be numbered among this kind of sinners.

But there are other sinners who are converted to God, and do not retain the purpose of sinning, or do not persevere in sins against conscience, but have the beginnings of penance and salutary amendment, truly tremble at the recognition of judgment and the wrath of God against sins, cast away the evil purpose, and cease to rush against conscience: and they have in their heart an ignited spark of faith, by which, being raised up, they seek consolation, and ask for the remission of sins, establishing that they are heard for the sake of the Mediator.

Such sinners are David, Peter, the repentant thief on the cross, etc. Let these be placed in this number, of which the Lord Himself cries out in Matthew 11: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Behold, here too the universal particle 'All' is expressly placed: nevertheless, 'All' in this place does not comprehend the secure, the arrogant, the proud, the fierce contemners, who willingly indulge in all furies, but the fearful, and those bringing to God a contrite heart, deploring their own uncleanness, and with great solicitude avoiding lapses against conscience.

To all these is promised, offered, and granted grace or gratuitous reconciliation, and consolation or vivification. In the same way you must understand the universal particle 'Everyone' in the present text, concerning all the fearful and contrite, who have the beginnings of penance.

To all these is proposed and offered grace, or the remission of sins, salutary consolation, and help, and liberation in the words of the divine oath in Ezekiel 33: I live: I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.

Another objection. But you continue to object: Yet I am a sinner. This certainly cannot be denied: but when, having turned to God, or performing repentance, you believe and acquiesce in God through trust in the Mediator, your sins have already been transferred to the Lord Jesus Christ, and God wills that you approach Him, and flee to Him with the Son as your guide, and expect and ask for gratuitous remission, and divine aid, through and because of Christ, not because of your own dignity, or your virtues, or your actions.

And do not be deterred from invocation because of the multitude of your sins and the magnitude of your infirmity: but set before yourself the express, manifest, and universal command of Christ, Matt. 11: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

And let us not be submerged in darkness, or be perturbed by false speculations and the delirious imaginings of particularity: as if this consolation did not pertain to us, or we were not in the number of those to whom Christ offers mercy, or grace, and consolation. But diligently remember and fix in your mind the universal particle 'All', which has been most often repeated in the sermons of Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles, just as the same is placed in the Prophet Joel, chapter 2: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.

Item John 3: So God loved the world, that He gave His only-begotten Son, that Everyone who believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life.

Item Rom. 10: The same Lord of all, rich to all who call upon Him: and a little before it precedes: Everyone who believes in Him shall not be confounded.

Of these most manifest testimonies there is a great number in Scripture, which it is indeed fitting to study to collect, attentively consider, and diligently fix in memory, so that by these universal sayings your faith may be excited and confirmed, and you may know that you are members of this assembly, and are comprehended in this very number of those calling upon Him, whom God certainly wills to hear and regard.

Now let us approach the following words, which contain the explanation or most sweet and full declaration of the consolation of this promise. The Lord adds a parable or similitude.

If a little child asks his parents for a morsel or fragment of bread, will a father or mother give him a stone? etc. But you know how true and ardent love is, how sweet and expressed the affection (storge) in parents toward their offspring, so that in the hunger, diseases, and calamities of their children, a father and mother feel huge, most bitter, and inestimable pains of soul, which experience in very many people testifies and confirms. And God wills that our hearts be so tormented by the sharp stings of pain because of the unhappiness of our children, and He has for that reason impressed such affections upon the nature of men, so that they may be illustrious reminders of the immense love of the eternal Father toward His Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and toward us who are received into grace because of the Son.

Thus the Lord here uses a parable taken from the singular and ardent love and benevolence of parents toward their offspring: so that we may think a similar fire of love exists in God toward us men. But, alas, how far from this most sweet image are our thoughts about God!

For when we perceive our uncleanness, miseries, and sins, we continually reason: that we are therefore neither regarded, nor are we a care to God, but that we are deserted and cast out, in hardships, destitution, persecutions, ignominy or infamy, and finally in death itself, perpetually dwelling, clinging, and wasting away. Which certainly in no way appears, as is evident, to be a sign or testimony of true and paternal love in God toward us.

And although by a singular counsel God wills His elect Church in this life to be subject to the cross, and wills the pious to be exercised by afflictions: yet it must be held as most true and with both hands, and more truly with the whole heart, that He truly and paternally loves us, just as the Son of God Himself so often testifies in John 3: So God loved the world, that He gave His only-begotten Son, etc. Item John 14: If anyone loves me, he will keep my words, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our mansion with him.

John 17: I have manifested to them your name, and will further make it known, that your love, with which you love me, may be in them, and I in them.

This is truly a serious, ardent, and admirable prayer, which our Lord Jesus Christ recited in His agony a little before His crucifixion, and the sacrifice by which He appeased the wrath of the eternal Father.

He asks, moreover, that the immense love with which the eternal Father loves the coeternal Son may also be in us. What revelation can be sweeter? What more illustrious indication of supreme love toward us can be thought of? than this commemoration of Christ.

in which He asserts and promises that the eternal Father will embrace us with the same love with which He embraces His coeternal Son. Since, therefore, there is such a burning fire of love in God, and since we are, as it were, spurred and driven by divine precepts and promises to pray: we certainly ought, ardently and seriously, in all dangers of soul and body, or in all necessities, both spiritual and corporal, to seek, ask, and expect grace—that is, the gratuitous remission of sins, the confirmation of faith, consolation, help, the mitigation of punishments, and eternal salvation—fleeing suppliantly to God with true groaning of heart, with prayers and tears, and to obtain them by daily and assiduous cries.

These few things may suffice for the explanation of this most sweet parable or similitude. Nevertheless, I wish to add a brief admonition concerning the clause or appendix of the prayer, namely, concerning the particle Amen.

Question.

For what reason is the particle Amen usually added at the end of a prayer in place of a clause or appendix? I answer. The particle Amen reminds the one praying of certainty, or the full assurance of faith, and the firmness of assent. For it is an asseveration: just as if you were to say: May this very truth confirm it, or, these things will most truly and certainly come to pass. And as often as you have said a prayer, so often, having diligently and attentively considered the particle Amen, you should, as it were, examine and question yourself whether you yourself believe and firmly establish that God receives and hears your prayers, and that they are not an empty murmur. For the one who invokes [God] to persevere in this doubt, and not to emerge or be raised by faith from these waves of a trembling mind, and thus reasoning: It is a vain labor to say prayers to God, God does not care for nor regard you. This incredulity, I say, or diffidence, is a huge and sad sin, which corrupts the invocation. For thus the Lord says in Matt. 21: "All things whatsoever you shall ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive." Likewise 1 Tim. 2: "Pray without anger and hesitation," that is, in afflictions, let not the mind, broken by impatience, be angry at God and rage against the judgment of God, nor, fleeing God and trembling in diffidence, fall into despair, or, persevering in doubt, be drowned: but with certain confidence establish that you are a care to God, that you are regarded, and approaching and fleeing to God with this faith, expect divine help and liberation. Rom. 10: "How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?" As if He were to say: There cannot exist true invocation without faith, by which, when hearts are not raised and sustained, they flee from God horribly; so far are they from invoking Him.

James 1: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all men abundantly, and it shall be given him; but let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavers is like a wave of the sea, which is moved and carried about by the wind; for let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord." Fix this very saying of James and turn it over in your mind, so that it may remind you that in every invocation faith is necessary, by which your heart, fleeing to God, may establish that He is appeased and propitious to you, and that for the sake of His Son He wills to hear your groans, and that your prayer will not be in vain.

Likewise to the Hebrews 4: "Having such a High Priest, who has experienced our sorrows and frailty, let us go with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may find mercy and grace and help in time of need." Eph. 3: "In Christ Jesus our Lord we have consolation, by which we dare to approach confidently, or in trust, through faith in Him."

Remember these and similar sentences, so that you may learn to stir up and kindle faith in prayer.

Many recite prayers by a certain habit, not even thinking what they are reciting, much less solicitous about being heard, but they place them with little discernment, however the matter may fall, whether the prayer is received or is in vain. Such cold and simulated battology and thoughtlessness is not prayer nor petition.

And for the most part, those very slothful and thoughtless ones are men who are intemperate, or drunk with pleasures, and secure, who experience no temptations, adversities, troubles, and miseries. Therefore they wander with idle minds, and mutter little prayers without attention.

But when the prayer is ardent, and attention is retained in true sorrows and the sense of miseries, then it is necessary, in true contemplation of the divine manifestations and promises, and by the pious motion of the heart, that this faith or trust, resting in God and certainly expecting divine help, be kindled and stirred up, according to the saying in Psalm 25: "All who wait for Thee shall not be confounded."

ctum: All who wait for you shall not be put to shame. Objection. But how shall I believe, someone might say, or wait? Since this weak nature cannot cast off or put aside the depravity born with us, and the hearts of all men are full of doubt and trepidation, fleeing from God? I answer: It is most true that in all of us there is and remains a great deal of infirmity and trepidation; but you should set before yourself, and consider in your mind, the voice of that miserable father, Mark 9, who weeping acknowledges the weakness of his faith, and asking to be confirmed, cries out: I believe, Lord, but bring help to my unbelief or weakness.

For it is necessary that the beginnings and sparks of true faith be kindled in each person, however languid, but gradually struggling and resisting doubt, diffidence, and the trepidations of a heart fleeing from God.

Indeed, in this struggle and fight, one must learn what true faith is, and how the languid beginnings of faith are to be confirmed, so that they may grow and increase; if faith is rather languid, let your heart look upon and set before itself some sayings or testimonies of divine promises, let it strive to assent to these, and asking for help, let it attribute to God this honor, this praise of truth and goodness, that He certainly wishes to hear us, and in this good hope or consolation let the soul acquiesce and be enlivened: namely, that God is about to help, and will not desert you, nor allow you to be submerged in eternal death, as long as you ask to be helped, and your breast is raised by faith.

Here also it is necessary to repeat and know the distinction of the promises or benefits which are asked for; for some promises speak of eternal and spiritual goods, others of corporal and present goods.

Concerning eternal benefits, that is, reconciliation and eternal life, it must be known that it is the eternal and immutable command of God that each person should ask for these very goods by name, and with firm faith determine that they are certainly given or happen to them: just as the Lord Himself affirms in John 6: This is the will of the Father who sent me, that everyone who knows the Son and believes in Him, may have eternal life.

The eternal God most severely commands that you believe in the Son, and indeed He demands that you believe without condition that He is about to give you these very goods by name: grace or the gratuitous remission of sins, righteousness, that is, the imputation of righteousness, vivification or the donation of the Holy Spirit and eternal life.

Faith must ask for and expect these eternal and spiritual goods specifically or by name.

In the same way, goods in general joined with the promise of grace and eternal life are to be asked for by name without condition, such as the propagation of saving doctrine and the preservation of the Church.

But concerning corporal goods—food, peace, good health, riches—it is true that these goods must be asked for, yet with this condition: that we offer ourselves, and be ready to render obedience to God, if He wishes us to be exercised longer by afflictions: just as we often see it happen that the Saints are not delivered in this life from the present punishments or calamities for which they ask, or at least that it is deferred, and deliverance does not happen immediately, nor does the outcome correspond to human imaginations and wishes.

For the rule concerning all corporal benefits and promises, whether expressed by name or not by name, must be held: that they have two conditions annexed or included: one of chastisement, the other of the cross.

For although God most truly grants even the goods of the body, nevertheless He chastises and punishes the disobedient.

He also wishes the pious to be exercised, and the Church to be subject to the cross, for many reasons: about which you have heard very often in their place.

David and Manasseh are chastised and punished for their certain faults; Joseph, Jeremiah, and Daniel are exercised by hardships and led into exile: even though they ask for and expect deliverance from God.

But here it must be known that the petitions for corporal benefits are by no means on that account void, but certainly obtain one or the other, namely: either deliverance, so that they are entirely removed, or mitigation, so that the calamities and punishments are eased.

Thus pray Isaiah, Jeremiah, and other Prophets, who, when they see that punishments are already roaming, and that it will not happen that they cease immediately or are entirely removed, nevertheless ask for and obtain mitigation.

For thus Jeremiah prays in chapter 10: Correct me, O Lord, but in judgment, not in fury, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing.

And Isaiah deprecates wrath with these words, chapter 64: Ah Lord, you are our Father and creator or molder, behold we are your clay and the works of your hands, do not be angry, O Lord, greatly, do not pour out your wrath.

And Habakkuk 3: Lord, we are your work, give life.

us in the midst of the years, when you are angry, O Lord, remember your mercy.

In this way you also ought daily to seek the mitigation or relief of present and impending punishments.

O eternal God, for the sake of your beloved Son, and so that your glory may be known and illustrated, remember your immense mercy in your most just anger; preserve us with the Church and in your Church; do not strike the land with a curse; do not allow an infinite devastation to occur, or Turkish and Cyclopean barbarism in these regions; preserve your good political regime, the salutary state of the Church, the holiness of public discipline; protect our little families; make them vessels of mercy; give them sustenance, success in the duties of their vocations, and other goods necessary for the body, etc.

Such a prayer is not empty and vain, just as the prayers of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others were not useless or vain. For even if the punishment is not entirely taken away and removed, it is nevertheless softened and mitigated.

Furthermore, it is necessary to hold most firmly to this rule: Even when we are stuck in bodily punishments, oppressed by whatever weight of calamities, we must nevertheless not fail in the meantime to look to God, nor despair of final or ultimate liberation and eternal salvation, just as Saul, having been defeated in several battles, with fortune blowing against him, fails entirely from God, feels that he is cast away into eternal destruction, and thus loses and casts away both the promise of grace and the hope of final, ultimate, and everlasting liberation. But David, stripped of his kingdom and all his glory, offers his obedience to God; he knows that reconciliation has been promised, and that this promise must be held by faith, even if the whole nature of things were to oppose it. Therefore, he does not fail to look to God, but awaits eternal salvation and liberation, even if he is not to be brought back and restored to his kingdom. Concerning this firm hope of eternal salvation, Job says most sweetly in chapter 13: Even if God should slay me, yet I will hope in him; that is: I know it is the will of God that I should certainly believe and firmly expect the remission of sins and eternal life, or the inheritance of eternal salvation, whether things in this life are favorable or adverse. Therefore, I will embrace and retain this eternal consolation by faith, even if all the goods of the body must be lost, and I must waste away in these torments of diseases and in poverty.

On the giving of thanks.

In the previous sermon I said that the designation of invocation, adoration, and prayer is attributed to two kinds or degrees: namely, petition and the giving of thanks. I have already discussed petition, and whenever mention is made of it, a reminder about the giving of thanks must be added.

You already know that ingratitude is a common or very vulgar vice. For when someone lies down oppressed by disease, he often indeed and ardently asks God for the recovery of his health; but the same person, having been restored by the benefit of God from a serious and long-lasting illness, completely forgets God, nay, he pretends that he has recovered, and that the disease was softened or driven away primarily by the efficacy of remedies and the help of physicians, or even that the force of the disease was overcome by the strength and firmness of nature, and he does not think that the restoration of health and bodily strength is truly the gift and work of God; nay, often afterwards he becomes much worse and more petulant. This is customary for most people in very many matters, and what is to be lamented is that all men are ungrateful.

It is certain, however, and most manifest, that gratitude is required and commanded by God, both toward himself and toward men; of which indeed these are the words in Psalm 50: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me; that is, having been liberated and helped, you will acknowledge my presence, you will conclude that I have heard your groans, that I have helped you when you called, and therefore with a true movement of the heart you will give thanks to me. God also affirms in the same Psalm that these are spiritual sacrifices, that these are the principal acts of worship, and that we cannot offer God anything else besides these highest honors. general appellation love: and he who performs obedience according to these precepts, he truly performs for men those things which he would wish to be performed for himself by them. And there is a most certain declaration of this saying: Whatsoever you wish that men should do to you, namely according to the law of God or the Decalogue rightly understood, the same also do you to them. So much I wished to say briefly concerning the meaning or understanding of this saying.

Now you hear very often concerning the divine law, that no man in this depraved nature can entirely fulfill the Decalogue, and perform the obedience which the law requires. Since, therefore, not even the reborn can in this mortal life satisfy the law of God, it is asked, for what purpose is it necessary to teach and learn the divine law? Concerning this question you often hear proposed the necessary and full doctrine of piety. It is most truly the eternal, severe, and immovable will of God that the Decalogue be proposed, taught, and learned: and there are three causes, that is, there are three offices, or a threefold use of the Decalogue.

The first office, or the first use, is political and pedagogical, namely the diligence of reason in governing external discipline, or the governance of external actions, which individual men, even in this weakness, can perform in some way by natural powers.

For although this weak and corrupt nature of men cannot satisfy the Decalogue with interior and perfect obedience of the heart, and fulfill the law: yet God most severely wills and commands that external members be restrained by this as it were bridle of discipline, lest they rush into homicides, adulteries, thefts, or commit other external crimes. And those who do not wish to perform this external obedience, but atrociously violate discipline, it is certain that they are punished by God with severe penalties even in this mortal life, as these sayings affirm: Matt. 26: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword. Heb. 13: God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Isa. 33: Woe to you who plunder, for you shall be plundered. Item, Ecclesiastes in chapter 8 says: It will not be well for the wicked, nor will his days be long. These rules speak of corporal punishments in this life, which God takes from the guilty either through magistrates or by other means. Even if robbers enjoy impunity for some time, and are thought to have escaped the hands of judges, yet in their own time they are divinely drawn to punishments in this corporal life: daily examples show this.

The second use of the Law is: or the second cause is why it is necessary to teach and learn the Decalogue: namely, that from it we may recognize the wrath of God against sin.

Because the moral law is a universal judgment accusing all sins in all men, interior and exterior, and the whole depravity. Therefore God terrifies by the voice of the Decalogue, according to the saying of Paul, Rom. 4: The law works wrath. As often as you hear this divine voice: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, it is necessary for you to confess that you have sin, and have deserved the wrath of God, because your heart by no means agrees with the law, it does not burn, it is not full of the love of God, as it ought to be. Here, on the other hand, you may look, and recognize the grace or benefit of Christ: that freely, that is, through mercy, on account of Christ we have remission of sins, we are reconciled, and received into the inheritance of eternal salvation; we are not righteous, that is, accepted, and pleasing before God on account of the law, but on account of the propitiator Christ.

The third use, or the third cause of the Law, is in those converted to God, or the reborn, who are already received into grace, and experience the help and efficacy of God: for these also it is necessary that the law be proposed, so that they may be taught and know what works, what worship pleases God, and not devise works and worship by their own counsel, as the Heathens, Monks, and all men in all ages have done, who have spurned the word of God written in the Prophetic and Apostolic books.

But although not even the reborn and truly holy can satisfy the Decalogue, they nevertheless have the beginnings of obedience or conformity with the law. As, your heart feels the beginnings of the fear of God, of faith, of love toward God: and although these beginnings are languid and weak, yet we know that God demands this inchoation of obedience, and that it pleases Him in the reconciled and children of God, and is grateful to God on account of the Mediator Christ. Indeed, God wishes to help us with present aid and efficacy, so that this obedience may be kindled and grow; He also wishes that it be sought from Him with true groans, with the shining confidence of the Mediator, so that He Himself, on account of Christ and through Him, having poured the Holy Spirit into us, may wish to kindle and confirm in our breasts true fear of God, firm faith, patience, chastity, and other virtues befitting the divine will, which God has expressed in His law. These huge gifts and benefits God certainly effects in us, when we seriously and ardently ask for them: so that Christ may clearly he says in Luke 22: How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

See, pious listeners, that you fix these words in the innermost senses of your soul and comprehend them; exercise your faith and invocation in this work, in this meditation and prayer. Thus you will understand more clearly, and you will experience in reality, that these things are not empty nor fabricated: Ask that God, through and for the sake of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, may illuminate, teach, rule, sanctify, and confirm your hearts with his Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, from these things which have been commemorated, it can be clearly understood that the preaching of the Law is not empty or idle, or that the Decalogue is not proposed and explained in the Church in vain, even if our hearts cannot provide the perfect obedience which the Decalogue requires.

Let these things suffice concerning the threefold use of the Law; it follows in the text:

This is indeed the Law and the Prophets.

These words are not only to be referred to the rule immediately preceding: Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do the same to them: because the Law and the Prophets do not speak only of the second table, but rather of the whole heavenly doctrine, revealed in the Law and the Gospel, of the first and second table of the Decalogue, and also of the divine promises.

Therefore this appendix or clause: This which I teach is the Law and the Prophets, ought to be understood concerning the whole preceding sermon: as if the Lord were saying: I have proposed to you an entire declaration or narration of both tables of Moses; learn this my declaration or interpretation, because it contains, so to speak, the kernel and the nerve, that is, the foundation and the sum of the whole doctrine concerning the law, comprehended in Moses and the Prophets.

And know that these words are opposed to Pharisaical persuasions and corruptions, and also to the superstitious trifles of new human traditions: as if he were saying: Behold, I call you back to the Law and the Prophets, from which the Pharisees called you away and led you astray.

Furthermore, that which is especially worthy of observation and memory is that the Lord himself alleges the testimony of Moses and the Prophets, wishing his Church to be bound to the writings divinely handed down, lest we invent, choose, and institute for ourselves acts of worship, departing by our own audacity from the word of God, just as the Heathens, Pharisees, Roman Pontiffs, Monks, and Anabaptists have done.

And in all ages in the human race there remain the seeds of this diabolical superstition, by which new and peculiar acts of worship, without the command of God and outside the word divinely handed down, are perpetually invented by the rashness of some: who indeed, as authors and defenders of idolatrous worship, judge this their superstitious curiosity to be a huge ornament of some exceptional and illustrious wisdom and holiness, when in reality it is a horrible blindness, a huge crime, and an audacity to be detested.

Wherefore, that saying of Christ, Matt. 15, you should diligently commit to memory and fix in your mind: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men.

But both things must be known and held: first, that human traditions, or ceremonies, and works, which are instituted in the Church by human authority, cannot be the worship of God.

Second, that your life ought to be ruled by the certain word of God, and instituted according to the prescription of the Decalogue in this order, that at the beginning faith may shine in the heart, apprehending Christ and receiving consolation, the remission of sins, and righteousness on account of the Son of God, the mediator.

Then that other good works may follow and be ruled according to all the commandments of God pertaining to us, just as the Prophet prays in Psalm 119: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths.

For you must by no means imagine that it is permitted for you to wander without the bonds of laws and discipline, as wild beasts wander in the woods, or as fierce horses with the rider thrown off.

This Cyclopean license is nothing less than Christian liberty, but let your heart and your work be governed and directed by the certain norm of the commandments of God: your marriage, your craft, your method of providing for your livelihood, must not cross the boundaries of the divine precepts, nor, by breaking out beyond the limits of the divine law, disturb the order prescribed by God and, as it were, tear it down by cutting the steps of the ladder.

All these things are comprehended and included in these words: This which I teach is the Law and the Prophets, as if he were saying: The Pharisees led you away from the Law and the Prophets, and thus from God himself, and they, having utterly taken away true consolation and the remission of sins, cast you into doubts, plunged you into darkness and horrible blindness, and afterwards superstitiously preached and boasted of the hypocrisy of empty works or exercises, and served avarice and their belly by accumulating sacrifices, etc.

Just as in our age the Papists bring Masses to market for gain.

On the contrary, says the Lord, my doctrine is divine truth, expressed in the Law and the sermons of the Prophets, by which God wills his people to be ruled, sanctified, and saved.

That this is the proper and genuine meaning of these words of the Lord, there is no doubt.

Furthermore, you have been reminded what is the sum of the doctrine contained in the Law and the Prophetic writings.

And let there always be before your eyes a common admonition, that the whole doctrine, immediately in the beginning, after our first parents, Adam and Eve, were received into grace, was distributed among the people of God, or the Church, into two main or principal heads, of which the first is the Law, or the doctrine of precepts, that is, the Decalogue, wherever it is proposed, explained, and repeated, which indeed is eternal and immovable wisdom, and the rule of justice in God, revealed to men at creation, commanding what kind of men we ought to be, and what to do, and what to omit, and promising good things to those who perform complete obedience, but condemning, that is, pronouncing that all who do not perform perfect obedience are to be punished with eternal torments, and destroying those not conformed to the Law in heart and work, unless there be remission and reconciliation through Christ the mediator.

And what the uses of the Law are, and for what causes it is necessary to teach the Decalogue in the Church, was said a little before.

Therefore, the other and principal head of Christian doctrine is the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is the preaching of repentance or conversion to God, and the gratuitous promise, brought forth from the secret counsel of the divinity through the Son, by which God exhibits the remission of sins, the imputation of justice, or reconciliation, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the restoration of justice and eternal life through Christ the mediator, and through him freely, that is, not on account of any merits of ours, to all who receive the promise by faith.

This is that sum and proper consolation of the Gospel, which the eternal God, in his immense goodness, has most clemently revealed and made known to us through the Son and on his account.

Moreover, it is absolutely necessary for every Christian to have both kinds of doctrine most familiarly known, and to hold the distinction of each rightly understood.

And both the sermon of the Law and the promise of grace are expressly delivered and repeated in the individual Prophets: as immediately in the beginning of the revelations in Gen. 3. When the first parents Adam and Eve are received into grace after the fall, the Son of God himself, the Logos, then openly addressing them as they tremble, begins the ministry of the preaching of repentance, by which, sounding the most sorrowful accusation, he argues sins, and afterwards consoles those who are terrified by the published or promulgated promise of the Gospel, that is, by absolution, contained in this saying: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the Serpent.

This was the first promulgation or revelation of the promise of the Gospel, and the beginning of the Church received in Paradise.

Then follow many sermons of the Law, such as that in the 4th chapter of Genesis concerning homicide, before Cain kills his brother Abel.

Likewise, afterwards, concerning the punishments of lusts in Genesis 19: When Sodom was burned on account of its nefarious impurity.

There follow by degrees more illustrious revelations concerning the coming redeemer and liberator, as when God renews the promise in Gen. 22 to Abraham: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed. So then, in all the Prophets, there exist similar sermons concerning the Law and the Gospel.

And any sane person will easily perceive that the doctrine of our Lord Jesus Christ is one, the same, and a voice consenting with the sermons of the Prophets: nay, all the Prophets were divinely sent, called, chosen, sent, excited, and illuminated through this Son, just as John affirms, saying: Of his fullness have we all received, that is, from Christ's most perfect wisdom and justice we have all received truth, or true light and spiritual knowledge, new justice and eternal life.

Furthermore, just as the Prophets exercised their faith in the recognition and invocation of the Messiah, to whom, fleeing and crying out, they sought and obtained light, or illumination, and divine justice, so we also ought to seek and expect from this Son, the Savior, true understanding or true knowledge of God, justice, and life.

What of the fact that not even can a new light be kindled, true understanding be confirmed, and salutary conversion be begun, so long as hearts retain this coldness and this stupor, such that they only idly hear these admonitions, nor does there follow at last a motion of the soul, which, crying out with true groans to the Son of God, may seek the illustrious and vivifying knowledge of God, the true understanding of the word, and grace or reconciliation, which are the beginning of salvation and eternal life.

That not even a new light can be kindled, true understanding confirmed, and salutary conversion begun, as long as hearts retain this coldness and this stupor, so that they only idly hear these admonitions, nor does there approach a serious movement of the soul, which, crying out with true groans to the Son of God, seeks the illustrious and vivifying knowledge of God, the true understanding of the word, and the grace or reconciliation, which are the beginning of salvation and eternal life. Moreover, although the Church is perpetually exposed to continuous dangers, and as if surrounded on all sides, subsequently it is attacked by the Devil, who tries to extinguish and destroy the pious congregations, on one side by slaughters, on the other by the madness of sects, and by the poisons of impious doctrine: yet in these times, so turbulent and most difficult, much sadder confusions, harsher struggles, and more horrible dangers seem to impend.

For are not the slaughters of bodies happening before the eyes of all?

Turkish robbers certainly rage cruelly in Hungary: this, alas, cannot be denied.

Nor let us dream that the slaughters and devastations in neighboring Pannonia have nothing to do with us.

For shortly, which God forbid, with the Turkish madness raging further, these regions could be devastated more quickly and more savagely than anyone expects, [and] these little churches, in which the little sheep of Christ are fed, in which you and the tender flock of your children dwell, could be devastated.

But there stands by us a helper and protector, the Son of God, crying out: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands.

Indeed, I beseech you, that you may lift up and fortify your hearts with this very consolation, and that you may most often repeat it in your memory, and place this saying before your eyes: Indeed, as often as you go to sleep, as often as you rise from bed, as often as you put your dearest little infants to bed in the evening, or take them out of the same in the morning when they have awakened, think of and recite these or similar words: Ah Lord Jesus Christ, this tender infant or little child is also a little sheep of your poor flock, I and my little family are in your hands, we stand subject to your hand, and we have no certain visible and human protections, no firm defense, but do you mercifully protect, guard, and rule us, drive away from us the Devils, the Turks, the Pope, the Anabaptists, and your other enemies who rage with lies and murders.

Assert the glory of your divine name, and do not permit that enemies, blasphemous and thirsting for blood, should utterly overturn and completely destroy these wretched little churches.

Repeat such prayers often: because certainly the fear of the evils pressing and encroaching at this time is so great that in this public sadness, if ever at any other time, it is now most necessary that we, with true movements of our souls and groans, sigh to our propitiator, our Lord Jesus Christ, take refuge, cry out, and pour forth most ardent prayers.

Besides that danger, impending from the most cruel Turkish nation, these territories are so greatly suffering from civil wars, difficulties of provisions, and the weight of other miseries, [and] are so urged and pressed, that the dissipation of the Churches and barbaric devastation is much to be feared.

Added to this are the manifold contagions of errors, and the corruptions of heavenly doctrine, which are as most insidious as they are most pernicious: which are being scattered everywhere in these customs and times most audaciously.

The patrons of the tyrants of the Pontifical or Roman dignity have already learned to paint their manifest errors with deceptive colors, which they confirm, and [enforce] by open force, or cruelty, and by tricks most craftily stitched together.

Fanatic Anabaptists arise again as if with renewed strength, nor do they fear to invent and circulate such foul and notable errors, that that blasphemous Spirit, by which that more than delirious sect is agitated and driven, seems to mock and insult the human race so insolently.

You ought to propose all these great dangers to your minds, and so much the more ardently and seriously implore the help of Christ, whose is this sweetest voice, John 10: My sheep hear my voice, and no one shall snatch them from my hands.

5. You see this very voice of the Lord to correspond entirely with the perpetual sentiment of the Gospel: it defines the members of the Church as little sheep hearing the divine voice, that is, embracing the heavenly doctrine, of which we speak in the present, comprehended in the Prophetic writings: therefore he adds afterwards: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands; and because he uses the word 'snatching,' he signifies that there is a huge struggle and a most bitter fight.

The Devil drives the Turks, the Pope, the Anabaptists, and various kinds of sects to utterly exterminate us all, and [to destroy] the narrowness of the time, [with] so much material comprehended in this sermon, [it is difficult] to be explained and declared as much and as far as there is need.

Nevertheless, fill [your minds] yourselves, and call back into memory those things in which you are daily diligently and clearly instructed, namely, what is the sum, what are the chief heads, what are the principal places of the doctrine of the Prophets and of the whole Church from the beginning to the end.

To this meditation add the exercises of true invocation and spiritual goods.

Thus it will come to pass that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, may himself instruct and illuminate you, so that you may persist in a sincere intellect, or in a right sentiment, may be strengthened, and may be confirmed, and thus may remain the little sheep of Christ, vessels of mercy, and heirs of eternal salvation, Amen. ...vessels of Christ, vessels of mercy, and heirs of eternal salvation. Amen. Enter through the narrow gate, for wide is the gate that leads to perdition, and many are those who enter through it, etc. Concerning the scandal that arises in the minds of many people, because the greatest multitude is impious, and because in the world and in the Church there are great varieties of opinions.

These two greatest scandals in the human race bring immense ruin, and confirm impiety or unbelief and Epicurean contempt for God in most people.

The first, namely, that such a multitude, so many thousands of myriads of profane people openly live and persevere in manifest and Cyclopean contempt for God, not a few of whom, meanwhile, abound in pleasures of every kind, flourish with successes, power, riches, and honors on earth.

The second, no less pernicious, is that so many and such great dissimilarities, varieties, and distractions of opinions and judgments exist and are observed in this very assembly that usurps the title of the people of God or the Church. You know that throughout the whole world, and in the greater part of the human race, many people embrace the more than fanatical delusions of the Mahometans.

In all of Africa, the Churches have been utterly destroyed; in Asia, there are very few remnants; the rest of the multitude, far more numerous, and more terrible in wealth, empires, armies, and weapons, are the Turks and Tartars, who openly mock and insult the Son of God, our Lord Iesus Christus.

Afterwards, in this very assembly, which is called Christian, do not many more live in manifest and Cyclopean contempt for God? Do not many attack and persecute the truth?

Is there not everywhere a great deal of intemperance, superstition, sophistry, ambition, Pharisaic hatreds, most venomous slanders, and other notable vices? When anxious minds contemplate this promiscuous flood of the greatest multitude in the human race, what else can they think? Than that it is not consistent that so many thousands of people, as have been, are, and will be impious from the beginning of the world until the resurrection of the dead, and who, neglecting the word of God, have loosened, loosen, and will loosen the reins to whatever desires, should after this life be in eternal torments.

And so these thoughts stir up such great commotions in the minds of many that, having strayed from true doctrine to the examples of the multitude, they reason thus: Behold, what is the point of being so greatly tormented about the life that will follow after the death of bodies? Should I refuse the common fate of so many thousands of thousands of people?

And demand some special and peculiar one for myself? Indeed, whatever is to become of so many thousands of myriads, with what face would I dare to deprecate that the same should happen to me? For if God cared for human affairs, He would by no means allow such a multitude of people to fall so horribly and to be entangled in such sad errors?

What then, that the corrupt contagions of opinions, morals, and examples spread most quickly? Especially among those whose intimacy and constant conversation are close. Just as it is clear that everyone is imbued and shaped by opinions and morals, whether good or bad, such as are seen and prominent in those whose company they enjoy: so we more easily imitate vices and embrace false opinions, both because of the depravity of nature, and because tender and weak minds are more quickly moved and attracted by the consensus and custom of the impious multitude.

Concerning such various offenses, scandals, and most pernicious contagions, Salomon says in Proverb. 5.: "I was almost in all evil in the midst of the congregation or multitude, where I saw and learned various kinds of corruptions, in rites and morals, or harmful examples, and false opinions." You know that innumerable young people, endowed with good talents and suitable for virtue, are corrupted and seduced by bad company, which by example invites otherwise good people to the fellowship or imitation of crimes.

Against so many and such manifold scandals and contagions, we are frequently warned and admonished by severe divine commands and threats: as in Exodi 23.

God expressly says: "You shall not follow the crowd or multitude to do evil, nor shall you answer in judgment, inclining to the inclining multitude." Let the rule of life be the word of God, by which, as a norm divinely handed down, opinions and morals are to be governed, not examples and rites departing from the Prophetic and Apostolic scripture. For you remember that this precept is repeatedly inculcated and repeated in the sacred scriptures, as in Matth. 17.: "This is my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him," Galat. 1.: "If anyone preaches another Gospel..."

let him be anathema. Psalm.

119.: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my paths. Item Psalm 1: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful, but his delight is in the Law of the Lord. Psalm 119: Cursed are they that decline from thy commandments.

Finally, very many [passages] exist everywhere divinely spoken to this effect.

Thus God often recalls us from judgments, customs, opinions, and examples that variously hallucinate—most notably, of course, the great multitude in the world—back to Himself, and to His word, expressly handed down in the Prophetic and Apostolic monuments.

Men ought to know and frequently meditate upon this necessary doctrine, and direct their thoughts and customs to the norm or prescription of the divine word, and not look around having abandoned the rule, and follow either examples or the multitude, and embrace now this, now that opinion.

Just as many do today, who wish to appear as men not so much of all hours as of all sects; among the Papists they feign the Papistic religion, among the Evangelicals the Evangelical, among the Jews they applaud Jewish superstitions, among the Turks the Turkish or Mahometan, when yet they believe or approve of none of these, but proudly deride God and all religions.

Concerning all of whom the Lord says here: Wide is the gate and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat.

This wide-open gate is to take for oneself the license to wander in opinions, and in works not to be surrounded, nor to be bound by certain limits divinely established; that is, to petulantly feel and invent whatever one pleases, likewise with the reins of discipline and the bonds of customs loosened, to indulge oneself in whatever one likes: just as the Heathens fashioned idols or deities according to their lust: and just as at this time many distorted and rabid minds invent opinions for blind and rapid affections.

Many thousands of men wander and rush rashly in works and customs, restrained by no reins, like fierce horses with the rider thrown off; they practice adulteries, indulge in gluttony, in lusts, they apply themselves to illicit things, to frauds and impostures, wherever the opportunity and occasions are at hand.

This vagabond license of customs and opinions is that open or wide gate, to which it is manifest that the greatest crowd or multitude of men, as it were, flow together and run in troops: but the end and outcome is very miserable, and the catastrophe more than tragic.

Therefore the Lord also says in this text: The wide gate leadeth to destruction or ruin.

The same is affirmed by Psalm 119: Cursed are all they that decline from thy commandments.

On the other hand, the eternal and narrow gate is the word of God itself, which binds both our faith and our works to one certain norm of doctrine, and to the one true God, who by certain and illustrious testimonies has revealed both His essence and His will.

Now the thing itself speaks and experience testifies that the human heart scarcely suffers itself to be bound as if reduced to straits, and to be enclosed by surrounding limits, and to be constrained by bonds.

For it indulges in curiosity entirely beyond measure and without end, so that, just as birds now here now there fly about everywhere and freely in the air, so the human heart, fluctuating, longs to wander about with both opinions and appetites, longs to be carried, snatched, and to rush now here now there like the wind, longs to loosen the reins of the contumacy of wandering desires.
