But such men cannot live unless the sustenance necessary for them is provided. Therefore, at all times, God has willed that they be fed by the Church, and by singular counsel has established certain revenues for them. And it is most true that the Church ought to provide sustenance and the necessary aids of life to pious teachers, just as the Lord says: The laborer is worthy of his hire. Thus it is said in this place that Moses commanded this as a testimony to them, that is, that it should be their right, or what is owed to them. With this simple exposition I am content. But yet another is also true, which some use in this place, that the Law is a testimony of both things, of our sins and of Christ the liberator, and that the Law itself testifies that sins are not taken away by the Law, but that it is only a testimony against us, judging and condemning us. And this explanation is comprised in the doctrine concerning the distinction between the Law and the Gospel or the grace of Christ, which is recited more copiously elsewhere. I will add, however, a few things.

It is most well known that there are two principal heads of heavenly doctrine: the Law and the Gospel concerning the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. The doctrine of the Law is comprised under the most common appellation of the Decalogue, and it is the eternal and immovable norm of wisdom in God, teaching what God is and what He is like—namely, wise, just, chaste, and truthful—and the Law demands that rational creatures, Angels and men, be conformable to this norm of divine wisdom and justice, and it denounces horrible wrath, and does not dissemble to all who are not conformable.

But you know that there is a twofold use of the Law. First, regarding discipline and the governing of the locomotive faculty. For it is the eternal and immutable will of God that there be some honest external governance of life. And the reason is manifest, because no society would be durable if it were permitted to individuals to seize the goods, wives, or children of others at their own whim. And what kind of life would it be if murders were promiscuously permitted? And although many are driven by Devils to such frenzies, and many even invite themselves to murders, lusts, and the license of all crimes, yet it is manifest that God Himself is the avenger, and that atrocious punishments immutably follow atrocious crimes even in this life, just as Christ affirms: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword. Thus God Himself compels some to provide for an honest governance of life.

But here it is necessary to know that this governance of discipline is far from the perfect fulfillment of the Law, nor is it a merit for the remission of sins, and that many sad doubts about God, many depraved inclinations, and other infinite filth remain in the heart: as all must necessarily confess.

But the other use of the Law is to show the wrath of God against sin in us, and to terrify hearts with the commination of God's wrath; just as Paul says: The Law works wrath, that is, hearts terrified by the judgment of the Law are plunged into death and are oppressed by the pains of the infernal regions, just as Hezekiah affirms concerning this judgment: Like a lion he has crushed all my bones.

These pains are known to many men, and some feel them greater, others lesser. And how great a thing the judgment of the Law is, is often seen in those who are to be subjected to capital punishment. And such men feel that sin, the wrath of God, and the pains of the infernal regions are not taken away by the Law, but that the Law is a judgment and a testimony accusing and condemning us. First in this way, when it testifies that God is just to judge and condemn sin: then, because the conscience, convicted by this testimony of the Law, is forced to confess that we are guilty, and that we have deserved the wrath of God and horrible punishments, and that God acts justly in that He sets forth examples of His justice in us, in that He abolishes and destroys a nature defiled by such great filth.

Those who hear these tables of the Law recited against themselves in true sorrow know that these sorrows are not empty or ridiculous terrors, and with David they consider this most sad complaint. they learn: The sorrows of death surrounded me, and the perils of hell found me.

Many, oppressed by these sorrows, rush into eternal destruction. Like Saul, Judas, Ahithophel, and other innumerable ones, feeling the testimony and judgment of the Law, they are utterly oppressed by the sorrows of the lower world, and they remain in these for all eternity.

But against this terrible judgment of the Law, one must seek the other voice of the Gospel concerning the Son of God, who appeased the wrath of the eternal Father and became a victim for us, so that He might certainly grant the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life freely, not because of any merits or works of ours.

It is necessary to acknowledge this Son of the eternal Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, as our savior and liberator, just as He revealed Himself in the promises He gave to the fathers and in the visible custom of assuming human nature.

And it must be held most firmly that this Jesus Christ, God and man, is to be extolled and exalted far above Moses. For this one Christ Jesus, our Lord and savior, brings forth true and certain consolation in this terrible judgment of the law, saying in John 3: God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life.

This consolation is the proper voice of the Gospel, preaching in the name and efficacy of our Lord Jesus Christ repentance and the remission of sins.

And you hear most often that this Lord Jesus Christ, and this ineffable grace of His, is to be received and embraced by faith, as it is said: He who believes in Him has eternal life. And how this very statement is to be understood is explained more fully elsewhere.

And first of all, this is most certain and true without any doubt: that a man should not remain secure in sins against his conscience, in Ethnic and Epicurean frenzies, or in a purpose of wickedness, but should tremble at the recognition of the wrath of God, just as the Lord says: The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin.

And in the oath which God Himself proposes in Ezekiel, it is a copulative statement, embracing both conversion and consolation: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Let us consider this oath concerning our conversion, and let us know that God wills that we be converted to Him.

And in the same way, it is said in the last chapter of Isaiah: To whom shall I look? Except to the poor and contrite in spirit and him who trembles at my words.

For it is absolutely necessary to hear even this terrible sentence of the law against us, so that we may know that we are guilty and have deserved the punishments.

In the sight of these punishments and this wrath, it is necessary that we be terrified. But after the heart has begun to be oppressed by these sorrows, consolation must also be added, which our Lord Jesus Christ brought forth from the bosom of the eternal Father with immense goodness.

For God does not wish us to be terrified by the voice of the law so that we might remain in all eternity in the contumelious roarings of the lower world against God, but so that we might be converted to Him and obtain the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life: which happens in this way: Let your heart certainly believe and determine that God, because of His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, certainly gives you the remission of sins, and that by this very faith He dwells in your heart and is efficacious, and powerfully snatches you from the sorrows of the lower world, and restores eternal life to you.

And although in this most sad and most squalid life there remains our huge infirmity and defilement: nevertheless, you should certainly determine that you are received by God through this very faith, and that the righteousness of the Son of God is imputed to you, and that you are clothed and covered by this very righteousness of the Son. For thus says Paul in 2 Corinthians 5: Him who did not know sin, God made sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.

Paul comprehends both: death and passion, and the immense grace of the Son. First, he says: God made the Son sin for us; this is, although He was without sin, yet He willed that this Son should bear the wrath against sin for us.

And thus this Son was an innocent and most pure victim for sin, and now in the arcane and unsearchable counsel of the eternal Father, He intercedes for us before all creatures, and by His intercession the eternal Father is reconciled with us, imputing to us the righteousness of the Son and remitting all sins: and the Father and the Son pour the Holy Spirit into our hearts, so that both eternal righteousness and life may be begun in us through this very Lord of ours, Jesus Christ.

And although a very sad infirmity remains in us, and innumerable depraved inclinations, yet the righteousness of the Son is imputed to us, and by this covering our filth is hidden.

Let us consider this consolation in every invocation, and let us know that it is necessary for both to grow in us in the perpetual exercises of repentance. acknowledging the terrors and fearing the wrath of God, and the consolation, by which the mind, seeking and expecting the remission of sins, raises itself by faith, and determines with certainty that we are thus joined to the Son of God as members, and thus we are heirs of life and eternal salvation.

You have heard, therefore, without ambiguity and without wrapping of words, what our faith and opinion is concerning the remission of sins and righteousness through and on account of the Son of God, and you have clearly heard mentioned also the efficacy of the whole divinity in the hearts of believers, and that this perpetual consolation is inseparably joined to it, which it is necessary to know: Even if the divinity is efficacious in us, and some obedience is begun, yet it must be believed and determined that we are pleasing to God, and are accepted for eternal life, on account of our Lord Jesus Christ, not on account of the following newness or efficacy.

A new writer in Prussia accuses us, that nothing is said by us about the efficacy of the divinity in the hearts of believers.

But you, on the contrary, shall be witnesses that we have also faithfully instructed you in this matter, as the saying of John sounds: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him.

And you know how often this voice of the Son of God is repeated: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself is present with you, is efficacious in you, giving righteousness and new life, and powerfully preserving and protecting you against the snares and furies of the devils.

And although all these things are most true, yet even in all the saints in this life (Christ alone excepted) there remains a huge and sad infirmity and the filth of sins.

And it is necessary for all to confess with David: No one living shall be justified in your sight.

And individuals feel their minds vehemently tormented, both by the terrors of past sins, and by the sight of present filth, which clings to us, and which we carry around constantly.

Here it is necessary to hold onto this consolation, about which the Psalms preach: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered, Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.

Understand, however, how they are covered, namely by the righteousness of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in the secret council of the divinity constantly intercedes for you, as it is written to the Hebrews 7: This High Priest always lives to intercede for us, and this High Priest is our Lord Jesus Christ, God and man, and on account of this High Priest's intercession, the eternal Father is propitious to us.

And do not allow this necessary consolation to be snatched from you by that new speculation, which feigns that a man is righteous, because the essential righteousness of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit dwells in him.

Learn, however, to acknowledge this eternal and supreme High Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, as mediator and propitiator perpetually, and call upon him with faith and true confidence, and approach the throne of mercy in all sorrows through this very High Priest from time to time: just as Daniel prays, for we do not prostrate our prayers before your face in our own justifications, but in your many mercies on account of the Lord: Hear, O Lord, be appeased, O Lord, attend and act.

Accustom yourselves to these very words of Daniel, and learn to imitate them in your invocation, and dwell on the thought of them, saying: Almighty, eternal, living and true God, eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of heaven and earth, of Angels and men, and of all creatures, together with your co-eternal Son our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, I call upon you with true groans, and with my whole heart I confess that I have horribly offended you with many sins and errors, and I truly grieve that you have been offended, and I fear your wrath, and I prostrate my prayers before your face, not in my own righteousness, but in your great mercy on account of your Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and I pray to you, have mercy on me and justify me, and through your Son save and protect me, teach, rule and help me with your Holy Spirit, who proceeds from you and your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

In such a form of prayer, which the Prophets use, both the chief doctrine is recited and many useful admonitions can be sought from it.

And there is in the invocation of the Prophets a singular emphasis of words, which, fixed in the mind, teach and admonish many things.

Wherefore I warn you again, that you should strive to imitate and express the invocation of the prophets.

Let these things suffice now concerning the words of Christ: Offer the gifts which Moses commands them for a testimony to them.

May our Lord Jesus Christ be with us and rule us, Amen.

A centurion approached him, praying to him, and saying etc.

In the recitation of all the miracles, first of all, the most common doctrine concerning miracles must be considered. Afterwards, individual miracles have peculiar, useful admonitions which, as much as is granted by God, are to be considered at the same time. And you often hear that the common doctrine of miracles is distributed into these three parts.

First are the testimonies, that this doctrine, which Christ professes and proclaims, is truly a divine voice, and that this Christ is a truthful teacher, sent by God, and that these very testimonies show this, and in this way reveal themselves, so that we may be certain that the voice of the Gospel is true, and is not fabricated or fabulous, such as are the fables and religions of the Heathens. Let us know, therefore, that our faith is to be confirmed by such testimonies.

Secondly, there are examples and testimonies of divine promises, which teach that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, certainly wishes to hear and help us, just as his promises sound, and these very examples testify to this. And in these, he addresses us in the same way as he invites the spectators of such miracles: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

Thirdly, there are examples of application, and they teach how the help of Christ is to be received, namely, by faith looking upon this Son. And in the variety of men whom Christ helps, he wants us to consider a rule often repeated elsewhere, that God is not a respecter of persons, but is equal toward all who call upon him, as the saying expressly affirms: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.

You see Christ helping without discrimination Gentiles and Jews, Samaritans, publicans, and women polluted by the shame of their lives: You see all who do penance and flee by faith to this Lord obtain help. Know, therefore, that for all of us, in all counsels and dangers, spiritual and corporal, we must flee to this Lord in the same way, this Lord must be called upon by faith, and it must be certainly established that these are the highest and true forms of worship, thus to flee by faith to God and the Lord Jesus Christ, and to certainly seek and expect help from him.

Therefore, let this common doctrine be most known to all in every invocation, in all counsels and dangers of life: and by the thought of it, let invocation and faith be stirred up: and let us all know that we are called in the same way to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, just as this centurion is called, or the Syrophoenician woman, or the Samaritan, or the leper, or the adulterous Samaritan woman. Only approach this Lord eagerly through faith, and thus, taught by your own experience, you will understand that this faith is never in vain. And let this brief admonition suffice for the beginning.

Now, certain peculiar and very significant documents of the present history are to be considered.

The centurion approaching the Lord was a Heathen man, and yet Christ testifies of him that he is holy and truly an heir of eternal life, and a member of the true Church. Wherefore, it must first be considered here how God has gathered an eternal Church in all times, and who are the true worshippers, discerning the true Church from the false.

Concerning this matter, the Lord himself preaches in this place: Many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. By this saying of Christ, you hear most expressly that the true Church is discerned from hypocrites.

Wherefore, we shall speak briefly first about the true Church.

God revealed himself with immense goodness, and immediately after the most sad fall of Adam and Eve, having issued the promise concerning the Messiah and Savior of the human race, he showed himself, saying: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. In this sermon, God promises that he will send his Son to assume human nature, so that through this Son of his, sin and death might be abolished, and justice and eternal life might be restored to all who would acknowledge this Son by faith, and by trust in this Son would seek and expect eternal justice. With this voice of promise, the Church began to be restored anew in Adam and Eve: and they, when they received this consolation by faith, felt that they were again snatched from death and the pains of the underworld by the efficacy of this voice.

And through them, the ministry of this promise concerning the Son, and of the true worship of God, began, and all their descendants, who embraced this voice of the promise concerning the Son by faith, at the same time also received the remission of sins and justice and eternal life, and were members of the true Church of God, such as many after Adam and Eve are recounted, Abel, Seth, Enoch, Noah, Sem, Abraham etc.

Many, having cast aside this promise and faith, separated themselves from the Church, as Cain and others after him, countless in number, and the Gentile multitude began to devise foul idolatrous frenzies, and openly practiced foul filthiness in their life.

But after God, in His immense goodness, established the polity of Israel, He simultaneously commanded this most severely, that they should be taught about the future liberator of the human race.

And although He instituted many sacrifices and rites, yet He declared by His own voice that all those were only external signs of the future liberation through the Son.

Nor must it be imagined that sin or death was abolished by those rites.

And in that whole kingdom of Israel, only those were heirs of eternal life, and members of the true Church, who embraced the promise concerning the future liberator by faith.

And this very liberator dwelt in the hearts of the believers with the voice of this promise, and kindled the knowledge of God and true invocation.

Such were, in the time of Zacharias, Zacharias himself, Simeon, Joseph, Mary, Elizabeth, Anna, and many other hearers of Zacharias and Simeon, who embraced their doctrine and voice.

Besides this true Church, there were many thousands of Pharisees, Sadducees, and others, who pretended that they obtained the remission of sins by their own sacrifices, and rejected the faith of the promised liberator, and added other dreams as well, that the Messiah would have only a corporal kingdom, in which they themselves, flourishing in wealth and power, would reign.

In these shadows, it was impossible for such people to invoke God, who did not yet have the remission of sins.

There was, therefore, a great multitude of the kingdom and people of Israel that was not holy, but only hypocritical, and yet with this very multitude, the impious seed, the holy seed was divinely preserved, of which Isaiah says: Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have become as Sodom.

But it very often happened that even some from the Gentiles learned and embraced the doctrine of the promises from the holy ones of the people of Israel, and acknowledged the true God of that people and the liberator of the human race, and worshipped Him with true faith and invocation and true cults, such as was Naaman, Cyrus, and many others.

Such were members of the Church and heirs of eternal life, even if they did not observe the rites and ceremonies of the people of Israel.

And in such people shone that great and arcane wisdom, that the remission of sins happens only on account of this liberator promised to the people of Israel, and that one must flee by faith to this redeemer, and this one God, revealed to the people of Israel, is to be acknowledged and invoked, and the will of this true God is to be learned and sought from the voice of the Prophets, and not elsewhere etc.

Such was also this centurion, who rightly understood and learned the promise, either from Jairus the Archisynagogue of his town, or from Joseph, or from their hearers, holy men and rightly instructed.

And the centurion understands that the Messiah is the Son of God, whom he knows will come for this purpose, that He may destroy sin and death, and restore righteousness and eternal life.

Nor is there any doubt that this very centurion had heard many of Christ's sermons, and had rightly worshipped and invoked God.

You will learn, therefore, in this place to distinguish the citizens of the true Church from idolatrous assemblies, such as the crowds of the Roman Pontiff, the Monks, and similar swine, who think that idolatrous masses or Monastic rites are merits for the remission of sins and eternal life etc.

Here, on the contrary, you shall constantly and firmly maintain that the heirs of eternal life and citizens of the true Church are only those who obey the saying and rule of Christ: Repent and believe the Gospel.

Wherever, therefore, minds truly tremble at the knowledge and fear of the wrath of God, and, looking with faith to the Mediator Christ, expect consolation from Him, and acquiesce in this consolation: in such people, immutably, true invocation and the righteousness of a good conscience also shine.

These are also certainly reputed as sons of God, and are members of the true Church, not dead or feigned, but true.

And such, if they persevere in this conversion to God, and retain the faith, are truly also heirs of life and eternal salvation.

You will diligently observe this distinction between the true and false Church, and at the same time you will learn to consider which are true and necessary cults, and which are feigned and prohibited and condemned.

For it is necessary for everyone to know which is the true Church, and it behooves everyone to join himself to its society, and with it to acknowledge and invoke God.

Just as in the flood no one was saved outside the ark of Noah, so let us know that this is the most true rule: outside the Church there is no salvation.

And it is no small benefit for you to understand which is the true Church, and to be a citizen of this host, so that in this society and assembly of the sons of God you may acknowledge, invoke, and celebrate the true God.

And concerning this benefit, David says in Psalm 27: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that is, that I may be a member and citizen of the true Church, and never be excluded from the number of the children of God. And you, give thanks to God with all your heart, even if the hardships of this life are sad, because you nevertheless live in such a congregation, which is truly the Church of God, which rightly calls upon and worships God. And pray to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, that He may perpetually gather, preserve, and rule the eternal Church among us, just as He Himself prays to the eternal Father: Father, keep them in thy name, sanctify them in thy truth, thy word is truth, Holy Father keep them in thy name, whom thou hast given to me, that they may be one, even as we are, that all may be one, as thou Father art in me, and I in thee, and that they may be one in us. Let us also pray the same with our Lord Jesus Christ, and let us ask with true groans and vows, that He Himself may preserve and rule the eternal Church in us.

Question.

But you will say: How do I know where or which is the true Church? I see there are infinite sects, and each one gloriously proclaims itself to be the Church and the people of God?

Response. There have been, alas, sad and horrible confusions in all times; as in the time when Zacharias, Simeon, Elizabeth, and Mary lived, there were at the same time huge crowds of Pharisees and Sadducees. After the Apostles, the Ebionites, Marcionites, Arians, Manichaeans, and others arose. In our time, there are huge crowds of Papists, Anabaptists, and Interimists. Let the pious mind therefore seek to whom it should approach. I answer that the distinction shown above must be sought and retained. For it is most certain that wherever the voice of the Gospel sounds uncorrupted, and the use of the Sacraments is legitimate and retained as instituted by Christ, and idols or other grim frenzies are not stubbornly defended, such a congregation is truly the Church of God. Therefore, you should approach this congregation and join yourself to it, according to the saying of the Son of God: My sheep hear my voice.

You will object here again: All sects cry out that they retain the voice of the Gospel uncorrupted: who then is the judge, as to which one teaches correctly? I answer: The Son of God Himself, in the voice of the Gospel and the writings of the Apostles and in the Creeds, is the judge. And if you faithfully seek the truth, the divine voice is by no means obscure or ambiguous, and you can understand whether our Churches or the Papist or the Anabaptist ones agree with the uncorrupted divine voice. Only retain in this investigation the immutable command of the eternal Father sounding from heaven: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, hear him. The voice is, as you see, of the eternal Father, neither obscure nor ambiguous, leading you to the one teacher and judge, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, whom you ought to hear. In the same way, Paul also says clearly: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. Let these rules be the norms which you follow in judging which is the true or false Church of God. When doctrine fights with the express voice of the Gospel, or with one or more articles of faith, or with the Decalogue, you may certainly conclude that such a congregation is not the Church of God. As the wicked scoundrels, the Anabaptists, affirm that adultery is not a sin. Such an assertion is a manifest and diabolical lie against the Decalogue.

Papists say: Our works are merits for the remission of sins, and they name as works idolatrous Masses, Monastic rites, satisfactions, and similar superstitions; afterwards, they affirm that one must perpetually doubt about the remission of sins. All these assertions fight with the most manifest voice of the Gospel, which clearly and without ambiguity affirms concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, that through this Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, we have remission of sins through faith in Him, not by our merits, not by idolatrous Masses, not by Monastic rites, or any other works whatsoever.

And pious minds understand that this very voice of the Gospel is not uncertain or obscure. And it is most manifest that it is commanded to us that we believe in this our Lord Jesus Christ, and that we certainly conclude that God, through and because of this beloved Son, certainly forgives sins and gives eternal life. Thus, in the recitation of the Creed, you assert: I believe in the remission of sins: and I believe this specifically, that remission is given not only to others, but to me also. The same is asserted by John, who says: He who does not believe God, has made Him a liar.

It is therefore manifest and most certainly true: the Papist article, in which doubt is confirmed, to treat the voice of the Gospel with horrible insult, and to destroy it entirely.

The Pontiffs also teach that dead men are to be invoked, Anna, George, and others. This directly fights with the first commandment of the Decalogue:... You shall adore the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve.

The Pontiffs also forbid the marriages of priests.

This fights most expressly with the sixth commandment. You can therefore judge from such a recitation and assert with certainty whether those who teach such things and stubbornly defend them are the true Church or a false one.

You know, therefore, that it is the command of God that you join yourself to the true Church, and that you wish to be a citizen of it, and that you serve God with true worship, in true conversion to God, in faith, in invocation, and in the militia of a good conscience, just as you see this centurion not joining himself to the Church of the Pharisees or Sadducees, but you perceive him to be a citizen of the Church of Christ and of His hearers and friends, who instructed him by the voice of the Prophets, and first led him to Christ.

There is in him an admirable and ardent light of faith, recognizing Christ, and resting with great confidence in Him.

He understands that this Christ is omnipotent, and that He is efficacious with His word, as he confesses: Only say one word, and my boy will be healed. Truly, it is a singular and immense light of faith, shining in this soldier, which instructs him so that he understands that the Messiah is God and man, and is the eternal λόγος (Word) of the eternal Father, through whom all things were created, through whom now also all things are sustained and vivified.

As John says: In Him was life, and the life was the light of men.

With such faith, it is necessary that many other virtues be joined.

And Luke 7: it is said of this soldier, that the elders of the town prayed solicitously to the Lord for him, and were witnesses of his integrity and beneficence in government.

For they say: He is worthy that You grant this to him, because he loves our nation, and he himself built the Synagogue for us. All these things sufficiently testify that this soldier was a disciple of the voice of the Prophets, and had embraced their doctrine.

And thus he is a citizen and member of the true Church, because through faith he is grafted into our Lord Jesus Christ, he understands and believes the promises concerning the Messiah to be true, and celebrates God with true worship: and although he is not circumcised, and does not observe the ceremonies and rites of the people of Israel, yet this wisdom shines in him, that through and because of the Messiah he has the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life, not through or because of the observations of the Mosaic law or any of his own good works.

And he rightly understands the promise given to Abraham, and indeed in this manner, that even the nations outside the polity of the people of Israel are to be heirs of eternal life and salvation through this promised seed of Abraham.

And he retains the τὸ ῥητὸν (the literal text) of the promise: In your seed shall all nations be blessed. The soldier understands these words more correctly than many in the people of Israel, namely, that even the nations outside the polity of Moses are to be blessed, not just that one people of Israel, and he knows that this blessing is not a corporal benefit, as many imagined, but is a liberation from sin, from the wrath of God and the power of the devil, with which benefit he recognizes that righteousness and eternal life are restored to us.

But the modesty of this soldier, by which he humbly submits himself to Christ, shows how reverently and honorably he felt about Christ, when he was indeed a Roman man, and a soldier, a prefect or captain of the city.

That kind of man rarely exercises modesty or beneficence toward inferiors and subjects. But this prefect is a holy man, having a singular light of faith. Wherefore he is also honorably commended by the Lord Himself: Amen I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.

Although the example pertains to all, yet it behooves governors especially to look upon him as an example of many virtues.

For first they will learn how much reverence and what duties they owe to Christ and His ministry. Then, how they ought to institute their government for the glory of God and the salvation of their subjects. The example also teaches this, that it is permitted for a Christian man to hold magistracy, and to exercise political offices, and that this kind of life is good in its own kind, and pleases God.

Concerning which matter, more abundant admonitions are proposed elsewhere. And it is necessary, from time to time, to warn the hearers, lest they allow themselves to be fascinated or deceived by the superstitions of the Anabaptists, who condemn the political order, and deny that it is permitted for Christians to hold or exercise political offices, and who seek and aid seditions, slaughters, and confusions of the divine order.

Consider therefore, most dear hearers, what copious doctrine is proposed in the history of this soldier, however brief it may be, concerning many things, concerning the Church, concerning faith, concerning good works, concerning political offices and magistracies, and concerning other things.

Would that all, and especially princes and governors, should consider the example of this soldier attentively and reverently. There are many other things remaining, which the brevity and narrowness of time does not allow to be explained, and the magnitude of the matters is so great that I would not dare to institute an account.

I cannot, however, omit an appendix, which embraces both a sweet consolation and a sad threat. The consolation is sweet, when the Lord says that the nations are to be received into the society of the Church. The threat is terrible, when He says: The children of the kingdom, who have this glorious name, that they are the Church and the people of God, shall be cast out. Therefore, regarding the first point, as often as it is said that even the nations are received by God to the knowledge of the Son of God, and to the society of life and eternal salvation, let us remember that this great and ineffable consolation is delivered, that by the immense and ineffable mercy of God the human race is received, and obtains the remission of sins freely on account of the Son of God without any merits of our own, etc.

Of Peter's mother-in-law.

Coming into Peter's house, Jesus saw his mother-in-law lying down and suffering from a fever, and He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she arose and served them, etc.

Some miracles are recounted in this eighth chapter, very briefly and very simply, because the bulk of the books would have grown to an immense size if the Apostles had commemorated each miracle at length. Therefore, in this place, it is first said briefly that the Lord cured Peter's mother-in-law, who was sick, and as the text says, πυρέσσουσαν (suffering from a fever). Afterwards it is said: They brought to Him many who had demons, and He cast out the spirits with a word, and cured all who were ill, so that what was said by the Prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, saying: He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses.

Here I warn you again, that you should repeat in your mind the common doctrine of miracles, and consider attentively and reverently what should be especially thought about in the recitation of them.

You know first that they are testimonies of doctrine, for God wishes to show in this way that He is delivering this word, which He Himself adorns and confirms with such great miracles. Therefore, looking upon these admirable examples, let them think that the word sounding through Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles is truly the immovable sentence and will of God Himself, which He wishes to be heard and received. For to raise the dead and restore life to them is a work proper to the divinity alone, inimitable by devils and all creatures.

Secondly, although miracles are bodily goods, yet they are examples and testimonies of all promises, both spiritual and bodily. And these examples show that God wishes to help those who call upon Him in both spiritual and bodily dangers. Thirdly, they are a doctrine of application, which reminds everyone and each individual about seeking and expecting the help of God, namely that one must approach our Lord Jesus Christ with faith and confidence in the promise, just as the Syrophoenician woman approaches with faith, bringing or showing no merits of her own.

In the same way, the will of God is immutable, and the command is most severe and pertains to all, that they should approach the Lord Jesus Christ with faith, and thus call upon God. Such an invocation is never in vain, but is truly effective, and obtains what it has asked for. And the most common sayings pertain to the doctrine of application: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands. And it is, as I said, a most severe command that you should call upon God with faith, and imitate the examples of faith proposed in the most sweet and innumerable miracles. You hear these things inculcated often, and it is necessary that these common and catechetical elements be repeated often, so that they may be in the sight of all, and be thought upon by all in constant invocation and in the reading or recitation of such miracles.

But you will say, these miracles were done with those whom the Lord helped, now miracles have ceased, and I see myself and others stuck in miseries, and not helped by God. What then is the use of this recitation? I answer: Minds must be diligently fortified against such blasphemous thoughts and voices.

For it is most certain that even now immense miracles are done daily, of which the saying in the Acts reminds us: In Him we live, and move, and have our being. For the fact that you live, that infants are preserved, that the Devil is hindered so that he does not overturn everything with his furies, all this happens by the benefit of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, protecting and saving you most miraculously.

This Lord, as Isaiah says, in His bosom and in his arms and bosom carries you, just as a shepherd carries and sustains a tender, newly-born lamb: this Lord calls you in the Psalm, saying: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you.

And all these deliverances are huge and stupendous miracles, even if the blinded eyes of men do not behold or recognize these miraculous deeds. Wherefore, cast far from your mind those blasphemous and insulting lies against God, that God does not show you miracles.

For such thoughts, as I have said, are insulting to God and are impediments to true invocation. On the contrary, believe for certain that God is present and effective among us through daily miracles, and that he most kindly helps those who call upon him in all counsels and dangers, both spiritual and corporal.

Know that you owe this honor to God, that you confess this, believe it, and thus call upon God. And these are the highest and chief acts of worship, which are to be learned and practiced in true invocation. And let this brief commemoration of miracles suffice in this place.

Now we approach the saying of Isaiah, about which we shall likewise give a few warnings.

Isaiah speaks not only of the infirmities or diseases of bodies, but he comprehends both: sin or the inner disease of the soul and all other evils, and all the burdens which have arisen through sin, and which have been its wages. And there are two distinct words in the saying of Isaiah, To carry and To take away, and the distinction is worthy of observation.

For they are distinct offices: to carry our miseries, and afterwards to take them away and remove them. First, Christ carries our infirmities and miseries, that is, he himself in his passion, in his death, and in horrible pains, which he underwent for our sake, in order to satisfy divine justice, felt the ineffable and horrible wrath of the eternal Father, and there was no fault or cause of his own in such great pains, but for our sake and for our salvation he derived all these things into himself, and by this obedience of his and reverence toward the eternal Father, he procured for us the remission of sins and reconciliation with God.

Just as it is said of this obedience of the Son in Psalm 40: In the beginning of the book it is written of me, I do your will, O Lord, willingly, and your law is always in the midst of my heart. And in that very chapter of Isaiah, from which the present words have been taken, it is written: When he shall have made his soul an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed. There are also many other similar testimonies, some of which ought to be in sight, so that we may know that the obedience of Christ in his passion and death is the propitiation for us, and that because of the obedience of this victim, as many as have been sanctified from the beginning of the Church have received the remission of sins and have been pleasing to God, and by faith have apprehended the merits of this victim. Let, therefore, this very merit of the Son of God, and the propitiation made through him, be your one and highest consolation against the sight of all your sins and filth.

And we warn pious minds not to allow themselves to be troubled by the tragic clamors and threats of Osiander, or to be deterred from this consolation, who vociferates that you are not pleasing to God because of the obedience or merit of the Son of God, but because of the essential justice or divinity dwelling in you and moving you to do just things. See to it that these speculations of Osiander do not shake away true consolation from you, but I hold most firmly to the words of John, chapter 1: The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sins: and indeed, inscribe these very words in the depths of your heart, and in every invocation behold and consider what John affirms: The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sins.

Attend, however, to how he speaks; he wants you to apprehend this consolation by faith, that the obedience of Christ is a propitiation for us, and that the eternal Father is certainly propitious to us, forgives sins, and receives us, because the beloved Son, in whom he is well pleased, in whom he rejoices and rests, has been made a victim for us. And think that Isaiah comprehends all these things in the word of carrying, when he says: He himself took our infirmities, that is, for our sake and for our salvation he underwent a most sorrowful death, and derived the wrath of the eternal Father into himself.

The other word has the meaning of taking away: He himself took away our sicknesses, that is, sin and all other evils which have followed sin. For both are the benefit of Christ: to appease the wrath of the eternal Father, and to sustain the punishment for us.

And by that very act he takes away and removes sin from us. First, because by his immense goodness sins are forgiven us and we are received into eternal life: secondly, because most truly in every conversion, that very Lord of ours Jesus Christ begins to abolish the mass of sin clinging to us, and in the resurrection of the dead he is about to render a new and clean mass without sin, with death and all pains deleted.

And that same Lord Jesus Christ will render to us life, wisdom, justice, and eternal joy, just as he says: I give eternal life to them.

And the Baptist, embracing all these things in one voice, says: Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

The Baptist names Christ the Lamb because he was to be a victim, as was the custom among the Jews, that they should slaughter and offer lambs daily morning and evening.

But he names this victim the Lamb of God, so that he may distinguish it from the lamb of Aaron and the Levitical victim.

And he wishes to signify that it is not a victim to be offered by the command or order of men, but that admirable and great victim, ordained and sanctified divinely, given to us and for our salvation by God out of immense goodness.

But what the Baptist adds: Who takes away the sins of the world, comprehends both: this victim sustains the punishment for us, and completely abolishes sin and death, with life, justice, and eternal joy restored.

And all these things come to pass in this way, when we look with faith upon the merits of this victim, and apprehend the consolation proposed, establishing this certainly and by name, that we receive the remission of sins on account of the obedience and merits of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was made a victim for us, etc.

Let these things suffice concerning the saying of Isaiah in this place.

But what Matthew cites concerning the diseases of bodies does not conflict with our exposition: for Christ takes away both, sin and all other evils, which are the wages of sin, diseases, death, eternal punishments, wars, and the remaining calamities.

And it must be most firmly established that he wishes to be invoked even in the dangers of this life, and that the mitigation of bodily calamities should be sought and expected from him.

For even if the Church is subject to the cross, yet the Son of God wishes to preserve it, and therefore he mitigates the punishments and miseries of this life, giving hospitality and necessary sustenance, and the necessity of these goods is evident and manifest.

For in the procreation and education of children it is necessary that there be some suitable little nests, and other moderate aids, just as we see that for little birds their own nests are necessary: afterwards, so that they may be advanced as men fit for teaching, [and for] many other similar causes, God wishes also to bestow the goods of the body by his most wise counsel, so that men may live who, by teaching and other labors, may serve the human race and especially the Church.

And the most beautiful image of all these things is proposed in the mother-in-law of Peter: the Lord heals her, being in danger from a most burning fever, so that she may serve him and the other guests in the preparation of food and hospitality.

But it behooves us to look upon and consider these very examples, so that we may understand why we should seek and expect peace, sustenance, comfortable health, and other goods of the body.

As often as you look upon your little children, consider of what and how many goods they are in need, which the duties of both parents, as much father as mother, require.

On account of these little children, know that you ought to pray that life may be prolonged for you, that necessary sustenance may be granted, that public government may be salutary.

Thus you see the years of life of King Hezekiah prolonged, so that his government and life may serve his whole kingdom and be salutary.

In such invocation and expectation of bodily goods, let us exercise our faith, and let us think to what dangers and miseries this wretched life is exposed.

There are in sight wars, famines, and other innumerable punishments, by which we are indeed harshly pressed; therefore God wishes us to be affected by some care for such dangers, he does not wish us to be iron-hearted, and to furiously heap evils upon us, but in true conversion he wishes us to seek help and mitigation of punishments from him, just as he addresses and calls us by his own voice: Turn to me, and I will turn to you.

He wishes us to do penance and amend our ways; thus he promises and pledges his help, thus he affirms that he will give eternal and bodily goods.

These groans of ours in true conversion will by no means be empty or vain, but will certainly obtain what we seek, just as the Lord most sweetly depicts and affirms in the image of the widow so often interceding with the unjust judge, who, as she finally extorts help by persistent intercessions and a certain pertinacity, so he also commands us to persistently seek and hope for eternal and bodily goods.

It behooves you to follow up this moving of the heart concerning the present miracle, even in other matters from time to time with pious meditation, so that it may be an exercise of penance and invocation.

For God is about to hear you, both invoking and approaching in faith, with the same kindness with which he brought help to those who were invoking him.

God is equal toward all, who also calls the others.

And for this very reason he invites and calls, so that he may have mercy on all who flee to him in faith.

And remember the universal vocation proposed in the sweetest saying: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

Of the scribe who is about to follow Christ, if he knows where he must finally settle, etc.

There follow some examples containing useful doctrine.

And the chief one is that of the scribe who is about to follow Christ, if he knows where the Lord finally wishes to settle. An image of a most common temptation is proposed, worthy of careful consideration.

The minds of all men are vehemently tormented by two things: first, what works are commanded and ordained, and second, what the outcomes of these works are. But the distinction is clear. It is necessary to know and follow the commands, whatever the outcomes may be, whether sad or pleasant.

For example, Moses must obey God, who commands him in the leading of the people out of Egypt, even if he does not foresee the mass of dangers that are to follow. Outcomes, however, are to be expected by faith, and we must not curiously inquire with our own speculations as to who and what kind they will be, whether sweet or unsweet. Because when we do what is necessary and commanded in our calling, we know for certain that salutary outcomes will eventually follow.

Meanwhile, however, adverse cases must be expected and overcome by faith, which, by the singular counsel of God, happen frequently even to the saints in their calling, as it is said in the Psalm: Many are the tribulations of the righteous, but the Lord will deliver them out of them all. Wherefore, as I have said, faith is necessary for the saints, which obeys God who calls, and expects salutary outcomes, even if something adverse intervenes in the meantime, just as Moses expects in the leading of the people, which is full of labors and dangers.

But this weak and fragile nature of men obeys God who calls with difficulty, and attempts to pre-measure all outcomes by its own counsels. Often, even when good counsels have been in good and commanded matters, with some adverse case intervening, many men, having deserted God, begin to murmur and grow indignant.

As many who at first sought marriage with right counsel, afterwards, with the miseries of marriage approaching, become either deserters, or, having deserted God, attempt illegitimate and forbidden things. So many who a little before received the preaching of the Gospel with joyful hearts, and professed it eagerly, now, with the impending dangers of persecutions, become more timid, and cast away the profession of the Gospel. But the Lord opposes a most severe rule: He who shall have persevered to the end, shall be saved.

And so that the end may be expected, faith is necessary, which may confirm the mind, lest it be broken before having deserted God, before the hope of a salutary outcome shines forth, just as this doctor of the Law is broken here, who, before he follows the Lord, seeks to establish for himself a certain place of lodging. Thus, innumerable others sin horribly, who, broken either by impatience or by other miseries, desert their calling: because they anxiously seek outcomes outside of certain and defined ones, and think it unjust, as if it were in darkness and blind night to follow God who calls confidently, and to rashly summon dangers to oneself, either to one's life or to one's sweetness. Examples are innumerable in wars, which, when they were not necessary, were moved only because the authors wished to establish tranquility for themselves and their affairs by their own counsel.

Against this audacity, which rashly moves things that are not necessary, the Psalm opposes a useful rule: Commit thy way unto the Lord, and pray to him, and he shall do it. He calls the duties of one's own and necessary calling the 'way'; this the Psalm commands to be thought of and done holily and solicitously. Afterwards it bids: Ask and expect also help and good outcomes from God, so he himself will do it, that is, he will give salutary outcomes to you, and useful ones to your calling.

This rule of life is very necessary for all men, which it behooves heads of families especially to think about diligently and attentively. Even if they are conflicted for some time by the dangers and miseries of poverty, wars, and other evils, yet let them serve their calling in the education of their children, and in other duties commanded by God, and at the same time call upon God, and expect good outcomes. No one, ever needy or miserable, expecting the Lord, has not experienced His help.

All this wisdom is most learnedly proposed here by Christ to that doctor of the law, when he says: The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests: but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head. What the Son of God affirms of himself, let the same be understood of the Church.

The Church has no certain or durable seat in the human race, and yet it is God's care that it has some modest little nests somewhere. Thus, let individuals also resolve that they will have some little huts somewhere, even if they do not yet foresee where in the world or in what places they will be. And let us individuals know that we must obey God who calls eagerly, with good hope and confidence, and that outcomes, whatever they may be, are to be commended to Him.

Great is this wisdom, but unsweet to our fragility, and ungrateful to the wisdom of the flesh, which, however, those who are inserted into the Church must always understand and exercise in true invocation.

tet. But let the most common saying of the Psalm, which we have cited, be before your eyes: Commit your way to the Lord, and pray to him, and he will act. I will not be more prolix in this commemoration, but I warn the listeners that, against the most common temptation—which, having deserted one's calling, seeks certain safeguards of tranquility by its own counsel—they should learn to oppose the command to retain one's calling, and with faith to ask for and await the outcomes, as we have said.

Another of his disciples says to him: Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father. But Jesus says to him: Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead, etc.

The main point that is proposed in this commemoration is this: That you should prefer your calling and the duties or works proper to your calling over all other works, however splendid and specious they may be, that do not pertain to your calling.

And the summary of this admonition is handed down in a most well-known rule: Only necessary things are to be done, unnecessary things are to be omitted entirely, and unnecessary things must by no means hinder necessary things.

But the courts of princes, and the individual families of private persons, abundantly testify that there is greater care for unnecessary things than for those which are very necessary, and it usually happens as it is said: more side-works than works [πλείω πάρεργα τῶν ἔργων].

As the first and highest care of princes should have been this concern, that the voice of the Gospel be handed down uncorrupted in churches and schools by suitable and faithful ministers and teachers; afterwards that the chancellery or political government be so constituted that it might faithfully recognize and judge the causes and complaints of subjects; then that there be public peace, prohibiting and severely punishing robberies on the roads, so that there might be public and severe penalties for rapine, thefts, murders, and similar crimes: but these great and necessary duties pertaining to the safety of princes and subjects are cared for much more lightly and coldly than the foolish and unnecessary preparations in empty pomps, in gluttony, in histrionic or gladiatorial gesticulations, in the preparation of which no expense, no labor, or care is spared.

What happens in courts, consider the same in your own life and family.

The concern and care of many for foolish and unnecessary splendid buildings, for delights and the choice of horses, and similar frivolous things, is much greater than for the pious education and instruction of the necessary poor infants, concerning whom, however, Paul in the 6th chapter to the Ephesians most severely commands parents: Bring up your children in the discipline and correction of the Lord.

Christ, however, in this place speaks principally and primarily about the calling of the ministers of the Gospel, whose proper and necessary duties are: to sound the voice of the Gospel uncorrupted, and to administer the sacraments divinely instituted, and to use and preserve them in the instituted use.

The Lord wills these duties to be performed by ministers in such a way that they execute them with greater care, concern, and faith than any others, however splendid or specious they may appear.

And how the Bishops have obeyed the command of Christ for many years, and still obey today, is in the sight of all.

For it cannot be denied that they have been and are now more concerned about the affairs of political government, and more anxious about the care of trivial matters, than about the concern of the most difficult and greatest ministry.

It is most manifest that many have cast aside the care of the ministry entirely, or have become enemies and persecutors of the Gospel.

The same happens even among us, for innumerable people serving the Gospel among us are more vehemently anxious about their own goods, or about advancing their own children and household, than they are anxious about the duties of their ministry, to which they were especially called.

Let us know, therefore, that in this narrative it is commanded to all and singular, that the first and chief care should be for the calling to be rightly and faithfully administered, which is to be preferred by far over all other unnecessary things, just as Paul most gravely warns about this very matter in 1 Thess.

4: We exhort you, brothers, that you study to excel in this, and do this ambitiously, that you may be quiet and do your own things.

And Peter in 1 Peter 4 says:

Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a malefactor, or a busybody [ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος].

Peter warns individuals that they should faithfully and constantly perform the proper duties of their calling, and not meddle in the affairs of others, and he affirms that punishments follow divinely upon the audacity that breaks into the calling of others.

And as he ascended into the boat, his disciples followed him.

And behold, a great commotion was made in the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves.

But he himself was sleeping, etc.

It is an example and image painting for us the face of the Church, as long as it is gathered in this miserable course of bodily life.

And it signifies both, with what great dangers and sorrows the Church in this life be conflicted.

Then, how and by whom he might be delivered.

Now, the state of the Church is almost always such in all times that it is shaken from time to time by horrible movements, and in these it is forced to fear and experience the furies of devils, the cruelty of tyrants, and the delusions of fanatical men, who all strive with all their might to oppress and destroy the Church.

And the narrative of the present danger, in which the head of the Church, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, is with his disciples, is a most expressive image of the furies of the devil, by which he wished to submerge and absorb both Christ and the Apostles in the waves.

And while these things are happening, and the Apostles are in danger, Christ sleeps, just as if he were taking no care of the Church, and neither could nor thought to repress the raging devils and restrain the other enemies, just as the narrative of the second Psalm also agrees entirely with this image: Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things?

The Kings of the earth stood by, and the Princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. Let us break their bonds, and cast away their yoke from us. He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them, etc.

It is necessary that these images and narratives be known, so that we may understand that in these dangers faith and invocation are necessary, just as in this place we hear the fear of the disciples and the weakness of their faith being rebuked by the Lord.

Let us know, therefore, that it is necessary in all those dangers that the confession of the Gospel be constantly retained, and that our spirits be fortified, so that they may eagerly and confidently seek help from the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and constantly wait for it.

Just as we see the Apostles, although trembling, nevertheless seeking help, and not abandoning the confession of the Gospel and of their Lord Jesus Christ.

Let us resolve that the same is required of us, as these sayings warn, in Psalm 37: Be subject to God and hope in him, and he himself will act.

Wait for the Lord, and keep his way, and he will exalt you, so that you may take the land as an inheritance: when the sinners have perished, you will see.

Let us learn these exercises of faith, and let us think of them in the dangers of the present times.

And let us strive to express this wisdom, proper to the Church, in true invocation and confession of the Gospel, and in other duties pertaining to the Church.

But let us also know the fruit and sweetness of these exercises: because when invocation is kindled, that which is called here the sweet tranquility finally shows itself.

For when the Lord is awakened by the groans and prayers of those who call upon him, it is most certain that he is present, and that he gloriously suppresses the furies and roarings against the Gospel, having repressed and destroyed the devils, tyrants, and fanatical men, so that the glory, presence, and kindness of the guardian and of his own saving and omnipotent Lord may appear to the Church.

This consolation is also proposed in Psalm 44: Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord?

Arise and do not repel us to the end, why do you turn away your face, and forget our poverty and our tribulation? And in Psalm 12: Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now it will be taught with confidence.

And when Jesus had come across the strait into the region of the Gerasenes, two men possessed by Demons met him, etc.

Gerasa is across the Jordan towards Arabia, about which Strabo writes, that there is in that place a foul pool carrying waters deadly to the living creatures that drink from it.

And it is likely that the pool was infected and corrupted by the Devils, whom the text here affirms were sent into the swine, and rushed headlong into the pool.

But although the image of the nation, of which mention is also made in the text, and of all those who despise the voice of the Gospel, or who, having spurned and rejected Christ, use foolish desires as a pretext.

The nation of the Gerasenes orders Christ to depart from their borders, lest they lose their swine.

Such are the Canons, more foul and filthy than any swine, who wherever they rush, fill everything with abominable poison.

There are also others similar to these Gerasenes, who, after they have heard the voice of the Gospel, furiously indulge in all their desires and lusts, so that by their foulness, poison, and contagion of crimes, they infest and fill everything nearby more than others, as there are (alas) innumerable examples.

The image of the Gerasenes, and the foul and poisoned lake of that nation, signifies all such people.

The very word Gerasa or גירשה signifies a valley of seditious scoundrels; perhaps the name was made from this, because a seditious multitude of Arab robbers or others, who had no fixed abode, fled there and found refuge there.

On the example.

The example itself signifies, first, that the Lord Jesus Christ casts out the Devils, and the kingdom destroys it, as it is said in 1 John 3: "For this the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil." And Genesis 3: "The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent." Regarding this matter, it is spoken of more fully elsewhere.

Next, the punishment for ingratitude is proposed. Christ sees that the people are ungrateful for the greatest benefit, therefore he afflicts them with this punishment, that he sends the Devil into the swine, so that the whole herd might rush headlong into the sea and die. I also believe that many Jewish apostates and deserters of the rites of the Israelite nation were hiding in this Gerasa, who, contrary to the custom of the nation and the commandment of God, ate swine's flesh. Christ wished to punish these as well.

But in this very punishment, let this be observed. The loss of the swine in itself is not great, but what is signified, this is sad and deplorable: namely, that men ungrateful for the Gospel are converted into swine by a terrible metamorphosis, and become the dwellings of devils; this, I say, is sad and deplorable, and it is signified in this image. And our age has seen horrible examples of the Anabaptists, who, with what foul furies and diabolical crimes they have polluted themselves, and are now polluting themselves, the facts themselves and the histories of our time clearly show, etc.

Latin:

Vade, ostende te Sacerdoti, et offer ei donum, quod constituit Moises in testimonium ipsis, etc.

Proxima concione recitata est communis doctrina de miraculis, in qua audivistis haec testimonia magna diligentia intuenda esse, ut his commonefacti et in nobis fidem et invocationem excitemus. Nam qui horum exemplorum usum in vera invocatione ipsi discunt, hi intelligere doctrinam paulatim incipiunt, non potest magnitudo rei ulla quantumvis evidenti oratione exprimi, nisi accedat invocatio, in qua corda exercere et intelligere doctrinam incipiunt. Estque utilissimum aliqua insignia exempla in conspectu habere, qualia sunt Syrophoenissae, centurionis, aut huius leprosi, ut tam illustribus testimoniis excitata ac confirmata mens petat auxilium, et fide ac spe indubitata exspectet.

Sunt autem in hoc exemplo reliqui duo: Sanat Dominus leprosum, sicut petivit, et testatur invocationem non esse inanem aut irritam. Postea interdicit ei, ne cuiquam dicat. Hic multa quaeri possunt, an prohibetur confessio fidei? An displicet tanti beneficii celebratio? Apud Sacerdotes necesse est huic sanato fateri se fuisse leprosum, et petere ut pronuntient se iam sanatum esse, necesse est offerre sacrificium in lege constitutum, agnum anniculum et reliqua quae lex postulat. Quomodo igitur caelari sanatio Christi miraculosa potest?

Respondeo. Non moveo disputationes, nec subtilitates quaero. Non prohibetur confessio aut grata celebratio. (Necesse enim est sanatum fateri sacerdotibus veritatem.) Sed proponit Dominus exemplum, in quo prohibet cupiditatem gloriae in operibus, quae a Deo per nos fiunt. Ac docet frenare animos, ne efferri ac superbirie incipiant, cum peculiari aliquo beneficio divinitus ornantur, ut superbiebat et efferebatur Saul post victorias, flagrans ira et odio adversus Deum, et cupiditate iniusta accensus, Davidem innocentem persequens, et miseros sacerdotes tyrannice interficiens.

Ac manifestum est, innumerabiles homines abuti donis divinitus attributis. Quam pauci sunt, qui non efferuntur, cum fortunae benevolentioris aura aliquantulum foventur? Quot millia hominum luce doctrinae coelestis ad suas cupiditates abutuntur, ad superbiam, ignaviam, stultam securitatem, aut gloriae cupiditatem, qua constantiam, labores, et pericula sua praedicant, et caeteros damnant ac persequuntur, cum pleni sint horribilium peccatorum, errorum, libidinum, ἀσωτίας et similium.

Illa vanitas et superbia propter dona divina quaecunque, prohibetur hic a Christo, cum inquit: Cave ne cui dixeris. Nec ero in hac quaestione prolixior. Celebremus dona Dei vera fide, pietate, ac timore Dei, nec his praetextibus cupiditati nostrae et petulantiae indulgeamus.

Secunda quaestio est: Cur hunc sanatum Christus ad Sacerdotes ablegat, et iubet offerre munus, quod constituit Moses in testimonium ipsis, ut Lucae 17. dicitur: Ite, ostendite vos sacerdotibus.

Ac notum est, Pontificis hunc ipsum locum ad confessionem detorsisse. De hac quaestione breviter dicemus.

Quanquam non potest ullius creaturae sapientia exhaurire magnitudinem mysteriorum, quae in concionibus et miraculis Christi recitantur, tamen initia discenda sunt, quantum et patefecit ipse, et immensa bonitate in discentibus adiuvat. Quare duas causas recitabo, propter quas Christus ad sacerdotes istos sanatos ablegat.

Prima causa est, vult ipsos et universum genus humanum commonefacere hoc mandato, ut ipsi et nos omnes ministerio Sacerdotum legitimo, et a se constituto, reverenter et ad sui nominis gloriam utantur. Ac sicuti hos sanatos ad Sacerdotes remittit, ita intelligas nos omnes, et singulos omnibus temporibus ad ministerium in Ecclesia deduci: ibi vocem Evangelii audias, et usu Sacramentorum fidem confirmes, hoc ministerio scias velle Deum Ecclesiam aeternam sibi colligere, et cum voce huius ministerii et usu Sacramentorum velle efficacem esse, et hoc modo et non aliter homines convertere et salvare, remittere peccata, et initia vitae aeternae in nobis accendere.

Haec esse vera certissimum est, ita enim ipse Dominus inquit: Sicut misit me Pater, ita ego mitto vos.

Et alibi: Qui vos audit, me audit, qui vos spernit, me spernit.

Rom. 1.: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Hunc ordinem Deus ipse immensa bonitate ita sancivit, sic vult esse efficax, et Ecclesiam aeternam colligere, et ad hoc ministerium a se sanctum omnes deducit, vultque intelligere omnes, ita se, et non aliter, efficacem fore, vult igitur vocem Evangelii et usum Sacramentorum magnificari.

Ac diserte ac severe prohibet, ne quis se ipsum aut suo exemplo alios ab hoc ministerio abducat.

Sicuti proh dolor contemptus Evangelii et Sacramentorum ingens in multitudine promiscua cernitur, et crescit in dies barbaries, ac multis tetris furoribus contemptus Evangelii in animis hominum confirmatur.

Nec dubium est, maximam partem tristissimarum calamitatum, bellorum, famis, crudelitatis Turcicae, et aliarum miseriarum, huius contemptus poenas esse.

Ita primum considerate Dominum deducere nos ad ministerium Sacerdotum, hoc est, ad vocem Evangelii et ad usum sacramentorum.

Ex his prorsus non sequitur, confessionem Papisticam a Domino sanctam esse, quae quidem multos tetros furores pugnantes cum voce Evangelii continet.

Sed non ero in hac commemoratione prolixior, nos exemplum intuemur, quod propositum est ideo, ut revereri, amare et ornare ministerium Evangelii studeamus.

Secunda causa, quod istos sanatos ad Levíticos Sacerdotes Dominus remittit, haec est: Vult hoc miraculo et aliis eos convincere, ut credant se esse Messiam, et in hac legatione commonefacit eos, ut ipsum agnoscant et recipiant, vult ipsos et nuntios et testes esse praesentis Messiae ac Redemptoris.

Fuit enim Sacerdotium veteris Testamenti propter hunc ultimum ac summum finem sanctum ac constitutum, ut doceret venturum esse Messiam, qui ipse futurus sit victima et propitiatio vera pro peccatis generis humani, et hanc venturam victimam umbris illis ac figuris Leviticorum sacrificiorum significari.

Ita docet Baptista, inquiens: Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi, ac sine agnitione et fide huius Messiae, mactationes victimarum et conciones Sacerdotum horribiles tenebrae et Idolomaniae fuerunt.

Resuscitat igitur mortuos, et editis aliis miraculis conspiciendum se praebet hic ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus verus Messias natus ex virgine Maria, et Sacerdotes his ipsis miraculis alloquitur, ut ipsum agnoscant, vera de ipso doceant, et testes sint suae praesentiae, de hoc ipso per hos sanatos leprosos commonefacit Sacerdotes.

Sed quantum profecerit Dominus, omnibus notissimum est.

Ac ne conqueri possint, Dominum abolere legem, ministeria eorum appetere, et stipendia divinitus ipsis attributa imminuere, expresse praecipit Dominus, ut offerant Sacerdotibus munera a Mose constituta.

Et exstant alibi similia praecepta de decimis: Haec oportuit facere, et illa non omittere, Matth. 23. Ita testatur, se nihil illis velle eripere.

Ac cum nondum abolitum sit Sacerdotium, et ipse huius Ecclesiae civis esse velit, et cum ipsis ritus institutos observet, vult et hac in re officiosus erga ipsos esse, cum mandat stipendia debita Sacerdotibus persolvi.

Vicissimet Sacerdotes sui ministerii propria intelligere et exequi oportebat.

Debebat enim docere, sacrificia sua non esse merita remissionis peccatorum, sed Messiae victimam veram propitiationem peccatorum, et irae Dei futuram esse.

Et hunc verum Messiam iam praesentem esse, et in oculis universi populi versari, videlicet, hunc natum ex Maria virgine, tot miraculis sese ostendentem etc.

Ad hunc doctorem deducere auditores, et de eo testificari debebant.

Hic est unus ille aeternus et summus Pontifex ac doctor Ecclesiae, qui Adae et Evae hanc promissionem tradidit: Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis.

Hic Messias est, quem vidit Moses facie ad faciem, hic Dominus est, qui fuit custos Ecclesiae in deserto, hic nunc assumta humana natura accedit ad nos, ut victima sit, et sacrificium suum offerat pro nobis etc.

Hoc inquam vicissim Sacerdotes facere decebat, et fuerunt tunc aliqui tales, sed paucissimi, qui vere hunc Dominum agnoverunt, et ad ipsum conversi sunt.

In nostro autem textu additur de munere, quod praecipit Moses in testimonium ipsis. Horum verborum simplicissima sententia est: Munus, quod est ius ipsorum, seu quod debetur ipsis. Saepissime enim vox Testimonium legem ipsam significat. Nec sine gravi consilio ita sancitum est, ut decimae et victimae sacerdotibus tribuerentur, necesse est enim aliquos esse ministros, qui legitime vocati ad ministerium, serviant Ecclesiae in propagatione verbi et usu Sacramentorum. Non possunt autem tales vivere, nisi victus eis necessarius tribuatur. Ideo omnibus temporibus ali eos Deus ab Ecclesia voluit, et singulari consilio reditus certos eis constituit. Ac verissimum est debere Ecclesiam piis doctoribus victum et necessaria vitae adiumenta, sicut inquit Dominus: Dignus est operarius mercede sua. Ita hoc in loco dicitur, Mosen praecepisse hoc in testimonium ipsis, hoc est, ut esset ius ipsorum, seu quod debetur ipsis. Hac simplici expositione ego contentus sum. Sed tamen vera est et altera, quam quidam hoc in loco usurpant, legem esse testimonium de utraque re, de peccatis nostris et de liberatore Christo, et legem ipsam testificari, non tolli peccata per legem, sed tantum esse testimonium contrarium nobis, iudicans ac damnans nos. Estque haec enarratio comprehensa in doctrina de discrimine Legis et Evangelii seu gratiae Christi, quae alibi recitatur copiosius. Adii-ciam autem pauca.

Notissimum est duo esse praecipua capita doctrinae coelestis, Legem et Evangelium de filio Dei Domino nostro Iesu Christo. Doctrina Legis comprehenditur communissima appellatione Decalogi, et est aeterna et immota norma sapientiae in Deo, docens quod sit Deus et qualis sit, videlicet, sapiens, iustus, castus et verax, et postulat lex, ut creaturae rationales, Angeli et homines, huic normae sapientiae et iustitiae divinae conformes sint, et denuntiat iram horribilem, et non simulat am omnibus, qui non sunt conformes.

Scitis autem duplicem esse usum Legis. Primum, quoad disciplinam et regendam locomotivam. Est enim voluntas Dei aeterna et immutabilis, ut sit aliqua honesta vitae gubernatio externa. Et est manifesta ratio, quia nulla esset futura societas durabilis, si singulis liceret aliorum bona, coniuges aut liberos pro arbitrio rapere. Ac qualis vita esset, si caedes promiscue concederentur? Et quamquam multi a Diabolis ad eiusmodi furores impelluntur, multi etiam ad caedes, libidines et omnium scelerum licentiam se ipsos invitant, tamen manifestum est, Deum ipsum vindicem esse, et poenas atroces etiam in hac vita immutabiliter sequi delicta atrocia, sicut affirmat Christus: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. Ita Deus ipse aliquos ad honestam vitae gubernationem praestandam adigit.

Sed hic necesse est scire, hanc gubernationem disciplinae procul abesse a perfecta legis impletione, nec esse meritum remissionis peccatorum, et manere in corde multas tristes dubitationes de Deo, multas pravas inclinationes, et sordes alias infinitas: sicuti omnes fateri necesse est.

Alter vero usus legis est, iram Dei adversus peccatum in nobis monstrare, et comminatione irae Dei corda perterrefacere; sicut inquit Paulus: Lex iram operatur, hoc est, iudicio legis perterrefacta corda demerguntur in mortem et doloribus inferorum opprimuntur, sicuti Ezechias affirmat de hoc iudicio: Tanquam leo contrivit omnia ossa mea.

Hi dolores multis hominibus noti sunt, et sentiunt alii maiores, alii minores. Et quanta res sit iudicium Legis, saepe in his conspicitur, qui capitalibus suppliciis afficiendi sunt. Ac sentiunt tales, peccatum, iram Dei et dolores inferorum non tolli per legem, sed esse legem iudicium ac testimonium accusans et damnans nos. Primum hoc modo, cum testificatur Deum iustum iudicare et damnare peccatum: deinde, quia hoc testimonio legis convicta conscientia cogitur fateri, nos esse reos, et iram Dei et poenas horribiles promeritos esse, et iuste Deum facere, quod suae iustitiae exempla in nobis statuit, quod abolet ac destruit naturam inquinatam tantis sordibus.

Has tabulas legis qui recitari contra se in vere dolores audiunt, hi sciunt non esse hos dolores inania aut ridicula terriculamenta, et cum Davide hanc querelam tristissimam discunt: Dolores mortis circumdederunt me, et pericula inferni invenerunt me.
