De paralytico. Fides aliena prodest ad multa bona corporalia aliis impetranda. Sed remissionem peccatorum oportet quemlibet accipere propria fide. Hic paralyticus et aliena fide adfertur ad Christum, et ipse habet propriam fidem, cum dicitur ei: Remittuntur tibi peccata tua.

Sequitur disputatio de remissione peccatorum. Pharisaei indocti nihil sciverunt de promissionis intellectu, non cogitarunt etiam Davidi dictum esse: Dominus abstulit peccatum tuum, et Danielem dicere ad regem: Erit sanatio delictorum tuorum, etc. Semper Levitae simul debuerunt declarare promissionem de Messia, sed non intellexerunt amplius officium suum. Hanc ignorantiam taxat Christus, et affirmat, quod velit instituere ministerium remittendi peccata, sicut dicit: Quorum remiseritis peccata.

Addit Christus miraculum, ut sit huius doctrinae testimonium. Iubet Christus, ut tollat grabbatum, id est, accepta remissione mitigantur poenae, possumus gestare grabbatum.

De vocatione Matthaei. Et cum transiret inde Iesus, vidit hominem sedentem in telonio, Matthaeum nomine etc. In exemplo Matthaei Christus ipse ostendit applicationem, quod sit testimonium communis doctrinae Evangelii, quod omnibus praedicat poenitentiam, arguit peccata in omnibus, et annuntiat remissionem peccatorum omnibus agentibus poenitentiam, et credentibus remittit gratis propter Christum, iuxta dictum: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Sit igitur Matthaeus exemplum, quod filius Dei vere recipiat omnes agentes poenitentiam, et gratis recipiat. Et regula sit nota: Non veni vocare iustos, sed peccatores ad poenitentiam.

Et diserte dicit: Ad poenitentiam, vult nos Deus ad se converti, non vult nos manere in delictis contra conscientiam. Haec est summa exempli. Nunc videamus partes.

Prima Pars. I. Status populi Iudaeorum fuit miserabilis, multae Levitae facti sunt scribae et ministri publicanorum, et publicani plerique fuerunt Ethnici, et valde onerarant homines usuris, et eorum scribae vixerunt Ethnico more apud eos etc. Hoc magnum dolorem attulit sanctis.

II. Evangelium arguit omnes homines, quod habeant peccata, sed ostendit discrimina.

Primo sunt multi, qui habent manifesta peccata externa, ut in hac historia publicani, seu ut semper sunt multi palam scortatores, et mala conscientia viventes.

Secundo sunt hypocritae, qui habent externam disciplinam, et putant se iustos esse; interea in corde sunt pleni idololatria, erroribus, non recte invocant Deum, sunt sine timore Dei et sine vera fide, sunt pleni odiis et invidia, etc. Sicut Pharisaei in hac historia, hi sunt superbi et alios iudicant, et sese anteferunt, et fingunt se esse sine peccato, et se sanctos esse; tales semper multi fuerunt, sunt et erunt, etiam cum desinent esse Cuculli et Monachi, tamen Monachorum natura non cessabit.

Hi iudicant in hac historia Christum, et reprehendunt eum, quod comedit apud publicanos, nec intelligunt se ipsos immundiores esse publicanis.

Utrosque vocat Christus ad poenitentiam, sed Pharisaei minus audiunt quam publicani.

Tertio sunt peccatores, qui convertuntur, sive habuerint manifesta peccata, sive arcana. Hi habent contritionem, fatentur se esse peccatores, et vere dolent, et desinunt facere contra conscientiam, et credunt remissionem peccatorum propter Christum. Tales homines quanquam conversi sunt, adhuc tamen habent peccata, sed non contra conscientiam, et tales homines fiunt salvi.

De aliis peccatoribus, non agentibus poenitentiam, omnibus dictum est 1. Corinth. 6.: Nolite errare, scortatores, idololatrae, adulteri etc. regnum Dei non possidebunt. Item: Qui non credit in Filium, ira Dei manebit super eum.

De dicto Esaiae.

Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium, et scientiam Domini magis quam holocausta.

Regula communis est, saepe repetita in Prophetis, quae ordinat opera.

Tres sunt gradus operum.

Primus est, notitia Dei, id est, vera agnitio, vera fides, verus timor Dei, opera primi et secundi praecepti immediate cum Deo agentia. Haec omnia nominat hic notitiam Dei. Haec sunt prorsus et simpliciter necessaria, sicut manifestum est ex primo praecepto et secundo.

Secundus gradus est dilectio proximi, id est, opera secundae tabulae erga proximum, haec omnia nominat hic misericordiam. Haec opera etiam sunt necessaria, sicut ex secunda tabula Decalogi manifestum est.

Tertius gradus est ceremoniarum, Eufferliche geberden, mit Opffer, Speiss, Kleider vnd Menschen sagung. Haec opera sunt longe infra duos gradus priores, de his dicit regula: Non sacrificium, etc.

Quare hoc dictum citat Christus?

Quia reprehendit omnem superstitionem in toto genere humano, praeferentem externos ritus mandatis summis primi praecepti et secundi, et secundae tabulae. Apud Papistas maius peccatum est comedere carnes die sexta, quam adulterium.

Ita tunc Iudaei damnabant Christum, quod non servabat traditionem, quae prohibebat comedere apud publicanos. Christus contra opponit praeceptum de dilectione, ait se misericordiam erga eos exercere, quia ideo ad eos accedat, ut convertantur.

Et bene observanda et discenda est haec regula, quae ostendit gradus operum, et taxat superstitionem negligentium necessaria opera.

## 9:2 The Nineteenth Sunday After Trinity
The Nineteenth Sunday after Trinity.

Gospel of Matthew

9. And getting into a boat, he crossed over and came to his own city.

And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed. And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic: Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven.

And behold, some of the Scribes said within themselves: This man blasphemes. And when Jesus had seen their thoughts, he said: Why do you think evil in your hearts?

For which is easier to say, your sins are forgiven, or to say, rise and walk?

But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins on earth, then he said to the paralytic: Rise, take up your bed, and go. into your house. And he arose, and went into his house. But the crowds seeing it were amazed, and glorified God, who gave such power to men.

There are three principal points.

I. The difference between the Old and New Testament. II. Concerning private absolution. III. Human calamities are the punishments of sinners, but they become exercises for the just, and are mitigated.

Concerning the first.

The Law of Moses neither remits sins, nor commands it to be said, Thy sins are remitted to thee.

For although it had sacrifices, which were called propitiations, yet those ceremonies only merited such a remission, so that he for whom it was sacrificed, might not be excluded from that people: and the Epistle to the Hebrews says: It was impossible for the blood of bulls to take away sins. Moreover, even if the law says something about remission, it does not give a gratuitous remission, but at the same time requires complete obedience. Furthermore, unless the remission is gratuitous, it will be void, for no one satisfies the law. Therefore Paul contends about the particle "Gratis" [freely], and establishes this difference between the Gospel and the law: the Gospel freely, on account of the Son of God, remits sins to those who believe, and a ministry has been instituted, in which remission is expressly announced, either to many, or to individuals.

But someone might ask: How then did the saints in the Old Testament obtain remission?

I answer: Besides the ministry of the law, there were revealed promises concerning Christ. The priests ought to have proposed these also to the people, so that they might know remission was offered on account of that coming victim, and that each one might believe that by this faith he obtained remission, just as David says: Blessed is he who trusts in him. And Isaiah: Because he will lay down his soul as a sacrifice for sin etc., and Zech.: In the blood of thy testament thou wilt send forth the bound from the pit. But because this understanding of the promises was often obliterated, therefore God through the Prophets restored it from time to time.

With these the priests contended, who meanwhile were heaping up their ceremonies with superstition and avarice, and contended that they merited remission. These opinions the Prophets often rebuke, as: Thou wilt not delight in burnt offerings. The Fathers therefore had remission wrapped up in the promises concerning Christ.

Concerning the second. In the Gospel a ministry has been instituted for expressly announcing the remission of sins to all who believe in Christ. And this announcement can not only be proposed to many in general, as doctrine, but also applied to individuals, as Christ says: If he asks, remit it to him.

So therefore the minister rightly speaks to individuals, so that each may believe in Christ, according to that: This is my beloved Son, Hear him. Thus the minister rightly says to anyone: I announce to you yourself that remission has truly been granted to the one who believes in Christ. This private application makes the promise more illustrious, and shows that the benefit of the Gospel pertains to you.

Concerning the third.

Calamities are a part of the law, that is, the prison of human nature, into which we have been shut on account of sin, as the Psalm says: On account of iniquity thou chastisest the sons of men, and Paul: The body is mortified on account of sin, namely, clinging in the flesh. Therefore Christ first here remits sins, afterwards he takes away the disease, so that he may admonish us that this nature is subject to death, and to calamities, because it is immersed in sin, and may testify that he is the deliverer, who wishes to take away both, the cause and the effect, sin and death, and to restore perpetual justice and life.

Why then do the saints obtain the remission of sins, yet are afflicted?

I answer, just as Paulus says: The body is mortified on account of sin, namely, clinging in the flesh. For because sin is now taken away by imputation, and in reality there remains the infirmity of the flesh, God wills it to be mortified, so that in those exercises faith may be exercised and shine. Likewise, that God may show his glory in our infirmity against the devil, whom he conquers through the infirm, according to that: Know that God makes his saint wonderful, that is, he delivers him miraculously, showing his glory in our infirmity, when he saves the deserted, the abject, beyond all human counsels, beyond the opinion of all.

Latin:

Dominica XIX. post Trinitatis.

Evangelium Matth.

9. Et ascendens in naviculam transfretavit, et venit in civitatem suam.

Et ecce, offerebant ei paralyticum iacentem in lecto. Et videns Jesus fidem illorum, dixit paralytico: Confide fili, remittuntur tibi peccata tua.

Et ecce quidam de Scribis dixerunt intra se: Hic blasphemat. Et cum vidisset Jesus cogitationes eorum, dixit: Ut quid vos cogitatis mala in cordibus vestris?

Quidenim est facilius dicere, dimittuntur tibi peccata, an dicere, surge et ambula?

Ut autem sciatis, quia filius hominis habet potestatem dimittendi peccata in terra, tunc ait paralytico: Surge, tolle lectum tuum, et vade in domum tuam. Et surrexit, et abiit in domum suam. Videntes autem turbae admiratae sunt, et glorificaverunt Deum, qui dedit potestatem talem hominibus.

Tres sunt praecipui loci.

I. Differentia veteris et novi Testamenti. II. De absolutione privata. III. Calamitates humanae sunt poenae peccatorum, sed fiunt iustis exercitia, et mitigantur.

De primo.

Lex Moisi nec remittit peccata, nec mandat dici, Remittuntur tibi peccata.

Quanquam enim habebat sacrificia, quae vocabantur placationes, tamen ceremoniae illae tantum merebantur talem remissionem, ne is pro quo sacrificabatur, excluderetur ex illo populo: et Epistola ad Ebraeos ait: Impossibile erat sanguine taurorum tolli peccata. Praeterea lex etiamsi quid dicit de remissione, tamen non dat gratuitam remissionem, sed simul requirit integram obedientiam. Porro nisi remissio sit gratuita, erit irrita, nemo enim legi satisfacit. Ideo Paulus dimicat de particula Gratis, et hanc constituit differentiam inter Evangelium et legem, Evangelium gratis propter Filium Dei remittit peccata credentibus, et institutum est ministerium, in qua expresse annunciatur remissio, aut multis, aut singulis.

Sed quaerat aliquis: Quomodo igitur sancti in veteri Testamento consequebantur remissionem?

Respondeo: Praeter ministerium legis erant revelatae promissiones de Christo. Has debebant sacerdotes etiam proponere populo, ut scirent remissionem offerri propter illam venturam victimam, et crederet quisque se hac fide consequi remissionem, sicut David ait: Beatus qui confidit in eo. Et Esaias: Quia ponet animam suam hostiam pro peccato etc., et Zach.: In sanguine testamenti tui emittes vinctos de lacu. Sed quia hic intellectus promissionum saepe obliterabatur, ideo Deus per Prophetas eum subinde restituebat.

Cum his dimicabant sacerdotes, qui interea suas ceremonias superstitione, et avaritia cumulabant, et contendebant eas mereri remissionem. Has opiniones saepe reprehendunt Prophetae, ut: Holocaustis non delectaberis. Habebant ergo Patres remissionem involutam in promissionibus de Christo.

De secundo. In Evangelio institutum est ministerium expressa voce annunciandae remissionis peccatorum omnibus credentibus in Christum. Et haec annunciatio non solum in genere multis proponi potest, ut doctrina, sed etiam applicari singulis, sicut dicit Christus: Si petet, remitte ei.

Ut igitur recte dicit minister ad singulos, ut quisque credat in Christum, iuxta illud: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, Hunc audite. Ita recte dicit minister cuilibet: Annuncio tibi ipsi vere donatam esse remissionem credenti in Christum. Haec applicatio privata reddit promissionem illustriorem, et ostendit beneficium Evangelii ad te pertinere.

De tertio.

Calamitates sunt pars legis, id est, carcer humanae naturae, in quem propter peccatum inclusi sumus, sicut Psal. inquit: Propter iniquitatem corripis filios hominum, et Paulus: Corpus mortificatur propter peccatum, scilicet, haerens in carne. Ideo Christus primum hic remittit peccata, postea tollit morbum, ut admoneat nos hanc naturam obnoxiam esse morti, et calamitatibus, quia est immersa peccato, et testetur se esse liberatorem, qui velit utrunque tollere, causam et effectum, peccatum et mortem, et reddere perpetuam iusticiam et vitam.

Cur ergo sancti consequi remissionem peccatorum, tamen affliguntur?

Respondeo, sicut Paulus inquit: Corpus mortificatur propter peccatum, scilicet, haerens in carne. Quia enim peccatum nunc imputatione sublatum est, et reipsa manet infirmitas carnis, vult eam Deus mortificari, ut in illis exercitiis exerceatur et luceat fides. Item, ut Deus ostendat suam gloriam in nostra infirmitate adversus diabolum, quem vincit per infirmos, iuxta illud: Scitote quod mirificat Deus sanctum suum, id est, mirabiliter liberat, ostendens gloriam suam in nostra infirmitate, cum desertos, abiectos, praeter omnia humana consilia, praeter omnium opinionem servat.

## 9:14 Sermons on Matthew
Why do your disciples not fast?

There follows the doctrine concerning Christian liberty.

Whenever God renews the Gospel, then false worships and human traditions are taxed, and when some retain traditions and others do not, then a dissimilarity arises which breeds contentions. Some who retain them grieve that laws are being relaxed, and they see in others a greater license following than there ought to be. Among others who do not retain them, there are good men who rightly understand liberty and rightly use it. There are also many evil ones who become more wild and neglect divine and human laws, just as (alas) in our time we see very many have abused and do abuse the doctrine of Christian liberty.

In this history, the Apostles do not retain the traditions of the Pharisees, and they rightly use their liberty, and they are excused by Christ, but the Lord at the same time warns what kind of people those who use liberty ought to be.

Learn, therefore, what Christian liberty is, of which the Lord says: If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed. It must be known, however, that there are four degrees of Christian liberty, which you should consider in order, and remember well.

The first is the gratuitous remission and reconciliation on account of Christ through faith, and justification not on account of the Law, but on account of the Mediator. Concerning this degree, Paul says: You are not under the law, but under grace.

The second degree is the liberation in the heart itself from the pains of hell, and the beginning of righteousness and eternal life through Christ by the Holy Spirit given, according to the saying: Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. This degree is a living and true consolation, in which the help and presence of God is felt, just as David in exile feels consolation, and Lawrence rejoices in the very roasting, etc.

These two degrees are properly and principally Christian liberty, namely, to be liberated from sin, from the wrath of God, from eternal death, to have consolation and joy in all tribulations, and to feel the presence and help of God. And this liberty is begun in this life in those who are truly converted to God and understand the Gospel.

Afterwards, it will be consummated in eternal life, where we shall be entirely free from sin, from death, and from all miseries, and God will be all in all, communicating Himself to us and His wisdom, righteousness, and eternal life. These two are the principal degrees; of these the Lord speaks properly when He says: If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed.

Consider what a great thing it is to be liberated from sin, from the wrath of God, from eternal death, and to have the Son of God present in all dangers, consoling and helping, and all these things are received in true repentance through faith. Thus David had liberty in flight.

Thus the three men in Babylon in the furnace had liberty, when the Son of God was openly among them. Thus Daniel had liberty among the lions, etc.

May you learn to understand this liberty and to consider it in true conversion and daily invocation. Afterwards, there are other degrees concerning external things.

There is, therefore, a third degree, that it is not necessary for a Christian man to use the polity of Moses, but he can live according to the honest polities of those nations in which he lives, wherever he is, just as Cyrus could use Persian laws, and Constantine Roman ones. And yet faith and invocation in the heart is the same toward the true God, on account of the Son, etc.

The fourth degree is to know that no traditions made by men in the Church are the worship of God. Likewise, that they are not necessary, and that they can be omitted without sin.

And concerning this degree of liberty, the Apostles show the example here; they know these fasts instituted by the Pharisees are neither the worship of God, nor are they necessary works. And by their own example, they teach others not to think they are the worship of God, and not to think they are necessary works.

Let us know, however, the rule, that before this fourth degree, there must be in us the two first degrees: liberation from sin, and the faith which apprehends the consolation and presence of God in us. Where these degrees are not, many abuse liberty.

Christ, therefore, teaches that the former degrees and the latter must be embraced together: The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them. He signifies then that men use liberty rightly when Christ the bridegroom is with them.

Then they are free from sin, then they rejoice, and joyfully they invoke and give thanks, and are not occupied with those foolish human ceremonies. Those Pharisaical fasts are not the worship of God, but my disciples will have far different fasts, namely, obedience in the cross commanded by God.

Afterwards, He adds an admonition, that many without the prior degrees do not rightly understand liberty, nor do they rightly use it. No man sews a new piece of cloth onto an old garment, no man pours new wine into old bottles, that is, the doctrine of liberty is not understood by men who are not converted to God, but are still impious and savage, not terrified by the law of God.

Such men, having heard the name of liberty, despise divine and human laws all the more, and become savage, like bears and other beasts in the woods, just as we manifestly see in our time, that many men become entirely beastly by the abuse of liberty. And God punishes this sad abuse with many calamities, war, and plunderings, and other evils, because we are gluttonous and are more negligent in governing ourselves; therefore, more sins come, and afterwards wars and other punishments.

Let us diligently consider these things, and let us learn to understand liberty rightly, and to use it rightly.

Latin:

Quare discipuli tui non ieiunant?

Sequitur doctrina de libertate Christiana.

Quandocunque Deus renovat Evangelium, tunc taxantur falsi cultus et traditiones humanae, et cum alii retinent traditiones, alii non retinent, tunc fit dissimilitudo, quae parit certamina. Aliqui retinentes dolent laxari leges, et vident sequi in aliis licentiam maiorem, quam esse deberet. Inter alios, qui non retinent, sunt boni recte intelligentes libertatem, et recte ea utentes. Multi etiam mali sunt, qui fiunt magis feri et negligunt divinas et humanas leges, sicut (proh dolor) nostro tempore, videmus, valde multos abusos esse et abuti doctrina de libertate Christiana.

In hac historia Apostoli non retinent traditiones Pharisaeorum, et recte utuntur libertate, et excusantur a Christo, sed Dominus simul monet, quales esse debeant, qui libertate utuntur.

Discatis igitur quid sit libertas Christiana, de qua dicit Dominus: Si vos filius liberaverit, vere liberi eritis. Sciendum est autem quatuor gradus esse libertatis Christianae, quos ordine considerate, et bene mementote.

Prima gratuita remissio et reconciliatio propter Christum per fidem, et iustificatio non propter Legem, sed propter Mediatorem. De hoc gradu ait Paulus: Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia.

Secundus gradus est ipsa in corde liberatio a doloribus inferorum, et inchoatio iustitiae et vitae aeternae per Christum dato Spiritu sancto, iuxta dictum: Ubi est Spiritus Domini, ibi est libertas. Hic gradus est viva et vera consolatio, in qua sentitur auxilium et praesentia Dei, sicut David in exilio sentit consolationem, Laurentius laetatur in ipsa torrefactione, etc.

Hi duo gradus sunt proprie et principalis libertas Christiana, scilicet liberari a peccato, ab ira Dei, a morte aeterna, habere consolationem et laetitiam in omnibus aerumnis, et sentire praesentiam et auxilium Dei. Et haec libertas in hac vita inchoatur in his, qui vere convertuntur ad Deum, et intelligunt Evangelium.

Postea consummabitur in vita aeterna, ubi prorsus erimus liberi a peccato, a morte, et omnibus miseriis, et erit Deus omnia in omnibus, communicans sese nobis et suam sapientiam, iustitiam, vitam aeternam. Hi duo sunt principales gradus, de his proprie loquitur Dominus, cum ait: Si Filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis.

Cogitate quanta res sit liberari a peccato, ab ira Dei, a morte aeterna, et habere praesentem filium Dei in omnibus periculis, consolantem et iuvantem, et haec omnia in vera poenitentia per fidem accipiuntur. Sic David habebat libertatem in fuga.

Sic tres viri in Babylone in fornace habebant libertatem, cum palam apud eos esset filius Dei. Sic Daniel habebat libertatem inter leones, etc.

Hanc libertatem discatis intelligere et eam in vera conversione et quotidiana invocatione considerare. Postea sunt alii gradus de rebus externis.

Est igitur tertius gradus, quod homini Christiano non necesse sit uti politia Mosi, sed potest vivere secundum honestas politias earum gentium, in quibus vivit, ubicunque est, ut Cyrus potuit uti legibus Persicis, Constantinus Romanis. Et tamen fides et invocatio in corde eadem est ad verum Deum, propter filium etc.

Quartus gradus est, scire quod nullae traditiones ab hominibus factae in Ecclesia, sint cultus Dei. Item, quod non sint necessariae, et quod possint omitti sine peccato.

Et de hoc gradu libertatis hic ostendunt exemplum Apostoli, sciunt haec ieiunia instituta a Pharisaeis neque cultus Dei esse, neque opera necessaria esse. Et suo exemplo docent alios, ne putent esse cultus Dei, et ne putent esse opera necessaria.

Sciamus autem regulam, ante hunc quartum gradum oportere esse in nobis duos primos gradus, liberationem a peccato, et fidem quae apprehendit consolationem et praesentiam Dei in nobis. Ubi hi gradus non sunt, multi abutuntur libertate.

Christus igitur docet complectendos esse simul priores gradus et postremum: Non possunt filii sponsi lugere, donec apud eos sponsus est. Significat tunc homines recte uti libertate, quando apud eos est sponsus Christus.

Tunc sunt liberi a peccato, tunc laetantur, laeti invocant et agunt gratias, et non sunt occupati illis stultis ceremoniis humanis. Ista Pharisaica ieiunia non sunt cultus Dei, sed mei discipuli habebunt longe alia ieiunia, scilicet, obedientiam in cruce a Deo praeceptam.

Postea addit admonitionem, quod multi sine prioribus gradibus non recte intelligant libertatem, nec recte ea utantur. Nemo adsuit veteri vesti novum pannum, nemo novum mustum infundit in utres veteres, id est, doctrina de libertate non intelligitur ab hominibus, qui non sunt conversi ad Deum, sed sunt adhuc impii et efferi, non perterrefacti lege Dei.

Tales audito nomine libertatis, magis contemnunt divinas et humanas leges, et fiunt efferi, sicut ursi et aliae bestiae in silvis, sicut manifeste videmus nostro tempore, multos homines prorsus fieri bestiales, abusu libertatis. Et Deus punit hunc tristem abusum multis calamitatibus, bello et expilationibus et aliis malis, quia helluamur et sumus negligentiores in nobis regendis, ideo veniunt plura peccata, et postea bella et aliae poenae.

Haec diligenter consideremus, et discamus recte intelligere libertatem, et recte ea uti.

## 9:18 Sunday XXIV After Trinity
Sunday XXIV after Trinity.

While He was speaking these things with them, behold, a certain ruler came, and worshipped Him, saying: My daughter has just now died, but come, and lay your hand upon her, and she will live. And Jesus, rising, followed him, and the disciples of him. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, coming up from behind, touched the fringe of his garment. For she had said within herself, If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved. But Jesus, turning and seeing her, said: Take heart, daughter, your faith has made you well. And the woman was made well from that hour. And when Jesus had come into the ruler's house, and had seen the flute players and the crowd making a tumult, he says to them: Depart, for the girl is not dead, but sleeps. And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put out, he went in, took her by the hand, and the girl arose. And this report went out into all that land.

There are four points.

I. Concerning the Synagogues. II. Common doctrine concerning miracles. III. Doctrine concerning faith and invocation. IIII. Allegory of the flute players, and others.

Concerning the first.

By a singular counsel, God willed that there be only one tabernacle or temple among the people of Israel, to which legitimate sacrifices, offerings, and slaughters should be made, and at which the high priest was always present, with some college. This arrangement was useful for retaining the concord of doctrine, opinions, and worship. Because diverse temples and diverse pontiffs would have sooner produced diverse worships and diverse opinions, as happened afterwards when Jeroboam and others, with human audacity, founded a new temple, from which discord of doctrine and great errors arose. For concord is more easily retained when the perpetual profession of doctrine is handed down by hands in one place, and doctrine is propagated by certain authority and certain testimonies, and there is always a grave senate as inspector, which considers what is publicly taught; and in that people, a divine promise had been made, that there would always be among these worships, and in this seat, some Church of God and truth. Wherefore, even if often the pontiffs and a great part of the college were impious, yet God preserved some remnants, such as Jeremiah, Simeon, Zechariah, and the like. There was, therefore, one place to which at a certain time all gathered from all the towns, and there they conferred on doctrine. Just as Christ also, as a youth, remained in Jerusalem, disputing about doctrine with the college, even though at that time the Pharisees and Sadducees had extinguished the light of true doctrine.

Although there was one seat, as the inspector and governess of doctrine, yet in all the remaining towns there were Synagogues, that is, established assemblies, not for offerings or slaughters of victims, but only for exercises of doctrine and public prayers. For God willed the voice of the Prophets to sound everywhere. But yet, so that consensus might remain, there was one supreme school as inspector at the temple. I recount these things so that we may recognize that God also wills the studies of doctrine, and that doctrine be propagated by grave authority through some assemblies, and that there be inspectors to retain the concord of doctrine.

Let us consider these things, so that we may be stirred to love, help, and defend the schools in which the Gospel shines, just as it was commanded to the people of Israel that they should defend their temple. Because God always wills that there be some studies of the Church, just as He preserves His own book of the Church, written by the Prophets and Apostles. And therefore He had commanded the tablets of Moses to be placed in the ark, to signify that the doctrine handed down by Him would remain in the Church. There was, therefore, an Archisynagogue in the town of Capernaum, a reader and interpreter of some of the Prophets, who is honored here by a notable miracle. For because few teachers believed in Christ, therefore Christ rewards this man's faith with a singular benefit.

Concerning the second. In one and the same way, we generally speak about miracles, that these three things are to be held concerning miracles.

First, that the wonders universally performed by the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles are testimonies of doctrine, by which God testifies that He is present with these teachers, and that this doctrine is proposed by His will. Just as all the miracles that were performed when the people were being led out of Egypt were testimonies of doctrine, namely, that this voice of the law was truly the voice of God.

Thus, the resurrections of the dead performed by Christ testify that He was sent by God, and that the kind of doctrine is undoubtedly divine. And let these miracles confirm us, so that we may embrace the Gospel and discern it from the doctrine of philosophers and from human opinions.

For although other nations also have certain miracles, yet these are proper to the Church, which no creature can imitate, namely, to restore life to the dead, to stop sun, to make the barren fruitful.

Let us oppose these to the empty deeds which the heathens recount, such as the cutting of the whetstone.

Let this, therefore, always be the primary thought concerning divine miracles: that testimonies concerning doctrine are proposed to us, in which God has so often revealed Himself.

Second doctrine.

The deeds of Christ show in a particular way what the kingdom of the Messiah is like. The Jews were expecting glorious victories, the partitioning of provinces, great wealth, and sweet tranquility, but Christ shows that His benefits are of a different kind: He announces the remission of sins, He promises and initiates eternal life and the restoration of human nature; and in order to show both, that He helps in reality and is the restorer of life, He heals all who ask. As often, therefore, as we think of His deeds, let us think of the perpetual kingdom of Christ, and what benefits He wishes to give to soul and body. Let us know that His kingdom is such even now, that He is always present, remitting sins to those who ask, hearing those who call upon Him, healing, and helping in many great dangers of the body.

Thirdly. Miracles are examples of promises, and applications to individuals. The promise is: Ask, and you shall receive. The examples are this Archisynagogue, the Centurion, the Syrophoenician woman, and all the rest who sought liberation in their distress.

Profane readers think in this way, as if it were about courtly liberality. I see indeed that Christ helps some, but His will is not the same toward all, just as in a court some who are closer to the princes experience liberality, while many others, although they have deserved better, are nevertheless neglected. This comparison must be extirpated from our minds, and the doctrine of promises must be opposed to it, in which these two things should be considered above all: that the promise of grace does not depend on our merits, but bids us look to the merit of Christ, and that the promises are universal: Come to me all you who labor, etc.

1 Tim. 2: God wishes all men to be saved. And Acts 10: There is no respect of persons with God. Let us join these statements with all the examples, and let us gather ourselves into this number of those who ask; let us know that these were helped so that others might be invited.

The Syrophoenician woman, a heathen, was helped, likewise the sinful woman in Luke 7, and the Samaritan woman in John 4. Finally, He Himself says that those who are healthy have no need of a physician.

Let us therefore put aside the human opinion concerning our own dignity and particularity, and let us all approach this high priest, Christ, with confidence in His mercy and His merits.

If you are distressed, like the Archisynagogue or the Syrophoenician woman, approach Christ, and do not dispute about your own merits, but know that this wretched nature has been horribly oppressed by sin, and that we can in no way rely on our own dignity. Acknowledge that God has revealed Himself in His immense goodness, and that He wishes to be invoked by all. No human mind can sufficiently consider and sufficiently value this wondrous counsel of God, that God revealed Himself, that He sent His Son, that He wishes to hear and save us. Let us confess that we are like infants, and do not attain to the magnitude of God's mercy, and that we bring sin and doubts, and that our hearts are not kindled by the knowledge and love of God as they ought to be, and yet let us approach this high priest, Christ, with that weak crowd; let us ask for benefits, and let us be confirmed by the examples of this crowd.

He heard the Syrophoenician woman, therefore He wishes to hear you too; for this reason, in order to invite others, He helped her. Thus Psalm 33 transfers examples to use: Approach Him, and be enlightened. This poor man cried to the Lord, and the Lord heard him, etc. Let this doctrine concerning application be always considered in the third place in miracles.

Third place. Concerning faith and invocation.

This application, of which we have spoken, requires the knowledge of the Gospel in invocation, and of faith. This thought always clamors against us: What great thing do I do, that God should look upon me? I am unclean and guilty; what should I expect from God but punishments? What does God care for my cries, and even if you wish to call upon Him, will He magnify these recitations with which you ask for something?

These doubts always torment the soul. Here it is necessary that we be well fortified with this doctrine concerning invocation, which is the chief part of the Gospel.

But first it must be known that God requires this worship above all things.

Therefore He revealed Himself, that He might be acknowledged. But He cannot be acknowledged without invocation.

Therefore, the command concerning invocation is given so often, as Christ says: Always pray, and do not grow weary. Item: Ask, and you shall receive. If men can give gifts to men, how much more the heavenly Father.

Philip. 4: Be not anxious, but in every prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. Psalm 68: I [direct] my prayer to Thee Lord, time of favor, O God, that is, may that time at last be, when you might wish to deliver me.

Therefore, let the mind first gather the precepts which command us to call upon Him, then let it add the promises: Ask, and you shall receive.

Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give to you. But here, in the promises, our unworthiness soon clamors against us; we have deserved punishments, as David, Manasseh, Samson, and finally many better men were not heard, such as Saul and countless others.

What would become of me? Who am an unclean mass, contaminated in many ways, more so than David, who says: Against you only have I sinned, that is, I am a guilty and cast-off thing, what can I obtain?

This struggle is difficult, but because we are constantly accused by this very voice of the law, let us learn that for this very reason the promises of the Gospel were given, concerning the remission of sins for the sake of the Son.

Although we are unworthy, yet God wishes to receive us for the sake of the Son.

Here the particle 'Freely' must be considered: We are justified freely, by His grace through faith.

We bring to God not merits, but a miserable and contaminated nature, just as David says: Against you only have I sinned.

And Daniel cries out: Not in our righteousness, but in your mercy do we prostrate our prayers.

And: Hear us for the sake of the Lord.

And Jonah: Those who do not flee to mercy, pursue vain things, that is, trust in one's own dignity is empty, but one must flee to mercy.

By this doctrine of the promises, let souls be confirmed, and let them know that it is the command of God that we bring this faith in prayer, and ask with the confidence of the Son, just as it was said: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, that is, naming me as mediator, who carries your prayers, He will give to you.

This doctrine concerning invocation and faith is nowhere known to any people outside the Church, and it has been revealed in the Church of God alone, and is understood only by those who hear and know the Gospel.

And God wishes the doctrine of the Gospel, and His mercy and presence, to become more visible through these exercises of invocation.

Therefore, in all dangers and daily affairs, let us run to this truly sacred anchor.

In the book of Wisdom, invocation is called our shield.

And Paul says: Whatever you do in the name of the Lord, that is, in the invocation of God, do it.

But a great part of mankind rushes on securely, where blind frenzies drag them, it begins and moves many things, without any thought of the judgment of God, without the fear of God, without invocation.

Therefore, miseries are heaped up.

Furthermore, when examples clamor against us, Why is Jeremiah not heard when he prays for help, and many similar things?

Here let faith prudently discern the promise of grace, and of the mitigation of temporal punishments.

It is the command of God that you believe by name that your sins are remitted to you, that you are received by God into the fellowship of eternal life, for the sake of Christ, John 6: This is the will of the Father, that everyone who believes in the Son, may have eternal life.

Whenever, therefore, you invoke, it must be truly established that God receives you, for the sake of the Son, and hears your prayers.

Thus, in every invocation, the Gospel shines forth, concerning repentance, and concerning the remission of sins, and it runs to meet this voice of the law, that God does not hear sinners, namely those persevering in sins, not doing repentance, not fleeing to the Son.

But concerning bodily benefits, let us know that the Church is subject to the cross, and that God demands obedience.

Let faith therefore be retained, that we are received into grace, even when calamity remains.

And yet God demands, not only obedience in afflictions, but also invocation, and He wishes to mitigate or remove miseries, just as He most sweetly says in Psalm 77: He does not kindle all His wrath, etc.

For He wishes His own band to be preserved even in this life.

He wishes some to be unharmed, so that they may sustain the labors of common life, He wishes the studies of the doctrine of the Gospel, polities, and economies to be preserved, for the sake of the propagation of the Gospel.

Finally, He wishes to be celebrated also in the mitigation of punishments and calamities.

Therefore, you ought always in invocation to ask and expect help, and the mitigation of calamity, even if it is not immediately removed, as Jeremiah cries: Correct me, O Lord, but in judgment, not in your fury, lest you reduce me to nothing.

And in the Psalm: The Lord has chastened me, and has not delivered me to death.

Item: I shall not die, but live, and I will announce the works of the Lord.

Therefore, the Lord delivers, so that we may afterwards be witnesses that God hears, and that He truly wishes to be worshipped in this way, and that we may learn and teach others about invocation, as Psalm 85: This poor man cried to the Lord,... and the Lord heard him.

Indeed, for this very reason all the examples of miracles have been proposed from the beginning, so that we may learn that invocation is not in vain.

But the greatest part of mankind, although because of custom calls upon [God] in [his] distress, yet remains in this imagination, that the invocation is void.

This diffidence must be most fiercely resisted, and promises must be opposed [to it], and the heart must be stirred up, so that it may find rest in the contemplation of the promises and believe that the invocation will be profitable, lest we accuse God of falsehood.

Thus Paul says in Rom. 8: The Holy Spirit bears witness to our spirit, in which we cry: Abba, Father.

Jeremiah knew that destruction was coming, but he prayed nonetheless, and he determined that prayer was profitable for mitigation.

Thus David, while in exile, saw that he was being chastised, yet he did not cast away prayer.

For he knew that he was obtaining help and mitigation, and he experienced meanwhile consolations, and new strength in his heart, and such a moderation of events, that he would not be utterly oppressed.

This doctrine concerning invocation and faith must be diligently considered, so that faith may be kindled in daily prayers, and your invocation may be distinguished from that which is heathen, Jewish, and Turkish.

Concerning the fourth [point].

Not all things are to be transformed into allegories, but sometimes facts and examples contain such illustrious images that there is no doubt that something else was signified.

As the offering of Isaac without doubt signified the offering of Christ.

The flood without any doubt signifies the final judgment.

Thus, there are many images of the greatest things throughout all sacred history, but prudence must be applied, lest inconsistent and absurd interpretations and comparisons be produced.

Here, a sufficiently consistent meaning of the Synagogue is the woman suffering from a flow [of blood], who had spent her resources in vain on a cure.

Such was the Church at that time among the Jewish people, which was in great misery, was torn by wars, and was involved in errors, and was unhappily cared for by princes and teachers.

For the teachers, the Pharisees and Sadducees, did not know the Gospel concerning the Messiah and true invocation: the princes, indeed, were entirely Epicureans; they did not care for doctrine and discipline, they only plundered the people, and disturbed the government with foolish tumults.

When the state of the people was such, Christ came and helped this woman, that is, His Church, which He gathered among this people.

Thus also the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is an image of the Church extinct among the people.

She is raised up again by Christ, but Christ is laughed at by the flute players who had been hired for the funeral.

This is an illustrious picture of the wise, who only know the doctrine of the law and of external discipline.

For just as flute players sing funeral songs, so the teachers of the law, without the knowledge of Christ, as if at a funeral, lament human miseries, propose discipline and punishments, and yet they often feel that this doctrine of theirs is overcome by the infirmity of men, and that even if the most perfect doctrine could be obtained: yet the law does not bring consolation concerning the remission of sins, concerning gratuitous reconciliation, concerning eternal life, concerning true invocation.

But it leaves men in doubt and in death, and that discipline is like the apparatus of a funeral.

Heathen governors and philosophers knew the wisdom of the law, whose doctrine, because it does not contain firm consolation concerning the reconciliation of God, is only a sad complaint about human miseries.

Finally, what else is philosophy, if not a consideration of human infirmity, and some kind of bridle restraining overly foolish impulses, and it itself confesses that this whole bridle is weak, and is often torn by the depravity of nature.

It is therefore a funeral complaint, just as Plato says, that Philosophy is a meditation on death, that is, the recognition of our miseries, and the moderation of desires, so that miseries are not increased.

But hypocrites, ignorant of the Gospel, attribute too much to this bridle, they accumulate laws with superstitious opinion, and when they hear the Gospel, which takes away from these observances the praise of justice, and proposes another justice, they think their bonds are being loosened, and they execrate the Gospel, because it seems to weaken the zeal for doing good, to diminish [the honor of] God, and seditiously to undermine the authority of laws.

These opinions in the minds of the wise, who are ignorant of the Gospel, are the causes of most bitter hatred.

For a wise man ought to strive to kindle the zeal for doing good, and to protect the worship of God, and to maintain the modesty of men and tranquility.

These ends a wise governor ought to consider the highest, but in such a way, however, that he understands and protects the true worship of God.

But true worship is not understood without the Gospel; therefore, impious governors, fascinated by the opinions of the law and ignorant of the Gospel, go astray and are inflamed with hatred of the Gospel.

This is signified in this place by the flute players.

But let us learn to distinguish the kinds of doctrines, the law and the Gospel, and let us assign to each kind its own place.

Let the law govern discipline, and let it govern severely.

But at the same time let us know that there is need of another justice, namely, which the Gospel proposes, concerning trust in the Son of God. Let us also avoid the false judgments of hypocrites, and let us not, because of their hatreds, cast away the confession of the Gospel.

Latin:

Dominica XXIIII. post Trinitatis. Evangelium Matth. 9.

Haec cum illis loqueretur, ecce Primas quidam venit, et adoravit eum, dicens: Filia mea modo defuncta est, sed veni, et impone manum tuam super illam, ac vivet. Et surgens Iesus, secutus est eum, ac discipuli illius. Et ecce mulier quae sanguinis profluvio laboraverat duodecim annos, accedens a tergo, tetigit fimbriam vestimenti illius. Dixerat enim intra sese, Si tantum tetigero vestimentum illius, ero salva. At Iesus conversus, ut vidit illam, dixit: Confide filia, fides tua te salvam fecit. Et salva facta fuit mulier a tempore illo. Et cum venisset Iesus in aedes Primatis, vidissetque tibicines et turbam tumultuantem, dicit illis: Secedite, non enim mortua est adolescentula, sed dormit. Et deridebant illum. Cum autem esset eiecta turba, introgressus, tenuit manum illius, et surrexit adolescentula. Et emanavit rumor hic in totam terram illam.

Quatuor sunt loci.

I. De Synagogis. II. Doctrina communis de miraculis. III. Doctrina de fide, et invocatione. IIII. Allegoria tibicinum, et aliae.

De primo.

Singulari consilio Deus in populo Israël, tantum unum esse tabernaculum seu templum voluit, ad quod fierent legitima sacrificia oblationes et mactationes, et ad quod semper praesto erat summus sacerdos, cum aliquo collegio. Haec ordinatio proderat ad retinendam concordiam doctrinae, opinionum et cultuum. Quia diversa templa, diversi pontifices citius peperissent diversos cultus et diversas opiniones, sicut postea accidit, quando Ieroboam et alii humana audacia condiderunt novum templum, hinc discordia doctrinae, et magni errores orti sunt. Facilius enim retinetur concordia, cum in uno loco perpetua doctrinae professio per manus traditur, et propagatur doctrina certa autoritate et certis testimoniis, et semper est gravis senatus inspector, qui considerat, quid publice doceatur, et in illo populo promissio divina facta erat, semper apud hos cultus, et in hac sede futuram aliquam Dei Ecclesiam, et veritatem. Quare etiam si saepe pontifices et magna pars collegii erat impia, tamen Deus servavit aliquas reliquias, ut Ieremiam, Simeonem, Zachariam, et similes. Erat igitur unus locus, ad quem certo tempore omnes conveniebant ex omnibus oppidis, et ibi doctrinam conferebant. Sicut et Christus adolescens mansit Hierosolymis, de doctrina disputans cum collegio, etsi tunc quidem Pharisaei et Sadducaei extinxerant lucem verae doctrinae.

Quanquam autem una sedes erat, tanquam inspectrix et gubernatrix doctrinae, tamen in omnibus oppidis reliquis Synagogae erant, id est, conventus instituti, non ad oblationes aut mactationes hostiarum, sed tantum ad exercitia doctrinae et publicas precationes. Voluit enim Deus ubique sonare vocem Prophetarum. Sed tamen ut maneret consensus, erat una summa schola inspectrix ad templum. Haec ideo recito, ut agnoscamus Deum velle etiam studia doctrinae, et gravi autoritate, per coetus aliquos, propagari doctrinam, et esse inspectores, ad retinendam doctrinae concordiam.

Haec consideremus, ut excitemur ad amandas, juvandas et tuendas scholas, in quibus Evangelium lucet, sicut populo Israël mandatum erat, ut suum templum tuerentur. Quia semper vult Deus aliqua esse Ecclesiae studia, sicut servat suum librum Ecclesiae, scriptum per Prophetas et Apostolos. Ideoque mandaverat imponi tabulas Moisi in arcam, ut significaret in Ecclesia mansuram esse doctrinam a se traditam. Fuit igitur Archisynagogus in oppido Capernaum, lector et interpres quispiam Prophetarum, qui ornatur hic insigni miraculo. Quia enim pauci doctores credebant Christo, ideo huius fidem Christus singulari beneficio remunerat.

De secundo. Uno et eodem modo plerumque de miraculis dicimus, tria haec de miraculis tenenda esse.

Primum universaliter facta Prophetarum, Christi et Apostolorum miranda, esse testimonia de doctrina, quibus Deus testatur, se adesse his docentibus, et hanc doctrinam sua voluntate proponi. Ut miracula omnia, quae facta sunt, cum populus educeretur ex Aegypto, testimonia erant doctrinae, videlicet, hanc vocem legis vere esse vocem Dei.

Sic resuscitationes mortuorum factae a Christo, testantur eum a Deo missum esse, et genus doctrinae haud dubie divinum esse. Nosque haec miracula confirment, ut amplectamur Evangelium, et discernamus a philosophorum doctrina, et ab humanis opinionibus.

Quanquam enim et aliae gentes quaedam miracula habent, tamen haec sunt propria Ecclesiae, quae nulla creatura imitari potest, scilicet, reddere vitam mortuis, sistere solem, foecundas facere anus.

Haec opponamus inanibus factis, quae narrant Ethnici, ut de dissecta cote.

Sit igitur semper haec de miraculis divinis prima cogitatio, testimonia de doctrina nobis proponi, in quibus toties se Deus patefecit.

Secunda doctrina.

Christi facta peculiariter ostendunt, quale sit regnum Messiae. Iudaei expectabant gloriosas victorias, partitiones provinciarum, magnas opes et dulcem tranquillitatem, sed Christus ostendit sua beneficia alterius generis esse: annunciat remissionem peccatorum, pollicetur et inchoat vitam aeternam, et instaurationem humanae naturae, et ut ostendat utrunque, se et re opitulari, et esse instauratorem vitae, sanat omnes petentes. Quoties igitur eius facta cogitamus, de perpetuo regno Christi cogitemus, quae beneficia dare velit animae et corporis. Sciamus tale esse nunc quoque eius regnum, semper eum adesse, remittere peccata petentibus, exaudire invocantes, sanare, iuvare in multis magnis periculis corporum.

Tertio. Miracula sunt exempla promissionum, et applicationes ad singulos. Promissio est: Petite, et accipietis. Exempla sunt, hic Archisynagogus, Centurio, Syrophoenissa, et reliqui omnes, qui in suis aerumnis liberationem petiverunt.

Prophani lectores sic cogitant, ut de liberalitate aulica. Video quidem Christum aliquibus opitulari, sed non est similis voluntas erga omnes, ut in aula liberalitatem experiuntur aliqui propiores principibus, multi alii, quamvis melius meriti, tamen negliguntur. Haec collatio ex animis extirpanda est, et opponenda doctrina promissionum, in quibus praecipue haec duo considerentur, quod promissio gratiae non pendet ex nostris meritis, sed iubet intueri meritum Christi, et quod promissiones sint universales: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis etc.

1. Tim. 2.: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri. Et Act. 10.: Non est acceptio personarum apud Deum. Has sententias coniungamus omnibus exemplis, et nos ipsos ad hunc numerum petentium aggregemus, sciamus ideo hos adintos esse, ut caeteri invitentur.

Adiuta est Syrophoenissa ethnica mulier, item mulier peccatrix Luc. 7. et mulier Samaritana Iohan. 4. Denique ipse dicit, sanis non esse opus medico. Deponamus igitur humanam opinionem de nostra dignitate et de particularitate, et ad hunc pontificem accedamus omnes fiducia misericordiae, et meritorum ipsius.

Si angeris, ut Archisynagogus aut Syrophoenissa, accede ad Christum, nec disputa de tuis meritis, sed scito, hanc miseram naturam horribiliter oppressam esse peccato, et nequaquam nos posse nostra dignitate niti. Agnosce Deum se patefecisse immensa sua bonitate, et velle invocari ab omnibus. Nulla mens humana hoc mirandum Dei consilium satis considerare, et satis magni aestimare potest, quod Deus se patefecit, quod misit Filium, quod vult nos exaudire et servare.

Fateamur nos infantum esse similes, et non assequi magnitudinem misericordiae Dei, et adferre peccatum ac dubitationes, nec accensa esse corda agnitione et dilectione Dei, ut debebant, et accedamus tamen ad hunc pontificem Christum, cum illa imbecilli turba, petamus beneficia, et confirmemur exemplis huius turbae.

Exaudiit Syrophoenissam, ergo te quoque vult exaudire, ideo enim, ut caeteros invitet, illam adiuvit. Sic Psal. 33. exempla ad usum transfert: Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini. Iste pauper clamavit ad Dominum, et Dominus exaudivit eum etc. Haec doctrina de applicatione tertio loco semper in miraculis consideretur.

Tertius locus. De fide et invocatione.

Haec applicatio, de qua diximus, requirit cognitionem Evangelii invocatione, et de fide. Semper obstrepit nobis haec cogitatio: Quid facio magni, ut Deus me respiciat: sum immundus et reus, quid expectem a Deo, nisi poenas, quid curat Deus meos clamores, etiamsi velis eum invocare, an magnificiet istas recitationes, quibus aliquid petis?

Hae dubitationes semper cruciant animos. Hic oportet nos bene munitos esse hac doctrina de invocatione, quae est Evangelii praecipua.

Primum autem sciendum est, quod Deus hunc cultum omnium maxime requirat. Ideo se patefecit, ut agnoscatur.

Non potest autem agnosci sine invocatione. Ideo toties praecipitur de invocatione, ut Christus inquit: Semper orate, et non defatigemini.

Item: Petite, et accipietis. Si homines possunt dare dona hominibus, quanto magis pater coelestis.

Philip. 4.: Non sitis solliciti, sed in omni precatione et petitione, cum gratiarum actione postulationes vestrae notae fiant Deo. Psalm. 68.: Ego orationem meam ad te Domine, tempus beneplaciti Deus, id est, sit aliquando illud tempus, quod velis me liberare.

Primum igitur colligat mens praecepta, quae iubent invocare, deinde et promissiones addat: Petite, et accipietis. Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis.

Sed hic in promissionibus mox obstrepit nobis indignitas nostra, sumus meriti poenas, ut David, Manasses, Samson, denique multi meliores non sunt exauditi, ut Saul, et alii innumerabiles.

Quid de me fieret? qui sum massa immunda, contaminata multipliciter, magis quam David, qui inquit: Tibi tantum peccatum sum, id est, res rea et abiecta, quid impetrare possum?

Difficile est hoc certamen, sed quia hac ipsa voce legis assidue accusamur, discamus hanc ipsam ob causam promissiones Evangelii traditas esse, de remissione peccatorum propter Filium.

Quanquam sumus indigni, tamen Deus vult nos propter Filium recipere.

Hic cogitanda est particula Gratis: Iustificamur gratis, per gratiam eius fide.

Afferimus ad Deum non merita, sed miseram et contaminatam naturam, sicut David dicit: Tibi tantum sum peccatum.

Et Daniel clamat: Non in iusticia nostra, sed misericordia tua prosternimus preces nostras.

Et: Exaudi nos propter Dominum.

Et Ionas: Qui non confugiunt ad misericordiam, sectantur vana, id est, fiducia propriae dignitatis est inanis, sed confugiendum est ad misericordiam.

Hac doctrina promissionum confirmentur animi, et sciant mandatum Dei esse, ut hanc fidem in precatione afferamus, ac petamus fiducia Filii, sicut dictum est: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, id est, me nominantes mediatorem, perferentem preces vestras, dabit vobis.

Haec doctrina de invocatione et fide nusquam ulli genti extra Ecclesiam nota est, ac in sola Ecclesia Dei patefacta est, et tantum ab iis intelligitur, qui audiunt et norunt Evangelium.

Vultque Deus nobis Evangelii doctrinam, et suam misericordiam et praesentiam, fieri conspectiorem his exercitiis invocationis.

Ideo in omnibus periculis et quotidianis negotiis decurramus ad hanc vere sacram ancoram.

In libro Sapientiae invocatio vocatur scutum nostrum.

Et Paulus inquit: Quicquid facitis in nomine Domini, id est, invocatione Dei, facite.

Sed magna pars hominum secura ruit, quo coeci furores trahunt, multa incipit ac movet, sine ulla cogitatione de iudicio Dei, sine timore Dei, sine invocatione.

Ideo aerumnae cumulantur.

Porro cum obstrepunt exempla, Cur non exauditur Hieremias deprecans auxilium, et similia multa?

Hic fides prudenter discernat promissionem gratiae, et mitigationis poenarum temporalium.

Mandatum Dei est, ut nominatim credas tibi remitti peccata, recipi te a Deo ad societatem vitae aeternae, propter Christum, Iohan. 6.: Haec ect voluntas patris, ut omnis qui credit in Filium, habeat vitam aeternam.

Quandocunque igitur invocas, vere statuendum est, quod Deus te recipiat, propter Filium, et tuas preces audiat.

Sic in omni invocatione praelucet Evangelium, de poenitentia, et de remissione peccatorum, et uccurrit huic voci legis, Deus peccatores non exaudit, scilicet perseverantes in peccatis, non agentes poenitentiam, non confugientes ad Filium.

Sed de beneficiis corporalibus sciamus, Ecclesiam subiectam esse cruci, et Deum postulare obedientiam.

Retineatur igitur fides, quod recipiamur in gratiam, etiam cum manet calamitas.

Et tamen postulat Deus, non solum obedientiam in afflictionibus, sed etiam invocationem, et vult mitigare aut tollere aerumnas, sicut dulcissime inquit Psal. 77.: Non accendit totam iram suam etc.

Vult enim servari et in hac vita suum aliquod agmen.

Vult esse aliquos incolumes, ut communis vitae labores sustineant, vult conservari studia doctrinae Evangelii, politias, oeconomias, propter propagationem Evangelii.

Denique vult et in mitigatione poenarum et calamitatum celebrari.

Ideo semper in invocatione petere et expectare debes auxilium, et mitigationem calamitatis, etiamsi non statim tollitur, ut clamat Ieremias: Corripe me Domine, veruntamen in iudicio, non in furore tuo, ne ad nihilum redigas me.

Et in Psalm.: Castigans castigavit me Dominus, et morti non tradidit me.

Item: Non moriar, sed vivam, et annunciabo opera Domini.

Ideo liberat Dominus, ut postea testes simus, quod exaudiat Deus, et vere sic velit coli, et discamus ac doceamus alios de invocatione, ut Psal. 85.: Iste pauper clamavit ad Dominum, et Dominus exaudivit eum.

Imo hanc ipsam ob causam omnia exempla miraculorum, inde usque ab initio proposita sunt, ut discamus invocationem non esse irritam.

Sed maxima pars hominum, quamvis propter consuetudinem invocat, tamen manet in hac imaginatione, invocationem esse irritam.

Huic diffidentiae acerrime repugnandum est, et opponendae sunt promissiones, et excitandum cor, ut acquiescat cogitatione promissionum et credat profuturam invocationem, ne accusemus Deum mendacii.

Ita Paulus inquit Rom. 8.: Spiritus sanctus testimonium dat spiritui nostro, in quo clamamus: Abba pater.

Sciebat Ieremias venturum esse excidium, sed orabat tamen, ac statuebat orationem prodesse ad mitigationem.

Ita David exulans castigari se videbat, neque tamen abiiciebat precationem.

Sciebat enim se impetrare auxilium et mitigationem, et experiebatur interim consolationes, et novum robur in corde, et talem moderationem eventuum, ne penitus opprimeretur.

Haec doctrina de invocatione et fide diligenter consideranda est, ut accendatur fides in quotidianis precibus, et discernatur invocatio vestra ab ethnica, Iudaica et Turcica.

De quarto.

Non sunt omnia in allegorias transformanda, sed interdum facta ac exempla, adeo illustres imaginationes continent, ut non dubium sit, aliud quiddam significatum esse.

Ut oblatio Isaac sine dubio significabat oblationem Christi.

Diluvium sine ulla dubitatione significat ultimum iudicium.

Sic passim multae sunt imagines maximarum rerum in tota sacra historia, sed prudentia adhibenda est, ne interpretationes et collationes inconcinnae et absurdae gignantur.

Hic satis concinna significatio Synagogae est mulier laborans fluxu, quae suas facultates in curatione frustra impenderat.

Talis tunc fuit Ecclesia in populo Iudaico, quae erat in magnis miseriis, lacerabatur bellis, et versabatur in erroribus, et infeliciter a principibus et doctoribus curabatur.

Nam doctores, Pharisaei et Sadducaei, non norant Evangelium de Messia et de vera invocatione: principes vero prorsus erant Epicurei, doctrinam et disciplinam non curabant, tantum expilabant populum, et stultis tumultibus perturbabant gubernationem.

Talis cum esset populi status, venit Christus, et opitulatur huic mulieri, id est, suae Ecclesiae, quam in hoc populo collegit.

Sic et Archisynagogi filia imago est Ecclesiae extinctae in populo.

Haec rursus excitatur per Christum, sed ridetur Christus a tibicinibus, qui ad funus conducti erant.

Haec est illustris pictura sapientum, qui tantum norunt doctrinam legis et disciplinae externae.

Sicuti enim tibicines canunt funebria carmina, ita doctores legis, sine agnitione Christi, tanquam in funere deplorant miserias humanas, proponunt disciplinam et poenas, et tamen sentiunt saepe vinci hanc suam doctrinam infirmitate hominum, et ut maxime obtineri perfectissima doctrina posset: tamen lex non adfert consolationem de remissione peccatorum, de reconciliatione gratuita, de vita aeterna, de vera invocatione.

Sed relinquit homines in dubitatione et in morte, et disciplina illa est veluti apparatus funeris.

Norant ethnici gubernatores et philosophi sapientiam legis, quorum doctrina, quia non continet firmam consolationem de reconciliatione Dei, tantum est tristis querela de miseriis humanis.

Denique quid aliud est philosophia, nisi consideratio humanae infirmitatis, et qualecunque frenum nimis stolidos impetus coërcens, et fatetur ipsa, totum hoc frenum infirmum esse, et saepe lacerari naturae pravitate.

Est igitur querela funebris, sicuti Plato dicit, Philosophiam esse meditationem mortis, id est, agnitionem nostrarum miseriarum, et moderationem cupiditatum, ne augeantur miseriae.

Sed hypocritae ignari Evangelii, nimium tribuunt huic freno, cumulant leges superstitiosa opinione, cumque audiunt Evangelium, quod detrahit his observationibus laudem iusticiae, et proponit aliam iusticiam, putant laxari sua vincula, et Evangelium execrantur, quod videatur languefacere studium bene operandi, diminuere Dei, et seditiose labefactare legum autoritatem.

Hae opiniones in animis sapientium, qui ignorant Evangelium, sunt causae acerbissimi odii.

Nam homo sapiens contendere debet, ut accendat studium bene operandi, et cultus Dei tueatur, et modestiam hominum et tranquillitatem retineat.

Hos fines debet sapiens gubernator summos ducere, sed ita tamen, ut veros cultus Dei intelligat et tueatur.

Veri autem cultus non intelliguntur sine Evangelio, ideo impii gubernatores fascinati opinionib. legis et ignari Evangelii, aberrant, et inflammantur odio Evangelii.

Id hoc loco per tibicines significatum est.

Nos vero discamus discernere genera doctrinarum, legem et Evangelium, et tribuamus suum cuique generi locum.

Lex regat disciplinam, et severe regat.

Sed simul sciamus alia iusticia opus esse, videlicet, quam Evangelium proponit, de fiducia Filii Dei. Vitemus etiam falsa iudicia hypocritarum, nec propter eorum odia, confessionem Evangelii abiiciamus.

## 9:18 Sermons on Matthew
While he was speaking these things to them, behold, a certain ruler came and worshipped him, saying: Lord, my daughter is just now dead, etc.

First, let the doctrine concerning the causes of miracles be recited. In the beginning, God revealed Himself through ordinary works. And ordinary works are always a testimony of God to individual men, now also and at all times. Besides these, He revealed Himself through extraordinary works for these four causes.

I. That miracles may be testimonies that God is a free essence not bound to nature, omnipotent, which can save even against the order of nature.

II. That they may be testimonies concerning doctrine, that this doctrine in the Church is most truly from God.

III. They are examples of spiritual and bodily promises, and just as God, having heard the word, commands us to ask and receive spiritual and bodily goods through faith, so He commands by these very examples that we ask and believe that we are helped, because the examples are illustrious testimonies of the word.

IIII. The cause, that they may teach us about application, that application is made by faith, not on account of our merits, and that there is no respect of persons in God, but that He receives Jews and Gentiles, and demands faith, and does not receive on account of our merits.

These causes are known, and let us always know that the Church has miracles not imitable by the Devils, namely, the resuscitation of the dead.

Christ raised three dead persons. In the first year, the widow's son. In the second year, the daughter of Jairus. In the third year, Lazarus. These examples are testimonies of the doctrine, and at the same time they teach that the Messiah is the Lord of life, and can and will restore life, and was sent to restore eternal life, according to the saying: O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy plague.

In Luke, the temptations of Jairus are described; the servants come to him and say the girl is dead, but the Lord commands him to believe. Thus, let us not be broken by impediments.

Finally, also consider this, what a beautiful government there was in Capernaum at that time. Christ was a citizen there, and his friends were the Roman captain and the pastor Jairus, and undoubtedly these made use of Christ's counsel in many great matters. Thus that town was truly Capernaum, that is, Schöndorff. Thus think that it must be asked of God that there be such a government among us, that pastors and princes and captains may be friends of Christ.

Other miracles follow soon in the same chapter, concerning which the same doctrine should always be considered as you have just heard concerning miracles, and they can be briefly repeated.

At the end is a general saying concerning the ministry of the Gospel. And three sayings are placed: First, concerning the misery of the Church, that the Church is languid, and like sheep which do not have a shepherd.

II. The saying that the harvest is great; this is a sweet consolation, that nevertheless many are elect, and the labor of those who teach is not in vain.

III. Concerning prayer, that God may send salutary teachers.

This whole doctrine concerning the ministry must be thought upon often and much, and thanks must be given to God, because in His immense goodness He sent His son, and instituted and preserves the ministry, because thus and not otherwise He gathers and preserves the Church, namely by the voice of the Gospel. Nor must one think: What is weaker than these miserable men who teach the Gospel? but it must be known that the son of God himself is powerful, who began this ministry, and is always effective in it. And thus he says: As the father sent me, so I send you. Likewise: I will be with you even unto the consummation of the age. Likewise: He sits at the right hand of the eternal Father, giving gifts to men, Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors, Doctors, etc. Let us know, therefore, that we ought to believe the voice of the Gospel, and let us know that God himself is truly effective through the Gospel, as it is said: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Against these, Stenckefeld and the Anabaptists furiously cry out, who are ungrateful to God; they say that the vocal word, or the contemplation of the written word, etc., profits nothing.

Now concerning those three members.

The Church is like sheep without a shepherd; the complaint is that, very often and in many places, suitable pastors are lacking, and tyrants drive away suitable pastors, and the teachers themselves contend with ambitions and hatreds, disturb the Churches, etc. These evils are in sight, nor is there need for a long declaration.

II. Consolation that there is a great harvest, that is, many elect; truly we have need of this consolation, because in this great human malice, very few seem to be elect, just as Elias complains, and Esaias says: Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have been as Sodom and Gomorrah.

But God consoles Elias, and Paul says: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord. And the Lord says: You will bear abundant fruit, John 15. And your fruit will remain, etc. Let us all diligently consider this consolation, in this sad confusion of the world and of kingdoms.

III. Prayer; you see it is a divine command that we should pray, that God may gather the Church, give suitable ministers, and preserve the Church, just as the Son of God himself prays assiduously. Let the prayer of the Son of God, spoken before his agony, be repeated, John 17.

Latin:

Haec illo loquente ad eos, ecce princeps unus accessit et adorabat eum, dicens: Domine, filia mea modo defuncta est, etc.

Primum recitetur doctrina de causis miraculorum. Deus initio patefecit se ordinariis operibus. Et semper ordinaria opera sunt testimonium de Deo singulis hominibus, nunc quoque et omni tempore. Praeter haec patefecit se extraordinariis operibus propter has quatuor causas.

I. Ut miracula sint testimonia, quod Deus sit essentia libera non alligata naturae, omnipotens, quae potest servare etiam contra naturae ordinem.

II. Ut sint testimonia de doctrina, quod haec doctrina in Ecclesia verissime sit a Deo.

III. Sunt exempla promissionum spiritualium et corporalium, et sicut Deus nos audito verbo, iubet petere et accipere per fidem spiritualia et corporalia bona, ita iubet ipsis exemplis, ut petamus et credamus nos iuvari, quia exempla sunt illustria testimonia verbi.

IIII. Causa, ut doceant nos de applicatione, quod fide fiat applicatio, non propter nostra merita, et quod in Deo non sit acceptio personarum, sed quod recipiat Iudaeos et Ethnicos, et postulet fidem, non recipiat propter nostra merita.

Hae causae sunt notae, et semper sciamus, quod Ecclesia habet miracula non imitabilia Diabolis, scilicet resuscitationem mortuorum.

Christus tres mortuos resuscitavit. Primo anno viduae filium. Secundo anno filiam Iairi. Tertio anno Lazarum. Haec exempla sunt testimonia doctrinae, et simul docent, quod Messias sit Dominus vitae, et possit et velit restituere vitam, et sit missus ut restituat vitam aeternam, iuxta dictum: O mors ero mors tua, o inferne, ero pestis tua.

In Luca describuntur tentationes Iairi, veniunt ad eum domestici, et dicunt puellam mortuam esse, sed Dominus iubet eum credere. Ita nos non frangamur impedimentis.

Postremo etiam hoc considerate, quam pulcrum regimen fuerit in Capernaum illo tempore. Christus fuit ibi civis, et fuerunt eius amici capitaneus Romanus, et pastor Iairus, et haud dubie hi de multis magnis rebus usi sunt consilio Christi. Sic erat illud oppidum vere Capernaum, id est, Schöndorff. Ita cogitate a Deo petendum esse, ut sit tale regimen inter nos, ut pastores et principes et capitanei sint amici Christi.

Sequuntur mox et alia miracula in eodem capite, de quibus eadem doctrina semper consideretur, quam de miraculis proxime audivistis, et possunt breviter repeti.

In fine est dictum generale de ministerio Evangelii. Et ponuntur tria dicta: Primum de miseria Ecclesiae, quod Ecclesia sit languida, et similis ovibus, quae non habent pastorem.

II. Dictum, quod messis magna sit, haec est dulcis consolatio, quod tamen multi sint electi, et non sit irritus labor docentium.

III. De precatione, ut Deus mittat doctores salutares.

Haec tota doctrina de ministerio saepe et multum cogitanda est, et agendae Deo gratiae, quod immensa bonitate misit filium, et instituit et servat ministerium, quia sic et non aliter colligit et servat Ecclesiam, videlicet voce Evangelii. Nec est cogitandum: Quid est infirmius his miseris hominibus, qui docent Evangelium? sed sciendum est, ipsum filium Dei potentem esse, qui inchoavit hoc ministerium, et semper in eo est efficax. Et sic dicit: Sicut misit me pater, sic ego mitto vos. Item: Ego ero vobiscum usque ad consummationem seculi. Item: Sedet ad dexteram aeterni Patris, dans dona hominibus, Apostolos, Prophetas, Evangelistas, Pastores, Doctores etc. Sciamus ergo nos debere credere voci Evangelii, et sciamus ipsum Deum vere efficacem esse per Evangelium, sicut dictum est: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Contra haec furenter clamat Stenckefeld et Anabaptistae, qui sunt ingrati Deo, dicunt nihil prodesse verbum vocale, aut cogitationem verbi scripti, etc.

Iam de tribus illis membris.

Ecclesia est sicut oves sine pastore, querela est, saepissime et in multis locis desunt idonei pastores et tyranni pellunt idoneos pastores, et doctores ipsi certant ambitionibus et odiis, turbant Ecclesias, etc. Haec mala sunt in conspectu, nec opus est longa declaratione.

II. Consolatio quod multa messis sit, id est, multi electi, profecto hac consolatione nobis opus est, quia in hac tanta malitia humana, paucissimi videntur esse electi, sicut Elias queritur, et Esaias inquit: Nisi Dominus reliquisset nobis semen, sicut Sodoma et Gomorra essemus.

Sed Deus consolatur Eliam, et Paulus inquit: Labor vester non erit inanis in Domino. Et Dominus inquit: Copiosum fructum feretis, Iohann. 15. Et fructus vester manebit etc. Hanc consolationem diligenter cogitemus omnes, in hac tristi confusione mundi et regnorum.

III. Precatio, videtis mandatum divinum esse, ut petamus, ut Deus colligat Ecclesiam, det idoneos ministros, et servet Ecclesiam, sic filius Dei ipse petit assidue. Repetatur precatio filii Dei ante agonem dicta Iohann. 17.

## 10:1 Sermons on Matthew: Argument
Chapter X.

And calling his twelve disciples, etc. Here, and after the resurrection, the calling of the Apostles is described, because God wants us to be certain about the doctrine, he wants us to know through whom and how it has been propagated, just as he has called Prophets from the beginning, and we have often said elsewhere what Prophets, Apostles, Pastors, and Doctors are.

And first it is well to be noted, what is written in Luke 6, that Christ remained on the mountain in prayer for the whole night before this election of the Apostles.

Now let us consider how great a work the Lord himself judged it to be, to send certain doctors; he asked the eternal Father that he himself might govern them, just as he also prays in his agony: Sanctify them in truth, your word is truth, etc. Thus let us pray that suitable ministers be given.

II. Let us consider, however, the immense benefits of God, and let us give thanks to God.

God calls Ministers in two ways: immediately and mediately.

Immediately, the Prophets and Apostles, and he adds testimonies to them, so that we may be certain.

Mediately, through the Church, other Pastors and Doctors, who ought to hand down the doctrine delivered through the Prophets and Apostles without any change.

In both callings, the Son of God is effective, as is said in Ephesians 4, and Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes.

III. After he called them and added the power of performing miracles, so that the doctrine might have testimonies, he also delivered commands, where and what they ought to teach.

Not among the Gentiles, because God first wished to gather the Church in Israel. Afterward, however, among the Gentiles after three years; in the meantime, however, many from the Gentiles were also converted.

What ought they to teach? Just as he says elsewhere: Repent and believe the Gospel, and here he says: The kingdom of heaven is at hand. What does he name the kingdom of heaven? The kingdom promised on account of the Son of God, in which sin and death will be blotted out, and righteousness and eternal life will be restored. This kingdom is begun in this life by the preaching of the Gospel, repentance, and faith; after the resurrection, righteousness and eternal life will be consummated, in which God will be all in all, and we shall be without sin and death.

Thus he says elsewhere: Go, preaching repentance and remission in my name.

IV. Concerning defense. When something new is instituted, when legates are sent, it is necessary for them to have provisions and defense. And to wish to make a change in the whole world through the Apostles, and indeed while the Roman Empire was flourishing, the matter seems to be impossible. Therefore, Christ first confirms the Apostles here, he promises them defense and provisions, just as he says elsewhere: I will be with you even to the consummation of the age. Item, John 15: I chose you, that you might go and bear fruit, and your fruit might remain. And here he says: I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves, but all the hairs of your head are numbered.

And first concerning provisions he says: Do not possess gold in your belts, nor shoes, etc.

Here some fanatical men have argued that Pastors and other preachers ought to have nothing of their own, and they make a singular worship of God out of not having property.

Christ does not say this, that it is not permitted to have property, but he speaks of the fact, that it so happens. Pious doctors do not have riches and defense. And he adds consolation, so that they do not abandon their office because they do not have defense and riches, and he promises that he will take care that they nevertheless have lodging and food. lodging and food.

Such is the Church; wherever it is in the world, it has a lodging which God protects, and it has no human defense. Therefore it is said in Isaiah: I will give you a teacher and bread and water, with tribulation.
