Just as a mustard seed is small, and yet produces a large body and leaves, and has a sharp power for cleansing, so the voice of the Gospel is something despised before the world, and yet it effectively gathers an eternal Church for God, and is the instrument by which eternal life is begun in us.

Here let an antithesis be made.

The Jews understood the promises concerning a political kingdom.

Christ says the contrary, that this kingdom is to be gathered by the word.

And here let us learn against the Enthusiasts the doctrine of the efficacy of the word.

First, let us learn that the voice of the Gospel is not empty, but that some are always converted by it, indeed all who assent to it.

Second, let us learn to acquiesce in the promises, and let us hold this rule, that God can neither be seen, nor apprehended otherwise, except by the contemplation of this word.

Whenever we call upon him, minds ask where God is, and who God is, and they would gladly address the true God, not to stray from the true God, not to address anything else, which is not God.

In this contemplation and temptation, the mind looks at the word and the testimonies, through which God has revealed himself, and you think that this is the true God, who has handed down this Gospel to the Church, who has testified by the resurrection of the dead, that he is to give this voice and these promises, address this God and you think.

Third, let the similitude also be considered.

Just as mustard is sharp, and purges the brain, so the Gospel bites false opinions, and depraved desires.

Latin:

Cum dormientes homines etc.

In priore parabola dixit qualis sit Ecclesia, et iam plantavit Ecclesiam. Nunc de plantata dicit, quas habeat tentationes, et monet, semper in Ecclesia bonos et malos mixtos esse.

Haec doctrina necessaria est, quia saepe accidit, sicut in regno Monasteriensi, ubi volebant facere Ecclesiam, in qua nulli essent peccatores. Sed tales postea eo delabuntur, ut nullos recipiant, nisi suos adulatores, et hos fingunt sanctos esse, etiamsi sunt pessimi nebulones. Sit ergo haec doctrina ex hac similitudine, quod in hac vita, usque ad resurrectionem mansura sit Ecclesia Dei, et quod semper in ea sint mixti boni et mali.

Quid igitur dicis de excommunicatione? An non sunt excommunicandi mali?

Respondeo: Illi qui vivunt in manifestis delictis, si non velint agere poenitentiam, sunt excommunicandi.

Sed praeter hos tamen adhuc multi manent hypocritae, et variis vitiis laborantes, qui tolerandi sunt, sed assidue praedicamus poenitentiam, ut aliqui convertantur.

Quare igitur dicit? Sinite utraque crescere.

Primum refutat opinionem Apostolorum de mundano regno Messiae.

Nam et Apostoli sperabant talem pulcrum statum fore, ut domitis et deletis omnibus impiis, soli una viverent sancti, in hac mortali vita etc. Reprehendit ergo eos, et docet Ecclesiam non fore regnum mundanum, et non vult, ut Apostoli gerant gladium, aut gladio puniant delinquentes.

Sed contra manifesta delicta tradit alibi excommunicationem.

Postea tamen multa vitia manent.

Hic sciamus non propterea nullam esse Ecclesiam, etiam permixti sunt bonis multi mali.

Haec doctrina consolatio utilis est, quia multi nunc quoque propter multa scandala clamitant: Si Lutherani essent Ecclesia, nulli essent inter eos adulteri, ebriosi, fures, etc.

Adversus hoc scandalum scias, Ecclesiam quaerendam esse ibi, ubi sonat vox Evangelii, et nusquam alibi.

Nec deterreat te, etiamsi non omnes convertuntur, etc. quia nusquam est Ecclesia Dei, nisi in coetu vocatorum, id est, ubi sonat vera vox Evangelii.

Rom. 8.: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit etc.

Tertia parabola.

Simile est regnum coelorum grano sinapis.

Summa est concionis, et similitudinis, de ministerio Evangelii et eius effectibus.

Sicut granum sinapis est parvum, et tamen gignit magnum corpus et folia, et acrem vim habet ad purgandum, sic vox Evangelii est quiddam spretum coram mundo, et tamen est res efficacissima, colligit Deo aeternam Ecclesiam, et est instrumentum, quo in nobis inchoatur vita aeterna.

Hic fiat antithesis.

Iudaei intelligebant promissiones de regno politico.

Christus contra dicit, hoc regnum verbo colligendum esse.

Et hic discamus contra Enthusiastas doctrinam de efficacia verbi.

Primum discamus quod vox Evangelii non sit inanis, sed semper aliqui per eam convertantur, imo omnes, qui ei assentiuntur.

Secundo discamus acquiescere in propositionibus, et teneamus hanc regulam, quod Deus nec cerni, nec adprehendi aliter possit, nisi cogitatione huius verbi.

Quandocunque invocamus, quaerunt mentes ubi sit Deus, et quis sit Deus, et libenter vellent compellare verum Deum, non aberrare a vero Deo, non alloqui aliud, quod non est Deus.

In hac cogitatione et tentatione mens intuetur verbum et testimonia, per quae Deus se patefecit, et cogites hunc esse verum Deum, qui hoc Evangelium Ecclesiae tradidit, qui resuscitatione mortuorum testatus est, se edere hanc vocem et has promissiones, hunc Deum alloqui te cogites.

Tertio, similitudo etiam consideretur.

Sicut sinapi est mordax, et purgat cerebrum, ita Evangelium mordet falsas opiniones, et pravas cupiditates.

## 13:33 Sermons on Matthew
The kingdom of heaven is like leaven.

The same argument is concerning the ministry of the Gospel, and its efficacy.

And again let the antithesis be considered.

The Jews expect a political kingdom, but Christ opposes another form.

Indeed, he says, it will be such a kingdom, in which the hearts of men will be changed by the word.

Here also let these two be considered, first that the voice of the Gospel is not an empty thing, but that it is truly efficacious, and that some are always converted by it.

Indeed all who assent to it.

Second, let us learn what the effect is.

The Gospel is signified in this place by leaven.

And just as leaven is mixed with flour, and inflates the bread, so the word is mixed with the hearts of men, and at the same time the Holy Spirit is given, so that those moved hearts may be incited toward God.

What the affections may be.

But there are three ...measures, that is, three bushels.

It is certain that in general it signifies human nature.

And although in number it is not a matter of question, yet since there are three principal powers in man, the mind, the will, and the heart,

Understanding, Will and Heart, to this number three seeds correspond well.

The Gospel kindles a new light in the mind, and the knowledge of God, firm assent and faith.

In the will, the fear of God, trust, hope, love of God, and a firm purpose of obeying God.

In the heart, it represses evil desires, and kindles there the love of God, and chastity, and patience, and other virtues, because the heart is the instrument of the will, and in serious actions the heart acts together with the will, when it is truly serious, as when a youth seriously loves a girl, then the will and the heart act together.

Thus, when a man is reborn through the Gospel, and is purged, then hypocrisy is corrected again, and true fear of God, true invocation, true love, etc., begin, and the will and the heart act together.

This exposition concerning the three seeds shows what kind of effects the Holy Spirit has in us.

And in sum, both similitudes teach what the kingdom of Christ is like. And that the ministry of the word is efficacious.

Latin:

Simile est regnum coelorum fermento.

Idem argumentum est de ministerio Evangelii, et de efficacia eius.

Et rursus consideretur antithesis.

Iudaei exspectant regnum politicum, sed Christus opponit aliam formam.

Imo, inquit, erit regnum tale, in quo per verbum corda hominum mutabuntur.

Hic quoque haec duo considerentur, primum quod vox Evangelii non sit inane quiddam, sed vere sit efficax, et quod per eam semper aliqui convertantur.

Imo omnes qui ei adsentiuntur.

Secundo quales sint effectus discamus.

Evangelium hoc loco significatur per fermentum.

Et sicut fermentum miscetur farinae, et inflat panem, sic verbum miscetur cordibus hominum, et simul datur Spiritus sanctus, ut illo mota corda incitentur ad Deum.

Quales sint... affectus.

Sunt autem sata tria, id est, drey scheffel.

Certum est in genere significari humanam naturam.

Et quanquam de numero non est opus subtili quaestione, tamen cum tres sint in homine praecipuae vires, mens, voluntas et cor,

Berstand, Will vnd Herz, ad hunc numerum tria sata bene congruunt.

Evangelium in mente accendit novam lucem, et notitiam Dei, firmam adsensionem et fidem.

In voluntate timorem Dei, fiduciam, spem, dilectionem Dei, et firmum propositum obediendi Deo.

In corde reprimit malas cupiditates, et accendit ibi amorem Dei, et castitatem, et patientiam, et alias virtutes, quia cor est instrumentum voluntatis, et in actionibus seriis simul agit cor cum voluntate, wenn es recht ernst ist, ut quando iuvenis serio amat puellam, tunc simul agunt voluntas et cor.

Ita quando per Evangelium renascitur homo, et repurgatur, tunc rursus emendatur hypocrisis, et incipit verus timor Dei, vera invocatio, vera dilectio etc. et simul agunt voluntas et cor.

Haec de tribus satis expositio ostendit, quales sint effectus Spiritus sancti in nobis.

Et in summa, utraque similitudo docet, quale sit regnum Christi. Et quod ministerium verbi sit efficax.

## 13:36 Sermons on Matthew
Concerning the tares.

That in this life in the congregation, which is called the Church, there are many hypocrites and wicked people.

Latin:

De zizaniis.

Quod in hac vita in congregatione, quae vocatur Ecclesia, multi sint hypocritae et mali.

## 13:44 Sermons on Matthew
It is like a treasure.

It is like one seeking pearls. The Gospel is a treasure and a pearl.

A pearl, a little bead, is a noble white growth in an Indian sea-shell, like a fish's eye, beautiful, white, transparent, and has great power against all poison, and gives the heart special strengthening, more than all other medicine.

This beautiful little grain grows thus. In the spring the shell becomes very thirsty and lustful, and comes forth in the morning, and opens its mouth, snapping for the dew. Now the body of the shell is a particularly pure, subtle flesh; the same draws the dew to itself, and thus from the same flesh and dew this precious little grain becomes like gold or silver, and as the dew is purer, the pearl becomes nobler and more powerful, and more beautiful in color.

And it becomes especially precious when great storms come afterwards, so that the air is purified.

And if one wants to take out the pearl, one must do it with special skill. For if the shell grabs the fingers of men, it bites them off.

Meaning.

The Gospel is the heavenly dew, from which a pearl becomes [formed] in the heart that has a thirsty and lustful desire for it, and thus a new grain, a new birth, becomes [formed] in the heart, that is, joy in God.

And this pearl grows and becomes purer in the storm, that is, in persecution.

And the shell, that is, the people or Church, in which the pearl is, does not let it be taken from it, but with cunning it is taken from it. גרית Garith crustula (little cakes) בר Bar γνήσιον purum (pure).

Christ is the purest little cake.

The Gospel is a pure little cake of doctrine.

The Church also becomes a pure little cake. גרית Garith crustula (little cakes) מר Mar amara, moesta (bitter, sorrowful).

Christ is a most bitter, that is, most sorrowful little cake.

The Gospel is a bitter little cake, that is, the doctrine of the cross.

The Church is a bitter little cake, that is, under the cross.

Thus Theophrastus writes that the pearl is born in shells: At the beginning of spring, by a certain wonderful nature, the shells thirstily crave the heavenly dew. When they have crawled onto the shore and, gaping, have drunk this in, there is born from that dew and the flesh of the shell, whose odor is excellent, a pellucid gem, sometimes of golden, sometimes of silver color, and having a miraculous power in dispelling poisons and in the medication of the human heart.

It becomes, however, more generous when there are frequent great tempests, until the shells are pregnant. These things correspond beautifully. The Gospel is the heavenly dew, which when thirsty souls drink in, a gem is born in them, that is, their hearts are reborn, the Son of God restoring life and light to them.

They say also that the shells have a leader, like bees; that corresponds to the Church, which has the Son of God as its leader. When, however, the Son of God wishes this pearl to be bought, he commends to us the studies of heavenly doctrine, which we should cultivate piously and constantly, nor should we cast them away because of the hardships which must be endured by those who teach and confess. As the gem becomes purer in tempests, so doctrine is more wholesome in difficulties and dangers. PHIL. MEL. EXEGETICAL WRITINGS. 872 storms, so doctrine is more salutary in difficulties and dangers.

It is like a net cast into the sea. Preface. All these parables generally contain this doctrine: that this new kingdom of the Messiah is not political, nor will that just society of men without sins, etc., exist in this mortal life, as the Jews imagined a golden age.

So here it speaks of the net, and it contains three parts.

I. That the Church is to be gathered by the voice of the Gospel, and the Gospel is that net which gathers and unites men.

And here let that necessary doctrine be held: Whom He chose, these He also called. There are no members of the Church without a calling, that is, even if there is great virtue in Socrates, Xenophon, or similar figures, yet because they are not called, they are not members of the Church of God, because it is necessary to know the promise concerning the Son: No one comes to the Father except through the Son.

II. In this congregation in this life, there are good and bad.

And this doctrine and consolation are necessary.

The Donatists denied the validity of the administration of the Sacraments performed by the wicked, and there were great commotions about this matter.

Likewise, individual people are often disturbed by this scandal.

When they see many being wicked, they think that God does not regard us, that we are not heard, that the Church is nothing.

Against all these temptations, many things said in this chapter must be held, as above concerning the seed, and here concerning good and bad fish, that indeed in this life, in the assembly of the Church of God, there are reborn and not reborn, and often the not reborn are in the administration of the Sacraments, etc.

Therefore, let us not be disturbed by the multitude of wicked in our congregation, but let us know that such is the external appearance of the Church of God, and meanwhile, in this assembly of the called, there are always some good fish, and let all who are doing penance know that they are certainly received by faith, that God certainly hears them, and wills to fulfill His promises, even if many are wicked, just as God comforts Elijah: Still seven thousand men have not bowed their knees to Baal.

Likewise, Unless God had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and Gomorrah.

This consolation must often be considered, because there are very many who, because of this scandal, become weaker or completely fall away from God, because they see a very great multitude of the impious everywhere.

Against this scandal, let us be raised by faith, and let us invoke God more ardently, lest we be led into temptation, as is often said in the Psalms: Do not destroy my soul with the wicked, Psalm. 26. 28. Likewise, in Proverbs 5.

I was almost in all evil in the midst of the Church and the Synagogue, that is, when I saw the examples of the greatest multitude, I almost imitated their customs and opinions.

Nor is it a light struggle to resist this temptation.

III. Finally, separation occurs.

God in this life purifies the Church, as when He destroyed the Jews, when He destroyed the Arians and other heretics, so now He will be judge between us and the Papists.

Afterwards, another universal judgment will follow, where the Church will be glorified and the punishments of the damned will be seen, etc.

Another sermon.

So every scribe who is taught will be.

This sermon properly instructs preachers or teachers in the Church.

And it is a useful admonition for all people, and first it teaches that it is necessary to learn.

Here, let the distinction between Ethnic religions and Christian religion be considered.

Ethnic religions are known to be without doctrine, because they are a part of the law, and then whatever deity anyone had imagined, this was thought to be truly a deity, and the more gods they imagined, the greater holiness was thought to exist, etc.

On the contrary, the Church of God is founded on the Word of promise, and no one would have known the promise of grace concerning the Son if God had not revealed it, and God afterwards willed the revelation to be written.

Therefore, it is absolutely necessary to learn, hence it is commanded so often: Hear Him.

Likewise Jeremiah: I did not command you concerning burnt offerings, but hear me, etc.

So here it is said: A scribe who has received and learned doctrine.

Second part.

But what should one learn and teach? From the treasure, that is, from the books handed down by God.

Let the treasure be understood not as one's own wisdom, but as the books handed down to the Church, because we ought to be guardians of these books, as Paul says: Guard the deposit. Thence let him take old and new, that is, the Law and the Gospel.

Latin:

Simile est thesauro.

Simile quaerenti margaritas. Evangelium thesaurus est et margaritum.

Margaritum, ein Perlein, ist ein edel weis gewechs in einer Indischen Meer schnecken, wie ein Fisch aug, schön, weis, durchsichtig, vnd hat grosse krasst wider alle Gisst, vnd gibet dem Herzen sonderliche sterckung, mehr denn alle andere Arkney.

Dieses schön Körnlein wechst also. Im Lengen wird die Schneck sehr dürstig vnd geil, vnd that sich morgens herfur, vnd thut das maul vff, schnapt nach dem Thaw. Nu ist der Schnecken leib ein besonder rein subtil fleisch, dasselbig ziehet den Thaw an sich, vnd wird also aus demselbigen Fleisch vnd Thaw dieses köstlich Körnlein, wie Gold oder Silber, vnd so der Thaw reiner ist, wird das Perlein edler vnd kresstiger, vnd schöner von farb.

Vnd besonder wird es köstlich, wenn hernach grosse Ungewitter komen, das die lusst gereinigt wird.

Vnd so man das Perlein wil ausnemen, mus mans mit besonderer kunst thun. Denn so die Schneck die finger der Menschen ergreisst, beist sie dieselbigen ab.

Bedeutung.

Das Euangelium ist der Himlische Thaw, daraus wird ein Perlein im herken, das hesstigen durst vnd lust darzu hat, vnd wird also im Herzen ein newes Körnlein, newe geburt, das ist, freud in Gott.

Vnd dieses Perlein wechst vnd wird reiner im Ungewitter, das ist, in der Verfolgung.

Vnd die Schneck, das ist, das Volk oder Kirch, darin das Perlein ist, lest es jr nicht nemen, Aber mit listen wird es jr genomen. גרית Garith crustula Küchlein בר Bar γνήσιον purum.

Christus est purissima crustula.

Evangelium est pura crustula doctrinae.

Ecclesia etiam fit pura crustula. גרית Garith crustula מר Mar amara, moesta.

Christus est amarissima, id est, moestissima crustula.

Evangelium est amara crustula, id est, doctrina crucis.

Ecclesia est amara crustula, id est, sub cruce.

Sic scribit Theophrastus nasci in conchis margaritum: Initio veris sua quadam natura mirabili siti conchae appetunt rorem coelestem. Hunc cum in littus repentes, et hiantes hauserunt, nascitur ex eo rore et conchae carne, cuius odor optimus est, gemma pellucida, alias aurei, alias argentei coloris, et mirificam vim habens in pellendis venenis, et medicatione cordis humani.

Fit autem generosior, cum crebrae sunt magnae tempestates, donec conchae sunt gravidae. Haec pulcre congruunt. Evangelium est ros coelestis, quem cum sitientes animi hauriunt, gemma in eis nascitur, id est, renascuntur corda, filio Dei reddente eis vitam et lucem.

Aiunt etiam conchas ducem habere, ut apes, id congruit ad Ecclesiam, quae ducem habet filium Dei. Cum autem hoc margaritum emi vult Filius Dei, studia doctrinae coelestis nobis commendat, quae pie et constanter colamus, nec abiiciamus ea propter aerumnas, quae docentibus et confitentibus tolerandae sunt. Ut purior fit gemma in tem- pestatibus, ita doctrina in difficultatibus et periculis salubrior est.

Simile est sagenae missae in mare. Praefatio. Omnes hae similitudines continent generaliter hanc doctrinam, quod novum hoc regnum Messiae, non sit politicum, nec sit futura in hac mortali vita, illa societas hominum iusta sine peccatis etc. sicnt fingebant auream aetatem Iudaei.

Ita hic dicit de sagena, et continet tria membra.

I. Quod Ecclesia colligenda sit voce Evangelii, et Evangelium est illud rete, quod colligit et coniungit homines.

Et hic teneatur illa necessaria doctrina: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Nulla sunt Ecclesiae membra sine vocatione, id est, etsi est magna virtus Socratis, Xenophon-tis aut similium, tamen quia non sunt vocati, non sunt membra Ecclesiae Dei, quia oportet nosse promissionem de Filio: Nemo pervenit ad Patrem, nisi per Filium.

II. In hac congregatione in hac vita sunt boni et mali.

Et haec doctrina et consolatio necessaria est.

Donatistae negabant valere administrationem Sacramentorum, quae fit per malos, et fuerunt magni tumultus de hac re.

Item, singuli homines saepe turbantur hoc scandalo.

Cum videant plurimos esse malos, cogitant non respici nos a Deo, non exaudiri, nihil esse Ecclesiam.

Contra has tentationes omnes tenenda sunt dicta multa in hoc capite, ut supra de semine, et hic de bonis et malis piscibus, quod revera in hac vita sint in coetu Ecclesiae Dei, renati et non renati, et saepe non renati sint in administratione Sacramentorum etc.

Ideo non turbemur multitudine malorum in nostra congregatione, sed sciamus talem esse speciem externam Ecclesiae Dei, et interea in hoc coetu vocatorum tamen semper aliquos bonos pisces esse, et sciant omnes agentes poenitentiam, certo se recipi fide, certo Deum exaudire, et velle praestare promissa, etsi plurimi sint mali, sicut consolatur Deus Eliam: Adhuc septem millia virorum non curvarunt genua ad Baal.

Item, Nisi Deus reliquisset nobis semen, sicut Sodoma et Gomorra essemus.

Haec consolatio saepe cogitanda est, quia valde multi sunt, qui propter hoc scandalum fiunt languidiores, vel omnino a Deo deficiunt, quia valde magnam esse multitudinem impiorum ubique vident.

Contra hoc scandalum fide erigamur, et eo ardentius Deum invocemus, ne inducamur in tentationem, sicut in Psalmis saepe dicitur: Ne perdas cum impiis animam meam, Psalm. 26. 28.

Item, in Proverb. 5. Pene fui in omni malo in medio Ecclesiae et Synagogae, id est, cum viderem exempla maximae multitudinis, pene et ego mores et opiniones eorum imitatus essem.

Nec leve certamen est, huic tentationi resistere.

III. Tandem fit separatio.

Deus in hac vita repurgat Ecclesiam, ut quando Iudaeos delevit, quando delevit Arianos et alios haereticos, ita et nunc erit iudex inter nos et Papistas.

Postea sequetur et alterum iudicium universale, ubi glorificabitur Ecclesia et conspicientur poenae damnatorum etc.

Alia concio.

Sic erit omnis scriba doctus.

Haec concio proprie instituit concionatores seu doctores in Ecclesia.

Et est utilis commonefactio pro omnibus hominibus, et primo docet, quod necesse sit discere.

Hic discrimen consideretur inter Ethnicas religiones et Christianam.

Ethnicae sciuntur sine doctrina, quia sunt particula legis, et deinde qualecunque numen quilibet finxerat, hoc putabatur vere esse numen, et quo plures Deos fingebant, eo maior sanctitas esse putabatur, etc.

Econtra Ecclesia Dei est condita Verbo promissionis, et promissionem gratiae de filio nemo scivisset, si Deus non revelasset, et Deus postea voluit scribi revelationem.

Ergo prorsus necesse est disci, ideo toties mandatum est: Hunc audite.

Item Ieremias: Non mandavi te holocausiis, sed audite me, etc.

Ita hic dicitur: Scriba qui doctrinam accepit et didicit.

Secunda pars.

Quid autem discere et docere debet? Ex thesauro, id est, ex libris a Deo traditis.

Intelligatur thesaurus non propria sapientia, sed libri traditi Ecclesiae, quia nos debemus esse custodes librorum istorum, ut Paulus dicit: Cu- stodi depositum. Inde sumat vetera et nova, id est, Legem et Evangelium.

## 13:57 Sermons on Matthew
A prophet is not despised, except in his own country.

Proposition.

The complaint is that the chief enemies of the Gospel are in the very body which is called the Church, as it is said in John 1: He came unto his own, and his own received him not. And Isaiah 65: All day long I have spread out my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.

Moreover, it contains a twofold doctrine. The former is that it warns us not to be deceived by the title of Church, just as now also Bishops and Monks boast that they are the Church, but they are so just as the Pharisees and Sadducees were the Church, and other persecutors among the people of the Jews, while Christ was preaching. This admonition is necessary, so that we may not be deceived by a title.

There is also a consolation, which warns us not to be moved by the scandal of the fewness of believers, so as to assent rather to the greater part, but that we should always know that the rule must be kept, that we judge of the Church from the word of God. Those are the Church who believe the uncorrupted word of God.

Secondly, the accusation must be considered, so that we may do penance. Not only are the Pharisees accused in this text, but other good men and hearers of Christ, who nevertheless were negligent, and did not do penance, and heard without true faith.

Such are many among us, and in this very assembly, which says it embraces the Gospel. Let us therefore do penance, and stir up true faith, and exercise it in invocation, in hope of divine aid, in patience. Sufficiently great dangers now impend, perhaps there will be new wars, and we see churches being disturbed in many places.

Against these evils let us fight with prayer and penance, lest the Gospel be taken away from us, as the Lord threatens elsewhere, where He says: The last state becomes worse than the first.

Latin:

Non est Propheta contemtus, nisi in patria.

Propositio.

Querela est, quod praecipui hostes Evangelii sint in ipso corpore, quod vocatur Ecclesia, sicut Ioh. 1. dicitur: In propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Et Esa. 65. Tota die expandi ma- nus meas ad populum non credentem, sed con- tradicentem.

Duplicem autem doctrinam continet. Prior est, quod monet, ne decipiamur titulo Ecclesiae, sicut nunc quoque gloriantur Episcopi et Mona- chi, quod sint Ecclesia, sed sic sunt, sicut fue- runt Ecclesia Pharisaei et Zadducaei, et alii per- secutores in populo Iudaeorum, praedicante Chri- sto. Haec commonefactio necessaria est, ne titulo decipiamur.

Est et consolatio, quae monet, ne scandalo paucitatis credentium moveamur, ut potius maiori parti assentiamur, sed semper sciamus regulam servandam esse, ut iudicemus de Ecclesia ex ver- bo Dei. Illi sunt Ecclesia, qui credunt verbo Dei incorrupto.

Secundo, accusatio consideranda est, ut aga- mus poenitentiam. Non tantum Pharisaei accu- santur in hoc textu. Sed alii boni et auditores Christi, qui tamen erant negligentes, et non age- bant poenitentiam, et sine vera fide audiebant.

Tales multi sunt inter nos, et in hoc ipso coetu, qui dicit se amplecti Evangelium. Aga- mus igitur poenitentiam, et veram fidem excite- mus, et exerceamus eam in invocatione, in spe auxilii divini, in patientia. Satis magna pericula nunc impendent, fortassis nova bella erunt, et videmus turbari Ecclesias in multis locis.

Contra haec mala pugnemus oratione et poe- nitentia, ne auferatur a nobis Evangelium, sicut alibi minatur Dominus, ubi ait: Fiunt novissima peiora prioribus.

## 14:1 Sermons on Matthew: Argument
Chapter XIV.

On the death of John the Baptist.

Here is a great question, to which human wisdom cannot answer: Why is the Church subjected to the cross? Why are John, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the highest lights of the Church killed? This doctrine is revealed in the Gospel, and delivered immediately at the beginning in Paradise: I will put enmity between the serpent and the seed of the woman, and the serpent shall lie in wait for his heel. The chief and primary cause of death and of all the calamities of the whole human race is that the nature of men is contaminated by sin, which God shows that He horribly hates. Therefore He burdens this whole nature with such great miseries, as it is written: The wages of sin is death. This is the first thing it is necessary to know about the common punishment of the whole human race. But why is the Church more burdened than other men? There are several chief causes. The first, because God wishes His wrath to be seen more in His Church, and thus He invites us to penance. The second, because the Devil rages more atrociously against the Church than against his own instruments. The third, because even many saints fall, therefore great punishments come, as David, Manasseh, and many others have horrible falls, on account of which both they and at the same time many others are punished. The fourth, but the Prophets, such as Jeremiah and the Baptist and the Apostles and many others, are killed in confession, not on account of any certain offenses. This happens for these reasons, so that that death may be a testimony to the doctrine, so that it may be established that there was no simulation, because they prefer confession to their own life. Likewise, by this death they testify that another life remains, and that they expect another life; likewise our head Christ wishes the chief teachers to become like himself, and he wishes this so that they may consider how great the wrath of God is against the common sin of the human race. All these things must be considered whenever we recite the histories of the punishments of the Prophets and Apostles, and by their examples we ought to strengthen ourselves. God spares the weak, and does not wish for all to be killed in this way, but nevertheless all suffer some persecution. And meanwhile God preserves some assembly in life, because it is written: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord. It is necessary for some to live, so that there may be some Church in this life, and there may be procreation and instruction; it is necessary for women in childbirth to have little nests. All these things are a care to God, as it has been said: Do not be anxious, your heavenly Father knows that you need these things.

First, let the cause and occasion of the hatred in Herod against John be considered; John, as a faithful preacher, rebukes Herod because he had snatched away the wife of his living brother. Thus it happens, truth begets hatred. This is the common danger of all who teach rightly, as it is written: You will be hated by all men for my name's sake.

The manner: how does he kill? By the false pretense of the religion of an oath, and indeed with a dancing girl. I do not know if any Prophet has been killed on such a trivial and scurrilous occasion. But it is a signified sophistry, craft and deceit, just as it happens now; hypocrisy plays before the highest kings, and asks for the head of John.

Let it be concluded. That such examples are testimonies of doctrine, as has been said, they also teach us that we should also bear our own persecutions patiently.

Christ withdrew, having heard of the death of John. These things happened in the second year of Christ's preaching, around Passover.

And consider first the wonderful counsel of God. Some have a longer time to preach, others a shorter. John had two years, Elijah twenty or somewhat more years, Elisha about seventy, Paul thirty-five, John the Evangelist about ninety.

Latin:

Caput XIV.

De nece Iohannis Baptistae.

Hic est magna quaestio, de qua sapientia hu- mana non potest respondere: Quare Ecclesia sub- iecta est cruci? Quare Iohannes, Prophetae, Apo- stoli, et summa lumina Ecclesiae interficiuntur? Haec doctrina est revelata in Evangelio, et statim initio in Paradiso tradita: Ponam inimici- tias inter serpentem et semen mulieris, et ser- pens insidiabitur calcaneo eius. Causa praecipua et prima mortis et omnium calamitatum totius generis humani est, quia na- tura hominum contaminata est peccato, quod ostendit se Deus horribiliter odisse. Ideo onerat hanc naturam universam tantis miseriis, sicut scriptum est: Stipendium peccati mors. Hoc primum scire oportet de poena communi totius generis humani. Sed quare Ecclesia magis onerata est, quam alii homines? Causae praecipuae plures sunt. Prima, quia Deus in Ecclesia sua magis vult conspici iram suam, et sic invitat nos ad poeni- tentiam. Secunda, quia Diabolus atrocius grassatur contra Ecclesiam, quam contra sua organa. Tertia, quia etiam sancti multi labuntur, ideo veniunt magnae poenae, ut David, Manasse et alii multi habent horribiles lapsus, propter quos et ipsi et simul alii multi puniuntur. Quarta, sed Prophetae, ut Ieremias et Bapti- sta et Apostoli et multi alii in confessione inter- ficiuntur, non propter aliqua certa delicta. Hoc fit propter has causas, ut illa mors sit testimo- nium doctrinae, ut constet non fuisse simulatio- nem, quia confessionem anteferunt vitae suae. Item ista morte testantur, quod restet alia vita, et quod exspectent aliam vitam, item caput nostrum Christus vult praecipuos doctores fieri si- miles sibi, et hoc ideo vult, ut hi cogitent, quanta sit ira Dei adversus commune peccatum generis humani. Haec omnia cogitanda sunt, quandocunque recitamus historias de suppliciis Prophetarum et Apostolorum, et horum exemplis debemus nos confirmare. Deus parcit infirmis, et non vult omnes isto modo interfici, sed tamen omnes ali- quam persecutionem patiuntur. Et interea servat Deus aliquem coetum in vita, quia scriptum est: Non mortui laudabunt te Domine. Oportet ali- quos vivere, ut sit in hac vita Ecclesia aliqua, et sit procreatio et institutio, oportet puerperas ha- bere nidulos. Haec omnia Deo curae sunt, sicut dictum est: Ne sitis soliciti, scit Pater vester coe- lestis, quod his rebus indigeatis.

Primum consideretur causa et occasio odii in Herode contra Iohannem, Iohannes ut praedicator fidelis arguit Herodem, quod rapuerit fratris viventis coniugem. Ita fit, veritas odium parit. Hoc commune periculum est omnium recte docentium, ut scriptum est: Odio eritis omnibus hominibus, propter nomen meum.

Modus: quomodo interficit? Falsa specie religionis iurisiurandi, et quidem saltante puella. Nescio an aliquis Propheta tam levi et scurrili occasione interfectus sit. Sed significata est sophistica, list vnd betrug, sicut nunc fit, ludit hypocrisis coram summis regibus, et petit caput Iohannis.

Concludatur. Quod talia exempla sint testimonia doctrinae, ut dictum est, item docent nos, ut etiam nostras persecutiones patienter feramus.

Christus secessit, audita morte Iohannis. Haec facta sunt anno secundo praedicationis Christi circa Pascha.

Et cogita primum mirabile consilium Dei. Alii longius tempus habent ad praedicandum, alii brevius. Iohannes habuit biennium, Elias viginti aut aliquanto plures annos, Elisaeus circiter septuaginta, Paulus quinque et triginta, Iohannes Evangelista circiter nonaginta.

## 14:25 Sermons on Matthew
On Christ's walking upon the sea.

In this history, the principal thing is the example of Peter, and it is an admonition concerning πολυπραγμοσύνη [meddlesomeness], that is, what the outcomes are when we attempt unnecessary and dangerous things, when we undertake dangerous and unnecessary things, just as Josiah moves a war that is not necessary, which he could have avoided, and often men sin in this way, because they do irregular things without necessity. As when young men bring dangers upon themselves by climbing or swimming, when parents betroth daughters to strangers. But it is sinned against most in government, when curious rulers make dangerous innovations without necessity.

But that we may consider this doctrine well, first let the division of works be held. Some are commands, which it is simply necessary to do, as, Keep the marriage vow, etc. Regarding these, deliberation is not difficult. Others are prohibitions, which it is simply necessary to flee, as, Do not kill, Do not invoke an idol. Regarding these also, deliberation is easy.

The third degree is of intermediate works, which are neither necessary nor expressly prohibited. I have already said, to swim, or to move a war for a probable cause, which nevertheless could be omitted. Here let us learn a rule: In great and dangerous matters, nothing is to be done unless it is necessary; and things that are not necessary, although they are specious, and the intention is good, yet they are to be omitted.

This is a singular wisdom, and necessary for all men, because it is written: He who loves danger will perish in it. Item: You shall not tempt the Lord your God, that is, do not, for the sake of your own wisdom, move a dangerous business without necessity, without a command of God, without a calling, having left the common way, which is consistent with the command of God, just as Josiah could have had peace, which was offered to him, but he preferred to have war.

So here Peter, with good zeal and good intention, wishes to run to the Lord, but it is an unnecessary and dangerous work, having left the common way, without necessity, and without utility to his neighbor. Therefore, his foolishness is shown to him, because the Lord lets him sink.

This, therefore, is the first doctrine: let us not do unnecessary and dangerous things. And for the most part in such dangers, even if there were beginnings of faith, yet there was more of human audacity, and faith afterwards languished in an adverse outcome.

Although it was foolishness that he wanted to walk upon the waters, yet because the Lord commanded that he should come, he ought to have believed that he would not perish. But the Lord wishes to show him both: that he acted foolishly, wishing to walk upon the waters without necessity, and that his faith was weaker than he thought. Peter therefore has this infirmity as well, namely, that he begins to doubt in the midst of danger.

Here now let a second doctrine be learned, namely, that God heals the errors of the Saints when they flee to Him. David, when he had ordered the people to be numbered, even afterwards acknowledged his error, when God was punishing the people for it with a pestilence, but yet he afterwards obtained forgiveness. Moses also trembled when he struck the rock, but he was raised up again, and afterwards is helped by God.

Such are many of the errors of all the Saints, which God in His immense goodness amends and heals. Let us learn this doctrine well, that we may not trust in our own wisdom, likewise, that we may not fall away from God after a lapse, but return to Him, and ask for and expect deliverance.

Latin:

De ambulatione Christi super mare.

In hac historia principale est exemplum Petri, et est admonitio de πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, id est, quales sint eventus, quando non necessaria periculosa tentamus, wen wir fehrliche unnötige ding fürnemen, sicut Iosias bellum movet non necessarium, quod vitare poterat, et saepe sic peccant homines, quod faciunt irregularia sine necessitate. Ut quando iuvenes scandendo vel natando accersunt sibi pericula, quando parentes elocant filias ignotis. Maxime autem sic peccatur in gubernatione, quando curiosi regentes faciunt novitates periculosas sine necessitate.

Ut autem hanc doctrinam bene consideremus, primum teneatur divisio operum. Alias sunt mandata, quae simpliciter necesse est facere, ut, Serves fidem coniugalem etc. De his non difficilis deliberatio est. Alia sunt prohibita, quae simpliciter fugere necesse est, ut, Ne occidas, Ne invokes idolum. De his etiam facilis deliberatio est.

Tertius gradus est operum mediorum, quae nec necessaria sunt, nec expresse prohibita. Iam dixi, natare, vel bellum propter probabilem causam movere, quod tamen omitti possit. Hic discamus regulam: In magnis rebus et periculosis nihil faciendum esse, nisi necessaria; et non necessaria, quamquam sunt speciosa, et est bona intentio, tamen omittenda esse.

Haec est singularis sapientia, et necessaria omnibus hominibus, quia scriptum est: Qui amat periculum, peribit in eo. Item: Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum, id est, ne propter tuam sapientiam moveas periculosum negotium sine necessitate, sine mandato Dei, sine vocatione, relicta via communi, conveniente cum mandato Dei, ut Iosias poterat habere pacem, quae ei offerebatur, sed maluit habere bellum.

Ita hic Petrus bono zelo, bona intentione vult occurrere Domino, sed est opus non necessarium et periculosum, relicta via communi, sine necessitate, et sine utilitate proximi. Ideo ostenditur ei stultitia, quia Dominus sinit eum mergi.

Est igitur haec prima doctrina, ne faciamus non necessaria periculosa. Et plerumque in talibus periculis, etiam si quae fuerunt initia fidei, tamen plus fuit audaciae humanae, et fides postea languefit in adverso eventu.

Quamquam autem stultitia fuit, quod voluit incedere supra aquas, tamen quia Dominus iussit, ut veniret, iam debuit credere, se non interiturum esse. Sed vult ei Dominus utrumque ostendere, quod stulte fecerit, volens incedere super aquis sine necessitate, et quod fides eius fuerit infirmior, quam putavit. Habet ergo Petrus et hanc infirmitatem, scilicet, quod incipit dubitare in medio periculo.

Hic iam secunda doctrina discatur, videlicet, quod Deus sanat errata Sanctorum, quando ad eum confugiunt. David cum iussisset numerari populum, etiam postea agnovit errorem suum, cum Deus puniret propterea populum pestilentia, sed tamen deinde veniam impetravit. Moses etiam trepidavit, quando percussit saxum, sed rursus erectus est, et postea adiuvatur a Deo.

Talia multa sunt omnium Sanctorum errata, quae Deus immensa bonitate emendat et sanat. Hanc doctrinam bene discamus, ne confidamus nostrae sapientiae, item, ne a Deo deficiamus post lapsum, sed ad eum redeamus, et petamus et exspectemus liberationem.

## 15:1 Sermons on Matthew: Argument
Chapter XV.

An excellent doctrine is contained in this place, concerning the distinction between true and false worships, or concerning the distinction between divine commandments and human traditions, which doctrine is very necessary. Because it is a most common superstition of the human race, having abandoned the commandments of God, to place religion in human traditions, as all the elders remember, this opinion existed: That it was a greater sin if a Priest took a wife than if he killed a man. Likewise, it was considered a greater sin to eat meat on the sixth day than to commit adultery. This foolish and impious opinion often wanders through the Church. And God has refuted it time and again through the Prophets, Christ, the Apostles, and other pious teachers.

But in order that this doctrine may be rightly understood, we wish to proceed in order, and first to say what are the true worships of God, which God demands and approves, and which are absolutely necessary. And we wish to propose to ourselves the saying of Paul, which you ought always to remember: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience.

Therefore, the necessary worships are, first, faith, which is the true knowledge of God according to the whole Creed, and is the trust in mercy, by which we receive the remission of sins, and are accounted righteous, and are heard on account of the Son of God. This light in the heart is the first and principal and highest worship, because it is necessary to approach the Father through the Son according to that: No one comes to the Father, except through the Son. Likewise, He who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father. And this light ought always to shine, in every invocation, and in all other works. A man ought not to live in this opinion: I am displeasing to God, I doubt whether I please Him, I doubt whether He receives me, I doubt whether He receives my prayers. These doubts are naturally in the mind, but a man ought to perform repentance, and afterwards determine that he is certainly received, and that he pleases God through obedience, on account of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in this trust he ought to approach God, and invoke Him.

Secondly, the necessary worships are a good conscience, according to the commandments of God, that is, that a man according to all the commandments may have a good conscience. Let him not be an adulterer, not a fornicator, not a thief, not a liar, not a murderer, let him not harbor in his heart, knowingly and willingly, unjust hatred against his neighbor, etc. Such works commanded by God are true worships of God when accompanied by faith.

Ezekiel 20: Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, but walk in my statutes. Here He expressly draws us back to the commandments of God, and commands that we do those things which He Himself has commanded.

And this doctrine has been often repeated, and it is a great consolation to the pious to know that the worships of God are these very works necessary for common life, an honest married life, honest works of another vocation. Likewise, our patience in the cross, just as the Psalm says: A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit. And in all these things faith and invocation ought always to shine, in all works and dangers. Invoke and ask and expect the help of God, as the Psalm says: Commit your way to God, and He will act.

Second part.

After I have said what are the necessary worships, I will now speak about traditions.

And know that there are two kinds of traditions, some are against God, such as all those which command impossible or impious things, such as the prohibition of marriage. Likewise, the orders of Monks, and masses, which they have preserved as worships, and as merits for the remission of sins. These impious things are simply to be abolished.

Concerning such traditions Christ says here: Why do you violate the commandment of God because of your tradition? By these words He signifies that the commandment of God is to be preferred to human commandments, and when the commandments of men command something to be done against the commandments of God, then we ought to keep the rule: It is necessary to obey God rather than men. This rule is immovable, and it is necessary that this most well-known rule always be in the Church.

And concerning these traditions it is manifest that they are not worships of God, but as Paul says, they are the doctrine of demons. And on the contrary, it is the worship of God to resist such worships and doctrines.

Secondly, there are other traditions concerning indifferent matters, which are not against God, and are made for the sake of good order, such as that the day of Easter is observed at a certain time, the day of Christ’s birth at a certain time, that this hour is appointed for the sermon, because there must be order in human life. And this order is to be observed just as, having observed an honest order in a house, in the morning the children say a prayer, afterwards they eat, then they go to school. Thus let good ordinances also be observed in the Church, not because they are righteousness or things necessary for righteousness, but for the sake of good order and tranquility.

It is necessary for this doctrine to be known, and let the opinion, such as it was of old, never be received, where they thought abstinence from meat to be a holy work, by which God wishes to be honored, and they thought it to be a necessary thing.

This opinion is simply false and is to be rejected, and meanwhile true worship, faith, and a good conscience in works commanded by God are to be sought.

Application.

This is the sum of the doctrine in this text, Christ teaches that worship consists of works commanded by God, and not works of human traditions, just as He says below: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men.

And He censures the Pharisaic tradition. They used to say it was better to offer to the temple than to support parents, just as they now say: It is better to endow a mass, or to support many monks for the sake of a mass, than to help poor students or other miserable people from the goods of the Church. The understanding of the Pharisaic tradition was entirely similar.

Therefore Christ rejects this tradition, because it fights against the divine command.

He also excuses His disciples for not washing their hands, and rejects the foolish opinions that they thought such works were necessary and were holiness.

But when these things are said, then the Pharisees are offended; here is the work of the doctrine concerning scandal.

Not that which enters into the mouth.

Again, at the beginning, I admonish you concerning the weakness of the Apostles. There is error even in the Apostles, who still think that distinctions of foods are great and singular acts of worship of God, and that this people of Israel excels the nations for this reason, that they do such holy works, namely, that they abstain from swine’s flesh and from hares, etc. Indeed, the Apostles have this persuasion, not only concerning ceremonies, but also concerning human traditions.

Let us learn, therefore, from this example, that it is no wonder that there were also some errors in Augustine, Ambrose, and the like. Always in all men there are some sins and some ignorance, in some more, in others less.

But let us hold to two precepts here.

First, that it is necessary to hold the foundation, that is, the articles of faith, as it is said in 1 Corinthians 3: Other foundation can no man lay than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

It is necessary that this be held in such a way that no article of faith is completely ignored, or that the contrary is not asserted. But those who pertinaciously assert the contrary are undoubtedly damned, according to that: He who does not believe is already condemned.

II. Second doctrine: But when the foundation is held, and then some error is added, even if this obscures some article of faith, nevertheless a man can be saved, as it is said there in 1 Corinthians 8: Another builds upon it with stubble, he shall be saved, yet so as through fire.

But such a man ought to be teachable, and when God reveals errors, just as God from time to time restores the Church and purges doctrine, he ought not to pertinaciously oppose. Because these errors, even if they seem to be about small matters, nevertheless are great, and always obscure some articles of faith, and hinder faith and true worship of God. And God is an enemy of lying; He does not want us to defend lies, as it is written: Lying is an abomination before God, Proverbs 12: Indeed, when such pertinacity is added that one does not wish to be corrected, then it becomes blasphemy and a sin against the Holy Spirit, because such people knowingly resist the truth, etc.

I have said these things so that you may know that true doctrine is to be retained even concerning these traditions, such as concerning foods, clothing, and the like. You may use meat or fish, but nevertheless know this, that such a work is not worship of God. Likewise, that it does not merit the remission of sins. Likewise, that they are not necessary things, and can be omitted outside the case of scandal.

Now I come to the other part of the sermon.

First He says: A man is not defiled by foods, that is, it is not a sin before God to eat things ordained by God.

I. Let us know this doctrine, so that consciences may not be ensnared.

II. Item, that we may know that the worship of God is not distinctions of foods or garments, or any human traditions, but only works commanded by God, according to the rule handed down here: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. Item Psalm 119: A lamp to my feet etc.

Secondly he says: Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts.

Here he teaches what is the source of sins, namely, disobedience in the heart against God.

And first he names evil thoughts, so that it may be understood concerning all commandments, especially concerning the first, namely, concerning Epicurean opinions, contempt of God, and carnal security, doubts, and many false opinions which continually disturb faith and fear and hope. Item, let it be understood concerning all vicious affections. And this passage testifies that sins are not only external deeds, but also internal diseases.

The doctrine concerning these diseases must be held, that it is necessary to resist evil affections, lest they be completed in deed, and at the same time to ask that on account of the Mediator these evils may be forgiven us, as the doctrine at Rom. 7. 8. teaches:

And Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the parts of Tyre etc.

Concerning the Canaanite woman.

In this history three doctrines are contained. I. Concerning miracles. II. Concerning temptations, which clamor against one praying. III. Concerning faith and the chief worship.

I. Concerning miracles.

First, the general doctrine here must be repeated, that miracles are testimonies that this teacher was truly sent by God. Item, that this teacher is the Lord and the promised savior, such as he proclaims himself to be, destroying the works of the Devil, sin, the tyranny of the Devil, and death.

A peculiar image is proposed here. Nowhere does he pass by so harshly, or reject prayers arising from true and great pain, as here. And two things are objected: first, that she is not from Israel; second, that she is unworthy, like a dog. Yet she struggles out of these temptations, and at length by faith obtains what she seeks. Here, therefore, let us learn that the minds of individuals are attacked by similar temptations, and that faith is not to be cast away on that account, but rather to be raised up amidst these waves.

There are, however, two chief temptations, the other concerning unworthiness, the other concerning election. The former arises from the law. For the law always cries out in our consciences that God regards, hears, and saves the worthy and the just, but that we are unjust, unworthy, polluted, and cast away, like dogs. To this temptation the Gospel concerning gratuitous justification and concerning the exclusive 'freely' must be opposed, and testimonies must be gathered which show that the unworthy and unjust are received. We are justified freely by faith. Item: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven. Item: To you I am only a sinner. Item, in this place sin and grace ought to be compared, just as Paul compares them: Grace abounds over sin. Let the Son of God and the sacrifice of the Son of God be valued more than our sin, so that we may conclude that we are forgiven, that sin is remitted, and we may begin to obey God. These are firm and true consolations against the temptation concerning unworthiness.

The second concerns election. Because men, when they see many well-deserving people rejected, such as Saul, Augustus, Cicero, and far worse people received, such as Magdalene, the thief on the cross, they dispute about particularity, namely, that God has a certain catalog of those whom He wishes to save, while the others are neglected, like dogs. Thus they attribute inequality to God, which in reality is to accuse Him of tyranny. This is a most harsh temptation.

But against this temptation must be opposed the doctrine that the promises are universal. And the universals must be diligently collected, such as: Everyone who believes in the Son shall not perish. Likewise: Come to me, all. Likewise, Rom. 10: God is the same to all, rich to all who call upon Him. To this should be added the immutable command, which is placed far above all laws, namely, that He commands that all believe in the Son of God, and it is necessary for all to obey this command. Nor ought we to seek or scrutinize the will of God, having set aside this command and rejected the promises. And since Christ says: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Likewise: He who sees me, sees also the Father: the will of God must necessarily be sought in the Son given to us, and in the Gospel, which the Son of God brought forth from the bosom of the Father.

…Let us remember these consolations, so that we may have firm refutations of those temptations which exercise the minds of many, and let us bring forth these consolations daily in our invocation. For if you examine your own mind, you will see that you are hindered by these two temptations from calling upon him, because you think yourself unworthy. Likewise, you think that God has chosen some of His own, but that you are neglected. And human arguments are added to this, because we are not the equals of Abraham, Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, and the like; we are weak, without great gifts, without authority, and therefore we judge that we are neglected, and out of a certain despair we omit prayer.

But here we must look with our minds at the doctrine of the Gospel, which commands faith, as has already been said. We must also look at this Canaanite teacher, who, having refuted her unworthiness and particularity, reasons that the promises pertain not only to Israel, but also to the Gentiles; 'The dogs,' she says, 'eat of the crumbs.' Thus, with faith awakened, we must call upon God in the acknowledgment of His Son.

And this faith and invocation in those who practice repentance is the highest worship of God, and the chief worship of the Church, as it is said here: 'O woman, great is your faith.'

And that this is not in vain, but obtains good things, this very voice testifies: 'Let it be to you as you wish.' According to that: 'Ask and you shall receive.'

Therefore, there is proposed to us in this Gospel an example of faith, struggling out of the most grievous temptations and obtaining good things, so that we too may learn to overcome diffidence and to awaken faith and invocation. Nor do we have lesser causes than this Canaanite, who labors for her daughter; so too do we for our own necessities and for public ones.

There follows in the text the history of the four thousand hearers of Christ, satisfied with seven loaves.

In this history, these things are to be considered and learned.

I. The distinction between promises concerning eternal things and concerning present or bodily things.

II. That to a bodily promise, the doctrine of the cross must always be added, to which the Church is subject for reasons that have been recited elsewhere.

III. Why promises concerning present things were given, namely: I. So that we may establish that these good things do not happen by chance, nor are they prepared only by human industry, but that we may believe them to be the benefits of God.

II. The cause: since God wills that there always be some Church of His in this life, the body needs food, lodging, defense, government, and some peace, so that offspring may be educated and studies may be cultivated.

Therefore, He added these promises, and God provides these benefits, but miraculously. For although the Devil always rages against the Church, and there are constant tumults in the world, by which the sins of the human race are constantly and horribly punished: yet among these tumults, God preserves His Church, just as He preserved the standing people of Israel in the Red Sea. And the body remains, even if some members are slaughtered, just as David's army remains, even if some soldiers are killed while fighting.

III. The third cause why these promises were given is that they might be exercises of faith and invocation. God wills to be acknowledged through invocation. Therefore, He has proposed many things that might admonish us concerning invocation. He wills us to flee to Him, even when we seem deserted and cast out by the whole nature of things, just as David says: 'My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up.'

IIII. In what order they are to be sought. This is taught by the saying in Matthew 6: 'Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you.' But let honest labor be added, and that which is suitable to each according to their vocation.

V. How faith is to be exercised in the petition for bodily goods. First, it must be known that faith must always shine before the petition for bodily things, by which we believe that we are received and heard on account of Christ. Indeed, so that this faith may be kindled and grow in us, so many various external occasions, dangers, and afflictions are proposed.

Let us know, therefore, that the first and highest promise concerning the Mediator and reconciliation must always be embraced at the same time. Daily, therefore, when you recite these words at the table: 'Give us this day our daily bread,' because our infirmity soon clamors: 'God does not hear you, unworthy one, He does not want you to be fed or nourished': here the promise concerning Christ must be looked at, and faith must be added, that on account of the Mediator we are received and heard.

Therefore, it soon follows: 'And forgive us our debts.' Afterwards, let that faith think of the three things I recounted above: that God wills that the goods of the body be asked of Him.

First, that we believe they are given divinely, not thinking they happen by chance. Second: Because He wills the Church to be preserved in this life, He gives food, defense, and lodging miraculously, etc. Third, He wills to be acknowledged and worshipped by this invocation, therefore He has proposed many things which He wills to be asked for.

He also wills faith to be confirmed petition for corporal things, since experience shows that the prayer was not in vain, as it is said in the Psalm: This poor man cried to the Lord, and God heard him.

Finally, God also wishes to be worshipped with thanksgiving for deliverances, as is most sweetly said in 2 Corinthians 1, where Paul commands many to pray for him, so that many may give thanks.

But here human weakness objects: What is the point of praying, when we know that we must be afflicted? Just as it is written: But the body is subject to death because of sin. Likewise, it is manifest that the saints are often not delivered from present calamities, such as Jonathan, the Maccabee. Since, therefore, we must offer obedience, as Christ prays, yet not my will, but thine be done, what is the benefit of petition, and indeed with doubt?

I answer: A rule must be held most firmly, that God has commanded and requires invocation, and that the invocation of the pious is never empty or in vain, even if deliverance is deferred, or the outcomes do not respond as we imagine, and it is not for us to prescribe to God the manner of helping, and we are bound to obedience, as Christ says: Thy will be done. Next, let us know that two objects must always be included in the petition for corporal things: the universal Church, and private necessity. The petition of the pious always obtains for the universal Church, and thus let faith establish that this petition is ratified, and let it not doubt that the petition is received by God for the universal Church. But privately, we must pray for ourselves with this condition, that we offer ourselves to obedience, just as Christ offers himself.

VI. Application of the history.

That Christ feeds his hearers is shown as an example of the promise: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you.

With this faith let us follow Christ, let us be faithful in the study and propagation of the Gospel, and in each one's own calling, and let us expect from the Son of God help, sustenance, and defense. But that he commands the Apostles to propose [this], he warns the governors of the Church to take care that alms are given, and to know that resources are not diminished, but increased by alms.

He also covertly signifies doctrine, that teachers should propose this, and gather the remnants, and take care that true narrations are propagated, lest the light of doctrine be extinguished for posterity, and by this study the teachers themselves become more learned.

Chapter XVI. And the Pharisees with the Sadducees came, and tempting asked him that he would show them a sign from heaven, etc.

First topic.

Concerning signs, as above in chapter 12, one must judge rather according to the word of God, handed down, from then on from the beginning in the Church through the Fathers, Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, etc. Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees.

Second topic.

II. Solicitude about bread.

At the beginning of the second year after John was killed, he withdrew, lest he be captured by Herod. There are two admonitions. One prohibiting solicitude about sustenance and defense, and leading us to his own examples.

This passage testifies that examples were made for this reason, that we might know they were also proposed to us, so that we might expect similar consolations, just as we have often said elsewhere concerning miracles, that they are examples of promises. And let us learn here that God wishes faith and invocation to be exercised by the expectation of corporal benefits, which are necessary. But the rule must be held, which we often repeat: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you.

First, let the heart be faithful and the conscience good. Afterwards, let us pray and expect defense and help from God, and let us know that he wishes these to be prayed for and expected, and that he wishes to bring help. Thus scripture often teaches: Commit thy way unto the Lord, and he shall bring it to pass. Cast thy care upon God, and he shall nourish thee.

You ought to remember such notable sentences, so that by the thought of them faith and invocation may be kindled, and you may have consolation, and hearts must acquiesce in God, and have firm hope and expectation, and know that such hope and expectation is not in vain. Second admonition. Concerning avoiding the leaven of false doctrine.

Whenever God has handed down true doctrine, an admonition has always been added, that false doctrine should be prudently avoided, because falsehood extinguishes faith, the true knowledge of God, true invocation, true worship, and is the cause of eternal death, and of great [evils]. of madnesses in the human race. Just as formerly on account of false doctrine the Gentiles worshipped idols, and slaughtered men, and did many horrible things, as if they were the best forms of worship.

Thus among those who are called Christians, there have been and are those who have worshipped statues and dead saints. Likewise, those ignorant of the doctrine of faith rushed into despairs. Likewise, many perished on account of celibacy. Likewise, many perished on account of Masses and other foul superstitions. Thus, corrupt doctrine always brings many present and eternal damages. Wherefore let us highly value this often-repeated admonition, and let us be firm and vigilant, lest either manifest errors or the seeds of errors be received, just as many are attempting to plant errors again.

And by name he says: Beware of the leaven, where he signifies a small mass, which nevertheless afterwards draws with it many other errors. As in the worship of saints, if only the beginnings were received again, just as they are now being depicted, their entire idolatry would immediately follow.

And he recites three kinds, the leavens of the Pharisees, the Sadducees, and the Herodians.

Concerning the appearance of the Church.

Here let us learn again what the appearance of the Church is often like, and what in the meantime is the true Church. And let us learn to seek the Church, not from titles, but according to the word of God. This consolation is very necessary, because it behooves us to know whether we are members of the true Church, and to take care that we invoke God in the true Church, as it is written in Proverbs 26: I hate the church of the malignant, and I will not sit with the impious, etc.

Therefore, the true Church is that which rightly teaches the Gospel and rightly administers the sacraments. And the enemies of true doctrine are not members of the Church, whether they be called Bishops, or Priests, or Monks.

And Christ affirms that God wishes to dwell in the true Church, as it is written in John 14: We will come to him, and will make our abode with him. Therefore, let us rejoice that we are in the true Church, just as at that time in Judea the true Church consisted of Mary, Joseph, Zacharias, John, Anna, Elizabeth, and many of their listeners. And yet, in the meantime, the Pharisees, Sadducees, Herod, and other impious men were reigning.

Let us hold to this doctrine and consolation, lest we be moved by the titles and power of the Bishops and

the Pope, who shout that they themselves are the Church. And let us console ourselves with the example of the Saints who existed at that time when the Pharisees and Sadducees were reigning, etc.

But Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, and was asking his disciples, saying: Whom do men say that the son of man is, etc.

Place.

After John was killed, Christ withdrew into the desert beyond Galilee, towards Sidon, where the territory of Philip was, who was the brother of Herod. This Philip had restored the town of Dan, and named it Caesarea. In that desert this question is proposed: Whom do men say that I am? Some John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah.

Here it must first be considered, whence is this diversity of opinions?

Response: Natural reason understands in some way the law of God. Wherefore it also thinks that the sent Prophets are great men, sent to restore the law, and to establish or restore polities.

Just as Moses was sent to restore the polity of Israel. Then the Prophets Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah were sent, so that they might be supports for a while, hülffens ein zeitlang halten, like one places a piece of wood against a bad wall, so that it does not collapse.

These things are understood in some way by reason, and the Jews thought the Messiah would be such, a great Prophet and King indeed, but only an amplifier of a political kingdom etc.

The Lord censures these errors in this place. And He teaches us to think far otherwise about the Messiah.

These articles are far above and outside the natural wisdom of angels and men.

I. God from the beginning after the fall sends the son to the Church, who is the λόγος of the eternal father.

II. And this son brings forth the promise from the bosom of the eternal Father.

III. The Son himself vivifies believers by this promise.

IIII. Sin is remitted and taken away on account of this son, whom they understand is to assume human nature, and to be a victim.

V. Adam and Eve, vivified from death, feel themselves to live on account of this coming Lord, and by faith expect complete liberation from sin and death.

VI. Here the Son assumes human nature, and if this decree concerning the Son had not been made, that He should assume human nature, Adam and Eve would have been utterly destroyed then, and no human would have been born, and this work of God, namely human nature, would have been created in vain.

VII. Here the Son becomes a victim, and always remains the vivifier through the Gospel in the Church; He is present in the Gospel, and thus He is effective.

Just as John 10 says: I give them eternal life. Item: No one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him. VIII. It is not enough to know about the Son, that He is a victim, but it is necessary for you to know also that this Son is effective through the Word, that He may vivify you and be present with you, and give you the Holy Spirit.

All impious men are ignorant of this whole doctrine concerning the Messiah. This is the summary of this question.

Peter therefore answers: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Here Peter embraces the whole doctrine concerning Christ.

Concerning His two natures, and His offices. He calls Him the Son, namely the one sent from the beginning to the Church, and the person through whom the eternal Father immediately issues the promise. And he knows this Son by nature to be the Son above all angels. Because the angels did not know from their own natural wisdom this secret decree concerning redemption. Also, angels cannot take away sin and death. But the promise says: He shall crush the head of the serpent.

He also calls Him Christ or Messiah. This name comprehends two natures: the divine, which is the second person of the divinity sent from the beginning to the Church. The other, the human, assumed from the virgin. This whole Person, in whom are two natures, is the Messiah, that is, our King and supreme Priest.

Here, as Priest, He has these offices: I.

He preaches the Gospel. II. He offers sacrifice for us. III. He always prays for us, in His passion, and afterwards, indeed from the beginning after the fall, according to the saying of Psalm 2: Ask of me, etc. IIII. Item, He has the office of blessing, and He blesses not only by announcing the remission of sins, but also because He Himself in reality takes away sin and death, and restores life, since He is the vivifying λόγος (Word) of the eternal Father.

He is King. Because He frees us from sin, death, and the Devils, destroys the kingdom of the Devil, and restores to us righteousness and eternal life.

Such is the King, restoring the eternal kingdom, not a political one, but in such a way that at a certain time He becomes a victim, as the Prophet says: Because He shall lay down His soul for sin, He shall see a long-lived seed.

Peter's confession embraces all these things.

Text. Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven. I say to you: You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build my Church. And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you shall bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven. And whatever you shall loose, shall be loosed in heaven. After the confession is recited, the doctrine concerning the Church follows.

And the following part contains four principal articles. The first is that the Church is not gathered by human wisdom and human powers, but that the living members of the Church are born, with the Father revealing the Word, and drawing hearts to believe and confirming them. The second is concerning the ministry, that God wills there to be a ministry of confession in the Church, and it distinguishes the proper doctrine of the Church from all sects. The third, the promise and consolation, is concerning the perpetuity of the Church, that it cannot be destroyed, and that it is to endure after this life in all eternity. The fourth is concerning the keys, concerning the express announcement of the remission of sins, which was then unknown to the Pharisees. And in the ministry of the law, there was no command concerning express remission.

Concerning these four matters, even though they are very extensive, I will nevertheless speak briefly, so that you may remember so that you may more easily grasp these summaries.

And this text should often be pondered for common consolation.

But first, remember the definition of the visible Church, as you often hear, because this text will pertain to this definition.

The visible Church is a visible assembly of people embracing the uncorrupted doctrine of the Gospel, and using the sacraments according to the institution of Christ, in which assembly the Son of God himself regenerates many through the Gospel, and yet there are in the same assembly many who are not holy, but who nevertheless agree on the doctrine.

Think of such a Church when you recite the article of faith: I believe in the Holy Catholic Church.

And know that God preserves among men such a Church, which is at times larger, at times smaller, at times more, at times less pure, and think that individual men who wish to be saved must be in this Church, and it is rightly said: Outside the Church there is no salvation.

Everyone, wherever he is, even if he is in Turkey in prison, must join himself to the true Church by confession and will, that he wishes the true Church not to be destroyed, wishes it well, and when he can, he must show, by the use of the sacraments and other duties, that he approves of that Church.

These things must be well considered against errors, and many evil men who run through the world and wish to be citizens of no Church.

Now I come to those four articles which I proposed.

On the first article.

The principal and living members in the Church are those reborn by the Son of God through the voice of the Gospel.

Here let us know that for this reason the promise was issued in the beginning, and that the Son himself is effective through the promise, and the words spoken here to Peter: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my heavenly Father.

These words are best understood if you look at Adam and Eve.

Flesh and blood did not reveal to them the promise concerning the mediator.

Indeed, flesh and blood were ignorant of it, and they were in the midst of death.

But the Son brought forth the voice, and at the same time was effective in their hearts, vivified them, and drew them out of hell, and thus the Church was begun, and in the same way the Son of God always has been, is, and will be effective in his Church.

He himself is the head perfecting all things in all.

And he does this by divine power, therefore he says here: Your heavenly Father has revealed it, namely through the Son.

And through the Son he gives the Holy Spirit to confirm hearts.

On the second article.

In order for the Son to be effective through the Gospel, there must be a ministry of the Gospel, of which he says: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.

Here the Pope, the Anabaptists, Stenckefeld, and many fanatical spirits are to be condemned.

The Pope deletes the promise of grace and turns the whole ministry of the Gospel into a political empire; he says he is Peter, and thus declares that he is a king and can establish laws, the observance of which makes the Church, and meanwhile he is an idolater and a blasphemer; he deletes the promise of the Gospel and fashions idols, commands the invocation of the dead, and the adoration of the bread which he carries around, etc.

In sum, the Pope makes a pagan kingdom.

The Anabaptists and Stenkefeld reject the external ministry and command men to seek other illuminations and fantasies.

This is the meaning: You are Peter, namely, thus confessing, and preaching to others the promise and your confession concerning the Messiah.

Here the preaching minister is Peter, that is, the rock upon which the Church is built, as Eph. 1. it is said: The Church is founded upon the foundation, namely upon the Prophets and Apostles, but in such a way that the cornerstone is Christ himself, just as it is said to the Corinthians: No other foundation can be laid than that which is Christ Jesus.

But this must be preached through the voice of the Prophets and Apostles.

Thus let this statement about the building of the Church be understood most simply as referring to the true ministry.

There is no Church where there is no true ministry.

Nor is Peter there where the promise of grace does not sound, and where idols are confirmed.

It is manifest, however, that in the Pope's synagogue there is no true ministry, there is no voice of the Gospel, and there idols are manifestly confirmed by the sword and cruelty, just as in the kingdom of the pagans.
