And this voice can be administered either simultaneously for many, or for individuals, just as is done in private absolution. Wherefore private absolution is by no means to be abolished or neglected.

And they destroy this text who destroy private absolution. Item John 20. Whose sins you shall remit, they shall be remitted to them.

Concerning the public congregation.

Where two or three shall have been gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.

Men must be diligently taught that God wills there to be public congregations, and why He wills this, and that on account of these He preserves governments, cities, and empires.

That He wills there to be public congregations: It is proved first by the commandment of the Decalogue: You shall sanctify the Sabbaths. And God had so ordained the Sabbath, that a public congregation might take place.

2. Thus the Lord's Supper is instituted, that it may take place in a public congregation.

3. Psalm 22 says: In the midst of the Church I will praise you, in the great people I will celebrate you. Item: His praise in the Church of the saints.

And such are innumerable sayings, as Psalm 2, 68, 109, 149, 102.

But why does He will there to be public congregations?

1. The heathens had secret conventicles. But God wills the voice of His Gospel concerning the Son to sound publicly in the human race; He wills the Son, and Himself, to be acknowledged by all men.

2. He wills there to be public congregations on account of decency, because in secret conventicles many shameful things are done.

3. Indeed, our public assemblies are an image of eternal life. Thus in eternal life we shall decently gather to see and hear God and our Lord Jesus Christ.

That God on account of these congregations preserves cities etc. Jeremiah 17. If you shall not sanctify the Sabbath, God will destroy Jerusalem etc. He therefore grants empires, so that there may be such honest assemblies, as Psalm 122 teaches: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord, etc. Here let there also be considered the promise, specifically added to the common congregation: Wherever two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them. Likewise: If two shall agree, etc.

Now let there be a rebuke. From this admonition learn that it is the will of God that you gather in the public temple to hear the voice of the Gospel, and for common invocation, and thanksgiving, and for the use of the sacraments, just as it is said in Isaiah, chapter 56: My house shall be called a house of prayer.

Those who do not wish to help the preservation of such congregations sin against the commandment: Keep the Sabbath holy. They offend God by contempt of the ministry and the sacraments, and they draw down punishments.

What is more beautiful than an assembly in temples, where the voice of the Gospel sounds without lies? If you do not wish to preserve even this great good by your diligence, God will allow your temples to be reduced to stables for soldiers, just as has happened in Asia and in Greece, where the Turks have now turned temples into stables.

Second admonition.

But let us also know for what purpose we are to gather, namely for these four things: 1. To hear the voice of the Gospel. 2. For invocation. 3. For thanksgiving. 4. For the use of the sacraments.

Latin:

Amen Amen dico vobis: Quaecunque ligaveritis super terram, ligata erunt et in coelo, etc.

Postea in textu sequuntur doctrinae generales de remissione peccatorum, et de communi congregatione Ecclesiae.

Christus expresse dat mandatum remittendi peccata, et affirmat, in coelo veram esse vocem absolutionis: Quicquid ligabitis super terram, erit ligatum in coelo.

Item: Quicquid solvetis super terram, erit solutum in coelo. Hic discant omnes pii, vocem Evangelii esse hanc ipsam vocem, annuntiantem, remitti peccata agentibus poenitentiam.

Et haec vox potest administrari vel simul pro multis, vel pro singulis, sicut fit in privata absolutione. Quare privata absolutio nequaquam abolenda vel negligenda est.

Et hunc textum delent, qui delent privatam absolutionem. Item Ioann. 20. Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur eis.

De publica congregatione.

Ubi duo aut tres congregati fuerint in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio eorum.

Diligenter docendi sunt homines, quod velit Deus esse publicas congregationes, et quare hoc velit, et quod propter has servet regimina, civitates et imperia.

Quod velit esse publicas congregationes: Probatur primum per praeceptum Decalogi: Sabbata sanctifices. Et Deus sic ordinaverat Sabbatum, ut publica congregatio fieret. 2.

Sic instituta est coena Domini, ut fiat in publica congregatione.

3. Psalm. 22. dicit: In medio Ecclesiae laudabo te, in populo magno celebrabo te. Item: Laus eius in Ecclesia sanctorum.

Et talia sunt innumerabilia dicta, ut Psalm. 2. 68. 109. 149. 102.

Quare autem vult publicas congregationes esse?

1. Ethnici habuerunt arcana conventicula. Sed Deus vult sui Evangelii vocem de filio publice sonare in genere humano, vult agnosci filium, et se, ab omnibus hominibus.

2. Vult esse publicas congregationes propter honestatem, quia in arcanis conventiculis multa turpia fiunt.

3. Imo nostri publici coetus sunt imago vitae aeternae. Sic in vita aeterna decenter conveniemus ad videndum et audiendum Deum et Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Quod Deus propter has congregationes servet civitates etc. Ierem. 17. Si Sabbatum non sanctificabis, Deus destruet Ierosolymam etc. Ideo dat imperia, ut sint tales honesti congressus, ut Psalm. 122. docet: Laetatus sum in his, quae dicta sunt mihi: In domum Domini ibimus, etc. Hic consideretur et promissio, peculiariter addita communi congregationi: Ubicunque duo aut tres conveniunt in nomine meo, in medio eorum sum. Item: Si duo consenserint, etc.

Iam fiat obiurgatio. Ex hac commonefactione discatis, voluntatem Dei esse, ut conveniatis in publico templo ad audiendam vocem Evangelii, et ad communem invocationem, et gratiarum actionem, et ad usum sacramentorum, sicut in Esaia dictum est, cap. 56. Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur.

Qui non volunt adiuvare conservationem talium congregationum, peccant contra praeceptum: Sabbata sanctifices. Offendunt Deum contemtu ministerii et sacramentorum, et attrahunt poenas.

Quid pulcrius est congressu in templis, ubi sonat vox Evangelii sine mendaciis? Si hoc tantum bonum non velitis vestra diligentia etiam conservare, Deus sinet vestra templa redigi in stabula militum, sicut in Asia et in Graecia factum est, ubi iam Turci verterunt templa in stabula.

Secunda admonitio.

Sed sciamus etiam, ad quid conveniendum sit, nimirum ad haec quatuor: 1. Ad audiendam vocem Evangelii. 2. Ad invocationem. 3. Ad gratiarum actionem. 4. Ad usum sacramentorum.

## 18:21 Sermons on Matthew
Then Peter came and said: How often shall I forgive?

This passage contains a doctrine most necessary in the Church, and a most ample consolation. Therefore, let it be diligently learned and fixed in the heart. All fearful minds are tormented: since our falls are so frequent, does God forgive sins as often? Just as here it also seems strange to Peter if God forgives so often. Therefore Meletius of Alexandria and Novatus of Rome denied that the lapsed should be received who had manifest offenses, such as those who had committed adultery, or homicide, or who had failed the Gospel in the danger of confession due to fear of punishments. And although the authority of Meletius was so great that a large multitude in Egypt and Syria embraced this harsh error, yet the Alexandrian Bishop Peter constantly opposed him. And he cited this passage of scripture: Forgive seventy times seven.

And he added testimony from the rite of the Church, which even then was receiving the lapsed and pronouncing absolution to them. Just as we still retain the custom of absolving individuals. And indeed, for this very reason it is useful for the custom of individual absolution to be retained, so that this testimony may remain in the Church, that the lapsed are to be received.

Thus let us also hold to this doctrine, that the lapsed are to be received, and let us know that the Lord speaks here of the ministry and true remission before God, when Christ says: Forgive seventy times seven, that is, whenever we ask. Because the number, seventy times seven, is put for an infinite multitude. Now seventy times seven make four hundred and ninety.

Some have badly corrupted this text and contended that it speaks only of fraternal reconciliation between men, not of remission before God. But these do injury to the text and deprave it with great impiety. Because Christ clearly said before: Whatever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

2. Likewise: You have gained your brother. If the remission were not valid before God, he would not gain his brother.

3. And indeed it is a manifest and impudent lie to say that this does not speak of remission before God, when the text afterwards clearly says: So shall my heavenly Father do.

4. And the following parable signifies that very many things are forgiven us by God.

Let us therefore approach the parable, which contains excellent doctrine. The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a king, who would take account with his servants. Here first observe that the kingdom of heaven, that is, the Church, is called to account, and likewise the king's own servants. We are called to account.

We are called to repentance. Therefore it is written in 1 Peter 4: Judgment begins at the house of God.

Therefore, the horrendous security of men is to be greatly detested.

See how great the debt of the first servant is, ten thousand talents, that is, sixty tons of gold. This is as much money as the annual revenues of the French kingdom, and it is not the money of one citizen, or of one prince.

But such a great sum is set forth so that we may know that we have very many and great sins before God. Just as you will easily find many, if you look at your own life. Great is carnal security, then great negligence in invocation, great distrust and many doubts about God. Likewise, various desires wander without end. In sum, we are full of filth and dung.

Now compare the two debts. You owe God sixty tons of gold. Your fellow servant owes you ten crowns. See how unequal the sum is. And God wishes to remit so much, etc.

II. Here let us also learn consolation.

Sins are great and many, but grace abounds over the transgression, Rom. 5: These so many and so great sins God wishes to remit for you assiduously. Here let faith be awakened, so that we may truly believe this. And with this faith let us approach God, and with true invocation let us celebrate Him, and give Him thanks.

But why does He remit such great and so many sins? He remits them not because of our merits, but by His immense mercy because of the Son. This price is so great that it surpasses our sins. Do not think, my sins are greater and more powerful than the Son of God. Rather, most certainly conclude that the Son of God is greater than the whole kingdom of sin is. And remember well the rule: Grace abounds over the transgression, Rom. 5.

III. But afterwards let our obedience follow.

We see here it is most severely commanded that we remit to our neighbors, that we be studious of peace. Let us not hold onto hatreds, and desires for vengeance, etc.

This work of love is necessary, especially in governors and teachers, because among them offenses easily arise, which afterwards beget wars, and discords of the Churches.

Let us omit our pride. Since God remits so much to us, let us also remit much smaller offenses to our brothers.

This is the doctrine concerning good works, which you often hear. And it does not follow that God remits because of our remission, or because of our works. He Himself remits because of the Son, and afterwards our obedience must follow, as you often hear.

Latin:

Tunc accedens Petrus inquit: Quoties remittam?

Hic locus continet doctrinam in Ecclesia maxime necessariam, et amplissimam consolationem. Ideo diligenter discatur, et infigatur pectori. Omnes pavidae mentes excruciantur, an cum tam crebri sint lapsus nostri, Deus toties remittat peccata? Sicut hic Petro etiam videtur mirum, si toties Deus remittat. Ideo Meletius Alexandriae, et Novatus Romae, negaverunt lapsos recipiendos esse, qui habebant delicta manifesta, ut, qui fecerant adulterium, aut homicidium, aut qui in periculo confessionis defecerant ab Evangelio propter metum suppliciorum. Et quanquam Meletii tanta erat autoritas, ut magna multitudo in Aegypto et in Syria hunc durum errorem amplecteretur, tamen Episcopus Alexandrinus Petrus constanter ei adversatus est. Et citavit hunc locum scripturae: Remitte septuagies septies.

Et addidit testimonium ex ritu Ecclesiae, quae tunc quoque lapsos recipiebat, et pronuntiabat eis absolutionem. Sicut nos adhuc retinemus morem singulos absolvendi. Et quidem hanc ipsam ob causam utile est retineri morem absolutionis singulorum, ut maneat in Ecclesia hoc testimonium, quod lapsi sint recipiendi.

Sic et nos teneamus hanc doctrinam, quod lapsi sint recipiendi, et sciamus hic loqui Dominum de ministerio et vera remissione coram Deo, quando dicit Christus: Remitte septuagies septies, id est, quandocunque petimus. Quia numerus, septuagies septies, ponitur pro infinita multitudine. Faciunt autem septuaginta septem, quadringenta et nonaginta.

Aliqui hunc textum male corruperunt, et contenderunt eum tantum loqui de reconciliatione fraterna inter homines, non de remissione coram Deo. Sed hi faciunt iniuriam textui, et magna impietate depravant eum. Quia Christus clare dixit prius: Quicquid solveritis super terram, erit solutum et in coelo.

2. Item: Lucratus eris fratrem tuum. Si remissio non valeret coram Deo, non lucraretur fratrem.

3. Et quidem manifestum et impudens mendacium est, dicere quod hic non dicatur de remissione coram Deo, cum textus postea clare dicat: Sic faciet Pater meus coelestis.

4. Et sequens similitudo significat, nobis plurima remitti a Deo.

Accedamus igitur ad similitudinem, quae continet egregiam doctrinam. Simile est regnum coelorum regi, qui voluit subducere rationes cum servis suis. Hic primum observa, regnum coelorum, id est, Ecclesiam, vocari ad rationes, item proprios servos regis. Nos vocamur ad rationes.

Nos vocamur ad poenitentiam. Ideo scriptum 1 Petr. 4.: Iudicium a domo Dei incipit.

Valde igitur detestanda est horrenda securitas hominum.

Vide quantum sit debitum primi servi, decem millia talentorum, id est, sexaginta tonnae auri. Haec est tanta pecunia, quanti sunt reditus annui regni Gallici, et non est pecunia unius civis, aut unius principis.

Ideo autem tanta summa ponitur, ut sciamus, nos valde multa et magna peccata habere coram Deo. Sicut facile invenies multa, si vitam tuam adspicies. Magna est securitas carnalis, postea magna negligentia in invocatione, magna diffidentia et multae dubitationes de Deo. Item vagantur sine fine cupiditates variae. In summa, pleni sumus sordium et stercoris.

Iam confer duo debita. Tu debes Deo sexaginta tonnas auri. Conservus debet tibi decem coronatos. Vide quam inaequalis summa sit. Et Deus tam multum vult remittere, etc.

II. Hic discamus et consolationem.

Peccata sunt magna et multa, sed gratia exuberat supra delictum, Rom. 5.: Haec tanta et tam multa peccata Deus adsidue tibi vult remittere. Hic fides exsuscitetur, ut hoc vere credamus. Et hac fide accedamus ad Deum, et vera invocatione eum celebremus, et ei gratias agamus.

Quare autem tam magna et tam multa peccata remittit? Remittit non propter nostra merita, sed immensa misericordia propter filium. Hoc pretium tantum est, ut superet nostra peccata. Noli cogitare, mea peccata sunt maiora et potentiora, quam filius Dei. Imo certissime statuas, filium Dei maiorem esse, quam sit totum regnum peccati. Et bene memineris regulam: Gratia exuberat supra delictum, Rom. 5.

III. Sed postea sequatur nostra obedientia.

Videmus hic severissime praecipi, ut remittamus proximis, ut simus studiosi pacis. Non retineamus odia, et cupiditates vindictae, etc.

Hoc opus dilectionis est necessarium, praesertim in gubernatoribus et doctoribus, quia inter illos facile oriuntur offensiones, quae postea pariunt bella, et discordias Ecclesiarum.

Omittamus nostram superbiam. Cum Deus tam multa nobis remittat, remittamus et nos fratribus multo minores offensiones.

Haec est doctrina de bonis operibus, quam saepe auditis. Et non sequitur, Deum remittere propter nostram remissionem, seu propter nostra opera. Ipse remittit propter Filium, et postea debet sequi nostra obedientia, ut saepe auditis.

## 18:23 The 22nd Sunday After Trinity
The 22nd Sunday after Trinity.

Gospel of Matthew 18. Therefore the kingdom of heaven is likened to a king, who wished to settle accounts with his servants.

And when he had begun to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. But since he did not have the means to pay, his lord ordered him to be sold, and his wife and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made. But that servant, falling down, begged him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will pay you everything.

And the lord of that servant, having compassion, released him, and forgave him the debt. But that servant, having gone out, found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. And holding him, he choked him, saying: Pay what you owe. And his fellow servant, falling down, begged him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will pay you everything.

But he would not, but went away, and put him in prison until he should pay the debt. But his fellow servants, seeing what was happening, were very saddened, and came and told their lord all that had been done. Then his lord called him, and said to him: You wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt, because you asked me; ought you not therefore to have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I also had mercy on you?

And his lord, being angry, delivered him to the torturers, until he should pay the whole debt. So also will my heavenly Father do to you, if you do not forgive each one his brother from your hearts.

There are four principal points.

I. These two differ: the public ministry of remitting sins, and the private forgiveness of offenses.

II. The ministry is twofold: the announcement of the Gospel concerning the remission of manifest and unknown sins. And ecclesiastical jurisdiction instituted concerning manifest sins, so that there may be some correction of sinners in the Church.

III. The distinction between ecclesiastical and political government.

IIII. How defense can be joined with private forgiveness, and when defense should be used.

On the first.

The public ministry of remitting sins is the very command of Christ delivered through the Gospel, so that in the Church the remission of sins may be expressly announced to individuals or to many believers, according to that: Whose sins you shall remit, they shall be remitted to them. The Levitical priests did not preach this voice, but they were bound to preach in general, because of the coming Messiah, that the remission of sins was to be believed, as Peter says in Acts ch. 2: Let everyone be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of sins. And 2 Corinthians 5: He has placed in you the word of reconciliation. And here Matthew 18: How often shall I forgive? Seventy times seven. For that former part of the text speaks not only of private forgiveness, but of the ministry, since it clearly says before: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. And this sentiment is to be faithfully retained, that that part speaks of the ministry through which God remits sins. And let us not think it is merely a civil precept about private forgiveness, having nothing to do with divine remission, as many pervert this text.

But private forgiveness is not to hate him who offended you, nor to seek revenge. Just as Jacob loved his brother Esau, although he had been affected by great injuries. Even the heathens know some semblance of this virtue, because this gentleness is necessary in life, not to pursue all injuries, but to forgive many for the sake of public tranquility. Just as at Rome, enemies who were to hold the same magistracy at the same time were publicly compelled to return to favor. And the Attic state made a most humane decree concerning ἀμνηστία (amnesty), that is, the oblivion of injuries. And Scipio used to overlook the injuries of the Tribunes.

But the Church has many more reasons for sparing. The first is because it knows that God commands this forgiveness, and indeed so severely that it has been said: If you do not forgive, your heavenly Father will not forgive you.

The second, because revenge is an honor belonging to God, according to that: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay. God therefore wishes us to omit private revenge.

The third, because we ought to acknowledge that we also have sins worthy of punishment, and since we wish to be spared, we should be so affected toward others, according to that: What you wish to be done to you, do to another. Thus David spared the cursing Shimei, adding a very memorable saying: The Lord will repay me with good for these curses. For it signifies that this patience is pleasing to God, and that it is God's concern that we be adorned again, even when we have been unjustly deformed.

The fourth reason is because God wishes us to spare the common tranquility of the Church, which is disturbed when conflicts are nourished.

The fifth, prayer is disturbed by growing hatreds in revenge.

The sixth, other more necessary business is hindered. Let us diligently consider these causes, and accustom ourselves to this virtue, namely to gentleness, and not indulge in hatreds and the desires of revenge.

On the second. The ministry is twofold. One is the announcement of the Gospel, by which known and unknown sins are remitted. Of this ministry it was properly said: Whose sins you shall remit, they shall be remitted to them. Likewise: Go, preach repentance and the remission of sins in my name. Finally, this is the proper voice of the Gospel, through which God forgives believers, administered either to many or to individuals, as in private absolution.

The other matter is jurisdiction, which pronounces upon manifest offenses. For Christ wished there to be public correction of sinners in his Church.

But because the Church is not a polity like worldly ones, that is, the ministers of the Gospel do not bear the sword: Christ instituted such correction, which does not so much seek punishment as it strives to heal; he orders the fallen one to be admonished first, so that he may return to the way of his own accord. If he returns, he orders him to be received, as it was said: Seventy times seven, because Christ knows many more falls than we imagine. But if he does not return, he orders him to be cast out of the Church, i.e., to be struck with the threat of divine wrath.

This is the nerve of discipline, which Christ established in the Church, and wishes to be kept, just as the Apostles, and then the pious Bishops, executed it in this way by excommunication. The Corinthians excommunicate the incestuous person, and Paul says he was delivered of Satan, that he may torment his body. For some vexation of the body invaded that incestuous man, just as the scribe of Stilicho, whom Ambrose excommunicated, was seized by madness: because true excommunication is not an empty thunderbolt, but by the judgment of God bodily punishments and calamities follow, as it is written in Genesis: I will curse those who curse you.

Concerning the third.

There is a huge difference between ecclesiastical and political government, which must always be in our sight, for confusion brings great darkness. What political government is, human reason easily understands and judges, because God has implanted in the human mind the laws according to which polities must be established. Political government is, therefore, a divine mandate through certain magistrates for the preservation of external discipline, the maintaining of peace, and the punishing of the contumacious with bodily punishments, or the sword. It is a great and wonderful work of God that He not only implanted in our minds the laws by which empires are to be ruled, but that He also Himself in a singular way establishes and transfers them, as is said in Daniel, and especially cares for that part which provides hospitality to the Churches: for to this end He principally establishes empires, that they may be hospices for the Church. But just as many abuse marriage, so many kings and princes abuse empires; they commit unjust slaughters, seize the property of their subjects, and indulge in lusts without measure. When governors thus run rampant in empires, God shakes them off and transfers the kingdoms. For these have always been the causes of changes. Cyrus punished Astyages, who had offered his son to Harpagus to be eaten. Alexander punished the cruelty of the Persians, then the Romans punished the petulance of the Greeks. Julius punished the tyrannies of the Roman nobility. Afterwards, frequent changes were made. And empires in the end will have more confusion and injuries. On the contrary, Solomon says: By justice the throne is established. These things must be thought about concerning empires, so that we may know that men are not associated by chance, but that this political order is the work of God, and that the thing must be distinguished from the persons, that the order is torn apart by the furies of men, and that the tearing apart is punished by God, and that some hospices are preserved for the Churches, some more, some less tranquil.

Therefore, let us faithfully commend to God those empires which are hospices of the Church: for in these, too, many cruel storms arise. Therefore Paul commands to pray for them in 1 Timothy 2. And he shows the end, that you may have tranquility with piety. He commands that peace be sought, not so that we may abuse peace for luxury, but that it may serve education, the protection of discipline, and pious studies. Thus the Psalm teaches to pray, Let there be peace in your strength: and it is placed among the rewards of piety, flourishing, as it is said in the Psalm: That you may see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life.

And Isaiah 33: They will see the king in his beauty, that is, the pious will see the flourishing state of the Republic. But what is ecclesiastical government? It is a mandate of God, which commands to teach the Gospel, to call ministers of the Gospel, to administer the sacraments, to punish the contumacious with excommunication, without bodily force.

This government must be prudently distinguished from the political, and the ends must be considered. This governs not only external morals, but teaches one to invoke God with the heart, and imparts eternal goods to the pious, even when they lose their lives and empires, just as David, although he had been shaken from his kingdom, nevertheless knew that he ought to seek the remission of sins from God, and expect help in present miseries. Let us feel the same now, when the pious are oppressed by the Turks, that they do not therefore fall away from God because they have lost their polities. Let us know that the heavenly kingdom, the ministry of the word, is one thing; let us acknowledge that we are being punished, with the comforts of our bodies snatched away, and let us sustain ourselves with the word of God in these miseries.

Here let us learn that the Gospel is the ministry of the spirit, that is, not an external polity, but the consolation of the mind, which imparts eternal goods, just as David and Manasseh did not lose the ministry of the spirit, even when they were expelled from their kingdom. This admonition is necessary because of those who imagine that only flourishing polities are the people of God, like the Turks, and judge doctrine by the fortune of polities, which must not be done.

I have said that the ministry of the remission of sins is one thing, and private forgiveness is another. The ministry preaches concerning the divine will. Private forgiveness testifies to your will toward another, namely, that you forgive another and do not seek vengeance, and in turn embrace him with true benevolence for God's sake, as David forgave Saul, and Jacob his brother Esau. God requires this duty in the Church for the reasons I have recounted above, and it has rewards, just as other good works, according to that saying: Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you, namely, by the mitigation of punishments.

But here the question is asked concerning the Magistrate, and concerning private defense. The Magistrate is compelled by divine command to punish crimes. First, because of justice, because the justice of God wills that the wicked be removed. Second, to protect the innocent. Third, for the sake of example. And God wills that the magistrate in this his office not be slothful and negligent; he wills that discipline and peace be severely defended, as the law says: You shall not spare him, but you shall remove the evil from the land. And therefore, when the magistrate pollutes himself with the society of crimes, that is, when he is negligent in punishing, whole nations are destroyed. Therefore, let not the sentences concerning private remission be mixed with the office of the magistrate, as Julian mixed them, and mocked the Gospel, as if these sayings concerning remission take away the defense of peace and the sinews of civil society. And the Anabaptists have long spread such delusions. But the rule must be held: In the Gospel, the magistrate and political laws are truly approved, when they are congruent with reason, as is evident from the 13th chapter to the Romans.

As for what is asked concerning defense, the pious must be diligently warned that there is a great difference between defense and private vengeance. As if someone should move an unjust lawsuit against you concerning a field, it is just to use legitimate defense, that is, the aid of the magistrate, by which you retain your property, but let not hatred and the desire to harm the adversary be added. Thus, concerning insults, it is just to respond for the sake of defense, as Christ responds: I do not have a demon. But let not hatred and a more atrocious rage to act against the adversary be added. This difference between defense and private vengeance must be prudently considered.

For the world wickedly mixes them. After a lawsuit has been started, we are not content with legitimate defense, but we are inflamed by hatreds and the desire to harm, and we attempt atrocious things, not so that we may protect ourselves, but so that we may harm the adversary, nay, so that we may destroy him. And from the struggle of a few, sometimes great movements, great dissipations, and civil wars arise. As from the rivalry of Pompey and Caesar, civil war flared up. But let the pious discern these two, defense and private vengeance, and keep themselves within the bounds proposed in the Gospel.

To defend is to retain fame, life, and property in a certain order, without the desire to harm another. Vengeance is the desire to harm in an irritated mind. If anyone attempts to unjustly take away your life or property, it is just to implore the aid of the magistrate, just as Paul appeals to Caesar. But do not add the desire to harm.

If insults are spoken, consider when refutation is necessary, and when it is not necessary. Then refutation is necessary when the Gospel is treated with contumely, or when they brand it with marks of scandal that deform the Church, or when they harm peace or the concord of friends. Just as Athanasius refuted the crimes of magic objected against him, and the machination against the emperor. In such cases, defense is necessary, according to that saying: We have need of a good conscience for our own sake, and a good reputation for the sake of our neighbor. And such defense agrees with this saying: Bless those who curse you. For the one refuting is without the desire to harm, and he blesses, that is, he either teaches the adversaries, or even prays for some, and yet in the meantime is compelled to extinguish the insult of others, as if it were a kindled fire.

But there are many other insults, such as those of ignorance, ignobility, stupidity, and the like, which neither harm the Gospel, nor brand it with marks of scandal, nor harm peace. These it is not necessary to refute.

But for the most part, refutation arises from arrogance or pride, according to that saying: He who would yield in wit, there will be none. And contention, growing little by little, increases dissensions, which, when they wander more widely, often overturn whole republics. Let the pious understand this danger, and repress anger, and altogether dissimulate some injuries, and forgive them for the sake of public tranquility, and not think that one must fight over all small and great matters. For in small matters, there is no need for defense. But let them know that this moderation pleases God, and is necessary for common tranquility, nay, necessary in prayers, namely, to restrain the desire for vengeance, and to altogether dissimulate certain injuries.

As Ecclesiastes 28, many

XII. ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPELS. sentences teach. Abstaining from strife will diminish sins. And for this reason these precepts are repeated so often in the Old and New Testaments, because in every government the desire for revenge excites the greatest disturbances, as it is also said in the verse: For other kingdoms Luxury turns to vices, and pride to hatreds.

Latin:

Dominica XXII. post Trinitatis.

Evangelium Matth. 18. Ideo assimilatum est regnum coelorum homini regi, qui voluit rationem ponere cum servis suis.

Et cum coepisset rationem ponere, oblatus est ei unus, qui debebat ei decem millia talentorum. Cum autem non haberet unde redderet, iussit eum dominus eius venundari et uxorem eius et filios, et omnia quae habebat, et reddi. Procidens autem servue ille, rogabat eum, dicens: Patientiam habe in me, et omnia reddam tibi.

Misertus autem dominus servi illius, dimisit eum, et debitum remisit ei. Egressus autem servus ille, invenit unum de conservis suis, qui debebat ei centum denarios. Et tenens eum suffocabat eum, dicens: Redde quod debes. Et procidens conservus eius, rogabat eum, dicens: Patientiam habe in me, et omnia reddam tibi.

Ille autem noluit, sed abiit, et misit eum in carcerem, donec redderet debitum. Videntes autem conservi eius, quae fiebant, contristati sunt valde, et venerunt et narraverunt domino suo omnia quae facta fuerant. Tunc vocavit illum dominus suus, et ait illi: Serve nequam, omne debitum remisi tibi, quoniam rogasti me, nonne ergo oportuit et te misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego misertus sum?

Et iratus dominus eius, tradidit eum tortoribus, quoadusque redderet universum debitum. Sic et pater meus coelestis faciet vobis, si non remiseritis unusquisque fratri suo de cordibus vestris.

Quatuor sunt loci praecipui.

I. Differunt haec duo, ministerium publicum remittendi peccata, et privata condonatio offensionum.

II. Ministerium est duplex, annunciatio Evangelii de remissione manifestorum et ignotorum delictorum. Et iurisdictio ecclesiastica instituta de manifestis delictis, ut sit in Ecclesia correctio aliqua peccantium.

III. Discrimen ecclesiasticae gubernationis et politicae.

IIII. Quomodo cum condonatione privata coniuncta esse possit defensio, et quando defensione utendum sit.

De primo.

Ministerium publicum remittendi peccata, est ipsum mandatum Christi traditum per Evangelium, ut in Ecclesia expresse annuncietur remissio peccatorum, singulis aut multis credentibus, iuxta illud: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur eis. Hanc vocem non praedicabant levitici sacerdotes, sed in genere concionari debebant, propter venturum Messiam credendum esse remissionem peccatorum, ut Petrus inquit in Act. cap. 2.: Baptizetur unusquisque in nomine Iesu Christi, ad remissionem peccatorum. Et 2. Corinth. 5.: Posuit in vobis sermonem reconciliationis. Et hic Matth. 18.: Quoties remittam? Septuagies septies. Nam prior illa pars textus, non de privata condonatione tantum, sed de ministerio loquitur, cum clare prius dicat: Quicquid ligabitis supra terram, erit ligatum in coelo, et quicquid solveritis super terram, erit solutum in coelo. Estque haec sententia fideliter retinenda, quod illa pars de ministerio loquatur, per quod Deus remittit peccata. Nec tantum putemus esse civile praeceptum de privata condonatione, nihil pertinens ad remissionem divinam, ut multi hunc textum depravant.

Sed privata condonatio est, non odisse eum, qui te offendit, nec vindictam expetere. Sicut Iacob fratrem Esau diligebat, quanquam magnis iniuriis affectus erat. Huius virtutis simulacrum aliquod etiam Ethnici norunt, quia necessaria est in vita haec mansuetudo, non omnes iniurias persequi, sed multas publicae tranquillitati condonare. Sicut Romae publice cogebantur redire in gratiam inimici, qui eosdem magistratus eodem tempore gesturi erant. Et Attica civitas humanissimum decretum fecit de ἀμνηστίᾳ, id est, oblivione iniuriarum. Et Scipio dissimulabat iniurias Tribunorum.

Sed Ecclesia multo plures causas habet parcendi. Prima est, quia scit Deum praecipere de hac condonatione, et quidem adeo severe, ut dictum sit: Si non remiseritis, non remittet vobis pater coelestis.

Secunda, quia vindicta est honos Deo competens, iuxta illud: Mihi vindictam, et ego retribuam. Vult igitur Deus nos omittere privatam vindictam.

Tertia, quia nos agnoscere debemus, nos quoque habere peccata digna poenis, et cum nobis parci velimus, sic simus affecti erga alios, iuxta illud: Quod tibi vis fieri, alteri feceris. Sic David pepercit maledico Simei, addens valde memorabile dictum: Reddet mihi Dominus bonum pro his maledictis. Significat enim hanc patientiam Deo gratam esse, et Deo curae esse, ut rursus ornemur, etiam cum iniuste deformati sumus.

Quarta causa est, quia vult nos Deus parcere communi tranquillitati Ecclesiae, quae turbatur cum aluntur certamina.

Quinta, interturbatur precatio crescentibus odiis in vindicta.

Sexta, impediuntur alia negocia magis necessaria. Has causas diligenter consideremus, et nos ad hanc virtutem, videlicet ad mansuetudinem assuefaciamus, nec indulgeamus odiis, et cupiditatibus vindictae.

De secundo. Duplex est ministerium. Quoddam est annunciatio Evangelii, qua nota et ignota peccata remittuntur. De hoc ministerio proprie dictum est: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur eis. Item: Ite, praedicate poenitentiam et remissionem peccatorum in nomine meo. Denique haec est propria vox Evangelii, per quam Deus credentibus ignoscit, administrata seu multis, seu singulis, ut in privata absolutione.

Alia res est iurisdictio, quae pronunciat de manifestis delictis. Voluit enim Christus in Ecclesia sua correctionem esse publicam peccantium.

Quia vero Ecclesia non est politia similis mundanis, hoc est, ministri Evangelii non gerunt gladium: Christus instituit talem correctionem, quae non tam quaeret poenam, quam sanare studet, iubet primum admoneri lapsum, ut ultro redeat in viam. Si redit, iubet eum recipi, sicut dictum est: Septuagies septies, quia Christus scit multo plures lapsus, quam nos existimamus. Sin autem non redit, iubet eum eiici ex Ecclesia, i. e. feriri comminatione divinae irae.

Hic est nervus disciplinae, quem Christus in Ecclesia constituit, et vult servari, sicut et Apostoli, et deinde pii Episcopi excommunicatione hoc modo executi sunt. Corinthii excommunicant incestum, et Paulus inquit, traditum esse Satanae, ut corpus eius excruciet. Aliqua enim corporis vexatio incestum illum invasit, ut Stilliconis scriba, quem excommunicavit Ambrosius, furore correptus est: quia vera excommunicatio non est inane fulmen, sed iudicio Dei sequuntur corporales poenae et calamitates, ut in Genesi scriptum est: Maledicam maledicentibus tibi.

De tertio.

Ingens discrimen est inter gubernationem ecclesiasticam et politicam, quod semper in conspectu nobis esse debet, nam confusio magnas tenebras affert. Quid sit gubernatio politica, facile intelligit ac iudicat humana ratio, quia Deus indidit humanae menti leges, iuxta quas constituendae sunt politiae. Est igitur politica gubernatio mandatum divinum per certos magistratus custodiendae externae disciplinae, et retinendae pacis, et puniendi contumaces poenis corporalibus, seu gladio. Magnum et mirandum Dei opus est, quod non solum nostris mentibus indidit leges, quibus regenda sunt imperia, sed quod etiam et ipse singulari modo constituit, et transfert, sicut in Daniele dicitur, et praecipue eam partem curat, quae praebet hospitium Ecclesiis: nam ad hunc finem constituit principaliter imperia, ut sint hospitia Ecclesiae. Sicut autem coniugio multi abutuntur, sic multi reges et principes abutuntur imperiis, faciunt iniustas caedes, rapiunt facultates subditorum, sine modo indulgent libidinibus. Cum ita grassantur in imperiis gubernatores, Deus eos excutit, et regna transfert. Nam hae semper fuerunt causae mutationum. Cyrus punivit Astyagen, qui filium vescendum Hapargo praebuerat. Persarum saevitiam punivit Alexander, deinde petulantiam Graecorum Romani punierunt. Romanae nobilitatis tyrannides Iulius punivit. Postea crebrae mutationes factae sunt. Et imperia ad extremum plus confusionis habitura sunt, iniurias. Contra Salomon dicit: Iustitia stabilitur thronus. Haec cogitanda sunt de imperiis, ut sciamus homines non casu consociatos esse, sed hunc politicum ordinem esse Dei opus, et discernendam esse rem a personis, lacerari ordinem furoribus hominum, et a Deo puniri dilacerationes, et aliqua hospitia Ecclesiis servari, alias magis, alias minus tranquilla.

Illa igitur imperia, quae sunt hospitia Ecclesiae, fideliter Deo commendemus: nam in his quoque oriuntur multae saevae tempestates. Ideo Paulus pro his precari iubet 1. Timoth. 2. Et finem ostendit, ut habeatis tranquillitatem cum pietate. Iubet expeti pacem, non ut pace ad luxum abutamur, sed ut serviat educationi, tuendae disciplinae, piis studiis. Sic Psalmus docet orare, Fiat pax in virtute tua: et ponitur inter praemia pietatis florens Resp. ut in Psalmo dicitur: Ut videas bona Ierusalem omnibus diebus vitae tuae.

Et Esai. 33.: Videbunt regem in decore suo, id est, pii videbunt florentem statum Reipublicae. Quid est autem ecclesiastica gubernatio? Est mandatum Dei, quod praecipit docere Evangelium, vocare ministros Evangelii, administrare sacramenta, punire contumaces excommunicatione, sine vi corporali.

Haec gubernatio prudenter discernenda est a politica, et fines considerandi sunt. Haec regit non tantum externos mores, sed docet corde invocare Deum, et aeterna bona impertit piis, etiam cum vitam et imperia amittunt, sicut David, quanquam excussus erat regno, tamen sciebat se a Deo petere debere remissionem peccatorum, et expectare auxilium in praesentibus aerumnis. Ita nunc sentiamus, cum opprimuntur pii a Turcis, non propterea deficiant a Deo, quod politias amiserunt. Sciamus aliud esse regnum coeleste, ministerium verbi, puniri nos agnoscamus, ereptis commodis corporum, et nos verbo Dei in his aerumnis sustentemus.

Hic discamus Evangelium esse ministerium spiritus, id est, non externam politiam, sed consolationem mentis, quae aeterna bona impertit, ut David, Manasses, non amiserunt ministerium spiritus, etiam cum regno expulsi erant. Haec admonitio necessaria est propter eos, qui tantum florentes politias imaginantur populum Dei esse, sicut Turci, et de doctrina iudicant ex fortuna politiarum, quod non est faciendum.

Dixi aliud esse ministerium remissionis peccatorum, aliud privatam condonationem. Ministerium concionatur de divina voluntate. Privata condonatio de tua voluntate erga alterum testificatur, videlicet te remittere alteri, et non expetere vindictam, ac rursus te vera benevolentia complecti eum propter Deum, ut David condonabat Sauli, Iacob fratri Esau. Hoc officium Deus requirit in Ecclesia propter causas, quas supra recensui, et habet praemia, sicut alia bona opera, iuxta illud: Remittite, et remittetur vobis, scilicet mitigatione poenarum.

Sed hic quaeritur de Magistratu, et de privata defensione. Magistratus mandato divino cogitur punire scelera. Primum, propter iusticiam, quia iusticia Dei vult tolli sceleratos. Secundo, ad tuendos innocentes. Tertio, exempli causa. Et vult Deus magistratum in hoc suo munere non esse ignavum et negligentem, vult disciplinam et pacem severe defendi, ut lex inquit: Non parces ei, sed tolles malum de terra. Ideoque cum magistratus polluit se societate scelerum, hoc est, cum est negligens in puniendo, totae gentes delentur. Non igitur misceantur sententiae de remissione privata, muneri magistratus, sicut miscuit Iulianus, et derisit Evangelium, quasi haec dicta de remissione tollant defensionem pacis, et nervos civilis societatis. Et Anabaptistae diu talia deliria sparserunt. Sed tenenda est regula: In Evangelio vere comprobari magistratum, et leges politicas, cum ratione congruentes, ut constat ex 13. capite ad Romanos.

Quod autem quaeritur de defensione, pii diligenter monendi sunt, magnum discrimen esse defensionis et privatae vindictae. Ut si quis iniustam litem tibi moveat de agro, iustum est uti legitima defensione, hoc est, auxilio magistratus, quo res tuas retineas, sed non accedat odium, et cupiditas nocendi adversario. Sic de conviciis, iustum est respondere defensionis causa, ut Christus respondet: Non habeo daemonium. Sed non accedat odium, et rabies atrociora faciendi contra adversarium. Hoc discrimen defensionis et vindictae privatae prudenter considerandum est.

Nam mundus flagitiose commiscet. Postquam lis mota est, non sumus contenti legitima defensione, sed accendimur odiis et cupiditate nocendi, et tentamus atrocia, non ut nos tueamur, sed ut noceamus adversario, imo ut eum deleamus. Et ex paucorum certamine interdum magni motus, magnae dissipationes et bella civilia oriuntur. Ut ex Pompeii et Caesaris aemulatione exarsit bellum civile. Sed pii discernant haec duo, defensionem, et vindictam privatam, et intra metas in Evangelio propositas se contineant.

Defendere, est famam, vitam, res retinere certo ordine, sine cupiditate nocendi alteri. Vindicta, est cupiditas nocendi in animo irritato. Si quis tibi vitam aut res iniuste eripere conatur, implorare auxilium magistratus, iustum est, sicut Paulus provocat ad Caesarem. Sed non addas cupiditatem nocendi.

Si convicia dicuntur, considera quando necessaria sit refutatio, quando non sit necessaria. Tunc est necessaria refutatio, cum Evangelium contumelia afficitur, aut cum inurunt notas scandali, quae deformant Ecclesiam, aut cum nocent paci, vel amicorum concordiae. Sicut Athanasius refutavit obiecta crimina magiae, et machinationem contra imperatorem. In talibus defensione necessaria est, iuxta illud: Bona conscientia nobis opus est nostra causa, bona fama propter proximum. Et talis defensio congruit cum hoc dicto: Benedicite maledicentibus. Nam refutans est sine cupiditate nocendi, et benedicit, id est, vel docet adversarios, vel etiam pro aliquibus orat, et tamen interim cogitur convicium aliorum causa, tanquam excitatum incendium restinguere.

Sed alia multa sunt convicia, ut inscitiae, ignobilitatis, stoliditatis, et similia, quae nec laedunt Evangelium, nec scandali notas inurunt, nec nocent paci. Haec non necesse est refutari.

Sed plerumque ex arrogantia aut superbia oritur refutatio, iuxta illud: Qui velit ingenio cedere, nullus erit. Et contentio paulatim crescens, auget dissidia, quae cum latius vagantur, saepe totas respub. evertunt. Hoc periculum pii intelligant, et reprimant iracundiam, et aliquas iniurias prorsus dissimulent, ac condonent publicae tranquillitati, neque de omnibus parvis et magnis rebus pugnandum esse existiment. Nam in parvis defensione nihil opus est. Sed sciant hanc moderationem Deo placere, et necessariam esse communi tranquillitati, imo necessariam in precationibus, videlicet, frenare cupiditatem vindictae, et quasdam iniurias prorsus dissimulare.

Sicut Ecclesiast. 28, multae

XII. ANNOTATIONES IN EVANGELIA. sententiae docent. Abstinens a lite peccata minuet. Ideo autem toties in veteri et novo testamento haec praecepta repetita sunt, quia in omni gubernatione maximos motus excitat cupiditas vindictae, ut in versu etiam dictum est: Nam caetera regna Luxuries vitiis, odiisque superbia vertit.

## 19:1 Sermons on Matthew: Argument
Chapter XIX. The Pharisees came to Jesus, tempting him, and saying: Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?

In this chapter the question concerning divorce is treated. And Christ approves and repeats the necessary doctrine concerning marriage, and restricts the opinion concerning divorce.

But since the question concerning divorce pertains more to the Consistory than to sermons in the Church, I wish to say in order some necessary things concerning marriage.

Christ repeats the institution of marriage, made with these words: They shall be two in one flesh.

This saying is the perpetual law concerning marriage, sanctioning that it be the perpetual and indissoluble union of one male and one female, and prohibiting every commixture outside this instituted order.

First, therefore, from this saying of Genesis let it be held what marriage is. And let it be known that God ordained such a union, and approves it.

Secondly, let it be known that the law concerning marriage was given immediately in Paradise, because God wished human nature to obey Him, especially in this work, in preserving chastity in marriage, and before marriage.

And afterwards, after the fall of men, He horribly punished sins committed against chastity, such as adulteries and other wandering commixtures. And always and universally in the human race until the end God punishes, and will punish, wandering lusts with many public and private punishments. This is most certain, as it is written: God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Let us know these things, and fearing the wrath of God, let us take care to preserve chastity, either in marriage, or in the celibate life, as the age of the young or the old requires. And let us diligently consider the severity of God in this matter. Do not think that God makes little of sins against chastity. Consider the examples of punishments from the beginning. The cause is alleged for the flood, that they took and seized women, whom each one wanted. Afterwards He destroyed

Sodom. Likewise, in the desert, the princes of the tribes were hanged because of whoredom. And twenty-four thousand men were killed. Likewise: The tribe of Benjamin was almost entirely destroyed because of the defiled wife of the Levite. Likewise, David was expelled from the kingdom, and many thousands were slaughtered. The Ethnic histories are manifest in many ways; Troy was destroyed because of the abducted Helen. In Rome, kings were expelled because of the violated Lucretia. And many such histories of our own time could be recited, which show that adulteries and other wandering lusts are horribly punished. And let us not doubt, each one who is guilty will experience the punishments in himself. This is most certain, but God mitigates the punishments for those who do penance. Let us know this first, that it is the command of God that we live chastely, whether in marriage, as God ordained, or outside of marriage. And let us know that sins against chastity are horribly punished. Secondly, let us also know why God wishes chastity to be kept so severely. This is the cause: Since God is a chaste Spirit, He wishes chastity to be understood in the human race, and He wishes Himself to be distinguished from unclean spirits and men. For we cannot embrace God with our arms, but He must be recognized by thought, that He is such an essence—wise, truthful, just, beneficent, chaste—which revealed itself by sending His Son. Therefore, in every invocation, one must think about what you are invoking, and which God you are invoking; this God must be separated from all unclean natures. The Ethnics worshipped gods who favored wandering lusts. Indeed, they held the lusts themselves to be pious works; God horribly condemns these frenzies and wishes His Church to greatly abhor such frenzies. Let us often think of this cause in invocation, why God demands chastity, and let us think of Him as a chaste mind; indeed, thinking of our own uncleanness, let us the more deplore our uncleanness, and let us pray that He may also bend us toward chastity, because He Himself loves chastity. This doctrine concerning chastity and the punishments of lusts must be thought about often and much. Here now must be added a complaint against the doctrines of demons; the Devil has always vexed the human race, horribly impelling it so that it might be polluted by various lusts. And wherever there was idolatry, there were foul lusts, as is signified in Rom. 1. Thus, in the Papacy there are unclean celibate canons and monks, and such will always be.

The Pope once sent a dispensation concerning the marriage of priests into Germany, but in such a way that the priests might retain their wives, but not be in the ministry. This is, in reality, to restore celibacy as it was before, so that there might be whoremongers and adulterers in the ministry. But the Pope will always be a defender of the most shameful lusts, nor should we expect better things from the Papacy, because it is a blinded and condemned kingdom. But God, loving chastity, will defend the Church, in which there is true doctrine concerning other articles, and concerning chastity. This I wished to warn first concerning chastity, just as we ought often to speak of this virtue. Next, I will say a few things concerning divorce.

Concerning divorce.

Let us learn what marriage is, which God ordained, and let us avoid all things that fight against that ordinance, because it is certain that all sins fighting against this law of His are horribly punished by God. What is marriage? It is the lawful and indissoluble conjunction of one male and one female, instituted by God for the sake of procreation, and so that all other commixtures of bodies outside this ordained conjunction might be avoided. This definition is contained in this saying: They shall be two in one flesh, that is, inseparably joined. The first institution, therefore, prohibits polygamy, that is, to have many spouses at the same time, because the text says most plainly: They shall be two. And Christ recalls His Church to this first institution. For although God permitted another Ethnic custom even to the fathers in the Law, yet that custom was contrary to the first institution. And it is nowhere approved by the command of God, but only permitted. Now, however, Christ recalls us to the first institution, which we should consider most diligently. Secondly, Christ prohibits divorces. And here it must be considered how great is the malice of men. All Ethnics and Jews shamefully abused divorces. Just as the Turks do now. Whenever anyone wished, whether there was a cause or there was no cause, he cast out his wife. It often happened also that someone would practice so that another would make a divorce, so that he might possess the other's spouse. Just as Hortensius asked Cato to make a divorce with his wife Martia, so that he himself might marry her. And he married her afterward. Such levities conflict with the institution of marriage, which ought to be a perpetual will to retain one's spouse. Since, therefore, the Jews were playing around in this way, Christ openly restricts divorces to this one case: when the other person becomes an adulterer. For then, by the very act of adultery, the bond of marriage is dissolved, and the person who sinned becomes guilty of death and ought to have been put to death. Let this suffice to have said here. More things, which ought to be said here, I commend to the Consistory and the courts.

The preacher ought to teach this especially, so that the people may know what marriage is, and what it ought to be, and that he may take care that this bond is preserved, so that it is not dissolved, and that spouses may have patience with one another, even if there is some infirmity in the husband or wife, on account of which the other person would willingly seek a dissolution. Here we preachers propose the voice of the Gospel to men, so that they do not make unjust separations. Likewise, that the other person may not exercise such cruelty that they appear to want to torment the other for so long and so harshly that they either flee or die. For there are many murderers in marriage, sometimes husbands, sometimes wives. Let them learn to curb this bitterness and cruelty, and let them know how to fight it with the commandment.

After this sermon on marriage, when the disciples hear that divorces are restricted, they begin to murmur and complain that marriage is a hard bond. Here Christ meets their question: whether one must live in celibacy. And he says clearly: Not all grasp this word. That is, he wants the rule to be kept, that all men should live in marriage who are not in a singular way or by a gift suitable for chaste celibacy. Paul also hands down this rule: Let each one have his own wife for the sake of avoiding fornication. Let us not tempt God, nor against this ordinance of God let us institute another kind of life, just as the Pope forces a huge multitude into celibacy, and Monks and Nuns instituted another kind of life, from which horrible sins have arisen, on account of which God punishes the whole human race, just as he punished Sodom.

However, he excepts three kinds of men. First are those excepted who are born by nature in such a way that they are not suitable for the marital custom. Secondly, those who have been castrated by iron or similar violence. Thirdly, those who have a singular gift, so that they can live as celibates without impurity, like John the Baptist, Christ, John the Evangelist. The text itself shows that these are few, saying: Not all grasp this word. Likewise, he who can grasp it, let him grasp it.

Let other men, according to nature, as it is in the majority, know that the rule handed down by God must be kept, which in Genesis says clearly: The Lord said, it is not good for man to be alone, I will make him a helper like him. Hear, O all you pious ones, consider these words well; in Genesis the Lord said: Who commands marriage? God himself, who said—that is, by an eternal and immovable decree he sanctioned—that there should be such a conjunction of male and female. Now see the audacity of the Pope, who deletes this word: The Lord said, and puts the contrary: The Pope says, it is good for man to be alone. Nay, the most shameful law of the Pope says that marriage is an impurity, and on the contrary praises the most impure celibacy. God has uncovered this impiety, and let us pray to him that he may be present to his own ordinance, and defend and govern spouses.

Then little children were brought to him, so that he might lay his hands on them and pray. But the disciples were rebuking them. But Jesus said to them: Let the little children be, and do not forbid them to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.

This is a sermon about children, very worthy of memory, which we distribute into four parts. The first part should be about the duty of parents. For we want to start with the parents, because the text here also speaks of those bringing the children. The second part should be about the baptism of infants. The third part should be about the instruction and education of infants, whose age is already capable of discipline. The fourth part should be about the will of God toward the first age, that those who retain the gifts of baptism are pleasing to God, and are protected and guarded by God against the furies of the devil, and in wars and many dangers: and let them take care that the younger ones retain God's gifts.

Of the first part. Of the duty of parents.

We will speak of two groups of children. Of the first age which is to be brought to baptism is, even if he is not yet capable of instruction, and about children who are already capable of instruction. I speak of both, that it is the duty of parents to bring both to Christ, as the age of each permits. Let them bring infants of the first age to baptism, and take care that they become members of the Church of God. Because here they learn that such infants are also truly and certainly received by God. And that God wills that such should become members of the Church through the ministry, and that they should be brought to the ministry, namely, to baptism. And let it be a great consolation to parents that they know this age is an heir of eternal life, and they know that that weak age is pleasing to God and is guarded by God, and that they have in their cradles citizens of the heavenly kingdom. Let them know, therefore, that it is the command of God that the parents themselves take care that their offspring be brought to baptism. Then, after the age is capable of instruction, let them also educate them, as Paul commands in Eph. 6: Bring up your offspring in the discipline and divine doctrine. Let parents also commend their offspring to God with assiduous prayers. All these things are comprehended in the word: Bring your offspring to Christ.

Concerning the second part.

You know that the Anabaptists have horribly disturbed the Church by denying the baptism of infants. And they have done injury to God, to the infants, to the Church, and to parents.

1. They did injury to God, because they denied that He receives infants, which would be most harsh, and is manifestly false, because Christ says: It is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should perish. Likewise, they corrupted the divine promises, because they excluded infants from them. 2. They did injury to the infants themselves, they condemned those who should not be condemned, since Christ clearly says: Of such is the kingdom of heaven. 3. They did injury to the Church of God, because they condemned a great part of the Church, and prevented infants from becoming members of the Church. 4. They did injury to parents, whose invocation for their infants was hindered, and it would be a great sorrow if infants were rejected by God. Therefore, you ought to be fortified against the error of the Anabaptists, and with certain faith establish that infants are received by God through baptism. And you ought to commend them to God with your prayers and your faith. But hold fast to the confirmation from this text.

First confirmation.

Christ commands that infants be brought to Him, and most clearly affirms that of such is the kingdom of heaven. And the kingdom of heaven does not belong to those who are outside the Church. Therefore, it is necessary that they be inserted into the Church and become members of the Church through baptism. Second confirmation. God made this admonition, that He wills to save only those called to the Church, upon whom the name of the Son has been invoked. Therefore He says: Whom He chose, these He also called, Rom. 8. And nowhere does He wish the elect to be sought, except in the assembly of the called, which is of great consolation: Nowhere are the elect, except in the assembly of the called. And always in the assembly of the called there are some elect. Some infants are elect, because the text clearly says: It is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should perish. Therefore, it is necessary that they become members of the assembly of the called through the ministry, that is, through baptism.

Third confirmation. The promise of the remission of sins and of the Holy Spirit and of eternal life pertains to infants. Nor do I wish to add more arguments; it is enough for you to consider these, and I exhort you to consider them diligently, and to give thanks to God for such a great benefit, that He receives infants, and that you come to baptism with greater reverence, and there with the whole Church of the whole world commend the infants to God. Do not think it to be an empty game, but know that your offspring truly become there citizens of the heavenly kingdom and children of God. We are too negligent, because we do not consider such great benefits more diligently, and do not give thanks. Therefore I exhort you, that you both consider these works of God more diligently, and give thanks to God.

Third part.

Just as I said before that parents ought to educate the age that is already capable of doctrine, so now I say again: You ought not only to take care that infants are baptized, but this is also necessary afterwards is to instruct children about God and the Son of God, and to instill the whole doctrine of His Gospel little by little, and to accustom them to the invocation and recognition of the Son of God. This voice embraces all these things: Suffer the little children to come unto me. You are not parents only so that you may care for their bodies, but you ought also to lead their souls to God. And the families of individuals ought to be like Churches. You, father, you, mother, ought to be like pastors of your children, and to instruct them, and to accustom them to invocation. And if you do not do this, God will punish this negligence, just as He punished Eli for not chastising his sons.

The Fourth Part.

Consolation for the younger ones, and an exhortation that they may preserve the gifts of God.

Consider, I pray, when you are in your chambers with your little children, what a great good this is, that you know these little ones born of you, your own blood, are pleasing to God, are citizens of the heavenly kingdom, are guarded by the Son of God and by the holy Angels, and that because of them, the Angels dwell with you. Devils lie in wait for them horribly, but the Son of God protects His members, just as He also says: Their angels behold the face of the Father. Parents themselves confess: there are so many dangers to children that no human diligence would suffice to save them, unless they were guarded by God. These things are often to be pondered, and prayer is to be added, and that invocation of your domestic Church is most pleasing to God—the groaning of parents and the voice joined with the voice of the children. And in every chamber these sayings ought to be written: Of such is the kingdom of heaven. Item: It is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should perish.

Exhortation to the younger ones.

But listen, you younger ones, the diligence of parents is not enough if you yourselves also do not wish to retain the gifts of God, if you do not wish to learn. Item, if you wish to offend and grieve the Holy Spirit. Therefore, take care that you retain the gifts of God. Consider what a great good it is that you are pleasing to God, that God hears you, as long as you retain the Holy Spirit received in baptism. On the contrary, what a horrible misery it is not to be pleasing to God, not to be heard by God, to be a captive of the Devil. Avoid these greatest evils with all care. And also diligently inculcate these sayings to yourselves: It is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should perish. Give thanks to God, and kindle invocation in your hearts, and the care of retaining the gifts of God. Item, inculcate to yourselves also this saying: Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings Thou hast perfected praise. God wishes to be acknowledged and invoked by you.

And behold, one approaching said to Him: Good Master, what good shall I do, that I may have eternal life, etc. In this history, manifold doctrine is contained. The first article is the reproof of hypocrisy, when Christ says: Why callest thou me good? For although this man was speaking the truth, yet because he was not speaking with a true heart, he is reproved. For he does not ask in order to obey, but immediately departs again, and does not judge Him to be a good master, because he soon deserts His doctrine. But God requires the truth of the heart, and does not wish to be invoked with a false heart, even if true praises are attributed to Him, just as it is written: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart.

The second article concerning the saying: If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments. Many disputations have been handed down concerning this saying, and the Monks have built up from it this fantasy, that men can satisfy the law of God, and that men are saved on account of the fulfillment of the law. But whenever mention of the law is made, one must immediately look to the saying of Paul: Christ is the end of the law, that is, without the recognition of the Son of God, there is neither law, nor does it profit. But the law was given so that it might show us sin, and signify the Messiah who was to come, so that He might take away sin, and truly satisfy the law, and restore it in us. Just as the victims manifestly signified the death of the Messiah for our sins. And all who were rightly instructed knew that those victims, lambs and calves, did not take away sins.

Therefore, this saying: If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments, is to be understood in such a way that the commandment concerning hearing the Son of God, or concerning faith in the Son of God, is included. Keep the commandments, namely, also the first commandment concerning faith in the Son of God. This being understood, the declaration is easy: If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments, namely, also first believe in the Son of God, then do the other works of the ten commandments, which, although they will be imperfect and very languid, on account of our great infirmity, yet they will be pleasing to God, because you believe in the Son, and have the remission of sins, and have been made an heir of eternal life, on account of the Son. This is the simplest and true declaration of this saying, and one to be well observed, because Papists greatly deprave this saying. And yet they themselves must also admit that they do not keep the commandments of the Decalogue. But it is customary for them to speak a lie in hypocrisy.

The third article is about the ignorance of the Pharisees of that time, and it is a similar ignorance to that of many in all times.

He thought he was satisfying the law of God, and boldly answers: All these I have kept. Thus then the Pharisees taught, and thus the Monks taught, that a man can satisfy the law of God, and that external works are the fulfillment of the law, and merit the remission of sins and eternal life: and that men can do more, and that it is perfection to do works of supererogation, and in sum, many foul and pernicious errors about the law exist today in the doctrine of the Monks.

But let us know our misery in the Church. The law of God is the wisdom and justice of God, demanding that our minds and hearts conform to that rule of the divine mind. Nor does it only demand external deeds, but we are all forced to admit that our hearts are full of evil desires, and in no way conform to the law of God. Therefore the law indicates and condemns all, just as Paul says: That the whole world may be guilty before God. It is necessary that this doctrine be well understood in the Church. And let us learn to approach God by the faith of the Son of God, and let us confess that we are unclean, and in no way satisfy the law of God.

The fourth article is again a rebuke of hypocrisy.

This man had boasted that he kept the law. And Christ commands him to sell his inheritance and become a minister of the Gospel. Here hypocrisy is revealed, because he does not want to obey this Lord, whom he had previously called a good teacher: and he values riches more than the ministry of the Gospel. Let us consider this rebuke, and let us also search our own hearts, whether we are willing to lose our possessions and our life for the sake of the Gospel. Here we will find great weakness in ourselves as well, but yet let us not depart, as this man departed, but let us ask that the Son of God may confirm us.

The fifth article, concerning perfection.

Here the Monks have disputed much about perfection, because of the saying: If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all, and give to the poor, and follow me.

Here it must first be known that all that insanity of the Monks, that they feigned that it is perfection to leave one's property and become a Monk, are diabolical errors, because perfection is not in works not commanded by God, of which it is said: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. Secondly, no man perfectly keeps the law of God, except Christ. Indeed, we all have sins, as the Psalm says: No one living shall be justified in your sight. Item: If we say that we have no sin, we are liars. Therefore that pride of those who boast and attribute perfection to themselves, die vollkommenheit [perfection], is to be detested. And the word 'perfect' here does not mean vollkommen [perfect], to whom nothing is lacking, but it is the opposite of a hypocrite; if you wish to be perfect, that is, rechtschaffen [upright], on heucheley [without hypocrisy], because Christ wants to signify this, that this man is a hypocrite. He does not want to concede that he had kept the law, and that only something was lacking for perfection.

Sixth article: Is it perfection, or a good work, to leave one's property?

I answer first. I have already said it is not perfection. Secondly, there is a twofold desertion: one which has the command of God, as in confession, where God commands one to depart from property rather than cast away the confession of doctrine. This desertion of property is a good work. Another desertion is without the command of God, as when Monks or Anabaptists leave their possessions. This is not a good work; indeed, God wants there to be households, and He wants us to serve in this common life; He does not want us to flee into the woods, etc.

Amen I say to you: A rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven etc. Here consciences must be taught about the general rule, that the Gospel does not abolish economic or political ordinances. But it is a doctrine of faith and true invocation of God, and true obedience of the heart toward God. He allows us, however, to have property, to have households, to become magistrates, to exercise judgments.

And He approves of this external political or economic life, and wants to see in it invocation, confession, love toward husband, wife, children, parents, and towards other men, so that the whole life, interior and exterior, may serve God, and God may be celebrated. This rule being known, it must also be known that it is the will of God that some should be rich, others poor. Because it is necessary that some be rich for the utility of the republic, for empires cannot be maintained without resources. But here both must be learned: to use riches rightly, and to bear poverty rightly. A poor man can be much worse than a rich man, as the robber hanging on the cross, and mocking Christ, was truly poor and miserable. Nor does poverty merit eternal life. I shall say, therefore, first, how poverty is to be rightly tolerated, because the greater number is of the poor.

1. Let the poor man know that he is neither just nor unjust because of his poverty, but let him seek justice by faith in the Son of God. 2. Let him know that it is the will of God that some be rich, others poor, just as Solomon says: The rich and the poor dwell together, God made them both. Let him also know that it is the will of God that a man should obey in poverty, just as in bodily weakness, and not murmur against God because he is poor, just as it would be insanity if you were to murmur against God because he did not give you a body as robust as the body of Samson was. 3. Let the poor man know that because of poverty, evil arts, thefts, lies, and flatteries are not to be sought, just as many come into courts, and because of poverty they basely flatter; therefore Solomon says: Give me neither riches nor poverty, lest fullness make me proud and forgetful of God. And on the contrary, lest poverty make me become a thief or a flatterer, failing God. 4. Let him seek honest labors, and in these exercise faith and invocation. If he does this, God will bless his labors and his family, so that he may live more comfortably than many who are very rich. For what do riches profit the foolish Nabal, who fills himself, so that he may die? etc. Let him not be a sturdy beggar, like the Monks; such sturdy beggars are thieves.

Concerning the rich man.

Now we shall also provide rules for the rich man. First, let him also seek here justice by faith in the Son of God. Secondly, let him know that riches are a gift of God, and that he does not possess more by chance than others possess, but that God, by a certain counsel, gives greater resources to some, and lesser to others. Let him therefore give thanks to God. Thirdly, let him not be proud, let him not trust in his riches. Let him not think that he can therefore justly oppress the poor because he himself is rich. But rather let him know that he ought to do good to the poor, just as it is commanded to the rich: Let your fountains be derived abroad, and you remain the Lord of them. This most sweet saying commands both, that we should help others, and it shows the manner, namely, that you do not lose your estates, but remain the Lord of your house and fields. And thus it confirms that it is permitted to have property and riches.

Fourthly, let him not practice gains prohibited by God, and usury, nor set unjust prices. Amen I say to you: A rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven, etc. Christ says: He shall hardly enter. And afterwards he exaggerates the difficulty: It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle etc. Let the rich fear this threat, and be more cautious in the use of riches, and in their gains. But on the contrary, let the poor also know that many abuse poverty, becoming flatterers of the powerful for a fragment of bread, etc.

However, having heard this sentence concerning the difficulty, the Apostles are terrified, because they were still dreaming of the kingdom of the Messiah, and great riches, but nevertheless they first ask about eternal life: Who can be saved? Here a useful doctrine and consolation is proposed. The doctrine is: With men it is impossible to be saved. Here he teaches generally that men are not saved by their own diligence, wisdom, justice, or by their own strength, just as scripture often cries out: By the works of the law shall no flesh be justified. Item: He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him, John 3.

On the contrary, the consolation: With God all things are possible. Here he leads us to acknowledge God, as he has revealed himself, with promises given, the Mediator sent, and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

It is necessary to embrace all these things here.

The saying is general: With God all things are possible. But it must be known that God is effective in such a way as he promised he would be effective.

But it is a good and sweet consolation when he says "All things." We always think, he could and would save others, but I am too great a sinner, I have too many sins, He does not want to save me; rather, He says: All things are possible, namely, in that way, as He promised: If you believe in the Son and are converted.

Keep this consolation well in mind.

Behold, we have left all things, and have followed You; what will there be for us?
