Postquam autem dixit de illa nova Ecclesia collecta ex gentibus, hic rursus ostendit discrimen vere credentium et hypocritarum, qui secundum externam speciem sunt in Ecclesia et in convivio, et tamen non vere credunt, non vere adorant sponsum, non habent, inquit, vestem nuptialem.

Omitto autem longas et multiplices disputationes de veste, et dico simpliciter: Vestis nuptialis est vera et viva fides, quae in vera poenitentia sentitur, et erigit corda, et accendit invocationem veram, spem et confessionem, et alios fructus, qui sequi debent. Haec fides vera, non simulata, est vestis nuptialis, sicut in Hosea dicitur: Desponsabo te mihi in fide.

Et in hoc ipso Psalmo dicitur: Audi filia, et vide, et inclina aurem tuam. Hic sponsus vult se audiri, vult nos aures inclinare, id est, vera fide amplecti Evangelium etc.

Discamus igitur hoc loco haec tria:

1. Quod veri cultus in Ecclesia sint, haec fides et vera poenitentia, vera invocatio, spes et dilectio.

2. Quod in Ecclesia, in hac vita sint mixti vere credentes et hypocritae, et non offendamur, quod non omnes in Ecclesia sint sancti et firmi, sed sciamus Ecclesiam tale corpus esse, quod multos continet malos. Et tamen certum est, nunquam esse Ecclesiam Dei electam, nisi in hoc ipso coetu vocatorum, in quo simul multi sunt hypocritae. Non igitur currendum est in solitudinem, ut eremitae fecerunt, nec faciendae aliae congregationes clam, sicut Anabaptistae fecerunt. Sed maneas in hac Ecclesia, ubi audis filium Dei, huic inclina aurem.

3. Sequitur poena impiorum, et nominat tenebras, quae foris sunt, id est, extra regnum coelorum sunt tenebrae, et stridor dentium, id est, horribiles pavores et dolores, de quibus cogitemus, ut timentes iudicium et iram Dei, convertamur ad Deum, et quaeramus hunc nostrum sponsum, filium Dei, vere nos diligentem ardenti amore.

## 22:14 Sermons on Matthew
Many are called, few are chosen.

There is consolation and there is threatening.

Consolation for the pious, who, when they see many falling away, and likewise many living in the Church in manifest wickedness, are offended, and dispute with themselves whether such a gathering can be the true Church of God, in which there are so many who are light-minded, inconstant, and likewise otherwise contaminated by manifest sins.

But in many sermons Christ paints such a picture of the Church, to signify that in this life the Church is and will be a great gathering, in which there are and will be many hypocrites. But yet in this very gathering where the Gospel sounds, there is and will be the Church of the elect, and nowhere else. This consolation is to be considered first in this saying.

There follows a threatening against the negligent.

All threats in the whole heavenly doctrine from the beginning of the world to the end are proposed for this reason, that some, moved by the admonition and threat of God, might be converted, as the history of Jonah shows. And let all threats be understood with this exception, that God is willing to remit sins to those who do penance. And let the oath be compared to this: As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner.

But here many object: If the election of God saves, there is no need for our conversion. And if anyone is not elected, conversion profits him nothing. Against this pernicious error it is necessary that all men be rightly taught, and well confirmed.

And first, let this rule be held: We must judge concerning the will of God from the revealed word, and not from any other imaginations. Nor must we seek God without his Gospel. Already in the Gospel he has taught how he receives a man, and how he rejects him. It is certain that he receives one who does penance and believes. You should hold fast to this most firm sentiment, which is also most true without any doubt.

And when a man departs from this life in this way, doing penance and believing, then without any doubt he is elected. However, it is necessary that conversion take place in this life, according to that: Be faithful even unto death.

That is: Begin in this life, and in death do not cast away faith.

On the contrary, it is most certain from the Gospel that all those in whom there is no penance or conversion, and who despise the Gospel, are displeasing to God. And if anyone departs in this way without penance and without faith, he is without doubt rejected, as John says: He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him. To know this concerning the will of God and concerning election or rejection is enough, nor should you seek another will, but judge according to this word, which is truly the lamp of the saints.

Secondly, when you know this, that it is most true that one who does penance and believes is received, and is elected if he departs in this way, and that it is necessary that conversion take place in this life: you should begin conversion, and console yourself with the oath of God: As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, etc., and do not be a blasphemer against the Son of God, do not think that he was sent in vain.

Confirm yourself also with these universal promises: Come to me all you who labor, etc.

Everyone who shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. God wills all men to be saved.

Thirdly, let not this imagination delay you, that you cannot effect conversion.

Nay, you can, with God helping, and he himself truly wills to help, and he helps those who ask, according to that: How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask? God does not force, he does not drag you like a stone, resisting and unwilling, but it is necessary that you also will. And when you will and ask, it is most certain that you are helped by him. These consolations are truly necessary for all, and it is a great and clear argument that God truly helps those who flee to the Son.

In God there are no contradictory wills.

The promises are universal. Therefore it is most true that he receives all and wills to help them, when he says: Everyone who shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. You, therefore, should see to it that you include yourself in that promise, and do not doubt that you too are received and heard. And he who feels otherwise about the will of God departs from His word, and does not judge of the will of God according to the word, but according to human and foreign imaginations. Then the Pharisees went and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk.

Latin:

Multi sunt vocati, pauci electi.

Consolatio est et comminatio.

Consolatio pro piis, qui cum vident multos deficere, item multos in Ecclesia vivere in manifestis sceleribus, offenduntur, et disputant secum, an talis coetus possit esse vera Ecclesia Dei, in qua tam multi sunt leves, inconstantes, item alioqui contaminati manifestis delictis.

Sed in multis concionibus pingit Christus talem speciem Ecclesiae, ut significet, in hac vita Ecclesiam esse et fore coetum magnum, in quo sunt et erunt multi hypocritae. Sed tamen in hoc ipso coetu sonante Evangelium, est et erit Ecclesia electorum, et non alibi. Haec consolatio primum in hoc dicto consideranda est.

Sequitur comminatio contra negligentes.

Omnes comminationes in tota doctrina coelesti a principio mundi usque finem ideo proponuntur, ut aliqui moti admonitione et comminatione Dei convertantur, sicut ostendit historia Ionae. Et omnes comminationes intelligantur cum hac exceptione, quod agentibus poenitentiam Deus velit remittere peccata. Et conferatur huc iusiurandum: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris.

Sed hic obiiciunt multi: Si electio Dei salvat, nihil opus est nostra conversione. Et si quis non est electus, nihil prodest ei conversio. Contra hunc perniciosum errorem necesse est omnes homines recte doceri, et bene confirmari.

Ac primum teneatur haec regula: Nos de voluntate Dei debemus iudicare ex verbo revelato, et non ex ullis aliis imaginationibus. Nec debemus quaerere Deum sine ipsius Evangelio. Iam in Evangelio docuit, quomodo recipiat hominem, et quomodo reiiciat. Certum est, quod recipiat agentem poenitentiam et credentem. Hanc sententiam firmissimam retineas, quae etiam sine ulla dubitatione verissima est.

Et quando homo sic discedit ex hac vita, agens poenitentiam, et credens, tunc sine ulla dubitatione est electus. Oportet tamen in hac vita fieri conversionem, iuxta illud: Sis fidelis usque ad mortem.

Id est: Incipias in hac vita, et in morte non abiicias fidem.

Econtra certissimum est ex Evangelio, displicere Deo omnes, in quibus non est poenitentia seu conversio, et qui contemnunt Evangelium. Et si quis sic discedit sine poenitentia et sine fide, is haud dubie reiectus est, sicut Iohannes inquit: Qui non credit in Filium, ira Dei manet super eum. Haec scire de voluntate Dei et de electione vel reiectione satis est, nec aliam voluntatem quaerito, sed iuxta hoc verbum iudicato, quod vere est lucerna sanctorum.

Secundo, cum haec scias, quod verissimum sit, agentem poenitentiam et credentem recipi, et electum esse, si sic discedit, et quod oporteat in hac vita fieri conversionem: incipias conversionem, et iureiurando Dei te consoleris: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, etc. et non sis blasphemus contra filium Dei, non cogites, quod frustra missus sit.

Confirmes te etiam his promissionibus universalibus: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis etc.

Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri.

Tertio non remoretur te haec imaginatio, quod non possis efficere conversionem.

Imo potes, Deo iuvante, et ipse vere vult iuvare, et iuvat petentes, iuxta illud: Quanto magis Pater coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus? Deus non cogit, non trahit te sicut lapidem, repugnantem et nolentem, sed te quoque velle oportet. Et quando vis et petis, certissimum est, te ab ipso iuvari. Hae consolationes vere sunt et necessariae omnibus, et magnum et perspicuum argumentum est, quod Deus vere iuvet confugientes ad filium.

In Deo non sunt contradictoriae voluntates.

Promissiones sunt universales. Ergo verissimum est, quod omnes recipit et vult iuvare, cum dicat: Omnis, qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Tu igitur videas, ut in illam promissionem te includas, nec dubites te quoque recipi et exaudiri. Et aliter de voluntate Dei sentiens discedit ab eius verbo, et non iudicat de Dei voluntate iuxta verbum, sed iuxta humanas et peregrinas imaginationes. Tunc euntes Pharisaei consilium inierunt, ut eum caperent in sermone.

## 22:15-22 The 23rd Sunday After Trinity
The 23rd Sunday after Trinity. Gospel

Matthew 22. Then the Pharisees went and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk. And they send unto him their disciples with the Herodians, saying: Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth, neither carest thou for any man: for thou regardest not the person of men. Tell us therefore, What thinkest thou? Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not? But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said: Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites? Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny. And he saith unto them: Whose is this image and superscription? They say unto him: Caesar's. Then saith he unto them: Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's. When they had heard these words, they marvelled, and left him, and went their way.

There are four principal points.

I. Concerning the distinction between corporal and eternal promises.

II. Concerning the time of Christ's advent. III. Concerning the true worship of God, and the rule that it is necessary to obey God rather than men. IIII. Concerning corporal duties, which authority either demands by right or extorts by force.

On the first.

It is often profitable for men to be reminded of the distinction between promises, because in all times even great men have fallen through a wrong interpretation of corporal promises.

When Jeremiah foretold the destruction of the temple and the city, the priests argued that he was in manifest error, because it is written: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah. Since God had promised this people a kingdom and the preservation of its worship, they argued that Jeremiah's preaching was in manifest conflict with the clearest promises, and these outcries moved not a few. It is also said of the sons of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7, that they invaded the promised land long before Moses and were killed; they were undoubtedly moved by the promise, and argued that they ought, relying on the divine voice, to take up arms and occupy their own, that God did not wish them to neglect the promises through idleness.

Who would not be moved by so specious a reason? Thus we argue: The Church will never be destroyed, therefore it is necessary that the Turks be defeated, it is necessary that the state of the Church remain in these places. So also in this case the Jews argued: Liberty is promised to the seed of Abraham, therefore we also ought to defend it, and shake off the Romans.

To explain this argument, one must hold to the distinction between commandments and promises, and likewise between corporal and eternal promises. Concerning commandments, there is no doubt; those things which God has commanded must be done. Concerning promises, it must also be known universally that one must believe the promise, but not presume the mode or the time, unless it is expressed by the voice of God, just as we must believe that we shall rise again, but we are ignorant of the time and the mode.

Afterwards, a distinction of promises is necessary. One is of reconciliation and eternal things, which is proper to the Gospel, and is given freely for the sake of the Son of God. And it is a commandment that we believe this promise, and now receive reconciliation by faith, and at all times return to it, according to that saying: As I live, I desire not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.

Others are promises of corporal benefits, which are either expressed by name or not expressed by name. And the rule to be held concerning all corporal promises is that they are not to be snatched by our own counsels, without a divine calling. A condition must also be added, that the Church is subject to the cross.

Thus, even though the land was promised to Abraham, yet he never occupied it. Therefore it is said to the Hebrews: They died not having received the promise, awaiting the eternal promise. Likewise, the fathers in Egypt knew that the land was promised to them, yet they did not occupy it, but awaited the calling. A kingdom was promised to David, yet he did not seize it while Saul was alive. Christ says: They shall have a hundredfold in this life, which you must understand as not to be seized by human counsel, as the Anabaptists pretended that they ought to occupy the wealth of others.

But understand it as God will give it by His own counsel, and Christ himself adds the interpretation, when tribulation.

The Church will be preserved, but miraculously, even if it is variously exercised in the meantime.

This wisdom of the Church is singular: not to snatch at promises by human counsel.

Likewise, to distinguish corporal things from eternal ones; even when corporal things are snatched away, one must know that the eternal ones are not lost, just as when David was driven from his kingdom, he knew that he owed obedience in his punishment, but yet that the promise concerning the remission of sins and eternal life was not to be cast away, that it remained unmoved on account of the promised Lord.

As it is said: The Lord has sworn, and will not repent.

Saul, having lost his kingdom, also casts away the promise concerning the remission of sins, just as many in calamities utterly cast away the promise of eternal things, once corporal things are lost.

It must be known, therefore, that two conditions are included in all corporal promises, namely the condition of the cross, and likewise the condition of the punishment of disobedience, just as legal promises depend on the condition of obedience.

Liberty was promised to the people, but in such a way that it is also exercised by the cross, and likewise that the impious are also punished.

Thus Jeremiah answered his adversaries: A kingdom is promised to the people, therefore it will be preserved.

He concedes both.

The kingdom is promised, but with the condition that the impious are also punished, and likewise that the cross is not removed.

And the kingdom will be preserved, but otherwise than according to human imaginations, because the Church is not ruled by human counsels, as it is written: Without me you can do nothing.

And in Jer. ch.

10: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his, nor is it for a man to walk and direct his steps; that is, man does not have all events in his power, and as he does not understand all sins, so he does not foresee punishments, and because he does not foresee the counsel of God concerning the afflictions of the Church: therefore he cannot foresee and rule all cases.

Many things happen otherwise, to Jacob, to David, and to others, than they themselves had thought.

There is another argument agitated in this cause, that the temple must be defended.

There was a tax for the temple.

For the Romans had transferred to themselves the didrachma that was to be paid annually to the temple by each person.

Therefore the Jews ought not to have permitted the revenue to be taken away from the temple.

One must respond to the major premise: The temple must be defended, namely, as far as it pertains to doctrine and true worship, not as far as it pertains to money or stones.

Just as Jeremiah wanted doctrine and true worship to be defended and retained, he did not want stones or money to be defended.

Thus, the seizure of money had to be tolerated among the evils of servitude, just like the other burdens of servitude.

At the same time, however, the people ought to have recognized the benefit of God in this very servitude, and the time of the advent of the Messiah.

It was a great benefit of God that the Romans had not overturned the temple, were not polluting it with statues, and had not led colonies there after the people had been abducted.

These things often happened among other nations, and shortly after occurred in Judea, after the resurrection of Christ.

But it had been predicted by Daniel that the city would remain until the advent of the Messiah.

They ought to have compared these predictions to their servitude, because it had also been predicted that the Messiah would come in the fourth monarchy, when the people had lost their kingdom.

But the multitude was fascinated by foolish persuasions, and by the error concerning the royal power of the Messiah.

Therefore they neither understood the prophecies, nor recognized Christ.

Thus impiety, fascinated by its own delusions, departs from the word of God.

Concerning the second.

Concerning the time of the advent of Christ.

This very servitude, in which the Jews were at that time, under the fourth monarchy, was a testimony of the advent of Christ.

Because Jacob predicted that the kingdom of Judah would remain until the advent of Christ, according to that: The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, until the Messiah comes.

But now a part of Judea had been reduced to the form of a province.

Galilee had King Herod the Idumean.

And Daniel had predicted the years, which were already running to their end.

These things collected were certain testimonies for the pious of the advent of the Messiah.

Therefore, they recognized this preacher, who was raising the dead, and purifying doctrine, and to whom John had given testimony, to be the Messiah.

But the impious, fascinated by the opinion of an earthly kingdom, did not want to recognize him.

Furthermore, it is useful for us to consider the testimonies that the Messiah has come.

The prophets clearly predict that he would come during the Jewish polity.

Now it lies utterly destroyed, longer than it stood; it is necessary, therefore, that the Son of God has come.

Concerning the third.

Render to God the things that are God's.

This is the principal response in this disputation, and it explains the objected arguments.

The Pharisees were arguing that this money should be given to the temple, not to Caesar.

Christ responds: Render to God, which are God's, that is, true doctrine and true worship, these are not to be yielded to any creature, just as the three men in Babylon did not allow their goods and bodies to be taken from them, but they did not allow true doctrine and true worship to be taken from them. You, on the contrary, dispute about money, you yourselves cast away true doctrine and true worship, you oppose the Gospel, you accumulate traditions, and the snares of gain, you invent false dogmas, you follow the Sadducees and Pharisees.

Wherefore, let the distinction be carefully considered in this place, of things which we can yield to others, and which it is not permitted to yield. Regarding doctrine and true worship, one must not yield, but let us leave our life and fortunes to the adversaries who seize them, especially if no one defends us, as we are taught in many sayings of the Gospel, Matt. 10: He who has confessed me, etc.

On the fourth. Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

Tributes are of two kinds. Some are justly imposed, because God, who is the author of political order, wills that there be governors, and wills that money be contributed for common defense, and that stipends be given even to magistrates and soldiers; therefore, moderate and tolerable tributes are justly requested. And John approves of them, saying: Be content with your wages. But the same man commands soldiers that they should be content, and not seize more than moderate tributes from the people's resources, as much as they please.

And as God is the author of political order, so He Himself by His own voice, "You shall not steal," distinguishes the resources of individuals; let governors hold their own, and let citizens hold their own resources, lest the rapacity of governors disturb this distinction. God punished Ahab for seizing the field of the citizen Naboth; so He will punish others who decree unjust exactions.

I said that some tributes are justly imposed, which it is most just to pay, because we ought to contribute not only our fortunes but also our bodies for the common defense, as John says: Just as He laid down His life for us, so each one ought to lay down his life for his brother. I also said that some immoderate tributes are unjustly decreed. What, therefore, shall subjects do about unjust exactions?

I answer. All difficulties of government are punishments for our sins, as Solomon said: Because of the sins of the people, governments are changed.

Although, therefore, the action is unjust, and the extortioners will be punished, yet the suffering is just, that is, let us feel that we are being punished by the just judgment of God, as Daniel says: To Thee, O Lord, is justice, we are justly punished, and let us bear the acknowledged punishment, let us pay the tributes, even those unjustly imposed, just as other servitude, which is manifold, is to be endured, and let us do penance, that God may mitigate public calamities.

Thus Christ wanted the Jews to think about all the times of their polity. In the time of David and Solomon, there was great glory for this people; afterwards, servitude grew. But those calamities were always punishments for sins, and God again delivered the remnants of the people, who were doing penance, and miraculously preserved the worship and the temple in such great servitude.

Thus, then, He also wanted them to be warned by servitude, so that they might think about penance, and meanwhile bear the calamity, and expect liberation from God, as if He were saying: Give to Caesar, bear the burden and bodily servitude, because by your own counsels and strength you cannot shake it off, but if the remnants do penance, they will be delivered divinely.

But as the Church in the last time of the Jewish people was in a certain bitter and sad servitude, Ptolemy Lathyrus, having slaughtered a great multitude of Jews, had ordered the bodies of women and children to be dissected, and the dissected limbs to be cooked, and had forced the Jews to eat them. That extreme age was subject to such great calamities. Thus let us know that now, in the extreme time of the world, the Church will be in servitude, either under the Turks or under other kings and princes, and will have little defense. Therefore, let us learn to bear the difficulties of polities, and let us do penance, that God may mitigate them. Meanwhile, however, let each one do his own duty diligently and prudently, so that we may retain the Churches, which God will miraculously preserve, even in such great changes of kingdoms. Let us also pray to God that He Himself may mitigate the changes of kingdoms.

Latin:

Dominica XXIII. post Trinitatis. Evangelium

Matth. 22. Tunc abeuntes Pharisaei, consilium inierunt, ut caperent eum in sermone. Et mittunt ei discipulos suos cum Herodianis, dicentes: Magister, scimus quia verax es, et viam Dei in veritate doces, et non est tibi cura de aliquo, non enim respicis personam hominum, Dic ergo nobis, quid tibi videtur, Licet censum dare Caesari, an non? Cognita autem Iesus nequicia eorum, ait: Quid me tentatis hypocritae? Ostendite mihi numisma census. At illi obtulerunt ei denarium. Et ait illis Iesus: Cuius est imago haec, et superscriptio? Dicunt ei: Caesaris. Tunc ait illis: Reddite ergo quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, Et quae sunt Dei, Deo. Et audientes mirati sunt, et relicto eo, abierunt.

Loci sunt quatuor praecipui.

I. De discrimine promissionum corporalium et aeternarum.

II. De tempore adventus Christi. III. De vero cultu Dei, et de regula, quod oporteat Deo magis obedire, quam hominibus. IIII. De officiis corporalibus, quae vel iure petit potestas, vel vi extorquet.

De primo.

Prodest saepe commonefieri homines de discrimine promissionum, quia omnibus temporibus etiam magni homines lapsi sunt mala interpretatione promissionum corporalium.

Cum Ieremias praediceret templi et urbis excidium, arguebant eum sacerdotes manifesti erroris, quia scriptum est: Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda. Cum huic populo regnum et huius cultus conservationem Deus promisisset, disputabant praedicationem Ieremiae manifeste pugnare cum promissionibus clarissimis, nec paucos movebant hi clamores, Dicitur et de filiis Ephraim 1. Paral. 7. longe ante Moisen invasisse eos terram promissam, et interfectos esse, ii haud dubie moti sunt promissione, et disputaverunt se debere fretos voce divina arma capere, et sua occupare, Deum non velle ut ociosi negligerent promissa.

Quem non moveret tam speciosa ratio? Sic nos disputamus: Nunquam delebitur Ecclesia, ergo necesse est vinci Turcas, necesse est in his locis manere statum Ecclesiae. Ita et in hoc casu Iudaei argumentabantur: Semini Abrahae est promissa libertas, ergo etiam tueri debemus, et excutere Romanos.

Ad hoc argumentum explicandum, tenendum est discrimen mandatorum et promissionum, item promissionum corporalium et aeternarum. De mandatis nihil dubium est, facienda esse quae Deus praeceperit. De promissionibus etiam universaliter sciendum est, credendum esse promissioni, sed non praesumendum modum, aut tempus, nisi voce Dei exprimatur, ut credere debemus nos resurrecturos esse, sed tempus et modum ignoramus.

Postea necessarium discrimen est promissionum. Alia est reconciliationis et rerum aeternarum, quae est propria Evangelii, et datur gratis propter Filium Dei. Estque mandatum, ut huic promissioni credamus, et iam accipiamus reconciliationem fide, et omni tempore ad eam redeamus, iuxta illud: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed convertatur et vivat.

Aliae sunt promissiones corporalium beneficiorum, quae vel nominatim expressa sunt, vel non nominatim expressa. Estque tenenda regula de omnibus promissionibus corporalibus, non rapiendas esse nostris consiliis, sine vocatione divina. Addenda etiam conditio, Ecclesiam subiectam esse cruci.

Sic etsi Abrahae promissa erat terra, tamen nunquam eam occupavit. Ideo ad Ebraeos dicitur: Mortui sunt non accepta promissione, expectantes aeternam promissionem. Item patres in Aegypto sciebant sibi promissam terram, nec tamen occupabant, sed expectabant vocationem, Davidi promissum est regnum, neque tamen rapuit vivo Saul. Christus inquit: Habebunt centuplum in hac vita, quod intellige non rapiendum humano consilio, sicut Anabaptistae fingebant se debere aliorum opes occupare.

Sed intellige, sicut Deus suo consilio dabit, et Christus ipse addit interpretationem, cum tribulatione.

Servabitur Ecclesia, sed mirabiliter, etiamsi interea varie exercebitur.

Singularis est haec sapientia Ecclesiae, non rapere promissiones humano consilio.

Item, discernere corporalia ab aeternis, etiam cum corporales eripiuntur, tamen sciendum est non amitti aeternas, ut cum David excussus erat ex regno, sciebat se debere obedientiam in poena, sed tamen non esse abiiciendam promissionem de remissione peccatorum et vita aeterna, hanc manere immotam propter promissum Dominum.

Sicut dictum est: Iuravit Dominus, et non poenitebit eum.

Saul amisso regno etiam abiicit promissionem de remissione peccatorum, ut multi in calamitatibus, penitus abiiciunt promissionem rerum aeternarum, amissis corporalibus.

Sciendum est igitur omnibus promissionibus corporalibus inclusas esse conditiones duas, videlicet conditionem crucis, item conditionem poenae inobedientiae, sicut promissiones legales pendent ex conditione obedientiae.

Promissa est populo libertas, sed ita, ut etiam exerceatur cruce, item ut puniantur etiam impii.

Sic Ieremias respondebat suis adversariis: Promissum est populo regnum, ergo servabitur.

Concedit utrunque.

Regnum promissum est, sed cum conditione, ut etiam puniantur impii, item, ne crux tollatur.

Et servabitur regnum, sed aliter quam iuxta humanas imaginationes, quia Ecclesia non regitur humanis consiliis, sicut scriptum est: Sine me nihil potestis facere.

Et apud Ierem.

cap. 10.: Scio Domine, non est hominis via eius, nec viri est, ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos, id est, homo non habet omnes eventus in sua potestate, et ut peccata non intelligit omnia, ita nec poenas prospicit, et quia consilium Dei de afflictionibus Ecclesiae non prospicit: ideo non potest omnes casus prospicere et regere.

Multa accidunt aliter, Iacob, Davidi et aliis, quam ipsi cogitaverant.

Est aliud argumentum in hac causa agitatum, templum defendendum esse.

Census erat templi.

Nam Romani didrachmum quotannis pendendum templo viritim ad se transtulerant.

Ergo Iudaei non debebant permittere, ut reditus templo adimeretur.

Respondendum est ad maiorem, Templum defendendum est, scilicet quod ad doctrinam et veros cultus attinet, non quod ad pecuniam aut lapides attinet.

Sicut Ieremias voluit defendi et retineri doctrinam et veros cultus, non voluit defendi lapides aut pecuniam.

Ita iam ereptio pecuniae toleranda erat inter mala servitutis, sicut reliqua onera servitutis.

Simul autem debebat populus agnoscere beneficium Dei in hac ipsa servitute, et tempus adventus Messiae.

Magnum beneficium Dei erat quod Romani non everterant templum, non polluebant statuis, non deduxerant eo colonias abducto populo.

Haec saepe apud alias gentes fiebant, et paulo post acciderunt in Iudaea, post resurrectionem Christi.

Praedictum autem erat a Daniele mansuram civitatem, usque ad adventum Messiae.

Has praedictiones ad servitutem conferre debebant, quia etiam praedictum fuerat, in quarta monarchia venturum esse Messiam, cum populus amisisset regnum.

Sed multitudo fascinata erat stultis persuasionibus, et errore de regia potentia Messiae.

Ideo nec vaticinia intelligebant, nec agnoscebant Christum.

Ita impietas fascinata propriis deliriis discedit a verbo Dei.

De secundo.

De tempore adventus Christi.

Haec ipsa servitus, in qua tunc erant Iudaei, sub quarta monarchia, testimonium erat adventus Christi.

Quia Iacob praedixit regnum Iuda mansurum esse usque ad adventum Christi, iuxta illud: Non auferetur sceptrum de tribu Iuda, donec veniat Messias.

Iam autem pars Iudaeae redacta erat in formam provinciae.

Galilaea habebat regem Herodem Idumaeum.

Et praedixerat Daniel annos, qui iam decurrebant ad finem.

Haec collecta piis erant certa testimonia adventus Messiae.

Ideo hunc concionatorem, qui resuscitabat mortuos, et repurgabat doctrinam, et cui Iohannes dederat testimonium, agnoscebant esse Messiam.

Sed impii fascinati opinione de regno mundano nolebant eum agnoscere.

Caeterum nobis utile est cogitare testimonia, quod venerit Messias.

Prophetae clare praedicunt venturum esse durante politia Iudaica.

Nunc funditus deleta iacet, diutius quam stetit, necesse est igitur venisse Filium Dei.

De tertio.

Date Deo, quae Dei sunt.

Haec est praecipua responsio in hac disputatione, et explicat obiecta argumenta.

Pharisaei disputabant templo dandam esse hanc pecuniam, non Caesari.

Respondet Christus: Date Deo, quae sunt Dei, id est, veram doctrinam et veros cultus, haec non sunt cedenda ulli creaturae, ut tres viri in Babylone sinebant sibi eripi res et corpora, sed veram doctrinam et verum cultum non sinebant sibi eripi. Vos econtra de pecunia disputatis, veram doctrinam et veros cultus ipsi abiicitis, Evangelio adversamini, cumulatis traditiones, et aucupia quaestus, fingitis falsa dogmata, sectamini Sadducaeos et Pharisaeos.

Quare diligenter hoc loco discrimen consideretur rerum, quas cedere aliis possumus, et quas non licet cedere. De doctrina et de vero cultu non est cedendum, sed vitam et fortunas rapientibus adversariis relinquamus, praesertim si nemo nos defendat, sicut in multis dictis Evangelii docemur, Matth. 10.: Qui me confessus fuerit etc.

De quarto. Date Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris.

Duplicia sunt tributa. Quaedam iuste imposita, quia Deus, qui est autor politici ordinis, vult esse gubernatores, et vult conferri pecuniam ad communem defensionem, etiam magistratibus et militibus dari stipendia, ideo mediocria et tolerabilia tributa iuste petuntur. Et Iohannes ea approbat, inquiens: Estote contenti stipendiis vestris. Sed idem praecipit militibus, ut sint contenti, non supra mediocria tributa rapiant ex populi facultatibus, quantum ipsis libet.

Et ut Deus est autor politici ordinis, ita ipse sua voce, Non furtum facies, discernit singulorum facultates, teneant suum gubernatores, teneant et cives proprias facultates, ne conturbet hoc discrimen rapacitas gubernatorum. Punivit Deus Achab eripientem civi Naboth fundum, ita puniet caeteros, qui iniustas expilationes indicunt.

Dixi quaedam esse tributa iuste imposita, quae iustissimum est etiam pendere, quia singuli pro communi defensione, non solum fortunas, sed etiam corpora nostra conferre debemus, sicut Iohannes inquit: Sicut ipse animam suam pro nobis posuit, sic unusquisque pro fratre suo animam ponere debet. Dixi etiam quaedam immodica tributa iniuste indici. Quid igitur facient subditi de iniustis expilationibus?

Respondeo. Omnes difficultates gubernationis sunt poenae nostrorum peccatorum, sicut Salomon dixit: Propter peccata populi mutantur principatus.

Quanquam igitur actio iniusta est, et expilatores punientur, tamen passio est iusta, id est, nos sentiamus nos iusto iudicio Dei puniri, sicut Daniel inquit: Tibi Domine iusticia, iuste punimur, et agnitam poenam feramus, solvamus tributa, etiam iniuste imposita, sicut reliqua servitus, quae multiplex est, toleranda est, et agamus poenitentiam, ut Deus mitiget publicas calamitates.

Sic Christus volebat Iudaeos cogitare omnia tempora suae politiae. Tempore Davidis et Salomonis magna gloria huius populi fuit, postea servitus crevit. Semper autem calamitates illae fuerunt poenae peccatorum, et Deus rursus liberavit reliquias populi, agentes poenitentiam, et mirabiliter servavit in tanta servitute cultum et templum.

Ita tunc quoque volebat eos servitute admoneri, ut cogitarent de poenitentia, et ferrent interim calamitatem, ac a Deo liberationem expectarent, quasi diceret: Date Caesari, feratis onus et servitutem corporalem, quia vestris consiliis et viribus non potestis excutere, sed si reliquiae agent poenitentiam, liberabuntur divinitus.

Ut autem Ecclesia ultimo tempore populi Iudaici in quadam acerba et tristi servitute fuit, Ptolemaeus Lathurus trucidata magna multitudine Iudaeorum, iusserat dissecari corpora mulierum et puerorum, et dissecta membra coqui, et his vesci Iudaeos coëgerat. Tantis calamitatibus illa extrema aetas fuit obnoxia. Ita sciamus nunc extremo mundi tempore Ecclesiam in servitute fore, vel sub Turcis, vel sub aliis regibus et principibus, et habituram exiguam defensionem. Ideo discamus ferre difficultates politiarum, et agamus poenitentiam, ut Deus eas mitiget. Interim tamen suum quisque officium diligenter et prudenter faciat, ut retineamus Ecclesias, quas Deus mirabiliter servabit, etiamsi in tantis regnorum mutationibus. Oremus etiam Deum, ut ipse regnorum mutationes mitiget.

## 22:17 Sermons on Matthew
Of the tribute.

Before I speak of the question of the Pharisees, I must first speak of that very history, what the money was, and what the tribute is, about which they ask; from this it will be possible to understand what a specious cause the Jews had for not giving this tribute to the Romans.

History of Exodus 30.

God commanded individual men in Israel, who had reached their twentieth year, to give a didrachma to the temple every year, which is worth one quadrant of our Rhenish gold coin.

With this money, God willed that the building of the temple be preserved, and the repair of books and instruments, likewise, that poor priests, widows, and orphans be helped, and in sum, this was the principal treasury in this whole administration. And it was a great sum of money. I believe that in the time of Christ there were about three tons of gold annually, because in a great administration money is needed.

But when the Romans saw that so much money was being contributed to the temple every year, they feared that the Jews, who otherwise easily stirred up seditions, being instructed by this money, might rebel more easily; they transferred this money to the Roman treasury, because from it they could easily support garrisons. But the Jews, bearing it ill that so much money was being taken from their republic, were arguing everywhere that this money should not be given to the Romans, and they alleged a specious cause: That the temple and the rights of the temple ought to be defended, and that God would be present for a pious cause, just as in the time of the Maccabees He had been present for the defenders of the temple.

Now this money was by divine law attributed to the temple. Therefore, they reasoned that because of this money, war ought to be moved. This argument is very specious, and can be solved with difficulty.

Since, therefore, it was a dangerous question, they propose it to Christ, for they knew that it would offend one side or the other, the Romans or the people. But the Lord answers them acutely. And at the same time, He teaches them about two most important matters; He rebukes them because they were in an uproar about money, and were neglecting other principal rights of the temple, namely, true doctrine and true invocation, and He commands them to bear servitude in a corporal matter.

This is the briefest summary of this question, in which many things are to be learned.

First, just as God commands by that law that something be given to the temple every year, so let men know that individuals ought to help the preservation of the Evangelical ministry according to their means. And very many men act impiously, who are willing to contribute nothing to the preservation of the ministry. And because of this sin, God punishes men, as it is expressly written in Haggai: Therefore the harvests are thinner, because they neglect the building of the temple, and care only for private buildings.

Secondly, to understand the argument of the Pharisees, it is necessary to know: that there are two kinds of promises. One is the principal promise of grace, which is universal, and promised freely on account of the Son, to all who receive it by faith. This promise God certainly wills to be valid for all, at any time, when they receive it by faith, whether we have corporal goods, or whether corporal goods are taken from us.

Therefore Job rightly says: Even if He kills me, I will hope in Him. And the Lord says: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Likewise Isaiah: Where will the Lord dwell?

In the contrite and afflicted. Therefore, man is not cast off by God on account of calamities. And it is necessary wisdom for the Church to know that God wills us to retain this most true consolation, that it is necessary to believe in God, and to retain the promise of grace, even when they are oppressed by great punishments.

As David rightly does, because he retains the promise of grace, even when he is overwhelmed by just punishments. Saul does not act rightly, because he casts away the promise of grace, and fails God after he feels the punishments. Indeed, God for this reason strips us of all corporal goods, so that He may test our faith, whether we adhere more firmly to His word than to corporal goods.

These things must be diligently considered, and this brief saying Let this be fixed in your minds: Even if he kills me, I will hope in him.

There are other promises of bodily goods, because it is true that this bodily life of the Church is also a care to God, as the Psalm says: The dead will not praise you, O Lord.

Therefore, he has promised bodily goods, and he wishes them to be sought from him and expected.

But these promises must always be understood with the exception of the cross and chastisement.

God often punishes the saints and, on account of certain sins, takes away from them temporal goods.

Just as he takes away the kingdom from David, and sends the whole people into exile in Babylon.

And daily he punishes many saints as well on account of sins.

Regarding these promises, it must be known that we owe God obedience in punishment, and we must show our conversion and faith in that obedience, and seek the mitigation of punishments.

Thus God mitigates punishments in turn.

Thus, liberty and a secure fatherland were promised to the people of Israel.

But on account of sins, they often came into servitude and into exile.

There in exile they were required to be obedient, and to turn to God, and to seek liberation.

Nor was it a sin, or anything against the law, to suffer exile.

Thus in the time of Christ, the loss of that money was not a sin, but it was a bodily punishment, which they were required to tolerate.

Let this be said enough about the distinction of the promises, and you ought to remember this doctrine well.

Now let us speak about the argument of the Pharisees.

The rights of the temple must be defended, namely, doctrine and true worship must be defended and retained in due ways, by teaching and confessing and suffering.

When, however, money is taken away, it is not a sin to endure the punishment; indeed, it would be a sin to stir up seditions then, when God does not provide suitable leaders.

The Pharisees were shouting much about money, and were neglecting doctrine and true invocation.

Therefore Christ inverts the argument against them: The rights of the temple must be defended, namely, by teaching rightly, and by true worship.

Give these to God, these are owed to God; why do you clamor about money, and neglect true doctrine?

The rights of the temple are immutable: true doctrine and true worship.

But the collection of money is a mutable thing; when God punishes us with the loss of money, the punishment must be borne.

And yet, true doctrine and pious worship must be retained.

Therefore Christ looks at the coin, to convince them that they are already in servitude: You are servants, and already the victor has taken this money from you.

Remember, therefore, that you are being punished, and turn to God.

And because Caesar is named there, two reminders are also signified at the same time.

The first reminder: Since it is the fourth Monarchy, and you have in the very land foreign magistrates, a Roman governor, consider that the time is at hand when the Messiah was predicted to come.

The second reminder: Consider that it is the end of your entire polity, and of your temple.

Therefore you dispute in vain now about money.

There is, therefore, also this other solution to the argument: The rights of the temple must be defended, and God will be present, namely, as long as he wishes this temple to remain.

These are the rights of the temple, namely, until the Messiah comes, but now the Messiah is present, therefore there is no longer a need to contend about tribute.

This is the sum of this narrative, in which observe especially these two things: First, that a collection is necessary for the ministry of the Gospel.

Second, that there is a difference between the promise of grace and the promises of bodily goods.

On these sayings. Render to God the things that are God's, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

Three things are contained here.

1. The order of commandments, so that the commands of God are preferred to human ones.

2. What the true forms of worship of God are.

3. What obedience is to be rendered to authority, and what things belong to the authority.

Concerning the order, the doctrine is clear, according to the rule: It is necessary to obey God rather than men.

Whenever the commands of men do not agree with divine commands, then it is necessary to omit human commands and obey divine ones, as the Israelites did in Babylon, not wishing to adore the statue.

Thus we must also do now, when it is commanded that the Popish Mass be restored, or the invocation of the dead be performed, or false doctrine be received, it is necessary to contradict.

Likewise, pious Priests, who do not are fit for celibacy, they ought to contract an honest marriage.

From such examples the rule can be understood: It is necessary to obey God rather than men. This rule ought to govern and discern all laws.

Render unto God the things that are God's.

Which are the proper forms of worship of God?

The brief and most ample answer is: The works of the entire Decalogue, by rightly understanding the Decalogue, are true worship of God. And these acts of worship are to be rendered to God in a just order, according to that saying: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Likewise: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet.

Likewise Ezek. 20. Walk in my statutes, not in the statutes of your fathers.

Remember this sentence well. It expressly prohibits following human traditions, and conversely binds us to the commandments of God.

Now set before yourself the whole Decalogue, and learn in order in the individual commandments what works God demands, and how they please Him, and how they can be done.

In the first commandment He demands the knowledge of true doctrine revealed by God, and handed down through Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles. And let us embrace this whole doctrine with firm faith.

Then He demands fear, faith, which is trust in mercy, love, hope, patience, humility. And this obedience pleases Him by faith on account of Christ.

In the second commandment He demands preaching, invocation, confession, thanksgiving, the religion of the oath.

In the third, the preservation of the Evangelical ministry and the sacraments.

In the fourth, the obedience due to parents and magistrates, but only so far as we do not comply with commands that conflict with the commands of God.

And these following works please God when those acts of worship of the first table precede them, and faith shines forth, which is trust in the mercy promised on account of the Son.

In the fifth He demands that we do not inflict injuries upon the bodies of others, and that we do not kill others without the order of trials.

In the sixth He commands chastity, that is, that bodies be not polluted by wandering lusts, but that men for whom marriage is necessary live chastely in marriage.

In the seventh He prohibits thefts, usuries, deceptions in buying and selling, etc.

In the eighth He prohibits all lies and slanders, and commands truth.

These works govern the whole life, and are true acts of worship of God, and they please God when they are done, as has been said, in true faith.

Here it is necessary that men be taught about other works, which men invent. Just as the Devil has always sown other works in the world to obscure true worship: so have Monasticism, private Masses, and the invocations of the dead been devised; concerning all these let us hold to these rules:

1. 1 Cor. 10. Flee from idolatry.

Likewise Matt. 15. In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. Let us therefore be cautious and vigilant, lest we receive other forms of worship which are not handed down in the word of God.

Latin:

De censu.

Priusquam de quaestione Pharisaeorum dicam, prius dicendum est de illa ipsa historia, quae fuerit pecunia, et quod tributum, de quo interrogant, inde poterit intelligi, quam speciosam causam habuerint Iudaei, non dandi huius tributi Romanis.

Historia Exodi 30.

Deus mandavit singulis hominibus in Israë, qui attigerant vicesimum annum, dare quotannis templo didrachmum, quod valet nostra pecunia unum quadrantem aurei Rhenani.

Hac pecunia voluit Deus conservari aedificium templi, et reparationem librorum, et instrumentorum, item, iuvari pauperes Sacerdotes, et viduas et orphanos, et in summa, hic erat praecipuus thesaurus in hac tota gubernatione. Et erat pecunia magna. Credo illo tempore Christi circiter tres tonnas auri quotannis fuisse, quia in magna gubernatione opus est pecunia.

Cum autem Romani viderent, quotannis tantam pecuniam ad templum conferri, metuebant, ne Iudaei, qui alioqui facile movebant seditiones, instructi hac pecunia, facilius rebellarent, hanc pecuniam ad Romanum fiscum transtulerunt, quia inde facile praesidia alere poterant. Iudaei autem aegre ferentes suae reipublicae tantam pecuniam eripi, passim disputabant, hanc pecuniam Romanis non dandam esse, et speciosam causam allegabant: Templum et iura templi oportere defendi, et Deum piae causae adfuturum esse, sicut tempore Maccabaeorum adfuerat defensoribus templi.

Haec autem pecunia iure divino erat attributa templo. Ergo propter hanc pecuniam bellum movendum esse ratiocinabantur. Hoc argumentum valde speciosum est, et difficulter solvi potest.

Cum igitur esset periculosa quaestio, proponunt eam Christo, sciebant enim, offensurum esse alterutros, Romanos aut populum. Sed Dominus respondet eis acute. Et simul de duabus maximis rebus eos docet, obiurgat eos, quod tumultuabantur de pecunia, et negligebant alia principalia templi iura, scilicet veram doctrinam, et veram invocationem, et iubet eos servitutem ferre in re corporali.

Haec est brevissuma huius quaestionis, in qua multa sunt discenda.

Primum sicut Deus ea lege praecipit, dari quotannis aliquid ad templum, ita sciant homines singulos debere adiuvare conservationem ministerii Evangelici, pro suis facultatibus. Et impie faciunt plurimi homines, qui nihil volunt conferre ad ministerii conservationem. Et propter hoc peccatum Deus punit homines, ut in Aggaeo expresse scriptum est: Ideo messes esse tenuiores, quia negligant aedificationem templi, et tantum privatas aedificationes curent.

Secundo, ad intelligendum argumentum Pharisaeorum opus est scire: Duo genera esse promissionum. Una est praecipua promissio gratiae, quae est universalis, et promissa propter filium gratis, omnibus fide accipientibus. Hanc promissionem certo vult Deus ratam esse omnibus, quolibet tempore, cum accipiunt eam fide, sive corporalia bona habeamus, sive eripiantur nobis corporalia bona.

Ideo recte dicit Iob: Etiamsi occidet me, sperabo in eum. Et Dominus inquit: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Item Esaias: Ubi habitabit Dominus?

In contritis et adflictis. Non igitur abiectus est homo a Deo, propter calamitates. Et sapientia necessaria est Ecclesiae, scire, quod Deus velit nos retinere hanc verissimam consolationem, quod necesse sit Deo credere, et promissionem gratiae retinere, etiam cum magnis poenis opprimuntur.

Ut David recte facit, quod retinet promissionem gratiae, etiam cum iustis poenis obruitur. Saul non recte facit, quod abiicit promissionem gratiae, et deficit a Deo, postquam sentit poenas. Imo Deus ideo exuit nos omnibus bonis corporalibus, ut fidem probet, an firmius adhaereamus suo verbo, quam bonis corporalibus.

Haec diligenter consideranda sunt, et hoc breve dictum Iob sit infixum animis: Etiam si occidet me, sperabo in eum.

Aliae sunt promissiones bonorum corporalium, quia verum est, hanc vitam corporalem Ecclesiae etiam curae esse Deo, sicut Psalmus dicit: Non mortui laudabunt te Domine.

Promisit igitur bona corporalia, et vult ea a se peti et exspectari.

Sed hae promissiones semper intelligendae sunt cum exceptione crucis et castigationis.

Deus saepe punit sanctos et propter aliqua peccata eripit eis bona temporalia.

Sicut eripit Davidi regnum, et totum populum mittit in exilium in Babylonem.

Et quotidie multos etiam sanctos punit propter peccata.

De his promissionibus sciendum est, quod Deo debemus obedientiam in poena, et nostram conversionem et fidem in illa obedientia ostendere, et petere poenarum mitigationem.

Ita Deus mitigat rursus poenas.

Sic populo Israël fuit promissa libertas et patria certa.

Sed propter peccata saepe venerunt in servitutem et in exilium.

Ibi in exilio debebant esse obedientes, et converti ad Deum, et petere liberationem.

Nec fuit peccatum, aut aliquid contra legem, pati exilium.

Sic tempore Christi non fuit peccatum, amissio illius pecuniae, sed fuit poena corporalis, quam tolerare debebant.

Hoc satis sit dictum de discrimine promissionum, et hanc doctrinam bene meminisse debetis.

Nunc dicamus de argumento Pharisaeorum.

Iura templi sunt defendenda, scilicet, doctrina et verus cultus debent defendi et retineri debitis modis, docendo et confitendo et patiendo.

Cum vero pecunia eripitur, non est peccatum, sustinere poenam, imo peccatum esset, tunc movere seditiones, quando Deus non dat duces idoneos.

Pharisaei multum vociferabantur de pecunia, et negligebant doctrinam et veram invocationem.

Ideo Christus invertit argumentum contra ipsos: Iura templi sunt defendenda, scilicet, recte docendo, et veris cultibus.

Haec date Deo, haec sunt debita Deo, cur de pecunia clamatis, et negligitis veram doctrinam?

Iura templi immutabilia sunt, vera doctrina et veri cultus.

Sed pecuniae collatio est res mutabilis, cum Deus punit nos amissione pecuniae, ferenda est poena.

Et tamen veram doctrinam et cultus pios retineri oportet.

Ideo Christus inspicit numisma, ut eos convincat, quod iam sint in servitute: Estis servi, et iam victor abstulit vobis hanc pecuniam.

Mementote igitur, vos puniri, et convertimini ad Deum.

Et quia ibi nominatur Caesar, etiam duae commonefactiones simul significantur.

Prior commonefactio: Cum sit quarta Monarchia, et vos habeatis in ipsa terra peregrinos magistratus, Romanum praesidem, cogitate tempus adesse, quo Messiam venturum praedictum est.

Altera commonefactio: Cogitate finem esse totius politiae vestrae, et templi vestri.

Ideo frustra iam de pecunia disputatis.

Est ergo et haec altera solutio argumenti: Iura templi sunt defendenda, et Deus aderit, scilicet, donec vult manere hoc templum.

Haec sunt iura templi, scilicet, donec venit Messias, sed iam adest Messias, ergo iam non dimicandum est de tributo.

Haec est summa huius narrationis, in qua praecipue haec duo observate: Primum quod necessaria est collatio ad ministerium Evangelii.

Secundum, quod differentia est inter promissionem gratiae, et promissiones bonorum corporalium.

De dictis istis. Date Deo, quae Dei sunt, et Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris.

Tria hic continentur.

1. Ordo praeceptorum, ut mandata Dei anteferantur humanis.

2. Qui cultus veri sint Dei.

3. Quae obedientia potestati tribuenda sit, et quae res sint potestatis.

De ordine perspicua doctrina est, iuxta regulam: Oportet Deo magis obedire, quam hominibus.

Quandocunque cum congruunt mandata hominum cum mandatis divinis, tunc necesse est omittere humana mandata et obedire divinis, ut fecerunt Israëlitae in Babylone non volentes adorare statuam.

Ita et nunc debemus facere, cum mandatur, ut Papistica Missa restituatur, vel fiat invocatio mortuorum, vel falsa doctrina recipiatur, necesse est contradicere.

Item pii Sacerdotes, qui non sunt idonei ad coelibatum, debent honestum coniugium contrahere.

Ex talibus exemplis potest intelligi regula: Oportet Deo magis obedire, quam hominibus. Haec regula debet regere et discernere omnes leges.

Date Deo, quae Dei sunt.

Quinam sunt cultus proprii Dei?

Brevis et amplissima responsio est: Totius Decalogi opera, recte intelligendo Decalogum, sunt veri cultus Dei. Et hi cultus iusto ordine sunt tribuendi Deo, iuxta illud: Si vis ingredi in vitam, serva mandata. Item: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum.

Item Ezech. 20. In praeceptis meis ambulate, non in praeceptis patrum vestrorum.

Hanc sententiam bene mementote. Expresse prohibet sequi traditiones humanas, et contra alligat nos ad mandata Dei.

Iam propone tibi totum Decalogum, et ordine in singulis praeceptis discas, quae opera Deus postulet, et quomodo ei placeant, et quomodo fieri possint.

In primo praecepto postulat cognitionem verae doctrinae revelatam a Deo, et traditam per Christum, Prophetas et Apostolos. Et hanc totam doctrinam firma fide amplectamur.

Deinde postulat timorem, fidem, quae est fiducia misericordiae, dilectionem, spem, patientiam, humilitatem. Et placet haec obedientia fide propter Christum.

In secundo praecepto postulat praedicationem, invocationem, confessionem, gratiarum actionem, religionem iurisiurandi.

In tertio conservationem ministerii Evangelici et sacramentorum.

In quarto obedientiam debitam parentibus et magistratibus, sed eatenus, ne obtemperemus in mandatis pugnantibus cum mandatis Dei.

Et haec sequentia opera placent Deo, quando praecedunt illi cultus primae tabulae, et praelucet fides, quae est fiducia misericordiae propter Filium promissae.

In quinto postulat, ne aliorum corpora iniuriis adficiamus, et ne alios sine ordine iudiciorum interficiamus.

In sexto praecipit castitatem, id est, ne polluantur corpora vagis libidinibus, sed ut in coniugio caste vivant homines, quibus coniugio opus est.

In septimo prohibet furta, usuras, deceptiones in emendo et vendendo, etc.

In octavo prohibet omnia mendacia et calumnias, et praecipit veritatem.

Haec opera regunt totam vitam, et sunt veri cultus Dei, et Deo placent, quando fiunt, ut dictum est, in vera fide.

Hic necesse est doceri homines de aliis operibus, quae fingunt homines. Sicut semper Diabolus in mundo alia opera seminavit, ut obscuraret veros cultus: ita sunt excogitati Monachatus, privatae Missae, invocationes mortuorum, de his omnibus teneamus has regulas:

1. Corinth. 10. Fugite idololatriam.

Item Matth. 15. Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. Simus igitur cauti et vigilantes, ne alios cultus recipiamus, qui non sunt traditi in verbo Dei.

## 22:17 Sermons on Matthew
Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

Here the obedience due to authority is confirmed. And at the same time a boundary is set. He commands that some things be given to Caesar, but specifically those things which are Caesar's.

Not all things are Caesar's; namely, the doctrine concerning God is not Caesar's, that is, Caesar does not have the power of establishing new doctrine, nor of commanding that men embrace false doctrine and impious forms of worship.

Secondly: Not all corporal things are Caesar's. Your wife is not Caesar's, your daughter is not Caesar's. Indeed, not even all those things which are valued by money are Caesar's. Your house, your field, your garden is not Caesar's. And Caesar and Princes are also bound by this commandment: You shall not steal.

What things, therefore, are Caesar's and the Princes'?

There are three kinds. 1. Honor, that is, true reverence toward superiors, so that you submit yourself to them, and plot nothing against them, so that you are not seditious or abusive toward them.

2. Obedience in external commands, pertaining to corporal peace, which do not conflict with the commands of God, such as when they command the labors of military service, or watches, or establish statutes concerning purchases and sales and similar things.

Likewise obedience in legitimate punishments.

safe regarding purchases and sales and similar matters. Item, obedience in legitimate penalties.

3. Stipends are owed to them, that is, ordinary tributes and other legitimate tributes, the manner of which ought to be such that they are stipends, as John says: Be content with your stipends, that is, let them be tributes which are contributed for the preservation of peace, and let them not be such great extortions that the miserable people, along with their small children, are forced to suffer hunger, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus 38: Food, a rod, and a burden for a donkey: so bread, discipline, and work for a servant. Princes ought to rule the people in such a way that they maintain discipline and take care that the people are not corrupted by idleness. And they ought to leave them a moderate livelihood. Let them not drive miserable children to hunger, nor drink the blood of miserable girls and boys. And princes ought to consider well this word: What belongs to Caesar, so that they may learn that not everything belongs to the princes, because they themselves also ought to obey this commandment: You shall not steal.

Latin:

Date Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris.

Hic confirmatur obedientia debita potestati. Et simul meta circumdatur. Iubet ut dentur Caesari aliqua, sed illa nominatim, quae sunt Caesaris.

Non omnia sunt Caesaris, videlicet, doctrina de Deo non est Caesaris, id est, Caesar non habet potestatem condendi novam doctrinam, nec mandandi, ut falsam doctrinam et impios cultus amplectantur homines.

Secundo: Non omnia corporalia sunt Caesaris. Tua uxor non est Caesaris, tua filia non est Caesaris. Imo etiam non omnes illae res, quae aestimantur pecunia, sunt Caesaris. Tua domus, tuus ager, tuus hortus non est Caesaris. Et tenentur Caesar et Principes etiam hoc praecepto: Non furtum facies.

Quae res igitur sunt Caesaris et Principum?

Tria genera sunt. 1. Honos, id est, vera reverentia erga superiores, ut te eis subiicias, et nihil contra eos moliaris, ne sis seditiosus aut contumeliosus contra eos.

2. Obedientia in externis mandatis, pertinentibus ad pacem corporalem, quae non pugnant cum mandatis Dei, ut quando praecipiunt labores militiae, aut vigiliarum, aut condunt statuta de emtionibus et venditionibus et similibus rebus.

Item obedientia in legitimis poenis.

Item obedientia in legitimis poenis.

3. Debentur eis stipendia, id est, tributa ordinaria, et alia legitima tributa, quorum talis debet modus esse, ut sint stipendia, sicut Iohannes inquit: Estote contenti stipendiis vestris, id est, sint tributa, quae ad pacis conservationem conferantur, non sint expilationes tantae, ut miser populus cum parvis liberis cogatur famem pati, sicut scriptum est Ecclesiastici 38.: Cibaria, virga, et onus asino: ita servo panis, disciplina et opus. Principes debent populum ita regere, ut tueantur disciplinam, et curent, ut populus non corrumpatur otio. Et debent eis relinquere mediocrem victum. Ne adigant miseros pueros ad famem, ne bibant sanguinem miserarum puellarum et puerorum. Et deberent principes bene considerare hoc verbum: Quae sunt Caesaris, ut discerent, non omnia esse principum, quia ipsi etiam debent obedire huic mandato: Non furtum facies.

## 22:23 Sermons on Matthew
On that day the Sadducees came to him.

Here again, let it be considered what the form of the Church was at that time, and let us learn in such a great variety of sects to seek what and where the true Church is, and let us know that we individually ought to be members of the true Church, and let there be in us a care that we join ourselves to the true Church of God, as it is written in Psalm 27: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life. And Psalm 84: Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord. And Psalm 92: Planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God they shall flourish.

These and similar sayings command that we seek where and what the true Church is, so that we may take care that we ourselves also join it.

Now see what its appearance was at that time. They all had the name of the people of God in that polity, and yet many were enemies of the true Church; there were two powerful sects, the Pharisees and the Sadducees. And the Sadducees were so impious that they denied that souls are immortal, and they denied the resurrection of the dead; finally, they completely denied that another life remained after this one, but believed that the life of men ended in death, just like the life of cattle, and that no judgment remained after this life. And since they denied this chief foundation of the articles of faith concerning life after this life and concerning the future judgment, they were manifestly enemies of God and the Church.

Others were the Pharisees, who corrupted the doctrine concerning the Messiah and knew nothing of the righteousness of faith.

They were such as the Mahometans are now. Since, therefore, neither the Sadducees nor the Pharisees were the Church of God, God nevertheless preserved some true members of His Church, namely, Zechariah, Simeon, Joseph, Elizabeth, Anna, Mary, and many others who retained the foundation of sound doctrine.

So now there are Papists, Monks, Canons, fanatics; some are entirely Epicureans, some take away certain articles of faith and establish manifest idols, and yet they call themselves the Church, and the highest Bishops of the Church.

Where, therefore, is the Church? And what men are the Church? I answer: God always preserves some assembly in the human race which is the true Church, the guardian of the Gospel; this assembly embraces the pure and uncorrupted doctrine of the Gospel in all articles of faith, and has the true use of the sacraments, and does not stubbornly defend idols.

Indeed, it condemns and flees all idolatry, insofar as it recognizes and understands it. Such an assembly is without any doubt the Church of God, in which men are heard and saved by God, according to these sayings: John 14: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Item, John 17: Father, sanctify them in your truth; your word is truth.

Item, Galatians 1: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema.

These sayings teach both things: that the Church of God is there where the voice of the Gospel is uncorrupted, and that those men are not the Church who are enemies of the true doctrine.

Hold this consolation, and know that the Church of God truly exists wherever the Gospel is taught rightly and without corruptions, and the sacraments are rightly administered, and idols are not stubbornly defended. And when you have learned what the true Church is, you also join yourself to that Church in the use of the sacraments and in your confession.

Such is the Church by the grace of God in this very town, and in others, wherever the same doctrine is taught.

And know that you are in the true Church of God when you are joined to this congregation.

Do not let this consolation be snatched from you. This admonition is necessary at this time, and must be repeated often, and thought upon by you often.

Now I come to Christ's argument concerning life after this life.

See how sad the darkness was in that people. The Sadducees openly denied life after this life, and sought ridiculous arguments. Thus men become insane when they depart from the word of God, and seek out cavils for their own opinions. Christ solves their argument, and says that in eternal life there will not be such a commixture as occurs in marriage in this life.

Afterwards he opposes an excellent argument: God is the God of the living, not of the dead. God is the God of Abraham. Therefore Abraham lives.

This argument contains excellent consolation, not only concerning future life, but also concerning this life, namely that God truly cares for us, because to say that God is the God of the living is to say that He cares for, benefits, and saves those whose God He calls Himself, just as it is said in the first commandment: I am the Lord thy God, that is, caring for thee, hearing thee, helping thee, saving thee.

Consider this well, and in your invocation let faith always be stirred up, that you invoke not an idle God, but one who most truly wishes to care for, hear, help, and save you, if you believe in the Son.

Furthermore, the Sadducees were well refuted by the very resurrection of Christ, and of many others who were resurrected and seen by many.

But the Pharisees, hearing that he had imposed silence on the Sadducees, etc. A lawyer asked him one of them.

You have heard the battle with the Sadducees. Now follows the battle with the Pharisees; Christ refutes and overcomes these also, and taxes their chief error, that they were ignorant of who the Messiah was, and what his true benefits are, and what kind of kingdom it would be. And just as they were ignorant of the true doctrine concerning the Messiah, so they were ignorant of the doctrine of the righteousness of faith. Christ will tax such great darkness here. And there are two disputations here: the former concerning the Law, the latter concerning the Gospel. Here it is first necessary for us to think about the distinction between Law and Gospel. It is necessary that this distinction be seen in the Church.

Law is the doctrine delivered by God, commanding what we ought to be, and what we ought to do or not do, and requiring perfect obedience, and promising good things for perfect obedience, and truly being angry at all who do not perform perfect obedience, and punishing all disobedience, just as it is written: Cursed is he who remains not in all things which are written in the law. And in sum, the law is the very voice of the Decalogue, which condemns all men in this corruption of nature, because no one is without many and great sins, and God is truly angry at sins, just as it is said there: God is a consuming fire.

Or: The Law of God is the eternal and immovable wisdom of God, and the norm of righteousness in the will of God, discerning good and evil, communicated to the rational creature in creation, and revealed afterwards by His word, so that we may know what kind of God He is, and binding all rational creatures, and He wishes all to be conformable to Himself, and condemning all not congruent to that eternal and immovable wisdom of God, etc.

But the Gospel is the preaching of repentance, and the promise of the remission of sins, and of righteousness and eternal life, to be exhibited on account of the mediator the Son of God, freely, and to be received by faith.

These distinctions having been established, it must now be known that man does not receive the remission of sins, nor is he righteous on account of the law or his own merits, and much less on account of Monasticism and similar ceremonies.

But the law is therefore to be preached, so that it may show and accuse sin, and we, terrified by the acknowledged wrath of God, may flee to the Son of God, so that we may be healed by Him.

They begin therefore the disputation concerning the law: the Pharisee asks, what is the great commandment in the law? Christ answers most wisely concerning the sum of the law and the chief commandments: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart. And the second is like unto this: Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.

Why did Christ add: The second? Here he taxes the Pharisee, because the Pharisee imagines that ceremonial commandments, which were profitable to them, are far greater than the commandment concerning the love of the neighbor. And the Prophets and Christ often tax this error. And such dreams always remain among men. Papists once thought it a greater sin to eat meat on the sixth day than to kill a man. Against these ravings the Prophet speaks.

Hosea 6: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. That is, I desire the true recognition of God, fear, and faith. Then mercy, that is, love of the neighbor; these, he says, are to be preferred to ceremonies.

Thus here Christ places the word 'like'. Why does he speak thus? Certainly this second seems to be far inferior to the first.

I answer: He speaks against that pharisaical opinion, because they thought that the love of the neighbor could be neglected, and that ceremonies and offerings were much more important. Indeed, many even did this: They committed adulteries, and afterwards wanted to compensate with sacrifices, just as the opinion of the Papists concerning the Mass still is.

Therefore Christ shows that this commandment concerning love is by no means to be neglected, and says it is like the first, namely. nes, quam occidere hominem.

Against these ravings the Prophet speaks. Hosea 6: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. That is, I desire the true recognition of God, fear, and faith. Then mercy, that is, love of one's neighbor, he says, is to be preferred to ceremonies.

Thus here Christ uses the word "like." Why does he speak thus?

It certainly seems that this second [commandment] is far inferior to the first. I answer: He speaks against that Pharisaical opinion, because they thought that the love of one's neighbor could be neglected, and that ceremonies and offerings were much more important.

Indeed, many even did this: they committed adultery, and afterwards wanted to compensate with sacrifices, just as the opinion of the Papists about the Mass still is today. Therefore Christ shows that this commandment about love is by no means to be neglected, and says it is like the first, namely, because the obligation is similar under the penalty of eternal damnation, and obedience also becomes a worship of God, just as the worship of the first commandment.

On the second question.

After the Lord answered the Pharisees about the law, he now wants to show their ignorance concerning the chief foundation of the Church, namely, the Messiah. Because in the Church, it is not enough to know the law, nor does the knowledge of the law make a distinction between the Gentiles and the Church of God, but the knowledge of the promise of the Messiah, and faith according to that promise.

This Mediator must be acknowledged in the Church, according to those sayings: No one comes to the Father except through the Son. Item: He who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father. Item: This is eternal life, that they may know you alone, the true God, and whom you sent, Jesus to be the Christ.

Item 1 Corinthians 3: No other foundation can be laid than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. These testimonies and similar ones ought to be most well-known to all men, so that they may learn what the true Church of God is, and learn to separate the true Church of God from the Gentiles.

But the Pharisees were ignorant of this whole doctrine about the Messiah. This disputation shows this impious and condemned ignorance in them.

And first we will recite the question of the Lord, and afterwards we will speak about the offices of the Messiah. The Pharisees knew that the Messiah was to come, and indeed from the descendants of David, but they imagined that he would only be an earthly king, and would divide the empire of the world among the Jews: they knew nothing about the passion of the Messiah, nothing about the remission of sins, nothing about the imputation of righteousness.

In sum, there was a horrible darkness in the Pharisees. The Lord therefore asks: Whose son is the Messiah?

They rightly answer: David's, but they cannot say how this agrees with the Psalm, in which the Messiah is named the Lord of David. Therefore Christ opposes: How does David in the Spirit call him Lord, if he is his son?

Declaration.

Here the unskilled need a declaration.

How the argument or objection holds. For a rude man can think that it is not unusual in speech for the son of a peasant who has become a doctor or a powerful Canon to be called Lord. But the sayings of Scripture do not speak only of an empty title, but David understands "Lord" as one who is truly superior to himself.

And such is the Syllogism: No son in the same order of a kingdom is the Lord of his father or grandfather, just as Charles is never more worthy than Maximilian, nor does he rule over Maximilian. The Messiah is the son of David: Therefore he cannot be the Lord of David, as you Pharisees imagine.

This argument could not be solved if the Messiah were only a man, and only established an earthly kingdom. Then truly David would be more worthy than the Messiah, and would be the Lord of the Messiah, as a King prior in the same kingdom.

Christ therefore proposed a most firm argument to the Pharisees. But this is the solution: For two reasons the Messiah is the Lord of David, although he is his son.

The first reason is because the Messiah is at the same time by nature the Son of God, and always was and is the Lord of the Church, and has always been acknowledged in the Church, because he was present with it, guarded it, and saved it. He was with Abraham, who also calls him Lord, and worships this Lord.

He was with Moses in the desert. David also speaks with him, and names him Palmoni and Michael. Palmoni, that is: wonderful, wonder-doer, wonderful. Michael, who is like God? as if he were saying: This Lord is like God, equal to the Father, and through him and because of him God receives and preserves us, and makes us safe. All these great testimonies the Pharisees neglected and corrupted, and they thought that the Messiah was not yet in that Church of Israel, nor had he been among the Fathers.

These darknesses were truly great.

Second solution, the Messiah is therefore truly the Lord of David, because he instituted another eternal kingdom, which far surpasses the kingdom of David, and gives eternal liberation, and eternal goods, not, as David did, merely repressing present and mortal enemies. Therefore the Messiah is the Lord of David, because in that eternal kingdom he deletes sin and death, and restores to David and to all believers righteousness and eternal life. Indeed, even in this very political government of David, this Lord Messiah is present, he rules the right hand of David in battles, he is the guardian of this whole Church, and he loves it greatly, for it he prays to the eternal Father, defends it, and saves it even then, when David and other kings reign, who all are only Ministers and organs of that superior Lord, who is the Son of God. These things the Pharisees did not know. Wherefore, since they were ignorant of the chief article of faith concerning the Son of God, and concerning the remission of sins, it is manifest that they were not members of the Church, but were hypocrites similar to the Turks and the impious Jews of this time. Let this brief declaration now suffice.

But let us now consider these two things.

First, concerning the great blindness in the people of God.
