In filio Dei causa, cur velit pati, est bona, scilicet, quia scit hanc obedientiam esse pretium, quo iustitiae Dei satis fit, et ira placatur, et Deus recipit genus humanum, sicut in Psalmo scriptum est: In capite libri scriptum est de me, ut faciam voluntatem tuam, Deus meus, volo, et lex tua in medio cordis mei etc. Tota scriptura loquitur de hoc mirando consilio Dei, quod Deus hoc modo voluerit salvare genus humanum, et saepe haec miranda deliberatio cogitanda est, Filius est deprecator pro Adam et Eva, et fit decretum, ut poena in ipsum derivaretur, quia ordo iustitiae erat, ut non reciperetur genus humanum, nisi facta compensatione, et poenam aequivalentem solveret redemptor. Hoc mirandum consilium quotidie cogitandum est, et Deo gratiae agendae pro donato filio. Sed causa passionis in hostibus Christi, erant odium Dei in Diabolo, et odium Christi in Pharisaeis, qui nolebant suos errores et peccata accusari, et eodem modo semper oderunt veram Ecclesiam hypocritae.

3. Acta recitabimus ordine, quomodo simul mendaciis et manifesta violentia Christum perdere conentur. 4. Personarum socii, ut dixi. Socii Christi sunt pauci auditores, Apostoli, Maria, et pauci alii, qui dolent cum eo patiente, et laetantur cum resurgente. Sed socii impiorum Pontificum et Pharisaeorum sunt tyranni, qui armis adiuvant persecutionem. Item proditor Iudas, et reliqui blasphemi et impii, qui perseverant in impietate. His omnibus dicetur: Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum.

5. Poenae impiorum etiam in hac vita incipiunt, ut poena Iudae, et haud dubie multi alii, Pilatus, Herodes, et Pontifices habuerunt etiam poenas in hac vita, sed postea sequuntur aeternae poenae multo maiores. 6. Econtra liberatio iustorum inchoatur in resurrectione, ibi manifeste vident Apostoli, qualis sit futura totius Ecclesiae liberatio in resurrectione. Haec de Iuda satis sit dixisse, et oremus Deum ardenter, ut nos regat Spiritu suo sancto, ne Diabolus implicet nos laqueis suis, ut a Christo deficiamus, ipsum etiam Christum oremus, ut ipse nos regat, et pro nobis intercedat, sicut pro Petro intercessit, et eum confirmavit.

Prima Azymorum.

Sequitur historia de agno Paschali, et de institutione coenae Domini. Non volumus autem iam dicere de veteri ritu agni Paschalis. Sed volumus dicere de nostris Sacramentis, et de causis, cur semper fuerint in Ecclesia Sacramenta, et quis sit eorum usus. Hanc doctrinam necesse est saepe repeti, et haec est prima causa institutionis Sacramentorum omnibus temporibus. Cum Deus immensa misericordia velit colligere aeternam Ecclesiam ex genere humano, edidit inde usque ab initio suam promissionem de reconciliatione, et addidit externa visibilia signa, quia vult illam promissionem sonare in genere humano, et ut promissio fiat insignior, oculis etiam proposita sunt externa visibilia signa. Item cum velit Ecclesiam esse certum coetum distinctum ab aliis gentibus, vult esse signa distinguentia, ut circumcisio discernebat Israëlitas a caeteris gentibus omnibus, Baptismus discernit nos ab illis gentibus. Vult etiam aliqua signa esse vincula publicorum congressuum, quia certissimum est, Deum velle, ut publici honesti congressus fiant, et servat eos ipse in genere humano, et non placent ei dissipationes, quales faciunt Anabaptistae, aut alii, qui currunt in latebras, et faciunt distractiones sine necessaria causa.

Vult Deus esse Ecclesiam distinctam a caeteris gentibus, et vult eam conspici et exaudiri in toto genere humano. Ideo vult esse honestos congressus, et servat eos, et addidit signa, ut discerni et conspici Ecclesia possit. Hanc causam bene considerate, ut postea melius intelligatis ea, quae de coena Domini dicentur. Quia haec ita instituta est, ut sit illa publica ceremonia connectens publicum congressum.

Post hanc causam, quae de publico congressu aut distinctione loquitur, est et haec causa pro sua cuiusque conscientia cognoscenda, Sacramenta sunt etiam testimonia voluntatis erga te, et sunt applicationes promissionum per fidem. Quando sumis corpus et sanguinem Domini, cogita et crede, ad te quoque pertinere promissionem gratiae. Alias cogitant homines, ecce promissio est generalis sermo, fortassis ad te nihil pertinet, sed scito in hoc ipso ritu testari Deum, quod promissio ad te pertineat. Dat tibi Dominus corpus et sanguinem, facit te membrum sui corporis, vult igitur et promissiones vere tibi tribuere.

Hanc causam diligenter considerate, et simul hic discite magnum et horrendum abusum, qui semper in mundo vagatus est, de merito operis, seu de usu Sacramentorum sine fide. Sicut Pharisaei docebant, remitti peccata propter sua sacrificia et mactationes, et de fide prorsus nihil dicebant: ita populus in Papatu currit ad coenam Domini, et putavit se hoc opere, et hac obedientia mereri remissionem peccatorum. Haec insania est magna idololatria. Sed debes scire, quod haec tua sumtio vel obedientia nequaquam sit meritum remissionis peccatorum, sed quod filius Dei sua morte meruerit nobis omnibus remissionem, et hanc oportere fide accipi in vera poenitentia. Postea vero haec sumtio tibi est testimonium, quod promissio etiam ad te pertineat, et mens tua intueatur Filium Dei sedentem ad dextram aeterni Patris, qui te iam facit membrum sui corporis, et multo ante meruit tibi remissionem, et vult, ut te promissione sua consoleris. Hic verus usus discernendus est a papistico et ethnico abusu, qui ceremonias ita faciebant, quasi essent merita remissionis peccatorum.

Postquam dixi de causis, et de usu Sacramentorum, generaliter, proxime etiam de textu et de Missa dicemus.

## 26:26 Sermons on Matthew
Taking bread, Jesus, etc.

First, I want to say a few things about the papistic Mass, so that you may know what kind of error has been in the whole world, and still is among the Papists, and that you may be warned to detest that great error and idolatry. The Papists said and say that their mass is an offering or sacrifice, which is necessary for the Church, and merits for the one performing it and for others for whom it is done, the remission of sins, just as the Pharisees said that they merited remission for themselves and others by the slaughtering of cattle. This opinion is an error, and it fights against the saying to the Hebrews: "By one offering He has perfected the saints." Likewise, it fights against the saying: "The just shall live by his faith." Now if the work of the sacrificer merits remission, remission is not received by faith. Most firmly, therefore, it must be held that the work of the sacrificer does not merit remission, and that all papistic Masses for the living and the dead are idolatrous. And no one ought to approach them, and it is horrible to think that such great idolatry has pervaded the Church and has been so widely accepted. But let us pray to God that He Himself may amend it, because no wisdom or power of men can remove this great error, but it is the work of God alone to destroy this idolatrous worship, and we ought to grieve on account of such great error of the world, and on account of such great insult to God, and we ought to pray to God often that He Himself might destroy this great abomination.

Nor do I wish to dispute at greater length.

For although crafty men now invent many sophistical glosses to defend the papistic Mass, yet they are only sophistries, and are devised to stabilize errors, nay, they accumulate errors, like the book Interim and the writings of Sidonius. Let this suffice to have said about the papistic Mass.

I also wish to confess this, that there is no Sacrament except in its use, as the institution sounds. And since the Lord's Supper is instituted for the taking, it must be known that that custom of carrying the bread around is idolatrous and to be avoided. Secondly, I will speak about the true use. Principally, as I have said, this supper was instituted so that it might be the sinew of the public congregation.

And those taking the body and blood of the Lord should be such, namely, men doing penance; they should not be secure, having an evil purpose, because it is written: Let a man prove himself, and so let him eat of that bread.

Likewise: He has filled the hungry with good things.

In sum: Let no one approach while retaining an evil purpose, because it is given to be a pledge of the remission of sins for those who believe.

But he who retains an evil purpose does not seek the remission of sins, but despises God, and if he approaches knowing this, he mocks our Lord Jesus Christ.

This horrible and not rare sin exists even among us, who call ourselves Evangelicals.

But in this very reception we ought to excite faith, that this reception was instituted to be a testimony that the goods promised in the New Testament are truly given to you on account of the Son of God, who died and rose again, because the text says: This is the chalice of the New Testament.

A testament, however, is an ordinance in which one who is about to die assigns an inheritance to another; thus the Son of God, dying, merited for us the remission of sins.

And this He assigns to us, and added this ministry, the preaching of the Gospel and the Sacraments, so that through this ministry we might receive these goods, but through faith.

And let this faith not think thus: you receive remission on account of this work of yours, or this reception of yours, but on account of the Son of God, who suffered for you on the cross, and rose again, and reigns at the right hand of the eternal Father, and is the mediator for us, and in this reception makes us His members and joins us to Himself, and testifies that He has washed us with His blood.

Let this faith be the true consolation of one doing penance.

And then a living and ardent faith is felt, when there is true sorrow, in which consolation is felt.

Where there is security and sloth, there consolation is not felt, and this saying is not considered: He has filled the hungry with good things.

You ought to learn this doctrine rightly, and think about what the difference is between you and the Papists, why the Papists approach, and why you approach.

The Papists approach without penance, and afterwards pretend that by this obedience they merit the remission of sins, and that by this work sins have been wiped away.

This error must necessarily be censured.

You, however, ought to approach with penance, and bring this faith, that sins are remitted to you, not on account of your reception, but on account of the Son of God, who merited remission by His passion: yet He wills this reception to be a memorial and testimony of His promise, and He wills to excite and confirm us to faith by this testimony.

Thirdly, in that consolation, invocation and thanksgiving must also approach; you ought to think: Behold, the Son of God has made you a member of His body, He wants you to approach the Father with Him, not to flee; He wants you to invoke, to ask for the remission of sins, eternal life, help in this life against the Devil, and against other evils; ask that the Church be preserved, ask for peace and other necessary goods.

Likewise, give thanks to God for this immense mercy, that He received the human race in this way on account of the Son; give thanks to the Son Himself, that He was an intercessor for us, that He was made a victim, that He gathers and preserves the Church, that He receives you, that He helps you, and think about all the benefits which you receive daily.

It is a great blindness to want to be helped by God, and not to want to give Him thanks, and never to profess that those goods which you receive are given to you by God.

Paul says in 1.

Thessal. last chapter: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in all things give thanks.

He commands three things: First, he bids us to rejoice, that is, not to be angry with God, but to obey Him in favorable and adverse things.

Secondly, he bids us always to ask for necessary things.

Thirdly, he bids us always to give thanks, and to acknowledge and confess that those goods which you receive are given by God.

And let this gratitude be declared not only by words, but also by the will to obey.

Therefore, obey God more diligently, lest you be stubborn like an ungrateful person.

Remember these things well concerning the use of the Sacrament, and think about them with yourselves every Sunday, when communion takes place.

That these three ought to be joined: penance, faith in consolation, invocation and thanksgiving.

I also wish to add this admonition: It is written in Paul: Do this until I come.

Remember these words most diligently, because they contain the sweetest consolation, that the Church is to remain until Christ comes and shows Himself in the final and visible judgment.

Likewise, that in the meantime

may be remaining public and honest assemblies of the Church, doctrine and ministry. And although these are sometimes disturbed, yet God restores them from time to time. Give thanks, therefore, to God who preserves the Church, and ask that He may preserve it. And with this hope, be more diligent in learning, and in helping the Church, etc. And when they had sung a hymn, they went out.

In this history at the Mount of Olives, these four things are to be considered.

1. The beginning of the passion in this place. The cause of the passion has been spoken of before, which, however, it is always necessary to have in view. 2. The security, sleep, and flight of the Apostles. 3. Peter's fight. 4. The captivity of the Lord.

On the first.

Concerning the passion itself. Although the Lord in all His life often suffered great terrors and sorrows in His heart, as John 12 cries out while preaching: Father, save me from this hour, yet now on the Mount of Olives the sorrow is singular, and this is recounted by the writers of the Gospel as a singular part of the passion of Christ. But what that sorrow is, we cannot clearly say, because we could not even endure it. But we must believe that there were great sorrows because of the wrath of God against our sins; then the Son of God felt the wrath of God poured out upon Himself against our sins, as if He Himself had been defiled by your sins, and mine, and those of others. Therefore He is named the Lamb of God, that is, the victim, because He is slaughtered in the place of others. And Isaiah says: And the Lord has laid on Him the iniquity of us all. Likewise: For the transgressions of my people He struck Him.

These things are to be thought upon with pious meditation, and the wrath of God against sins is to be acknowledged. And thanks are to be given to God, and to our Lord Jesus Christ, that He so willed to save the human race. Then consider the magnitude of the sorrow. It is necessary that the sorrow was great, in which the powers of the heart are dissolved, so that blood flows out instead of sweat. And He Himself prays: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what You will, let it be done. This struggle shows that there were the greatest sorrows; it is also confirmed by the angel. Although we do not understand all these things, yet they must be thought upon in some way, as I said, so that we may think upon the wrath of God against sins, and give thanks to Him.

On the second. When the Lord is in such great sorrow, the Apostles sleep, and they still have good hopes of victory and of an earthly kingdom.

Here we discern an example of infirmity in the Saints. They themselves are negligent, and in error concerning an earthly kingdom.

But at the same time let us consider this: the Lord speaks to them sorrowfully, He taxes their negligence, and commands them to pray, that they may not enter into temptation.

There is negligence in the Saints, but yet it is rebuked, and being warned, let us pray, lest our negligence harm us, and lest the Devil precipitate us into some more serious falls.

Furthermore, let us know this: although the Apostles are infirm, yet there were some persons in the Church who understood the passion of Christ, and at the same time suffered true and great sorrows, namely Mary the mother, and her sister Mary of Cleophas.

And there are always some in the Church who suffer with Christ. And let us be more patient in our own afflictions, and let us think that we suffer with our head, Christ.

On the third.

Another sin is depicted in the Apostles, which very often happens in the Church. We want to fight in persecution, and defend the Gospel with the sword. Thus Peter draws his sword, and cuts off the servant's ear, and he has this opinion that Christ is about to put everyone to flight, because all had fallen away, when Christ was speaking to them.

Often similar things have been done, and similar things will be done, as Münzer, Straus, and others wanted to propagate the Gospel with the sword.

I do not want, however, to speak now of the office of Princes, but I want to speak of the office of preachers.

This is most certain, that we preachers ought not to fight with the sword, and here the Lord adds a rule.

He who takes the sword will perish by the sword. Know that this rule is not an empty sound, but that it truly happens so. God regularly draws all murderers to punishment, even if the magistrate does not

punishes.

As God punished Saul, who had killed the Priests: God punished David, who suffered much harder than death, because he had snatched another man's wife, and ordered the man to be taken away craftily. And we must not doubt that God keeps this rule, He punishes with the sword all who unjustly draw the sword, whether they be Kings, or Princes, or men among the people, and homicides which are committed unjustly do not remain unpunished.

Let us learn, however, that it is expressly said: He who takes the sword, namely, not given by the laws, shall perish by the sword. He speaks therefore of the seditious and such like, who are not magistrates, and of magistrates, when they kill others against the laws, out of their own fury, just as Nero, Caligula, Domitianus, and many other tyrants did.

Thus you see that Christ, even in this His passion, nevertheless teaches the Church about the temptations which happen to the Church in the time of persecution.

On the fourth.

Finally, the Lord is taken willingly, and although there is a traitor and cohorts there, yet they could have accomplished nothing, unless the Lord willingly allowed Himself to be taken and bound, but yet the Devil and impious men rage, and attempt by fraud and violence to destroy the Church, and God allows this up to a certain point, but yet He sets limits, and the rule is kept: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands.

Latin:

Accipiens Iesus panem, etc.

Primum pauca volo dicere de Missa papistica, ut vos sciatis, qualis fuerit error in toto mundo, et apud Papistas adhuc sit, et sitis moniti, ut illum tantum errorem et idololatricum detestemini. Papistae dixerunt et dicunt, suam missam essa oblationem seu sacrificium, quod sit necessarium Ecclesiae, et mereatur facienti et aliis, pro quibus fit, remissionem peccatorum, sicut Pharisaei dicebant, se mereri remissionem sibi et aliis, mactione pecudum. Haec opinio est error, et pugnat cum dicto ad Ebraeos: Una oblatione consummavit Sanctos. Item pugnat cum dicto: Iustus fide sua vivit. Iam si opus sacrificuli meretur remissionem, non accipitur remissio fide. Firmissime igitur tenendum est, quod opus sacrificuli non mereatur remissionem, et quod omnes Missae papisticae pro vivis et mortuis, sint idololatricae.

Et nemo debet ad eas accedere, et horrendum est cogitare, tantam idololatriam pervasisse in Ecclesiam, et tam late receptam esse. Oremus autem Deum, ut ipse emendet, quia nulla sapientia aut potentia hominum hunc tantum errorem tollere potest, sed solius Dei opus est, hunc idololatricum cultum delere, et nos debemus dolere propter tantum errorem mundi, et propter tantam contumeliam Dei, et deberemus Deum saepe orare, ut ipse hanc tantam abominationem deleret. Nec volo prolixius disputare.

Quanquam enim nunc homines astuti fingunt multas sophisticas glossas ad defendendam Missam papisticam, tamen tantum sunt sophisticae, et excogitantur ad stabiliendos errores, imo cumulant errores, sicut liber Interim, et scripta Sidonii. Haec satis sit dixisse de Missa papistica.

Volo et hoc confiteri, quod nihil est Sacramentum, nisi in suo usu, sicut institutio sonat. Et cum coena Domini instituta sit ad sumtionem, sciendum est, illam consuetudinem circumgestandi panem esse idololatricam et fugiendam. Secundo dicam de vero usu. Principaliter, ut dixi, haec coena instituta est, ut sit nervus publicae congregationis.

Et sumentes corpus et sanguinem Domini sint tales, videlicet homines agentes poenitentiam, non sint securi, habentes malum propositum, quia scriptum est: Probet se ipsum homo, et sic de illo pane edat.

Item: Esurientes implevit bonis.

In summa: Nemo accedat retinens malum propositum, quia est donatum, ut sit pignus remissionis peccatorum, credent.

Sed qui retinet malum propositum, non expetit remissionem peccatorum, sed contemnit Deum, et si sic sciens accedit, irridet Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Hoc peccatum horrendum et non rarum est etiam apud nos, qui vocamus nos Evangelicos.

Sed in hac ipsa sumtione debemus fidem excitare, quod haec sumtio sit instituta, ut sit testimonium, quod vere tibi dentur bona promissa in novo Testamento propter filium Dei mortuum et resuscitatum, quia textus inquit: Hic est calix novi Testamenti.

Testamentum autem est ordinatio, in qua moriturus alteri attribuit hereditatem, ita filius Dei moriens, meruit nobis remissionem peccatorum.

Et hanc attribuit nobis, et addidit hoc ministerium, praedicationem Evangelii et Sacramenta, ut per hoc ministerium accipiamus haec bona, sed per fidem.

Et haec fides non sic cogitet, tu accipis remissionem propter hoc tuum opus, aut hanc tuam sumtionem, sed propter filium Dei, qui pro te passus est in cruce, et resurrexit, et regnat ad dextram aeterni Patris, et est mediator pro nobis, et in hac sumtione facit nos membra sua et adiungit nos sibi, et testatur, quod abluerit nos sanguine suo.

Haec fides sit vera consolatio agentis poenitentiam.

Et tunc sentitur viva et ardens fides, quando est verus dolor, in quo consolatio sentitur.

Ubi est securitas et pigritia, ibi non sentitur consolatio, et non consideratur hoc dictum: Esurientes implevit bonis.

Hanc doctrinam recte debetis discere, et cogitare, quid intersit inter vos et Papistas, cur accedant Papistae, et cur vos accedatis.

Papistae accedunt sine poenitentia, et postea fingunt, se hac obedientia mereri remissionem peccatorum, et hoc opere deleta esse peccata.

Hic error necessario taxandus est.

Vos autem debetis accedere cum poenitentia, et adferre hanc fidem, quod peccata vobis remittantur, non propter vestram sumtionem, sed propter filium Dei, qui meruit remissionem sua passione: velit autem hanc sumtionem memoriale et testimonium esse suae promissionis, et velit nos hoc testimonio ad fidem exsuscitare, et confirmare.

Tertio, in ista consolatione etiam debent accedere invocatio et gratiarum actio, debes cogitare: Ecce filius Dei fecit te membrum sui corporis, vult te secum accedere ad Patrem, non fugere, vult ut invoces, petas remissionem peccatorum, vitam aeternam, auxilium in hac vita contra Diabolum, et contra alia mala, petas servari Ecclesiam, petas pacem et alia bona necessaria.

Item agas gratias Deo, pro hac immensa misericordia, quod genus humanum hoc modo receperit propter filium, agas gratias ipsi filio, quod fuit pro nobis deprecator, quod sit factus victima, quod colligat et servet Ecclesiam, quod te recipiat, quod tibi opituletur, et cogita de omnibus beneficiis, quae quotidie accipis.

Magna coecitas est, velle iuvari a Deo, et non velle ei gratias agere, et nunquam profiteri, quod illa bona, quae accipis, sint tibi a Deo donata.

Paulus dicit 1.

Thessal. ultimo: Semper gaudete, incessanter orate, in omnibus gratias agite.

Tria praecipit: Primum iubet gaudere, id est, non irasci Deo, sed ei obedire in secundis et adversis rebus.

Secundo iubet semper petere necessaria.

Tertio iubet semper agere gratias, et agnoscere et fateri, quod illa bona, quae accipitis, sint data a Deo.

Et haec gratitudo declaretur non solum verbis, sed etiam voluntate obediendi.

Ideo diligentius Deo obedias, ne velut ingratus sis contumax.

Haec de usu Sacramenti bene mementote, et singulis dominicis, quando fit communio, cogitate vobiscum.

Haec tria oportere coniungi, poenitentiam, fidem in consolatione, invocationem et gratiarum actionem.

Volo et hanc admonitionem addere: In Paulo scriptum est: Hoc facite donec veniam.

Haec verba diligentissime mementote, quia continent dulcissimam consolationem, quod Ecclesia mansura sit, donec veniet Christus, et se ostendet in novissimo et visibili iudicio.

Item, quod interea

sint mansuri publici et honesti coetus Ecclesiae, doctrina et ministerium. Et quanquam haec aliquando turbantur, tamen Deus subinde restituit. Agatis igitur gratias Deo servanti Ecclesiam, et petatis, ut servet. Et hac spe sitis magis diligentes in discendo, et in iuvanda Ecclesia etc. Et hymno dicto egressi sunt.

In hac historia ad montem Oliveti sunt haec quatuor consideranda.

1. Passionis initium in hoc loco. De causa passionis prius dictum est, quam tamen semper oportet in conspectu esse. 2. Apostolorum securitas, somnus et fuga. 3. Petri pugna. 4. Captivitas Domini.

De primo.

De ipsa passione. Quanquam Dominus in omni vita saepe passus est in corde suo magnos pavores et dolores, ut Iohan. 12. inter concionandum clamat: Pater salva me ex hac hora, tamen iam in monte Oliveti singularis est dolor, et hic recitatur ab Evangelii scriptoribus, tanquam singularis pars passionis Christi. Quid autem sit iste dolor, nos non possumus clare dicere, quia nec sustinere possemus. Sed debemus credere, fuisse magnos dolores propter iram Dei adversus peccata nostra, tunc filius Dei sensit effundi in se iram Dei, contra peccata nostra, quasi ipse se polluisset tuis et meis et aliorum peccatis. Ideo nominatur agnus Dei, id est, victima, quia mactatur loco aliorum. Et Esaias inquit: Et posuit Dominus in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Item: Propter scelera populi mei percussit eum. Haec pia meditatione cogitanda sunt, et agnoscenda ira Dei contra peccata.

Et agendae gratiae Deo, et Domino nostro Iesu Christo, quod sic velit salvare genus humanum. Deinde cogitate magnitudinem doloris. Necesse est magnum dolorem fuisse, in quo resolvuntur vires cordis, ut sanguis effluat pro sudore. Et ipse precatur: Pater, si fieri potest transeat a me calix iste, veruntamen non quod ego volo, sed quod tu vis, fiat. Haec lucta ostendit, fuisse maximos dolores, item confirmatur ab angelo. Haec omnia etsi non intelligimus, tamen aliquo modo cogitanda sunt, ut dixi, ut cogitemus iram Dei contra peccata, et agamus ipsi gratias.

De secundo. Cum Dominus est in tanto dolore, Apostoli dormiunt, et habent adhuc bonas spes de victoria, et de regno mundano.

Hic cernimus exemplum infirmitatis in Sanctis. Ipsi sunt negligentes, et in errore de regno mundano.

Sed simul hoc consideremus, Dominus dolenter alloquitur eos, taxat negligentiam eorum, et praecipit, ut orent, ne intrent in tentationem.

Est negligentia in Sanctis, sed tamen reprehenditur, et commonefacti oremus, ne nostra negligentia nobis noceat, nec Diabolus praecipitet nos in aliquos graviores lapsus.

Praeterea hic sciamus: Quanquam Apostoli sunt infirmi, tamen in Ecclesia fuerunt aliquae personae, quae intellexerunt passionem Christi, et simul veros et magnos dolores passae sunt, scilicet Maria mater, et eius soror Maria Cleophae.

Et semper sunt in Ecclesia aliqui, qui cum Christo patiuntur. Et nos in nostris afflictionibus simus patientiores, et cogitemus nos cum capite Christo pati.

De tertio.

Aliud peccatum in Apostolis pingitur, quod valde saepe accidit in Ecclesia. Volumus in persecutione pugnare, et Evangelium gladio defendere. Ita Petrus stringit gladium, et praecidit servo auriculam, et habet hanc opinionem quod Christus sit fugaturus omnes, quia omnes lapsi erant, cum Christus eos alloqueretur.

Saepe similia facta sunt, et fient similia, ut Monetarius, Straus, et alii volebant gladio propagare Evangelium.

Non volo autem iam loqui de Principum officio, sed de officio praedicantium volo loqui.

Hoc certissimum est, nos praedicantes non debere gladio pugnare, et addit hic Dominus regulam.

Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. Hanc regulam scitote non esse inanem sonitum, sed vere sic fieri. Deus regulariter omnes homicidas retrahit ad poenam, etiamsi magistratus eos non

punit.

Ut Deus punivit Saulem, qui interfecerat Sacerdotes: Deus punivit Davidem, qui multo duriora morte passus est, quia rapuerat alterius conjugem, et iussit astute virum tolli. Et non debemus dubitare, quin servet Deus hanc regulam, punit gladio omnes, qui iniuste gladium stringunt, sive sint Reges, sive Principes, sive homines in populo, et non manent impunita homicidia, quae fiunt iniuste.

Discamus autem expresse dici: Qui gladium acceperit, scilicet non datum a legibus, gladio peribit. Loquitur ergo de seditiosis et talibus, qui non sunt magistratus, et de magistratibus, quando contra leges, ex proprio furore alios interficiunt, sicut fecit Nero, Caligula, Domitianus, et alii tyranni plurimi.

Ita videtis, quod Christus etiam in hac sua passione tamen docet Ecclesiam de tentationibus, quae accidunt Ecclesiae tempore persecutionis.

De quarto.

Tandem Dominus volens capitur, et quanquam sunt ibi proditor et cohortes, tamen nihil potuissent efficere, nisi Dominus volens sineret se capi et ligari, sed tamen Diabolus et impii homines insaniunt, et conantur fraude et violentia Ecclesiam delere, et Deus hoc aliquo usque permittit, sed tamen metas constituit, et servatur regula: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis.

## 26:57 Sermons on Matthew
Those taking Jesus led Him to Caiaphas.

This is the second act of the passion. The first was in the garden, the second is before the Pontiffs. And here at the same time is contained the history of Peter's denial.

But why is Christ led first to the Pontiffs? I answer: Such is the process in the persecution of the Church. First, Christ is condemned by the Priests and by the Doctors; these are the first who accuse and condemn Him of two things: of blasphemy and of sedition.

And although it is harsh to be named seditious before the world, yet it is much harsher to be called a blasphemer. It is much harsher for us that we are called heretics and authors of errors, than that we are called disobedient to the Emperor, or seditious.

How great these great crimes are, let everyone think to himself, and let us know that similar things happen in the Church, whenever persecution occurs, just as now also similar things happen, we are called authors of errors, and at the same time we are called disobedient to the Emperor.

But let us be instructed and confirmed by the true excuse.

Consider, however, this history; to some things the Lord answers, to some He does not answer.

First, He does not answer where the objection is trivial, not pertaining to doctrine, and where the vanity of the witnesses is manifest in itself, as when they object about the destruction of the temple.

Secondly, He answers where mention is made of doctrine. For this is the chief article of faith, that this Jesus, born of a virgin, is the Messiah, and is the Son of God promised to the Fathers, so that He may be the redeemer and savior of the human race.

Interrogated about this great article, He gives an express confession; Luke 22 says: I am.

After this confession, they all expressly condemn Him, nay, they shout: What need is there of witnesses? We ourselves have heard from His mouth.

And after the condemnation made by the Pontiffs, now those scoundrels, the ministers of the Pontiffs, mock Christ, and strike Him, etc.

In this first condemnation before the Pontiffs, now another evil is added. Peter himself falls horribly, so not only does persecution happen through enemies, but also in the Church itself scandals follow.

And in both ways the Devil rages, he impels the Pontiffs, and at the same time he tempts the weak members of the Church, so that they also may fall.

But where is the Church? What kind of appearance is it? Does it not always behoove the Church to remain in the human race? And indeed, does it not behoove it to be seen and heard?

Truly, it is now a tearful appearance; Peter denies, the Apostles are scattered and doubt, and yet it is necessary for the Church to remain; Christ Himself still performs miracles, even in the garden He performed miracles, He struck down the soldiers, He healed the wounded one.

And the remnants remain constant in faith, Mary the mother, and her sister Mary of Cleophas, and certain others confirmed by them. But yet the Church is now small and languid and deformed, but after Easter it becomes great and glorious again. Let us consider these things, lest we fail because of temptations.

Now let us also consider Peter's fall and conversion.

Three distinct denials are described here.

History. The first denial took place in the vestibule of the house of Caiaphas, where they had made a fire, so that they might warm themselves at night. Here Peter, terrified by the voice of the maidservant, denied that he knew Christ, "I do not know him, and I do not know what you are saying." This is the first denial, and immediately after this first denial Peter went out, perhaps dismayed by fear. And after he had gone out, he heard the cock crowing for the first time. And such things happened not without danger in the middle of the night, when the cocks are accustomed to crow, for they had led the LORD around all night long, from Annas to Caiaphas, and they had gathered the great prelates together at Caiaphas's house, and held counsel there for a long time, etc.

Second denial. A while later Peter returned to the fire, and there he denied him again, when another maidservant said that he had been with Jesus, and one of the cohort of ministers also challenged him, and said: "And you are one of them." Here Peter not only denied it, but added an oath. This is the second denial, made after midnight around the second hour. Meanwhile, there were great contentions of the Pontiffs and Prelates with Christ; false witnesses were heard against him, he was interrogated as to whether he was the Messiah, the Son of God, and he was struck by the ministers of the Pontiffs. Thus for several hours from midnight the Lord was in the house of Caiaphas. Therefore, the third denial followed in the morning around the fourth hour according to our clock.

Third denial.

For the third time, some ministers of the Pontiff came and said that he had been with Jesus, and specifically his kinsman, whose ear had been cut off, affirmed that he had seen him in the garden. Here Peter denies much more strongly, swears, and curses himself. But meanwhile, while he is speaking, the cock crows for the second time. And the Lord turned toward him and looked at him. Here Peter remembered the words that Jesus said: "Before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times." And having gone out and dwelling upon that thought, he wept bitterly.

This is the history of Peter's denial, very significant, and diligently recounted by all the Evangelists, which we ought to think about often for these two reasons: so that it may warn us ourselves of our own infirmity. And then, so that we do not despair when we have fallen, but so that we may know that it is the will of God that we return, but so that we may know that it is the will of God that we return through repentance and faith to God, and not fall into despair and the eternal hatred of God, like Judas.

And let us diligently consider these causes: The first is concerning infirmity. Let no one be secure, let no one trust in his own wisdom and constancy, but let us always think that we are infirm, and let us ask for help from God, as the Church sings: "Without your divine power, there is nothing in man." Item: "Without me you can do nothing." Item: "Ask and you shall receive." And see the excellent Saints, how horribly they have fallen.

Aaron consented that a calf should be made. David snatched away another man's wife, and took care that the husband should be killed. Manasses was multiply polluted by the worship of idols and by homicides; he had sacrificed his own sons. Peter denied him three times.

These falls are manifest and great. But we also, each one of us, have many and great sins. Therefore, let us not be proud and secure, but let us do penance, as the Lord cries out: "Do penance," let there be in us true sorrow for our uncleanness and for our many sins, as the Prophet cries out: "Rend your hearts," etc.

And you often hear that there are three parts of repentance or conversion: contrition, faith, and new obedience. Aaron had great contrition, just as it is written of him, the Lord wished to crush him. David also was in great sorrow when Nathan rebuked him, and often afterwards, and when he was driven into exile. Manasses was led away captive, and there he also began to acknowledge his sins and to grieve. Peter also weeps bitterly here.

This bitterness signifies immense sorrow of heart. And how does this contrition come about? The Lord looks at him, and by this look he reminds him to think about what he has done. And Mark says explicitly: ἐπιβαλών, thinking intently, he wept.

Let there not be such hardness in us, that we are unwilling to think about our sins and about the wrath of God,

 Christ looks upon us, admonishes us with the voice of the Gospel, and draws us with His Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Apocalypse: I stand at the door and knock. Let us therefore listen, and let us not repel the Holy Spirit. But let us think about the magnitude of our sins, and about the just wrath of God, and let us grieve, just as Aaron, David, and Peter grieved.

On the second part, on faith. But let there not only be grief in us, but let there also be faith; let us know this promise and this oath of God: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Let us know that the Son of God has appeared, so that He may receive sinners who are doing penance. Let us know this saying of the Lord: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

Peter thought upon this very doctrine during these two days in his grief, and he sustained himself with this consolation; there were in him the beginnings of faith, otherwise he would have perished like Judas, and there was a great struggle of grief and faith: therefore Christ consoles him very lovingly after the resurrection. And undoubtedly Peter thought upon these words of the Lord, spoken the day before: Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And however he raised himself up, thinking upon many sayings of the Lord until the day of the resurrection, there the Lord consoles him in His presence, and receives him with a manifest absolution.

And this is the second reason why these examples must be considered most diligently, because they are testimonies of the rule and the principal promise of the Gospel, that God wishes to receive all who are doing penance and believing, just as Aaron, David, and Peter; their falls were manifest and great, and yet they were received. Therefore, let not the multitude of our sins deter us from believing that they are remitted to us.

And these histories are examples of this rule: Grace abounds over the offense. The Son of God is more powerful than the whole kingdom of sin and the Devil. Do not think that the death of the Son of God is not a sufficient price for your sins. Do not treat the Son of God and His passion with contempt. But believe that it is truly a sufficient price for us all, and that God is truthful, and truly wishes to receive us freely on account of the Son, not on account of our own dignity. And with this faith approach God, and know that you are then received, and are an heir of eternal life.

After this faith, a new obedience must also follow, just as Peter was afterwards obedient and faithful in his ministry and his whole life.

Latin:

Capientes Iesum duxerunt ad Caipham.

Hic est secundus actus passionis. Primus fuit in horto, secundus est coram Pontificibus. Et hic simul continetur historia de negatione Petri.

Quare autem prius ducitur Christus ad Pontifices? Respondeo: Talis est processus in persecutione Ecclesiae. Primum condemnatur Christus a Sacerdotibus et a Doctoribus, hi sunt primi, qui accusant et condemnant eum de duabus rebus: de blasphemia et de seditione.

Et quanquam durum est, nominari seditiosum coram mundo, tamen multo durius est, dici blasphemum. Nobis est multo durius, quod dicimur haeretici et autores errorum, quam quod dicimur inobedientes Imperatori, aut seditiosi.

Haec magna crimina quanta sint, unusquisque apud se cogitet, et sciamus similia accidere in Ecclesia, quandocunque fit persecutio, sicut nunc quoque similia fiunt, dicimur autores errorum, et simul dicimur inobedientes Imperatori.

Sed simus instructi et confirmati vera excusatione.

Considerate autem hanc historiam, ad aliqua respondet Dominus, ad aliqua non respondet.

Primum, non respondet, ubi levis est obiectio, non pertinens ad doctrinam, et ubi vanitas testium per se manifesta est, ut cum obiiciunt de destructione templi.

Secundo respondet, ubi fit mentio doctrinae. Nam hic est articulus fidei praecipuus, quod hic Iesus natus ex virgine, sit Messias, et sit Filius Dei promissus Patribus, ut sit redemtor et salvator generis humani.

De hoc tanto articulo interrogatus, edit expressam confessionem, Lucae 22. dicit: Ego sum.

Post hanc confessionem expresse damnant eum omnes, imo clamant: Quid opus est testibus? Ipsi audivimus ex ore eius.

Et post condemnationem factam a Pontificibus, iam nebulones illi ministri Pontificum illudunt Christo, et percutiunt eum etc.

In hac prima condemnatione coram Pontificibus accedit iam aliud malum. Ipse Petrus labitur horribiliter, ita non solum fit persecutio per hostes, sed etiam in ipsa Ecclesia sequuntur scandala.

Ac utroque modo Diabolus furit, impellit Pontifices, et simul infirma membra Ecclesiae tentat, ut etiam labantur.

Ubi autem est Ecclesia? Qualis species est? An non semper oportet in genere humano manere Ecclesiam? Et quidem conspici eam et audiri oportet?

Profecto iam lacrymabilis species est, Petrus negat, Apostoli dissipati sunt et dubitant, et tamen necesse est reliquam esse Ecclesiam, Christus ipse adhuc miracula facit, iam in horto fecit adhuc miracula, prostravit milites, sanavit vulneratum.

Et manent reliquiae constantes in fide, Maria mater, et eius soror Maria Cleophae, et alii quidam ab his confirmati. Sed tamen iam parva et languida et deformis est Ecclesia, sed post Pascha rursus fit magna et gloriosa. Haec consideremus, ne deficiamus propter tentationes.

Iam et Petri lapsum et conversionem consideremus.

Tres distinctae negationes hic describuntur.

 

Historia. Prima negatio facta est in vestibulo domus Caiphae, ubi fecerant ignem, ut se calefacerent noctu. Hic Petrus territus voce ancillae, negavit se nosse Christum, Ich kenne ihn nicht, und weis nicht was du sagest, haec est prima negatio, et statim post hanc primam negationem exivit Petrus fortassis metu consternatus. Et postquam exivisset, audivit gallum primo canentem. Und ist solches geschehen ongefehrlich in mitternacht, da die Han pflegen zu schreien, denn man hat den HERRN die gange nacht also vmbgeführt, von Hanna zu Caipha, Und hat man bey Caipha die grossen Prelaten zusammen gefordert, und lang da rath gehalten, etc.

Secunda negatio.

Aliquanto post rediit Petrus ad ignem, ibi rursus negavit, cum et alia ancilla diceret eum fuisse cum Iesu, et unus ex cohortem ministrorum etiam eum compellaret, et diceret: Et tu ex illis es. Hic Petrus non solum negavit, sed addidit iusiurandum. Haec est secunda negatio, facta post mediam noctem circa horam secundam. Interea magnae contentiones fuerunt Pontificum et Praelatorum cum Christo, auditi sunt contra eum falsi testes, interrogatus est, an sit Messias, filius Dei, percussus est a ministris Pontificum. Ita per aliquot horas a media nocte fuit Dominus in domo Caiphae.

Secuta est igitur mane circa quartam iuxta nostrum horologium, tertia negatio. Tertia negatio. Tertio venerunt aliquot ministri Pontificis, et dicunt, eum fuisse cum Iesu, et nominatim cognatus eius, cuius praecisa erat auricula, affirmat, se vidisse eum in horto. Hic multo magis negat Petrus, iurat, et seipsum exsecratur. Sed interea dum loquitur, canit gallus secundo. Et Dominus versus ad eum, intuitus est eum. Hic Petrus recordatus est verba, quae dixit Iesus: Priusquam gallus bis cantabit, ter me negabis. Et egressus et incumbens in eam cogitationem, flevit amare.

Haec est historia de negatione Petri, valde insignis, et diligenter ab omnibus Evangelistis recitata, quam saepe cogitare debemus propter has duas causas, ut nos ipsos de nostra infirmitate admoneat. Et deinde, ut lapsi non desperemus, sed ut sciamus, voluntatem Dei esse, ut redeamus, sed ut sciamus, voluntatem Dei esse, ut redeamus per poenitentiam et fidem ad Deum, et non ruamus in desperationem et aeternum odium Dei, sicut Iudas.

Et diligenter has causas consideremus: Prior est, de infirmitate. Nemo sit securus, nemo confidat propria sapientiae et constantia, sed semper cogitemus, nos esse infirmos, et petamus a Deo auxilium, sicut canit Ecclesia: Sine tuo numine nihil est in homine. Item: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Item: Petite et accipietis.

Ac vidite excellentes Sanctos, quam horribiliter lapsi sint. Aaron adsensit, ut fieret vitulus. David rapuit alterius coniugem, et curavit, ut vir interficeretur. Manasses fuit multipliciter pollutus, idolorum cultu et homicidiis, immolaverat filios suos. Petrus ter negavit. Hi lapsus sunt manifesti et magni.

Habemus autem et singuli multa et magna peccata. Ideo non simus superbi et securi, sed agamus poenitentiam, sicut clamat Dominus: Agite poenitentiam, sit in nobis verus dolor propter nostram immunditiam et propter multa peccata nostra, sicut clamat Propheta: Scindite corda vestra, etc.

Ac saepe auditis, partes poenitentiae vel conversionis tres esse, contritionem, fidem, et novam obedientiam. Aaron habuit contritionem magnam, sicut de eo scriptum est, Dominus voluit eum conterere. David etiam fuit in magno dolore, quando obiurgavit eum Nathan, et saepe postea, et quando pulsus est in exilium. Manasses abductus est captivus, ibi etiam coepit agnoscere sua peccata, et dolere. Petrus etiam hic flet amare.

Haec amaritudo significat ingentem dolorem cordis. Et quomodo fit haec contritio? Dominus aspicit eum, et hoc aspectu commonefacit eum, ut cogitet, quid egerit. Et Marcus expresse dicit: ἐπιβαλών, intente cogitans, flevit.

Non sit talis durities in nobis, ut nolimus cogitare de peccatis nostris, et de ira Dei, Christus aspicit nos, commonefacit nos voce Evangelii, et trahit Spiritu suo sancto, sicut in Apocalypsi scriptum est: Sto ad ostium et pulso. Audiamus igitur, et non repellamus Spiritum sanctum. Sed cogitemus de peccatorum magnitudine, et de iusta ira Dei, et doleamus, sicut Aaron, David, Petrus doluerunt.

De secunda parte, de fide. Sed non tantum sit dolor in nobis, sed sit etiam fides, sciamus hanc promissionem et hoc iuramentum Dei: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Sciamus filium Dei apparuisse, ut peccatores agentes poenitentiam recipiat. Sciamus hoc dictum Domini: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos.

Hanc ipsam doctrinam Petrus hoc biduo in dolore suo cogitavit, et hac consolatione se sustentavit, fuerunt in eo initia fidei, alioqui periisset sicut Iudas, et fuit magna lucta doloris et fidei: ideo Christus post resurrectionem eum valde amanter consolatur. Et haud dubie cogitavit Petrus haec verba Domini, dicta pridie: Petre, oravi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Et utunque se erexit, multa dicta Domini cogitans usque ad diem resurrectionis, ibi Dominus coram eum consolatur, et absolutione manifesta eum recipit.

Et haec est secunda causa, propter quam haec exempla diligentissime consideranda sunt, quia sunt testimonia regulae et principalis promissionis Evangelii, quod velit Deus omnes agentes poenitentiam et credentes recipere, sicut Aaronem, Davidem, Petrum, horum fuerunt manifesti lapsus magni, et tamen recepti sunt. Ergo nec nos multitudo peccatorum nostrorum deterreat, quo minus credamus nobis remitti.

Et haec historiae sunt exempla huius regulae: Gratia exuberat supra delictum. Filius Dei potentior est toto regno peccati et Diaboli. Non cogites mortem filii Dei non esse sufficiens pretium pro tuis peccatis. Non contumelia afficias filium Dei, et passionem eius. Sed credas, quod sit vere sufficiens pretium pro nobis omnibus, et quod Deus sit verax, vere velit nos propter filium gratis, non propter nostram dignitatem recipere. Et hac fide ad Deum accedito, et scias te tunc receptum esse, et haeredem esse vitae aeternae.

Post hanc fidem debet et nova obedientia sequi, sicut Petrus postea fuit in ministerio suo et tota vita obediens, et fidelis.

## 27:1 Sermons on Matthew: Argument
Chapter XXVII.

I. 1. Jesus is led to Pilate; where the punishment of Judas is first recounted. 2. Afterwards the accusation, and the confession of Christ. 3. Then the confession of Pilate, that Christ is innocent. 4. Fourthly, the scourging and crowning with thorns. 5. The condemnation and crucifixion. 6. The conversion of the thief, and other testimonies.

Latin:

Caput XXVII.

I. 1. Ducitur Iesus ad Pilatum; ubi primum recitatur poena Iudae. 2. Postea accusatio, et confessio Christi. 3. Deinde confessio Pilati, quod Christus sit innocens. 4. Quarto flagellatio et coronatio cum spinis. 5. Condemnatio et crucifixio. 6. Conversio latronis, et alia testimonia.

## 27:3 Sermons on Matthew
First, on the punishment of Judas.

Previously he recounted the example of the fall of Peter, who nevertheless was converted and returned to penance. This example, therefore, contains the sweetest consolation. Now another example follows, that of Judas, who was not converted, did not perform true penance, but was oppressed by grief and fell into eternal destruction, into eternal wrath, and horrendous torments, which no tongue of men or angels can express.

And this example is proposed so that we may be vigilant, so that we ourselves do not seek out the sins of blasphemy. Peter fell through infirmity, although it is a horrendous fall, yet he did not seek this out of his own will, he did not want Christ to be killed, but only feared for himself. Judas, however, was a blasphemer, and willingly and knowingly sought this, that Christ should be killed.

Here let us be cautious, lest we fall into such sins, but let us assiduously pray to God, that He may rule and confirm us, and not allow us to slip so far, as it is written concerning Judas: Satan entered into his heart. Let us think upon the magnitude of this great evil, with great fear, and let us pray to God with assiduous groans, that He may rule us, and not allow us to fall, but may drive the Devil away from us; let us cry out also to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, that He may be present with us, because the Son of God came to destroy the works of the Devil, and to crush the head of the serpent: Ah Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, crucified for us and resurrected, sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, and reigning with him, you who said: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands: We pray to you, that you may rule and preserve us, and do not allow us to fall, but preserve your Church among us for yourself.

Think on these things regarding Judas, and do not be so hard-hearted that your hearts are not moved by fear when you consider such a horrible example.

Afterwards, consider the hypocritical holiness of the Pontiffs.

They do not want to receive money into the treasury, and yet they dare to kill Christ.

But this confession was made by both Judas and the Pontiffs, so that both might admit that they had acted unjustly.

Judas admits that he sold that blood: They admit that they corrupted him with money.

Regarding the accommodation of the saying in Zechariah, there is no need for an anxious dispute.

That Jeremiah is named here, perhaps the hand of some scribe erred.

Secondly, let us be content that Matthew understands this history to be signified in that image which the Prophet Zechariah recites, and the number of the money certainly agrees here, because God says that he himself was valued at this price; this was manifestly and according to the letter completed in Christ, who is God.

That he also says he was valued by the sons of Israel leads us to the history of Joseph, which is also a type of the selling of Christ, just as that whole deliberation about killing Joseph was a figure of the passion of Christ.

Let these things suffice regarding the accommodation of the saying of Zechariah, and reading such sayings, let us consider what deep falls follow in man when he is not guarded by God, and when the Devil has occupied his heart.

Thirty pieces of silver make fifteen thalers in our currency.

But even if it were more, it is still a horrible and diabolical fury to sell Christ for any amount of money, to oppose the acknowledged truth, to kill the members of Christ, just as many do at this time, who oppose the acknowledged truth and kill the Saints.

But the end of Judas shows the punishments that hang over such traitors and persecutors.

Second part. Are you the King of the Jews?

Matthew briefly recites this part; in John and Luke there are certain members that pertain to this confession.

Previously, Christ had issued his confession before the Pontiff, that he is the Messiah, that he is the Son of God, that he taught rightly.

He was accused of these articles, and Christ responded expressly concerning them.

Now another accusation is instituted before Pilate.

This judge does not care much what Jesus taught, and as a pagan man, he laughs at those things they said about the Son of God, and he laughs at disputes about doctrine, but he cares about the affairs of government, lest sedition be stirred up against the Romans, and lest someone become king and join the multitude to himself.

Therefore, they bring forward these crimes first: They accuse the Lord, because he said he was a king, and also because he forbade tribute to be given to Caesar.

Also, because he stirred up the people throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to Jerusalem.

These are great crimes, and often this appearance weighs heavily on teachers; we are called seditious because we do not obey the Emperor when he commands us to receive impious doctrine.

And it must be diligently considered: Christ does not respond to all the lies, but he leaves aside those that were completely manifest.

However, he responds to the question about the kingdom; he affirms that he is a king, and he distinguishes the kingdom of the world, in which Pilate served, from his own kingdom, of which he himself, the Son of God, is king.

Thus the Church must clearly purge the crime of sedition; it must say that it wishes to provide all legitimate obedience in political affairs.

But regarding doctrine, it wishes to obey God, just as it was commanded: It is necessary to obey God rather than men.

And here let all the pious consider the difference between the political kingdom and the eternal kingdom, in which the Son of God calls us through the Gospel to eternal goods, and gives the remission of sins and eternal life.

And these kingdoms must not be mixed, just as the Pope, under the pretext of ministry, wants to be king of the world and Lord of Kings, as is written in canon law, and as the Pope removed emperors from the empire, and forced the emperor Frederick Barbarossa to lie before him, and placed his feet upon his neck.

To see and hear such diabolical pride in the Church is horrible.

Now also in another way the powers are mixed; the Emperor and the Princes want to propose a new doctrine to the Churches; they made the Interim and want to establish impious cults, the Mass, the invocation of Saints, and other idolatrous things in the Church, they themselves they wish to be Doctors and Pastors, while yet they do not understand the doctrine, and are enemies of the true doctrine.

This is by no means to be approved, but let the offices be distinguished, and let each one labor faithfully in his own office.

Afterwards Pilate himself confesses that Jesus is innocent.

Thus it is always made clear that the Church is innocent, and does not covet the kingdoms of the world, nor stir up seditions.

And yet an impious power, against conscience, aids persecution, with impious Doctors urging it on.

First, he orders him to be beaten with scourges and crowned with thorns.

Pilate confesses that Jesus is innocent, and yet he afflicts him with such insults and torture, just as now, even those who do not kill Jesus, who do not utterly remove those who teach rightly, because they cannot, yet show their hatred against them in many signs, neglect the needy Pastors, and allow them to be vexed in various ways.

Now let this scourging and crowning be considered.

The Pope and all his Bishops scourge Christ, crown and mock him, and clothe him in purple, who defend false doctrine, and scourge the miserable minds of men, nay, even kill many.

Then, when they establish a kingdom for themselves, they crown Christ with thorns, and clothe him in purple, that is, they afflict Christ himself and the true Church with pain, through that false and impious domination which they arrogate to themselves, against the will of God and against the salvation of the Church.

Whenever you see the Pope depicted with his crown and golden mantle, you should think on the contrary of Christ standing crowned with thorns and clothed in purple in mockery.

And pray to God that he may destroy those idols and that impious domination, and that he himself may gather the Church among us mercifully, and rule us; let Christ himself be King, not the Pope.

Afterwards Pilate is moved to also kill Christ, when he hears those words: If you do not crucify him, you are not a friend of Caesar.

Such are those who collude with the impious: even if at the beginning they are not most cruel, yet little by little they become worse.

Therefore, beginnings must be guarded against, according to those sayings: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees.

Item: Do not be yoked together with the Gentiles.

What fellowship has Christ with Belial?

2 Cor.

6. Item Ecclesiasticus 13: He who touches pitch will be defiled by it.

Item: To avoid sins is to avoid the occasions of sins.

After Pilate first began to gratify the Chief Priests against his conscience, the Devil entered into his heart; therefore he rushed further and passed an unjust sentence against Jesus.

Let us consider these horrendous examples, so that we may flee far from such collusions with enemies, and always clearly profess that we dissent from them, and let us not approach them when they attempt compromises.

Moved therefore, Pilate, against his conscience, passes sentence for Christ to be crucified, and the miserable men, the Chief Priests and other Jews, cry out: His blood be upon us and upon our children.

Here these miserable men condemn themselves, and the outcome even in the calamities of this life responds to their voice; they and their descendants paid horrendous penalties when Jerusalem was destroyed, and a great multitude was killed, and the rest were scattered, and even now they wander most miserably.

Afterwards, indeed, they will also have eternal punishments.

But when Jesus is led out, on the way a certain Simon of Cyrene is added to him, to help him in carrying the cross.

This Simon signifies that there will be some in the Church who will carry the cross, that is, who will help the Church a little in the midst of afflictions, just as now some pious Princes and some cities help the Churches, and on that account are in various dangers.

But God will save and does save his promise: Whoever gives a cup of water to one of the least of mine for the sake of the doctrine, shall have his reward.

Item: Blessed is he who understands the needy and the poor; in the day of evil the Lord will deliver him.

And let this much be said concerning the accusation before Pilate, and the sentence of Pilate up to the crucifixion.

Third act.

Crucifixion.

In this, let the following be observed:

1. The crucifixion itself.

2. The words of Christ hanging on the cross.

3. The persons, the Church and the persecutors, who either crucify or mock the crucified one besides.

4. The two thieves.

5. The miracles, the eclipse of the Sun; the earthquake, in which many rise from opened graves.

6. The death of Christ.

First, let the history be known, and let us know what is written singularly in the law: Cursed is he who hangs on a tree.

The Lord endured this kind of punishment, which was the most ignominious of all. But let us consider not only the external lacerations of the body, although these too were atrocious and caused the greatest torments, but let us also consider his internal sorrows. Just as outwardly he endured a punishment that was most ignominious, and for that reason the law says that one crucified is cursed: so he himself felt inwardly in his heart the supreme wrath of God against our sins, as the Prophet says: We saw him struck by God. It is not the greatest pain to be struck by men, as Lawrence was only tortured outwardly in his body by a tyrant, he did not feel the wrath of God inwardly, but the Son was struck by God, and he felt the wrath of God inwardly. We do not understand these things, but nevertheless they must be considered piously. Great sorrows are signified when the Son of God is named a curse, as Paul says: He was made a curse for us, that he might redeem us from the curse of the law.

These things must first be thought upon regarding the very mode of the punishment.

Here also the doctrine concerning the fruit of the passion and its application must be repeated. The whole life of Christ was full of passions, and when we speak of the passion of Christ, let us not think only of the crucifixion, but of his whole life; yet this crucifixion and death was the final part, and the most atrocious. And here Christ hangs, and is the Priest, and the cross is his Altar, upon which he offers himself. Now it pertains to the office of a Priest offering for another, that he should apply the sacrifice to that person, that is, that he should ask that God receive this sacrifice for that person.

What, therefore, are the words of application? Those words of application are expressly written in John 17: For their sake I sanctify myself, that is, I offer myself to you. Likewise: I pray for them. And not for them only, but also for all who will believe through their word. These are the words of application, which must be thought upon often.

They require, however, faith in us at the same time, so that we may apply this very benefit to ourselves. He himself gives you his merits, and cries out to the Father that He may receive you and grant you these merits, so that you may have the remission of sins and be righteous. You must receive these things by faith. This admonition must be repeated often during the passion.

Here again, in the words of Christ hanging on the cross, this very admonition is proposed.

Of the words. The first words spoken on the cross are these: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.

Behold, here too he performs the office of a Priest; he prays for others. And although he now prays by name for those who are crucifying him, yet you should know that he had previously prayed for all in John 17. And at the same time you should understand that the same prayer is repeated here, because his heart wished to gather the Church not only from those who were present there, but from the whole human race. Therefore, the groaning of Christ's heart is for all in the same way as he prays for them. Again, therefore, let us know here that faith is required, so that we may believe that this intercession truly benefits us, and that on account of this Priest of ours we are received and saved. Do not learn only this moral example here, that we must forgive those who inflict injury upon us. Another much greater doctrine concerning the priesthood of Christ and the intercession for us should be thought upon here. And let faith be stirred up, that on account of this Priest we are received. He does not hang here only to teach us patience by his example, but to be the price for us, and the cause of our salvation. And so much for the first words; later I will speak of the others as well.

3. The persons: The Church, such as Mary, his sister, John, and some others.

There are many enemies; some crucify with their own hand, others mock. It happens thus in the world, as I shall say again later.

4. The two thieves.

Among those spectators, however, some are converted, such as the thief and the centurion. And let us especially learn the doctrine concerning the thieves in this place.

These two thieves signify the whole human race, in the midst of which hangs Christ, who becomes a victim for us, although he himself is innocent. All others are destined to death because of the sins that are in us. Yet from that whole multitude of the entire human race, some are converted to Christ, some are not converted, but remain in fury, and although they are in death, they nevertheless mock Christ, just as this hardened thief does. Others, however, who are converted, are like the thief who is converted here. And this thief is a testimony that we are not saved because of our merits, but because of this Lord. See, however, what he is like, and whether all parts of repentance or conversion are in him.

The first is contrition in him. He acknowledges himself to be a sinner, and says: We suffer justly. Likewise, he has no merits, and boasts of no merits, but rather confesses his sins. You have now heard the first part, namely, contrition, nay, even confession before God, and before Christ hanging beside him, and before the Church standing by, Mary, and his sister, and John, and before heaven and earth and the angels.

The second part is Faith.

Remember me, when you come into your kingdom, etc. Behold, here he knows already by faith that this one is King, and not in this life, but soon in the other life. He knows more about the kingdom of the Messiah than the most learned men of that time knew, who dreamed of a worldly empire; he knows that the Messiah suffers in this way, and is a victim, and yet will reign; he knows him to be the Son of God, giving righteousness and eternal life. This he now preaches while hanging on the cross; while the Apostles are silent, this thief becomes an Apostle.

Thus God always gathers the Church miraculously; if the learned and wise do not wish to confess, then other unlearned and despised men will come, who nevertheless will be witnesses for God. And when this thief dies, and can no longer speak, afterwards heaven and earth begin to speak; the sun is darkened, the earth brings forth the living returning from death, who now begin to preach. And then the centurion begins to preach. Thus God always raises up witnesses against the Devil and against the world.

Afterwards follows absolution, when the thief has already shown his faith in his petition, Christ absolves him with an express consolation: Today you will be with me in Paradise. That is: You will not be in eternal death, but you will have true joys in God. And as Christ said this, the heart of the thief was already feeling the beginnings of that joy. He was already an heir of eternal life, he was already rejoicing in God, he was already learning this sentence: This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God, and whom you sent, Jesus, to be the Christ.

The third part, namely, New life, was it in the thief?

I have already said that because he felt consolation in his heart, there was already a new life, which is new righteousness. Where there is true faith, there are at the same time all those virtues: hope, love, invocation, good purpose, patience, and at the same time many good works concur. He confesses his sins, he invokes Christ, and shows his confession; he is patient in this punishment, and willingly renders obedience to God. He rebukes the impious thief, and defends the innocence of Christ. All these are excellent works, and yet it is not to be thought that he is saved because of these works, but he knows that he is saved freely because of this Messiah.

May you know that all these things must happen in the same way in all who are converted, and they are made in the same way. Therefore, I show you this teacher, the thief, and I exhort you that you often look upon him, and diligently consider his sermon, which is most full of erudition.

Concerning Mary.

Concerning the persons who are present at the crucifixion.

After the fall of Adam and Eve, there are always two distinct parts in the human race. One is chosen by God, which is gathered through the word of God, through the voice of the Gospel, and is only in the true Church. And this part truly acknowledges God, truly invokes him, is ruled by the word of God and the Holy Spirit, and begins to serve him, and to do some things pleasing to him, and is saved because of the Son. The other part is a despiser of God, and is a companion of the devils; it rushes into all crimes against the will of God, pollutes itself with lusts, murders, robberies, lies, despises the word of God, feigns impious worship, or considers all worship to be entirely fabricated. These two greatest parts of the human race must be distinguished, and much is proposed daily regarding their distinction in the doctrine of the Church, and they are depicted here also in the history of the greatest matter. Here are the enemies of Christ, Jews and Gentiles, showing in various ways hatred and contempt for Christ; the Priests were the accusers, Pilate passes an unjust sentence, the ministers crucify Christ with their hands, the Jews blaspheme and mock Christ, etc.

But besides these impious ones and enemies, there are also other persons present, who are the Church, because it was necessary that some in the true Church itself be witnesses of this work of the Son of God. There are present, therefore, the highest members of the Church: the Mother, the sister of the mother, and Magdalene and Salome, and they are named distinctly, Mary the mother of James. Likewise the mother of the sons of Zebedee, likewise the Apostle John was present. This group is now small, because the Church was then very much weakened, but suddenly in this very affliction it begins to grow; the thief and the centurion are converted. Thus, there are in such a great work some witnesses, who are members of the Church. But these persons are not only present as witnesses, but they also suffer at the same time, because the Church is made conformable to the Son of God, suffers with him, and is glorified through him and because of him.

Now consider both: How great was the sorrow of the mother, seeing her son hanging there, and such a son, through whom the dead had been raised, and she herself knew the causes of this passion, that this son was a victim and was suffering for the human race, and that the wrath of God against the sins of the human race was poured out upon him. And she herself also felt some part of the divine wrath. No other woman in the whole human race could have sustained this sorrow. There was great sorrow in Eve looking upon the slain Abel, but this sorrow in Mary was much greater. Since, however, the sorrow is immense, and yet Mary does not die, there is no doubt that she is meanwhile sustained divinely, and feels some sparks of consolation in her heart.

These things are to be considered piously and often, nor let us be so iron-hearted and without feeling that we do not accept these wonderful examples divinely proposed to us. Let us know also that all things which happen in the person of Mary happen similarly in the Church in some, because Mary is a type of the whole congregation, which is called the Church of God. Whenever, therefore, we think of the crucifixion, let us think at the same time of our own afflictions, and let us sustain ourselves with this consolation. You should think that you must stand under the cross with Mary, because God wants us all to be made conformable to the image of the Son. And do not think only of the necessity, that it is necessary to suffer, but at the same time of the consolation. Mary herself is divinely sustained, because otherwise she could by no means sustain such great sorrows. Thus you too should know that God wants to sustain you, and not to let us be submerged into death and eternal punishments, as the Psalm says: The Lord is near to those who are of a contrite heart.

I said, however, that God wants this wonderful passion of the Son to happen in such a way that He is present to the Church, and it is a witness and suffers at the same time; He Himself is also present, and shows testimonies in all of nature, which show that God was not unaware of what was then happening: the sun was darkened, the earth was shaken, the graves were opened, the dead were coming back to life. These great things were testimonies of the presence of God, and that God was magnifying that death and passion of His Son. Thus also let us know that God is present when the Church suffers, as the Lord says: All the hairs of your head are numbered.

Concerning the words on the cross.

The first saying I reviewed: Father forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. I spoke there, however, about the priesthood of Christ.

The second saying. Woman, behold your son. To John: Behold, this is your mother, and immediately he began to care for her and to serve her.

This saying commends to all of us the Church and the ministers of the Gospel; Christ, hanging on the cross, commands the mother, that is, the Church, to care for those who teach. And again, he commends to us every mother, namely, the Church. This admonition teaches us that in all things we should be more diligent in fostering teachers, and in fostering the peace of the Church.

The third saying to the thief. Today you will be with me in Paradise. Regarding this, I said before that it was the absolution of the thief, and a proclamation in which Christ himself, even then hanging on the cross, testifies that he is the Messiah and will soon possess an eternal kingdom.

The fourth saying.

Eli, Eli, Lama asabthani. This is the saddest voice, surpassing the wisdom of all creatures. Here the Lord shows that he is struggling with great and ineffable sorrows, in which he grieves as if he were deserted by the Father, but afterwards he struggles out of this great sorrow when he says: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.

We do not understand the magnitude of these sorrows, but nevertheless, we ought to know the cause of the passion and the victory. He was struck for our sins, as it is written in the Prophet: The wrath of God against our sins is poured out upon him, and thus the justice of God is satisfied. Again, the eternal Father, because he loves the Son, does not allow him to succumb in this struggle, but afterwards glorifies him, and glorifies him in such a way that he receives us on account of him.

Regarding this great struggle, the text says in Heb. 5: Offering up with crying and tears, he was heard because of his obedience. Let us consider these things reverently, and give thanks to the eternal Father and the Son, and by faith apply the benefit to ourselves.

The fifth saying. I thirst. It is a fitting sign for the previous cry: Eli, Eli, because it signifies the immense sorrows of the heart, which so burn the heart and lungs, and the best juices in the whole body, and dry up the marrow in the bones, that a great thirst is kindled, as we see in those who are led to execution. It must be considered, however, as an example, how Christ, seeking refreshment in the height of pain, is even more tormented by mockery, and is given vinegar to drink.

Thus, for the most part, other men torment the afflicted Church, who ought to have been moved by mercy toward her, and they increase her pain through mockery, and give her vinegar to drink.

The sixth saying.

It is finished. Consider this saying well; it was necessary for us to be redeemed through the Son of God, who would at the same time be man, as it is written: The seed of the woman will crush the head of the serpent. And because man had sinned, it was necessary for someone in the human race to pay the penalty. Likewise, Scripture always says that the redeemer is the propitiator through his blood. And all the victims in the Law signified this death and the shedding of blood. Although, therefore, the whole life of Christ is a perpetual passion and a continuous sacrifice, yet this final passion and death is the principal sacrifice and the consummation of the whole and continuous sacrifice of Christ.

Therefore he says: It is finished. And it is a voice of victory, by which he gives thanks to God, and shows the Church that he has now completed the sacrifice which was decreed in the secret counsel of the divinity, with wonderful wisdom, and was afterwards signified by the victims in the Law, and was predicted by the Prophets, and signified by the death of Abel, by the offering of Isaac, by the death of John the Baptist, and of other Saints.

I believe also that this voice was a consolation to Mary, who understood this passion. Hearing this, she knows that this sacrifice is now finished, by which the wrath of God is appeased, and the Church is received. And she herself understood that she, on account of this finished sacrifice, was an heir of eternal life, as it is written: By one offering he has perfected the Saints. She herself also, now hearing the consummation, gives thanks to God for these highest and wonderful benefits.

And let us think daily about this consummation, and let us also give thanks that our salvation was finished then.

The seventh saying.

Father, into your hands I commend my spirit. The words are in Psalm 30: Into your hands I commend my spirit; you have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth. The text, however, says: He cried with a loud voice. Here again, victory is signified, because the cry signifies that his strength is now restored. And when he commends his spirit to the Father, he now joyfully knows that he is approaching the Father.

Therefore also with a great cry he utters this final voice, so that the whole Church may know that he is departing not as one condemned, but as one pleasing to God, and as a victor who has overcome the devils and death.

He teaches us to depart from this life in the same way. And thus we can depart confident in this very victory, in which Christ conquered the devils and death, and appeased the wrath of God for us. And let us often in our whole life think of this voice: Into your hands I commend my spirit. And at the same time let us think of Christ himself crying out thus, let us know that we always have life only in this way, with God preserving our life for us, and that we live in him on account of Christ. We are always in dangers of death, death always looms, therefore let us always cry: Into your hands I commend my spirit.

Concerning the title and the garments.

The history of the passion contains so much that the wisdom of no creature could exhaust it.
