Est et hic congressus Mariae, Elisabeth, Zachariae, imago verae piae et Christianae synodi: nam hoc primum fuit concilium novae Ecclesiae. Puella Maria venit per 20 miliaria, tantum enim fere fuit iter a Nazareth Hierosolymam usque, ibi narrat cognatae Elisabeth et familiae de suo conceptu, et testimonio angeli, Elisabeth vicissim illi testimonium perhibet, et accedit Zacharias senex, cuius pietas publice nota est, et ex muto subito loquens, sua voce confirmat haec testimonia. Ita in hoc conventu concluditur de summo et gravissimo articulo, de concepto et exhibito Messia, et vera est rata definitio sanctissimae synodi, etiamsi non accedit decretum aut approbatio Pontificum et Pharisaeorum.

His testimoniis adduntur et Cantica, seu gratiarum actio, ut extet confessio etiam ad posteritatem, et praedicetur hoc ingens Dei beneficium, quod misertus populi sui, miserit Filium. Hoc vult Maria agnosci et palam celebrari. Non vult occultari, aut obrui veritatem, sed extare noticiam verae doctrinae, ut agnoscatur et glorificetur Deus, ut recte colatur et invocetur.

ΧΙΙ. ΑΝΝΟTATIONES IN EVANGELIA. agnoscatur et glorificetur Deus, ut recte colatur MELANTH, OFER. VOL. XIV. 481 agnoscatur et glorificetur Deus, ut recte colatur et invocetur. Talia concilia approbat Deus, quae quaerunt veritatem, et iuxta verbum Dei testimonium perhibent de Christo, non quae praestigiis sophismatum et fucosis articulis obruunt veritatem.

De tertio. De Cantico Mariae.

In hoc cantico Maria gerit personam totius Ecclesiae. Est enim confessio de Messia et gratiarum actio, et descriptio victoriae Ecclesiae, contra mundum, tyrannos, et omnia membra diaboli. Quare et nos sciamus a nobis postulari, ut vere una canamus et sequamur hanc praecentricem, quae ut in choro incoatrix est huius carminis, ac ingenti animo edit confessionem. Tria ergo comprehendit.

I. Gratiarum actionem. Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Id est, ex tota anima, tota anima, toto corde glorifico Deum. Non dubito vitam in discrimen offerre, propter confessionem.

Sic debemus et nos adfecti esse, ut confessionem anteferamus omnibus rebus, vitae, facultatibus, liberis. Qui sic affectus est, vere canit hunc hymnum, Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Quando trahebantur ad mortem Iohannes Baptista, Paulus et similes, tunc vere dicebant: Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Sic sunt Christiani fortissimi milites, cogitant, Magnificat anima mea regem, pro quo pugno, vitam meam et omnia coniicio in discrimen, ut dimicem pro rege, ut sit magnus et victor.

Secunda pars Cantici.

Respexit humilitatem ancillae suae. Fecit mihi magna qui potens est etc. Haec est narratio beneficiorum, quae in Ecclesia Deus efficit. Ecclesia sit sprèta, humilis, parva, Deus tamen dat ei victorias, conservat eam contra tyrannos et sapientiam mundi. Haec est summa huius partis. Loquitur Maria de se, sed non tantum de se sola, sed de toto corpore Ecclesiae. Respexit Deus humilitatem, id est, miseriam ancillae suae.

Quamvis simus abiecti, quamvis simus imbecilles, sine praesidiis, sine defensione humana, tamen respicit nos Deus, exaudit, iuvat contra tyrannos et sapientes mundi. Hic discamus, quod in sola Ecclesia sic agnoscatur Deus, quod sit Deus remittens peccata, et miseros credentes exaudiens. Humana ratio et omnes religiones, praeter evangelicam, aliter sentiunt de Deo. Habent talem opinionem, quod Deus non curet, non respiciat adflictos. Et est singularis et arcana sapientia, et solorum credentium in Christum, erigere se fide, et credere remissionem peccatorum, et petere et expectare auxilium etc.

Tunc haec fiunt, Fecit potentiam brachio suo etc., servat Ecclesiam inter pericula, sicut servavit electos cum ducerentur in captivitatem Babylonicam. Dispergit superbos confidentes sua sapientia, sicut confudit magos Pharaonis, sic nunc confundit sapientia sua confidentes Papistas, et alios. O magnum peccatum, quod non intellegunt sapientes: quod volunt Ecclesiam suis consiliis regere et mutare. De his est dictum: Perdam sapientiam sapientum. Deponit potentes de sede, sicut Romanos perdidit persequentes Christum. Exaltat humiles. Esurientes implet bonis, consolatur, servat Ecclesiam.

Tertia pars, Confessio de Messia.

Tertia pars est propria illius concilii confessio, quod Messia dato, recordatus est Deus promissionum. Haec est summa Cantici. Ita et nos agamus gratias, et cum recitamus hoc Canticum, intuemur animo totam Ecclesiam, cogitemus qualia sint certamina in Ecclesia, propter confessionem, quam mirabilibus operibus Deus defendat Ecclesiam. Cogitemus requiri a nobis confessionem, cogitemus hunc esse summum cultum, quem haec puella, id est, tota vera Ecclesia, praestat, praedicare Deum quod dederit Messiam, quod elegerit Ecclesiam perpetuo victuram, quod eam defendat et servet, non humanis viribus aut consiliis. Haec discenda sunt in lectione huius historiae, qualis sit vera Ecclesia, et qui sunt veri cultus, et repetenda sunt animo, testimonia de Christum, ut nostram fidem confirmemus, et nos ad invocandum excitemus.

Reliquum est exemplum de infante Iohanne, qui in utero sensit adesse Dominum et Messiam. Quanquam autem hoc de Iohanne peculiare est, tamem est testimonium, quod Spiritus sanctus etiam in parvulis sit efficax, et quod habeant motus quosdam, quanquam nobis incognitos, tamen Deo placentes. Ideo cum audis, Talium est regnum coelorum, cogites in infantibus Spiritum sanctum, certos motus efficere, quales sunt sanctorum, qui sunt membra regni coelorum, id est, Ecclesiae verae. Et hi motus pii excitantur verbo, ut hic dicitur: Postquam sonuit vox tua etc.

## 1:57-80 John the Baptist
John the Baptist.

Gospel of Matthew 3. In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the desert of Judea, and saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.

For this is he of whom it was spoken by Isaiah the Prophet, saying: The voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare the way of the Lord, make His paths straight. And John himself had a garment of camel's hair, and a leather belt around his loins.

And his food was locusts and wild honey. Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region around the Jordan went out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.

But seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: Brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore, bear fruits worthy of repentance, and do not wish to say within yourselves: We have Abraham as our father.

For I say to you, that God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham. And now the axe is laid to the root of the trees.

Every one, therefore

tree, which does not produce good fruit, is cut down, and cast into the fire. I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear, He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire, whose fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly purge his floor, and will gather his wheat into the garner, but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.

There are seven principal points.

I. Why the feast day of the Baptist is celebrated.

II. Concerning the nature of the Church, and how God from time to time renews it, lest the whole human race should perish.

III. Concerning the peculiar calling and office of the Baptist.

IIII. Concerning his whole doctrine: He taught not only the law, but also the Gospel concerning Christ, he preached concerning repentance, concerning faith in Christ, and the remission of sins.

He adds also a sermon concerning good works, concerning kinds of life, concerning the distinction of moral works and ceremonies: finally, he was a purifier of doctrine, and a beginner of baptism, and he receives the Gentiles.

V. John is a witness of the doctrine concerning the Trinity, also concerning the two natures in Christ: finally, the history of John embraces all the articles of faith.

VI. Why he says: I baptize you with water, but he who comes after me, will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.

VII. Concerning his diet, concerning the time of his preaching, and concerning his death.

Concerning the first.

Although the Church of God is a small part of mankind oppressed in the world and miserable: while empires are eminent and are looked upon, and are thought to be the principal and most flourishing part of the human race, and so turn the eyes of men upon themselves, so that men think that either the highest empires please God, or that the whole human race is neglected, yet God wills that even His Church be heard in the world, He wills that the knowledge of God should shine. Therefore He commanded that there be public preaching and confession of doctrine, and that through such gatherings and assemblies doctrine should be handed down by public voice to posterity, lest there be secret conventicles, in which lurking places might provide an opportunity for corrupting doctrine and for other evil things. Finally, since human nature is especially created for celebrating God, it is most just that there be public assemblies, in which men may be taught about God, and God may be invoked with the one voice of all. Wherefore Christ also adorned these gatherings with a great testimony: Wheresoever two or three are gathered in my name, there will I be in the midst of them.

This is the first reason why feast days were divinely instituted. Furthermore, let us cast away those heathen opinions, that the leisure of the day and pomp are the worship of God. But let us seek other ends, namely, that men may be taught publicly, and that a public confession of doctrine and invocation may be made, and let us cast away also this error, which is simply heathen, concerning the invocation of the dead. The feast of the Baptist is not celebrated so that he himself may be invoked, but so that we may learn publicly what the Church is, how God has from time to time sent restorers, how the Church is governed, and so that we may give thanks to God for these benefits. Also, that we may learn what the doctrine of the saints was. Also, that we may be confirmed by their testimonies and examples.

Concerning the second. Although the human mind is offended when it hears that the Church of God is always a very small assembly, if it is compared to the rest of the multitude, and many things are argued against it, yet let us know that the matter is truly so, and that the cause of this smallness is the very malice of men, who either neglect the word handed down by God with certain testimonies, or petulantly cast it away.

And consider the example in the very people of the Jews, in whom was the true Church of God, yet the greater multitude was of the impious. King Herod was impious, and had destroyed the principal council of the people, who were called the Sanhedrin, the doctors were distracted into three sects. There were the Sadducees with a most arrogant title, as if you would say, Justiciaries, who utterly rejected the Prophets, and professedly defended Epicurean opinions: they denied that souls were immortal: they denied also the resurrection of the dead. But who would not wonder that such madnesses were defended among the people of God, and indeed under the pretext of the doctrine of Moses?

But others were the Pharisees, that is, interpreters, who nevertheless retained the Prophets, defended the immortality of the soul and the resurrection. but they added many human traditions, fascinated by this opinion, that external discipline is righteousness before God, and that it merits the remission of sins.

Therefore, they taught the law only regarding external discipline, and they did not know the doctrine of faith, of the passion of the Messiah, of the remission of sins, but they imagined that the Messiah would propagate the law of Moses into the whole world, and would occupy empires. Thus the great multitude of them felt, but it is consistent that among them there were some sounder ones, who sought the doctrine of the Messiah, having been informed by the true remnants of the Church, by Simeon, Zacharias, John the Baptist, and others.

The third sect was the Essenes, that is, the workers, who contributed their things in common, and strove to overcome others with fasts and alms. But this sect was small, and had errors similar to the Pharisees, concerning the righteousness of works and the worldly kingdom of the Messiah.

Although the great multitude was profane, and there was great confusion of opinions, and Herod was raging with constant slaughters, and the pontiffs were godless (ἄθεοι), yet God preserved remnants for the Church, Zacharias, Simeon, Joseph, Elizabeth, Anna, Mary, and many such.

These gave testimony to the true doctrine, and reproved public errors. But afterwards John was raised up, who with a clearer reproof condemned errors, and by the wonderful work of God gathered a new Church. Thus God has from time to time purged the Church.

When idols were worshipped in Israel, Prophets were raised up to condemn false worship and to propagate true doctrine: the hearers of these were the Church.

The impious kings and the multitude given to idols were not the Church, and by the wonderful goodness of God there was a continuous succession of Prophets.

Elijah presided for about twenty years, soon followed by Elisha, who presided for about seventy years. Isaiah as a young man could see him, and he presided for about eighty years; Jeremiah saw him as an old man, and he presided for forty years. Daniel followed immediately, who presided for seventy years: then there were Zacharias, Malachi, Ezra, Nehemiah, up to the times of Alexander the Great: afterwards, under Antiochus Epiphanes, very many elders were killed: but yet God preserved some remnants.

Let us therefore acknowledge the goodness of God, and give thanks, because from time to time He raised up teachers, and exhibited testimonies of doctrine.

Thus, after the Apostles, some pious teachers were raised up from time to time, who censured public errors, as Methodius refuted the errors of Origen, Malchion [refuted] the Samosatene, Athanasius [refuted] Arius, Augustine [refuted] the Manichaeans and Pelagius: and by many the errors of the Pope have been censured, as by Wessel and others.

But the glory of the people of Israel was far more illustrious than that of this last age of the world. However, this whole course of the Church must be considered, so that we may learn what the Church is, and what parts we ought to embrace.

Perhaps now, because a greater dispersion is happening through the Turks, God is kindling the light of the Gospel for this very reason, so that in this dispersion the pious may have certain doctrine and consolation, and wherever they are dispersed, they may be able to propagate it with their own voice, even if they do not have ordinary Bishops or Teachers as before.

On the third.

There is a twofold calling. One is ordinary, as when the Church chooses ministers; thus in the law there was an ordinary calling of priests, because God had commanded this office to a certain tribe. And although many abuse this ordinary calling, yet the authority of the calling is not to be rejected universally. But because teachers in an ordinary calling often do not teach correctly, therefore God adds an extraordinary calling: He raised up great men to correct public errors and to gather the Church, as He called Elijah, Elisha, and thus John in a singular way, and as the pontiffs ought to have heard Elijah, although they were in the place of an ordinary calling, so the pontiffs ought to have heard John, because God had provided him with certain testimonies, an angel had appeared to his father, and had predicted his calling.

Those who do not consider what a great thing such a calling is, and what the government of the Church is, do not understand the office of such men, like Elijah, Elisha, John, Paul; indeed, wise politicians hated them as morose and seditious men.

Other foolish people think they were simple men who, like monks, sought hiding places because of superstition. But it is by no means to be thought so of them; let us know that these are the highest leaders, through whom God was effective, and restored and increased the Church, and through whom He suppressed false doctrine and renewed the true: in short, whose ministry was salutary to many called to eternal life. The unlearned dream that John only handed down certain precepts concerning good morals, just as Phocylides or Theognis handed down, but as we often warn, the doctrine of the Church must be distinguished from philosophy, and from pharisaical doctrine.

Philosophers teach a portion of the law concerning good morals. The Pharisees teach the same, and add many ceremonies. But the Church preaches concerning repentance, and concerning the remission of sins, concerning the judgment of God, concerning reconciliation, and eternal life.

When he speaks of repentance, he expounds the law, and testifies that the law of God does not only command external discipline, but that all are accused; he says the law is the voice of God, showing and condemning sin in the whole human nature. Therefore he says to all: Do penance, and he adds a prophecy concerning the end and destruction of this people, which such a man, foreseeing, lamented with great sorrow.

They already saw foreigners reigning, and he knew well that the destruction of all cities would follow, and he deplored not only the deaths of so many thousands of men, women, and children, but also eternal destruction. How much sorrow this thought brought to such a man, no one can explain in words. And although this prediction was derided by the impious, yet it moved the pious. And it is inculcated in these words: He will purge his threshing floor, he will gather the wheat, and he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.

He also added the doctrine concerning the remission of sins.

For it must not be imagined that John preached the law only, or repentance without the remission of sins. It is a pagan imagination to think of the doctrine of repentance without the Gospel concerning the remission of sins: because repentance without consolation is angry at God, and flees from God. Therefore Luke says clearly: He preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins: and John sounded the Gospel most clearly, and indeed he showed Christ himself, and added these sermons proper to the Gospel: This is the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.

Item: He who believes in the Son, has eternal life. Item: From his fullness we have all received grace for grace. Item: The law was given through Moses, Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, that is, reconciliation is given to us on account of him and through him, and truth, that is, true and eternal justice and life is restored through him.

The law contained shadows signifying future and eternal goods. Item, the justice of the law, that is, discipline, is a certain vanishing shadow. But this Son begins eternal things in us, and will afterwards perfect them. And although these sentences are brief, yet they comprehend the sum of the Gospel, as a mediocre reader can understand.

Nor is there any doubt that these sentences were copiously expounded by him. As often, therefore, as we speak of John, this diligence must be applied, that his sermons be sought, which properly contain the Gospel and the doctrine of faith.

Nor should we think that he only handed down certain precepts of morals, of which will be spoken later. For he had another primary office. For God wished him to be a public witness, who would show Christ, and at the same time renew doctrine. John was primarily called to these duties, therefore he showed the present Christ, he spoke of repentance, of the judgment of God, of the remission of sins, of faith in Christ, and of eternal life.

At the same time he also taxed the errors of the Pharisees, concerning their sacrifices and traditions. They thought they were just by the law, they thought they deserved the remission of sins by their discipline. He refutes this, nay he says: This lamb takes away the sins of the world.

You receive grace, that is, reconciliation, not on account of your justice, but for grace, that is, because he himself is beloved. Item: From his fullness you receive, that is, he himself will endow you with new light, justice, and life. He also refutes errors concerning the empire of the world; when he testifies that this Christ will be the lamb, that is, the victim.

Item, when he predicts the destruction of the nation. After you have diligently considered this part of the doctrine of faith, another part must also be sought, namely the doctrine concerning good works.

This also he hands down, saying: Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, and when asked he does not show the works of ceremonies, as the Pharisees, but moral works, just as the Prophets always condemned the common superstition of men, by which ceremonies are preferred to moral works, as in Isaiah 1, 58, Psalm 50, and elsewhere we are often warned.

Item, the passage also contains useful doctrine, concerning the approval of political life and military service, and indeed he hands down memorable laws, which restrain the desires of governors, and distinguish the faculties of inferiors from the affairs of superiors: Do not think, he says, that it is permitted for you to seize as much as you like from the goods of citizens, but be content with your wages.

Item: Exact no more than what is appointed etc.

The same passage testifies that the nations were received.

Thus John begins.

she said: Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb. And whence is this to me, that the mother of the Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of thy salutation sounded in my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy, And blessed is she that believed, because those things shall be accomplished, which were spoken to her by the Lord.

And Mary said: My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour, Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed. Because he that is mighty hath done great things to me; and holy is his name. And his mercy is from generation unto generations, to them that fear him. He hath shewed might in his arm: he hath scattered the proud in the conceit of their heart. He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away. He hath received Israel his servant, being mindful of his mercy. As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever. And Mary abode with her about three months, and returned to her own house.

This is a most beautiful history, and full of spiritual and Christian doctrine. It has, however, three principal points.

I. The testimony concerning the Messiah.

II. The image of the Church and of a true synod.

III. The Canticle of Mary.

Concerning the first.

There is a great difference between the Church and the empires of the world. The Church is a small gathering of those who retain the pure doctrine of the Gospel and believe in Christ, scattered, despised, and rejected in the world, which admires the power, glory, victories, and triumphs of great empires. And yet this small gathering of the Church truly performs the greatest things. Although, therefore, the actions of Christ are not seen in the world like the deeds of Alexander or Caesar, yet He is not entirely unknown, and He has His testimonies: because there must be some Church in which God wills that He and His Son be known, and wills that some gathering be saved, in which He Himself is celebrated in eternal life; therefore He has exhibited many testimonies, which Christ, having been exhibited according to the promises, [has given to] our faith.

Thus, here, immediately upon the conception of Christ, testimonies are recited. The witnesses come together: Mary, Elisabeth, an old woman pregnant by a singular miracle of God, the infant leaping in the womb, Zacharias, to whom, though hitherto mute, speech is suddenly restored, and others in this family. For Mary sets out to her kinswoman, not for the sake of private friendship, but for the sake of this illustrious testimony, and for the confirmation of her own faith and that of other saints.

Concerning the second. One must consider the image of the Church, and seek consolation from this passage, so that we may not fall away from the truth, deceived by the appearance and title of the Church. The Pontiffs, Bishops, Kings, and those addicted to them call themselves the Church; just as once Caiphas, Annas, the Pharisees, and the Sadducees did, but they are not the Church. Meanwhile, there is another small, true Church, as Paul says: Not all who are of Israel are Israel. As, therefore, there were then the Church—Zacharias, Elisabeth, Mary, and a few others—so now there is a small number of those who believe in Christ and rightly worship God, and this gathering is persecuted by the pontiffs and bishops, just as then the enemies of the saints were Caiphas and his like. For it is said that even Zacharias was killed because he affirmed that the Messiah had come, as Epiphanius writes.

There is also in this meeting of Mary, Elisabeth, and Zacharias an image of a true, pious, and Christian synod: for this was the first council of the new Church. The maiden Mary comes for 20 miles—for that was about the distance from Nazareth to Jerusalem—there she tells her kinswoman Elisabeth and the family about her conception and the testimony of the angel; Elisabeth in turn bears witness to her, and Zacharias the elder approaches, whose piety is publicly known, and, being suddenly loosed from his muteness, confirms these testimonies with his own voice. Thus, in this assembly, a conclusion is reached concerning the highest and most grave article, concerning the conceived and exhibited Messiah, and the definition of this most holy synod is true and ratified, even if the decree or approval of the Pontiffs and Pharisees does not accompany it.

To these testimonies are added the Canticles, or thanksgiving, so that a confession may exist even for posterity, and this great benefit of God may be preached, that He, having had mercy on His people, has sent His Son. Mary wills that this be acknowledged and celebrated openly. She does not will that it be hidden or that the truth be overwhelmed, but that the knowledge of true doctrine should exist, so that so that God may be acknowledged and glorified, that He may be rightly worshipped and invoked. God approves of such councils that seek the truth, and according to the word of God bear witness to Christ, not those that overwhelm the truth with the deceits of sophistries and specious articles.

Concerning the third. Concerning the Canticle of Mary.

In this canticle, Mary bears the person of the whole Church. For it is a confession concerning the Messiah and an act of thanksgiving, and a description of the victory of the Church against the world, tyrants, and all the members of the devil. Wherefore let us also know that it is required of us that we truly sing as one and follow this precentor, who, as in a choir, is the leader of this song, and with a great spirit brings forth the confession.

It therefore comprehends three things.

I. An act of thanksgiving.

My soul doth magnify the Lord. That is, with my whole soul, with all my soul, with my whole heart I glorify God. I do not hesitate to offer my life into danger for the sake of the confession. Thus we also ought to be affected, that we prefer the confession to all things, to life, to faculties, to children. He who is thus affected truly sings this hymn, My soul doth magnify the Lord. When John the Baptist, Paul, and those like them were being dragged to death, then they truly said: My soul doth magnify the Lord. Thus are Christians most valiant soldiers, thinking: My soul doth magnify the King for whom I fight; I cast my life and all things into danger, that I may fight for the King, that He may be great and victorious.

The second part of the Canticle.

He hath regarded the lowliness of His handmaiden. He that is mighty hath done to me great things, etc.

This is a narrative of the benefits which God effects in the Church. Although the Church is despised, humble, and small, God nevertheless gives it victories, preserves it against tyrants and the wisdom of the world. This is the sum of this part.

Mary speaks of herself, but not only of herself alone, but of the whole body of the Church. God regarded the lowliness, that is, the misery of His handmaiden. Although we are abject, although we are weak, without protection, without human defense, yet God regards us, hears us, helps us against the tyrants and the wise of the world.

Here let us learn that in the Church alone God is thus acknowledged, that He is the God who forgives sins and hears the miserable who believe. Human reason and all religions, except the evangelical, think otherwise of God. They have such an opinion that God does not care, does not regard the afflicted. And it is a singular and secret wisdom, and of those only who believe in Christ, to raise themselves by faith, and to believe in the remission of sins, and to seek and expect help, etc.

Then these things come to pass: He hath showed strength with His arm, etc., He preserves the Church amidst dangers, just as He preserved the elect when they were being led into the Babylonian captivity. He scatters the proud who are confident in their own wisdom, just as He confounded the magicians of Pharaoh; so now He confounds the Papists and others who are confident in their own wisdom. O great sin, that the wise do not understand: that they wish to rule and change the Church by their own counsels. Of these it is said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.

He puts down the mighty from their seat, just as He destroyed the Romans who were persecuting Christ. He exalts the humble. He fills the hungry with good things, He consoles, He preserves the Church.

The third part, Confession concerning the Messiah.

The third part is the confession proper to that council, that the Messiah having been given, God was mindful of His promises. This is the sum of the Canticle.

So let us also give thanks, and when we recite this Canticle, let us look with our mind upon the whole Church, let us think what kind of struggles there are in the Church for the sake of the confession, which God defends by His marvelous works. Let us think that confession is required of us, let us think that this is the highest worship, which this maiden, that is, the whole true Church, performs: to preach God because He has given the Messiah, because He has chosen the Church to live forever, because He defends and preserves it, not by human strength or counsels. These things are to be learned in the reading of this history, what the true Church is, and who are the true worshippers, and they are to be repeated in the mind, the testimonies concerning Christ, so that we may confirm our faith and stir ourselves up to invocation.

It remains to consider the example of the infant John, who in the womb felt that the Lord and Messiah was present. Although this is peculiar to John, yet it is a testimony that the Holy Spirit is effective even in infants, and that they have certain motions, although unknown to us, yet pleasing to God.

Therefore, when you hear, Of such is the kingdom of heaven, you should think of the Spirit in infants. this Church to be gathered from the Gentiles and the Jews: he therefore had a greater office than the other Prophets. He was the demonstrator of the present Christ: he had the mandate of beginning the new Church, of baptizing and receiving the Gentiles.

On the fifth.

Therefore some revelations of the highest teachers have been written, so that they may instruct and confirm the rest of the Church. Wherefore in the histories of the Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles, those confirmations should be diligently sought.

Moreover, a most clear testimony was exhibited to John concerning the three persons of the divinity at the baptism of Christ. The voice of the Father is heard, and the Father and the Son are distinctly named by that voice: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. The Son is seen standing in the river with the eyes. The form of a dove is also beheld, in which was the Holy Spirit. For the Father had also said to John that the Holy Spirit was in this form. Therefore John also understood the article concerning the Trinity, and delivered it to the Church. For he made this revelation known to others for this reason, that he might teach them about the nature of God, about the eternal Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and show the distinctions of their offices.

He also teaches about the two natures in Christ, when he says that the Son was before him, and is now sent, so that he may become a victim. Concerning the Holy Spirit, he knows that he is the mover, who is given on account of the Son, and kindles new motions in believers that are pleasing to God, a new light and life. Therefore he says: He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.

Now if you review the whole symbol in order, you see that John has preached about all the articles. Thus let us learn to contemplate the whole John, that is, to embrace the universal body of doctrine. But especially in our invocation, let the mind think upon the revelation made to John, so that we may distinguish our invocation from the Jewish and Turkish; let us invoke the eternal God, who made himself known through the Son, and said of him, This is my beloved Son, let us ask to be heard and received on account of the Son, and to be ruled by the Holy Spirit.

On the sixth.

That he says: I baptize you with water, but he who will come after me will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire, is a necessary distinction. But it is very profitable to know that it is not the external baptism that is distinguished, but the persons. The person of Christ differs far from the ministers. John often inculcates this; so that we may learn that Christ is not only a teacher, as all those ignorant of the Gospel imagine: but let us know that he is a savior. When you hear John preaching, or Paul, let faith look upon Christ, not these teachers, and let it know that the remission of sins is given on account of Christ, and let it seek the Holy Spirit and eternal life from Christ, not from John or Paul. Therefore John said most significantly: I am a voice, as if he were saying: I am only a minister sounding the Gospel, through which another is effective, namely, Christ. Thus he says that he baptizes with water, that is, he applies the external ministry, but that another is effective, namely, Christ, who baptizes with the Holy Spirit, that is, he gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life to those who believe and invoke him.

On the other hand, however, he will baptize all the impious with fire, that is, he will overwhelm them with eternal wrath and torments, just as he says later: He will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. He calls true and horrible terrors fire, as scripture often speaks. The pious taste these in repentance, but are delivered. The impious, however, are oppressed by eternal dread and pain.

On the seventh.

After it has been spoken about the ministry and the doctrine of the Baptist, let it then be spoken about his private virtues. But as often as examples are proposed, let us know that there are distinctions of vocations and degrees of virtues; let each one imitate those things which befit his own vocation, and let him imitate according to his own mediocrity. Nor let him think that he attains the degrees of those excellent men, but that mediocrity itself is a great honor in those things which befit our vocation, just as Paul says: This is required, that we be faithful.

But that John lives in the desert, this was fitting for his vocation, it does not fit yours. Because since he had been born into the priestly tribe, he ought to have sacrificed in the temple. Since therefore God was beginning another ministry through him, he wanted him to depart from the temple, therefore he dwells in the desert, and the priests understood that a new thing was being done, and contrary to the law....

Let these causes of deeds be considered in examples, and let us know that not all things fit all people. But because he was in the desert, the situation brought it about that his diet was more sordid: although I think concerning the locusts, that John acted against the law, because departed from the temple, so he acted against the law concerning food, in order to show that the end of the Jewish polity had come, and that the Gospel also pertains to the Gentiles, and that the distinctions of foods are removed.

For locusts usually signify crabs, which it was not permitted for the people of the law to eat; it is consistent, however, that John used things available at the Jordan, where fishermen gave him crabs, which they otherwise would not sell.

I am also moved by the signification of the locust.

There is a natural discord between the locust and serpents, and it is said that in battle it skillfully seizes the neck of the serpent.

Thus, John had a discord with the Pharisees, and he strangled their necks, that is, their doctrine.

If, however, anyone prefers that the locust be understood as the insect, I do not object.

But the death of such a man must be considered most of all.

And not only should these precepts be taken from it, that one ought to teach the truth and rather face death than cast away the confession of the true doctrine, according to that saying: He who will not confess me before men, I will not confess him before my heavenly Father.

But this must be considered much more: why God does not always defend his own against tyrants.

This aspect greatly offends human judgments.

But let us learn here that it is the proper wisdom of the Church to understand that it is subject to the cross, and why it is subject to the cross.

But concerning these leaders in the ministry of the word, there is something singular.

The primary cause is that God wishes through them to show a testimony concerning the future judgment.

It is established from the previous testimonies that Isaiah, Jeremiah, John, Paul, and the like truly please God.

Nor did he approve of them only so that they might be miserable and reduced to nothing, nor does he reject the impious so that they might always be flourishing: rather, there will be a distinction at some time.

Therefore, when he allows his own to be killed, he testifies that another judgment remains, in which he will reveal his wrath against the impious and will adorn his own with glory, just as it was said to Cain: If you do well, you will receive: but if you do evil, your sin will rest, until it is revealed.

For God testifies that he truly receives the just and is angry at sin, but he defers the judgment, and this delay confirms security in the impious: therefore he says, Sin will rest, but yet afterwards wrath will be revealed against sin.

The illustrious testimonies of this coming judgment are the deaths of those whom God shows by certain testimonies to please him.

You have the primary cause.

Afterwards there are also other causes.

God wishes to show them, because they feel seriously and from the heart that the doctrine is true.

For if the profession of doctrine brought no danger, it could not be known whether they feel so seriously.

Now, since they prefer it to life, they show that they feel so seriously; they show also this, that the profession is more necessary than life.

The third cause is, he also wishes it to be seen that they do not serve God servilely, not seeking the tranquility of this life, but that with true love they prefer the knowledge of God to all things.

The fourth cause is, that they may become similar to the image of the Son of God.

The fifth cause is, that the death of the saints universally testifies that sin remains in the nature of man, on account of which we are all subject to all calamities, which, however, God mitigates for the weak, as it is said in the Psalm: If you should observe iniquities, O Lord, who shall endure? that is, if you were to pour out your wrath against the mass of our sins, and wished to punish everything according to merit, all would suddenly perish and fall into eternal punishments, but you spare them on account of the mediator, the Son.

Altogether, the consideration of the death of the saints is a distinguished school, and it admonishes us concerning the highest things, concerning the future judgment, concerning the common sin of human nature, concerning the wonderful counsel of God, by which he wishes the Church to be subject to the cross.

What is more dissimilar than Nero and Paul? And yet Paul, having been saved so many times before, is torn apart by that most foul beast.

What is more dissimilar than Herod and the Baptist? Whom, born by the singular work of God, and called to the highest ministry, and adorned with the singular light of the Gospel, the tyrant kills so quickly: for John did not preach in the desert for a full two years, because he was killed about the second Passover after he began his preaching, as the series of evangelical history indicates.

Latin:

Iohanne Baptista.

Evangelium Matth. 3. In diebus illis veniebat Iohannes Baptista, praedicans in deserto Iudaeae, et dicens: Poenitentiam agite, appropinquavit enim regnum coelorum.

Hic est enim, de quo dictum est per Esaiam Prophetam dicentem: Vox clamantis in deserto, Parate viam Domino, rectas facite semitas eius. Ipse autem Iohannes habebat vestimentum de pilis camelorum, et zonam pelliceam circa lumbas suos.

Esca autem eius erat locustae et mel sylvestre. Tunc exibat ad eum Ierosolyma et omnis Iudaea, et omnis regio circa Iordanem, et baptizabantur ab eo in Iordane confitentes peccata sua.

Videns autem multos Pharisaeorum et Sadducaeorum venientes ad baptismum suum, dixit eis: Progenies viperarum, quis ostendit vobis fugere a ventura ira? Facite ergo fructus dignos poenitentia, et Ne velitis dicere intra vos ipsos: Patrem habemus Abraham.

Dico enim vobis, quoniam potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae. Iam autem et securis ad radicem arborum posita est.

Omnis ergo

arbor, quae non facit fructum bonum, exciditur, et in ignem mittitur. Ego quidem baptizo vos aqua in poenitentiam: qui autem post me venturus est, fortior me est, cuius non sum dignus calciamenta portare, Ipse vos baptizabit Spiritu sancto et igne, cuius ventilabrum in manu sua, et permundabit aream suam, et congregabit triticum suum in horreum, paleas autem comburet igne inextinguibili.

Septem sunt loci praecipui.

I. Cur festus dies Baptistae celebretur.

II. De specie Ecclesiae, et quomodo Deus eam subinde renovet, ne humanum genus totum pereat.

III. De peculiari vocatione et officio Baptistae.

IIII. De tota eius doctrina: Docuit non solum legem, sed etiam Evangelium de Christo, concionatus est de poenitentia, de fide in Christum, et remissione peccatorum.

Addit et concionem de bonis operibus, de vitae generibus, de discrimine moralium operum, et ceremoniarum: denique fuit repurgator doctrinae, et incoator baptismi, et recipit gentes.

V. Iohannes est testis doctrinae de Trinitate, item de duabus naturis in Christo: denique Iohannis historia complectitur omnes articulos fidei.

VI. Cur dicat: Ego baptizo vos aqua, sed qui post me veniet, baptizabit vos Spiritu sancto et igni.

VII. De victu eius, de tempore praedicationis, et de nece eius.

De primo.

Etsi Ecclesia Dei est exigua pars hominum oppressa in mundo et misera: imperia vero eminent et conspiciuntur, et existimantur esse praecipua et florententissima pars generis humani, et ita convertunt in se hominum oculos, ut existiment homines, aut summa imperia Deo placere, aut negligi totum genus humanum, tamen Deus vult etiam suam Ecclesiam in mundo audiri, vult lucere noticiam de Deo. Ideo praecepit, ut sint publica praedicatio et confessio doctrinae, et ut per tales congressus et panegyres tradatur doctrina publica voce posteris, nes sint secreta conventicula, in quibus latebrae praebeant occasionem corrumpendae doctrinae et aliis malis rebus. Denique cum natura humana praecipue condita sit ad celebrandum Deum, iustissimum est esse publicos coetus, in quibus doceantur homines de Deo, et una omnium voce invocetur Deus. Quare et Christus magno testimonio ornavit hos congressus: Ubicunque sunt duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, ibi ero in medio eorum.

Haec est prima causa, cur festi dies divinitus instituti sint. Porro illas ethnicas opiniones abiiciamus, ocium diei et pompas esse cultum Dei. Sed alios fines quaeramus, scilicet, ut publice doceantur homines, et fiat publica confessio doctrinae, et invocatio, abiiciamus et hunc errorem simpliciter ethnicum de invocatione mortuorum. Non celebratur festum Baptistae, ut ipse invocetur, sed ut publice discamus, quid sit Ecclesia, quomodo Deus subinde miserit instauratores, quomodo regatur Ecclesia, et ut Deo pro his beneficiis gratias agamus. Item, ut discamus quae fuerit sanctorum doctrina. Item, ut confirmemur ipsorum testimoniis et exemplis.

De secundo. Etsi offenditur humana mens, cum audit Ecclesiam Dei semper valde exiguum coetum esse, si conferatur ad reliquam multitudinem, et multa contra disputantur, tamen sciamus vere rem sic se habere, et causam esse exiguitatis ipsam hominum maliciam, qui verbum a Deo certis testimoniis traditum, vel negligunt, vel petulanter abiiciunt.

Et considera exemplum in ipso populo Iudaeorum, in quo erat vera Ecclesia Dei, tamen maior multitudo fuit impiorum. Rex Herodes erat impius, et deleverat praecipuum concilium populi, qui vocabantur Sanhedrin, doctores erant distracti in tres sectas. Erant Zadducaei arrogantissimo titulo, quasi dicas, Iusticiarii, qui prorsus reiiciebant Prophetas, et ex professo defendebant epicureas opiniones: negabant animas esse immortales: negabant et resurrectionem mortuorum. Quis autem non miretur, in populo Dei defensos esse tales furores, et quidem praetextu doctrinae Moisi?

Alii autem erant Pharisaei, id est, interpretes, qui tamen retinebant Prophetas, defendebant animae immortalitatem et resurrectionem. sed addebant multas humanas traditiones, fascinati hac opinione, disciplinam externam esse iustitiam coram Deo, et mereri remissionem peccatorum.

Tantum igitur legem docebant de externa disciplina, nec norant doctrinam de fide, de passione Messiae, de remissione peccatorum, sed fingebant Messiam propagaturum esse legem Moisi in totum mundum, et occupaturum imperia. Sic sentiebat maxima eorum multitudo, sed consentaneum est inter hos fuisse aliquos saniores, qui quaesiverunt doctrinam de Messia, commonefacti a veris reliquiis Ecclesiae, a Simeone, Zacharia, Iohanne Baptista, et aliis.

Tertia secta fuit Essaei, id est, operarii, qui conferebant res suas in commune, et studebant vincere caeteros ieiuniis et eleemosynis. Sed haec secta fuit exigua, et habuit errores similes pharisaicis, de iustitia operum et de regno mundano Messiae.

Quanquam autem magna multitudo erat prophana, et magna erat opinionum confusio, et Herodes grassabatur caedibus assiduis, et pontifices erant ἄθεοι, tamen Deus servavit Ecclesiae reliquias, Zachariam, Simeonem, Ioseph, Elisabeth, Annam, Mariam, et multos tales.

Hi testimonium dabant verae doctrinae, et reprehendebant publicos errores. Sed postea excitatus est Iohannes, qui clariore reprehensione damnavit errores, et mirabili opere Dei collegit novam Ecclesiam. Ita Deum subinde repurgavit Ecclesiam.

Cum in Israël idola colerentur, excitati sunt Prophetae, ut falsos cultus damnarent, et veram doctrinam propagarent: horum auditores erant Ecclesia.

Reges impii, et multitudo dedita idolis non erat Ecclesia, et mira Dei bonitate continua successio fuit Prophetarum.

Elias praefuit circiter viginti annos, hunc mox secutus Elisaeus, praefuit circiter annos septuaginta. Hunc videre potuit Esaias adolescens, qui praefuit circiter octoginta annos, hunc senem vidit Ieremias, qui praefuit annos quadraginta. Secutus est statim Daniel, qui annos septuaginta praefuit: deinde fuerunt Zacharias, Malachias, Esdras, Nehemias, usque ad Alexandri Magni tempora: postea ab Antiocho Epiphane plurimi senes interfecti sunt: sed tamen reliquias aliquas Deus servavit.

Agnoscamus ergo bonitatem Dei, et gratias agamus, quod subinde excitavit doctores, et exhibuit testimonia doctrinae.

Sic post Apostolos subinde excitati sunt aliqui pii doctores, qui publicos errores taxaverunt, ut Methodius refutavit Origenis errores, Malchion Samosatenum, Athanasius Arium, Augustinus Manichaeos et Pelagium: et a multis errores Papae taxati sunt, ut a Wesselo et aliis.

Sed longe fuit illustrior gloria populi Israël, quam huius ultimae aetatis mundi. Considerandus est autem hic totus cursus Ecclesiae, ut discamus qualis sit Ecclesia, et quas partes amplecti debeamus.

Fortassis nunc, quia fit maior dispersio per Turcas, accendit Deus lucem Evangelii, hanc ipsam ob causam, ut in hac dispersione pii certam doctrinam et consolationem habeant, et quocunque dispergentur, sua voce propagare possint, etiam si non habebunt ordinarios Episcopos aut Doctores ut antea.

De tertio.

Duplex est vocatio, Alia ordinaria, ut cum Ecclesia eligit ministros, ita in lege erat ordinaria vocatio sacerdotum, quia Deus certae tribui mandaverat hoc officium. Et quanquam multi hac ordinaria vocatione abutuntur, tamen vocationis autoritas non est universaliter reiicienda. Quia vero saepe doctores in vocatione ordinaria non recte docent, ideo Deus addit extraordinariam vocationem: excitavit magnos viros ad publicos errores emendandos, et ad colligendam Ecclesiam, ut Eliam, Elisaeum, sic Iohannem singulari modo vocavit, et ut Eliam debebant audire pontifices, quanquam essent in loco ordinariae vocationis, ita Iohannem debebant audire pontifices, quia Deus ei certa testimonia praebuerat, angelus patri apparuerat, et eius vocationem praedixerat.

Qui non considerant, quanta res sit talis vocatio, et qualis sit Ecclesiae gubernatio, hi non intelligunt talium virorum officium, ut Eliae, Elisaei, Iobannis, Pauli, imo sapientes politici oderunt eos tanquam homines morosos et seditiosos.

Alii inepti putant fuisse homines simplices, qui, ut monachi, propter superstitionem quaesiverint latebras. Sed nequaquam de eis ita sentiendum est, sciamus hos esse summos duces, per quos Deus fuit efficax, et restituit et auxit Ecclesiam, et per quos oppressit falsam doctrinam, et renovavit veram: denique quorum ministerium salutare fuit multis vocatis ad vitam aeternam. Indocti somniant Iohannem tantum tradidisse aliqua praecepta de bonis moribus, sicut tradidit Phocylides aut Theognis, sed ut saepe monemus, discernenda est doctrina Ecclesiae a philosophia, et a pharisaica doctrina.

Philosophi docent particulam legis de bonis moribus. Idem et Pharisaei docent, et addunt multas ceremonias. Sed Ecclesia concionatur de poenitentia, et de remissione peccatorum, de iudicio Dei, de reconciliatione, et vita aeterna.

Cum de poenitentia dicit, enarrat legem, et testatur legi Dei non tantum praecipi externam disciplinam, sed omnes accusari, dicit legem esse vocem Dei, monstrantem et condemnantem peccatum in tota natura humana. Ideo omnibus dicit: Agite poenitentiam, et addit prophetiam de fine et interitu huius populi, quem talis vir prospiciens, ingenti dolore luxit.

Videbant iam regnare peregrinos, et sciebat bene secutura esse excidia omnium urbium, et deplorabat non solum neces tot millium virorum, mulierum, puerorum, sed etiam aeternum exitium. Haec cogitatio quantum dolorem attulerit tali viro, nemo verbis explicare potest. Et quanquam haec praedictio deridebatur ab impiis, tamen pios movebat. Estque inculcata his verbis: Purgabit aream suam, colliget triticum, et paleas comburet igni inextinguibili.

Addidit et doctrinam de remissione peccatorum.

Non enim fingendum est, Iohannem praedicasse legem tantum, aut poenitentiam sine remissione peccatorum. Ethnica imaginatio est, cogitare doctrinam poenitentiae, sine Evangelio de remissione peccatorum: quia poenitentia sine consolatione irascitur Deo, et fugit Deum. Ideo Lucas diserte inquit: Praedicabat baptismum poenitentiae ad remissionem peccatorum: et Iohannes clarissime sonuit Evangelium, et quidem ipsum Christum monstravit, et addidit has conciones proprias Evangelii: Hic est agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi.

Item: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam. Item: Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus gratiam pro gratia. Item: Lex per Moisen data est, Gratia et veritas per Iesum Christum facta est, id est, reconciliatio nobis propter eum et per eum donatur, et veritas, id est, vera et aeterna iustitia et vita per eum restituitur.

Lex continebat umbras significantes futura et aeterna bona. Item, iustitia legis, id est, disciplina, est quaedam umbra evanescens. Sed hic Filius res aeternas incoat in nobis, et postea perficiet. Etsi autem hae sententiae sunt breves, tamen summam Evangelii comprehendunt, ut mediocris lector intelligere potest.

Nec dubium est has sententias copiose ab ipso enarratas esse. Quoties igitur de Iohanne loquimur, adhibenda est haec diligentia, ut quaerantur conciones eius, quae proprie continent Evangelium et fidei doctrinam.

Nec putemus eum tantum quaedam morum praecepta tradidisse, de quibus postea dicetur. Fuit enim aliud eius praecipuum officium. Voluit enim Deus publicum esse testem, qui monstraret Christum, et simul renovaret doctrinam. Ad haec munera Iohannes praecipue vocatus est, ideo monstravit praesentem Christum, dixit de poenitentia, de iudicio Dei, de remissione peccatorum, de fide in Christum, et de vita aeterna.

Simul etiam taxavit errores Pharisaeorum, de suis sacrificiis et traditionibus. Hi putabant se lege iustos esse, putabant se mereri remissionem peccatorum sua disciplina. Haec refutat, imo inquit: Hic agnus tollit peccata mundi.

Gratiam accipitis, id est, reconciliationem, non propter vestram iusticiam, sed pro gratia, id est, quia ipse dilectus est. Item: Ex plenitudine eius accipitis, id est, ipse vos nova luce, iusticia, et vita donabit. Refutat et errores de imperio mundi; cum testatur hunc Christum fore agnum, id est, victimam.

Item, cum praedicit gentis interitum. Postquam hanc partem doctrinae de fide diligenter consideraveris, quaerenda erit etiam altera pars, videlicet doctrina de bonis operibus.

Hanc quoque tradit, inquiens: Facite dignos fructus poenitentiae, et interrogatus non monstrat opera ceremoniarum, ut Pharisaei, sed moralia opera, sicut semper Prophetae damnarunt superstitionem communem hominum, qua ceremoniae anteferuntur moralibus operibus, ut Esaiae 1.

58. Psalm, 50. et alias saepe monemur. Item locus etiam utilem doctrinam continet, de approbatione vitae politicae et militiae, et quidem leges tradit memorabiles, quae frenant cupiditates gubernatorum, et discernunt facultates inferiorum a rebus superiorum: Non putate, inquit, licere vobis ex civium bonis rapere quantum libet, sed estote contenti stipendiis vestris.

Item: Non plus exigite, quam constitutum est etc.

Idem locus testatur receptas esse gentes.

Ita incoat Iohannes.

dixit: Benedicta tu inter mulieres, et benedictus fructus ventris tui. Et unde hoc mihi, ut veniat mater Domini ad me? Ecce enim, ut facta est vox salutationis tuae in auribus meis, saliit prae exultatione infans in utero meo, Et beata quae credidit, quoniam perficientur ea, quae dicta sunt ei a Domino.

Et ait Maria: Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Et exultavit spiritus meus in deo salvatore meo, Quia respexit ad humilitatem ancillae suae, ecce enim ex hoc beatam me dicent omnes generationes. Quia fecit mihi magna qui potens est, et sanctum nomen eius. Et misericordia eius in progeniem et progeniem, timentibus eum, Fecit potentiam in brachio suo, dispersit superbos mente cordis sui. Deposuit potentes de sedibus, et exaltavit humiles. Esurientes implevit bonis, et divites dimisit inanes, Suscepit Israël puerum suum, recordatus misericordiae suae. Sicut locutus est ad patres nostros, Abraham et semini eius in secula. Mansit autem Maria cum illa quasi mensibus tribus, et reversa est in domum suam.

Pulcerrima est historia, et plena spiritualis, et Christianae doctrinae. Habet autem tres praecipuos locos.

I. Testimonium de Messia.

II. Imago Ecclesiae et verae synodi.

III. Canticum Mariae.

De primo.

Magnum discrimen est inter Ecclesiam, et inter imperia mundi. Ecclesia est exiguus coetus eorum, qui retinent puram doctrinam Evangelii, et credunt in Christum, dissipatus, contemtus et spretus in mundo, qui miratur potentiam, gloriam, victorias et triumphos magnorum imperiorum. Et tamen hic parvus coetus Ecclesiae vere gerit res maximas. Etsi igitur Christi actiones non sic conspiciuntur in mundo, ut Alexandri aut Caesaris res gestae, tamen non est prorsus ignotus, et habet sua testimonia: quia oportet esse aliquam Ecclesiam, in qua Deus vult se et Filium suum cognosci, et vult aliquem coetum salvum fieri, in quo ipse celebretur in vita aeterna, ideo exhibuit multa testimonia, quae fidem nostram Christus exhibitus iuxta promissiones.

Ita hic statim a concepto Christo recitantur testimonia. Conveniunt testes, Maria, Elisabeth anus gravida singulari miraculo Dei, infans exultans in utero, Zacharias cui hactenus muto subito redditur loquela, et alii in hac familia. Nam Maria proficiscitur ad cognatam, non propter privatam amicitiam, sed propter hoc illustre testimonium, et propter confirmationem suae fidei et aliorum sanctorum.

De secundo. Consideranda est imago Ecclesiae, et petenda consolatio ex hoc loco, ut non deficiamus a veritate, decepti specie et titulo Ecclesiae. Vocant se Ecclesiam Pontifices, Episcopi, Reges, et his addicti; sicut olim Caiphas, Annas, Pharisaei, Sadducaei, sed non sunt Ecclesia. Interim est alia parva Ecclesia vera, sicut Paulus inquit: Non omnes qui sunt ex Israël, sunt Israël. Ut igitur tunc erant Ecclesia, Zacharias, Elisabeth, Maria, et pauci alii, ita nunc est exiguus numerus credentium in Christum, et recte colentium Deum, et hunc coetum persequuntur pontifices et episcopi, sicut tunc erant hostes sanctorum, Caiphas et similes. Dicitur enim, et Zacharias interfectus esse, propterea quod adfirmavit Messiam venisse, sicut scribit Epiphanius.

Est et hic congressus Mariae, Elisabeth, Zachariae, imago verae piae et Christianae synodi: nam hoc primum fuit concilium novae Ecclesiae. Puella Maria venit per 20 miliaria, tantum enim fere fuit iter a Nazareth Hierosolymam usque, ibi narrat cognatae Elisabeth et familiae de suo conceptu, et testimonio angeli, Elisabeth vicissim illi testimonium perhibet, et accedit Zacharias senex, cuius pietas publice nota est, et ex muto subito loquens, sua voce confirmat haec testimonia. Ita in hoc conventu concluditur de summo et gravissimo articulo, de concepto et exhibito Messia, et vera est rata definitio sanctissimae synodi, etiamsi non accedit decretum aut approbatio Pontificum et Pharisaeorum.

His testimoniis adduntur et Cantica, seu gratiarum actio, ut extet confessio etiam ad posteritatem, et praedicetur hoc ingens Dei beneficium, quod misertus populi sui, miserit Filium. Hoc vult Maria agnosci et palam celebrari. Non vult occultari, aut obrui veritatem, sed extare noticiam verae doctrinae, ut agnoscatur et glorificetur Deus, ut recte colatur et invocetur. Talia concilia approbat Deus, quae quaerunt veritatem, et iuxta verbum Dei testimonium perhibent de Christo, non quae praestigiis sophismatum et fucosis articulis obruunt veritatem.

De tertio. De Cantico Mariae.

In hoc cantico Maria gerit personam totius Ecclesiae. Est enim confessio de Messia et gratiarum actio, et descriptio victoriae Ecclesiae, contra mundum, tyrannos, et omnia membra diaboli. Quare et nos sciamus a nobis postulari, ut vere una canamus et sequamur hanc praecentricem, quae ut in choro incoatrix est huius carminis, ac ingenti animo edit confessionem.

Tria ergo comprehendit.

I. Gratiarum actionem.

Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Id est, ex tota anima, tota anima, toto corde glorifico Deum. Non dubito vitam in discrimen offerre, propter confessionem. Sic debemus et nos adfecti esse, ut confessionem anteferamus omnibus rebus, vitae, facultatibus, liberis. Qui sic affectus est, vere canit hunc hymnum, Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Quando trahebantur ad mortem Iohannes Baptista, Paulus et similes, tunc vere dicebant: Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Sic sunt Christiani fortissimi milites, cogitant, Magnificat anima mea regem, pro quo pugno, vitam meam et omnia coniicio in discrimen, ut dimicem pro rege, ut sit magnus et victor.

Secunda pars Cantici.

Respexit humilitatem ancillae suae. Fecit mihi magna qui potens est etc.

Haec est narratio beneficiorum, quae in Ecclesia Deus efficit. Cum Ecclesia sit spreta, humilis, parva, Deus tamen dat ei victorias, conservat eam contra tyrannos et sapientiam mundi. Haec est summa huius partis.

Loquitur Maria de se, sed non tantum de se sola, sed de toto corpore Ecclesiae. Respexit Deus humilitatem, id est, miseriam ancillae suae. Quamvis simus abiecti, quamvis simus imbecilles, sine praesidiis, sine defensione humana, tamen respicit nos Deus, exaudit, iuvat contra tyrannos et sapientes mundi.

Hic discamus, quod in sola Ecclesia sic agnoscatur Deus, quod sit Deus remittens peccata, et miseros credentes exaudiens. Humana ratio et omnes religiones, praeter evangelicam, aliter sentiunt de Deo. Habent talem opinionem, quod Deus non curet, non respiciat adflictos. Et est singularis et arcana sapientia, et soloro credentium in Christum, erigere se fide, et credere remissionem peccatorum, et petere et expectare auxilium etc.

Tunc haec fiunt, Fecit potentiam brachio suo etc., servat Ecclesiam inter pericula, sicut servavit electos cum ducerentur in captivitatem Babylonicam. Dispergit superbos confidentes sua sapientia, sicut confudit magos Pharaonis, sic nunc confundit sapientia sua confidentes Papistas, et alios. O magnum peccatum, quod non intelligunt sapientes: quod volunt Ecclesiam suis consiliis regere et mutare. De his est dictum: Perdam sapientiam sapientum.

Deponit potentes de sede, sicut Romanos perdidit persequentes Christum. Exaltat humiles. Esurientes implet bonis, consolatur, servat Ecclesiam.

Tertia pars, Confessio de Messia.

Tertia pars est propria illius concilii confessio, quod Messia dato, recordatus est Deus promissionum. Haec est summa Cantici.

Ita et nos agamus gratias, et cum recitamus hoc Canticum, intuemur animo totam Ecclesiam, cogitemus qualia sint certamina in Ecclesia, propter confessionem, quam mirabilibus operibus Deus defendat Ecclesiam. Cogitemus requiri a nobis confessionem, cogitemus hunc esse summum cultum, quem haec puella, id est, tota vera Ecclesia, praestat, praedicare Deum quod dederit Messiam, quod elegerit Ecclesiam perpetuo victuram, quod eam defendat et servet, non humanis viribus aut consiliis. Haec discenda sunt in lectione huius historiae, qualis sit vera Ecclesia, et qui sunt veri cultus, et repetenda sunt animo, testimonia de Christo, ut nostram fidem confirmemus, et nos ad invocandum excitemus.

Reliquum est exemplum de infante Iohanne, qui in utero sensit adesse Dominum et Messiam. Quanquam autem hoc de Iohanne peculiare est, tamem est testimonium, quod Spiritus sanctus etiam in parvulis sit efficax, et quod habeant motus quosdam, quanquam nobis incognitos, tamen Deo placentes.

Ideo cum audis, Talium est regnum coelorum, cogites in infantibus Spiritum hanc Ecclesiam colligendam ex gentibus et Iudaeis: habuit igitur maius officium caeteris Prophetis. Fuit monstrator praesentis Christi: habuit mandatum incoandae novae Ecclesiae, baptizandi et recipiendi gentes.

De quinto.

Ideo revelationes aliquae summorum doctorum scriptae sunt, ut erudiant et confirment reliquam Ecclesiam. Quare in historiis Patrum, Prophetarum et Apostolorum, confirmationes illae diligenter quaerantur.

Est autem Iohanni clarissimum testimonium exhibitum de tribus personis divinitatis in baptismo Christi. Patris vox auditur, et nominatim discernuntur ea voce pater et Filius: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, quo delector. Filius stans in flumine cernitur oculis. Conspicitur et species columbae, in qua erat Spiritus sanctus. Nam et pater dixerat Iohanni, in hac specie esse Spiritum sanctum. Ergo et intellexit Iohannes articulum de Trinitate, et Ecclesiae tradidit. Nam hanc revelationem ideo patefecit aliis, ut eos de natura Dei, de aeterno patre, Filio et Spiritu sancto doceret, et discrimina officiorum ostenderet.

Docet et de duabus naturis in Christo, cum ait, Filium ante se fuisse, et nunc missum esse, ut fiat victima. De Spiritu sancto scit eum agitatorem esse, qui datur propter Filium, et novos motus Deo placentes in credentibus, novam lucem et vitam accendit. Ideo dicit: Baptizabit vos Spiritu sancto.

Iam si ordine recenseas totum symbolum, vides Iohannem de omnibus articulis concionatum esse. Ita discamus totum Iohannem intueri, id est, universum doctrinae corpus complecti. Praecipue vero in nostra invocatione mens cogitet revelationem Iohanni factam, ut discernamus invocationem nostram a Iudaica et Turcica, invocemus Deum aeternum, qui se patefecit per Filium, et de eo dixit, Hic est Filius meus dilectus, petamus nos exaudiri et recipi propter Filium, et regi Spiritu sancto.

De sexto.

Quod inquit: Ego baptizo vos aqua, sed qui post me veniet, baptizabit vos Spiritu sancto et igni, necessarium discrimen est. Sed valde prodest sciri, non externum baptismum discerni, sed personas. Longe differt Christi persona a ministris. Id saepe inculcat Iohannes; ut discamus Christum non tantum esse doctorem, ut imaginantur omnes ignari Evangelii: sed sciamus salvatorem esse. Cum audis praedicantem Iohannem, aut Paulum, fides intueatur Christum, non istos doctores, et sciat propter Christum dari remissionem peccatorum, et a Christo petat Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam, non a Iohanne vel Paulo. Ideo Iohannes significantissime dixit: Ego sum vox, quasi dicat: Sum tantum minister sonans Evangelium, per quod alius est efficax, scilicet, Christus. Ita dicit se baptizare aqua, id est, adhibere externum ministerium, sed alium esse efficacem, scilicet Christum, qui baptizat Spiritu sancto, hoc est, dat Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam credentibus et invocantibus.

Econtra vero baptizabit igni omnes impios, id est, aeterna ira et cruciatibus obruet eos, sicut postea inquit: Paleas comburet igni inextinguibili. Veros et horrendos terrores vocat ignem, ut saepe scriptura loquitur. Hos degustant pii in poenitentia, sed liberantur. Impii vero opprimuntur aeterno pavore et dolore.

De septimo.

Postquam de ministerio et de doctrina Baptistae dictum est, deinde de eius privatis virtutibus dicatur. Sed quoties exempla proponuntur, sciamus discrimina esse vocationum et gradus virtutum, imitetur unusquisque ea quae suae vocationi competunt, et imitetur pro sua mediocritate. Nec existimet se illorum excellentium virorum gradus assequi, sed ipsam mediocritatem magnum decus esse in his quae competunt nostrae vocationi, sicut Paulus inquit: Hoc requiritur, ut fideles simus.

Quod vero Iohannes vivit in deserto, hoc illius vocationi conveniebat, tuae non convenit. Quia cum natus esset in tribu sacerdotali, debebat sacrificare in templo. Cum igitur Deus incoaret per eum aliud ministerium, voluit eum discedere a templo, ideo versatur in deserto, ac intelligebant sacerdotes rem novam agi, et contrariam legi....

Hae causae factorum in exemplis considerentur, et sciamus non omnia convenire omnibus. Quia autem erat in deserto, res ita ferebat, ut victus esset sordidior: etsi de locustis ego arbitror, ut contra legem fecit Iohannes, quod discessit a templo, ita contra legem de cibo fecisse, ut ostenderet finem esse politiae Iudaicae, et Evangelium ad gentes quoque pertinere, et tolli discrimina ciborum.

Locustae enim usitate cancros significant, quibus non licebat vesci populo legis, consentaneum est autem Iohannem usum esse rebus ohviis ad Iordanem, ubi piscatores ei cancros dabant, quos alioqui non vendebant.

Moveor et significatione locustae.

Naturale dissidium est locustae cum serpentibus, et dicitur in pugna arte prehendere collum serpentis.

Sic Iohanni dissidium fuit cum Pharisaeis, et horum colla, id est, doctrinam, strangulavit.

Si quis autem mavult locustam intelligi insectum, non repugno.

Maxime vero mors talis viri consideranda est.

Nec tantum inde sumantur haec praecepta, quod oporteat vera docere, et potius oppetere mortem, quam abiicere confessionem verae sententiae, iuxta illud: Qui non confitebitur me coram hominibus, non confitebor eum coram patre meo coelesti.

Sed multo magis hoc considerandum est: quare non semper Deus defendat suos adversus tyrannos.

Haec species valde offendit humana iudicia.

Sed hic discamus propriam Ecclesiae sapientiam esse, intelligere quod sit subiecta cruci, et cur sit subiecta cruci.

Sed de his ducibus in ministerio verbi, est singulare quiddam.

Praecipua causa est, quod Deus per hos ostendere vult testimonium de futuro iudicio.

Constat ex priorib. testimoniis, Deo vere placere Esaiam, Ieremiam, Iohannem, Paulum, et similes.

Nec approbavit eos tantum ut sint miseri, ac redigantur in nihilum, Nec ideo reiicit impios, ut semper sint florentes: imo erit aliquando discrimen.

Ergo cum suos interfici sinit, testatur restare aliud iudicium, in quo patefaciet iram suam adversus impios, et ornabit gloria suos, sicut dictum fuit ad Cain: Si bene feceris, recipies: sin autem male feceris, peccatum tuum quiescet, donec revelabitur.

Testatur enim Deus vere se recipere iustos, et irasci peccato, sed differre iudicium, et haec mora confirmat securitatem in impiis: ideo dicit, Quiescet peccatum, sed tamen postea patefiet ira adversus peccatum.

Huius venturi iudicii illustria testimonia sunt neces eorum, quos Deus sibi placere certis testimoniis ostendit.

Habes praecipuam causam.

Postea sunt et aliae causae.

Deus vult eos ostendere, quod serio et ex animo sentiant veram esse doctrinam.

Nam si professio doctrinae nihil adferret periculi, non posset sciri an serio sic sentiant.

Nunc cum vitae anteferunt, ostendunt se serio sic sentire, ostendunt et hoc, professionem magis necessariam esse, quam vitam.

Tertia causa est, vult etiam conspici, quod Deo non serviant serviliter, non captantes huius vitae tranquillitatem, sed quod vero amore noticiam Dei anteferant omnibus rebus.

Quarta causa est, ut fiant similes imaginis Filii Dei.

Quinta causa est, quod universaliter sanctorum mors testatur, reliquum esse peccatum in natura hominis, propter quod omnes omnibus calamitatibus subiecti sumus, quas tamen Deus infirmis mitigat, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Si iniquitates observaveris, Domine, quis sustinebit? id est, si effunderes iram tuam adversus molem peccatorum nostrorum, et omnia pro merito punire velles, omnes subito interirent, et ruerent in aeternas poenas, sed parcis propter mediatorem Filium.

Omnino insignis schola est consideratio necis sanctorum, et de summis rebus nos admonet, de futuro iudicio, de peccato communi naturae humanae, de mirabili consilio Dei, quo Ecclesiam vult esse subiectam cruci.

Quid est dissimilius, quam Nero et Paulus? et tamen Paulus toties antea servatus, laceratur ab illa foedissima bestia.

Quid dissimilius Herode et Baptista? quem natum singulari Dei opere, et vocatum ad summum ministerium, et ornatum singulari luce Evangelii, interficit tyrannus tam cito: Iohannes enim non toto biennio concionatus est in deserto, quia circiter secundum Pascha, post incoatam praedicationem interfectus est, ut indicat series historiae evangelicae.

## 2:21 The Day of the Circumcision of the Lord
The Day of the Circumcision of the Lord. Gospel of Luke 2.

And after eight days were accomplished, that the child might be circumcised, his name was called JESUS, which was called by the angel, before he was conceived in the womb.

I. Topic. Comparison of the rite and the word of God.

II. What the Sacraments are.

III. Why Circumcision was instituted, and of what benefit it was a pledge.

IV. What it signified, and why God wanted the sign to exist in this part of the body.

V. Why Christ was circumcised.

On the first [point].

Of the comparison of the rite and the word of God. We vituperate ethnic ceremonies on account of their absurdity, because the luperci ran about clad in skins, and others. Circumcision seems to have more absurdity: but first let us learn here, that in divine ceremonies the work is not to be considered without the word, but together with the word of God. The ethnics had rites without any word of God, and many peoples retained circumcision without the word of God, as the Colchians, Egyptians, and now the Turks and Jews retain it. But a work without the word of God is nothing, indeed it is a thing condemned by God. Remember this rule diligently er this rule of all works, what word is to be required, and there the will of God is to be recognized, afterwards in the work some signification is to be sought.

Concerning the second. What the Sacraments are.

God from time to time restored the collapsed doctrine of his promises, and so that this restoration might be more illustrious, new signs were instituted.

And generally a sacrament properly so called, is a sign of the promised reconciliation.

Therefore, the promise added to the signs must be sought.

But two promises were handed down to Abraham: one concerning reconciliation, the other concerning the cause of reconciliation, namely concerning the seed, in whom all nations shall be blessed.

These promises are to be joined: I will be their God.

Item: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed.

The mark of these promises was that circumcision, instituted in that part of the body, so that it might admonish the circumcised concerning the seed to come.

Concerning the third. Why circumcision was instituted.

Circumcision is therefore a Sacrament with added promises, namely the promise of reconciliation, and the promise of the seed.

For the promise of the land, and of the kingdom or polity, was given on account of the seed.

For it was necessary that there be a certain people, in whom the savior would be born, and on account of these promises circumcision brought grace, because God says: I will be their God.

Hence it can be understood that it truly was a sacrament, and adults admonished by this sign, looked by faith to the promise of grace, and of the savior to come.

By this faith they were pleasing to God, and called upon him.

This faith and invocation are the highest worship, unknown to carnal judgments, which the pious performed when admonished by circumcision, even if the work itself seemed absurd to the impious.

But it was a pleasing pledge, and a notable testimony to those who from it determined that God was propitious.

Concerning the fourth. What it signified.

All ceremonial and moral works are symbols, and images of those principal things, which are signified in the promises.

Then also other significations of heavenly things are added.

And indeed those things, which are properly called Sacraments, are principally signs of the will of God towards us, proposed in the promises.

Afterwards other significations can be added.

Circumcision therefore principally signified the promised reconciliation, because God says, I will be their God: and the place admonished concerning the cause of reconciliation.

For because the seed was promised, in whom all nations would be blessed, therefore a sign was added to that part of the body.

This was the principal signification.

But to this others are added, because a particle is cut off from the member of generation, it was signified that this nature was fallen, and now destined for death, and that this skin was to be cast away.

But yet the seed to come, which with the curse removed would restore a new and eternal nature and life.

The saints saw these things as if they were painted in this image.

Other admonitions also were added, the world most miserably contaminates those parts, and abuses generation, God on the contrary placed a mark in this very part, so that we might think that God wills that these members be holy, and that we use generation holily.

For us, baptism principally signifies the reconciliation proposed in the promise: but afterwards the image admonishes much.

We are immersed, so that sin may be washed away by immersion, namely by the death of Christ, and we inserted into the death of Christ may be mortified, and overwhelmed by all storms: but we rise again and emerge with Christ.

Thus the Lord's supper is principally a pledge of reconciliation, but the image itself testifies that we are made members of Christ.

Item, that we are mutually members of one body.

Thus also Christ willed moral things to be symbols: Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you.

The love of parents towards children is στροργή [natural affection] divinely implanted in the human breast, and an image of the love of God towards us.

Concerning the fourth. Why Christ was circumcised.

It pleased the Son of God even without circumcision, nor was he bound by that law: If anyone shall not have been circumcised, he shall be rooted out.

But just as Christ universally willed to be subject to the law, so also he was to be circumcised.

And many causes concur.

He willed that there be a testimony, that he was born from the descendants of Abraham in this people, that he was a companion and member of this Church: but the principal cause is subjection under the law, which is not to be understood only civilly, that he willed to be an obedient citizen, but subjection under the law in that person, who was not a debtor, signifies a singular benefit, pertaining to us. For he is subjected to the law for us, namely, not only to legal duties, but also to the curse and punishment, which we had deserved, so that he might become a sacrifice for us, appeasing the Father, and freeing us from the curse of the law. Thus, Christ being circumcised signified that he was subjected to the law for us, when he himself was not a debtor, and was now obligated to death for us. Let us learn to acknowledge, understand, and celebrate these benefits, namely that we have been redeemed from the curse of the law, that is, from the wrath of God on account of the Son subjected to the law, and by this faith let us call upon God, and obey him: let us likewise learn that this old fallen nature has been amputated and cut off, and a new and perpetual nature and life has been promised.

Latin:

Die Circumcisionis Domini. Evangelium Lucae 2.

Et postquam consummati sunt dies octo, ut circumcideretur puer, vocatum est nomen eius IESUS, quod vocatum est ab angelo, priusquam in utero conciperetur.

I. Locus. Collatio ritus, et verbi Dei.

II. Quid sint Sacramenta.

III. Quare sit instituta Circumcisio, et cuius beneficii fuerit pignus.

IV. Quid significaverit, et quare in hac parte corporis voluerit Deus extare signum.

V. Quare Christus circumcisus sit.

De primo.

De collatione ritus, et verbi Dei, Vituperamus ethnicas ceremonias propter absurditatem, quod discurrebant luperci pelliti, et alias. Plus videtur absurditatis habere circumcisio: sed primum hic discamus, in ceremoniis divinis non opus sine verbo, sed una cum verbo Dei considerandum esse. Ethnici habuerunt ritus, sine ullo verbo Dei, et multae gentes circumcisionem retinuerunt sine verbo Dei, ut Colchi, Aegyptii, et nunc Turcae et Iudaei retinent, Sed opus sine verbo Dei nihil est, imo est res damnata a Deo.
