Hanc regulam diligenter memine rimus de omnibus operibus, quod verbum requirendum sit, et ibi voluntas Dei agnoscenda, postea in opere significatio aliqua quaerenda est.

De secundo. Quid sint Sacramenta.

Deus subinde instauravit collapsam doctrinam suarum promissionum, et ut haec instauratio esset illustrior, nova signa instituta sunt.

Et generaliter sacramentum proprie dictum, est signum promissae reconciliationis.

Quaerenda est igitur promissio addita signis.

Duae autem traditae sunt promissiones Abrahae: altera de reconciliatione, altera de causa reconciliationis, videlicet de semine, in quo benedicentur omnes gentes.

Hae promissiones coniungendae sunt: Ero Deus eorum.

Item: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes.

Harum promissionum nota fuit illa circumcisio, instituta in illa parte corporis, ut de venturo semine admoneret circumcisos.

De tertio. Quare sit instituta circumcisio.

Est igitur circumcisio Sacramentum additis promissionibus, videlicet promissione reconciliationis, et promissione seminis.

Nam promissio terrae, et regni seu politiae, data est propter semen.

Oportuit enim certum esse populum, in quo salvator nasceretur, et propter has promissiones circumcisio adferebat gratiam, quia Deus inquit: Ero Deus eorum.

Hinc potest intelligi vere fuisse sacramentum, et adulti admoniti hoc signo, fide intuebantur promissionem gratiae, et venturi salvatoris.

Hac fide placebant Deo, et invocabant eum.

Haec fides et invocatio sunt summi cultus, ignoti carnalibus iudiciis, quos pii praestabant admoniti per circumcisionem, etiamsi opus ipsum videbatur impiis absurdum.

Erat autem gratum pignus, et insigne testimonium his, qui inde statuebant Deum propicium esse.

De quarto. Quid significaverit.

Omnia opera ceremonialia et moralia sunt symbola, et imagines praecipuae earum rerum, quae in promissionibus significantur.

Deinde accedunt et aliae significationes rerum coelestium.

Et quidem ea, quae proprie Sacramenta dicuntur, praecipue sunt signa voluntatis Dei erga nos, propositae in promissionibus.

Postea possunt addi aliae significationes.

Circumcisio igitur principaliter significabat promissam reconciliationem, quia Deus dicit, Ero Deus eorum: et locus admonebat de causa reconciliationis.

Quia enim fuit promissum semen, in quo benedicerentur omnes gentes, ideo illi parti corporis additum est signum.

Haec fuit praecipua significatio.

Sed ad hanc accedunt aliae, quia praeciditur particula a membro generationis, significabatur hanc naturam lapsam esse, et nunc destinatam morti, et hanc pelliculam abiiciendam esse.

Sed tamen venturum semen, quod sublata maledictione redditurum esset novam in et aeternam naturam et vitam.

Haec sancti videbant tanquam pictae esse in hac imagine.

Accedebant et aliae admonitiones, mundus miserrime contaminat eas partes, et generatione abutitur, Deus econtra in hac ipsa parte posuit notam, ut cogitemus Deum velle, ut haec membra sint sancta, et sancte utamur generatione.

Nobis baptismus praecipue significat reconciliationem in promissione propositam: sed postea multam monet imago.

Mergimur, ut peccatum abluatur mersione, videlicet morte Christi, et nos inserti morti Christi mortificemur, et omnibus procellis obruamur: sed resurgimus et emergimus cum Christo.

Sic coena Domini praecipue pignus est reconciliationis, sed imago ipsa testatur nos effici membra Christi.

Item, nos mutuo membra esse unius corporis.

Sic et moralia voluit Christus esse symbola: Remittite, et remittetur vobis.

Amor parentum erga liberos est στοργὴ divinitus indita humano pectori, et imago amoris Dei erga nos.

De quarto. Quare Christus sit circumcisus.

Placebat Filius Dei etiam sine circumcisione, nec tenebatur illa lege: Si quis non fuerit circumcisus, eradicabitur.

Sed sicut universaliter Christus voluit esse subiectus legi, sic etiam circumcidendus erat.

Et concurrunt multae causae.

Voluit extare testimonium, quod natus esset ex posteris Abrahae in hoc populo, quod esset huius Ecclesiae socius et membrum: sed praecipua causa est subiectio sub legem, quae non est intelligenda tantum civiliter, quod voluerit esse obsequens civis, sed subiectio sub legem in illa persona, quae non erat debitrix, singulare beneficium significat, ad nos pertinens. Est enim subiectus lege pro nobis, videlicet, non tantum officiis legalibus, sed etiam maledictioni et poenae, quam nos eramus meriti, ut fieret hostia pro nobis, placans patrem, et liberans nos a maledictione legis. Ita circumcidi Christum, significabat eum subiici legi pro nobis, cum ipse non esset debitor, et iam obligari ad mortem pro nobis. Haec beneficia agnoscere, intelligere et celebrare discamus, videlicet nos redemptos esse a maledictione legis, hoc est, ab ira Dei propter Filium legi subiectum, et hac fide Deum invocemus, et ei obediamus: discamus item hanc veterem naturam lapsam, amputatam et praecisam esse, et promissam novam et perpetuam naturam et vitam.

## 2:22-35 The Purification of Mary
The Purification of Mary. The Gospel of Luke 2.

After the days of their purification were fulfilled, according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord, that every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord. And to give a sacrifice, according to what was said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon. And this man was just and pious, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit, that he would not see death, unless he first saw the Christ of the Lord. And he came by the Spirit into the temple. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do according to the custom of the law for him, he himself took him into his arms, and blessed God, and said: Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace. Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a Light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel. And his father and mother were wondering at these things, which were said about him. And Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary his mother: Behold, this one is set for the ruin and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted. Yea, and a sword shall pierce through your own soul, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

There are six principal topics.

I. What the law concerning the unclean and purification in Leviticus 14 signifies.

II. Why Mary, although she was not bound by that law, nevertheless obeyed it.

III. What the law concerning the firstborn signifies.

IIII. Testimonies concerning the born Messiah from Simeon and Anna.

V. Doctrine in the sayings of Simeon concerning the kingdom of Christ.

VI. Doctrine concerning the cross.

Concerning the first.

This whole law of Moses is a pedagogy or discipline, not indeed taking away sin, but admonishing the people about many great things, namely about sin, and about future liberation. Thus this law concerning the unclean, who nevertheless had brought forth a conception from male seed, signified that sin is propagated with this regeneration, and that human nature is guilty. The ceremony therefore admonished the pious to think about propagated sin, and about the causes of human calamities, and about the wrath of God: then that they should bring the promises to this sad meditation. sions concerning future liberation, concerning the election of this people, and that they might call upon God by faith, or trust in the promises, etc. For these uses these symbols were especially instituted; afterwards, other reasons for this custom were added. The law serves the utility of the body and restrains wandering lusts. The birth itself is a great miracle, by the wonderful ordination of God; the hips, which otherwise do not move from their place, are nevertheless opened in birth, and immense pain follows. Finally, great bodily weakness follows the birth, which itself admonishes us of the first fall. Therefore, so that the body of the woman in childbirth might be spared, God ordained some days during which He wills her to attend to her health, and God wills that the work of generation be ruled by His word, and not wander rashly. He wills, therefore, that in the meantime the woman in childbirth abstain from her husband, and He decrees a capital punishment for this matter. These moral [precepts] are also to be observed in this place, because moral [laws] pertain to all men; God now also wills that women in childbirth take care of their health; therefore, although the certain number of days and those sacrifices do not pertain to us, nevertheless the kind [of duty] pertains to us. But as for the fact that they offered a lamb or turtledoves, this rite did not take away sins, but was a testimony of the observance of that childbirth, and an occasion for teaching the people when they came to the temple and sacrifices were offered, because the priests were to be supported by such duties. Furthermore, the coming sacrifice was signified covertly. Concerning the second. Mary was not bound by this law concerning the unclean, because the law speaks explicitly of her who has brought forth a conception from male seed. This addition would have been superfluous unless it covertly signified that one would bring forth without male seed. Therefore, God does not wish to accuse the mother of His Son. Why, then, did Mary observe the rite? I answer. There are four causes why Christ observed circumcision and all the other rites. First, because He subjected Himself to the law, so that He might undergo the punishment which the law threatens for the sins of the human race. Second, so that it might be established that this Messiah was from the seed of Abraham; it was necessary for Him to live among this people and to observe the same rites, especially since it was necessary for Him to be exhibited to that people. Third, because it was necessary for the Messiah to be a companion of the Church of God, and not to be absent from the rest of the body of the Church, so that clear testimonies concerning Him might be spread in the Church. Fourth, so that illustrious testimonies concerning Him might be spread through the ministry itself, as through Zacharias, Simeon, Elisabeth, Anna, and others. Therefore, when the parents knew these causes, they obey the law and warn us that we should assist in the preservation of the ministry and declare that we are members of the true Church. And that Mary and Joseph acted rightly, God Himself testifies, who here by a notable miracle moves Simeon and Anna to prophesy. For it is said explicitly: He came by the motion of the Spirit into the temple. Let us learn, however, that God is present to this endeavor of preserving the common ministry, because He Himself is effective through the ministry, just as He says: He who hears you, hears me. Concerning the third. Three times in Moses the law concerning the firstborn males is repeated. Exod. 13. Item 34, and Num. 8. And an antithesis (ἀντίθεσις) is added, because the firstborn of Egypt were struck down, I demand your firstborn. Generally, however, it was signified that this people was chosen by God, so that the Church might be in it. But just as a subject testifies by a certain duty that he is addicted to his Lord, so God wills that He be acknowledged as the Lord of this people. The Turkish tyrant takes every tenth boy from individual villages and towns and chooses at his own discretion. By this great duty the people confess that this is their lord: but this is a miserable servitude instituted for destruction, which I recite for the sake of example. God willed that the firstfruits of the newborn also be handed over to Him, so that the people might acknowledge that they were thus truly the people proper to God. And on the contrary, that the firstborn of the Egyptians and other nations were rejected. What does this whole image signify? Namely, that all nations are rejected which do not worship God according to this word delivered to this people, and that these are truly the people of God who worship Him according to the word by which He revealed Himself in this people. And as that Turkish servitude is destructive, so this one is salutary. And the rite is opposed to impious opinions, which either pretend that all religions are equally fabulous, or that all are equally to be approved. But here God rejects the firstborn of the Egyptians, that is, He rejects other nations, other cults and religions, and by a clear sign testifies that He is truly the Lord of this people, and that He cares for this people, who embrace the word delivered by Him.

And this very rite is to be referred to the promise added to circumcision, in which it is clearly said: I will be their God, that is, those who call upon me because of the promised seed, I will receive, I will hear, I will save, etc. The symbols and repetitions of this promise were many other ceremonies, just as this very service, or the tradition of the firstborn. This truly, as in a public forum, was a mutual testimony, by which it was shown that God was the lord of this people, and that this people was the own property of God, just as the tradition of children among the Turks signifies lordship.

Secondly, but as the reason for lordship first embraces this, that the Lord receives this people, hears them, saves them, so in return the service signified due duties. The doctrine of God is to be learned and retained, and it is to be obeyed; children are to be instructed in the doctrine, bodies and resources are to serve in war, and elsewhere for the preservation of the doctrine.

That this is the meaning of the law, God himself testifies, because he says: All the firstborn are owed to me, I have chosen for myself the tribe of Levi in their place. He requires, therefore, especially the duties of preserving the doctrine. This, in sum, is what the law concerning the firstborn signifies, namely, a peculiar people, chosen so that it may be saved, and truly celebrate God.

But here it must be added, that in this people there is a certain firstborn who excels all others, for whom principally the firstborn were dedicated to God, namely the Messiah, who is the first heir, for whom the others are received. This doctrine concerning the Messiah Mary understood very well in the offering of the firstborn, and therefore she came principally into the temple, so that she herself might testify that this was that chief firstborn, for whom all the significations were instituted. Just as also the Holy Spirit himself testifies that this is that firstborn, just as Simeon, Anna, and others preach him.

Now let us learn here, that we are grafted into the olive tree of the people of God, and have been made co-heirs of Christ, and the own people of God, provided that we call upon him according to this word, in which he revealed himself, and that we also owe certain duties: to learn the doctrine, to obey him, to offer our bodies and resources for the preservation of the doctrine.

Concerning the fourth.

As has been said often elsewhere, testimonies are observed concerning the born Messiah, so that our faith may be confirmed, because God wants the Church to have certain testimonies. Before, there were the witnesses Zacharias, Elisabeth, the Angels, Joseph, the Shepherds, the Magi: now Simeon and Anna approach, so that the article that the Messiah has been born may be widely spread.

Concerning the fifth.

Doctrine is delivered in the sayings of Simeon concerning the kingdom of Christ; he calls Christ his salvation, he calls him a light for the revelation of the Gentiles, that is, a light shining to the Gentiles, or providing light to the Gentiles, so that they may see God.

He understands, however, salvation, not of an earthly empire, but of true salvation, by which God, having abolished sin and abolished death, restored true goods, and thus he speaks concerning the Gentiles: That the Gentiles would have the light of the Gospel, in which they will recognize God, and will truly call upon him.

Concerning the sixth.

There is added also the doctrine concerning the cross, from which it is clear that the old man understands that Christ's kingdom would not be political, because he says that many would contradict him, and he alludes to the sayings of the Prophets concerning the passion of Christ. Afterwards he adds that the mother would be in great sorrow, namely, because she will see her Son crucified.

Moreover, the mother everywhere represents the Church, whose afflictions are painted here, when he says: A sword will pierce your own soul, while the thoughts of hearts are revealed, that is, while the impiety previously hidden under the appearance of wisdom and justice brings itself forth and shows itself. Just as men fascinated by the admiration of their own wisdom and justice most bitterly hate the Gospel, as it is said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.

A brief narration of the same history.

I. Concerning the obedience to be rendered to the ministry.

II. Testimonies concerning the born Christ.

III. The Canticle of Simeon.

IIII. Concerning persecution.

Concerning the first.

Two laws are to be considered here, which contain a most serious doctrine...: The former concerning the uncleanness of the woman who has given birth, the latter concerning the firstborn consecrated to God. The former law speaks explicitly of one born from male seed, Leviticus 12, and signifies that men are born with uncleanness, and commands the mother to offer for sin, that she may be purified.

This law warned this people of the uncleanness of human nature, and of original sin.

And, because it speaks explicitly of one born from male seed, it... pertained in no way to Christ, or his mother: and yet Mary obeys the law. Why? So that by her example she might preserve the public ministry, and show that she, and this child, are members of this Church.

From this let us learn that the preservation of the ministry is a concern for the saints, and that it is to be aided by the examples and obedience of all.

Another law concerning the firstborn requires all firstborn males to be consecrated to God, and redeemed.

This law signified many things. First, that men are born primarily to serve God.

Likewise, that the primary part of life, of labors, and of fruits is owed to God. It also contained a hidden promise, because God demanded the firstborn, he testified that this people would be his concern, and that they pleased him.

Finally, there was a secret signification concerning Christ, that the firstborn would come, who would be properly consecrated to God, namely the Messiah.

Although, therefore, the prior law concerning the unclean pertained in no way to Mary, yet she understood this law concerning the firstborn to be a witness concerning Christ, and to signify this firstborn.

Therefore, although he was consecrated to God without ceremony, she nevertheless brings him to the Church, so that she may signify that the law concerning the consecrated firstborn has now been truly fulfilled. And she wishes this very ceremony to be a witness of the exhibited and consecrated Christ.

And therefore the testimony of the Holy Spirit is added, who through Simeon and Anna proclaims that this infant is the Messiah consecrated to God. Great glory therefore follows, after Mary performed the customary duty in the ministry.

Wherefore let us also learn to venerate and protect the ministry of the Church, and let us remember that that firstborn has now been exhibited, who is truly consecrated to God, and through whom others are consecrated, etc.

Concerning the second. It has often been said that all testimonies are to be collected, because God wished this nativity to be made manifest and to become clear, so that the Church might be certain. For although the deeds of the Church do not so strike the eyes of all, as the battles of emperors, of Alexander, and the like: yet God wishes there to be certain testimonies concerning Christ, and concerning his word in the Church.

Thus here are the witnesses: Mary, Joseph, Zacharias, Elizabeth, the Shepherds, the Magi, Simeon, Anna.

Nor was the authority of these witnesses light: for without doubt Simeon and Anna were the remnants of the saints who had taken part in the battles of the Maccabees: because from Judas Maccabaeus to the nativity of Christ are 161 years.

And Simeon and Anna, having passed their hundredth year, had seen the holy elders of the previous century. Thus, true faith remained with a few people in a perpetual series among this people.

Furthermore, let these testimonies confirm our faith, and at the same time let us consider here the appearance of the Church, which was a small assembly, despised and oppressed by the tyranny of Herod and the high priests, and yet this small assembly shone in this people, nor was it entirely unknown.

Concerning the third.

The canticle is a testimony concerning the Messiah, and an act of thanksgiving. Likewise a prophecy concerning the calling of the Gentiles, and a doctrine concerning the benefits of Christ.

Having seen Christ, the old man says that he will depart in peace, because he recognizes that the immense mercy of God has been given, he thinks of the future restoration of the Church, he knows that through this Messiah sin and death are to be abolished, eternal life is to be begun, he recognizes that his sins have been forgiven, he recognizes that he will have eternal life: thus he is exhilarated by manifold consolation. Let us also think of these things, having recognized Christ.

"A light for the revelation of the Gentiles," that is, he will be a light illuminating, enlightening the Gentiles, or shining for the Gentiles, by which, having recognized him, they will perceive God, and the immense mercy of God willing to receive and save the Gentiles: or a light, that is, a consoler, to be revealed to the Gentiles, who frees them from sins and eternal death.

Concerning the fourth.

Another description of the Church follows; Simeon warns that the polity of the people will not remain, and that the princes will be opposed to Christ; hence there was a great distraction. These things always happen in the Church, when disputes are stirred up concerning the Gospel, and when the wise abhor discord, many, moved by this appearance, are more hostile to the Gospel: but yet some pious assembly remains, therefore it is said: "He will be for the resurrection of many."

But these very people endure the most sorrowful persecutions, therefore here he says concerning Mary:

A sword shall pierce through thy soul. He prophesies that Christ will suffer, and at the same time signifies that the Church will perpetually have afflictions in this life, because Mary is the image of the whole Church.

Latin:

Die purificationis Mariae. Evangelium Lucae 2.

Postquam impleti sunt dies purgationis eorum, secundum legem Moisi, tulerunt illum in Ierusalem, ut sisterent eum Domino, sicut scriptum est in lege Domini, quod omne masculinum adaperiens vulvam, sanctum Domino vocabitur. Et ut darent hostiam, secundum quod dictum est in lege Domini, par turturum, aut duos pullos columbarum. Et ecce, homo erat in Ierusalem, cui nomen Simeon. Et homo iste iustus et pius, expectans consolationem Israël, et Spiritus sanctus erat in eo. Et responsum acceperat a Spiritu sancto, se non visurum mortem, nisi prius videret Christum Domini, Et venit spiritu in templum. Et cum inducerent puerum Iesum parentes, ut facerent secundum consuetudinem legis pro eo, et ipse accepit eum in ulnas suas, et benedixit Deum, et dixit: Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secundum verbum tuum in pace. Quia viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum, quod parasti ante faciem omnium populorum, Lumen ad revelationem gentium, et gloriam plebis tuae Israël. Et erant pater et mater eius mirantes super his, quae dicebantur de illo. Et benedixit illis Simeon, et dixit ad Mariam matrem eius: Ecce positus est hic in ruinam et resurrectionem multorum in Israël, et in signum cui contradicetur. Quin et tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius, ut revelentur ex multis cordibus cogitationes.

Sex sunt praecipui loci.

I. Quid lex de immundis et de purificatione Levitici 14. significet.

II. Cur Maria, cum non teneretur ea lege, tamen ei obtemperaverit.

III. Quid lex de primogenitis significet.

IIII. Testimonia de nato Messia Simeonis et Annae.

V. Doctrina in dictis Simeonis de regno Christi.

VI. Doctrina de cruce.

De primo.

Tota haec lex Mosi est paedagogia seu disciplina, non quidem tollens peccatum, sed de multis magnis rebus admonens populum, scilicet de peccato, et de futura liberatione. Ita haec lex de immundis, quae tamen conceptum ex virili semine pepererant, significabat propagari cum hac regeneratione peccatum, et naturam humanam ream esse. Admonebat igitur ceremonia pios, ut cogitarent de peccato propagato, et de causis humanarum calamitatum, et de ira Dei: deinde ut ad hanc tristem meditationem conferrent promissiones. siones de futura liberatione, de electione huius populi, et invocarent Deum fide, seu fiducia promissionum etc. Ad hos usus haec symbola praecipue instituta erant, postea accedebant et aliae rationes huius moris. Lex servit utilitati corporis, et coërcet errantes libidines. Magnum miraculum est ipse partus, mirabili Dei ordinatione, coxae quae alioquin non moventur suo loco, tamen in partu aperiuntur, et accedit ingens dolor. Denique sequitur partum magna corporis debilitas, quae ipsa nos de primo lapsu admonet. Ut igitur parcatur corpori puerperae, Deus aliquos dies ordinavit, quibus vult illam servire suae valetudini, et vult Deus suo verbo regi opus generationis, nec temere vagari. Vult igitur interim a puerpera virum abstinere, et sancit capitalem poenam de hac re. Haec mortalia etiam hoc loco observanda sunt, quia moralia ad omnes homines pertinent, Deus nunc quoque vult puerperas curare suam valetudinem, ideo etsi certus numerus dierum, et sacrificia illa ad nos non pertinent, tamen genus ad nos pertinet. Quod vero offerebant agnum, aut turtures, hic ritus non tollebat peccata, sed erat testimonium observati illius puerperii, et occasio docendi populi, cum veniebant ad templum, et hostiae offerebantur, quia talibus officiis sacerdotes alendi erant. Caeterum tecte significabatur ventura hostia. De secundo. Maria non tenebatur hac lege de immundis, quia lex diserte dicit de ea, quae peperit conceptum ex virili semine, Haec additio supervacanea fuisset, nisi tecte significaret quandam parituram esse sine virili semine. Non igitur vult Deus accusare matrem Filii sui. Cur igitur observavit Maria ritum? Respondeo. Quatuor sunt causae, cur Christus circumcisionem et caeteros ritus omnes servavit. Prima, quia subiecit se legi, ut subiret poenam, quam minatur lex pro peccatis generis humani. Secunda, ut constaret hunc Messiam esse ex semine Abrahae, oportebat eum in hoc populo versari, et servare ritus eosdem, praesertim cum oportuerit exhiberi eum isti populo. Tertia, quia oportuit Messiam esse socium Ecclesiae Dei, et non abesse a reliquo corpore Ecclesiae, ut clara testimonia in Ecclesia de eo ederentur. Quarta, ut testimonia de eo illustria spargerentur per ipsum ministerium, ut per Zachariam, Simeonem, Elisabeth, Annam, et alios. Parentes ergo cum has causas scirent, legi obtemperant, et monent nos, ut conservationem ministerii adiuvemus, et declaremus nos esse membra verae Ecclesiae. Et quod Maria et Ioseph recte fecerit ipse Deus testatur, qui hic insigni miraculo movet Simeonem et Annam, ut vaticinentur. Dicitur enim diserte: Venit motu Spiritus in templum. Discamus autem Deum adesse huic studio conservandi communis ministerii, quia ipse est efficax per ministerium, sicut dicit: Qui vos audit, me audit. De tertio. Ter in Mose est repetita lex de primogenitis masculis. Exod. 13. Item 34. et Num. 8. et est adiuncta ἀντίθεσις, quia percussi primogenita Aegypti, posco vestra primogenita. Generaliter autem significatum est, hunc populum electum esse a Deo, ut in eo sit Ecclesia. Sicut autem subditus certo munere testatur, se suo Domino addictum esse: ita vult Deus se agnosci esse Dominum huius populi. Turcicus tyrannus ex singulis pagis et oppidis sumit decimum quemque puerum, et deligit suo arbitrio. Hoc magno munere populus fatetur hunc esse dominum: sed haec est misera servitus ad exitium instituta, quod exempli causa recito. Voluit Deus et sibi tradi primitias nascentium, ut agnosceret populus, sic vere proprium esse Dei populum. Econtra vero Aegyptiorum, et aliarum gentium primogenita reiecta esse. Quid haec tota imago significat? Hoc videlicet omnes gentes reiectas esse, quae non colunt Deum iuxta hoc verbum traditum huic populo, hos vere esse populum Dei, qui eum colunt iuxta verbum, quo se patefecit in hoc populo. Et ut Turcica illa servitus exitiosa est, ita haec salutaris est. Ac opponitur ritus opinionibus impiis, quae aut omnes religiones pariter fingunt fabulosas esse, aut omnes pariter probandas. Sed hic reiicit Deus primogenita Aegyptiorum, id est, reiicit caeteras gentes, caeteros cultus et religiones, et claro signo testatur, se vere esse Dominum huius populi, et curare hunc populum, qui amplectitur verbum ab ipso traditum.

Et hic ipse ritus referendus est ad promissionem additam circumcisioni, in qua clare dicitur: Ego ero Deus eorum, id est, hos qui me invocant propter semen promissum, recipiam, exaudiam, salvabo etc. Huius promissionis σύμβολα et repetitiones erant multae aliae ceremoniae, sicut haec ipsa servitus, seu traditio primogenitorum. Haec vere, ut in foro, testimonium erat mutuum, quo ostendebatur Deum esse dominum huius populi, et hunc populum esse proprium Dei, sicut traditio puerorum apud Turcas dominium significat.

Secundo, ut autem dominii ratio primum haec complectitur, Dominum recipere hunc populum, exaudire, salvare, ita e regione servitus significabat debita officia. Discenda et retinenda est doctrina Dei, et ei obediendum, instituendi liberi ad doctrinam, corpora et facultates serviant in bello, et alibi ad conservationem doctrinae.

Hanc esse legis sententiam Deus ipse testatur, quia inquit: Debentur mihi omnia primogenita, delegi mihi pro illis tribum Levi. Requirit ergo praecipue officia conservandae doctrinae. Haec in summa lex de primogenitis significat, videlicet populum peculiarem, delectum ut salvetur, et vere celebret Deum.

Sed hic addendum est, in hoc populo esse quendam primogenitum omnibus antecellentem, propter quem principaliter Deo dicata sunt primogenita, videlicet Messiam, qui est primus haeres, propter quem caeteri recipiuntur. Hanc doctrinam de Messia optime intelligebat Maria in oblatione primogeniti, ideoque principaliter venit in templum, ut ipsa testaretur hunc esse primogenitum illum praecipuum, propter quem omnes significationes institutae fuerunt. Sicut etiam Spiritus sanctus ipse testatur, hunc esse illum primogenitum, sicut eum praedicant, Simeon, Anna, et alii.

Iam hic discamus, nos insertos oleae populi Dei, et factos cohaeredes Christi, et proprium populum Dei, modo ut invocemus eum iuxta hoc verbum, in quo se patefecit, debere item nos certa officia, discere doctrinam, obedire ei, corpora et res offerre ad doctrinae conservationem.

De quarto.

Ut saepe alias dictum est, testimonia observantur de nato Messia, ut fides nostra confirmetur, quia Deus vult Ecclesiam habere certa testimonia. Ante fuerunt testes Zacharias, Elisabeth, Angeli, Ioseph, Pastores, Magi: nunc Simeon et Anna accedunt, ut late spargatur articulus, quod natus sit Messias.

De quinto.

Doctrina traditur in dictis Simeonis de regno Christi, vocat Christum salutare suum, vocat lumen ad revelationem gentium, id est, lumen lucens gentibus, seu praebens lucem gentibus, ut videant Deum.

Intelligit autem salutare, non de imperio mundano, sed de vera salute, qua Deus abolito peccato, et abolita morte, restituit vera bona, et sic de gentibus loquitur: Gentes habituras lumen Evangelii, in quo Deum agnoscent, et vere invocabunt.

De sexto.

Additur et doctrina de cruce, ex qua perspicuum est senem intelligere, Christi regnum non fore politicum, quia dicit, Multos ei contradicturos esse, et alludit ad dicta Prophetarum de passione Christi. Postea addit matrem in magno dolore futuram esse, scilicet, quia videbit Filium crucifigi.

Caeterum mater ubique repraesentat Ecclesiam, cuius afflictiones hic pinguntur, cum ait: Animam tuam penetrabit gladius, dum revelantur cogitationes cordium, id est, dum se profert et ostendit impietas antea tecta specie sapientiae et iusticiae. Sicut acerrime oderunt Evangelium homines fascinati admiratione suae sapientiae et iusticiae, ut dictum est: Perdam sapientiam sapientium.

Eiusdem historiae brevis enarratio.

I. De obedientia praestanda ministerio.

II. Testimonia de nato Christo.

III. Canticum Simeonis.

IIII. De persecutione.

De primo.

Duae leges hic considerandae sunt, quae gravissimam doctrinam continent: Prior de immunditia puerperae, Posterior de primogenitis consecratis Deo. Prior lex diserte loquitur de nato ex virili semine, Levit. 12. et significat nasci homines cum immunditie, et iubet matrem offerre pro peccato, ut purgetur.

Haec lex admonebat hunc populum de immunditie humanae naturae, et de peccato originis.

Et, quia diserte loquitur de nato ex virili semine, nihil pertinebat ad Christum..., aut matrem: et tamen Maria obtemperat legi. Quare? ut exemplo suo conservet ministerium publicum, et ostendat se, et hunc natum, esse membra huius Ecclesiae.

Hinc discamus conservationem ministerii sanctis curae esse, et adiuvandum esse omnium exemplis et obedientia.

Altera lex de primogenitis postulat omnia primogenita mascula Deo consecrari, et redimi.

Haec lex multa significabat. Primum nasci homines praecipue, ut Deo serviant.

Item deberi Deo praecipuam partem vitae, laborum et fructuum. Continebat et tectam promissionem, quia Deus postulabat primogenita, testabatur sibi curae fore hunc populum, et placere.

Denique arcana significatio erat de Christo, venturum primogenitum, qui esset proprie consecratus Deo, scilicet Messias.

Quanquam igitur prior lex de immundis, nihil prorsus ad Mariam pertinebat, tamen hanc legem de primogenitis intelligebat testem esse de Christo, et significare hunc primogenitum.

Ideo, etsi sine ceremonia erat consecratus Deo, tamen adfert eum ad Ecclesiam, ut significet iam vere impletam esse legem de primogenito consecrato. Et hanc ipsam ceremoniam vult testem esse exhibiti et consecrati Christi.

Ideoque accedit testimonium Spiritus sancti, qui per Simeonem et Annam concionatur hunc infantem esse Messiam consecratum Deo. Magna igitur gloria sequitur, postquam ministerio praestitit Maria usitatum officium.

Quare discamus et nos venerari, et tueri ministerium Ecclesiae, et meminerimus iam exhibitum esse illum primogenitum, qui vere consecratus est Deo, et per quem caeteri consecrantur, etc.

De secundo. Saepe dictum est omnia testimonia colligenda esse, quia Deus patefieri et inclarescere hanc nativitatem voluit, ut Ecclesia esset certa. Etsi enim Ecclesiae facta non sic incurrunt in omnium oculos, ut imperatorum, Alexandri, et similium praelia: tamen vult Deus esse certa testimonia de Christo, et de verbo suo in Ecclesia.

Ita hic sunt testes, Maria, Ioseph, Zacharias, Elisabeth, Pastores, Magi, Simeon, Anna.

Nec levis fuit auctoritas horum testium: nam haud dubie Simeon et Anna fuerunt reliquiae sanctorum, qui Maccabaeorum praeliis interfuerant: quia a Iuda Maccabaeo ad nativitatem Christi sunt anni 161.

Et Simeon et Anna egressi centesimum annum viderant sanctos senes prioris seculi. Ita mansit penes aliquos paucos vera fides perpetua serie in hoc populo.

Porro haec testimonia fidem nostram confirment, et simul hic speciem Ecclesiae consideremus, quae erat coetus exiguus, spretus et oppressus tyrannide Herodis et pontificum, et tamen hic exiguus coetus fulgebat in hoc populo, nec erat prorsus ignotus.

De tertio.

Canticum est testimonium de Messia, et gratiarum actio. Item prophetia de vocatione gentium, et doctrina de beneficiis Christi.

Conspecto Christo senex ait se discessurum in pace, quia agnoscit ingentem Dei misericordiam datam esse, cogitat futuram instaurationem Ecclesiae, scit per hunc Messiam abolendum esse peccatum et mortem, incoandam vitam aeternam, agnoscit sibi remissa esse peccata, agnoscit se habiturum vitam aeternam: ita multiplici consolatione exhilaratur. Haec et nos cogitemus agnito Christo.

Lumen ad revelationem gentium, id est, erit lumen illustrans, illuminans gentes, vel lucens gentibus, quo agnito cernent Deum, et ingentem misericordiam Dei volentis recipere, et salvare gentes: vel lumen, id est, consolator, patefaciendus gentibus, qui eos liberat a peccatis et aeterna morte.

De quarto.

Sequitur alia descriptio Ecclesiae, praemonet Simeon non mansuram politiam populi, et principes adversaturos esse Christo, hinc secura erat magna distractio. Haec semper fiunt in Ecclesia, motis certaminibus de Evangelio, et cum sapientes abhorreant a discordiis, multi hac specie moti, sunt iniquiores Evangelio: sed tamen manet aliquis pius coetus, ideo dicitur: Erit in resurrectionem multis.

Sed hi ipsi sustinent tristissimas persecutiones, ideo hic dicit de Maria:

Gladius penetrabit animam tuam. Vaticinatur Christum passurum esse, et simul significat perpetuo in hac vita Ecclesiam habituram afflictiones, quia Maria est imago totius Ecclesiae.

## 2:41 First Sunday After Epiphany
First Sunday after Epiphany.

Gospel of Luke 2.

And his parents went every year to Jerusalem, at the feast day of the Passover.

And when he was twelve years old, they going up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, and having fulfilled the days, when they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem; and his parents knew it not.

Thinking however that he was in the company, they came a day's journey, and sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance.

And not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him.

And it came to pass after three days, they found him in the temple sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions.

And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.

And seeing him, they were astonished.

And his mother said to him: Son, why hast thou done so to us?

Behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing.

And he said to them: How is it that you sought me?

Did you not know, that I must be about my Father's business?

And they understood not the word that he spoke to them.

And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.

But his mother kept all these words in her heart.

And Jesus increased in wisdom and age, and grace with God and men.

There are seven points.

First.

Example concerning the keeping of ceremonies divinely instituted.

Mary, Joseph and Jesus come to the Passover, although they were righteous, and had no need of this discipline for themselves, but they provide an example, so that we may learn that ceremonies are to be kept, which are profitable for the preservation of the ministry, both so that we ourselves may learn, and so that others may be invited, and the Gospel propagated.

Second.

The Son remains in the temple without consulting his parents, and confers with the doctors concerning doctrine, undoubtedly disputing about the kingdom of the Messiah, which they thought would be worldly, and reproving their error concerning the cults, which they thought to be righteousness.

Third.

When is it lawful for children to decline the authority of parents?

I answer, The commandment of God is to be preferred to the will of parents, as Christ says: He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me.

As when parents forbid the study of true doctrine, confession, or marriage.

Again, outside of this case, obedience is owed to parents.

As here Christ returns home with his parents, once the duty of his vocation was completed.

Fourth.

Concerning the negligence and sorrow of Mary.

The world does not understand that there are sins, except for external civil sins.

It does not acknowledge how great an evil is natural infirmity, and negligence in any commandment of God whatsoever.

But the saints understand the magnitude of this interior weakness, and often experience that huge punishments follow slight negligence, as it seems: and the magnitude of the calamities, by which the saints are especially oppressed, convicts and convinces them that they still carry sin about with them, and indeed in those calamities they acknowledge their own vices, security, negligence, diffidence, etc.

Thus here Mary acknowledged her negligence, she thought that the custody of this son had been especially entrusted to her, that she had forgotten her duty, she compared herself with Eve, who had previously lost the human race, now she herself thinks that she is another Eve who, having lost her son, had again lost the human race, she thought of all the miracles by which God had stirred her to the care of this son.

Since therefore she saw how great a sin this negligence was, it is necessary that there were huge sorrows during the entire three days, the magnitude of which no man understands.

Here therefore let us learn what the sins of the saints are like, and let us not extenuate the vice of natural infirmity or negligence.

Just as the magnitude of calamities ought to warn us, lest we extenuate it.

There is, however, in individual saints a manifold negligence, which afterwards also brings on huge miseries.

Fifth.

Christ is found in the temple, that is, in the ministry: by which it is signified that Christ is to be sought among the Church, that the Church is to be heard, but that it is to be judged by the ministry, that is, by the word of God.

That at last is the Church, which has the ministry of the Word of God, and by the Word showing, Christ is found.

Sixth. As Christ, having completed the office of his calling, returns home with his parents, so let us remember that it is also commanded to us that we obey our parents, but in such a way that we prefer the commandment of God, according to our calling. Seventh. How does the Son of God progress? I answer: In all the saints, gifts become more illustrious and more excited by use, just as on the contrary they become more languid and are extinguished by negligence, as the parable of the Talent teaches. And Paul says to Timothy: Stir up the gift which is given to you, etc. The Apostles had the gift of tongues, but they nourished it by reading and exercise. Let these examples also exhort us to intention and care, and to exercise in all spiritual gifts, that is, in studies and in restraining wicked desires, in exciting good motives, in invocation, and in other things.

Latin:

Dominica I. post Epiphania.

Evangelium Lucae 2.

Et ibant parentes eius quotannis in Ierusalem, in die festo Paschae.

Et cum factus esset annorum duodecim, ascendentibus illis Ierosolymam secundum consuetudinem festi, consummatisq; diebus cum redirent illi, remansit puer Iesus in Ierusalem, et non cognoverunt parentes eius.

Existimantes autem eum esse in comitatu, venerunt iter diei, et requirebant eum inter cognatos et inter notos.

Et non invenientes eum, regressi sunt in Ierusalem, requirentes eum.

Et factum est post triduum, invenerunt illum in templo sedentem in medio doctorum, et audientem illos, et interrogantem eos.

Stupebant autem omnes, qui eum audiebant, super intelligentia et responsis eius.

Et videntes eum, stupebant.

Et dixit mater eius ad illum: Fili, quid fecisti nobis sic?

Ecce pater tuus et ego dolentes quaerebamus te.

Et ait ad illos: Quid est quod me quaerebatis?

Nesciebatis, quod in his, quae Patris mei sunt, oportet me esse?

Et ipsi non intellexerunt verbum quod locutus est eis.

Et descendit cum eis, et venit Nazareth, et erat subditus illis.

Mater autem eius conservabat omnia verba haec in corde suo.

Et Iesus proficiebat sapientia et aetate, et gratia apud Deum et homines.

Loci septem sunt.

Primus.

Exemplum de servandis ceremoniis divinitus institutis.

Maria, Ioseph et Iesus veniunt ad Pascha, tametsi erant iusti, nec pro sese habebant opus hac disciplina, sed praebent exemplum, ut discamus ceremonias servandas esse, quae prosunt ad conservationem ministerii, tum ut ipsi discamus, tam ut alii invitentur, et propagetur Evangelium.

Secundus.

Filius inconsultis parentibus manet in templo, et confert cum doctoribus de doctrina, haud dubie disputans de regno Messiae, quod ipsi arbitrabantur fore mundanum, et reprehendens errorem eorum de cultibus, quos putabant esse iusticiam.

Tertius.

Quando licet filiis detrectare auctoritatem parentum?

Respondeo, Mandatum Dei anteferendum est voluntati parentum, ut Christus inquit: Si quis patrem aut matrem plus diligit quam me, non est me dignus.

Ut quando parentes prohibent studium verae doctrinae, confessionem, coniugium.

Rursus extra hunc casum debetur obedientia parentibus.

Ut hic Christus redit domum cum parentibus, absoluto vocationis officio.

Quartus.

De negligentia et dolore Mariae.

Mundus non intelligit esse peccata, nisi externa civilia peccata.

Non agnoscit quantum malum sit naturalis infirmitas, et negligentia in quocunque mandato Dei.

Sed sancti intelligunt magnitudinem huius interioris imbecillitatis, et saepe experiuntur ingentes poenas sequi levem negligentiam, ut videtur: et magnitudo calamitatum, quibus praecipue oppressi sunt sancti, coarguit et convincit eos, quod adhuc circumferant peccatum, et quidem in illis calamitatibus agnoscunt sua vitia, securitatem, negligentiam, diffidentiam etc.

Ita hic Maria agnovit suam negligentiam, cogitabat sibi praecipue mandatam esse custodiam huius filii, se esse oblitam officii sui, conferebat se cum Eva, quae antea perdiderat genus humanum, nunc ipsa cogitat se alteram Evam esse quae amisso filio, rursus perdiderit genus humanum, cogitavit omnia miracula, quibus Deus ipsam ad curam huius filii excitaverat.

Cum igitur videret quantum peccatum esset haec negligentia, necesse est fuisse ingentes dolores toto triduo, quorum magnitudinem nemo hominum intelligit.

Hic igitur discamus, qualia sint peccata sanctorum, nec extenuemus vitium naturalis infirmitatis aut negligentiae.

Sicut magnitudo calamitatum monere nos debeat, ne id extenuemus.

Est autem in singulis sanctis multiplex negligentia, quae postea etiam accersit ingentes aerumnas.

Quintus.

Christus invenitur in templo, id est, in ministerio: quo significatum est, quaerendum esse Christum apud Ecclesiam, Ecclesiam audiendam esse, sed iudicandam esse ex ministerio, hoc est, ex verbo Dei.

Illa demum est Ecclesia, quae habet ministerium verbi Dei, et verbo monstrante, reperitur Christus.

Sextus. Ut Christus officio vocationis absoluto domum redit cum parentibus, ita meminerimus et nobis praecipi, ut obediamus parentibus, sed ita ut anteferamus mandatum Dei, iuxta vocationem. Septimus. Quomodo proficit Filius Dei? Respondeo: In omnibus sanctis dona fiunt illustriora, et excitatiora usu, sicut econtra fiunt languidiora, et extinguuntur negligentia, ut parabola de Talento docet. Et Paulus inquit ad Tim.: Excita donum quod tibi est collatum etc. Habebant Apostoli donum linguarum, sed id alebant lectione et exercitatione. Haec exempla nos quoque hortentur ad intentionem et curam, et ad exercitationem in omnibus donis spiritualibus, hoc est, in studiis et coërcendis pravis cupiditatibus, in excitandis bonis motibus, invocatione et aliis.

## 5:1 Fifth Sunday After Trinitatis
Fifth Sunday after Trinitatis.

Evangelium of Lucae 5.

Now it happened that as the crowd pressed in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Genesareth.

And he saw two boats standing by the lake; but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets.

And he got into one of the boats, which was Simon's, and asked him to put out a little from the land.

And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat.

When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon: "Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch." And Simon answered and said to him: "Praeceptor, we have toiled all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net." And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish, so that their net was breaking.

And they signaled to their partners who were in the other boat to come and 324 help them.

And they came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.

But when Simon Petrus saw it, he fell down at Iesu's knees, saying: "Depart from me, Domine, for I am a sinful man." For fear had seized him and all who were with him, because of the catch of fish that they had taken.

Likewise also Iacobum and Iohannem, the sons of Zebedaei, who were partners with Simon.

And Iesus said to Simon: "Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men." And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

There are two main points.

I. An example of the exercise of faith in bodily terrors.

II. An example of the exercise of faith in spiritual terrors.

The first point, concerning bodily goods, teaches from the saying of Christi: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." For it commands that our first care should be for the word of God and the preservation of its ministry, so that God will defend us, and supply us with what is necessary for food and for this life, even if it is not done without our labor and without some difficulties.

This consolation is necessary in the Ecclesia, which we see to be in need and afflicted in the world.

Ministers almost perish from hunger, and therefore the ministry is abandoned, and everyone thinks about providing for themselves.

Here the spirit must be uplifted by this promise, that to those who seek the kingdom of God, all other things will be added.

If anyone wishes to extend this, it can also apply to other kinds of vocations, for every vocation has its dangers which press upon and weary men.

There, the kingdom of God must be sought first, that is, care must be taken that from the word we learn of God's good will towards us, so that by faith we may flee to him in all of life, in all dangers.

Then, that each one in his own vocation, which indeed has God's command, may serve God, do his duty for God's glory, and the benefit of the Ecclesia and the Reipub.

The rest he should commit to God, for God promises that these things will be added of their own accord.

Such are many sentences of scripture, such as: "Cast your thought upon the Dominum, and he will nourish you." Likewise: "Reveal your way to the Domino, and he will do it," etc.

XII. ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPELS.

These sentences teach both that without faith and invocation our labors are unhappy, and even if many adverse things happen in our calling, nevertheless our spirits must be excited by trust in Christ, and it must be known that He Himself will be present for us, and will give, so that our labor may not be vain and without fruit.

The other passage is about spiritual doctrine, that is, about the remission of sins.

For that former bodily benefit now becomes a sacrament for Peter.

He understands divinely that this benefit has happened to him, and that this Lord is sent by God, having divine power, just, good, etc.

This recognition produces in him new movements; first, it leads him to the recognition of himself; he sees that he is a sinner unworthy of such a benefit: for he does not become worse or more secure, as otherwise successes make men more insolent, but there exists in his mind, first contrite, that is, terror from the sight of his own unworthiness, and from the sense of the judgment of God or wrath against sin, from which he could not be freed unless he were recalled by the voice of Christ, who commands him to trust, that is, to determine that he is received by God, and has the remission of sins, and adds as a sign, by which he testifies that He truly receives him called to the society of the ministry of the Gospel.

Thus Peter, terrified by the magnitude of the benefit, and judging himself unworthy of the presence of the Lord, and of such an immense and sudden good, which he saw had happened to him not by his own labor, but by the benefit of the Lord, is an example of how everyone should be affected, even when he experiences that God is not angry, but merciful.

For the human mind, whether it fears the wrath of God or sees His mercy, nevertheless, as much as is in it, flees both.

For this thought clings to the minds of all, that we are worthy of punishment, but unworthy of mercy. Here it is necessary for us, like Peter, to be recalled by the voice of Christ: Do not fear, as if He were saying, Because you are a sinner, and are terrified by your unworthiness, I want you to have hope in my mercy and goodness, and to be at peace.

Trust therefore, and you will not only feel my benefit in this matter, but I will make you a fisher of men, that is, an Apostle and teacher in my kingdom, far different from the teachers who have been in the people of God until now.

The allegory of both passages has much sweetness concerning the Church.

When she seeks the kingdom of God, even if she is in need in the world, yet she is sustained in the midst of afflictions, and endures perpetually, while meanwhile the wicked with their power and their wealth perish.

The other passage can be transferred to this allegory, that the ministry of the Gospel is a fishing not idle, but of great labor and much trouble.

But how fruitful the ministry is, and how long the labor of the ministry will endure, is not seen.

For just as fish lie hidden in a net under water, so the Church in this life lies hidden, overwhelmed by afflictions and infirmity of every kind.

But at the end, after the net has been drawn out of the water, the fruit will appear richer than everyone's opinion, so that the future admiration of all will be immense.

There is also proposed consolation against scandal, because many fail from the Gospel and relapse into errors.

For even if some, like fish when the net is broken, fall out, yet in the rest the ministry is effective; many are saved and remain in the society of the members of the Church and in the confession of the pure doctrine of the Gospel.

Latin:

Dominica V. post Trinitatis.

Evangelium Lucae 5.

Factum est autem cum turba irrueret ad eum, ut audiret verbum Dei, et ipse stabat secus stagnum Genesareth.

Et vidit duas naves stantes secus stagnum: piscatores autem descenderant ex illis, ac lavabant retia.

Ascendens autem in unam navim, quae erat Simonis, rogavit eum ut a terra re-duceret pusillum.

Et sedens docebat de navi turbas.

Ut cessavit autem loqui, dixit ad Simonem: Duc in altum, et laxate retia vestra in ca-pluram. Et respondens Simon, dixit illi: Praeceptor, per totam noctem laborantes nihil cepimus, in verbo autem tuo laxabo rete. Et cum hoc fecissent, concluserunt piscium multitudinem copiosam: rumpebatur autem rete eorum,

et innuerunt sociis, qui erant in alia navi, ut venirent et 324 adiuvaret se.

Et venerunt, et impleverunt ambas naves, ita ut mergerentur.

Videns autem Simon Petrus, procidit ad genua Iesu, dicens: Exi a me Domine, quia vir peccator sum. Pavor enim circum-dederat eum, et omnes qui cum illo erant, super captura piscium quam coeperant.

Similiter autem et Iacobum et Iohannem filios Zebedaei, qui erant socii Simonis.

Et ait ad Simonem Iesus: Noli timere, posthac homines eris capiens. Et subductis ad terram navibus, relictis omnibus secuti sunt eum.

Duo sunt praecipui loci.

I. Exemplum exercitii fidei in terroribus corporalibus.

II. Exemplum exercitii fidei in terroribus spiritualibus.

Prior locus de bonis corporalibus docet, de dicto Christi: Primum quaerite regnum Dei et iusticiam eius, et caetera adicientur vobis. Prae- cipit enim, ut prima nobis cura sit de verbo Dei, eiusque ministerio conservando, ita futurum, ut Deus defendat nos, suppeditet nobis ea, quae ad victum et ad hanc vitam necessaria sunt, etiamsi id non fiat sine nostro labore, et sine aliquibus difficultatibus.

Haec consolatio necessaria est in Ecclesia, quam videmus egere, et affligi in mundo.

Mini- stri tantum non fame pereunt, propterea deseritur ministerium, et quique pro se de victu parando cogitat.

Hic erigendus est animus hac promissione, quod quaerentibus regnum Dei caetera omnia adiciantur.

Id si quis velit extendere, ire potest etiam per alia genera vocationum, quaelibet enim vocatio sua habet pericula, quae premunt et fatigant homines.

Ibi primum quaerendum est regnum Dei, id est, curandum est, ut ex verbo discamus de bona voluntate Dei erga nos, ut fide ad eum confugiamus in omni vita, in omnibus periculis.

Deinde, ut in sua quisque vocatione, quae quidem habet mandatum Dei, serviat Deo, faciat suum officium ad Dei gloriam, et utilitatem Ecclesiae et Reipub.

Reliqua Deo committat, illa enim ultro se Deus adiectorum esse promittit.

Quales sunt multae sententiae scripturae, ut: Iacta cogitatum tuum in Dominum, et ipse te enutriet. Item: Revela Domino viam tuam, et ipse faciet etc.

XII. ANNOTATIONES IN EVANGELIA.

Hae sententiae utrunque docent, et quod sine fide ac invocatione nostri labores sint infelices, et etiamsi in nostra vocatione multa accidunt adversa, tamen animos excitandos esse fiducia Christi, et sciendum ipsum nobis adfuturum esse, et daturum, ne labor noster sit irritus, et sine fructu.

Alter locus est de doctrina spirituali, id est, de remissione peccatorum.

Nam illud prius corporale beneficium, nunc Petro fit sacramentum.

Intelligit divinitus sibi contigisse hoc beneficium, et hunc dominum esse missum a Deo, habentem potentiam divinam, iustum, bonum etc.

Haec agnitio parit in eo novos motus, primum traducit eum ad agnitionem sui, videt se esse peccatorem indignum tanto beneficio: non enim fit deterior aut securior ut alioqui successus reddunt homines insolentiores, sed existit in eius animo primum contrito, id est, terror ex conspectu suae indignitatis, et sensu iudicii Dei seu irae adversus peccatum, a quo non posset liberari, nisi revocaretur voce Christi, qui iubet eum confidere, id est, statuere quod recipiatur a Deo, et habeat remissionem peccatorum, et addit tanquam signum, quo testetur se vere illum recipere vocatum ad societatem ministerii Evangelii.

Ita Petrus territus magnitudine beneficii, et iudicans se indignum esse praesentia Domini, et tam immenso et repentino bono, quod videbat sibi non ex labore suo, sed Domini beneficio contigisse, exemplo est, quo quisque modo sit affectus, etiam cum experitur Deum non iratum, sed misericordem esse.

Nam mens humana sive iram Dei metuit, sive misericordiam videt, tamen quantum in ipsa est, utrunque refugit.

Haeret enim in omnium animis haec cogitatio, quod poenam meriti simus, misericordia vero indigni simus, Hic necesse est nos sicut Petrum, revocari voce Christi: Ne metuas, quasi dicat, Ideo quia tu es peccator, et terreris tua indignitate, volo te in mea misericordia et bonitate spem habere, et acquiescere.

Confide igitur, et non tantum in hac re meum beneficium senties, sed faciam te piscatorem hominum, hoc est, Apostolum et doctorem in regno meo, longe alium, quam hactenus fuere doctores in populo Dei.

Allegoria utriusque loci plurimum habet suavitatis de Ecclesia.

Haec cum quaerat regnum Dei, etiamsi eget in mundo, tamen sustentatur in mediis afflictionibus, duratque perpetuo, cum interim impii cum sua potentia, suis opibus pereant.

Alter locus ad hanc allegoriam transferri potest, quod ministerium Evangelii sit piscatio non ociosa, sed magni laboris et multae molestiae.

Quam vero frugiferum sit ministerium, et quam diu duraturus labor ministerii, non cernitur.

Sicut enim pisces in reti sub aqua latent, ita Ecclesia in hac vita latet obruta afflictionibus, et infirmitate omnis generis.

Ad extremum vero postquam rete ex aqua extractum fuerit, apparebit fructus uberior omnium opinione, ut ingens sit omnium futura admiratio.

Proponitur item consolatio adversus scandalum, quod multi deficiunt ab Evangelio, et relabuntur ad errores.

Nam etsi aliqui, ut pisces rupto reti, excidunt, tamen in reliquis efficax est ministerium, multi servantur et manent in societate membrorum Ecclesiae et confessione purae doctrinae Evangelii.

## 6:36-42 Sunday IV. After Trinity
Sunday IV. after Trinity. Gospel of Luke 6.

Be therefore merciful, as your father is merciful. Do not judge, and you shall not be judged. Do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned. Forgive, and it shall be forgiven to you. Give, and it shall be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom. For with the same measure, with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you. And he spoke to them a similitude: Can the blind lead the blind? Do they not both fall into the ditch? The disciple is not above his master: but every one shall be perfect, if he be as his master. And why do you see the mote in your brother's eye, but the beam in your own eye you do not consider? Or how can you say to your brother: Brother, let me cast the mote out of your eye, and you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, cast first the beam out of your own eye, and then you shall see clearly to cast the mote out of your brother's eye.

There are four principal points.

I. Doctrine concerning good works. II. Precepts concerning four duties of love: mercy, not judging, forgiving, giving. III. Promises and threats. IIII. Reproof of those who judge perversely, not keeping the rule of Proverbs 10. The just man in the beginning is his own accuser, afterwards he explores his neighbor.

Concerning the first.

Paul's voice is well known: Brethren, we are debtors, not to live according to the flesh. If you have lived according to the flesh, you shall die: but if by the spirit you mortify the flesh, you shall live. Item 1 John 3: Let no man deceive us, he who does sin, is of the devil.

Let these sayings be fixed in our minds, so that we may know that it is necessary for those who are to be saved to have an inchoate [begun] obedience, and that without it men cannot be saved, but faith in Christ must precede and shine forth, and it must be known that inchoate obedience is pleasing to God in this way, when those reconciled by faith acknowledge that they do not satisfy the law. And yet they begin this obedience, and believe that it is pleasing on account of the high priest Christ, after the person has been accepted on account of the mediator Christ. These things have been said often elsewhere, and this summary must always be repeated in sermons about good works.

Concerning the second. The present sermon delivers the doctrine concerning good works, and indeed concerning certain duties of love, pertaining to the fifth commandment. And the sermon would be long, if one were to speak entirely about these virtues. But there are other sayings in this place, clearer than others. The commandment about giving can be understood in some way, but those about not judging, and about the perversity of judgments, are more obscure, and contain necessary doctrine for retaining the peace and concord of the Church. I will speak briefly about each. Mercy in general is to be affected by the sense of another's calamity, especially an unjust one, and to help those unjustly oppressed, according to one's vocation.

Also, to mitigate a just calamity by a probable reason, and it has two degrees. It is mercy that Constantine helps the Church oppressed by tyrants. Another degree is ἐπιείκεια [equity/clemency] in the punishments of those who have deserved ill, as David after victory spares the citizens who had been seditious, and yet were now returning to their duty. He preaches about this ἐπιείκεια, when he says: Be merciful, as your father is merciful. He admonishes us what we have deserved; it is madness, however, to insult the calamitous with the same punishments that one has deserved.

Furthermore, we have all deserved punishments, therefore let us not insult one another, but rather let us alleviate them with common sorrow. Also, let us be grateful to God, who was merciful towards us, and delivered us, and wants us by his example to be merciful towards others. Concerning this ἐπιείκεια it is said in James: Mercy is above judgment, that is, rigor, but this has its limits, as is said elsewhere. Do not judge.

An unlearned man of Christian doctrine is offended by this voice, because it seems to abolish polities, but Christ speaks only of private judgments. First, therefore, it must be known that there are three judgments which do not pertain to this place. The ministry of the Gospel, which judges and reproves sins, as Paul says: Admonish, rebuke, with all authority. Also the judgments of the magistrate,

Item, vituperation, which is done for the sake of healing, or for the sake of admonishing others in a manifest crime, as when I say: 'You should abstain from the company of this man, because I know him to be a drunkard,' and the law rightly says in the ff. [Digest]: 'He who denounces a guilty person is not to be punished, because it is expedient that known crimes be made public so that they may be amended.'

These judgments are not prohibited. What, therefore, does Christ prohibit here? I answer, private and calumnious ones, namely, when we interpret either a good deed, or an ambiguous one, in the worse light, or exaggerate a slight error out of malevolence, and do not strive to heal. The unlearned crowd does not understand how easily huge discords and disturbances of kingdoms arise from such beginnings, when malevolent, suspicious men, greedy for revenge, contend among themselves with hatreds and calumnies, as is now the custom to judge: 'This priest takes a wife, therefore he is a fickle man, not constantly maintaining the custom of his order.' Item, 'I saw another speaking more familiarly with my enemy, therefore he is plotting something against me.' These things are very widespread in life, and especially in government they stir up great tumults. Therefore, Christ preaches on a most important matter in this place, to the rest, but especially to governors, so that they may learn to curb these impulses.

Forgive. This precept is close to the neighbor; we ought not only to avoid calumnious judgments, but also to forgive those who are suspicious of us, to overlook their injuries, not to fight with the malevolent bitterly, but rather to heal them, if they are curable, or to spare them for the sake of the Republic. But just as I said above concerning not judging, that divinely instituted ministries are not prohibited, but private and calumnious judgments are, so here concerning remission, let it be known that it is not commanded regarding ministries, lest they fail to tax or punish crimes which are punished by the word of God and the laws, but private remission is commanded, which has three degrees.

The first is, when we are provoked by slight injuries, we pretend that we have just causes, and we are inflamed by emulation, or ambition, or a desire for revenge, so that we may crush our adversary. Here Christ commands concerning remission: for from such beginnings great tumults and great dissensions often arise in government.

The second degree is, when we are provoked by true causes, yet not atrocious ones; in these also epieikeia [equity/clemency] must be applied, so that we do not pursue all injuries, as when David spares the citizens, for the consideration of maintaining public tranquility is always to be held more important than private pain, and these sayings pertain to this: 'Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you.' 'Charity covers a multitude of sins,' etc.

The third degree is, when there are atrocious injuries, where the defense of the magistrate is needed, or otherwise for the sake of public peace unjust impulses must be coerced, it is right to flee to the office of the magistrate, but yet let there be remission in the heart before God, which does not impede the penalties.

Give. This precept can be understood more easily, but it embraces two degrees: to give what is owed, which is owed by civil or natural obligation, and to give alms, which is owed by divine obligation. For in both kinds men sin. There are great frauds in contracts, when yet God wishes us to exercise obedience in maintaining equality in contracts. Then also there is a divine obligation concerning alms, that we should help the calamitous, the needy, and especially the associates of the same confession and faith. This duty has degrees and limits, as Paul says, 'Not that there should be idle leisure for others, and affliction for you.' Item, 'Let your fountains be derived abroad, but you remain the master of them.'

Concerning the third.

Let us look at the threats and promises added, so that we may excite fear and faith. And the sum of the threats and promises is in this saying: 'With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again,' and indeed the text says that it will be that it is returned in full measure, so that Constantius, although he was a pagan, yet because he was merciful and did not rage against the Christians, was not cast out of the empire. Diocletian, although he was a wise prince, yet at length brought death upon himself, for fear of Constantine.

And universally let us remember that the law of retaliation is a divine ordinance, which God regularly maintains, even if human judgments neglect it, or men do not consider it. Therefore, even the most ancient laws religiously sanctioned the law of retaliation, as appears from Moses, as in the verse of Rhadamanthus: 'If he suffers what he did, the punishment is to be considered just.' For the first fathers diligently proposed this ordinance of God to the people, so that they might remind men of the fear of God, and hence many sayings have been: 'He who takes up the sword, by the sword' will perish.

First, therefore, let the threats exhort us to the fear of God, and let us know that they are spoken concerning present and future punishments. Second, the promises also speak of future rewards, just as Paul clearly says in 1 Timothy 6: Godliness has promises of the present life and of the life to come. And Christ says: He will receive a hundredfold in this life, and after this life, eternal life.

Now let us learn here to exercise faith. Corporal promises have been given so that faith may be exercised simultaneously in seeking reconciliation before God and in the expectation of corporal aid.

Therefore, let us always add to the corporal promises, at the beginning, the chief promise of the Gospel, concerning the remission of sins. David expects victory from God, but first he feels that God is propitious to him.

Thus God wants you to exercise faith in a twofold way. First, believe that God is propitious to you on account of the Son, then obey and expect aid from Him, give to the poor, and expect in turn that God will give you sustenance, peace, and other goods. 2 Corinthians 9. Many lie in wait for David in his kingdom. Now, if he wanted to remove all suspects in the manner of tyrants, there would be no end to the rampaging. What, therefore, does he do? First, he believes that he has a propitious God. Then, he diligently performs his duty. Third, he expects defense from God with a great and tranquil mind, nor is he moved by suspicions to exercise cruelty. Every individual can adapt this example to their own vocation, because no vocation, however humble, is without dangers. And let us diligently consider these exercises of faith: for the highest and the lowest in life sin greatly by this diffidence, because, not expecting aid from God, they seek forbidden protections, some in one way, some in another.

Concerning the fourth.

The parable of the beam in the eye and the speck is an illustrious picture and rebuke of human judgments concerning the Church.

Naturally, the world judges the Church calumniously, sometimes without any cause, sometimes calumniously exaggerating causes, as now, if a priest takes a wife, which hypocrites abhor, although they have no cause at all, nay, they disparage a just matter. Then, if at any time pious men sin through some infirmity, as there are also many lapses of the pious, and many scandals, what exultation and ἐπιχαιρεκακία (malicious joy), what sarcasm among the impious? As it is said in Solomon: A troubled fountain is the just man's fall before the impious. Meanwhile, the impious themselves have far greater sins: idolatry, blasphemies, homicides, stains of lusts, rapines. For the pontifical status is manifestly polluted by all these vices, and the defenders of the society of these crimes contaminate themselves. Therefore,

the precept of Proverbs 10 is delivered concerning the order of judgment, which exhorts individuals to repentance. The just man is in the beginning his own accuser, afterwards he examines his neighbor.

Moreover, the disease of all men, φιλαυτία (self-love), is common; we favor our own customs, we forgive ourselves, we either do not see our own vices or we deem them light, we look more diligently at the vices of others, and we pass a harsher censure upon them.

This unjust inequality has been condemned by many maxims, which ought always to be in our sight, so that we may govern our minds and tongues as if with these reins, not that we may judge others rashly, but that we may recognize and amend our own vices. These are the maxims: Know thyself. Live with yourself, and you will know how short your supply is. Thales, being asked what is difficult? He answered, to know oneself. Again, being asked what is easy? He answered, to rebuke others. The same is also signified in the fable of the two wallets: we carry the vices of others in the front wallet, we carry our own in the other, which hangs on our back.

All these maxims are referred to the saying of Solomon: The just man is in the beginning his own accuser. Afterwards he examines another. Item, to this Parable of the speck, so that we may know that this curiosity, petulance, and perversity of judgments are also divinely prohibited.

But so many things are said about this vice because not only is the inequality in itself unjust, but it is also often the cause of public discords, especially when the vices of governors are traduced. For this disease is common to men, to bear rule with difficulty, and these always have some inconveniences and vices, and good governors often also sin, as it is said: ὃ πολλὰ πράττων, πολλὰ καὶ ἁμαρτάνει (he who does many things, sins many things).

Here it must be considered why governments become more difficult, and the chief cause is that the morals of the people rush into the worse. Luxury, license, and petulance grow in the people, therefore God allows governments to be exasperated. Servitude grew as sins increased. of the world, as indicated by the statue seen by the king in his dream in Daniel. And Salomon says: "Because of the frequent sins of the people, there are frequent changes of kings."

Let us therefore endure the harshness of empires, and acknowledge that it is a punishment for our sins, and let us not curse the governors themselves, but consider these sayings: "Judge not."

Let those who are in the office of judging see to it; God will demand an account from them; let us not arrogate to ourselves another's office.

Likewise, let us know that many public difficulties are alleviated by our fairness.

Therefore it is written: "Forgive, and you will be forgiven."

Likewise: "Christ washing the disciples' feet signifies that the faults of others are not to be exacerbated, but covered, or gently washed away."

And Petrus says: "Love covers all sins," signifying that the sins of others are to be covered among men, and healed skillfully.

Finally, many things are commanded, especially by Christus and the Apostoli, concerning this virtue, which is called ἐπιείκεια, which is the nurse of public concord, and most necessary in the Ecclesia.

But nevertheless, all these things are to be understood as tolerating the curable manners of men, not as approving errors, concerning which the rule is to be held: "If anyone preaches another Evangelium, let him be anathema."

Likewise: "Whoever confesses me before men, I will confess him before my father," etc.

Latin:

Dominica IIII. post Trinitatis. Evangelium Lucae 6.

Estote ergo misericordes, sicut et pater vester misericors est. Nolite iudicare, et non iudicabimini. Nolite condemnare, et non condemnabimini. Dimittite, et dimittetur vobis. Date, et dabitur vobis. Mensuram bonam, confertam, et coagitatam et superfluentem dabunt in sinum vestrum. Eadem quippe mensura, qua mensi fueritis, remetientur vobis. Dicebat autem illis similitudinem: Nunquid potest coecus coecum ducere? Nonne ambo in foveam cadunt? Non est discipulus supra magistrum suum: perfectus autem omnis erit, si sit sicut magister eius. Quid autem vides festucam in oculo fratris tui, trabem autem in proprio oculo non consideras? Aut quomodo potes dicere fratri tuo: Frater, sine, eiiciam festucam de oculo tuo, et ipse in oculo tuo trabem non vides? Hypocrita, eiice primum trabem de oculo tuo, et tunc dispicies, ut eiicias festucam de oculo fratris tui.

Quatuor sunt praecipui loci.

I. Doctrina de bonis operibus. II. Praecepta de quatuor officiis dilectionis, misericordia, non iudicando, remittendo, dando. III. Promissiones et comminationes. IIII. Vituperatio perverse iudicantium, non servantium regulam Proverb. 10. Iustus in principio est accusator sui, postea explorat proximum.

De primo.

Nota est vox Pauli: Fratres, debitores sumus, ne secundum carnem vivamus. Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini: si spiritu carnem mortificabitis, vivetis. Item 1. Iohan. 3.: Nemo nos decipiat, qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est.

Haec dicta sint infixa animis, ut sciamus oportere in salvandis existere inchoatam obedientiam, nec sine ea posse homines salvari, sed oportet fidem in Christum praecedere, et praelucere, et sciendum est, ita placere Deo inchoatam obedientiam, cum reconciliati fide agnoscunt se non satisfacere legi. Et tamen inchoant hanc obedientiam, et credunt eam placere propter pontificem Christum, postquam persona propter mediatorem Christum recepta est. Haec alias saepe dicta sunt, et semper in concionibus de bonis operibus haec summa repetenda est.

De secundo. Praesens concio tradit doctrinam de bonis operibus, et quidem de certis officiis dilectionis, pertinentibus ad quintum praeceptum. Ac longa esset concio, si quis integre de his virtutibus dicturus esset. Sunt autem alia dicta hoc loco, aliis clariora. Praeceptum de dando utcunque intelligi potest, sed illa de non iudicando, et de perversitate iudiciorum, sunt obscuriora, et continent doctrinam necessariam, ad retinendam Ecclesiae pacem et concordiam. Dicam breviter de singulis. Misericordia in genere est affici sensu alienae calamitatis, praesertim iniustae, et opitulari iniuste oppressis, pro vocatione.

Item probabili ratione mitigare iustam calamitatem, et habet duos gradus. Misericordia est, quod opitulatur Constantinus Ecclesiae oppressae a tyrannis. Alius gradus est ἐπιείκεια in poenis male meritorum, ut David post victoriam parcit civibus, qui fuerant seditiosi, et tamen iam redibant ad officium. De hac ἐπιείκεια concionatur, cum inquit: Estote misericordes, sicut pater vester misericors est. Admonet nos quid meriti simus, insania est autem meritum easdem poenas insultare calamitoso.

Porro omnes homines meriti sumus poenas, ideo non insultemus alii aliis, sed potius communi dolore leniamus.
