Item simus grati Deo, qui erga nos fuit misericors, ac liberavit nos, et vult nos suo exemplo erga alios misericordes esse. De hac ἐπιείκεια in Iacobo dicitur: Misericordia sit supra iudicium, id est, rigorem, sed haec habet suas metas, ut alibi dicitur. Nolite iudicare.

Homo imperitus doctrinae Christianae offendit hac voce, quia videtur politias tollere, sed Christus tantum de privatis iudiciis loquitur. Primum igitur sciendum est tria esse iudicia, quae non pertinent ad hunc locum. Ministerium Evangelii, quod iudicat et arguit peccata, sicut Paulus inquit: Admone, increpa, cum omni imperio. Item iudicia magistratum,

Item vituperatio, quae fit sanandi causa, aut aliorum admonendorum causa in flagitio manifesto, ut cum dico: Abstineas a consuetudine huius hominis, quia scio ebriosum esse, et recte dicit lex in ff.: Eum qui nocentem infamat non esse puniendum, quia expedit crimina nota fieri ut emendentur. Haec iudicia non sunt prohibita.

Quae igitur hic prohibet Christus? Respondeo, privatae et calumniosae, scilicet, cum aut bonum factum, aut ambiguum, interpretamur in deteriorem partem, aut leve erratum malevolentia exaggeramus, non studemus sanare. Non intelligit vulgus imperitum, quam facile oriantur ingentes discordiae, et perturbationes regnorum ex talibus initiis, cum homines malevoli, suspicaces, cupidi vindictae, inter se certant odiis et calumniis, ut nunc usitatum est iudicare, hic sacerdos ducit uxorem, ergo est homo levis, non constanter retinens sui ordinis morem. Item, vidi alium familiarius loquentem cum meo inimico, ergo aliquid machinatur adversus me. Haec in vita latissime patent, et praesertim in gubernatione cient magnos tumultus. Ideo Christus de re maxima concionatur hoc loco, cum caeteris, tum vero maxime gubernatoribus, ut discant hos impetus frenare.

Remittite. Vicinum est hoc praeceptum proximo, non solum vitare calumniosa iudicia debemus, sed etiam illis male suspicantibus ignoscere, dissimulare eorum iniurias, non pugnare cum malevolis amarulente, sed potius eos sanare, si sunt sanabiles, aut parcere eis Reipub. causa. Sicut autem supra dixi de non iudicando, non prohiberi ministeria divinitus instituta, sed privatae et calumniosae iudicia, ita hic de remissione sciatur, non praecipi de ministeriis, ne taxent, neve puniant delicta, quae verbo Dei et legibus puniuntur, sed praecipitur privata remissio, quae habet tres gradus.

Primus est, cum levibus iniuriis lacessiti, fingimus nos habere iustas causas, et aemulatione, vel ambitione, vel cupiditate vindictae incendimur, ut premamus adversarium. Hic praecipit Christus de remissione: nam ex talibus initiis magni tumultus, magna dissidia saepe in gubernatione oriuntur.

Secundus gradus est, cum veris causis lacessiti sumus, non tamen atrocibus, in his etiam ἐπιείκεια adhibenda est, ne omnes iniurias persequamur, ut cum David parcit civibus, semper enim potior est habenda ratio tuendae publicae tranquillitatis, quam privati doloris, et huc pertinent haec dicta: Remittite, et remittetur vobis. Universa delicta operit caritas, etc.

Tertius gradus est, quando sunt atroces iniuriae, ubi defensione magistratus opus est, aut alioqui pacis publicae causa coërcendi sunt iniusti impetus, recte confugitur ad officium magistratus, sed tamen accedat in animo remissio coram Deo, quae non impedit poenas.

Date. Hoc praeceptum facilius intelligi potest, complectitur autem duos gradus, dare debita, quae civili vel naturali obligatione debentur, et dare eleemosynas, quae divina obligatione debentur. Nam in utroque genere peccant homines. Magnae fraudes sunt contractuum, cum tamen Deus velit nos exercere obedientiam, in servanda aequalitate in contractibus. Deinde et de eleemosynis divina obligatio est, ut calamitosis, egentibus, et praecipue sociis eiusdem confessionis et fidei opitulemur. Hoc officium habet gradus et metas, ut Paulus inquit, Non ut aliis sit ignavum ocium, vobis afflictio. Item, Fontes tui deriventur foras, tu autem dominus illorum maneto.

De tertio.

Comminationes et promissiones additas intuemur, ut timorem et fidem excitemus. Estque summa comminationum et promissionum in hoc dicto: Qua mensura mensi fueritis, eadem reddetur et vobis, et quidem textus ait, fore ut cumulate reddatur, ut Constantius, etsi fuit ethnicus, tamen quia erat misericors, nec saeviit in Christianos, non est excussus ex imperio. Diocletianus etsi fuit sapiens princeps, tamen tandem sibi ipsi mortem conscivit, metu Constantini.

Et universaliter meminerimus poenam talionis ordinationem divinam esse, quam Deus regulariter servet, etiamsi humana iudicia eam negligunt, aut homines eam non considerant. Ideo et vetustissimae leges religiose sanxerunt poenam talionis, ut ex Moise apparet, ut in versu Radamanthi: Si patitur quae fecit, poena est iusta putanda. Nam primi patres hanc Dei ordinationem diligenter proposuerunt populo, ut commonefacerent homines de timore Dei, et hinc multa dicta sunta sunt: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. Item: Vae qui praedaris, quia et tu spoliaberis.

Primum ergo comminationes nos hortentur ad timorem Dei, et sciamus de poenis praesentibus et futuris dici. Secundo promissiones etiam loquuntur de futuris praemiis, sicut clare dicit Paulus 1. Timoth. 6.: Pietas habet promissiones praesentis vitae et futurae. Et Christus inquit: Recipiet centuplum in hac vita, et post hanc vitam, vitam aeternam.

Iam hic discamus exercere fidem. Corporales promissiones traditae sunt, ut fides exerceatur simul in quaerenda reconciliatione coram Deo, et in expectatione auxilii corporalis.

Quare semper addamus promissionibus corporalibus initio promissionem praecipuam Evangelii, de remissione peccatorum. David expectat victoriam a Deo, sed prius sentit sibi Deum propicium esse.

Ita vult vos Deus fidem exercere dupliciter. Primum crede tibi Deum propicium esse propter Filium, deinde obtempera et expecta ab eo auxilium, da pauperi, et expecta vicissim Deum tibi daturum esse victum, pacem, et alia bona. 2. Corinth. 9. Davidi multi in regno insidiantur. Iam si more tyrannorum omnes suspectos tollere vellet, non esset finis grassandi. Quid igitur agit. Primum credit se habere Deum propicium. Deinde diligenter facit officium suum. Tertio expectat a Deo defensionem magno et tranquillo animo, nec movetur suspicionibus, ut saevitiam exerceat. Hoc exemplum singuli ad suam vocationem accommodare possunt, quia nulla quamvis humilis vocatio est sine periculis. Et diligenter haec exercitia fidei consideremus: plurimum enim in vita peccant summi ac infimi hac diffidentia, quod non expectantes a Deo auxilium, quaerunt inconcessa praesidia, alii aliter.

De quarto.

Parabola de trabe in oculo, et festuca, est illustris pictura et reprehensio humanorum iudiciorum de Ecclesia.

Naturaliter mundus calumniose iudicat de Ecclesia, alias sine ulla causa, alias calumniose exaggerans causas, ut nunc, si sacerdos ducat uxorem, quam abhorrent hypocritae cum nullam prorsus causam habeant, imo rem iustam vituperent. Deinde si quando peccant homines pii infirmitate aliqua, ut sunt etiam multi lapsus piorum, et multa scandala, quanta exultatio et ἐπιχαιρεκακία, qui sarcasmi apud impios? Sicut dicitur in Salomone: Fons conturbatus est iustus lapsus coram impio. Interim ipsi impii habent longe maiora peccata, idololatriam, blasphemias, homicidia, libidinum maculas, rapinas. Nam his vitiis omnibus manifeste pollutus est status pontificius, et contaminant se defensores societatis horum scelerum.

Traditur ergo praeceptum Proverb. 10. de ordine iudicii, quod singulos ad poenitentiam hortatur. Iustus in principio accusator est sui, postea explorat proximum.

Caeterum et communis est omnium hominum morbus φιλαυτία, nostris moribus favemus, nobis ignoscimus, nostra vitia aut non videmus, aut levia ducimus, aliena diligentius contuemur, et censuram de eis acerbiorem agimus.

Haec iniusta inaequalitas multis sententiis vituperata est, quae semper in conspectu nobis esse debent, ut tanquam his frenis mentes et linguas regamus, ne de aliis temere iudicent, sed ut nostra vitia agnoscamus et emendemus. Sunt autem hae sententiae: Nosce teipsum. Tecum habita, et noris quam sit tibi curta supellex. Thales interrogatus, quid sit difficile? Respondit, seipsum nosse. Rursus interrogatus, quid facile? respondit, reprehendere alios. Idem et in Apologo de duabus manticis significatum est, vitia aliorum gerimus in priore mantica, nostra gerimus in altera, quae in tergo pendet.

Haec sententiae omnes referantur ad dictum Salomonis: Iustus initio accusator est sui. Postea explorat alium. Item, ad hanc Parabolam de festuca, ut sciamus etiam divinitus prohiberi hanc curiositatem, petulantiam et perversitatem iudiciorum.

Ideo autem tam multa de hoc vitio dicuntur, quia non solum inaequalitas per sese est iniusta, sed etiam causa est saepe publicarum discordiarum, maxime cum vitia gubernatorum traducuntur. Nam est hic morbus communis est hominum, aegre ferre imperia, et haec semper aliqua habent incommoda et vitia, ac boni gubernatores saepe etiam peccant, ut dicitur: ὃ πολλὰ πράττων, πολλὰ καὶ ἁμαρτάνει.

Hic cogitandum est, cur imperia fiant difficiliora, ac praecipua causa est, quia populi mores ruunt in deterius. Crescunt in populo luxus, licentia, petulantia, ideo sinit Deus imperia exasperari. Crevit servitus crescentibus peccatis. mundi, ut indicat statua visa regi in somno apud Danielem. Et Salomon inquit: Propter peccata populi crebrae sunt mutationes regum.

Feramus igitur imperiorum asperitatem, et agnoscamus poenam esse nostrorum peccatorum, nec maledicamus ipsis gubernatoribus, sed cogitemus haec dicta: Non iudicate.

Ipsi viderint qui sunt in officio iudicandi, ab ipsis Deus rationes reposcet, non arrogemus nobis alienum officium.

Item, sciamus nostra aequitate leniri multas publicas difficultates.

Ideo scriptum est: Remittite, et remittetur vobis.

Item: Christus lavans discipulis pedes, significat non exulcerandos esse aliorum naevos, sed tegendoos, aut suaviter abluendos.

Et Petrus inquit: Universa delicta operit dilectio, significans aliena delicta tegenda esse inter homines, et arte sananda.

Denique multa praecipiuntur, praesertim a Christo et Apostolis de hac virtute, quae vocatur ἐπιείκεια, quae est nutrix publicae concordiae, et in Ecclesia maxime necessaria.

Sed tamen haec omnia intelligantur de tolerandis moribus sana-bilibus hominum, non de approbandis erroribus, de quibus teneatur regula: Si quis aliud Evangelium docuerit, anathema sit.

Item: Qui confitetur me coram hominibus, confitebor eum coram patre meo, etc.

## 7:11-17 The Sixteenth Sunday After Trinity
The Sixteenth Sunday after Trinity.

The Gospel of Luke 7.

And it came to pass afterwards, that He went into a city which is called Naim; and there went with Him His many disciples, and a great crowd. And when He drew near to the gate of the city, behold a dead man was carried out, the only son of his mother; and she was a widow: and a great crowd of the city was with her. And when the Lord saw her, He was moved with mercy towards her, and said to her: Weep not. And He came near and touched the bier. And they that carried it stood still. And He said: Young man, I say to thee, arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And He gave him to his mother. And there came a fear on them all: and they glorified God, saying: That a great prophet is risen up among us: and, That God hath visited His people. And this rumour of Him went forth throughout all Judea, and throughout all the country round about.

There is one principal point of this Gospel, the miracle of Christ, which a great part of men think pertains only to that widow whose son was raised. But let us establish that it pertains also to us, and indeed to each one of us. For it is a testimony that Christ wishes to be acknowledged as the vivifier, the consoler, and the high priest, who is truly and spontaneously affected by our troubles and miseries, and likewise as the victor over sin, and death, and the whole kingdom of the devil.

For this is the proper and peculiar doctrine of the Gospel, that God truly looks upon the miserable and afflicted, who are oppressed by troubles and terrified by the sight and sense of their own unworthiness, and by the voice of the law, which cries out that God is angry on account of sin, and in such punishments shows nothing but the wrath of God.

Nor is there any doctrine that shows true consolation in these troubles, except the sole voice of the Gospel brought forth through the Son of God; this testifies that God truly looks upon the troubled, and does not cast them away because they are unworthy and have deserved the punishments of the law, but that He wishes to have mercy on those who flee to the Son the mediator, and believe that they are forgiven on His account according to the promises, and that He wishes to hear those who call upon Him with this faith, as it is said: Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall receive consolation.

And so that the testimony may become more evident, for this reason it is especially necessary for the Church to be subjected to the cross and troubles of every kind, because He wishes it to exercise repentance in these, and to acknowledge and hate sin; likewise, He wishes invocation to be exercised, and faith in the mercy and presence of God to grow; finally, He wishes it to be made so similar to the image of the Son of God, and that these very afflictions be testimonies of the future of liberation and glorification in eternal life, as is often said elsewhere.

A notable testimony of this doctrine is expressed in this history, and the Evangelist amplifies the affection of both persons, the widow and Christ, with many circumstances.

How great the grief of the poor woman, especially the widow, was at the death of her son, and an only son at that, even those who have experienced it cannot grasp in their minds: but the greater the force of grief in the widow, the greater in turn is the grief by which Christ is moved, and He comes of His own accord to help her, and in such a way that the magnitude of the joy, which she receives from her son being raised to life, far exceeds the grief which she had begun to feel from his death. Moreover, there is a significant emphasis in the word ἐσπλαγχνίσθη [he was moved with compassion], by which the Evangelist testifies that Christ was not affected by a light movement of the mind, but was moved by an incredible grief of heart, just as John writes that He did at the tomb of Lazarus. Then, also moved by a great ardor of spirit, He raises the dead.

But here someone might object: God is ἀπαθής [impassible], therefore in God there is no mercy, joy, and similar affections.

I answer: I deny the antecedent. For God is not a Stoic, but He is affected by our evils, and it is His greatest pleasure to help us and to hear us. And because στοργαὶ [natural affections] are most clearly expressed in excellent natures, it is necessary that in God also these στοργαὶ be so much the more ardent, as He is more excellent than all other natures created by Him.

Since, therefore, God is most vehemently affected by our evils, we ought to willingly flee to Him and call upon Him, according to that passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 4: Let us approach with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and grace for timely help. But these things are easier to say than to put into practice when there is need, and that indeed is by far the most difficult of all. For such is the infirmity of human nature even in the pious, that it can scarcely raise itself above the sense of its own unworthiness in afflictions, and in others there is a blindness as great as that in Epicurus, so that they think all things happen by chance, and that there is no God who looks upon us.

Is it a sin to doubt about mercy? It is. On the contrary. Whatever the law commands is right, but the law commands that we feel that God is angry at sin, and does not forgive: therefore it is right to feel so. I answer: I concede the whole argument, but to feel so is not enough. For the Gospel concerning Christ must be added, and indeed in such a way that we feel that grace abounds over sin, as Paul teaches in Romans 5. Wherefore, not only must that be felt, that God is angry at sin, in such a way that no one could bear that anger or appease it, except the Son, but also in those very terrors the mind must be lifted up above sin, so that it may determine that the grace by which God remits our sins, as we believe in Christ, is far greater.

Another question. Is it lawful to mourn the dead? It is. On the contrary. Christ says to the widow: Do not weep. Therefore He forbids mourning. I answer the antecedent:

Christ by these words consoles the mourner, which is in itself a pious duty, and He forbids mourning to the woman, not because the son is dead, but because he is about to live. Indeed, by the example of Christ, it is lawful for us also to follow our dead with tears, just as He Himself wept for the death of Lazarus, and here He mourns together with the widow. For if anyone is not affected by the evils of others, especially of his own, he is unworthy of the name of man. But yet we ought to differ from others who mourn, in that we moderate our grief, just as Paul commands to the Thessalonians: Do not mourn, as others who have no hope. He does not forbid mourning at the death of those who are dear to us: for although we hope that it will be well for them after this life, yet that bitterness which is in this separation of soul from body cannot but move us, but because we have the hope of which I spoke, therefore grief ought to be more moderate in us than in others. And this, finally, is true fortitude, not that by which men are not affected by sad things, but by which they restrain themselves, so that, moved by grief in this corrupt nature, they do not act basely, as Virgil writes of Aeneas: The mind remains unmoved, the tears roll down in vain, that is, the judgment remains in its purpose, so that it may obey the command of God, as Virgil imagines, even if it is torn away with great grief of mind.

Finally, in this miracle, one must look at the image of the dead man coming back to life, which if we truly perceived, there would be no calamities anywhere that we would not endure with a cheerful and willing mind. For the magnitude of the joy, which we would perceive from that glorification which is to be after this life, when we shall behold face to face the image of God, to which we were created, would easily overwhelm them. The recognition of Christ is followed by confession and preaching, and finally new movements in the minds of men. To this pertains what the Evangelist says: Fear seized all, and they were glorifying God.

Latin:

Dominica XVI. post Trinitatis.

Evangelium Lucae 7.

Et factum est deinceps, ibat in civitatem, quae vocatur Naim, et ibant cum eo discipuli eius multi, et turba copiosa. Cum autem appropinquaret portae civitatis, ecce defunctus efferebatur, filius unicus matris suae, et haec vidua erat, et turba civitatis multa cum illa. Et cum vidisset eam Dominus, misericordia motus est erga eam, et dixit illi: Noli flere. Et accessit ac tetigit loculum. Hi autem, qui portabant, steterunt. Et ait: Adolescens, tibi dico, surge. Et resedit mortuus, et coepit loqui, et dedit illum matri suae. Accepit autem omnes timor, et glorificant Deum, dicentes: Quia Propheta magnus surrexit in nobis, et quia Deus visitavit plebem suam. Et exiit hic sermo in universam Iudaeam de eo, et in omnem finitimam regionem.

Huius Evangelii locus unus est principalis, miraculum Christi, quod magna pars hominum existimat tantum ad viduam illam pertinere, cuius filius resuscitatus est. Sed nos statuamus etiam ad nos, et quidem singulos, pertinere. Est enim testimonium, quod Christus velit agnosci, tanquam vivificator, consolator, et pontifex, qui vere et ultro afficiatur nostris aerumnis atque miseriis, item tanquam victor peccati, et mortis, et totius regni diaboli.

Est enim haec propria et peculiaris doctrina Evangelii, quod Deus vere respiciat miseros et afflictos, qui sunt oppressi aerumnis, et perterrefacti conspectu et sensu propriae indignitatis, et voce legis, quae clamat Deum irasci propter peccatum, et in talibus poenis nihil nisi iram Dei ostendit.

Nec ulla est doctrina, quae ostendat veram consolationem in his aerumnis, nisi sola vox Evangelii prolata per Filium Dei, haec testatur Deum vere respicere aerumnosos, nec propterea eos abiicere, quod sint indigni, et meriti poenas legis, sed velle eorum misereri, qui confugiunt ad Filium mediatorem, et credunt sibi propter ipsum ignosci iuxta promissiones, et hac fide invocantes velle exaudire, sicut dicitur: Beati qui lugent, quia hi consolationem accipient.

Et ut testimonium fiat evidentius, ideo praecipue Ecclesiam oportet esse subiectam cruci et aerumnis omnis generis, quia vult eam et poenitentiam in his exercere, et agnoscere ac odisse peccatum, item vult exerceri invocationem, et crescere fidem misericordiae et praesentiae Dei, postremo vult eam ita similem fieri imaginis Filii Dei, et ipsas afflictiones esse testimonia futurae liberationis et glorificationis in vita aeterna, ut alias saepe dicitur.

Huius doctrinae insigne testimonium expressum est in hac historia, ac Evangelista utriusque personae, viduae et Christi affectum multis circumstantiis amplificat.

Quantus fuerit dolor mulierculae, praesertim viduae, mortuo filio, et quidem unico, ne quidem illi, qui sunt experti, animo complecti possunt: sed quo maior est vis doloris in vidua, eo maiore vicissim Christus dolore commotus ultro venit, ut opituletur ei, atque ita, ut magnitudo gaudii, quod ex filio resuscitato percipit, longe superet dolorem, quem ex morte coeperat. Insignis autem est emphasis in verbo ἐσπλαγχνίσθη, quo testatur Evangelista, Christum non levi motu animi affectum fuisse, sed incredibili quodam dolore cordis motum esse, sicut ad Lazari monumentum eum fecisse scribit Iohannes. Deinde etiam ingenti ardore animi motus resuscitat mortuum.

Sed hic obiiciat aliquis: Deus est ἀπαθής, ergo in Deo non sunt misericordia, laeticia, et similes affectus.

Respondeo: Nego antecedens. Deus enim non est Stoicus, sed afficitur nostris malis, et summa ei voluptas est iuvare nos et exaudire. Et quia στοργαὶ in praestantibus naturis sunt expressissimae, necesse est etiam in Deo στοργὰς tanto ardentiore esse, quanto est omnibus aliis naturis a se conditis praestantior.

Cum igitur Deus vehementissime afficiatur nostris malis, libenter ad eum confugere, eumque invocare debemus, iuxta illud Epistolae ad Hebraeos cap. 4.: Accedamus cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae, ut consequamur misericordiam et gratiam ad auxilium oportunum. Sed haec facilius dici, quam ad usum cum opus est, transferri possunt, id vero est longe omnium difficilimum. Tanta est enim infirmitas humanae naturae etiam in piis, ut supra sensum suae indignitatis sese erigere vix possit in afflictionibus, in aliis coecitas tanta quanta est in Epicuro, ut existiment omnia casu fieri, neque Deum esse ullum, qui nos respiciat.

Estne peccatum dubitare de misericordia? Est. Contra. Quicquid iubet lex, rectum est, sed lex iubet, ut sentiamus Deum irasci peccato, non ignoscere: ergo ita sentire rectum est. Respondeo: Concedo totum argumentum, sed ita sentire non satis est. Addendum enim est Evangelium de Christo, et quidem ita, ut sentiamus gratiam exuberare supra peccatum, ut docet Paulus Rom. 5. Quamobrem non tantum illud sentiendum est, quod Deus irascatur peccato, ita, ut nemo illam iram ferre, aut placare potuerit, nisi Filius, sed etiam in illis ipsis terroribus animus extollendus est supra peccatum, ita, ut statuat gratiam longe maiorem esse, qua Deus remittit nobis peccata credentibus in Christum.

Alia quaestio. Licetne lugere mortuos? Licet. Contra. Christus inquit ad viduam: Noli flere. Ergo prohibet luctum.

Respondeo ad antecedens: Christus his verbis consolatur lugentem, quod est per se pium officium, et prohibet luctum mulieri, non quia mortuus est filius, sed quia victurus est. Imo exemplo Christi licet nobis etiam lacrymis prosequi nostros mortuos, sicut ipse deflevit mortem Lazari, et hic una cum vidua luget. Nam si quis non afficitur malis aliorum, maximo suorum, hic indignus est nomine hominis. Sed tamen hoc debemus a caeteris, qui lugent, differre, ut nostrum dolorem moderemur, sicut praecipit Paulus ad Thess.: Nolite lugere, sicut caeteri, qui spem non habent. Non prohibet luctum, in morte eorum qui nobis cari sunt: etsi enim speramus eis bene fore post hanc vitam, tamen illa acerbitas, quae est in ista separatione animi a corpore, non potest nos non commovere, sed quia spem, quam dixi, habemus, ideo dolor moderatior esse in nobis, quam in aliis debet. Atque haec demum est vera fortitudo, non qua non afficiuntur homines rebus tristibus, sed qua cohibent sese, ne quid in hac corrupta natura dolore commoti turpiter faciant, sicut Virgilius de Aenea scribit: Mens immota manet, lacrymae volvuntur inanes, id est, iudicium manet in proposito, ut obtemperet mandato Dei, sicut fingit Virgilius, etiamsi cum magno animi dolore avellitur.

Postremo in hoc miraculo intuenda est imago reviviscentis mortui, quam si vere cerneremus, nihil esset ubique calamitatum, quod non hilari ac lubenti animo pateremur. Facile enim eas obrueret magnitudo gaudii, quod perciperemus ex illa glorificatione, quae post hanc vitam futura est, cum de facie ad faciem intuebimur imaginem Dei, ad quam conditi sumus. Agnitionem Christi sequitur confessio et praedicatio, denique novi motus in animus hominum. Hue pertinet quod ait Evangelista: Timor cepit omnes, et glorificabant Deum.

## 7:36 Mary Magdalene
The Gospel of Mary Magdalene, Luke 7.

A certain one of the Pharisees asked Jesus to eat with him, and having entered into the house of the Pharisee, he reclined.

And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she knew that he had reclined in the house of the Pharisee, brought an alabaster jar of ointment, and standing behind at his feet weeping, she began to water his feet with tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment.

But the Pharisee who had invited him, seeing this, said within himself, saying: If this man were a Prophet, he would surely know who and what kind of woman she is who touches him, for she is a sinner.

And Jesus answering, said to him: Simon, I have something to say to you.

But he said: Master, speak.

Two debtors were to a certain moneylender, one owed five hundred denarii, but the other fifty.

But when they had nothing with which to pay, he forgave both.

Which therefore of them, tell me, will love him more?

But Simon answering, said: I suppose that he to whom he forgave more.

But he said to him: You have judged rightly.

And turning to the woman, he said to Simon: Do you see this woman?

I entered into your house, you gave me no water for my feet, but she has watered my feet with tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head. You gave me no kiss, but she, from the time she entered, has not ceased to kiss my feet.

You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.

For which reason I say to you: Her many sins are forgiven, because she has loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loves less.

But he said to her: Your sins are forgiven.

And they who reclined together began to say within themselves: Who is this, who even forgives sins?

But he said to the woman: Your faith has made you safe, go in peace.

It has three principal points.

I. The whole history is an example of the doctrine of repentance, which is the proper doctrine of the Gospel.

II. At the same time, a comparison of the pious to the hypocrites is proposed.

III. Finally, the whole history is a wonderful image of the Church.

On the first.

We always say that in conversion there must exist contrition, that is, terrors born from the recognition of the wrath of God against sin, as is seen in Adam, David, Hezekiah, Peter, Paul, and many others, and Joel says: Rend your hearts into lamentation. And Isaiah 66: To whom shall I look? except to the humble and contrite in spirit, and him who trembles at my words. And 2 Cor. 7: Sorrow according to God effects repentance unto salvation. Item, Rom. 7: Sin through the law killed me, that sin might become exceedingly sinful, that is, that the guilt and wrath of God might be seen. For when human security does not see what a great thing sin is, God judges hearts by his word, and shows his wrath; here we recognize that God is truly angry, and we are terrified, thus sin becomes exceedingly guilty, etc.

But how great a thing it is to offend God, let it be estimated from the first sin, what a horrible punishment followed the first disobedience of men, namely, the perpetual misery of the entire posterity: what punishment followed the fall of David? But the human mind, as it does not comprehend the immense justice and wrath of God: so it cannot comprehend the magnitude of sin, but we see it a little when hearts are truly terrified, as Jeremiah says: After you showed me, my thigh was struck. Therefore also this huge mass of calamities has been imposed on the human race, that it might admonish us concerning repentance, as Paul says: We are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world. Let there exist, therefore, in us contrition and recognition of the wrath of God, as is seen in this woman, who stands weeping at the feet of Christ.

On the second. But it is not enough that terrors exist, nor that we flee from God, as Cain, Saul, Judas, but let us know that a propitiator has been given to us, to whom God wills us to take refuge, and indeed let us know that the chief of all commandments is to acknowledge this Son of God, to honor him, and through him to desire to return to the Father, as it is written: Kiss the Son. Blessed are all who trust in Him.

Let us also know that the promises concerning the remission of sins and liberation from sin and eternal death have often been confirmed by God with an oath. Truly, therefore, God wants us to be saved, as: I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live. Item: The Lord has sworn, and He will not repent, etc.

And Psalm 88, Augustine says: Christ will reign forever among His saints; this God said, this He promised; if that is a small thing, He swore it; because, therefore, the promise is firm not according to our merits, but according to His mercy, let us believe and call upon Him, etc.

Therefore, the woman comes to this Lord and seeks consolation. She hears, therefore, the voice concerning the remission of sins: Your faith has saved you, go in peace.

These words preach about the other part of conversion, namely, faith. Christ expressly names faith; He says that through faith one is received into grace and saved.

Thus, the two parts of repentance are clearly proposed here. Contrition, by which sin is judged: but here fear would overwhelm the mind with eternal death, unless consolation were to approach. Therefore, the other part approaches, namely faith, which is the trust that lifts up the soul, that God, through mercy on account of the Mediator, receives the believer, truly forgives, hears, and will make him an heir of eternal life.

By this trust, the heart conceives new light and life, as it is said: The just shall live by his faith. Item, that we may receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

On the third point.

But why did He say before: Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much, and to whom much is forgiven, he loves much?

Here, love seems to be called the cause of remission. The easiest and simplest answer is: Christ testifies that she has been converted, and certainly conversion is necessary, and He attributes to this miserable woman that very excellent praise which the people of the law falsely arrogated to themselves, as if Christ were saying: This woman fulfills the law, and is a member of the people of God. You neither fulfill the law, nor are you a member of the people of God.

It is certain, however, and we always say this, that conversion is necessary, or begun obedience, and yet when He says: Your faith has saved you, Christ also testifies that remission is received by faith, not on account of obedience or love.

Another answer is more expeditious. There is a twofold absolution. One of the conscience, which is done by faith. Another public before the Church, which is done on account of works.

But more on these solutions later.

First, let the very sermon of Christ be considered, which is the sweetest consolation to the pious, to be joined to this sentence: Grace abounds over sin, and it must be opposed to temptation, by which the heart is tormented by the magnitude of some certain sin, as Peter is tormented by the sight of his denial, or David by the sight of his adultery and murder. Here this voice must be opposed: Grace abounds over sin, and here: To whom much is forgiven, he loves much, as if to say, the more you acknowledge the remission, the more you will acknowledge the magnitude of God's benefit toward you. A greater flame of faith and love therefore arises, and conversely, God loves the one who loves more, more. Thus God consoles the one who is deeply mourning, and embraces both; He testifies that God truly forgets our sins and does not bear a grudge [μνησικακεῖν], and He attributes to the woman the praise of true obedience, so that she may be able to retain faith, and know that she henceforth pleases God even if she previously offended horribly.

Therefore, this consolation of Christ must be diligently observed and opposed to the magnitude of the fall, lest we later think that we are loved less, received less, etc. And let it be referred to this saying: Grace abounds over sin.

On the contrary, the pride of the Pharisee is censured; Christ signifies that he is ignorant of the remission of sins, and therefore is without love. But I return to the solutions.

It is most expeditious to say that there is a twofold remission. One before God, this is done by faith. Another before the Church, this is done on account of good works.

And this solution is supported by the fact that it is said to the woman: Your faith has saved you. But to the Pharisee who accuses and condemns the woman, works and love are alleged, so that she may be absolved before him as well.

If anyone, however, demands another answer, the true and infallible sentence is that faith cannot rely equally on the promise and on the condition of our dignity; if it is to be thought that you will have remission when you have enough merits, as the narrative in the text clearly shows, He does not want us to transfer it to our works, nor can faith wander, and having left the propitiator, seek its own dignity.

Why then is it said elsewhere: Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much?

I answer, that a synecdoche is being used, as if it said, because she is converted. For it is most true that conversion is necessary, and yet in the meantime remission is received by faith, and not because of our dignity. These synecdoches are most common. Isaiah 1: Cease to do evil. Item: Turn to me, and I will turn to you. Item: Redeem your sins with justice, and there shall be healing for your transgressions. These sayings and similar ones contain a synecdoche, in which several parts of conversion are comprehended, which how they are to be discerned, must be learned from other places.

For it is certain that remission is given because of the propitiator, not because of our dignity, and yet it is true that love ought to follow, that is, new obedience, which he here adorns with great praises, so that he may testify that it pleases God.

Allegory.

There are two congregations in the Church. One is of hypocrites, who are secure and puffed up by the persuasion of justice; they neither know sin, nor the remission of sins, nor faith, and in the meantime, because perhaps they perform discipline moderately, they admire themselves, and boast that they are just; Christ sits at the table of these, that is, these are the pontiffs, the governors, they have the title of the Church, wherefore under them the voice of the Gospel sounds somewhere. There is also another congregation, namely, one hearing the Gospel, acknowledging sin, truly mourning its errors, seeking Christ with true faith: to this congregation, performing repentance and believing, Christ attributes the testimony that it is the true Church, he also attributes the praise of true obedience, that it fulfills the law, that it loves. Hypocrites falsely arrogate this praise to themselves, therefore Christ transfers it to this congregation, which the hypocrites despise, because the life of this congregation is less showy.

But the chief duty, which Christ preaches so much, is this, that the woman washed and anointed his feet. But the feet signify especially the ministry of the Gospel: the true Church cares for this and strives to protect and preserve it with every duty, it fosters pious teachers with all offices. On the contrary, the Pharisees, the Pontiffs, neglect the ministry of the Gospel, they seek empires, they establish laws useful for protecting wealth and dignities, they kill pious teachers.

Latin:

Evangelium die Mariae Magdalenae, Lucae 7.

Rogabat Iesum quidam de Pharisaeis, ut manducaret cum ipso, et ingressus in domum Pharisaei, discubuit.

Et ecce mulier in civitate quae erat peccatrix, ut cognovit quod accubuisset in domo Pharisaei, attulit alabastrum unguenti, et stans retro secus pedes eius flens, lacrymis coepit rigare pedes eius, et capillis capitis sui extergebat, et osculabatur pedes eius, et unguento ungebat.

Videns autem Pharisaeus qui vocaverat eum, ait intra se, dicens: Hic si esset Propheta, sciret utique, quae et qualis est mulier quae tangit eum, quia peccatrix est.

Et respondens Iesus, dixit ad illum: Simon, habeo tibi aliquid dicere.

At ille ait: Magister, dic.

Duo debitores erant cuidam foeneratori, unus debebat denarios quingentos, alter autem quinquaginta.

Non habentibus autem illis unde redderent, donavit utrisque.

Quis ergo eorum, dic eum plus diliget?

Respondens autem Simon, dixit: Existimo, quod is, cui plus donavit.

At ipse dixit ei: Recte iudicasti.

Et conversus ad mulierem, dixit Simoni: Vides hanc mulierem?

Intravi in domum tuam, aquam pedibus meis non dedisti, haec autem lacrymis rigavit pedes meos, et capillis capitis sui extersit, Osculum mihi non dedisti, haec autem ex quo intravit, non cessavit osculari pedes meos.

Oleo caput meum non unxisti, haec autem unguento unxit pedes meos.

Propter quod dico tibi: Remittuntur ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum, Cui autem minus dimittitur, minus diligit.

Dixit autem illi: Remittuntur tibi peccata multa.

Et coeperunt qui simul accumbebant, dicere intra se: Quis est hic, qui etiam peccata remittit?

Dixit autem ad mulierem: Fides tua salvam te fecit, vade in pace.

Tres habet praecipuos locos.

I. Tota historia est exemplum doctrinae de poenitentia, quae est propria Evangelii doctrina.

II. Simul etiam proponitur collatio piorum ad hypocritas.

III. Denique tota historia est mirifica imago Ecclesiae.

De primo.

Semper dicimus in conversione oportere existere contritionem, hoc est, pavores ortos ex agnitione irae Dei adversus peccatum, sicut in Adam, Davide, Ezechia, Petro, Paulo, et aliis multis cernitur, et Ioël inquit: Scindite corda vestra in planctum. Et Esaiae 66.: Ad quem respiciam? nisi ad humilem et contritum spiritu, et trementem sermones meos. Et 2. Cor. 7.: Tristitia secundum Deum efficit poenitentiam ad salutem. Item, Rom. 7.: Peccatum per legem occidit me, ut fieret excellenter peccatum, id est, ut conspiceretur reatus et ira Dei. Cum enim humana securitas non videat, quanta res sit peccatum, Deus verbo suo corda iudicat, et ostendit iram suam, hic agnoscimus Deum vere irasci, et expavescimus, sic peccatum fit excellenter reum etc.

Quanto vero res sit offendere Deum, aestimetur ex primo peccato, quam horribilis poena secuta est primam inobedientiam hominum, videlicet, perpetua miseria posteritatis universae: quanta poena secuta est lapsum Davidis? Sed humana mens, ut immensam iusticiam et iram Dei non comprehendit: ita nec magnitudinem peccati comprehendere potest, sed aliquantulum aspicimus, cum corda vere expavescunt, ut inquit Ieremias: Postquam ostendisti mihi, percussifemur meum. Ideo etiam haec ingens moles calamitatum imposita est generi humano, ut nos de poenitentia admoneat, sicut Paulus inquit: Corripimur a Domino, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. Existat igitur in nobis contritio et agnitio irae Dei, sicut in hac muliere conspicitur, quae flens astat ad pedes Christi.

De secundo. Sed non satis existere pavores, nec fugiamus Deum, ut Cain, Saul, Iudas, sed sciamus donatum nobis esse propiciatorem, ad quem Deus vult nos confugere, et quidem sciamus omnium mandatorum praecipuum esse, hunc Filium Dei agnoscere, honore afficere, et per eum velle ad patrem redire, sicut scriptum est: Osculamini Filium. Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.

Sciamus item saepe iureiurando a Deo confirmatas esse promissiones, de remissione peccatorum, et liberatione a peccato et morte aeterna. Vere igitur vult Deus nos salvos fieri, ut: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Item: Iuravit Dominus, et non poenitebit eum etc.

Et Psal. 88. inquit Augustinus: In aeternum regnabit Christus in sanctis suis, hoc dixit Deus, hoc promisit, si parvum est, hoc iuravit, quia ergo non secundum merita nostra, sed secundum illius misericordiam firma est promissio, credamus et invocemus etc.

Venit ergo ad hunc Dominum mulier, et quaerit consolationem. Audit igitur vocem de remissione peccatorum, Fides tua salvam te fecit, vade in pace.

Haec verba concionantur de altera parte conversionis, scilicet de fide. Christus expresse nominat fidem, dicit eam fide recipi in gratiam et salvari.

Ita duae partes poenitentiae hic clare proponuntur. Contritio, qua iudicatur peccatum: sed hic pavor opprimeret mentem aeterna morte, nisi accederet consolatio. Accedit ergo altera pars, scilicet fides, quae est fiducia erigens animum, quod Deus per misericordiam propter mediatorem recipiat credentem, vere ignoscat, exaudiat, faciet haeredem vitae aeternae.

Hac fiducia concipit cor novam lucem et vitam, ut dicitur: Iustus fide sua vivet. Item, ut promissionem Spiritus accipiamus per fidem.

De tertio.

Sed cur antea dixit: Remittuntur ei multa, quia dilexit multum, et cui multum remittitur, multum diligit?

Hic videtur dilectio dici causa remissionis. Facilima et simplicissima responsio est: Christus testatur conversam esse, et certe conversio necessaria est, et tribuit huic miserae mulieri iam illam eximiam laudem, quam sibi falso arrogabat populus legis, quasi dicat Christus: Haec mulier implet legem, et est membrum populi Dei. Tu nec imples legem, nec es membrum populi Dei.

Constat autem, et semper haec dicimus, conversionem necessariam esse, seu incoatam obedientiam, et tamen cum dicat: Fides tua salvam te fecit, testatur etiam Christus, remissionem accipi fide, non propter obedientiam aut dilectionem.

Alia responsio est expeditior. Duplex est absolutio. Alia conscientiae, quae fit fide. Alia publica coram Ecclesia, quae fit propter opera.

Sed de his solutionibus postea.

Prius ipsa concio Christi consideretur, quae est dulcissima consolatio piis, adiungenda huic sententiae. Gratia exuberat supra peccatum, et opponi debet tentationi, qua cor magnitudine certi alicuius peccati angitur, ut Petrus angitur conspectu negationis, aut David conspectu adulterii, caedis. Hic opponenda est vox: Gratia exuberat supra peccatum, et hic: Cui multum remittitur, multum diligit, quasi dicat, quo magis agnoscis remissionem, eo magis agnosces magnitudinem beneficii Dei erga te. Maior ergo flamma fidei et dilectionis oritur, et vicissim magis diligit Deus magis diligentem. Sic consolatur Deus valde lugentem, et utrunque complectitur, testatur Deum vere oblivisci peccata nostra, et non μνησικακεῖν, et tribuit mulieri laudem verae obedientiae, ut possit retinere fidem, et sciat se deinceps placere Deo etiam si antea horribiliter offendit.

Diligenter igitur observanda est haec Christi consolatio, et opponenda magnitudini lapsus, ne postea existimemus, nos minus diligi, minus recipi etc. Et referatur ad hoc dictum: Gratia exuberat supra peccatum.

Econtra taxatur superbia Pharisaei, hunc significat Christus ignarum esse remissionis peccatorum, ideoque sine dilectione esse. Sed redeo ad solutiones.

Expeditissima est, dicere, duplicem esse remissionem, Alteram coram Deo, hanc fieri fide. Alteram coram Ecclesia, hanc fieri propter bona opera.

Et huic solutioni patrocinatur, quod ad mulierem dicitur: Fides tua salvam te fecit. Sed Pharisaeo accusanti mulierem et damnanti, allegantur opera et dilectio, ut apud hunc quoque absolvatur.

Si quis autem flagitat aliam responsionem, vera est et infallabilis sententia, fidem non posse niti pariter promissione, et conditione nostrae dignitatis, si cogitandum erit, tunc habebis remissionem, cum satis habebis meritorum, ut clare ostendit narratio in textu, non vult nos eam transferre in nostra opera, nec potest vagari fides, et relicto propiciatore quaerere propriam dignitatem.

Cur igitur alibi dicitur: Remittuntur ei multa, quia dilexit multum?

Respondeo, Synecdochen esse usitatam, ac si dicat, quia conversa est. Verissimum est enim, conversionem necessariam esse, et tamen interim fide accipitur remissio, et non propter nostram dignitatem. Hae synecdochae sunt usitatissimae. Esaiae 1.: Desinite male facere. Item: Convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos. Item: Redime peccata tua iusticia, et erit sanatio delictis tuis. Haec dicta et similia continent synecdochen, in qua plures partes conversionis comprehenduntur, quae quomodo sint discernendae, ex aliis locis discendum est.

Certum est enim remissionem dari propter propiciatorem, non propter nostram dignitatem, et tamen verum est, sequi oportere dilectionem, id est, obedientiam novam, quam hic magnis laudibus ornat, ut testetur eam placere Deo.

Allegoria.

Duo sunt coetus in Ecclesia. Unus est hypocritarum, qui securi tument persuasione iusticiae, ii nec peccatum norunt, nec remissionem peccatorum, nec fidem, et interim quia fortassis mediocriter praestant disciplinam, admirantur sese, et gloriantur se iustos esse, ad horum mensam assidet Christus, id est, hi sunt pontifices, gubernatores, habent titulum Ecclesiae, quare sub eis sonat alicubi vox Evangelii. Est et alius coetus, scilicet, audiens Evangelium, agnoscens peccatum, vere lugens errata sua, vera fide quaerens Christum: huic coetui agenti poenitentiam et credenti, tribuit Christus testimonium quod sit vera Ecclesia, tribuit item laudem verae obedientiae, quod impleat legem, quod diligat. Hanc laudem arrogant sibi falso hypocritae, ideo Christus transfert eam in hunc coetum, quem hypocritae despiciunt, propterea quia minus est speciosa vita huius coetus.

Praecipuum autem officium, quod Christus tantopere praedicat, hoc est, quod mulier lavit et unxit pedes. Significant autem pedes praecipue ministerium Evangelii: hoc curat et omni officio tueri et conservare studet vera Ecclesia, fovet pios doctores omnibus officiis. Econtra Pharisaei, Pontifices negligunt ministerium Evangelii, quaerunt imperia, condunt leges utiles tuendis opibus, dignitatibus, interficiunt pios doctores.

## 7:36-38 Day of Mary Magdalene
Gospel for the day of Mary Magdalene, Luke 7.

A certain one of the Pharisees asked Jesus that he might eat with him, and entering into the house of the Pharisee, he reclined. And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she knew that he had reclined in the house of the Pharisee, brought an alabaster jar of ointment, and standing behind at his feet weeping, she began to wet his feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment.

But the Pharisee who had called him, seeing it, said within himself, saying: If this man were a Prophet, he would surely know who and what kind of woman she is who touches him, because she is a sinner.

And Jesus answering, said to him: Simon, I have something to say to you. But he said: Master, speak.

There were two debtors to a certain moneylender, one owed five hundred denarii, but the other fifty. And when they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both.

Which of them, therefore, will love him more? But Simon answering, said: I suppose that he to whom he forgave more. But he said to him: You have judged rightly.

And turning to the woman, he said to Simon: Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, you gave no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head. You gave me no kiss, but she, from the time she entered, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. For which reason I say to you: Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loves less.

But he said to her: Many sins are forgiven you.

And those who were reclining together began to say within themselves: Who is this, who even forgives sins? But he said to the woman: Your faith has made you safe, go in peace.

It has three principal parts.

I. The whole history is an example of the doctrine of repentance, which is the proper doctrine of the Gospel.

II. At the same time, a comparison of the pious to the hypocrites is also proposed.

III. Finally, the whole history is a wonderful image of the Church.

On the first.

We always say that in conversion there must exist contrition, that is, terrors arising from the recognition of the wrath of God against sin, as is seen in Adam, David, Hezekiah, Peter, Paul, and many others, and Joel says: Rend your hearts in lamentation. And Isaiah 66: To whom shall I look? Except to the humble and contrite in spirit, and him who trembles at my words.

And 2 Cor. 7: Sorrow according to God produces repentance unto salvation.

Likewise, Rom. 7: Sin through the law kills me, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful, that is, so that the guilt and wrath of God might be beheld. For since human security does not see what a great thing sin is, God judges hearts by His word, and shows His wrath; here we recognize that God is truly angry, and we are terrified, thus sin becomes exceedingly guilty, etc.

But how great a matter it is to offend God, let it be estimated from the first sin, what a horrible punishment followed the first disobedience of men, namely, the perpetual misery of the entire posterity: what punishment followed the fall of David?

But the human mind, just as it does not comprehend the immense justice and wrath of God, so it cannot comprehend the magnitude of sin, but we see it a little when hearts are truly terrified, as Jeremiah says: After you showed me, I struck my thigh.

Therefore, this huge mass of calamities has also been imposed upon the human race, to admonish us about repentance, as Paul says: We are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world.

Let there be, therefore, in us contrition and recognition of the wrath of God, as is seen in this woman, who stands weeping at the feet of Christ.

On the second. But it is not enough for terrors to exist, nor should we flee from God, like Cain, Saul, Judas, but let us know that a propitiator has been given to us, to whom God wills us to take refuge, and indeed let us know that the chief of all commandments is to acknowledge this Son of God, to honor him, and through him to desire to return to the Father, just as it is written: Kiss the Son. Blessed are all who trust in Him.

Let us also know that promises have often been confirmed by God with an oath, concerning the remission of sins, and liberation from sin and eternal death. Truly, therefore, God wants us to be saved, as: I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live. Item: The Lord has sworn, and He will not repent, etc. And Psalm 88, Augustine says: Christ will reign forever in His saints; God said this, He promised this; if that is a small thing, He swore this; because, therefore, the promise is firm not according to our merits, but according to His mercy, let us believe and call upon Him, etc.

The woman therefore comes to this Lord, and seeks consolation.

She hears, therefore, the voice concerning the remission of sins: Your faith has saved you, go in peace. These words preach about the other part of conversion, namely, faith. Christ expressly names faith; He says that by faith she is received into grace and saved. Thus, the two parts of repentance are clearly proposed here. Contrition, by which sin is judged: but here fear would overwhelm the mind with eternal death, unless consolation were to approach. Therefore, the other part approaches, namely faith, which is the trust that lifts up the soul, that God, through mercy on account of the Mediator, receives the believer, truly forgives, hears, and will make him an heir of eternal life. By this trust, the heart conceives new light and life, as it is said: The just shall live by his faith. Item, that we may receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

Concerning the third.

But why did He say before: Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much, and to whom much is forgiven, he loves much? Here love seems to be called the cause of remission. The easiest and simplest answer is: Christ testifies that she is converted, and certainly conversion is necessary, and He attributes to this wretched woman now that excellent praise which the people of the law falsely arrogated to themselves, as if Christ were saying: This woman fulfills the law, and is a member of the people of God. You neither fulfill the law, nor are you a member of the people of God.

It is established, however, and we always say this, that conversion is necessary, or begun obedience, and yet when He says: Your faith has saved you, Christ also testifies that remission is received by faith, not on account of obedience or love. Another answer is more expeditious. Absolution is twofold. One is of the conscience, which is done by faith. The other is public before the Church, which is done on account of works.

But concerning these solutions later.

First, let the very sermon of Christ be considered, which is the sweetest consolation to the pious, to be joined to this sentence. Grace abounds over sin, and it ought to be opposed to the temptation by which the heart is tormented by the magnitude of some certain sin, as Peter is tormented by the sight of his denial, or David by the sight of adultery and murder. Here the voice must be opposed: Grace abounds over sin, and here: To whom much is forgiven, he loves much, as if to say, the more you acknowledge the remission, the more you will acknowledge the magnitude of God's benefit toward you. A greater flame of faith and love therefore arises, and in turn, God loves the one who loves more, more. Thus God consoles the one who is deeply mourning, and embraces both; He testifies that God truly forgets our sins, and does not bear a grudge [μνησικακεῖν], and He attributes to the woman the praise of true obedience, so that she may be able to retain faith, and know that she henceforth pleases God even if she previously offended horribly. Diligently, therefore, this consolation of Christ must be observed, and opposed to the magnitude of the fall, lest we later think that we are less loved, less received, etc. And let it be referred to this saying: Grace abounds over sin.

On the contrary, the pride of the Pharisee is censured; Christ signifies that he is ignorant of the remission of sins, and therefore is without love.

But I return to the solutions. The most expeditious is to say that there is a twofold remission. The one before God, this is done by faith. The other before the Church, this is done on account of good works. And this solution is supported by the fact that it is said to the woman: Your faith has saved you. But to the Pharisee accusing and condemning the woman, works and love are alleged, so that she may be absolved before him as well. If anyone, however, demands another answer, the true and infallible sentence is that faith cannot rely equally on the promise and on the condition of our own dignity; if it is to be thought, then you will have remission when you have enough merits, as the narrative in the text clearly shows, He does not want us to transfer it to our works, nor can faith wander, and having left the propitiator, seek its own dignity.

Why then is it said elsewhere: Many sins are forgiven her, for she loved much? I answer, that a synecdoche is being used, as if it said, because she has been converted. For it is most true that conversion is necessary, and yet in the meantime remission is received by faith, and not because of our dignity. These synecdoches are most common. Isaiah 1: Cease to do evil. Item: Turn to me, and I will turn to you. Item: Redeem your sins by justice, and there shall be healing for your transgressions. These sayings and similar ones contain a synecdoche, in which many parts of conversion are comprehended, which how they are to be distinguished, must be learned from other places. For it is certain that remission is given because of the propitiator, not because of our dignity, and yet it is true that love ought to follow, that is, new obedience, which he here adorns with great praises, so that he may testify that it pleases God.

Allegory.

There are two congregations in the Church. One is of hypocrites, who are secure and puffed up by the persuasion of justice; they neither know sin, nor the remission of sins, nor faith, and meanwhile because perhaps they perform discipline moderately, they admire themselves, and boast that they are just; Christ sits at their table, that is, these are the pontiffs, the governors, they have the title of the Church, wherefore under them the voice of the Gospel sounds somewhere. There is also another congregation, namely, one that hears the Gospel, acknowledges sin, truly mourning its errors, seeking Christ with true faith: to this congregation, which is doing penance and believing, Christ attributes the testimony that it is the true Church, he also attributes the praise of true obedience, because it fulfills the law, because it loves. Hypocrites falsely arrogate this praise to themselves, therefore Christ transfers it to this congregation, which the hypocrites despise, because the life of this congregation is less showy. But the chief duty, which Christ preaches so much, is this, that the woman washed and anointed his feet. But the feet signify especially the ministry of the Gospel: the true Church cares for this and strives to protect and preserve it with every duty, it fosters pious teachers with all services. On the contrary, the Pharisees, the Pontiffs, neglect the ministry of the Gospel, they seek empires, they establish laws useful for protecting wealth and dignities, they kill pious teachers.

Latin:

Evangelium die Mariae Magdalenae, Lucae 7.

Rogabat Iesum quidam de Pharisaeis, ut manducaret cum ipso, et ingressus in domum Pharisaei, discubuit. Et ecce mulier in civitate quae erat peccatrix, ut cognovit quod accubuisset in domo Pharisaei, attulit alabastrum unguenti, et stans retro secus pedes eius flens, lacrymis coepit rigare pedes eius, et capillis capitis sui extergebat, et osculabatur pedes eius, et unguento ungebat.

Videns autem Pharisaeus qui vocaverat eum, ait intra se, dicens: Hic si esset Propheta, sciret utique, quae et qualis est mulier quae tangit eum, quia peccatrix est.

Et respondens Iesus, dixit ad illum: Simon, habeo tibi aliquid dicere. At ille ait: Magister, dic.

Duo debitores erant cuidam foeneratori, unus debebat denarios quingentos, alter autem quinquaginta. Non habentibus autem illis unde redderent, donavit utrisque.

Quis ergo eorum, dic eum plus diliget? Respondens autem Simon, dixit: Existimo, quod is, cui plus donavit. At ipse dixit ei: Recte iudicasti.

Et conversus ad mulierem, dixit Simoni: Vides hanc mulierem? Intravi in domum tuam, aquam pedibus meis non dedisti, haec autem lacrymis rigavit pedes meos, et capillis capitis sui extersit, Osculum mihi non dedisti, haec autem ex quo intravit, non cessavit osculari pedes meos. Oleo caput meum non unxisti, haec autem unguento unxit pedes meos. Propter quod dico tibi: Remittuntur ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum, Cui autem minus dimittitur, minus diligit.

Dixit autem illi: Remittuntur tibi peccata multa.

Et coeperunt qui simul accumbebant, dicere intra se: Quis est hic, qui etiam peccata remittit? Dixit autem ad mulierem: Fides tua salvam te fecit, vade in pace.

Tres habet praecipuos locos.

I. Tota historia est exemplum doctrinae de poenitentia, quae est propria Evangelii doctrina.

II. Simul etiam proponitur collatio piorum ad hypocritas.

III. Denique tota historia est mirifica imago Ecclesiae.

De primo.

Semper dicimus in conversione oportere existere contritionem, hoc est, pavores ortos ex agnitione irae Dei adversus peccatum, sicut in Adam, Davide, Ezechia, Petro, Paulo, et aliis multis cernitur, et Ioël inquit: Scindite corda vestra in planctum. Et Esaiae 66.: Ad quem respiciam? nisi ad humilem et contritum spiritu, et trementem sermones meos.

Et 2. Cor. 7.: Tristitia secundum Deum efficit poenitentiam ad salutem.

Item, Rom. 7.: Peccatum per legem occidit me, ut fieret excellenter peccatum, id est, ut conspiceretur reatus et ira Dei. Cum enim humana securitas non videat, quanta res sit peccatum, Deus verbo suo corda iudicat, et ostendit iram suam, hic agnoscimus Deum vere irasci, et expavescimus, sic peccatum fit excellenter reum etc.

Quanto vero res sit offendere Deum, aestimetur ex primo peccato, quam horribilis poena secuta est primam inobedientiam hominum, videlicet, perpetua miseria posteritatis universae: quanta poena secuta est lapsum Davidis?

Sed humana mens, ut immensam iusticiam et iram Dei non comprehendit: ita nec magnitudinem peccati comprehendere potest, sed aliquantulum aspicimus, cum corda vere expavescunt, ut inquit Ieremias: Postquam ostendisti mihi, percussifemur meum.

Ideo etiam haec ingens moles calamitatum imposita est generi humano, ut nos de poenitentia admoneat, sicut Paulus inquit: Corripimur a Domino, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur.

Existat igitur in nobis contritio et agnitio irae Dei, sicut in hac muliere conspicitur, quae flens astat ad pedes Christi.

De secundo. Sed non satis est existere pavores, nec fugiamus Deum, ut Cain, Saul, Iudas, sed sciamus donatum nobis esse propiciatorem, ad quem Deus vult nos confugere, et quidem sciamus omnium mandatorum praecipuum esse, hunc Filium Dei agnoscere, honore afficere, et per eum velle ad patrem redire, sicut scriptum est: Osculamini Filium. Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.

Sciamus item saepe iureiurando a Deo confirmatas esse promissiones, de remissione peccatorum, et liberatione a peccato et morte aeterna. Vere igitur vult Deus nos salvos fieri, ut: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Item: Iuravit Dominus, et non poenitebit eum etc. Et Psal. 88. inquit Augustinus: In aeternum regnabit Christus in sanctis suis, hoc dixit Deus, hoc promisit, si parvum est, hoc iuravit, quia ergo non secundum merita nostra, sed secundum illius misericordiam firma est promissio, credamus et invocemus etc.

Venit ergo ad hunc Dominum mulier, et quaerit consolationem.

Audit igitur vocem de remissione peccatorum, Fides tua salvam te fecit, vade in pace. Haec verba concionantur de altera parte conversionis, scilicet de fide. Christus expresse nominat fidem, dicit eam fide recipi in gratiam et salvari. Ita duae partes poenitentiae hic clare proponuntur. Contritio, qua iudicatur peccatum: sed hic pavor opprimeret mentem aeterna morte, nisi accederet consolatio. Accedit ergo altera pars, scilicet fides, quae est fiducia erigens animum, quod Deus per misericordiam propter mediatorem recipiat credentem, vere ignoscat, exaudiat, faciet haeredem vitae aeternae. Hac fiducia concipit cor novam lucem et vitam, ut dicitur: Iustus fide sua vivet. Item, ut promissionem Spiritus accipiamus per fidem.

De tertio.

Sed cur antea dixit: Remittuntur ei multa, quia dilexit multum, et cui multum remittitur, multum diligit? Hic videtur dilectio dici causa remissionis. Facilima et simplicissima responsio est: Christus testatur conversam esse, et certe conversio necessaria est, et tribuit huic miserae mulieri iam illam eximiam laudem, quam sibi falso arrogabat populus legis, quasi dicat Christus: Haec mulier implet legem, et est membrum populi Dei. Tu nec imples legem, nec es membrum populi Dei.

Constat autem, et semper haec dicimus, conversionem necessariam esse, seu incoatam obedientiam, et tamen cum dicat: Fides tua salvam te fecit, testatur etiam Christus, remissionem accipi fide, non propter obedientiam aut dilectionem. Alia responsio est expeditior. Duplex est absolutio. Alia conscientiae, quae fit fide. Alia publica coram Ecclesia, quae fit propter opera.

Sed de his solutionibus postea.

Prius ipsa concio Christi consideretur, quae est dulcissima consolatio piis, adiungenda huic sententiae. Gratia exuberat supra peccatum, et opponi debet tentationi, qua cor magnitudine certi alicuius peccati angitur, ut Petrus angitur conspectu negationis, aut David conspectu adulterii, caedis. Hic opponenda est vox: Gratia exuberat supra peccatum, et hic: Cui multum remittitur, multum diligit, quasi dicat, quo magis agnoscis remissionem, eo magis agnosces magnitudinem beneficii Dei erga te. Maior ergo flamma fidei et dilectionis oritur, et vicissim magis diligit Deus magis diligentem. Sic consolatur Deus valde lugentem, et utrunque complectitur, testatur Deum vere oblivisci peccata nostra, et non μνησικακεῖν, et tribuit mulieri laudem verae obedientiae, ut possit retinere fidem, et sciat se deinceps placere Deo etiam si antea horribiliter offendit. Diligenter igitur observanda est haec Christi consolatio, et opponenda magnitudini lapsus, ne postea existimemus, nos minus diligi, minus recipi etc. Et referatur ad hoc dictum: Gratia exuberat supra peccatum.

Econtra taxatur superbia Pharisaei, hunc significat Christus ignarum esse remissionis peccatorum, ideoque sine dilectione esse.

Sed redeo ad solutiones. Expeditissima est, dicere, duplicem esse remissionem, Alteram coram Deo, hanc fieri fide. Alteram coram Ecclesia, hanc fieri propter bona opera. Et huic solutioni patrocinatur, quod ad mulierem dicitur: Fides tua salvam te fecit. Sed Pharisaeo accusanti mulierem et damnanti, allegantur opera et dilectio, ut apud hunc quoque absolvatur. Si quis autem flagitat aliam responsionem, vera est et infallabilis sententia, fidem non posse niti pariter promissione, et conditione nostrae dignitatis, si cogitandum erit, tunc habebis remissionem, cum satis habebis meritorum, ut clare ostendit narratio in textu, non vult nos eam transferre in nostra opera, nec potest vagari fides, et relicto propiciatore quaerere propriam dignitatem.

Cur igitur alibi dicitur: Remittuntur ei multa, quia dilexit multum? Respondeo, Synecdochen esse usitatam, ac si dicat, quia conversa est. Verissimum est enim, conversionem necessariam esse, et tamen interim fide accipitur remissio, et non propter nostram dignitatem. Hae synecdochae sunt usitatissimae. Esaiae 1.: Desinite male facere. Item: Convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos. Item: Redime peccata tua iusticia, et erit sanatio delictis tuis. Haec dicta et similia continent synecdochen, in qua plures partes conversionis comprehenduntur, quae quomodo sint discernendae, ex aliis locis discendum est. Certum est enim remissionem dari propter propiciatorem, non propter nostram dignitatem, et tamen verum est, sequi oportere dilectionem, id est, obedientiam novam, quam hic magnis laudibus ornat, ut testetur eam placere Deo.

Allegoria.

Duo sunt coetus in Ecclesia. Unus est hypocritarum, qui securi tument persuasione iusticiae, ii nec peccatum norunt, nec remissionem peccatorum, nec fidem, et interim quia fortassis mediocriter praestant disciplinam, admirantur sese, et gloriantur se iustos esse, ad horum mensam assidet Christus, id est, hi sunt pontifices, gubernatores, habent titulum Ecclesiae, quare sub eis sonat alicubi vox Evangelii. Est et alius coetus, scilicet, audiens Evangelium, agnoscens peccatum, vere lugens errata sua, vera fide quaerens Christum: huic coetui agenti poenitentiam et credenti, tribuit Christus testimonium quod sit vera Ecclesia, tribuit item laudem verae obedientiae, quod impleat legem, quod diligat. Hanc laudem arrogant sibi falso hypocritae, ideo Christus transfert eam in hunc coetum, quem hypocritae despiciunt, propterea quia minus est speciosa vita huius coetus. Praecipuum autem officium, quod Christus tantopere praedicat, hoc est, quod mulier lavit et unxit pedes. Significant autem pedes praecipue ministerium Evangelii: hoc curat et omni officio tueri et conservare studet vera Ecclesia, fovet pios doctores omnibus officiis. Econtra Pharisaei, Pontifices negligunt ministerium Evangelii, quaerunt imperia, condunt leges utiles tuendis opibus, dignitatibus, interficiunt pios doctores.

## 8:4 Dominica Sexagesimae
Dominica Sexagesimae. The Gospel of Luke 8.

And when a very great crowd was gathering, and they were hurrying to him from the cities, he said by a similitude: A sower went out to sow his seed.

And while he sows, some indeed fell beside the way, and it was trampled, and the birds of the air ate it.

And another fell upon rock, and having been born it withered, because it did not have moisture.

And another fell among thorns, and the thorns having sprung up together, choked it.

And another fell into good ground, and having sprung up, it made fruit a hundredfold.

Saying these things, he cried out: He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

But his disciples were asking him, saying, what this parable was?

But he said: To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to others in parables, that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

But this is the parable: The seed is the word of God.

But those beside the way, these are they who hear, then the devil comes, and takes the word from their heart, lest believing they be saved.

But those upon the rock, these are they who, when they have heard, receive the word with joy, And these have no roots, because they believe for a time, but in the time of temptation they recede.

But that which fell among thorns, these are they who have heard, and are choked by the anxieties, and riches, and pleasures of life as they go, and do not bring forth fruit.

But that which fell into good ground, these are they who, hearing the word with a sincere and good heart, retain it, and bring forth fruit in patience.

But no one lighting a lamp, covers it with a vessel, or puts it under a bed, but puts it upon a lampstand, that those entering may see the light.

For there is nothing hidden, which shall not be manifested, nor secret, which shall not be known, and come into the open.

See therefore, how you hear.

For he who has, to him it shall be given, and whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has, shall be taken away from him.

The summary of the Gospel, and the principal proposition is the consolation concerning the Church, that there is certainly some Church, wherever the Gospel is taught.

There is also consolation against the scandal of the paucity of believers.

There is therefore the first point.

The Gospel is never entirely without fruit, but is always effective in some, as Isaiah 55 testifies:

The word shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed.

Second. Always in that assembly where there is true doctrine, it is necessary that there be some true members of the Church, because the word of God is not without fruit, and it is necessary that there be some Church. This [Church] does not belong to those defending impious opinions; therefore, it is necessary that it be in the other assembly.

Third. Since the Church is small, as Isaiah says: Unless God had left us a seed, we would be as Sodom. The minds of many doubt whether there is any Church of God, or whether God still hears and grants his promises. Against this scandal, this parable confirms us; it commands that we believe there is a Church, and that God truly hears and grants the promises to the Church. And it testifies that those who do not fall away from the Gospel are good soil.

Fourth. He recounts the ways of those who fall away: where it must be diligently observed that he does not only enumerate the common sins of human infirmity, such as illicit gains, and unlawful pleasures, and the fear of persecution, but he adds other obscure temptations, namely, when the devil shakes the correct opinion from minds and instills Epicurean opinions, or others. Against these snares, the pious must be vigilant.

Fifth. A most sweet consolation is proposed in the saying, "To him who has, it will be given": namely, that God receives the weak, that he wishes to advance them, that he does not despise beginnings. As it is said elsewhere: "A smoldering wick he will not quench." Likewise Paul concerning the weak: "God has received them." Now, those who have are those who have the beginnings of repentance, and these very ones he calls here the good soil, namely, those not falling away from the word of God, because he enumerated those who fall away above.

Sixth. A doctrine is also handed down which commands that we strive to progress, that we be those who have, that we retain the word, which cannot be done without care and without struggle.

Seventh. There are degrees of the pious; some produce fruit a hundredfold, etc., which is to be understood generally concerning the gifts of individuals and concerning ministries, just as Joseph bore more abundant fruit than the remaining brothers; that is, he both excelled in gifts and converted more people. And the chief fruit is to confess and to teach, as Christ says: "So the heavenly Father will be glorified, if you are my disciples and bear more abundant fruit," that is, you will propagate and preserve the Gospel.

Eighth. Many threats are proposed here against the contemners of the word of God and the persecutors. For it is a wonder how it happens that with such obstinacy they oppose the acknowledged truth. But here we are admonished not to be broken by their obstinacy or judgments, because it was predicted that there would be such enemies of the true Church who, though seeing, would yet be blind. Wherefore those obstinate enemies of the Gospel are to be fled, and minds are to be raised up against them, so that we may retain the word of God, be good soil, and bear some fruit, each one in his own vocation.

The same Sunday of Sexagesima. Gospel of Matthew 13. I. The passage, an image of the Church, which admonishes and confirms the pious, and rebukes the slothful. II. Concerning the growth of the pious, and the blinding of those who contemn and persecute. III. How the fathers knew the kingdom of Christ. IIII. Concerning the manifold fruit.

Concerning the first. Many things offend weak minds: the fewness of the pious, daily desertions, and perfidies. Against these scandals, we hold the consolation proposed in this image, which warns that such confusion and dissimilarity will exist in the Church, and let us raise ourselves up, lest on account of the falls of others, we ourselves also fall away.

And the causes of confusion and desertion are recounted here. The first is more obscure than the others, but more common and powerful, namely, when minds are captured by the deceits of the devil and the word of God is shaken out, just as Eve was first seduced. Thus, very many become Epicurean, or Academic, or heretical, to whom the devil offers some false persuasion, and then holds and urges them, entangled and ensnared, just as we see how he gradually overturned Eve. Paul often describes these snares and calls them fiery darts.

Now this age has very many and various examples, partly because of the petulance of talents, which is growing, and partly because the devil, in the last time, sensing that the judge will soon be present, rages more madly. Therefore, there are now more atheists [ἄϑεοι], and more monstrous sects arise, such as the manifold delusions of the Anabaptists.

Let us think, therefore, that we must be vigilant and must resist the snares of the devil, who seeks wondrous occasions by which he may draw minds into errors and to defection, etc. And let us be stirred by the saying of Peter: Watch, for your adversary goes about like a roaring lion. The remaining causes of desertion are less obscure, such as the fear of punishments, immoderate anxieties about retaining wealth, power, and dignity.

On the second. A very useful doctrine is taught here concerning the growth of the pious. Luke 8. See how you hear: For to him who has, it will be given, and from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away. Let us learn, therefore, that spiritual gifts must be exercised, because they grow in these exercises, just as Paul says elsewhere: Those who serve faithfully are confirmed in faith. And Augustine: Love merits the increase of love. Therefore Christ says: If men can give good things, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him: which signifies not to the idle, not to the secure, not to those who despise, but to those who hear the word of God, who desire to obey, and who ask for help. There exist promises, there exist commands which order us to ask, therefore He wishes to give and to accumulate gifts, just as the prayer itself testifies, which Christ delivered.

Hallowed be thy name, that is, grant that we may truly acknowledge God, truly invoke Him, take away idolatry and all impious opinions. Thy kingdom come, that is, rule us with Thy Holy Spirit, do not grant the kingdom to the devil. Thy will be done, just as the angels obey in heaven, and each one does his own duty, so make it that on earth all teachers, princes, governors, and private citizens obey Thee, each in his own place; take away all scandals of governors and others which offend Thy will. Give us this day our daily bread, that is, all the comforts of the body, peace, provisions, good government. Forgive us our debts, do not let us succumb to the devil in temptations. Deliver us from all evils, and lead us into eternal life. Here we see Christ commanding that we ask for goods of every kind, spiritual and corporal, and He wishes to accumulate these for those who ask and exercise them.

But a warning against the negligent is also added here. That seeing they may not see. Item: From him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away, that is, those who despise will be punished with blindness and manifold madness.

On the third.

But blessed are your eyes, etc. Christ says of Abraham, Abraham saw my day and rejoiced: thus all the saints from the beginning of the world were saved by faith in the coming liberator, whom they knew to be promised, and some had clearer light than others. But that they are said here not to have seen, let it be understood only of bodily conversation. The fathers marveled at this beginning of the kingdom, and certainly they desired to hear Him preaching in person, they desired to see their Lord, they desired to grow in the knowledge of their Lord.

On the fourth.
