Different fruits signify that some excel others in gifts. Item, that in individual vocations some labor more than others, as Paul preached to more people than anyone else.

Latin:

Dominica Sexagesimae. Evangelium Lucae 8.

Cum autem turba plurima conveniret, et de civitatibus properarent ad eum, dixit per similitudinem: Exiit qui seminat seminare semen suum.

Et dum seminat, aliud quidem cecidit secus viam, et conculcatum est, et volucres coeli comederunt illud.

Et aliud cecidit supra petram, et natum exaruit, quia non habebat humorem.

Et aliud cecidit inter spinas, et simul exortae spinae, suffocaverunt illud.

Et aliud cecidit in terram bonam, et ortum, fecit fructum centuplum.

Haec dicens, clamabat: Qui habet aures audiendi, audiat.

Interrogabant autem eum discipuli eius, dicentes, quae esset haec parabola?

Ille autem dixit: Vobis datum est, nosse mysteria regni Dei, caeteris autem in parabolis, ut videntes non videant, et audientes non intelligant.

Est autem haec parabola: Semen est verbum Dei.

Qui autem secus viam, hi sunt, qui audiunt, deinde venit diabolus, et tollit verbum de corde eorum, ne credentes salvi fiant.

Qui autem supra petram, hi sunt, qui cum audierint, cum gaudio suscipiunt verbum, Et hi radices non habent, quia ad tempus credunt, sed in tempore tentationis recedunt.

Quod autem inter spinas cecidit, hi sunt, qui audierunt, et a solicitudinibus, et divitiis, et voluptatibus vitae euntes suffocantur, et non referunt fructum.

Quod autem in bonam terram, hi sunt, qui corde sincero et bono audientes verbum, retinent, et fructum afferunt in patientia.

Nemo autem lucernam accendens, operit cam vase, aut subter lectum ponit, sed super candelabrum ponit, ut intrantes videant lumen.

Non est enim occultum, quod non manifestetur, neque absconditum, quod non cognoscatur, et in apertum veniat.

Videte ergo, quomodo audiatis.

Qui enim habet, illi dabitur, et quicunque non habet, etiam quod putat se habere, auferetur ab illo.

Summa Evangelii, et principalis propositio est consolatio de Ecclesia, quod certo sit aliqua Ecclesia, ubicunque docetur Evangelium.

Est et consolatio adversus scandalum paucitatis credentium.

Est ergo primus locus.

Evangelium nunquam prorsus est sine fructu, sed semper in aliquibus est efficax, ut testatur Esai. 55.:

Non revertetur verbum ad me vacuum, sed faciet, quaecunque volui.

Secundus. Semper in eo coetu, ubi est vera doctrina, necesse est aliqua esse vera membra Ecclesiae, quia verbum Dei non est sine fructu, et necesse est aliquam esse Ecclesiam. Haec non est defendentium impias opiniones, ergo necesse est eam in altero coetu esse.

Tertius. Cum Ecclesia sit exigua, sicut inquit Esaias: Nisi Deus reliquisset nobis semen, essemus sicut Sodoma. Animi multorum dubitant, an sit aliqua Ecclesia Dei, an Deus adhuc exaudiat, praestet promissa. Adversus id scandalum confirmat nos haec parabola, praecipit, ut credamus esse Ecclesiam, et vere Deum exaudire, et praestare promissa Ecclesiae. Et testatur illos bonam esse terram, qui non deficiunt ab Evangelio.

Quartus. Modos recenset deficientium: ubi diligenter observandum est, quod non tantum enumerat vulgaria peccata humanae infirmitatis, ut inconcessos quaestus, et illicitas voluptates, et metum persecutionis, sed addit alias obscuras tentationes, videlicet cum diabolus excutit animis rectam sententiam, et instillat Epicureas opiniones, vel alias. Adversus has insidias oportet pios esse vigilantes.

Quintus. Dulcissima consolatio proposita est in dicto, Habenti dabitur: quod videlicet infirmos Deus recipiat, quod velit eos provehere, quod initia non contemnat. Sicut alibi dicitur: Linum fumigans non extinguet. Item Paulus de infirmis: Deus eos recepit. Sunt autem habentes qui habent initia poenitentiae, et hos ipsos hic vocat honam terram, scilicet non deficientes a verbo Dei, quia supra enumeravit deficientes.

Sextus. Traditur et doctrina quae praecipit, ut studeamus proficere, ut simus habentes, ut retineamus verbum, quod sine cura et sine dimicatione fieri non potest.

Septimus. Gradus sunt piorum, alii fructum faciunt centuplum etc. quod generaliter intelligendum est de donis singulorum, et de ministeriis, ut Ioseph copiosiorem fructum tulit, quam reliqui fratres, hoc est, et donis excelluit, et plures convertit. Estque praecipuus fructus confiteri et docere, sicut Christus inquit: Sic pater coelestis glorificabitur, si eritis mei discipuli, et copiosiorem fructum feretis, id est, propagabitis et conservabitis Evangelium.

Octavus. Comminationes multae hic propositae sunt adversus contemtores verbi Dei, et persequutores. Mirum est enim, qui fiat, ut tanta pertinacia agnitam veritatem oppugnet. Hic autem admonemur, ne illorum pertinacia vel iudiciis frangamur, quia praedictum est, tales aliquos fore hostes verae Ecclesiae, qui videntes, tamen sunt coeci futuri. Quare fugiendi sunt pertinaces illi hostes Evangelii, et contra erigendae mentes, ut retineamus verbum Dei, simus bona terra, feramus aliquem fructum, unusquisque in sua vocatione.

Eadem Dominica Sexagesimae. Evangelium Matth. 13. I. Locus, imago Ecclesiae, quae admonet et confirmat pios, et obiurgat ignavos. II. De incrementis piorum, et excaecatione contemnentium et persequentium. III. Quomodo patres noverint regnum Christi. IIII. De multiplici fructu.

De primo. Multa offendunt infirmos animos, paucitas piorum, quotidianae desertiones et perfidiae. Adversus haec scandala tenemus consolationem in hac imagine propositam, quae admonet futuram talem confusionem, et dissimilitudinem in Ecclesia, et erigamus nos, ne propter aliorum lapsus, et ipsi deficiamus.

Et causae confusionis et desertionis hic recitantur. Prima est obscurior caeteris, sed communior et potentior, videlicet cum praestigiis diaboli capiuntur animi, et excutitur verbum Dei, sicut Eva primum seducta est. Ita plurimi sapientes fiunt Epicurei, aut Academici, aut haeretici, quibus diabolus offert aliquam falsam persuasionem, ac deinde implicatos et irretitos tenet et urget, sicut videmus, quomodo paulatim Evam everterit. Has insidias saepe Paulus describit, et vocat tela ignita.

Habet autem haec aetas plurima et varia exempla, partim propter ingeniorum petulantiam, quae crescit, partim, quia diabolus postremo tempore sentiens brevi affuturum esse iudicem, rabiosius grassatur. Ideo iam plures sunt ἄϑεοι, et monstrosiores sectae oriuntur, ut deliria Anabaptistarum multiplicia.

Cogitemus igitur vigilandum esse, ac repugnandum insidiis diaboli, qui miras quaerit occasiones, quibus pertrahat animos in errores et ad defectionem etc. Ac dicto Petri excitemur: Vigilate, quia adversarius vester tanquam leo rugiens circumit. Reliquae causae desertionis minus sunt obscurae, ut metus suppliciorum, immoderatae solicitudines retinendarum opum, imperii, dignitatis.

De secundo. Valde utilis doctrina hic traditur, de incrementis piorum. Lucae 8. Videte quomodo audiatis: Habenti enim dabitur, et a non habente, quod videtur habere, auferetur. Discamus igitur exercenda esse dona spiritualia, quia in his exercitiis crescunt, sicut alibi Paulus inquit: Qui fideliter serviunt confirmantur in fide. Et Augustinus: Dilectio meretur incrementum dilectionis. Ideo Christus inquit: Si possunt homines bona dare, quanto magis pater vester qui in coelis est, dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus: quod significat non ociosis, non securis, non contemnentibus, sed audientibus verbum Dei, cupientibus obedire, et petentibus auxilium. Extant promissiones, extant mandata, quae iubent petere, ergo vult dare et cumulare dona, sicut et precatio ipsa testatur, quam Christus tradidit.

Sanctificetur nomen tuum, id est, da ut vere agnoscamus Deum, vere invocemus, tolle idololatriam et omnes impias opiniones. Adveniat regnum tuum, id est, rege tu nos Spiritu sancto, non concedas regnum diabolo. Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in coelo obtemperant angeli, et suum quisque facit officium, ita fac ut in terra obtemperent tibi omnes doctores, principes, gubernatores, privati, suo quisque loco, tolle omnia scandala gubernatorum et aliorum, quae offendunt tuam voluntatem. Da panem quotidianum, id est, omnia corporis commoda, pacem, annonam, bonum regimen. Remitte debita, ne sinas nos succumbere diabolo in tentationibus. Libera nos ab omnibus malis, et traduc in vitam aeternam. Hic videmus praecipere Christum, ut omnis generis bona, spiritualia et corporalia petamus, et haec cumulare vult petentibus et exercentibus.

Additur autem et hic comminatio contra negligentes. Ut videntes non videant. Item: A non habente, quod videtur habere, auferetur, id est, contemtores punientur caecitate et multiplici amentia.

De tertio.

Vestri autem beati oculi etc. Christus inquit de Abraham, Abraham vidit diem meum et laetatus est: ita omnes sancti ab initio mundi salvati sunt fide venturi liberatoris, quem norant promissum esse, et alii habuerunt lucem clariorem aliis. Quod autem hic dicuntur non vidisse, intelligatur tantum de conversatione corporali. Hanc incoationem regni patres mirati sunt, et certe coram cupiebant audire praedicantem, cupiebant videre suum Dominum, cupiebant crescere agnitione sui Domini.

De quarto.

Diversi fructus significant, alios excellere aliis donis. Item, in singulis vocationibus alios plus laborare aliis, ut Paulus pluribus praedicavit, quam aliquis alius.

## 10:23-24 The Thirteenth Sunday After Trinity
The Thirteenth Sunday after Trinity. The Gospel of Luke 10.

And turning to His disciples apart, He said: Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I say to you, that many Prophets and Kings have desired to see what you see, and have not seen, and to hear what you hear, and have not heard.

And behold, a certain Lawyer stood up, testing Him, and saying: Master, what must I do to inherit eternal life? But He said to him: What is written in the Law? How do you read it? And he answering said: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself. And He said to him: You have answered rightly; do this, and you shall live.

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: And who is my neighbor? And Jesus answering said: A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers, who also stripped him, and having added wounds, went away, leaving him half-dead.

And by chance a certain Priest was going down the same way, and seeing him, passed by. Likewise also a Levite, when he had come to the place and saw him, passed by. But a certain Samaritan, while traveling, came near him, and seeing him, was moved with mercy. And approaching, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine. And setting him on his own animal, he led him to an inn, and took care of him. And the next day, going out, he brought out two denarii, and gave them to the innkeeper, and said to him: Take care of him, and whatever you spend more, I, when I return, will repay you. Which therefore of these three seems to you to have been a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?

But he said: He who showed mercy to him. Jesus therefore said to him: Go, and do you likewise.

There are four principal points.

I. The point is the doctrine of faith.

II. The doctrine of the law.

III. The definition of a neighbor.

IV. The allegory of the example.

On the first.

The following discourse must be included: All things have been given to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is, except the Father, and who the Father is, except the Son, and to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him. To this discourse add the epiphonema: Blessed are the eyes, etc. This whole discourse first proposes the proper doctrine of the Gospel concerning faith. Christ clearly says that the Father is known by no one, except by the Son revealing Him: therefore, unless the Son reveals Him, it is impossible to do the law. And thus, the objection is answered, which follows later when mention is made of the law: Do this, and you shall live.

To these words, another discourse must be added. It is not enough to hear the law, but the Son must be heard, revealing the Father, that is, the will of the Father concerning the Son; not only concerning the law, but the will of the Father must be known, why He sent the Son, and what He has delivered to Him, namely, the power to liberate the human race.

Concerning the fourth. from sin and from death, to be given eternal life.

This sermon on faith is placed before the disputation on the law, so that by faith we may apprehend the benefits of the Son of God. Afterwards, when we have acknowledged the Father through the Son, obedience to the law should follow, which will be pleasing on account of the Son, although it may be imperfect.

Concerning the second. To the Pharisee, who was asking not for the sake of learning but for the sake of testing, Christ shows his empty arrogance, so that he might acknowledge sin.

And perhaps this hypocrite was one of those very ones who passed by the wounded man, of whom it is spoken here in the example. Now Christ had ordered the questioner to consult the scripture; he leads him to the word, but the Pharisee knows nothing except the law, neglects the promises, and alleges the law without understanding it.

Christ adds, in order to tax his ignorance: Do this, and you will live; for he signifies that he neither does the law nor will he live, but that he is oppressed by sin and death. For the sentence is: If you do it, you will live, but neither you nor others do it; therefore, life must be sought elsewhere.

The saying is true: He who does the law shall live.

For if there were no sin, there would be no death. Thus he convicts the Pharisee, because he does not know what the law is, what sin is, what death is, which is a certain terrible evil sprung from sin, and it is not taken away by the law, because the law is not fulfilled in human nature oppressed by sin.

This whole disputation is entirely similar to the disputations of these times. We are litigating with adversaries who are fascinated by philosophical opinions about the law; they do not know what sin is, what death is.

Concerning the third.

Our neighbor is the wretch in need of our benefit, and especially he who is joined by the society of the name of God, who is a member of the people of God: thus here he says that the wounded man was judged to be the neighbor by the Samaritan.

On the contrary, the flesh leads [us to consider] the flourishing and powerful as neighbors, it flees the wretched. As Menander says most charmingly: Fortune paints friends in various ways. But this example teaches us that we ought to embrace the wretched as neighbors.

Furthermore, these things must be mutual, gratitude and beneficence. This is the sum of the example, in which those who boasted of the righteousness of the law, like the Priests and Levites, are falsely rebuked, and yet they were surpassed in true works by the Samaritan.

Concerning the fourth.

Christ rightly answers the Pharisee, depicting the magnitude of sin, and signifying that sin is not taken away by the ministry of the law, but in some other way.

The wounded man signifies the whole human race, which is stripped of the spiritual gifts it had in the beginning, and wounded, multiply depraved and distorted by ignorance of God, by contempt of God. The powers of nature are also corrupted, and death has been added.

And these very wounds are far greater than reason can judge. For just as we do not understand the magnitude of the wrath of God against sin, so we do not sufficiently understand sin, nor death.

The Priest and the Levite pass by this wounded man; the wounded man is not helped by the ministry of the law; sin and death are not taken away through the law, but the Samaritan, Christ, comes, rejected by the people of the law. He binds the wounds, pours in wine, that is, the preaching of repentance, and oil, that is, the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, by which eternal life is begun, and he places him on his own beast, that is, either his body or his ministry, and commends him to the Church, and gives the minister two denarii, that is, the preaching of the law and the Gospel, and adds, if you have spent anything more, I will pay it, as if to say, labors, dangers, lack of counsel will arise; in all these I will be present, and I will help you.

In this image he shows how we are healed, namely by Christ through the ministry of the Gospel. Here they trifle about works of supererogation, as if the allegory signified private works not commanded by God, when it signifies the works which the healing requires, which are divinely commanded.

Mention is made of such works, that is, of labors, dangers, and struggles, in which he signifies that he will be present, that he will supply the expenses, because there is a constant need for divine help in governance.

For there occur infinite things, where our counsels, our strengths, are surpassed by the magnitude of the dangers, where one must pray, as is said in 2 Chron.

20: When we do not know what we ought to do, we have this alone remaining, that we direct our eyes to you. In the darkness of our mind, and in the thick gloom, When there is no counsel in the whole heart: Troubled, we raise the eyes of our heart to you, O God, Our faith prays for your help alone.

Do you, best Father, rule our deeds with your counsels, So that all our work may serve your praise.

Latin:

Dominica XIII. post Trinitatis. Evangelium Lucae 10.

Et conversus ad discipulos seorsim, dixit: Beati oculi qui vident, quae vos videtis. Dico enim vobis, quod multi Prophetae et Reges voluerunt videre, quae vos videtis, et non viderunt, et audire quae auditis, et non audierunt.

Et ecce quidam Legisperitus surrexit, tentans illum, et dicens: Magister, quid faciendo, vitam aeternam haereditabo? At ille dixit ad eum: In Lege quid scriptum est, quomodo legis? Respondens autem dixit: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua, et ex omnibus viribus tuis, et ex tota mente tua, et proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Dixit autem ille: Recte respondisti, hoc fac, et vives.

Ille autem volens iustificare seipsum, dixit ad Iesum: Et quis est meus proximus? Respondens autem Iesus, dixit: Homo quidam descendebat ab Ierusalem in Iericho, et incidit in latrones, qui etiam despoliaverunt eum, et plagis additis abierunt semimortuo relicto.

Casu autem Sacerdos quidam descendit eadem via, et viso illo, praeterivit. Similiter et Levita cum venisset secus locum, et videret eum, pertransivit. Samaritanus autem quidam iter faciens, venit secus eum, et videns eum, misericordia motus est. Et accedens, obligavit vulnera eius, infundens oleum et vinum. Et imponens illum in iumentum suum, duxit eum in hospitium, et curam eius egit. Et altera die egrediens, protulit duos denarios, et dedit hospiti, et ait illi: Curam illius habe, et quodcunque supererogaveris, ego cum rediero, reddam tibi. Quis ergo horum trium videtur tibi proximus fuisse illi, qui incidit in latrones?

At ille dixit: Qui fecit misericordiam in illum. Ait ergo illi Iesus: Vade, et tu fac similiter.

Quatuor sunt praecipui loci.

I. Locus est doctrina de fide.

II. Doctrina legis.

III. Definitio proximi.

IIII. Allegoria exempli.

De primo.

Complectenda est proxima concio: Omnia mihi data sunt a patre meo, et nemo novit quis sit Filius, nisi pater, et quis sit pater, nisi Filius, et cui voluerit Filius revelare. Huic concioni addite epiphonema: Beati oculi etc. Haec tota concio primum proponit doctrinam propriam Evangelii de fide. Christus clare dicit, Patrem a nemine agnosci, nisi revelante Filio: ergo nisi revelante Filio, impossibile est legem facere. Et sic respondetur ad objectionem, quae postea sequitur, cum fit mentio legis: Hoc fac, et vives.

His verbis addenda est altera concio. Non satis est audire legem, sed Filius audiendus est, revelans patrem, hoc est, voluntatem patris de Filio, non tantum de lege, sed cognoscenda est voluntas patris, cur Filium miserit, quid ei tradiderit, scilicet potentiam liberandi genus humanum.

De quarto. a peccato et a morte, dandae vitae aeternae.

Haec concio de fide praeponitur disputationi de lege, ut fide apprehendamus beneficia Filii Dei. Postea cum agnovimus patrem per Filium, sequatur obedientia legis, quae placebit propter Filium, quanquam sit imperfecta.

De secundo. Pharisaeo non discendi, sed tentandi causa interroganti, ostendit Christus inanem ipsius arrogantiam, ut agnoscat peccatum.

Et fortassis hic hypocrita fuit unus ex illis ipsis, qui praeterierunt saucium, de quibus hic in exemplo dicitur. Jusserat autem Christus interrogantem consulere scripturam, deducit eum ad verbum, sed Pharisaeus nihil scit nisi legem, promissiones negligit, et allegat legem non intellectam.

Christus addit, ut eius ignorantiam taxet: Hoc fac, et vives, significat enim eum nec facere legem, nec victurum esse, sed oppressum esse peccato et morte. Est enim sententia: Si feceris, vives, sed nec tu facis, nec alii, ergo vita aliunde petenda est.

Verum est dictum, Faciens legem vivet.

Si enim non esset peccatum, mors non esset. Ita coarguit Pharisaeum, quod nesciat quid sit lex, quid peccatum, quid mors, quae est quoddam terribile malum ortum a peccato, et non tollitur lege, quia lex non fit in natura humana oppressa peccato.

Haec tota disputatio prorsus similis est disputationibus horum temporum. Litigamus cum adversariis qui sunt fascinati philosophicis opinionibus de lege, nesciunt quid sit peccatum, quid sit mors.

De tertio.

Proximus nobis est miser indigens beneficio nostro, et praesertim is, qui coniunctus est societate nominis Dei, qui est membrum populi Dei: ita hic dicit saucium judicatum esse proximum a Samaritano.

Econtra caro ducit proximos florentes et potentes, fugit miseros. Sicut venustissime dicit Menander: Fortuna varie pingit amicos. Sed hoc exemplum docet nos debere complecti miseros tanquam proximos.

Caeterum haec debent esse mutua, gratitudo et beneficentia. Haec est summa exempli, in quo false reprehenduntur illi, qui iactabant iusticiam legis, ut Sacerdotes et Levitae, et tamen veris operibus vincebantur a Samaritano.

De quarto.

Christus recte respondet Pharisaeo, pingens magnitudinem peccati, et significans peccatum non tolli ministerio legis, sed alio quodam modo.

Saucius significat totum genus humanum, quod est spoliatum donis spiritualibus, quae habuit initio, et vulneratum, multipliciter depravatum et distortum ignorantia Dei, contemtu Dei. Sunt et naturae vires corruptae, et accessit mors.

Et haec ipsa vulnera longe maiora sunt, quam iudicare ratio potest. Sicut enim magnitudinem irae Dei non intelligimus adversus peccatum, ita nec peccatum, nec mortem satis intelligimus.

Sacerdos et Levita praetereunt hunc saucium, saucius non iuvatur ministerio legis, peccatum et mors non tolluntur per legem, sed venit Samaritanus Christus, reiectus a populo legis. Hic obligat vulnera, infundit vinum, id est, praedicationem poenitentiae, et oleum, id est, Evangelium et Spiritum sanctum, quo incoatur vita aeterna, et imponit eum suo iumento, id est, seu corpori seu ministerio, et commendat Ecclesiae, et dat ministro duos denarios, id est, praedicationem legis et Evangelii, et addit, si quid supererogaveris solvam, quasi dicat, accedunt labores, pericula, inopia consilii, in his omnibus adero, et iuvabo te.

In hac imagine ostendit quomodo sanemur, scilicet a Christo per ministerium Evangelii. Hic nugantur de operibus supererogationis, quasi allegoria significet privata opera non mandata a Deo, cum significet opera quae requirit curatio, quae sunt divinitus mandata.

Talium operum, hoc est, laborum, periculorum et certaminum mentio fit, in quibus significat se adfuturum esse, suppeditaturum sumtus, quia assidue opus est in gubernatione divino auxilio.

Incidunt enim infinita, ubi nostra consilia, nostra vires, magnitudine periculorum superantur, ubi precandum est, ut dicitur 2. Paral.

20.: Cum ignoramus quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te. In tenebris nostrae, et densa caligine mentis, Cum nihil est toto pectore consilii: Turbati erigimus Deus ad te lumina cordis, Nostra tuamque fides solius orat opem.

Tu rege consiliis actus, pater optime, nostros, Nostrum opus ut laudi serviat omne tuae.

## 11:14-22 Dominica Oculi
Dominica Oculi. Gospel of Luke 11.

And He was casting out a demon, and it was mute. But it came to pass when the demon had gone out, the mute spoke, and the crowds were amazed. But some of them said: By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, He casts out demons. Others, however, testing Him, sought a sign from heaven from Him. But He, knowing their thoughts, said to them: Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house. If then Satan is also divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? because you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub.

If, however, I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has surely come upon you. When a strong man armed guards his atrium, those things which he possesses are in peace. But if a stronger one than he coming upon him overcomes him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils. He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me, scatters.

When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through waterless places, seeking rest, and not finding it, he says: I will return to my house, from whence I came out. And when he has come, he finds it swept with brooms and adorned, then he goes and takes seven other spirits, more wicked than himself, and entering in, they dwell there. And the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.

And it came to pass, as he was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd, lifting up her voice, said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you have sucked. But he said: Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it.

I. Topic, the principal disputation is concerning miracles.

II. Concerning blasphemers, and concerning the middle or neutral ones.

III. Doctrine concerning the fear of God, against the security which is accustomed to follow liberation.

Concerning the first.

There have been at all times, from the very beginning of the world and the Church, some miracles of the impious, just as among the Gentiles specters often denounced something. Likewise, statues have spoken. Likewise, Calchas predicted that it would come to pass that Troy would be captured in the tenth year. It may therefore be asked, if doctrine is to be judged by miracles, which one is true? I answer: True [miracles] are distinguished from false ones in two ways, first by impossibility, second by their ends.

For first, the Church has certain proper miracles which the devil cannot imitate, such as the resuscitation of the dead, stopping the course of the sun, making a sterile and worn-out woman fruitful. These and similar things belong to the Church alone, and are impossible for the devil. Therefore, the miracles of the Church are to be preferred to those of the Gentiles, and they are certain and firm testimonies of doctrine divinely handed down. To these must be added that which is also handed down here: casting out the resisting devil. For although the devil sometimes, as if colluding, yields even to jugglers and impostors, yet this ejection, which Christ and the Apostles performed, was dissimilar: for they were casting out a resisting, not a colluding one, because the devil cries out so often that he is being tormented before the time. Rightly, therefore, does Christ argue: I cast out the devil resisting and unwilling, and I cast him out everywhere, although he is raging atrociously: therefore, I cast him out by divine power overcoming the resisting devil.

The second distinction is to be taken from the ends. The end of the miracles of the devil is regularly the confirmation of some error or crime. Conversely, the end of the miracles of the Church is the confirmation of true worship, and it agrees with the word already revealed before, concerning true worship and the Son of God. As for the prophecies of Tiresias or Calchas, what ends did they have? They commanded the slaughter of human sacrifices, and they confirmed the existing idol-mania. Since, however, these errors are manifest madnesses, and indeed have established many other vices of the Gentiles, it sufficiently appears that these miracles are not divine. Such miracles are performed even now in the invocation of the dead, so that impiety and error may be confirmed.

These distinctions of miracles must be diligently observed, so that we may confirm our minds with the testimonies of true miracles, and discern them from deceptions. For the power of the devil is great, and he casts many errors into human minds: and at all times he has confirmed impious superstitions with certain prodigious events. Therefore, the pious must be fortified with firm testimonies; as Moses overcame the Magicians, so the Church overcomes the devil in two ways. It has certain proper miracles which the devil cannot imitate. Likewise, it refers them not to establishing crimes, but to confirming the true recognition of God, and [that which is] consistent with the word of God handed down. Let us remember these rules.

Concerning the second.

It is said here that a certain sin is not forgiven. Nor is there a need to define *a priori* which one it is: because we have the command that we should do penance, and believe that all sins are forgiven. It is necessary to obey this rule, because the sentence is universally true: Grace abounds over sin. Likewise: And he himself is the propitiation for our sins, not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world. But it is manifest that some stubbornly hold to a perpetual contention, or hatred of Christ, even against their conscience. These neither wish to accept the offered remission, nor do they wish to believe, but either securely and most proudly mock the Gospel, or furiously hate it. Concerning these, let us judge *a posteriori* that they have the sin against the Holy Spirit, because in that perpetual contention or hatred of Christ they depart, and rush into eternal wrath, just as Judas and those like him.

And here both are to be embraced, the enemies who fight against the Gospel against their conscience, and the middle ones, who proudly mock all religions against their conscience; of these he says: He who is not with me, scatters. For such are many. Such also are those who fashion religions for themselves by their own judgment, and take from the Gospel what they like, and reject what they do not like.

On the third.

After Christ had spoken the above things concerning the most secret and sublime matters against his adversaries, he now turns his speech to the Church, to whom he preaches about the fear of God, as if he were saying: The power of the devil is greater than you understand, the wrath against blasphemy is greater than you can think. Now, therefore, I forewarn you, that having acknowledged the Gospel, and having obtained liberation, you should retain the fear of God, because many after liberation become secure and idle: and idleness nourishes and inflames wicked desires, as it is written: My servant has grown fat, and has kicked. Likewise: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. And Sodom, six years or thereabouts after the enemies had been divinely defeated by Abraham, began to fall into horrendous vices. And in Matthew it is specifically said about idleness: He finds the house empty, etc. Therefore, let us shake off security by the proposed examples, which show what vices and what punishments have followed after security.

Latin:

Dominica Oculi. Evangelium Lucae 11.

Et erat eiiciens daemonium, ei illud erat mutum. Factum est autem egresso daemonio, locutus est mutus, et admiratae sunt turbae. Quidam autem ex eis dixerunt: In Beelzebub principe daemoniorum eiicit daemonia. Alii autem tentantes, signum de coelo quaerebant ab eo. Ipse autem sciens cogitationes eorum, dixit eis: Omne regnum contra seipsum divisum, desolabitur, et domus supra domum cadet. Si autem et Satanas contra seipsum divisus, quomodo stabit regnum eius? quia dicitis, in Beelzebub me eiicere daemonia. Si autem ego in Beelzebub eiicio daemonia, filii vestri in quo eiiciunt? Ideo ipsi iudices vestri erunt. Si autem in digito Dei eiicio daemonia, profecto pervenit in vos regnum Dei. Cum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum, in pace sunt ea quae possidet. Si autem fortior eo superveniens vicerit eum, universa arma eius aufert, in quibus confidebat, et spolia eius distribuit.

Qui non est mecum, me est, et qui non colligit mecum, dispergit.

Cum immundus spiritus exierit de homine, ambulat per loca inaquosa, quaerens requiem, et non inveniens, dicit: Revertar in domum meam, unde exivi. Et cum venerit, invenit eam scopis mundatam et ornatam, tunc vadit et assumit septem alios spiritus, nequiores se, et ingressi, habitant ibi. Et fiunt novissima hominis illius peiora primis.

Factum est autem, cum haec diceret, extollens vocem quaedam mulier de turba, dixit illi: Beatus venter qui te portavit, et ubera quae suxisti. At ille dixit: Quinimo, beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud.

I. Locus, Disputatio principalis est de miraculis.

II. De blasphemis, et de mediis seu neutralibus.

III. Doctrina de timore Dei, contra securitatem, quae sequi solet liberationem.

De primo.

Fuerunt omnibus temporibus inde usque ab initio mundi et Ecclesiae, et impiorum aliqua miracula, ut apud Ethnicos saepe spectra aliquid denunciarunt. Item, Statuae locutae sunt. Item, Calchas praedixit fore, ut primum decimo anno Troia caperetur. Quaeri igitur potest, si doctrina ex miraculis iudicanda est, utra est vera? Respondeo: Vera discernuntur a falsis dupliciter, primum impossibilitate, secundo finibus.

Primum enim habet Ecclesia quaedam propria miracula, quae diabolus non potest imitari, ut resuscitationem mortuorum, sistere cursum Solis, anum sterilem et effoetam efficere foecundam. Haec et similia sunt solius Ecclesiae, et sunt impossibilia diabolo. Ideo miracula Ecclesiae anteferenda sunt Ethnicis, et sunt certa, et firma testimonia doctrinae divinitus traditae. His adnumerandum est, quod et hic traditur, eiicere repugnantem diabolum. Etsi enim diabolus interdum quasi colludens, cedit etiam praestigiatoribus et impostoribus, tamen haec eiectio, quam Christus et Apostoli faciebant, erat dissimilis: eiiciebant enim repugnantem, non colludentem, quia toties clamitat diabolus, se ante tempus cruciari. Recte igitur argumentatur Christus, Eiicio diabolum repugnantem et invitum, et ubique eiicio, quamvis atrociter saevientem: ergo eiicio divina potentia superante diabolum repugnantem.

Secundum discrimen sumendum est a finibus. Finis miraculorum diaboli est regulariter alicuius erroris aut sceleris confirmatio. Econtra, finis miraculorum Ecclesiae est confirmatio veri cultus, et consentit cum verbo iam ante revelato, de vero cultu et Filio Dei. Ut vaticinia Tiresiae, aut Calchantis, quos fines habebant? Iubebant mactare humanas hostias, et confirmabant praesentem idolomaniam. Cum autem hi errores sint manifesti furores, et quidem multa alia vitia Ethnicorum stabilierint, satis apparet haec miracula non esse divina. Talia miracula fiunt etiam nunc in invocatione mortuorum, ut confirmetur impietas et error.

Haec discrimina miraculorum diligenter observanda sunt, ut confirmemus animos nostros testimoniis verorum miraculorum, et discernamus ea a praestigiis. Magna est enim diaboli potentia, et multos offundit errores humanis mentibus: et omnibus temporibus confirmavit impias superstitiones prodigiosis quibusdam eventibus. Ideo muniendi sunt pii firmis testimoniis, ut Moses superabat Magos, sic Ecclesia superat diabolum dupliciter. Habet quaedam propria miracula, quae imitari diabolus non potest. Item, refert ea non ad stabilienda scelera, sed ad confirmandam veram agnitionem Dei, et consentientem cum verbo Dei tradito. Has regulas meminerimus.

De secundo.

Dicitur hic quoddam peccatum non remitti. Nec opus est a priori definire, quodnam sit: quia nos habemus mandatum, ut agamus poenitentiam, et credamus omnia peccata remitti. Huic regulae necesse est obtemperare, quia universaliter vera est sententia: Gratia exuberat supra peccatum. Item: Et ipse est propiciatio pro peccatis nostris, non pro nostris tantum, sed pro peccatis totius mundi. Sed manifestum est, quosdam mordicus tenere perpetuum contentum, vel odium Christi, etiam contra conscientiam. Hi nec volunt oblatam remissionem accipere, nec volunt credere, sed aut securi superbissime derident Evangelium, aut furenter oderunt. De his a posteriore iudicemus, habere eos peccatum contra Spiritum sanctum, quia in illo perpetuo contentu, vel odio Christi discedunt, et ruunt in aeternam iram, sicut Iudas, et similes.

Et hic utrique complectendi sunt, hostes qui contra conscientiam Evangelium oppugnant, et medii, qui superbe contra conscientiam derident omnes religiones, de his dicit: Qui non est mecum, dispergit. Tales enim pluri sunt. Tales sunt etiam, qui sibi suo arbitrio fingunt religiones, et sumunt ex Evangelio quod libet, quod non libet reiiciunt.

De tertio.

Postquam Christus de rebus maxime arcanis, et sublimibus contra adversarios superiora dixit, iam vertit sermonem ad Ecclesiam, cui concionatur de timore Dei, quasi dicat, maior est potentia diaboli, quam vos intelligitis, maior ira adversus blasphemiam, quam cogitare potestis. Iam igitur vos praemoneo, ut agnito Evangelio, et consecuti liberationem, retineatis timorem Dei, quia multi post liberationem fiunt securi et ociosi: et ocium alit ac incendit pravas cupiditates, sicut scriptum est: Incrassatus est servus meus, et recalcitravit. Item: Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et resurrexit ludere. Et Sodoma sexennio aut circiter, postquam hostes divinitus profligati erant per Abraham, coepit ruere in horrenda vitia. Et in Matthaeo nominatim dicitur de ocio: Invenit domum vacantem etc. Ideo excutiamus securitatem propositis exemplis, quae ostendunt, quae vitia, et quae poenae post securitatem secutae sint.

## 14:1-11 Seventeenth Sunday After Trinity
Seventeenth Sunday after Trinity.

The Gospel of Luke 14.

And it came to pass, when Jesus went into the house of one of the chief Pharisees on the Sabbath, to eat bread, and they watched him. And behold, there was a certain man before him who had the dropsy. And Jesus answering spoke unto the lawyers and Pharisees, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? But they held their peace, and he took him, and healed him, and let him go. And answering them, he said: Which of you shall have an ass or an ox fall into a pit, and will not straightway pull him out on the Sabbath day? And they could not answer him to these things. And he spoke also a parable to those who were bidden, marking how they chose out the chief rooms; saying unto them: When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; and he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room. But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher. Then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee. For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

There are three principal topics.

I. Concerning the Sabbath, what is the proper and principal meaning of the commandment. II. What are the proper works of the Sabbath. III. Concerning humility, concerning vocation, and concerning ambition.

Concerning the first.

As the first commandment speaks of the acknowledgment of God, and the motions of the heart toward God; the second of the confession of the mouth, and the preaching of doctrine; so the third speaks of public ceremonies divinely instituted, that is, of the whole public ministry. For a certain day is appointed to this end, that there may be public assemblies, in which congregations may be taught by the preaching of the Gospel and by ceremonies. For both must be understood, because ceremonies without doctrine are transformed into superstition. Wherefore, when the Sabbath is named, let all ceremonies divinely instituted be understood, and let us know that the preservation of the public ministry, of the doctrine, and of the ceremonies which God has instituted, is commanded. For that public ministry, there is need of some certain time; therefore, the observance of the Sabbath is not the idleness of that day, but, as the text says, sanctification, that is, the placing of oneself in holy works, namely, in the divine ministry.

They therefore violate this third commandment, first, those who are in charge, if they do not teach, or neglect the doctrine, or do not teach correctly. Then, those who neglect or corrupt the ceremonies divinely instituted, such as those who read Masses, that they may offer them for others, or for the sake of gain, or who exercise other superstitions. The people also sin, who either never hear, or rarely hear pious sermons, or never or rarely attend public ceremonies. For although in the New Testament a certain day is not commanded, as it is in the divine law, yet he who is absent out of contempt, or by his own example confirms the negligence of others, he sins gravely. Just as a memorable example exists in Jeremiah 17, where the Prophet rebukes those who on the Sabbath were carrying goods through the gates, that is, were trading while neglecting the ministry, and a threat is added: I will kindle a fire in the gates, etc. And again a promise is added: if you will sanctify the Sabbath, kings and princes shall enter through the gate, that is, you shall have a flourishing kingdom, etc.

Because God wishes to help individuals in the preservation of the ministry. The people also sin, who by their presence confirm impious worship. They also sin who hinder the public ministry, who either take away the stipends due to the ministers, or refuse to contribute them.

He also sins who, having neglected the care of meditating on the doctrine of the Gospel, spends the Sabbaths in profane occupations, or games, or other things which lead minds away from pious meditation. Now let everyone consider how widely the violation of the Sabbath extends, and let us not think it a light sin, the contempt of the public ministry.

Concerning the second. The history of the man cured of the dropsy shows what the observance of the Sabbath is. For the law does not command simply the idleness of the Sabbath, but forbids works that hinder the public ministry. Furthermore, it commands sanctification, that is, certain works of the divine ministry. Wherefore this action of Christ was truly the observance of the Sabbath and sanctification.

For Christ here preaches, and adds a work, which is a testimony of the doctrine. testimony of doctrine. For these are the proper works appropriate to the Sabbath: the sermon of the Gospel, the meditation of the Gospel, and pious examples, which properly assist the ministry. Christ also preaches at other times about certain other works that are appropriate for the Sabbath, such as the necessary duties of love. The Maccabees fought on the Sabbath, and indeed those battles were appropriate for the Sabbath in two ways: both because they were a confession of doctrine and a preservation of the Sabbath and the law, and because they were works necessary for love.

On the third.

Humility is the fear of God, that is, having acknowledged our own weakness, to truly fear the wrath of God, lest He cast away those who are unworthy or ill-suited, but nevertheless to obey God in one's calling, and to judge that gifts are given to us for the common utility, and that outcomes are not happy without God, nor are others to be despised, since they can become more useful instruments of God. To this virtue, faith must be added, which in one's calling seeks and expects help from God, just as the Prophets often teach, Psalm 26: "Wait for the Lord, act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord." Such was the great-hearted warrior David, and yet he was humble; he acknowledged his own infirmity, and did not despise others, as Goliath despised those who were lesser, but David obeyed his calling and expected help from God.

Conversely, pride is a trust in one's own industry, with God neglected, or the goal of one's calling neglected, as Goliath and Sennacherib trusted in their own strength while despising God; Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander were pleased with themselves and thought that such great empires were gained by their own virtue, and they neither acknowledge nor fear God. Therefore, they also rush securely into other sins, as Alexander defiled himself with manifold baseness. Others seek higher callings: for pride declares itself in many ways, as in Absalom, Cassius, and Antony. Others sin by not acknowledging superior gifts in others, as Agamemnon, who is superior in position, does not acknowledge Achilles to be superior in virtue.

Concerning all these, this rule is handed down here: Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled. And the tragic falls of most excellent men show this, such as those of Saul, Goliath, Sennacherib, Pompey, Agesilaus, Alexander, and Antony. Indeed, in the Church, the chief humiliation occurs because judgment begins at the house of God, as the notable examples of the saints show—Samson, David, Nebuchadnezzar, and others who fell from a high pinnacle so that they might acknowledge their own infirmity, and so that the power of God and the mercy of God might be seen, as in David, who was cast down and restored. From these examples, let us learn both things: namely, the fear of God, having acknowledged our own infirmity, and faith in obedience to our calling. Let us also learn to keep ourselves within the bounds of our calling.

Latin:

Dominica XVII. post Trinitatis.

Evangelium Lucae 14.

Et factum est cum introisset Jesus in domum cuiusdam principis Pharisaeorum Sabbato, ad manducandum panem, et ipsi observabant eum. Et ecce, homo quidam hydropicus erat ante illum. Et respondens Jesus dixit ad Legisperitos et Pharisaeos, dicens: Si licet Sabbato curare? At illi tacuerunt, et apprehensum sanavit eum, ac dimisit. Et respondens ad illos, dixit: Cuius vestrum asinus aut bos in puteum cadet, et non continuo extrahet illum die Sabbati? Et non poterant ad haec respondere illi. Dicebat autem et ad invitatos parabolam, intendens, quomodo primos accubitus eligerent, dicens ad illos: Cum invitatus fueris ab aliquo ad nuptias, non discumbas in primo loco, ne forte honoratior te sit invitatus ab illo, et veniens is, qui te et illum vocavit, dicat tibi: Da huic locum, et tunc incipias cum rubore novissimum locum habere. Sed cum vocatus fueris, vade, recumbe in novissimo loco, ut cum venerit qui te invitavit dicat tibi: Amice, ascende superius. Tunc erit tibi gloria coram simul discumbentibus. Quia omnia qui seipsum exaltat, humiliabitur, et qui seipsum humiliat, exaltabitur.

Tres sunt praecipui loci.

I. De Sabbato, quae sit propria et principalis sententia praecepti. II. Quae sint propria Sabbati opera. III. De humilitate, de vocatione, et de ambitione.

De primo.

Ut primum praeceptum loquitur de agnitione Dei, et motibus cordis erga Deum. Secundum de confessione oris, et praedicatione doctrinae. Ita tertium loquitur de publicis ceremoniis divinitus institutis, hoc est, de toto publico ministerio. Nam dies certa constituta est ad hunc finem, ut sint publici congressus, in quibus doceantur coetus praedicatione Evangelii et ceremoniis. Utrumque enim intelligendum est, quia ceremoniae sine doctrina transformantur in superstitionem. Quare cum nominatur Sabbatum, intelligantur omnes ceremoniae divinitus institutae, et sciamus praecipi conservationem publici ministerii, doctrinae et ceremoniarum, quas Deus instituit.

Ad illud publicum ministerium opus est aliquo tempore certo, est igitur Sabbati observatio non ocium eius diei, sed ut textus inquit, sanctificatio, id est, collocatio in opera sancta, videlicet in ministerium divinum. Violant igitur hoc tertium praeceptum, primum hi qui praesunt, si non doceant, aut negligant doctrinam, aut non recte doceant. Deinde qui negligunt aut depravant ceremonias divinitus institutas, ut qui Missas legunt, ut offerant pro aliis, aut quaestus causa, aut qui alias superstitiones exercent. Peccat item populus, qui vel nunquam audit, vel raro audit pias conciones, aut nunquam, aut raro interest publicis ceremoniis. Etsi enim in novo Testamento dies certa non est praecepta, ut in lege divina, tamen qui ex contemptu abest, aut suo exemplo confirmat aliorum negligentiam, is graviter peccat. Sicut memorabile exemplum extat Ieremiae 17. ubi Propheta obiurgat eos, qui in Sabbato per portas convehebant merces, id est, negociabantur neglecto ministerio, et additur comminatio, succendam ignem in portis etc.

Et rursus additur promissio, si sanctificabis Sabbatum, intrabunt per portam reges et principes, id est, habebitis regnum florens etc. Quia Deus vult singulos adiuvare conservationem ministerii. Peccat item populus, qui sua praesentia confirmat impios cultus.

Peccant et illi, qui impediunt ministerium publicum, qui stipendia debita ministris aut eripiunt, aut conferre nolunt. Peccat item, qui neglecta cura meditandae doctrinae Evangelii, conferunt Sabbata in occupationes prophanas, aut ludos, aut alia, quae abducunt animos a pia meditatione. Iam cogitet quisque quam late pateat violatio Sabbati, nec putemus leve peccatum esse, contemptum publici ministerii.

De secundo. Historia de curato hydropico ostendit quid sit observatio Sabbati. Non enim praecipit lex simpliciter de ocio Sabbati, sed prohibet opera impedientia ministerium publicum. Caeterum praecipit sanctificationem, id est, certa opera divini ministerii.

Quare haec actio Christi, fuit vere observatio Sabbati et sanctificatio. Nam Christus hic concionatur, et addit opus, quod est te stimonium doctrinae. Haec enim sunt propria opera convenientia Sabbato, concio Evangelii, meditatio Evangelii, exempla pia, proprie adiuvantia ministerium. Alias etiam concionatur Christus de aliis operibus quibusdam, quae conveniunt Sabbato, ut necessaria officia dilectionis. Maccabaei in Sabbato pugnabant, et quidem praelia illa dupliciter Sabbato conveniebant, et quia erant confessio doctrinae, et conservatio Sabbati et legis, et erant opera necessaria dilectionis.

De tertio.

Humilitas est timor Dei, hoc est, agnita nostra imbecillitate, vere metuere iram Dei, ne indignos aut parum idoneos abiiciat, sed tamen in vocatione Deo parere, et iudicare dona nobis dari ad communem utilitatem, nec eventus sine Deo felices esse, nec caeteros despiciendos esse, cum possint fieri utiliora organa Dei. Ad hanc virtutem accedere debet fides, quae in vocatione petat, et expectet auxilium a Deo, sicut saepe docent Prophetae, Psalm. 26.: Expecta Dominum, viriliter age, et confortetur cor tuum, et expecta Dominum. Talis erat bellator magnanimus David, et tamen erat humilis, agnoscebat infirmitatem suam, nec despiciebat caeteros, ut Goliath despiciebat minores, sed David vocationi parebat, et expectabat a Deo auxilium.

Econtra, superbia est fiducia propriae industriae, neglecto Deo, aut neglecta meta vocationis, ut Goliath, Sennaherib, confidunt viribus suis contemto Deo, Nabugdonosor, Alexander placent sibi, et existimant sua virtute parta esse tanta imperia, nec agnoscunt nec timent Deum. Ideo et in alia delicta securi ruunt, ut Alexander polluit se multiplici turpitudine. Alii appetunt superiores vocationes: nam superbia multipliciter se declarat, ut Absalon, Cassius, Antonius. Alii peccant non agnoscentes dona superiora in aliis, ut Agamemnon qui superior est loco, non agnoscit Achillem virtute superiorem esse.

De his omnibus traditur hic regula: Omnis qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Idque ostendunt tragici casus praestantissimorum virorum, ut Saulis, Goliath, Sennaherib, Pompeii, Agesilai, Alexandri, Antonii. Imo in Ecclesia praecipua fit humiliatio, quia iudicium a domo Dei incipit, ut ostendunt insignia exempla sanctorum, Samsonis, Davidis, Nabugdonosor, et aliorum qui ex alto fastigio delapsi sunt, ut agnoscerent suam infirmitatem, et conspiceretur potentia Dei et misericordia Dei, ut in Davide deiecto et restituto. His exemplis utrunque discamus, videlicet timorem Dei, agnita nostra infirmitate, et fidem in obedientia vocationis. Discamus item nos continere intra metas vocationis.

## 14:16-17 Second Sunday After Trinity
Second Sunday after Trinity. Gospel of Luke 14.

A certain man made a great supper, and invited many, and sent his servant at the hour of supper, to say to them that were invited: Come, for now all things are ready.

And they began all at once to make excuses. The first said to him: I have bought a field, and I must needs go out, and see it, I pray thee, have me excused. And another said: I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them, I pray thee, have me excused. And another said: I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.

And the servant returned and reported these things to his lord. Then the master of the house being angry, said to his servant: Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the feeble, and the blind, and the lame. And the servant said: Lord, it is done as thou hast commanded, and yet there is room. And the lord said to the servant: Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled. For I say unto you, that none of those men, which were bidden, shall taste of my supper.

The reproof is the contempt of the Gospel, in those who are especially called, that is, who seem to be the principal part of the Church. And a horrible sentence is added concerning their condemnation: None of them shall taste of my supper.

Although Christ preached concerning the rejection of the Jewish people, yet he does not speak of them alone, but the sermon pertains generally to all times, and accuses the contempt of the Gospel in teachers, rulers, and the more prominent part of the people. But human blindness is to be acknowledged and deplored, that men care less for God and eternal things than for any other business of the body. Just as often in the countryside, rustics are more officious toward a cowherd than toward a pastor of souls, and when asked, they respond that they have more need of the cowherd.

This example depicts similar affections in the highest ranks. How great is the contention for glory, for wealth, while in the meantime men care most coldly for those things which pertain to the glory of God or the salvation of their own souls. Men are more troubled by the loss of money than by the conscience of any sin.

This preposterous solicitude and depravity of men is signified by the examples recited here. One alleges that he has bought fields; this man, because of family matters, neglects his own salvation. Another alleges that he has bought oxen; this man values civil power and civil business more than the Gospel. Just as political men now say that they are more occupied with other necessary businesses than to have time to know the Gospel. Likewise, they neglect it because of civil peace, etc. Another alleges a marriage; this man prefers his spouse and children to confession, and does not want to put his own in jeopardy for the sake of the Gospel.

Thus, in sum, the examples point to this: that they rebuke the perversion of human nature, which neglects God and with greater solicitude cares for inferior businesses, which even if they are necessary, yet were not to be preferred to God, according to that: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you. A second point is proposed: the image of the Church, when the more prominent part having been rejected, the lame and the blind are called. It warns, therefore, that God preserves the Church by gathering some here and there who do not excel in wealth and authority, just as Isaiah says: Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have been made as Sodom and Gomorrah.

Third point.

Concerning compulsion.

Three things are to be observed.

First, it is a most sweet consolation that God even commands us to be compelled, for it signifies that He truly seeks our salvation and truly wills to save, just as when a father is seriously affected by the care of governing his Son, he uses not only cold admonitions but also a certain severity of authority toward him, and compels him to do his duty. Secondly, Christ signifies that the ministry is truly effective, because compulsion in this place properly signifies that which is done through the ministry of the Gospel, which proposes the command of God and eternal punishments, and is effective with God's help. Wherefore this sentence also adorns the authority of the ministry and signifies that God is effective through the ministry.

Thirdly, although Christ here says nothing about bodily compulsion or the office of magistrates, but only about the ministry of the Gospel, which compels by the proposed command of God, by proposed eternal punishments, and also by God's help: yet the magistrate also has his own compulsion, namely, that which pertains to external discipline, as we have often said elsewhere, that the Magistrate is the guardian of the law, so that he may remove external idolatry and punish external offenses.

Latin:

Dominica II. post Trinitatis. Evangelium Lucae 14.

Homo quidam fecit coenam magnam, et vocavit multos, et misit servum suum hora coenae, ut diceret invitatis: Venite, quia iam parata sunt omnia.

Et coeperunt simul omnes excusare se. Primus dixit ei: Agrum emi, et necesse mihi est exire, et videre illum, Rogo te, habe me excusatum. Et alter dixit: Iuga boum emi quinque, et eo ad probandum illa, Rogo te, habe me excusatum. Et alius dixit: Uxorem duxi, et ideo venire non possum.

Et reversus servus nunciavit haec domino suo. Tunc iratus paterfamilias, dixit servo suo: Exi cito in plateas et vicos civitatis, et pauperes ac debiles, et claudos et coecos introduc huc. Et ait servus: Domine factum est ut imperasti, et adhuc locus est. Et ait dominus servo: Exi in vias et sepes, et compelle intrare, ut impleatur domus mea. Dico enim vobis, quod nemo virorum illorum, qui vocati sunt, gustabit coenam meam.

Reprehensio est contemptus Evangelii, in his qui praecipue sunt vocati, hoc est, qui videntur esse praecipua pars Ecclesiae. Et adiecta est horribilis sententia de illorum condemnatione: Nemo illorum gustabit coenam.

Quanquam autem de reiectione populi Iudaici concionatus est Christus, tamen non de illis solis loquitur, sed generaliter pertinet concio ad omnia tempora, accusat contemptum Evangelii, in doctoribus, regentibus, et praestantiore parte populi. Est autem agnoscenda et deploranda coecitas humana, quod levius curant homines Deum, et res aeternas, quam ulla reliqua corporis negocia. Sicut plerunque in pagis rustici magis officiosi sunt erga bubulcum, quam animarum pastorem, et interrogati, respondent se magis opus habere bubulco.

Hoc exemplum pingit similes affectus in summis. Quanta est contentio de gloria, de opibus, cum interim frigidissime curent homines, ea quae ad gloriam Dei, aut propriam animarum salutem pertinent. Magis anguntur homines iactura pecuniae, quam conscientia alicuius peccati.

Hanc praeposteram solicitudinem et depravationem hominum, significant exempla hic recitata. Alius allegat se emisse agros, hic propter rem familiarem negligit salutem suam. Alius allegat se emisse boves, hic pluris facit civilem potentiam et civilia negocia, quam Evangelium. Sicut iam politici viri dicunt, se esse occupatiores caeteris negotiis necessariis, quam ut vacet Evangelium cognoscere. Item, negligunt propter pacem civilem etc. Alius allegat nuptias, hic praefert conjugem et liberos confessioni, non vult in discrimen venire suos propter Evangelium.

Ita in summa huc spectant exempla, ut reprehendant perversionem humanae naturae, quae negligit Deum, et maiori solicitudine curat negocia inferiora, quae etiamsi sunt necessaria, tamen non erant anteferenda Deo, iuxta illud: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis. Secundus locus proponitur imago Ecclesiae, cum praestantiori parte reiecta vocantur claudi et coeci. Monet igitur Deum conservare Ecclesiam, colligendis aliquibus passim, qui non antecellunt opibus et autoritate, sicut inquit Esaias: Nisi Deus reliquisset nobis semen, essemus facti sicut Sodoma et Gomorra.

Tertius locus.

De coactione.

Tria sunt observanda.

Primum dulcissima est consolatio, quod Deus etiam cogi nos iubet, significat enim vere se expetere salutem nostram, et vere velle salvare, ut cum pater serio afficitur cura regendi Filii, non tantum frigidis admonitionibus, sed etiam severitate quadam imperii erga eum utitur, cogit eum facere officium. Secundo, Significat Christus ministerium vere esse efficax, quia coactio proprie hoc loco significat eam, quae fit per ministerium Evangelii, quod proponit mandatum Dei et aeternas poenas, et est efficax adiuvante Deo. Quare et haec sententia ornat autoritatem ministerii, et significat Deum esse efficacem per ministerium.

Tertio, Quanquam Christus hic nihil loquitur de coactione corporali, seu de officio magistratuum, sed tantum de ministerio Evangelii, quod cogit proposito mandato Dei, propositis aeternis poenis, item, adiuvante Deo: tamen et magistratus suam habet coactionem, scilicet, quod ad disciplinam externam attinet, sicut alias saepe diximus, Magistratus esse custodem legis, ut tollat externam idolatriam, puniat externa delicta.

## 15:1 Sunday III. After Trinity
Sunday III. after Trinity.

Gospel of Luke 15. And all the publicans and sinners were drawing near unto him to hear him.

And The Pharisees and Scribes murmured, saying, "This man receives sinners and eats with them." But He spoke this parable to them, saying: "What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one which is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!' I say to you that likewise there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine just persons who need no repentance.

Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls her friends and neighbors together, saying: 'Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I lost!' Likewise I say to you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents. There are six main topics. I. Concerning mercy and the promise of grace. II. Concerning repentance. III. Concerning the prodigal son. IIII. That calamities call one to repentance. V. Concerning the remission of sins, and new gifts. VI. Concerning the pride of hypocrites. Concerning the first. When the first humans had sinned, God immediately preached repentance to them, and at the same time delivered the promise, by which He revealed His mercy and reconciliation, and received them; and both messages were afterwards more illustrated, as that voice clearly testifies: "As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may turn and live." But human reason, even though it confesses that God is merciful, nevertheless resists in this imagination; it favors the just, and neither receives those who have fallen enormously, nor receives them unless some merits and some compensation have first intervened.

Thus reason, ignorant of the Gospel concerning gratuitous reconciliation, imagines these things, and they reason from the law that Christ admits those guilty of manifest crimes.

They magnified their own discipline, and thought that the Church was to be taken only from that number which retains discipline. Thus all imagine. Although discipline is the most beautiful of all human things, and commanded by God, yet the immense mercy of God calls all to repentance, and offers grace to all who perform repentance, even if they were not previously restrained by discipline. And it is useful in these very histories to consider the magnitude of the mercy of God. We are less surprised that God sent His Gospel to the Jewish people, in whom some true doctrine concerning God had remained, and there was an honest discipline.

But let us compare Rome in the time of Nero to Nazareth. First, in Rome, the true God was entirely unknown; many were openly atheists [ἄθεοι], the rest wickedly worshipped idols. Then the whole city was full of the foulest lusts, which were thought to be permitted pleasures, not worthy of punishment; afterwards, embezzlement and usury were even led to praise. Finally, there was no reverence for God, no modesty, no study of truth and justice. In such a city, God commands that a Church also be gathered for Himself, and such were the customs in almost the whole world.

In this example, the magnitude of the mercy of God is discerned, that to such people, where discipline is so extinct, the voice of God also sounds, calling to repentance and offering salvation. And the matter at first seemed unworthy to the Jews, that the Gospel should be spread among those execrable men who had lived in the highest turpitude without any discipline. Hence are those struggles of Paul, when he affirms that the Gospel pertains to the Gentiles, and that the remission of sins is offered freely for Christ's sake to all who perform repentance. It is a great and salutary consolation for the pious to think of this amplitude of mercy, which is most seen when we think of God spreading the Gospel among those monsters of men, as the Gentiles were then, and as many are now.

Concerning this great mercy, He also preaches here, and proposes images: of the lost sheep, of the lost coin, of the prodigal son. Let this whole sermon be referred to this voice: "As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may turn and live," and let us hold the sum of the Gospel, that to all who perform repentance, the remission of sins is certainly given

of sins freely, for Christ's sake, because God demands that we believe in this voice of the Gospel, and by this faith call upon Him, etc.

Christ seeks the lost sheep; we are all lost sheep, but the misery of those who have lived without discipline is more clearly seen, such as the harlot, the thief, and the innumerable ones who have been converted from the Gentiles. And in the text there is a sweet significance inserted regarding the passion of Christ. Christ places the found sheep upon His shoulders, that is, He Himself transfers our burden onto Himself, He becomes a victim for us. Then, carrying us, He brings us to His flock; He carries us, feeds us, cherishes us, and governs us.

On the second point. But thus Christ receives and gathers the Church, even from those who have lived without discipline, if they perform repentance. He does not receive those who persevere in sins against their conscience, as it is clearly said: Fornicators, adulterers, shall not possess the kingdom of God. And 1 John 3: He who commits sin is of the devil. Let us know, therefore, that repentance is necessary, and let us learn what things it embraces. Since, however, repentance or conversion to God contains three parts: Contrition, faith, and new obedience, one must diligently think about each one.

Contrition is truly to tremble at the recognized wrath of God against sin, and truly to grieve that we have offended God by our contempt and contumacy. Here, let it first be considered when a man is without repentance, namely, when he lives without any sense of the fear of God, as Paul says in Ephesians 4 concerning those who are secure: Who after they had ceased to feel pain, gave themselves up to impurity. This profound security is often most gravely accused, as in Jeremiah 6: They knew not how to blush. Item: This people has a forehead of bronze. Wherefore, against this security, let us gather testimonies of the wrath of God, the voice of the law, examples of punishments, the passion of Christ, and our present and impending calamities. And let us know that the whole human race is burdened with such great calamities so that we may learn to recognize the wrath of God against sin, as it is said in Psalm 38: Because of iniquity you correct man. Item, Micah 7: I will bear the wrath of God, because I have sinned against Him.

Nor can human nature sufficiently understand how great an evil sin is, and how great the wrath of God is. It seemed a light thing to taste the apple: but contempt of God and contumacy against God is an infinite and horrendous evil. God shows this by the magnitude of the punishments that followed. And the first parents themselves began to understand the magnitude of their fall more when they saw the murder of Abel, and the crime of Cain, and then many slaughters, and many sins.

Thus, in us, let the recognition of the wrath of God grow, let sorrow grow, by the sight of punishments. And let not the thought of punishments be omitted, because some argue with sufficiently idle minds that repentance should not be begun from the fear of punishment, or the preaching of the law.

Rather, it is necessary that the law be inculcated, because it is the eternal and immutable judgment of God, by which God testifies that He is angry at sin. For even when He forgives, He does not approve of sin, but receives His miserable creature for the sake of the Son, as it is said in Habakkuk 3: O Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years; but punishments, He both imposes and wished to be written, so that His wrath might be seen. These things concerning contrition must be diligently thought about, and security must be rooted out from the soul, because without some fear and sorrow it is impossible for repentance to exist.

Therefore it is said in Isaiah: Where will the Lord dwell? In a contrite spirit, and one who trembles at my words. But it is not enough to teach about contrition, which in calamity often so oppresses men that they are extinguished by grief, and fleeing from God, they rush into eternal destruction.

Therefore, the doctrine of faith must be added, namely, that it is the eternal and immutable command of God that we believe that sins are forgiven us for the sake of the Son, that God has constituted His Son as a victim for our sins, that He has testified that He is truly affected by care for us, that we are truly received, because He joined human nature to Himself by an eternal covenant, when the Son humbled Himself and assumed human nature. This great work of God is treated with contempt, because one does not believe that he is received by God for the sake of the Son.

But human reason opposes many things. Even if God is merciful, yet He is also just; He has mercy on those who compensate for their falls by their own merits. Item, He has mercy on those who have not sinned so atrociously; my sins are too many and great. These are legal and rational imaginations, against which the Gospel must be opposed, which cries out certainly that one is not received freely for the sake of the Son of God; it cries out also that grace abounds above sin. Christ is greater than our sins, provided that you recognize Him by faith, believe that He is the mediator, and through this mediator approach God again, and call upon Him again. Although it is most true that some sins are greater than others, yet we do not perceive the magnitude of those which are thought to be light; always in one sin many things are contained, and one fall begets many, as appears in the fall of Adam, David, Solomon, and finally, daily experience is a witness to this matter. Wherefore, to the magnitude and multitude of sins, let us oppose this saying: grace abounds over sin.

Let us also come to the ministry of the Gospel in the Church, let us confess before the Church that we are guilty, let us show the signs of our conversion, and let us seek absolution, so that by the voice of the Gospel faith may be confirmed, establishing the remission of sins. After we have established the remission of sins, let a new obedience begin, let there be a purpose to do right, let invocation begin, and let no sin be admitted against the conscience. Let us consider that there is no greater evil for man than to live without the invocation of God, that is, not to have God as propitious and a protector, but as an enemy casting one into punishments of every kind. Let us therefore be vigilant and firm, lest we fall against our conscience, lest God be alienated from us again. These things have been briefly said concerning the doctrine of repentance, which must always be thought upon, because it is a secret wisdom, concerning the greatest matters: concerning justice, concerning the wrath of God, concerning human infirmity and contumacy, concerning the punishments of sins, concerning mercy, concerning the Son of God, concerning the miseries of the human race, subject to huge calamities, infirmity, and scandals, even after conversion. This wisdom is something greater than all the wisdom of the world.

Concerning the third.

As he recounted above the images of the lost sheep and the lost drachma: so here he adds a more illustrious one concerning the prodigal son. Although the image is rightly compared to the Jews and the Gentiles, yet universally by the appellation of the prodigal son are understood men without discipline, living in manifest turpitude. And on the contrary, the more frugal son is a man who is governed by honest discipline.

But it is true that discipline is commanded by God, and that the contempt of discipline is severely punished, as public punishments, wars, diseases, poverty, infamy, and very many human calamities testify; and among the goods of nature, no good is greater than honest discipline; yet God, in His immense mercy, calls to Himself not only those who are restrained by discipline, but also the others contaminated by horrendous crimes, just as the voice of the Gospel sounded not only in Nazareth, but also in Rome in the time of Nero and in other places, where all things were full of horrendous turpitude. Let us diligently consider these historical examples, so that we may more clearly perceive the magnitude of the mercy of God, who gathers the Church from such people.

And these examples show to what Christ was looking while preaching here about the prodigal son. For He was looking at the greatest part of the human race living without discipline. And when we consider this image, let us add the doctrine of the Gospel concerning gratuitous remission on account of Christ, as was said above.

And look at the image itself: the son sins twice; he asks for the inheritance before the time, when there is no inheritance for the living, then he removes himself from the father's power, he departs, and he does not want to be ruled by paternal admonitions. Thus all the unbridled invade their inheritance before the time; the goods of talent and other things which God gave so that they might serve Him, we transfer to ourselves, and we abuse them turpitudinously; the mind is not the domicile of God, the body is polluted and becomes an organ of the devil, riches are conferred upon base pleasures. Finally, in sum, think of obscene men, or robbers before conversion, and weigh how great an evil it is to fail from God, and to abuse the gifts of God to the contumely of God.

Observe here also the grammatical annotation, ἐπιβάλλον μέρος. It is a geometric term, and usually signifies a proportional part, according to Ptolemy, Aristotle, and Demosthenes.

But regularly and for the most part, bodily punishments follow in this life the contempt of discipline, for three causes: for the justice of God, to coerce men, and so that we may be called to repentance. These three causes are often repeated in the scriptures.

Concerning the first, it is said in the Decalogue: I am a God visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons, unto the third and fourth generation. Concerning the second, in the Psalm: Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle. Concerning the third, Isaiah 28: Vexation alone gives understanding. And Jeremiah 31: Thou hast chastised me, O Lord, and I have been instructed.

Thus here the Prodigal, after he is now pressed by calamity, begins to think of causes and remedies, and as the text says, returning to himself, he said, that is, admonished by calamity, he thought of the causes and the remedies. But few return to themselves in this way; Pharaoh, Saul, Nero, and many others, oppressed by calamity, nevertheless rage against God, and rush into blasphemy. inias, despairs, and eternal destruction.

But those who return to the Father, with what great clemency He receives them, is most clearly signified in this image. Basil says of this very place: You have only to wish, and God anticipates you. Thus here the father sees him approaching from afar; we approach trembling and languidly, and we bring not merits, but a polluted conscience and great filth. Although, however, we are such, yet the Father meets us, provided we approach; He sees from afar, that is, He knows our miseries, He cares for us, He utters the Word, and calls us, He is moved with mercy, He seriously wishes to save us, as it is said in Hosea 11: My heart is turned within me, my compassion is kindled, I will not execute the fierceness of my anger.

Then He meets us, that is, to us who are languishing, He Himself draws us by the Word and the Holy Spirit. As it is said in Revelation 3: Repent, Behold I stand at the door, and knock; if any man hear my voice, I will enter unto him.

He falls upon our neck, embraces us, sustains David and those like him in sorrow and punishments. For we would be extinguished by grief and pain, unless we were helped and saved by God. Finally, He gives a kiss, that is, He announces the remission of sins, and with new light and consolation mitigates terrors and punishments.

On the other hand, the son submits himself to the father, confesses his guilt, and acknowledges a double offense, namely, that he had been contumacious to God and to his father. In this recognition and reconciliation, renewal or regeneration takes place.

Therefore, this new adornment is described: a robe, a ring, sandals. For in conversion, the Holy Spirit is given back, as it is said in Romans 8: As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.

The ring signifies the Gospel and faith, by which the one received recognizes that the honor of a son of the family is restored to him, and his former nobility is returned to him. For the Gospel is a testimony of reconciliation, and faith is the apprehension and application, as if by a ring the application of some honor were signified. Finally, the ring is a sign of some covenant. Now, however, this reconciled one makes a covenant again with God, which is done by the recognition of the Gospel and faith.

The robe signifies a good conscience universally. The sandals signify the works of one's calling, in which confession ought especially to shine.
