Et ingressus transibat per Iericho, et ecce, vir nomine Zachaeus, et hic princeps erat publicanorum, et ipse erat dives, et quaerebat videre Iesum, quis esset, et non poterat prae turba, quia statura parvus erat. Et praecurrens ante, ascendit in sycomorum, ut videret eum, quia illac erat transiturus. Et cum venisset ad locum, suspiciens Iesus vidit illum, et dixit ad eum: Zachaee, festinans descende, hodie enim in domo tua oportet me manere. Et festinans descendit, et excepit illum gaudens. Et qui videbant, omnes murmurabant dicentes, quod ad virum peccatorem ingressus divertisset. Stans autem Zachaeus, dixit ad Dominum: Ecce dimidium bonorum meorum Domine do pauperibus, et si quo aliquem defraudavi, reddo quadruplum. Ait autem Iesus ad eum: Hodie salus huic domui facta est, eo quod et ipse est filius Abrahae. Venit enim filius hominis quaerere et salvum facere, quod perierat.

Exemplum est gratuitae vocationis, poenitentiae et absolutionis, et adiecta est concio de remissione peccatorum.

I. Locus de vocatione.

Matth. 9. dicitur: Non veni vocare iustos, sed peccatores ad poenitentiam. Haec est doctrina Evangelii propria, quod propter Christum donetur remissio peccatorum credenti, gratis, non propter nostra merita, et quod hac fide velit Deus invocari, sicut ait Paulus: Per hunc habemus accessum ad patrem. Hanc consolationem in Evangelio propositam discamus et amplectamur. Et cogitemus diligenter causas, quare necesse sit in Ecclesia retineri hanc doctrinam de gratuita remissione, seu de exclusiva, Gratis: sunt autem quatuor causae.

Prima, ut tribuatur debitus honos Filio Dei, videlicet, quod propter ipsum detur remissio peccatorum, non propter nostra ulla merita. Secunda causa, ut conscientia habeat firmam consolationem, ac certo statuere possis, quod habeas remissionem peccatorum, et Deus iam sit tibi propicius, ac vere velit accipere tuas preces, et dare vitam aeternam credenti. De hac causa loquitur Paulus Rom. 4. Ideo ex fide gratis, ut sit firma promissio.

Tertia causa est, ut possimus Deum vere invocare, quia cor dubitans fugit Deum, irascitur Deo, sicut Saul, Achas et similes, non igitur invocat. Scriptum est autem: Per hunc habemus accessum fide. Quare ut veri cultus Deo tribui possint, necesse est tenere doctrinam, quod placeamus et exaudiamur propter Filium Dei, gratis, non propter nostram dignitatem. Ideo dicitur: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis etc.

Quarta causa est, ut discrimen legis et promissionis evangelicae perspicue conspiciatur. Quia lex etiam dicit, Deum misericordem esse, sed ait iustis et dignis esse misericordem. Evangelium vero clamat, omnes iniustos et indignos esse, et promittit omnibus remissionem peccatorum gratis, propter Filium Dei, et praecipit hanc fide accipi, ut Iohan. 3. et Rom. 3. clare scriptum est.

Haec est summa doctrinae, quae et in hac historia traditur, cum ait Christus: Venit Filius hominis quaerere, et salvare quod perierat. Sciamus et nos quaeri, sicut admirabili bonitate rursus tenebras Ecclesiae discussit, et restituit lucem Evangelii, sciamus nobis offerri beneficia Christi, remissionem peccatorum, gratiam et vitam aeternam, et summum Dei cultum esse, agnoscere Filium Dei, petere et accipere haec beneficia, sicut pater aeternus inquit: Hunc audite, et 1. Iohan. 5.: Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum, quia non credit in testimonium, quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo, et hoc est testimonium, quod vitam aeternam dedit nobis Deus, et haec vita in Filio eius est, et qui habet Filium, habet vitam, qui non habet Filium, vitam non habet.

Haec conspiciuntur in hoc exemplo. Zachaeus erat homo iniustus, vectigalia supra leges exigens, et habens iniusta aucupia quaestus, ut plerumque fit in praefecturis. Talem virum vocat Christus ad gratiam, ut testetur se vocare peccatores. Sed hic addendum est. Hic publicanus non habebat meritorum praerogativam, sed hoc aderat, Christum audiebat, erat in hoc populo, ubi sonabat Evangelium, quia non sit vocatio sine Evangelio. Idque significatur per hunc stantem in arbore sycomoro. Significatur enim primum vocatos esse eos, qui stabant in populo Israël, iuxta illud: Ex Sione egredietur lex. Haec doctrina vere est Evangelium Dei perpetuum, quae in isto populo Prophetis commendata est, de venturo Messia.

Nam sycomorus est typus populi Israël. Similis est enim arbor illa fico et moro, et est admodum foecunda et lactea, et gignit fructus copiosos, qui tamen non maturescunt, nisi scalpantur et ungantur oleo, ut scribit Theophrastus. Vides ipsissimam imaginem populi legis, qui est foecundus, potens, habet regnum. Deinde etiam est lacteus, habet etiam promissiones et cultum, et gignit copiosos fructus. Magni labores, egregia opera fuerunt Moisi, Iosuae, Gedeonis, Saulis, Davidis, et multorum aliorum. Sed hi fructus non maturescebant sine sectione et oleo, id est, sine crebris castigationibus et sine divina consolatione. Secabantur Israëlitae, quoties vexabantur ab hostibus Palaestinis, Assyriis, Chaldaeis. Sed Deus infundebat oleum, restituebat et sanabat eos, missis bonis ducibus, ut Samuele, Davide, Iosaphat, Elia, Daniele. Stans igitur in sycomoro, significat stantem in populo legis, ubi sonat doctrina, ubi Prophetae tradiderant promissiones, ubi Christus ipse concionaturus erat. Ita et nos in sycomoro stamus, cum illud idem Evangelium audivimus, traditum per Prophetas et Apostolos, et maxime cum sumus in eo coetu, ubi sonat vere vox Evangelii. Nam sine Evangelio non fit vocatio ad salutem.

De secundo. Exemplum poenitentiae proponitur. Zachaeus fatetur peccata, et promittit emendationem, et absolvitur hac voce Christi: Hodie salus facta est huic domui, quia ipse filius est Abrahae, et habiturus benedictionem, et promissionem vitae aeternae factam Abrahae. Et in ipsa absolutione adiicitur integra concio Evangelii: Veniet Filius hominis quaerere et salvare quod perierat.

## 19:41-48 The 10th Sunday After Trinity
The 10th Sunday after Trinity. The Gospel of Luke 19.

And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: If thou also hadst known, and that in this thy day, the things that are to thy peace; but now they are hidden from thy eyes. For the days shall come upon thee: and thy enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and straiten thee on every side, and beat thee flat to the ground, and thy children who are in thee: and they shall not leave in thee a stone upon a stone, because thou hast not known the time of thy visitation. And entering into the temple, he began to cast out them that sold therein, and them that bought, saying to them: It is written, My house is the house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves. And he was teaching daily in the temple. And the chief priests and the scribes and the rulers of the people sought to destroy him: and they found not what to do to them: for all the people was very attentive to hear him.

There are four points.

The principal point is the threatening of punishments, which hang over all enemies and contemners of the Gospel. Here let the horrible examples from the beginning of the world be compared, by which God declared His wrath against sin. And conversely, let the deepest security of human minds be considered, which is moved by no such horrible examples: the punishment of Adam, the flood, the conflagration of Sodom, the destruction of Pharaoh, the dissipation of the kingdom of Israel, the frequent destructions of Jerusalem, the overthrow of all monarchies, and of all great cities. By the thought of these examples, let us stir up our minds, and remember how foully men have been slaughtered, infants and old men killed, women subjected to insult and slain. How often also has the multitude perished by famine, how often in sieges have legions been decimated for food, when the army fed on human flesh. Yet such is the blindness that these things are thought to happen by chance, just as Christ says here: But now they are hidden from thy eyes.

And Jeremiah rebukes those who deny that punishments happen by the counsel of God, in Lamentations 3: Who is he that hath commanded a thing to be done, when the Lord commandeth it not? And Zephaniah 1: I will visit upon the men that are settled on their lees, that say in their hearts: The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil.

Let us acknowledge this blindness, and correct it, and let us think that punishments hang over us too, and indeed judgment begins at the house of God.

Of the second. The sorrow and tears of Christ are a testimony of true and not feigned love towards us. But since human blindness neglects wrath when such terrible examples are set forth, it recognizes the love of God even less. But let us struggle out of such darkness, and acknowledge both, and amidst our troubles let us firmly believe that He punishes not to destroy, but to recall to repentance, or to exercise us, as He says: As I live, I desire not the death of the sinner, etc.

Of the third.

Christ casts out the buyers and sellers from the temple. The principal sin is idolatry, but wherever this reigns, there it is necessary that horrible crimes and tyrannies follow, since such a state is truly the kingdom of the devil. As the examples of all nations testify, where, once idolatry was increased and accumulated, there followed most monstrous crimes and foulest lusts, as in Egypt, Syria, and Greece, and from thence arose wars and destructive changes. But it is asked, since Christ cast out the buyers and sellers, is it lawful for other preachers to drive out idolatrous priests by force? I answer: Christ casts them out by a singular motion, just as Peter slew Ananias; He is not surrounded by a cohort, He does not rely on human guards. Whatever is done by such a divine or heroic motion is the work of God. It is signified, however, that in the last times there would reign in the Church such merchants of ecclesiastical wealth and dignities, who are cast out from their kingdom divinely, and on account of whom the world will pay the penalties of impious worship.

Of the fourth.

My house is the house of prayer. In this saying, the entire ecclesiastical government and true worship are briefly and significantly described. For when He names prayer, the doctrine of the Gospel must be added correlatively. For without promises and faith, no prayer exists. And let the antithesis be established: You think this house was built for the sake of sacrifices, to increase your wealth, and you pervert both, government and worship; you seek wealth and kingdom for yourselves, and you think sacrifices are worship.

I, on the contrary, proclaim that government is rightly to teach, and to call upon God in faith and a good conscience as the one and proper worship.

Now, as these things are said publicly concerning the house of God and the ministry, so let each one apply them to himself; let us each know that we are the house of God. And so we shall be, when true doctrine sounds within us, and invocation in faith and a good conscience. And let this saying exhort us to invoke and to pray, because it testifies that this is the proper worship of the people of God and the house of God, which God most especially demands.

Latin:

Dominica X. post Trinitatis. Evangelium Lucae 19.

Et ut appropinquavit, videns civitatem, flevit super illam, dicens: Quia si cognovisses et tu, et quidem in hac die tua, quae ad pacem tibi, nunc autem abscondita sunt ab oculis tuis. Quia venient dies super te, et circundabunt te inimici tui vallo, et circumcingent te, et coangustabunt te undique, et solo aequabunt te, et filios tuos in te: et non relinquent in te lapidem super lapidem, eo quod non cognoveris tempus visitationis tuae. Et ingressus in templum, coepit eiicere vendentes in illo et ementes, dicens illis: Scriptum est, Domus mea domus orationis est, vos autem fecistis illam speluncam latronum. Et erat docens quotidie in templo. Principes autem sacerdotum, et scribae, et primores plebis, quaerebant illum perdere, et non inveniebant quid facerent. Omnis enim populus suspensus erat audiens illum.

Quatuor sunt loci.

Praecipuus locus est comminatio poenarum, quae omnibus hostibus et contemtoribus Evangelii impendent. Hic conferantur ab initio mundi horribilia exempla, quibus Deus iram suam adversus peccatum declaravit. Et vicissim consideretur altissima securitas humanarum mentium, quae tam horribilibus exemplis nihil movetur, poena Adae, diluvio, conflagratione Sodomae, Pharaonis exitio, dissipatione regni Israëlis, crebris excidiis Ierosolymae, eversione omnium monarchiarum, et omnium magnarum urbium. Horum exemplorum cogitatione excitemus animos, et recordemur, quam foede trucidati sint homines, necati infantes et senes, mulieres contumeliae affectae et occisae. Quoties etiam fame perierit multitudo, quoties in obsidionibus decimatae sint legiones in cibum, cum exercitus humanis carnibus vesceretur. Tanta autem coecitas est, ut haec putentur casu accidere, sicut hic inquit Christus: Nunc autem abscondita sunt ab oculis tuis.

Et Ieremias increpat eos, qui negant Dei consilio accidere poenas, Threno. 3.: Quis est qui dicit haec fieri, Domino non iubente? Et Sophoniae 1.: Visitabo defixos in fecibus suis, qui dicunt, Nec bene nec male faciet Dominus.

Hanc coecitatem agnoscamus, et corrigamus, et cogitemus nobis etiam impendere poenas, et quidem iudicium a domo Dei incipit.

De secundo. Dolor et lacrimae Christi sunt testimonium veri et non simulati amoris erga nos. Sed humana coecitas cum iram propositis tam terribilibus exemplis negligat, multo minus agnoscit amorem Dei. Sed eluctemur ex tantis tenebris, et utrumque agnoscamus, et inter aerumnas diliginos statuamus, quia punit non ut perdat, sed ut revocet ad poenitentiam, vel exerceat, sicut inquit: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, etc.

De tertio.

Christus eiicit ementes et vendentes ex templo. Praecipuum peccatum est idolatria, sed haec ubicunque regnat, ibi necesse est sequi horrenda scelera, et tyrannides, cum talis status vere sit regnum diaboli. Sicut exempla omnium gentium testantur, ubi aucta et cumulata idololatria secuta sunt immanissima scelera, foedissimae libidines, ut in Aegypto, Syria, Graecia, et inde extiterunt bella et mutationes exitiales. Sed, quaeritur, cum Christus eiecerit ementes et vendentes, an liceat aliis concionatoribus vi pellere idolatricos sacrificulos? Respondeo: Christus eiicit motu singulari, sicut Petrus Ananiam occidit, non est stipatus cohorte, non nititur praesidiis humanis. Quicquid autem fit tali motu divino seu heroico, Dei opus est. Significatum est autem, et postremis temporibus regnaturos esse in Ecclesia tales mercatores opum et dignitatum ecclesiasticarum, qui eiiciuntur e regno suo divinitus, et propter quos mundus dabit poenas impiorum cultum.

De quarto.

Domus mea domus orationis est. In hoc dicto breviter et significanter totum regimen ecclesiasticum, et verus cultus describitur. Nam cum nominat orationem, correlative addenda est doctrina Evangelii. Nam sine promissionibus et fide nulla existit oratio. Et constituatur antithesis: Vos putatis hanc domum conditam esse sacrificiorum causa, ad augendas opes vestras, et utrunque depravatis, regimen et cultum, vobis quaeritis opes et regnum, et sacrificia putatis esse cultum.

Ego contra clamito, regimen esse recte docere, et unicum cultum et proprium, in fide et bona conscientia invocare Deum.

Iam ut haec publice de domo Dei et ministerio dicuntur, ita unusquisque ad se ipsum transferat, singuli sciamus nos esse domum Dei. Sic autem erimus, cum in nobis sonabit vera doctrina, et invocatio in fide et bona conscientia. Et hortetur nos hoc dictum ad invocandum et orandum, quia testatur hunc esse proprium cultum populi Dei et domus Dei, quem Deus maxime flagitet.

## 21:25-33 Of Advent
Of Advent. Gospel of Luke 21. On the signs of the final judgment.

There will be signs in the Sun and Moon and Stars, and on earth distress of nations in despair, with the roaring of the sea and the waves, men fainting from fear and expectation of those things which are coming upon the world: for the powers of the heavens will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near. And he told them a parable: See the fig tree and all the trees, when they already put forth their buds, seeing them, you know from yourselves that summer is already near. So also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things have been done. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

Christ's sermon mixes two subjects: the prediction of the destruction of Jerusalem, and the calamities of the last time of the world.

He recounts, however, especially these calamities: tyrannies against the Gospel, sects, idolatry in the Church, the fall and changes of kingdoms, the ruins of the celestial bodies. He adds, however, two precepts: one about temperance and the care of piety, the other about prayer, and he teaches that calamities are mitigated by prayer. He also adds the consolation of the pious.

Secondly. Was there a need to foreknow anything future? I answer: God willed that both the future judgment and the calamities of the Church in this life be foreknown.

First, concerning the judgment. Because since punishments and rewards are deferred, men had to be warned about the future judgment, lest they think the world is ruled by chance, and that there are no punishments for crimes, no rewards for justice. Therefore, so that we may know that human affairs are a care to God, and that we may be stirred to obedience by the fear of punishments and the expectation of rewards, it was necessary for these things to be predicted.

Wherefore, from the beginning of the world, there has existed a doctrine concerning the final judgment, as in the first sermon to Cain: Sin will rest, until it is revealed. When he says, Sin will rest, he signifies that it will come to pass that punishments are deferred, but afterwards he says, Sin will be revealed, that is, the wrath of God against sin will be shown. Now, since most sins are not revealed here, and are not punished, it is necessary that another judgment follow.

And afterwards Enoch preached about the final judgment, as it is written in the Epistle of Jude: The Lord will come to execute judgment. And then the Prophets, as Isaiah in the last chapter: All flesh will come to worship before my face, says the Lord, and they will go out, and they will see the corpses of the men who have transgressed against me. Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished. Then Christ and the Apostles handed down this doctrine more clearly.

Now let us stir ourselves to fear and faith by the thought of the judgment. For this reason the prediction was divinely proposed, and it will not fail. Human minds are naturally greedy for the knowledge of future things, and God wills that some things be foreseen; he wills that we extend our minds to the recognition of things to come. Therefore he predicted the greatest and most necessary things. But with these neglected, human curiosity seeks light and useless things.

Thirdly. Why were the calamities of the Church and the world predicted?

First, so that we may know that the world is not ruled by chance, and that it does not happen without God's knowledge that the just are afflicted here. Likewise, if the calamities of the Church had not been predicted, we would doubt whether this were the Church, which is oppressed, especially since all were joyfully expecting the coming of the Messiah.

Item, predictions were to be published concerning errors, so that we might beware of them, as when Paul says, The prohibition of marriage is a doctrine of demons, or when Christ says, In the temple there shall be an abominable desolation. Item, it was necessary for the saints to be forewarned that the end of miseries would come, so that they would not despair. Item, predictions concerning monarchies are testimonies which prove the doctrine of this people to be divine. Item, they admonish the saints concerning the time of the advent of both.

Let us consider these causes of predictions, and let us confirm our souls with the thought of their certainty, so that we may resist the impious, and expect the liberation, which the very mutations of kingdoms signify is not far off. Daniel testifies that after the fourth monarchy is destroyed, the judgment will come. Ezekiel testifies that a little before the final judgment, Gog and Magog (that is, the Scythian nations) will devastate the Church, which the Turks are already manifestly doing, and the speed of their course and the magnitude of their successes signify that the last day is accelerating. And the time predicted by Elias is almost complete: Six thousand years for the world, and afterwards destruction. Just as Christ says concerning the summer, that a conjecture is made from the fig tree, so by a collation of the Prophets let us admonish ourselves concerning the end of the world, or concerning the final judgment. It is useful to think about these things regarding predictions, so that minds may be prepared, and confirmed in faith, and excited to fear and obedience.

Fourthly. Precepts should also be considered. Christ signifies that it will come to pass that in the last time luxury, pride, and avarice will increase. That this is happening is in plain sight. Therefore Christ forewarns, saying: Beware lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of life.

The second precept concerning prayer contains the sweetest consolation, because it testifies that calamities are mitigated by prayer. But let us remember that God cannot be invoked with an evil conscience. Therefore repentance must be performed, and the course of a good conscience in faith must be urged, lest we be overwhelmed by the huge ruins of the last time, especially when we see Gog and Magog already in sight, raging, who attempt to destroy the Church utterly. Against these let us fight with prayer.

Latin:

Dominica II. Adventus. Evangelium Lucae 21. De signis novissimi iudicii.

Erunt signa in Sole et Luna et Stellis, et in terris anxietas gentium per desperationem resonante mari et fluctu, extabescentibus hominibus prae timore et expectatione eorum, quae supervenient orbi terrarum: nam virtutes coelorum movebuntur. Et tunc videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nube cum potestate et gloria magna. His autem fieri incipientibus, suspicite et attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemtio vestra. Et dixit illis similitudinem: Videte ficum et omnes arbores, cum protrudunt iam gemmas, cernentes, ex vobis ipsis scitis, quod iam instet aestas. Ita et vos, cum videritis haec fieri, scitote, quod instet regnum Dei. Amen dico vobis, non praeteribit aetas haec, antequam omnia facta fuerint. Coelum et terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt.

Concio Christi miscet duas materias, praedictionem excidii Hierosolymae, et calamitates postremi temporis mundi.

Recenset autem praecipue has calamitates, tyrannides contra Evangelium, sectas, idolatriam in Ecclesia, regnorum casus et mutationes, corporum coelestium ruinas. Addit autem duo praecepta, alterum de temperantia et cura pietatis, alterum de oratione, et docet mitigari calamitates oratione. Addit et consolationem piorum.

Secundo. Fuitne opus aliqua futura praescire? Respondeo: Deus et iudicium futurum praesciri voluit, et calamitates Ecclesiae in hac vita.

Primum de iudicio. Quia cum differantur poenae et praemia, praemonendi fuerunt homines de futuro iudicio, ne cogitarent mundum casu regi, et nullas esse scelerum poenas, nulla praemia iusticiae. Ergo ut sciamus Deo curae esse humana, et metu poenarum et expectatione praemiorum exuscitemur ad obedientiam, haec praedici necesse fuit.

Quare ab initio mundi extitit doctrina de novissimo iudicio, ut in prima concione ad Cain: Peccatum quiescet, donec revelabitur. Cum ait, Peccatum quiescet, significat futurum ut differantur poenae, sed postea inquit, Revelabitur peccatum, id est, ostendetur ira Dei adversus peccatum. Iam cum plurima peccata hic non revelentur, non puniantur, necesse est aliud iudicium sequi.

Et postea Enoch concionatus est de novissimo iudicio, ut scriptum est in Epistola Iudae: Veniet Dominus facere iudicium. Et deinde Prophetae, ut Esaias capite ultimo: Veniet omnis caro, ut adoret coram facie mea, dicit Dominus, et egredientur, et videbunt cadavera virorum, qui praevaricati sunt in me. Vermis eorum non morietur, et ignis eorum non extinguetur. Deinde Christus et Apostoli hanc doctrinam clarius tradiderunt.

Iam nos cogitatione iudicii ad timorem et fidem excitemus. Ideo enim praedictio divinitus proposita est, et non fallet. Humanae mentes naturaliter avidae sunt cognitionis futurorum, et Deus vult quaedam praevideri, vult nos extendere animos in agnitionem venturarum rerum. Ideo res maximas et necessarias praedixit. Sed his neglectis humana curiositas quaerit levia et inutilia.

Tertio. Quare calamitates Ecclesiae et mundi praedictae sunt?

Primum, ut sciamus non regi mundum casu, non fieri Deo nesciente, quod hic iusti affliguntur. Item, si non essent praedictae calamitates Ecclesiae, dubitaremus, an haec esset Ecclesia, quae est oppressa, praesertim cum veniente Messia omnes laeta expectarent.

Item, de erroribus fuerunt edendae praedictiones, ut eos caveremus, ut cum Paulus ait, Prohibitionem coniugii esse doctrinam daemoniorum, seu cum Christus ait, In templo fore desolationem abominandam. Item, sanctos oportuit praemoneri, quod finis miseriarum futurus sit, ne desperarent. Item, praedictiones de monarchiis sunt testimonia, quae probant doctrinam huius populi divinam esse. Item, admonent sanctos de tempore adventus utriusque.

Has causas praedictionum consideremus, et nostros animos cogitatione certitudinis earum confirmemus, ut repugnemus impiis, et expectemus liberationem, quam ipsae mutationes regnorum significant, non procul abesse. Daniel testatur destructa quarta monarchia venturum iudicium. Ezechiel testatur paulo ante extremum iudicium Gog et Magog (id est, gentes Scythicas) pervastaturos esse Ecclesiam, quod iam manifeste faciunt Turci, et celeritas cursus eorum, ac magnitudo successuum significat accelerare novissimum diem. Et pene completum est tempus praedictum ab Elia: Sex millia mundus, et postea destructio. Sicut igitur Christus de Vere ait, coniecturam fieri ex ficu, ita collatione Prophetarum nos admoneamus de fine mundi, seu de novissimo iudicio. Haec de praedictionibus utile est cogitare, ut animi praeparentur, et confirmentur in fide, excitentur ad timorem et obedientiam.

Quarto. Praecepta etiam considerentur. Significat Christus futurum, ut postremo tempore crescant, luxus, superbia et avaricia. Id fieri in conspectu est. Ideo praemonet Christus, inquiens: Cavete ne corda vestra graventur crapula, ebrietate, et curis victus.

Secundum praeceptum de oratione, dulcissimam consolationem continet, quia testatur mitigari calamitates oratione. Sed meminerimus non posse Deum invocari mala conscientia. Ideo agenda est poenitentia, et urgendus cursus bonae conscientiae in fide, ne opprimamur ingentibus ruinis postremi temporis, praesertim cum videamus iam in conspectu grassantes Gog et Magog, qui delere Ecclesiam funditus conantur. Adversus hos dimicemus oratione.

# John

## 1:1-14 On the Birthday of Christ
On the Birthday of Christ, the Gospel of John 1.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him, and without him was not anything made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came to bear witness, that he might bear witness of the light, that all might believe through him. He was not that light, but was sent that he might bear witness of the light. That was the true light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not. He came unto his own, and his own received him not. But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name, which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.

The beginning of the Gospel of John teaches who Christ is, and for what cause he came into the world, what the difference is between the Law and the Gospel, and what the proper benefits of Christ are. These things are set forth in proper order.

And just as other Evangelists describe at the beginning the nativity from a virgin, so that they may testify that Christ was born of the seed of David: so John describes at the beginning the eternal nativity, and says what the person of the Son of God is before the assumption of human nature.

But John wished to preach more clearly concerning this article, so that he might refute the error of Hebion [Ebion] and Cerinthus, who had taught that there was only a human nature in Christ, just as the Jews also dream about the Messiah now: so that John might refute them, he testifies that there are two natures in Christ, divine and human, and concerning the divine he says thus: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

Let us believe the voice of the Holy Spirit concerning the nature of God, not human reasonings, and let us acknowledge the immense magnitude of divine goodness toward us, when we understand that it was constituted by the admirable counsel of the eternal Father, that this Son, who was with him from eternity, should descend to us, and become a victim for us, and our king, defender, helper, and savior.

By what pledge could God testify more that he truly cares for and loves us, than by giving his Son, to whom he truly communicated his own essence?

Just as Christ himself says concerning the counsel of the Father: So God loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, etc.

It is useful to think on these things, so that we may know to ask and to will God, and that these things are to be believed concerning his will, that because of this Son he truly loves us, that he wills to be invoked by the trust of this Son, that he has delivered this norm, which distinguishes true worship from false.

Although the Jews and Mahometans invoke the creator of heaven and earth, yet because they do not invoke him by the mention and trust of the Son, he repudiates and abominates their worship: thus he wills to be invoked and worshipped, as he himself has revealed himself, by the mention and trust of the Son the mediator.

It is necessary that these things be warned of in the Church, and therefore let us meditate on the sermon of John teaching these things, and as Basil says, let us imprint them on our hearts as a seal.

But because the devil hates the Son of God, and has impelled many light minds to deprave this doctrine of John, especially since it is otherwise placed outside the sight of reason: therefore pious minds must be diligently admonished, so that they may retain the true, certain, and perpetual sentiment of the catholic Church of God, and hand it down to posterity. The narrative is taken from Gen. 1. There God is described as saying, so here John says, that in the beginning the Word was with God. First, therefore, you may learn from that passage what God is.

For because he says [he] is an intelligent substance: and because he is before all things, he is eternal: and because he created all things, he is omnipotent, and he is good, willing good and giving to creatures.

Secondly, because John says here that the Word was in the beginning, you may learn that he means by this that he was coeternal with the Father.

He was, he says, in the beginning, as if he were saying: He was not created, but was before creation.

But why does he call him the Word?

Here let us retain with the firmest hearts the sentiment that λόγος signifies a person, as the text clearly shows afterward.

But why he is called λόγος, others have handed down a different exposition.

John took it from Moses, who says: God said.

But first I will review the explanation, afterwards we will refute the slanderers who have corrupted this passage.

Irenaeus says the Son is called the Logos, because he is the person speaking with the fathers, just as John here says: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us. And Ambrose and Hilary say that the Son spoke with the fathers.

Basil and others say that the Son is called the Logos, because he is the image of the Father, begotten by the Father thinking of himself: for the Father, looking at himself, begets a thought, which is called the Word, which thought is the image of the Father, into which image the Father, so to speak, transfuses his own essence. This substantial image of the Father is another person, and is called the Word.

It follows in the text.

And the Word was with God. Here the persons are distinguished, Father and Son.

Then, so that we may know, however, that the Son was not created out of nothing, but truly born from the substance of the Father, and is light from light, as the creed says, therefore it is added: And the Word was God. Here he clearly affirms the Logos to be God, therefore the Logos himself is also a person having the divine essence. For Logos is placed in the subject position, and God, as if describing what the Logos is, is placed in the predicate position.

Just as John calls the Son the Logos, so in the Epistle to the Hebrews he is called the brightness of glory, and the image of the Father's substance. These words describe in some way the Son and his generation: for because he is called an image, he is another person similar to the Father, wisdom, justice, power, and because he is the brightness of the paternal essence, a communicated essence is signified.

But it follows in John: All things were made through him; And without him was not anything made that was made. This sentence is often repeated in the scriptures, as to the Colossians and Hebrews: Through whom he made the ages, and in John: The world was made through him.

It is, however, an illustrious testimony that the Logos is omnipotent, and with the Father the creator of things. But it is explicitly said: Through the Son he created all things, as if the Father were deliberating with the Son and ordaining, as when he says: Let us make man in our image. But let us not discuss the manner, let us only remember the testimonies, so that we may know the Son to be omnipotent, and given to us by the Father as a helper, and to be invoked with the Father.

Why is it added: Without him was not anything made that was made.

I do not doubt that he here distinguishes created things from non-created things, as if he were saying: You see in the world celestial bodies, elements, plants, living creatures, men, the certain laws of celestial bodies, the powers of plants, generations, and you see men endowed with mind and intelligence. You acknowledge all these things to be most beautiful, most excellent, and to testify that there is some eternal architectonic mind.

But besides these, in such a beautiful nature of all things, you see in men sin and death, do you marvel at the infinite confusion of human life, what the tearing apart of religions and empires is? How much of vicious desires, error, and falls there is in individual men? How many innocent and deserving people perish in tragic accidents? These evils are so great that the profane, looking at them, forget the beauty of the world, and begin to doubt the cause of the world. For they are moved more by the sight of huge evils than by the beauty of nature.

Hence those Epicurean ideas. But uncertain fate wanders, and brings and carries back changes, and mortal things have their chance.

It was necessary, therefore, for John to distinguish the works of God from that mass of miseries not created by him. Therefore John says that only those things were made through the Son which are created, that is, the very most beautiful and excellent nature of things, but other things which have crept in, namely sin and death, not being created, did not arise from God willing and effecting them, as it is written: You are not a God who wills impiety: and Hosea 13: Your destruction is from yourself, O Israel, only in me is your help.

Therefore John, in order to distinguish and exclude evils from the works of God, spoke thus: Without him was not anything made that was made, as if he were saying, only the works which were created were created through him, not others which later arrived not created, namely sin and death, which are the destruction of nature and of the works of God. Furthermore, when he says: All things were made through him, let it not only be understood as the fabrication of the world, but let it also comprehend all the wondrous liberations made in the Church from the beginning.

Because this Logos is Emmanuel, that is, God acting with us, defending us against the devil.

quit: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has revealed [him] to us. This Son spoke with the fathers, gave promises, saved Noah, Abraham, Joseph, Moses snatched from the waters, was present with the people when they were led out of Egypt, just as Paul says concerning the accompanying rock, guided the hands of Joshua, of Gideon, of David against the devil. Therefore, just as they recognized him as the one who was to come, so let us recognize him as the one who has been exhibited, and let us invoke him so that he may help us, just as John preaches concerning him: The Son of God came, that he might destroy the works of the devil. Therefore, let us invoke the Son of God, that he may defend his Church against the Turks and other enemies. Likewise, that he may rule our minds and sanctify [us] with the Holy Spirit, just as he says: We will come to him, and we will make our dwelling [with him]. It follows:

In him was life.

That is, this Word (λόγος) is the life-giver, not only giving natural life and motion to things, but also specifically liberating the Church from eternal death: for in the meantime it signifies that he is speaking of the liberations in the Church. Jacob was saved against his brother, Moses was snatched from the waters.

Thus, the other saints were also saved and made alive through the Son of God, through whom they were also liberated from eternal death. And the life was the light of men. This same life-giver is also always from the beginning the illuminator of the Church, just as it was said before: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has revealed [him] to us, and afterwards when he appeared, he illuminates the Church.

For he imparts the same Word both to the fathers and to us, and creates by this Word a new light, that is, a firm, illustrious, and life-giving knowledge of God in the minds of believers, just as it is said elsewhere: This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God, and whom you sent, Jesus Christ. This is the simple meaning concerning the light: others here dispute about bodily light. Although it is true that bodily light was also created through him, as were other bodies, yet the following words indicate that John is speaking here especially of another light, which is the knowledge of the will of God and the beginning of eternal life, when it is said: And the darkness did not comprehend the light.

For here the true Church is distinguished from the impious who do not recognize the light, namely the Son of God, and who do not have the true knowledge of God. But it must be diligently observed that he calls the whole human race darkness, except for those alone in whom is the knowledge of the Son of God, or in whom he kindles his light through the Gospel.

You have, therefore, the first doctrine in this text concerning the Son of God, that he is a person begotten from the eternal Father of his substance and coeternal, and that he is not idle: but that through him all good things were created, and wondrous liberations were made in the Church, and that he is the life-giver, liberator, and illuminator of the Church.

The following discourse will describe the assumption of human nature.

But he first inserts the testimony of John the Baptist, and explicitly says that John the Baptist is far below the Messiah, namely a minister of doctrine, and is not the life-giver or illuminator, which properly belong to the Son of God, who is efficacious in our minds and who gives the Holy Spirit. Afterwards follows the repetition concerning the Son of God: He was in the world, and the world was made through him.

Here, when he speaks of Christ who appeared, he manifestly shows that the divine nature is in him, because he says: The world was made through him. But the world was not created through human nature.

What he says: He illuminates every man, signifies first that the Word is revealed through him, which pertains to all. Or, he illuminates every man, namely, who is illuminated, just as he says below: From his fullness we have all received.

There is also inserted a statement concerning the appellation: how we obtain life and light, namely by faith.

He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.

And he adds that our regeneration is not carnal, as the Anabaptists imagine, that children are born from saints without sin, because he says:

Not of blood. That is, they become children not by carnal generation.

Nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man. That is, not by human or legal adoption, nor by human effort or imitation.

But John looks to the people of the law, signifying that the people of God are not only the seed of Abraham, nor legal children, that is, the circumcised from the nations, that is, those inserted into the Mosaic polity, who were to be the people, but that they are simply the Church of God, all those reborn by faith of the Son of God, whether they were Jews or Gentiles, without distinction of places or nations, etc.

And the Word was made flesh.

When he says: The Word was made flesh, he testifies that the Son of God assumed human nature, ...and that Christ is a person in whom are two natures, the λόγος (Word) shining in the whole nature, and the human nature assumed, that is, body and soul. John used the term 'flesh' to signify the infirmity of the nature assumed, which was without sin, but yet subject to death, as it is said to the Philippians: Being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. Although, therefore, 'flesh' here signifies the whole man, yet the emphasis must be observed, that 'flesh' is used to signify mortality. Afterwards, John alleges testimonies: We saw his glory, that is, his wonderful works, the resurrection of the dead, and other things; he was therefore the giver of life and omnipotent.

Now that this narrative of John is known, the refutation of Samosatenus and Arius is easy.

Samosatenus craftily evaded the text, denying that 'Word' signifies a person, but rather the purpose of God willing to create the human race and to save it through a certain excellent man. To this imagination he twisted John's narrative.

But the refutation is firm when it is said: The Word was made flesh; this cannot be understood of a vocal word, or of a thought, which is the eternal Father himself, but it must be understood of some person. Likewise, it is said of Christ: The world was made by him. Now if Christ were only a man, and the divine nature did not remain in him, it could not be said so; therefore, λόγος signifies a remaining person.

Nor is the refutation of Arius difficult if we consider what the principal question was. Arius conceded that the Word is a person, but denied that he was of the substance of the eternal Father, and contended that he was created out of nothing. Here it was necessary to contradict him.

And he is refuted by this testimony; John says: The Word was God; he speaks here of God properly, not metaphorically. Likewise, it is said to the Hebrews: The brightness and image of the Father's substance; therefore, he is truly of the substance of the eternal Father. Likewise, he is so often called the only-begotten Son of God, so that he may be distinguished from sons by adoption. Why, therefore, he is properly a son by birth, it is necessary that he be of the substance of the Father.

Afterwards follow descriptions of his gifts and office.

Full of grace, that is, pleasing to the Father above all, as he says: This is my beloved Son. And Eph. 1: Because of this beloved one, he loved us. Full of truth, that is, of the true knowledge of God, and of true justice.

Before me he is, or prior to me, that is, more excellent in vocation, and in glory or power. Because he was before me, that is, co-eternal with the Father and from eternity ordained to this office, and the first for whose sake God loved the Church, and who was effective in the Church from the very beginning, that is, he was the helper and liberator of all the elect.

Of his fullness we have all received. All the fathers, Prophets, and saints, by his revealing, have received the Gospel; by his giving, we have received the remission of sins. By his moving and governing, we have received light, or spiritual knowledge, new justice, and eternal life.

Thus he himself narrates, Grace for grace, that is, the acceptance of us, because he himself is accepted or beloved. And he says it this way so that he may testify that we are not pleasing because of our own dignity, but because of the beloved Son.

There follows the distinction between Moses and the Messiah, of the Law and the Gospel. The Law was given by Moses, as if he were saying, there is a great distinction between the offices of Moses and the Messiah.

Moses was a minister of the Law, which does not take away sin and death: but Christ brings grace and truth.

Grace, that is, the remission of sins and reconciliation. Truth, that is, the true knowledge of God, true justice; with sin and death removed, he makes the people of God just and eternal. No man hath seen God.

The Law is naturally known, and a certain knowledge of the Law is born with us concerning God, that he is God, and that he punishes the guilty. But that will, concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, concerning the admirable salvation of man through the Son, is by no means naturally known to men, but only revealed through the Son.

Therefore he says: No man hath seen God at any time. The interpretation is true, whether you understand it of his substance or of his secret will to save men. But here he speaks of the knowledge of the secret will, and by the wonderful counsel of saving men. This certainly no man saw or perceived, but the Son alone, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared it, namely that in this wonderful way, at which the world is amazed, He willed to save men, with the Son sent, that He might become a victim, that having been resurrected He might reign, might restore eternal life, might sanctify for Himself a perpetual Church. All of which are full of wonderful works, which the astonished reason cannot comprehend. Therefore the greatest part of men neglect it on account of incredulity, and afterwards, fascinated by the devil, hate and persecute it, just as was signified above: The darkness did not comprehend the light. But let us hear this Son, just as it was commanded, Hear Him, and let us learn to discern His word from the law, and from the wisdom of the world, and let us receive from His fullness grace and truth, and let us know for certain that these things happen to those who believe, and let us excite faith, looking into so many promises and commands, which enjoin that we believe in the Son, just as the Baptist says afterwards: Everyone who believes in the Son has eternal life.

The history of the nativity of Christ.

Luke 2. And it came to pass in those days, that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus, that the whole world should be described. This first description was made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria. And all went, that they might be described, each into his own city. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth into Judea, into the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, that he might be described with Mary, his espoused wife, who was pregnant. And it came to pass, when they were there, the days were fulfilled, that she should bring forth. And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn. And there were shepherds in the same region watching, and keeping the night watches over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the brightness of the Lord shone round about them, and they feared with a great fear. And the angel said to them: Do not fear, For behold I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people, because there is born to you this day a savior, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this shall be a sign to you, You shall find the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, laid in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God, and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, to men of good will. And it came to pass, as the angels departed from them into heaven, the shepherds spoke to one another: Let us go over to Bethlehem, and see this word, which has come to pass, which the Lord has made known to us. And they came with haste, and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant laid in the manger. And seeing, they made known the word, which had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard wondered at those things, which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told to them.

The principal topics of this history.

I. Why mention is made of Augustus, the census, and the town. II. That the promises are wonderfully fulfilled. III. The political duties of the saints. IV. God cares for the manger, that is, some hospice for His Church. V. Witnesses to the birth of Christ, angels and shepherds. VI. The doctrine in the sermon and song of the angels. VII. Why the angel thus confirms his statement: Know that I have spoken the truth, because you will see the infant lying in the manger. VIII. The study of Mary, who commits these testimonies to memory and repeats them.

On the first. Therefore mention is made of Augustus, the census, and the town, because it was predicted that the Messiah would come in the fourth monarchy, and indeed while the polity of Moses was standing, but yet subject to servitude. Augustus signifies the fourth monarchy, the Census signifies servitude, the description of the town and family testifies that the polity still stands.

The reader is therefore admonished, that when he sees the event agree with the prophecies, he may believe more firmly: and the Jews are refuted, who after the fourth monarchy, and after the overthrow of the polity of Moses, still expect the Messiah, when it was necessary for him to be born while this polity stood, nay, while the second temple stood, as Haggai, Daniel, and Micah testify. On the second. But the promises are fulfilled in a wonderful way; God had promised that He would give the land of Canaan to Jacob, but first He leads him into Egypt, and there for a long time He harshly afflicts his miserable posterity; He had promised that He would defend the temple, but yet He allows it to be destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, and afterwards restores it.

Thus, for the most part, promises are exhibited in a way other than we imagine. We ought to know this, so that we do not cast away the word of God when impediments occur which seem to fight against the promise: just as the Church is promised life, yet we are first plunged into death.

Therefore, in this place too, the promise was fulfilled otherwise than men imagined. Everyone knew that Christ was to be born in Bethlehem, but they thought there would be some wealthy citizen living there, fortified by the alliance of nobles, in whose family Christ would be born, so that he might have associates afterwards for managing affairs.

Although Joseph is a citizen and a noble, yet he does not live there, nor is he surrounded by a guard of friends; he only has the hospitality of an inn for a short time. On the third. The Messiah was to come when the people were in servitude, and yet they had autonomy [αὐτονομίαν].

But these two persons, born of royal lineage, declare the servitude most of all; for the memory of the lineage was not yet extinct, but a hundred and sixty years before, Jannaeus still held the government, who was killed by Antiochus, whom Luke recounts as the great-grandfather of Joseph. Wherefore the old men had seen many to whom that Jannaeus was known: for in order that the series of the family might be certain, God did not wish the memory of the succession in that family to be entirely extinct. But two things may be learned from this example.

That the saints ought to perform political duties according to their vocation, and direct them to the utility of the Church: as happens here, the saints obey, and this path serves most of all the utility of the Church; nay, God so governs the time of the edict, that Augustus, although ignorant, serves this great work. Admonished by these examples, let us know that it is God's care that empires do not entirely overwhelm the Church.

On the fourth.

As therefore in this place God cares for the manger for the newborn Christ, so He has always provided and provides some hospitality for the Church, sometimes more, sometimes less tranquil.

And this spectacle reminds us of both things, of the miseries of the Church and of the hospitality. It is full of hardships, but yet God provides some hospitality, just as He saved the ship for Paul, for so long until he should come into port, Acts 27.

On the fifth. Even if those things which are done in the Church do not strike the eyes in the same way as the deeds of Alexander or C. Caesar, which are seen by the eyes of all nations: yet God wills the Church to be certain, and exhibits many testimonies.

Therefore, here too, testimonies concerning the Nativity are diligently recited, which we ought to inculcate in ourselves, so that they may confirm faith in us.

In the beginning, there are witnesses concerning the time and place, Daniel and Micah. Since, therefore, the event responds, it is certain that those prophecies were divine.

Now, indeed, from the conception there are witnesses: Mary, Joseph, Zacharias, Elisabeth, and their families. From the birth: shepherds, Magi, Simeon, Anna, and many others.

Therefore, the Church is a visible assembly, having certain testimonies of men truly asserting those things which God shows, even if these testimonies are despised because of the weak persons. As the narrative of the shepherds was scorned by many, and yet some, even in the ordinary function of priests, were witnesses, as Zacharias and Simeon.

But let us diligently propose these things to ourselves, because faith is confirmed by the example of the members of the Church concerning all articles. At the same time, let us also consider the dissimilarity between the Church and empires, and let us know that the Church is not without testimonies, even if the things which are done in it do not strike the eyes of all in the same way as the great armies of empires, which roam the world. On the sixth.

There is a doctrine especially to be observed, and an application of the history in this saying: Behold, I announce to you great joy, today a savior, Christ, is born to you.

No creature can sufficiently weigh the causes and the magnitude of this admirable counsel; nay, human reason, hearing these things, that the Son of God was sent so that He might be subjected to punishment, is stunned and flees.

Therefore the Prophet says: Who will believe our report? But let us consider these things: Since it is certain that the human race was created by God, so that He Himself might be known, it is also certain that God has revealed Himself in some word.

But this prophetic doctrine is the first and unique one, which has had testimonies in all ages, that it was handed down by God.

In this doctrine this counsel concerning the Son of God has been revealed. Therefore let us assent to so many divine testimonies, to the resurrection of the dead and to others, and let us not resist the voice of God, even if we do not perceive such great things.

Then let us think about the causes, for not in vain has such a great thing been decreed and established by the counsel of God, but it is necessary that there be great causes.

There are, however, three things for us to think about especially. The magnitude of the wrath of God against sin: And the immense mercy of God, And the love of the Son toward us.

Man had been created for an excellent dignity, and he was to be the image of God, that is, so that in man the knowledge of God might always shine, and God might dwell in him, and might delight in him, and might rest there and keep the Sabbath, and men might truly praise God.

Adam lost this great dignity by his fall, and he had already deserved eternal wrath, just like the devils: nor could any creature appease God, nor was there any equal price for sin. Therefore the Son of God interceded against that great and horrible wrath, and this admirable decree concerning redemption through the Son of God was made.

If we understood in some way the wrath of God, we could better think that this counsel had a great cause: but human blindness neither sees nor cares for these things, but the Church ought to kindle and excite itself to the contemplation of these things.

I think the angels estimate the magnitude of sin and the wrath of God more from this counsel than from the eternal punishments of the devil.

And it is necessary for a pious heart to shudder in its spirit at the thought of these things.

The impious do not care for these things, because they do not see how foul a thing sin is. But let us think how horrible evils are the contempt of God, Epicurean frenzies, doubts about God, idolatries, and the manifold confusion and contumacy against God.

These things stirred up that great wrath in the mind of God, which no creature could appease, and on account of which the Son became the intercessor.

This is the first cause.

The second is the immense mercy of the eternal Father: He had created the work in which He wished to delight, and He did not wish it to perish entirely, nor could He turn away the Son who was interceding, therefore the decree concerning sending the Son was made.

And indeed it must be known that grace abounds over sin, as Paul says: There is immense wrath, but it is appeased through this intercessor.

The third cause is the love of the Son Himself toward us, which it is necessary to be true and immense, since He was both the intercessor, and afterwards underwent the punishment for us, and perpetually is the propitiator.

We would value all these things more, if we could think of the wrath of God and the magnitude of the punishments.

The angels proclaim that they are announcing great joy, because they themselves understand how great a thing the wrath of God and eternal punishments are, therefore they know that this benefit is truly going to produce great gladness for those to be saved: but the world is little affected by these things, each one has his own business, which brings pleasures or pains.

Few care for this chief matter, the reconciliation of God and eternal life: but to those who do care and know sin, to them the recognition of the Son is a great consolation.

Let them hold to the doctrine of faith concerning the appellation of this benefit, which is signified here in the particle "To you": I announce joy to you, to you a Savior is born, that is, let each one determine for himself that the Son of God was made a victim, that the Father has been reconciled to him, that eternal life has been restored to him.

Concerning the canticle of the angels.

Just as the Prophets, speaking of the kingdom of the Messiah, generally speak of the consummation, namely of that very future state in which, having been resurrected, we shall enjoy eternal glory with Christ, so if you refer the hymn of the angels here to that state, which the angels certainly embrace, the explanation will be most easy.

And the hymn is a description of that eternal kingdom, as if they were saying: The Messiah will bring to you henceforth not the empire of the world, as you think, but another kind of kingdom, which will be such: God will be known openly, and then He will be celebrated with eternal and true praise without any doubts, we shall understand how man was created, we shall understand the wrath of God against sin, and we shall preach mercy, we shall behold the Son of God, and we shall see what that wonderful society of divine and human nature is, we shall discern how He has always been present to the Church, and how wonderful liberations have been made, intercession after the fall, liberation in the flood, in the sea in red, and from then on in all times.

We shall therefore praise the power, wisdom, justice, goodness, and mercy of God. There will also be peace on earth, because the devils and all the impious will be in eternal punishments, and death will be abolished. The Church will burn with the love of God, and will be most sweetly associated in benevolence and in the studies of doctrine; there will be no hatreds, dissensions, tumults, and factions. Nor will there be only peace, but also joy for men, because it will be well for the men themselves, and they will sweetly enjoy the sight of God and Christ, the knowledge of such great things, and mutual companionship.

If you look at that state, which the angels certainly embrace, the song can easily be understood. Compare, however, the kingdoms of the world to this state.

First, they ought to have illustrated the glory of God, but they have almost always defended and will defend idols, and the contempt of God is manifest in the greatest part of kings: as in Alexander, Antiochus, Caesar, Caligula, etc. Nor do they make peace on earth, because new wars, new tumults, and new confusions arise at all times, so that it is not without cause that Plato says that peace is an empty name, which governors easily understand why it is said, for they know there is nothing of leisure and quiet. Furthermore, hatreds, injuries, and perpetual discords always remain in the world among princes and among the people. Finally, there is no lasting joy in this life, which is subject to infinite calamities and to death, and eternal punishments are added.

This antithesis declares the hymn of the angels.

Although this interpretation concerning the consummation of the kingdom of Christ is most convenient and most illustrious, yet because that kingdom is begun in this life, we also accommodate this hymn to the Church before the resurrection.

The same glory is to be attributed to God in this life, even if it is not yet seen with bodily eyes. The same peace and joy will be in the souls, but in the meantime many impediments occur: great miseries from without cause those begun goods not to be seen in the souls. Finally, this future kingdom, which is begun here, is still veiled.

These questions signify the same thing: What does the advent of Christ bring? What are the benefits of the Gospel? What kind of kingdom is the Church's? Christ brings these things, or the Gospel distributes these benefits; it causes us to attribute glory to God, that there may be peace on earth, and that men may truly rejoice, or have true and imperishable joys.

Concerning glory.

To attribute glory is to attribute power, wisdom, justice, goodness, and mercy: just as Epicurus does not attribute glory to God, because he feigns that there is no God, or that God is idle. Nor did Saul attribute glory to God, for even if he judges that there is a God, and feels that He is angry at sins: yet he does not resolve that he is forgiven, he flees from God, and is horribly angry at Him. Therefore, neither reason nor law without the Gospel attributes glory to God.

So that glory may be truly attributed to God, it was necessary for the Gospel to be brought through Christ from the bosom of the Father, upon hearing which, we attribute mercy to God, because He truly receives us, truly remits our sins, cares for us, and wills to restore eternal life to us. Here, therefore, we recognize that God is not idle, but we feel His anger in repentance and punishments, and we discern His mercy in the remission of sins, which, as we believe, we simultaneously resolve that we are truly looked upon, heard, cared for, helped, and defended by Him. Thus, the glory attributed to God is exactly the same as that which will be attributed in eternal life, but then all things will be more illustrious.

Now, miseries from without prevent the glory from being seen. A truly pious man, surrounded by Turks, even if he sees that the Turkish power is great and such a spectacle is offered to the eyes, as if God cares nothing for us, yet he retains this conviction: Christ, crucified and resurrected for us, is truly the Son of God and our savior; on account of Him, God has received you, cares for you, and will save you eternally.

And now, indeed, the Church is dispersed and subject to the cross, by the just judgment of God, but yet God will preserve some members in this life, even if He allows some to be killed. Thus, the pious man attributes glory to God, because he hears, receives, cares, and is about to save, even if external miseries prevent those things from being seen yet, and the glory will be seen in its own time.

And on earth peace.

Peace in the present Church is such: there is peace between God and the Church, because God,... now appeased through Christ, is not angry at us, and we do not flee from Him. There is also peace against enemies to the extent that we have a certain guardian against the devil and his organs, and we know that they cannot rage the enemy for his cruelty, but that he is restrained by Christ, and does not harm more than he is permitted, just as Christ says: The hairs of your head are numbered, etc.

However, since the death of the body still remains, and other calamities common to the human race remain, and the devil does not cease to attack the Church, peace is not yet consummated. The enemies are held back, even if they are not yet entirely oppressed. But there will be complete peace when the Church, after the resurrection, is adorned with its glory.

Joy.

All men seek some ultimate thing in which they rest, and in which they truly rejoice. Just as for the miser the highest good, in which he truly rejoices, is a huge increase of money, and he truly grieves at a huge loss. So for Scipio, the highest good is glorious victory; in this he rejoices most, and conversely, he would grieve most if he were defeated. These examples show what this affection is like, seeking some ultimate thing in which the mind may rejoice.

But above the common affections of men, there is in the Church, as in Jeremiah, in Paul, a peculiar affection: to rest in God, or to rejoice in the knowledge of God, whom they now know to have as propitious and a guardian, wherefore they willingly and joyfully obey Him, and by this joy they overcome the fear and sorrow which the dangers of the body, reputation, or property bring, as when Lawrence lies on the gridiron, yet retains the greatness of a mind resting in God, which cannot exist unless the mind rejoices and delights in God.

Thus David says: My father and mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up. Likewise: You have given joy in my heart, from the fruit of the grain they are multiplied. Furthermore: Without the knowledge of Christ, the mind cannot rejoice in God, because it still flees from Him as angry. Likewise: It does not know how to please God with obedience, in such great infirmity of ours.

But joy accompanies those former parts of the hymn.

Glory signifies the true knowledge of God revealed in the Gospel. Peace signifies peace with God, and being guarded by God. From these arises joy and voluntary obedience. But this joy in this life is often disturbed by great terrors and sorrows, from which, however, it struggles out, but after this life it will be complete.

So that you may understand that the hymn preaches about the highest goods and about eternal life, look at the first commandment, for the hymn entirely embraces the principal works and the highest worship of the first commandment, namely, the true knowledge of God, peace with God, that is, to believe that God is reconciled on account of the Son, and joy, that is, the true love of God.

When these are consummated, they will be eternal life itself. The hymn is therefore a description of the benefits of Christ, or the sum of the Gospel, or a description of the eternal kingdom of the Church, which nevertheless begins in this life. Furthermore, as the angels are the precentors, so let all pastors know that they ought to precent this hymn to the Church, that is, to deliver the true doctrine by which God is known, to announce peace to the conscience on account of the Son of God, and to be authors of peace and concord in the Church, and also to retain the joy of consciences, that is, to take care that consciences are not wounded or disturbed, by which thing invocation is hindered.

Impious teachers disturb all the members.

First, because false doctrine harms the glory of God. Then, it disturbs the concord of the Church. Third, it wounds minds, so that they do not rightly invoke God. Julius disturbs in the second degree, contending about a non-necessary matter, about the time of Easter.

Although David was a good teacher and had retained concord, yet he saddened the good by his scandal, having snatched the wife of another. Therefore, let teachers be intent on these three degrees, so that they may truly precent the angelic hymn to the people, that is, that they may teach the truth, announce peace to pious consciences, protect concord, and avoid scandals, lest in any way they hinder the invocation of God by wounded minds.

On the seventh.

Signs are generally called unusual works done by God, so that they may testify that something is announced divinely, as the resuscitation of Lazarus was a work done by God, so that it might testify that Christ was truly sent by God.

Does he also understand the sign in this way in this place, when he says: You will find the infant in a manger? Otherwise, signs are understood differently. Here it is most simple to say that he calls a sign, not a miracle which might testify about the narration, but the thing by which he wishes this infant to be recognized and distinguished from others, as if he were saying, This infant is the Messiah, whom you will find placed in a manger, in swaddling clothes; thus the infant is distinguished from all others, because God certainly wished Christ to be shown, He wished it to be known who he was, where he was, who the mother was.

For God wishes certain testimonies of such a great matter to exist in the Church. Moreover, the very sight of the angels was a sign, that is, a miracle testifying about the narration.

It was difficult to believe that this was the Messiah, born of a poor woman; therefore, so that this might be believed, the shepherds are confirmed by an unusual event, the sight of angels, but so that they might recognize and distinguish the infant from others, circumstances are added.

Furthermore, let an allegory be considered here. That he commands the infant to be sought in a manger wrapped in swaddling clothes signifies that the Messiah is to be sought in the sayings of the Prophets, in the very people of the law, and the sayings of the Prophets are the swaddling clothes, upon the unfolding of which the Son of God is seen and recognized. Why do you believe that the Son of God put on human nature? Because you believe only this word, which exists in the Church, to have been handed down by God, and in this word God promised that he would send such a Messiah. This confirmation, this testimony must be held with one's whole heart, that God shows by most clear testimonies that he handed down this word to the Prophets, to Christ, and to the Apostles, which they sound forth, and in this word it is affirmed that such is the Messiah, therefore you assent.

All miracles, therefore, from the beginning, all the sayings of the Prophets, are signs and testimonies about this Messiah: these are those swaddling clothes in which he is wrapped, these God wants us to consider; he gave testimony to the word of Moses, and then of the other Prophets, who all repeated the same promise. Isaiah says: A child is born to us etc. God, the father of eternal life. Micah says: His goings forth are from before the beginning of the world. John says: In the beginning was the word. They also add why he was given, such as: Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. When, therefore, swaddling clothes are named, let us know that we are led to such sayings in which the knowledge of the Messiah is truly wrapped, and these swaddling clothes are signs; that is, wondrous testimonies about the Messiah.

On the eighth [point].

That he says Mary remembered all these things and pondered them in her heart warns the whole Church that we should imitate this study of considering testimonies. The mother had heard the narration of the angels from the shepherds: she compared this to the other miracles she knew, and by the comparison of all things she confirmed her faith. Again, Joseph also explained to the shepherds the miracles known to him, so that he might confirm their faith. Thus we ought to nourish and confirm our faith by the comparison of all these things, the prophetic sayings, the miracles, and the deeds which are narrated in the Gospel. This meditation is useful to the pious, and let the final thought always be added that it was decreed by God that the Son should put on human nature: the magnitude of the causes is placed far above the sight of all creatures, for the causes are the true and ineffable wrath of God against sin, and the immense mercy toward the human race, which God had created, so that in it he might be celebrated. Therefore he did not want the whole to perish.

Wherefore let us recognize the will of God, and give thanks to him, because he sent his Son, and as it is written in the Psalm: Kiss the Son. Thus let us embrace him with true piety, let us learn that this is the chief worship of God, to call upon God with confidence in the Son, and let us determine that those who call upon him in this way are truly heard. By such exercises God wants true faith to be kindled in us, and this faith is the recognition of the Messiah, which is the beginning of eternal life, as it is written: This is eternal life, that they may know you to be the true God, and whom you sent, Jesus to be the Christ.

Latin:

Die natali Christi, Evangelium Iohan. 1.

In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine eo factum est nihil quod factum est. In ipso vita erat, et vita erat lux hominum, et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebrae eam non apprehenderunt. Erat homo missus a Deo, cui nomen Ioannes. Hic venit ad testificandum, ut testaretur de luce, ut omnes crederent per ipsum. Non erat ille lux, sed missus erat, ut testaretur de luce. Erat lux illa vera, quae illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum. In mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In sua venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, videlicet his, qui credunt in nomen ipsius, qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt. Et Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis, et conspeximus gloriam eius, gloriam velut unigeniti a Patre, plenum gratia et veritate.

Initium Evangelii Iohannis docet, quis sit Christus, et quam ob causam venerit in mundum, Quod sit discrimen legis et Evangelii, Quae sint propria Christi beneficia. Haec apto ordine exponuntur.

Ac ut alii Evangelistae initio describunt nativitatem ex virgine, ut testentur Christum esse natum ex semine David: ita Iohannes describit initio nativitatem aeternam, dicit, quae sit persona Filius Dei ante assumptionem humanae naturae.

Ideo autem Iohannes de hoc articulo clarius concionari voluit, ut Hebionis et Cerinthi errorem refutaret, qui docuerant in Christo tantum esse humanam naturam, sicut nunc quoque Iudaei de Messia somniant: hos ut refutaret Iohannes, testatur in Christo duas esse naturas, divinam et humanam, ac de divina sic dicit: In principio erat verbum, et verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat verbum.

Credamus voci Spiritus sancti de Dei natura, non humanis cogitationibus, et agnoscamus immensam magnitudinem bonitatis divinae erga nos, cum intelligimus admirabili consilio aeterni Patris constitutum, ut hic Filius, qui apud ipsum ab aeterno fuit, ad nos descenderet, ac fieret victima pro nobis, et rex noster, defensor, adiutor et salvator.

Quo pignore potuit Deus magis testari, quod vere nos curet et diligat, quam dato Filio, cui vere communicavit essentiam suam?

Sicut de consilio Patris et ipse Christus inquit: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret etc.

Haec cogitare utile est, ut sciamus postulare et velle Deum, credi haec de sua voluntate, quod propter hunc Filium vere nos diligat, quod velit invocari fiducia huius Filii, quod hanc tradiderit normam, quae veros cultus a falsis discernit.

Quanquam Iudaei et Mahometistae invocant conditorem coeli et terrae, tamen quia non invocant eum mentione et fiducia Filii, repudiat et abominatur eorum cultus: sic vult invocari et coli, ut ipse se patefecit, mentione et fiducia Filii mediatoris.

Haec in Ecclesia moneri necesse est, et propterea Iohannis concionem haec docentem meditemur, et sicut inquit Basilius, imprimamus cordibus tanquam sigillum.

Quia vero diabolus odit Filium Dei, et impulit multa levia ingenia, ut hanc doctrinam Iohannis depravarent, praesertim alioqui extra conspectum rationis positam: ideo piae mentes diligenter admonendae sunt, ut veram, certam et perpetuam catholicae Ecclesiae Dei sententiam retineant, et tradant posteris. Sumta est autem narratio ex Gen. 1. ibi describitur Deus dicens, ita hic Iohannes ait, In principio fuisse verbum apud Deum. Primum ergo discas ex eo loco, quid sit Deus.

Quia enim dicit, est substantia intelligens: et quia ante omnia est, est aeternus: et quia condidit omnia, est omnipotens, et est bonus, bona volens et dans creaturis.

Secundo, quod hic ait Iohannes, Verbum fuisse in principio, discas eum hoc velle, quod fuerit coaeternum Patri.

Erat, inquit, in principio, quasi diceret: Non est conditum, sed erat ante conditionem.

Quare autem vocat Verbum?
