Dicebant ergo: Quid est hoc, quod dicit, modicum? Nescimus quid loquatur. Cognovit autem Iesus, quia volebant ipsum interrogare, et dixit eis: De hoc quaeritis inter vos, quod dixi, modicum, et non videtis me, et iterum modicum, et videbitis me.

Amen amen dico vobis, Plorabitis et flebitis vos, mundus contra gaudebit. Vos autem contristabimini, sed tristitia vestra vertetur in gaudium.

Mulier cum parit, tristitiam habet, quia venit hora eius. Cum autem peperit puerum, iam non meminit pressurae propter gaudium, quia natus est homo in mundum. Et vos igitur nunc quidem tristitiam habetis, sed iterum videbo vos, et gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis.

Et in illo die me non interrogabitis quicquam. Duo sunt loci.

I. Praedicatio de afflictionibus Ecclesiae.

II. Consolatio in his afflictionibus.

## 16:23-27 Sunday of the Voice of Joy
Sunday of the Voice of Joy.

Gospel of John 16.

Amen, amen I say to you, whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give to you. Hitherto you have not asked anything in my name. Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be perfect. These things I have spoken to you in proverbs. The time will come when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but I will announce to you plainly of my Father; in that day you shall ask in my name. And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you. For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me, and have believed that I came out from God.

Always concerning prayer, these four things must be held: The commandment of God, the divine promise, faith, and the thing to be asked.

Concerning the Commandment.

Let us know that this is the highest duty for which we were created: to acknowledge and call upon God; therefore the chief and first law is concerning the acknowledgment of God and invocation, as the saying testifies: You shall adore the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve. And so the commandment concerning invocation has been often repeated, as in Luke 18: It is necessary always to pray. And in Psalm 49: Call upon me in the day of tribulation. And in Matt. 7: Ask and you shall receive, etc. Let these commandments teach us that invocation is the chief and highest worship.

This work distinguishes the true Church, or people of God, from all other men. Although men understand by nature the commandment that bids us call upon God, nevertheless the ungodly neither call upon him nor know how he is to be called upon. Therefore it is said in the Psalm: They have not called upon God. And although it is a great thing to know the commandment concerning invocation, yet it is not yet enough, but the promise must be added.

Concerning the second. Let the promise therefore be a...added, which testifies that God hears our prayers and grants what we ask. The nations know the commandment, but they doubt whether they are heard, as Virgil says: And we cherish a vain fame. But to the Church are handed down the promises other rites of the impious.

This thoughtlessness is similar to the custom of fools, who run to statues and murmur something there, not thinking what or why they are invoking. And since such is the invocation of the greater part of mankind, this error must often be censured, and minds must be taught to invoke correctly.

A certain Hermit said that there is no greater labor than prayer, which is most true, because it is difficult to retain attention—that is, to think of God as He has revealed Himself, and to separate our invocation from that of the Heathen and the Turk, and at the same time to look to the promise, so that faith may be excited.

This entire attention is greater when we are in pain, but when minds are idle, drunk with pleasures, they wander more. Yet the pious and moderate should learn the doctrine of invocation and accustom themselves to it correctly: thus, in true sorrows, they will feel an even more ardent consolation.

And first, indeed, when we begin prayer, we must think about who God is.

The Turks and other impious people invoke, but they err from God in two ways.

First, because they stubbornly retain a false opinion about the essence of God. Second, because they are ignorant of His will. For the Turks and those like them, even if they say that this is God, who created heaven and earth, yet they deny that He is truly God—He who revealed Himself through the Son, who delivered the Gospel to us; they deny that the Son and the Holy Spirit are of the essence of the Father. Thus, first, they err concerning the essence. Afterward, also concerning the will, because they have cast away the word revealed by God, they are ignorant of the promise of grace, and they cannot believe that they are regarded and heard. Wherefore, thinking about the will of God, they rush into horrible darkness and eternal doubt.

Our invocation must therefore be separated from their opinions, and first we must think about who God is—namely, He who is such, who revealed Himself in His word from the beginning, after the creation and the fall of Adam.

But God revealed Himself in His Gospel thus: One is the omnipotent and eternal Father, who with His Son, who is the co-eternal image of the Father, and the Holy Spirit, created all good things, and revealed Himself by the given word and the sent Son.

Then, because indignation clamors against you, and we doubt whether God receives us or cares for our prayers, set before your mind the promises of the Gospel: Think that God has commanded us to invoke Him, and that we should believe that our prayers are pleasing and received on account of the Son.

And that this invocation is the highest worship, and the greatest of all works, and most pleasing to God. Therefore, Christ cries out so often: Ask and you shall receive. Item: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you. It is necessary to think of this daily in praying.

Nor is prayer the murmuring of some words without this thought.

Therefore, prayer is a difficult work: for first, this attention is difficult, but it is a much greater labor to excite faith, so that you may rest in the promise of the Gospel, and conclude that prayers are not an empty murmur, not said in the heathen manner out of custom, but that they are truly sought from God, approved, received, and heard.

Here the heart must be instructed so that it may rest in so many promises, sanctified by the blood and resurrection of the Son, as: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

These things are often repeated elsewhere. Now, indeed, I have reviewed this so that we may look more diligently at this text, in which it is shown who God is, and mention is made of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

As often, therefore, as you begin prayer, first think whom you wish to address, and propose to yourself the testimonies concerning both matters, namely, the testimonies by which God revealed Himself, who He is, and the promises, that He hears on account of the Son.

Behold with your mind the eternal Father sounding this voice: This is my beloved Son, hear Him. Acknowledge Him to be the Creator with His Son, the co-eternal image, and the Holy Spirit poured out upon the Apostles. And remember the promises: On account of this Son, Jesus Christ the propitiator, God wishes to hear us, to receive us, and to rule us by the Holy Spirit.

I have often recited an example of the form: Omnipotent, eternal, and living God, eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who revealed Yourself in the human nature, and cried out concerning Your Son our Lord Jesus Christ: Hear Him: Creator and preserver of all things, with Your co-eternal Son, Your Word (λόγῳ) and image, and the Holy Spirit poured out upon the Apostles, fostering Your creature, wise, good, merciful, judge, and strong, on account of Jesus Christ Your Son, our Lord, whom You willed to be a victim for us, mediator and intercessor (μεσίτην καὶ ἱκέτην), by a wonderful and ineffable counsel, and sanctify, inflame, teach, rule, help my heart and soul with Your Holy Spirit, just as the Son said: How much more will the heavenly Father give the ...Holy Spirit to those who ask.

In such prayer we profess who God is, and what He is like, and we separate our prayer from the Heathen, Jewish, and Turkish, and we suggest the promises to ourselves, so that faith may be excited. Acknowledge we that this is God, the creator of all things, who revealed Himself by His word and by sending the Son, and we acknowledge that He is not idle, or bound by secondary causes, but wise, good, just, a judge, strong, merciful on account of the Son, helping us, and ruling by the Holy Spirit: it is necessary to embrace all these things in prayer. For who God is, and why He hears, cannot be conceived unless we embrace all these things. Let good minds therefore accustom themselves to some such form, and oppose it to Ethnic and Turkish opinions.

On the second.

Descriptions of the persons of the divinity are often repeated.

The Father is an intelligent, eternal, omnipotent substance, acting freely, good, just, merciful, begetting from eternity the image of Himself: with whom and with the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, He created heaven and earth, and all natures which it contains. The Son is a substance begotten by the Father, coeternal, the image of the eternal Father, and because He was established as propitiator by a wonderful counsel, He therefore assumed human nature, and was made a victim, and a pledge that God is willing to receive us, to restore to us justice, and eternal life. But as the image is begotten by thought, so the Spirit is said to proceed from the will of the Father and the Son, because He is the breath and agitator, moving the creature, and kindling light, and new motions in the hearts of those hearing the Gospel. To this agitation which is from the will, the word 'proceed' is appropriate.

Now see in this place how great the goodness of God is described, and how great a promise is handed down to the Church. Christ promises that He will send the Holy Spirit, and at the same time affirms that the Father wills that He be sent. Therefore the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit will that the human race should not perish, but that new light, the knowledge of God, new justice, faith, love, and eternal life be restored to men: for since they will the Holy Spirit to be given, there is no doubt that these things are kindled in the hearts of men.

When it is said that the Holy Spirit proceeds, the property of the person is indicated: then when He is called the Spirit of truth and παράκλητος (Paraclete), His offices or proper gifts are described, which the divinity imparts through Him. The Spirit of truth, that is, He who through the Gospel makes the true knowledge of God shine in the mind, and kindles in the heart motions congruent to the will of God, reverence toward God, trust, invocation and love of God, hatred of sin, consolation and joy in God, beginning eternal life.

These goods are better understood by comparison. Although Cato has this knowledge by natural judgment, that there is some eternal mind, the creator of things, and caring for empires, yet when he sees the confusion of the human race, and sees himself in a cause, as they suppose, justly neglected, he is again plunged into immense darkness, loses all persuasion about God, and thinks that He is either nothing, or idle, or unjust. Then he becomes angry at all religions. The hearts of all men who do not know the Gospel are oppressed by this darkness and this lie, from which alone we learn why and how God hears, and why the human race is subject to death and other punishments.

But often greater furies are kindled in the impious, because there is darkness in minds ignorant of the Gospel, and the devil impels many to invent insulting things against God, as Epicurus with horrible petulance vociferates that there is no God. The common people invent idols and many gods, as those who run to the statues of the dead. Heretics also invent their own delusions. Manichaeus imagines two Gods. Let us think on these examples, and consider how great is the misery of men who are without the Gospel and without the Holy Spirit, and let us know that the Holy Spirit is given so that, these furies and lies having been repelled, He may kindle in us the truth, that is, the true knowledge of God, who He is, and how He hears, how He wills to be worshipped, how He is about to judge.

Another appellation in this place is παράκλητος, which signifies an advocate, namely, one ruling us by counsel, and consoling us in sorrows, and confirming us in various struggles. Thus Christ says: The Holy Spirit will lead you into all truth.

Human minds are too wandering, and easily stray from God, easily admit plausible opinions, fighting against the word of God, as Eve was deceived, and Paul calls them the fiery darts of the devil, the specters of opinions which the devil pours into weak minds. Against these evils, we cannot be safe unless the Holy Spirit confirms our minds. Wherefore it must always be prayed: Confirm this, O God, which You have worked in us. And the promise concerning the Holy Spirit must be thought upon, who is therefore promised to the Church, and to individuals who call upon Him, so that He may confirm and retain the truth in us. ness, and the will of God made manifest, as it is said in Deut. 4: There is no other nation so glorious, which has God drawing near, as our God is present to all of us who call upon Him.

Here now all the promises in the whole scripture are gathered together. But the chief one is proposed in today's lesson, confirmed by the oath of the Son of God.

Amen, amen I say to you, Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give to you. Ask and you shall receive. Everyone who asks receives.

Item: If men can give good things to men, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Item: Come to me all you who labor. Item: Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you. Item, the constant prayer of the just will greatly avail. Item, Matt. 18, concerning common prayer: Amen I say to you, Concerning whatever matter two shall agree, whatever they ask, it shall be done.

It is necessary to look upon these promises, because doubt in prayer, whether God receives our prayers, is impious. Therefore it is written, Let him ask in faith.

Now let us consider here how few men perform this worship to God. Therefore there is a great cause why the Psalm says, They do not call upon God. For few approach to pray in this way, with a good conscience and faith, so that they may determine that their prayers are received.

Concerning the third.

The third is faith. Here it must be known what is called faith. First, let faith be understood as the confidence of reconciliation granted on account of Christ, and that on account of this mediator and high priest, the eternal God receives our prayers. It is necessary that this general faith be brought into every invocation.

Therefore it is expressly added here: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, that is, not with confidence in your own dignity, but with confidence in the mediator Christ, because it is necessary to hold the rule that there is no access to the eternal Father except through the Son, as it is said in Rom. 5: Through Him we have access. Item: Having such a high priest, let us approach the throne of grace. Item: Always living, so that He may intercede for us.

This faith, therefore, distinguishes the sinners, the Jews and the Turks, and all who have an evil conscience, from hypocrites and Christians who truly call upon Him. The Jews and Turks boast that they call upon God the creator of all things, and indeed they are very proud of this doctrine, that they name one God, but they do not call upon God the eternal Father of the Son who was sent and appointed as mediator; nay, they treat the mediator Himself, the Son of God, with contempt, and therefore they do not call upon Him.

Furthermore, having a purpose to sin, they cannot call upon God, they do not approach God through a mediator, and they are without faith, as John says, 1 John 3: If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, etc. Finally, hypocrites, that is, those approaching with confidence in their own dignity, or doubting because they recognize their own unworthiness, do not approach God, they do not truly call upon Him.

But against these, it is necessary to bring this faith, which recognizes that God is appeased through the Son, and with confidence in this mediator, it calls upon and asks, and determines that our prayers are received, and that they please God, and are not in vain, even if the outcomes are either delayed or do not respond to our thought.

Here also the doctrine must be held, that some faith asks without condition, but some with a certain condition. Those things are to be asked and expected without condition, concerning which the will of God is specifically and expressly stated, that He will give these very things by name, namely, those which are proper to the Gospel: the remission of sins, reconciliation, the gift of the Holy Spirit and eternal life. When we ask for these, it must be determined that they are truly granted to us, and received by that very faith which consoles us in our terrors, according to that: Being justified by faith we have peace, etc.

In the petition for corporal things, it is necessary to bring a general faith, that God is propitious to you and receives your prayers, but concerning the thing itself, which is asked by name, it is not determined without condition, because in corporal afflictions, we owe obedience to God, just as David, driven into exile, indeed asks to be restored, but nevertheless adds: If God does not wish to restore me, let that be done which pleases Him. Nay, this is the singular wisdom of the Church, even if corporal liberation does not happen, yet not to rush into desperation, into blasphemies, or hatred of God, but to be raised up by faith, and to retain the remission of sins, and the certain hope of eternal life, because since the wrath of God is just against our sins, we owe obedience in punishment.

But it is difficult in such a struggle to retain faith, so that Saul, frustrated in his hope of victory, is utterly overwhelmed by desperation, thinks he is cast off by God, and does not believe that his sins are forgiven him, and in this desperation he brings death upon himself. Thus very many, out of impatience and because of delay, rush into desperation and eternal destruction.

But it must be inculcated

is a doctrine for souls, that God wills the Church to be afflicted for many causes, and wills that invocation should be approached, so that faith may be excited, receiving the remission of sins. Next, that it may establish that God is the author of bodily benefits, and that He wills to give them, so that the Church may not be utterly destroyed in this life, just as He saved Noah, Abraham, and Moses in miraculous ways, so that the Church might remain.

Thus, therefore, let us exercise faith in both ways in the petition for bodily things. First, let us know that we must establish the petition for the remission of sins through the mediator: next, let us know that bodily benefits are to be sought and expected from God, and that the Church is God's care, even if He exercises other members differently, and wills us to be prepared for obedience. God saved the Church, even though tyrants were killing Paul and Timothy after their course was finished. He will save the Church, even if He allows some pious ones to be killed by the Turks. Thus let us seek and expect help, and yet be most prepared for obedience. And indeed, let us know that prayers are not in vain, but always obtain some good things, nay, even the mitigation of bodily miseries, as it is said in Luke 21: Pray that you may be able to escape all these things that are to come, etc.

On the fourth.

The fourth is the thing to be sought. There are, however, as has already been said, some things spiritual, others bodily, such as counsel, success in one's calling, and other comforts of life. God wills that all these things be sought from Him, and indeed it is said concerning one's calling: Without me you can do nothing.

And faith is exercised in a twofold way in the petition for bodily things. First, it seeks the remission of sins. Next, it acknowledges God as the author of good successes and of other bodily benefits, and that He wills to give them for the sake of the Church being preserved, as it is written: Your Father knows that you have need of all these things. Item: The rest shall be added unto you. Item: Cast your care upon God, and He shall nourish you.

Here let us each contemplate our sins, our callings, and our public and private calamities. Admonished by these great necessities, let us invoke God, as He says: Ask, and let not your prayer be an empty babbling (βαττολογία) without petition. Soldiers seek success in battle, Senators seek wisdom in giving counsel and government, Doctors and students in their studies, etc.

Next, also for peace, the fruitfulness of the earth, and an honest and tranquil civil government, as it is said in 1. Timothy 2: That we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all piety and honesty.

Finally, as often as we think about prayer, let thanksgiving be added; let us acknowledge that the benefit received has proceeded from God, and that we owe Him gratitude, which is to be shown in a twofold way: by the celebration of Him, and by our obedience. And daily we receive many benefits from God; we are often defended against the devil, his snares being repelled by the Son of God, which we are entirely ignorant of.

And there are other innumerable benefits; therefore Paul says, 1. Thessalonians last: Pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks.

Latin:

Dominica Vocem Iucunditatis.

Evangelium Iohannis 16.

Amen amen dico vobis, quaecunque petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Hactenus non petiistis quicquam in nomine meo. Petite et accipietis, ut gaudium vestrum sit perfectum. Haec per proverbia locutus sum vobis, Veniet tempus, cum iam non per proverbia loquar vobis, sed palam de patre meo annunciabo vobis, in illo die in nomine meo petetis. Et non dico vobis, quod ego rogaturus sim patrem pro vobis. Ipse enim pater amat vos, quia me amastis, et credidistis quod a Deo exiverim.

Semper de oratione haec quatuor tenenda sunt: Praeceptum Dei, Promissio divina, Fides, et res petenda,

De Praecepto.

Sciamus hoc summum officium esse, ad quod conditi sumus, agnoscere et invocare Deum, ideoque praecipua et prima lex est de agnitione Dei et invocatione, ut testatur dictum: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et ei soli servies. Itaque saepe repetitum est praeceptum de invocatione, ut Lucae 18.: Oportet semper orare. Et in Psalm. 49.: Invoca me in die tribulationis. Et Matth. 7.: Petite et accipietis etc. Haec praecepta nos doceant, praecipuum et summum cultum esse invocationem.

Hoc opus discernit veram Ecclesiam, seu populum Dei, ab omnibus reliquis hominibus. Quanquam homines naturaliter intelligunt praeceptum, quod iubet Deum invocare, tamen impii nec invocant, nec norunt, quomodo sit invocandus. Ideo in Psalmo dicitur: Deum non invocaverunt. Etsi autem magnum quiddam est, nosse praeceptum de invocatione, tamen nondum satis est, sed oportet adiungi promissionem.

De secundo. Accedat ergo promissio, quae testatur Deum audire nostras preces, et praestare, quae petimus. Norunt gentes praeceptum, sed dubitant, an audiantur, ut Virgilius inquit: Famamque fovemus inanem. Sed Ecclesiae sunt traditae promissiones aliis impiorum ritibus.

Haec incogitantia similis est consuetudini stultorum, qui currunt ad statuas, et ibi aliquid murmurant, non cogitantes, quid aut cur invocent. Cumque talis sit invocatio maximae partis hominum, hic error saepe taxandus est, et docendae sunt mentes, ut recte invocent.

Quidam Eremita dixit, nullum esse maiorem laborem precatione, quod verissimum est, quia et attentionem retinere est difficile, hoc est, cogitare Deum sicut se patefecit, et seiungere nostram invocationem ab Ethnica et Turcica, et simul respicere ad promissionem, ut fides excitetur.

Haec tota attentio maior est, cum sumus in dolore, sed cum animi sunt ociosi, ebrii voluptatibus, magis vagantur. Sed tamen pii et moderati, doctrinam de invocatione discant, et se recte assuefaciant: ita in veris doloribus etiam ardentiorem consolationem sentient.

Ac primum quidem cum precationem incoamus, cogitandum est, quis sit Deus.

Invocant Turci et alii impii, sed aberrant a Deo dupliciter.

Primum quod de essentia Dei falsam opinionem mordicus retinent. Secundo quod voluntatem ignorant. Turci enim et similes, etsi dicunt hunc esse Deum, qui condidit coelum ac terram, tamen negant vere esse Deum, hunc, qui se per Filium patefecit, qui tradidit nobis Evangelum, negant Filium et Spiritum sanctum esse de essentia patris. Ita primum de essentia errant. Postea et de voluntate, quia verbum revelatum a Deo abiecerunt, ignorant promissionem gratiae, nec possunt credere se respici exaudiri. Quare cogitantes de voluntate Dei, in horribiles tenebras et dubitationem aeternam irruunt.

Seiungenda est igitur ab illorum opinionibus nostra invocatio, ac primum cogitandum, quis sit Deus, is videlicet ac talis, qui se in verbo suo patefecit ab initio, post conditionem et lapsum Adae.

Sic autem patefecit se Deus in Evangelio suo: Unus est omnipotens et aeternus pater, qui cum Filio suo, qui est coaeterna imago patris, et Spiritu sancto, condidit omnes res bonas, et patefecit se dato verbo et misso Filio.

Deinde, quia obstrepit tibi indignatis, et dubitamus, an Deus recipiat nos, an curet preces nostras, propone animo promissiones Evangelii: Cogita Deum mandasse, ut invocemus, et credamus placere et recipi nostras preces propter Filium.

Et hanc invocationem summum esse cultum, et operum omnium maximum, et Deo gratissimum. Ideo toties clamat Christus: Petite et accipietis. Item: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Haec quotidie in precando cogitare necesse est.

Nec est precatio demurmurare aliqua verba sine hac cogitatione.

Ideo difficile opus est precatio: nam primum haec attentio est difficilis, sed multo maior labor, fidem excitare, ut acquiescas in promissione Evangelii, ac statuas preces non esse inane murmur, non dici ethnico more propter consuetudinem, sed revera eas a Deo flagitari, approbari, recipi, exaudiri.

Hic cor erudiendum est, ut acquiescat in tot promissionibus, sanctitis sanguine et resuscitatione Filii, ut: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, ego reficiam vos.

Haec alias saepe repetuntur. Iam vero recensui, ut hunc textum diligentius aspiciamus, in quo ostenditur, quis sit Deus, fit mentio, Patris, Filii et Spiritus sancti.

Quoties ergo incoas precationem, primum cogites quem velis alloqui, et testimonia de utraque re tibi proponito, videlicet, testimonia quibus se patefecit Deus, quis sit, et promissiones, quod propter Filium exaudiat.

Intuere mente aeternum patrem sonantem hanc vocem: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, Hunc audite. Hunc agnosce creatorem esse cum Filio suo, coaeterna imagine, et Spiritu sancto effuso in Apostolos. Et memento promissiones: Propter hunc Filium lesum Christum propiciatorem vult nos exaudire Deus, recipere, et regere Spiritu sancto.

Exemplum formae saepe recitavi: Omnipotens aeterne et vive Deus, aeterne pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui te patefecisti in mensa hominate, et clamasti de Filio tuo Domino nostro Iesu Christo: Hunc audite: Conditor omnium rerum et conservator, cum Filio tuo coaeterno, λόγῳ et imagine tua, et Spiritu sancto effuso in Apostolos, fovente creaturam tuam, sapiens, bone, misericors, iudex, et fortis, propter Iesum Christum Filium tuum, Dominum nostrum, quem voluisti pro nobis esse victimam, μεσίτην καὶ ἱκέτην, mirabili et inenarrabili consilio, et sanctifica, inflamma, doce, rege, iuva cor et animam meam Spiritu sancto tuo, sicut dixit Filius: Quanto magis pater coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus.

In tali precatione profitemur quis sit Deus, et qualis sit, et seiungimus nostram precationem ab Ethnica, Iudaica, et Turcica, et promissiones nobis suggerimus, ut fides excitetur. Agnoscimus hunc esse Deum creatorem rerum, qui se patefecit verbo suo, et misso Filio, et agnoscimus non esse ociosum, aut alligatum secundis causis, sed sapientem, bonum, iustum, iudicem, fortem, miserentem propter Filium, iuvantem nos, et regentem Spiritu sancto: haec omnia complecti in precatione necesse est. Nam quis sit Deus, et cur exaudiat, nisi haec omnia complectamur, cogitari non potest. Assuefaciant ergo se bonae mentes ad talem aliquam formam, et opponant eam Ethnicis et Turcicis opinionibus.

De secundo.

Saepe repetuntur descriptiones personarum divinitatis.

Pater est substantia intelligens, aeterna, omnipotens, libere agens, bona, iusta, misericors, gignens ab aeterno imaginem sui: Cum qua et cum Spiritu sancto procedente a Patre et Filio, condidit coelum et terram, et omnes naturas, quas continet. Filius est substantia genita a patre, coaeterna, imago aeterni patris, et quia mirabili consilio constitutus est propiciator, ideo assumsit humanam naturam, et factus est victima, et pignus, quod Deus velit nos recipere, nobis reddere iusticiam, et vitam aeternam. Ut autem imago gignitur cogitatione, ita spiritus dicitur procedere a voluntate Patris et Filii, quia est flatus et agitator, movens creaturam, et accendens lucem, et novos motus in cordibus audientium Evangelium. Huic agitationi quae a voluntate est, convenit vocabulum procedere.

Iam vide hoc loco, quanta Dei bonitas describitur, et quanta traditur promissio Ecclesiae. Christus pollicetur, se missurum esse Spiritum sanctum, et simul affirmat patrem velle ut mittatur. Volunt igitur pater aeternus, Filius et Spiritus sanctus, non perire genus humanum, sed reddi hominibus novam lucem, agnitionem Dei, novam iusticiam, fidem, dilectionem, et vitam aeternam: quia enim volunt dari Spiritum sanctum, haec accendi in cordibus hominum non dubium est.

Cum dicitur Spiritus sanctus procedere, personae proprietas indicatur: deinde cum vocatur Spiritus veritatis et παράκλητος, officia seu propria munera describuntur, quae per eum divinitas impertit. Spiritus veritatis, id est, qui per Evangelium facit lucere in mente veram agnitionem Dei, et in corde accendit motus congruentes voluntati Dei, reverentiam erga Deum, fiduciam, invocationem et dilectionem Dei, odium peccati, consolationem et laetitiam in Deo incoantem vitam aeternam.

Haec bona melius intelliguntur ex collatione. Cato etsi iudicio naturali habet hanc noticiam, quod sit aliqua mens aeterna, conditrix rerum, et curans imperia, tamen cum videt confusionem humani generis, et videt se in causa, ut arbitrantur, iusta negligi, iterum mergitur in immensas tenebras, amittit totam persuasionem de Deo, cogitat aut nihil esse, aut ociosum, aut iniustum esse. Deinde omnibus religionibus irascitur. His tenebris et hoc mendacio omnium hominum corda oppressa sunt, quae non norunt Evangelium, ex quo solo discimus, cur et quomodo Deus exaudiat, et cur genus humanum subiectum sit morti, et aliis poenis.

Saepe vero accenduntur in impiis maiores furores, quia sunt tenebrae in mentibus ignaris Evangelii, et diabolus impellit multos, ut fingant contumeliosa adversus Deum, ut Epicurus horribili petulantia vociferatur, nihil esse Deum. Vulgus fingit idola et multos Deos, ut qui currunt ad statuas mortuorum. Haeretici etiam fingunt sua deliria. Manichaeus duos Deos comminiscitur. Haec exempla cogitemus, et consideremus quanta sit miseria hominum, qui sunt sine Evangelio et sine Spiritu sancto, ac sciamus dari Spiritum sanctum, ut depulsis his furoribus et mendaciis, accendat in nobis veritatem, id est, veram agnitionem Dei, quis sit, et quomodo exaudiat, quomodo coli velit, quomodo iudicaturus sit.

Altera appellatio hoc loco est παράκλητος, quae significat advocatum, scilicet, nos consilio regentem, et consolantem in doloribus, et confirmantem nos in variis certaminibus. Sic albi Christus inquit: Spiritus sanctus ducet vos in omnem veritatem.

Nimis vagabundae sunt mentes humanae, ac facile aberrant a Deo, facile admittunt plausibiles opiniones, pugnantes cum verbo Dei, ut Eva decepta est, et Paulus vocat tela ignita diaboli, opinionum spectra, quae diabolus infirmis animis offundit. Adversus haec mala, non possumus esse tuti nisi Spiritus sanctus confirmet mentes. Quare semper petendum est: Confirma hoc Deus, quod operatus es in nobis. Et promissio de Spiritu sancto cogitanda est, qui ideo promittitur Ecclesiae, et singulis invocantibus, ut veritatem in nobis confirmet, retineat nes, et patefacta voluntas Dei, ut Deut. 4. dicitur: Non est alio natio tam gloriosa, quae habeat Deum appropinquantem, sicut Deus noster adest omnibus nobis invocantibus eum.

Huc iam promissiones omnes colligantur in tota scriptura. Praecipua vero proponitur in hodierna lectione, confirmata iureiurando Filii Dei.

Amen amen dico vobis, Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Petite et accipietis. Omnis qui petit accipit.

Item: Si homines possunt hominibus bona dare, quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Item: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis. Item: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te. Item, multum iuvabit deprecatio iusti assidua. Item, Matth. 18. de precatione communi: Amen dico vobis, De quacunque re consentient duo, quicquid petent, fiet.

Has promissiones necesse est inspici, quia dubitatio in precatione, an Deus recipiat nostras preces, est impia. Ideo scribitur, Petat in fide.

Iam hic cogitemus, quam pauci homines praestent hunc cultum Deo. Ideo magna causa est, cur dicat Psalmus, Deum non invocant. Pauci enim sic accedunt ad precandum, cum bona conscientia et fide, ut statuant recipi suas preces.

De tertio.

Tertium est fides. Hic sciendum est, quid vocetur fides. Primum fides intelligatur fiducia reconciliationis donatae propter Christum, et quod propter hunc mediatorem et pontificem aeternus Deus accipiat nostras preces. Hanc generalem fidem necesse est adferri in omni invocatione.

Ideo hic diserte additum est: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, id est, non fiducia dignitatis vestrae, sed fiducia mediatoris Christi, quia necesse est teneri regulam, quod non sit accessus ad patrem aeternum, nisi per Filium, sicut Rom. 5. dicitur: Per hunc habemus accessum. Item: Habentes talem pontificem, accedamus ad thronum gratiae. Item: Semper vivens, ut interpellet pro nobis.

Haec igitur fides discernit peccantes, Iudaeos et Turcas, et omnes habentes malam conscientiam, hypocritas et Christianos vere invocantes. Iudaei, Turcae gloriantur se invocare Deum conditorem rerum, et quidem valde superbiunt hac doctrina, quod unum Deum nominent, sed non invocant Deum aeternum patrem Filii missi et constituti mediatoris, imo mediatorem ipsum Filium Dei contumelia afficiunt, ideo non invocant.

Deinde habentes propositum peccandi, non possunt Deum invocare, non accedunt ad Deum per mediatorem, et sunt sine fide, ut Iohannes inquit, 1. Ioh. 3.: Si cor nostrum non condemnat nos, fiduciam habemus ad Deum, etc. Postremo, hypocritae, id est, accedentes fiducia suae dignitatis, vel dubitantes, quia agnoscunt suam indignitatem, non accedunt ad Deum, non vere invocant.

Sed adversus haec necesse est adferri hanc fidem, quae agnoscit Deum placatum esse per Filium, et fiducia huius mediatoris, invocat et petit, et statuit accipi preces nostras, et Deo placere, nec irritas esse, etiamsi eventus vel differuntur, vel non respondent nostrae cogitationi.

Hic etiam tenenda est doctrina, quod fides quaedam petat sine conditione, quaedam vero cum aliqua conditione. Sine conditione petenda et expectanda sunt illa, de quibus nominatim, et specialiter expressa est voluntas Dei, quod haec ipsa nominatim daturus sit, videlicet, quae sunt propria Evangelii, remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, donationem Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae. Haec cum petimus, statuendum est vere ea nobis praestari, et illa ipsa fide accipi, quae nos in pavoribus consolatur, iuxta illud: Iustificati fide pacem habemus etc.

In petitione rerum corporalium necesse est adferri fidem generalem, quod Deus tibi sit propicius et accipiat preces tuas, sed de re ipsa, quae nominatim petitur, non statuitur sine conditione, quia in corporalibus aerumnis, debemus obedientiam Deo, sicut David pulsus in exilium, petit quidem se reduci, sed tamen addit: Si non volet me Deus reducere, fiat quod ipsi placet. Imo haec est singularis sapientia Ecclesiae, etiamsi non contingit liberatio corporalis, tamen non ruere in desperationem, in blasphemias, aut odium Dei, sed erigi fide, ac retinere remissionem peccatorum, et spem vitae aeternae certam, quia cum ira Dei sit iusta adversus peccata nostra, debemus obedientiam in poena.

Sed difficile est in tali certamine retinere fidem, ut Saul frustratus spe victoriae prorsus opprimitur desperatione, cogitat sibi abiectum esse a Deo, nec credit sibi remitti peccata, et in hac desperatione sibi mortem consciscit. Ita plurimi ex impatientia, et propter moram ruunt in desperationem et aeternum exitium.

Sed inculcanda

est animis doctrina, quod Deus velit affligi Ecclesiam, propter multas causas, ac velit accedere invocationem, ut excitetur fides, accipiens remissionem peccatorum. Deinde, ut statuat Deum autorem esse beneficiorum corporalium, eaque velle dare, ne in hac vita penitus deleatur Ecclesia, sicut servavit Nohae, Abraham, Mosen, mirabilibus modis, ut reliqua esset Ecclesia.

Sic igitur exerceamus fidem utroque modo in petitione corporalium. Primum sciamus statuendum esse de remissione peccatorum propter mediatorem: deinde sciamus a Deo petenda et expectanda esse beneficia corporis, et Deo curae esse Ecclesiam, etiam si alia membra aliter exercet, ac vult nos ad obedientiam paratos esse. Servabat Ecclesiam Deus, etiam si tyranni Paulum et Timotheum confecto curriculo interficiebant. Servabit Ecclesiam, etiam si aliquos pios sinet a Turcis interfici. Sic nos petamus et expectemus auxilium, et tamen ad obedientiam paratissimi simus. Et quidem sciamus non esse irritas preces, sed semper impetrare aliqua bona, imo et mitigationem corporalium aerumnarum, ut Lucae 21. dicitur: Orate ut possitis effugere omnia haec, quae ventura sunt etc.

De quarto.

Quartum est res petenda. Sunt autem, ut iam dictum est, aliae res spirituales, aliae corporales, ut consilium, successus in vocatione, et ceterae vitae commoda. Haec omnia vult Deus peti a se, et quidem de vocatione dicitur: Sine me nihil potestis facere.

Ac fides dupliciter exercetur in petitione corporalium. Primum petit remissionem peccatorum. Deinde agnoscit Deum autorem esse bonorum successuum, et aliorum beneficiorum corporalium, et velle ea dare servandae Ecclesiae causa, sicut scriptum est: Scit pater vester quod opus habeatis his omnibus. Item: Reliqua adiicientur vobis. Item: Iacta curam tuam in Deum, et ipse te enutriet.

Hic singuli intuemur peccata nostra, vocationes, calamitates publicas et privatas. His tantis necessitatibus admoniti invocemus Deum, sicut dicit: Petite, nec sit precatio inanis βαττολογία sine petitione. Milites petunt successus in praelio, Senatores sapientiam in dando consilio et gubernatione, Doctores et discipuli in studiis etc.

Deinde et pacem, foecunditatem terrae, honestum et tranquillum regimen civile, ut 1. Timoth. 2. dicitur: Ut tranquillam et quietam vitam agamus in omni pietate et honestate.

Postremo, quoties de precatione cogitamus, adiungatur gratiarum actio, agnoscamus acceptum beneficium a Deo profectum esse, et ei debere gratitudinem, quae ostendenda est dupliciter, celebratione ipsius, et nostra obedientia, et quotidie multa beneficia a Deo accipimus, saepe defendimur adversus diabolum, depulsis eius insidiis a Filio Dei, quas nos prorsus ignoramus.

Et sunt alia innumerabilia beneficia, ideo Paulus inquit, 1. Thessal. ultimo: Incessanter orate, in omnibus gratias agite.

## 18:1-40 Good Friday. Concerning the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ
Good Friday. Concerning the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The meditation on the passion of the Son of God is threefold: Pedagogical, Spiritual, and Exemplary.

Pedagogical is to often read the narratives themselves for the sake of learning or teaching the history, and to seek the testimonies of the Prophets, and the causes, whether God willed the Son to suffer, why he willed him to suffer, how human nature is subject to sin, whether it is redeemed by the Son alone, etc., and to confirm by such reading the faith by which we assent to the history. This diligence is also useful, and without it the following uses cannot be had. Therefore, let this reading and reflection be frequent, so that the following uses may arrive at the same time.

Spiritual meditation is this: because it behooved the Son of God to become a sacrifice, to recognize the magnitude of the wrath of God against sin, and truly to tremble, and again to recognize the mercy, and by faith to be raised up and vivified, because this sacrifice is more excellent than the whole mass of sin, and the Son is a certain pledge that God loves us and wills to make us saved. When these true motions, terrors and consolation, fear and faith, the sense of the wrath of God and vivification through faith in the Son of God arrive, this is the principal and salutary meditation, and the application of the benefit of God to us.

But it is necessary to contemplate both in the mind, wrath and mercy. Men think of God with idle minds; they do not think that he is truly angry at sin, because the levity of human minds does not magnify its own errors. But God wills this madness to be corrected: therefore he has burdened the whole human race with huge calamities. All the miseries of individuals, death, and punishments, wars, destructions, devastations, such as the flood, the conflagration of Sodom, the slaughters of all kingdoms, of all ages, are testimonies set forth, so that they may convince us that God is truly angry at sin. But an evident testimony for the impious, who in this life despise the word and testimonies of God, will be eternal torment after this life. Truly, in this visible world, the most evident testimony of the wrath of God was that it could be appeased by nothing, except the death of the only-begotten Son: it could not be appeased, not even by the hardships of the saints, such as Abel, and others. Now consider, what man sufficiently considers the magnitude of this wrath, and esteems the benefit of God as much as it truly ought to be esteemed: all therefore are ungrateful, ignorant, both of the wrath of God and of the benefit. Let us recognize this security, ingratitude, ignorance, and in some way correct it.

Again, when true terror has arisen in the heart, let consolation arrive, and let us recognize the magnitude of the mercy, that God willed the Son to suffer for this reason, that, appeased through him, he might truly receive us and save us: and let us learn the application, that we do not otherwise obtain the remission of sins, eternal life, except by this very faith, determining that on account of the Son of God made a victim for us, the eternal father receives us and saves us.

Concerning this application, let testimonies be held in readiness: Rom. 3: We are justified however freely through the redemption of Jesus, whom God made a propitiator, through faith in his blood, etc. Rom. 8: For sin he condemned sin. 2 Cor. 5: Him, who knew no sin, he made sin, that we might become the righteousness of God through him. This application learn the lesson, so that the blood of Christ may not have been shed in vain for you, and that you may give thanks to God, and obey Him for such a great gift. This meditation, namely to tremble while beholding the wondrous [love] of God in the passion of the Son, and again to be raised up by faith, acknowledging His mercy, and to give thanks, is truly the worship of God, which ought to be perpetual. Now consider how many men there are who care for this great gift, who do not prefer their own desires to the blood of the Son of God. Very many confess that they doubt whether this great gift pertains to them: but against this doubt let us confirm ourselves with the Gospel, and with constant exercise in prayer.

The third kind of meditation is exemplary, where we now use this example, as a law or rule, that just as Christ suffered, so it behooves us also to suffer. And this is the singular wisdom of the Church, to understand the causes of human calamities, and the true consolations. Wise men from the very beginning of the world have wondered what the cause is, why this excellent nature of men is burdened with such great miseries, indeed how it happens that the best are oppressed by the saddest events, and others have thought of other causes. But the word of God shows the true causes. In the beginning, as Paul says, "Through sin death passed into all men," and the great bites of the devil followed, as it is said of the serpent: "The serpent shall bite thy heel."

Causes of afflictions.

I. Sin and the bites of the devil.

II. The acknowledgment of sin in the Church.

III. The will of God, who wishes to recall [us] to repentance and the acknowledgment of promised mercy.

IIII. The occasion for confirming faith.

V. The acknowledgment of God's help, and the exercise, so that trust in God may be confirmed, and trust in ourselves may be cast off.

VI. That the power of God may be seen in our weakness.

VII. That we may be made like the Son of God.

VIII. That affliction may be a testimony of the future life.

But why was Christ, when He was without sin, subjected to the cross? Because death is the penalty of sin. Since therefore Christ was the victim, that is, was about to undergo the penalty of sin for us, death and the saddest afflictions had to be undergone by Him. And God wishes the Church to become like this Head of hers, therefore the chief members, Abel, Isaiah, the Prophets, the Apostles, and many others were killed, so that they might become like the Head. But in these and other men, afflictions have this cause also, that they themselves may acknowledge their own sin and that of the human race. For the Church is especially subjected to the cross, so that it may acknowledge the sin which the ungodly despise. Then there are added other causes, which I have recounted.

And especially the end of afflictions must be considered, namely, that God wishes us to be afflicted, not that we may perish, but that we may be saved, that is, that we may be recalled to the acknowledgment of sin and mercy, according to that: "As I live, I desire not the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live." Human reason does not see this will of God and these causes by itself: when things are adverse, we immediately think that we are cast off by God. Again, we think those are loved who flourish in glory and power. But this error must be removed from our minds, and the image of Christ must be set against it, and the perpetual sentence of the Gospel must be learned, that the Church is subjected to the cross, and why it is subjected, and the sentences must be held which teach us about this will of God, such as: "Whoever wishes to follow me, let him take up his cross, and follow me." Item: "Many are the tribulations of the righteous." Item: "Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God," namely, which both powerfully humbles and powerfully delivers.

Chapter LIII. of Isaiah.

This chapter has eight chief points.

I. The point is history.

II. The cause. III.

The application of the benefit. The knowledge of Him shall justify many.

IIII. The preaching of universal repentance.

V. The universal promise.

VI. Concerning the priesthood of Christ.

VII. Concerning the resurrection and the kingdom.

VIII. Concerning the punishments of the ungodly.

Who believes our report, and to whom shall the arm of the Lord be known? He shall grow up before God as a tender plant, and as a root out of a thirsty ground. There is no beauty in Him nor comeliness, when we looked at Him, there was no beauty that we should desire Him. He was despised and the most abject of all, oppressed by grief and miseries. Thus we abhorred Him, so that we turned our faces from Him: therefore we esteemed Him as nothing.

He himself bore our infirmities, and he himself sustained our sorrows; we regarded him as afflicted, and struck by God and cast down. But he was wounded for our sins, and afflicted for our iniquities. He himself sustains the punishment, so that peace and forgiveness may be granted to us, and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, everyone in his own ways, and the Lord has cast upon him the iniquities of us all. When he was afflicted and humbled, he did not open his mouth, like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that is silent before the one shearing it, and does not open its mouth. From affliction and punishment he was delivered, and who shall declare his generations? When he was cut off from the land of the living, for the wickedness of the people he was struck, and he was buried like the wicked, and died like the rich. He did not act unjustly, nor was there deceit in his mouth, but it pleased God to crush him with affliction. Because he gave his soul as a sacrifice for sin, he shall see a long posterity, and the counsel of God shall be happily perfected by his hand, because his soul labored, he shall enjoy pleasure. And my righteous servant shall justify many by the knowledge of himself, because he himself sustained their sins. Therefore I will distribute to him a great inheritance, and he shall spoil the strong, because he delivered his soul unto death, and was reputed with the wicked, and he himself sustained the sins of many, and prayed for the transgressors.

Of the Lamb slaughtered at the Passover. From chapter 12.

Exodus.

It is certain that the ancient rite of the slaughtering of the lamb, instituted with such great miracles, was not only a sign warning of the past liberation, but also of the future, and of the lamb, that is, the victim, through whom a true and eternal liberation was to be given.

Therefore Paul also compares the old Passover with Christ, saying: Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.

But as in our Passover, that is, the passion of Christ, the magnitude of God's wrath against sin is seen: and again, mercy in the beginning of eternal life, through the resurrection, and the promise of liberation from sin and death.

Thus in the old Passover the whole history is to be considered, so that both the wrath of God against the sins of the Egyptians, and mercy in the liberation of the Church may be recognized.

It was a sad example, that kingdom, most flourishing of all in the whole world, to be suddenly dissipated and overturned by tumult, with the greatest part of the men consumed, by continuous manifold plagues, with the princes destroyed, and the whole form of the kingdom changed. These were the punishments for idolatry, magic, lusts, and cruelty against the saints.

But first the time is described, in the first month, that is, the lunar month, which immediately followed the vernal equinox, for that was the beginning of the year. On the tenth day a whole lamb is to be chosen, a yearling, a male, and from the lambs and the kids, that is, to be taken from the rest of the flock, and to be kept until the 13th day, then in the evening it is to be slaughtered. This description agrees with Christ. Generally, a lamb and especially one slaughtered signifies a victim: wherefore the Israelites themselves understood that another certain victim was signified, through whom they were to obtain a true and eternal liberation, and that victim had to be whole, without sin, male, strong: taken from the rest of the flock, that is, from the people of Israel.

It was necessary, therefore, for Christ to be born in this people, and not elsewhere, it was necessary for him to preach in this people, and to suffer: therefore the lamb was set apart beforehand, so that it might be signified that Christ would preach for some time beforehand.

II. In the evening they shall slaughter, and they shall sprinkle the doorposts

with blood: it was signified that Christ would come in the evening, towards the end of the world, and that the Church was to be sprinkled with his blood, that is, that sin was to be washed away by the blood of Christ.

III. Let the roasted flesh be eaten. Our eating is described in John 6.

As the Israelites were nourished by eating the lamb, so we are built up with confidence in Christ in true terrors, we are made members of Christ, we are vivified through him: for he ascends, that he may give gifts to men, and truly be effective, that he may give the Holy Spirit.

But let the roasted flesh be eaten: there is no doubt that the passion is signified by the very appellation of the lamb and the slaughtering. But the passion of the lamb is also signified here: because Christ truly experienced the fire, that is, the judgment of God, undergoing punishments for us. But it is customary to interpret these things regarding the quality of those who eat. They eat the lamb raw, who themselves retain carnal crudity, namely, Epicurean or hypocritical security, which is to be without repentance, without recognition of the wrath of God. Likewise, to retain human opinions about God, not to amend errors from the Word of God, just as many bend Christian doctrine toward human philosophy.

And the loaves shall be unleavened. This manifestly signifies the purity of doctrine. Let us not invent other opinions about God, like heathen idolaters, nor about Christ, like Mahometans and heretics, nor other cults, like Papists, but let the purity of doctrine be preserved.

But what is added, when the text generally calls the food bitter with wild lettuce, it signifies the doctrine of repentance, or even the very sense of present afflictions, which warns us that the human race, because of sin, is subject to the wrath of God, and cannot be liberated except through the lamb, whom God had signified through these rites, that is, through the Son, whom He exhibited to us.

IIII. Not raw. I interpret this concerning our crudity. For they eat it raw who themselves retain carnal crudity, as was said before, that is, along with carnal opinions about God and religion, also security and contempt for the judgment of God, such as is in those who are without repentance, without recognition of the wrath of God, without sorrow and fear of the punishments of sin. Now let us consider how many men in the Church are raw, and disdain Christ and the Gospel.

V. Roasted with fire. I do not doubt that the passion of Christ is signified, who truly felt the fire of divine judgment and the wrath of God against sins. And those who eat it roasted, let them recognize the roasting, that is, let them also recognize the judgment of God against sins, namely that God is so angry at sin that no victim could appease Him except the death of the Son. And let us not dilute this food by maceration in water, that is, by security and carnal opinions.

VI. You shall eat the whole. The doctrine concerning Christ must be held entire. For it is customary for heretics to retain a part of the doctrine concerning Christ, just as Samosatenus retained this part, that Christ is a man, and Mahomet also retained the same: finally, others have retained another particle. Our adversaries retain the articles about the two natures, but not about the office; they do not want God to be invoked by this faith, so that we believe we are truly received freely on account of the Son, the mediator. But the Church of Christ retains the entire doctrine.

VII. You shall gird your loins, and you shall be shod. There is no doubt that the people of the law, eating thus in the attire of a traveler, were warned by this very rite that another greater liberation was still to be expected, that in the meantime they would be travelers, would have great dangers, exiles, and changes of their kingdom: but then they would have rest, this pilgrimage being completed, when another liberation would come, which will lead into life and eternal glory.

VIII. It is called the Passover of the Lord, because God passed over, struck the Egyptians, and spared the families where the threshold was sprinkled with blood: this is the principal signification. Having sent the Son, God will judge the world, will pass through all nations, and will cast them into eternal torments, but will spare His Church sprinkled with the blood of the Son of God.

This part manifestly testifies that in this noted image Christ and the passion of Christ are depicted, because it is clearly said here that the families were spared where the threshold was sprinkled with blood. It is certain, however, that we are not liberated otherwise from eternal death except by the blood of the Son of God. The image openly corresponds to this signification.

Furthermore, the attire of the traveler also warns us of the struggles, exiles, and hardships to be undertaken in this life. For although the liberation has begun, it is not yet perfect, but will be perfected when we have been led through death into eternal life. But just as the sea did not overwhelm the Israelites going through the waves, so death does not absorb those who believe in the Lamb Christ.

In this way the type warns us about the liberation to be perfected, just as it warned the Israelites that another liberation remained. And there is no doubt that wise men among the people of Israel, when they stood at the feast girded, warned their own with such words: You see what this our attire signifies; God commands us to be girded for exiles, for struggles, for dangers. Let us therefore take this up with a pious mind, and expect the other liberation, which will lead us into eternal rest, signified by this liberation.

IX. Finally, it is again commanded concerning unleavened bread, and leavened. And there is no doubt that unleavened bread signifies the purity of doctrine, of invocation, of faith, of cults, so that cults may be unleavened, not fermented with human opinions outside the Word of God, just as the gentiles, Mahomet, monks, and now many learned men mix leaven, that is, their own beautiful thoughts and plausible opinions, alien to the Word of God and the doctrine of faith.

Let us diligently contemplate this comparison of the Paschal lamb with the Lamb Christ; let the slaughter and the sprinkling of blood come before our eyes. The slaughter signifies the death of Christ. The sprinkling signifies the application, by which individuals by faith apply to themselves the benefit of Christ, and thus are sprinkled with his blood, as Peter says. Let the causes of God's wrath against the sin of the human race be considered, and his mercy, that he redeemed us with the blood of his Son; let faith be retained in invocation, that we are truly accepted on account of this Son, not on account of our own dignity. Let the punishments of Egypt also be considered, signifying the destruction of all the impious.

On the Resurrection of Christ.

The Gospel of Luke 24.

And behold, two of them were going on that same day to a village, which was sixty stadia away from Jerusalem, named Emmaus. And they were talking to each other about all these things that had happened.

And it happened that while they were talking, and questioning among themselves, Jesus himself approached and walked with them: but their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him. But he said to them: What are these words that you are exchanging with each other as you walk, and are sad?

But one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering, said to him: Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known what has happened there in these days? And he said to them: What things?

But they said, about Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man and a Prophet, powerful in work and word, before God and all the people, and how the chief priests and our leaders handed him over to the sentence of death, and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.

And yet, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened. But also some women from our group terrified us, who were at the tomb before dawn, and not having found his body, they came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive.

And some of those who were with us went to the tomb, and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see. And he said to them: O foolish and slow of heart to believe in all that the Prophets have spoken.

Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things, and to enter into his glory? And beginning from Moses and from all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things that were about himself.

And they approached the village where they were going, and he pretended to go further, and they compelled him, saying: Stay with us, for it is getting toward evening, and the day is now far spent. And he went in to stay with them.

And it happened, while he was reclining with them, he took bread, blessed it, and broke it, and was offering it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him, and he vanished from them.

And they said to each other: Was not our heart burning within us, while he was speaking to us on the way, and while he was opening the scriptures to us? And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered, and those who were with them, saying that the Lord has truly risen, and has appeared to Simon.

And they were recounting what had happened on the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of bread. While they were speaking these things, Jesus stood in their midst, and says to them: Peace be with you.

But terrified and made fearful, they thought they were seeing a spirit. And he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?

See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having.

And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. But while they still did not believe for joy and were wondering, he said to them: Do you have anything here that can be eaten?

But they offered him a piece of broiled fish, and a honeycomb. And taking it, he ate before them.

But he said to them: These are the words which I spoke to you, while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms concerning me. Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures, and said to them: Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

This chapter has six principal points.

I. Pious conversations.

II. The infirmity of the disciples.

III. Even infirm but teachable persons are pleasing to God.

IIII. Confirmation of the Gospel from prophetic testimonies.

V. Concerning the resurrection, namely that faith ought to look upon the resurrected and reigning Christ.

VI. Concerning the benefits of the resurrection.

Concerning the first.

Christ intervenes twice in the conversations of the disciples, who were disputing about the resurrection. Therefore, the example warns and testifies that God favors pious meditation and discourse, and that through these it is effective. Therefore it is written: Let the word of God abound among you. Likewise: Let your speech be seasoned with salt.

Concerning the second. The infirmity in the disciples is notable. For they doubt the resurrection, even though it had indeed been predicted beforehand. Therefore, there are sins in the saints, infirmity of faith, doubts, ignorances, security, many vicious impulses, diffidences, etc. As it is said in the Psalm: Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from my hidden ones. And everyone will detect in himself the infirmity of his own faith, thinking about eternity, about our resurrection, etc. Likewise, [they detect] too great a security, and many errors which arise from diffidence or carnal confidence. Here, therefore, let us learn that there ought to be perpetual repentance in the saints, and that the saints are not righteous by the law, because they do not satisfy the law, and the confidence in works is to be condemned; and again it must be learned that those who perform repentance obtain remission by faith, and are pleasing to God on account of Christ. Sins are also to be distinguished here: for faults against conscience shake off faith, grace, and the Holy Spirit.

Concerning the third.

It is a useful consolation, the example of the infirmity of the Apostles in the whole history of the Gospel. For it testifies that the infirm, if they are teachable and hold to the foundation, are pleasing to God, just as Paul also says: Him that is weak in the faith receive, for God receives him. And in the Church, the greatest part always has notable infirmities. However, teachable infirm persons are to be distinguished from arrogant, stubborn, and contumacious hypocrites. Teachable infirm persons are those who hold the foundation, that is, the articles of faith, even if in some things they do not yet hold a sufficiently explained doctrine, about which, however, they hear other more learned men, seek testimonies of scripture, do not resist, do not defend private persuasions, or private affections, ambitions, or other cupidities, under the pretext of the word of God, with poorly twisted scriptures, etc. On the contrary, the contumacious are those who, in certain articles, oppose true opinions, either through ignorance or arrogance, and confidence in their own wisdom, admiration of their own opinions, or on account of some private cupidities, etc. Such contumacious persons are not pleasing to God, nor are they to be named infirm, but rather contentious, enemies to the Gospel.

Concerning the fourth.

Christ himself leads the Church to prophetic testimonies, and not only convinces the disciples by his miracles and his own resurrection, but adds testimonies of scripture: because he does not want us to judge from miracles alone, but miracles ought to consent with the delivered word. Now it is useful here to collect some testimonies, about which Christ undoubtedly discoursed when he taught about the passion, about the resurrection, about the victim for sin, about abolishing death, about restoring eternal life, and refuted the imaginations about a worldly kingdom of the Messiah. For the disciples had the common persuasion that the Messiah would have a kingdom of the world and political domination. But Christ teaches differently here, namely, that he was sent so that he might become a victim for sin, might promulgate the Gospel, and, having been resurrected, might give the Holy Spirit, might help those calling upon the Father through him, might send the Apostles, and might build and preserve the Church, and in the resurrection of the dead might glorify it. These things were said in the promises and sermons of the Prophets, as in the first promise: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent, that is, Christ shall destroy the works of the devil, sin, and death, And the serpent shall bite his heel, that is, the devil shall exercise cruelty against Christ and the Church, but yet he shall be conquered and crushed. To this pertains also the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah. Likewise, the victims in the law signified the true victim, just as the Epistle to the Hebrews says, it was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sin.

Concerning the fifth.

Our faith [ought] to look upon Christ resurrected, living, and in every prayer and invocation... reigning, he ought, and to hold the rule: Whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name etc. That is, the confidence of Christ, not the confidence of your own dignity. For Christ is the perpetual high priest, perpetually interceding for us, perpetually giving gifts to men. Nor must it be imagined that he is blessed for himself, that he is idle, but he rose again that he might reign, that is, that he might be effective in those who call upon him, just as he says to the Apostles: All power is given unto me, I am with you even unto the end of the world. And in the Psalm it is said: Sit at my right hand, by which it is signified that Christ would reign by divine power.

Of the sixth. Of the benefits of the resurrection.

In Rom. 4 it is said: Who was delivered for our offenses, and was raised again for our justification. Here he delivers the distinction of the penalty paid for us, and then of the justice and life to be exhibited to us. For because Christ died, he paid the penalty which we owed. But if he had remained in death, the benefit would not have been complete, nor would he himself have had the promised kingdom, nor would he have been effective in liberating his own from eternal death: therefore it was necessary for him to rise again, so that sitting at the right hand of the Father, that is, reigning by divine power, he might be effective. Therefore, the benefits of the resurrection are all the works of Christ reigning, namely, to justify believers, to sanctify them by the given Holy Spirit, to defend them against the power of the devil, to liberate them from eternal death, to begin eternal life in believers, and afterwards to raise them up, to restore the whole human nature to live with new light, wisdom, justice, and perpetual life. None of these things would happen from one dead and idle.

Concerning these works, the prophetic sayings preach, which speak of the resurrection, as Ose. 13: I will deliver them from the hand of death, and I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy death; O grave, I will be thy destruction. This sermon of Hosea declares the ancient promises, and signifies what kind of liberation is promised through the Messiah, namely, not the restitution and amplification of a political kingdom, but a far different thing, namely, the destruction of death and sin, and the restitution of eternal life. Therefore it is said: O death, I will be thy death, that is, I will destroy death, I will destroy the underworld, I will restore life and perpetual justice, namely, to believers. In these words the rest are contained, that is, Therefore the Messiah reigns, he intercedes for us before the Father, that he may receive us and pronounce us just, he gives us the Holy Spirit, he fights for us against the devil, he begins eternal life in believers, and he raises the dead, just as he himself rose again. Furthermore, we shall understand these benefits, and we shall obtain them, if we rouse ourselves to invocation, and ask for help in public and our own perils, from Christ reigning, and we shall not dream that he is idle.

A similar saying is found in Isaiah: In that day the root of Jesse shall stand, which shall be for a sign to the people, to him the Gentiles shall flee, and his burial shall be glorious. It is a description of Christ reigning. In that day he shall stand, that is, the promised liberator from the stock of Jesse shall not be overturned. And he shall be for a sign to the people, that is, he shall be as a leader bearing a banner: he shall be able to be seen in his sign, that is, the preaching of the Gospel: and the Gentiles shall flee to him, they shall call upon him. When?

Not only when he shall converse with us in this life, as a mortal man, but also afterwards, when his death shall be glorious, that is, when he shall have risen again. For if resurrection, or new life, did not follow death, it would not be true glory. The saying of the Prophet therefore testifies that this Lord would rise again, and would not remain in death, and that then the Gentiles would call upon him. Here he teaches what kind of worship will be in the New Testament, they shall not slaughter victims, but shall flee to this leader, from him they shall seek help. He shall liberate those who call upon him from the highest evils, from which they cannot be liberated in any other way, namely, from the wrath of God, from sin, from eternal death, from the power of the devil etc. Moreover, these sermons of the Prophets have been handed down, so that they may excite and confirm faith in us, and exhort us to these acts of worship, to the acknowledgment and invocation of Christ, and thus these sermons will grow sweet to us, and we shall understand the benefits of the resurrection, if we seriously exercise invocation, admonished by these sentences. Hither pertain all the sentences which speak of the perpetual kingdom of Christ etc.

Latin:

Die Parasceves. De passione Domini nostri Iesu Christi.

Triplex est meditatio passionis Filii Dei, Paedagogica, Spiritualis et Exemplaris.

Paedagogica, est saepe legere ipsas narrationes discendae aut docendae historiae causa, et quaerere testimonia Prophetarum, et causas, an Deus voluerit Filium pati, cur voluerit eum pati, quomodo natura humana sit subiecta peccato, an redemta per solum Filium etc. et confirmare tali lectione fidem, qua adsentimur historiae. Haec diligentia etiam est utilis, et sine hac sequentes usus haberi non possunt. Ideo haec lectio et cogitatio sit crebra, ut simul accedant sequentes usus.

Spiritualis meditatio haec est, quia Filium Dei oportuit fieri hostiam, agnoscere magnitudinem irae Dei adversus peccatum, et vere expavescere, ac rursus agnoscere misericordiam, et fide erigi et vivificari, quia haec hostia est praestantior tota mole peccati, et Filius est certum pignus, quod Deus diligat nos, et velit nos salvos facere. Cum hi veri motus, pavores et consolatio, timor et fides, sensus irae Dei et vivificatio per fidem in Filium Dei accedunt, haec est praecipua et salutaris meditatio, et applicatio beneficii Dei ad nos.

Sed utrumque oportet animo intueri, iram et misericordiam. Homines ociosis animis cogitant de Deo, non existimant eum vere irasci peccato, quia humani animi levitas non magnificat errata sua. Sed Deus hanc amentiam vult corrigi: ideo totum genus humanum ingentibus calamitatibus oneravit. Omnes miseriae singulorum, mors, et supplicia, bella, excidia, vastitates, ut diluvium, conflagratio Sodomae, clades omnium regnorum, omnium aetatum, sunt testimonia proposita, ut convincant nos, Deum vere irasci peccato. Sed evidens testimonium erit impiis, qui in hac vita verbum et testimonia Dei contemnunt, cruciatus aeternus post hanc vitam. Verum in hoc mundo visibili fuit evidentissimum testimonium irae Dei, quod placari nulla re potuit, nisi morte unigeniti Filii: non poterat placari, nec sanctorum aerumnis, ut Abel, et aliorum. Iam cogita, quis hominum satis consideret magnitudinem huius irae, et beneficium Dei tanti aestimet, quanti revera aestimandum est: omnes igitur sunt ingrati, ignari, et irae Dei, et beneficii. Hanc securitatem, ingratitudinem, ignorantiam agnoscamus, et aliquo modo corrigamus.

Rursus, cum verus pavor extitit in corde, accedat consolatio, et agnoscamus magnitudinem misericordiae, quod voluit Deus ideo pati Filium, ut per hunc placatus, vere nos recipiat, et salvet: et discamus applicationem, quod non aliter consequamur remissionem peccatorum, vitam aeternam, nisi hac ipsa fide, statuentes, quod propter Filium Dei factum pro nobis victimam, pater aeternus recipiat nos, et salvet.

De hac applicatione teneantur in promptu testimonia, Rom. 3.: Iustificamur autem gratis per redemptionem Iesu, quem fecit Deus propitiatorem, per fidem in sanguine eius etc. Rom. 8.: Pro peccato damnavit peccatum. 2. Cor. 5: Eum, qui non novit peccatum, fecit peccatum, ut nos fieremus iusticia Dei per ipsum. Hanc applicationem discas, ne sanguis Christi frustra pro te effusus sit, et Deo gratias agas, et ei obedias pro tanto munere. Haec meditatio, videlicet expavescere intuente miram Dei in passione Filii, et rursus erigi fide, agnoscentem misericordiam, et gratias agere, est vere cultus Dei, qui debet esse perpetuus. Iam cogita, quam multi homines sint, qui hoc tantum munus curent, qui non anteferant sanguini Filii Dei suas cupiditates. Plurimi fatentur se dubitare, an ad ipsos pertineat hoc tantum munus: sed contra hanc dubitationem confirmemus nos Evangelio, et assiduo exercitio in invocatione.

Tertii generis meditatio est exemplaris, ubi iam utimur hoc exemplo, ut lege, seu regula, quod sicut Christus passus est, ita oporteat et nos pati. Esque haec singularis sapientia Ecclesiae, intelligere causas calamitatum humanarum, et veras consolationes. Sapientes inde usque ab initio mundi mirati sunt, quid sit causae, cur haec praestans natura hominum tantis aerumnis onerata sit, imo qui fiat, ut optimi tristissimis casibus opprimantur, et alii alias causas cogitaverunt. Sed verbum Dei monstrat veras causas. Initio, ut Paulus inquit, Per peccatum pervasit mors in omnes homines, et secuti sunt morsus diaboli ingentes, sicut dicitur de serpente: Serpens mordebit calcaneum tuum.

Causae afflictionum.

I. Peccatum et morsus diaboli.

II. Peccati agnitio in Ecclesia.

III. Voluntas Dei, volentis revocare ad poenitentiam, et agnitionem promissae misericordiae.

IIII. Occasio confirmandae fidei.

V. Agnitio auxilii Dei, et exercitium, ut confirmetur fiducia Dei, exuatur fiducia nostri.

VI. Ut conspiciatur in nostra imbecillitate potentia Dei.

VII. Ut efficiamur similes Filii Dei.

VIII. Ut afflictio sit testimonium futurae vitae.

Sed cur Christus cum esset sine peccato, subiectus est cruci? Quia mors est poena peccati. Cum igitur Christus esset victima, hoc est, poenam peccati pro nobis subiturus esset, mors et tristissimae afflictiones ei subeundae fuerunt. Et vult Deus Ecclesiam huius sui capitis similem fieri, ideo praecipua membra, Abel, Esaias, Prophetae, Apostoli, et alii multi interfecti sunt, ut fierent similes capitis. Sed in his et caeteris hominibus afflictiones hanc quoque causam habent, ut ipsi suum et generis humani peccatum agnoscant. Nam Ecclesia praecipue subiecta est cruci, ut agnoscat peccatum, quod impii contemnunt. Deinde accedunt et caeterae causae, quas recensui.

Ac praecipue finis afflictionum considerandus est, videlicet, quod velit Deus nos affligi, non ut pereamus, sed ut salvemur, hoc est, ad agnitionem peccati et misericordiae revocemur, iuxta illud: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Hanc voluntatem Dei, et has causas humana ratio per sese non videt: cum sunt res adversae, statim cogitamus nos abiectos esse a Deo. Rursus hos putamus diligi, qui florent gloria et potentia. Sed hic error eximendus est animis, et opponenda imago Christi, et discenda perpetua sententia Evangelii, quod subiecta sit Ecclesia cruci, et quare subiecta sit, et tenendae sententiae, quae docent nos de hac voluntate Dei, ut: Qui vult me sequi, tollat crucem suam, et sequatur me. Item: Multae tribulationes iustorum. Item: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, videlicet, quae et potenter humiliat, et potenter liberat.

Caput LIII. Esaiae.

Hoc caput octo habet locos praecipuos.

I. Locus est historia.

II. Causa.

III. Applicatio beneficii. Noticia eius iustificabit multos.

IIII. Praedicatio poenitentiae universalis.

V. Promissio universalis.

VI. De sacerdotio Christi.

VII. De resurrectione, et regno.

VIII. De poenis impiorum.

Quis credit sermoni nostro, et brachium Domini quis agnoscet? Pullulabit coram Deo sicut virgultum, et sicut radix de terra sitiente.
